Enoch was translated up to the airy heaven, Elias was lifted up; because the Lord willed to have heralds and witnesses of his ascension, one before the law and another under the law, so that at length he might come who truly penetrated the heavens. Whence the order is also marked out by certain steps: Enoch translated, Elias carried up to heaven, so that afterwards he might come who, neither translated nor carried up, penetrated the ethereal heaven by his own power.
**“and they that provoked him in their envy, were reduced to a small number”** — the priests of Baal
48.6: **“Who broughtest down kings to destruction, and brokest easily their power in pieces, and the glorious from their bed”** — because he foretold to the sick king that he would not rise healthy from his bed
48.7: **“Who heardest judgment in Sina, and in Horeb the judgments of vengeance”** — namely, where he spoke with God and saw visions on Mount Horeb
48.8:
**“Who anointedst kings to penance”** — Hazael over Syria and Jehu over Israel
**“and madest prophets successors after thee”** — namely, Eliseus
48.9: **“Who wast taken up”** — namely, into heaven
48.10: **“Who art registered in the judgments of times to appease the wrath of the Lord, to reconcile the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob”** — who art to come before the day of judgment, according to the prophet Malachias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children
48.12:
**“Elias”** — namely, this is he
**“was indeed covered with the whirlwind”** — that he might not be seen by men
**“Elias was … covered with the whirlwind”** — Elias was covered with the whirlwind. Since the disciple is not above the master, Eliseus asks Elias, saying: “let thy double spirit be in me”; but unless the mystery is kept, the request is not fitting. For Elias signifies Christ our head, and Eliseus his body, that is, the Church. Elias gives the choice of asking, and Christ says: “Ask, and it shall be given you.” So Eliseus, that is, the Christian people, asks: “let thy double spirit be in me,” that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit twofold, namely for the remission of sins and the bestowal of virtues. Christ did not need the remission of sins, for he had no sin; but he does the works of the virtues. “If thou see me when I am taken from thee,” says Elias, “thou shalt have what thou hast asked: but if thou see me not, thou shalt not have it.” For he who can set the eyes of right faith on him and faithfully believes his passion, resurrection and ascension receives the fruit of his request. A dead man was cast into the tomb of Eliseus and came to life at the touch of his bones. For he who touches the death of Christ with firm faith is a sharer in his resurrection; whence: “I am the resurrection and the life: he that believeth in me … shall not die for ever.”
**“and his spirit was filled up in Eliseus: in his days he feared not the prince, and no man was more powerful than he”** — In Eliseus, etc. Who prayed, saying: “let thy double spirit be in me,” and obtained it. Hence he was unconquerable in patience and strength, and did many signs in life and in death.
48.13: **“No word could overcome him, and after death his body prophesied”** — it signifies that the raising of the dead man, who came to life when cast into the tomb of Eliseus, was mystical
48.15:
**“For all this the people repented not, neither did they depart from their sins till they were cast out”** — into captivity
**“And there was left but a small people”** — Because the house of David and the tribes of Juda and Benjamin did not wholly cast off the worship of God; but some of them were idolaters, like Joram and Achaz, and others clung to God, like Ezechias and Josias.
48.17:
**“Ezechias”** — Christ
**“fortified his city”** — repairing the wall that was broken down and building towers
**“and brought in water into the midst thereof”** — because he brought water into the city
**“and he digged a rock with iron, and made a well for water”** — of which it is said: “The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful”
**“Ezechias fortified his city”** — Ezechias fortified his city. That Ezechias stops up the spring and the brook that ran through the midst of the land, so that the kings of the Assyrians should not find water, signifies that the divine mysteries are to be veiled from heretics and gentiles. That Sennacherib king of the Assyrians sent a strong band against Jerusalem by Rabsaces to overthrow it, and that, as Ezechias and Isaias prayed with the people, the city was delivered and the enemies destroyed, is fully shown in Paralipomenon.
48.22: **“For Ezechias did that which pleased God”** — These things are fully set out in the books of Kings and Paralipomenon and in the book of Isaias
48.23:
**“In his days”** — of Ezechias
**“the sun went backward”** — by ten lines
**“and he lengthened the king’s life.”** — that is, he showed that it was lengthened
48.24:
**“With a great spirit”** — prophetic
**“he saw”** — Isaias
**“the things that are to come to pass at last”** — that is, what was to come in the last age
**“and comforted the mourners”** — by teaching and writing
48.25: **“He shewed what should come to pass for ever, and secret things before they came”** — the coming of Christ, the redemption of mankind, and many other things

49.1:
**“The memory of Josias”** — The memory of Josias: he compares the memory of King Josias to the work of a perfumer, to the sweetness of honey and to music, because the fame of his virtue, the sweetness of his modesty and his zeal for restoring the worship of God surpass every scent, sweetness and song; for he could say with David: “How sweet are thy words to my palate! more than honey to my mouth.”
**“The memory of Josias is like the composition of a sweet smell made by the art of a perfumer”** — Josias, which means ‘strength of the Lord’, signifies Christ, of whom it is said: “The Lord who is strong and mighty: the Lord mighty in battle.” And elsewhere: “he shall save his people from their sins.” With zeal for God he cleanses the land of Juda and Jerusalem from all abominations, he who says: “the zeal of thy house hath eaten me up”; and he has his fan in his hand and purges his floor.
49.2: **“He was directed by God unto the repentance of the nation”** — because he taught the Jewish nation to repent of its sins
49.4:
**“Except David, and Ezechias, and Josias”** — in comparison with these
**“Except David”** — Except David: these three are not said to have sinned in comparison with the others, for what they sinned they blotted out by worthy penance, and they pleased God by devotion and piety.
49.6:
**“They burnt the chosen city of holiness, and made the streets thereof desolate according to the prediction of Jeremias”** — as Jeremias had prophesied and written
**“They burnt the chosen city”** — They burnt the chosen city: some understand this place of the person of Christ. For Jeremias means ‘the exalted of the Lord’, who destroyed the kingdom of the devil and the opposing powers, blotting out the handwriting on the cross of the Lord. “Why have the Gentiles raged, and the people devised” etc. And when these were destroyed he built the Church of God.
49.7: **“to overthrow, and pluck up, and destroy, and to build again, and renew”** — whence: “Lo, I have set thee this day over the nations, and over kingdoms, to root up, and to pull down, and to waste, and to destroy, and to build, and to plant.”
49.8:
**“It was Ezechiel that saw”** — in a vision
**“It was Ezechiel that”** — It was Ezechiel that. Mystically. Ezechiel, which means ‘strengthened by God’, who, living in Babylon, foretold captivity to sinners and pardon to those converted and penitent, signifies Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, who visited us in the captivity of this world and foretold punishments to sinners and remedies to penitents.
49.9: **“under the figure of rain”** — Under the figure of rain: it signifies that he preached that a rain of vengeance would come upon sinners, and promised the consolation of mercy to those walking in the way of God’s commandments.
49.10:
**“And may the bones of the twelve prophets spring up out of their place”** — because they left a worthy memory to those who came after
**“for they strengthened”** — by their preaching
**“Jacob, and redeemed themselves by strong faith”** — namely, by announcing the word of God to the people they showed themselves free of the guilt of silence
49.11:
**“How shall we magnify Zorobabel?”** — Christ, who is the master of Babylon, that is, of the world
**“for he was as a signet on the right hand”** — the leader of the people of Israel, who, returning from Babylon, restored the temple of the Lord
**“for he was”** — For he was: which signifies Christ, who is the image of God, so that whoever believes in God is sealed by him as with a ring. Whence Aggeus: “I … will make thee as a signet, for I have chosen thee, saith the Lord of hosts.”
49.12:
**“Jesus the son of Josedec”** — the high priest
**“Jesus the son”** — Jesus the son: because through the grace of Jesus Christ, who is our king and priest, the Church is rebuilt after the captivity of the devil’s oppression.
49.13:
**“And let Nehemias be a long time remembered, who raised up for us our walls”** — the virtues
**“that were cast down, and set up the gates and the bars”** — the teachers, or works
**“Nehemias”** — Nehemias, ‘God the comforter’ or ‘comforted by the Lord’, here signifies Christ, who says: “I will ask the Father, and he shall give you another Paraclete”; who builds the city of God, that is, the Church, and comforts those who mourn. Whence: “The Lord buildeth up Jerusalem: he will gather together the dispersed of Israel. Who healeth the broken of heart,” etc.
49.14: **“No man was born”** — No man was born: Enoch, ‘dedication’, here signifies Christ, who built and consecrated the Church with his blood, who came into the world without sin and is to be taken up into heaven with glory. Of whom it is said: “Thou art beautiful above the sons of men.” And elsewhere: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive.”
49.15:
**“Nor as Joseph”**
• ‘increased’; he is Christ, who is most full of the grace of God, “of whose fulness we all have received”
• Nor as Joseph: Joseph, like Jacob his father, longed for the land of promise and loathed Egypt, teaching us to long for the land of the living, that we may rest in peace.
**“who was a man born prince of his brethren, the support of his family”** — of Judea
**“the ruler of his brethren”** — of the apostles; whence: “go, tell my brethren” etc.
**“the stay of the people”** — the Christian; he is “a light to the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel”
**“And his bones”** — And his bones: it signifies that Joseph before his death foretold to his brethren: “God will visit you, carry my bones with you out of this place”; and this was done, for the children of Israel carried his bones with them out of Egypt and buried them in Sichem, which is Neapolis, a city of the Samaritans.
49.16:
**“Seth and Sem obtained glory among men”** — in reversed order he has put first the prophets, and afterwards the ancient patriarchs
**“Seth and Sem”** — Seth and Sem: Seth the son of Adam and Sem the firstborn of Noe were preferred above the men of their time both in faith and in conduct; in them Christ is signified, who is God and man, to whom God gave “a name which is above all names: that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow,” etc.

50.1:
**“Simon”** — Simon: ‘put away grief’, or ‘hear sadness’
**“the high priest, the son of Onias, who in his life propped up”** — by the word of teaching
**“the house”** — the synagogue, as our teachers do
**“and in his days”** — in the times of the Church
**“fortified”** — Simon the son of Onias. He comes to men in time, for this Simon was the son of Onias, who was born of Simon surnamed the Just. Onias, as Josephus relates, was faint-hearted and greedy, and by not paying the tribute to King Ptolemy provoked him to anger. Onias at his death left the priesthood to his son Simon, and when he too died his son Onias succeeded. This Simon was high priest of the Jews when Ptolemy Euergetes reigned in Egypt and Seleucus in Asia and Syria. It is plain that Jesus, the writer of this book, and this Simon lived at the same time, since Jesus describes Simon’s life and conduct so exactly.
50.2:
**“By him also the height of the temple was founded”** — but the incarnation, passion and resurrection of Christ are established in the faith of believers
**“the double building and the high walls of the temple”** — those coming from both peoples
50.3: **“the wells of water”** — The wells of water: the depths of the Scriptures, which lie hidden under figures in the divine books but overflow from the mouths of preachers like a sea, to satisfy very many.
50.4:
**“He took care of his nation, and delivered it from destruction”** — from sins, from the slavery of the devil
**“He prevailed to enlarge the city”**
• through the grace of Christ the labour of the preachers prospers
• in the number of believers
50.5:
**“and obtained glory in his conversation with the people: and enlarged the entrance of the house and the court”** — the entrance of the house and the court is the order of teachers
**“the entrance of the house”** — The entrance of the house: because the merit of the teachers grows both in the beginners, whom the court signifies, and in the perfect, who are signified by the house.
50.6:
**“as the morning star in the midst of a cloud”** — it signifies the difference among teachers, to whom the Spirit grants various graces, “dividing to every one according as he will”
**“and as the moon at the full”** — by the word of teaching and the sacrament of baptism: in this way the teachers take care
50.7:
**“And as the sun when it shineth, so did he shine in the temple of God”** — because in the obscurity of the letter the splendour of wisdom shines out
**“as the rainbow giving light in the bright clouds”** — the knowledge of the Scriptures, through which the arrows of the divine testimonies
50.8:
**“and as the flower of roses in the days of the spring”** — the blood of the martyrs in the green springtime of the infant Church
**“as the lilies”** — continence and virginity
**“that are on the brink of the water”** — of the passing world
**“and as the … frankincense”** — pure prayer
**“sweet smelling … in the time of summer”** — in the brightness of faith
50.9:
**“As a … fire”** — of charity
**“bright …, and frankincense burning in the fire”** — of the passion
**“As a … vessel”** — the soul
**“of gold”** — of wisdom
**“massy …, adorned with every precious stone”** — with every kind of virtue
50.10:
**“As an olive tree budding forth, and a cypress tree”** — the light of faith and the love of mercy
**“rearing itself on high”** — the height of the perfection of good will, such as the saints have
**“when he put on”** — When he put on: the order of preachers, by taking the robe of glory and clothing itself with the perfection of virtues, shows the judgment of its dignity, the adornment of faith and the clothing of good works. For these ought to appear in priests, that they may be able to teach worthily; whence: “Jesus began to do and to teach”; and let him pour out prayers for them.
50.11: **“When he went up to the holy altar, he honoured the vesture of holiness”** — because he rightly keeps the laws of his priesthood, so as to teach those under him rightly
50.12:
**“And when he took the portions out of the hands of the priests, he himself stood by the altar”** — first in work and teaching
**“about him”** — that they may imitate
**“was the ring of his brethren: and as the cedar planted in mount Libanus”**
• of the priests and of those of lesser order, who follow the example of the good shepherd
• And when he took, etc. He takes the portions from the hand of the priest who requires the act of good work from the ministers.
50.13:
**“And the oblation of the Lord was in their hands, before all the congregation of Israel”**
• “So let your light shine before men,” etc.
• the multitude of the faithful
50.14: **“and finishing his service, on the altar, to honour the offering of the most high King”** — And finishing, etc. The finished offering is given to the most high King when the body of Christ is offered to God.
50.15:
**“He stretched forth his hand to make a libation, and offered of the blood of the grape”** — by offering the blood of Christ
**“He poured out at the foot”** — He poured out at the foot: in remembrance of Christ, who is the foundation of the Church. The odour of this offering is most sweet to almighty God.
50.17:
**“Then all the people”** — Then all the people: when the office of the Church is performed by the ministers of the altar in memory of Christ, the people, roused to the praise of Christ, fall down on their faces, that is, show the humility of their heart.
**“to pray”** — To pray: because whatever is done in the fear and love of God is prayer before God and an odour of sweetness.
**“and to pray to the Almighty God the most High”** — And to pray to the Almighty God: because the whole Church strives to persevere in prayer until the end of the world, when the body of Christ will be honoured with incorruption and the members will be joined to their head.
50.18: **“And the singers lifted up their voices, and in the great house”** — the Church
50.19: **“And … besought”** — And … besought: that whatever is offered to God in the unity of the faith is received by him, and whatever is outside it is counted as impiety. A great sound is made in the Church when to the prayers of the priests and those who bless, all the people answer Amen; and this sound belongs as much to the cry of the voice as to the devotion of the heart. “Man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart.”
50.20: **“Then coming down”** — Then coming down: the company of the saints, rejoicing, lifts up its hands over all the congregation of the children of Israel when it gives thanks for the completion of its labour in the salvation of all the people; then it multiplies praises and repeats its prayer, because it never ceases from praises.
50.21: **“to shew the power”** — To shew the power: namely, to preach the mercy of him who gives us joyfulness of heart and peace in everlasting times, so that all true Israelites and lovers of the eternal King may proclaim the power and goodness of God in the deliverance of his people.
50.25:
**“two nations”** — Two nations: a twofold ruin; namely, the gentiles, who are defiled by idolatry and by vain conduct.
**“and the third”** — namely, the heretical
**“is no nation, which I hate”** — not one and simple, but made up of various errors
50.26:
**“They that”** — the first
**“sit”** — namely, the Jews
**“on mount”** — of pride
**“Seir”** — ‘hairy’
**“and the Philistines”** — the second
**“and the foolish people”** — the third
50.27: **“the doctrine”** — The doctrine: he commends his work, showing how useful it is to one who reads, meditates and acts on it.
50.28: **“Blessed is he that is conversant in these good things”** — by meditating and fulfilling them in deed
50.29:
**“For if he do them, he shall be strong to do all things: because the light of God”** — wisdom
**“guideth his steps.”** — namely, through which we may be able to come to the kingdom

51.1:
**“A prayer of Jesus the son of Sirach.”** — A prayer of Jesus the son of Sirach. The prayer of Jesus is better applied to the whole Church than to one person, because in it many kinds of tribulations and various consolations are described.
**“I will give glory to thee, O Lord, O King”** — Christ, the Lord and King of the Church, who is her head and bridegroom
51.2:
**“for thou hast been a helper”** — For thou hast been a helper: Christ is the helper and protector of his bride, who delivered himself up for her to free her from the perdition of original sin.
**“And hast preserved my body from destruction”** — from the persuasion of idolatry, lest I should serve the creature rather than the Creator
**“from the snare of an unjust tongue”** — from persuasions
**“and from the lips of them that forge lies”** — of the philosophers and heretics
**“and in the sight of them that stood by, thou hast been my helper”** — of the persecutors, or of the faithful who awaited the coming of my passion
51.3:
**“And thou hast delivered me”** — from persecution
**“according to the multitude of the mercy of thy name”** — not of merits
**“from them that did roar, prepared to devour”** — namely, the persecutors, who rage to devour the people of God as they eat bread
**“Out of the hands of them that sought my life, and from the … afflictions”** — or: from the gates of afflictions
**“the gates of afflictions”** — The gates of afflictions: these are the mouths of princes and tyrants, from which come threats and deceits that compel the servant of God to deny the faith.
51.4: **“From the oppression”** — From the oppression: this happened bodily to the three children in the furnace of fire. But all the saints are delivered spiritually from the heat of persecution.
51.5:
**“From the depth of the belly of hell, and from an unclean tongue, and from lying words”** — of heretics, or of false witnesses
**“from an unjust king, and from a slanderous tongue:”** — understand: he delivered me, lest the power of the enemies should bring souls to destruction
51.6: **“my life”** — My life: because the life of the flesh, failing daily, tends to death. He calls death hell because the death of the flesh is the punishment of the first sin, as hell is the everlasting punishment of sinful souls.
51.7: **“They compassed me”** — They compassed me: the Church, seeing herself surrounded by enemies and human comfort lacking, seeks help from God, from whom is every good, and to whom she attributes her deliverance from her enemies.
51.9:
**“Thou hast exalted”** — by teaching and miracles
**“my dwelling place upon the earth and … for death”** — for passing punishments
51.10:
**“I called upon the Lord, the father of my Lord”** — Jesus Christ
**“that he would not leave me in the day of my trouble, and in the time of the proud without help.”** — the present life, in which the wicked are proud
51.11:
**“I will praise thy name continually, and will praise”** — in the death of the faithful
**“it with thanksgiving”** — of sin, or of praise
**“and my prayer was heard.”** — “Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity: for the Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping.”
51.12:
**“And thou hast saved me from destruction, and hast delivered”** — or: hast rescued
**“me from the evil time.”** — of the present life
**“Therefore I will give thanks”** — my sin
**“and praise thee, and bless the name of the Lord.”** — by doing well and speaking well
51.13:
**“When I was yet young, before I wandered about, I sought for wisdom openly in my prayer.”**
• When I was yet young, etc. Vices are strongest in youth or childhood. Whence: “The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember.”
• When I was yet young. After the common prayer of the Church he tells how he sought wisdom from his infancy.
**“before I wandered about”** — Before I wandered about: he signifies that before the error of childhood or youth he desired wisdom and asked it of the Lord, and persevered to the very end.
51.14: **“I prayed for her before the temple, and unto the very end I will seek after her, and she flourished as a grape soon ripe”** — a kind of wine or grapes called ‘early ripe’, because it is ripened by the sun before the others
51.15:
**“as a grape soon ripe”** — As a grape soon ripe: he compares the beauty of wisdom to the early-ripe grape, to show that there is delight with her; for the grape is called early-ripe because it ripens quickly.
**“My heart delighted in her, my foot walked”** — my affection
**“in the right way”** — of God’s commandments
**“By”** — or: in
**“my youth up I sought after her.”** — because I profited little of myself
51.16:
**“I bowed down … a little”** — because I profited little of myself
**“my ear”** — “every one that asketh, receiveth: and he that seeketh, findeth”
51.17:
**“I found much … in myself”** — in my unprofitableness
**“To him that giveth me”** — to God, not to myself
**“wisdom, will I give glory.”** — by praising and giving thanks
51.18: **“I have determined”** — I have determined: first he says that he took counsel to do it; then that he burned with zeal for good; afterwards that his soul wrestled for it and was confirmed in doing it. And understand that first comes counsel, so that good is distinguished from evil; then the good must be willed, so that it is loved; and lastly the pursuit of good work must be applied, and constantly. For so confirmed he will come to the fruit of wisdom. Whence Wisdom says: “Counsel and equity is mine, prudence is mine, strength is mine”; “I walk in the ways of justice, in the midst of the paths of judgment, That I may enrich them that love me.”
51.19: **“I stretched forth my hands on high”** — seeking the help of God with devout prayers
51.20:
**“my soul”** — meditating on her with my whole heart
**“I directed … to her, and in knowledge I found her.”** — of the enlightened mind
**“I possessed … with her”** — with the lovers of wisdom
**“the beast”**
• clean
• “Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God.”
**“from the beginning: therefore I shall not be forsaken.”** — by her who says: “I love them that love me”
51.21:
**“My entrails were troubled in seeking her: therefore shall I possess a good”** — wisdom
**“possession.”** — because all discipline for the present is bitter
**“My entrails”** — My entrails: moved to penance through the knowledge of wisdom.
**“therefore … a good”** — Therefore … a good: to come to the perfection of wisdom is not of human effort but of divine gift.
51.22: **“hath given”** — Hath given: a good reward is a learned tongue, which knows how to instruct and correct the brethren.
51.23: **“Draw near to me, ye unlearned, and gather yourselves together into the house of discipline.”** — the Church, where true discipline is learned
51.24: **“Why are ye slow? and what do you say of these things? your souls are exceeding thirsty.”** — for the word of God
51.25:
**“I have opened my mouth”** — as: “All you that thirst, come to the waters: and you that have no money make haste, buy”
**“and have spoken: buy her for yourselves without silver”** — material
51.26:
**“And submit your neck to the yoke”** — the stiffness of pride
**“and let your soul receive discipline: for she is near at hand to be found.”** — “The Lord is nigh unto all them that call upon him”
51.27:
**“Behold with your eyes”** — inner
**“how I have laboured a little”** — because I profited little of myself
**“and have found much rest to myself.”** — the delight of wisdom
51.28:
**“Receive ye”** — therefore
**“discipline as a great sum of money”** — of divine eloquence
**“and … abundance of gold”** — understanding
51.29:
**“Let your soul rejoice in his mercy, and you shall not be confounded in his praise.”** — he who is ungrateful is confounded
**“Let your soul rejoice”** — Let your soul rejoice: great is the joy of the heart if it remembers the mercy of the Judge on high.
51.30:
**“Work your work”** — “work … whilst you have the light”
**“before the time”** — of judgment
**“and he will give you your reward”** — the eternal reward
**“in his time.”**
• of judgment
• “in due time we shall reap, not failing”

1.1:
**“The vision of Isaias”**
• modestly, of himself as if of another
• spiritual
• that is
• of the Saviour the Lord
• The vision of Isaias, etc. There are three kinds of vision. The first is bodily, by which we see heaven and earth and the like. The second is spiritual, by which we see, as in every image, the likeness of men and the like. The third is intellectual, which is in reason, by which we know the Creator, and by the revealing of the Holy Spirit understand whatever it may be. To see also is often put for to understand. Whence we often ask, saying, “Do you see?” that is, “Do you understand?” The prophets also are hence called seers, that is, those who understand. This vision Isaias saw; the Holy Spirit, namely, inspiring him, he understood what was to come. Whence in the beginning he does not set down visions as Daniel does, nor does he say what he saw, but at once says: “Hear, O ye heavens,” and “give ear.”
*Jerome:* Not only Isaias but also the others who have in the title “the vision which this one or that one saw” do not bring in what they saw, for example, “I saw the Lord sitting,” but at once relate what was said, as here: “Hear, O ye heavens,” etc. And: “Thus saith the Lord to Idumea.” For the prophets are rightly called seers, whose eyes are always on the Lord, according to that: “To thee have I lifted up my eyes, who dwellest in heaven,” and elsewhere: “Lift up your eyes, and see the countries, for they are white already,” etc. Of these eyes it is said: “The light of thy body is thy eye.” And the people saw the voices, that is, understood. So those who saw thus were not, as Montanus would have it, without understanding.
*Rabanus:* Isaias means saviour of the Lord; Juda, confession; Jerusalem, vision of peace; Ozias, strength of the Lord; Joathan, perfection of the Lord; Achaz, holding or strong; Ezechias, rule of the Lord. For he who is saved with the Lord presiding, and is the son of Amos, that is, of the strong and robust, perceives spiritually the vision of confession while he mourns his former sins, and of peace when after penance he passes over to the light and rests in eternal peace; and all his times pass under the strength of the Lord, and in perfection and robustness. And when he has done all things, he says: I am an unprofitable servant; I have done that which I ought to do.
**“the son of Amos”** — strong or robust
**“The son of Amos”** — Amos, the father of Isaias, is not the third of the twelve prophets; for among the Hebrews they are written with different letters. This one has as first and last letters aleph and sade; the other, ain and samech. And this one, they say, is interpreted strength or robust; the other, a heavy or hard people. But this one was a prophet, if we agree with the Hebrews, who maintain that the fathers, grandfathers and great-grandfathers of the prophets, whose names are set down at the beginning of their prophecy, were prophets.
**“which he saw”**
• he understood
• spiritually
**“concerning”**
• others against
• as a weight of tribulation
**“Juda”** — confession
**“and Jerusalem”**
• a vision of peace
• Benjamin, in whose tribe Jerusalem [was]
• the people
• The vision of Isaias, etc. For Juda, in which the two tribes are signified, the Septuagint and Theodotion put Judea, which signifies the whole land of the twelve tribes. And where we translate from the Hebrew “concerning Juda and Jerusalem,” they put “against Judea and Jerusalem.” Symmachus more plainly: “of Juda and Jerusalem”; he wishes neither prosperity nor adversity to be shown in the title, but only that the prophet foretold concerning Juda and Jerusalem.
**“Concerning Juda and Jerusalem”** — Isaias speaks principally of the two tribes, that is, Juda and Benjamin, with the exception of the ten which are called Israel and Ephraim, which Phul, king of the Assyrians, had already begun to lay waste under Ozias, king of Juda. Finally, in the fifty-second year of his reign, while Phacee the son of Romelia was reigning in Samaria, Theglathphalasar, king of the Assyrians, took, with many others, Galilee and all the land of Nephtali, and carried them over to the Assyrians. From this it is shown that these things were foretold, with the overthrow of Samaria near at hand, for the correction of the two tribes.
*Jerome:* I know that some interpret Juda and Jerusalem as heavenly things, and that Isaias puts forward the person of the Lord, who foretells their captivity in our land and their return to the holy mount in the last days. We, judging these things contrary to the faith, despise them all, and following the truth of the history, whatever they dream about the heavenly Jerusalem, we refer to the Church of Christ and to those who either leave her because of sin or return through penance; of which it is said: “Arise, be enlightened, O Jerusalem: for thy light is come,” etc.
**“in the days of Ozias”** — of the strength of the Lord
**“Joathan”** — of the perfection of the Lord
**“Achaz”** — fearing or strong
**“Ezechias”** — of the rule of the Lord
**“In the days of Ozias”** — Ozias is the same who is also Azarias. It is easy to know, from the kings who are set down in the title, that Isaias, Osee, Joel and Amos prophesied at one and the same time. But the beginning of the word of the Lord was in Osee. As for what is said in the title, that he prophesied under Ozias, Joathan, Achaz and Ezechias, unlike the other prophets we do not know what was said specially under each one, because it is fully distinguished up to the end of the volume.
**“kings of Juda.”** — It should also be known that Ezechias began to reign in Jerusalem in the twelfth year of Romulus (who founded a city in Italy named after himself), so that our histories appear older than the Gentile ones.
1.2:
**“Hear”**
• makes attentive
• Mystically.
**“O ye heavens”** — heavenly
**“and give ear”** — Historically.
**“give ear, O earth”**
• earthly
• metonymy, the container for the contained: heaven, that is, the heavenly ones; earth, the inhabitants of the earth
• Hear, O ye heavens, etc. Above, it has been shown in the title who the prophet is, whose son, what he saw against Juda and Jerusalem, and in what time. Now he calls heaven and earth to hear. For the Lord, through Moses, calls heaven and earth when he gave his law to the people of Israel: “Hear, O ye heavens, and I will speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth.” After the people’s transgression he calls the same as witnesses, that all the elements may know that God is justly roused to anger in vengeance for his commandments. He wished, moreover, heavens to be said in the plural and understood in the singular, as we say or call single cities Thebes or Athens.
• Samayn in Hebrew signifies the heavens in the plural; so all words that end in a syllable are masculine and plural, as cherubim and seraphim; those in oth are feminine plurals, as Sabaoth. Hear, O ye heavens, etc. Things that are lofty have the greater understanding, those lower an earthly one. Whence: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.” Let him therefore who is heavenly hear the allegory; let him who is earthly hear the history.
• Some think heaven and earth are summoned to hear as if they were living things, in accord with that: “He looketh upon the earth, and maketh it tremble”; since this power is of God, and is not to be understood in an earthly way.
**“for the Lord hath spoken”**
• not to you who are unworthy, but to me
• namely this
**“The Lord hath spoken”** — Not to you but to me, so that I may report to you what I heard in the spirit, you who do not deserve to hear it yourselves.
**“children”** — the Jews, whom he deigns to call sons
**“I have brought up”**
• I have brought up, not begotten, according to some, as some codices have it; for whosoever is born of God sinneth not
• by benefits, as little children
**“and exalted them;”** — by miracles
**“but they have despised me.”**
• by casting off my precepts and despising the prophets
• who did such great things for them
• I have brought up children, etc. As if: I adopted them as sons and called them firstborn, yet they were not won by benefits, even as brute animals are, so as to understand their nourisher. Nor does he compare them to the dog, a most keen animal, which for a little food defends the houses of its masters, but to the dull sense of the ox and the ass, of which one turns up the earth, the other carries men. Whence they are also called beasts of burden, because they help men.
• I have brought up children, and, etc. From this place he relates what the Lord spoke to the children of Israel, whom he established as servants by the common law, but turned into sons, saying: “Israel is my son, my firstborn.” It is also said to the apostles that if they do the will of the Lord they shall not be called servants but friends. Israel is called firstborn lest he be proud, because there are also second sons from the Gentiles, and yet according to the mysteries of the Scriptures they do not receive the inheritance of the firstborn but of the second. Not Cain’s gifts but Abel’s were pleasing to the Lord. Nor did Ismael but Isaac receive the inheritance. Nor did Esau the firstborn but Jacob seize the blessing. Ruben also being set aside, the blessing of the seed of Christ is transferred to Juda. The Jews therefore, according to the order of the calling, were the first and the head called. We, the second and the tail, he says, have been turned into the head, and are called sons of God; whence: “He gave them power to be made the sons of God.”
1.3:
**“knoweth”** — by believing
**“The ox”** — those of the Jews who believed
**“his owner”**
• Christ
• The ox knoweth, etc. “Thou shalt not plough with an ox and an ass together,” as Ebion does, who confounds the Gospel and the Old Testament. Blessed is he that soweth upon all waters, where the ox and the ass tread, that is, in the divine sayings, namely of the holy Scriptures, of the old namely and new testament, and treads the water of the killing letter that he may reap the fruit of the life-giving spirit. The ox is referred to Israel, who bore the yoke of the law as a clean animal. The ass signifies the Gentile people, burdened with the weight of sins, to whom it is said: “Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened.”
**“The ass”** — A Gentile, or a convert, once wanton and unclean, burdened with sins, who believed in the incarnation of Christ, who, born, was at once laid in the manger, so that he might refresh all by the bridle of his flesh.
**“Israel”** — Scribes and Pharisees, having the key of knowledge and of the law. Whence those who saw God were called Israel.
**“but Israel hath not known me, and my people”** — whom I exalted
**“my”** — that is
**“hath not understood.”**
• to be pronounced with grief
• therefore
1.4:
**“Woe”** — Eternal damnation threatens eternal destruction, because they are unwilling to believe in the coming of the Son of God, who is to redeem the world
**“to the nation”** — not to sons
**“sinful, a people laden”** — unmoved
**“with iniquity, a wicked seed”**
• You are of your father the devil, and offspring of vipers; who has shown you to flee from the wrath to come?
• Woe to the nation, etc. In the title he recalls the person, the cause and the time. Second, he makes them attentive. Third, he relates what the Lord has said. Fourth, as if in excess, he rebukes the sinful nation.
• Woe to the nation, etc. He threatens eternal destruction because they reject the Son who brought salvation.
**“With iniquity”** — “Iniquity sits upon a talent of lead.” Whence elsewhere: “They are heavy upon me as a heavy burden.”
**“ungracious children.”**
• to the Jews who were first sons of God by benefit, and sons of iniquity by their own vice
• because
**“They have forsaken the Lord”** — worshipping idols, not receiving the Son of God
**“Wicked”**
• Others: the vice of the worst men, not of the seed, but of the malice of those who by their own will have forsaken God. For the nature of good and bad is not to be thought diverse.
• Others: the vice of the worst men, not of the seed, but of the malice of those who by their own will have forsaken God. For the nature of good and bad is not to be thought diverse.
**“have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel”** — worshipping idols, not receiving the Son of God
**“they are gone away backwards.”** — no one putting his hand to the plough and looking back
**“They are gone away”** — Those who were called a part and sons of God, it is said of them: “The children that are strangers have lied to me.” No one putting his hand to the plough, etc. Whence the Apostle: stretching forth himself to those things which are before, forgetting those that are behind.
1.5:
**“For what”** — or in which
**“shall I strike you any more, you that increase”** — multiplying
**“transgression?”**
• to transgression
• Why shall I strike you any more, etc. As if I had struck you in vain, since you did not receive correction; therefore my zeal will depart from you. Like that: “There is no soundness in their wound.”
• God often strikes that he may correct. But to those who are incorrigible he says: “For what shall I strike you?” as if to say: I find no medicine that I may apply to you; all your members are full of wounds; I have applied healing often; now I find no part of the body that is not already struck and full of wounds. Or: I find no strokes by which to break your hardness; for the hardness grows the more as I apply greater scourges. That there is now no place fit for medicine he shows thus: the whole head is sick.
**“The whole”** — metaphor
**“head”** — metaphor
**“is sick”**
• by the habit of sinning
• by impiety
**“and the whole heart is sad”**
• the wise, because wisdom is in the heart through affection; these, because they understand and lament both their own sins and those of others
• The whole head is sick, etc. As gladness of soul sometimes lessens the pains of the body, and if languor of mind is added the infirmity is doubled; and as, if the head aches, all the members are weak; so, if the princes and teachers had kept justice, the people would somehow have had medicine. But because all have been made sick, the medicine of souls is taken away; whence: from the sole of the foot, etc.
1.6:
**“From the sole of the foot unto the top of the head”** — from the least to the greatest
**“there is no ... therein”** — in the people, or in the head, or in the body
**“soundness.”** — of mind, because they killed the physician
**“wounds”** — of malice
**“and bruises”** — of envy
**“and swelling sores.”** — the pride of the Jews
**“they are not bound up”** — with the bandages of prayers
**“nor dressed, nor fomented with oil”** — of good works
**“nor fomented with oil.”**
• of penance, so that their hardness might be softened by the tears of compunction
• The Septuagint: there is no plaster to apply, neither oil nor bandages.
• therefore
• Wound and bruise, etc. As if bodies either gape with wounds, or are black and blue from blows, or swell with stripes. This properly suits the final captivity, for which there is no remedy, and in which it is fulfilled: “All have gone aside, they are become unprofitable together.”
• Wound: by a staff; bruise: by rods; stripe: by a sword; usually by a staff.
• It should be known that these things were foretold of the Lord’s coming and of the last captivity, when they had by then received no cure, because they killed the true and merciful physician sent to them.
**“Nor dressed”** — Whence: “We would have cured Babylon, but she is not healed”; the city, that is, of confusion and vices. We read also of the man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, wounded by robbers, cured by the Samaritan, and after the sharpness of the wine, the softness of oil poured in. And it must be noted that from where he said: “For what shall I strike you,” etc., up to here, “nor dressed, nor fomented with oil,” he kept the figure and expressed the irremediable captivity of the Jews.
1.7:
**“Your land”** — will be
**“Your cities are burnt with fire”** — of the Babylonians or the Romans
**“your country strangers before your face”** — Samaritans or Romans
**“devour, and it shall be desolate”** — indeed
**“as when wasted by enemies”**
• Your land is desolate, etc. These things were partly fulfilled under the Babylonians, when the cities of Jerusalem were burnt and the region of the Jews overthrown; with the Samaritans dwelling there, and lions also laying waste the land; but wholly under the Romans.
• Almighty God forsook Jerusalem, and the temple, and the people, whose guardian he himself was, while they bore the fruits of good works. Whence: “Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it.”
• Allegorically. Those who have fallen from their former health and been handed over to hostile powers, all their goods come into desolation, and God will not remember their former justice, and all things will be set on fire by the fire of the devil and become food for beasts, of whom it is said: “Deliver not up to beasts the souls that confess to thee.”
1.8:
**“And shall be left”** — by men or by God
**“Shall be left”** — Whence: “Arise, let us go hence”; and: “Your house shall be left to you desolate”; and elsewhere: “I have forsaken my house,” etc.
**“daughter of Sion”** — Jerusalem or the temple
**“as a covert in a vineyard”** — a vineyard stripped of its grapes, from which you carried the vine out of Egypt
**“and as a lodge”** — which, the fruit having been taken away, the keepers left empty
**“in a garden of cucumbers”** — the crops having been gathered
**“and as a city that is laid waste”**
• The daughter of Sion, etc. By the affection of a most loving father, all are by nature sons, and by fault strangers. Whence Babylon is often called a daughter.
• “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” Therefore, after the boar out of the wood has laid it waste, and those passing by the way have gathered its grapes, it is left by the Lord.
*Jerome:* Morally. By Sion, which means watching, and which is called a paradise of fruits, and a vineyard, the soul is understood, which ought to stand in contemplation and bring forth acceptable fruits; and if the mind, that is the nous, presides over it, it has God as the guardian of the mind. But if vices and sins, like little beasts, have eaten up the shoots of the virtues, it immediately loses God as its guardian.
1.9:
**“Except”** — therefore
**“the Lord of hosts”**
• in Hebrew, Sabaoth
• Christ, of whom the Lord of hosts is himself the King of glory
• Lord Sabaoth, which the Septuagint, according to the quality of the places, translate either Lord of powers or Lord almighty. For Christ, to whom it is said: “All power is given to me in heaven and in earth,” as he is God of God and Lord of Lord, so is he almighty Son of the Almighty.
**“had left us”** — the remnant of Israel will be made safe
**“seed”**
• or the gospel
• the apostles and their followers; whence others
• That is, in the apostles the remnant of the Jewish people was made safe, and on one day three thousand and five believed, and the gospel is spread abroad through the whole world.
**“as”** — likewise dead in sins
**“Sodom”** — dumb, from the praise of God. For Sodom is interpreted dumb, Gomorrha rough
**“we had been as Sodom, and we should have been like to Gomorrha”**
• rough through the enormity of sins
• Except the Lord of hosts, etc. This is spoken in the person of the prophet and of the faithful from the same people.
• Except the Lord, etc. Here it is shown that what was said against Juda and Jerusalem is to be referred to the captivity by the Romans, when in the apostles the remnant of the Jews were saved, and in one day three thousand believed, and the Gospel was sown in the whole world.
1.10:
**“Hear”**
• but that you not perish
• in mind
**“the word of the Lord, ye rulers of Sodom”**
• as you who boast yourselves to be sons of Abraham
• to whom your father is like, the Amorrhite, and your mother the Cethite
**“give ear”** — with the outward ears at least
**“to the law of our God, ye people of Gomorrha”**
• “You are of your father the devil.”
• The remnant of the people of Israel having been saved through the apostles, the prophet, speaking likewise, turns to the scribes and Pharisees and the people crying out: “Crucify him, crucify him,” and calls them princes of Sodom and people of Gomorrha, who devised the worst counsel and bound the just one, and said: “We have no king but Caesar.”
• The Hebrews say that Isaias was put to death for two reasons: that he called them princes of Sodom and people of Gomorrha, and that, when the Lord said to Moses: “Thou canst not see my face,” he dared to say: “We saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and elevated,” not considering that the seraphim covered the face and the feet of God, or their own, which is read ambiguously in the Hebrew, and that Isaias writes that he saw only the middle parts.
• Hear, etc. This pertains specially to the Jews of that time, to the scribes and Pharisees and to the people crying: crucify him, crucify him. For as the Sodomites sinned publicly, devising the worst counsel against the just man Lot, and without shame said: bring out the men that came in to thee, that we may abuse them; so these shamelessly said against Christ: come, let us devise devices against the just one; and he is guilty of death; and the like. Whence in what follows: “They have proclaimed their sin as Sodom, and they hide it not.”
• Hear the word of the Lord, etc. The Hebrews hand down that Isaias was put to death because he had said this, or because he had said: “I saw the Lord,” etc. Whereas the Lord said to Moses: “Man shall not see me and live,” and “Thou canst not see my face”; nor do they consider the face or the feet of the Lord, or their own. For in the Hebrew it is said ambiguously: the seraphim covered, and Isaias wrote that he saw only his middle parts. Yet the angels, even of the lesser ones in the Church, always see the face of God, but man cannot. “For we see now through a glass in a dark manner,” etc. But when we advance from men into angels, we behold the glory of God with face revealed, although according to the property of nature no creature can see the face of God; and he is now discerned by the mind when he is believed invisible.
**“Hear the word”** — The remnant being saved through the apostles, the word is turned to the scribes and Pharisees and to the people crying out, “Crucify him, crucify him.”
1.11:
**“To what”** — to what purpose
**“do you offer me the multitude of your victims”** — as if to say: since you do not keep the law, why do you offer?
**“of your victims”** — not mine, whom you offend
**“saith the Lord”** — who is to be feared
**“I am full, I desire not holocausts of rams, and fat of fatlings, and blood of calves, and lambs, and buck goats.”**
• ever
• “The holocausts of rams,” etc., down to: “Judge for the fatherless,” etc. He rejects the sacrifices of the Jews and commends the obedience of the gospel.
• Burnt offerings of rams, etc. It points to the last destruction of the temple, which lasts forever. For after the Babylonian captivity the temple was built by Zorobabel, and sacrifice was offered in it for a long time.
**“I am full”** — As if you think I need these or delight in them. But I am full, that is, I need nothing. For “the earth is mine, and the fulness thereof.” Or, I am full, that is, filled with loathing, because you do not offer rightly.
*Allegorically:* It can also be understood of those who, despising God’s commands, wish to appease him by a multitude of sacrifices and to buy licence to sin. Or of those who offer robbery and greed upon the altar and bestow them on the poor.
**“I desire not”** — Using the past tense, he shows that he never loved the sacrifices of the Jews, but endured them for a time because of what they signified, and once the true sacrifice was accomplished, counted them as nothing.
1.12:
**“When you came to appear before me, who required”** — as if it were a spiritual law
**“When you came”** — God did not require these sacrifices as though he had need of them, but so that they would not sacrifice to demons, and so that through fleshly and typical things they might more easily come to the spiritual and true sacrifice.
**“who required”** — Let the Ebionites hear this, who think the law must be kept after Christ’s passion. Let their associates hear this, who decree that it is to be kept only by the Israelite race.
**“these things at your hands, that you should”** — so
1.13:
**“Offer no more”** — therefore
**“Offer sacrifice no more in vain”**
• useless
• because
**“incense”** — your
**“is an abomination to me”** — because not with pure intention
**“The new moons, and the sabbaths, and other festivals”** — encaenia, jubilee
**“I will not abide”** — I will no longer endure, because your assemblies are wicked
**“The new moons”** — The feast of the new moon, which they celebrated at the beginning of the months. Neos, new; mene, moon. Whence: “Blow the trumpet in the new moon to the Lord.”
**“your assemblies are wicked”** — Because they do not offer spiritual sacrifices. Whence: “A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit.”
1.14:
**“new moons”** — new moons
**“your”** — not mine
**“and your solemnities”** — your
**“My soul hateth”**
• because you use them badly
• Anthropopathism: not that he has a soul, but he speaks in our manner, as if: I have utterly hated.
**“they are become troublesome to me”** — the things said above
**“I am weary of bearing”** — waiting for your conversion
**“I am weary of bearing them”** — Symmachus. I grew weary of pitying, as if I could no longer have mercy, because after the servants you killed the Son. As in Osee: “Destruction is thy own, O Israel: thy help is only in me.” Perish, Israel, who are saved not by your own merit but by my help alone.
1.15:
**“And when you stretch forth your hands”** — which they did, as if imitating Moses, who prayed against Amalec with hands raised
**“I will turn away my eyes”** — with a look of mercy
**“from you”** — to the wicked
**“And”** — also, or therefore
**“when you multiply prayer, I will not hear”** — that is: because
**“hands”** — works
**“for your hands are full of blood”**
• From sin. Whence: “Deliver me from blood, O God, thou God of my salvation”, that is, from sins.
• This testimony is to be used against those who, having bloody hands from their daily deeds, keep watch in prayer day and night.
**“Your hands full of blood”** — Of the prophets, at last, of their Lord. Whence: “Fill ye up then the measure of your fathers.” They slew the prophets; you slew the son of the householder.
1.16:
**“Wash yourselves”**
• with the tears of penance
• bring forth worthy fruits of penance
• As if: the truth of the gospel pleases what I hated. Wash yourselves: with the blood of Christ, in the water of baptism. Be clean: afterwards, remaining in innocence of life. For baptism alone can be for the remission of sin; whence: “Unless a man be born again,” etc. And elsewhere: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father,” etc.
**“be clean”**
• lest you fall back
• innocence of life
• The order is chief: “wash yourselves” is not enough unless “be clean” is added, that after the washing of water they may have purity of heart. For “blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God.” But having purity of heart, they must take away evil from their minds, not only in the sight of men but also in the sight of God, from whom nothing can be hidden. But what is added, “Cease to do perversely,” the gospel echoes: “Behold thou art made whole: sin no more.” Therefore, departing from vices, let him learn to do good, seek judgment, help the oppressed, defend the fatherless and the widow. But if he does these things, the sins that before were scarlet like blood will be forgiven, and the works of blood will be changed in the garment of the Lord, which is made of the fleece of the lamb, whom those follow in the Apocalypse who shine with the whiteness of virginity.
**“take away”** — take away evils; in this way wash yourselves
**“the evil”** — work
**“of your devices”** — if you at least think them, do not complete them
**“your”**
• of iniquities
• not of mine
**“from my eyes”** — because it is an abomination to me
**“cease”** — you who are baptized
**“to do perversely”** — turn aside from evil
1.17:
**“Learn to do well.”**
• do good
• in this way
**“Learn to do well”** — Virtue is to be learned and imitated, not trusting in nature; whence Jesus the son of Sirach: “If thou desire wisdom, keep justice, and God will give her to thee.” And Isaias: “Everyone who has not learned justice upon earth will not do truth.” Justice, therefore, is to be learned, and the thresholds of teachers are to be worn.
**“seek judgment”** — from the wise, whose office it is to judge; whence Solomon asked for wisdom to judge the people
**“relieve the oppressed”** — by force
**“judge”** — that is, help him in judgment if his cause is good, because it is said: “Spare not the poor man in judgment”
**“for the fatherless”** — that is, to the poor man
**“defend the widow”**
• from violence
• in judgment
**“Seek judgment”** — The evangelical commands succeed the sacrifices of the Jews. Provision is made for orphans and widows, so that, secure concerning their spouses and children, martyrs may go forth to war.
1.18:
**“And then come”** — when you have done these good things
**“and accuse me”**
• as one ungrateful
• if I shall not reward
**“saith the Lord”** — who does not lie
**“if your sins be”** — as if you had done these
**“they shall be made as white as snow”** — Whence: “Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, O Lord”; and elsewhere: “his raiment white as snow”
**“as scarlet”** — The same is coccus and coccinum and vermiculus: a great sin, namely such as murder and adultery, etc. But that which is signified by the snow, and likewise by the wool, is the cleansing, namely the washing away of sins.
**“and if they be red as crimson, they shall be white as wool”** — As snow, because they will be cold against the incentives of vices. And as wool, because they will be clothed against the cold of unbelief.
**“wool”** — From which the garment of Christ is made; whence: “As many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ.” And elsewhere: “As I live, saith the Lord, thou shalt be clothed with all these as with an ornament.”
1.19:
**“If you be willing”**
• through free will
• as if it lies in your own will
**“and will hearken to me”** — you obey
**“the good things of the land”** — of the living, or of the present; so that at least the Jews, invited by present things, may obey
**“you shall eat”** — If you be willing, etc. Free will is reserved, so that it may be shown that rewards or punishments follow not from God’s prejudgment but from the merits of individuals.
**“of the land”** — Since the other elements are in motion, the earth stands immovable. Therefore by it is signified the firmness of eternal blessedness.
1.20:
**“But if you will not, and will provoke me to wrath”**
• vengeance
• thus
**“the sword shall devour you”** — as if you should not doubt the truth
**“The sword”** — Of the Babylonians, or of the Romans, or of God: pestilence, namely death, famine, eternal punishment; for whatever afflicts is customarily called a sword.
**“because the mouth of the Lord”** — The Word of the Father, or the prophet through whom God speaks his secrets, whose judgment is not changed while sins remain.
1.21:
**“How”** — in wonder
**“become a harlot”** — not so much by deed as by mind, by withdrawing from God
**“faithful city”** — once
**“The faithful city”** — The Septuagint added Sion, for the sake of a clearer sense. Sion is the mountain on which Jerusalem was founded. But after it was taken by David it was called the city of David, in which there were holy men while it had the tabernacle of the Lord; and afterwards the temple, when Nathan and others prophesied, and Asaph and Idithun and Haneman and the sons of Core were set over the choirs, so that religion might pass little by little from the sacrifices of victims to the praise of God.
**“that was full of judgment”** — of truth
**“Justice”** — Justice in Hebrew is sedech, which signifies rather just, so that we understand the Lord dwelling in it, concerning whom; but what did the just man do? This is signified in Ezechiel by Oolibah, which is interpreted tabernacle, or my tabernacle in her.
**“dwelt in it”** — as in his own house
**“but now murderers”**
• because they killed the prophets and the Lord of the prophets
• How, etc. These things refer to the time of the prophet, but especially to the incarnation of Christ, when they wholly withdrew from God, choosing Barabbas and killing the Son of God; whence, wondering, he says: How, etc.
*Morally:* The faithful soul, full of judgment, while it obeys God, has God dwelling in it, who is justifying justice. But if it withdraws from God, it is inhabited not by place but by merit, by evil spirits, who are the murderers of souls.
1.22:
**“Thy silver”**
• truly: where justice is, there are murderers, because the silver, etc.
• the words of divine Scripture turned into the dross of the wicked teaching of the scribes and Pharisees
• Silver, etc. Namely, the bright and shining have turned back to vices. Thy silver. Whence: “The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver,” etc.
**“into dross”** — Dross in Hebrew is sygin, which is the rust of metals, or the refuse and dirt that are burned off by fire.
**“thy wine is mingled with water”** — the sternness of the law with the softness of the Pharisaic tradition, or of heretical perversion
**“Thy wine”** — Others: your innkeepers mix the wine with water. Symmachus: thy wine is mixed with water.
*Morally:* Thy wine is mixed with water: because he softens the precepts of holy Scripture, by which he ought to correct his hearers, to suit their will; by mixing in his own sense he corrupts the wine.
*Morally:* Thy wine, etc. Heretics too corrupt the gospel, like the worst tavern-keepers who make water out of wine, when the Lord turned water into wine, which the master of the feast marvelled at; and the queen of Saba, praising in the banquet of Solomon the cupbearers and servants of wine.
1.23:
**“Thy princes”**
• the scribes and Pharisees
• the priests who ought to judge the people
**“are faithless, companions of thieves”**
• of the scribes and Pharisees
• not believing in Christ, disobedient
• because
**“companions of thieves”** — Receiving gifts from the scribes and Pharisees, which they took away from the poor. Also in the Lord’s passion they were unbelieving, unwilling to believe in Christ, and companions of thieves: of the scribes and Pharisees, and of Judas the betrayer.
*Jerome:* Morally. Companions of thieves. We too ought to beware lest we receive gifts from those who gather riches from the tears of the poor, lest we become companions of thieves, and lest it be said of us: “If thou didst see a thief, thou didst run with him,” etc.
**“they all love bribes”** — For he does not say they receive gifts but that they love them; for sin lies in the will, not in the thing.
**“they run after rewards”**
• acquisitive
• Symmachus: vicissitudes or vengeances; so that he too is at fault who exacts evil for evil, tooth for tooth, eye for eye, not hearing that: “If I have rendered to them that repaid me evils,” or that: “He shall give his cheek to him that striketh him,” etc. For to the man of the gospel it is said: “Whosoever shall strike thee on thy right cheek, turn to him also the other,” that is, bear it patiently.
**“They run after rewards”** — Because they think only those friends who give, whose face they regard not but whose hand they consider. And only those whose purses they drain they judge holy. They give to those from whom they hope for things; they favour them, they extol them or praise their cause.
**“fatherless”** — from whom they hope for nothing
**“they judge not”** — and
**“the widow's cause”** — which is pitiable
**“cometh not in to them”** — they disdain to hear
1.24:
**“Therefore saith the Lord the God of hosts”** — who is mighty and to be feared
**“the mighty one of Israel”** — The Septuagint: Woe, strong ones of Israel. As if: the mighty will suffer mighty torments. From him to whom more is given, more is required. Which we can say against the princes of the Church who destroy dignity by their works or their manners.
**“Ah! I”** — By the feeling of a loving Father he laments or strikes them, though they are enemies, because they perish and are unwilling to repent.
**“will comfort myself over my adversaries”** — specially to the scribes and Pharisees, to whom it is said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees,” and elsewhere: “An evil and adulterous generation seeketh a sign,” etc.
**“I will comfort myself”** — He is consoled by vengeance over his enemies, namely those who in prosperity disdain to recognize God’s benefits; they are corrected by punishments and afflictions.
**“and”** — that is
1.25:
**“And I will turn”** — I will extend to punish
**“my hand”**
• vengeance
• which I have long held, as it were folded up, by patience
**“to thee”** — to be punished
**“and I will clean purge”** — purging with the fire of tribulation
**“thy dross”** — the filth of vices
**“And I will clean purge”** — Because above he had named silver, he keeps the metaphor. I will purge, etc.: purging filth and vices by the fire of tribulation, that, the tin being separated, pure silver may remain, which cannot be done without fire. Whence: “Like a refining fire, and like the fuller’s herb”; and elsewhere: “He will gather the wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” In which he signifies that they will suffer torments.
**“and I will take away all thy tin”** — Tin. The false teaching of the scribes and Pharisees, which is like the true, as tin is to silver. And I will give the pure and perfect knowledge of the law and the gospel.
1.26:
**“And I will restore thy judges as they were before”** — Moses, Aaron, Gideon, Josue and others
**“and thy counsellors as of old”** — who will reveal to you God’s counsels and secrets
**“And I will restore”** — Not only after the captivity, as Zorobabel, Esdras and others who presided over the people even to Hyrcanus, but also after the coming of the Lord, the apostles and other rulers of the Church.
**“After this”** — those being restored
**“thou shalt be called the city of the just”** — of Christ
**“the city of the just”** — The Church, in which men are called to live justly. For a city is a gathering of men to live justly.
**“city”** — a city cannot be hid, set upon a mountain
**“a faithful city”** — believing in Christ
1.27:
**“Sion”** — not all, but in the distinction of believers and unbelievers the remnant of Israel will be saved
**“shall be redeemed in judgment”**
• by the blood of the Son
• from unbelief
**“and they shall bring her back in justice”**
• which was led away through injustice
• but
1.28:
**“And”** — the Lord
**“shall destroy”** — by the Romans or in hell
**“the wicked”** — prelates
**“and the sinners together”**
• subjects
• who consented to the death of Christ and would not believe
• destruction for sinners who forsook the Lord
**“and they that”** — deservedly
**“have forsaken the Lord”** — remaining in their wickedness
**“shall be consumed”** — here and in the future
1.29:
**“shall be confounded”**
• within and without
• blushing
• with their goods saved
**“For they shall be confounded for the idols, to which they have sacrificed”** — in the prophetic manner, he quickly changes the person
**“the gardens”** — in places of pleasure
**“which you have chosen”** — of your luxury
1.30:
**“When you shall be”** — when the water of wisdom has failed you; when you are parched, and you will be barren
**“as an oak”** — unfruitful
**“with the leaves falling off, and as a garden”** — or paradise; another reading
**“without”** — you who ought to have been “a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed”
**“water”**
• of wisdom
• unfruitful
• As an oak, etc. As the leaves fall from an oak shaken by dryness, and as a garden cannot bring forth fruits of herbs unless it is watered, so you, unless you have the leaves of the words of God, which do not wither, and the water of spiritual understanding, cannot work good, but all your labours will fail through dryness.
• To this day the Jews, reading the holy Scriptures, are terebinths, or oaks according to Symmachus, or the fig tree according to the gospel, on which the Lord sought fruit and found none, and condemned it to eternal dryness. And they have already lost the very leaves and the show of words. Also the watered garden, that is, the knowledge of the Scriptures, or a paradise (another reading) of diverse trees, because without spiritual grace they bring forth not even the herbs that the weak man may eat.
1.31:
**“And your strength shall be”**
• then
• in persecution and captivity
**“your strength”**
• pride
• in which you trusted
**“as the ashes of tow”**
• Symmachus: the refuse of tow
• will quickly be consumed
**“As the ashes of tow”** — Allegorically or morally. All these things can be taken of contrary doctrines, because both masters and disciples are alike to perish, and their work is food for fire.
**“and your work”**
• of strength or of idolatry
• all fortifications
**“your work”** — or his
**“as a spark”** — of no importance
**“shall burn”** — by enemies or by the Lord
**“both shall burn together”** — strength, work, or idol; or Jerusalem, in which the idol [is]
**“and there shall be none to quench it”** — which the Lord kindles

2.1:
**“The word”** — about to come visibly in the flesh
**“that Isaias saw”** — understood
**“Isaias the son of Amos”** — proven nature, worthy that he saw it, to whom one must be believed
**“concerning Juda and Jerusalem”**
• that is, concerning Judah and Jerusalem
• The word that Isaias saw, etc. In the first vision, after the threat, prosperous things are promised: “I will restore thy judges as they were before,” etc. In this one, after prosperous things, adverse things are announced: “Behold the sovereign the Lord of hosts shall take away from Jerusalem and from Juda the valiant and the strong,” etc. Therefore, according to the Hebrew, both in that one and in this, it is to be understood not as against Juda and Jerusalem, nor as for Juda and Jerusalem, as the Septuagint wished, but, according to Symmachus, as concerning Juda and Jerusalem, in which both joyful and sad things can be contained. And it is to be noted that there he saw a vision, here the word that “was in the beginning with God.” And in that one, threatening the Jews, he comes to the salvation of the Gentiles; but in this one, beginning from the salvation of the Gentiles, Israel being punished, he gathers the believers from both walls into the Church.
• He shows when these things happen: when the Word will become flesh, which Isaias saw, that is, understood; for the other words are heard, not seen; this is said of this: “He was seen upon earth, and conversed with men.” Of this he adds: “And in the last days, etc.”
2.2:
**“And in”** — When the fulness of the time was come, God sent his Son
**“in the last days”** — in the last age
**“In the last days”** — Of which Jacob said to his sons: “Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you the things that shall befall you in the last days.” And a little after: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda, till he come that is to be sent,” etc. In John: “It is the last hour”; in which, namely, the stone cut out of the mountain without hands grew into a great mountain.
**“prepared”** — a lamb predestined by God, slain from the beginning of the world
**“mountain”** — which Daniel saw as a stone cut from the mountain without hands, etc.
**“Mountain”** — The mountains are angels, prophets, apostles, martyrs, and others who shone with miracles. Lesser hills receive light from the greater, whence: “leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills”; and elsewhere: “Mountains are round about it.”
**“the house of the Lord”** — of the Church
**“on the top of mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills”** — by desire of faith
**“Above the hills”** — Above all the saints, because all receive from his fullness (of whom: “mountains are round about it”), who are called mountains from Christ the mountain.
**“shall flow”** — quickly, abundantly
**“unto it”** — Incarnate.
**“all”** — many of the Gentiles
**“nations”** — Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles.
2.3:
**“And many people shall go”** — with the steps of faith
**“people”** — The Jews.
**“many”** — not all, because fewer of the Jews
**“and say: Come and let us go up”** — not content with their own salvation, they will urge one another: Come, etc.
**“to the mountain”** — Christ
**“of the Lord”** — of God
**“and to the house”** — the Church
**“of the God of Jacob”** — of the younger people, that is, the Christians signified by Jacob
**“To the house of the God of Jacob”** — This is said so that we may receive the Old Testament, and not, with the Manichean, seek another house than the house of Jacob.
**“and”** — when we are in the house of Jacob
**“he will teach us his ways”** — easier commandments by which we may advance to him
**“His ways”** — Which others have trodden. The Lord too, going up the mountain, taught his disciples. Therefore the ways are spoken of first, and walking in the paths comes after.
**“and we will walk in his paths”** — narrower ones
**“his”** — come, let us go up
**“for the law shall come forth from Sion”** — the old law, spiritually understood
**“From Sion”** — Not from Sina, the rock, but from Mount Sion, on which is Jerusalem, in which is the temple and the worship of God. The Lord too taught in the temple, as it was not fitting for a prophet to die outside Jerusalem.
**“and the word of the Lord”** — the gospel
**“from Jerusalem.”**
• the primitive Church, which is the watching and vision of peace
• in which is the religion
**“Law and word”** — As above he set word and law together, so that the princes might hear the word and the people take in the law by ear. For whoever shall have done the law will come to the word of God; the law will go out from the word as from a fountain, that it may water others.
2.4:
**“And he shall judge”** — concerning sins; for there will be a difference of punishments according to the difference of merits
**“nations”** — the Gentiles who are going to believe; he who does not believe is already judged
**“and rebuke many people”**
• the Jews
• he will rebuke the peoples by correcting them, because they did not receive the Son of God
**“and”** — therefore
**“they shall turn their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they be exercised any more to war.”**
• as before; for although afterwards wars were never so grievous
• And they shall turn their swords, etc. All zeal for warring will be turned into peace, which was plainly done when the Lord was incarnate; for so great was the discord in the world before him, until the twentieth year of Octavian Caesar, under whom he was born, that there was no passage from province to province. But when he was born who is our peace, who made both one, at whose birth the angels sang: “Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will,” all wars ceased and the works of agriculture were practised.
• Spiritually the swords are changed into ploughshares and the spears into sickles when the seditions of discord and of wrath are driven out, and the hardness of the heart is broken by the ploughshare, that is, by the word of God, and the thorns of vices are rooted out, that the seed of the word may grow, and at last we may eat the labours of our hands in the time of harvest, that is, of death.
2.5:
**“O house of Jacob, come ye”** — with me
**“and let us walk”** — from virtue to virtue
**“in the light of the Lord.”** — O house of Jacob, come ye, etc. After the calling of the Gentiles and the showing of the mountain of God, he invites his people who are of Jacob, that going out of the darkness of unbelief they may receive the light of Christ.
**“In the light”** — While you have the light, believe in the light. “Come ye to him and be enlightened,” etc. As if to say: he that doth evil hateth the light, but come with me, let us walk in the light of the Lord, who says: “I am the light of the world,” etc.
2.6:
**“For thou hast cast off thy people”** — nature
**“the house of Jacob”**
• that is
• to whom they ought to be like
• formerly
• and thou hast cast them off with reason, because
**“For thou hast cast off”** — After he had exhorted them, and saw their hardness in spirit, suddenly turning the eyes of his mind to the Lord, he says: “For thou hast cast off, etc.,” as if they were therefore to be exhorted, because thou hast cast off, etc.
**“because they are filled”** — with iniquity and deceits
**“as in times past”**
• in Egypt, or in the land of promise, in the times of the Judges
• Because they are filled, etc. Namely, while the Romans were casting out the Jews, foreigners dwelt in Judea, brought from wherever by Titus and Vespasian or other princes. Or they committed these things under impious kings before they were laid waste by the Babylonians.
**“and have had soothsayers”** — who foretell future things from the chattering of birds
**“as the Philistines”**
• The Seventy: foreigners; whence: foreigners have been made subject to me
• or Palestines, another reading, who most serve this superstition
**“As the Philistines”** — Philistines, who today are the Palestinians; because the Hebrew language has no such letter, but the Greek uses Philistiim in its place.
**“and have adhered to strange children”** — by departing from God, or with Gentiles whom they bought for abuse
**“have adhered.”** — lustfully
**“Have adhered to strange children”** — It signifies the lust of the victors upon the Jewish nation. For the Greeks and Latins also long laboured under this vice, but under the emperor Constantine, with the gospel shining forth, this foulness was destroyed along with the rest.
*Allegorically:* Strange children, or attendants of demons. For they have children, as Christ also has, who says: “Behold I and my children, whom the Lord hath given me.”
2.7:
**“Their land is filled with silver and gold”**
• as though, when they abound in riches, they are greedy and covetous
• Their land is filled with silver and gold, etc. The covetousness both of the Romans and of the Jews is branded. For Greek and Latin histories attest that nothing is more covetous than either nation. Among idols covetousness is condemned. Whence he says: “Covetousness, which is a serving of idols.”
**“and”** — yet
**“there is no end”** — the covetous always lacks
**“of their treasures.”** — the covetous man will not be filled with the riches of his treasures
**“And their land is filled with horses”** — of the victors or of the Jews
**“and innumerable”** — because what is against God is not worthy of number
**“their chariots”** — some in chariots, and some in horses; but we, etc.
**“With horses and innumerable”** — And this is against the Lord, who forbade chariots and horses to be multiplied; for these animals were given for help, not for pride; whence they are also called beasts of burden.
*Allegorically:* “A horse is a vain thing to save a man”; and elsewhere: “The horse and the rider he hath thrown into the sea.”
2.8:
**“And their land is filled”** — earthly
**“idols”**
• excessive abundance is followed by idolatry
• and
**“the work of his hands”** — statues and the like
**“they have adored what their fingers have made.”** — wondrous madness: what is better, what was made, or he who made it?
**“The work of the hands”** — Allegorically, etc. Every doctrine contrary to the truth. He adores the works of his own hands, and man, bound by the devil, is bent over and is not raised up except by the Lord, like the gospel woman whom Satan bound.
2.9:
**“And man hath bowed himself down”** — from his dignity; whence: man, when he was in honour, did not understand
**“man”** — earthly, weak in faith; why man is from the earth
**“and man hath been debased.”** — who seemed to be strong, because vir is from virtus
