**“Bowed himself down”** — Where once there was the temple and worship of God, there is a statue of Hadrian and an idol of Jupiter; whence: when you shall see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, etc.
**“not”** — others read: lest
**“therefore forgive”** — or: I will forgive, according to the Septuagint, in the person of God
**“them.”**
• because they committed such great things
• From the place where it is said: They are filled with iniquity, up to this place, some refer it to the Jews, as we have said, and others to the Romans and Chaldeans, who dwelt in their land after the Jews were taken captive; whence: And they are filled with idols, etc.
**“Therefore forgive them not”** — Isaias does not curse but blesses, because he calls down on them what is just, and everything just is good. But it is better understood of the Romans, lest the prophet seem to pray against his own people.
2.10:
**“Enter thou”** — because you do not wish to be converted
**“into the rock”** — then they will say to the mountains: Fall upon us, and to the hills: Cover us
**“and hide thee in the pit”** — in caves, which also happened, as the historians relate
**“from the face of the fear of the Lord”** — of the Babylonians or of the Romans, through whom God proved himself to be feared and glorified
**“and from the glory of his majesty.”** — and then
**“Enter into the rock”** — Allegorically. Flee for refuge to Christ, of whom: “and the rock was Christ”; and elsewhere: “the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs.” Hide thee in the pit, in the ground, in the protection of his flesh; the pits are on the cross, whence: “they have dug my hands and feet,” etc. From the face of the fear of the Lord, from the wrath of judgment; and from the glory of his majesty, because he will come “with great power and majesty.”
*Morally:* To hide in a pit of earth. “Enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father.” Or, he is hidden in a pit of earth who within the cave of the flesh hides the evil things he thinks in secret, lest they come forth outside through the working of the flesh.
2.11:
**“The lofty eyes of man”**
• pride
• of the powerful
**“are humbled”** — by the devastating Romans or Babylonians
**“and the haughtiness of men shall be made to stoop.”**
• nobility of birth
• The lofty eyes, etc. Neither riches nor power nor nobility will save anyone; one captivity will come upon all. These may also be taken of the judgment, when every creature will be humbled in the sight of God and will feel that it is nothing in comparison with him.
**“And the Lord alone shall be exalted”**
• because no one will escape his anger
• the proud being humbled
**“in that day.”**
• when he will avenge himself through the Romans or Chaldeans
• therefore
2.12:
**“Because the day of the Lord of hosts”** — who resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Whence: “He that exalteth himself shall be humbled.”
**“upon every one that is proud”**
• shall come
• the priests, scribes and Pharisees; or the day of judgment upon the devil and his members. Whence: “He that exalteth himself shall be humbled.”
**“and highminded,”** — shall come
**“upon every one that is arrogant, and he shall be humbled.”** — when praise is perfected out of the mouth of infants and sucklings, so that the enemy may be destroyed
**“Of the Lord of hosts”** — Wherever it speaks of the Lord’s victory or vengeance, it calls him the Lord of hosts, so that we may not doubt his victory, whose power is so great.
2.13:
**“and upon all the cedars of Libanus”** — proud in nobility
**“tall”**
• that is
• in nobility
**“and lofty”** — in pride
**“and upon all the oaks of Basan.”**
• the luxurious, who bear fruit for swine, that is, for demons
• Yet there are cedars of good odour, who can say with the Apostle: “We are the good odour of Christ.” Whence: “The cedars of Libanus, which he planted,” etc. And elsewhere: “I will set in the land the cedar and the box-tree.”
• Libanus is a mountain of the region of Phenicia, having cedars lofty above all trees. Basan is a region of Arabia, which king Og ruled; it has acorn-bearing oaks, whose fruit is the food of swine, not of men. By the cedars of Libanus are understood the nobility of the proud, for Libanus means whiteness; by the oaks of Basan, which means shame, those who wallow in the mire of lust, whose fruit is the food of demons, not of men.
**“The cedars of Libanus”** — “The voice of the Lord breaketh the cedars”; and: “I have seen the wicked highly exalted, and lifted up like the cedars of Libanus; and I passed by, and lo, he was not.”
2.14:
**“and upon all the high mountains”** — the higher ones
**“and upon all the elevated hills.”** — the proud
**“High mountains”** — For the variety of virtues, some of the good are called mountains, others hills. For the diversity of vices, some of the wicked are called mountains, others hills, to whom it is said: “I will bring upon you the sword.”
2.15:
**“And upon every high tower”** — Literally: when the Romans came, both towers and walls were utterly overthrown. Allegorically: those who excelled, or ought to excel, in life and virtues shall be overthrown in that day.
**“and upon every high tower and upon every fenced wall.”**
• A tower is built either for the defence of a city or as a lookout. We should all build one, after counting the cost. But if it becomes proud, it will fall upon him by whom it was built, like that one in Siloe or Jerusalem which killed eighteen men.
• The walls of the Church are wise men, strengthened by every reason, so that a perverse doctrine may not prevail over the truth; whence to Jeremias: “I have painted thy wall upon my hands.”
2.16:
**“and upon all the ships of Tharsis”**
• those who seek gain by ships
• The Hebrews think that in their language the sea is properly called Tharsis. If it is called otherwise, it is Syrum.
**“Ships”** — Josaphat had ships which he sent to Tharsis, but they were broken in Asiongaber. Solomon also had ships which went to Tharsis and returned with silver and gold and ivory and apes. But because each sinned, the one through the pleasure of Gentile women, the other through fellowship with the king of Samaria, each is referred to the heathen and to heretics, in whom there is only a glitter of eloquence and a sense built up by the devil’s art, and a dead speech, which is signified by the ivory, and a likeness of human reason, which we revere in the apes. Whence: “With a vehement wind thou shalt break in pieces the ships of Tharsis.” There are also good ships, of which it is said: “They that go down to the sea in ships,” etc.
**“Tharsis”** — Of any sea whatever. For the Hebrews call any sea Tharsis, and whatever gatherings of waters, seas; according to that: “the gathering together of the waters he called seas.” As Josephus relates, when the Romans arrived, those who were in the harbours were seized and their ships burned.
**“and upon all that is fair to behold.”**
• the temple, which is very beautiful; young men and virgins
• built by human reason, raising itself against the reason of God
2.17:
**“And the loftiness of men shall be bowed down”** — some sold, some slain, some dead of hunger
**“the loftiness of men”** — power and nobility
**“and the haughtiness of men shall be humbled, and the Lord alone shall be exalted”** — that is, he will appear high, or in judgment
**“in that day”** — when he has given his enemies into captivity
**“The loftiness of men shall be bowed down”** — Allegorically. Human speech seems reasonable if it is not compared with divine knowledge. But when falsehood approaches truth like straw to fire, it is devoured and perishes; and the doctrines of falsehood, which are called idols, if they were fabricated, are utterly ground to pieces by him as well.
2.18:
**“And idols shall be utterly destroyed”** — This was in the captivity of the Chaldeans, when the idols of the Jews were broken in pieces and the metals carried off to Babylon. For in the last captivity the Jews are not read to have worshipped idols. Therefore, though it is a mixture of both and of the day of judgment, since it says this specially, it is to be referred to the former.
**“and idols shall be utterly destroyed.”** — Bede. King Solomon built in Jerusalem Astarte, the idol of the Sidonians, etc., where, unless I am mistaken, it is shown that Solomon never fully repented, because he did not destroy the idols he had built.
2.19:
**“And they shall go”**
• idols
• this applies to both
**“into the holes of rocks”** — that is, into the hiding-places of hearts in which they are laid up
**“and into the caves of the earth”** — so that they may be hidden in the precipices of the inhabitant of the earth
**“from the face of the fear of the Lord”** — sent in by the Lord
**“and from the glory of his majesty”** — when he will appear glorious who was despised
**“when he shall rise up”** — who seemed to be sleeping
**“to strike”** — through the Romans or the Chaldeans, or in judgment
**“the earth.”** — earthly ones
2.20:
**“In that day”**
• of captivity
• Allegorically, etc. Silver is eloquence, gold wisdom, which are given by the Lord to men that they may serve God and speak of God. But those men misuse them in the making of idols. Whence: “I gave them silver and gold; but they made Baal of it.” When therefore one, terrified, has first hidden idols in the cave of his heart and concealed them in the pits of the earth, not daring to bring forth what he has wickedly fashioned, the second step is to cast them away and not suffer them to be in himself.
**“a man shall cast away his idols”** — false doctrines
**“his, of silver”** — of eloquence
**“and idols”** — in which they trusted
**“of gold, his”** — of wisdom
**“To adore moles”** — Not in fact. But as moles, the images of the Gentiles have eyes and see not; and as bats, which flee the light, for they are blind. So are all doctrines contrary to the truth; and when these are cast away, those who cast them away go into the clefts of the rocks and into the caverns, that is, that they may dwell not in dust and vile clay but in firm reason, and find for themselves the various openings of the virtues by which one comes to the truth.
2.22:
**“Cease ye therefore from the man”** — namely, to Christ
**“Cease ye therefore”** — That these things will happen unless you cease. Cease, then, lest you rage against Christ, who seems a mere man because he breathes through his nostrils and lives as other men do.
**“for ... high”**
• according to the divinity
• cease, because he is God
**“he is reputed”** — believed by the apostles and other saints
**“Reputed high”** — “The Lord is high above all nations.” And “the Highest himself hath founded her.” Yet the Hebrew signifies not “high” but “exalted”... For he is himself the height, not merely high.

3.1:
**“For behold”**
• because you would not cease from such a man, but shed innocent blood
• therefore I warn
• Up to this point, they think, it is said of judgment; what follows, of the coming captivity, which some refer to the Babylonians, others to the Romans. But it is better to refer all things to the passion of Christ, after all the gifts of grace were taken from the Jews.
**“The sovereign the Lord of hosts”** — whom no one resists
**“shall take away from Jerusalem”**
• of the two tribes
• from the priests
**“and from Juda”** — the princes
**“the valiant and the strong”** — everything will be weak for them, everything infirm, because they killed Christ, in whom alone is strength
**“the whole strength of bread”**
• by bread is meant whatever is eaten; the Lord so took this away from the Jews that they even devoured their sons
• who came down from heaven, who strengthens the heart of man
**“and the whole strength of water”**
• by water, whatever is drunk
• whoever drinks of this water shall thirst again
• The Jews have bread, they have waters also, but without strength or vigour. They read the Scriptures and do not understand; they hold the parchments but flee Christ who is written there. And they are fed with milk like little children, not with solid food, because they have lost strength; they are weak and eat herbs. The solid food of athletes is that which sustains life and strengthens the heart.
**“The whole strength of bread”** — Allegorically. Divine Scripture, when it needs the grinding of exposition, is food; when it is taken easily and without labour, drink. God took this away from the Jews and gave it to the Gentiles; whence: “the kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof”; and elsewhere: “I will send forth a famine into the land: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst of water, but of hearing the word of the Lord.”
3.2:
**“the strong man, and the man of war”** — so that no one may be able to resist visible or invisible enemies who rage even today.
**“the man of war”** — For among the Jews there is no one who fights for the law and judges according to it; for all are vain and foolish.
**“and the judge”** — because after the captivity they had Roman judges.
**“and the prophet”** — There is now no prophet, and he will know us no more.
**“and the cunning man”** — Those who at times divine truths, like Balaam, and the diviners of the five cities of the Philistines, by whose counsel the ark of the Lord was sent back. As if both true prophets and false ones will be taken away from the Jews.
**“and the ancient”** — in character.
**“the ancient”** — Whom the Septuagint translated presbyter. The glory of old men is grey hairs, that is, wisdom, of which: “the grey hairs of men are prudence.” Abraham alone was called presbyter, that is, old man, who lived fewer years than many from Adam down to himself. Roboam lost the kingdom because he would not hear the elders.
3.3:
**“The captain over fifty”** — The Levites, the gatekeepers, receive the head of fifty.
**“and the honourable in countenance”** — who is usually honoured by reverence of countenance alone.
**“and the counsellor”** — so that they rush headlong into everything without counsel.
**“and the skillful”** — the chief of craftsmen, as Beseleel was.
**“the architect”**
• With these lost, the grace of all building has been transferred to the Church. Whence: “As a wise architect I have laid the foundation.”
• The captain over fifty, etc. Allegorically. Christ is the head of penance and of those who are saved by penance. Whence it is said that if fifty just men be found in the city, it is to be saved. The number fifty also signifies the jubilee, of which Christ is the prince, as of the sabbath and of the other solemnities; whence: “The Son of man is Lord of the sabbath also.” The fiftieth psalm is set down as the penitential psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God.”
• By the man of fifty, understand the whole by a part. By these all princes, understand those taken away; and so it is no wonder if all dignity perishes among those to whom the power of waging war is not granted.
**“and the skillful in eloquent speech”**
• who, that is, has been trained in the law and the gospel.
• The Seventy: hearer. Necessary in the Church. Whence priests were once appointed to discern by what spirit the prophets spoke.
**“the skillful”** — A teacher or a hearer. For the first is blessed who is wise; the second, who hears the wise.
**“The architect”** — Christ himself is called the son of a craftsman, and in Paralipomenon we read of the valley of craftsmen. There indeed were craftsmen whom knowledge did not puff up, but who followed the humble Christ; whence: “I am the least of the apostles.”
3.4:
**“And I will give”** — these having been taken away: whom I had given.
**“children”** — in character, not in age.
**“to be their princes”** — Woe to the city whose prince is a child, and whose prince eats in the morning.
**“and the effeminate shall rule over them”**
• wanton, weak, unwarlike.
• I will give children, etc. Such was Roboam, who followed the counsels of the young men when he had received the kingdom at forty years of age. But Solomon, at twelve years, was not called young, because he was wise. Daniel also, before the judgment, was called a boy; after he judged, an elder and priest, because he was wise. Hence the apostle: a bishop ought not to be chosen a neophyte, lest he be puffed up with pride like the devil; whence: “I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven.”
• So also in the Church, because of the sins of the people, good princes, religious rectors, counsellors and prudent men are taken away. A boy rises against an old man, and no rank is honoured.
• The holy state of the Church is thrown into confusion.
**“And I will give children”** — Since he had said the rest in his own person, he suddenly introduces the Lord speaking, for greater authority.
**“The effeminate”** — The Seventy: mockers. Such as, namely, the concubines of the Levite mocked in Gabaa; the effeminate, luxurious, broken in the manner of a woman. Allegorically: the teachers of the people too are mockers, who devour the people of God as the food of bread and interpret the Scriptures perversely.
3.5:
**“And”** — then.
**“the people shall rush”** — where there is no governor, the people falls.
**“every man against”**
• against.
• against.
**“his neighbour”** — who ought to love as himself.
**“shall make it tumult”** — without reason.
**“the child against the ancient”** — in age or in manners
**“and the base against the honourable”** — in birth or in way of life
3.6:
**“For a man shall take hold of his brother”** — they do not choose one another in common
**“of the house of his father”**
• even
• a home-born slave
**“Thou hast a garment”** — therefore
**“be thou our ruler, and let this ruin”** — want
**“under thy hand”** — defence
**“shall take hold”** — Literally: when the Jews were shut in by the siege of the Romans, they were divided into three parts. Some held the temple and the citadel, others the upper part of the city, others the lower; and they set over themselves whom they wished, even the servants of their fathers, saying: “Thou hast a garment, be thou our ruler.” “And let this ruin be under thy hand,” that is, you have food and clothing; be our ruler, provided you deliver us from hunger, and our ruin be sustained by your help.
3.7:
**“he shall answer”** — chosen as prince
**“In that day, saying: I am no healer”**
• Christ alone heals the broken of heart, and binds up their bruises.
• I am not sufficient to heal your miseries.
**“and in my house there is no bread”** — who may suffice for me and for you.
**“nor clothing”** — therefore
**“He shall answer”** — This is not in the Hebrew but is added from the Septuagint. For according to the Hebrew it is joined thus: In that day he shall say, I am no healer, etc.
**“I am no healer”** — Morally. Let us not at once yield to the judgment of the multitude, but, when chosen for rule, let us know our own measure, because “God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.” Many who are hungry and naked, having neither spiritual food nor the tunic of Christ, promise others clothing and sustenance; and, full of sores, they boast that they are physicians, not fearing what is said: “Seek not to be made a judge, lest thou be not able to take away iniquities.”
3.8:
**“For is ruined”** — without help
**“Jerusalem”**
• Benjamin
• the city itself
**“and Juda”** — the province of Judea
**“For Jerusalem is ruined”** — Spoken in the person of the prophet. As if therefore they will find no one who is willing to help them, because they blasphemed the Lord, saying: You have a demon, and the like.
**“is fallen”** — therefore
**“because their tongue, and their devices”**
• I can destroy this temple made with hands, etc.
• Crucify him, crucify him. “His blood be upon us and our children.”
**“against the Lord”** — meek
**“to provoke”** — to anger
**“the eyes of his majesty”**
• regard of mercy
• because
**“because their tongue”** — although the Romans, as far as they were concerned, came to the siege over the tribute that was refused, yet the death of the Lord was chiefly the cause.
3.9:
**“The shew of their countenance”** — because seeing Christ in the flesh they were unwilling to believe.
**“The shew”** — They will acknowledge that this has happened because of their sins, or they will always have their sins before the eyes of the mind.
**“hath answered them”** — when placed in misery they will acknowledge that they suffer this because of the death of the Son of God.
**“and their sin as Sodom”** — defiled with the sodomitic vice
**“and their sin”** — Morally. He proclaims his sin as Sodom does and does not hide it, who by the example of his sin corrupts others as with a stench.
**“they have proclaimed abroad”**
• crying out, Crucify him, crucify him
• shamelessly
**“and they have not hid it”** — a second plank after shipwreck is to conceal impieties
**“Woe”** — therefore
**“to their souls”** — not only to the body
**“Woe to their souls”** — Septuagint. Woe to their souls, for they devised a most wicked counsel against themselves, saying: “Let us bind the just, because he is unprofitable to us.”
**“for”** — as they will be punished by their deserts
**“evils are rendered to them”** — for sins
**“evils”** — their own
3.10:
**“Say”** — readers, praise the justice of the Lord
**“to the just man”** — to Christ, to whom judgment has been given
**“that it is well”** — he has judged justly
**“for he shall eat the fruit”** — the reward
**“of his doings”** — “For what things a man shall sow, those also shall he reap.”
**“he shall eat”** — the wicked man
3.11:
**“Woe”** — Well: because woe to the wicked man, unto evil, which would ever last.
**“to the wicked unto evil”** — to the one laying snares
**“for the reward”** — For the recompense: he who delivered up his prince to Roman power is himself subject to it.
**“of his hands”** — of works
**“shall be given him”** — by the Lord
3.12:
**“my people”** — my people: the words of the Lord
**“their oppressors”**
• exactors, not teachers
• scribes and Pharisees, exacting the firstfruits and tithes, who ought to have taught
**“have stripped them, and women”** — of them; or they themselves effeminate
**“have ruled over them”**
• as if: do not believe them, because my people
• My people, etc. Let us take care that we not be exactors among the people, lest, according to the impious Porphyry, matrons and women become our senate, who rule in the churches, and the favour of women judge from the priestly rank.
**“O my people, they that call thee blessed”**
• O my people, who call you blessed: “let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head.”
• priests flattering those from whom they receive
**“the same deceive thee”**
• with flattering words
• that you not praise a man in his life
**“and destroy the way of thy steps”** — the uprightness of works
**“destroy”**
• by praising wrongly
• And the way of thy steps, etc. Whence Jeremias: “Ask which is the good way, and walk ye in it.” But if we have gone astray, let us hear the Lord saying in Ezechiel: I will give them another way, of which: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
3.13:
**“The Lord standeth up to judge”** — Now, as if angry, he does not sit, ready to render to each according to his works. Or, he does not yet sit so as to judge in the present, but stands considering and discerning the works of all, as if there is still a place for penance, and reserves a space.
**“The Lord standeth up to judge, and he standeth to judge the people”** — The people, who were deceived through ignorance and simplicity, are still called, that they may be saved. The Lord does not sit as one judging, but stands to judge, wishing the people to stand, whose way has been scattered. He comes against the princes and elders to judge, giving them place for defence; whence: “That thou mayst be justified in thy words,” etc.
3.14:
**“The Lord”** — at last
**“to judgment”** — eternal
**“will enter into judgment with the ancients of his people”** — prophets and patriarchs. Whence: when he sitteth among the senators of the land
**“and its princes”** — apostles, of whom: thou shalt make them princes over all the earth
**“for you”** — O Pharisees and scribes
**“have devoured”** — by violently exacting tithes and such like
**“for you have devoured”** — Jerome. I think this was among the elders and princes of the old people as it is among the priests and bishops of our time.
**“the vineyard”**
• of the house of Israel
• You have transferred a vine out of Egypt. “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.”
**“and the spoil of the poor”**
• of the innocent
• by tax, or by the spirit, one who could not pay nor defend himself
• is
3.15:
**“Why”**
• O princes
• as if for this he will condemn you in judgment
**“do you consume”** — or you afflict, another reading
**“my people, and grind the faces of the poor”** — of orphans and widows
**“grind”** — you wear down with hunger. Whence: for they wear away their faces, etc.
**“saith the Lord the God of hosts”**
• whom you ought to fear
• In whose houses is the plunder of the poor, while they store up for themselves the wealth of the Church and squander it in luxuries. What is given for the support of the poor, they keep for themselves or distribute to their kinsmen, and they make the want of others the riches of themselves or their own.
**“Why do you consume my people”** — Our princes too, when they publicly rebuke and shame poor offenders, do not so much as nod at the rich who sin worse.
3.16:
**“And the Lord said: Because the daughters of Sion are haughty”** — into pride
**“daughters of Sion”** — the lesser cities of Juda, towns which in the book of Josue are called daughters
**“and have walked”** — from vice to vice
**“with stretched out necks”** — in which pride is signified
**“and wanton glances of their eyes”** — by signs of wantonness
**“and made a noise as they walked”** — by playing
**“as they walked with their feet and moved in a set pace”**
• so that they might even entice those who see them by their gait
• adorned with the plunder of the poor
• Because the daughters of Sion are haughty, etc. This can be referred especially to the wives of the scribes and Pharisees, and also to others, on whose account, for their delights and luxury, their husbands despoiled the poor. Lest therefore they think themselves free from sin, the Lord says: Because, etc.
*Morally:* Because they are haughty, etc. Rebuked are the souls that are lifted up into pride, and pursue not manly hardness but womanish softness, and lose the ornaments of virtues, which are described under necklaces, collars, bracelets, and the like. These things are also said against the women of the Church, who walk with stretched out necks and speak by nods and signs.
3.17:
**“The Lord will make bald the crown of the head of the daughters of Sion”** — so that in place of adornment there is shame
**“Will make bald.”** — What is hidden will be laid open, and foul baldness will appear. For nothing is covered that shall not be revealed.
**“and the Lord will discover their hair.”** — by which sins are covered
3.18:
**“In that day”**
• with the Romans invading
• That is, of the Babylonian captivity. Or more truly, when they were taken by the Romans and lost all their ornaments. Or metaphorically, the ornaments of women, that is, of cities, were destroyed, which are in the streets, porticoes, the forum and the gymnasia, and in the public walls. We also refer these things to the soul in the moral sense.
**“the Lord will take away the ornaments of shoes, and little moons”** — the little moons: the ornaments of the Church, which are illumined by the sun of justice
**“of shoes”**
• Which in the wilderness were not worn out, but such as they brought out of Egypt they had for sixty years in the desert. By these are shod those who are to eat the flesh of the lamb; whence elsewhere: “Your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace.”
• These cannot last if one walks with a stretched-out neck. If garments are dragged with the feet, so that in place of matronly cleanness, the filth of the earth is turned up.
3.19:
**“And chains”** — an ornament of the neck hanging down to the breast, in which is the understanding of the mind
**“and necklaces”** — any ornaments whatever
**“and bracelets”** — of the arms, that is, good works; Rebecca received these at her betrothal
**“and bonnets”** — of the head, in which is all sense
3.20:
**“And bodkins”**
• of the hair, which are also called scrinones
• in which discernment is signified
**“and ornaments of the legs”** — of the ankles, like bracelets, whereby the foot does not stumble; and “deliver my feet from falling”
**“and tablets”** — of the neck, which are woven of rods of gold and silver, that is, of sense and speech
**“and sweet balls”** — in which they carried musk and other perfumes, as we are the good odour of Christ
**“and earrings”**
• from the ears
• that we may not hear the judgment of blood, but “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.”
3.21:
**“Rings”** — By which we are sealed for the warfare of Christ, whom the Father sealed; whence: “you, the seal of likeness.” The prodigal son also received a ring with the robe, and shoes.
**“Jewels hanging on the forehead”** — By which our face and head are adorned. Of which: “Like the precious ointment on the head, that ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron,” etc.
3.22:
**“and changes of apparel”** — of which they go from virtue to virtue
**“and short cloaks”** — by which the shoulders, and by which work, and the breasts in which the senses are protected
**“and fine linen, and crisping pins”** — by which the rule of all the precepts is smoothed
**“Fine linen”** — Jerome. That we may enjoy the delights in the Lord; whence: “And thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure.”
3.23:
**“And looking-glasses”** — for we see now through a glass in a dark manner, etc.
**“and lawns”** — fine veils
**“Headbands”** — Which bind the mind flowing hither and thither.
**“and fine veils”**
• with which the shoulders are covered
• with which we are covered against the heat of vices
**“Fine veils”** — A woman’s garment, very thin and fit to be seen through, suited to summer; and it is named from this, for summer is called teria.
3.24:
**“And instead of”** — for you
**“a sweet smell”**
• of virtues
• “My wounds have putrefied and are corrupted.”
**“stench”** — of vices and sins
**“and instead of a girdle”**
• golden
• of truth
• with which you stand girded, having your loins girded in virtue
**“a cord”**
• of lies
• of sins, by which each man is bound
**“instead of curled hair”** — twisted and turned back
**“baldness”**
• disfigurement of the head
• vice in place of virtue
**“and instead of a stomacher”**
• which holds in women the place that the rational holds in bishops
• lost
**“haircloth”** — the mourning of the penitent
**“Instead of a stomacher”** — By which the breasts are chastised, that they may not overflow. For I have betrothed you, etc. And elsewhere: in Egypt your breasts were broken.
3.25:
**“Thy fairest men”** — young men
**“Thy men also”** — the justice of the just will not deliver him
**“by the sword”** — of the Romans
**“shall fall, and thy valiant ones”** — warriors
3.26:
**“And her gates shall lament and mourn, and she shall sit desolate on the ground.”**
• which we see with our eyes
• a city utterly overthrown or a people wholly cast down
**“And shall lament”** — Whoever has given his place to the devil and has not kept his heart with all watchfulness, her gates will mourn, and with the bridegroom absent she will always be in bed, and falling into the dust she will sit.
**“Her gates shall lament and mourn”** — By metonymy: judges, kings, princes, who used to sit in the gate. Whence: They that sat in the gate spoke against me.

4.1:
**“And in that day seven women shall take hold of one man”** — Christ alone, who is without sin
**“In that day, saying”**
• when the height of men shall be bowed down
• The number seven and the number ten are familiar to the Jews because of the sabbath and the decalogue. Since, according to the ambiguity of the Hebrew language, by which the word saba is interpreted now as seven, now as many, and now as an oath, we can understand “many” in this place.
• Seven women. The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. “The spirit of wisdom and of understanding, the spirit of counsel and of fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and of godliness; and he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” They are called women because no one is begotten to God except through the Spirit. And in the plural, because the gifts are many, though the Spirit is one.
**“And seven women shall take hold of”** — When Nabuchodonosor took captive Sedecias the king and the princes of the Jews and the tribe of Juda and Benjamin (for the other ten had already been carried away beyond the mountains of the Medes and Persians and did not return afterwards), it could happen that far more women remained, and seven took hold of one man, saying: we have bread and clothing, lest we die without seed and incur this curse of the law, namely the curse of the barren woman who has not left seed upon the earth: take away from us the reproach of barrenness. “Let thy name be called upon us,” that thou mayst be called our husband.
*Allegorically:* The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are the seven women. Whence: “The spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom,” etc. And Christ is called man; whence Zacharias: “Behold a man, the Orient is his name.” In that day, that is, of the Lord’s incarnation, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit shall take hold of one man, namely Christ, because they found no other in whom to rest; whence: “He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending, and remaining upon him,” etc. These are the seven eyes of which Zacharias speaks: “Upon one stone are seven eyes,” and on the one golden candlestick are seven lamps and seven pipes. Nor did the Spirit fill him then for the first time, when he appeared upon him in the form of a dove at his baptism, but at the time of his conception.
*Morally:* They shall take hold, that they may hold firmly and not let go. They pass by all men; they take hold of none up to Christ, for “there is no man who sinneth not.” In other men the Spirit of tribulation has a lodging, not a dwelling of rest. For he was in the prophets and in other just men, but because they were men and therefore sinners, he was in them but did not remain; whence it is said of Christ alone: “Upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending, and remaining upon him, he it is that baptizeth.”
*Augustine:* The seven women are the seven churches to which John writes in the Apocalypse, through which all are designated. For in seven the whole is designated. These laid hold of Christ through faith, after the ascension, through the preaching of the apostles.
**“We will eat our own bread”**
• we do not need your bread or clothing
• our food is the bread that came down from heaven, the word; the bread of the women is the Father
• We will eat our own bread. The body of Christ. We will be covered with our own apparel: the ornaments of virtues. “Let thy name be called upon us”: from Christ may we be called Christians. “Take away our reproach,” which we suffer from the Jews, as being without God and without law; whence: “You are no more strangers and foreigners,” etc.
• We will eat our own bread, etc. Which is for the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son to possess all things equally and to need nothing. “Let thy name be called upon us”: that is, let them be called Christians from thee who desire to enjoy our dwelling. “Take away our reproach”: lest, driven out of the hearts of men, we be often forced by the stench of vices to change our lodging.
**“our own bread”** — Our bread is Christ, a rod from the root of Jesse; and the flower of the women’s bread is the Father, as also of Christ, who says: “My meat is to do the will of my Father.”
**“and wear our own apparel”** — with the word of God, with which each of these women is adorned
**“only let us be called”** — that we all may be called by your name, that is, all be called Jesus, so that your name may be all in all
**“by thy name”**
• Jesus
• that the imperfection of the law may be completed in the gospel
**“take away”** — Because false doctrines will rise up against wisdom, and against the other women, that is, the virtues. Each has its opposite rising up, when false virtues steal their names.
4.2:
**“In that day”** — of captivity
**“shall be the bud of the Lord”**
• the earth is opened and may bring forth the Saviour
• The Son
• the remnants of Israel will be made safe
**“in magnificence”**
• in this, that God
• “O Lord our Lord, how admirable is thy name in the whole earth!”
**“and glory, and the fruit of the earth”**
• The Son of Mary
• “of the fruit of thy womb I will set upon thy throne.”
**“high”**
• above all angels and men
• in that he is man
**“and a great joy”** — from him
**“to them that”** — who believed in him; to others, sorrow, as to the scribes and Pharisees
**“shall have escaped”** — by him
4.3:
**“And in”** — that is, these
**“every one”** — not all, but the remnant
**“that shall be left”** — cast off by unbelievers
**“in Sion”** — the Church, which contemplates God and enjoys the vision of peace
**“and that shall remain in Jerusalem, shall be called holy”** — Christian from Christ
**“every one that is written”**
• predestined
• Namely, although the apostles and other faithful, of whom: “Except the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we had been as Sodom.”
**“in life”**
• in the book of life
• “Rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven.”
• which will be
**“in Jerusalem”** — heavenly
4.4:
**“If the Lord shall wash away”** — Because it is affirmative: as if he will truly wash away in baptism.
**“the filth”** — of vices
**“of the daughters”** — of souls
**“Sion”** — of the Church
**“and the blood”** — of the prophets, whom they and their fathers shed, and of him of whom they said: “His blood be upon us and our children.”
**“of Jerusalem”** — through penance. Whence: “Wash ye, be clean.”
**“out of the midst thereof, by the spirit of judgment”** — lighter things
**“and by the spirit”** — heavier things
**“of burning”**
• of fervent charity, by which he shed blood.
• By the spirit of burning, which is given in baptism, where there is discernment. For from then it appears for whom punishment is predestined, and for whom a crown.
**“By the spirit of judgment, and by the spirit of burning”** — Namely, of tribulation and passion, by which the elect are purified. Whence: the furnace tries the potter’s vessels; whence John: I baptize you in water, he in the Holy Spirit and fire. For man gives water only; God gives the Holy Spirit, who washes away filth and the sins of blood.
4.5:
**“And the Lord will create”** — “Old things have passed away”; “in Christ there is a new creature.”
**“upon every place of mount Sion”** — of the Church, which is a mountain in contemplation
**“and where he is called upon”** — by the faithful, the sons of Israel
**“a cloud”** — a cloud was present by day, fire by night
**“by day”** — “The sun shall not burn thee by day, nor the moon by night.”
**“A cloud by day”** — That is, the overshadowing of the Spirit in prosperity, lest they be lifted up; as the cloud was for the children of Israel by day, and fire by night.
**“and a smoke”**
• of compunction, whence tears
• And smoke, etc. Whence: “The house was filled with smoke”; and elsewhere: “He toucheth the mountains, and they smoke.”
**“and the brightness”** — for enlightenment, lest they lose the way
**“of a flaming fire”** — “For our God is a consuming fire.”
**“in the night”** — by adversity, lest they be broken
**“for over all the glory”** — of the Church
**“shall be a protection”**
• of Christ
• Over all the glory, etc. Many of the Jews, and those associated with them, understand this of the captivity in Babylon and the return to Jerusalem under Zorobabel, Esdras and Nehemias.
• For over all, etc. The Jews refer this passage to Antichrist, whom they conjecture to be signified by whirlwind and tempest, and they trust that they will be defended from him by divine power. But we refer it to the first coming of Christ.
4.6:
**“And there shall be a tabernacle”** — The Church.
**“and”** — shall be.
**“for a shade”** — under the protection of God.
**“in the daytime from the heat”**
• of persecution.
• My God, my helper, etc.
**“and for a security and covert”** — I shall be protected under the covert of thy wings.
**“from the whirlwind”** — by the assault of persecutors.
**“and from rain”** — by a lesser persecution.

5.1:
**“I will sing to my beloved”** — to the people of the Jews, or to God the Father.
**“the canticle”** — a mournful song.
**“The canticle”** — A canticle, sometimes in gladness, sometimes in sadness; such as this one which he composed who, seeing the city, wept, saying: “If thou also hadst known.”
**“of my cousin”**
• the son of an uncle.
• of Christ, from the same people from which I was born, which canticle he himself composed for his vineyard.
**“concerning his vineyard”** — “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.”
**“My beloved had a vineyard”** — This is my beloved Son.
**“on a hill”** — in power, in strength.
**“in a fruitful place”** — God hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.
5.2:
**“And he fenced it in”** — The guard of angels.
**“and picked the stones”** — stone idols and all things that hinder divine worship.
**“the choicest vines”**
• cast out.
• from all nations.
• not from any sprout or kind.
• Another reading: a vine of sorech, which is a kind of the best and most abundant vine, with everlasting fruits.
• All the things that are said of the vineyard are referred to the state of the soul, which, planted by God, did not bring forth grapes but wild grapes, and, given over to the beasts to be trampled, did not receive the rain of doctrine, having despised the gifts of the past.
**“And he planted it”** — by instructing with the law.
**“and built a tower”**
• The temple.
• in which I might store the fruits and watch out for lurking beasts.
**“in the midst thereof, and set up a winepress”**
• altar, where the blood of victims was poured out.
• so that grapes might be pressed in the same place.
**“and set up a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth”** — the fruit of good works.
**“and it brought forth wild grapes”**
• Called wild grapes because they grow on the banks of roadways.
• by the bitterness of vices
**“wild grapes”** — In Hebrew: usin.
5.3:
**“And now”** — because I did what I ought.
**“O ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and ye men of Juda, judge”** — hears by my reason, to which the vineyard does not contradict.
**“between me and my vineyard”**
• by creation, by benefit
• Now therefore, etc. Similarly Nathan the prophet asks David, so that he pronounces judgment about himself as about another. Whence: “He will bring those evil men to an evil end; and will let out his vineyard to other husbandmen.” The husbandmen are the apostles.
5.4:
**“What”** — further
**“is there that I ought to do more”** — the things mentioned above
**“to my vineyard, that I have not done to it”**
• by cultivating well
• as if I seem to have done this, perhaps beyond what was due
**“that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes”**
• as if uncultivated
• Or that which I looked for, etc. According to some, he said this above to himself; here, however, he asks others what he had thought.
5.5:
**“And now”** — because he returns evil for good; he adds this judgment
**“And now I will shew you”** — As if, because you do not wish to answer, I will answer for you.
**“what I will do”** — whom no one resists
**“to my vineyard”** — no other
**“I will take away the hedge”**
• the help of angels
• let us pass from these seats
**“and it shall be wasted”** — to the nations
**“I will break down the wall thereof”** — It is the same, but repetition is confirmation.
5.6:
**“And I will make it desolate”** — Your house shall be left to you desolate.
**“it shall not be pruned”** — by the sickle of God’s word; and when he sins he will not be corrected
**“and it shall not be digged”** — by the admonition of fear he will not be humbled
**“and briers and thorns shall come up”**
• he will be overwhelmed by the multitude of sins
• I will take away, etc. That is, so that those who did not perceive God through benefits may perceive him through punishments; or he threatens punishment so that they may turn to penance.
**“and I will command the clouds to rain no rain upon it”** — to preachers, who rain with words, flash with miracles, shine with virtues
**“rain”**
• drops of doctrine
• And I will command the clouds, etc. Which under Elias (because all were idolaters) did not rain for three years and six months, lest instead of grapes they should bring forth thorns, but that in their dryness they might ask him who gives the rains of virtues. Whence: I will make for you a heaven of iron and an earth of brass; and elsewhere: The heaven that is over thy head shall be of brass, and the earth that is under thee of iron.
• And I will command the clouds. This after the Lord’s ascension, when they had no prophets and rejected the apostles, of whom it is said: “Who are these, that fly as clouds?”
5.7:
**“For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts”**
• He explains the metaphor.
• I will do this to my vineyard; for the vineyard
**“is the house of Israel”** — the ten tribes, or the whole people
**“and the man of Juda”** — the two tribes
**“his pleasant plant”**
• by comparison with Israel, who worshipped calves; whence he was first taken captive
• because, the other tribes having been separated, he afterwards sprouted
**“his”**
• of God
• The house of Israel, etc. Since the kingdom was divided, the ten tribes were called Israel, but the two were Juda, among whom kings of Juda reigned. Their men were a pleasant plant to God, because among them were priests, Levites, religious men, when Isaias spoke these things; or because Christ was born of them.
**“I looked that he should do judgment”** — grapes
**“and behold iniquity”** — wild grapes
**“and do justice”**
• would receive
• by receiving Christ
**“and behold a cry”**
• Take him away; crucify him
• And behold a cry, etc. Or they made a cry instead of justice, because they killed Christ, whose blood cries to the Lord from the earth. Whence: “The voice of the blood of thy brother crieth to me from the earth.”
5.8:
**“Woe to you that join house to house and lay field to field, even to the end of the place”**
• and with the earth failing, greed is not satisfied
• Woe to you that join. This is said against the heretics, who join house to house, that is, doctrines to doctrines, like the foolish man who built his house upon the sand. And they join new things to old until the land fails, namely sense and human speech.
**“Woe to you that join”** — This is said specially to the Jews, who were most greedy; generally, to all the greedy, who make the need of others their own pleasure.
**“shall you alone dwell”** — others being shut out
**“in the midst of the earth”**
• at large
• or was so great a land created for you alone?
5.9:
**“These things are in my ears”** — still sounding
**“saith the Lord of hosts”** — which are
**“in my ears”** — The prophet, as if he heard with his inner ears these words which are of the Lord of hosts.
**“Except”** — namely
**“many houses shall become desolate”** — after the captivity
**“great and fair”** — in which you delight
**“without an inhabitant”**
• as if my anger will not rest
• aposiopesis
• Unless many houses, etc. Namely the pomp and structure of the words of heretics, and dialectical arguments. The tilling also and the building of the heretics shall be rooted out. And from the tenfold and thirtyfold number in which Ezechiel prophesied and the Lord was baptized, they shall be reduced to an ephi, which in comparison with a manifold number is bound together in unity; because of the vineyard of the Sodomites is their wine, and their grape a grape of gall.
5.10:
**“For ten”** — which is a sacred number
**“acres”**
• a hundred and twenty feet in length
• others: ten yokes. Acres, where ten yoke of oxen worked
**“For ten acres”** — The barrenness of the land is shown, which was to follow the captivity.
**“of vineyard shall yield”** — others: a bath
**“one little measure”** — Not more.
**“and thirty”** — in which the Lord is baptized
**“bushels”**
• that is, the cor, which in Hebrew is gomer
• which used to multiply shall decrease
• by excessive barrenness
**“of seed shall yield three bushels”** — or ephi, which is a measure of dry goods
5.11:
**“Woe to you that rise up early in the morning”** — eagerly
**“to follow drunkenness”** — in Hebrew, sicera
**“and to drink till the evening, to be inflamed with wine”**
• to all vices
• Woe to you that rise up early in the morning, etc. Every disturbance of the soul is drunkenness, which is conceived of the wine of the fury of dragons and the venom of asps. Many drink this from morning till evening, that is, from youth to old age. Others at the third, sixth, ninth, or eleventh hour are roused from the feast, and it is said to them: Awake, you that are drunk with wine; upon this wine fire and brimstone are rained from the Lord; whoever therefore drink of it shall be burned up. Whence: You shall not drink wine and strong drink when you go into the tabernacle. They seek the harp and the psaltery, whose inventor was Tubal, of the stock of Cain. The king of Babylon had these musical instruments, at which the peoples, prostrate on the ground, adored the golden statue.
• But they are most unhappy who, occupied until old age with gluttony and drunkenness and various pleasures, do not understand the works of the Lord in themselves.
**“Woe to you that rise up early”** — As if captivity were threatening, yet you give yourselves to luxury. Whence: woe to you. These things are said also to our prelates, who drink from morning till evening, who, occupied with delights, do not understand the Creator from creatures. Nor do they consider his works. Whence: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.”
5.12:
**“The harp, and the lyre, and the timbrel, and the pipe”** — to increase luxury
**“and wine are in your feasts: and the work of the Lord you regard not, nor do you consider the works of his hands”** — you neglect to foresee why you were created yourselves, or what the Lord is going to do to you.
5.13:
**“Therefore”** — therefore
**“is my people led away captive”** — by the Romans or by the devil
**“because they had not”** — because he was unwilling to have it
**“knowledge”** — of things future or present
**“and their nobles have perished with famine”** — of hell
**“and their multitude were dried up with thirst”**
• Really, or of doctrine: “He hath brought me up, on the water of refreshment.”
• Therefore, etc. Morally. Whatever we have said of the people of the Jews, let us refer to those who are occupied with the delights of the world. Who, not regarding the works of God, are led captive into sin, and have no knowledge of God; and perishing with hunger and thirst for works and virtues, they are dragged down into hell, to be tormented for ever, wretchedly humbled for their power and pride.
5.14:
**“Therefore”** — as said above
**“hath enlarged”** — so that it may receive the multitude
**“hell her soul”** — the desire to devour; it is said not that it has a soul but according to human custom
**“and opened her mouth without any bounds”** — insatiably
**“and their strong ones shall go down”** — of the people
**“and their people, and their high”** — the proud
**“and glorious ones”** — the nobles
**“his”** — of the people
**“unto it”** — hell
5.15:
**“and”** — then
**“shall be brought down”** — from pride
**“man”** — the lesser, because they understand themselves to be mortal, who now run unbridled as though never to die.
**“and man shall be humbled”** — the greater
**“and the eyes of the lofty shall be brought low”** — of the proud
5.16:
**“And”** — when the things said above have been fulfilled
**“the Lord of hosts”**
• who was despised
• who seemed unjust
**“in judgment”**
• to the just
• judge not before the time
• Thou art just, O Lord, and thy judgment is right.
**“and the holy God”** — in himself
**“shall be sanctified”**
• he will appear holy
• Let thy name be sanctified.
**“in justice”** — done
5.17:
**“And”**
• and then
• by the doctrine of the Father
• those being removed
**“the lambs shall feed”**
• not eaten
• the chosen, the meek
**“according to their order”** — capacity
**“and the deserts”** — the scriptures deserted by the Jews
**“into fruitfulness”** — in spirit, to others of understanding
**“turned”** — the nations
**“shall eat”** — And the lambs shall feed, etc. Historically it is the same as what is above: strangers devour your region before your eyes.
**“Strangers”** — “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof.”
5.18:
**“Woe to you that draw”**
• These things are said to the leaders of the Jews, who, neglecting the prophecies of the prophets, joined sins to sins.
• Woe to you that draw: These things are said to the leaders of the Jews, who, though often called to penance, persist even today in blasphemies, and three times each day in all the synagogues under the name of Nazarenes curse the name of Christians.
**“iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as the rope of a cart”**
• the bond of sin
• a thong, according to the Seventy
**“sin as the rope of a cart”**
• burdened with sins
• “The cords of the wicked have encompassed me.” And each one is bound with the cords of his own sins. And rightly is iniquity drawn with cords of vanity, because sins are linked to sins, and are empty like the threads of spiders. But if we wish to get out, we are held as by the strongest bonds.
**“With cords of vanity”** — Among whom were those to whom the Lord said: Go out. The red heifer also neither drew the yoke nor was bound with cords. Achitophel also and Judas, of whom one betrayed David, the other Christ, drawing their sins with a long rope, perished by hanging, thinking they could end the evil of conscience by present death, supposing that after death there is nothing.
5.19:
**“That say: Let him make haste”** — do not think the wrath of God is coming, but that the prophets threaten in vain
**“and let his work come quickly”** — the captivity which you prophets preach
**“that we may see it”** — if it is true
**“and let the counsel come”** — which you alone behold
**“of the Holy One of Israel”** — of the one sanctifying
**“that we may know it”**
• counsel
• which we now do not believe
5.20:
**“Woe to you that”** — they mortify souls that are dying, and give life to those that are not living
**“call evil good”**
• the just
• Christ, who says, “I am the good shepherd”
**“and good evil”**
• the devil
• the unjust
• Barabbas
**“that put darkness for light”** — the devil, who is night and darkness, and who transformed himself into an angel of light; whence the fellowship of light with darkness
**“and light for darkness”** — Christ, “I am the light of the world”
**“that put bitter”** — falsehood
**“for sweet, and sweet”** — truth
**“for bitter”** — Woe to you that call, etc. This is said especially against the Jews, who chose Barabbas and condemned Christ. Generally, to all who justify the unjust and condemn the just. Evil, darkness, bitter, and the like are put with a like signification and figure. In Barabbas we understand the devil, of whom: deliver us from evil.
*Allegorically:* Woe, you who say, etc. All doctrines contrary to the truth are bitter; the truth is sweet. We must therefore beware lest we follow a lie in place of the truth, darkness in place of light. “There are ways that seem right to a man, and the ends thereof lead to hell.” He is a just man who perishes in his own justice, to whom it is said, “Be not over just.” Whence: “we will not turn aside neither to the right hand nor to the left.” But we hardly avoid this curse, since we both flatter the wicked because of their power and despise the good because of their poverty. Whence Aquila more significantly: Woe to you who say to the evil man, “You are good,” and to the good man, “You are evil.” The scribes also and Pharisees, not receiving the words of the Saviour but the traditions of men and old wives' fables, made good evil and evil good.
5.21:
**“Woe to you that are wise in your own eyes”** — of a proud heart
**“and prudent in your own conceits”** — be not wise in your own sight
**“Woe to you that are wise”** — Having despised the wisdom of God, you are lifted up among yourselves by your own. “For wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human.” Prudence, according to the Stoics, is of human things only. This is against the scribes and Pharisees, who have the key of knowledge, and neither enter to Christ nor permit others to enter.
5.22:
**“Woe to you that”** — Whence above: “Woe to you that rise up early in the morning to follow drunkenness.”
**“that are mighty to drink”** — he is judged the mightier who is more drunken
**“wine”** — the wine of the dragon
**“and stout men at drunkenness”**
• you boast of your strength in this
• To drink wine, etc. Allegorically. Wine is any vice. For the drunken themselves make the peoples drunk, so that raving they cry out against the Lord. Priests about to enter the tabernacle must not drink wine and strong drink; nor the Nazarites, to whom neither raisins nor vinegar made of wine is given. Whence in Proverbs: “Give not wine to kings,” lest, that is, they forget wisdom, and lest those who can do more than others harm their subjects by other vices and especially by anger. And he mingles strong drink who, being full of drunkenness, feigns certain shadows and images of virtues.
• From an abundance of bread and wine the sin of Sodom grew.
**“Drunkenness”** — Wine contains one vice. Drunkenness, which in Hebrew is signified by sicera, is all that overturns the state of the mind.
5.23:
**“That justify the wicked”** — you say they have justice
**“for gifts”** — not weighing the cause but the gifts
**“and take away the justice of the just from him”**
• which would be justly judged against him
• That justify, etc. It was said above that instead of grapes they brought forth thorns, and hay, and wood, and stubble, and briers, to be burned; because they did not do these things only, but cast away the law and blasphemed the word of God. Of whom: “the law shall go forth out of Sion, and the word of the Lord out of Jerusalem.”
5.24:
**“Therefore”** — on account of the aforesaid iniquities
**“as the tongue of the fire devoureth the stubble”** — the tongue
**“the heat of the flame consumeth it: so shall their root be as ashes”** — of eternal fire
**“and their bud”** — evil work
**“shall go up as dust”** — Not so the wicked, not so: but like the dust, which the wind driveth from the face of the earth.
**“They have cast away”** — and deservedly
**“for the law of the Lord of hosts”** — the new, namely the gospel
**“And”** — therefore
**“have blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel”** — Thou art a Samaritan, and hast a devil.
**“Their root”** — A wicked thought, from which the work proceeds as a sprout. Whence the apostle: “Lest any root of bitterness springing up, etc.”
5.25:
**“Therefore”** — on account of the sins of the princes
**“is the wrath of the Lord kindled”** — vengeance
**“of the Lord”** — O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation; and Jeremias: Correct us, O Lord, but yet with judgment, and not in fury.
**“against his people”**
• before, in the fathers
• Jacob, the cord of his inheritance
**“and hath stretched out”** — about to strike
**“his hand”** — The Son, the arm of the Lord, to whom it has been revealed; and elsewhere: “the hand of the Lord touched me”
**“upon them”**
• the people
• He who had been angry against the princes and the powerful, who are wise in their own eyes and follow bribes, whom the tongue of fire devoured, so that the powerful may suffer torments powerfully.
• He is angry. Not that he is subject to human passions, but we who sin do not fear unless we hear the Lord angry. Whence: “the patience of God leadeth thee to penance.” “But according to thy hardness thou treasurest up to thyself wrath, against the day of wrath.”
**“Therefore is the wrath kindled”** — It is to be noted that he does not reproach idolatry or the other sins, but that they have cast away the law of the gospel and blasphemed the law of the Lord.
**“And struck them”** — the people
**“and”** — thence
**“the mountains were troubled”** — hyperbolically, on account of the greatness of the evils
**“and their carcasses became”** — overthrown by the Romans
**“as dung in the midst of the streets”** — but
**“For all this his anger is not turned away”** — because they have not been converted
**“but his hand”** — the power of striking
**“stretched out”**
• as though about to strike still
• And he struck, etc. He speaks of future things as past, with prophetic certainty. Whence: “And they gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”
5.26:
**“And he will lift up a sign”**
• because they have blasphemed the word of the Lord
• of calling, who will gather the Romans against the Jews
**“to the nations”** — of the Romans
**“afar off, and will whistle”**
• will inspire
• this is the sign
**“to them from the ends of the earth”** — the Roman army to be gathered
**“and behold they shall come with speed”** — the sign having been received
**“shall come swiftly”**
• drawn not by its own power but by the power of God
• And he will whistle, etc. The Hebrews understand this place of the Babylonians; but we, attending to the sequence, understand the Romans, who dwell at the ends of the earth. Whence Italy, because Hesperus sets there, was once called Hesperia. For if the discourse were of the Babylonians, he would have said, in the prophetic manner, “I will call him that is from the north,” or would have pointed out the Babylonians and Assyrians more openly.
5.27:
**“There is none that shall faint”**
• hyperbolically
• anyone on so great a march
**“nor labour”** — as it seems, out of desire to accomplish
**“among them”** — in the army
**“shall not slumber”** — from eagerness to fight
**“nor sleep”** — by night, so that they are always ready
**“neither shall the girdle of their loins be loosed, nor the latchet of their shoes be broken”** — through age, all things will last longer than usual
5.28:
**“Their arrows are sharp”** — the quality of the arms is described
**“and all their bows are bent”** — not slack
**“The hoofs of their horses shall be like the flint”** — untiring
**“and their wheels”** — of chariots
5.29:
**“Their roaring”** — a metaphor: he will come not so much to fight as to plunder and devour, like a lion
**“like that of a lion, they shall roar like young lions: yea they shall roar, and take hold of the prey”** — the Jews and their possessions
**“and”** — eagerly
5.30:
**“And they shall make a noise”** — the noise of the victors
**“against them that day, like the roaring of the sea”** — then
**“we shall look”**
• in sympathy the prophet joins himself to his people
• who now are proud
**“towards the land, and behold darkness”** — despair
**“of tribulation, and the light”** — of the hope we had in the Lord
**“is darkened with the mist thereof”** — of tribulation
**“We shall look”** — Not daring to look up to heaven, whose inhabitant, God, we have offended.

6.1:
**“In the year that king Ozias died”** — the kingdom of sin
**“Ozias”**
• under whom the preceding visions were seen
• Jerome’s book on this vision survives
• In the year, etc. Ozias is the same as Azarias, who, when he rashly offered sacrifice, was struck with leprosy. In his reign the foregoing things were seen; when he was dead, Isaias saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne. Morally: for while the leprous king, that is the devil, reigns in us, we can neither see the Lord in his power nor know the mysteries of the Trinity; so the children of Israel, when Pharao was dead, were able to cry to the Lord; Ezechiel, when Phacias, a most wicked prince, was dead, falling on his face, cries to the Lord with a loud voice.
• King Ozias. That is, the king, a leper, who usurped the priesthood.
**“I saw”** — while the son of Joatham reigned, who did that which was right in the sight of the Lord
**“the Lord”** — the Son
**“sitting”**
• as reigning
• No man hath seen God at any time, that is, with the eyes of the flesh; but one can see him with the eyes of the heart, as Isaias saw. “Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God.” Or certainly, he was seen by the prophets not in his own nature but in a created thing that was subject to him.
**“I saw the Lord”** — That is, Christ; whence John: “These things said Isaias, when he saw his glory.” And Paul in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Holy Ghost spoke well by Isaias,” “with the ear you shall hear, and shall not understand,” etc. The Son was seen in the habit of one reigning; the Holy Ghost spoke on account of the fellowship of majesty.
**“concerning”** — upon; in the aspect of a reigning one
**“a throne high”** — the angels, in whom he sits and through whom he decides his judgments
**“and elevated”** — and lifted up; reigning not only among men
**“and his train filled the temple”** — and the house was full; that which builds upward, not that which is downward, which the wise woman builds and the foolish one tears down
**“his train”**
• from his majesty; reigning
• his majesty; the angels fill the higher places and the lower ones
**“Upon a throne”** — He who sees the Lord reigning among the heavenly powers sees him upon a high and elevated throne; these are the thrones and dominations, etc. Morally: Daniel saw the Lord sitting, but not upon a high throne; and elsewhere it is said: “I will sit and judge the people in the valley of Josaphat.” The sinner sees God sitting in the valley of Josaphat, that is, of judgment; the just man, like Isaias, upon a high throne. When you consider how he dispenses human things and for our salvation comes down to earth, you see his throne lowly and near the earth.
**“The temple: his train”** — The Church above fully knows his majesty, that is, how great he is; which does not do the things that are below.
**“and those”** — and those: the hosts of angels, or wonders
**“that were under him”** — which are under him; lower things, to God
**“filled”**
• were filling; by his service
• with various gifts
**“the temple”**
• The temple: that is, the Church which is below
• Morally: make yourself a temple that you may be filled
6.2:
**“stood the seraphims”**
• Two: that is, the two Testaments, which is better
• burning, or inflaming with the love of God
• Whence: “his ministers a burning fire.”
**“Upon it”**
• upon it: the temple
• angels over the Church as guardians
**“the one had six wings, and the other had six wings: with two they covered his face”** — six wings to the one and six wings to the other; with two they covered his face, of God, not their own
**“and with two they covered his feet”** — and with two they covered his feet: after these things, who will declare what is to come?
**“and with two they flew”**
• and with two they flew; opening the middle
• because through the two Testaments we are always drawn to the things above
• Some say the seraphim are powers in heaven, standing by God and praising, which are sent into service especially to those who need purification, and on account of some sins, in part to punishments.
• Each had six wings, etc. Jerome, Victorinus: He understood the twelve apostles. But we understand the twelve stones of the altar, which iron did not touch, and the twelve gems in the priest’s diadem.
• Angels are said to have wings because they dwell in the heights, or because of their swift running to all things, just as winds are also called wings.
• The seraphim, that is the aforesaid testaments, with two wings, namely their doctrine, which has wings because it lifts to heaven, and two because there are two testaments. Or two wings, because they teach the love of God and of neighbour; they veiled the face of God, that is, they teach nothing that was before the world. Angels also and preachers teach nothing of it; likewise they veil the feet.
**“Seraphims”** — Seraphim is interpreted burning. Of which: “I am come to cast fire on the earth,” etc. And: “Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he opened to us the scriptures?” And: “The words of the Lord are silver tried by the fire.” There is therefore a saving burning in the sacred scriptures, by which sins are purged. Or, the beginning of the mouth, which signifies the Hebrew tongue, in which the Old Testament was written. Burning, then, and the beginning of the mouth are the two testaments, which stand around God, and by them he is known.
*Allegorically:* The two seraphim are the two Testaments looking at each other in all things, that is, agreeing, by which we know only the middle things.
*Origen:* The two seraphim are my Lord Jesus and the Holy Spirit. Do not think that this divides the nature of the Trinity, but the offices of the names are kept, which Jerome calls impious.
*Jerome:* Cherubim: a multitude of knowledge, upon whom the Lord is shown sitting in the manner of a charioteer. Whence: “Thou that sittest upon the cherubims, shine forth before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasses.” But except for this place I do not remember having read of the seraphim in the canonical scriptures. Those therefore err who are accustomed to write in prayers: “Who sittest upon the cherubim and seraphim.”
**“Stood”** — That is, they stand, assisting God; they fly, showing God; they uncover, as it were, the middle: they do not reveal the things that are veiled, nor veil the things that are known.
**“With two they covered his face”** — What things were before these I do not know; from these I understand God. Whence Isaias: “Shew the things that are to come hereafter, and we shall know that ye are gods.” (Declare to me the former things and the last that shall be, and I will say that you are gods.)
**“They covered his feet”** — What will be after this world we do not know; yet we know only the middle things, which were made or are being made in six days or ages.
**“With two they flew”** — Because we have knowledge only of the present.
*Jerome:* My Hebrew went by a far different way. For he says that no one of the prophets besides Isaias saw the seraphim standing about God, and that the seraphim themselves are not mentioned elsewhere. Then, that it was a sign foretold of the consummation and captivity of Jerusalem, which was brought about under Nabuchodonosor. For from Ozias, under whom he began to prophesy, to Sedecias, who reigned last and who was led blind into Babylon, there were eleven kings, and a twelfth, Godolias, whom the king of Babylon had set over the land, whom Ismael the son of Nathanael slew in the midst of a feast, a murderer of his own country’s remnant. And these are the twelve wings, of which four cover the face; as is found in some copies, four fly, four cover the feet. For of these twelve kings it is agreed that only four were just: Ozias, Joatham, Ezechias, and Josias, who in the several captivities might lift themselves up and dare to glorify the Lord: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts.” The rest veil the face because of their sins, and the others veil the traces of their feet because they were led into captivity. The lintel taken away, and the house filled with smoke (as we said above), he explained as the overthrow of Jerusalem and the burning of the temple. The tongs, with which the coal of the altar was taken up and the lips purged, he declares to be the proper passion of Isaias, because he was slain under Manasses; and then, truly purged in his lips, he said to the Lord: “Behold, here am I, send me.”
6.3:
**“And they cried one to another”**
• exhorting one another to the praises of God
• The Old Testament is contained in the New, and conversely.
• and said:
**“Holy”**
• Father
• Son
• Holy Spirit
**“The Lord”**
• not of the Lord
• one in substance
**“of hosts”** — “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory.”
**“all the earth is full of his glory”**
• of Christ
• God once known in Judea. In the time of grace the whole earth is full. Whence: “O Lord our Lord, how admirable is thy name in all the earth!”
• not only Judea
• First the glory of the Lord is proclaimed in all the earth, and afterwards the temple is filled with smoke, because the gospel was first preached throughout the world; and then the temple was burned by the Romans forty-two years after the passion of the Lord.
**“And they cried”** — They do not speak lightly, but proclaim with a cry a confession saving to all: “Holy, holy, holy,” because the seraphim themselves are holy; for nothing is holier than they. But they marvel that the Son of God humbled himself so much, and underwent the cross, and made himself known to earthly beings.
**“Holy, holy, holy”** — The mystery of the Trinity. In both Testaments the Trinity is proclaimed, namely the Lord Christ, who here is of four letters, which is properly applied to God: iod, he, iod, he, that is, two ia, which doubled make the ineffable name of God.
**“All the earth is full”** — And it will be fulfilled when this has been fulfilled: “Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” As yet the Father’s will is in heaven, and on earth it is not yet fulfilled; so that it may be believed on earth, namely, what it has not yet had in all the earth.
6.4:
**“And”** — the veil being torn
**“were moved”** — the nearby overthrow of the temple by the Romans is signified; whence: “Behold, your house shall be left to you, desolate.”
**“the lintels”** — that they may be higher; whence: “Lift up your gates.”
**“of the doors”** — of the two Testaments
**“The lintels”** — In the Old Testament the Lord spoke at the door of the tabernacle, because he had not yet led them into the holy of holies, that is, to heaven; but when Christ came down to earth, the lintel, like some obstacle, was taken away, and the whole world was filled with smoke, that is, the glory of God. “Our God is a consuming fire,” but because we cannot take in his whole substance, a lighter and as it were thinner nature is spread abroad in the world like smoke, which, taking it in, we say: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part.”
**“at the voice”** — of Christ and of the Holy Spirit
**“of him that cried”**
• let us pass out of these abodes
• of the multitude
• enigmatic
**“and the house”**
• of Jacob
• the temple
**“was filled with smoke”**
• of ignorance and unbelief; or, by the smoke the burning of the temple is foretold
• by the emission of fire; for smoke is the vapour of fire
6.5:
**“And I said”** — Ozias being dead
**“Woe is me”** — because I did not freely rebuke Ozias and others, therefore I did not merit to praise God with the angels, and I fear lest it be said to me: Why dost thou declare my justices?
**“because I have held my peace”**
• from the praise of God
• see how much he humbles himself; he acknowledges his sins, and therefore is cleansed
**“because I am a man of unclean lips”**
• unworthy to praise God or to see him
• praise is not seemly in a polluted mouth
• like the apostles with polluted feet, which the Lord washed
**“Unclean”** — He says this on account of the people with whom he was compelled to speak. It is harmful to live with sinners. He who touches pitch is defiled by it.
**“and I dwell in the midst of a people that hath unclean lips”**
• by which they praise idols
• he accuses the people no more or less than himself
• an impenitent people, not knowing the uncleanness of its lips, does not deserve purification
**“I dwell”** — Note that one must not linger with sinners.
**“and”** — yet
**“I have seen with my eyes the King the Lord of hosts.”**
• to be pronounced with weight
• And the King, etc. So Abraham, after he saw the Lord and heard his voice, confesses that he is dust and ashes, because however great a man’s dignity is, it becomes worthless in comparison with him.
6.6:
**“And flew”**
• that is, he fulfilled the ministry
• willingly, because he was bound to this office
• yet
**“to me”** — to cleanse
**“one of the seraphims”** — Christ was sent by the Father for the taking away of sins
**“Of the seraphims”** — We say seraphim in the masculine with m, and in the neuter plural with n. Seraphim may however be said in the singular, as cherubim and cherub.
**“and in his hand”** — he saw the likeness of a man, so that he might not be afraid
**“And in his hand”** — That is, by his working, that is, Christ’s. The coal, that is charity, which he had taken with the tongs from the altar, that is, from the teaching of the two testaments, from the altar, and had placed as an example for Isaias.
**“a live coal”** — the word of God made fiery
**“A live coal”** — The Seventy: a carbuncle, a fiery stone which is called fiery because of its flame-coloured hue.
**“with the tongs”**
• by the two testaments, which are joined by the union of the Holy Spirit
• Having both commandments, namely its own and those of the Old Testament, it comprehends the word of God in the double edge of precepts.
**“With the tongs”** — This is the ladder of Jacob, the sword sharp on both edges. These are the two mites which the poor widow put into God’s gifts. This is the stater of two denarii, which was found in the mouth of the fish and paid for the Lord and Peter.
**“had taken”** — whereby he cut away from vices, so that no unclean speech should go out any more
**“off the altar”**
• the lips are cleansed by the fire of the altar
• which appeared in the vision
**“Off the altar”** — Which John saw in the Apocalypse, which is full of fiery coals by which your sins can be cleansed. Whence: “coals were kindled by it”; and elsewhere: “I am come to cast fire on the earth,” etc.
6.7:
**“And he touched”** — with the coal
**“my mouth, and said: Behold this hath touched”** — as if: do not fear
**“thy lips”** — by the fire of tribulation, that is, or by the burning of love
**“Behold this hath touched”** — Whence: “What shall be given to thee, or what shall be added to thee, to a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals that lay waste.” This is the word of God, of which it is said: “You have coals of fire; you will sit upon them; these will be a help to you.”
**“and”** — and so
**“thy iniquities shall be taken away”** — to others
**“and thy sin”** — to us
**“shall be cleansed”** — not the unworthy people, that is, those who do not confess as you do
**“And shall be taken away”** — Jeremias, who was a boy and therefore almost free from sin, is cleansed only in his hand by the touch. But to Isaias, who says, “I am a man of unclean lips,” the angel is sent with the coal.
6.8:
**“And I heard the voice of the Lord”** — of the Holy Spirit
**“saying: Whom shall I send?”** — unity of substance
**“and who shall go”** — to preach to my people, acquisitively
**“for us?”**
• plurality of persons
• A similar saying: “Let us make man to our image and likeness.” “I and the Father are one”: we are one on account of nature; we are distinct on account of the diversity of persons. Thus the Lord commanding, the Trinity commands.
**“Whom shall I send?”** — He does not compel but seeks the will; for the will alone merits reward. Isaias, however, as one cleansed, offers himself willingly.
*Origen:* Note: the Son, sent by the Father, here alone forgives sins, which the whole Trinity forgives. For whoever believes in one believes in all; lest you think the Son was sent as less than the Father.
**“And I said: Lo, here am I”** — I am here
**“send me.”** — because cleansed
