**“Send me.”** — He thinks he will bring good news, and therefore offers himself of his own accord. But because he heard, “Say to this people: With the ear you shall hear, and shall not understand,” etc., when afterwards it is said to him, “Cry,” he does not cry at once, but asks, “What shall I cry?” Jeremias also, to whom it was said, “Take the cup, and thou shalt make all nations drink,” and the rest, takes it willingly. But when he hears, “First thou shalt give drink to Jerusalem,” he answers, “Thou hast deceived me, O Lord,” etc. But we say that his offering himself was not rashness but obedience.
6.9:
**“And he said:”** — therefore
**“Go, and thou shalt say to this people: Hearing, hear”**
• Christ preaching
• permissively, not imperatively
**“and understand not”**
• as if: because you are unwilling, you will not understand
• God in man
**“and see the vision”** — man
**“and know it not.”**
• God
• Christ bodily
• Hear in hearing, etc. Luke, according to the Septuagint, in the Acts of the Apostles: “With the ear you shall hear, and shall not understand,” and the like. In this the interpretation is easy, which says what he is to do to the people. Paul also set down this interpretation in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Whence he is contradicted, because he does not use Hebrew testimonies. Nor had the Jews falsified the Scripture before; for the Lord and the apostles would not have kept silent about this, nor did the apostles or evangelists bring it forth as the Jews were going to falsify it. For they hand down that Luke was a physician and knew Greek letters better than Hebrew. Whence in both volumes he savors of worldly eloquence and uses Greek testimonies rather than Hebrew.
6.10:
**“Blind the heart of this people”**
• as if: If you wish the world to be saved, who? I wish; and I
• he prays what is just; he does not curse.
**“this”** — so wicked
**“and their ears”** — of heart
**“make their ears heavy”** — with sin
**“and their eyes”** — inner
**“shut”** — with the door of sins
**“Blind”**
• Compare: I raised you up that I might show you my power; and elsewhere: I gave them “eyes that they should not see; and ears that they should not hear,” etc.
• The prophet, foreseeing the blindness that would come upon Israel, that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter into the faith, says: Lord, blind the heart of this people; as if to say, if you desire to save the whole world, blind the heart of this people. For if this people is blinded, the Gentiles will be enlightened. For it is not cruelty in God but mercy, when the unbelieving are blinded, to enlighten the humble. Whence: “How often would I have gathered together thy children,” etc. Whence: God hath concluded all under sin, that he may have mercy on all; and a little after: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God!”
**“lest”** — as if he could, if he wished.
**“see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart”** — It is an exposition.
**“understand, and be converted”** — by understanding
**“and I heal them.”** — converted
**“And be converted”** — However grave the sin, if one is converted, he can be saved; but these, because of the greatness of their crime, are unworthy of penance. Whence: “I would have gathered together thy children, and thou wouldst not.”
6.11:
**“And I said:”** — comforting my people
**“How long”** — will be accursed
**“O Lord? And he said: Until the cities be wasted”** — are made desolate by the Romans; and this is “without inhabitant,” etc.
6.12:
**“And the Lord shall remove men far away”** — from their land
**“men”** — the Jews
**“and she shall be multiplied”**
• otherwise, deserted
• or indeed
**“that was left”** — was
**“in the midst of the earth”** — where she will be held captive
6.13:
**“And”** — yet
**“still a tithing therein”**
• that is, scarcely a tenth part will remain in it, either in the whole world or in Judea.
• And yet. And for “that is”: yet a tenth from that nation will remain, as if a tenth part of that people will still remain.
**“and she shall turn”**
• again under Hadrian
• the remnant of Israel will be made safe
**“and shall be made a shew as a turpentine tree”** — without leaves and fruit
**“and as an oak”** — dry
**“that spreadeth its branches: a holy seed shall be”** — the apostles and other believers. Whence: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we had been made as Sodom, and we had been like to Gomorrha.”
**“that which shall stand therein”**
• by faith, lest it fall through unbelief
• And there shall be still a tithing therein, etc. Under Adrian Judea was laid waste again, nearly fifty years after the Roman captivity.
• For they were forbidden by public laws to enter Judea.

7.1:
**“And it came to pass in the days of Achaz the son of Joathan, the son of Ozias, king of Juda, that Rasin king of Syria”** — that is, the king of Aram.
**“and Phacee”** — who had earlier struck down a hundred and twenty thousand fighting men of Judea and carried off to Samaria two hundred thousand women, boys and girls, with an immense booty.
**“The son of Romelia, king of Israel, came up to Jerusalem to fight against it, but they could not prevail over it.”**
• because the Lord helped, so that by this occasion he might announce his Son who was to be born of a virgin.
• And it came to pass, etc. What is written above, up to this place, was seen under Ozias and his son Joathan. What follows is under King Achaz, most impious, who, forsaken by God, is attacked by his enemies.
• The king of Syria came up: this is the king of Aram, which means “lofty,” puffed up, that is, with worldly wisdom. And Phacee the son of Romelia, king of the ten tribes according to the prophet Osee, the king of heretics. These, that is, agree together to storm the Church. The house of David, that is, the simple people of Christ, hearing this, is greatly afraid, because it is compared not to fruitful trees but to an unfruitful wood. For heretics and Gentiles fight with the swords of arguments against the house of David, although they disagree among themselves; whence Herod and Pilate were made friends in the passion of Christ.
**“Achaz”** — He who shut the doors of the temple, and worshipped Baalim, consecrated his son to an idol, removed the bronze altar and placed an altar of idols in the temple. Rightly therefore he was forsaken by the Lord, and his enemies rose up against him.
**“came up”** — The second time. For the first time the Assyrians had killed many of the tribe of Juda and led them captive to Damascus, and with this confidence they return in the time of Achaz; but they do not prevail, God helping, not by the merits of Achaz but by the sole mercy of God.
7.2:
**“And they told”** — of the royal house, that is.
**“the house of David, saying”** — that is, it was united in peace and friendship with the ten tribes, whose king was Phacee the son of Romelia.
**“Syria hath rested upon Ephraim”** — that is, the ten tribes who adhered to Roboam, who was of the tribe of Ephraim.
**“and was moved”** — because of this message.
**“his heart”** — of the king.
**“and the heart of his people”** — of the house of David.
**“as the trees of the woods are moved”**
• unfruitful
• the leaves of trees
7.3:
**“And the Lord said to Isaias: Go forth to meet Achaz, thou and Jasub thy son that is left, to the conduit of the upper pool”**
• namely
• that is, which was outside the city, for springs were rare in the mountains.
**“in the way of the fuller's field”**
• Go forth to meet, etc. Tropologically. It must be considered that Isaias is commanded to meet the wicked king, rising up from his place, not at the beginning of the conduit but at the farthest ends of the upper pool, which was in the fuller’s field, where filth and stains were cleansed. For although Achaz reigned over Juda, because he was wicked he lingered at the farthest ends of the pool. God therefore has mercy not so much on him as on his people. He calls worldly wisdom and heretical speech the tails of smoking firebrands, whose end is burning. For in vain they have taken counsel to go up against Juda and set over it the son of Tabeel, that is, a good god. For each thinks his own teaching best, but with God’s help their counsel will not stand. But as long as the world stands, it and what belongs to it hold sway within their bounds. But when the end of the world comes, that is, sixty-five years, and both the things of the world which were made in six days and all that pertain to the five senses have reached their end, all things will be dissolved. This the Gentiles and heretics do not believe, and therefore do not understand, according to the Septuagint, as they are called, who say, “With the ear you shall hear.”
• Left behind. By his brother Rapsaces, who had gone over to the Assyrians, as the Hebrews relate.
• There Rapsaces afterwards, by the command of Sennacherib, blasphemed the people of God.
**“Jasub”** — Who is interpreted as remnant and returning, because the people of Juda was to be delivered from the hands of two kings.
7.4:
**“And thou shalt say to him: See thou be quiet: fear not”** — that is, do not reveal the fear of your heart.
**“and let not thy heart be afraid”** — the evils you have already suffered.
**“of the two tails of these fire brands, smoking”** — to be ended now.
**“with the wrath of the fury”** — that is, do not fear.
**“of the two tails”** — The two tails of the firebrands: Rasin king of Syria and Phacee the son of Romelia, because in them the kingdom of Syria and Samaria was ended. For Teglathphalassar killed Rasin, and Osee killed Phacee and reigned in his place nine years, and, besieged by Salmanasar for three years, was taken and led with the ten tribes into the mountains of the Medes and Persians.
7.5:
**“Because Syria hath taken counsel against thee, unto the evil of Ephraim”** — subjects
**“and the son”** — the prelate
7.6:
**“Let us go up to Juda”** — because Judea is mountainous.
**“and rouse it up”** — at rest, sleeping.
**“and draw it away to us”** — let us draw it into our power
**“Tabeel”** — Tabeel: good God. As if we were to set up the idol of our god. Or literally: he calls the son of a man thus.
7.7: **“Thus saith the Lord God: It shall not stand, and this shall not be.”** — which he threatens
7.8:
**“But the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rasin”** — they will be
**“within threescore and five years, Ephraim shall cease to be a people”**
• Within threescore and five years, etc. As if meanwhile they will be content with their own borders, and Damascus, as the metropolis of Syria, will command Rasin, and the head of the cities of Ephraim will be Samaria, and in it meanwhile will reign the son of Romelia.
• Sixty-five, etc. From the twenty-sixth year of the reign of Ozias, when he was struck with leprosy, from then his son Joathan reigned twenty-seven years while his father was still alive; after his death sixteen; after which Achaz another sixteen; afterwards, Ezechias reigning, in the sixth year Ephraim, that is, the ten tribes led into captivity, ceased to be a people.
7.9:
**“And the head of Ephraim is Samaria and the head of Samaria the son of Romelia. If you will not believe”** — the Lord preaching these things through the prophet; Achaz and the people did not believe future things; whence he adds: if you will not believe
**“you shall not continue”** — in your land, but you also will be taken captive
7.11:
**“Ask thee a sign”**
• of deliverance or victory
• So that, because he did not believe the prophet, he may be struck with fear by the authority of the Lord. As if it seems hard to you that the most powerful kingdoms should be ended in a short time, and you and your people be delivered; but ask for a sign.
**“of the Lord”** — who promises help
**“thy God”** — not from the idols you worship
**“unto the depth”** — is set at your choice
**“of hell”** — from the underworld
**“or unto the height above”**
• from heaven, or as Elias comes from heaven and Moses from the underworld
• Ask thee a sign. Moses received a sign from the earth, whence: “He sent forth signs and wonders in the midst of thee”; he brought forth frogs, locusts, gnats and dog-flies; from heaven, hail, fire, and darkness of three days. Ezechias also received a sign from heaven, when the sun went back ten lines. And Josue at Gabaon and Aialon, when the sun and moon stood still. And very many think that Saul received a sign from the earth and the depth of hell, when by incantations he was seen to have raised up Samuel. Jonas, delivered from the abyss and the jaws of death, both received and gave a sign of hell.
• Because the prophet did not believe the former words, he is commanded to ask a sign, by whose authority he may be compelled to believe. As if to say: do you wish the earth to be split and hell to lie open, which is said to be in the heart of the earth? Or the heavens to be opened? Each of which regards the death of the Lord and his ascension; for he who descended is the same who ascended. Whence: “Say not in thy heart: Who shall ascend into heaven?” that is, to bring Christ down; “or who shall descend into the deep?” that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead.
7.12:
**“And Achaz said”** — when he ought to have obeyed
**“I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord”**
• or I will exalt; for the Hebrew signifies both
• I will not ask, etc. Not humbly but proudly. For many are read to have asked the Lord for signs and received them; but Achaz answered thus, as though having authority, “Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.” Or he feared that in the sign God would be glorified and the idols made worthless.
7.13:
**“And he said”** — Isaias
**“Hear ye therefore, O house of David”**
• because Achaz does not want to hear
• whence Christ was to be born
**“Is it a small thing for you”** — as if you not only despise the words of the prophets but also contradict the Lord commanding
**“to be grievous to men”** — to the prophets whose words you despise
**“that you are grievous to my God also”**
• envying his signs and glory
• burdensome; whence “laboring, enduring”
7.14:
**“Therefore”** — namely, that you not be troublesome
**“the Lord himself shall give you a sign”** — of salvation and deliverance
**“Behold”** — namely this
**“a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son”**
• of whom: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”; and the Lord of hosts, he is the King of Glory
• He will no longer speak to you by riddles: a virgin shall conceive; this will be new and marvellous. The Jews lie, saying that a young woman conceives; but “alma,” which is written in the Hebrew, in the Punic tongue means virgin. Among the Hebrews “alma” is said of a young girl, or of one hidden, that is, secret, who never lies open to the sight of men.
• Behold a virgin shall conceive. The Hebrews think this is said of Ezechias, because Samaria was taken in his reign. But Achaz, the son of Joathan, reigned sixteen years, and his son Ezechias succeeded him and reigned twenty-nine years, who was twenty-five years old when he began to reign. How then, in the first year of Achaz, was the prophecy spoken to him of Ezechias who was to be born, when he was already nine years old, unless perhaps they say that the sixth year of the reign of Ezechias, in which Samaria was taken, is called his infancy, not of age but of rule? That this is violently forced is plain even to fools.
**“Behold a virgin shall conceive”** — In Hebrew “alma”; in Latin also “alma” means holy. And the Hebrews use the words of almost all languages. Whence in the Canticles: “King Solomon made him a litter” (from the Greek “phorion,” that is, a dish); for so we read in the Hebrew. Otherwise what novelty of miracle is it if a young girl conceived, as the Hebrews falsely claim? Yet “alma” signifies a virgin of marriageable age and a young maiden.
**“and”** — and, O Juda
**“shall call”**
• in danger
• Or, she shall call. For in Hebrew each word means both. But “they shall call,” which is in Matthew, is not in the Hebrew; Matthew follows the sense, not the words.
**“his name shall be called Emmanuel”** — God with us: which will be made clear in the destruction of the two kings.
**“Emmanuel”** — Some say that Isaias had two sons, Jasub and Emmanuel. Emmanuel was begotten of his wife the prophetess, as a type of the Saviour; and Jasub, which is interpreted “left” or “returning,” as a type of the Jewish people, which was left and would afterwards return. Emmanuel, that is, “God with us,” signifies the calling of the Gentiles, for the sake of which the Word was made flesh.
7.15:
**“He shall eat butter and honey”** — From the part, the whole: all food suitable for man, in which true man is shown.
**“that he may know”** — Even God will be, so that he may know.
**“to refuse the evil”**
• Herod, the scribes and the Pharisees.
• He is never open to the passions of vices.
**“and to choose the good”**
• Shepherds, magi.
• By these words we perceive that the divine infancy of the Saviour did not diminish wisdom in him, although he is called a child; yet “Jesus advanced in wisdom and age,” so that the truth of the human body might be proved. For infancy did not prejudice divine wisdom.
**“To refuse the evil”** — As if placed in the swaddling clothes of infancy, he will have discernment of good and evil.
7.16:
**“For”** — Indeed I say: hear, house of David, the sign of your deliverance.
**“before”** — Before God is made man.
**“the child know to refuse the evil, and to choose the good, the land shall be forsaken”** — In the sixth year of the reign of Ezechias, Samaria was taken by the Assyrians.
**“which thou abhorrest, of the face of her two kings”**
• As if these are not to be feared by you, but the Assyrian.
• Be forsaken, the land, etc. As though the land of Syria and Samaria will be laid waste at the invocation of his name, and the house of Juda will be delivered from the two kings.
7.17:
**“The Lord shall bring upon thee”**
• When the Assyrian comes, those being overcome, you will be delivered in the presence of Emmanuel.
• Whence the land will be left by these kings.
**“and upon thy people, and upon the house of thy father, days”** — Of tribulation and captivity.
**“that have not come”** — Such evil.
**“since the time of the separation of Ephraim from Juda with the king of the Assyrians”** — Nabuchodonosor, with whom came the Medes and Persians and Egyptians and Chaldeans.
7.18:
**“And it shall come to pass in that day, the Lord shall hiss”** — He will inspire.
**“the Lord shall hiss for the fly, that is in the uttermost parts of the rivers of Egypt”** — Of the Nile.
**“and for the bee”** — Or the Assyrians or Chaldeans, very fierce and mighty with darts.
**“The fly”** — That is, for the Egyptians, a people unwarlike and foul with idolatry. We read that Josias was slain by the Egyptians and the people of Israel subjugated; and not long after, Nabuchodonosor with an innumerable army took Jerusalem, burnt the temple, and settled Assyrians as inhabitants in Judea.
7.19:
**“And they shall come”** — He pursues a metaphor; for flies and bees gather in such places.
**“and shall all of them rest in the torrents”** — In your land.
7.20:
**“In that day the Lord shall shave with a razor”** — Because Egypt is given to him as payment for the labor with which they serve the Lord at Tyre.
**“sharp”** — Or hired; another reading.
**“A sharp razor”** — The king of the Assyrians (who is called the dove of God in Jeremias): in him, and in those who are beyond the river, namely the Assyrians, the Lord will shave in Judea the head and the hairs, that is, all the strength of kings and princes and subjects.
**“by them that are beyond the river”**
• The Euphrates.
• That is,
**“by the king of the Assyrians, the head and the hairs of the feet”** — so that nothing strong, nothing beautiful may remain, but they may be compared to effeminate men, or rather to shameful women.
**“and the whole beard”** — comeliness and strength
7.21:
**“And it shall come to pass in that day”**
• that is, when all things shall have been carried over into Chaldea
• in the time of grace
• After the overthrow of the city, Nabuzardan, the captain of the army, whom the Septuagint call Archimarum, left the poor to till the vineyards and fields. Whence Godolias, of royal stock, who was set over them, says: Serve the king of Babylon and it shall be well with you; at which time there was so great a desolation in Judea that they had neither flocks of sheep nor herds of oxen.
**“a man shall nourish”** — a rare inhabitant
**“a young cow”**
• only one, because he is poor
• flesh
• a strong unity
**“and two sheep”**
• whence he is fed and clothed
• two simple affections, namely toward the Lord and toward the neighbour
**“Tropologically”** — Tropologically. A man shall nourish hardly one cow and two sheep; that is, the Jews have clean animals, so that infancies may be nourished with milk, not with solid food, so that they eat the honey of words from the lips of a harlot, and have no wine that maketh glad the heart of man. But let their works be turned into thorns, and let them be wounded by those who “shoot in the dark at the upright of heart,” if they wish to be wiser than they ought, that labouring in the Scriptures they may find the mystical sense. Let them bring forth no fruits, but be filled with briers and thorns, which spring up in the hands of a drunkard. Let their land, or doctrine, be trodden down not by a rational living creature but by oxen (of which God has no care) and by brute beasts.
7.22:
**“And for the abundance”** — because there is much pasture and few animals
**“of milk”** — of evangelical teaching
**“he shall eat butter: for butter and honey”** — wild
**“shall every one eat that shall be left in the midst of the land”** — for lack of bread
**“He shall eat butter”** — He will delight in the passion of Christ or in his own. For butter is made from many mixtures.
7.23:
**“And it shall come to pass in that day, every place where there were a thousand vines”** — with the wine failing and the vineyards deserted, single vines will be bought for single pieces of silver
**“at a thousand pieces of silver”** — will be bought
**“shall become thorns and briers”** — of the vineyard
7.24:
**“With arrows and with bows”** — from fear of robbers
**“they shall go in thither”** — into the fields to view them
7.25:
**“And as for all the hills”**
• they will be such
• Having left the plains through fear of the enemy, they will flee to the mountains, cultivating the rough mountains with their own hands and sustaining a wretched life; the rest will be pasture.
**“that shall be raked with a rake, the fear of thorns and briers shall not come thither, but they shall be”** — the rest of the land
**“for the ox to feed on, and the lesser cattle to tread upon”** — only not for human habitation

8.1:
**“And the Lord said to me”** — under another figure the birth of the virgin is described
**“Take thee”**
• O Isaias
• First the prophet foretells the future to Achaz; afterwards the Lord himself commands him to ask a sign; then the words are turned to the house of David, and a virgin is promised who shall bear a son, and a son who is to be born. At the calling upon this son, Samaria and Syria are overthrown, and by the king of the Assyrians, who afterwards takes Judea and turns it into a desert; whence again the virginal birth is described.
**“a great book”** — signifying great things
**“and write”** — that you not publicly preach the mystery of the new birth
**“in it with a man's pen”** — in the manner of men, so that it might indeed be understood
**“With speed”** — Words of the Father to the Son
**“the spoils”**
• men
• Bring back the captive captivity.
**“Take away”** — To the devil.
**“quickly take the prey”** — It is the same.
**“With speed, the spoils”** — This is the name of the boy, as if to say: Suffer not the devil to reign any longer; and send not angels, send not prophets, but come down yourself.
8.2:
**“And I took”** — I, Isaias.
**“unto me faithful witnesses”** — of this matter.
**“Urias”** — The light of the Lord.
**“the priest”**
• On account of the teaching of the law.
• The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge.
**“and Zacharias”**
• The memory of the Lord.
• whom it is established was a prophet.
**“the son of Barachias”**
• The blessing of the Lord.
• Urias, etc. Urias, the light of the Lord; Zacharias, the memory of the Lord; Barachias, the blessing of the Lord. By these witnesses the nativity of the Lord is proved. Whence: to the two witnesses going to Emmaus, beginning from Moses and the prophets, he expounded what had been said of himself.
8.3:
**“And I went”** — I made myself worthy to approach.
**“to the prophetess”** — who prophesied, saying: “My soul doth magnify the Lord.”
**“To the prophetess”** — To the Holy Spirit, from whom is all prophecy; and “prophecy” is neuter in Greek (pneuma), feminine in Hebrew (rua), masculine in Latin, and therefore it is assigned different positions, for it belongs to no one. Or to Mary, whom no one doubts to have been a prophetess.
**“and she conceived, and bore a son”**
• that is, caused her to conceive. Whence: “The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the most High shall overshadow thee”; and: “that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost.”
• And she conceived, etc. Tropologically. In a virgin soul, not defiled by any filth, the word of God conceived of the Holy Spirit despoils the demons and makes all things serve it. And though he sees in part and prophesies before he is perfect, and rightly calls God his Father and the heavenly Jerusalem his mother, by his infancy he overcomes the strength of Damascus, that is, secular wisdom, and takes away the spoils of Samaria, with which heretics despoil the Church, saying: “We have no part in David,” etc. With the king of the Assyrians, the devil, present, who cannot help them, such sons are begotten by the Virgin Mary and by holy women: Sara, that is, princess, and Rebecca, that is, patience, wives of the patriarchs.
**“And the Lord said to me”** — O Isaias.
**“call his name”** — of the boy.
**“Hasten to take away the spoils”** — “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive.”
**“Make haste to take away the prey”** — Hell.
8.4:
**“For before”**
• not yet born, he will save his people by invocation alone.
• before the man is made.
**“know”** — according to his humanity.
**“the child call his father”**
• God.
• or Joseph, putatively.
**“and his mother”** — Mary.
**“The child”** — Augustine. Of whom it is said: “Before the child know good or evil, he will despise malice.” These two are known in one way and another: good by prudence, and evil by experience. By the prudence of good, evil is known and not felt; for one holds to the good lest evil be felt. By the experience of evil, good is known; for he who has lost it feels how ill it is with him who has lost the good. The child therefore, before he knew by experience the good which he would lack, or the evil which he would feel after losing the good, despised evil that he might choose the good; he likewise was unwilling to lose what he had, or to feel, by losing it, what he ought not to lose.
*Allegorically:* The waters of Siloe, in which the blind man washed and saw. For the blindness of the Jews is not otherwise healed than by the teaching of Christ, which is gentle, without noise and clamour.
**“Anagogically”** — Anagogically. The heretic, who joins to himself the help of secular wisdom and wishes to assail Jerusalem, that is, the Church, has forsaken the waters of Siloe, which is interpreted “sent,” and which spring up unto life everlasting, and is handed over to the prince of the Assyrians, that is, the devil, to be led into the depth of sins; for he it is who dared to say: “All these will I give thee, if falling down thou wilt adore me.” He also tries to enter Juda, that is, the house of confession, and through the negligent comes up to the neck, desiring to strangle those who believe in Christ; but he cannot, for Juda has with him Emmanuel present.
**“shall be taken away”** — by Theglathphalasar.
**“the strength of Damascus, and the spoils of Samaria”** — through the king of the Assyrians, Salmanasar, namely.
**“before the king of the Assyrians”** — The Assyrian directing, or proud.
8.5: **“And the Lord spoke to me again, saying”** — Translative.
8.6:
**“Forasmuch as this people hath cast away”** — The ten tribes.
**“the waters of Siloe”** — which bubble up by the hours.
**“that go with silence”** — kings of Juda who reigned quietly and lawfully.
**“and hath rather taken Rasin”** — king of Syria.
**“and the son of Romelia”** — Phacee, king of Israel.
8.7:
**“Therefore behold the Lord will bring upon them the waters of the river”**
• of the armies of Senacherib
• the Assyrians.
**“The waters of the river”** — The army of Senacherib, whose power, occupying the land of Samaria, is compared to the flood of a river.
**“strong and many”** — violent and lasting.
**“the king of the Assyrians”**
• namely,
• as if they would not serve the kings they chose, but the Assyrian.
**“and all his glory: and he shall come up over all his channels”** — princes who ought to have resisted enemies.
**“his”** — of Samaria.
**“and shall overflow all”** — or: all.
**“banks”** — lands.
8.8:
**“And shall pass through Juda”** — because then it will not take him.
**“overflowing, and going over”** — signifies the nearby captivity.
**“shall reach even to the neck”** — suffocation.
**“And your strength shall be”** — it extends even from God.
**“the stretching out of his wings”** — of the princes.
**“shall fill the breadth of thy land”** — of Judah.
**“thy land, O Emmanuel”** — is mockery.
8.9:
**“Gather yourselves together”**
• Sarcasm.
• As if you could do nothing against Emmanuel; let all the earth also know this from afar.
**“O ye people, and be overcome”**
• of Syria or Samaria.
• Gather yourselves together, etc. We use this testimony against persecutors: for although they seem strong and to overcome us in the lapsed, yet they are overcome in those who shed their blood for Christ, and after the wars peace is restored to the Churches, and all counsels against Emmanuel are scattered. To those also who speak against the truth they listen profitably, because at last they are overcome by reason, and that they may not wish to conquer in a lie, because perversity cannot overcome the right.
**“and give ear”**
• Know.
• not only Syria and Samaria.
**“all ye”** — not only the neighbours.
**“lands afar off: strengthen yourselves, and be overcome, gird yourselves, and be overcome”** — although many, although strong, although girded, yet you will be overcome
8.10:
**“Take counsel together”** — Whence above: Let us go up against Juda, etc.
**“and it shall be defeated”** — by Emmanuel
**“speak a word”** — namely, let us set up as king the son of Tabeel
**“and it shall not be done: because God is with us”**
• Interpretation: Emmanuel
• against whom you can do nothing
8.11:
**“For thus”** — the things foretold
**“For thus saith the Lord to me: As he hath taught me, with a strong arm”** — in work and power
**“hath taught me”**
• Isaias
• Blessed is the man who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly.
**“that I should not walk”** — to this end, namely, he taught me
**“in the way”** — wrong
**“of this people, saying”**
• wicked
• The Lord: I say, speaking to me and to the other prophets.
8.12:
**“Offer no more”** — Otherwise: not
**“say ye: A conspiracy”**
• is to be feared
• but consider this rather, for all things
**“for all that this people speaketh”** — of Juda
**“is a conspiracy”** — against me
**“is, and neither fear ye their fear”** — of the people
**“neither fear ye”** — you and those with you, the peoples who seem to be feared
**“Say ye not”** — As if to say: Fear not the conspiracy of the two kings against Juda. A conspiracy is the agreement of many in evil.
**“Neither fear ye”** — You and the peoples who are with you, because they seem to be feared; for the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.
8.13:
**“the Lord of hosts”** — and
**“Sanctify himself”** — in you
**“himself”**
• let him be
• the Lord
• Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord.
**“your fear”** — in body

And it lighted upon Israel, that is, on the ten tribes, which, neglecting the commandment of God, cast off the house of David and chose Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim, whence they are also surnamed Ephraim. Spiritually, however, the Lord sent the word of the gospel into Jacob, that is, to the apostles and others, and it lighted upon Israel: that is, it was transgressed by the unbelievers. Or he sent the Word, that is, the Son, into Jacob, namely the people of the Jews, and it lighted upon Israel because the Gentiles received him.
• The Lord sent a word into Jacob, that is, into the Church, which supplanted the former people. And it lighted upon Israel, that is, upon the heretics, who boast that they see God. Therefore their princes and all who dwelt in Samaria shall know, that is, those who say they keep the law and are in abundance of virtues and bring forth the fruits of justice (for Ephraim is interpreted fruitfulness), who despise the Church and think its simplicity ignorance.

**“And the Lord shall destroy”** — Tropologically. The Lord will take away the head and the tail: the greater, that is, and the lesser. By saying “tail” of the heretics, he shows them to be not men but beasts of burden, which with this member cover their dung and keep off other small creatures. “Him that bendeth down” and perverts: those who subvert the words or precepts of the law and pervert the right way. The aged also, who is the head, and the false prophet, that is, the tail, he will destroy: teachers and disciples alike, both those who praise for the sake of gifts and those who, being praised, do not repent. Therefore the Lord does not rejoice in their young men, because “woe to the city whose king is a child,” and those who have lost God as true Father or Spouse will not obtain mercy. Every heretic is indeed a hypocrite, and whatever he speaks is folly. Therefore the Lord stretches out his hand to punish, and a devouring flame will consume the thorns of their impiety, and their words without virtues (which are compared to an unfruitful thicket) will be wrapped in the smoke of pride. At their punishments the earth will tremble, and the deceived peoples will be handed over to eternal fires or burnings, because for the sake of base gain they spare not even their own, but vie in plundering the deceived, leaving good things, following evil, and are never satisfied with errors; they devour themselves and likewise fight against the Church. But on account of lust and pleasure and the plunder of the deceived they are at discord among themselves, and out of one heresy make two.

10.1:
**“Woe to them that make”**
• The prophet against the scribes and Pharisees, who put their own traditions before the law of God.
• a threat against the two tribes.
• Anagogically. Every heretic writes iniquity and deceives the poor, not the rich; whence “the riches of a man are the redemption of his soul.” The poor man does not bear a threat, but the humble is quickly scandalized; and the widow who has lost her husband has lost God, and the orphan who has lost his father, the Creator; whence: “Thou hast forsaken the God that begot thee, and hast forgotten the Lord that created thee.” What then will they do in the day of judgment, when they have deceived so many, and of the calamity coming from afar? To the just man it is said: “The word of God is nigh in thy mouth,” and elsewhere: “The kingdom of God is within you.” On the other hand, the calamity of the heretics comes from afar and has been prepared for a long time. To whom will they flee for help, since they have a feigned God? To whom will they leave their glory, since all things are pretended? They will not be able to escape the bond with which they have bound very many; they will fall with the several slain, and perish in the death of others. And though they suffer much, and the day of visitation come, there will be no end of their destruction, but they will ever dread the hand of God hanging over them.
**“wicked laws: and when they write, write injustice”** — traditions. Whence: “Whatever gift is from me shall profit thee,” when the Lord said: “Honour thy father and thy mother.”

**“my indignation”**

But he, immoderately puffed up, ascribed this to his own strength and not to God. And he not only took them captive but partly destroyed them.

• When the Lord shall have performed, etc. Namely the overthrowings of the city, also the siege, when Rabsaces came and did those things which are recounted in what follows.
**“I will visit”** — Morally. When Samaria and Jerusalem have borne the wrath of the Lord and have perceived that they erred in the making of idols, then the great mind of the Assyrians will be destroyed, which is puffed up with such pride against the Lord that it thinks all things will yield to its wisdom. And although their doctrines are lofty and fortified with the art of dialectic, yet they must be shaken and utterly destroyed, so that (like chicks) they may not be able to rise to the heights, and, not yet animated, be senseless and torpid, which is signified in the eggs; and that they may not dare so much as to mutter or to move the tongue against the strength of his word.
10.13:

• The wolf shall dwell. Note that it is not the lamb and the kid that dwell with the wolf and the leopard, but the wolf and the leopard that imitate the innocence of the lamb and the kid, namely Christ.
• The calf and the sheep, humble and innocent, consecrating their flesh to God by mortifying it. For these animals are appointed for sacrifices. This union of diverse characters, in the sheet that was let down to Peter from heaven by four beginnings, through which we understand the four parts of the world, in which there were fourfooted beasts and serpents and wild beasts and fowls of the air, we do not doubt is figured, so that what the ark did in the flood, the Church does in the world.
*Jerome:* The wolf shall dwell, etc. The Jews and our Judaizers contend that at the coming of Christ, whom they await at the end of the world, all the beasts will grow tame. We ask them: if we take everything literally, how shall bodiless things (namely justice and truth) gird the reins of the Lord? and what is worthy of the majesty of the Lord, that the wolf and the lamb should feed together? and the like. But if they answer that these things are said for the future blessedness, that men may enjoy good things in security, let them hear that nothing is good but virtue, and nothing evil but vice. Whence: “Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile”; “turn away from evil, and do good.” But riches and health of bodies and abundance of all things, and their contraries, are called neither good nor evil even among the philosophers. Whence the Stoics, who in most things agree with our teaching, say that nothing is good but honour and virtue alone, nothing evil but baseness.

**“I will ascend into heaven”** — He was in the firmament and desired to ascend to heaven, where the Lord’s throne is.
**“Above”** — above; not below.
**“the stars of heaven”** — the stars of heaven; or: of God.
**“I will exalt my throne, I will sit in the mountain of the testament”**
• I will exalt my throne; I will sit on the mountain of the covenant. A city seated on a mountain cannot be hidden.
• Sion, where the temple is, in which the covenant is, which is on the north side.
**“In the sides of the north”** — Whence evils blaze up from the north, and the pot of Jeremias is kindled. Of which: “I will say to the north: Give,” that is, restore the captives.
14.14:
**“I will ascend”** — he was in the firmament and desired to ascend to heaven, where the Lord’s throne is.
**“above the height of the clouds”** — of devils.
**“I will be like the most High”** — that, as he did, I may have prophets and apostles.
**“of the clouds”** — Of the prophets, of whom: “I will command the clouds to rain no rain upon it,” and “thy truth reacheth, even to the clouds.” Judas was a cloud with the other apostles, but by his vice he received the devil as rider.
14.15:
**“But yet thou shalt be brought down to hell”**
• Nabuchodonosor, or devil.
• from so great a height.
• whosoever exalteth himself shall be humbled.
• You are brought down unwillingly; Christ descended willingly.
**“But yet to hell”** — You who could have ascended by virtues shall fall by vices. The saints have the wings of a dove and of an eagle, that they may fly and rest. The wicked are sunk like lead “in the mighty waters,” and go down “into the depth like a stone.” Whence: “Iniquity sitteth upon a talent of lead.”
**“the depth”** — To the lowest and worst punishments. For the higher the step, the heavier the fall.
**“into the depth of the pit”** — Of the pit, that is, of hell. Whence “with them that go down into the pit,” and “they have laid me in the lowest pit.” As a pit receives waters, so hell receives souls; into it Banaias went down in the time of snow and killed a lion. Heretics forsake the fountain of living water and dig to themselves broken pits that can hold no water. Whence, as a pit cools waters, so those who have malice, who are neither cold nor hot, that is, neither believe nor wholly disbelieve, but through lukewarmness and pretence of faith are rejected by the Lord.
14.16:
**“They that shall see thee”**
• in pains
• by the look of the heart
**“shall turn toward thee”** — humbled
**“and behold thee”** — saying
**“Is this the man”**
• saying: I will be like the Most High
• He is a man, not God. Whence: “An enemy man has sown tares over it.”
**“that troubled the earth”** — to earthly ones, to whom it is said: “Dust thou art, and unto dust thou shalt return.”
**“that shook”** — not overthrew; whence: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well nigh slipped.”
**“kingdoms”** — kings, whose heart is in the hand of God
14.17:
**“That made the world a wilderness”** — with the virtues put to flight
**“and destroyed the cities thereof”** — village
**“to his prisoners”**
• by sins
• to whom Christ said: “Come forth: and to them that are in darkness, shew yourselves.” Whence: “Thou hast broken my bonds”, and elsewhere: “The Lord looseth them that are fettered.”
**“To his prisoners”**
• His immense cruelty is shown, who not only burdened captives with chains but shut them up in darkness, so that he did not even open it for Evilmerodach his son.
• Those whom the apostles, imitators of the Master, loose, who said: “Whatsoever you shall loose upon earth, shall be loosed also in heaven.” They loose, however, by the word of God, the testimony of the Scriptures, and the exhortation of virtues.
**“the cities”** — Churches, that he might make them synagogues of the devil, and pollute the purity of faith with heretical perversity.
14.18:
**“All the kings of the nations have all of them slept”** — rested
**“in glory”**
• heavenly
• because
**“every one in his own house”**
• in the tomb
• slept
• “In my Father’s house there are many mansions.”
**“All the kings”** — Jerome. The kings of the nations, to whom God had entrusted the nations to be governed, who were shaken by Nabuchodonosor yet not overthrown, over whom sin does not reign because their heart was in the hand of God, have by no means fallen; for as Christ is the God of gods, so he is Lord of lords and King of kings. These have slept in their glory, every one in his own house, because with the Father there are many mansions, and according to the variety of virtues there is a variety of mansions; but Nabuchodonosor does not rest from torments even in death.
14.19:
**“But thou art cast out”**
• as the buried kings whom you slew; you will be cast out unburied; or if all souls at some time receive some rest, you never shall
• the burial of Nabuchodonosor
**“out of thy grave, as an unprofitable branch”** — which, growing from a root, brings barrenness to the tree, worthy of fire
**“unprofitable, defiled”**
• as with the filth
• with the blood of the slain
• with the gore of those, that is, who are
**“and wrapped up among them that were slain by the sword”** — of yours, namely
**“and art gone down to the bottom of the pit”** — of hell
**“as a rotten carcass”** — But thou, being as a corpse
**“rotten”** — which all shun
**“But thou”** — He seems to agree with the fable by which the Jews say that Nabuchodonosor, having returned to his former state, was put in prison by his son Evilmerodach (who reigned in that interval of seven years), and that he was there with king Joachim during his father’s life. When he was dead, Evilmerodach, not daring to take the kingdom, saying: My father dies when he wishes and rises again, by the counsel of Joachim sought out three hundred birds from different parts of the world, and bound a part of the body, dug up and scattered into small pieces, to each. For Joachim said: When these birds come together, your father will come to life again.
**“As a rotten carcass”** — By the multitude of sins my scars have rotted and been corrupted. Virtue is a sweet odour. Whence: as ointment on the head, and thy odour sweet, and thy face beautiful.
14.20:
**“Thou shalt not keep company with them, even in burial”** — That is, thou shalt not be a companion in burial with those whom thou hast slain.
**“keep company”** — Namely, of burial: for the punishment of the author is one thing, and another that of him who was compelled by authority. This is the sword by which very many were wounded and slain; whence: he brandished his sword.
**“for thou”** — This is said of the devil and Nabuchodonosor.
**“thy land”**
• also thine
• not only another’s
**“For thou hast destroyed thy land”** — As if through thy pride the kingdom of the Chaldeans was destroyed, which would still have remained had thy pride not been.
**“thy people”** — Which God had entrusted to thee to be corrected and governed; whence he dares to say: all these things have been delivered to me.
**“thou hast slain”** — Not keeping them alive for God, but preparing companions for thy punishment.
**“not”**
• Now the prophet speaks in the third person of Nabuchodonosor.
• It can also be said of the devil: shall not be called.
**“shall be named”**
• as if the power of that one has utterly perished
• thy
**“for ever the seed of the wicked”**
• of demons
• Not that the seed is evil in itself, for God made all things good; but from those who are most wicked by will an evil seed has arisen, which comes about by will, not by nature. Whence: “O thou seed of Chanaan, and not of Juda.” Of the good it is said through the gospel: I have begotten you.
• All histories agree that after Balthasar was slain none of the seed of Nabuchodonosor reigned afterwards; the whole progeny was blotted out for the pride and impiety of the father.
**“shall not be named”** — Therefore he shall not be called for ever, because he himself is the seed of the most wicked.
14.21:
**“Prepare his children”** — thoughts and evil deeds born of impious fathers
**“his”** — Nabuchodonosor
**“for slaughter”** — for
**“for the iniquity of their fathers: they shall not rise up”** — as if they were slain, that they may not rise again
**“nor inherit”** — into the kingdom
**“the earth”**
• of the father
• of the saints
**“nor fill the face of the world”** — of the Lord
**“with cities”**
• or: of the city
• “Unless the Lord keep the city.”
**“With iniquity”** — The Septuagint: For the iniquity of thy father. Some, not understanding this, want the dragon who reigns in the sea, whom the Hebrews call Leviathan, to be the father of the devil, according to that: “he is a liar, and the father thereof”; which they distort by misunderstanding.
14.22:
**“And”**
• for because
• the victory of man is not perfect
**“I will rise up”** — in Cyrus and Darius
**“against them”** — that is, the sons of Nabuchodonosor
**“saith the Lord of hosts: and I will destroy the name of Babylon”** — that it may not be named the mistress of kingdoms
**“and the remains”**
• that is, the sons
• lest they sprout any more in the cities of the Lord
**“and the bud, and the offspring, saith the Lord”** — or he says
14.23:
**“And I will make it”** — not content with these
**“a possession for the ericius”** — from this understand also the other monsters
**“and pools”** — or: to pools
**“of waters”** — with which the rich are surrounded
**“And I will sweep”** — a likeness: that all of them, that is, are carried away as filth
**“and wear it out with a besom”**
• that the seeds of Babylon may perish
• that nothing remain except the hedgehog
**“saith the Lord of hosts”** — And I will make it, etc. There is nothing in it but a royal hunting-ground, enclosed by walls of baked brick, rebuilt after many years.
**“A possession for the ericius”** — The world too is possessed now by the hedgehog and the pools, that is, by unclean spirits; but at the end of the world the Lord will sweep it, that is, purge it, with purgatorial fire.
14.24:
**“The Lord of hosts hath sworn”**
• he firmly decreed
• as if the oath of the Lord will be fulfilled by these agreements
**“The Lord of hosts hath sworn, saying: Surely”** — as if it cannot be done otherwise
**“as I have thought”** — or I decreed
**“so shall it be”** — an aposiopesis, as if you would not believe me if I did not do it
**“and as I have purposed”** — The Lord hath sworn, etc. Thus far of Babylon and its kings and peoples; now of Sennacherib and what then threatened the Assyrians, who laid waste Samaria and Judea except Jerusalem, and were lifted up in pride against the Lord; whence one hundred and eighty-five thousand of them were struck down in one night by an angel. And this in the land of Juda and on its mountains, as the Lord had foretold.
14.25:
**“So”** — that is, or and
**“shall it fall out: That I will destroy the Assyrian in my land”** — a contrary strength
**“and upon my mountains tread him under foot”** — Behold, “I have given you power to tread upon serpents.”
**“shall be taken away from them”**
• to the saints
• to the Jews
**“his yoke”** — heavy of affliction
**“his burden shall be taken off their shoulder”** — of the Assyrians and of Sennacherib, or of the devil
**“shall be taken away”**
• that they may serve no longer
• The rash enemy, hastening, seeks to occupy not only God’s land and the lower places, but also those who have advanced in virtues, of whom it is said: “His foundations are in the holy mountains.”
**“Upon my mountains”** — Note the peculiarity: he is trodden down in the land; on the mountains he is trampled by the Lord himself. For when all enemies have been placed under the feet of Christ, so that the last enemy, death, is destroyed, then the yoke of the Assyrian will be taken away from the saints.
14.26:
**“This is the counsel”**
• if I have not thought, etc.
• That is, that his yoke be taken away: this is my counsel.
**“that I have purposed upon all the earth”** — to protect the whole earth
**“and this is the hand that is stretched out”** — this is the hand, that is, Sennacherib; or, the hand, namely mine, is stretched out to protect all nations
**“upon all nations”**
• This counsel which I have thought upon all the earth: the nations of the Assyrians, namely, or of all who are subject to Sennacherib or to the devil.
• At the end of the vision what was hidden is revealed: that the Lord had thought out a counsel over all the earth, and his raised hand over all nations, not only Babylon; whence it is shown that what has been said pertains generally to the whole world.
14.27:
**“For the Lord of hosts hath decreed”** — as if the prophet says: and this cannot be changed
**“and who”**
• as if no one
• no one
**“can disannul it”** — his decree
**“and his hand is stretched out”** — to strike
14.28:
**“In the year that king Achaz died”**
• the impious one
• contention or possession
**“was this burden”**
• that is, this vision
• Septuagint: word
**“In the year that died”** — From the beginning of the book up to here, Isaias prophesied under Ozias, Joatham and Achaz; from here to the end, under Ezechias; the things foretold were partly fulfilled.
**“Achaz”** — While Achaz was living and reigning among sinners, neither a burden against foreigners nor the word of God (according to the Septuagint) could be delivered to the prophet.
14.29:
**“Rejoice not”**
• concerning the death of Achaz
• falling by a potion
• With the king dead, enemies rejoice as if about to gain something from the new state of affairs. Hence the Philistines, whom Achaz afflicted, rejoice at his death and mock the Jews, because with the king lost in his prime they are subject to his son; under whose reign he thought he could invade their borders.
**“whole Philistia, thou”** — from this
**“for the rod is broken in pieces”** — your rod and your staff
**“of him that struck thee”** — Achaz
**“for out of the root of the serpent”** — Achaz, who bit the Philistines but did not swallow them
**“shall come forth a basilisk”** — Ezechias
**“and his seed shall swallow the bird”**
• like a basilisk, by breath alone or by sight; for he struck the Philistines more than all others
• Septuagint: flying serpents
• Whom the Lord loveth he chastiseth, etc. God instructs us as sons, who visits iniquities with the rod. This is the rod and yoke which the Saviour wishes to lay upon the necks of all, so that, the yoke of the Assyrian being laid aside, they may bear the yoke of Christ; and if anyone has cast it off or broken it, at once from the root of the crooked serpent there will come forth the basilisk, and asps, according to the Septuagint, and from them flying serpents, or such as swallow birds.
**“The rod of him that struck”** — When the yoke of God is cast off, first the seed of the serpent takes root in our thoughts; afterwards from the evil seed the basilisk is born, who is the king of serpents, and is said to kill men by his breath and sight. These are vain sins, bursting forth from the evil treasure of thoughts into the worst of deeds; when these have reigned in those who are estranged from God, winged serpents will come forth, so that it is not enough for them to have thought or done what is evil, but they seek defences of evils and invent heresies. By winged serpents heretics can be understood, who lift themselves up against the knowledge of God and with poisoned mouth swallow the birds, that is, those who desire to fly to the heights.
14.30:
**“shall be fed”**
• “The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing.”
• when he has swallowed you up
**“of the firstborn”**
• The Jews, of whom: my firstborn son Israel
• the spirit, who do not cast off the yoke
**“of the poor and the poor shall rest with confidence”**
• without fear
• with a shepherd anxious for them
**“shall rest”** — in peace, with Lazarus, in Abraham’s bosom
**“and I will make perish with famine”** — of the word of God
**“thy root”** — your stench
**“and thy remnant”**
• who will be left by Ezechias
• lest anything sprout from the evil seed
• casting off the yoke
**“I will kill”**
• by the Assyrians and Chaldeans
• therefore
14.31:
**“Howl, O gate”** — you who dwell in the gate of the city of the Philistines
**“cry, O city”**
• or citizens
• nothing in it of divine wisdom
• because
• Howl, O gate; cry, O city. The Philistines fall by drink, made drunk, that is, with the cup of Babylon and the wine “wherein is luxury.” Yet they lost the kingdom of God both on account of their other vices and on account of drunkenness. They are therefore commanded that their gate howl: the gate of heretics is the blasphemous mouth; the city, the soul filled with evil thoughts.
**“Howl”** — As if the Philistines: weep for your misery, which comes through Sennacherib.
**“is thrown down”** — by the Assyrians
**“all Philistia is thrown down: for a smoke shall come from the north”** — the great army of Sennacherib, or report
**“and there is none that shall escape his troop”**
• of smoke
• for no one is without sin, not even an infant of one day
• From the north, for, etc. With the arrows of the devil blazing, who is harmful to the eyes and contrary to the light. The pot of Jeremias is kindled from the north. Whence in Proverbs: the north wind is harsh, but by name it is fair.
**“There is none that shall escape his troop”** — None except Jerusalem. And the angels who preside over the Assyrians asked why she alone is saved. It will be answered: because the Lord hath founded Sion, etc. And as Jeremias put chains of wood upon the necks of those who had been sent to him, Isaias says to the Lord: What shall be answered to the messengers of the various nations, if they ask concerning the coming of Sennacherib? To whom the Lord answers that they themselves are to be taken, and Jerusalem alone is to be delivered.
14.32:
**“And”** — when Philistia has fallen and its smoke has pervaded everything
**“what shall be answered to the messengers of the nations”** — namely, this is to be answered
**“messengers”** — To the angels who preside over cities and individual nations, wondering why Sion alone has avoided or escaped the bitterness of the smoke.
**“That the Lord hath founded Sion, and the poor of his people shall hope in him”** — and therefore they are saved
**“the poor”** — in spirit
**“Hath founded Sion”** — Upon the foundation of prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, which are Christ. Whence: “For other foundation no man can lay, but that which is laid,” etc.; but he who is foolish builds upon the sand.

15.1:
**“The burden of Moab”**
• Rightly, because Moab was conceived of the incest of a daughter at night, or the night signifies the greatness of sorrow.
• This is the vision of Isaias, given concerning the burden, that is, the destruction of Moab.
• Moab was the son of Lot, whose offspring and province were called Moab; in it is Ar, which is now Ariopolis, the metropolis.
• The burden of Moab. There is a carnal circumcision and a spiritual one. Whence: “We are the circumcision, who in spirit serve the Lord.” In distinction from the spiritual, it is called Israel: “Behold Israel according to the flesh.” So Moab is taken spiritually, which is interpreted “from the father” or “paternal water,” begotten of incest and drunkenness, as it were with the father absent and not knowing.
• Moab is the author of sense, which seems to be born of God the Father. But because he is an adversary to the people of God, he is begotten of incest in a cave and by night. By the sorrow of night, therefore, he has perished for ever, like the Egyptians in the morning watch, that is, in the time of night. Lot also, when Sodom was perishing, came into Segor, and the sun rose; whence: “We are not the children of night, nor of darkness,” etc. And elsewhere: “The night is passed, and the day is at hand,” etc.
**“Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste”**
• metropolis
• Historically. Because the Moabites rejoiced at the captivity of the Israelites, as the Philistines did, it is foretold to them that they are to suffer it. And it should be known that they were laid waste first by the Assyrians, afterwards by the Chaldeans.
**“Ar”** — That is: the adversary, namely worldly wisdom, which is adversary to God. Its wall, built by the art of dialectic, is laid waste in the night and falls silent.
**“Moab”** — the province of Arabia
**“it is silent”** — not daring to rebel
**“because the wall of Moab is destroyed in the night”** — built by the art of dialectic
**“Moab ... it is silent”** — for ever
15.2:
**“is gone up”** — to weep, where before it was to sacrifice
**“came up”** — To the high places in which it had been proud, that it may not sacrifice but mourn where it had sinned.
**“The house”** — royal
**“and Dibon”**
• noble city
• of adverse wisdom
• Dibon. Their flux is a lie: it passes and flows, and never remains in the same state; but the word of the Lord is firm and stable. Whence: manna is seen as if ice; it does not flow but stands firm.
**“to the high places”** — of idols
**“to mourn”** — to lament evils
**“over Nabo”**
• which is interpreted as sitting or prophecy
• noble city
**“and over Medaba”** — from the woodland
**“Moab”** — the whole province
**“hath howled: on all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard shall be shaven”** — the ancients in affliction and mourning shaved their heads and beards; whence Job, his head shaved, fell to the ground
**“Over Nabo”** — Jerome. Which is that all this prophecy has one sense; I have not torn it into parts.
15.3:
**“In their streets”** — in public
**“are girded with sackcloth”** — of penance
**“on the tops of their houses, and in their streets all”** — in every way
**“All shall howl”** — Another reading: “Every Moab howls,” that is, and so he will go down into weeping. As if he went up to the heights so that he might weep before the idols. But when he found no help there, he went down to weeping in the land or his own house.
15.4:
**“Hesebon shall cry”**
• thoughts
• From the beginning of the kingdom, which is in Hesebon, as far as the city Jasa, where it ends: everywhere a cry, everywhere mourning.
**“and Eleale”**
• ascent
• cities of the province of Moab
**“their voice is heard even to Jasa”** — deed or command
**“their voice”** — of the Moabites
**“For this”** — evil
**“the well appointed men of Moab”** — also, not only the old men
**“The well appointed men”** — Strong warriors free from wives. Hence it is said that Abraham chose the servants born in his house, unencumbered, that is, without wives.
15.5:
**“My heart”** — compassion, because he is a creature of God, because he is to be pitied, and an enemy
**“shall cry to Moab, the bars thereof”** — that is, the strength or its borders; they will be deserted as far as Segor, which is at the end
**“unto Segor”**
• to Segor, that is, they will come to the little one, so that they appear not strong but fragile
• Jerome. Segor is one of the five cities of the Sodomites, which was delivered for Lot’s sake. A heifer, because of lust, “three years old” (conternantem), not “consternating” (consternantem) as some read, but falsely. The Hebrews report that, twice shaken, it fell at the third earthquake. Or he says “conternating” for strong; for animals are strong in the third year, as a man at thirty; and it can be understood that it would have remained strong if after its deliverance it had not sinned.
**“a heifer of three years old”** — of three years
**“for by the ascent of Luith”**
• gene
• For Chus, who met the captives by whom they were being led, and through his city Aronaim.
**“they shall go up weeping: and in the way of Oronaim”** — the hole of sorrow
**“a cry”** — mourning
**“My heart shall cry to Moab”** — Namely, that I may provoke them to penance. Their bars, that is, the strongholds which they seemed to have in their heresies, will come to Segor, that is, to the little one, that they may appear not strong but frail. And Segor, that is, little penance, if it persevere, will lead them to perfect salvation, which is signified in the heifer of three years. Whence Abraham is commanded to offer a heifer and a ram and a goat of three years, namely a perfect sacrifice, that he may deserve to be the heir of the Lord. But when they have done penance, through Luith, that is, the tears of the cheeks, they ascend to higher things, and as through an opening and entrance of sorrow they will raise the cry of contrition to the Lord, saying: “A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit: a contrite and humbled heart.” And this will come to pass because the doctrine of the heretics (who are compared to leopards and transgressors) will be desolate. Every herb also and shoot, and whatever seemed green in their speech, has withered, and according to the greatness of their sins they have been visited by God, that him whom they had not perceived through benefits they may know through scourges. Finally they are led to the valley or torrent of willows, that no fruit of the heretics may remain in them. For they say that the nature of the seed of these trees is such that whoever drinks it in a cup becomes childless. Whence the saints: “On the willows in the midst thereof we hung up our instruments” in Babylon. A cry goes round all the borders of the Moabites, of those calling to penance, that through their wailing they may be able to offer the calves of their lips and come to the fountain of the Lord’s rams or of the strong, because Helym signifies both. And the waters of Dibon (which is interpreted sufficient sorrow or grief), which had defiled many by their sprinkling, will be shown to the deceived peoples to have been not for salvation but for blood. Whence the prophetic word promises that over the flowing tears (which is the interpretation of Dibon) they will redouble not one sorrow but many additions of sorrow, that when they have done full penance and fled from Moab they may deserve to have as prince the lion, whom the Septuagint called Ariel, which is interpreted lion of God.
15.6:
**“For the waters of Nemrim”** — leopards or transgressors
**“shall be desolate, for the grass is withered away, the spring is faded, all the greenness is perished”** — of trees, of vineyards
**“The waters of Nemrim”** — Nemrim is a town on the sea, and has many springs and waters, but false and bitter, and therefore barren. And it must be noted that the grass did not wither in Moab because the waters were false and bitter in all Moab, but the waters will be false and bitter in all Moab as the water of Nemrim, and therefore the grass will wither.
15.7:
**“According to the greatness”** — according to the extent of the disease, the physician’s cure
**“of their work”** — of sin
**“is their visitation also”** — vengeance
**“they shall lead them to the torrent of the willows”** — the rivers of Babylon. Whence: “On the willows in the midst thereof we hung up our instruments.”
**“Is their visitation also”** — Visitation in evil: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod.” Visitation in good: “the Orient from on high hath visited us.”
**“To the torrent of the willows”** — Thus far concerning the captivity of the Moabites by the Assyrians; now concerning that which is by the Chaldeans.
15.8:
**“For the cry is gone round about the border”** — town
**“of Moab unto Gallim”** — calves or heaps of sand
**“the howling thereof”**
• Moab
• As if Moab will therefore howl because where before there was luxury and delight on account of the watered places and the pleasantness of the springs, there are now streams of blood.
**“and unto the well of Elim”** — rams or strong ones
15.9:
**“For the waters of Dibon”** — sufficient sorrow
**“are filled with blood”** — Moab
**“for I will bring more upon Dibon”** — flowing tears
**“Additions”**
• of sorrow
• these, namely
**“the lion upon them that shall flee of Moab”** — a raging enemy or beasts that devour the Chaldeans
**“and upon the remnant of the land”**
• that remained; I will send them against the Chaldeans
• Nabo: sitting or prophecy. Medaba: from the leap. Esebon: thoughts. Eleale: ascent. Jasa: a deed without command. Segor: small. Luith: cheeks. Oronaim: pit of sorrow. Nemrim: leopards or transgressors. Gallim: calves or heaps of sands. Elym: rams or strong ones. Dibon: sufficient sorrow. Therefore the perverse doctrine, which without the inspiration of God is born in the human sense in the darkness of error, is laid waste by night, and its arguments, that is, its walls, are destroyed by ecclesiastical discourse, and are silent, and are turned to penitence; and over Nabo, that is, prophecy, and sitting, that is, their teachers, and Medaba, where is a barren leap and the dwelling of beasts, there will be howling and lamentation; and from their heads the ornaments of eloquence will be taken away, that they may remain naked and deformed; and if they seemed to have any manliness in the beard, it will be shaved off by the ecclesiastical man and shown to be effeminate and weak. In their crossroads also and the byways of errors, while each one invents what he wishes, he will be girded with the sackcloth of penitence; and upon the housetops, that is, the doctrines in which they believed themselves to be lofty, and in the streets, because they enter the broad way that leadeth to death, there will be howling; neither will they go up into pride, but will go down into weeping. Then they will understand their vain thoughts (which Esebon signifies) and the vain ascent of pride, which Eleale sounds. And their voice will be heard even to the evil works they have done, and the command which they thought to be of God, condemning themselves by their own confession. Therefore the bars, that is, those who were weak in Moab and understood their error, will howl, and will begin to have hope of progress when their soul has howled for itself. Whence the prophet, with the affection of one who suffers with them: “My heart shall cry to Moab.”
**“The waters of Dibon”** — Dibon means silence. Dibon means weeping, and yet it is one city.

16.1:
**“Send forth the lamb”** — Christ.
**“the ruler”** — “All power is given to me in heaven and in earth.”
**“of the earth, from Petra of the desert, to the mount of the daughter of Sion”**
• Ruth the Gentile; for the Gentiles worshipped stones as God, and therefore were deserted by God.
• Petra of the desert. That is, Ruth, because by God’s precept the Moabites do not enter the Church of God until the tenth generation.
• Ruth the Moabitess: Booz married her, of whom he begot Obed, of whom Jesse was the father of David, from whose seed the virgin Mary came forth, who conceived and bore Christ. For just as Christ came for both peoples, so he willed to be born of both.
**“Send forth”** — Therefore the prophets are scarcely understood, because they suddenly change persons and numbers and times, and from any one pass over again to another. For when Isaias was speaking just now of the captivity of Moab and its miseries, unexpectedly he turned the eye of the mind to the birth of Christ and began to address Moab, as if to say: do not despair, do penance, because although you are to be made captive, yet from your offspring will be born the lamb “who taketh away the sins of the world,” who will rule over the whole world.
**“to the mount”** — To Jerusalem, or rather to the Church, which is in contemplation, as it were a daughter of watching. Also in Jerusalem above all he preached, worked miracles, suffered, died, rose again, and redeemed the human race.
16.2:
**“And”**
• That is, these.
• returns to the captivity of Moab.
• as.
**“shall come to pass, that as a bird”** — who has fled from Moab.
**“fleeing away”** — the hawk.
**“young ones”** — lest they be devoured by the Moabite serpents.
**“flying out of the nest”** — most swiftly.
**“so shall the daughters of Moab be”** — cities or men, women.
**“in the passage”** — Moabite souls.
**“So shall be”** — So they will pass into captivity across Arnon, which is the boundary of the Moabites and Amorites.
**“Arnon”** — Which is interpreted as the illumination of those who, having left errors behind, pass over to knowledge of the truth.
16.3:
**“Take counsel”**
• O Moab.
• Do nothing without counsel, nor be carried about by “every wind of doctrine”; follow “the angel of great counsel.”
**“gather a council”** — foresee how you may escape.
**“Gather a council”** — That is, making the Church out of the wandering and erring.
**“make thy shadow as the night”** — a secure hiding place.
**“in the midday”**
• in open persecution.
• Place it at noon, while there is persecution of the Jews. Place, O you Moab, your shadow, that is, your defence, as if night, that is, a secure hiding place, for the Jews.
• It is to be noted that Jerusalem was laid waste first by the Assyrians and afterwards by the Chaldeans, before Moab; and therefore he is commanded to receive the fleeing people of God with him and hide them.
**“Make as the night”** — That is, the tabernacle in which you thought to rest, which was of night and darkness: place it at noon, that is, in the brightest light, in which you ought to hide those fleeing from error, and no longer betray those who once wandered.
**“hide them that flee”** — The Jews.
**“and betray not them that wander about”**
• from place to place
• to the enemies
16.4:
**“shall dwell”** — Jerusalem laid waste
**“with thee”** — because he is a neighbour to them
**“My fugitives shall dwell with thee: O Moab, be thou a covert to them from the face of the destroyer”**
• when the devil has begun to pursue
• the Assyrians and the Chaldeans
• because
**“My fugitives”** — Those who fled from me, who went out of the Church, who followed their own sense and not the teaching of the Holy Spirit.
*Mystically:* Let us consider from the beginning of this burden how the Moabites, by the steps and order of penance, become Israelites, and flee like a bird and fly like young ones from the nest, that they may cross over by Arnon and dwell on the mount of the daughter of Sion; and, the power of the devil or of antichrist being crushed, Christ may reign in these and set his throne among those who are saved by mercy and justice. “For neither doth the Father judge any man, but hath given all judgment to the Son.”
**“is at an end”**
• of the devil
• consumed, killed
• Sennacherib
• who at the coming of the lamb, who sprang from the rock of the desert, came to mount Sion
**“for the dust”** — the power of the devil is compared to dust
**“the wretch is consumed”** — because he made them wretched
**“he hath failed, that trod”** — by laying waste
**“the earth”** — earthly ones
**“Is at an end”** — He suddenly passes to the slaying of Sennacherib, who was dust and wretched, because his glory was like dust which the wind drives from its face, etc. He wretchedly departed from this light, slain by his own sons in the temple of his god.
16.5:
**“And shall be prepared”**
• of the first coming
• that having been consumed
• The Jews expound this of Ezechias, who reigned in peace after the death of Sennacherib. But it is better referred to Christ, and some things to his first coming, some to the second coming.
**“in mercy”**
• of the Father
• for all have sinned and need the glory of God
**“A throne”**
• of the Son
• an everlasting kingdom
**“and one shall sit upon it in truth”** — so that, after mercy, he may judge, and seek justice, and render to each according to his works
**“in the tabernacle”**
• in the Church
• which had fallen and has been raised up
**“of David, judging and seeking judgment”** — at the second coming
**“and quickly rendering”** — saying to the wicked, “Depart into the fire”; and to the good, “Come, ye blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom.”
**“that which is just”** — to each one according to his works.
**“Shall sit”** — Resting, and judging over the hearts of the good.
16.6:
**“We have heard of the pride”**
• this again concerning Moab.
• the voice of the saints who were saved out of Moab and have experienced his pride.
**“Moab”** — of the heretics, mocking the simplicity of the Church.
**“he is exceeding proud: his pride and his arrogancy, and his indignation”** — headlong audacity dares more than it can.
**“is more than his strength”**
• it is proud beyond its strength.
• because it is proud against God.
**“We have heard”** — Scripture goes on: because he had said it joyfully, lest he make the negligent careless, he frightens them with a threat.
**“and his indignation”** — He set his mouth against God in heaven, slandering the prophets, adding that gospel saying: “All, as many as have come before me, are thieves and robbers.” He calls Moses and David murderers, and Josue a bloodthirsty man.
16.7:
**“Therefore shall Moab howl to Moab”** — to one another.
**“shall howl”** — One to another: all, that is, the diversities of heretics and philosophers against one another will bellow in torments.
**“Every one”** — Moab.
**“shall howl to them that rejoice”** — who trust and boast in the fortification of walls.
**“upon the brick walls, tell ye”** — O prelates of the Church, or those of Moab who are saved.
**“their stripes”**
• death, captivity.
• made by the darts of heretics.
**“upon the brick walls”** — Not built of square stone, like the temple of God, in which the stones were so polished that neither hammer nor axe was heard.
16.8:

**“are desolate”** — by God’s help, or burned by divine fire.

**“the vineyard of Sabama”**
• especially.
• the multitude of the people.
