**“the lords of the nations”**
• the princes of the Assyrians or of the Chaldeans.
• the apostles or apostolic men.
• or distinguish thus: and the vine of Sabama, the lords of the Gentiles.
**“have destroyed”** — the inhabitants, that is, of Sabama, have fallen
**“the branches thereof”**
• lest from other heresies others should be born without end, its scourges have cut off, etc.
• very bad roots
• the shoots having been cut off
**“even”** — even
**“to Jazer”**
• city
• which is their strength, that is, to the strongest doctrines of heretics in which they trust
**“have reached, have wandered”** — lords of the nations
**“They have wandered”** — Roaming through all the land of Moab.
**“in the wilderness”** — so that at last they might not have those whom they would kill
**“In the wilderness”** — That at last they might not have whom they would kill.
**“The branches”** — He continues the metaphor of the vine.
**“are left”**
• by God
• understand fugitives
• but
**“They have passed in haste”**
• lords of the nations
• led into Babylon
**“the sea”** — of the temptation of the world: I am come into the depth of the sea, and a tempest hath overwhelmed me
**“They are gone over the sea”** — That, freed from the temptations in the depths, they might see the wonders of the Lord.
16.9:
**“For this”** — by evil
**“I will lament”**
• Isaias
• that they may weep with me
**“with the weeping of Jazer”**
• that is, weeping Jazer
• namely the strength of heretics, which exalts itself against the knowledge of God
**“the vineyard of Sabama: I will water thee with my tears”**
• I will weep abundantly over your captivity
• Sabama: one who exalts himself against the sentence of God.
**“the vineyard”** — The vineyard of Moab, from the neighbourhood of the place, is such as Sodom’s. Whence: “Their vines are of the vineyard of Sodom,” etc.
**“Hesebon”** — their thoughts, by which they have climbed to lofty things
**“and Eleale”** — ascent
**“for the voice of the treaders hath rushed in upon thy vintage, and upon thy harvest”** — which grows in the valleys of Raphaim
**“the voice of the treaders”**
• of the lords of the nations
• of the Assyrians and Chaldeans plundering the goods of the Moabites
16.10:
**“And gladness and joy shall be taken away”** — of heretics, that they may hear “Blessed are they that mourn”
**“from Carmel”** — from the knowledge of the false name
**“From Carmel”** — Carmel is a mountain between Phoenicia and Palestine, overhanging Ptolemais, in which Elijah prayed. It is often put for any fertility; whence here also “gladness and joy shall be taken away from Carmel,” that is, the fertility in which the Moabites rejoiced.
**“there shall be no rejoicing nor shouting in the vineyards”** — Moab
**“Rejoicing”** — Because heretics boast that they have the knowledge of spiritual circumcision.
**“nor shouting”**
• they will be silent in eternal silence
• because
**“He shall not tread out wine in the press”** — Moab
**“that was wont to tread it out: the voice of the treaders I have taken away”** — a shout which the grape-gatherers were accustomed to sing
**“the voice”** — Lest the poisons of the dragon be pressed out from there and those drinking be killed.
16.11:
**“For this”**
• misfortune
• with Moab destroyed and false joy turned into mourning
**“my bowels”**
• feeling
• turned
**“for Moab”** — penitent
**“shall sound like a harp”**
• lamenting
• mourning
**“My bowels”** — The prophet, who like a harp is composed by musical art, and conceiving from the fear of God begets many children, so that every heart gives back its sound.
**“and my inward parts”**
• the inner parts of the heart
• Whence: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me.”
**“to the wall”** — fragile
**“of baked brick”** — of the city which is made of bricks
**“my inward parts”** — As a harp does not give forth a harmonious sound if even one string is broken, so spiritually the belly of the prophet, if one string of the virtues is lacking, will not resound a sweet melody, nor will it cry out with all its inward parts for the brick wall. It is also the opinion of the philosophers that the virtues cling to one another. And James: he who lacks one is lacking in all.
16.12:
**“And it shall come to pass, when it is seen”**
• that it is vain
• for him
**“that he is wearied”** — in vain
**“Moab on his high places”**
• on the mountains and roofs
• by the doctrines which he thought lofty
• then
**“he shall go in to his sanctuaries”** — the idols which he thought holy
**“his sanctuaries”** — To the holy things, namely of the Church, which he will try to make his own; he will not prevail, for we do not at once grasp virtue perfectly.
**“to pray”** — for deliverance
**“shall not prevail”** — That is, he will not find help in those things in which he hoped; and so it appeared that he worshipped in vain.
16.13:
**“This is the word that the Lord spoke to Moab from that time”**
• from the time that he was created, saying: Behold the Lord; the Moabites and Ammonites will not enter into my Church; or, from the time that he foreknew them
• This word, etc. In the prologue, where it is said: the burden of Moab. From then, that is, from when he began to speak, so that everything he said may be one word, that is, one sentence.
• This word. The prologue answers to the epilogue; for what was begun there is completed here.
16.14:
**“And now”** — against
**“the Lord hath spoken, saying”** — this concerning Babylon
**“In three years”**
• not more
• As a few grape-clusters remain after the grape-gatherers, so out of the multitude of Moab few will escape the enemy.
• In three years. The prophecy against the Philistines and the Moabites began to be directed after the death of Achaz, and it can be understood that from then in the third year the Moabites would be laid waste; as if he said: as a hireling waits for the end of the year to receive the wages of his work, so Moab after three years will be destroyed by the Assyrians. It can also be understood of Babylon, that after the capture of Jerusalem it was to be laid waste in the third year by the Chaldeans; or that in three years no rest is to be given them.
• As the mercy of God is in weight and measure, so in the Jews are torment and punishment, so that when three years have passed, in which one is left small and feeble, he may cease to be inglorious. Moab therefore, which was a foreigner and not of the people of God, but turned back after leaving error, is left for three years only small and feeble and inglorious; of whom: “I thought upon the days of old: and I had in my mind the eternal years.”
**“as the years of a hireling, the glory of Moab shall be taken away”** — Moab has departed, so that he who had many companions in error is left with few.
**“for all the multitude of the people, and it shall be left small and feeble”** — in humility
**“as the years of a hireling”** — False doctrine does everything for the sake of gain; for the hireling “seeth the wolf coming, and flieth.” Therefore it was said that a stranger and a hireling of the priests should not eat of the holy things, but the servants of the holy ones should be partakers, because they do all things not for love of the Lord but for pay, to be clothed with wool and to milk the milk. Likewise he who gives alms to be praised by men receives his reward, because he is a hireling. He who feigns chastity, having something else in his heart, receives the punishments of a sinner. Therefore, in comparison of two evils, it is a lighter sin to sin openly than to feign holiness.

17.1:
**“The burden of Damascus”** — of the Gentiles who before the faith of Christ were friends of blood and cruelty, and did works worthy of mourning and sackcloth
**“Behold Damascus”** — namely the converted nations will not be in their former way of life; here it is treated of the calling of the Gentiles
**“shall cease to be a city”** — powerful, noble
**“and shall be as a ruinous heap”** — a faithful flock gathered from many
**“of stones”** — of living [stones]
**“a ruinous”**
• of the blinded Jews
• Behold Damascus. Damascus, the metropolis of Syria, which Eliezer, Abraham’s servant, founded; whose king Rasin always gave help to the ten tribes against Judah. Therefore the Holy Spirit threatens it with captivity through Isaias; by it, moreover, we understand the whole province.
• Damascus: shedding blood, or drinking it, or the kiss of blood, because there Cain killed Abel; or the blood of sackcloth. For those who shed much blood ought to do penance, which is signified by sackcloth. But since they did not do penance, they were taken captive.
17.2:
**“shall be left”**
• that overthrown
• by men
**“The cities of Aroer”**
• the region of Syria in which are many cities
• myrica
• that is, unfruitful
**“shall be left for flocks”**
• ecclesiastical
• to pasture
**“Aroer”** — The myrica is an unfruitful tree growing in deserts and salty places. As if all the Syrians will be unfruitful and desolate. Others say that from this tree hatreds are stirred up by wicked arts.
**“and they shall rest there”** — with a calm mind
**“and there shall be none”** — So great will be the desolation that not even a robber is to be feared.
**“to make them afraid”** — because the Lord is among them; with the shepherd present they will not fear wolves.
17.3:
**“And aid shall cease”**
• of Damascus.
• of God.
**“from Ephraim, and the kingdom”**
• the scribes and Pharisees, who are opposed to the people of God.
• shall cease.
**“from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria”**
• of those from the nations who believed.
• The remnant, etc. Ironically. For ignominy; as the children of Israel were led into captivity because they placed their hope not in God but in man, so also the Syrians, who promised them aid, to separate them from the worship of God, which they also did. Both therefore to an ignominious captivity.
**“and the kingdom”** — That sin may not reign in her, who previously loved blood.
**“as the glory of the children of Israel”** — namely, as formerly the children of Israel were, the kingdom having been taken from the Jews and handed over to the nations.
**“saith the Lord of hosts”** — he promised through the prophets, namely, saith the Lord of hosts.
17.4:
**“And”** — then.
**“And it shall come to pass in that day, the glory of Jacob shall be made thin”** — Syria and Damascus, in which it boasted.
**“the glory of Jacob”**
• of the Jews.
• for they were glorious throughout the whole world.
• the strength of confidence.
• Three similitudes, almost one meaning. For as the ears of corn very rarely escape the hands of the reapers, and few grapes (called from remaining) escape the hands of the grape-gatherers, and few olives remain after the shaking of the olive tree, so few will remain in Damascus and in all Syria, first when the Assyrians come and afterwards the Chaldeans. For under the Assyrian captivity few remained to till the land. Others were transferred to Cyrene, which is a region beyond Egypt.
**“And it shall come to pass”** — When Syria has been laid waste by the Assyrians and Damascus has ceased to be a city.
**“and”** — that is.
**“the fatness of his flesh shall grow lean”** — others read: its fat flesh will wither, but falsely.
**“shall grow lean”** — They will have no prophets, nor signs, nor miracles, nor kingdom, nor priesthood. But the whole body of the nation will wither.
17.5:
**“And”** — this, namely.
**“in the harvest”** — It is said of the nations. The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few. They gather the remnants of the harvest, which were saved through the apostles, and the very rare ears. Not on the mountains but in the valley of Raphaim, that is, in the lowliness of the letter; for Raphaim means giants.
17.6:
**“And the fruit thereof that shall be left upon it, shall be as one cluster of grapes”** — those who shall be saved.
**“And”** — and it will be.
**“as the shaking of the olive tree, two or three berries in the top of a bough, or four or five upon the top of the tree, saith the Lord the God of Israel”**
• namely, the salvation of the Jews.
• who knows not how to lie.
• Two: of Paul and Barnabas. And again of Peter, James and John, who saw the Lord transfigured on the mountain and saw the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue raised.
**“as the shaking”** — When the Jewish people were struck down, the olive that under Moses had six hundred thousand armed men, and under David when Joab counted, an innumerable people, offered the Saviour scarcely a few fruits.
**“or four”** — These are the nine remaining, among whom Matthias obtained the place of Judas the betrayer. These, according to a diversity of graces unknown to us, were divided into four or five, that they might show in themselves the number of the gospels and the volumes of the law, as preachers of both testaments.
17.7:

**“and his eyes shall look to the Holy One of Israel”** — temple
17.8:

**“such as groves and temples”** — in which they were accustomed to sacrifice
17.9:

**“cities shall be”** — strong
**“his strong”** — Israel
**“shall be left”** — forsaken by men

**“and the corn that were left”** — forsaken by the Amorrhites
**“before the face”** — by the onslaught
**“of the children of Israel, and thou shalt be desolate”** — people

17.10:
**“Because thou hast forgotten”**

**“of inheritance”**

• therefore

**“Woe to the multitude”** — The prophetic word threatens Sennacherib and his army, whom he had gathered against the people of God. For he comes with so great a multitude that its noise is compared to the noise of the sea.
**“like the multitude of the roaring sea: and the tumult of crowds, like the noise of many waters”** — many waters: many peoples
17.13:
**“shall make a noise”**

• with a voice in agreement of impiety

**“like the noise of waters overflowing, but he shall rebuke”** — the Lord, by slaying the army
**“him”**
• the devil, the author of sedition
• Sennacherib, the lord of that army
**“and he shall flee”**
• from the people of God
• into Nineve
**“far off: and he shall be carried away”**
• that he may be bound in the abyss
• from Jerusalem, or from the world
• the more strongly, the higher he was
**“as the dust of the mountains before the wind, and as a whirlwind before a tempest”**
• separated from the people of God
• who rises from the earth
**“He shall be carried away”** — He was taken from Jerusalem when with a few he fled to Nineve. He was taken from the world when he was quickly slain by his own sons.
17.14:
**“In the time”** — that is, in the last part of the night
**“of the evening”** — of the consummation

Egypt, which is sorrow or darkness, is the world, changed into Chanaan. The five cities are the five senses of the body, of which one is of the sun, that is, the eyes, by which we behold the light. Those who serve vices and do not guard the senses of the body from evil pleasures speak the Egyptian language, because they dwell in the darkness of sins; but those who give their effort to virtues speak the language of Chanaan, that is, they speak a changed language, because they are changed from vices to virtues.

**“the language of Chanaan”** — The question is asked why the five cities of Egypt speak not the Hebrew language but that of Chanaan. Because, namely, Hebrew means “one who passes over,” who passes from place to place. So as long as we are in the Egypt of this world we cannot speak the Hebrew language, but the language of Chanaan, which is midway between the Hebrew and the Egyptian language and for the most part borders on the Hebrew. Chanaan is interpreted “commotion,” or “as it were answering.” When we depart from Egypt we are moved, and as it were answer the will of the Lord. But because we are still in the world, we cannot speak the Hebrew language.

**“but Israel is my inheritance”** — because there he was born, nurtured, suffered, and completed the other mysteries of our redemption
**“Israel”**
• he alone who beholds God in mind can say, God is my portion
• Blessed, etc. These regions abounded in monks beyond all others, and therefore deserved to be blessed.

20.1:
**“In the year that Tharthan entered”** — tower; overflowing or prolonging
**“into Azotus”** — fire of generation
**“when Sargon the king of the Assyrians had sent him”** — prince of gardens
**“and he had fought against Azotus, and had taken it”**
• In the year, etc. These are Assyrian names: Tharthan means tower, or superfluous, or removing far off. Sargon, prince of the garden. The king of the Assyrians, that is, the great sense, has very many leaders, of whom one is Tharthan, lifted up in pride, going far forward in wickedness, who is sent to take Azotus by storm, which in Hebrew is called Esdor, that is, fire of generation. For the leader of the king of the Assyrians storms those who serve generation and lust.
• In the year, etc. Azotus, the most powerful city of the Philistines of the five, which Sargon, who is also Sennacherib (for he was called by seven names, according to Jerome), by sending Tharthan as leader of his army, took by storm and held. But when it was taken, the Lord spoke “by the hand of Isaias,” with a work agreeing with the words. For the works bore witness to what the Lord spoke through him.
**“When Sargon had sent him”** — Fittingly the king of the Assyrians is called Sargon, that is, prince of the garden; like him is Achab, who desired to turn the vineyard of Naboth into a garden; which that man, understanding tropologically, preferred to die rather than do, lest his paternal inheritance and ancient possession be changed into the delights of an impious king.
20.2:
**“At that same time the Lord spoke by the hand of Isaias the son of Amos”** — with the deed agreeing with the words
**“saying: Go, and loose the sackcloth from off thy loins”** — sackcloth; for this is the dress of a prophet mourning the sins of the people
**“and take off thy shoes from thy feet”** — Put off the shoes from thy feet: for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.
**“And he did so, and went naked, and barefoot”**
• For three days.
• The prophets foretold the future not only by words but also by deeds, as in this place.
• Go and loose, etc. The prophet is commanded to lay aside sackcloth and shoes and to walk naked and barefoot, as a sign to the Egyptians and Ethiopians, who persecuted the people of God. For Egypt is persecuting or afflicting; the Ethiopians are humble and cast down; for he that exalteth himself shall be humbled. These are to be led into captivity for three years, to suffer torments, concerning which: “I had in my mind the eternal years.” Nor let us think the punishments small, but they will be prolonged for great times. And in that very captivity of Egypt, the young men, that is, strengthened in malice, and the old men, who have come to the vices of perfect age, will go naked, that all their crimes may be laid open; for there is nothing hidden that shall not be revealed.
• And he did so. A wonderful obedience: the most noble man, whose daughter King Manasses took in marriage, as the Hebrews relate, was clothed only in sackcloth; he was not ashamed to go naked, judging nothing more honourable than to obey the Lord.
• Barefoot, etc. To be noted: before Azotus is taken, the prophet is clothed in sackcloth with shoes on his feet, that he may lament those who have been wounded by the burning arrows of the devil and serve lust, and that he may be able to tread upon serpents and scorpions, which are in the desert of this world, where there is thirst for all good things. But after Azotus has been taken, as a sign of the captivity of Egypt and Ethiopia, he goes barefoot and naked. For clothed in sackcloth, and with his feet covered with skin, he cannot either stand or walk in the holy land, to which he hastens.
20.3:
**“And the Lord said: As my servant Isaias hath walked, naked and barefoot”** — Not that he went naked for three years, but days can be understood as years. Whence the Lord says to Ezechiel: “I have given thee a day for a year.”
**“it shall be a sign and a wonder upon Egypt, and upon Ethiopia”** — Humble and cast down, because it has been humbled on account of its pride.
20.4:
**“So”** — Three years, as my servant walked naked; three days.
**“shall the king of the Assyrians lead away the prisoners of Egypt, and”** — He will lead away.
**“the captivity of Ethiopia”** — The Ethiopians were allied with the Egyptians.
**“young”** — Strong in wickedness.
**“and old”** — Grown old in evil days.
**“naked”**
• Nothing covered that shall not be revealed.
• I mean captivity.
**“and barefoot, with their buttocks uncovered”** — Through which dung comes out.
**“to the shame of Egypt”** — To be shown.
**“to the shame”** — Because they could not eat the Lord’s passover, which he eats girded in the loins, holding a staff in his hand, with shod feet, lest, passing through the desert of this world, he be bitten by serpents.
20.5:
**“And they shall be afraid”** — The Jews.
**“and ashamed”**
• With shame.
• When they see her confounded.
**“of Ethiopia their hope”** — In whom they hoped.
**“and of Egypt their glory”** — In whose help they gloried.
20.6:
**“And”** — Therefore.
**“shall say”** — Not a newcomer and stranger but a resident.
**“the inhabitants of this isle”**
• Jerusalem, which was incessantly battered by persecutions and waves.
• An island, as it were in the sea.
**“this”** — Of the world.
**“in that day: Lo”** — Behold, so fragile.
**“this was our hope, to whom”** — To such as: to the fragile and infirm, who could not free themselves.
**“we fled for help, to deliver up from the face of the king of the Assyrians, and how”** — As if in no way.
**“shall we be able to escape?”** — Since these have been taken captive.
**“Lo, this was”** — The wonderful providence of God has destroyed all the kingdoms that were proud against one another. Israel hoped, against the will of God, in Damascus and the Syrians, and therefore both were taken captive by the Assyrians. Juda, in the Ethiopians and Egyptians, and these also were conquered by the Assyrians and Chaldeans. The Assyrians, because they presumed on themselves, perished by the Chaldeans. The Chaldeans and Babylonians, lifted up against the Lord, were subjugated by the Medes and Persians, and these by Alexander the Great, who, when he had exalted himself as a god, was killed by poison, and his kingdom was split into parts and afterwards subjugated by the Romans. The Roman empire, which as with iron teeth and claws tore the flesh of the saints, has already for the most part perished. In the end it will perish entirely, when the kingdom of Christ shall have shone forth.

21.1:
**“The burden of the desert”**
• in which God does not dwell
• by God and men
**“of the sea”** — of the world. Whence: “they that go down to the sea in ships”
**“The burden of the desert of the sea”** — Of Babylon: called a sea because of the multitude of its people. Whence: “the Lord will make her sea a desert.”
**“As”** — the voice of Babylon
**“whirlwinds”** — of temptations
**“from the south”** — whence the most violent winds
**“cometh from the desert”** — so from the desert of the Medes and Persians desolation rushed upon me
**“it cometh from a terrible land”** — to me
**“from the desert”** — In which the Lord was tempted; in which the Israelites were struck by serpents.
21.2:
**“A grievous vision”**
• with how many temptations the world is full
• of captivity
**“is told me”** — by God
**“me”** — Isaias
**“he that is unfaithful”**
• to God or to his lord
• Darius or Cyrus
**“He that is unfaithful”** — The general judgment is, as it were, the fault of individuals, that they are overwhelmed in the storm.
**“unfaithfully”** — against his lord, Balthasar, by killing him, though God permitted it
**“dealeth”** — He acts as befits an unbeliever
**“and he that is a spoiler, spoileth”** — me
**“Go up”** — the voice of the Lord to the Persians and Medes
**“Elam”**
• despising ones, who are wont, that is, to tempt and to scorn
• the province of the Persians and the city
• Go up, Elam. Septuagint: The Elamites and the envoys of the Persians. The Elamites despising, the Persians tempting.
• Go up, as if, O Persians and Medes, do not fear the horses; mount up and besiege Babylon.
• Go up, Elam: trusting in the strength of God, he speaks boldly against his adversaries.
**“besiege, O Mede”**
• Otherwise, Mede
• Babylon
• a city in Media
**“I have made all the mourning thereof to cease”** — of the sea or of the hard vision
**“All the mourning”** — By which he made you and the other nations to groan. Or, that no one now groan, oppressed by the power of Babylon. Or, that she be afflicted with such great evils that she dare not groan against you.
21.3:
**“Therefore”**
• The voice of the prophet, because Babylon is so crushed.
• because, namely, my loins, doing penance, are full not with pleasure as before but with pain.
**“my loins filled with pain”** — of so great misery.
**“anguish hath taken hold of me, as the anguish of a woman in labour”** — A woman when she gives birth has sorrow, because her hour has come.
**“I fell down”** — into sorrow, or into the earth.
**“at the hearing of it”**
• the misery of Babylon.
• the hard vision.
**“I was troubled at the seeing of it”** — in spirit.
21.4:
**“My heart failed, darkness”** — anguishes; or, the eyes grew dim with tears.
**“amazed me”** — my mind, so that, troubled, I hardly knew what to think.
**“Babylon”** — the world, which lies in evil.
**“my beloved”**
• formerly.
• each has its own holy appearance, as man to man.
**“my”** — of God, or of the prophet.
**“is become to me”** — of Isaias.
**“a wonder”**
• because overthrown.
• how could it be overthrown so quickly by the proud?
21.5:
**“Prepare”** — The Lord to the prophet.
**“the table”**
• of the Lord, by whose food, being filled, he beholds more keenly what is to come to the world.
• that you may announce what is to come, saying: eat and drink.
**“behold”**
• O Balthasar.
• O Babylon.
**“in the watchtower them that eat and drink”** — you, O Darius and Cyrus, eating and drinking with the king, arise and kill your lord.
**“arise, ye princes, take up”** — or take up.
**“the shield”**
• Prepare the table, etc. As if to say: O Persians and Medes, take food, preparing yourselves for war; contemplate from the watchtower; look at what has been written on the wall, for God has numbered the kingdom of this king. Arise, after you have eaten and drunk; seize arms; make war upon Babylon.
• Eat and drink, believing the blood and body of the Lord, that you may be princes of the Church, that you may take up the shield of faith and the armour of Paul, in which you may check the fiery darts of the devil.
**“Behold”** — What is to fall upon him after the table. Or, behold, O Balthasar, what was written on the wall: Mane, Thecel, Phares.
21.6:
**“For thus hath the Lord said to me: Go, and set”**
• in your heart, that is, diligently look upon what is to come to the world.
• yourself.
**“a watchman”** — Christ, in whom the things to come; the watchman.
**“A watchman”** — Prophets are called watchmen. Whence to Ezechiel: “Son of man, I have made thee a watchman to the house of Israel.”
**“and whatsoever he shall see”** — by the spirit of prophecy
21.7:
**“And he saw”** — I am a watchman.
**“a chariot with two horsemen”** — a chariot which is usually drawn by two horses
**“a rider upon an ass, and a rider upon a camel”** — that is, the rider, who in place of horses made use of an ass and a camel for riding
**“and he beheld them diligently”** — the watchman
**“A rider”** — Cyrus the prince ruled the Medes and Persians after the death of Darius his uncle. This rider, then, the prophet saw coming against Babylon with the Medes and Persians, together with Darius his uncle. The ass is that of the kings of the Persians, which before Cyrus was ignoble and of no dignity. The camel is the kingdom of the Medes, which was always most powerful.
21.8:
**“and cried like a lion”** — Christ, who is also the watchman
**“A lion”** — The lion is the same: for strength of soul; the watchman, by the privilege of contemplation.
**“upon the watchtower of the Lord I am”**
• Isaias
• explains what a watchman is
**“Upon the watchtower of the Lord I am”** — That is, placed in contemplation by day, ready by days and nights to hear and to speak what he has commanded.
**“standing continually in the daytime”** — namely, set in the light of the Lord, whence I may foresee things to come
**“and upon my ward I am standing”** — steadfast
**“all the night”**
• not only in prosperity
• the duty enjoined on me, namely, that I may foresee things to come in the darkness of the world
**“standing all the night”** — That I may guard myself from all sin and be worthy to hear the word of the Lord.
21.9:
**“Behold this man cometh, the rider upon the chariot with two horsemen”** — the lion who had cried out above
**“Behold this man cometh”** — What follows signifies that he saw the Saviour coming, seated upon a chariot and joining one chariot from two animals, that is, an ass and a camel.
**“and he answered”** — to me, desiring to hear his words
**“and said: Babylon is fallen, she is fallen”**
• already in the presence of God
• at my first coming, and utterly at the second
**“She is fallen, she is fallen”** — When Cyrus and Darius laid waste Babylon, the idols too were broken, the temple of Bel overthrown and burned with fire.
**“Babylon”** — the confusion of the whole world
**“and all the graven gods thereof”** — false doctrines, written with the sharp edge of dialectic and coloured with rhetorical paint
**“are broken unto the ground”** — he who is of the earth speaks of the earth
21.10:
**“O my thrashing”**
• The voice of the prophet or of Christ, as if to say: what I owed I have done for you; and do not say it was not spoken.
• O Jerusalem, threshed by many tribulations
• As if to say: O people who are to be stored in my barns, whom I have threshed with various straits, that I might shake out the chaff and bring the pure wheat into the barns: what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have declared to you.
**“and the children of my door”** — that is, of the temple built on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, who is also called Areuna
**“that which I have heard of the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have declared unto you”** — as if: my words are not mine; believe them, for they are the Lord’s, who does not know how to deceive
21.11:
**“The burden of Duma”** — Septuagint: Of Idumea, which is a province of the Saracens. Duma is a region of Idumea; its inhabitants are of the offspring of Esau, who is Edom and Seir. Now the Idumeans were overcome by the Assyrians and Chaldeans, as were the two tribes; who, seeing that after seventy years the two tribes were freed from servitude while they themselves were held in captivity, though they were of the same stock, implored the help of the Lord; and this is: he calleth to me.
**“calleth to me out of Seir”** — still a captive, who is from Seir
**“Watchman, what of the night? watchman, what of the night?”** — or: what
**“of the night”** — you free your people, as though you watch over them while they sleep; why then do you not likewise free us, who are of the same kind?
21.12:
**“The watchman said”** — Almighty God
**“The morning cometh”** — the time of release from the burden for my people
**“also the night”** — tribulation for the Edomites
**“if you seek”** — me
**“Seek”**
• with the whole heart
• leaving idols
• by doing penance
• He calleth to me, etc. That is, God, my watchman, calls me day and night to penance, that leaving Seir, which is interpreted bristly and hairy, I may return to dwell with him. Duma is likeness or silence. Idumea is earthly. We can therefore say that, after the likeness of the people of Israel, a multitude of the Gentiles is called, and where before there had been silence of the law of God, there may be the cry of confession. The Church too can relate that the Lord calls to me from Seir, that is, from earthly places, and summons me to salvation, and says to him: O watchman, who rising by night dwellest in the darkness, who art in the flesh without the sin of the flesh, for what cause didst thou will to take a human body? The watchman said: the Samaritan, who carried the wounded man on his own shoulders to the inn. The morning cometh, and the night: to the Gentiles, namely, the sun of justice; to the Jews, darkness; whence: that they who see not may see, and they who see may become blind. Then he speaks to the Gentiles: if you seek me, seek more earnestly.
• The morning cometh, etc. As for my people, I will give the light of joy to those returning from captivity; but you I will leave in the night of captivity, because you exulted over the affliction of my people. For since the Edomites rejoiced at the captivity of Israel, therefore they too have been taken captive.
**“If you seek”** — If you seek my help in necessity, seek it likewise in prosperity. Turn to me in heart. Come in deed, and so I will hear you.
**“return, come”**
• even so
• to me
21.13:
**“The burden”** — the burden of captivity
**“The burden in Arabia”** — The Arabs are the Saracens, from Ismael and Cedar his son; or more correctly Agarenes, from Agar their mother; but they preferred to be called Saracens, as if sons of Sara the free woman, not of Agar the handmaid. When they ought to have given bread and water to the Jews fleeing from the face of the Chaldeans, they offered bread but withheld water, that they might burn the more with thirst and perish. Wherefore they too were led into captivity. Hence God addresses the Jews who flee thus: In the forest at evening you shall sleep, in.
**“In the forest at evening you shall sleep”** — In the evening weeping shall have place, and in the morning gladness.
**“In the forest”** — O Jews, who will flee the Babylonian siege: you will sleep in the forest, that is, in the woods of the Saracens, fleeing the Chaldeans, in the paths of Dodanim, which is interpreted “to neighbours or kinsmen,” that is, on the way that leads to your kinsmen the Saracens.
**“at evening”** — Which is the beginning of the night. He who begins to sin in the evening is one who comes to the height at midnight. At midnight the firstborn of Egypt are slain; Peter denies, and repents when the light is already near.
**“In the paths”** — Because evening is the beginning of evils. The Seventy: in the way of Dedan, which is interpreted judgments. For the kinds of sinners are so many judgments.
**“in the paths of Dedanim”** — Those who enter the way of sinners do not sleep in sown fields but in an unfruitful wood, where at evening are thorns and beasts. This wood devoured more of Absalom’s army than the sword did, when he rebelled against his father.
21.14:
**“Meeting”**
• do not wait until he comes
• O Ismaelite
**“the thirsty bring”**
• to my people fleeing to you
• because he was in the wood
**“water”**
• of teaching
• of baptism
• not only bread
**“Meeting the thirsty bring him water”** — This can be said against those who have given themselves to leisure and idleness, and are content with their own salvation, and who offer no gift to the penitent and converted.
**“the thirsty bring him water”** — Bring water to the brothers wearied by the heat of the sun and by thirst, lest they perish in the wilderness.
**“you that inhabit”** — you who have the light of knowledge of the Scriptures and of charity
**“the earth”** — southern
**“of the south”** — “God shall come from the south”
**“with bread”**
• not only with water
• of the word of God
**“meet him that fleeth”** — to the weary people
21.15:
**“For they are fled from before the swords”** — the doctrine of heretics, the blasphemy of the Gentiles, of the Jews
**“they are fled”** — to your help
**“from before the sword”**
• of the Babylonians
• so that you see many slain and fallen in battle
**“that hung over them”** — upon the necks
**“from the bent bow”** — of the Elamites, who were the best archers and came with the Chaldeans
**“from the face of a grievous battle”** — meet the one fleeing, because
21.16:
**“For thus”** — future
**“saith the Lord to me”** — as if: do not despise the wretched, for your day will come quickly
**“Within a year”** — of their captivity; the Lord will sustain you
**“according to the years of a hireling, and shall be taken away”** — after a year
**“all the glory of Cedar”**
• Within a year, etc. As if: because you have not had mercy on them, you will soon endure the misery of captivity.
• After a year from the captivity of the Jews and the overthrow of Jerusalem, these also were laid waste; whence: as in the year of a hireling; for the hireling reckons his year swift and short, with all its labor, while he longs for his wages; so for you too the space that remains is very small, because the destruction is near.
• Namely, as the year of a hireling passes quickly, who only awaits the wages of his labor, or who always labors that he may receive the wages of labor, so the glory of Cedar, which is interpreted darkness; whence: “I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar.” Also the whole number of the archers, that is, of diverse doctrines, which wounded in the forest of Arabia, shall be brought to nothing, when the fugitives shall have been freed from the forest and have received the waters of baptism and eaten the heavenly bread.
21.17:
**“And the residue of the number of strong archers of the children of Cedar”** — Saracens left by the Assyrians, who are archers, as Ismael their father, because they dwell in the wilderness
**“shall be diminished”** — by the Babylonians
**“The Lord”** — of all
**“for the God of Israel hath spoken it”** — properly, who is the reward of those who see God

22.1:
**“The burden of the valley”** — Jerusalem, once the lady of the nations, the city of the great king, is now called a valley in contempt. For it is not a valley, since it is on a mountain, but because it has been made lowly and base, subject to idols; as also it is called a village in contempt: “Go ye into the village that is over against you”; and well is it called the valley of vision.
**“The burden of the valley of vision”**
• For there were prophets there who deserved to see visions; and these things pertain not to the siege made by Sennacherib in the time of Ezechias, but rather to that made by Nabuchodonosor in the time of Sedecias.
• A burden of heretics, who fell from the lofty sense of the Scriptures to the lowest things.
**“the valley of vision”** — The Seventy: Sion, that is, of the watchtowers, namely of the Church. Whence: “But I am appointed king by him over Sion his holy mountain.” “They that trust in the Lord shall be as mount Sion.” And: “The Lord loveth the gates of Sion above all the tabernacles of Jacob.”
**“What aileth”** — the voice of the prophet in the person of the Holy Spirit
**“thee”** — not only to others
**“also, that thou too art wholly gone up”**
• to high things
• in your opinion, whence you are rather humbled
**“thou too”** — among others
**“to the housetops”** — in the plural, because of the many varieties of heretics
**“What aileth thee also”** — As if worldly philosophy and wisdom, disputing of lofty things, despised the simplicity of the Church: why do you too pursue high things?
22.2:
**“Full of clamour”** — first joy, after sorrow
**“a populous city”** — by the multitude of the deceived
**“a city”** — populous
**“a joyous”**
• in the time of David and Solomon
• pride. For the puffed-up swell and boast that they have found holier things.
**“thy slain”** — by heretics the greater part is supplanted without fight or contention
**“are not slain by the sword”**
• but by hunger and thirst
• because all fled
**“Full”** — The teaching of heretics is full of much talk and clamour.
**“Thy slain”** — That is, the valley of Sion, by their own will, went over to the heretics.
**“nor dead in battle”** — By comparison with those who are conquered after battle, those who surrender of their own accord are wounded more unhappily. As in martyrdom, he who denies after the torments is punished more lightly than he who denies Christ without necessity.
22.3:
**“All”** — for
**“thy princes”** — of the heretics
**“are fled”**
• they went out from us but were not of us
• to the synagogue of Satan from the Church
**“are bound hard”** — by the chains of the devil, whence “Our soul hath been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers.”
**“all that were found”**
• whom the heretics deceive; they boast that they have found them
• with the princes
**“are bound”** — by snares
**“they are fled far off”**
• from the Lord
• because they stopped their ears so as not to hear the good
• All the princes, etc. As is read in Jeremias, Sedecias went out by night through a hole in the wall with the princes and fled; but in the plains of Jericho they were taken and brought to Nabuchodonosor (who was then in Reblata; for dwelling there he had sent his army ahead to take the city). He ordered the sons of Sedecias to be slain before him, put out his eyes, and, blinded, led him with him to Babylon. But the princes and others who were taken with them were either slain or hard bound and led to Babylon.
**“Are fled”** — In flight they agree, whose prince is the dragon, the fleeing, twisting serpent.
22.4:
**“Therefore”** — because they flee
**“have I said”** — I, Isaias
**“Depart from me”**
• comforters
• O fellow prophet
**“I will weep bitterly”**
• “Who is weak, and I am not weak?”
• the devastation of my people
• so Samuel mourned Saul, and Christ mourned Jerusalem
**“labour not”** — To be bowed down toward me, sick with excessive grief.
**“to comfort me, for the devastation of the daughter of my people”** — Not the sons, who have lost the dignity of manhood.
22.5:
**“For it is a day”** — That is, it hangs over, and shows the works of each one.
**“of slaughter and of treading down”** — Not Jerusalem, which is the vision of peace, but Jebus, the ancient name, which is interpreted as treading down.
**“and of weeping to the Lord the God of hosts”** — Arises.
**“in the valley of vision”**
• Not in the mount of vision.
• Jerusalem.
**“And of weeping”** — Septuagint: of error. Not that weeping and error come from the Lord, but the occasion of error arises from the scriptures which he gave them to read; and they can say, why hast thou made us err from thy way? Whence the Lord gave them the spirit of error, etc.
**“searching”** — Causing to be searched, so that it may be utterly destroyed.
**“the wall”** — The wall of heretics built against the Church.
**“and magnificent”** — Stood forth.
**“upon the mountain”**
• Or: mountains.
• Teachers who glory in standing firm on the mount, Christ; whence: Come, let us go up to the mountain, etc.
• The temple, which he caused to be overthrown.
22.6:
**“And Elam took the quiver”** — Against my people.
**“the chariot of the horseman, and the wall”** — Clothed with the gold of the temple.
**“the shield was taken down”**
• The strength of the Chaldeans.
• Elam took the quiver. Elam, that is, their ascent, that is, the pride of heretics, took the quiver, “that he may shoot in secret at the upright in heart.”
**“Elam”** — A city in the province of Persia, in which are the best archers.
**“the wall”** — He stripped the strongholds of the Church with his shield, that is, with attack.
22.7:
**“And thy choice valleys”**
• lowly teachings
• once delightful
**“shall be full”** — O Jerusalem
**“of chariots”** — which are drowned with Pharaoh
**“and the horsemen”**
• which the city could not hold
• who were able to enter
**“shall place themselves in the gate”**
• lest anyone escape and be saved
• lest they suffer those shut up within to go out
22.8:
**“and”** — then
**“shall be discovered”**

23.1:
**“The burden of Tyre”**
• which in Hebrew is Sor, in Latin distress, and signifies a soul occupied with vices.
• Tyre was the most noble city of the Chanaanites. When Isaias foretold these things it was an island of the great sea; but long afterwards Nabuchodonosor wished to make it joined to the mainland, but after much labor spent in vain he could not. Those who were in the city, since they could not resist, those who could have ships fled into Egypt and into Moab and into the neighboring regions; whence Nabuchodonosor, inflamed with fury, burned the ships, overthrew the city, and led away captives, as is clear in what follows. And when he returned to Chaldea, the kingdom of Egypt was given him by the Lord in place of Tyre, Tyre having been rebuilt. After seventy years, when Alexander was going on to take Egypt captive, he left there part of his army, and wished to level it with earth and could not; but when Egypt was subdued, he brought with him Ethiopians and many other nations, and made it joined to the mainland with stones and trees, took the citizens, and overthrew the city.
• But now Isaias treats of that captivity which Nabuchodonosor made. This happened because, when Jerusalem was taken and its people were led into captivity by the Chaldeans in the time of Sedecias, Tyre, which ought to have had compassion, began to insult. Isaias foretells this misery: The burden of Tyre, etc.

**“Howl, O ye ships”** — sailors
**“of the sea”** — in Hebrew Tharsis, which means consummation or joy

Whence: “The wise man hath scaled the cities of the mighty, and hath destroyed the strength of the confidence thereof.” For whatever is composed by the art of heretics and of worldly wisdom, the man of the Church destroys and subjects to himself.
23.15:

**“according to the days of one king”** — they quickly forget
**“but after seventy years, there shall be unto Tyre”** — rebuilt

**“Seventy years”** — Tyre, once afflicted, is left, so that when the time of solitude is fulfilled she may turn the song of harlots into the praises of God, take up the harp, and have all the strings sounding together; that after she has sung well, she who for fornication had been given over to oblivion may be in memory before God, be restored to her former state, and gather rewards for the Lord. Who, then, would not have hope of salvation, if he sing well, if he tune the strings well? Whence: “O daughter of Tyre, with gifts they shall entreat thy countenance,” etc., “and the king shall greatly desire thy beauty.”

**“to her traffic”**

**“Behold the Lord shall lay waste”** — After the special rebuke of the single nations, Juda, Babylon, the Philistines, Moab, Damascus, Israel, Egypt, the desert of the sea, Arabia, Idumea, the valley of vision, and Tyre, he describes what the whole world is to suffer at the consummation. Nor does he treat of the nations singly but of all alike. First, what are the torments of the wicked, how heaven and earth shall pass away and sinners be led down into hell; afterwards, how the saints shall be caught up to meet the Lord in the air. So from the special description he passes to the general, which is the fourth rule of Tyconius; for it deals with species and genus, and the person is not changed.
**“the inhabitants thereof”** — Behold, the Lord has stripped bare; he passes from the particular to the general. For having described the particular burden of the Babylonians, Assyrians, Egyptians and many others, he passes to the general burden of the last judgment.

• In that day shall visit, etc. The Hebrews hold that the devil (that is, the accuser, which is a Greek name) is called in Hebrew Satan, that is, adversary. Whence it is said: “Satan stood on his right hand to be his adversary”; and he is called Belial, that is, apostate, that is, transgressor, and without yoke. Whence: “What concord hath Christ with Belial?” He is also called by other names; whence: “Upon the asp and the basilisk,” etc. And elsewhere: he who shall take the great whale. Likewise: “Canst thou draw out Leviathan with a hook?” And elsewhere: “This sea dragon which thou hast formed to play therein.” For he was made so that the angels might mock him. Whence: the apostles receive power to tread upon serpents and scorpions. Since, therefore, from that place where the Lord “shall lay waste the earth, and shall strip it,” up to the present chapter, judgment has been foretold against the whole world at the consummation of the world, and the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed, against the devil the final sentence is that the sword be brought upon him.
• [a] Septuagint: Fugitive. [b] For then he will flee who did not know how to flee, not knowing that: “Whither shall I go from thy spirit?” etc. Whence someone wittily played in the Gigantomachy: “Whither dost thou flee, Enceladus? Whatever shores thou comest to, thou wilt always be under Jove.”
• Leviathan is interpreted as their addition, of whom if not of men? And rightly is he called their addition, since after he brought in the first guilt by evil suggestion, he does not cease daily to increase it by grievous persuasions. For this Leviathan, in that he promised to give himself to man, crept up to him by twisting cords. And while he falsely promises impossible things, he took away true and possible ones. We must ask why, having said serpent, and adding to it crooked, he put the bar in between. Unless perhaps because in the crookedness of the serpent there is slack softness, but in the bar the hardness of rigidity. So that he might mark him as both hard and soft, he names both the bar and the serpent. For he is hard through malice, soft through flattery. He is called a bar who strikes even to death; but a serpent, because he contrives snares and infuses them.

Now he deals with the ten tribes, which are called Ephraim, either from Jeroboam, who of the tribe of Ephraim first reigned over it, or from Josue, who succeeded Moses. This is the crown of pride, because they are proud of their multitude, which is as it were the crown of a king; for the multitude of the people is the glory of the king. The fading flower, because they quickly fall from their glory; whence the Holy Spirit says: woe to the crown of pride.
• According to prophecy. Woe to the crown of pride, etc. The scribes and Pharisees, who according to the Septuagint are called the hirelings of Ephraim, on account of Judas, who of the tribe of Ephraim and of the village of that same tribe, Scarioth, sold the Lord, and who truly, the flower of apostolic doctrine, fell upon the fattest mountain. Whence: “the beloved grew fat, and kicked”; on the top, namely, of the valley of Gethsemani according to the Hebrew, where he betrayed the Lord, which is called the valley of the fat on account of its fertility, and the scribes and Pharisees who there seized the Lord. • Of God’s counsel and of Jeremias
• After the prophecy against Ariel, etc., up to this place he prophesies what, after the hundred and fifty years between Isaias and Jeremias, is shown to have been fulfilled.
**“saith the Lord, that you would take counsel, and not of me”** — but against
**“and would begin a web”**
• a metaphor
• It shows a wicked counsel.
**“and not by my spirit”** — who advised to remain, not to flee.
**“that you might add sin”** — of contention and pride.
**“upon sin”**
• old.
• He speaks of those who, scorning the counsel of God and of Jeremias, after the death of Godolias, whom Nabuchodonosor had set over the remnant, fled into Egypt; and this is: Woe, sons.
**“Tropologically”** — Tropologically. Woe to you, apostate children. That is, all who, having despised the religion of God, take counsel, and not through the Lord, and add sins to sins, so that, overcome by the allurements of sins, they receive also perversity of doctrines, and go down into the darkness of Egypt, seeking the help of Pharao, who reigns in Egypt, whose strength leads to everlasting reproach. For in Thamnis, that is, in a humble and cast-down commandment, are his princes, who laboured in vain over the people. The salvation of the disciples helps the holy masters; the destruction of the seduced destroys the wicked.
