**“and his rebuke”** — “For I was hungry, and you gave me not to eat”
**“with flames of fire”** — a terrible sentence, which will devour them as fire
66.16:
**“For the Lord shall judge by fire, and by his sword unto all flesh, and the slain of the Lord shall be many.”** — many will be found who now seem few
**“the slain of the Lord”** — all the wicked, damned
**“By fire the Lord”** — In judgment. Or his discernment and justice are shown, while he divides the good from the wicked by just judgment, not by power.
**“By his sword”** — Sentence, whence Amos: “by the sword of God all the sinners of the earth shall perish”; for while he will render to each what he deserves, all will know him as the just judge and will praise his judgment.
66.17:
**“They that were sanctified, and thought themselves clean in the gardens behind the gate within”** — Others: after the gate.
**“within, they that did eat swine's flesh”** — against the law
**“and the abomination”** — the other things forbidden
**“and the mouse”** — which we call a dormouse
**“they shall be consumed together”** — all
**“They that were sanctified”** — In their own opinion, in fountains and baptisms, which they prepared for themselves in pleasant places, where they also indulged in lust more willingly, that they might at once cleanse and wash themselves, as though they could be cleansed in this way. There they indulged in lust before the idols with males and females, after the manner of dogs. And this is “behind the gate within,” that is, from behind, which is shameful to say, but yet is said, to the confusion of those who are not ashamed even to do it.
**“saith the Lord”** — They that were sanctified. According to tropology we can say that all lovers of pleasure rather than of God are said to be sanctified in gardens and on thresholds, according to the Septuagint, because they cannot enter into the mysteries of truth and eat the foods of piety, who are not holy in body and spirit. Nor do they eat the flesh of Christ that they may have eternal life; and indeed “Christ our pasch is sacrificed,” who is eaten not outside but in one house and within.
**“In the gardens”** — Not with the sacrifice of a red calf, as was commanded in the law.
66.18:
**“But I”**
• to whom all things are open
• As if therefore I come to judgment with all nations and tongues, that I may judge at once all their works and thoughts and render to them all that they deserve.
**“their works”** — which now lie hidden
**“and”** — or
**“their thoughts”** — which will also be judged; whence: “Whosoever shall look on a woman to lust after her,” etc.
**“I come that I may gather them together”** — whence all nations will be gathered together before him
**“with all nations and tongues”** — by whom their thoughts will accuse or defend them
**“tongues”** — Which, according to the apostle, belong not only to men but also to angels. Whence we understand that all creatures are to be judged by the Lord, not only on the earth but also in the sea and in the heavens. According to that: “My sword is inebriated in heaven,” and it came down even to the earth.
**“And they shall come”** — all nations, to judgment or to faith; for these pertain to the first coming and the faith of the Gentiles
**“and shall see”** — with the eyes of the heart
**“my glory”** — the divinity and humanity, which is above all
66.19:
**“And I will set ... among them”** — who believed
**“And I will set a sign among them”** — Of the cross, of Christianity, of salvation; by which those marked in Ezechiel are not slain, by which the doorposts are marked in Egypt and the Israelites saved. Achaz refused to ask for this sign, which Isaias puts forward: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive, etc.”
**“and I will send”** — the apostles
**“of them”** — the Jews
**“that shall be saved”** — they will be a saved remnant, unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed
**“to the Gentiles”** — to be converted
**“into the sea, into Africa”** — through these all parts of the world are signified
**“and Lydia”**
• For the Lydians are skilled archers
• that is, Athens
**“them that draw the bow: into Italy, and Greece”** — the west, namely
**“to the islands afar off”** — to the islands afar off, to them, namely
**“to them that have not heard of me, and have not seen my glory”** — whence: they to whom it has not been announced of him will see
**“And they shall declare”**
• faithful Jews
• sent to the nations
**“into the sea”** — The world, namely, whose parts he subjoins: Africa, etc.; namely the southern region in which Africa is.
**“And I will send of them”** — It seems to be contrary, since it was said earlier of the judgment, to return to the first coming, by which the apostles are sent to the Gentiles and they hear: “Go, teach all nations.” But the day of judgment is preached so that, terrified by fear of the punishment to come, they may receive the coming of the Saviour and the preaching of the apostles, who are to be sent ahead.
66.20:
**“And they shall bring”** — the apostles
**“all your brethren”** — the faithful
**“your”** — O Jews
**“out of all nations for a gift to the Lord, upon horses”** — “Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance”
**“upon horses”** — Those are brought in horses who believe quickly and run swiftly to the faith.
**“in chariots”** — Philosophers, namely shining in teaching and in honesty of morals, whence they came more quickly to the teaching of the four evangelists; and raised up by the four principal virtues, they reached heavenly things in mind.
**“and in litters”** — the weak, who are carried by others
**“and on mules”** — “Do not become like the horse and the mule”
**“on mules”** — Upon whom David and Solomon are read to have sat; for those who are barren of the world’s offspring are for the Lord, who is figured through them, serving as gentle beasts.
**“and in coaches”** — who, brought by the help of others and adorned with the gravity of morals, serve wisdom and preaching
**“in coaches”** — Septuagint. covered carriages; others, simply carriages. These are those to whom it is said: “Bear ye one another’s burdens.”
**“to my holy mountain Jerusalem”**
• The present and future Church.
• First to the present, then to the heavenly Jerusalem; and this is to my holy mountain.
**“saith the Lord, as if the children of Israel should bring”** — With what joy, namely, that is done which they are accustomed to do with the greatest gladness.
**“an offering”** — The spiritual fruits of the soul.
**“in a clean vessel”** — With an unspotted body.
**“into the house of the Lord”**
• The Church.
• They shall bring. This they did according to the law three times a year, namely at the Passover, at Pentecost, and at the feast of tabernacles. Whence: “neither shalt thou appear before me empty.”
**“As”** — As if with such joy the apostles bring your brethren, whose gifts are faith, hope, charity, prayer, clean good works, and the other vessels: pure hearts and unspotted bodies.
**“The house of the Lord”** — “The temple of God is holy, which you are.” And elsewhere: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwelleth in you.”
66.21:
**“And I will take of them”**
• To the Jews.
• Or from both.
• From the converted Gentiles, the ministry of the Jews being rejected.
**“to be priests”**
• Sanctifying themselves and others.
• Priests: the apostles and apostolic men.
• Who in secret do not follow the line of descent but the order of faith.
**“and Levites”** — Taken from the world as ministers of God.
66.22:
**“For as the new heavens”**
• The aerial heavens.
• As these renewed things will remain immovable for ever, so your seed, O apostles, renewed from every corruption of the flesh, will reign with me for ever.
**“new heavens, and the new earth”**
• According to the figure, renewed.
• “Blessed are the meek: for they shall possess the land.”
**“which I will make to stand”** — Immovable.
**“before me, saith the Lord: so shall your seed stand”**
• Freed from the bondage of corruption.
• Spiritual sons.
• Sons of God.
**“your work”** — O apostles.
**“and your name”**
• Christian, to which nothing else succeeds.
• O apostles.
• Because as the heavens. These things, up to the end of the book, pertain to the day of judgment.
66.23:
**“And there shall be month”**
• The heavenly Church, namely, built out of the present one.
• Spiritual.
• And there shall be month: that is, once the days in which the world was made have passed, we may rest in the true sabbath.
**“after month”** — carnal
**“Month after month”** — Mene in Greek is luna in Latin, whence neomenia, as it were “new moon.” From mene comes mensis, among those who both end and begin the start of the calends not according to the course of the sun and the diverse lengths of the months, but according to the circuit of the moon, which the Hebrews do. By the month, therefore, is understood the moon; by the moon, which now waxes, now wanes, and, as the naturalists and philosophers say, receives from the sun the light it does not have, the Church is understood, of whom it is said: “He shall continue with the sun, and before the moon,” and elsewhere: “Fair as the moon, bright as the sun”; and this is “month after month.”
**“and sabbath”** — the sabbath rest that is reserved for the people of God
**“after sabbath”** — as he will rest in the future who here rests from evil work
**“will come”** — on the day of judgment
**“all flesh”**
• all the nations whom you have made will come and adore
• all flesh shall see the salvation of God
• the saints with their bodies
**“to adore”** — even the wicked, terrified, will adore the almighty power of God
66.24:
**“And they shall go out”** — The elect go out as if to see, not by place but by understanding or manifest vision, so that they may be kindled the more to praise God.
**“and see the carcasses”** — Carcasses. Because they will fall into eternal damnation; in the way that demons too can be called carcasses, in the way that they are also called men: whence, “An enemy man hath done this.”
**“of men”** — of all the reprobate
**“And see”** — It is no wonder that the saints, now immortal, see the reprobate, since the prophets, while still mortal, merited to see all these things.
**“that have transgressed”**
• the natural or written law
• I have accounted all the sinners of the earth prevaricators
**“against me: their worm”** — material or of conscience
**“Their worm”** — Material or of conscience. Whence: As the moth eats a garment, and the worm gnaws wood, and fire devours wood, so grief and sadness torment the heart of a man.
**“shall not die”** — so neither its matter
**“and their fire”** — material or of conscience
**“shall not be quenched”** — because there will always be something for it to consume, that is, the wicked persisting in punishments
**“And there shall be”** — the reprobate to the elect
**“a loathsome sight to all flesh”**
• to the saints
• The just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge
**“a loathsome sight”** — Because, that is, the good will see them separated from themselves by the just judgment of God, with the power lost by which they raged against the good, and the vengeance of God upon them so great that they ask for no greater. They who now say: “How long, O Lord, dost thou not revenge our blood?” will also be satisfied, giving thanks for their own blessedness, at the ineffable punishment of the way of the wicked.

1.1:
Origen. God is quick to do good, slow to punish. For though he could punish the guilty without any warning of the judgment to come, he never does so; but even when he has condemned them, he foretells it, that those who had been condemned by their transgression may be set free by penance. The Ninivites were sinners condemned by God: “Yet three days, and Ninive shall be destroyed.” For God would not punish the condemned in silence, but, giving them room for penance, sent a Hebrew prophet to say: “Yet three days, and Ninive shall be destroyed,” that they might not perish (that is, because they had been condemned), but by doing penance might obtain mercy. The Sodomites also and the Gomorrhites were already doomed to divine destruction, as the word of God to Abraham shows; yet the angels did what was theirs to do, wishing to save those who had judged themselves unworthy of salvation, and saying to Lot: “Hast thou here any of thine, son in law, or sons, or daughters?” etc. Nor were they ignorant that those would not follow Lot, but they showed their own kindness and love, and equally that of him who had sent them. We find something like it in Jeremias. For the time of his prophecy is to be noted, when he began to prophesy and when he ended. Someone will say then: What is the time of the history to me? Because he began to prophesy in the days of Josias the son of Amon, king of Juda, up to the thirteenth year of his reign. Then he prophesied in the days of Joakim, the son of Josias king of Juda, to the completion of the eleventh year of Sedecias, the son of Josias king of Juda, and his prophecy was extended through three kings to the captivity of Jerusalem in the fifth month. For God had condemned Jerusalem for its sins, and this was his final sentence, that it should be left to captivity. But since God is a lover of men and wills not that any should perish, before the time of the devastation was at hand he sent this prophet also to invite to penance. He sent the same man also under the second king after the first, and sent him also under the third. Captivity was now imminent, and still God was exhorting to salvation, granting room for penance even one day before; whence it is written: “Even to the captivity of Jerusalem, and to the fifth month,” Jeremias prophesied. Already the chains of the enemy had bound their hands, and nonetheless God said this: ‘Behold, you are made captives. Come, though late, do penance. Ask me, and I will spare you. I who delivered you up can rescue you from captivity.’ This also we can understand of ourselves. If we sin, we shall be captives. For to be delivered up to Satan as a sinner differs nothing from the Jews' being delivered to Nabuchodonosor. As God gave them over to the adversary because of their frequent impieties, so we are delivered for our sins to a spiritual Nabuchodonosor. Whence: “Whom I have delivered up to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.” Think how great an evil it is to sin, that you be delivered to Satan, who takes captive the souls of those who are forsaken by God, not without cause, that is, nor without judgment. For when he has sent rain upon the vineyard, and it has brought forth thorns instead of grapes, what will he do but command the clouds not to rain upon the vineyard? Our captivity also is therefore near, if we do not do penance, that we be delivered, that is, to Nabuchodonosor and the Babylonians; and while they are already close by, the words of the prophets, of the law, of the apostles, and of Christ himself exhort us to penance and call us to salvation. If we hear, we believe him who said: “And I will do penance for all the evil that I had spoken to do to them.”
Jerome to Eusebius. Because the volume is very long, and in most places the history in Jeremias is plain, do not look for a wide explanation, especially of what has already been said in the other prophets. That nothing may be wanting in the senses though much is wanting in the words, I will prepare for you the warp and the woof and the threads; make the most beautiful garment yourself.
The other prophets, as Isaias, Osee, Joel, were before the captivity of the two tribes, that is, of Juda and Benjamin; others after, as Daniel, Aggeus and Zacharias. But Jeremias and Ezechiel prophesied when the captivity was imminent, the one in the land of Juda, the other in Babylon. Jeremias began to prophesy as a boy in the thirteenth year of Josias king of Juda, the son of Amon, and prophesied under him nineteen years, and under Joakim his son eleven years, and under Sedecias, who was the last of the kings of Juda, eleven years, to the fifth month in which Jerusalem was taken captive by the Babylonians. But the three months each of Joachaz and Jechonias (of whom the one was led into Egypt, the other with his mother into Babylon) are counted in the years mentioned above. And so from the beginning of his prophecy to the captivity of Jerusalem, in which he himself was taken, he prophesied sixty-one years, apart from that time in which he was led into Egypt and prophesied there in Taphnis, as is contained in this very volume.
**“The words of Jeremias the son of Helcias, of the priests that were in Anathoth”**
• Behold the place.
• It is a small village at the third milestone from the city.
**“The words of Jeremias”** — The Septuagint. The word of God, because the words of Jeremias are the word of the Lord.
*Jerome:* After the beginning of Jeremias’s prophecy, in the thirty-fifth year, Ezechiel began to prophesy in Babylon to those who had been carried captive with him.
1.2:
**“which”**
• That is, because.
• That is.
**“The word of the Lord which came”** — which was in the beginning with the Father.
**“In the days of Josias”** — Jerome. The mercy of God is wonderful. Though captivity is near and the Babylonian army is besieging Jerusalem, he nevertheless calls the people to repentance, preferring to save the converted rather than destroy the sinners.
1.3:
**“And which came to him in the days of Joakim the son of Josias king of Juda, unto the end of the eleventh year of Sedecias the son of Josias”** — who was the last of the kings of Juda.
**“king of Juda, even unto the carrying away”** — The Septuagint: captivity.
1.4: **“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:”** — which was in the beginning with God, in whom the prophets speak.
1.5:
**“Before I formed thee”** — in act.
**“in the bowels of thy mother”** — of the mother.
**“I knew thee”** — in foreknowledge.
**“and before thou camest forth out of the womb, I sanctified thee, and made thee a prophet unto the nations.”**
• in the womb he used free will.
• Before I formed thee, etc. Not that he existed before conception, as heretics suspect; but because the Lord foreknew him as one who was to come, for whom things to be done are already done, who “calleth those things that are not, as those that are.”
• Before thou camest forth out of the womb, etc. Jerome. According to that of Paul: “But when it pleased him, who separated me from my mother’s womb, and called me by his grace, to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles.” John also was sanctified in the womb, and receives the Holy Spirit, and in the womb is moved, and speaks through his mother’s mouth.
*Jerome:* Before I formed thee. Some understand this place of the Saviour, who was properly the prophet of the nations and called all nations through the apostles. Before he was formed in the virginal womb, before he came forth from the womb, he was sanctified in the womb and known to the Father, he who is always in the Father, and in whom the Father always is.
1.6: **“And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God: behold, I cannot speak, for I am a child.”** — Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, etc. He shrinks from the office, which he cannot bear because of his age. With the same modesty with which Moses says that he is slender and of a thin voice; but he is rebuked as one of a great and robust age, whereas pardon is given to this one as to a child, who is adorned with modesty and shame.
1.7:
**“And the Lord said to me: Say not: I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee: and whatsoever I shall command thee, thou shalt speak.”**
• As if to say: do not consider the age of a grey-haired man, but apply his wisdom to your will, that you may go; you will have me as companion, that you may accomplish all things; open your mouth, and I will fill it.
• Say not, etc. Gregory. Some laudably seek the office of preaching, to which others are laudably compelled. For Isaias offered himself of his own accord, saying: “Behold, here am I, send me.” Jeremias humbly resists, saying: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God,” etc. From each an outwardly different voice went forth, but not from a different fountain of love. For there are two precepts of charity: namely the love of God and of neighbour. Isaias, therefore, desiring to profit his neighbours through the active life, seeks the office of preaching. Jeremias, through the contemplative life, desiring to cling to the love of God, refuses to be sent to preach. The one, lest by speaking he should lose the gains of silent contemplation; the other, lest by keeping silent he should feel the losses of zealous work. But it must be noted that he who refused utterly did not persist, and he who wished to be sent saw himself first purged by the coal of the altar; lest anyone, unpurged, dare to approach the sacred mysteries, or lest one whom God has chosen proudly gainsay him under a show of humility. Since, therefore, it is difficult to know oneself purged, the office of preaching is more safely declined. Yet it ought not to be declined obstinately when the heavenly will is recognized to require its acceptance. Moses wonderfully fulfilled both, who both refused to be set over so great a multitude and obeyed. For perhaps he would have been proud if he had fearlessly taken up the leadership, or if he had refused to obey the one who commanded. On both sides, therefore, he was submissive; by measuring himself he refused to be set over the people, and yet by presuming on the strength of him who commanded he consented.
1.8:
**“Be not afraid at their presence”** — do not consider the multitude of those to whom you are to speak, but me who am with you.
**“for I am with thee”** — you will have me as companion, that you may accomplish all things.
**“to deliver thee”** — not that he is free from persecutions and distress, for he suffered many things; but that he may overcome all things patiently and not give way.
1.9:
**“And the Lord put forth”** — The Father.
**“his hand”**
• The Son, through whom all things.
• so that, seeing human likeness, he may not be afraid.
**“and touched my mouth”** — so that, seeing the likeness of human limbs, he may not fear to be touched.
**“and the Lord said”** — The Father.
**“to me: Behold I have given my words in thy mouth.”**
• as if to say: “do manfully, and let thy heart take courage.”
• And the Lord put forth his hand, etc. It must be noted that here the hand of God is put forth, which touches the prophet’s mouth, and it is said: “Behold, I have given my words in thy mouth.” But in Isaias it is written: “And one of the seraphims flew to me, and in his hand was a live coal, which he had taken with the tongs off the altar,” and he touched my mouth, etc. Because Isaias was of full age, and had unclean lips, and dwelt in the midst of a people that had unclean lips, one of the seraphims is sent, who touches his mouth not with the hand but with the tongs and the coal, and takes away his iniquities. But here the hand of God himself is sent, not to take away sins, which, because of his boyhood, he had not committed in great number, but to give the grace of speaking. Ezechiel, however, devours a book written within and without, that is, containing both the divine sacraments and the plain history. Jeremias’s mouth is touched, and the words of the Lord are given, that he may receive confidence for preaching.
1.10:
**“Lo”** — The Father to the Son.
**“I have set thee this day over the nations”** — “Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance.”
**“and over the kingdoms, to root up”** — evils.
**“and to destroy”** — the kingdoms of the devil.
**“and to pull down, and to waste, and to build”** — The Church.
**“to root up, and to destroy”** — Two joyful things follow four sad ones; for good things could not be built unless the evil were destroyed, nor the best planted unless the worst were rooted out. For “every plant which my heavenly Father hath not planted shall be rooted up,” and the building that is not built upon a rock but upon sand is undermined and destroyed by the word of God. But that doctrine which the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and destroy with the brightness of his coming, namely every sacrilegious and perverse doctrine, he will destroy forever. And those things that are lifted up against the knowledge of God, and trust in their own wisdom, which is foolishness with God, he will scatter and bring down, that in place of them humble things may be built, and in the place of the higher things that are destroyed and plucked up, things may be raised and planted that agree with the truth of the Church; of which: “You are God’s building, you are God’s husbandry.”
**“and to plant.”** — Many take this passage as said of the person of Christ. For Jeremias is interpreted “the exalted of the Lord,” who destroys the kingdoms of the devil, which he had shown him on the height of the mountain; he destroyed the adverse powers, blotting out the handwriting of errors on the cross; of whom, after the truth of the history, it is said in a figurative sense: “Why have the Gentiles raged, and the people devised vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes met together.” In place of these things plucked up, destroyed, lost, and dragged down to the lower places, the Church of God is built and planted. But as to the person of Jeremias there is no doubt, who takes in his hand “a cup full of unmixed wine,” and is commanded to give it to drink to all the nations.
1.11:
**“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: What seest thou, Jeremias?”** — he rouses by a question.
**“And I said: a rod”**
• others: an almond tree.
• of which: “Thy rod and thy staff, they have comforted me”; and elsewhere: “What will you? shall I come to you with a rod, or in simplicity and meekness?”
**“I see a rod watching”**
• that is, he considers sins, in order to strike and correct.
• Some understand the watching and nut rod as the Lord. Of him Isaias: “There shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse.” Whence the rod of Aaron, which was thought dead, is said to have flowered at the resurrection of the Lord.
**“a rod watching”** — A rod of watchings: the Septuagint. They translated it “a rod of nut-wood” because of the likeness of the word. For in Hebrew watching, a watcher, and to watch is called seched, and a nut is seded. Whence in what follows the watching leopard is set down with this name. Which is also written in Daniel according to Theodotion, that from trees, the cyno and prino, that is the holm-oak and the mastic, cutting and sawing are decreed for the adulterous elders. And in the beginning of Genesis, from the man who is called is the woman is called issa, as a kind of manlike woman.
**“Morally.”** — The watching rod, of which: “Thy rod and thy staff, they have comforted me.” For the Lord corrects to this end, that he may amend. And as the nut and the almond have a most bitter rind and a very hard shell, so that when the hard and bitter parts are removed a most sweet fruit is found, so all correction and the labour of continence are bitter for the present but bring forth a most sweet fruit. Whence there is that old saying: The roots of letters are bitter, the fruits sweet.
1.12: **“And the Lord said to me: Thou hast seen well: for I will watch”** — considering all things.
1.13:
**“And the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying: What seest thou? And I said: I see a boiling caldron”** — signifies the king of Babylon and the city of Jerusalem.
**“I see, and the face thereof from the face of the north.”**
• of the devil.
• Of which Solomon says: the north wind is a harsh wind; but by name it is called “the right” by those, that is, who through its cold have lost the warmth of faith.
• A heated pot. Hence the Lord says to Job: “Out of his nostrils goeth smoke, like that of a pot heated and boiling.” “His breath kindleth coals, and a flame cometh forth out of his mouth.”
• Some take this passage in a good sense: that those who have been boiled in the brazen pot and purged by torments are afterwards to be princes of Jerusalem, and after the Lord has had mercy on them he reproaches them that they forsook him and worshipped idols. But this is a forced and wrong interpretation.
**“And the word of the Lord came”** — Sinners are rebuked by degrees; those who would not be corrected or amended by the striking rod are sent into the heated pot, of which Ezechiel speaks more fully.
1.14:
**“And the Lord said to me: from the north shall an evil break forth”** — others: evils shall blaze forth.
**“upon all the inhabitants of the land.”** — that is, of Judea or of the whole earth.
**“the inhabitants of the land.”** — Of whom in the Apocalypse: “Woe to the inhabitants of the earth.” For the saints are not inhabitants of the earth but strangers and pilgrims. Whence one of them says: “I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner as all my fathers were.” And another: Equal and most evil are my days in which I am a pilgrim upon the earth. And Peter: “To the elect strangers of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,” etc.
1.15:
**“For behold I will call together all the families”** — subject to the king of Babylon.
**“of the kingdoms of the north: saith the Lord: and they shall come”** — called.
**“and shall set every one”** — the city being besieged.
**“his throne”** — a throne, his tent.
**“in the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem”** — so that no one can get out.
**“and upon all the walls thereof round about, and upon all the cities of Juda”**
• fenced round with a like siege.
• not only over Jerusalem.
1.16:
**“And I will pronounce my judgments”** — when the city has been taken I will show that my judgments were just, and that each received what he deserved.
**“against them, touching all their wickedness”** — no sin unpunished.
**“who have forsaken me”**
• their Lord.
• as if not for the other vices to which the human condition is subject, but chiefly for idolatry.
**“and have sacrificed to strange gods”** — whom their fathers did not worship.
**“and have adored the work of their own hands.”**
• what they made, not him by whom they were made.
• the work: “The idols of the Gentiles are silver and gold, the works of the hands of men.”
1.17:
**“Thou therefore gird up thy loins, and arise, and speak to them all that I command thee. Be not afraid at their presence”**
• who do not endure correction.
• as if to say: do what is yours; I am ready to do what is mine.
**“not”** — So.
**“for I will make thee not to fear their countenance.”**
• It seems to make those whom he leaves to dread fear.
• Gird up thy loins, etc. Job also is commanded to gird up his loins. And the Apostle: “Stand therefore, having your loins girt about,” in charity, etc.; that with loins girded, which Elias and John the Baptist mortified with leathern girdles, they may hold lamps in their hands, namely of evangelical preaching. Whoever is to preach the words of God ought to gird up his loins. For the devil’s strength is in the loins. Whence: “My loins are filled with illusions.” With loins girded let him hear what is written: Arise, thou that sleepest, and Christ shall enlighten thee; that, ever watching and rising from sleep, he may do and say what is commanded.
1.18:
**“For behold I”** — a companion and helper, under whose leadership you will be safe.
**“have made thee this day”** — as long as “today” is said, in the present life.
**“a fortified city”** — Glorious things are said of thee, O city of God; and elsewhere: I am a firm city that is not assailed.
**“And into an iron pillar”** — The Church.
**“And”** — as if even this were not enough.
**“into a brazen wall”** — which is not violated by any rust, does not yield to rains, and becomes stronger by age.
**“over all the land”** — You will be such to the kings of Juda, etc.
**“to the kings of Juda, to the princes thereof, and to the priests, and to the people of the land.”** — because they savour earthly things, who bear the image of the earthly and not of the heavenly.
**“A fortified city”** — Not one house, not a tower or some walls, but the whole city, which, set upon a mountain, cannot be hidden.
**“And a pillar of iron”** — Of which the apostle says: “a pillar and ground of the truth”; and Peter and James and John, who were thought to be the pillars of the Church, gave the right hands of fellowship to Paul and Barnabas.
**“To the kings of Juda”** — If ever the kings of Juda (which is interpreted “confession”), and the princes and priests of it, and the people—that is, bishops and priests and deacons, and the common crowd, base and ignoble—should wish to rise against the holy man, let him have firmness of faith, and not fear, but hope in God, that he may conquer.
1.19:
**“And they shall fight against thee, and shall not prevail”** — in which you conquer, stronger than all.
**“saith the Lord, to deliver thee.”** — so that you do not succumb in temptations.

2.2:
**“Go, and cry”** — loudly and openly, so that no one may have an excuse.
**“in the ears of Jerusalem”** — namely of the inhabitants.
**“saying: Thus saith the Lord: I have remembered thee, pitying”** — as if all this is of my mercy, not of your merit.
**“thy youth, and the love of thy espousals”** — by which, in the manner of betrothals, the adornments of the law and necklaces of words were distributed to you.
**“when thou followedst me in the desert, in a land that is not sown.”**
• there was nevertheless an abundance of food.
• Youth, etc. This is read more fully in Ezechiel, where God joins Jerusalem to himself in marriage, and under the person of a wife unites her to his embraces. Or, to show a more ardent affection, he calls her a girl, and a young maiden, and betrothed. For what we have not yet obtained we desire more ardently.
2.3:
**“Israel is holy to the Lord, the first fruits of his increase”** — for the people of the Gentiles is gathered after the firstfruits of the Jews.
**“all”** — Therefore.
**“All they that devour him”** — Jerome. As those who devour the first fruits, though not of the priestly race, are guilty of a crime, so are those who defile Israel. Whence: “Whilst the wicked draw near against me, to eat my flesh,” etc., unto “and have fallen.” Neither shall they be unpunished, because they have fulfilled the sentence of the Lord. “For it must needs be that scandals come: but nevertheless woe to that man by whom the scandal cometh.”
**“all they that devour him offend: evils shall come upon them, saith the Lord.”** — Firstfruits are owed to priests, not to enemies.
2.4:
**“Hear ye”** — as if: “O my people, what have I done to thee, or in what have I molested thee? answer thou me,” etc.
**“O house of Israel”** — Both names are used, Jacob and Israel, not with reference to the two and ten tribes but to the whole people, since Jacob himself was afterwards called Israel.
2.5:
**“Thus saith the Lord: What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me”** — that is, they forsook for a long time.
**“and have walked after vanity”** — idols, which do not profit their worshippers but make them like themselves, according to that: “Let them that make them become like unto them: and all such as trust in them.”
**“What iniquity have your fathers found”** — God says the offence was committed by the fathers; not that the sins of the fathers are imputed to the sons, but because the sons, having the likeness of their fathers, are punished for both their own and their parents’ wickedness.
**“and are become vain”** — God has mercy on the sons on account of the holy fathers.
2.6:
**“And they have not said: Where is the Lord, that made us come up out of the land of Egypt?”** — for as long as we are in this world, and are led out of Egypt, we gradually ascend.
**“that led us”** — first.
**“through the desert, through a land uninhabited”** — which a holy man ought not to inhabit
**“and unpassable”** — it marks the difficulty of the journey
**“through a land of drought”** — in which we always desire greater things, not content with the present
**“and the image of death”** — for we are always in danger, and the devil spreads snares on every side
**“through a land wherein no man walked, nor any man dwelt?”**
• of God
• a man of perfect age in Christ; for we shall all rise “unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fulness of Christ our Lord”
**“nor any man dwelt”** — He who always hastens to greater things; for perfection is not in the way but in the end, and in the dwelling that is prepared for the saints in heaven, to whom it is said: “You that stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.” In vain, then, do heretics suppose that perfect victory is here, where there is battle, and not victory but struggle, and the uncertain outcome of things to come.
2.7:
**“And I brought you into the land of Carmel, to eat the fruit thereof, and the best things thereof: and when ye entered in, you defiled my land”** — idolatry
**“And I brought you”** — As if, in return for the labour of a most hard journey, I gave you abundance of all things, which Carmel signifies, which in Hebrew is Chermel, in Latin “knowledge of circumcision.” But as that people defiled and violated with idolatry the holy land, fertile in all things, so we also, truly receiving the knowledge of circumcision, eat its fruit, and if negligence has crept in, we defile the inheritance of God and make his inheritance abominable.
2.8:
**“The priests did not say: Where is the Lord? and they that held the law knew me not, and the pastors transgressed against me: and the prophets prophesied in Baal, and followed idols.”**
• The priests did not say, etc. Gregory. The Truth complains that he is not known by the priests, and declares that he does not know the rule of those who know not; whence: “Depart from me, you workers of iniquity, I know you not.” For the wicked, while they do not know the things that are the Lord’s, are not known by the Lord; whence: “If any man know not, he shall not be known.” This ignorance of pastors often corresponds to the merits of their subjects, who, although by their own fault they have not the light of knowledge, yet by strict judgment it is so ordered that through the ignorance of those, those who follow them also offend; whence, if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit.
• As if, after many benefits, they turned the privileges of dignity into contempt, so that the priests did not seek the Lord, the teachers of the law, who ought to teach others, did not know him, and the pastors through negligence became transgressors. And the prophets dispute among the peoples; they do not speak in God but in the idol, and venerate their own inventions. These words are to be used against the masters of our order, who devour the people of God as the food of bread, and by evil works do not call upon the name of the Lord.
2.9:
**“Therefore”** — lest he seem to oppress by power, as if he contended with the fathers by reason. Whence: “that thou mayest be justified in thy words, and mayest overcome when thou art judged.”
**“Therefore will I yet contend in judgment with you”** — it signifies that he has done this often
**“saith the Lord, and I will plead with your children.”** — who likewise, persisting in evil, secretly signifies that their sons too followed the ancient denial of God at the coming of the Lord
2.10:
**“Pass over”** — he compares an incomparable thing and sets the true God against lies
**“to the isles of Cethim, and see: and send into Cedar”** — This is the region of the wilderness of the Ishmaelites, whom they now call Saracens, against which Jeremiah prophesies in the farthest parts, of which David says: “I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar.”
**“Cethim”** — Cethim: either Italy, that is, the western parts, because Cyprus, an island near Judea, has a city of this name nearby, from which came Zeno, prince of the Stoics.
**“and consider diligently”** — We can say this against those who pursue vices with greater zeal than virtues, to whom it is said: “I speak an human thing, because of the infirmity of your flesh. For as you have yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity, unto iniquity,” etc.
2.11:
**“If a nation hath changed their gods”** — of wood or stone, or of gold, as if it held to an ancient error received from its ancestors, though none of them is God but images made by hand
**“and indeed they are not gods: but my people have changed their glory into an idol.”**
• truth into a lie
• that is, it preferred an idol to me
**“My people”** — Like the Anthropomorphites, who on the occasion of this testimony, “Let us make man to our image and likeness,” obstinately contend that the immense and simple substance of the divinity is composed of our features and human form.
2.12:
**“Be astonished, O ye heavens, at this, and ye gates thereof, be very desolate, saith the Lord.”** — of which it is said: “Lift up your heads, O ye gates, and the King of glory shall come in.”
**“Be astonished, O ye heavens”** — Jerome. The Septuagint. The heaven is astonished, namely that of which it is said: “Attend, O heaven, and I will speak”; and “Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth.” Seeing the precepts of God trampled upon, it shudders, and cannot conceal its amazement; every creature trembles and grieves with compassion over the sins of men. Aquila and Symmachus interpreted it “heavens,” the Septuagint and Theodotion “heaven.” But the Hebrew samay is of common number, and “heavens” as well as “heaven” are called by the same name, like Thebes and Athens.
2.13:
**“For my people have done two evils.”** — these, namely
**“They have forsaken the fountain of living water, and have digged to themselves cisterns”** — demons
**“broken cisterns”** — because they do not keep God’s commandments
**“They have forsaken me”** — Who, [transgressing] the precept of God, saying: “I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt”; and according to what is written in the same place, “There shall not be to thee strange gods in my sight”; in place of whom he followed demons.
**“the fountain of living water”** — It is a perpetual fountain and has living waters. Cisterns and pools are filled from torrents and muddy waters in the rains.
2.14:
**“Is Israel a bondman, or a homeborn slave? why then is he become prey?”** — He asks so that he may answer.
**“Is Israel a bondman”** — From this place the Jews, lifted up in pride, said: “We are the seed of Abraham, and we have never been slaves to any man: how sayest thou: you shall be free?” Not knowing that “whosoever committeth sin, is the servant of sin,” and will serve him by whom he is overcome. Born of Abraham, the friend of God, by their own vice they have become as the sons of Cham, to whom it was said: Cursed be Chanaan, he shall be a servant to his brethren.
2.15:
**“The lions have roared upon him”** — the princes of Babylon
**“and have made a noise”** — for they shout and gather what they have not begotten; they make riches not with judgment
**“they have made his land a wilderness: his cities are burnt down and there is none to dwell in them.”** — they do not have God as their inhabitant
**“The lions”** — According to the anagogical sense we understand the lions as adverse powers or princes of heretics, who, laying waste the land of the Church, have ravaged all its cities with the fire of heretics, that fire of which it is said: “all adulterers, like an oven is their heart.”
2.16:
**“The children also of Memphis, and of Taphnes have deflowered thee, even to the crown of the head.”** — he names the two greatest cities of Egypt
**“Even to the crown of the head”** — According to that: “From the sole of the foot unto the top of the head, there is no soundness therein.” So great was the lust of the Egyptians, who are “of great flesh,” that they spared no member. According to the letter, this refers to the idols of the Egyptians. Spiritually, to the masters of perverse doctrine, who defile the purity of the Church with their own baseness.
*Gregory:* To the top of the head. Tropologically: to be deflowered is, after the habit of evil working, to be corrupted even in the very height of faith. For when the most wicked spirits entangle the soul of each in impious works, but cannot spoil the integrity of faith, they defile, as it were, only the lower members. But he who is corrupted in faith is now deflowered even to the top of the head. For the malign spirit reaches as it were from the lower members to the highest, when, defiling the active life, he corrupts with the disease of distrust the chaste height of faith.
2.17: **“Hath not this been done to thee, because thou hast forsaken the Lord thy God at that time”** — that is, when you ought to have followed him.
2.18:
**“And now what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the troubled water?”**
• In Hebrew Syor; the common edition has Geon.
• That is, the Nile, whose water is muddy.
**“And what hast thou to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the water of the river?”** — That is, of the Euphrates, which is the river of the Assyrians.
**“To drink”** — Morally. Those who have forsaken Christ, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves the cisterns of the heretics, which cannot hold the waters of doctrines; it is necessary that they be subjected to lions, which reduce their land to a wilderness and destroy whole Churches, defile them to the top of the head, and drink the troubled waters, and those of the Assyrian river and of the north, whence evils blaze forth upon the earth.
2.19:
**“Thy own wickedness shall reprove thee”** — Others: Thy transgression shall instruct thee.
**“and thy apostasy shall rebuke thee. Know thou, and see that it is an evil and a bitter thing for thee, to have left the Lord thy God, and that my fear is not with thee”** — who is the beginning of wisdom.
**“with thee, saith the Lord the God of hosts”**
• who is to be feared.
• Thy own wickedness shall reprove thee, etc. Jerome. Note that wickedness and transgression, after they have sated the transgressor and, like quails, have brought him even to loathing, instruct him who does penance; and he is commanded to see what he has left and what he has followed, how, spurning good and sweet things, he has chosen evil and bitter ones; and all this was done because he forsook the Lord his God.
2.20:
**“Of old time thou hast broken my yoke”** — as if speaking to a harlot.
**“thou hast burst my bands”**
• or thy.
• of marriage.
**“and thou saidst: I will not serve”** — To the Lord or to the husband.
**“For on every high hill”** — Pleasant and high places are always dedicated to idols.
**“and under every green tree thou didst prostitute thyself”**
• of idolatry.
• as if.
**“Of old time thou hast broken”** — Jerome. This can be said of one who, a Christian from the beginning and in part devoted to the sacred writings, afterwards, through desire of secular literature, which is signified by the hills, and of pleasing eloquence, which is shown in the leafy trees, prostrates himself to demons, who under pretext of learning and lofty knowledge defile the souls of believers, so that they make them spread their feet to every passer-by.
2.21:
**“Yet I planted thee a chosen vineyard, all true seed: how then art thou turned unto me into that which is good for nothing, O strange vineyard?”**
• The Seventy: in the bitterness of the strange vine.
• How then art thou turned, etc. Let no one be secure, if both the planting of the Lord and the true seed and the vine Soreth are so changed by their own fault that through bitterness they depart from God and become a strange vine. And the clemency of the Creator, who is the true vine, is to be noted. For he himself gave to his disciples and to the people who believe in him that they be a true vine, a chosen vine, if they remain in that in which they were planted.
**“A chosen vineyard”** — In Hebrew soreth, which is a kind of very good vine, from whose shoot Israel planted; and he wonders how a true seed and chosen vineyard has been turned into bitterness and made strange.
2.22:
**“Though thou wash thyself with nitre, and multiply to thyself the herb borith”** — Borith: the Hebrew word itself. The Seventy, however: the herb of fullers, which grows in Palestine in damp and green places, and for washing away dirt has the same power as nitre.
**“thou art stained”** — although clean in the sight of men.
**“in thy iniquity before me, saith the Lord God”** — who know the thoughts of men; whence: “In thy sight no man living shall be justified.”
*Jerome:* Allegorically. Our nitre and the fuller’s herb is penance. The word of the Church also, which reproves and rebukes and corrects the offender, has the likeness of a more biting nitre. He who is stained with a light filth of sins is cleansed by lighter means. But grave sins, which draw to death, cannot be washed away by nitre or by the herb borith, but need heavier torments. “The fire shall try every man’s work, of what sort it is.”
2.23:
**“How canst thou say”** — as if you boast of cleanness in vain, and deny the uncleanness by which you have been polluted by the filth of idolatry.
**“I am not polluted, and I have not walked after Baalim? see thy ways in the valley”** — The Seventy: polyandrion, which is the tomb of a multitude.
**“know what thou hast done”** — know what you have done; he opens the closed eyes of the denier, so that he may see what he blushes to look at.
**“as a swift runner”**
• a roe.
• so that it is carried swiftly to pasture.
**“Unfolding thy ways”**
• because, as he was speaking to a harlot, he describes her fornication.
• How canst thou say, etc. According to the tropological sense, he reproves the shamelessness of the brow of those who will not confess their vices; by their very works it is plain that they do not walk in the narrow and strait way that leads to life, but in the wide and spacious one, which many go out by, which leads to death, and which is significantly named the burial-place. Or according to the history, because a multitude of the people was destroyed and slain there by the evil of idolatry.
**“See thy ways”** — That is, look at the valley of the sons of Ennon, which is watered by the springs of Siloe; there you will see the shrine of Baal, which you worshipped having abandoned God.
2.24:
**“A wild ass accustomed to the wilderness in the desire of his heart”** — Thus Israel is carried along with such impetus and desire of lust, and burns with all love of idols.
**“snuffed up the wind of his love: none shall turn her away”** — by wholesome warnings.
**“her”** — obstinate.
**“all that seek her shall not fail: in her monthly filth they shall find her”** — filth.
2.25:
**“Keep thy foot from being bare, and thy throat from thirst”** — Whence: “If any man thirst, let him come and drink.”
**“But thou saidst: I have lost all hope”** — By despair of the better or the worse, he denies that he will do what the Lord commanded.
**“I will not do it”** — because
**“for I have loved strangers”** — gods
**“and I will walk after them”** — heretics or demons
**“I will walk”** — Keep thy foot, etc. Those about to keep the Pasch are commanded to have shoes on their feet. And the apostle proclaims that their feet are shod who are prepared for the gospel; lest, while they go through the wilderness of this world, they lie open to venomous creatures, which ought to be trodden and crushed by the gospel foot.
**“I have lost all hope”** — Jerome. These things apply to those who follow heretics, who despair of the good and are strengthened in their own error. It is necessary, however, that he who follows another’s teaching should love strangers.
**“I have loved”** — By shameless confession he thinks he avoids his sins.
2.26:
**“As the thief is confounded”**
• although shameless and insolent
• Jerome. We may use this testimony when our wise men, and those who are thought to be leaders in the Church, are caught in shameful sins.
**“when he is taken, so is the house of Israel confounded”** — caught in idolatry
**“the house of Israel”** — those who are of the house
**“they and their kings”** — not only the people
2.27:
**“Saying to a stock: Thou art my father: and to a stone: thou hast begotten me: they have turned their back to me, and not their face: and in the time of their affliction they will say”**
• It is shameless to seek help in time of need from him whom one despised in peace.
• Whom they did not perceive through benefits, they perceive as Lord through torments.
**“They have turned”** — Casting my words behind them. For when the master commands, it is the mark of one who obeys if he hears with head bowed; if he turns his back, of one who despises. Whence: “they have turned their back to me,” going away. As if they so despised the commands that they did not even deign to hear, but show the swelling of their mind by the gesture of the body.
2.28:
**“Where are the gods, whom thou hast made thee?”** — Reproachfully: as if God is the creator of men, and man made himself a god; necessity itself proves what they can do, whom you worshipped more carelessly.
**“whom thou hast made thee? let them arise and deliver thee in the time of thy affliction: for according to the number of thy cities were thy gods, O Juda.”**
• in time of affliction
• According to the number, etc. Either the same or different gods; each city worshipped gods, so that they did not seem to agree even in impiety, but superstition, fighting against itself, pursued a different error.
2.29:
**“Why will you contend with me in judgment?”**
• As if in vain you raise complaints and turn an unjust cause back on the judge, when what you suffer is due to your own impiety.
• because
**“you have all forsaken me, saith the Lord”** — Why do you wish, etc. Human perversity is prone to excuse itself, and what it deservedly endures it seems to itself to endure unjustly.
2.30:
**“In vain have I struck your children”** — I struck that they might receive correction, but I accomplished nothing.
**“your children”** — So that by the blows on your sons you might learn that you needed a harsher remedy for healing, and lest perhaps you should say: you were unwilling to spoil sinners.
**“they have not received correction”** — they did not receive correction; the Septuagint: you did not receive it
**“your sword hath devoured”** — which you endure for your sins
**“your”**
• not mine
• not mine
**“prophets”** — Baal and soothsayers
**“like a ravaging lion”** — Yet you persist in wickedness and do not return to better things through fear of the prophets.
2.31:
**“your generation”** — with wonder
**“See ye the word of the Lord”** — Moses saw the voice of the Lord. And the apostle John says he saw and handled the Word of God.
**“Am I become a wilderness to Israel”** — that does not receive the rain of doctrine
**“or a lateward springing land”** — full of briars, not rejoicing, namely
**“why then have my people said”** — Once
**“We are revolted”** — which is wicked
**“we will come to thee no more”** — which is more wicked
**“to thee”** — a grave offence: to be unwilling to appease the one you have offended
2.32:
**“Will a virgin forget”**
• The Church, which is a mother who bears and a virgin, is without spot or wrinkle.
• Jerome. She loses her ornament because she withdraws from the Lord, and the understanding of doctrine, which is signified in the breast. Whence John lay back on the breast of the Lord at supper; and among the other things kept for the priests is the breast of the sacrificed victims.
**“her ornament, or a bride her stomacher? but my people hath forgotten me days without number”** — Jerome. The longer we forget God, the greater the sin, since we cannot be tamed even by the length of ages.
2.33:
**“Why dost thou endeavour to shew thy way good”** — as if you strive in vain to defend yourself by the art of words, as if to show your good works so that you may deserve love; and moreover, etc.
**“to seek my love, thou who has also taught thy malices to be thy ways”** — Others: that you might be an example of wickedness to others.
2.34:
**“And in thy skirts”** — Others: in the hands.
**“is found the blood of the souls of the poor and innocent”** — whom you sacrificed to idols or destroyed by example
**“not in ditches have I found them”**
• slain
• which often happens through the ambushes of robbers
**“but in all places”** — or in these
**“which I mentioned before”** — which I said above, namely
**“in all places”** — In these, or “under every oak”: another reading. For the Hebrew means both oak and these. But they sacrificed in pleasant places, in shade and leaves.
2.35:
**“And thou hast said”** — O Jerusalem
**“I am without sin and am innocent: and therefore let thy anger be turned away from me”** — since you deny it
**“Behold, I”** — says the Lord
**“in judgment”** — not by power
**“I will contend with thee, because thou hast said: I have not sinned”**
• since it is a greater sin to have one thing in conscience and another in the mouth
• And thou hast said: I am without sin, etc. This must be used against those who will not acknowledge their sins but in the time of affliction say that they suffer undeservedly. And they provoke the anger of God the more, since it is another, indeed a greater sin, not to mourn what you have done but to put forward excuses.
**“Behold, I will contend”** — Jerome. Let the new heresy hear from the old that the wrath of God is at its greatest when one is unwilling to confess sin humbly but shamelessly boasts of righteousness.
2.36:
**“How exceeding base art thou become, going the same ways over again”** — often
**“going the same ways”** — your sins
**“and thou shalt be ashamed of Egypt, as thou wast ashamed of Assyria”** — in which you found no help
**“and thou shalt be ashamed of Egypt”** — To escape the onset of the Egyptians they fled to the Assyrians, who profited them nothing; for they were conquered by the Egyptians. Again, to escape the wrath of the Assyrians they fled to the Egyptians, but were overcome none the less. They are therefore rebuked because, having left God, they put their hope in men.
2.37:
**“For from thence”** — from Egypt as from the Assyrians
**“thou shalt go”** — often frustrated
**“and thy hand”** — of the one mourning, who in vain hoped for help
**“shall be upon thy head: for the Lord hath destroyed thy trust”** — in whom you placed it: in strangers.
**“and thou shalt have nothing prosperous”** — with God adverse.
**“upon thy head”** — In the manner of mourners: Thamar, violated by Amnon, sprinkled ashes on her head and laid her hands upon it.

3.1:
**“It is commonly said: If a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and marry another man, shall he return to her any more? shall not that woman be polluted, and defiled”**
• Others: the land; because she likened the land of Israel to an adulteress.
• If he put away, etc. Behold, an argument of justice is set forth from the fornicating and forsaken woman, and yet to us returning after a fall not justice but mercy is shown; that we may gather, if you who offend are spared by us with so great mercy, and not even when you return after the offence, how great is the wickedness with which sin is committed. Or what pardon will there be from him upon the wicked, who does not cease to call after the fault? Whence: “and thy eyes shall see thy teacher,” and thy ears shall hear the word of one admonishing behind thy back. We ought therefore to blush at the mercy of him who calls, if we are unwilling to fear justice; because he is despised with so much the graver wickedness, in that, though despised, he still does not disdain to call.
**“If a man put away his wife”** — This we can say against those who, forsaking the faith of the Lord and ensnared by the errors of heretics, after many fornications and the deception of their own souls, pretend to return to the former truth, not to lay aside the poisons of the heart but to instil them into others.
**“but thou hast prostituted thyself to many lovers”** — or shepherds: for in Hebrew remi signifies shepherds, and romi lovers.
**“But thou hast prostituted thyself”** — Or you had many shepherds, to your offense, so that you would offend God; and those who ought to have been teachers, to keep others from every error, became authors of impiety.
**“nevertheless return to me, saith the Lord”** — after the fornication he receives the penitent and exhorts her to return to him.
**“Nevertheless return”** — “If you were returning to me,” says the Lord. He rebukes the shamelessness of the harlot, who after adultery dares to return to her husband.
3.2:
**“Lift up thy eyes”** — According to anagogy, it is commanded to those who promise to abandon heretical errors that they lift up their eyes straight ahead. For unless they see what is right, they cannot condemn their former wickedness.
**“as a robber in”** — As robbers are wont at evening in deserted places to lie in wait for travellers, so you, that by your intercourse you might kill the souls of fornicators.
**“and see where thou hast not prostituted thyself. Thou didst sit in the ways, waiting for them as a robber in the wilderness”** — For robber the Hebrew has Arabe, which can also signify Arabs, a people given to robberies, which raids as far as the borders of Palestine and beset the ways of those going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. Whence: “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers.”
**“and thou hast polluted the land with thy fornications, and with thy wickedness”** — or you killed, because many perished by the evil of idolatry.
3.3:
**“Therefore”** — the blessing of all things was taken away, namely, so that they might suffer the drought of God’s word.
**“the showers were withholden, and there was no lateward rain. Thou hadst a harlot's forehead”** — The Seventy: face.
**“thou hadst a harlot's forehead”** — The Seventy: it has become for all.
**“thou wouldst not blush”**
• Let heretics blush, because they are unwilling to be turned to better things.
• Because above she said, “I have not sinned,” he rebukes her as a shameless woman who does not blush to turn aside to any man.
**“Therefore the showers were withholden”** — Gregory. Sometimes by the name of the sun the brightness of preachers is signified. Whence: “the sun became black as sackcloth of hair,” etc. For in the last time the sun is shown as sackcloth of hair, because the shining life of preachers is shown rough and despised before the eyes of the reprobate. They are also figured by the brightness of the stars, because when they relate right things to sinners, or preach woes, they light up the darkness of the night; whence: “therefore the showers were withholden” (the stars of the rains). But since the sun shines by day, and the stars by night, and the present life is for the most part signified by the night, and the eternal country by the day, holy preachers become a sun to us when they open the contemplation of the true light, and stars when through the active life they look to the needs of the present life.
**“Thou hadst a harlot's forehead”** — This we can say to heretics who glory in their errors.
3.4: **“Thou art my father, the guide of my virginity”** — God has betrothed the soul to his embraces and teaches how it ought to pray and do penance. But the more merciful he who shows the way of salvation after fornication, the more wretched is the harlot who does not want to receive healing.
3.5: **“Wilt thou be angry for ever, or wilt thou continue until the end? Behold, thou hast spoken, and hast done evil things, and hast been able”** — The passage from “and for words” to “you have dealt with” is lacking in most copies.
3.6:
**“And the Lord said to me in the days of king Josias”** — This prophecy was made in the days of King Josias the just, under whom Jeremias began to prophesy.
**“Hast thou seen what rebellious Israel hast done? she hath gone out of herself upon every high mountain, and under every green tree”** — where the greater pleasure is.
**“and hath played the harlot there”**
• And the Lord said, etc. Jerome. This prophecy was made in the times of Josias, a just king, under whom Jeremias began to prophesy. If you have understood the two peoples, namely Israel and the Gentiles, understand the transmigration of Israel in the people of the Jews, and of the same it was said: “I put her away and gave her a bill of divorce,” that is, that by leaving her he might establish an example. The law of Moses commands that a bill of divorce be given to a woman who displeases her husband, and that she be put away, and that then it be lawful for the husband to take another. So understand the Jews as receiving a bill of divorce, and therefore as being altogether forsaken by God. For where among them are the prophets, the signs of power, where the manifestation of God? No temple, no victims, no other worship of his expressed in the law. They were cast out of their lands, and so God gave them a bill of divorce.
• After them we, who in the Scriptures are called Jews on account of the tribe of Juda, from whose stock the Saviour descended, have been converted to the Lord; and our last days, in the consummation of the world, will be like the sins of Juda, nay, worse. Whence: “when iniquities shall have abounded, the charity of many shall grow cold. But he that shall persevere to the end, he shall be saved.” And do you think that the Son of man, when he cometh, shall find faith on earth? If even now we judge our faith, and not the multitude and the will of men, and not the gathering, we shall see that in so great a number of churches faith is found with the greatest difficulty; for it is difficult for many to be good; whence: “many are called, but few chosen.” If therefore he says first: I put her away for the sins of Israel and left her in her defilement, but Juda, hearing what befell Israel, was unwilling to be converted to me; he speaks of our sins, who, reading what the people of the Jews suffered, neither fear nor say: if he spared not the natural branches, how much more will God not spare us? For he is not only kind and not severe. If he were only kind, we would despise his goodness. If only severe, we would despair. We need goodness for repentance and severity for our offences.
• Hast thou seen, etc. He makes a comparison between the two and the ten tribes, which were already carried captive by the Assyrians. And although the two tribes had seen this, they did not amend themselves but acted worse. And this is what he says: Hast thou seen, etc.
**“rebellious Israel”** — Under the figure of two sisters he speaks, who were begotten of one stock, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The first he calls the adversary, she who set up golden calves in Dan and in Bethel.
3.7: **“And when she had done all these things, I said: Return to me, and she did not return. And her treacherous sister Juda saw”** — in which the temple and worship, by imitation of her sister, gradually withdrew from the Lord.
3.8:
**“That because the rebellious Israel had played the harlot, I had put her away, and had given her a bill of divorce: yet her treacherous sister Juda was not afraid, but went and played the harlot also herself”** — She went of herself, etc. According to the anagogical sense it is a prophecy about heretics, who think they follow “knowledge falsely so called” with heretical subtlety, and to climb the mountain of pride, and, steeped in the pleasures of the flesh, display their fornication under every leafy and pleasant tree. When these are handed over to the devil for the destruction of the flesh, it frequently happens that the house of Juda, that is, of confession and true faith, is not frightened by the example but commits far greater things, and with its fornication defiles the land of the Church, and commits adultery with wood and stone, following doctrines contrary to God. But if a churchman wishes to correct the erring, and to cut away the rotten flesh, and to draw back to repentance those who have followed falsehood, they nonetheless, under the appearance of ecclesiastical truth, follow the old error.
**“And her treacherous sister Juda saw”** — The torments of some are the remedies of others. And when a murderer is punished, he indeed receives what he did, but others are frightened from crime. When the ten tribes that were called Israel were taken by the Assyrians and carried over into Media, the two tribes, Juda and Benjamin, who ought to have feared the like and turned to God with their whole mind, surpassed the crimes of the ten tribes, so that they set up a statue of Baal in the temple of God, which in Ezechiel is called an idol set up to provoke the jealousy and emulation of the Lord.
3.9: **“And played the harlot”** — Origen. And she committed adultery with stone and with stock, etc. When we sin with a hard heart against God, we commit fornication with the stone; when we sin in pleasure, we commit adultery “under every leafy tree.” “And in all these things her treacherous sister Juda hath not returned to me with her whole heart, but with falsehood.” We too have been converted to the Lord, but not with our whole heart, but with falsehood. Nor indeed does he say, “Juda hath not returned to me,” and keep silent, but he added “with her whole heart, but with falsehood,” to show that those who are converted not with the whole heart are converted in falsehood, not in truth.
3.11:
**“And the Lord said to me: The rebellious Israel hath justified her soul, in comparison of the treacherous Juda”** — because at once in the beginning she perished.
**“rebellious Israel, in comparison of the treacherous Juda”** — who could be amended by the torments of that one.
**“hath justified her soul”** — Sodom your sister has been justified by you. And elsewhere: “this man went down into his house justified rather than the other.”
3.12:
**“Go”** — Others: read.
**“and proclaim”** — the Hebrew word carathat means: call, cry out, and read.
**“these words toward the north, and thou shalt say: Return, O rebellious Israel, saith the Lord”** — Whence: “Turn away thy face from my sins.”
**“from you: for I am holy, saith the Lord, and I will not be angry for ever”** — Go and proclaim, etc. Jerome. The discourse is directed against the north and the Assyrians, both to the ten tribes and to the two tribes, and their return is proclaimed.
**“and I will not turn away”** — Whence: turn away thy face. Others, however: “I will harden my face against you,” that is, I will receive you not with the severity of a judge but with the countenance of mercy. For I am holy and merciful, so that I will no longer remember your iniquity. This can be referred to heretics and the negligent in the Church, who are called to repentance daily by churchmen, to whom it is properly applied. “And you have not heard my voice.” Every heretic dwells in the north, without the heat of faith, and cannot hear that word of the Apostle, “fervent in spirit,” etc. And because he has given himself to pleasures he has departed from the Lord, and has scattered his ways among strange doctrines, and has followed pleasure. For there is no heresy except one leading itself for the sake of gluttony and the belly, with little women laden with sins, “ever learning, and never attaining to the knowledge of the truth,” of whom it is truly said: “who devour my people as they eat bread.”
3.13:
**“But yet acknowledge thy iniquity, that thou hast transgressed against the Lord thy God, and thou hast scattered thy ways to strangers”** — idols
**“under every green tree”** — where religion is delicate and pleasant
**“But yet acknowledge”** — Because when I have had mercy on you, do not think yourself just, but always remember your iniquity, and lay down the neck of pride, so that you who have offended by arrogance may be able to appease God by humility.
3.14:
**“Return, O ye revolting children”** — others, wandering and withdrawing
**“saith the Lord: for I am your husband”** — or ruler of you
**“and I will take you, one”**
• in the unity of faith
• for all men have not faith
**“of a city”** — of the world
**“and two”** — in the love of God and neighbour
**“of a kindred”** — of the flesh
**“and will bring you into Sion”**
• of which: “Glorious things are said of thee, O city of God.”
• Return, etc. Jerome. The Jews think this was fulfilled after the return from Babylon under Zorobabel, and that in this it is signified that not all returned. “I will take you,” etc. But it is better fulfilled in the coming of Christ, when the remnants are saved. Whence the Apostle: “Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed.”
3.15:
**“And I will give you pastors”** — apostles and apostolic men
**“according to my own heart, and they shall feed you”** — believers
**“with knowledge”** — of Christ
**“and doctrine”** — not by Jewish ceremonies
3.16:
**“And when you shall be multiplied”**
• when the gospel has been multiplied throughout the whole world
• Jerome. Others refer these things to the end of time, when, the fullness of the Gentiles coming in, all Israel shall be saved.
**“and increase in the land”** — “Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth,” etc.
**“The ark of the covenant of the Lord”** — Jerome. In the ark, which was the guardian of the Mosaic law, they will not have confidence; but they themselves will be in the temple of God. Nor, like the erring Nazarenes, will they serve the abolished sacrifices, but they will follow spiritual food.
3.17:
**“At that time Jerusalem shall be called”**
• the Church
• vision of peace, of which: “And his place is in peace.”
• Between the two cherubim on the mercy seat of the Lord the majesty appeared and spoke to Moses and the priests; but now, in the time of faith, it is otherwise.
**“shall be called”** — Those who once said: “Thou that sittest upon the cherubims, shine forth before Ephraim,” etc.
**“the throne of the Lord, and all the nations shall be gathered together to it”** — all who believe perfectly will be the throne of God
**“all the nations”** — the faithful
**“in the name of the Lord to Jerusalem”** — the Church
**“and they shall not walk after the perversity of their most wicked heart”** — doing their own desires and following their errors; but they will say: “My soul hath stuck close to thee: thy right hand hath received me.”
3.18:
**“In those days the house of Juda shall go to the house of Israel, and they shall come together out of the land of the north”** — of most severe cold
**“to the land”** — of promise
**“which I gave”** — as I promised
**“to your fathers”** — Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
**“In those days”** — This is properly fulfilled at the coming of Christ, when the twelve tribes together believe the gospel and leave the land of the north and the rule of the devil.
3.19:
**“But I said”**
• Christ
• the voice of Christ
**“How shall I put thee among the children”** — that there may be one fold
**“and give thee a lovely land”** — of the living
**“the goodly inheritance of the armies of the Gentiles”**
• that is, of the strong
• Theodotion. Of the most robust, namely Christ
**“And I said”** — he who believes in me believes in God the Father
**“Thou shalt call”** — O Israel
**“me, and shalt not cease to walk after me”** — by imitating
**“shalt not cease to walk after me”** — by obeying
**“among the children”** — In the number of the sons who believed from the Gentiles. For “as many as received him, he gave them power to be made the sons of God.”
3.20:
**“But as a woman that despiseth her lover”** — but as if a woman should despise her lover; not her husband
**“so hath the house of Israel despised”** — so it despised, to its own ruin
**“me”** — me: the Saviour
**“a woman that despiseth her lover”** — Having once mingled with him, seeing him serve his own lust, and the law of nature changed in her, by which she had once been subject to a husband, the Lord saying: and her turning is from thee.
3.21:
**“A voice was heard in the highways”** — a voice in the ways; or in the streets
**“was heard, weeping and howling of the children of Israel: because they have made their way wicked”** — was heard, the weeping and howling of the children of Israel, because they made their way wicked; by their own vice
**“they have forgotten the Lord their God”** — A voice in the ways. The Lord gladly receives the penitent. He meets the son worn out with want and squalor, clothes him in his former garments, and restores grace to him as he returns, provided that he returns to the Father with weeping and howling.
3.22:
**“Return, O ye revolting children”** — turn back, children, returning; because, having understood the sins of their fathers, they return to the Father with weeping and howling
**“and I will heal your rebellions”** — and I will heal your apostasies; by which you have turned away from the Lord
**“Behold we come to thee”** — behold, we come to you; let the penitent say this, leaving behind all pride
**“your rebellions”** — Others: conversions. Although we are converted to him by our own will, yet unless he draws us and strengthens our desire by his help, we cannot be saved. We understand it both of the people of the Jews returning to him and of the heretics who have forsaken the Lord.
3.23:
**“In very deed the hills were liars, and the multitude of the mountains”** — truly the hills were liars, the multitude of mountains; or the height by which one is proud against God
**“truly in the Lord our God”** — truly in the Lord; not in others
3.24:
**“Confusion hath devoured the labor of our fathers from our youth”** — confusion; whence it is written: “They have failed in searching a search.”
**“hath devoured the labour of our fathers”** — has devoured the labour of our fathers; of heretics
**“from our youth, their flocks”** — from our youth, their flocks; whom they deceived
**“and their herds, their sons and their daughters”** — and their herds, their sons and their daughters; who had advanced in heresy
3.25:
**“We shall sleep in our confusion, and our shame shall cover us, because”** — Christ
**“we have sinned”** — not only when he appeared in the flesh but also before he came
**“we and our fathers from our youth even to this day, and we have not hearkened”** — For if you did believe Moses, you would perhaps believe me also; for he wrote of me.
**“to the voice of the Lord our God”** — who spoke to our parents
**“We shall sleep”** — The voice of Israel, who did not hear his God, and of the penitent heretic. For part of salvation is to know and confess sins. Whence: “Be thou first to tell thy iniquities, that thou mayest be justified.”

4.1:
**“If thou wilt return”**
• if you return from captivity
• The Seventy: another reading is “if you return,” that is, if you desire salvation and say you have sinned, return fully, that is, believe him whom you denied.
**“O Israel, saith the Lord, return to me”** — first by doing penance
**“if thou wilt take away thy stumblingblocks”** — idols
**“If thou wilt take away”** — It is clear, since we are moved when we say: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well nigh slipped.” We suffer this not from weakness of nature but because we set up our stumblingblocks and idols against God.
4.2:
**“And thou shalt swear: As the Lord liveth”**
• the oath of the Old Testament
• Jerome. Namely, in the disgrace of the dead gods by whom every idolater swears.
**“in truth, and in judgment, and in justice”**
• the idols, despised, by which you swore before
• these are the true companions of an oath; if they are lacking, it is perjury
**“and the Gentiles shall bless him”** — namely, when Israel has done these things, when the teacher of the Gentiles has been through the apostles
**“the Gentiles”** — because salvation is from Israel
4.3:
**“For thus saith the Lord to the men of Juda”** — of true faith
**“and Jerusalem”** — of the Church
