**“Break up anew your fallow ground, and sow not upon thorns”**
• which choke the seed
• be cleansed
**“Break up anew”** — By rooting out brambles and thorns, that the clean fields may receive clean seeds; and cast not your pearls before swine, nor give that which is holy to dogs. A mind full of the troubles of the world cannot receive the seed of God and bear fruit.
4.4:
**“Be circumcised”** — Symmachus: be purified
**“to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your hearts”**
• vices
• Symmachus: wickednesses
**“ye men of Juda, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem: lest my indignation come forth like fire, and burn, and there be none that can quench it: because of the wickedness of your thoughts”** — all these things will come to pass
**“Be circumcised to the Lord”** — Jerome. It is commanded to the men of Juda and the inhabitants of Jerusalem that they abandon the killing letter and follow the life-giving Spirit.
**“lest”** — Jerome. He warns and foretells, lest he be forced to do what we see was done, which we prove in the Ninevites, to whom the sentence was foretold, that by penance they might turn aside the impending fury.
4.5:
**“Declare ye in Juda”** — in which is the confession of God
**“and make it heard in Jerusalem”** — in which is peace
**“speak, and sound with the trumpet in the land: cry aloud, and say”** — to which is similar: lift up your voice in strength, etc.
**“Assemble yourselves”** — into one faith
**“and let us go into strong cities”** — as the wars of heretics rise up, let the defences of Christ hold us
4.6:
**“Set up the standard”** — of the cross
**“in Sion”** — in the watchtower and height of the Church
**“Strengthen yourselves”** — you who fear
**“stay not”** — run to the help of Christ
**“for I bring evil from the north, and great destruction”** — that is, Nabuchodonosor, who is therefore permitted by me in this world, so that your strength may be proved
4.7:
**“The lion is come up”** — Nabuchodonosor, the venom, who like a lion goes about “seeking whom he may devour”
**“out of his den”** — that is, from wickedness or from hell, where he is thrust back
**“and the robber of nations hath roused himself: he is come forth out of his place, to make thy land desolate”** — namely the Church; so that those who have gone out of the Church may fight against it. Whence: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.”
**“thy cities”** — of the Church
**“shall be laid waste”** — while the conventicles of heretics flourish
**“remaining without an inhabitant”** — The lion has come up, etc. Jerome. If anyone is the maker and author of perverse doctrines, it can be said of him: “The lion has come up out of his den, and the robber of nations has roused himself.”
**“and the robber of nations”** — Of whom it is said: He shall rule over all his enemies. He who boasts, saying: “I have gone round about the earth, and walked through it.” For who is there whom the poisons of the devils do not touch, except him who says: “The prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not any thing.”
**“out of his place”** — From the abyss in which he is to be bound, he prays that he may not be sent.
4.8:
**“For this gird yourselves with haircloth, lament and howl: for the fierce anger of the Lord is not turned away from us”** — The Septuagint: from us
**“For this gird yourselves”** — Without penitence we cannot avoid the most savage beast; and unless we turn to God not only in mind but also in body. For while the Church is laid waste, the wrath of God is open.
4.9:
**“And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord”** — with the robber laying waste the Church and the wrath of God remaining against us
**“shall perish”** — all counsel will be useless
**“the heart of the king”** — which ought to be in the hand of God
**“of the princes”** — Who ought to teach the law and defend their subjects from the lion.
**“the priests shall be astonished”** — Who were thought to be wise. For God has made foolish the wisdom of this world, because through it they did not know God.
**“the prophets shall be amazed”** — Aquila: they will be out of their minds. For who would not lose his mind and heart, when he has seen his princes, kings and priests, once his own, under the lion?
4.10:
**“And I said: Alas, alas, alas, O Lord God, hast thou then deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying: You shall have peace: and behold the sword reacheth”** — who cuts away and purges vices; for otherwise peace and promise do not follow
**“even to the soul”** — because nothing living is kept in the soul
**“And I said: Alas”** — What he said above: “At that time Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the Lord,” etc. Now he says: the heart of the king will perish, etc. The prophet is troubled; he thinks God has lied, and does not understand that the one is to come long after this, while this is to come in the near future.
4.11:
**“At that time”** — when the sword has come even to the soul, and the threshing floor has been finished
**“it shall be said to this people, and to Jerusalem: A burning wind”**
• Nabuchodonosor or the devil
• not one who cleanses and winnows
**“in the ways that are in the desert”** — where there is no dwelling of God
**“of the way of the daughter of my people, not to fan, nor to cleanse”** — A burning wind, etc. That is, when the sword shall have reached even to the soul, and the threshing-floor shall be finished, then a burning wind will come from the desert, to cleanse and winnow it, so that, the chaff being scattered hither and thither, the grain may be laid up in the barns. But a wind full of spirit will come by no means to the people but to me, that my wheat may be scattered.
4.12:
**“A full wind from these places shall come to me”** — and not to the people
**“and now I will speak”** — that they may know they justly bear what they bear
**“A full wind”** — Some expound this place thus: after the threshing floor has been cleansed, the remnant will be saved. Whence it is written: “A spirit of fulness shall come to me”; whence the evangelist: “Of his fulness we all have received.”
**“my judgments with them”** — And now I, etc. Aposiopesis, as Virgil says: “Whom I—but it is better to calm the troubled waves.” About to speak of good fortune, he holds himself back, and joined sad things to sad.
4.13:
**“Behold”** — as if he pointed with a finger
**“Behold he shall come up as a cloud”** — He discerns future things as present, and describes the army of the Babylonians, whose chariot and noise of wheels is compared to a most fierce tempest, and the speed of whose horses to eagles.
**“he shall come up as a cloud, and his chariots as a tempest: his horses are swifter than eagles: woe unto us, for we are laid waste”** — The army of the devil, namely the chariots and riders of Pharaoh; which the ecclesiastical man understanding says: “Woe to us, for we are laid waste,” believing that sentence. When you have turned and groaned, you will be saved.
**“Woe unto us”** — What the prophet showed as if with a finger, the people groan at. And they feel not things future but things already done, saying “Woe to us,” etc.
4.14:
**“Wash thy heart from wickedness, O Jerusalem”** — metropolis of the Jews
**“that thou mayst be saved: how long shall hurtful thoughts abide in thee?”** — which proceed from the heart; but heart in the holy Scriptures we ought to take for soul and senses
**“Wash from wickedness”** — The prophet answers. Rather, in the prophet the Lord speaks. “Wash,” etc. Whence Isaias: “Wash yourselves, be clean,” namely with the water of baptism, the water of saving penance.
4.15:
**“For a voice of one declaring from Dan”** — judgment
**“and giving notice of the idol from mount Ephraim”** — abundance
**“For a voice of one declaring”** — He speaks according to the situation of Judea. For the tribe of Dan, which lies beside Mount Libanus and the city now called Paneas, looks toward the north, whence Nabuchodonosor was to come.
**“from mount Ephraim”** — For after the tribe of Dan comes the land of Ephraim, through which one comes to Jerusalem. Allegorically, the judgment of the Lord comes into the land that sins against the Lord, with all the abundance of punishment.
4.16:
**“Say ye to the nations”**
• the Lord saw all nations round about
• Namely adversaries who besiege so diligently and close the city with fortifications that you would think them guards of vineyards and fields rather than adversaries.
**“Behold it is heard”** — namely often
**“in Jerusalem, that guards are coming from a far country, and give out their voice against the cities of Juda”**
• of wailing
• army
• The Lord wills all the nations round about to know his sentence, and, Jerusalem having been scourged, all to receive discipline.
4.17: **“They are set round about her, as keepers of fields: because she hath provoked me to wrath, saith the Lord.”** — your actions
4.18:
**“Thy ways”** — O Jerusalem
**“and thy devices have brought these things upon thee: this is thy wickedness, because”** — by themselves
**“because it is bitter, because it hath touched thy heart.”**
• or: heart
• has pierced the inner parts of the soul
• I suffer affliction of mind
• Whatever evil befalls us is of our vice, not of God, who turn the sweet God into bitterness and compel him, though willing, to rage.
• Let this not be imputed to the strength of enemies, but to the fault of Jerusalem. For if demons have no power over swine, how much less over men, and men once of the city of God?
4.19:
**“My bowels”** — Jerome. The Lord speaks this when he sees sedition and discord in the Church and in his conventicles, the partridge crying out and the rest of God turned into wars. Whence follows: “How long shall I see the fleeing,” etc.
**“My bowels, my bowels are in pain, the senses of my heart are troubled within me, I will not hold my peace, for my soul hath heard the sound of the trumpet, the cry of battle.”** — The voice of the prophet, and through the prophet of God, grieving over the crushing of his people, whose bowels are torn like a man’s. As the Saviour wept at the death of Lazarus and over Jerusalem, nor does he hide his sorrow in silence; and the blast of the trumpet and the din of battles trouble his heart, while evils are heaped upon evils and the whole land of the two tribes is laid waste.
4.20:
**“Destruction upon destruction is called for, and all the earth is laid waste”** — Inspired.
**“laid waste”** — With the Babylonian rushing in.
**“my tents”**
• that is, once their dwellings fell as prey to the enemy.
• once
4.21: **“How long shall I see men fleeing away, how long shall I hear the sound of the trumpet?”** — the Babylonian king, or those withdrawing from my service.
4.22:
**“For my foolish people”**
• He gives the cause of the evils foretold.
• not by nature but by eagerness for pleasure.
• because
• The Seventy: because the princes of my people have not known. So that the fault of the teachers is greater than that of the people who do not have knowledge of God.
**“have not known me: they are foolish and senseless children”** — that is, made so.
**“and senseless”** — for the wise.
**“they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge.”** — What greater folly is there than that, the ox knowing its owner and the ass its master’s crib, Israel should not know the Lord, and should despise him present, whom it always desired to see?
**“They are wise”** — They are wise, the malicious. Like to this: the children of this world are wiser than the children of light in their generation. And the steward of iniquity is told to have acted somewhat more wisely, and the serpent in paradise is read to have been more prudent than all the beasts. That, therefore, is true wisdom which is joined with the fear of God. But where there are snares and evasion, it is called not wisdom but cunning and craftiness.
4.23:
**“I beheld the earth, and lo it was void”** — with the inhabitant destroyed.
**“and nothing: and the heavens, and there was no light in them.”**
• the greatness of the terror, the people not seeing it.
• Whatever is said according to history of Judea and Jerusalem, let us refer to the Church of God: when it has offended God and been laid waste by vices and persecution, where once there was a band of virtues and joy, there a multitude of sins and mourning is found.
**“I beheld the earth”** — The prophet discerns in spirit what is to come, so that the people, hearing, may be terrified and do penance, so that they may not suffer what they dread.
4.24:
**“I looked upon the mountains, and behold they trembled”** — hyperbolically
**“and all the hills were troubled.”** — seem to be troubled.
4.25:
**“I beheld”** — on every side.
**“and lo there was no man: and all the birds of the air”**
• which usually follows the inhabitants.
• the elements feel the wrath of God, and the irrational animals are terrified.
**“were gone”** — departed with the man, and with the one perishing.
4.26:
**“I looked, and behold Carmel was a wilderness”** — which overhangs the great sea, planted with olive trees and shrubs, with vines either low or thick.
**“and all its cities were destroyed at the presence of the Lord”** — by the presence of the Lord
**“and at the presence”** — presence
**“of the wrath of his indignation.”** — stirred up by the sin of the people, which is the cause of all evils.
4.27: **“For thus saith the Lord”** — The Lord’s mercy is mingled with his wrath: the land is deserted but not consumed, so that there may remain those who understand his mercy.
4.28: **“I have purposed”** — The Lord threatened through Jonas so that he might remove the foretold sentence, and the wrath of the raging one should not reach its end; but the magnitude of tears and groans overcame the impending sword.
4.29:
**“At the voice of the horsemen”** — He describes the army of the raging, from whose fear the people leave the city and climb the heights; yet they could not turn aside the wrath of God.
**“At the voice of the horsemen, and the archers, all the city is fled away; they have entered into thickets and have climbed up the rocks: all the cities are forsaken, and there dwelleth not a man in them.”** — All this can be referred to the Church, when it has offended God and been handed over to adversaries in time of persecution, or to vices and sins.
**“And thou”** — What fault have you made the merciful God bitter?
**“when thou shalt be adorned with a golden ornament”** — By meditation on the sense and by spiritual understanding.
**“and paintest thy eyes with stibium”** — If you have had zeal for the ministries and for knowing the secrets of God.
**“At the voice of the horsemen, and the archers”** — For you prepare these things for your lovers, and a narrow bed cannot hold both. Nor does God receive the ornaments by which you once pleased your lovers.
4.30:
**“And thou when thou shalt be wasted, what wilt thou do?”** — Under the figure of an adulteress he speaks to her.
**“when thou shalt be clothed in scarlet”** — By faith in the blood of Christ.
**“in vain shalt thou adorn thyself”** — When you have offended God as if he were your husband.
**“thy lovers have despised thee”** — Demons.
**“they will seek thy life”** — Not the filth of fornication.
**“And thou when thou shalt be wasted”** — Jerome. The same must be said against those who have lost conjugal affection and the chastity of true faith.
4.31:
**“For I have heard the voice”** — For he describes Jerusalem awakening and crying out.
**“as of a woman in travail, anguishes as of a woman in labor”**
• As of one in labour, I have heard the anguish, as of a woman giving birth, among which she can scarcely breathe.
• One who has not yet experienced such pain.
**“The voice of the daughter of Sion”** — Is such, namely.
**“dying away”** — Dying among her own.
**“For I have heard the voice as of”** — Two examples are set down, of the woman in labour and of the mourner; and whatever a woman suffers either in childbirth or in the death of her children, Jerusalem will suffer among the peoples.

5.1: **“Go about through the streets of Jerusalem”** — Great is the love of justice: it is not, as in Abraham’s question and God’s answer, that God would free the city already about to perish for ten righteous men, but if he finds one who will do judgment and seek faith.
5.2: **“And though they say: The Lord liveth; this also they will swear falsely”** — Some among the people could feign the worship of God and swear by the Lord. But God does not delight in speech but in truth, and he loves those whose words and lips agree.
5.3:
**“O Lord”** — After the words in which he says, Go about the streets of Jerusalem, etc., the prophet speaks to the Lord.
**“thy eyes are upon truth”** — Elsewhere: they look upon.
**“thou hast struck them”** — Yet.
**“thou hast bruised them”** — Yet.
**“they have refused to receive correction; they have made”** — Above all.
**“their faces”** — Shameless, so that they would not blush at their vices.
**“harder than the rock, and they have refused to return”**
• At least in shame.
• Thinking with me.
• Thou hast struck, etc. Gregory. Every divine stroke is for us either a cleansing of the present life or the beginning of the punishment that follows. On account of those who make progress it is said: “who framest labour in commandment.” For when the wicked man is scourged, he who would not hear the commandment is corrected; he has heard sorrow, and is restrained from evils by sorrow as by a commandment. But of those whom the scourges condemn and do not amend it is said: “Thou hast struck them, and they have not grieved,” etc. These scourges begin in this life and last forever. Whence: “a fire is kindled in my wrath, and shall burn even to the lowest hell.” And it is one scourge that begins in time and is consummated in eternal punishments.
**“O Lord, thy eyes”** — The works of the Jews (in which they rejoiced according to the ceremonies of the law) are condemned by the faith of Christians, through which we have been made saved by grace.
**“and they have not grieved”** — Punishments are inflicted so that vices may be corrected, but Jerusalem is not amended, nor by torments.
5.4:
**“But I said: Perhaps these are poor and foolish”** — In the common people, namely.
**“that know not”** — The ignoble, unlearned crowd: if it cannot know the commandments of God, it is excusable.
**“Perhaps these are poor”** — Like that: “I will send my son; perhaps they will reverence him.” God uses the language of doubt, so that through the ambiguity of the sentence and the suspension of the words, the freedom of man’s choice may be shown.
5.5:
**“I will go therefore to the great men”** — who preside over the people
**“and I will speak to them: for they know the way of the Lord, the judgment of their God: and behold these have together broken the yoke more”** — of the law
**“and have burst the bonds”** — The teachers are worse than the disciples, and the greater the authority among the rich, the greater the arrogance of sinners.
**“and behold these”** — According to the tropology: those who are thought great in the Church, because they loosen the yoke and break the bonds, are handed over to the shame of sufferings, so that they do what is not fitting.
**“the bonds”** — Of the precepts of God, not of the Pharisees, of whom it is said: “Let us break their bonds asunder, and let us cast away their yoke from us.”
5.6:
**“Wherefore a lion out of the wood hath slain them”** — the kingdom of the Babylonians
**“a wolf in the evening”** — the Medes and Persians, which in Daniel is signified by the bear
**“hath spoiled them, a leopard watcheth for their cities: every one that shall go out thence shall be taken, because”**
• all these things they will suffer
• But because he weaves a history not of the future but of the past, or of what is already about to be, he is therefore silent about the Roman empire, of which perhaps it is said: “Every one that shall go out,” etc.
**“a leopard watcheth”** — It signifies the onset of Alexander, who, having subjected various peoples to himself, took up arms against the Medes and Persians like a leopard of many spots.
**“their transgressions are multiplied, their rebellions are strengthened”** — by constant practice
**“their rebellions”** — by the Lord
5.7:
**“How can I be merciful to thee? Thy children”** — not mine
**“How can I be merciful to thee”** — A catalogue of the sins of Jerusalem, while God says he does not know by what reason he could show mercy to them.
**“Thy children have forsaken me, and swear by them”** — those to whom they give the honour of God
**“that are not gods: I fed them to the full, and they committed adultery”** — Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold; the belly and the genitals are friends.
**“I fed them to the full”** — Let him who serves lust with the riches he has received hear this.
5.8:
**“They are become as amorous horses and stallions”**
• Not men: “Man when he was in honour did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts, and made like to them.”
• In Hebrew mosechim, that is, drawing, to show the size of the genitals; whence in Ezechiel: “their flesh is as the flesh of asses.” And elsewhere: “he is compared to senseless beasts, and is become like to them.”
**“amorous horses and stallions”** — When horses do not see a mare, their genitals do not appear; but when they see her, they bear down and rush upon her.
**“every one neighed after his neighbour's wife”**
• metaphor
• like a horse full of lust
5.9:
**“Shall I not visit”** — When you have done this, you are worthy of visitation.
**“Shall I not visit for these things”** — “I will visit their iniquities with a rod.”
**“saith the Lord; and in such a nation”** — as though no longer the people of God
**“shall not my soul take revenge”** — which in the Old Testament is put for affection, in the New for truth: “I have power to lay down my life.”
5.10:
**“Scale down”** — You nations, by whom the lion of the wood struck, etc.
**“the walls thereof”** — Jerome. For the true soul.
**“and throw them down”**
• O Jerusalem.
• that the remnants may be saved, and there may be some who proclaim the glory of God among the nations
**“but do not utterly destroy”** — he mixes mercy with severity
**“take away the branches”** — others: supports, that is, helps
**“thereof, because they are not the Lord's”** — And destroy, etc. Let the Church hear that the walls and bulwarks of those who have no hope in the Lord and transgress against him will soon be destroyed. Yet let there be no utter destruction, on account of the mercy of the judge and not on account of the merit of the sinners.
5.11:
**“For the house of Israel has greatly transgressed against me”** — the ten tribes
**“and the house of Juda”** — two
5.12:
**“They have denied the Lord, and said, It is not he”** — all things are done by his judgment, but they happen by chance
**“and the evil shall not come upon us”** — which the prophets threaten
**“the sword and famine”** — of siege
**“we shall not see”** — They have denied, etc. Let the careless Church hear this, and those who reject the providence of God, that they will endure both sword and famine unless they believe the things that are foretold.
5.13:
**“The prophets have spoken in the wind”** — all these things passed away in vain
**“and there was no word of God in them”** — of the Lord
**“these things therefore shall befall them”** — which the following words describe
5.14:
**“Thus saith the Lord the God of hosts: Because you have spoken this word”** — the prophets spoke in the wind
**“behold I will make my words in thy mouth as fire”** — O Jeremias
**“as fire”** — that is, that fire may have power
**“As fire”** — So that the unbelievers may be burned by your word. As God is called a consuming fire, so that he may consume in us wood, hay and stubble, if we build upon the foundation of Christ.
5.15:
**“Behold, I”** — as if the prophets had not spoken in the wind
**“I will bring”** — now already
**“upon you a nation”** — of Babylon
**“from afar, O house of Israel, saith the Lord: a nation”** — for which in Hebrew it is ethan
**“a strong”** — over whom Nemrod the giant once ruled
**“Whose language thou shalt not know”** — In Hebrew you will not understand what they say. For it is a comfort in evils if you have enemies whom you can ask, who understand your prayers.
5.16: **“Their quiver”** — the armour of the Babylonians; for the Assyrians and Babylonians, the Persians and Medes are archers
5.17:
**“And they shall eat up thy corn, and thy bread: they shall devour”** — the aforesaid nation
**“thy sons, and thy daughters: they shall eat up thy flocks, and thy herds: they shall eat thy vineyards, and thy figs: and with the sword they shall destroy thy strong cities, wherein thou trustest.”** — by the hostile sword
**“And they shall eat up thy corn”** — He describes the desolation of the land: the slaughter of many, the driving off of cattle, the overthrow of cities and walls, because by the hostile sword all things are taken.
5.18: **“Nevertheless in those days, saith the Lord, I will not bring you to utter destruction.”** — Nevertheless, etc. Remnants will certainly be saved, either of those who were led into Babylon or left to cultivate the land of Judea, or of those who, after the heat of persecution, kept faith with God by flight or by confession.
5.19:
**“And if you shall say”**
• it is great foolishness not to know why they suffer, since they have committed such great evils
• Tropologically. This can be taken of heretics, of whom “they went out from us, but they were not of us,” etc. For the Lord casts heretics out of the Church, who for a long time under his name have venerated the idols of their own lies, that they may worship them outside, and the chaff be separated from the wheat.
**“why hath the Lord our God done all these things to us? Thou shalt say to them”** — a brief answer
**“As you have forsaken me, and served a strange god”** — Baal, or the strange gods of all nations
**“in your own land”** — Judea
**“so shall you serve strangers in a land that is not your own.”** — To strange gods, etc. To the Babylonians and Chaldeans, as if to say: if a foreign religion delights you, why is it necessary to take up error from afar? Dwell rather, and serve those whose gods you worship.
5.21:
**“Hear, O foolish people”** — in many ways he calls sinners back to salvation, and calls the people foolish, who have forsaken the author of wisdom
**“who have eyes, and see not”** — like the idols, like them
**“Hear, O people”** — He speaks properly to Judah and to the house of Jacob. But Israel had already been in exile among the Assyrians for a long time.
**“and ears, and hear not”** — Who have no heart, etc. It shows that we ought naturally to understand what is right without a precept.
**“who have eyes”** — To which is similar: “They have eyes, but they see not,” etc. “Let them that make them become like unto them: and all such as trust in them.”
5.22:
**“Will not you then fear me”** — who have done such great things for you
**“will not you fear”** — as if I seek not the love of the perfect but the fear of beginners
**“saith the Lord: and will you not repent at my presence? I have set the sand”** — he recounts the benefits so as to reprove the ungrateful
**“a bound for the sea”**
• that it not go out beyond the shores
• so powerful an element
**“an everlasting ordinance, which it shall not pass over: and the waves thereof shall toss themselves, and shall not prevail: they shall swell, and shall not pass over it.”** — as if they feel me, though they have no sense
5.23:
**“But the heart of this people is become”** — my own, formerly, that is
**“hard of belief and provoking”** — not only despising
**“they are revolted”** — they have turned their backs to me
**“and gone away”** — with quick step
5.24:
**“And they have not said in their heart”** — nor did a silent conscience restrain them
**“let us fear the Lord our God, who giveth us the early”** — by these he signifies all good things
5.25:
**“Your iniquities have turned these things away”** — from us
**“and your sins have withholden good things from you.”** — Your iniquities, etc. If ever the sea passes its bounds and the rain is withheld, the hand of the Lord is not shortened so as not to prevent this. But our sins have turned aside these things that were coming to us, that they may go to others who have not sinned. Whence: “I will command the clouds to rain no rain,” etc. We can take the early and the latter rain as the law and the gospel, or the diverse callings from the first hour to the eleventh, in which the reward of the eternal vineyard is promised to the workmen.
5.26: **“For among my people are found wicked men, that lie in wait”** — because they openly deny God; iniquity and sin, if they confess their error, easily bend God to mercy
5.27: **“As a net”** — While they hunt one another to death and fill their houses with the losses and ruin of others, according to that saying of the philosophers: Every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man. And would that these things were done only by those who are outside and not by us, and that the hand of those coming to us were not regarded, but the mouth.
5.28:
**“They are grown gross and fat”** — To which is similar: “He grew fat, thick and gross, and forsook God,” etc. And “The beloved grew fat, and kicked,” etc.
**“and have most wickedly transgressed”** — despising all
**“And have most wickedly transgressed”** — Trusting in riches, as if they say: “Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thy rest; eat, drink, make good cheer.”
**“my words. They have not judged the cause of the widow”** — because he cannot give
**“they have not judged the cause of the fatherless”** — because he cannot give
**“they have not managed”** — it is the judge’s part to give an advocate to the orphan and to direct his cause
**“they have not judged the judgment of the poor.”** — what is just
5.29:
**“Shall I not visit for these things”** — sins
**“saith the Lord? or shall not my soul take revenge on such a nation?”** — so evil
**“shall not my soul take revenge”** — affected
5.31:
**“The prophets”**
• concerning whom I will go to the chief men
• who foretell the future
**“prophesied falsehood”** — no one among all these who thinks rightly
**“and the priests”** — who decree what is to be done according to the law
**“clapped their hands: and my people”** — as if the people too is not without blame
**“loved such things”** — formerly, but after he loved such things, he ceased to be mine
**“what then shall be done”** — by them
**“in the end thereof”** — that is, by judgment or captivity

6.1:
**“Strengthen yourselves, ye sons of Benjamin”**
• Jerusalemites
• sons of the right hand
• Let us refer all these things to the Church, so that if it has forsaken, and the assault of persecution comes, it prepares itself to resist.
**“Strengthen yourselves”** — Because even now Nabuchodonosor is about to come from the north. O inhabitants of Jerusalem, take up arms that you may be able to resist the enemies.
**“in the midst of Jerusalem, and sound the trumpet in Thecua”** — trumpet
**“Jerusalem, and sound the trumpet in Thecua”** — Jerome. Jerusalem is situated in the tribe of Benjamin. We see daily Thecua, a little village situated on a mountain, separated twelve miles from Jerusalem. Among these is another village which in the Syriac and Hebrew tongue is called Bethacarem, placed on a mountain.
**“sound the trumpet in Thecua, and ... over Bethacarem”** — the vineyard village
**“set up the standard ... for evil is seen out of the north”** — from which evils blaze up over the earth
6.2: **“Beautiful”** — The beauty of Jerusalem is described, which is Sion itself, so that one term denotes the whole city, another the citadel of the city. For Sion is interpreted as citadel, that is, watchtower, and is compared to a beautiful woman.
6.3:
**“to her”** — as to lovers of women
**“The shepherds shall come”** — princes
**“The shepherds”** — Quite elegantly a Hebrew word is set down here, which is written with four letters: res, ayn, lamed, mem. For if it be read reim, it means lovers; if roim, shepherds. Either, according to the metaphor of a beautiful woman, let lovers be understood, or, according to the overthrow of the city, shepherds, of whom some hasten to defile a harlot, others to the destruction of the city.
**“with their flocks”** — the army of the Chaldeans
**“they have pitched their tents against her round about”** — for the siege of the city
**“every one shall feed”** — prince
**“them”** — their troops
**“that are under his hand”** — power
6.4:
**“Prepare ye”**
• that is, the shepherds will say to their flocks
• for it is the Lord’s command
**“against her”** — Jerusalem
**“war ... arise”** — quickly
**“let us go up at midday”** — not by night, not by ambush; let us fight in full light, for no one will resist us
**“woe unto us, for the day is declined, for the shadows of the evening are grown longer”**
• others have failed
• like to which the greater shadows fall from the high mountains
• Woe unto us, for the day is declined, etc. Jerome. When those saying “Arise and let us go up” answer “Woe unto us,” etc., the sense is: if we suffer this by day, what shall we suffer by night?
6.5:
**“Arise, and let us go up in the night, and destroy her houses”**
• or foundations
• which are fortified by the strength of walls
**“Arise”** — Those who said “Rise up and go up,” etc., challenge themselves to war with those words. “Let us rise and go up in the night,” so that the adversaries may know that victory is not of time but of virtues.
6.6:
**“For thus saith the Lord of hosts”** — as if we were certain of the victory, because the Lord has commanded
**“Hew down her trees, cast up a trench”**
• or: pour out
• here it signifies the city to be taken not at once but by a long siege
**“cast up a trench about Jerusalem”** — by constructing siegeworks
**“this is”** — for
**“the city”** — of God
**“to be visited, all”** — I will visit their iniquities with a rod
**“oppression”**
• false accusation
• this is the greatest of sins
6.7:
**“As”** — therefore
**“As a cistern maketh its water cold”** — Without the heat of faith, the Church of those fervent in spirit. But evils are cold; whence: “the charity of many shall grow cold.” And that: “I shall be like them that go down into the pit.” Let it suffice to have said once that the word means a pit, not a pool, according to the Greeks, but a cistern, which in the Syriac and Hebrew tongue is called gab.
**“wickedness”** — Septuagint. Impiety and misery shall be heard in her before her face, through all pain and scourge; you shall be taught, Jerusalem, etc.
6.8: **“Be thou instructed”** — Jerome. By this we learn that God scourgeth every son whom he receiveth, and therefore Jerusalem is instructed by blows and torments, that she may be corrected and the soul of God not depart from her. Whenever, then, we lie under frequent afflictions, let us remember this verse: Through every sorrow and scourge thou shalt be instructed, O Jerusalem.
6.9: **“even to one cluster”** — As when Jerusalem has been laid waste, remnants will be saved. Or thus: let not even one cluster remain; and as a grape-gatherer does, whatever you find, draw it away into Babylon, as into a basket or into a winepress.
6.10:
**“To whom shall I speak? and to whom shall I testify, that”** — or, or
**“hear”** — that
**“behold, their ears are uncircumcised, and they cannot hear”**
• because they will not; for not being able descends from contempt and unbelief
• Uncircumcised ears, etc. It is to be noted that circumcision is spoken of in Scripture in three ways: in the foreskin, in the heart, and in the ears, whence: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.”
**“Behold”** — therefore
**“the word of the Lord”** — which was given to them for salvation
**“is become unto them a reproach”** — by their fault it was turned into punishment
6.11:
**“Therefore am I full of the fury of the Lord, I am weary with holding in: pour it out”**
• the fury
• the prophet, to the Chaldean
**“upon the child”** — let no age be spared
**“abroad, and upon the council of the young men”** — who had seized arms to resist
**“together: for man and woman shall be taken”** — Man: his sweetest names; together they feel captivity.
**“the ancient”** — It is clear that old age is not the last age.
**“he that is full of days”** — Whom we call decrepit or worn out.
**“Therefore am I full of the fury”** — As one who sees the coming wrath of God, I am full of his fury and anger, and cannot bear it any longer. Nor do I dare to pray to God for sinners.
6.12:
**“And their houses shall be turned over to others”** — We refer all these things spiritually to the Church, if it offends the Lord.
**“with their lands and their wives together”** — That is, spouse and property.
**“for I will stretch forth my hand upon the inhabitants of the land”** — Who are always in vice; whence: woe to the inhabitants of the earth.
**“I will stretch forth”** — The Seventy: I will lift up. But the posture of one striking is in both: whence, “and yet his hand is stretched out,” or raised high.
6.13:
**“For from the least of them even to the greatest, all are given to covetousness”** — Covetousness, the root of all evils.
**“all are given to covetousness: and from the prophet”** — Who prophesies falsehood.
**“even to the priest, all are guilty of deceit”** — Who interpret the law perversely; for he says in another place, through the prophet: “Seek the law from the priests.”
6.14:
**“And they healed the breach of the daughter of my people disgracefully, saying: Peace, peace: and there was no peace”** — Altogether.
**“And they healed the breach”** — As though, when they did so many evils, they yet announced every prosperity to my people. And as though they desired to heal the wound, and with disgrace to the daughter of my people, saying: Peace, peace. This is to be understood properly of the priests and teachers, who promise prosperity to the rich and honoured and preach a merciful God, thereby preparing them rather for punishment and the wrath of God.
6.15:
**“They were confounded, because they committed abomination: yea, rather they were not confounded with confusion, and they knew not how to blush”**
• They had neither knowledge nor sense of repentance.
• Were they confounded, etc. This is to be read in a lower tone here, according to the Hebrew. And when they had done such great things, he says, were they confounded? Did they blush for their sins? Nay, rather they increased their sin by contempt.
**“they knew not”** — They were not willing, but through excessive contempt and the vice of violent evil they could not even understand. Great impiety: not only not to guard against sins, but not even to wish to understand them, and to have no distinction between good and evil works.
**“wherefore they shall fall”** — Those who stood before.
**“among them that fall”** — By their own vices.
**“in the time of their visitation”**
• Punishment.
• By Nebuchadnezzar.
**“they shall fall down”** — Joined with those who are falling.
6.16:
**“Thus saith the Lord: Stand ye on the ways”** — The prophets.
**“and hear”** — Or: see.
**“And”** — Thus.
**“Interrogate”** — Inquire diligently.
**“Of the old paths”** — Which are worn by the footsteps of many saints.
**“Which is the good way”** — In the Gospel.
**“And walk ye in it, and you shall find refreshment for your souls”**
• As if this way, when found, gives refuge to the souls of believers.
• Stand ye on the ways, etc. Let us read the Gospel parable in which the merchant sold all his good pearls to buy one precious one; that is, through the patriarchs and prophets we may come to him who says, “I am the way”; whence: Stand ye on the ways, etc.
**“And they said”** — On the contrary.
**“We will not walk”** — That is, by the way of the Gospel.
6.17:
**“And I appointed watchmen over you”**
• The prophet, speaking properly of the faithlessness of the Jews, at once adds: I appointed over you a watchman.
• Namely the choir of the apostles; whence: “Son of man, I have made thee a watchman to the house of Israel.”
**“Hear ye”** — Saying.
**“To the sound of the trumpet, and they said: We will not hearken”** — Invited to the feast, they would not come.
**“The sound of the trumpet”** — Jerome. The trumpet’s voice: the commands of the gospel, or the teaching of the apostles; whence: “Get thee up upon a high mountain, thou that bringest good tidings to Sion: lift up thy voice like a trumpet, thou that bringest good tidings to Jerusalem.”
6.18:
**“Therefore hear, ye nations”** — Whence: turn ye quickly to the Gentiles.
**“And know”** — Others: Know, you who feed the flock of the bishop, namely also the priests.
**“O congregation”** — Not of the Jews but of all nations.
**“What great things I will do to them”** — To the unbelievers.
6.19:
**“Hear, O earth”** — The whole world, as in that of Isaias: “Hear, O ye heavens, and give ear, O earth”; namely what the Lord is about to do to the people of the Jews.
**“Behold I will bring evils”** — The punishments.
**“Upon this people”**
• Who answered: “We will not hearken.”
• Not upon the nations that are called to the truth.
**“The fruits of their own thoughts”** — Or of their aversions; whence: “For thou shalt eat the labours of thy hands.”
**“Because they have not heard my words”** — With the ear of the heart.
**“And they have cast away my law”** — With an untameable neck.
6.20:
**“To what purpose do you bring me frankincense”** — Whence frankincense comes, according to Virgil: “And a hundred altars glow with Sabaean incense.”
**“And the sweet smelling cane”** — In Hebrew it is canen, for which the Seventy and Theodotion translated cinnamon.
**“From a far country”** — India, namely, from which many spices come by way of the Red Sea.
**“Your holocausts”** — Not mine.
**“Are not acceptable”** — So far as it lies in you.
**“Nor are your sacrifices pleasing to me”**
• So far as it lies in you.
• To what purpose do you bring me, etc. As though in vain you bring me the spices of sweetest odour for making the ointments commanded in the law, and kindle holocausts, you who do not do my will in the law; whence above: “they have not heard my voice,” etc. Allegorically: this applies properly to those who offer sacrifices and alms from the plunder and stripping of the wretched. They think to redeem their sins by iniquity, though the Scripture says: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches.”
6.21:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord: Behold, I will bring destruction upon this people”** — We see all these things fulfilled daily.
**“By which shall fall”** — Nothing in them; perhaps, namely, all weakness is among them.
**“Fathers and sons”**
• “His blood be upon us.”
• The sons follow the blasphemies of the fathers, taking up daily that curse: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”
**“Together”** — Because they have sinned alike.
**“Neighbour and kinsman”** — Not only those, but all who follow the law according to the letter, which kills.
6.22: **“Behold a people”** — This is properly said of the Babylonians, who were to come against Jerusalem; and the whole order of armed men is described, and the onset of those fighting, so that, moved by terror, they may do penance and please the most merciful God.
6.23:
**“They shall lay hold on arrow and shield; they are cruel, and will have no mercy”** — That he may terrify even by his voice.
**“They shall mount upon horses, prepared as men for war, against thee, O daughter of Sion”** — gives occasion for asking the Lord and for appeasing him
**“Their voice”** — Allegorically. Jerome. We can abuse this testimony in a time of persecution, when the whole rage of the devil is stirred up against us, which has no mercy; and like the waves of a very violent sea, they overwhelm those who resist.
6.24:
**“We have heard”** — the answer of the people, to whom the Lord threatened through the prophet
**“The fame thereof”** — the Babylonians
**“Our hands grow feeble”** — that is, through fear we cannot lift up our hands
**“Anguish hath taken hold of us, as a woman in labor”** — they affirm, with the pain of a woman in labor, that they have felt nothing more grievous
6.25: **“Go not out”** — The Gospel also teaches that we are not to go out into the field, nor come down from the height of the roofs, but to hear that word: “In the mountain save me.” To which, in Isaias and Micheas, we are bidden to run. According to the letter he commanded that they should not go out abroad, nor leave the walls, but defend them most firmly with fortifications.
6.26:
**“Gird thee with sackcloth, O daughter of my people”** — he teaches what they ought to do: let them turn, that is, to penance, and have this most firm armour
**“And sprinkle thee with ashes; make thee mourning as for an only son”**
• in Hebrew: of the solitary ones
• nothing is more painful than to lose an only or sole son
**“Make thee a bitter lamentation, because the destroyer shall suddenly come upon us”**
• Nabuchodonosor or the devil
• or another misery; the letter
**“Upon us”** — affectionately: he testifies that God is to come upon himself what is to come upon the people
6.27:
**“I have set thee for a strong trier”** — the Lord to the prophet
**“Among my people”** — unbelieving
**“My people”** — formerly
**“Strong”** — so that you fear nothing, no snares of the people
**“And thou shalt know and prove”** — As if to say: when you have tried and known the way of the sinning people, then you may understand that silver mixed with brass is purged by no method. For as lead is mixed with metals that are adulterated, that the foreign matter may be separated, and if perchance they have been purged the lead is wholly consumed and reduced to nothing, so the word of teaching and the prophetic speech perishes in those who scorn to hear. Let us say this also of those who, like deaf asps, stop their ears that they may not hear the voice of the charmers.
6.28:
**“All of these princes go out of the way”** — by the Lord
**“All of these princes”** — Gregory. The princes are those who depart from the Lord and are disobedient, who walk perversely and deceitfully. For of this melting it is read in Job: “Silver hath beginnings of its veins, and gold hath a place wherein it is melted.” In silver eloquence is signified; in gold, life or the brightness of wisdom. And because heretics so pride themselves on the polish of their speech that they are grounded on no authority of the sacred books, which are to us for speaking as veins of silver, because from them we draw the origin of speaking, he calls them back to the pages of sacred authority, that if they truly desire to speak, they may take from there what they are to say. And “gold hath a place wherein it is melted”: as if the true wisdom of the faithful, whose place is the universal Church, suffers tribulation from us who persecute it, but is purged from all the filth of sins by the fire of our persecution. Whence “gold and silver are tried in the fire, but acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation.” Or, gold has a place wherein it is melted, because whoever suffers outside the unity of the Church can indeed suffer, but cannot become a martyr. Seek, therefore, O heretics, this place of melting; find this furnace in which gold is rightly purged. If you endure any bitterness or any tribulation for God outside it, you can be burned, but not purged. Whence: “The founder hath melted in vain, for their wickedness is not consumed,” etc.; and elsewhere: “If I should deliver my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.” For some think wrongly of God, others dissent from the fellowship of their neighbors. The former are divided by error of faith, the latter by schism. Whence at the beginning of the decalogue the fault of both is repressed, when it is said with the divine voice: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart,” etc., and immediately it is added: “Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.” For he who thinks wrongly of God does not love him. He who is at discord with the unity of the Church does not love his neighbor.
6.29:
**“The bellows have failed”** — accomplishing nothing
**“The lead is consumed in the fire”** — the word of God
**“The founder hath melted in vain”** — or the silversmith
6.30:
**“Silver”**
• therefore
• not gold
**“Call them reprobate silver, for the Lord hath rejected them”** — far from himself

7.2: **“In the gate”** — Through which the multitude of the people enters to pray to the Lord, that on this occasion they may hear what the Lord has commanded. By this we understand the hardness of the Jewish people, who held the prophets as liars and madmen, and yet are compelled by the occasion and the celebrity of the place to hear the word of the Lord.
7.3:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts the God of Israel: Make your ways and your doings good”** — which now are evil
**“Make your ways”** — the most merciful physician of life desires to heal all
**“and your doings; and I will dwell with you in this place”** — because it is natural to love one’s native soil, and nothing sweeter than one’s homeland is promised; rewards to the obedient: I will dwell with you in this place
7.4:
**“The temple of the Lord”** — This may suit those virgins who boast of modesty and with shameless face put forward chastity, while they have something else in conscience. But the true virgin is chaste both in body and in spirit. For what does bodily modesty profit when the mind is corrupted? Or if the virtues are lacking which the prophetic speech enumerates.
**“Trust not in lying words, saying: The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, it is”** — He commanded then the people of the Jews, and today us who seem to be established in the Church, that we should not have confidence in the splendor of buildings, and gilded ceilings, and marble walls, and say, “The temple of the Lord,” etc. For that is truly the temple of the Lord in which there is true faith, holy conduct, and a choir of all the virtues.
7.5:
**“For if you will order well”** — or: you will have directed
**“your ways”** — works
**“and your doings”** — thoughts
**“if you will execute judgment between a man and his neighbour”** — Jerome. If you will have followed justice
7.6:
**“the stranger”** — if you do not do evil to the stranger
**“the fatherless, and the widow”** — who cannot defend themselves
**“oppress not”** — by defending
**“oppress not the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, and shed not innocent blood in this place”** — the simple, that is, by scandalizing
**“and walk not after strange gods”** — by worshipping the perverse doctrines which you have feigned to your own harm
7.7:
**“I will dwell with you in this place”** — which you called, or call, the temple of the Lord
**“in the land, which I gave to your fathers”** — to the apostles and apostolic men
7.8:
**“Behold you put your trust in lying words”** — or: words
**“Behold you put your trust”** — These sins show that they have confidence in the temple in vain. For what does it profit to enter boldly the threshold of the house of the Lord, and to stand with neck erect, and to have defiled not only the heart but also the hands? No one doubts that these things happen spiritually in the Church when, considering the happiness of the present time, men do not amend their sins. But they think that God does not see, because vengeance does not follow at once. And they break out into such madness that they boast of being set free because they have withdrawn from the worship of God.
7.10: **“And you have come, and stood before me in this house, in which my name is called upon, and have said”** — after evil works
7.11:
**“Is this house then, in which my name hath been called upon, in your eyes become a den of robbers? I, I am he: I have seen it, saith the Lord”** — what you think is hidden
**“A den”** — Jerome. I think what is said in the Gospel is taken from this place: “My house shall be called the house of prayer; but you have made it a den of thieves.” Or, as it is in another Gospel, a house of traffic. The Church of God is turned into a den of thieves when thefts, murders, adulteries, perjuries, sacrilege, heresies, and other crimes are practiced in it, when the princes burn with the firebrands of avarice, and possesses a cheap cloak, or at least not a cheap one, once the wealth of kings; whence he adds: “I, I am he,” etc.
7.12: **“Go ye to my place”** — Where, that is, my tabernacle was. Whence: “He rejected the tabernacle of Silo.” For as it fell into ashes, so also will the temple, when it has become the dwelling of like sinners. But as Silo is an example for the temple, so is the temple for us. Whence: “When the Son of man cometh, shalt thou think he will find faith on earth?”
7.13:
**“And now, because you have done”** — that is, similar things
**“all these works, saith the Lord; and I have spoken to you rising up early”** — so that I might free you from darkness
**“and speaking, and you have not heard; and I have called you, and you have not answered”** — “Rising up early, and speaking to you,” etc. Not that with him there is any time without dawn, but because after the quiet of the night, the strength of the body being restored, the soul of men is more vigorous, and, not occupied with pleasures, is able to hear and do what is said; whence: “In the morning I will stand before thee, and will see.” And in Isaias: “My spirit riseth to thee by night, or at dawn, O God, for thy precepts are a light upon the earth”; whence they are called children of light, and not of night nor of darkness, nor sleepers, those namely who keep the commandments of God.
7.14:
**“I will do to this house”** — the temple in which you trust
**“in which my name is called upon”** — so that similar sins may be struck with an equal sentence
**“As I did to Silo”** — He cast off Silo, about to cast off the temple also; he cast off the ten tribes, about to cast off the two tribes also. Let us fear whatever is threatened to that people, and for ourselves as well if we do similar things.
7.15: **“And I will cast you away from before my face, as I have cast away all your brethren, the whole seed of Ephraim”** — the ten tribes over which Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim ruled
7.16:
**“Therefore, do not thou pray for this people”** — Jerome. Lest the prophet seem, in praying, to fail to obtain what he asks, the Lord commands him not to pray for a sinful people who do no penance.
**“and do not withstand me”** — The prayers of the saints can withstand the anger of God; whence it is said to Moses: “Let me alone, that I may strike this people,” etc. And “Phinees stood up, and pacified him,” etc. Aaron too, seizing the censer, stood between the fire and the people about to be burned, and the wrath of God ceased.
*Jerome:* There are two things which hinder prayers so that they are not heard by the Lord: namely, uncorrected and persisting error, and an impenitent heart. For error never merits pardon, except in him who is truly absolved from it. But the impenitent heart sins against the second spirit, by which the people of God is gathered into one, by which the unclean spirit is cast out, by which we are baptized, by which all sins are forgiven, and which the Church receives, that to whom she has forgiven sins they may be forgiven. For he speaks a word exceedingly evil and most impious against the Holy Spirit, in thought or tongue, so that according to the hardness of his heart he treasures up to himself wrath. This impenitence, this blasphemy, or word against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness for ever.
7.17:
**“Seest thou not what they do”** — within and without
**“Seest thou not”** — Lest we think God cruel, who does not allow himself to be asked, he gives the cause why he does not hear. Seest thou not?
7.18:
**“The children gather wood”** — as if there is no age and no sex that dissents from this very impiety
**“and the fathers kindle the fire and the women knead the dough, to make cakes to the queen of heaven”**
• of the moon, or of the host of heaven, or of all the stars
• Jerome. Or preparations, every kind of sacrifice
**“and to offer libations to strange gods”** — who are not gods, but under the names of gods they sacrifice to demons
**“And”** — and
**“to provoke me to anger”** — so; which I do not have, namely
7.19:
**“Do they provoke me to anger, saith the Lord”** — as if the wretches doing this do not understand that this contempt does not harm me, whom anger does not change, but them
**“Is it not themselves, to the confusion of their countenance”** — they will be in everlasting shame
**“upon this place”** — or will drip, that is, will inflict a moderate punishment; but if in a drop there is so great hardness, what will there be if the whole shower is poured out? What will it be in the future?
**“upon men and beasts, and upon the trees of the country and upon the fruits of the earth; and it shall be kindled”** — fury
**“and it shall not be quenched”** — because the people does nothing by which it could be quenched
**“is kindled”** — Jerome. As though what I was unwilling to do for a long time, I am compelled to do by the multitude of your sins: upon men and upon beasts. When God is angry, both men and the things that belong to man feel a similar severity.
7.20: **“Thus saith the Lord God: Behold my fury and my indignation is kindled”** — as if I were not angry by nature, but they provoke me to anger, so that I seem to change my nature; let them therefore feel me angry, which they strive as much as they can to bring about
7.21: **“Thus saith the Lord of hosts the God of Israel: Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices”** — whose temple he rejected; he rejects the sacrifice and publicly accuses them, because they offered not out of reverence for him but out of desire for feasting
7.22: **“For I spoke not to your fathers, and I commanded them not, in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning the matter of burnt offerings and sacrifices”** — For I spoke not, etc. He shows plainly that he first gave the decalogue, written on tables of stone with the finger of God; and that after the offence of idolatry and the head of the calf, he commanded sacrifices to be made to himself rather than to demons, taking away the pure religion of God’s commandments and conceding the blood of victims and the desire for flesh.
7.23:
**“But this thing I commanded them, saying: Hearken to my voice”** — commands in which pure religion lies
**“and I will be your God, and you shall be my people; and walk ye”** — advancing
**“in all the way that I have commanded you, that it may be well with you”** — as though I provide for you, not for myself; I am the true Lord; I do not need the services of servants
7.24:
**“But they hearkened not”** — I saying: hear my voice
**“nor inclined their ear, but walked in their own will, and in the perversity of their wicked heart, and went”** — against that of the apostle: forgetting the things that are behind, and stretching forth myself to those that are before
**“backward”** — desiring the past things
**“and not forward”** — despising the future things
7.25:
**“From the day that their fathers came out of the land of Egypt, even to this day. And I have sent to you all my servants the prophets from day to day, rising up early and sending”** — as above
**“From the day that I brought them out”** — He says that they spent all the time in between in offence against the Lord. Therefore the grace of the Gospel was necessary, which would preserve them not by merit but by the mercy of God.
7.26: **“And they have not hearkened to me”** — it is plain that the wrath of God justly dripped down upon the people, despisers of a stiff neck
7.27:
**“And thou shalt speak to them all these words, but they will not hearken to thee; and thou shalt call them”** — nevertheless
**“but they will not answer thee”**
• such is their pride that they disdain to answer
• And thou shalt speak to them, etc. Do not doubt that they have hardened their necks, etc. Behold, God gives a place for repentance; nor do I speak for this reason, that what I say may be done, but because I foretell future things. Now at least speak to them with my words.
7.28:
**“And thou shalt say to them: This is a nation”** — not the people of God
**“which hath not hearkened to the voice of the Lord their God, nor received instruction: Faith is lost”** — the faith of Christians
**“and is carried away out of their mouth”**
• the sons of God and the confession of faith
• This is the nation, etc. This happened in the time of the prophets and went before in shadow. It was fully completed in Christ, whose discipline they were unwilling to hear. Whence it is elegantly added: faith has perished, which is properly that of Christians.
7.29:
**“Cut off thy hair, and cast it away: and take up a lamentation on high: for the Lord hath rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath,”** — the people of the Jews; and this is properly to be referred to the time of Christ, when faith perished and was carried away from the mouth of the people blaspheming the Lord
**“Cut off thy hair”** — Among the ancients it was the custom of mourners to shave the hair; now, on the contrary, to let the hair grow long is a sign of mourning.
7.30:
**“Because the children of Juda have done evil in my eyes, saith the Lord”** — from whom nothing is hidden, even in my temple
**“saith the Lord. They have set their abominations”** — the idols of Baal
7.31:
**“And they have built the high places of Topeth”**
• which in Hebrew is Ramath
• or Aramtophet, with another letter
**“The high places of Topeth”** — Jerome. Tophet in Hebrew is “breadth” in Latin; it is a place in the valley of the sons of Ennon. And in Hebrew it is called Geennon. For Ge means valley; Ennon sounds the name of a man, or “grace.” And the Hebrews hold that Gehenna was named from this place, because all the people of the Jews perished there, offending the Lord. In which place they also consecrated their sons to idols in the fire.
**“which is in the valley”** — It signifies a place watered by the springs of Siloe, pleasant and wooded, and even today it offers the delights of gardens. But the error of the Gentiles occupied all the provinces, so that they sacrificed victims at the heads of springs and in the most pleasant groves.
**“and their daughters”** — If Jephte offered his virgin daughter, it was not the sacrifice that pleased God but the mind of the offerer. For if a dog or an ass or any unclean animal had first come to meet him, he ought not to have offered it to the Lord.
7.32:
**“Therefore behold the days shall come, saith the Lord”** — namely of the siege, which they suffered from the ninth year of king Sedecias to the eleventh
**“and it shall no more be called Topeth, nor the valley of the son of Ennom: but the valley of slaughter”** — because of the slaughter of many
**“and they shall bury in Topeth”**
• there will be so great a slaughter
• in the place of its worship
**“because there is no place”** — Behold the days shall come, etc. When he withdrew from the faithfulness of his Lord, then it began. But when the king of Egypt came to free Jerusalem, Nabuchodonosor put him to flight. Afterwards Nabuzardan besieged it and took it, and led Sedecias into Antioch, and there he was blinded.
7.33:
**“And the carcasses shall be”** — who could not be buried
**“of this people, meat for the fowls of the air, and for the beasts of the earth, and there shall be none to drive them away”** — because each will fear for himself, or be too worn out for the duty of burying
7.34:
**“And I will cause to cease”** — Jerome. We pass over the manifest things so that we may linger on the hidden ones
**“And cease”** — When the place of idolatry was turned into graves, so that where they had offended God, there their unburied corpses would lie.
**“out of the cities of Juda”** — which were subject to Jerusalem
**“and out of the streets of Jerusalem, the voice of joy, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride”** — so that all things may be filled with mourning and lament

8.1:
**“At that time, saith the Lord, they shall cast out the bones of the kings of Juda, and the bones of the princes thereof, and the bones of the priests”** — which greed dug up
**“They shall cast out the bones”** — We see in our time that all that the prophets' word describes has happened, not to Jerusalem alone, which suffered this from the Chaldeans and Romans, but to the whole world, so that now tears have dried up and everything is filled with the bones of the dead.
**“and the bones of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, out of their graves”** — Seeking gold and silver and the other things that were placed in tombs according to ancient custom.
8.2:
**“And they shall spread them abroad to the sun, and the moon, and all the host of heaven”** — so that those whom they served, God having been forsaken, be exposed to their sight
**“whom they have loved, and whom they have served, and after whom they have walked, and whom they have sought, and adored: they shall not be gathered, and they shall not be buried: they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth”** — unburied
8.3: **“And death shall be chosen rather than life”** — if any could flee
8.4:
**“And thou shalt say to them: Thus saith the Lord: Shall not he that falleth”** — by sinning
**“Shall not he that falleth rise again”** — by repenting
**“and he that is turned away”** — from the Lord
**“shall he not turn again”** — to him
**“And thou shalt say”** — After so many evils he calls to repentance those who remained. Or, before the things he threatened come, he exhorts them to conversion, and grants a place for penance.
8.5:
**“Why then is this people in Jerusalem turned away with a stubborn revolting? they have laid hold”** — stubbornly
**“lying”** — idols or whatever is perverse and contrary to truth and justice
**“and have refused to return”**
• who, though they could, eagerly pursued wickedness
• Why then, etc. As if: the more I provoked them to penance, the more they withdrew, not so much from zeal for sinning as from zeal to overcome me.
**“is turned away”** — Or, he has turned away. As one turned, he can resist and turn away by the prayers of God.
8.6:
**“I attended, and hearkened”** — whether they would return, whether they said anything good
**“no man speaketh what is good, there is none that doth penance for his sin, saying”** — in mouth or heart
**“What have I done? They are all turned to their own course, as a horse”** — with neck raised against God
**“rushing to the battle”** — No man speaketh what is good, etc. Every kind of men is prone to evil. In the time of the Saviour “all have turned out of the way; they are become unprofitable together: there is none that doth good.” Whence he himself says: “Save me, O Lord, for there is now no saint.” Where then are those who say that it is placed in our power to be without every sin?
8.7:
**“The kite”** — to which it is like: “The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master’s crib,” etc.
**“in the air”** — Jerome. In the air.
**“hath known her time: the turtle, and the swallow, and the stork have observed the time of their coming: but my people”** — It is to be pronounced with grief.
**“have not known the judgment of the Lord”** — about to come upon.
**“The kite in the air”** — As if the birds too know their seasons, so that, hastening to warm places, they know when they ought to avoid the rigor of winter, and at the beginning of spring return to their accustomed regions.
8.8:
**“How do you say”**
• O you scribes and Pharisees.
• as if boasting of knowledge of the law, and you write iniquity.
8.9:
**“The wise men are confounded”** — who, of course, can be condemned by their own judgment; the wisdom of these is foolishness. Whence: you who teach another do not teach yourself.
**“they are dismayed, and taken: for they have cast away the word of the Lord, and there is no wisdom in them”** — but he boasts of knowledge of the law in vain who by his works destroys the teaching.
8.10:
**“Therefore I will give their women”** — or wives.
**“to strangers”** — to enemies.
**“their fields”** — possessions.
**“to others for an inheritance”** — who will hold them forever.
**“because”** — as if they themselves are the cause, not my cruelty.
**“from the least even to the greatest all follow covetousness”** — which is the root of all evils.
**“from the prophet even to the priest”** — who ought to have restrained.
**“all deal”** — by seizing what belongs to others.
**“lying”** — so that truth is not in their mouth.
**“Therefore I will give”** — They have received their reward; and those who cast off the word of the Lord have themselves been cast off.
8.11:
**“And they healed”** — such men.
**“the breach of the daughter of my people disgracefully, saying Peace”** — of the mind.
**“Peace”** — of the body.
**“when there was no peace”** — rather, war hangs over sinners.
**“And they healed the breach”** — Like good physicians they desired to heal the wounds of others with words, though they themselves were wounded with every crime. This too we see daily among our people. Whence: “Thou that preachest that men should not steal, stealest,” etc. For when sinners and rich men see such people, they desire to heal the breach of the daughter of my people, that is, of the Church, and the disgrace of those who deceive, saying Peace, peace, etc.
8.12:
**“They are confounded”** — understanding the abomination which they committed.
**“because they have committed abomination”** — namely in their own crimes.
**“yea rather they are not confounded with confusion”** — not indeed; rather they have broken out into such madness that they desire neither by shame to amend their faults nor by hope of pardon to confess.
**“and they have not known how to blush: therefore shall they fall among them that fall in the time of their visitation”** — of captivity.
**“they shall fall, saith the Lord”** — to us.
**“Therefore shall they fall”** — So that those whose dignity was eminent are mixed in also in the fall of the people; as though, namely, all from the least to the greatest are of themselves.
8.13:
**“Gathering”** — in Jerusalem, namely that they may be besieged by the Chaldeans for a long time and tormented by famine.
**“I will gather them together, saith the Lord; there is no grape on the vines”** — to us.
**“and there are no figs”** — the people being besieged, because the figs are the enemies
**“on the fig tree, the leaf”** — in winter
**“is fallen: and I have given them the things that are passed away”**
• which they might see as things past and not dare to touch, and grieve the more
• There is no grape on the vines, etc. As though the seasons passed away and autumn followed summer, and in winter the leaves of the trees fell: you will see all things from afar and will take no food from them.
8.14:
**“Why do we sit still? assemble yourselves, and let us enter”** — The Septuagint, or cities
**“into the fenced city, and let us be silent there”** — because we do not dare to entreat
**“for the Lord our God”** — whom we have offended
**“hath put us to silence, and hath given us water of gall to drink”** — because we make sweet God bitter to ourselves
**“Why do we sit still”** — The voice of the people is introduced, answering, confessing its faults, and exhorting one another: “Assemble, and let us enter the fenced cities.” Or, one city, Jerusalem; for the others had already been taken.
*Jerome:* A change of persons especially makes the prophets difficult to understand; which, if they are rendered in their own places, causes and times, become plain, where they seemed obscure.
8.15:
**“We looked for peace”** — who have done no good
**“and no good came: for a time of healing”** — our
**“and behold fear”** — all full of fear
8.16:
**“The snorting of his horse was heard from Dan”** — as though he narrates things already past, for the truth of the matter
**“his”** — Nabuchodonosor
**“at the sound of the neighing”** — otherwise: of neighings
**“of his warriors, all the land was moved”** — hyperbole
**“and they came and devoured the land, and all that was in it: the city”** — Jerusalem
**“and its inhabitants”** — or the inhabitants of the land
**“From Dan”** — Where the river Jordan rises. Nabuchodonosor is described coming from Dan through Phoenicia with his army.
8.17:
**“For behold I will send among you serpents, basilisks”** — the eagle, the basilisks
**“against which there is no charm: and they shall bite you, saith the Lord”** — I will send among you serpents, etc. So that I may strike them incurably. Those who have despised God’s commands pour out prayers in vain against the ancient serpent, the crooked dragon. So likewise those who despise the words of the Lord are handed over to the adverse powers.
8.18: **“My sorrow is above sorrow”** — These things are to be read as spoken in the person of the Lord, lamenting the overthrow of Jerusalem and not bearing its misery.
8.19:
**“Behold the voice of the daughter of my people from a far country: Is not the Lord”** — The Father
**“Is not in Sion”** — as though therefore there is a voice of crying in Jerusalem, because its king has withdrawn from it
**“or is not her king in her”** — The Son, of whom it is said: “Give to the king thy judgment, O God: and to the king’s son thy justice.”
**“why then”** — why then did the king withdraw from them, because they provoked me to wrath
**“have they provoked me to wrath with their idols”** — idols
**“and strange vanities”** — the ceremonies of the nations
**“And behold the voice”** — He describes the weeping and wailing of the city when the enemies have entered.
8.20: **“The harvest is passed”** — The words of the people shut up in Jerusalem by a long siege, because the seasons are changed and the circle of the year has been completed. But our hope is in vain.
8.21:
**“For the affliction of the daughter of my people I am afflicted”** — anthropospathos
**“For the affliction”** — The Lord’s answer: he who seems afflicted in the affliction of Jerusalem.
8.22:
**“Is there no balm”** — the medicine of penance
**“Is there no physician there”** — a prophet or priest, by whose remedy it ought to have been cured
**“Why then is not the wound closed”** — of sin

9.1: **“Who will give water to my head”** — The king of Jerusalem, the city being besieged by enemies, at night broke the wall of the city and fled into the plain of Jericho; he was taken with his followers and led to Antioch; he was blinded before his sons.
9.2: **“Who will give me in the wilderness a lodging place of wayfaring men, and I will leave my people, and depart from them? because they are all adulterers, an assembly of transgressors”** — Who will give, etc. As if to say: it is better to dwell in the wilderness than to stay among such great crimes of men. Whence in the gospel: “How long shall I suffer you?” And elsewhere: “He that understandeth shall sit and keep silence, for it is an evil time.”
9.3:
**“And they have bent their tongue, as a bow, for lies, and not for truth; they have strengthened themselves upon the earth, for they have proceeded from evil to evil”** — that they may deserve to hear: “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt go.”
**“and me they have not known, saith the Lord”** — because this is the cause of evils
**“For they have proceeded from evil to”** — Sinners pass from evil to evil when they exchange one idol for another, and fall from sin into a worse sin; or from siege into captivity. Of the saints it is said: “they shall go from virtue to virtue”; but of sinners, “they have proceeded from evil to evil.” The cause of the evils is that they have not known the Lord, and are a company of transgressors, and a tongue arming itself for blasphemy.
9.4:
**“Let every man take heed of his neighbour”** — beware of kinsman, brother, and dear companion
**“and let him not trust in any brother of his: for every brother will utterly supplant, and every friend will walk deceitfully”** — The name of friendship is empty; the name of faith is empty.
**“Let every man”** — Jerome. The crafty enemy, when he sees himself driven out of the hearts of the good, seeks out those who are greatly loved by them, and speaks flatteringly through the words of those who are loved more than the rest, so that while the force of love pierces the heart, the sword of persuasion may easily break into the inmost parts of the innermost rectitude.
**“of his neighbour”** — Which is also: “And a man’s enemies are they of his own household.” The favour of brothers is also rare. And the father will betray the son, and the son the father. And two will be divided against three, and three against two.
9.5:
**“And a man shall mock his brother, and they will not speak the truth: for they have taught their tongue to speak lies: they have laboured to commit iniquity”** — use makes a master; custom is a second nature
**“for they have taught their tongue to speak lies”** — lying words
**“they have laboured to commit iniquity”** — that is, they strive to do iniquity
9.6:
**“Thy habitation is in the midst of deceit”**
• O Jeremias
• or Jerusalem
**“in the midst of deceit”** — of a deceitful people
**“Through deceit they have refused to know me”** — daily increasing sins
**“to know me, saith the Lord”** — I who forbade this
9.7:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts: Behold I will melt”** — or I will test by fire
**“and try them: for what else shall I do before”** — shamelessness
**“the daughter of my people”**
• Jerusalem
• And I will test, etc. In the furnace of tribulation. The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, so that whatever is of adulterated matter in us may be burned out; for the silver of the Lord, tried by fire, is proved in the earth.
9.8:
**“Their tongue is a piercing arrow”** — of heretics, who wound the hearts of hearers and of the ignorant; against whom it is said: “With all watchfulness keep thy heart.”
**“it hath spoken deceit: with his mouth”**
• not of God
• because he speaks in heart and with heart. Whence: “Who speak peace with their neighbour, but evils are in their hearts,” and “the venom of asps is under their lips.”
9.9:
**“Shall I not visit for these things”** — so many and so great
**“Shall I not visit them”** — with a rod
**“saith the Lord? or shall not my soul be revenged on such a nation”** — so wicked
**“Shall I not visit them for these things”** — He often repeats this verse, so that, having listed their evils, he may show that he justly does what he does.
9.10:
**“For the mountains”**
• With the Babylonian laying waste everything, the desolation of the province is prophesied.
• Tropologically. Weeping is taken up over the mountains, and lamentation over the beautiful places of the desert, when the princes of the Church sin, and nothing of the substance of God is found in it, nor is heard the voice of Christ, who possesses the Church through apostolic men. And “from the fowl of the air even to the beasts”: that is, from those who can ascend to the heights even to the simple, they have departed from God.
**“I will take up”** — or take up
**“weeping and lamentation, and for the beautiful places”** — or paths
**“of the desert, mourning: because they are burnt up”** — or have failed
**“for that there is not a man”**
• man
• there is none who walks through the land
**“that passeth through them”** — all having been cut down, nothing remained that could live
**“and they have not heard the voice of the owner”** — or of any substance, namely possession
**“from the fowl of the air”** — all things feel the wrath of God
9.11:
**“And I will make Jerusalem”**
• the Church
• or the transmigration
