• When the ecclesiastical teachers fail, Jerusalem is given into heaps of sand, or into transmigration, so that heretical speech may prevail in it. And thus the den of dragons, and its cities are made desolate, that the divine word may not dwell in it, he who says: “I will dwell in them, and walk among them.”
**“to be heaps of sand, and dens of dragons”** — of heretics
**“the cities of Juda”** — of confession
**“desolate, for want of an inhabitant”** — God
9.12:
**“Who is the wise man”** — the prophet
**“that may understand this”** — namely in Jerusalem
**“and to whom the word of the mouth of the Lord may come”** — worthily
**“that he may declare this”** — to others
**“why the land hath perished”** — he opens the cause
**“is burnt up”** — laid waste
**“like a wilderness”** — by God
**“which none passeth through”** — all having been slain
9.13:
**“and the Lord said”** — The prophet introduces the Lord answering and giving the reasons
**“Because they have forsaken my law, which I gave them, and have not heard my voice”** — precepts
9.14:
**“But they have gone after the perverseness of their own heart, and after Baalim”** — Baalim is plural; Baal singular; an idol of the Sidonians
**“which their fathers taught them”** — The error of parents is not to be followed, but the authority of the Scriptures and the command of God teaching
**“of their own heart”** — We must trust not in our own heart but in the Lord. The heart of man is depraved, from which come depraved thoughts.
9.15:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts the God of Israel: Behold I will feed this people with wormwood, and give them water of gall to drink”** — with necessities and distresses
**“give them water of gall”**
• the greatness of the evils and everlasting exile, or ignorance of the law; for instead of Christ they are going to receive Antichrist
• “Therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts,” etc. It can be prophesied of the near time when they were taken by the Chaldeans, and properly of this, that they are scattered among all the nations and divided through the whole world.
9.16: **“the sword”** — Either a material or a spiritual sword, by which they are divided, so that they do not consent to evil but perish in that they are evil.
9.17:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts the God of Israel: Consider ye, and call for the mourning women, and let them come: and send to them that are wise women, and let them make haste”** — that they may speak
**“and call for”** — Call for the mourning women, because of the coming captivity and the overthrow of the city. He bids them call the mourning women, who with a tearful voice and beaten arms invite to tears. For this custom remains to this day in Judea, that women with hair dishevelled and breasts bared, with a measured voice, pour the people into tears.
9.18:
**“Let them hasten and take up a lamentation for us: let our eyes shed tears”** — or yours
**“shed tears, and our eyelids run down”** — or yours
**“let our eyes shed tears”** — The prophet, or God himself, joins himself with the affection of one who suffers, so that he himself is said to bear and feel what the people endure.
9.19:
**“For a voice of wailing is heard out of”** — or in
**“Sion: How are we wasted”** — it is the voice of those lamenting in Sion
**“and greatly confounded”** — they answer themselves
**“because we have left”** — by our own fault
**“the land, because our dwellings are cast down”**
• which they once possessed as if passing through, or were possessing
• “How are we wasted,” etc. Let the crowd of believers say this under persecution, who are therefore laid waste and confounded because they have forsaken the law of the Lord and abandoned their tabernacles.
9.20:
**“Hear therefore, ye women”** — to negligent men
**“the word of the Lord: and let your ears receive the word of his mouth: and teach your daughters wailing: and every one her neighbour mourning”** — “Hear therefore,” etc. Above he said, call for the mourning women, etc. Now he addresses them as if present, to shame the priests and teachers and all men, so that while those men cease from teaching, the women may hear the word of the Lord.
9.21:
**“because”** — the cause of tears
**“death is come up”** — of sinners
**“through our windows”** — of the senses
**“it is entered”** — to the destruction of the soul
**“into our houses”** — minds
**“to destroy”** — for destroying
**“the children”** — by sense
**“from without”** — outside the Church
**“young men”** — the light-minded who walk the broad way that leads to death
**“from the streets”** — when these things have been accomplished
**“For death is come up”** — That the strength and speed of the enemies will be so great that they will not wait for the gates but will climb in through the windows and roofs.
9.22:
**“Speak: Thus saith the Lord: Even the carcass of man shall fall”** — corpses of the dead
**“of man as dung upon the face of the country, and as grass behind the back of the mower, and there is none to gather it”** — Speak: Thus saith the Lord, etc. The Hebrew word, which is written with three letters, daleth, beth, resh, has no vowels in the middle, and by the reader’s choice in what follows: if it is read dabar it signifies “word”; if deber, “death”; if daber, “speak.” Whence the Septuagint and Theodotion joined it to the end of the chapter, which they ended so as to read: “the young men from the streets, by death.” Aquila and Symmachus translated “speak,” so that the Lord commands the prophet.
**“As grass”** — “As grass.” That behind the back of the reaper it is neglected as useless. In which it is shown that there will be so great a slaughter in the city and round about that there will be no one to bury the falling.
9.23: **“Thus saith the Lord: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom”** — all pride is removed; the only and true glorying is to know God and understand
9.24: **“But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, for I am the Lord that exercise mercy, and judgment, and justice in the earth: for these things please me, saith the Lord.”** — That exercise mercy, etc. Although some things seem unjust, yet he does all things justly, all things providently. Where then are those who say that man is ruled by his own choice, and that the power of free will is so given that they take away the mercy and the justice of God? The apostle sets down this testimony, saying: “He that glorieth, may glory in the Lord.”
9.25: **“Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, and I will visit upon every one that hath the foreskin circumcised.”** — Behold, the days come, etc. Many nations, and above all those bordering on Judea and Palestine, are circumcised to this day, especially the Egyptians and Edomites, Ammonites, Moabites, and all the region of the Saracens who dwell in the wilderness, and who are shorn in the hair. Therefore Juda ought not to glory if he is circumcised according to the law; for circumcision profits not unless you keep the law.
9.26:
**“Upon Egypt”** — namely
**“and upon Juda”** — circumcised in the flesh, not in the heart
**“and upon Edom, and upon the children of Ammon, and upon Moab, and upon all that have their hair polled round”** — It signifies a nation, not the strength of fighters
**“that dwell in the desert: for all the nations”** — other nations
**“are uncircumcised in the flesh”** — of the flesh
**“but all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart.”** — not in the flesh, which leads to death

10.1: **“Hear ye the word”** — He speaks properly against those who worship the heavenly bodies, which were set as signs of years and seasons and months and days, as if the human race were ruled by them and earthly things were governed by the causes of the heavenly bodies.
10.3:
**“For the laws of the people”** — human wisdom
**“are vain”**
• they are useless
• a description of idols
**“for ... a tree”** — base and corruptible matter
**“the works of the hand of the workman hath cut a tree out of the forest with an axe”**
• who, being mortal, cannot make immortal things
• Wood, etc. What we have said of idols let us refer to heretics. For they promise great things and fashion images of a vain worship out of their own heart. They boast of grand things, and as if with golden senses and silver speeches they bind the edge of the unlearned; their teachings are carried by their own inventors, in whom there is no profit; their cult is proper to the Gentiles and to those who know not God.
10.4:
**“He hath decked it with silver and gold: he hath put it together with nails and hammers”** — the wonderful power of idols, which cannot stand by itself
**“With silver and gold”** — Jerome. That he may seize and deceive the simple with the brightness of the matter. This error has come down even to us, so that we think religion lies in riches.
10.5:
**“They are framed after the likeness of a palm tree”** — as if they had the beauty of matter and painting, but nothing useful or living
**“and shall not speak”** — whence they have a mouth and do not speak
**“they must be carried to be removed”** — therefore he who carries them is stronger
**“Therefore, fear them not”** — Many of the nations are accustomed to worship demons, lest they harm, and to beg others that they may profit. Whence Virgil: “A black sheep for winter, and a white one for the kindly west winds.”
10.6:
**“There is none like to thee, O Lord”** — These are not found in the Septuagint, but in many copies they are added from Theodotion.
**“There is none like”** — There is none like to thee, O Lord, of the gods, namely those that are feigned by heretics.
10.7:
**“Who shall fear thee, O king of nations?”** — The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.
**“for thine is the glory”** — beauty is in truth, deformity in falsehood
**“among all the wise men of the nations, and in all their kingdoms there is none like unto thee.”** — For thine is the glory, etc. Although heretics, according to the wisdom of the world which is destroyed, seem wise to themselves, yet in all the kingdoms that tear the Church, none is like the Lord. Whence: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject.”
10.8:
**“They shall be all proved together to be senseless and foolish”** — together
**“the doctrine of their vanity is wood”** — vile
10.9:
**“Silver”** — like silver: in the charm of eloquence
**“spread into plates”** — by the craft of words
**“from Tharsis”** — a region of India according to Josephus, or any sea
**“is brought from Tharsis, and gold from Ophaz”** — or: Ofaz
**“the work of the artificer, and of the hand of the coppersmith: violet and purple is their clothing: all these things are the work of artificers.”**
• or of the wise
• supposedly, for before God they are foolish
**“all these things”**
• Wrapped up, etc. Otherwise: it does not deceive; falsehood is wrapped up, and truth is opened.
• Hyacinth, etc. So that they deceive those who look at the surface, while they show the colour of heaven to themselves and promise heavenly things.
**“Ophaz”** — One of the seven names by which gold is called among the Hebrews, which we may call refined gold, so that what lies hidden within shines on the surface.
10.10:
**“But the Lord is the true God”** — those lies
**“he is the living God”** — those dead
**“and the everlasting king”** — those transitory
**“at his wrath the earth shall tremble”** — earthly
**“and the nations shall not be able to abide”** — not the people of God
10.11:
**“Thus then shall you say to them: The gods”** — these things are to be said to the false gods
**“that have not made heaven and earth”** — Which the co-workers of Christ, who are called gods and lords, have partly made through ecclesiastical teaching.
10.12:
**“He that”** — the Father
**“maketh the earth by his power”** — to the Son, who is called the power and wisdom of God
**“that prepareth the world”** — The Seventy: and he set up the world.
**“by his wisdom”** — To the Son: “For he spoke, and they were made: he commanded, and they were created.” Speaking to the Son: “Let us make man,” etc.
**“He that maketh the earth”** — Origen. The Lord, who maketh the earth by his power, etc. The prophet, taking in a certain manner three powers of God, power, wisdom, prudence, assigns to each its proper works: to power the earth, to wisdom the world, to prudence the heaven. In our earth, then (of which it was said, “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt return”), we have need of the power of God, without which it is impossible to carry out what is repugnant to the flesh. But when the members that are upon the earth have been mortified, then the spirit obeys the will. For by the spirit the deeds of the flesh are mortified. The Lord therefore maketh the earth by his power, which (as it is written in Job) he hath set upon nothing; whereby it is established that by the power of God the earth is held balanced in the middle of the world. I come also to the world, which in Greek is here called oikoumene, that is, the inhabited. I know a soul inhabited. I know one deserted. If then it has not God the Father and the Son saying: I and the Father will make our abode with him, and the Holy Spirit, it is truly deserted. But that soul is inhabited which is full of God and has Christ and the Holy Spirit. Hence David in the psalm of confession: “Strengthen me with a principal spirit.” “Renew a right spirit within my bowels.” “Take not thy holy spirit from me.” These things we have said in proof of this, that the inhabited, that is, the world, was built by the wisdom of God. For wisdom helpeth the just man, “having power over ten cities.” For “he that rejecteth wisdom and discipline is unhappy, and his hope is vain, and their labours without fruit, and their works unprofitable.” Let us labour, then, that our soul, being inhabited, may be raised up by the wisdom of God. For it fell from on high when we came into the place of miseries; it fell after we sinned. Finally, whoever or whatever is in this world fell before being raised up. For we all fell through sin into the world. But the Lord lifted up those who lay fallen, and by his prudence stretched out the heaven. Neither power nor wisdom is taken up in the stretching out of the heaven. Whence: The Lord by wisdom founded the earth, and prepared the heavens by prudence. There is therefore some prudence of God, which I would not have you seek outside Christ. For all things that are of God are Christ. He is his wisdom, he is power, justice, holiness. He is also prudence. But though it is one in the underlying reality, it is called by different names according to the variety of senses. For wisdom signifies one thing, justice another. For when it is called wisdom, it instructs you in the disciplines of things human and divine. When justice, he is signified as the distributor and judge of merits. So understand his prudence here, when it is teaching and demonstration of things good or bad or neither. And so now he is said to have stretched out the heaven by his prudence; whence: I stretched out my words, and you did not attend. For it asserts that there is a certain stretching out of words, as of the heaven. Whence: who stretcheth out the heaven like a skin. For our soul is stretched out, which before had been contracted. Those who bear the heavenly man are heavens. For if to the sinner it is said, “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt return,” why should it not be said to the just man: heaven thou art, and into heaven thou shalt return? Or if, on account of the earthy, it is said to him who bears the image of the earthy, earth thou art and into earth thou shalt return, why on account of the heavenly is it not said to him who bears the image of the heavenly: heaven thou art, and into heaven thou shalt return? Each of us has either heavenly or earthly things made for him. If they are earthly, they lead down to the earth, akin to them, the man who laid up treasure for himself on earth and not in heaven. But if heavenly, they bear their treasurer up to the region near to them.
10.13:
**“At his voice he giveth a multitude of waters”** — All the teaching of the Lord flows from heavenly things. Whence: “A free rain thou shalt separate, O God, to thy inheritance.”
**“in the heaven, and lifteth up the clouds”** — Concerning which: “I will command my clouds that they rain no rain upon it.”
**“from the ends”**
• not from consuls, not from leaders, not from the rich; for “blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”
• when with bright teaching he satisfies the parched hearts of men
• He who wishes to be first among you, let him become last. Otherwise, no one becomes a cloud.
**“of the earth”** — before frail, now firm by the strength of God
**“he maketh lightnings for rain, and bringeth forth the wind out of his treasures.”**
• in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge
• Lightnings for rain, etc. Origen. It is said that lightnings are generated from the collision of clouds or showers, as from harder flints struck together fire slips out between them. Moses was a cloud, and Jesus Nave also; while they strike against each other, lightnings flash from their words. Jeremias also and Baruch, conversing together, send forth gleaming lightnings.
**“the clouds”** — Which they know, namely, by whom they hang up the rains and to whom they bestow them.
**“and bringeth forth the wind out of his treasures”** — That is: The winds which blow through the lands are not from the treasures of God, because their nature is manifest; but there are treasures of winds, that is, of spirits: namely the spirit of wisdom and of understanding, the spirit of counsel and of fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and of godliness, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord. These treasures are before this hidden in Christ. Hence it comes about that one is wise, another faithful, and the like.
10.14:
**“Every man is become a fool for knowledge”** — holy
**“in them”** — heretics
**“Is become a fool”** — A fool by comparison with God. For “the foolishness of God is wiser than men,” namely wise men. For God made foolish the wisdom of the world, not in his own wisdom; for the wisdom of the world cannot grasp the wisdom of God, nor does the wisdom of God deign to descend in its whole to convince the wisdom of the world. But some small thing was necessary, which was the foolishness of God. For God took on all contraries that he might dissolve contraries.
**“For what he hath cast is false”** — Origen. What he feigns in his heart. For what he has cast is false, just as every man is foolish “by knowledge”; for what he makes is foolish.
**“There is no spirit in them”** — It is to be noted that in this chapter wind and spirit are called by one name among the Hebrews, ruach.
10.15:
**“They are vain things”** — For they are either rustic, like wood; or ringing with high-sounding speech, like silver; or feigned from their own sense, they lie like gold.
**“They are vain things and a ridiculous work: in the time of their visitation they shall perish”** — In the time of visitation, etc. Heresy has force for a time, that they who are approved may be made manifest. When the visitation of God has first come and has looked on all things with his eyes, all things will fall silent.
10.16:
**“The portion of Jacob is not like these”** — namely of those who have supplanted the Jews and destroy heretics. Whence: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.”
**“For it is he who formed all things”** — both in the soul and in the body
**“And Israel is the rod”** — every one who is upright in God, or, discerning God in his understanding, is the sceptre of his inheritance
**“Of his inheritance the Lord of hosts is his name”** — Sabaoth
10.17:
**“Gather up”**
• O Jerusalem
• Jerusalem is commanded to gather up into the most strongly fortified city whatever substance it has outside, and to prepare food far off for the siege. For God does not threaten, as before, things far in the future, but things immediately to come.
**“out of the land”** — fields
**“thy shame, thou that dwellest in a siege”** — your substance; for whatever you have is worthy of shame
10.18:
**“For thus saith the Lord: Behold”** — not another
**“I will cast away far off”**
• from their land
• as from a sling
**“the inhabitants of the land at this time: and I will afflict them, so that they may be found”** — namely, not being able to flee in the city
10.19:
**“Woe is me for my destruction, my wound is very grievous. But I said: Truly”** — the words of Jerusalem confessing its guilt
**“this is my own evil”** — patiently
**“and I will bear it”**
• or I will endure the anger of God
• Woe is me, etc. Jerusalem laments that it has been violently afflicted and with an incurable wound.
10.20:
**“My tabernacle”**
• dwelling
• Jerusalem laments its overthrow, made so easy that you would think not walls were torn down but a tabernacle taken away.
**“is laid waste”** — because I have sinned against him
**“all my cords”** — of the tent
**“are broken: my children are gone out from me, and they are not”** — slain
**“there is none to stretch forth my tent any more”** — that is, one who would restore me and lay the foundations of the walls
**“And they are not”** — For they were not carried away into Chaldea, but a great part of them was slain and destroyed.
10.21:
**“Because the pastors have done foolishly”**
• metaphorically
• the princes, through whose fault the people are scattered
**“and have not sought the Lord; therefore have they not understood, and all their flock”** — the people
**“Flock”** — Jerome. The Septuagint: flocks. This cannot stand according to history; for in so long a siege the flocks would not have lasted.
10.22:
**“Behold the sound of a noise cometh, a great commotion”** — of the coming Babylonians
**“out of the land of the north: to make the cities of Juda a desert”** — with the inhabitants slain
**“and a dwelling for dragons”** — The voice of hearing, etc. All these things which the former and present discourse describes let us refer to the times of the persecution of the Church, when the tabernacles of the Lord are overthrown and the dwelling of the Church is reduced to desolation. All of which happens through the fault of the shepherds, who acted foolishly and sought not the Lord.
**“Dragons”** — Or ostriches. Symmachus: sirens. So that dragons and all poisonous things dwell in place of men. Or ostriches, which are born and reared in the wilderness, familiar with desolation. Or sirens, that is, certain monsters and phantoms of demons.
10.23:
**“I know, O Lord, that the way of a man is not his”** — of the Babylonians, but of my merit and your indignation
**“to walk, and to direct his steps”** — I know, etc. Let them blush who say that each one is ruled by his own will. For “the way of a man is not his,” etc. Whence David: “By the Lord shall a man’s steps be directed.”
10.24:
**“Correct me, O Lord, but yet with judgment: and not in fury, lest thou bring me to nothing”**
• David agrees with this: O Lord, rebuke me not in thy fury, nor chastise me in thy wrath, etc.
• In judgment, etc. As if to say: what we suffer is great, and we remember greater; but correct as a father a son, do not afflict as an enemy a foe. For you chastise every son whom you receive, and with every pain and scourge you amend Jerusalem. But the nations, which have not known you, deserve not judgment but indignation.
10.25:
**“Pour out thy indignation”** — not judgment
**“upon the nations that have not known thee, and upon the provinces that have not called upon thy name: because they have eaten up Jacob”** — as if you had delivered us that we might be amended; but they made their yoke heavier, and spared neither age, nor sex, nor rank, nor place.

11.1:
**“The word”** — Namely that which was in the beginning with God. For this is the profit of preachers, if the word of God comes to individuals. For what does it profit me that he came into the world, if I do not have him who was made to the prophets, and the disciple says: I am with you even to the consummation of the world.
**“The word that came from the Lord to Jeremias, saying”** — The word that came, etc. It is not set down in the title at what time, or under what king, or in what year of his reign this prophecy was made; but we understand that it is to be joined to the former prophecy and time. Or that after an interval of time this word of the Lord was made to the prophet. But properly the word is now directed to the men of Juda and Jerusalem.
11.2:
**“Hear ye the words of this covenant”** — The word berith: Aquila and Symmachus always render it pactum (covenant); the Seventy and Theodotion render it testamentum.
**“and speak to the men of Juda, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem”**
• To the men of Juda, etc. Allegorically: namely Christians. For Christ sprang from Juda, of whom it is truly said: “Juda, thee shall thy brethren praise: thy hand shall be upon the back of thy enemies,” etc.
• Jerusalem, etc. Of the Church, which is the city of the great King and the vision of peace. For peace is multiplied and discerned in her.
11.3: **“Cursed”** — Origen. For the Jews are cursed, who did not hear the testament of God when he led them out of the land of Egypt. But we who believe in Christ obey his testament, which is handed down through Moses; and this is said to us, that we may not be cursed.
11.4:
**“Which I commanded your fathers in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, saying: Hear ye my voice, and do all things that I command you: and you shall be my people”** — so, that is, not otherwise
**“I brought them out”** — Jerome. Origen. God led us also out of Egypt and the iron furnace, namely out of the world and its distress; for the place where the Lord was crucified is specially called Sodom and Egypt.
**“From the iron furnace”** — It signifies the greatness of tribulation and punishment, not some place made of iron material prepared for punishment.
**“Hear ye my voice”** — As if he said: not by privilege of race, not by the prerogative of circumcision, not by the rest of the sabbath, but on account of obedience I become the God of Israel, and he my people. And here indeed he speaks to servants; in the gospel to friends: “You are my friends, if you do the things that I command you.” “I will not now call you servants,” etc. But when they have been friends, they pass from friends into sons. “But as many as received him, he gave them power to be made the sons of God.” But to friends and sons he commands: “Be perfect, as your Father is perfect.” He commands likeness, not equality. In the law, obedience to the commandments is the likeness of God.
**“And I”** — He is not the God of all, but only of those to whom he gives himself. Whence: “I am thy God”; and elsewhere he says of others also: “I will be their God”; and “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Expounding which the Saviour says: “But God is not of the dead, but of the living.” The dead man, namely, is the sinner.
11.5:
**“That I may accomplish the oath which I swore to your fathers”** — The fathers are received in their sons, and the promises to Abraham are fulfilled in the sons.
**“to give them a land flowing with milk and honey”** — hyperbolically
**“Milk and honey”** — Honey and milk signify abundance of all things, as Virgil says: “Honey flows for them, and the bramble bears the rough mulberry.” Or tropologically: the land flowing with milk and honey is the Church, in which little ones are nourished with milk until they can take solid food.
**“as it is this day”** — that is, as is proved today by the things themselves
**“And I answered and said: Amen, O Lord”** — The Seventy: “Let it be, O Lord,” which is the same.
11.6:
**“And the Lord said to me”** — God often foretells the future so that the unbelieving may be softened; and he foretells it both in the city and outside, so that those whose danger is one may have one and the same penance.
**“And the Lord said”** — The voice of the prophet longing for the Lord’s promise to be fulfilled, as if to say: Truly, O Lord, you have fulfilled what you promised. Or: Let it be, O Lord, that is, let what you have given always remain.
11.7:
**“For protesting I conjured your fathers in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt even to this day: rising early”** — as above
**“I conjured them, and said: Hearken ye to my voice”** — Because protesting, etc. The words “until they did these things” are not found in the Septuagint. What follows, “and they did not,” is placed by them at the end of the previous chapter. Hear the words, etc.
11.9:
**“And the Lord said to me: A conspiracy is found among the men of Juda, and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem”** — Others read colligatio: as if with one mind and eagerness they despise the commandments of God.
**“A conspiracy is found”** — Origen. “A conspiracy is found among the men of Juda,” etc. If we have sinned, we who are called men of Juda because of Christ, it is said of us: A bond, or conspiracy, is found among the men of Juda and among the inhabitants. Jerome: since in the Church there are such persons in whom the snare of iniquity and the chains of sin are found, of whom it is said: “Everyone is bound with the chains of his own sins.” “They are returned to the former iniquities of their fathers.” He does not say simply of their fathers, but added “of their fathers, the former.” For we have two kinds of fathers, and there is one kind of the worst fathers. Before we believed, the devil was our father. Whence: “You are of your father the devil.” But when we have believed, we are made sons of God. If afterwards we sin, we return to the iniquities of the former fathers. “For everyone who commits sin is born of the devil.” So as often as we sin, we are born of the devil. Unhappy is he who is always begotten by the devil; but happy is he who is always born of God. For I will not say that the just man is born of God once only, but by each work of virtue he is always born of God. Our Saviour also is the brightness of glory. And brightness is not born once and then ceases; but as often as the light from which the brightness arises is kindled, so often the brightness of glory also arises. Our Saviour is the wisdom of God, and wisdom is the brightness of eternal light. So then our Saviour is always being born. Whence he says: “Before all the hills he begetteth me,” not, as some wrongly read, “he begot.” You also, in his likeness, if indeed you have the spirit of adoption, are always begotten of God, through each understanding, through each work, and are made a son of God in Christ Jesus.
11.10:
**“They are returned to the former iniquities of their fathers, who refused to hear my words; so these likewise have gone after strange gods, to serve them; the house of Israel have made void my covenant”** — the ten tribes
**“and the house of Juda”**
• two
• so that, as their zeal is shared, their punishment is shared
11.12: **“shall cry”** — In their necessities; and I will not hear, because they would not hear me, which Saul also suffered. For when he feared the Philistines and had not deserved to receive the word of God, he turned to the witch, so as to learn from idols what he ought to have wrung from the Lord by urgent prayer and tears. Whence we learn that if the Lord does not hear, we must not cease. For he is quickly turned from anger, and changes his sentence, if those with whom he is angry are changed. But all that is now said pertains to Juda and Jerusalem, on whom captivity is pressing.
11.13: **“For according to the number of thy cities were thy gods, O Juda; and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem thou hast set up altars of confusion, altars to offer sacrifice to Baalim”** — According to the number, etc. In the book of Kings and Paralipomenon we find that Juda and Jerusalem did far worse things than Israel: that as many cities as they had, so many kinds of idols they had; and as many as were the streets and crossways in the city, so many altars they had, to their own confusion, at which to sacrifice to idols.
11.14: **“Therefore, do not thou pray for this people, and do not take up praise and prayer for them; for I will not hear them in the time of their cry to me, in the time of their affliction”** — Therefore, etc. The prophet is commanded not to pray for those against whom sentence has already been completed, lest his prayer seem weak and deservedly unheard. “Do not take up praise for them,” etc. As if: do not, by repeating the clemency of the old history, in which I am accustomed to have mercy, and by praising my mercy, strive to change my sentence. “For I will not hear them,” who cry out compelled by affliction. From this we learn that it is in vain to ask for one who does not deserve to receive.
11.15:
**“What is the meaning that”** — the people of Juda
**“my beloved hath wrought much wickedness in my house”** — by venerating idols
**“shall the holy flesh”** — as if by a multitude of such sacrifices your sins are not blotted out
**“What is the meaning”** — Jerome. Let us say this to the princes of the Churches, or to the rich, who, while they seize what belongs to others and do not remove the wickedness of their heart, think they deserve the clemency of God. “Shall the holy flesh,” namely, etc. But now the names of the offerers are publicly recited, and the redemption of sins is turned into praise; nor is the memory of the widow of the gospel celebrated, who put more than all into the treasury.
11.16:
**“The Lord called thy name a plentiful olive tree, fair, fruitful, and beautiful; at the noise of a word a great fire was kindled in it”** — or: fire in it
**“and the branches thereof are burnt”**
• the people
• by the sword of enemies. Whence: “The boar out of the wood hath laid it waste”; and “The Lord called thy name a plentiful olive tree, fair, fruitful, and beautiful: at the noise of a word, a great fire was kindled in it, and the branches thereof are burnt.”
• At the noise of a word, etc. As one exalted through pride, you did not humbly understand your Creator and Lord, but having spoken grandly against the Lord, kindled by his fire you shall be reduced to nothing.
11.17:
**“And the Lord of hosts that planted thee hath pronounced evil against thee; for the evils of the house of Israel, and the house of Juda”** — not undeservedly, since God could do what he wills, yet he sets out the causes, lest he seem unjust. Whence: “That thou mayest be justified in thy words, and mayest overcome when thou art judged.”
**“which they have done”** — Zealously.
**“to provoke me, offering sacrifice to Baalim”** — And the Lord, etc. “The Lord called thy name a plentiful olive tree, fair, fruitful, and beautiful”; and he planted thee; but “at the noise of a word, a great fire was kindled in it.”
11.18:
**“But thou”**
• The Father.
• The Jews and our Judaizers refer this to the person of Jeremias, and assert that he endured these things from the people on account of his prophecy of evils to come. But how do they prove that he was crucified, since scripture does not say this, unless perhaps they say that the people thought it and did not do it?
**“But thou, O Lord”** — according to the man.
**“hast shewn me”**
• how I ought to speak.
• To the Son.
**“and I have known; then thou shewedst me their doings”**
• of the Jews.
• As the wood sent by Moses into the bitter water made it sweet. For before the wood was put into his bread, when there was only bread and not wood, their sound had not gone out into all the earth.
*Origen:* “But thou, O Lord,” etc. Or: “Make it known to me, O Lord, and I shall know,” according to the Psalmist: the Lord teacheth man knowledge; whence: “Be not called masters upon earth.” For “one is your master, who is in heaven”; who, namely, instructs man either by himself or through the Son. He instructs also through Paul, through Peter, or any of the saints. Only let God the Spirit and God the Word come down and teach. “Make it known to me, O Lord, and I shall know,” as if: I cannot know unless thou reveal it. But with thee showing, I shall see the thoughts of each, and what they do, or what their will is. “Let us put wood on his bread,” etc. The bread of Jesus by which we are nourished is his word. Because, while he was teaching, some wished to place a stumbling block against his doctrine, crucifying him, they said: “Let us put wood on his bread,” etc. For when the crucifixion of the master is joined to his word and teaching, wood is put on the bread; and they indeed, plotting, say: Let us put wood on his bread. But I shall bring in something invisible or wonderful: the wood put on his bread made his bread better, that is, his doctrine sweeter.
11.19:
**“And I was as a meek lamb that is carried to be a victim”** — of the cross.
**“and I knew not”** — sin; whence: “him, who knew no sin, he hath made sin for us.”
**“that they had devised counsels against me, saying: Let us put wood”** — of the cross.
**“on his bread”**
• the body of the Saviour, who is “the bread that came down from heaven.”
• it was a proverb in Israel.
**“and cut him off from the land of the living”**
• that his name be blotted out.
• Origen. If a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it brings forth much fruit.
11.20:
**“But thou, O Lord of Sabaoth”** — The Son according to the flesh speaks to the Father and calls down his judgment.
**“who judgest justly”** — rendering to each what he deserves.
**“and triest the reins and hearts; let me see thy revenge”** — namely of those who persist in wickedness, not of those who repent.
**“on them”** — the obstinate; for for the others he says: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.
**“for to thee”** — Because I am crucified not by my merit but by their wickedness. Whence: “For the prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not any thing.”
11.21:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord to the men”** — the Jews.
**“of Anathoth”** — Obedience.
11.22: **“Therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts: Behold I will visit upon them; their young men shall die by the sword, their sons and their daughters shall die by famine”** — Therefore thus saith the Lord, etc. This seems contrary to the above, in which we fit what is said to the person of Christ, not of Jeremias, who properly dwells in the little village of Anathoth. But by Anathoth (which is interpreted obedience) we understand the Jews, and especially the people of Jerusalem, who once obeyed the commands of the Lord. But because they departed from the Lord, the final sentence came upon them, that their young men should die by the sword, etc. But to free ourselves from all trouble of interpretation, let us follow this rule: that all the prophets did very many things as a type of the Saviour, and that what is fulfilled in the present in Jeremias is prophesied for the future of the Lord.

12.1:
**“Thou indeed, O Lord, art just, if I plead with thee; but yet I will speak what is just to thee: Why doth the way of the wicked prosper”** — of heretics.
**“why is it well with all them that transgress”** — in the law.
**“and do wickedly”**
• by despoiling the Church.
• Just indeed, etc. The disputation is against all who act wickedly, as in that psalm: “How good is God to Israel, to them that are of a right heart,” etc. But especially against heretics.
12.2:
**“Thou hast planted them”** — as they boast.
**“and they have taken root; they prosper and bring forth fruit”** — by deceiving.
**“thou art near in their mouth, and far from their reins”** — Whence: “This people honoureth me with their lips: but their heart is far from me.”
12.3:
**“And thou, O Lord”** — Father.
**“thou hast known me, thou hast seen me”** — The Son: “No one knoweth the Son but the Father; neither doth any one know the Father but the Son.”
**“and proved my heart with thee; gather them together”** — in Jerusalem, or in assemblies.
**“as sheep for a sacrifice, and prepare them”** — from vices.
**“for the day of slaughter”**
• by slaying, sanctify; for whom the Lord loves, he rebukes, he scourges.
• And thou, O Lord, etc. As if he said: it is no scandal if the wicked or heretics flourish for a time. For though they prosper, though they bring forth children, though thou art near in their mouth and far from their reins, that is, from their conscience, yet it is no small consolation that they are marked out or sanctified for the victim, like sheep.
• In the day of slaughter. The slaying of heretics is the salvation of the deceived, when they have been slain, that is, by the sword of the Church.
**“gather them together”** — At Passover, when all were gathered for the festival day, then they were besieged and led into captivity.
12.4:
**“How long”** — until, that is, the mind of sinners is changed.
**“shall the land mourn”** — barren.
**“and the herb of every field”** — which were created for the use of men are consumed for their sins.
**“wither for the wickedness of them that dwell therein”** — namely the cause.
**“The beasts and the birds are consumed, because they have said”** — since all things are done by the providence of God.
**“He shall not see our last end”** — what we are about to suffer.
12.5:
**“If thou hast wearied with running with footmen”**
• by weariness.
• As if to say: if the captivity of neighboring peoples has worn you out, namely of the Moabites, Philistines, Ammonites and Idumeans, who because of the difficulty of the places are fit more for robbery than for battle.
**“how canst thou contend with horses? and if thou hast been secure in a land of peace”** — that is, if you have had some confidence in your land, what will you do when you have crossed the Jordan, when you have endured its swirling waters?
**“what wilt thou do in the swelling”** — swelling.
**“of the Jordan”** — How, etc. That is, what will you do when you come into captivity in Chaldea? For the Chaldeans and Persians delight in horses.
12.6:
**“For”** — Even.
**“even thy brethren”** — The Idumeans.
**“and the house of thy father”** — Moab and Ammon, who are of Lot.
**“Even they have fought against thee”** — with the Chaldeans.
**“And have cried after thee with full voice: believe them not when they speak good things to thee”**
• as kinsmen: no one is more harmful than a familiar enemy.
• For even thy brethren, etc. This can be understood of Christ, against whom the brethren cried out: “Crucify him”; “We have no king but Caesar.”
12.7:
**“I have forsaken my house”**
• coming into this earthly place.
• Whence: “Your house shall be left to you desolate; arise, let us go hence.”
**“I have left my inheritance”**
• the heavenly Jerusalem.
• Jacob, the cord of inheritance.
• that is, “as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee.”
**“I have given my dear soul”** — whence I have power to lay down my soul.
**“into the hand of her enemies”** — of the Jews.
12.8:
**“My inheritance is become to me”** — the people of Israel
**“as a lion in the wood”** — together roaring, Crucify him.
**“it hath cried out against me, therefore have I hated it”** — that she who was once beloved may be called hateful
**“My inheritance”** — Origen. It is no wonder that the inheritance was then likened to a fierce beast, since even to this day there are lions in the wood, anathematizing Christ and blaspheming and lying in wait for the faithful.
12.9:
**“Is my inheritance to me as a speckled bird?”** — Israel had such great beauty that there was no good thing which did not shine in it; but now, come, etc.
**“my inheritance to me as a speckled bird? Is it as a bird dyed throughout?”** — yet
**“come ye, assemble yourselves, all ye beasts of the earth”** — diverse nations
**“make haste to devour”** — because they did not know their God.
**“Is it as a bird dyed throughout?”** — Septuagint. Is my inheritance to me a den of the hyena? The hyena is a nocturnal beast that devours the corpses of the dead, digs bodies out of tombs, and feeds on all filth; Israel is compared to it in its uncleanness.
12.10:
**“Many pastors have destroyed my vineyard”** — Israel
**“they have trodden my portion under foot”** — lot
**“they have changed my delightful portion”** — once
**“into a desolate wilderness”** — without God
**“desolate wilderness”** — Many pastors, etc. Jerome. Let those hear this who wish to be rulers, and to render an account in the day of judgment for what is committed to them; for because of them the portion of the Lord is trodden under foot and defiled, and where once was the lodging of God is the dwelling of beasts. Others understand not the rulers of the people and the priests, but the princes of the enemy, who have scattered the people of God.
12.11:
**“They have laid it waste, and it hath mourned for me. With desolation is all the land made desolate”** — that is, deprived of my help
**“all the land, because there is none that considereth”** — God
**“in the heart”** — With desolation, etc. Origen. When the Jews filled up the measure of their fathers and added to the killing of the prophets even that of the Saviour, then all their land was laid waste with destruction.
*Origen:* Consider the earth that is in thee, how it has been laid waste, and thou wilt see that after the coming of Christ the things have been fulfilled which were said: “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth.” Since now the earth does not work its works, nor are those things done among the just by which the flesh was formerly cherished, namely fornication, uncleanness, lust, etc. Whence: “I came not to send peace, but the sword.” Before he came there was no sword upon the earth, neither did the flesh lust against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh. But when he came, and we were taught what belongs to the flesh or to the spirit, his teaching, like a sword sent in, divided the earth, that is, the flesh from the spirit, and laid it waste, because we bear about the mortification of Jesus in our body, and we do not live according to the flesh, but the spirit lives. And we sow not in the flesh but in the spirit, that we may reap not corruption from the flesh but life everlasting from the spirit.
12.12:
**“The spoilers are come upon all the ways of the wilderness”** — enemies
**“for the sword of the Lord shall devour from one end of the land”** — from end to end
**“to the other end thereof”** — other end
**“there is no peace for all flesh”**
• also of those fleeing from the city
• There is no peace, etc. The flesh cannot receive God’s peace in itself. For the wisdom of the flesh is an enemy to God, and those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
12.13:
**“They have sown wheat, and reaped thorns”** — as though they looked for good things and evil came; prosperity, and behold, adversity.
**“they have received an inheritance”** — they received abundance of all things from the Lord.
**“and it shall not profit them”** — which, namely of the clergy, will not profit them.
**“you shall be ashamed of your fruits, because of the fierce wrath of the Lord”**
• They have sown, etc. This too is said to churchmen who destroy the word of the Lord by an evil way of life. Of whom it is added by the Septuagint: the things of clerics shall not profit them. For the name of bishop, priest and the like will profit them nothing, but rather they will be burdened by their dignities, and the mighty will mightily suffer torments, and from him to whom more is committed, more is required.
• Of your fruits, etc. Septuagint. Of your glorying, namely in precious garments, adorned houses, many possessions, worldly wisdom; but “he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord,” and in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in his infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in him.
12.14:
**“Thus saith the Lord against all my wicked neighbours, that touch”** — or lay waste
**“the inheritance”** — that is, the Church
**“my wicked neighbours”** — Literally: the Idumeans, Philistines, Moab and Ammon. Allegorically: heretics who are called Christians and become kin by marriage to the holy land rather than its inhabitants.
12.15:
**“And when I shall have plucked them out”** — from the jaws of the enemy heretics
**“I will return, and have mercy on them: and I will bring them back, every man to his inheritance”** — the Church
**“every man to his land”** — of the living
12.16:
**“And it shall come to pass, if they will be taught”** — returning from heretics
**“will learn”** — in the Church
**“the ways of my people, to swear by my name”** — not of idols, which they have fashioned in their heart
**“The Lord liveth, as they have taught my people to swear by baal: that they shall be built up in the midst of my people”** — by the Lord, a part of his people
12.17:
**“But if they will not hear”** — my words
**“I will utterly pluck out that nation”**
• remaining in heresy
• from my people
**“pluck out and destroy”** — with perpetual uprooting and destruction, so that no place of penance is left. This we see every day and prove by experience: that heretics feign the truth of the faith in order to deceive the simple, yet they themselves never return.

13.1:
**“Thus saith the Lord to me: Go, and get thee a linen girdle”** — as I the sons of Israel
**“linen”** — linen, or a girdle
**“and thou shalt put it about thy loins, and shalt not put it into water”**
• lest it be spoiled
• Go and get, etc. A holy man is called the girdle of God, who was taken from the slime of the earth and is joined to his fellowship. And in a certain way he surrounds with greater diligence what seems unseemly in the Church, lest it lie open to the bites of the Gentiles and heretics. If this girdle touches water and crosses the streams of the Euphrates, steeped in Assyrian moisture it loses its former strength and rots. And although it returns to the use of God, yet it will not be able to have its former fullness, not through the hardness of God but through its own fault, because it would not hear the word of the Lord. Let him therefore beware who can say: “But it is good for me to adhere to my God,” lest perhaps through negligence he be separated from his loins and cross the Euphrates and be given into the power of the king of the Assyrians, and be taken up not in the most solid rock but in a hole of the rock, corrupt and defiled, that is, in the filth and vices of heretics, and come to such rottenness that he can no longer return to the use and girdle of the Lord.
• The girdle is the people of Israel, who, like linen taken from the earth and unwashed, had neither softness nor whiteness, and yet through the mercy of God clung to God. But when it had sinned, it was led across the Euphrates, that is, into the Assyrians, and was hidden there, that is, swallowed up in a way by the multitude of innumerable nations and reckoned as nothing.
13.2: **“And I got a girdle”** — or a girdle
13.3: **“And the word of the Lord came”** — after he sinned
13.4:
**“Take the girdle”** — from you, as it was taken from me
**“which thou hast got, which is about thy loins, and arise”** — because I will rise up to take vengeance
**“go to the Euphrates”** — to the Assyrians
**“and hide it”** — the aforesaid, to be swallowed up
**“there in a hole of the rock”** — And hide it, etc. Origen. The Jews showed themselves unworthy of God and were cast away by him; in their place God has girded himself with us. For it is not to be thought that he who cast away the girdle remained ungirded; as soon as he cast away some, he wove others for himself, that is, the Church from the Gentiles, which from black was made bright and white. Whence: “Who is this that cometh up” made white? Let her know, however, that if he spared not the natural branches, neither will he spare her, if she is not worthy of his loins, that is, if, not adhering to the Lord, she is not one spirit in Christ.
13.5: **“And I went, and hid it”** — in the type of the Lord
13.6: **“And it came to pass after many days, that the Lord said to me: Arise, go to the Euphrates, and take from thence the girdle”** — as I will bring back the sons of Israel
13.7:
**“And I went to the Euphrates, and digged, and took the girdle out of the place where I had hid it”** — as a sign of captivity
**“And took the girdle”** — Into captivity. It signifies, however, that the prophet frees the people in the type of the Lord, yet nonetheless sins. Afterwards he follows strange gods; at last he lays hands on the Son of God, and therefore wastes away in eternal destruction.
13.9:
**“Thus saith the Lord God”** — adapts the likeness
**“will I make the pride of Juda to rot”** — of the two tribes of Judah
13.10: **“This wicked people, that will not hear my words, and that walk”** — following their own vices
13.11:
**“For as the girdle sticketh close to the loins of a man, so have I brought close to me all of the house of Israel”** — the ten tribes
**“and all the house of Juda”** — the two tribes
**“saith the Lord: that they might be my people, and for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory, and”** — yet
**“but they would not hear.”** — me, who did all these things
13.12:
**“Thou shalt speak therefore to them this word: Thus saith the Lord God of Israel: Every bottle”** — that is, good or bad
**“shall be filled with wine, and they shall say to thee: Do we not know that every bottle shall be filled with wine?”**
• suited to the merits of each.
• Every bottle, etc. This is the drunkenness by which we forget the commandments of God, and the human condition is filled with vices and sins. Whence: “in thy sight no man living shall be justified.” Not in comparison with God, as the old and new heretics and their patrons wish, but according to his knowledge; for man sees the face, God the heart, and what seems clean to us is found unclean to him.
• The Hebrew word is nebel; the first edition of Aquila has “bottle,” the second nebel itself. Symmachus has “bowl,” the Septuagint “wineskin,” Theodotion “vessel”; they interpreted that everything is filled only with wine and drunkenness. For we are a fragile vessel and we have a treasure in earthen vessels, in which this is fulfilled: “in my flesh dwelleth no good”; “for the good which I will, I do not; but the evil which I will, that I work”; and “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?”
13.13:
**“And thou shalt say to them: Thus saith the Lord: Behold I will fill all the inhabitants of this land”** — not only the common, lowly people.
**“and the kings”**
• of the churches.
• that is
**“of the race of David that sit upon his throne”** — lying back, with the neck held up and the belly stretched out, that is, the stomach.
**“and the priests”** — the second rank in the Church.
**“and the prophets”** — who seem to have knowledge of the Scriptures.
**“and all the inhabitants”** — for the variety of sins.
13.14:
**“And”** — that is
**“I will scatter”** — so that the pain of punishment may grow, while they do not console themselves with mutual words.
**“them”** — the drunken.
**“every man from his brother, and fathers and sons in like manner”** — that they may be defiled by diverse errors and heresies, so that under the name of Christ they may fight against their mother, the Church.
**“And I will scatter”** — With reasonable anger, that I may lead back from error by pains and torments those who cannot be turned by words.
**“I will not spare”** — Not by cruelty of sentence but by the truth of judgment. For those who have slain shall perish forever. According to the history we take this simply: that the kings and priests and prophets and all the people of Jerusalem were to be made drunk with the cup of Babylon and overwhelmed by captivity.
13.15:
**“Hear ye”** — as much inwardly as outwardly, as much in mind as in body.
**“and give ear: Be not proud”** — into pride, as if to say: consider your frailty, for there is no one who, according to the quality of sin, is free from this drunkenness.
13.16:
**“Give ye glory to the Lord your God”** — that is, do penance; whence elsewhere: “Give glory to your God.”
**“before it be dark”**
• in the day of judgment.
• for you in Babylon.
**“before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains”**
• Babylon and every region of the Chaldeans are called dark mountains; whence Isaias: “Upon the dark mountain lift ye up a banner.”
• the shadowy demons, who are set over the torments.
**“you shall look for”** — here
**“light, and he will turn”** — there
**“it into the shadow of death, and into darkness”** — Give glory to the Lord, etc. He calls them to penance before they are led into Babylon.
**“Allegorically.”** — Give glory to the Lord, etc. As if to say: work while it is day; the night will come when you cannot work. Whence also Isaias: “The stars of heaven shall not give their light, and they shall be darkened at the rising of the sun,” etc. And Sophonias: “a day of darkness and whirlwind.”
13.17:
**“But if you will not hear this, in secret”** — so that not even groaning and weeping are free, lest the victors be offended.
**“my soul shall weep”** — of God or of the prophet.
**“for your pride”**
• of the victors
• of the unrepentant
• whence
**“weeping it shall weep”** — that is, I will not be able to hide my grief.
**“and my eyes shall run down the tears, because”** — by the devil or Nabuchodonosor
**“the flock of the Lord is carried away captive”** — ironically
**“But if you will not hear this”** — Let us say to the Jews and to our judaizers, who follow the letter that killeth: Unless you hear in secret, that is, in mystery, or according to Aquila in the darkness which he made his hiding place, and according to Solomon you understand the parable and the dark speech, the soul of the prophet shall weep for their pride.
**“is carried away captive”** — By the devil or Nabuchodonosor, or crushed. Sometimes Israel was the flock of the Lord, but because they judged themselves unworthy of salvation, the word was turned to the Gentiles. Let the wild olive, grafted contrary to nature into the good olive, beware lest it too be crushed.
13.18:
**“Say”** — the voice of the Lord to the prophet
**“to the king”** — to Jechonias
**“and to the queen”** — to his mother
**“Humble yourselves, sit down”** — in the dust
**“for the crown of your glory is come down from your head”**
• royal dignity handed over to the Babylonian
• Say to the king and to the mighty. He raves in this place who understands the king as Christ and the mighty as angels, that they may take the body of humility, and sit in the dust, and lose from their head the crown and the glory of strength. Also that the cities of the south are shut up, and hell, so that they may be opened to none; and that all the glory has been transferred to Juda, when in the passion it was fulfilled: “all have turned out of the way; they are become unprofitable together.”
• Say to the king and to the queen, etc. The Manichean said that a good nature was created by God, but an evil one by the devil. And that certain angels suffered for the redemption of the demons, and that after the judgment the gates of hell are shut and no one is punished there; which Origen seems to think, and which is frivolous.
**“Say to the king, and to the queen”** — The Hebrew word gebiza: Aquila and Symmachus translated it as “mistress” and “lady.” The Septuagint, thinking it was geburoth, said “the powerful.”
13.19:
**“The cities of the south”** — Judea and Jerusalem, which is to the south, has been turned
**“are shut up, and there is none to open them”** — shut up by siege
13.20:
**“Lift up your eyes”** — O inhabitants of Jerusalem
**“and see, you that come”** — the Chaldeans
**“from the north”** — O Jerusalem
**“where is the flock”** — the people
**“that is given thee”** — by God
**“thy beautiful cattle”** — a glorious multitude, as if the whole province were gathered into one
13.21:
**“What wilt thou say when he shall visit thee?”** — by handing you over to the Babylonians with the rod
**“for thou hast taught them against thee”** — by fleeing to their help and worshipping idols, who under the pretext of friendship learned by which way they might come to you
**“and instructed them against thy own head: shall not sorrows”** — of captivity
**“lay hold on thee, as a woman in labour”**
• suddenly, while you do not know
• For thou hast taught them against thee, etc. Let the negligent Church hear this, which teaches its adversaries how they may seize her with spiritual captivity and tear her flock with bestial cruelty.
**“For thou hast taught”** — When Ezechias showed the treasure to the messenger of the king of Babylon.
13.22:
**“And if thou shalt say in thy heart”** — that is, if you seek the cause
**“Why are these things come upon me?”** — I answer
**“For the greatness of thy iniquity, thy nakedness is discovered”**
• with garments lifted up
• as of a harlot, so that your fornication may lie open in public
**“Thy shame is uncovered, thy heels are defiled”** — For the greatness, etc. Jerome. Hence we learn that so long as sins are lesser, God acts patiently and awaits our penance. But if we join sins to sins and make heaps of sins, our shameful parts will be revealed, either in this world or in the next. For there is nothing covered that shall not be revealed, when that word of Daniel shall be fulfilled: these shall rise “to life everlasting, and the others to reproach and everlasting confusion.”
13.23:
**“If he can change”** — as if they cannot, God can
**“The Ethiopian”** — black in sins
**“his skin, or the leopard his spots”** — the diversities of vices
**“you also may do well, when you have learned evil”**
• by effort, not by nature
• If the Ethiopian can change his skin, etc. Those use this testimony who try to assert diverse natures, saying that the blackness or variety of sins is so great that it cannot pass into whiteness and the beauty of one color. They do not attend to this: “when you have learned evil.” For whatever is spoken of is not of nature but of study and of one’s own will, which by the custom of sinning in a manner passes into nature. But what is impossible to men is possible to God, so that it is not the Ethiopian or the leopard who seems to change his nature, but he who works in them. Whence the apostle: “I can do all these things in him who strengtheneth me.” And “yet not I, but the grace of God,” and “I live, now not I; but Christ liveth in me.” And “what hast thou that thou hast not received? And if thou hast received, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?” Let not the wise man therefore glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, and the like, which the power of Christ works in all.
13.24:
**“And I will scatter them”** — as by the effort of sinning they could not change nature
**“as stubble, which is carried away by the wind in the desert”** — whence as dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth
13.25:
**“This is thy lot”** — O Jerusalem
**“and the portion of thy measure from me, saith the Lord”** — which you have chosen for yourself. Whence: “In what measure you have meted, it shall be measured to you again.”
**“because thou hast forgotten me”** — the cause of the dispersion of Israel
**“and hast trusted in falsehood”** — in temporal things
13.26:
**“Wherefore I have also bared thy thighs”** — or your hinder parts; that she may indeed see her shame, and what ought to be behind come to be in front
**“against thy face, and thy shame hath appeared”** — to all
**“thy shame”** — I have bared thy thighs, etc. Let us pray Christ that he reveal not our hinder parts, neither in the present nor in the future, but blot out our iniquities and not suffer our crimes to appear.
13.27:
**“thy adulteries and thy neighing, the wickedness of thy fornication”** — as of mares that rage for coupling; whence Virgil: “A slow poison drips from the groin.”
**“upon the hills in the field”** — not only in the city
**“I have seen thy abominations”** — idols
**“Woe to thee”** — therefore
**“Jerusalem. Wilt thou not be made clean after me”**
• though you boast that you follow my footsteps and flaunt the confession of my name
• I will wait as long as I bear it
**“Upon the hills”** — Allegorically. He who, with head held high through pride, is not humbled under the mighty hand of God, but trusts in his crimes, fornicates upon the hills and in the fields and is never cleansed.

14.1: **“which”** — that is, because
14.2:
**“Judea hath mourned”** — for the famine of the word of God
**“and the gates thereof are fallen”** — boasting that it previously had the worship of God and the confession of true faith
**“and are become obscure”** — by sins
**“on the ground, and the cry of Jerusalem is gone up”**
• confused, unreasonable
• And the gates, etc. Namely the senses, through which instruction is taken into the soul.
• And they are become obscure, etc. All things agree with the wrath of God; whence the sun goes down upon sinners at noon, and the moon and stars do not give their light. But it is to be thought that in the time of the siege there were no rains, that the besieged might endure a barrenness of water. For the city uses one spring, Siloe, and that not perpetually, and even to the present day the barrenness of rains causes want not only of crops but of drink.
14.3:
**“The great ones”** — the great ones, who themselves ought to go
**“sent their inferiors”**
• in whom there are no grey hairs of wisdom
• which the patriarchs are read to have found
**“to the water: they came to draw, they found no water, they carried back”** — the lesser ones; not because there was no water, but because those could not find it
**“their vessels empty: they were confounded and afflicted, and covered their heads”** — because with unveiled face they do not contemplate the glory of God
14.4:
**“For the destruction of the land, because there came no rain upon the earth”** — for the desolation of the land, because no rain came upon the earth; the cause being that indeed a command was given to the clouds not to pour rain upon it
**“the husbandmen were confounded”** — the husbandmen were confounded, not understanding that without the grace of God they make no progress
**“Husbandmen”** — One of them said: “You are God’s husbandry; we are God’s coadjutors.”
14.5:
**“For”** — great is the barrenness
**“the hind also brought forth in the field”** — which poisonous things kill
**“and left it”** — to which they are likened
**“because there was no grass”**
• the pasture of grace
• For the hind also, etc. Gregory. For the hind also. Either the hind brought forth in the field, or the hinds brought forth. This sentence is spoken of teachers who incautiously forsake the sons they have begotten. But hinds are well likened to teachers, who after the manner of hinds, vices being slain as serpents killed, live, and from that burn more keenly for the fountain of life. Whence: “As the hart panteth after the fountains of water, so my soul panteth after thee, O God.” They also, while the passing moments of this time go by like rivers, bearing with one another in charity, lay their burdens upon each other, because with careful observance they keep what is written: “Bear ye one another’s burdens: and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ.”
14.6:
**“And the wild asses stood”** — Whence Job, who let the wild ass go free
**“upon the rocks”** — leaving the plains, not able to run
**“they snuffed up the wind like dragons”** — are drawn by the smell of their nostrils
**“their eyes failed, because there was no grass”** — They snuffed up the wind like dragons, etc. Gregory. The perverse, like dragons, draw in the wind when they are puffed up with wicked pride.
**“Their eyes failed”** — Not able to discern the clear light, the rational food being withdrawn. This dryness often befalls the Church when stags and wild asses are found among the peoples, and through lack of teachers they waste away; there are those who learn, not those who teach.
14.7:
**“If our iniquities have testified against us”** — as though our iniquities are the cause of all these things
**“O Lord, do thou it for thy name's sake”** — not according to our works
**“for our rebellions are many”** — we cannot overcome them; you overcome, who can overcome
**“our rebellions”** — the sins by which we are turned away from you, and you from us
**“we have sinned against thee”** — who searchest the hearts and reins
14.8:
**“O expectation”**
• true
• in you alone we hope; we await you
**“of Israel, the Saviour thereof in time of trouble”** — Whence: “In my trouble I cried to the Lord: and he heard me.”
**“why wilt thou be a stranger in the land”** — “He came unto his own, and his own received him not.”
**“and as a wayfaring man”** — who rejoiced as a giant to run the way
**“turning in to lodge”**
• The expectation of Israel, etc. Let us also say, in the time of dryness and lack of water: “To thee we have sinned, and have done evil before thee”; he awaits thy coming, thou who savest Israel, not by his own merit but by thy grace.
• As a husbandman, etc. Gregory. For he, who was not heard as Lord, is believed not to be the owner of the field but a tenant, who as a wayfarer has only turned aside to stay, because he took away few from Judea; and going on to the calling of the Gentiles, he completed the journey begun.
**“And as a wayfaring man”** — The Jews expound this place thus: Why dost thou separate thyself from my people, and, as a wayfarer, for the refreshment of one hour, carest not what lodging thou usest? But being about to pass on to other things, dost thou not save thy people and thy once renowned temple? Ours think it is said of the incarnation, that Christ would be a stranger on earth, and for a short time would use the lodging of the earth, and like a man passing through and strong, leaving Israel, would hasten to the Gentiles; from place to place, from people to people, from the temple to the Church.
14.9:
**“Why wilt thou be as a wandering man”** — among the Gentiles
**“as a mighty man that cannot save”** — Israel
**“But thou, O Lord, art among us”**
• leaving the Jews
• among the Gentiles
**“and thy name is called upon”** — Christian
**“by us”** — therefore
**“forsake us not”** — to whom the prophets sang of your coming
14.10:
**“Thus saith the Lord to this people”** — to one asking why you would be as a husbandman, etc.
**“that have loved”**
• from the Lord
• as if you want to know the reason, listen: as if my people loved, etc.
**“to move their feet”** — affection
**“their”** — not of God
**“and have not rested”** — in God, who are the true rest, in whom Jacob rests; Esau wanders at home like a hunter
**“And”** — therefore
**“have not pleased the Lord: He will now remember”** — who has long endured
**“their iniquities”**
• of innumerable [sins]
• because the impenitent are obstinate
**“and visit their sins”**
• because they are sick and do not perceive God, so that they may cease to sin
• To move their feet, etc. It is to be noted in the holy scriptures that the feet of sinners are always moved, while to the saints it is said with Moses: “But thou stand thou here with me.” And elsewhere: “Praise the Lord, ye servants, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.” And those who built the tower of Babylon moved their feet from the east.
14.11:
**“And the Lord said to me: Pray not”** — in vain
**“for this people for their good”**
• for the most wicked, obstinate one
• which they are unworthy of
• Pray not, etc. It is foolish to pray for him who has sinned unto death. Whence John: “There is a sin unto death: for that I say not that any man ask,” and there is a sin not unto death. Fasts and prayers and victims and holocausts then profit when we withdraw from vices and weep for our old sins. But if we remain in crimes, thinking the ears of God are bought off by vows and sacrifices, we greatly err, because we judge God to be unjust. For those who are once destined to the sword and famine and pestilence are rescued by no prayers; whence: pray not, etc.
14.12:
**“When”** — for
**“they fast”** — the impenitent
**“I will not hear”** — just
**“their prayers”** — unjust
**“and if”** — even
**“they offer holocausts”** — which are worthier
**“and victims, I will not receive them: for I will consume them by the sword, and by famine, and by the pestilence”** — as those who have sinned unto death, once delivered to death
14.13:
**“And I said: Ah, ah, ah”** — three times, against sword, famine and pestilence
**“O Lord God, the prophets”** — false
**“say to them: You shall not see the sword”** — of God’s torments
**“and famine”** — of the word of God
**“there shall be no among you, but he will give you true peace in this place”**
• of the Church or of Jerusalem
• The prophets say, etc. Let these teachers hear, who promise prosperity to sinners and to those who persist in vices.
• There are many such today who care not whence the offering comes, consulting their own avarice, as a certain man is said to have done, who persuaded men to confess their secret sins before God before the altar, while he sat opposite and heard; and he gave this assurance: that nevertheless to give large alms was enough.
14.14:
**“And the Lord said to me: The prophets prophesy falsely in my name: I sent them not”** — they came of their own accord; not to be heard
**“neither have I commanded them, nor have I spoken to them: they prophesy unto you a lying vision, and divination”** — not prophecy
**“and deceit”** — that by flatteries they may seduce, removing the fear of the Lord
**“and the seduction of their own heart”** — not of God
14.15:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord concerning the prophets that prophesy in my name”** — saying: Thus saith the Lord
**“whom I did not send, that say: Sword and famine shall not be in this land: By sword and famine shall those prophets be consumed”** — Thus saith the Lord, etc. Let false prophets beware, lest those who by deceiving allure the people of God themselves perish with the deceived, and lie unburied, and there be none to cover their shame with the dust of penance.
14.16:
**“And the people”** — who have trampled the commandments of God
**“to whom they prophecy, shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem because of the famine and the sword”** — as many as we see lying unburied in the streets of Jerusalem, and receiving their own evils
**“and there shall be none to bury them”** — with the dust of penance
**“they and their wives”** — the deceived common people
**“their sons and their daughters”** — the unlearned
**“their”** — broods of vipers
**“and I will pour out”** — abundantly
**“their wickedness upon them”** — which they have deserved
14.17:
**“And thou shalt speak this word to them: Let my eyes shed down”** — or yours
**“tears night and day”** — continually
**“and let them not cease”** — tears have the weight of voice
**“because the virgin daughter of my people is afflicted with a great affliction”** — not light, not worthless, is what is lamented
**“the virgin daughter of my people”**
• once not polluted by idolatry
• for whose age, tenderness and integrity one naturally grieves
**“with an exceeding grievous evil”** — intolerable
**“exceeding”**
• Let my eyes shed down tears, etc. This place is understood in two ways: either that God himself laments his people and does not cease to weep, or that he commands the people to overflow with tears. Others think these words are spoken in the person of the prophet.
• Because with a great affliction, etc. A just cause for lamenting: the virgin daughter crushed, the people wiped out.
14.18:
**“If I go forth”** — the Church
**“into the fields, behold the slain with the sword: and if I enter into the city”** — the Church
**“behold them that are consumed”** — scarcely clinging to the bones
**“with famine”** — of the word of God
**“The prophet also and the priest”** — as though you should not wonder at the common people and the lowly crowd
**“are gone”** — from the Lord
**“into a land”** — into hell
**“which they knew not”**
• with the due dignity and office
• If I go forth, etc. Let our prophets and priests hear this: that neither outside nor inside is there any safety because of their negligence.
• Those who are outside are scandalized by them, and they suffer those who are inside to perish of hunger. But let those who were the authors of sin be the first in torments.
**“The prophet also”** — Those who prophesied prosperity, and ought to have opened the commands of the law, went into a land they did not know, that is, they were taken captive.
14.19:
**“Hast thou utterly cast away”** — The prophet marvels that God had thus cast away Juda.
**“cast away”** — so suddenly
**“Juda”** — the two tribes in which were the worship and the temple of the Lord
**“or hath thy soul abhorred Sion? why then hast thou struck us”** — with an incurable wound
**“so that there is no healing for us? we have looked for peace, and there is no good: and for the time of healing, and behold trouble”**
• where worship had been
• Hast thou utterly cast away, etc. So that where there had been the worship of God and tranquillity, there may be sedition and the roaring of enemies. If ever our Sion and our Juda is cast off as abominable, let us in no way wonder, but say what follows: “We acknowledge, O Lord, our wickedness,” etc.
14.20:
**“We acknowledge, O Lord, our wickedness, the iniquities of our fathers, because we have sinned against thee”** — We acknowledge, O Lord, our wickedness, etc. As if: both we and our fathers have neglected the precepts of God with the same madness, and the measure of our fathers is filled up in us, and what was lacking to them is heaped up by our sin. Whence it is said of Juda: “May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered in the sight of the Lord: and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out; let them be before the Lord continually,” etc.
**“of our fathers”** — Whence: “Fill ye up then the measure of your fathers.” They had not yet come to the full heap of iniquity, which was completed in the death of Christ.
14.21:
**“Give us not to be a reproach, for thy name's sake, and do not disgrace in us the throne”** — of the temple
**“of thy glory”** — of any saint
**“Remember, break not thy covenant”** — of the promised salvation
**“The throne of thy glory”** — Of the temple, or of any saint, in which, as it is written, “thou hast broken down his throne on the earth,” it is then dashed down and destroyed when God is offended by it through a multitude of sins. But he who is lost by his own fault is sustained by the Lord’s clemency, which is changed by the severity of the sentence, if the Lord makes void his covenant, by which he promised us salvation.
14.22:
**“Are there any among the graven things of the Gentiles that can send rain? or can the heavens give showers?”** — of themselves
**“give showers? art not thou the Lord our God, whom we have looked for? for thou hast made all these things.”**
• in whom our hope is, to whom we turn our prayers
• Are there any, etc. After many and various discourses he returns to the title of the prophecy, where it is written: “The Word of the Lord that came to Jeremias concerning the words of the drought.”
• As if to say: the idols of demons cannot give rain; do thou therefore give it, from whom is every good, without whom it cannot be given. Heretics also cannot give the rain of doctrine, though they boast that they are the heavens, of whom it is said: “The heavens shew forth the glory of God.” Thou alone art he who canst instruct thy people and give divisions of graces to those who wait for thee.

15.1:
**“And the Lord said to me: If ... shall stand”** — for the people
**“Moses”** — to whom it was said: Let me alone, etc.
**“and Samuel”** — who are read to have withstood the wrath of God for the people and to have turned aside the sentence already hanging over them
**“before me, my soul is not towards this people”**
