• because the sins of the people are complete
• therefore
**“cast them out”** — show them cast out
**“from my sight”** — because unworthy
**“and let them go forth”** — not by place but by will, although we read that both Adam and Cain were cast out from the face of the Lord
**“Moses and Samuel”** — Gregory. Passing over so many fathers, Moses and Samuel alone are brought forward, whose wonderful power of obtaining is shown when even they are said not to be able to intercede. As if to say: I do not hear even those whom, because of the great merit of their petition, I least despise. What is it then that Moses and Samuel are preferred to the other fathers in petitioning, except that these two alone in the whole course of the Old Testament are read to have prayed even for their enemies? One is attacked by the people with stones, and yet prays for those who stone him. The other is cast out of his rule and says: “Far be this sin from me, that I should cease to pray for you.” “If Moses,” he says, “and Samuel shall stand before me, my soul is not towards this people.” As if to say: I do not now hear even them on behalf of friends, whom I know by the merit of great virtue to pray even for enemies. The power therefore of true prayer is the height of charity, and each one then obtains what he rightly asks when his mind is not darkened in the petition by hatred of an enemy.
15.3: **“And I will visit them with”** — The prophet Ezechiel also shows the four plagues by which the people of Juda was delivered up: the sword, pestilence and famine, beasts, and captivity. Among the beasts, understand also the dogs and the fowls, to whom their bodies were given to be torn, devoured and scattered. For it could not be that, the Creator being neglected, the whole creation would not rise up against sinners.
15.4:
**“And I will give them up to the rage of all the kingdoms of the earth: because of Manasses the son of Ezechias the king of Juda, for all that he did in Jerusalem.”**
• And I will give them, etc. This was in part fulfilled under the Babylonians, and is now fulfilled in the whole, when an impious people imitated a most wicked king, who filled Jerusalem from gate to gate with the blood of the just. From this we learn that peoples are for the most part destroyed by the crime of kings, princes and rulers.
• Because of Manasses, etc. We read in the book of Days that Manasses, after captivity and penance, returned to Jerusalem and reigned. But since the merits of the saints, as of David and the others, descend to posterity, so too the crimes of sinners come down to posterity, if their children and grandchildren have done like things.
• This Manasses was most wicked; he sawed Isaias with a wooden saw, and made his son Amon pass through fire to the honour of idols and Topheth.
15.5: **“For who shall have pity”** — No one can pray for the crimes of sinners when God is offended, because no creature can be as merciful as the Creator, nor can a stranger show mercy to outsiders as the Lord does to his own.
15.6:
**“But thou”** — because
**“Thou hast forsaken me, saith the Lord, thou art gone backward”** — “No man putting his hand to the plough, etc.”
**“and I will stretch out my hand against thee”** — the outstretched hand signifies striking; the slaying of sinners, wrath brought to completion
**“and I will destroy thee”** — The Septuagint: I will by no means spare them any longer.
**“I am weary of entreating”** — as if I had grown weary, forgiving them again and again; or I am wearied with them in urging them to salvation
**“thou art gone backward”** — Whereas, according to the Apostle, “forgetting the things that are behind, and stretching forth myself to those that are before,” he ought to have stretched himself forward; he longed for the Egyptian flesh.
15.7:
**“And I will scatter them”** — I scattered them that I might cleanse my threshing floor.
**“with a fan in the gates of the land”** — so that in some way they might tread the thresholds of hell
**“I have killed and destroyed my people”** — that, forced by the necessity of evils, they might flee the evils hanging over them
**“and yet they are not returned from their ways”**
• evils
• as though it does not profit to pray for them, because they neither turn back nor repent
15.8:
**“are multiplied”** — the men having been slain
**“Their widows unto me above the sand of the sea: I have brought upon them against the mother of the young man a spoiler”** — that is, the mothers felt the destroyer when their children were lost
**“at noonday”** — in clear light, not by night, not by ambush, but by an open way
**“I have cast upon the cities”** — of Juda, of a sinning people
**“a terror on a sudden”**
• so that the sooner the evil, the harder the escape
• Their widows are multiplied unto me, etc. God desires to save sinners by diverse remedies, so that those who scorned him when he flattered may fear him when he threatens.
15.9:
**“is become weak”**
• bereft of children
• or she has cast off, or has become empty
**“She that hath borne seven”** — or very many
**“her soul hath fainted away: her sun is gone down”** — of joy
**“while it was yet day”** — in clear light
**“she is confounded”** — in her solitude
**“and ashamed: and the residue of them I will give up to the sword”** — so that no one may escape death and the wrath of God
**“seven”** — The Hebrew word sabe sounds as either seven, or an oath, or very many; whence the Septuagint, Aquila and Theodotion translate it seven; in Symmachus it is rendered very many. Others refer this to the synagogue, which was weakened as the Church grew. Whence the barren “hath borne many,” seven or very many, and she that had many children “is weakened.” The sun of justice, in whose wings is health, went down upon Juda; she is confounded for ever, destroying her people by the spiritual sword.
15.10:
**“Woe is me, my mother”**
• wisdom, or the synagogue
• Woe is me, etc. This can be understood by synecdoche of Jeremias, who was judged not in the whole world but in Judea. But it truly befits the Lord, who says: “For judgment I am come into this world; that they who see not, may see; and they who see, may become blind.” Of whom it is written: “Behold this child is set for the fall, and for the resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be contradicted.” For which of the philosophers, which of the Gentiles, which of the heretics does not judge Christ, by imposing on him a law of being born, suffering and rising again, and by holding various opinions about his essence?
**“why hast thou borne me a man of strife, a man of contention”** — or that I should be judged
**“to all the earth? I have not lent on usury, neither hath any man lent to me on usury”** — I have not lent on usury; or, I have not profited. For no one wished to receive as much as I to give, nor did anyone profit me. The salvation of the creature is the gain of the Creator. Whence: I did not owe, that is, no one gave me as much as I wished, nor made me a debtor to himself, nor did anyone owe me. How could he owe me usury who is not worthy to receive a loan? All the heretics curse me, that is, by believing perversely and blaspheming more perversely.
**“any man: yet all curse me”**
• Woe is me, etc. It is no wonder that Christ, according to his humanity, says Woe is me, etc., when elsewhere he plainly says: “Woe is me, for I am become as one that gleaneth in autumn the grapes of the vintage,” etc. And lest we think the lowliness of the groanings is referred to the Word of God, he at once shows who this is that laments: woe is me, my soul, for it has perished returning from the earth. Not that we divide the persons, as the impious do, but that one and the same Son of God and of man speaks now according to the flesh, now according to the divinity.
• All curse me, etc. Jerome. Where we have translated according to the Hebrew “all curse me,” up to “in the time of tribulation against the enemy,” in the Vulgate edition I found: My strength hath failed in those who curse me; let it be done, Lord, to them that are being set right, if I stood not before thee in the time of their affliction, and in the time of their tribulation, for good against the enemy. As if to say: My strength has failed in those who curse me. For they do not understand my power, which is made perfect in infirmity, and the more they cursed me, the more my strength failed in them. And the prophet, or the Lord, adds and says: Let it be done, Lord, to them that are being set right; and this is it: Let the curses which the enemies speak come upon me, and let them be set right unto good, if I did not stand in thy sight in the time of their tribulation and distress, when the enemy was laying them waste, and pray to thee for them, and say: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. But we also find that Jeremias often in this book prayed for the people.
**“I have not lent on usury”** — Septuagint. I have not profited, and no one has profited me. Theodotion: I have not owed, and no one has owed me. The sense of all of them here is: no one has worthily taken my money, nor has anyone lent to me, making me his debtor, by cherishing the poor.
15.11:
**“Assuredly it shall be well with thy remnant”** — The Lord’s answer to what Jeremias had said above: Woe is me, my mother, etc. As if to say: do not consider only the present but the future. For “assuredly it shall be well with thy remnant,” etc. In the present too, when enemies wished to crush you, I ran to you and protected you.
**“saith the Lord: Assuredly it shall be well with thy remnant, assuredly I shall help thee in the time of affliction, and in the time of tribulation against the enemy.”**
• Assuredly it shall be well with thy remnant, etc. These things can also be said of Christ according to his humanity.
• Assuredly it shall be well with thy remnant, etc. These things can be taken of Jeremias, who was compelled to prophesy in the worst time, with captivity impending, and to suffer hard things from an unbelieving people.
15.12: **“Shall iron be allied”** — As if to say: Do not grieve that thy people is an enemy; for since thou announcest hard things, he who is hard cannot love thee. Or: The Babylonians, who come from the north and are the hardest iron, cannot be joined in friendship to this harder and untamed people, which is like brass. Or: the hardest iron, that is, the people of Israel, is unworthy of recognition, having come to such great wickedness that it is surrounded by what is harder than metal, that is, brass.
15.13:
**“Thy riches and thy treasures”** — all substance
**“I will give unto spoil for nothing”** — to your enemies
**“and thy treasures”** — Origen. There is one treasure: Jeremias is one, Isaias another, or Moses and the rest. These treasures God took away from the Jews and gave to us. Whence: “the kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof.” First “the words of God were committed to them,” and afterwards they were given to us; they have indeed the law and the prophets, but they do not understand.
**“because of all thy sins”** — That is, because of your sins, which have reached into all your borders, you who, as far as in you lies, have killed wisdom and truth; for Christ is indeed wisdom and truth. They have therefore lost all things, and Christ, rising again, appeared no more to his slayers, but only to believers.
15.14: **“it shall burn”** — It cannot be quenched, because you have supplied the matter of the heat, so that your mind’s fire consumes what is in you: wood, hay and stubble. The cause of the burning is therefore not in the Lord but in those who supply fuel to the fire.
15.15:
**“O Lord, thou knowest”** — happy the conscience that suffers reproach for the sake of God
**“do not defend me in thy patience”** — The voice of Christ. As if to say: you have always been long-suffering toward this sinning people. But since it has raised its rashness even against me, be long-suffering no longer. But if you consider the times of the Lord’s passion and of the ruin of Jerusalem, you will see that he was not patient. For from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar to the overthrow of the temple forty-two years are counted; for a space of penance had to be given on account of those who were to believe through the apostles.
15.16:
**“were found”** — true
**“Thy words”** — you who spoke them through my mouth
**“and I did eat them”** — that is, they were turned to me into food. Symmachus: I will receive them, understood: into joy, which had been into reproach.
**“and thy word was to me”** — otherwise: thy
**“a joy and gladness of my heart: for thy name is called upon me, O Lord God of hosts”** — as if I therefore rejoiced, because for thy name I suffered hard things
15.17:
**“I sat not in the assembly of jesters”** — I have not sat with the council of vanity: neither will I go in with the doers of unjust things; hence Jesus, teaching that he had risen, said: Behold your house shall be left to you desolate; for the divine word has left the council of the Jews
**“nor did I make a boast”** — to have no fellowship with the wicked
**“of the presence of thy hand”** — while I always await thy hand hanging over me
**“I sat alone”** — I am solitary until I pass over
**“because thou hast filled me with threats”**
• As it were, I was unwilling to sit in the council of jesters, but I swallowed my bitterness, that in the future I might prepare joy for myself
• I sat not in, etc. The Hebrews think that this is said in the person of Jerusalem, that she sat alone, filled with bitterness, and her sorrow is perpetual, and as waters pass away, so the words of the prophets who promised prosperity passed away falsely. But it is better said by the prophet or a holy man, who did not sit in the assembly of jesters.
• May the Lord grant us not to sit in the assembly of jesters and of those who do not think of the things to come; may he grant us not to yield to adversities, but always to fear the sentence of God, and to say with the prophet, who am filled with bitterness. Let them rejoice in their sports; but for us it is good to adhere to God, and to place our hope in him, to be filled with reproaches, and to await the sentence of the judge, which will show by the deed that all bitterness was like flowing waters.
• From the face of thy hand, etc. Origen. The face of the hand of God is the very stroke of just judgment, which drove proud man out of paradise into this blindness of the present exile. His threatening is the terror of the punishment still present. After the face of the hand, therefore, threats still terrify us, because after the experience of judgment the punishment of the present exile has struck us, and if we do not cease to sin, it adds still eternal punishments.
• I sat alone, etc. Gregory. As if he said: while I consider what I now suffer through the experience of judgment, I, trembling in mind, seek a retreat from the tumult of temporal desires, because I still fear more sharply those eternal punishments which you threaten.
15.18:
**“Why is my sorrow become perpetual”** — as if I had no respite from pain, nor did I await any remedies
**“and my wound desperate so as to refuse to be healed”** — they who afflicted me have prevailed
**“it is become to me as the falsehood of deceitful waters”** — In this is consolation: for as waters run off, so the assault of enemies, with thee helping, will perish
15.19:
**“Therefore”** — Hence it is plain that the prophet said the foregoing, to whom the Lord answered
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord: If thou wilt be converted”** — the people from sins
**“I will convert thee”** — from tribulation into joy
**“and thou shalt stand before my face”** — as the angels stand in the sight of God, seeing his face
**“and if thou wilt separate”** — with thy words
**“the precious”** — holy
**“from the vile”** — the sinner
**“thou shalt be as my mouth”**
• as if lest you should think there is no reward for good work
• thou shalt be joined to my precepts
**“they shall be turned to thee”** — they will be imitators of thee, not thou of them
**“and thou shalt not be turned to them”** — If thou wilt separate, etc. Gregory. For the present world is vile to God; a clean soul is precious to him. He therefore who separates the precious from the vile is called as it were the mouth of the Lord, since through him the Lord utters his words, who by speaking what he can tears a human soul away from the love of the present age.
**“As my mouth”** — Thou shalt be as my mouth. Let us consider how great a reward the speech of a teacher has, if he wishes to free someone from error and call him back from the number of sinners.
15.20:
**“And I will make thee to this people”** — that you not dread, saying: Why is my sorrow become perpetual?
**“a strong wall of brass”** — so that you may resist the adversary with all strength
15.21: **“And I will deliver thee out of the hand of the wicked, and I will redeem thee out of the hand of the mighty.”** — by my blood, or by my present help

16.2:
**“Thou shalt not take thee a wife, neither shalt thou have thee sons and daughters in this place.”** — not that he forbade the prophet to take a wife, but it was said to the people
**“Thou shalt not take thee a wife”** — Thou shalt not take a wife. With captivity at hand, lest you be tormented over your own grief, and also over the miseries of your wife and children. Well, therefore, the apostle commands, because the time is short and the end is near, that those who have wives be as though they had none.
16.4:
**“They shall die by the death of grievous illnesses: they shall not be lamented, and they shall not be buried”** — because of the multitude of the dying
**“as dung”** — As if the corpses will lie on a dunghill, to be torn by birds and beasts of the earth
**“By the death of grievous illnesses”** — By the death of grievous illnesses. Note that to waste away with long infirmity is the wrath of God; whence Joram son of Josaphat is consumed by infirmity, and the apostle says: Therefore are there many infirm and weak among you, etc.
16.5:
**“For thus saith the Lord: Enter not into the house of feasting, neither go thou to mourn, nor to comfort them: because I have taken away my peace from this people, saith the Lord, my mercy and commiserations.”**
• because they are unworthy of mercy
• Jeremias was sent by the Lord to preach while still young. Whence he says: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord, I know not how to speak.” And he was a virgin and chaste, without children, so that he might preach more freely.
**“Enter not”** — Whence with such a man you ought neither to take food nor to say to him “Hail”; to the apostles also it was forbidden to greet anyone on the road, whence also Eliseus forbade Giezi to greet. It is the custom of mourners to bring food and prepare a banquet, which are called parentalia, because the due rites are celebrated by the parents. Whence elsewhere: give wine to them that are in sorrow, that they may forget their grief. The prophet is therefore commanded not to comfort anyone of the people, not to be mingled with the banquets of the enemies of God, not to celebrate the due rites at the funerals of the dead. For it is one thing to die by the common law of nature, another to have fallen by the sentence of God.
16.6:
**“Both the great and the little shall die”** — I will spare no age.
**“in this land: they shall not be buried”** — they shall also lack burial.
**“nor lamented”** — It was a custom among the ancients, and in some of the Jews it remains to this day, to cut the arms in mourning, which we read that Job also did. The prophet is therefore forbidden to break bread among them, to enter the house of feasting, to be mingled with those whom the sentence of God has cursed. But if this is said of mourners, what will become of heretics, whose speech creeps like a cancer, and who daily lay low in the Church the corpses of the deceived?
16.9:
**“For thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold I will take away out of this place in your sight, and in your days the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride.”** — he who has the bride is the bridegroom.
**“Behold I will take away”** — Thus too God takes from the sinful Church every joy and every gladness. Of which it is said: “Rejoice in the Lord always,” etc.
16.11:
**“Thou shalt say to them: Because your fathers forsook me”** — those who preside in the Church.
**“saith the Lord: and went after strange gods”** — of whom “their god is the belly”: avarice, lust, and such like.
**“and served them”** — he by whom anyone is overcome is his slave.
**“and adored them”** — each one adores what he loves.
**“and they forsook me, and kept not my law”** — It is proper to priests not only to teach but also to keep the law, and to teach the flock not only by words but also by examples.
16.12:
**“And you also have done worse than your fathers: for behold every one of you walketh”**
• once forsaken by the Lord, they do what is not fitting.
• But you also, etc. Lest perhaps they should say: “The sentence is unjust: the fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the children are set on edge.”
**“after the perverseness of his evil heart”** — from which the most evil thoughts come forth; therefore they are separated from the Church, so that they go into a distant land which neither they nor their fathers knew before they sinned.
16.13:
**“So I will cast you forth out of this land, into a land which you know not, nor your fathers: and there you shall serve strange gods”** — which are not gods but are thought to be.
**“day and night”** — He shows perseverance in sinning, while by day they serve shameful deeds, by night lust.
**“which shall not give you any rest”** — Gods; so whatever we sin is the rule of demons, who never give us rest but always compel us to heap sins upon sins.
16.14:
**“Therefore behold the days come”** — plainly the restoration of the people is proclaimed.
**“saith the Lord, when it shall be said no more: The Lord liveth, that brought for the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt”**
• through Moses and Aaron.
• Behold the days come, etc. Miracles are foretold which, according to the letter, were partly fulfilled under Zorobabel and the high priest Jesus. To be fulfilled more fully spiritually in Christ.
• Behold the days come, etc. We can say this of the persecutions which befell our people from the days of Nero to the times of Maximian. For the Lord, having mercy on his people, brought them back into their own land, that is, the Church, which he gave to their fathers, that is, to the apostles and apostolic men.
16.15:
**“But, the Lord liveth, that brought the children of Israel out of the land of the north”** — under Cyrus king of the Persians, releasing the captives.
**“and out of all the lands”** — which was fulfilled not under Cyrus but under Christ. Whence: “until the fulness of the Gentiles come in; and so all Israel shall be saved.”
**“to which I cast them out”** — Or: I will cast out.
16.16:
**“Behold, I”** — For.
**“I will send many fishers”** — the apostles: “Come ye after me, and I will make you to be fishers of men.”
**“saith the Lord, and they shall fish them: and after this I will send them many hunters”** — ecclesiastical men, or angels, who, after the consummation has come, will hunt the saints.
**“and they shall hunt them from every mountain”** — of doctrines.
**“and from every hill”** — of good works.
**“and out of the holes of the rocks”** — Behold I, etc. The Jews think that by the name of fishermen the Chaldeans are signified, and by the hunters the Romans, who hunted the unhappy people from the mountains and hills and from the caves of rocks.
**“the holes of the rocks”** — To the apostles and apostolic men. For Christ is the rock, but he also gave to Peter that he should be called a rock; those who rest in his senses are rightly said to be transferred from the rock; and he shows that either the apostles or those who are afterwards to be hunted had sins, and received their double iniquities.
16.18:
**“And I will repay first”** — because afterwards they will receive good things.
**“their double iniquities, and their sins: because they have defiled my land”** — so that all the world may be made subject to God, and be preserved not by merit but by mercy.
**“Their double iniquities”** — Because the servant who knows the will of the Lord and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes. For it is fitting that those who are of the Gentiles receive simple sins, and we double ones; whence, for us sinning willingly, no sacrifice for sins is left.
16.19:
**“O Lord”** — Christ the Lord, you have been made our refuge.
**“my might, and my strength, and my refuge in the day of tribulation”** — whence “redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”
**“to thee the Gentiles shall come from the ends of the earth, and shall say: Surely our fathers have possessed lies, a vanity which hath not profited them.”** — To thee the Gentiles, etc. After Israel was cast out, and the multitude of the Gentiles was brought over from fishers and hunters, it is consequently called, and confesses its former error.
**“from the ends of the earth”** — The first of the earth are the wise of the world, the noble, the rich, the great men. But God hath chosen the last, that is, the foolish things of the world, that he may confound all the strong. The Gentiles come from the ends of the earth, that is, from those who are the lowest upon the earth, the foolish, the ignoble, and the despised.
16.20:
**“Shall a man make gods unto himself, and they are no gods?”** — They expose the ignorance both of themselves and of their ancestors, who thought that men make gods, whereas God makes men.
**“gods”** — Not only from bodily images do men make gods for themselves, but they also fashion them in the heart. All the philosophers and heretics who put forth various doctrines made idols for themselves, and thought the will of the soul to be god, and “adored the work of their own hands,” thinking that what they had fashioned was true.
16.21:
**“Therefore, behold I will shew”**
• not in shadow and image, as before.
• the passion being completed.
**“this once cause them to know, I will shew them my hand”** — Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God.
**“my power: and they shall know”** — the hand having been shown.
**“that my name is the Lord”** — Hearing that, Father: I have manifested your name to men.

17.1:
**“The sin of Juda”**
• Of the Jews.
• As though the sins of the nations have been blotted out, of whom it is said to Moses: “Let me alone, that I may destroy this people, and I will make thee a great nation”; but the sin of Juda is indelible, as if written with a pen of iron on a nail of adamant, which in Hebrew is called samur; not that any nail is called samur, but the adamant, which receives this name because it is untamed and unbreakable; it has so much brightness and smoothness that without any hindrance it can be written upon with an iron pen, so that the hard material of iron writes on a harder tablet, and the writing remains forever, according to that: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”
**“is written with a pen of iron”** — indelibly: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”
**“with the point of a diamond”** — Where then is that which the old woman of the lyre invents, that a man can be without sin if he wishes, and God’s commands are easy?
**“it is graven upon the table of their heart”** — so that the works of sacrilege may be in eternal memory.
*Jerome:* The sin of Juda, etc. This was said of the converted nations. Therefore I will show them, etc. Now he speaks of the cast-off Israel: the sin of Juda, etc. But why this was passed over by the Septuagint I do not know, unless they spared their own people. As in that place of Isaias: “Cease ye from the man, whose breath is in his nostrils.”
*Origen:* Perhaps the sin of Juda is our sin, we who believe in Christ of the tribe of Juda. Before I commit sin, no image of sin is turning in my heart. But when the conscience has taken on the image of sin, it takes its form from it, and the pomp of the offence is painted before the eyes of my heart. Now if the sin were written in ink, it could be blotted out. But it is written with a pen of iron, on a nail of adamant, upon the breast of the heart, that it may be fulfilled: “Nothing is covered that shall not be revealed, nor hid that shall not be known.” The conscience of my breast will be laid bare, and with the heart open the letters of my sins will be seen, which were written with an iron pen and a nail of adamant, and the whole multitude of beholders will read the images of my sins stamped upon my breast. If you wish to understand the sin as that of Juda the betrayer, what follows, “of them,” is against it, since it is written “Juda.”
17.3: **“high places”** — Which in Hebrew is ramoth; and by them are signified heretics, who “set their mouth against heaven,” and have broken out into such madness that they have remained alone without the grace of the Holy Spirit, and have lost the former inheritance of the Lord, that is, the truth of the faith. Whence an eternal fire is likened to them, and the servitude of demons, who are enemies and avengers.
17.4:
**“inheritance, which I gave thee: and I will make thee serve thy enemies”** — by the Babylonians, or rather by the Romans.
**“in a land which thou knowest not: because thou hast kindled a fire in my wrath”** — provoking the most merciful God to wrath.
**“it shall burn for ever”**
• fire.
• This is not in the Septuagint, so that the eternal sentence may not remain on his nation.
17.5:
**“Thus saith the Lord: Cursed be the man that trusteth in man”** — only man, for Christ is both man and God.
**“and maketh flesh his arm”** — not God.
**“his arm”** — that is, the strength of his own goods.
**“And”** — thus.
**“whose heart departeth from the Lord”** — claiming that he can do what he cannot.
**“whose heart”** — Cursed be the man, etc. Cursed, then, are Paul of Samosata and Photinus, who, though Christ is holy and exalted in all virtues, yet preach him to be only a man. But we are blessed, who believe in him who says: “You seek to kill me, a man who have spoken the truth to you.” For “if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer.” Of whom it is said: “Paul, an apostle, not of men, neither by man, but by Jesus Christ.” For if death is swallowed up in victory, why should the lowliness of the flesh, which was assumed for our sake, not have passed over into the majesty of the divinity, that both might become one, and that we might not adore the creature but the Creator?
17.6:
**“For he shall be like tamaric”**
• in Hebrew, aroer.
• Symmachus: like a fruitless tree in the wilderness.
**“in the desert, and he shall not see when good shall come”** — which the Gentiles are to see.
**“but he shall dwell in dryness in the desert”** — as the Jews, who are deserted by God and bear no fruit.
**“in a salt land”** — fruitless, which has not God for a guest, nor the protection of angels, nor the grace of the Holy Spirit, nor the knowledge of teachers.
17.7:
**“Blessed”** — or blessed.
**“the man”** — Ecclesiastical.
**“that trusteth in the Lord”** — Of whom: “Know ye that the Lord, he himself, is God.”
**“and the Lord shall be”** — Not man.
**“his confidence”**
• True.
• Blessed be the man, etc. As if to say, cursed are the Jews and heretics, who have no hope in the Lord, that is, in Christ, whom they think not the Son of God but a mere man.
• For he who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord is his confidence, in the time of Jewish drought will not fear but will always bear fruit, believing in him who died once and dies no more. And he says: “I am the life.”
17.8:
**“And he shall be as a tree”** — Of whom: and he shall be like a tree planted near the running waters.
**“that is planted by the waters”** — The divided graces of the Holy Spirit; that is transplanted over the waters.
**“towards moisture”** — Grace.
**“spreadeth out its roots”** — So that it may receive abundance from the Lord.
**“it shall not fear when the heat cometh”** — Of persecution or of judgment.
**“And the leaf thereof”** — And the leaf of Juda. Other reading: its.
**“shall be green”** — Green; not fearing the drought.
**“in the time of drought it shall not be solicitous”** — And in the time of drought it will not be anxious; when the angry Lord commands the clouds that they not send rain upon Israel.
**“neither shall it cease at any time to bring forth fruit”**
• Nor will it ever cease to bear fruit; of virtues.
• Like the fig tree which the Lord cursed.
• That spreadeth out its roots towards moisture, etc. As if he passes from the Jewish drought to the grace of baptism.
17.9:
**“The heart is perverse above all things”** — The heart of all is perverse; or of men.
**“and unsearchable, who can know it?”**
• The heart of men is small, etc. Septuagint: The heart is deep above all things, and it is man, who shall know him? The Hebrew word enos is written with four letters: aleph, nun, vau, sin. If then it is read enos, it means man; but if enos, it means unsearchable or past hope, because no one can find out the heart of men. Symmachus: The heart of men is unsearchable. But who is the man that can find it? Our people are wont, with a zeal of God but not according to knowledge, to say this against the Jews: that Christ is man according to the flesh, and no one can know his birth, according to that: “Who shall declare his generation?” And he searches out secrets and renders to every one according to his works.
• Because he said: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man,” and “blessed be the man that trusteth in the Lord,” lest we think the judgment of men to be sure, he adds that the hearts of all are perverse. Whence: “From my secret sins cleanse me,” that is, from thoughts. And in Genesis: “All the thought of men is bent upon evil.” And again: “The imagination and thought of man’s heart are prone to evil,” etc. It is clear therefore that God alone knows the thoughts of men; therefore Christ is God, who saw thoughts.
17.11:
**“The partridge”** — Partridge: the devil.
**“hath hatched”** — Hatched; or gathered.
**“which she did not lay”**
• Which she did not lay; saying: “All these things will I give thee, if falling down thou shalt adore me.”
• The Septuagint: the partridge cried out, gathered what she did not lay.
**“hath gathered riches, and not by right: in the midst of his days he shall leave them”** — Has made riches, and not in judgment; in the middle of his days he will leave them; or they will leave him, because they will be converted to the Lord through the apostles.
**“and in his latter end”** — In judgment.
**“he shall be a fool”**
• He shall be foolish, who seemed wise to himself.
• The partridge hath hatched, etc. The writers of natural history, of beasts and birds as well as of trees and herbs (whose chief authors are, among the Greeks, Aristotle and Theophrastus; among us, Pliny the Second), say that this is the nature of the partridge: that she steals the eggs of another partridge, sits on them and warms them; but the young, when grown, fly away and leave the foreign parent. Such are the rich who seize what belongs to others and make riches without regard to the judgment of God, which they leave in the midst of the time, overtaken by death. Whence: “Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee; and whose shall those things be?” And nothing is more foolish than not to foresee the last things and to think brief things everlasting. They also say the partridge is quarrelsome and unclean, so that it is the victor’s palm to have defiled the vanquished; in which it signifies the devil.
**“The partridge hath hatched”** — What the Septuagint says, the partridge cried out, is to be referred to heretics, through whom the devil cries out and gathers riches, which will leave him.
*Origen:* This partridge, that is, the devil, by crying out through heretics gathers creatures which he did not beget, and makes others’ his own; that is, he entangles the simple among the faithful in the snare of heretical decree. The partridge has become rich. Behold how many thousands there are, but they are not with judgment. For he does not think on judgment, nor has he justice in his heart, but all things without law. But Christ makes his riches with judgment; his wealth is tested and raised up. In the midst of his days, etc. His days are the days of this world. Christ plucks us out of this wicked world, and so we leave the partridge. His end shall be foolish, when all things shall have been made subject to Christ: “the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.”
17.12:
**“A high and glorious throne”** — The partridge being left behind.
**“high”** — Of the Lord, namely, who dwells in the saints.
**“from the beginning is the place of our sanctification”** — As if wherever there is a holy place, it is.
17.13:
**“O expectation”** — Is.
**“of Israel”** — you see God
**“O Lord”** — on the contrary
**“all that forsake thee shall be confounded”** — forever
**“they that depart from thee, shall be written in the earth”**
• blotted out of the book of life
• blotted out of the book of the living, whose manner of life is in heaven; they are written in heaven; those who depart from the Lord are written in the earth with those who savour earthly things
**“because they have forsaken the Lord, the vein of living waters”**
• who says: “If any man thirst, let him come and drink.”
• Whence: “Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.”
17.14: **“Heal me”** — Many physicians tended the woman with an issue of blood in the Gospel, but she could be healed by none except by him who is the true physician. Whence the prophet, who suffered reproaches from the people and was beset by snares, desires to be cured and healed by him whose praise is true and whose medicine is true.
17.15: **“Behold they say to me”** — who do not believe the things to come that I speak, thinking that the sentence is a pretence and a delay
17.16:
**“And I”** — they saying so
**“I am not troubled, following thee for my pastor, and”** — also
**“the day of man”** — a long life or the prosperity of this age, but of the Lord, that is, of the resurrection
**“I have not desired, thou knowest”** — as you, who are witness and also judge
**“That which went out of my lips, hath been right”** — not false
**“in thy sight”**
• by your good pleasure
• not of men
• And I have not, etc. The more you follow Christ, the less you labour. For there is no weariness in Jacob, nor pain in Israel. Whence: “Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you.”
17.17: **“Be not thou a terror unto me, thou art my hope in the day of affliction”** — Be not thou, etc. Septuagint: Be not made a stranger to me, sparing me in the evil day. As if to say: Do not spare me in the present age, which is evil, but render to me according to my sins, that I may have everlasting rest; for “whom thou lovest thou chastisest, and scourgest every son whom thou receivest.” Or: the day of judgment is evil for those who suffer torments.
17.18:
**“Let them be confounded”** — well, unto salvation
**“that persecute me”** — who reproach and say: where is the word of the Lord, etc.
**“and let not me be confounded”** — who preach the truth
**“let them be afraid”** — God or punishments
**“and let not me be afraid; bring upon them the day of affliction”** — of vengeance
**“And”** — then
**“with a double destruction”** — by sword and famine, in soul and body
17.19: **“Thus saith the Lord to me: Go, and stand in the gate of the children of the people, by which the kings of Juda come in, and go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem”** — Go and stand, etc. As if to say: Because they scorn to hear thy words and do not seek the sentence of God, go to the most frequented place, where all go in and out; preach in season and out of season, that they may not be able to excuse themselves as though they had not heard, but let them hear, willing or unwilling.
17.20: **“And thou shalt say to them: Hear the word of the Lord, ye kings of Juda, and all Juda, and all the inhabitant of Jerusalem, that enter in by these gates”** — of the temple or of the city
17.21:
**“Thus saith the Lord: Take heed to your souls and carry no burdens”** — of sins
**“on the Sabbath day”**
• of rest
• for they are not to be carried but rather to be cast away
**“and bring them not in by the gates”** — virtues
**“of Jerusalem”** — Take heed to your souls, etc. We set the whole thing together at once, lest we tear apart the precept of the sabbath renewed through Jeremiah, so that we may know all things together.
17.22:
**“And do not bring burdens”** — to be carried at all
**“out of your houses”** — bodies, minds
**“on the sabbath day, and any work”** — servile, of which it is said: “Labour not for the meat that perisheth,” etc.; but the work that does not perish
**“do ye not; sanctify the sabbath day”** — leading all your time in sanctification
17.23:
**“But they did not hear, nor incline their ear”** — of the mind
**“but hardened their neck”** — rejecting the yoke of the law, like untamed bulls
**“that they might not hear me”** — teaching
17.24: **“That you bring in no”** — If our Judaizers reject the figurative explanation, they will either be forced to be Jews and to circumcise the foreskins along with the observance of the sabbath, or to reproach the Saviour, who commanded the paralytic to take up his bed on the sabbath, for which the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he did not only break the sabbath, but also said God was his Father, etc.
17.25:
**“shall enter in by the gates of this city”** — that is, the reward of obedience
**“kings and princes”** — whose heart is in the hand of God, who reign in their own bodies
**“sitting upon the throne of David”** — imitating the example of Christ
**“and riding in chariots”** — of whom: “The chariot of God is attended by thousands,” etc.; and elsewhere: “thy riding is salvation”
**“and on horses, they and their princes, the men of Juda”** — who confess the Lord
**“and the inhabitants of Jerusalem”** — of which it is said: “And his place is in peace,” etc.; that is, in Salem, which is peace
**“and this city shall be inhabited”** — The Church
17.26:
**“And they shall come from the cities of Juda, and from the places round about Jerusalem, and from the land of Benjamin”** — which is “son of strength and of the right hand”
**“and from the plains”** — which in Hebrew is Sephela, which signifies the plain of history
**“and from the mountains”** — by lofty doctrines
**“and from the south”** — from the south, of which it is said: the Lord will come from the south, whence heat and full light come, and all cold is driven out
**“bringing”** — consecrating themselves
**“holocausts, and victims, and sacrifices, and frankincense”** — a sacrifice to God, a contrite spirit; or incense, of which: “we are the good odour of Christ,” etc. “Let my prayer be directed”
**“and they shall bring in an offering”**
• an offering or praise, according to the Septuagint; which in Hebrew is toda, that is, thanksgiving
• of which: “To what purpose is frankincense brought to me from Saba?”
**“into the house of the Lord”** — The Church
**“Sacrifice”** — For which the Septuagint put the Hebrew itself, manaa, which in our copies is read, through the carelessness of scribes, as manna.
17.27:
**“But if you will not hearken to me, to sanctify the sabbath day, and not to carry burdens, and not to bring them in by the gates of Jerusalem on the sabbath day: I will kindle a fire”** — of which: all adulterers, their hearts are like an oven
**“in the gates thereof, and it shall devour the houses of Jerusalem, and it shall not be quenched”**
• “Every man’s work shall be manifest … and the fire shall try every man’s work, of what sort it is”; and “if any man’s work burn, he shall suffer loss”
• If you will not hearken, etc. As if these were the rewards of those who sanctify the sabbath and are burdened by no weight. But if, etc.

18.1: **“The word that came from the Lord to Jeremias, saying”** — The word that came to Jeremias from the Lord, etc. Through all the senses the mind attains judgment and understanding: hearing, smell, taste, touch; but what is seen with the eyes is more firmly retained in the mind. Whence the prophet is commanded to go to the potter’s house and there to hear the commands of the Lord.
18.3: **“And I went down into the potter's house, and behold he was doing a work on the wheel”** — The Septuagint: upon stones, deceived by ambiguity. For the Hebrew, because of the difference of place and pronunciation, signifies both the instrument, that is, the potter’s wheel, and stones.
18.4: **“And the vessel was broken”** — Broken by divine providence, so that the craftsman, unknowing, through his own error might give form to a parable.
18.6:
**“Cannot I do with you, as this potter”** — who seem to have perished
**“O house of Israel, saith the Lord? behold as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel”** — that I may both destroy and restore
18.7: **“I will suddenly speak against a nation, and against a kingdom, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy it”** — I will suddenly speak, etc. He signifies free will, saying that he announces evils to a kingdom and nation, and again goods, yet these are not to come, but when they are changed, the opposite things befall. Not that he is ignorant of these future things, but that he leaves man to his own will, that he may receive by his merit either rewards or punishments. Yet the good is not wholly man’s, but of divine bounty. For the freedom of choice is so preserved that in all things the grace of the giver excels. Whence: “Unless the Lord build the house,” etc. “So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth,” etc.
18.8:
**“If”** — yet
**“shall repent of their evil”** — evil
**“that nation”** — by turning away from its evil
**“against which I have spoken, I also will repent of the evil that I have thought to do to them”** — that is, I will not bring it on
18.10:
**“If it shall do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice: I will repent of the good that I have spoken to do unto it”** — because I see all things
**“that it obey not my voice”** — commands
**“I will repent of the good”** — that is, I will not give it, because I did not promise it to such people, but to the good and the penitent
18.11:
**“Now therefore tell the men of Juda, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying: Thus saith the Lord: Behold I frame evil against you”** — as the potter the clay
**“evil”**
• that is, I will bring on the sentence deserved
• whence “making peace and creating evil”: not that it is evil in itself, as it seems to those who suffer
**“and devise a device against you: let every man of you return”** — that is, change your works so that the sentence may be changed
**“every man of you return from his evil way, and make ye your ways and your doings good”** — Behold I, etc. He fulfils the parable which he taught both by sight and by speech.
18.12:
**“He that”** — on the contrary
**“they said: We have no hopes”**
• salvation
• or we shall be strengthened in evils, that is, or we fail, that is, we cannot appease God
**“for we will go after our own thoughts”** — by working
**“and we will do every one”** — serving idols
**“according to the perverseness of his evil heart”** — After our own thoughts, etc. Where, without the grace of God, is the power of free will and the judgment of one’s own will, since it is an offence to God to follow thoughts and do the will of an evil heart? Whence he adds: “Ask among the nations,” etc., that is, all the nations round about her.
18.13:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord: Ask among the nations: Who hath heard such horrible things, as the virgin of Israel hath done to excess?”** — beyond the nations
**“the virgin of Israel”**
• formerly
• betrothed to God; whence God is known in Judea
18.14:
**“Shall the snow of Libanus fail from the rock of the field? or can the cold waters that gush out and run down, be taken away?”**
• Shall it fail from the rock? etc. Virgil says the like: “Sooner shall the light stags feed in the air, and the seas leave the fishes bare on the shore, than his face fall away from my heart.” And elsewhere: “While rivers run into the seas, while shadows move over the mountains, while the heaven feeds the stars, always shall thy honour and thy name and thy praises remain.”
• Shall it fail from the rock? etc. As the snow cannot fail from the summits of Libanus, nor be overcome by any heat of the sun, and the streams flowing from the mountains are not dried up, so thy name, stable and everlasting, cannot be changed. For while the rest keep their order, “my people have forgotten me.”
18.15:
**“Because my people have forgotten me”** — who am the way
**“my people have forgotten me, sacrificing in vain”** — uselessly
**“sacrificing”** — to idols
**“and stumbling”** — offending
**“in their ways”** — not of God
**“in ancient paths, to walk by them in a way not trodden”** — the footsteps of the saints who worshipped God, that they might walk in them on an untrodden road; who, having left God, worshipped idols; whence he adds the punishment that follows, that their land might become
18.16:
**“That their land might be given up to desolation”**
• a desolation, a solitude
• because they abandoned the worship of God, having followed the path of idolatry
**“and to a perpetual hissing”** — for astonishment of mind
**“every one that shall pass by it, shall be astonished”** — formerly most flourishing
**“and wag his head”**
• as a sign of a confused mind
• That their land might become, etc. This seems to have been fulfilled more fully after the coming of the Lord, when no Jew is permitted by law to enter the holy land and city. But when they come to the lamentation, they marvel and weep that the prophecies of the prophets are fulfilled.
18.17: **“As a burning wind”** — To this day this sentence remains upon the Jews scattered over the whole world, before the enemy, that is, the devil, or the enemies, that is, the demons. And though day and night in the synagogues of Satan they call upon the name of the Lord, he shows them the back and not the face, that they may understand that he is departing and never coming to them. But the day of the Jewish destruction is all the time after the Saviour’s passion until the consummation of the world, that after the fulness of the Gentiles shall have come in, then all Israel may be saved.
18.18:
**“And they said: Come, and let us invent devices against Jeremias: for the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet: come, and let us strike him with the tongue, and let us give no heed to all his words.”** — Come, etc. This is the thought, then, of the Jews against Jeremias or Christ, and now of heretics against the servants of God: to devise calumnies and to oppress the saints with accusation, not considering what truth those men speak, but what falsehood they may contrive. For they boast that in their priests and wise men and false prophets the law of God, counsel and speech remain, though wisdom does not enter into a malicious soul.
*Jerome:* We pass over the plain things so as to linger on the obscure ones; not interpreting the ravings of certain men and the captivity of the heavenly Jerusalem, but pursuing the clear history and most manifest prophecy with every confidence in words and senses.
18.19:
**“Give heed to me, O Lord, and hear the voice”** — “Crucify him,” etc.
**“of my adversaries”**
• of the Jews
• Give heed, O Lord, etc. In type of the Saviour, Jeremias suffers all this from the Jews, who afterwards are laid waste when the Babylonian comes. But it is more fully completed in Christ, when the city was overthrown by the Roman sword, not on account of idolatry, which then there was none, but because they cried out for the death of the Son of God: “Away with him, away with him: we have no king but Caesar.” And their imprecation is fulfilled for ever: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”
18.20:
**“Shall evil be rendered for good, because they have digged a pit”** — deceit
**“for my soul”** — taking away
**“Remember that I have stood in thy sight, to speak good for them”** — “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.”
18.22:
**“Let a cry be heard out of their houses: for thou shalt bring the robber upon them”** — Nabuchodonosor or the Roman army
**“suddenly: because”** — deservedly
**“they have digged a pit”** — he explains what they did against the Son of God and what they suffered
18.23:
**“But thou, O Lord, knowest all their counsel against me unto death: forgive not their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from thy sight: let them be overthrown”** — or stumbling against the stone, namely of offence, and the rock of scandal; of which: “The stone which the builders rejected,” etc.
**“before thy eyes, in the time of thy wrath do thou destroy them”** — Forgive not their iniquity, etc. It is not contrary to the previous sentence, in which he prays for the people. But because the time of repentance has passed, those remaining in their crimes are punished not so much for themselves as for others, lest sin go unpunished in them, as an example.

19.1:
**“Thus saith the Lord: Go, and take a potter's earthen bottle, and take of the ancients of the people”** — so that those who ought to understand may see
**“Go, and take”** — Divine Scripture wishes to teach the people not only by ears but also by eyes. For what is perceived by sight is retained more by the mind than what is heard.
**“a potter's earthen bottle”** — For the potter’s bottle (which in Hebrew is called bodioc) the Septuagint translated: a jar. For the earthen gate, Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion put the Hebrew itself, harsith. The Septuagint in their way, for the aspiration of the letter heth, added the Greek chi, so as to say charsith, as for Hebron Chebron, and for Jericho Hiericho.
19.2:
**“And go forth into the valley of the son of Ennom”** — where there is the temple of Baal and the grove of Siloe, watered by fountains
**“which is by the entry of the earthen gate: and there thou shalt proclaim”** — or you will read, or you will cry out; for the Hebrew charath signifies these three things
19.3:
**“And thou shalt say: Hear the word of the Lord, O ye kings of Juda”** — of the royal stock
**“and the inhabitants of Jerusalem”** — the people, so that all may be inexcusable who have been unwilling to hear
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold I will bring an affliction upon this place”** — the temple of God, where Baal is, and his altar, upon which they sacrificed and burned their sons
19.4: **“Because they have forsaken me, and have profaned this place: and have sacrificed therein to strange gods, whom neither they nor their fathers knew, nor the kings of Juda: and they have filled this place with the blood of innocents.”** — Because, etc. Every heretic forsakes God and makes strange the place of God’s dwelling, which he pollutes by his fraud, and sacrifices to strange gods, whom his fathers, that is, the apostles and apostolic men, did not know. But the kings of Juda, that is, the heresiarchs, once filled the place of God with the blood of the deceived and of the innocent. For no one is quickly overthrown except the foolish and simple. And they build the high places of Baalim, while they dispute about lofty things. And they burn to idols their sons, whom they have begotten in heresy.
19.5: **“which I did not command”** — Which I commanded not, nor thought of, etc. Not that the Lord does not know future things, but he says he does not know what is unworthy of his knowledge, as to them: “Depart from me, I know you not.” For “the Lord knoweth who are his,” and he who ignores shall be ignored. Or these things are to be taken of God anthropopathically, as are others.
19.6: **“Therefore behold the days come, saith the Lord, that this place shall no more be called Topheth, nor the valley of the son of Ennom, but the valley of slaughter.”** — Topheth and the valley, etc. Jerome. What the valley of the son of Ennom is, which in Hebrew is called gehennon, whence they think Gehenna is named, we have said above. But I wonder what the Septuagint mean by putting for Topheth “ruin,” and for the valley “polyandrion,” that is, a multitude of men, unless perhaps because there the people fell and a multitude of men was slain; either spiritually by the error of idolatry, or historically by the Babylonian laying waste.
19.7: **“And I will defeat the counsel of Juda and of Jerusalem in this place: and I will destroy them with the sword in the sight of their enemies, and by the hands of them that seek their lives: and I will give their carcasses to be meat for the fowls of the air, and for the beasts of the earth.”** — And I will give their carcasses, etc. Although these things befell the people in the Babylonian captivity, yet more truly in the times of Christ, when the city was besieged by Vespasian and Titus and Adrian and fell into everlasting ashes, so that those who had offered their sons to idols devoured them, driven by necessity; and those who had abused the gifts of God in impiety, and sacrificed their own bowels to idols, made their own bellies the tombs of their children.
19.10: **“And thou shalt break the bottle”** — wholly in the Roman captivity
19.11:
**“And thou shalt say to them: Thus saith the Lord of hosts: even so will I break this people”** — so that it will not be restored after the Roman captivity, as it was after the Babylonian
**“and this city, as the potter's vessel is broken, which cannot be made whole again”** — into its former state
**“even so will I break”** — Under Aelius Hadrian the city lost both its name and its state, to break the pride of its inhabitants. But the names of the holy cross and resurrection signify not the city but the place.
*Jerome:* The Jews think that Jerusalem will be restored, gilded and jewelled, with victims and sacrifices and the marriages of the saints, and a kingdom in the land of the Saviour. Although we do not follow these things, we cannot condemn them, because many churchmen and martyrs bear witness to them; let each abound in his own sense, and let all things be reserved to the true judge.
**“and they shall be buried in Topheth, because there is no other place to bury in”** — And they shall be buried in Topheth, etc. What he had said before, “this place shall no more be called Topheth, and the valley of the son of Ennom, but the valley of slaughter,” he here makes plain: that so great a slaughter will be in that very ground that the people will be buried there in heaps, and a place of religion will become a tomb of the dead, and the city itself, which overhangs this place, will become as Topheth.
19.12: **“Thus will I do to this place, saith the Lord, and to the inhabitants thereof: and I will make this city as Topheth.”** — Septuagint: ruin
19.13:
**“And the houses of Jerusalem, and the houses”** — palaces
**“of the kings of Juda shall be unclean as the place of Topheth”**
• in ruin
• deservedly
**“unclean”** — idolatry
**“all the houses upon whose roofs they have sacrificed to all the host of heaven”** — to the sun, the moon, and the stars
**“And”** — not content with these
**“And the houses”** — All the houses of the kings of Juda as the place of Topheth. This is not found in the Hebrew but is inserted by the Septuagint.
19.14:
**“Then Jeremias came from Topheth”** — where he broke the flask in the presence of the elders whom he had brought with him
**“whither the Lord had sent him to prophecy, and he stood in the court of the house of the Lord, and said to all the people”** — who would not go with him into Topheth
19.15:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold I will bring in upon this city, and upon all the cities thereof”** — subject
**“all the evils that I have spoken against it: because”** — not unjustly
**“they have hardened their necks”** — with a stiff neck and uncircumcised of heart, and after many impieties they do not do penance

20.1:
**“Now Phassur heard”** — The Septuagint: Phassur, which is interpreted “blackness of the mouth”
**“the son of Emmer, the priest”** — the name from which blackness is derived, not by the fault of the parent but by the crime of the one who begot him
**“And Phassur heard”** — This man was the high priest of the temple, and perversely abused the dignity of the priesthood, not to teach and rebuke with speech, but to terrify with tortures. The Lord also, and the apostle Paul, were beaten by order of the high priest; nor is it a wonder if to this day the servants of God are beaten by Phassur and sent to prison, for this power is given by the Lord that the faith of the saints may be shown. Nor does he conquer who strikes, but he who is struck and humbly suffers the judgment of the Lord, and does not cry out against the one who beats him but considers him who commands.
20.2:
**“And Phassur struck Jeremias the prophet, and put him in the stocks”** — a kind of torture
**“that were in the upper gate of Benjamin”** — son of the right hand
**“upper”** — upper, which indicates not truth but the unjust power of the priest
20.3:
**“And when it was light”** — The patience and prudence of the prophet are to be noted: sent into prison, he is silent, and overcomes the injury by silence; yet he does not conceal what he knows is to come, that at least the priest of God may cease to sin and may entreat the clemency of God.
**“when it was light the next day, Phassur brought Jeremias out of the stocks. And Jeremias said to him: The Lord hath not called thy name Phassur, but fear on every side.”**
• Not Phassur, etc. According to the interpretation above, by which the name Phassur had been changed so as to be called Phaschor, all have translated likewise, that they might signify either fear, or sojourning, or taking away, or transference.
• The Lord hath not called thy name Phassur, etc. The name of the high priest is changed to show the punishment to come. As if to say: you will not have blackness of face and the unjust sway of power, but you will be led captive to Babylon. For this is what fear on every side means: that trembling and uncertain of safety you may look about here and there and dread the adversaries who come.
20.6: **“But thou, Phassur, and all that dwell in thy house, shall go into captivity, and thou shalt go to Babylon, and there thou shalt die, and there thou shalt be buried, thou and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied a lie.”** — not true and sorrowful things, but false and prosperous ones, by promising
20.7:
**“Thou hast deceived me, O Lord, and I am deceived”** — or, “You have deceived me, O Lord, and I was deceived”
**“thou hast been stronger than I”** — or, you prevailed and were able
**“and thou hast prevailed. I am become a laughing-stock all the day”** — because they think I have lied in everything
**“all scoff at me”**
• The Apostle: “having damnation, because they have made void their first faith”
• Thou hast deceived me, O Lord, etc. The prophet says he was deceived by the Lord, to whom it was said above: “I have made thee a prophet unto the nations,” and “I have set thee this day over the nations, and over the kingdoms,” etc. By these words he supposed that he would say nothing against the Jews but against the nations, and therefore willingly took up prophecy. But now the matter has fallen out the opposite way, so that preaching the captivity of Jerusalem he endures persecutions and distresses.
• I am become, etc. The prophet had thought that what the Lord threatened would come at once; and the people reckoned that what had not come at once would not come.
**“Augustine.”** — Concerning adulterous marriages. A penitent cannot be reconciled while persevering in the same wickedness. Those who chose continence by their will made it a matter of necessity, since they can no longer turn aside from it without damnation.
20.8:
**“For I am speaking now this long time, crying out against iniquity”** — of the enemies
**“and I often proclaim devastation”** — Babylon
**“and I often proclaim devastation: and the word of the Lord is made a reproach to me, and a derision all the day.”** — since they think the delay of the prophecy is a lie
**“and the word of the Lord is made a reproach to me”** — Gregory. Because he saw that he was scarcely heard, he desired silence; but when he saw the evil growing, or the evil conscience, he did not remain in that same silence. For he who outwardly grew weary from the tedium of speaking bore within a fire from zeal of charity. For the hearts of the just are inflamed when they see uncorrected things growing, and they believe themselves sharers of the evil and of their guilt, whom by keeping silent they permit in iniquity. Whence David: “My heart grew hot within me: and in my meditation a fire shall flame out.”
**“Septuagint”** — Because with my bitter word I shall laugh at transgression, and call upon misery. As if to say: I know that present sadness is to be exchanged for future joy (whence “blessed are they that weep, for they shall laugh”); therefore I willingly endure misery and iniquity and affliction, I desire it, I call upon it, compensating the brevity of injury with the eternity of happiness.
20.9:
**“Then I said: I will not make mention of him”** — that is, I will no longer speak words to them nor name his name
**“nor speak any more in his name”** — he resolved this, indeed modestly, but foolishly
**“and there came”** — a word not uttered by the mouth
**“in my heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones”** — Whence Paul: “If I preach the gospel, it is no glory to me, for a necessity lieth upon me”; elsewhere also he was stirred up in spirit and burned with his whole mind.
20.11:
**“the Lord”** — by grace.
**“But the Lord is with me”**
• let us too in like persecution say the same.
• by free will.
**“as a strong warrior: therefore”** — because they persecute.
**“they that persecute me shall fall”** — or therefore they persecuted and could not understand the prophet, namely whence confusion will be to them.
**“and shall be weak: they shall be greatly confounded, because they have not understood the everlasting reproach”** — which will be blotted out by no forgetting.
20.12:
**“And thou, O Lord of hosts, prover of the just”** — or who tests what is just.
**“And thou, O Lord”** — God alone is he who proves justice, as he alone is he who sees the conscience of the heart. Whence Jesus, knowing the thoughts of men, is God not from advancement, as some think, but by nature. Like to this: “In thy sight no man living shall be justified,” that is, in virtues; much less, then, one dead in sins.
**“who seest the reins and the heart: let me see, I beseech thee, thy vengeance on them: for to thee I have laid open my cause.”** — Let me see, I beseech thee, etc. Although the just man knows he has God as his fighter, nevertheless in the patience of human frailty he already now desires to see what he knows is to come.
**“for to thee”** — For to thee, etc. You who say to me, “Revenge is mine, and I will repay,” etc. Happy the conscience whose cause is revealed to the Lord; whence, as the apostle says, everything that is made manifest is light.
20.13:
**“Sing ye to the Lord, praise the Lord: because he hath delivered the soul of the poor”** — in spirit, who has not the riches of this age; whoever has them receives his consolation.
**“because he hath delivered”** — Because he hath delivered. Poor in spirit, having obtained vengeance from the Lord, he praises and glories that he has been snatched from the hand of the wicked. This however does not come about by merit but by the grace of him who freed the poor man, who does not love the riches of falling pride but the humility of the freed poor man.
20.14: **“Cursed be the day”** — Jeremias was born in the fifth month, that is, in August; and on that same day the city was laid waste by the Chaldeans and Romans, on the very day on which he had been born; and on account of this misery which he had foreseen he says, Cursed be the day, etc.
20.15:
**“Cursed be the man”** — rightly the man who announces the birth of a male child is cursed, because by his announcement our corrupter’s base joy is made known.
**“that brought the tidings to my father, saying: A man child is born to thee: and made him greatly rejoice.”**
• Cursed be the man, etc. Those who think that souls were in the heavens and were cast down from a better state into a worse, use testimonies of this kind, namely, that it would have been better to dwell in the heavens than in earthly things and to be clothed with a body. But we, according to that of blessed Job, “Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man child is conceived,” and “cursed be the man that brought the tidings to my father, saying: A man child is born to thee.” We expound this testimony thus: that it is better not to be than to be in torments. Whence “death is rest to a man whose way is hid,” for whom God hath shut his way, and “why is light given to him that is in misery?” etc., and it was better for him if he had not been born; not that one who has not been born is anything, but that it is better not to be than to be ill. For it is one thing not to be at all, another to be tormented without any intermission, just as we prefer quiet death to a miserable life. Whence Amos calls it a day of darkness, a day of affliction; and Jacob, because he lived in labor and distress, calls the days of his life few and evil. And Paul: “that he might deliver us from this present wicked world,” and “redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”
• Cursed be the man, etc. In the person of the prophet the changeableness of the wavering human race is signified; by his father, this world from which we are born is expressed. The man who announces our birth to our father is the ancient enemy, who, when he sees us wavering in our thoughts, incites the minds of the wicked to persuade our deception. And when he has seen us do weak things, he lifts them up with favors as if they were strong, and speaks of us as born males when he rejoices that we have become corrupters of truth or innocence through falsehood. Therefore he announces to the father that a male is born when he shows to this world the one he has persuaded to be made a corrupter of innocence. For when it is said to any sinner and proud man, “You have acted like a man,” what else is announced in the world but a male born?
20.16:
**“Let that man be as the cities”** — Sodom and Gomorrha.
**“that the Lord hath overthrown, and hath not repented: let him hear a cry in the morning”** — that for all time he may be in mourning.
**“and howling at noontide”** — all by hyperbole.
20.18: **“Why came I out of the womb”** — he explains the reasons why he prefers death to life.

21.1:
**“The word that came to Jeremias from the Lord, when”** — wishing secretly for either the people or the prince to know what the Lord answers.
**“king Sedecias sent unto him Phassur, the son of Melchias, and Sophonias, the son of Maasias the priest, saying:”**
• When he sent to him, etc. It is to be noted that in the prophets, and especially in Ezechiel and Jeremias, the order neither of events nor of times is kept; but out of order, what according to history was done later is related first, and conversely. For it is one thing to write history, another to write prophecy. Whence in the present place Sedecias, who was taken with the city of Jerusalem, is written as sending to Jeremias, at the time when Jerusalem was besieged; and afterwards the history is told of his brother Joakim, who reigned before him, and of Joakim, that is, of Jechonias, who was the son of Joakim, of whom it is said in what follows.
• Phassur the son of, etc. Above, the high priest Phassur or Phashur, who struck Jeremias, had as father Emmer; this Phassur, however, is the son of Melchias, for they are not the same.
21.2: **“Inquire of the Lord for us, for Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon”** — for the city was already besieged.
21.4:
**“Thus saith the Lord, the God of Israel: Behold I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands, with which you fight against the king of Babylon, and the Chaldeans, that besiege you round about the walls: and I will gather them together in the midst of this city.”** — I will gather them, or those things.
**“Behold I will turn back”** — As if you wished to fight in vain and prepare warlike arms, of which you will have such use in the middle of the city that you seem to be armed. For the enemies did not have whom they might conquer but only whom they might capture.
21.5:
**“And I myself will fight against you”** — not the Chaldeans.
**“with an outstretched hand, and with a strong arm”** — open vengeance.
**“and in fury”** — against the worst.
**“and in”** — or for.
**“indignation”** — against the less sinning.
**“and in great wrath”** — against the middling.
21.6:
**“And I will strike the inhabitants of this city”**
• earthly
• woe upon the inhabitants of the earth
**“men”** — rational
**“and beasts”** — simple
**“a great pestilence”**
• double
• of the soul, not of the body only
21.7:
**“And after this, saith the Lord, I will give Sedecias the king of Juda, and his servants, and his people, and such as are left in this city from the pestilence, and the sword, and the famine, into the hand of Nabuchodonosor the king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of them that seek their life, and he shall strike them with the edge of the sword, and he shall not be moved to pity, nor spare them, nor shew mercy on them”**
• I will give Sedecias, etc. First it was prophesied of the whole city; now properly of Sedecias and his people who survive the pestilence, famine and sword: that he is to be taken by Nabuchodonosor and so also killed with his friends, and let him hope for no mercy, since he violated the covenant by perjury.
• Neither shall he spare, etc. The Septuagint has it thus: “I will not spare, nor have mercy.” But it is better, according to the Hebrew, that the sentence be cruel and unbending as the king’s, rather than the Lord’s.
**“Into the hand”** — Into the hand of Nabuchodonosor the king of Babylon, and into the hand of his enemies. These are not in the Septuagint.
21.8:
**“And to this people”** — To the king’s messengers who had come to the prophet to ask the Lord, he answered above what they should report to the king; now he exhorts him to answer the people, and gives counsel that they flee over to the Chaldeans against the will of the king, which no one doubts was dangerous to the prophet; whence he also calls down death upon himself, saying: “Cursed be the day wherein I was born.”
**“And to this people thou shalt say: Thus saith the Lord: Behold I set before you the way of life, and the way of death”** — Behold I set, etc. There are those who expound this place according to the tropological sense thus: it is better to give oneself over to secular disciplines, and above all to philosophical ones, than to remain in that Church in which there is a famine of the word of God, and every people dies by the sword of heretics, and by want of doctrine, and by the heretical plague.
21.9: **“He that shall abide in this city, shall die by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence”** — as if this is indeed grievous, but it is lighter to live in captivity than to die by the sword and by famine and by pestilence
21.11:
**“And to the house of the king of Juda”**
• you who speak above to the people
• This is said properly to the royal house, for whose fault the city is chiefly besieged, that by penance they may amend the error and obtain the mercy of the Lord.
21.12:
**“O house of David, thus saith the Lord: Judge ye judgment in the morning”** — in the light of justice
**“and deliver him that is oppressed by violence”** — the poor man
**“out of the hand of the oppressor”**
• the rich
• as if you should not respect persons in judgment
**“lest my indignation go forth”** — as if, if you do this, the fire of my wrath will not find in you the matter it may consume
**“like a fire, and be kindled, and there be none to quench it, because of the evil of your ways”**
• This is not found in the Septuagint.
• Judge in the morning, etc. In this place the clemency of God is shown; for when he had said above, “I have set my face against this city for evil,” etc., now he calls them to salvation, though the sentence is already pressing; not that he is ignorant that the city is to be taken, but he shows the free choice of man, that he may be seen to undergo the danger by his own will. As the Saviour knew that the people would deny him and that he was to be crucified, and had often said this to the apostles, and nonetheless warned them to repentance, so that whatever they afterwards suffered might befall them by their own fault, not by the harshness of him who threatened.
21.13:
**“Behold I come to thee that dwellest in a valley upon a rock above a plain, saith the Lord: and you say: Who shall strike us? and who shall enter into our houses?”** — Behold I, etc. I will speak against Jerusalem, which is besieged. Or, as Tyre is girt by the sea, so is she girt by the Babylonian army and cannot escape. Or, as the hardest rock, she thinks herself impregnable and strong, because of the solidity and size of her walls.
**“to thee that dwellest in a valley”** — The Septuagint: “Who dwellest in the valley of Sor and of the plain”; for which Symmachus has “rock,” Theodotion “oppressed,” Aquila’s first edition “solid,” the second “Tyre.” For Sor or Sur in the Hebrew tongue means Tyre and a compacted stone.
21.14:
**“And”** — I, if no one else can, whose eye you cannot escape
**“But I will visit upon you according to the fruit of your doings, saith the Lord: and I will kindle”** — I, not the Babylonian
**“a fire in the forest thereof: and it shall devour all things round about it”** — I will visit upon you, etc. Gregory. That they added to their other sins the sins which are committed through perverse counsel. The Lord pursues not so much evil deeds as the devices of wickedness. For in deeds one often sins through weakness, often through negligence; but in devices always with malicious intent. Whence also “he sat not in the chair of pestilence.” He sits in the chair of perverse counsel who is lifted up with such pride of iniquity that he attempts to accomplish evil even by counsels.
**“in the forest”** — Jerusalem and the surrounding region, which had no fruitful trees of good works and therefore was worthy of burning. How beautifully he calls it a plain valley, as open to enemies, not a lofty mountain that is hard to climb. Whence Isaias: “The vision of the valley of Sion.”

22.1:
**“Thus saith the Lord”** — This word of the Lord came to the prophet before Sedecias sent messengers to him, or after he instructed the messengers what they should announce to the king.
**“Thus saith the Lord: Go down to the house of the king of Juda, and there thou shalt speak this word,”** — Thus saith the Lord. Jeremias is commanded to speak to the king not through messengers but by himself. And the divine wisdom is to be noted: through messengers he orders sad things to be reported; through the prophet himself, not sad things but what the king ought to do, namely, that he may escape the impending sentence of God.
22.3:
**“Thus saith the Lord:”** — what belongs to the king he commands
