**“Execute judgment and justice, and deliver him that is oppressed out of the hand of the oppressor: and afflict not the stranger, the fatherless, nor the widow”** — these are more easily oppressed by the powerful
**“afflict not, nor oppress them unjustly”** — as if you should not only rescue them but not allow them to be grieved or oppressed by others
**“and shed not innocent blood”** — for to punish murderers, sacrilegious persons and poisoners is not the shedding of blood but the office of the law
**“Execute judgment”** — Whatever was said to the royal house, let bishops, priests, deacons and every ecclesiastical order understand. If they do the commandments of God, and do not shed innocent blood by scandalizing the little ones and wounding the consciences of individuals, let them keep their own dignity; otherwise they reduce the Church to desolation. And they enter, of the race of David, by the gates of Jerusalem, and sit upon his throne, whose name is interpreted “strong of hand,” and ride in chariots and on horses, when they restrain both their own disturbances and those of the people, and walk in the Church with measured step.
22.4:
**“For if you will do this thing indeed, then shall there enter in by the gates of this house”** — that is, you will keep your former power and will enter with pomp through the gates of Jerusalem
**“For if you will do this thing indeed”** — Allegorically. Whatever is prophesied of the royal house and of the metropolis city, let us refer to the ecclesiastical order and the princes of the Churches, who have given themselves over to pride, and riches, and wantonness. Nor are they at once delivered because they are of the royal house; for of those who were of the royal stock of David, few were found who pleased the Lord, such as David himself, Ezechias, Josias. But a great part of the princes and of the royal stock provoked the wrath of God against the whole people.
22.5:
**“But if you will not hearken to these words”** — as if the cruelty will not be so much the Lord’s as of your own will
**“I swear by myself”** — as though I had no one greater
22.6:
**“For thus saith the Lord to the house of the king of Juda: Thou art to me Galaad the head of Libanus: yet surely”** — I, not the king of Babylon
**“Galaad”** — Galaad. Which is in the half tribe of Manasses beyond the Jordan, on which mount Laban overtook the fleeing Jacob; and it was called the heap of witness, because there Jacob and Laban swore upon a heap gathered of stones. It is also the head, or the chief, of Mount Libanus the lofty, which is planted throughout with cedars. Whence: “The Lord will shake the cedars of Libanus.” And: “I have seen the wicked highly exalted, and lifted up like the cedars of Libanus.” And in Zacharias: “Open thy gates, O Libanus, and let fire devour thy cedars.” Since, then, he was speaking to the royal house, he speaks by metaphor to the temple or to the royal house, either because it is itself on a height, or because all sinners seek remedies for their sins from the temple. Whence: “Is there no balm in Galaad? or is no physician there?”
**“yet surely I will make”** — He threatens the royal house, and the city of Jerusalem, and the temple, which he calls the head of Lebanon, that it is to be reduced to desolation with all its cities.
**“thee a wilderness, and cities not habitable”** — Let the royal house of our city hear these things, and its princes, and the cedars that are lifted up to heaven and speak pride: “Who shall see us?” For they will quickly be consumed by the flame of the Lord if they will not submit to his precepts. One is the sanctification of the slayer and his arms, another that of the priests and of those who minister to the Lord.
22.7:
**“And I will prepare against thee the destroyer”** — Nabuchodonosor, who carries out the Lord’s sentence
**“and his weapons: and they shall cut down thy chosen cedars”** — the mighty and the princes of the city
**“and shall cast them headlong into the fire”** — the devouring flame will consume everything
22.8:
**“shall pass by”** — all being destroyed
**“And many nations shall pass by this city: and they shall say every man to his neighbour: Why hath the Lord done so to this great city?”** — Most wickedly
22.9:
**“And they shall answer”** — to the one asking
**“Because they have forsaken the covenant of the Lord their God, and have adored strange gods”** — for the true God
22.10:
**“Weep not for him that is dead, nor bemoan him with your tears: lament him”** — the three sons of Josias, or more properly Sedecias
**“that goeth away, for he shall return no more, nor see his native country”** — Weep not, etc. Jerome. This seems to me to be said properly of Sedecias, of whom is the prophecy both of the present chapter and of the past one; under him the kingdom truly came to an end, under him the city was taken, and he himself was led to Babylon and died. This is Sellum, that is, consummation and completion, the son of Josias, king of Juda, who reigned after Josias his father. But Jechonias was not the son but the grandson of Josias, the son of Joachim; so that from the beginning of this vision, when Sedecias sent to Jeremias Phassur the son of Melchias and Sophonias the son of Maasias the priest, up to this chapter, we understand everything of Sedecias. Woe to him that buildeth his house, etc.
22.11: **“to Sellum the son of Josias”** — Josias, a just king, had three sons: Joachaz, Joachim, and Sedecias. Pharao Nechao carried the first into Egypt, and he died there, and set up his brother Joachim in his place; when he died, his son Jechonias reigned, who was led into captivity by Nabuchodonosor with his mother and the princes; in his place his uncle Sedecias reigned, who, when Jerusalem was taken, was led to Babylon. Since, then, three were taken captive, the Hebrews think this fits all of them, and they call all the sons of Josias Sellem or Sellum, that is, consummation or completion, because in them the kingdom of Juda came to an end.
22.13:
**“Woe to him that”** — a heretic
**“buildeth up his house”** — a conventicle
**“by injustice”** — because he plunders what belongs to others
**“and his chambers not in judgment: that will oppress his friend”** — whom he deceives under the name of friendship
**“without cause, and will not pay him his wages”** — whom you promise
**“will not pay him”** — Woe to him, etc. Of Joachim the son of Josias, whom Pharao upheld in place of Joachaz his brother, who reigned eleven years impiously and cruelly; the history relates that he died and was not buried, although it tells of other kings who were dead and buried; but of this one it properly relates that he died and was not buried, of which we shall speak in what follows.
22.14:
**“Who saith: I will build me a wide house”** — thinking that he will reign forever
**“and large chambers: who openeth to himself windows”** — for he does not have a solid and lasting building
**“and maketh roofs of cedar”** — for it seems to have a most beautiful building
**“and painteth them with vermilion”** — with the blood of Christ
22.15:
**“Shalt thou reign”**
• forever
• heretics do not reign forever
**“because thou comparest thyself to the cedar”**
• to Josias, the just father, king
• by contending against the Church
**“thy father”** — Josias your father
**“did not thy father eat”** — partaking of the body of Christ, enjoying royal works, yet not offending God
**“and drink”**
• the blood
• ecclesiastical: all heretics began from the Church
**“and do judgment and justice, and it was then well with him”** — as if: he did not grow proud from abundance, therefore it was well with him both in the present and in the future, or will be
22.16:
**“judged the cause of the poor and needy for his own good”** — of the poor and needy, or of himself
**“was it not therefore because he knew me”** — he had these good things
22.17:
**“But thy eyes and thy heart”** — Joakim, of body and of soul.
**“to covetousness”** — that you may snatch away what belongs to others.
**“and upon shedding innocent blood”** — of the deceived.
**“shedding, and upon oppression, and running after evil works”** — or: running.
22.18:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord concerning Joakim the son of Josias king of Juda: They shall not mourn for him, Alas, my brother, and Alas, sister: they shall not lament for him, Alas, my Lord,”** — but
**“They shall not mourn for him”** — Jerome. What we have put from the Hebrew, “they shall not mourn for him, Alas, brother, and Alas, sister,” is not properly found in the Septuagint; it is said against Joakim king of Juda, and it is made plain which of the brothers was in doubt, so that the discourse is not about Joachaz or Sedecias but properly about Joakim, whom the Hebrew history tells was slain by bands of robbers of the Chaldeans, Syrians, Ammonites and Moabites. Whence in Kings it is written that he died, but his burial is passed over in silence. In the Book of Chronicles we read that he was bound in chains and led to Babylon, and nothing more is related of him after that.
**“Alas, the noble one”** — Led away in chains by Nabuchodonosor; but he also made peace on the way, under tribute. But afterwards he rebelled, and at last robbers killed him. Whence: “the burial of an ass,” etc.
22.19: **“He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, rotten”** — that is, unburied, he will be torn by beasts and birds; for this is the burial of an ass.
22.20:
**“Go up to Libanus, and cry: and lift up thy voice in Basan, and cry to them that pass by, for all thy lovers are destroyed.”** — Go up to Libanus, etc. Through the metaphor of Libanus and Basan, a region and mountains beyond the Jordan, he prophesies to Jerusalem that she has trusted in vain in the Egyptians. Or to Joakim, who was then resisting and had been set up as king by the Egyptians: that he hopes in vain for help from them, for they themselves were taken captive by the king of Babylon.
*Jerome:* What we render “cry to them that pass by,” as is also written in Hebrew, meabalim; the Seventy and Theodotion rendered “beyond the sea,” Symmachus “from across,” so as to signify that the voice of the prophet ought to reach as far as Mount Lebanon and Bashan.
22.21:
**“I spoke”** — God through the prophets; or the prophets spoke, that is.
**“to thee in thy prosperity”** — being proud against me from your abundance.
**“thou saidst: I will not hear: this hath been thy way”** — that is, pride, since you were brought out of Egypt.
22.22:
**“all thy pastors”** — the princes scattered hither and thither.
**“The wind shall feed, and thy lovers shall go into captivity”** — to Babylon.
22.23:
**“Thou that sittest in Libanus”** — it signifies arrogance.
**“and makest thy nest in the cedars, how hast thou mourned when sorrows came upon thee”** — of sudden captivity.
22.24:
**“As I live, saith the Lord, if Jechonias the son of Joakim the king of Juda were a ring on my right hand”** — who is with difficulty snatched from the hand of the one carrying him.
**“thence”** — Yet.
**“I would pluck him”**
• As I live, etc. Above he had said: “to the house of the king of Juda you shall speak this word”; then, “go down to the house of the king of Juda”; and again, “thus saith the Lord to the house of the king of Juda.” And in a reversed order, after he has spoken of Sedecias, who was the last king, he returns to Joakim his brother, who reigned before him; and when this prophecy is finished he now speaks to Jechonias the son of Joakim, grandson of Josias, who by another name is called Joachin, who was taken captive with many nobles, and led into Chaldea, and died there.
• Also his mother, that is, the synagogue, captured and cast down; and he does not fear what follows, “Thus saith the Lord.” Write this man, ab omniatum, etc., to be understood of the majesty of the Lord.
• For if he were, etc. Jerome. Wretched Grunnius translated into Latin a single book of Sextus, a Pythagorean, a Gentile, and divided it into two volumes under the name of Sixtus the martyr. In it no mention is made of Christ, none of the Holy Spirit, none of God the Father, none of the patriarchs, prophets or apostles; and with his usual rashness and madness he named this book the Ring, which is read in many provinces, and especially by those who preach apathy and sinlessness. Since therefore the Lord threatens that he will cast Jechonias away from his hand like a ring, so I beseech the reader to cast away this wicked book. If he wishes to read it, let him read it as a philosopher, not as a churchman.
*Jerome:* In commentaries and expositions, whose custom is to set out the differing opinions of interpreters, I am accustomed to mix in speech of this sort: “some say this, others maintain this, some think thus”; and Grunnius, and after many years the disciples of Jovinian and of that man, have slandered me as putting my own opinions under other men’s names; which I do out of good will, lest by naming a certain person I seem to tear anyone to pieces. I say therefore openly that their master Origen refers this passage to Christ, who like a ring was plucked from the hand of God the Father and sent into the land of captivity, into the valley of tears, and handed over to the cross.
22.25: **“And I will give thee into the hand of them that seek thy life”** — of the Babylonians.
22.27:
**“into the land”** — Judea.
**“whereunto they lift up their mind”** — with longing.
22.28:
**“why are they cast out”** — That this was done concerning Jechonias, no one doubts.
**“he and his seed, and are cast into a land which they know not”** — Is it an earthen vessel, etc. Jerome. Since this is said of Jechonias the son of Joakim, how can it be referred to Christ? And how, from the fact that the apostle says he is “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature,” can he be called a ring that is cast away from the hand of the Lord and handed over to the king of Babylon?
**“This man Jechonias”** — Jerome. Jechonias means “preparation of the Lord,” from which in the present place the first syllable, ie, that is, the name of the Lord, is taken away, and it is called Conias, as if it were understood: prepared for destruction and perishing.
22.30:
**“Thus saith the Lord: Write this man barren, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for there shall not be a man of his seed that shall sit upon the throne of David”** — only; but Christ, God and man, whose kingdom will not be earthly and brief like the kingdom of David, but perpetual and heavenly.
**“and have power any more in Juda”** — Write this man, etc. Jerome. Christ was born of this man’s seed. Whence Gabriel: “The Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father,” etc.; but not in his days, but much later. Of Joakim was born Jechonias, of whom Salathiel, of whom Zorobabel, and in order it comes down to Christ. But in the days of Joakim no son succeeded him as king, as he himself had succeeded his father; and until Christ none obtained royal power. For all were captives, and of the stock of David none reigned in Judea. Whence Josephus relates that the rulers were of the tribe of Levi, to whom Herod succeeded, the son of Antipater the proselyte; and afterwards, under Vespasian, the government of this race, or rather the semblance of a kingdom, was utterly destroyed.
**“barren”** — Aquila’s first edition: sterile. Second: not growing. Symmachus: empty. The Seventy and Theodotion: abominable and disowned.

23.1:
**“Woe to the pastors, that destroy and tear the sheep of my pasture, saith the Lord.”** — Woe to the pastors, etc. Because all hope of the Jewish kingdom has failed, the word passes to the leaders of the Church; the synagogue with its shepherds is abandoned and condemned. The discourse is about the apostles, of whom it is said: “And I will set up pastors over them,” etc.
*Jerome:* We can understand this, according to the tropological sense, of the rulers of the Church who do not worthily rule the sheep of the Lord; when they are cast out and condemned, the people handed over to good shepherds is saved, and the remnant are saved. Shepherds destroy the sheep by teaching heresy. They tear and scatter them by making schisms; they cast them out of the Church by unjustly separating them; they do not visit the sick; they withhold the hand from the penitent. God has mercy on them all, restoring the former pastures and taking away the evil shepherds.
23.2: **“Therefore thus saith the Lord the God of Israel to the pastors that feed my people”** — the scribes and Pharisees of the synagogue.
23.3: **“And I will gather together the remnant of my flock, out of all the lands”** — that there may be one fold.
23.4:
**“And I will set up pastors over them”** — the apostles.
**“and they shall feed them”**
• with the bread of the word of God.
• The flock of the Church.
23.5:
**“Behold the days come, saith the Lord, and I will raise up to David a just branch”** — Christ.
**“and a king shall reign, and shall be wise, and shall execute judgment”** — For neither doth the Father judge any man, but hath given all judgment to the Son.
**“and justice in the earth”** — Behold the days, etc. The shepherds of the synagogue, namely the scribes and Pharisees, having been cast out, Christ, the shepherd of shepherds, is brought in and put in their place, and the apostles.
23.6:
**“In those days”** — That from two rods there will be one.
**“shall Juda be saved”** — The two tribes.
**“and Israel”** — The ten tribes.
**“shall dwell confidently: and this is the name that they shall call him”** — as also in Isaias he is called Emmanuel.
**“the Lord our just one”** — Whence: who of God is made unto us wisdom, and justice.
23.7:
**“Therefore behold the days to come”** — when the sun of justice shall rise.
**“saith the Lord, and they shall say no more: The Lord liveth, who brought up”** — says the Lord; and they shall no longer say: The Lord liveth, who brought up, by Moses.
**“the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt”** — Therefore, etc. This whole chapter is not found in the Septuagint, and its sense is this: that the people of God is to be freed from Egypt not through Moses but through Christ from the whole world; which will be fulfilled entirely when “from the east and the west and the north and the south” they shall come and sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so that after the fulness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel may be saved.
23.8:
**“But the Lord liveth, who hath brought out”** — through Christ.
**“and brought hither the seed of the house of Israel from the land of the north, and out of all the lands, to which I had cast them forth: and they shall dwell in their own land.”** — The Church.
23.9:
**“To the prophets”**
• False.
• The word is addressed.
**“My heart is broken within me”** — He offers to God the victim of humility; whence: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise”; concerning which all my bones will say: “Lord, who is like to thee?”
**“all my bones tremble: I am become as a drunken man, and as a man full of wine, at the presence of the Lord, and at the presence of his holy words.”**
• or of the comeliness of his glory.
• And as a man full of wine, etc. Of no understanding, of no wisdom. For the Lord knoweth the thoughts of men, that they are vain. Where then are those who preach perfect justice in man? If they answer that they say this of the saints, not of themselves: who is holier than Jeremias, a virgin and prophet, sanctified in the womb, bearing the Saviour in his name? For Jeremias means “the exalted of the Lord.”
• From the presence of the Lord, etc. The prophet, considering the countenance of almighty God, that is of the Father, and the countenance of the Son, who is the brightness of glory and the figure of his substance, shudders in soul and body, and understands himself to be nothing; whence: “I am become as a beast before thee.”
23.10:
**“Because the land is full of adulterers”** — We do not have this in the Septuagint.
**“by reason of cursing”** — Septuagint: of his vain oath.
**“the land hath mourned”** — therefore.
**“the fields of the desert are dried up”** — Made barren.
**“the fields of the desert are dried up: and their course is become evil, and their strength unlike.”** — Mourned the land, etc. Whatever you understand of the land of Judea according to the letter, you can refer to the congregation of believers. For because of adulteries, lies, and perjuries, barrenness of virtues and of graces follows.
23.11:
**“prophet”** — teacher.
**“For ... and the priest”** — of the ministry of doctrine.
**“are defiled: and in my house”** — Church.
**“The prophet also”** — When evils are found in the Church of God, and especially among its leaders, we know this to be fulfilled. For the prophet and the priest are defiled.
23.12:
**“Therefore their way”** — the error of heretics.
**“shall be as a slippery way in the dark”**
• Whence they may not see; he who says, “I am the light of the world.”
• against which is written: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us.”
**“for they shall be driven on”** — every wind of doctrine
**“and fall therein: for I will bring evils upon them, the year of their visitation, saith the Lord.”** — I will bring upon them, etc. Not that they are evils, or that the Lord brings evils; but they seem evils to those who endure the punishments, since otherwise the same things are both good and evil: evils to those whom they torment, good to those whom they correct. And it should be noted that the year of the Lord’s visitation is called the correction and torment of the sinner; whence: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod,” etc. “But my mercy I will not take away from him.”
23.13:
**“And in the prophets of Samaria”**
• heretics, and all who boast of the knowledge of a false name, are the prophets of Samaria
• Since the prophets of Samaria, whatever they say, prophesy in Baal, so heretics, within the Church or outside it, prophesy to supplant the people of Israel, who formerly perceived God; he speaks in demons.
**“I have seen folly: they prophesied”** — who do not have Christ, the power of God, the wisdom of God
**“in Baal”** — consecrated to Baal, an idol consecrated to demons
23.14:
**“And in the prophets”**
• teachers
• not only among heretics
**“of Jerusalem”** — of the Church
**“I have seen the likeness”** — or horrible things
**“adulterers”** — that is, of the word of God
**“and the way of lying”** — going by the way of lying, agreeing with heretics
**“and they strengthened the hands of the wicked”** — whom they ought to have corrected
**“that no man should return from his evil doings: they are all become unto me as Sodom, and the inhabitants thereof as Gomorrha.”** — as if they will not bear it unpunished; their end is like that of Sodom and Gomorrah
**“For from the prophets”** — For from the prophets. For we use this testimony against those who send out into the world letters full of lying, fraud and perjury, and thereby defile the ears of those who hear. For it does not suffice them to devour their own iniquity or to hurt their neighbours, but those whom they have once hated they strive to defame throughout the whole world and to sow blasphemies everywhere.
23.15: **“Therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts to the prophets: Behold I will feed them with wormwood”** — either with sorrows or with bitterness
23.16:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts: Hearken not”** — O people, do not think yourself free of guilt if you have consented; for the punishment of the disciple and the master is equal
**“the words of the prophets that prophesy to you, and deceive you: they speak a vision”** — which they have feigned
23.17:
**“They say to them”** — to heretics and the perverse
**“that blaspheme me: The Lord hath said”** — what we shall say
**“the Lord”** — not we
**“You shall have peace: and to every one that walketh”** — as if you should not fear, terrified by empty threats
**“in the perverseness of his own heart, they have said: No evil shall come upon you.”** — what you fear because of an evil conscience, but the good that the Lord has spoken
23.18:
**“For who hath stood in the counsel of the Lord, and hath seen and heard his word? Who hath considered his word and heard it?”** — For who, etc. Do not believe the false prophets who say these things; whence can they know the counsels of the Lord? Who saw and announced them to them?
*Jerome:* Where we have “in the counsel of the Lord,” the Hebrew is written bassod. Aquila interpreted it as “secret,” Symmachus as “word,” the Seventy and Theodotion as “substance” or “subsistence” of God.
23.19:
**“Behold the whirlwind of the Lord's indignation shall come forth, and a tempest shall break out and come upon the head”** — not upon others
**“come upon the head of the wicked”**
• of the people, or of those who announce falsehoods
• Behold the whirlwind, etc. By contrast it is clear that the prophets do not know what they ought; for the storm of Babylon comes in place of the peace and security they promise.
23.20:
**“The wrath of the Lord shall not return”** — that is, it will not be appeased as before, but it will fulfil what it has often threatened
**“till he execute it, and till he accomplish the thought of his heart: in the latter days”** — when the last time of captivity has come
**“you shall understand his counsel”** — which you do not understand, but you boast that you understand
23.21:
**“I did not send prophets, yet they ran: I have not spoken to them, yet they prophesied.”**
• from their own heart
• I did not send, etc. Hence the apostle: as they did not think fit to have God in their knowledge, “God delivered them up to a reprobate sense, to do those things which are not convenient,” being filled with iniquity, malice, and fornication. For when false teachers have once given themselves over to lies and perjuries and to the deaths of the deceived, they fall headlong to their own destruction and that of others.
• Let us consider the heretics: since once they have despaired, they give themselves over to gluttony, seek delights, frequent the baths, smell of musk, anointed with various ointments, seeking the beauty of their bodies, not believing in the resurrection; which, if they do not say it in words, they speak in deeds.
23.22:
**“If they stood in my counsel”** — that is, they would have consented to my will.
**“and had made my words known to my people”** — not flattering them nor fawning, and saying: “In your righteousness you shall live.”
**“I should have turned them from their evil way and from their wicked doings.”** — so that they would not do what is not fitting, following their own thoughts.
23.23:
**“Am I, think ye, a God at hand, saith the Lord”**
• that I may know all things only when present, not distant; I am everywhere and I know all things.
• Septuagint: God drawing near, I, etc.
23.24:
**“If”** — as if
**“Shall a man be hid”** — “Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy face?”
**“in secret places, and I not see him, saith the Lord? do not”** — as if I am present everywhere, because I fill all things.
23.25:
**“I have heard what the prophets said, that prophesy”** — against whom is the higher heading, to the prophets.
**“lies in my name, and say: I have dreamed, I have dreamed.”** — I have heard what, etc. There are many kinds of prophesying, one of which is of dreams, as in Daniel. Therefore the prophetic word is directed to those who believe in dreams, and think that everything they see is a divine revelation, which is properly opened to the saints. Yet Pharao and Nabuchodonosor, impious kings, saw true dreams, not on account of their own merit, but that on such an occasion Joseph and Daniel might become renowned, and that the untamable hearts of tyrants might feel, by their own conscience, the majesty of the Lord.
23.27:
**“Who seek to make my people forget”** — who now is
**“my name through their dreams, which they tell every man to his neighbour: as their fathers forgot”** — the ancient people who came out of Egypt.
**“my name for Baal.”**
• as if they prophesied not in my name but in Baal.
• Their dreams, etc. There are dreamers today in the Church who make their own errors into prophecies of the Lord, often saying: “I have dreamed.” Against whom it is said: “How long will this be?” etc.
23.28:
**“The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream.”** — It belongs to those who have the word of God, in which is truth and not lies, to interpret the dream.
**“and he that hath my word, let him speak my word with truth: what hath the chaff”** — to heretics
**“to do with the wheat”** — the saints
**“saith the Lord”** — What is the chaff to do with the wheat, etc. Beautifully, the doctrine of heretics is compared to chaff, which has no marrow and gives no nourishment.
23.29:
**“Are not my words”** — not of heretics
**“as a fire”** — as if they announce coming punishments; they do not flatter the chaff, they threaten fire.
**“saith the Lord: and as a hammer that breaketh”** — Septuagint: an axe, of which it is said: “The axe is laid to the root of the tree,” etc.
**“the rock”** — the hard hearts of heretics; that the stony heart may be taken away and a heart of flesh put in, which can receive and perceive the commands of God.
**“Are not”** — Because among the former people the prophets lied, saying: Thus saith the Lord, and I saw the Lord, and the word of the Lord which was made to him or to her. So heretics take up testimonies of the scriptures from both testaments, and steal the words of the Saviour, “every one from his neighbour,” from the prophets, apostles, and evangelists, and “take up their tongues,” that they may utter with the mouth the poisons of the heart, “and sleep a sleep.” Whence: “They have slept their sleep; and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands.” The Lord therefore threatens that he will come against such.
**“As a hammer”** — It is written of churchmen that hammer and axe were not heard in the house of the Lord.
23.30: **“who steal my words”** — For a lie always imitates the truth; otherwise it cannot deceive.
23.31: **“Behold I am against the prophets, saith the Lord: who use their tongues”** — or have slept the sleep of slumber
23.32:
**“Behold, I”** — or the divine word
**“against the prophets that have lying dreams, saith the Lord: and tell them, and cause my people to err by their lying, and by their wonders”** — they promise great and incredible marvels, teaching what is not fitting for the sake of shameful gain, announcing prosperity to the wicked and adversity to the good.
23.33:
**“If therefore this people, or the prophet, or the priest shall ask thee, saying: What is the burden of the Lord?”** — or what is the taking up
**“thou shalt say to them: You are the burden: for I will cast you away, saith the Lord.”** — If therefore, etc. The Hebrew word massa Aquila translates “burden”; Symmachus and the Septuagint and Theodotion, “taking up.” Where therefore a thing is grievous and full of weight and labour, it is called a burden. But where prosperity is promised, or better things after a threat, it is called a vision or the word of the Lord; and it is plain from the very title of the prophecy, of burden or vision or word of the Lord, what kind of prediction follows. Since therefore the prophets were accustomed to announce sad things to sinners and so to provoke them to penance, but the Lord in mercy put off the sentence, the people, deceived by the fraud of the false prophets, thought that what the Lord threatened would not come, and turned a serious matter into a jest, and in mockery said to the prophets as they prophesied: Here again he sees the weight and burden of the Lord; and so it came about that it was no longer called a vision, but by way of jest a burden. The Lord therefore commanded that if the people or the prophet or the priest should ask Jeremias what is the burden of the Lord, he should say: You are the burden, and you the taking up. “For I will take you up and cast you away,” etc. “But if anyone shall dare to name the burden of the Lord, I will visit upon that man,” etc. Let every one therefore say to his neighbour: Not what is the burden of the Lord, but “What hath the Lord answered? and what hath the Lord spoken?” Because to each his own word and his own work will be reckoned as a weight. Whence: “By thy mouth thou shalt be justified, and by thy mouth thou shalt be condemned.”
23.34:
**“and the prophets”** — or: the prophet
**“and the priests”** — or: the priest
**“and the people”** — Or: people
23.36:
**“And the burden of the Lord shall be mentioned no more, for every man's word shall be his burden: for you have perverted”**
• being unwilling to obey
• and you have perverted, up to: But if you shall say, The burden of the Lord; this is not found in the Septuagint
23.37: **“Thus shalt thou say to the prophet: What hath the Lord answered thee?”** — not the burden of the Lord
23.38: **“But if you shall say: The burden of the Lord: therefore thus saith the Lord: Because”** — but
23.39:
**“Therefore behold I will take you away carrying you”** — or taking up your word, fulfilling it in deed, dashing you down from the height to the depths
**“and will forsake you”** — also
**“And will forsake”** — And I will forsake. We know this was done at the time of the Babylonian captivity, but more fully and perfectly after the Saviour’s passion; whence: “Your house shall be left to you desolate.” According to the Septuagint, lemna signifies not only “taking up” but also “house.” Since therefore the people promised themselves prosperity, he says they ought by no means to say this any more; this is fitting, that they are unworthy of the gifts of God, and are to be cast away and left without the help of God. Moreover, from words and from the interpretation of names things are often shown: as the names of Abraham, Sara, Peter, and the sons of Zebedee, being changed, signify a change of things; and in this prophet, phashur is called fear, or translation, or tenant, or stranger. It is to be noted that the words “of the living Lord of hosts, your God” the Latin and Greek copies do not have, but the Hebrews read them in their own books against themselves, which properly signifies the mystery of the Trinity.

24.1:
**“The Lord shewed me: and behold two baskets full of figs, set before the temple of the Lord: after that Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon had carried away Jechonias the son of Joakim the king of Juda, and his chief men, and the craftsmen, and engravers of Jerusalem”** — the interpreters of the law, that is, teachers; or craftsmen, setters of gold and gems, who are held in high esteem among the barbarian nations
**“and had brought them to Babylon”** — He showed, etc. It is to be noted that this vision was made in the time of Sedecias, after Jechonias was led into exile, not into captivity, because he surrendered himself willingly.
**“Set before the temple”** — Not outside, that is, outside the Church, because all things lie open to the Lord. Nor have the things that are outside so great a bitterness as those that, after so great a confession of faith, were changed through transgression; nor have the good figs that are not in the sight of the temple of God so great a sweetness (such as the Pharisees were, who by natural good and understanding of the creator strove not so much to follow as to praise virtues) as those that are in the temple of God, namely the prophets and apostles, one of whom says: “I gave you milk,” etc., and “My little children, of whom I am in labour again, until Christ be formed in you.” Whence it is said: the good figs very good, and the bad figs very bad.
24.2:
**“One basket had very good figs, like the figs of the first season”** — Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and other saints, of whom it is said: “As grapes in the wilderness I found Israel; as the first ripe fig in the fig tree, I saw your fathers.” Whence we too are called sons of Abraham; and on the contrary it is said to the Jews: “If Abraham were your father, you would do his works.”
**“and the other basket had very bad figs, which could not be eaten, because they were bad.”**
• The two baskets, etc. Some interpret the two baskets or hampers of bad and good figs, in the law and the gospel, as the synagogue and the Church; the people of the Jews and of the Christians; hell and the kingdoms of heaven. Of these, the one belongs to the punishments of sinners, the other to the dwelling of the saints. But we, thinking with the apostle that the law is good and holy and the commandment good and holy, and that the God of both testaments is one, would rather refer it to those Jews who at the coming of the Lord believed or did not believe: so that those who cried out, saying, “Crucify him, crucify him,” are the basket of bad figs; but those who believed are referred to the good figs and the best basket.
• And one, etc. Rabanus. Jerome. We who are simple, seeking the histories, say that the basket of good figs is Jechonias, who by the counsel of Jeremias gave himself up to the king of Babylon, and to whom prosperity is promised by the Lord; but the basket of the bad is Sedecias, who, contradicting the sentence of the Lord, was taken and blinded and led into Babylon, and died there.
24.4:
**“And the word of the Lord came”** — Jerome. The allegorical interpreter raves in this place, wishing to do violence to the history, and relating that from the heavenly Jerusalem some were taken captive and carried into the land of the Chaldeans, and would return again to their former place, such as Jeremias and the other prophets; but that those who were sinners in this land would die in this vale of tears.
**“of Juda”** — or Judea
**“whom”** — that is, Jechonias and his princes
24.5:
**“Thus saith the Lord the God of Israel: like”** — explains the parable
**“these good figs, so will I know the captivity”** — These good ones: so I will recognize the exile which was made by my counsel under Jechonias
**“I have sent out of this place”** — Jerusalem
24.6:
**“And I will set my eyes upon them to be pacified”** — captivity
**“and I will bring them again”** — from captivity
**“And I will set my eyes”** — In the captivity he set his eyes upon them, and gave them the land to till, to build houses, to plant orchards. Daniel from a captive became a prince; the three children were gloriously delivered from the furnace. When the seventy years were completed, under Zorobabel and Jesus the high priest, a great part returned to Jerusalem.
*Jerome:* I have set out the whole passage of this vision at once, so as not to divide the sense in the exposition.
24.7: **“And I will give them a heart”** — Similarly: God is he who works in us both to will and to accomplish; for not only works but our will rests on the help of God.
24.8: **“And as the very bad figs, that cannot be eaten, because they are bad: thus saith the Lord: So will I give Sedecias the king of Juda, and his princes, and the residue of Jerusalem, that have remained in this city, and that dwell in the land of Egypt.”** — that is, who fled over into Egypt
24.9: **“And I will deliver them up to vexation, and affliction”** — because they were also taken captive in Egypt, and Nabuchodonosor set his throne in Thamnis
24.10: **“And I will send among them the sword, and the famine, and the pestilence: till they be consumed out of the land”** — of the promise, that is

25.1:
**“The word that came to Jeremias concerning all the people of Juda, in the fourth year of Joakim the son of Josias king of Juda, (the same is the first year of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon,)”**
• that is the first year of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon; this is not found in the Septuagint
• The word which was spoken, etc. These things are earlier than the vision just past. For that one was made under Sedecias, Jechonias having already been carried over to Babylon; but this under Joakim, the son of Josias and father of Jechonias. For it is not the prophet’s concern to preserve the times, which the laws of history require, but to write what ought to profit hearers and readers; whence in the Psalter: Some wrongly seek the order of the psalms according to the text of history, which the lyric poet does not observe.
**“In the fourth year”** — In the fourth year of king Joakim, the son of Josias and father of Jechonias, Nabuchodonosor received the empire of Babylon; and so it happened that the year which was the first of Nabuchodonosor in Babylon was the fourth of king Joakim in Jerusalem. In the eighth year of his reign he finally led Jechonias into captivity, with his mother and the princes; he reigned only three months after the killing of his father Joakim. Joakim was killed in the twelfth year of his reign.
25.3: **“From the thirteenth year of Josias the son of Ammon king of Juda until this day: this is the three and twentieth year, the word of the Lord hath come to me, and I have spoken to you, rising before day, and speaking, and you have not hearkened.”** — From the thirteenth year, etc. From the thirteenth year of the reign of Josias, who reigned in Jerusalem thirty-one years, Jeremias began to prophesy; under him he prophesied nineteen years. His son Joachaz succeeded him, who was at once taken by Pharao Nechao; Joakim his brother obtained the kingdom. In the fourth year of his reign this word of the Lord came to Jeremias. So then it was the twenty-eighth year of the prophet Jeremias since he began to speak to the people; and he never ceased, but every day, at earliest dawn and rising by night, he exhorted, and yet they did not hearken. But if, as the heretics will have it, the law was given once as a help, and precepts were established which by our own choice we either do or neglect, why does the prophet thrust himself in and daily repeat the commandments of God, if once received they suffice? But he shows that we always need the help of God, and that what was given once does not suffice unless it is constantly recalled by the admonition of the Lord.
25.4:
**“and the Lord hath sent to you all”** — not one
**“his servants the prophets, rising early, and sending, and”** — yet
**“you have not hearkened, nor inclined your ears to hear”**
• And he sent, etc. Not through one prophet but through all he warned his people; and as one set on watch and guard he rose at dawn to admonish, and they did not hear, so that the more frequent the admonition, the greater the contempt.
• Nor did you incline, etc. Such was their hardness that they did not even take on the posture of one who hears, and did not incline their ears, though the Lord admonished them to return; and the infinite divine clemency of God is to be noted: he does not inflict punishment for the crime.
25.5:
**“When he said: Return ye, every one from his evil way”** — by work
**“and from your wicked devices”** — which without deed are counted as sin
**“and you shall dwell in the land which the Lord hath given to you”** — he promises a reward if they keep the command
**“and your fathers”** — but it is taken away by the fault of the sons.
**“for ever and ever”** — He shows that God’s gifts are perpetual if those to whom they are given are worthy.
25.6: **“And go not after strange gods to serve them, and adore them: nor provoke me to wrath by the works of your hands, and I will not afflict you.”** — And go not after strange gods, etc. As if he were warning, together with what went before, that you should not serve strange gods nor provoke me to anger, and compel me, unwilling, to your punishment.
25.7: **“And you have not heard me, saith the Lord, that you might provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, to your own hurt.”** — saith the Lord, that you might provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, to your own hurt; this is not found in the Septuagint.
25.8: **“Therefore”** — because you provoked me to anger and despised me calling you to penance.
25.9:
**“Behold I will send”** — angels who stir up the nations.
**“and take all the kindreds of the north”** — according to the position of Jerusalem, the Chaldeans are in the north.
**“saith the Lord, and Nabuchodonosor the king of Babylon my servant: and I will bring them against this land, and against the inhabitants thereof, and against all the nations that are round about it: and I will destroy them, and make them an astonishment and a hissing, and desolations”** — which is the judgment of wonder and astonishment.
**“perpetual”**
• so that they have not God as their ruler.
• And I will take, etc. Not as the prophets and other saints who serve God, but because in the overthrow of Jerusalem they serve the Lord’s will, according to that: “Whom I have delivered up to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.”
• And I will bring them upon this land, etc. These are the rewards of those who despise and will not hear God. Whatever evil, therefore, is brought upon us, our sins deserve it; and as the nations were brought against Jerusalem, so today they rage against the negligent Church.
25.10:
**“And I will take away from them the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride”** — Of Christ: “He that hath the bride, is the bridegroom.”
**“the sound of the mill”**
• of the church’s faith.
• that in it the grain is not ground, and is given to the peoples to eat.
**“and the light of the lamp”**
• “Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths.”
• the teaching of the prophets; John too was “a burning and a shining light.”
• I will take away from them, etc. This is proved in the assembly of the wicked, that their masters do not teach the word of God but are enchanters to themselves, like a serpent, in whom the voice of joy and gladness has perished, so that they do not hear that of the apostle: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice.”
25.11:
**“And all this land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment”** — of heretics, when its end appears, the foolish one.
**“And all these nations shall serve”** — As Jerusalem after seventy years receives back its former inhabitants, and, its punishments fulfilled, enjoys its former happiness, obeying the sentence of God; so the king of Babylon, puffed up into pride and ascribing to his own strength the nations over which he reigns, is destroyed by the Medes and Persians. Finally, to this day the remains of Babylon abide, which God set in everlasting solitude, who fulfilled all the words of Jeremias, who in what follows describes in prophetic speech what Babylon is to suffer.
25.12: **“And when the seventy years shall be expired, I will punish the king of Babylon, and that nation, saith the Lord, for their iniquity, and the land of the Chaldeans: and I will make it perpetual desolations.”** — And when the seventy years are fulfilled, etc. Note that Jeremias prophesies not only against Babylon but against all the nations that were in Babylon’s army and fought against the people of God; whence in what follows, against Egypt, and the Philistines, and Moab, etc.
25.15: **“For thus saith the Lord of hosts the God of Israel: Take the cup of wine of this fury at my hand: and thou shalt make all the nations to drink thereof, unto which I shall send thee.”** — Take the cup, etc. The cup of the fury of the Lord is propitiated by judgment: that all the nations that fought against the people of God drink of the cup of the fury of the Lord; whence Isaias: “Thou hast drunk of the cup of the Lord’s fury, and hast emptied it; therefore arise.” But this cup is drunk by all the nations so that they may vomit and rave; which a certain perverse interpreter takes in a good sense, after the manner of a purging draught, that it may force out whatever bile and phlegm and noxious humour is in the chest and restore the former health. He also takes Jeremias for a saviour, who gives the cup to all the nations to which he was sent, that, casting away idolatry, they might dedicate themselves to the worship of God; and what follows would show that this is contrary to holy Scripture. For the cup is not propitiated for a remedy, as that man raves, but for punishment.
25.18: **“Jerusalem, and the cities of Juda, and the kings thereof, and the princes thereof: to make them a desolation, and an astonishment, and a hissing, and a curse, as it is at this day.”** — Jerusalem and the cities, etc. As if I thought I would give the cup to the nations alone, and therefore I had gladly offered myself to this ministry; but among the other nations, nay before the other nations, I gave it to Jerusalem and the cities of Juda, etc.; whence above: “Thou hast deceived me, O Lord, and I am deceived.”
25.19: **“Pharao the king of Egypt, and his servants, and his princes, and all his people,”** — Pharao, etc. After Jerusalem, Pharao king of Egypt drinks, and his servants and princes and all the people, who are indeed not Egyptian but dwell in his regions.
25.20:
**“And all in general: all the kings of the land”** — which in Hebrew is Hus, of which it is said: “There was a man in the land of Ausitis named Job.” However, this verse is not found in the Septuagint, and Theodotion translated Hus as island.
**“Philistines”** — By the general name he signifies the land of the Philistines; its cities he names specifically: Solam. Geth he passes over, which he understands among the remnant of Azotus, to which it is related; but Isaias writes that the Philistines were taken and laid waste by the Babylonians.
25.21:
**“Edom”** — in which are the mountains of Seir, which in Hebrew is Edom.
**“and Moab, and the children of Ammon”** — these are the sons of Lot, near the Dead Sea.
25.22:
**“and all the kings of Tyre, and all the kings of Sidon, and the kings of the land of the islands”** — of Cyprus, Rhodes, and of the others which the Babylonians conquered.
**“that are beyond the sea”** — And all the kings of Tyre, etc. Tyre and Sidon are on the shore of Phoenicia, and were overcome by the Babylonians. Of these, Carthage is a colony, whence the Poeni are called, as if Pheni by corrupted speech. Their language is for the most part akin to Hebrew.
25.23: **“and Dedan, and Thema, and Buz”** — these nations in the desert are neighbours and mingled with the Ismaelites, whom they now call Saracens, who are shorn in the hair.
25.24: **“and all the kings of Arabia”** — after Dedan, Theman, Buz, and the Ismaelites, he follows the order of regions.
25.25:
**“and all the kings of Zambri, and all the kings of Elam”** — the region of Persis beyond Babylon; hence the Elamites.
**“and all the kings of the Medes”**
• by whom Babylon was taken; for they truly could offer the cup to Alexander.
• having specifically enumerated these, he generally puts all the kings of the north.
**“kings of Elam”** — What follows, Elam and the kings of the Medes, is thought to be Zambri, a faithless region. Unless perhaps, because Arabia went before, they are understood to be kings of the wilderness.
25.26:
**“and all the kings of the north”** — The Septuagint: those toward the sunrise.
**“far and near, every one against his brother”** — I gave the unmixed wine so that they go mad, that is, and fall by mutual wounds.
**“and all the kingdoms of the earth”** — in general, so as not to make it long and tedious by counting each one singly.
**“which are upon the face thereof, and the king of Sesac”**
• And the king of Sesac, etc. And the king of Sesac: as it were, all the nations round about will lie under the Babylonian empire and serve and drink of his cup. Whence: the golden cup, Babylon, making all the earth drunk. The last Babylonian king will drink, the Medes and Persians pouring it out.
• Babylon, which in Hebrew is Babel, is also called Sesac. For as we read the Greek alphabet in order to the last letter, that is, alpha, beta, etc., to omega, and again, for the memory of children, we reverse the order of reading and mix first and last, for example: alpha - omega, beta - psi, so among the Hebrews the first is aleph, the second beth, the third gimel, and so on to the twenty-second, that is the last letter, thau, before which is syn. We read therefore aleph - thau, beth - syn; and when we come to the middle, lamech meets caph; and, as we rightly read Babel, so, the order being changed, we read Sesac. But the vowel letters between beth and lamech, syn and caph, according to the idiom of the Hebrew tongue, are not put in this name; which perhaps the prophet prudently veiled, lest he stir up the madness of the Babylonians against himself, as the Apostle, writing of Antichrist against the Roman empire, says: “Only that he who now holdeth, do hold, until he be taken out of the way,” signifying the Roman empire, which according to Daniel is to be destroyed before Antichrist.
**“and thou shalt say to them”** — when you have made all the nations drink.
25.27:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink, and be drunken, and vomit, and fall”** — It is clear that this draught is not taken in a good sense.
**“Drink and be drunken”** — Jerome. The allegorical interpreters refer this whole passage to all the nations whom the devil made drunk with the cup of sins; and last of all the king of Babylon himself will drink punishments and torments; whence: “whom the Lord Jesus shall kill with the spirit of his mouth”; and elsewhere: “The last enemy, death, shall be destroyed.”
25.28:
**“And if they refuse to take the cup at thy hand”** — It is hinted that those who were unwilling to do God’s command will be made to do it by necessity.
**“to drink, thou shalt say to them: Thus saith the Lord of hosts: Drinking you shall drink”** — whether you will or no.
25.29:
**“For behold in the city wherein my name is called upon”** — God is known in Judea, etc.
**“I begin to afflict, and you”** — you who worship idols in place of God.
**“as innocent and escape free? you shall not escape free: for I will call for the sword”** — the draught.
**“for I call”** — Whence: I will send Nabuchodonosor the king of Babylon my servant, etc.
**“upon all the inhabitants of the land.”** — not only Israel.
25.30:
**“And thou shalt prophesy unto them all these words, and thou shalt say to them”** — as if you were prophesying to all the nations, and say to them.
**“The Lord shall roar from on high”** — by the judgment of his wrath; whence: The lion shall roar, who will not fear? etc.
**“and shall utter his voice from his holy habitation”** — so that he may terrify all who hear.
**“roaring he shall roar upon the place of his beauty”** — the temple.
**“the shout”** — that is, when they roar like men treading in the winepress, a shout of joy will be sung, and in the outpouring of mutual blood they will sing a mournful dirge over the flesh.
**“as it were of them that tread grapes shall be given out against all the inhabitants of the earth”** — The Lord from on high, etc. Jerome. The allegorical interpreters, following the Septuagint, refer this passage to the good side. The Lord, they say, from on high will give answer to those, namely, whom he is about to save, and from his holy place will give his voice, and will answer a word in his place. But they, like men gathering the vintage, full of the fruits of that sentence, will answer upon all the inhabitants of the earth, etc. But destruction will come not upon the whole earth but upon a part of the earth, namely of those who do not believe. For there will be judgment among the nations, and he will be judged with all flesh. But the wicked will be given to the sword.
25.31:
**“The noise is come”** — of the shout.
**“even to the ends of the earth: for the Lord entereth into judgment with the nations; he entereth into judgment with all flesh”** — so that no one goes unjudged.
**“the wicked”** — who do not believe.
**“I have delivered up to the sword”** — with the everlasting sword.
**“for the Lord entereth into judgment”** — That there are also different merits among the nations: he who does not believe is already judged in this, namely that he does not believe. For “he that doth not believe, is already judged”; but those who do not believe will be afflicted with various punishments.
25.32:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts: Behold evil shall go forth from nation to nation: and a great whirlwind shall go forth from the ends of the earth”** — Behold evil, etc. Let them blush who, doing violence to holy Scripture, take the Lord’s threats in a good sense.
*Jerome:* Behold I, etc. I think the Lord said this from this passage: “Nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom,” etc. Now these things were done according to the history when all the nations round about were subjugated by the king of Babylon; but according to the prophecy they are to be at the consummation of the world.
25.33: **“And the slain of the Lord”** — not that the Lord himself strikes, but in the destruction of the wicked his rule and will are fulfilled.
25.34:
**“Howl, ye shepherds”** — the rational ones.
**“and cry: and sprinkle yourselves with ashes, ye leaders of the flock”** — the rich, who are part of the flock.
**“for they are accomplished”** — with sins completed.
**“the days of your slaughter and your dispersion, and you shall fall like precious vessels”**
• whose loss is greater.
• broken, which could not be restored
• Howl, ye shepherds, etc. The Septuagint has: the howling of the leaders of the flock, the shouting of the rams. Now the difference between shepherds and rams is this: the shepherds rule the flock of the Church with wisdom and doctrine; but the rams seem to be princes among the people, yet have no wisdom and no doctrine, and by too great simplicity are almost fools. But when you have peace, and they have not understood it, given over to the showy things of peace, to luxury and idleness, the good things of peace will fall silent, and will be taken away in the fury of the Lord. Whence: when they shall say, “peace and security,” then “shall sudden destruction come upon them.”
25.35: **“And the shepherds shall have no way to flee”** — because they did not do penance. Whence: “Ye offspring of vipers, who hath shewed you to flee from the wrath to come?” And elsewhere: “flight hath failed me.”
25.37: **“And the fields of peace have been silent”** — Others: beautiful things.
25.38:
**“He has forsaken”** — the Lord
**“as the lion”** — under whose guard no one dares to approach
**“his covert”** — in Hebrew, socoth
**“his”** — whence his place has been made in peace
**“because”** — the lion leaving
**“the land is laid waste”** — of the Jews, or of all nations
**“because of the wrath of the dove”** — by the beasts that lay waste
**“and at the presence”** — Nabuchodonosor, who is called above the servant of the Lord, or Jerusalem, which in anger grieves to have lost the guardianship of its lion
**“the fierce anger of the Lord”** — From the face of the anger of the dove, etc. Gregory. Because no inequality of wrath is found in God, he named the wrath of the Lord the wrath of the dove; for in order to show the force of the divine severity as undisturbed, he said also the wrath of a dove, as if to say: he who remains gentle exerts a strict judgment unshaken, and punishes while remaining meek; whence also at the last judgment, remaining unchangeable in himself, he is varied by no change or mutability. Yet he is by no means shown to the elect and the reprobate under the appearance of this same unchangeableness; for he will appear both calm to the just and angry to the unjust. For, their conscience bearing witness, they have failed within themselves; whence their minds look equally upon one and the same, but are not equally affected, because past justice shows him kindly to the former, and guilt shows him terrible to the latter.

26.1: **“In the beginning of the reign of Joakim the son of Josias king of Juda, came this word from the Lord, saying”** — In the beginning of the reign, etc. This prophecy is earlier than the former, though under the same king. For that was made in the fourth year, this in the beginning of the same reign. Therefore in the prophets the order of history is not to be followed, since earlier things are said later and later things earlier.
26.2:
**“Thus saith the Lord: Stand in the court of the house of the Lord”**
• “You that stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.”
• as one about to speak the word of the Lord
**“and speak to all the cities of Juda, out of which they come, to adore in the house of the Lord, all the words which I have commanded thee to speak unto them: leave not out one word”** — although they rage against you, though it is sad
**“In the court”** — That you may speak also to the foreign cities. But it is fittingly that he stands in the court, and in the vestibule of the temple, so that those who gather to pray may be compelled to hear his words.
26.3:
**“If so be they will hearken and be converted every one from his evil way”** — when they repent and are changed, I, repenting, will change the sentence
**“that I may repent me of the evil that I think to do unto them for the wickedness of their doings”** — If so be they will hearken, etc. As if to say: perhaps they will hear and be converted. The word is doubtful and does not befit the divine majesty, but he speaks according to our feeling, and man’s free choice is preserved, lest by the foreknowledge of God we be compelled by necessity, as it were, to do something or not to do it. For it is not because God knows something to be future that it is future, but because it is future God knows it, as foreknowing things to come. And yet according to Jeremias, if God has foretold evils and the people have repented, or if he has promised prosperity and the people have neglected it, he would neither bring in the evils nor confer the prosperity. Like this is that: “perhaps they will reverence my son.”
26.4: **“If you will not”** — It is placed in our will either to do or not to do, so indeed that whatever good we wish, desire, and accomplish, we refer to the grace of God, who gives both to will and to accomplish. But if it suffices to walk once in the law given through Moses, as a foolish heresy supposes, how is it added, that the words of my servants the prophets be heard, who were sent after the law, and not once and by one secure, but always and by one careful?
26.5:
**“to give ear to the words of my servants the prophets, whom I sent”** — daily
**“to you rising up early”** — diligently
26.6:
**“I will make this house”** — the temple
**“like Silo”** — where the tabernacle was
**“And”** — the temple having been destroyed
**“I will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth”** — I will make this house, etc. As when the temple was built on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, and on mount Moria, that is, of vision, on which Abraham is told to have offered his son, the religion of Silo ceased, nor were sacrifices afterwards celebrated there; so when the Church was founded and spiritual victims were sacrificed, the ceremonies of the law ceased, and the city of the Jews was given for a curse, from which the Lord has freed us, redeeming us from the curse of the law, “being made a curse for us.”
26.7: **“And the priests, and the prophets, and all the people heard”** — Septuagint: false
26.9:
**“Why hath he prophesied in the name of the Lord, saying: This house shall be like Silo; and this city shall be made desolate, without an inhabitant? And all the people were gathered together”** — by delay, by sedition
**“all the people were gathered together against Jeremias”** — seized
**“into the house of the Lord”** — where Jeremiah was
26.10:
**“And the princes of Juda heard”** — who dwelt in the royal house
**“these words: and they went up from the king's house into the house of the Lord”** — note that the ascent is into the house of the Lord
**“and sat”** — which is their office, that they should learn the truth of the business and the sedition
**“In the new gate”** — It is called new because those who sat in it and presided over judgment resisted the calumnies of the priests and false prophets.
26.11:
**“And the priests and the prophets spoke to the princes, and to all the people, saying: The judgment of death is for this man: because he hath prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your ears”**
• And the priests and the prophets spoke, etc. While the princes of the city were sitting in the gate of the temple, who had run together from the king’s palace to quell the sedition of the people, the assembly being gathered, the priests and false prophets accuse him, and if they had had the power of judgment they would have condemned the prophet also; whence we understand that those who seemed to be religious were more cruel, out of envy of holiness, than those who were attending to public necessities.
• Angry because he foretold that religion would perish, and the gains coming from religion. If at any time, on account of the commandments of God and the truth of the faith, priests or false prophets or a deceived people are angry with us, let us not greatly care, but let us carry out the sentence of God, thinking not of present evils but of future goods.
26.12: **“Then Jeremias spoke to all the princes, and to all the people, saying: The Lord sent me to prophesy concerning this house, and concerning this city all the words that you have heard”** — And Jeremias said, etc. While they were accusing him and aiming at a charge of death, Jeremias speaks to the princes and to the people whom they had stirred up, prudently and humbly and constantly: he says he was sent by the Lord to speak against the temple and the city, and gives counsel that they do penance and the Lord change his sentence. He speaks humbly, saying: “Behold, I am in your hands,” etc. Constantly: “for in truth the Lord sent me to you.”
26.13: **“Now therefore amend your ways, and your doings, and hearken to the voice of the Lord your God: and the Lord will repent him of the evil that he hath spoken against you”** — Now therefore, etc. As if to say: if you are angry that I have spoken against the temple and the city, and you love the safety of the city and the temple, why do you heap sins upon sins, and make the city and its inhabitants guilty of my blood? If, then, at any time humility is needed by us from necessity, let us so take it up that we do not abandon truth and constancy. For it is one thing to insult a judge proudly, which is a sign of folly; another so to avoid an impending danger that nothing is taken away from the truth.
26.16:
**“Then the princes, and all the people said to the priests, and to the prophets”** — as though the people had not been led astray by the priests and false prophets; but the people, having heard the reasoning, quickly changes its judgment, because the Lord promised pardon if they make their ways good; but the priests and false prophets persevere in accusation
**“There is no judgment of death for this man: for he hath spoken to us in the name of the Lord our God”** — And the princes said, etc. The princes of the city and the people understand the truth of the judgment. But the elders, whose business it is to know true things, recount the history and compare Micheas to Jeremias, and show that he said graver things and suffered nothing from a just king; but all being converted to penance, the Lord changed his sentence. They also break the rage of the accusers, counting themselves among them: “We are doing a great evil against our souls.” As if to say: we shall not harm the accused, but our own souls, which we can free by a change of sentence.
26.20: **“There was also a man”** — There was also a man. It is asked, since Urias prophesied the same things as Jeremias, and fled into Egypt, and was drawn back from there and killed, how could Jeremias, who boldly persisted in his sentence, escape the judgment of the crowd and of the princes and the counsel of the elders? To this it must be answered: the judgment of God cannot be known, when in the same cause one is punished and another set free. But perhaps Urias was killed for the condemnation of the accusers and of the people. Jeremias, however, was reserved for the judgment of God, that he might preach to the remaining peoples and provoke them to penance; as James was at once crowned with martyrdom, while Peter and the other apostles were reserved for preaching. And the constancy of the prophet is to be noted, because Urias, though drawn back from Egypt, does not change his sentence, and with death imminent nonetheless speaks what the Lord had commanded. But that he feared and fled is a judgment not of unbelief but of prudence, that we may not offer ourselves in vain to dangers; Christ also slipped from the hands of those who persecuted him, as the apostle says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another.”
26.22: **“And king Joakim sent men into Egypt, Elnathan the son of Achobor, and men with him into Egypt”** — And the king sent, etc. The question is asked how Joakim, a king of small dominion and of weakness, on the point of perishing, could send into Egypt and bring Urias out. But we ought to consider that Nechao, king of Egypt, had appointed him prince, and that this prophecy was made when he had begun to reign.
26.24: **“So the hand of Ahicam the son of Saphan was with Jeremias, that he should not be delivered into the hands of the people, to put him to death”** — So the hand of Ahicam, etc. Although Jeremias was delivered by the help of the Lord, it is nevertheless reckoned as a reward to him through whom he delivered his prophet; we believe this was in the reign of Joakim.

27.1: **“In the beginning of the reign of Joakim the son of Josias king of Juda, this word came to Jeremias from the Lord, saying”** — In the beginning of the reign, etc. Many thought this was the beginning of the following chapter, but it is to be joined to the preceding one, so that whatever is reported as said or done at the beginning of Joakim’s reign, we believe, happened then.
27.2:
**“Thus saith the Lord to me: Make thee bands, and chains”** — which he calls by the common name boias
**“and thou shalt put them on thy neck”** — Thus says the Lord, etc. The vision above was at the beginning of Joakim’s reign, but this one is under Sedecias, who reigned last in Jerusalem, under whom the city was taken and overthrown.
27.4: **“And thou shalt command them to speak to their masters”** — their own
27.5:
**“I made the earth, and the men, and the beasts that are upon the face of the earth, by my great power, and by my stretched out arm”** — Whence: “to whom the arm of the Lord hath been revealed”
**“and I have given it to whom it seemed good in my eyes”**
• The earth and man, etc. The order is reversed: in Genesis the animals are made first and man afterwards; here, however, he names man first and afterwards what is subject to him.
• And I have given, etc. It signifies that all things are bestowed on the human race through the grace of God.
**“By my great power”** — In strength. Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, whence: “in wisdom hast thou made all things”; and elsewhere, “All things were made by him.”
27.6:
**“And now I have given all these lands into the hand of Nabuchodonosor”** — of the devil, who says: all these things have been delivered to me
**“king of Babylon my servant: moreover also the beasts of the field I have given him to serve him”**
• Into the hand of Nabuchodonosor, etc. How great is the unhappiness of Israel, in comparison with whom Nabuchodonosor is called the servant of God.
• Moreover the beasts, etc. Every kind of animal: for together with man all things subject to him are handed over, or wild nations, so that they may serve him who had not known how to serve.
27.7:
**“And all nations shall serve him”** — Evulmoradach
**“and his son's son”** — Balthasar
**“till the time come for his land and himself: and many nations”** — not all; for this properly belongs to Christ
**“and great kings shall serve him”** — Until the time comes, etc. Lest the kingdom of Nabuchodonosor be thought to be everlasting, it signifies that he is to be taken by the Medes and Persians.
27.8:
**“But the nation”** — or therefore
**“But the nation and kingdom that will not serve Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, and whosoever will not bend his neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon: I will visit upon that nation with the sword, and with famine, and with pestilence”** — of the Gentiles, who pretended to foretell the future by a divine spirit
**“saith the Lord: till I consume them by his hand”**
• But the nation and, etc. Not only does the Lord subject sinners to Nabuchodonosor, but Paul also, who says: “whom I have delivered up to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme,” for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved; he also admonishes us to obey the powers, “not only for wrath, but also for conscience’ sake.”
• The allegorical interpreter, fleeing the truth of the history, interprets this place of the heavenly Jerusalem: that its inhabitants ought of their own will to take up bodies and go down into Babylon, that is, the confusion of the world, which is “seated in wickedness,” and serve the king of Babylon, that is, the devil. But if they will not, he would say, they will not bear heavy bodies, but will perish by the sword, famine and pestilence, and will not be men but demons. Let us follow the simple history, lest we be wrapped in certain deceptions.
27.9:
**“Therefore hearken not”** — or: therefore
**“to your prophets, and diviners, and dreamers”** — who imitate Joseph and Daniel
**“and soothsayers”** — who bear witness, by the flight of birds and the voices of birds of omen, that something is to be done or not to be done
**“and sorcerers”** — serving the illusions of demons
27.12:
**“And I spoke to Sedecias the king of Juda”** — lest the envoys and kings of the aforesaid nations answer: why do you not order this to your people? He speaks similar things also to Sedecias, and to the prophets and priests.
**“And I spoke to Sedecias”** — After all the nations he turns to Sedecias and threatens the same things; for the Jews do not merit a privilege, who have sinned in ways similar to, or graver or greater than, the nations; and those who disdain to hear are consumed by pestilence and famine.
27.14:
**“Hearken not to the words”** — In this place the allegorical interpreter exhorts those placed in the heavenly Jerusalem not to hear their prophets and diviners, but to serve Nabuchodonosor by taking a body of lowliness, the wailing of infants and the cradles of little ones. For if they do this, when the service is fulfilled and the condition of mortality ended, they will return to their own land. He adds also his suspicion that those who have despised the commandments of God, weighed down with human bodies, will become demons and unclean spirits and will not recover their former seat.
**“You shall not serve”** — It is better to serve willingly, and to have God as friend and to till the land of the Gentiles, than to serve as a captive out of necessity.
**“the words of the prophets”** — It is to be noted that in the holy Scriptures false prophets are called prophets.
27.16:
**“I spoke also to the priests, and to this people, saying: Thus saith the Lord: Hearken not to the words of your prophets, that prophesy to you, saying: Behold the vessels of the Lord”** — which had been carried off with Jeconias
**“shall now in a short time be brought again from Babylon: for they prophesy a lie unto you”** — And to the priests, etc. After the nations and kings he speaks to the priests and to the people, to whom he had already announced ruin through the prophets, saying: “and I will cast you out,” etc. He speaks, however, the same things as above.
27.17: **“that you may live”** — Note the mercy of God: he wishes to hand them over to a lighter punishment, so that they do not undergo a heavier one.
27.18:
**“But if they be prophets”** — He who is a true prophet can meet the Lord with prayers, as Moses, to whom it was said: “Let me alone, that I may strike this people.” In which it is shown that God can be held back by the prayers of the saints.
**“let them interpose themselves before the Lord”** — Let them meet him, and show by the work accomplished what they predict; and then the prophecy will be proved true.
27.19: **“to the pillars”** — He lists the vessels that were carried to Babylon, Sedecias’s city having been taken, the city burned and the temple overthrown.

28.1:
**“And it came to pass in that year, in the beginning of the reign of Sedecias king of Juda, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, that Hananias the son of Azur spoke to me”** — as it seemed to the people
**“And the word of the Lord came”** — Ezechiel had not yet prophesied in Babylon to those who had been carried away with Jechonias.
**“a prophet of Gabaon”** — The Seventy: a false prophet, more clearly. For in Hebrew nebia means prophet, not false prophet; and they translate thus nearly everywhere, following not the word but the sense.
**“in the house of the Lord”** — In which he speaks confidently, because he promises the people prosperity; and lies are gladly heard, especially those that promise what is desired.
28.2:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts the God of Israel: I have broken”** — destroyed
**“the yoke”** — rule
28.3:
**“As yet two years of days”** — so that the short time would increase the greatness of joy
**“and I will cause all the vessels of the house of the Lord to be brought back into this place, which Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon took away from this place, and carried them to Babylon”** — All the vessels, etc. Jeremias had said that the remaining vessels were also to be brought; here he affirms that what was carried away is to be brought back.
28.5: **“And Jeremias the prophet said to Hananias the prophet in the presence of the priests, and in the presence of all the people that stood”** — or stood
28.6: **“And Jeremias the prophet said: Amen, the Lord do so: the Lord perform thy words, which thou hast prophesied: that the vessels may be brought again into the house of the Lord, and all the captives may return out of Babylon to this place.”** — Amen, etc. He wishes that to be done which the other lies about. This is what “amen” signifies, which the Lord often uses in the gospel; and he desires, for the prosperity of affairs, that the other rather than himself should speak the truth. Whence another prophet: “Would God I were not a man that hath the spirit, and that I rather spoke a lie.” But Jonas is saddened because he had lied, and is rebuked by the Lord that a lie was more useful than the ruin of so great a multitude. Yet lest he should seem to approve a false prophecy, he asserts the truth, without injury to the one who lies, by the example of others.
28.7: **“Nevertheless hear this word that I speak in thy ears, and in the ears of all the people”** — Nevertheless hear this word, etc. He could have said: You lie, you deceive the people, you are a false prophet. But the other could have turned the same back upon Jeremias. So he does no injury; he speaks as to a prophet, as if to say: not only are we prophets, but there were many others before us, Isaias, Osee, Joel and Amos, who prophesied against many lands, announcing war and adversity and want; others also announced peace and prosperity, and these the outcome of events tested, not the flattery of a lie. The Lord also says through Moses that a prophet is shown by the end of his prophecy. And it must be noted that he rebukes the liar not with threats, not cruelly, but with confidence in the truth; and he puts it off to the future, that those who hear may await the outcome.
28.10:
**“And Hananias the prophet took”** — supposedly
**“the chain”** — or a yoke-bar, which in Hebrew is michohath
