But it is ours to follow, more earnestly or more slackly, the exhortation and help of God, and by this to merit either reward or punishments.
32.40:
**“And I will make an everlasting covenant with them”** — The New Testament
**“and will not cease to do them good: and I will give my fear in their heart”** — not in the mouth
**“and I will give my fear”** — He thus gives free will, so that the fear which is repaid is from the grace of the giver.
32.41:
**“And I will rejoice over them”**
• I will love my gifts in them.
• to the saved, who are my creature; whence there is also joy of the angels in heaven over one sinner doing penance
**“when I shall do them good: and I will plant them in this land”** — in the present Church or the future one.
**“with my whole heart”** — If these are the Saviour’s words, then rightly is his heart and soul believed to be his, who says: “I have power to lay down my soul,” etc. But if they are the Father’s, they must be understood anthropopathically, as that: “My soul hateth your solemnities.”
32.42:
**“For thus saith the Lord: As I have brought upon this people all this great evil: so will I bring upon them all the good that I now speak to them.”** — For thus saith the Lord, etc. These things, according to the letter, in type, after the return from the Chaldeans, when the people of the Jews returned at the command of king Cyrus. But spiritually they were more fully fulfilled in Christ and the apostles.
**“Rabanus.”** — It was said above that Sedecias shut up Jeremias in the court of the prison because he prophesied, saying: “Thus saith the Lord: Behold I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon,” etc. There, shut up, he bought a field from the son of his father’s brother. There also now, a second time, a word of consolation is given to him concerning the return of the people.
32.43:
**“And fields shall be purchased in this land: whereof you say that it is desolate, because there remaineth neither man”** — rational
**“nor beast”** — simple men; “Men and beasts thou wilt preserve, O Lord”
32.44:
**“Fields shall be bought for money”** — that we may make friends for ourselves of the mammon of iniquity, that they may receive us into everlasting dwellings
**“and deeds shall be written”** — of the living
**“and sealed”** — of the cross and of victory
**“and witnesses shall be taken”** — the martyrs and the company of saints
**“in the land of Benjamin”** — where the strength of the Lord is
**“and round about Jerusalem”** — in which is the vision of peace and eternal security
**“in the cities of Juda”** — where is the true confession of Christ
**“and in the cities on the mountains”** — of one of which it is said: “A city seated on a mountain cannot be hid.”
**“and in the cities of the plains”** — which in Hebrew is sephela; so that out of the depths and the straits we may come forth, through the evenness of the plains, to the heights
**“and in the cities that are towards the south”** — The Seventy: vageb, where namely is midday and the full light of truth
**“because”** — these things being fulfilled
**“I will bring back their captivity, saith the Lord”** — “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.”

33.1:
**“And the word of the Lord came to Jeremias the second time, while he was yet shut up in the court of the prison”** — where Sedecias had shut him up
**“And the word of the Lord came”** — He foretells that as vengeance is prepared for sinners, so medicine is prepared for the penitent; for where by the indignation of the Lord corpses had lain, there the tabernacles of the converted will be rebuilt, with abundance of all good things, so that thence the glory of the Lord may be proclaimed, and praise and joy arise among all nations. Some refer this to the ending of the Chaldean captivity, but it seems better referred to Christian times, where spiritually the Lord grants all good things to his faithful, that they may live in all peace and concord; whence: “My peace I give unto you, peace I leave with you,” and elsewhere: “Behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation.” But when they had returned from Babylon, the neighbouring nations harassed them, forbidding them to rebuild the temple and the city. In the times of the Machabees also they suffered very many adversities and never had full security, until they were dispersed by the Romans throughout the whole world.
33.2: **“Thus saith the Lord”** — whose servants all are
33.3:
**“Cry to me and I will hear thee: and I will shew thee great things, and sure things which thou knowest not.”**
• Cry to me, etc. He shows that through the prayers of the prophets and saints who were among the people, the Lord was appeased, and revealed to them their return to their land, which had until now lain hidden.
• Above it was said: “Therefore, do not thou pray for this people,” etc. But now it is said: “Cry to me and I will hear thee”; because the Lord was unwilling to avert the impending captivity, so that they might first pay the penalty of their sin; but afterwards he did not deny the return, which he now promises.
33.8: **“And I will cleanse them from all their iniquity, whereby they have sinned against me”** — at the coming of Christ
33.10:
**“There shall be heard again”** — So that the Jews may not despair because of the threats and the future captivities, he promises the good things of restoration, so that the place which had been deserted on account of the sins of its inhabitants may be inhabited, for their correction and amendment.
**“Thus saith the Lord: There shall be heard again in this place (which you say is desolate, because there is neither man nor beast: in the cities of Juda, and without Jerusalem, which are desolate without man, and without inhabitant, and without beast)”** — Mystically. The Church of the Gentiles, which had been forsaken by the Lord through idolatry and the monstrousness of crimes, is inhabited through the faith of Christ and is filled with a multitude of believers from diverse nations; to her it is said through Isaias: “The land that was desolate and impassable shall be glad, and the wilderness shall rejoice,” etc.; and elsewhere: “Give praise, O thou barren, that bearest not: sing forth praise, and make a joyful noise, thou that didst not travail with child: for many are the children of the desolate.”
33.11:
**“The voice of joy”** — the preaching of the gospel
**“and the voice of gladness”** — alleluia
**“the voice of the bridegroom”** — of Christ
**“and the voice of the bride”** — of the Church
**“the voice of them that shall say: Give ye glory to the Lord of hosts, for the Lord is good, for his mercy endureth for ever: and of them that shall bring”** — themselves
**“vows into the house of the Lord”** — not made by hand
**“for I will bring back”** — of the Gentiles
**“of the land as at the first”** — that all may have one faith, and one lip in confession
33.12:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts: There shall be again in this place that is desolate without man, and without beast, and in all the cities thereof, an habitation of shepherds causing their flocks to lie down.”** — of the apostles and evangelists and teachers of the New Testament
**“causing their flocks to lie down”**
• or: of flocks
• Flocks lying down, etc. The flocks of the Church, namely those gathered from the Gentiles, who stand on the summit of virtues and yet do not forsake humility, but through the fervour of the Holy Spirit practise zeal for good works and keep the laws of love; with them are joined the flocks or nations that dwell in the land of Benjamin round about Jerusalem and in the cities of Juda, because of that former people there are many who belong to the faith of Christ and to the number of his sheep, of whom it is said: “My sheep hear my voice: and I know them, and they follow me.”
33.13:
**“And in the cities on the mountains, and in the cities of the plains, and in the cities that are towards the south”** — the fervor of the Holy Spirit
**“and in the land of Benjamin, and round about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Juda shall the flocks pass again”** — the way of this life
**“under the hand”** — living at hand, that is, according to the arrangement of the true shepherd, who says: “rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven”
**“of him that numbereth them”** — who counts the multitude of the stars
33.14:
**“Behold the days come, saith the Lord, that I will perform the good word”** — the coming of the Son, by which “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us”
**“that I have spoken to the house of Israel, and to the house of Juda.”** — the prophets
**“to the house of Israel”** — Of these Isaias says: “And in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of mountains,” etc.
33.15: **“In those days, and at that time, I will make the bud of justice to spring forth unto David, and he shall do judgment and justice in the earth.”** — Christ, who did judgment and justice in the earth; for justice is the girdle of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins
33.16:
**“In those days shall Juda be saved, and Jerusalem”** — the apostles and the primitive Church
**“shall dwell”** — in the faith of Christ
**“securely”** — under the protection of God
**“and this is the name that”** — which is elsewhere called Emmanuel, that is, God with us, because “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us”
**“they shall call him, The Lord our just one.”** — rendering to each according to his works
33.17:
**“For thus saith the Lord: There shall not be cut off from David a man”** — Christ and his members
**“to sit upon the throne of the house of Israel.”** — of the Church
**“There shall not be cut off”** — Rabanus. This testimony cannot be fitted to the kingdom of the Jewish people, nor to the priesthood; it must therefore be transferred to the kingdom and priesthood of Christ, of which it is said: “I will make his seed to endure for evermore: and his throne as the days of heaven,” and elsewhere: “The Lord hath sworn, and he will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech.” The members of this priest are the children of the Church; whence Peter: “You are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood,” etc. He offers holocausts and sacrifices most acceptable to the Father.
33.18: **“Neither shall there be cut off from the priests and Levites”** — because the priesthood of Christ is eternal
33.19: **“And the word of the Lord came to Jeremias, saying:”** — And the word of the Lord came, etc. Rabanus. By a fitting comparison he confounds the enemies who insult the people of God: for as the laws of heaven and earth, of day and night, stand immovably in their order, so the promise of God will remain unshaken. The two families chosen by the Lord we can understand as the royal and the priestly tribe; or the two that were in Jerusalem and the ten that were in Samaria. The Lord chose these when he promised their fathers a land flowing with milk and honey. But although very many of them erred from the truth, yet many were found approved in right faith and good works, because from them came the apostles and the primitive Church.
33.20: **“Thus saith the Lord”** — Above he had spoken of the creation of the sun, moon and stars and of their course, that their laws cannot be changed; now in like manner he says that the covenant of day and night cannot be made void, nor the covenant of the Lord with David. For when the legal priesthood is ended, the kingdom and priesthood of Christ will remain for ever.
33.22: **“As the stars of heaven cannot be numbered, nor the sand of the sea be measured: so will I multiply the seed of David my servant”** — spiritual, whose sum is known to God alone, who counts the multitude of the stars, etc.
33.24:
**“Hast thou not seen what this people”** — of the enemies
**“hath spoken”** — by mocking
**“saying: The two families”** — the priestly and the royal, or Judah and Israel
**“which the Lord had chosen”** — to whom he had promised a land flowing with milk and honey
**“are cast off”** — altogether
**“so that it is no more a nation before them”** — in their estimation
33.26: **“Surely I will also cast off the seed of Jacob, and of David my servant, so as not to take any of his seed to be rulers of the seed of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob”** — of whom it is said: “Sons are born to thee: thou shalt make them princes over all the earth.”

34.1: **“The word that came to Jeremias from the Lord”** — Rabanus. Although the wicked king is unworthy of mercy, yet because the mercies of God are many and exceedingly great, he warned him often through the prophets: through Jeremias, namely, in Judea, and Ezechiel, prophesying in Babylon, foretelling the coming captivity, if in some way he might provoke him to penance. But a hardened mind chooses rather to persevere in wickedness than to amend its life; whence he found the penalty due, being taken captive with his people.
34.10:
**“And all the princes, and all the people who entered into the covenant, heard that every man should let his manservant, and every man his maidservant go free, and should no more have dominion over them: and they obeyed, and let them go free.”**
• All the princes heard, etc. Rabanus. It is plain from this place that it profits a man nothing to begin any good, if he has not striven to bring it to a good end. For “he that shall persevere to the end, he shall be saved.” It was commanded in the law that the children of Israel should not sell their brethren into the condition of slaves nor afflict them, but at the appointed time they should return to their kindred and to the possession of their fathers; and they were to have manservants and maidservants from the nations that were round about them. Sedechias and the people of the Jews promised that they would do this, but turning back they took again the manservants and maidservants whom they had let go free; whence the Lord, being angered, delivered them to all the kingdoms of the earth, and sent the sword, the pestilence and the famine upon them, and set their cities on fire.
• Tropologically, however: when we have taken our brethren under our protection, being subject to us for God’s sake, let us not oppress them by power, nor lay upon them the burden of unwilling servitude, but treat them with brotherly affection, help them by word and example, that they may be able to render worthy service to the true Lord, who redeemed them with his blood, until the true jubilee comes and each one is restored to his own dignity and possession; whence Peter: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, ... willingly, ... neither as lording it over the clergy,” etc.
34.15:
**“And you turned”** — from the iniquities of your fathers
**“you today, and did that which was right in my eyes, in proclaiming liberty every one to his brother: and you made a covenant in my sight”** — by my good pleasure
34.16: **“And you are fallen back”** — to your iniquity
34.18: **“And I will give the men that have transgressed my covenant, and have not performed the words of the covenant which they agreed to in my presence, when they cut the calf in two and passed between the parts thereof”** — of the victim which they sacrificed to the Lord according to the condition of the covenant which they had entered into
34.20: **“And I will give them into the hands of their enemies, and into the hands of them that seek their life: and their dead bodies shall be”** — carcass

35.1: **“The word that”** — Rabanus. Since in the preceding chapter the prophet had dealt with Sedechias and what was done under him, he now turns the narrative to the times of Joakim the son of Josias. Whence it is plain that he did not keep the order of time in the narrative, but according to the dispensation of the Holy Spirit, who spoke in him, he wished his prophecy to be written as the occasions required and as the matters fitted, as is done in many places, and most of all in the gospel, so that the reader may know that the sacred Scriptures were not composed by human arrangement, but by divine inspiration and ordering.
35.2: **“Go to the house”** — Rabanus. To confound the pride of the Jews, who resisted the commandments of God, he sets before them the obedient Rechabites, who obeyed the precepts of Jonadab in all things, until by the necessity of the Babylonian army they were forced to enter Jerusalem; whence the Lord promises them that there shall not be wanting a man of the race of Jonadab standing in his sight all days. Mystically, however, the Rechabites signify those who by desire of perfection have gone beyond the commandments of the law. For the just, for whom the law is not made, are thus proved not to be under the law, but strive not only to fulfil the justices of the law but even to surpass them, so as to add voluntary things to what is owed. Hence Abraham would not accept what was rightly due to him of the victory, though he whose spoils he had brought back himself humbly offered it; hence David wept for his slain persecutors; hence Elias and Jeremias remained virgins; hence the sons of Jonadab are praised by the Lord for the obedience shown to their father, and good things to come are promised them, who, not content to offer tithes of their possessions, but rejecting the possessions themselves, offered their souls to God; for what exchange shall a man give for his soul? We ought therefore to know those from whom the legal commandment is not required, but to whom the gospel word sounds: “If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast,” etc. When we offer tithes, we are in a way held under the burden of the law, and do not reach the gospel height, which promises to those who obey not only the rewards of the present life but of the future. But the law promises the comforts of this life, saying: He that shall do these things shall live in them. The gospel, however, says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” It is not great if we abstain from unlawful things, but it is if we abstain from them out of reverence for him who, on account of our weakness, permitted them to us. For what could not be grasped by all was not to be commanded generally; for those who are great in the perfection of virtues can be crowned. But those who are little, and do not fill the measure of the age of the fulness of the body of Christ, although they seem to be hidden by the brightness of the greater, are nevertheless free from the darkness of the curses that are in the law, and are neither added to present evils nor punished with eternal punishment.
35.6:
**“And they answered: We will not drink wine: because Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, saying: You shall drink no wine”** — in which is luxury, which overturns the mind
**“neither you, nor your children, for ever”** — because he who perseveres to the end is saved
35.7:
**“Neither shall ye build houses”** — as those thinking of tomorrow
**“nor sow seed, nor plant vineyards, nor have any: but you shall dwell in tents all your days”** — as sojourners and strangers upon the earth
**“all your days, that you may live many days”** — may lead a life of holy conduct
**“upon the face of the earth, in which you are strangers”** — by the Lord
35.10: **“But we have dwelt in tents, and have been obedient”** — because if we have done anything less, it is to be ascribed not to will but to necessity
35.11: **“But when Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon came up to our land, we said”** — as by common counsel, not hastily, we did this
35.14:
**“The words of Jonadab the son of Rechab, by which he commanded his sons not to drink wine, have prevailed”** — who is greater than Jonadab, and the one Father of all
**“but I have spoken to you, rising early and speaking”** — by the prophets
35.15:
**“And I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, rising early,”** — by the prophets
**“sending and saying: Return ye every man from his wicked way, and make your ways good”** — by work, by thought, by speech
35.17:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts the God of Israel: Behold I will bring upon Juda, and upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the evil that I have pronounced against them, because I have spoken to them, and they have not heard: I have called to them”** — by the prophets
**“and they have not answered me.”** — by obeying
35.18: **“And Jeremias said to the house of the Rechabites: Thus saith the Lord of hosts the God of Israel”** — whom you obeyed in Jonadab
35.19: **“Therefore thus saith the Lord of host the God of Israel: There shall not be wanting a man of the race of Jonadab the son of Rechab, standing before me for ever.”** — immovable, acting manfully

36.3: **“If so be, when the house of Juda shall hear all the evils that I purpose to do unto them, that they may return every man from his wicked way: and I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin.”** — If so be they will hear, etc. The immense clemency of the Maker, when despised, brings not vengeance but promises pardon to the penitent; and he directs the word of preaching through the prophet not only to the Jews but to all nations, if in some way they may be converted, that through the mercy of God they may obtain pardon.
36.4:
**“So Jeremias called Baruch the son of Nerias: and Baruch wrote”** — lest anything perish
**“So Jeremias called”** — The prophet’s ready obedience accords with the divine clemency: for as God provides for human weakness by warning them to be converted, so the prophet by obeying exercises the office of preaching for the salvation of his neighbours; and though shut up in prison he could not do this himself, through an interpreter he fulfilled what had been commanded. What then shall they say who, free and at liberty, neglect to spend the word of God on their neighbours?
36.5: **“And Jeremias commanded Baruch, saying: I am shut up, and cannot go into the house of the Lord.”** — as if: though I am shut up, the word of the Lord is not bound
36.6:
**“Go thou in therefore, and read out of the volume, which thou hast written from my mouth, the words of the Lord, in the hearing of all the people in the house of the Lord on the fasting day”** — so that the people may hear more attentively
**“and also thou shalt read them in the hearing of all Juda”** — so that no one may be without excuse
36.9: **“And it came to pass in the fifth year of Joakim the son of Josias king of Juda, in the ninth month, that they proclaimed a fast before the Lord to all the people in Jerusalem, and to all the people that were come together out of the cities of Juda to Jerusalem.”** — They proclaimed a fast, etc. That those who have sinned through luxury may wash away their sins by abstinence and affliction, and those who have committed unlawful things may abstain even from lawful ones, that by this they may make satisfaction to the Maker; and that those who have committed forbidden things may cut off from themselves what is permitted, and reprove in the least things what they have left undone in the greatest.
36.16: **“And when they had heard all the words, they looked upon one another with astonishment, and they said to Baruch: We must tell the king all these words.”** — And when they had heard, etc. The grace of the Holy Spirit is necessary even for the hearers; for unless the Holy Spirit be present, the teacher’s speech is idle. When one speaks, we all in the Church hear one voice alike, but we do not all understand alike, but as the anointing of God teaches us of all things. The teacher or maker himself also does not speak for the instruction of man if he does not speak by the anointing of the Spirit. For it was said to Cain: “Thou hast sinned, be quiet”; but because, his faults preventing it, he was not anointed, he could hear the words of God but not keep them; so Joakim and his servants could hear the words of God with the ear of the body but not of the heart.
36.18: **“And Baruch said to them: With his mouth he pronounced all these words as if he were reading to me: and I wrote in a volume with ink.”** — And with his mouth he pronounced, etc. It signifies that the apostles and prophets suffered no need of thinking out or lack of speaking, but brought forth everything readily and easily; whence: “Take no thought how or what you shall speak.”
36.23: **“And he cast it into the fire”** — And he cast it into the fire. Astounding is the wickedness of a hardened heart: those who ought to have been pricked to penance by the wholesome warnings delivered the words of the Lord to the fire, and heaped insults on the prophet who was teaching and correcting them, whom they ought to have honoured; because the wicked spirit, who is always adverse to the spirit of grace, hardened their hearts that they might not believe and do penance.
36.26: **“And the king commanded Jeremiel the son of Amelech, and Saraias the son of Ezriel, and Selemias the son of Abdeel, to take up Baruch the scribe, and Jeremias the prophet: but the Lord hid them.”** — But the Lord hid them, etc. Against him human presumption strives in vain. For “The Lord keepeth all them that love him; but all the wicked he will destroy.”
36.30: **“Therefore thus saith the Lord against Joakim the king of Juda: He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David: and his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day, and to the frost by night.”** — Therefore thus saith the Lord, etc. A fitting vengeance, because he burnt the words of the Lord; so whoever resists the commandments of the Lord will suffer vengeance according to the hardness of his heart; for “what things a man shall sow, those also shall he reap.” It is to be noted, however, that in Paralipomenon it is read that Nabuchodonosor led this Joakim bound to Babylon, and in the Book of Kings that Joakim slept with his fathers, and Joakim his son reigned in his stead. But Josephus seems to agree more with the words of Jeremias, asserting that Joakim himself, the father of Jechonias, was killed in Jerusalem by the king of Babylon, not led captive to Babylon. In the tenth book of the Antiquities he says thus: When the king of Babylon had entered the city he by no means kept faith, but killed the strongest and comeliest young men together with king Joakim, whom he also ordered to be cast unburied before the walls. But his son Joakim he made king of the whole province; and those who were established in dignities, to the number of three thousand, he led captive to Babylon, among whom was the prophet Ezechiel, still a boy. This then was the end of king Joakim, who lived thirty-six years. He reigned, however, eleven years. The successor of the kingdom, Joakim, reigned three months and ten days. But whether the aforesaid Joakim perished in Jerusalem or in Chaldea need not be inquired, since according to the prophet it is established that his dead body was cast out to the heat by day and to the frost by night, so that he who burnt the prophetic writing with fire should be scorched by the heat of the sun and the frost of the night.
36.32: **“And Jeremias took another volume, and gave it to Baruch the son of Nerias the scribe: who wrote in it from the mouth of Jeremias all the words of the book which Joakim the king of Juda had burnt with fire: and there were added besides many more words than had been before.”** — And Jeremias took another, etc. Rabanus. After the burning, that is, of the first; because, Judea being reprobated for its faithlessness, the books of the law and the prophets were preserved for the salvation of the Gentiles, to whom all the glory of the old testament has been transferred; because “all these things happened to them in figure: and they are written for our correction,” etc. And there were added many more words than had been before, because they have the history only, but we with the history have the mystical sense. For they have a veil over their heart when Moses is read, but we with open face behold the glory of God.

37.1: **“Now king Sedecias the son of Josias reigned instead of Jechonias the son of Joakim: whom Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon made king in the land of Juda.”** — And he reigned, etc. That Sedechias reigned eleven years after Joakim, who was surnamed Jechonias, not only Jeremias but also the Book of Kings and of Paralipomenon relate. For after Josias his father reigned Joachaz three months; after him Eliachim, who is also Joakim, his brother, eleven years; after him also Joakim’s son Joakim, three months and ten days; and after him Sedecias, his uncle, eleven years; but all were wicked and idolaters, and therefore they perished.
37.3: **“And king Sedecias sent Juchal the son of Selemias, and Sophonias the son of Maasias the priest to Jeremias the prophet, saying: Pray to the Lord our God for us.”** — Pray to the Lord, etc. That the Chaldeans lifted this siege when the Egyptians approached, Josephus makes plain, saying that Vaphres, king of Egypt, came to the help of the Jews: and so when the king of Babylon learned this, he moved his camp against him, and having afflicted the province and plundered its fortresses, he was coming with a great army to besiege the city of Jerusalem itself. But the Egyptian king, hearing that Sedechias his friend was besieged, having gathered the greatest strength of warriors, came to Judea as if to raise the siege; but the Babylonian, departing from Jerusalem, met the Egyptians, and having overcome them all in battle, put them to flight and forced them to leave Syria. And when the king of the Babylonians had departed from Jerusalem, false prophets deceived Sedechias, saying that the Babylonians would not fight against him again, but would return, namely those who were captives in Babylon, with the vessels of God which the king had carried off. Jeremias prophesied the contrary, and the truth.
37.15: **“Wherefore the princes were angry with Jeremias, and they beat him, and cast him into the prison that was in the house of Jonathan the scribe: for he was chief over the prison.”** — Wherefore, etc. Rabanus. They excuse Sedecias in vain, as though he sent Jeremias into prison not willingly but compelled by the violence of the people and the request of the princes, adducing in confirmation of this opinion that in the necessity of famine he ordered food to be given him out of pious affection; for he who was unfaithful and opposed to God could not keep faith with a man. For it is clear from his works that he did nothing pleasing to God, either in the fear of God or in love of neighbour, and therefore he justly suffered the vengeance for his sins.

38.7:
**“Now Abdemelech the Ethiopian, an eunuch that was in the king's house, heard”**
• the king’s servant
• As those princes who put the prophet into the pit signify the demons, who always desire to plunge Christ’s faithful into the mire of vices and the filth of sins, so this Ethiopian eunuch, who, pricked by the fear and love of God, rescued the prophet, signifies the preachers from among the Gentiles, who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven, and who, by the impulse of true charity, strive in word and deed and example to draw those unjustly oppressed out of the pit of perdition; which his name also bears witness to, for Abdemelech is interpreted “servant of the king”: of him, namely, of whom it is said, “a great King above all gods.” Whom the order of preachers serves by the word of the gospel, joining the Gentiles to the faith. But that, helped by divine admonitions and the examples of those before us, we are delivered from the depth of this life, is well figured through Jeremias, for when he is lifted out of the pit, ropes and old rags are let down to him. For by the ropes are figured the precepts of God, which, because they convict and rescue us when set in sins, as it were bind and draw, constrain and lift. But lest, bound with these ropes, he be also hurt while being drawn, old rags are also put with them, because, lest the divine precepts terrify us, the examples of the ancient fathers comfort us, so that by comparison with them we may presume that we can do what we dread from our weakness. If therefore we hasten to be lifted out of this depth, let us be bound with ropes, that is, constrained by the Lord’s precepts. Let the old rags also be there, that the ropes may be better held, that is, let us be conformed to the examples of those before us, lest subtle precepts wound us in our weakness. Whence: “Remember your prelates who have spoken the word of God to you; whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.”
**“the Ethiopian, an eunuch”** — made a eunuch for the kingdom of heaven
38.9:
**“My lord the king, these men have done evil”** — as rulers of darkness
**“in all that they have done against Jeremias the prophet, casting him into the dungeon”** — of vices
**“to die there with hunger”** — of the word of God
38.10: **“Then the king commanded Abdemelech the Ethiopian, saying:”** — that is, preachers from among the Gentiles
38.11: **“So Abdemelech taking the men with him, went into the king's house that was under the storehouse: and he took from thence old”** — that is, the examples of the ancient fathers
38.12: **“And Abdemelech the Ethiopian said to Jeremias: Put these old rags and these rent and rotten things under thy arms, and upon the cords”** — the precepts of the Lord
38.17: **“And Jeremias said to Sedecias: Thus saith the Lord of hosts the God of Israel: If thou wilt take a resolution and go out to the princes of the king of Babylon, thy soul shall live, and this city shall not be burnt with fire: and thou shalt be safe, and thy house.”** — If thou wilt take a resolution and go out, etc. The prophet, foreseeing that the city was to be handed over into the hands of the Chaldeans, advised the king to surrender himself into the hands of the king of Babylon, so that he might thus soften his furious mind and receive a lighter sentence; but the hardened mind could not be corrected.
38.18:
**“But if thou wilt not go out”** — of his own accord
**“to the princes of the king of Babylon”** — by the Lord
**“this city shall be delivered into the hands”** — power
38.19: **“And king Sedecias said to Jeremias: I am afraid because of the Jews that are fled over to the Chaldeans: lest I should be delivered into their hands, and they should abuse me.”** — And king Sedecias said, etc. It is clear that Sedecias showed mercy to Jeremias without pure affection. For if he truly loved him, he would not hand him over to the princes. Fruitless therefore was his feigned mercy, like that of Pilate, who in the passion of the Lord washed his hands before the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this man.” But afterwards he handed him over to the Jews, scourged, to be crucified.
38.22:
**“Behold all the women that are left in the house of the king of Juda, shall be brought out to the princes of the king of Babylon: and they shall say: Thy men of peace have deceived thee, and have prevailed against thee”** — pleasure-seeking counsellors
**“Thy men of peace, they have plunged thy feet in the mire”** — of vices
**“in a slippery place”** — of carnal desires
**“thy feet”** — the steps of works
**“Behold all the women”** — It signifies that fleeting thought and voluptuous counsellors sink the steps of our works in the slipperiness of carnal desires and the mire of vices, and when they see us sunk they depart from us, because to the lost they can give no counsel, since they strove for this alone, to cast us headlong into the abyss of sin. If therefore we are unwilling, by the counsel of the divine Scriptures, to correct our sins and free our souls from perdition by penance, we shall be led out to the Chaldeans, which is interpreted “demons,” with our wives, that is, with carnal concupiscences, and our sons, that is, with depraved acts, and we shall be handed over bound into the hand of the king of eternal confusion, who will burn our city, that is, flesh and soul together, with unquenchable fire.
38.23:
**“And all thy wives”** — carnal lusts
**“and thy children”** — wicked deeds
**“shall be brought out to the Chaldeans”** — demons
**“and thou shalt not escape their hands, but thou shalt be taken by the hand of the king of Babylon”** — of the devil of everlasting confusion
**“thou shalt be taken by the hand of the king of Babylon: and he shall burn this city”** — that is, the soul together with the body
**“he shall burn this city with fire”** — with inextinguishable

39.11: **“Now Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon had given charge”** — Rabanus. To the proud and contemptuous God renders punishments, to the meek and humble consolations, which is clear in king Sedecias and in the prophet Jeremias and in the sentence of king Nabuchodonosor. Nor is it wonderful if through the same things he renders different things to different men, since through the same elements, chosen according to the quality of merits, he repays the elect and the reprobate differently: the water of the Red Sea preserved the Israelites unharmed, the same killed the Egyptians; the flame of the furnace burned the ministers of the king of Babylon, and preserved the children blessing God in the midst of the fire. Whence the wise man says in the praises of God: “For the creature serving thee the Creator, is made fierce against the unjust for their punishment; and abateth its strength for the benefit of them that trust in thee.”
39.17: **“And I will deliver thee”** — They that hope in the Lord shall not be confounded. Let all that do unjust things be confounded. Behold, the princes who sought the life of Jeremias are made captives; the eunuch who had delivered him obtained perfect liberty. So also, when the holy preachers are delivered, their persecutors will be punished with eternal vengeance.

40.1: **“The word that came to Jeremias from the Lord, after that Nabuzardan the general had let him go from Rama, when he had taken him, being bound with chains, among all them that were carried away from Jerusalem and Juda, and were carried to Babylon.”** — The word that was made, etc. It is asked how this word of the Lord is said to have been made to Jeremias the prophet. For it is not shown what this word was or what it made known; whence, unless I am mistaken, it is given to be understood that the prophet wished to signify secretly, by this word spoken to him, that his deliverance had been brought about through the captain of the soldiery by the divine will, as Nabuzardan himself says: “The Lord thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place,” etc. If therefore those who sinned against the Lord and did not obey were taken captive according to the word of the Lord, he who rebuked sinners and obeyed the Lord was set free according to the word of the Lord.
40.2: **“Taking”** — The devastation of the city, the destruction, and the captivity of the people and of the faithless king having been described, there follows what was done concerning Jeremias, and concerning the remnant of the people, whom the prophet warned, by the word of the Lord, to stay in their own land and serve the king of Babylon. But they preferred to go into Egypt, where Nabuchodonosor afterwards slew them and laid Egypt itself waste.
40.5: **“But dwell with Godolias”** — Rabanus. The mercies of the Lord are many, and his judgments are a great deep; as he justly rebuked the transgressors of the law, so he mercifully gave comfort to the humble and obedient. For through those very enemies by whom he punished the faithless king and his ministers, he appointed Godolias as protector of the remnant of the people. Mystically, moreover, Godolias, which is interpreted “magnified by the Lord,” signifies the preachers of the Lord, who are set in authority by the divine will, so that those who fear God may have refuge and comfort. These lay down their life for those under them, and set against the faithless the shield of protection, persisting faithfully in their office even to death, as Godolias, the innocent, was slain by the faithless Ismahel.

41.1: **“And it came to pass in the seventh month, that Ismahel the son of Nathanias, the son of Elisama of the royal blood, and the nobles of the king, and ten men with him, came to Godolias the son of Ahicam into Masphath: and they ate bread there together in Masphath.”** — And it came to pass, etc. Gregory. This deceit was done historically then by Ismahel, but is done spiritually every day by the devil. It must be known that the devil pursues our good deeds in three ways, so that what is rightly done before men may be spoiled in the sight of the eternal judge. Sometimes he defiles the intention, so that the action that follows is unclean from its origin. But if he does not prevail in this, he sets himself against it in the action itself, as on the way, so that when someone walks more securely by the purpose of his mind, a vice secretly joined to it destroys him as if from an ambush. Sometimes, however, he neither spoils the intention nor trips him on the way, but at the end of the action [he strikes] the good work; whence: “In this way wherein I walked, the proud have hidden a snare for me.” Which Jeremias well hints at, who, while he related what was done outside, showed what is done within, saying: “There came eighty men from Sichem,” etc. They shave the beard who withdraw from themselves confidence in their own strength. They rend their garments who do not spare themselves the tearing of inward beauty. They come to offer incense and gifts in the house of the Lord who promise to present prayer with works in the sacrifice of God. But yet if they do not know how to look carefully to themselves on the way of holy devotion, Ismahel the son of Nathanias comes to meet them; because any malignant spirit, begotten by the examples of its former self, that is, Satan, in the error of pride, sets itself against them to deceive. Of whom it is said: “Weeping all along as he went,” because thou devourest minds [that he may prevail to destroy by striking], he hides himself under the veil of virtue, and while he pretends to agree with those who truly mourn, admitted more securely to the inmost parts of the heart, he kills what lies hidden within of virtue; because for the most part he promises to carry them on to higher things; whence: he is said to have said, “Come to Godolias the son of Ahicam”; and while he promises greater things, he takes away even the least; whence it is said: “When they were come to the midst of the city, he slew them.” Therefore he slew in the midst of the city the men coming to offer gifts to God; because intentions given to divine things, unless they guard themselves with great circumspection, while the enemy steals upon them, lose life on the very way, when they carry the offering of devotion. From his hand there is no escape unless one quickly returns to penance. Whence it is plainly added: “Ten men were found among them,” etc. For the treasure in the field is hope in penance, which, because it is not seen, is held as if dug into the earth of the heart. Those therefore who had treasures in the field were saved. For those who afterwards return to lamentation after the fault of their incaution do not die as captives. But when the ancient enemy neither strikes at the beginning of the intention nor kills on the way of the action, he stretches harder snares at the end, and besieges him the more wickedly the more he sees that this alone remains to him to deceive. These snares set at his end the prophet saw when he said: “They shall watch my heel”; for by the heel, which is the end of the body, the end of the action is signified.
41.5:
**“There came some from Sichem, and from Silo, and from Samaria, fourscore men, with their beards shaven”** — not having confidence in their own strength
**“and their clothes rent, and mourning”** — not sparing their own comeliness
**“offerings”** — works
**“and incense”** — prayer
41.6:
**“And Ismahel went forth”** — any malign spirit
**“the son of Nathanias”** — that is, of Satan
**“from Masphath to meet them, weeping all along as he went”** — because he hides himself under a veil of virtue and pretends to agree with the mourning men
**“and when he had met them, he said to them: Come to Godolias, the son of Ahicam”** — because he promises to lead them to higher things, he who even takes away the least.
41.7: **“And when they were come to the midst of the city”** — in the very course of the action.
41.8: **“But ten men were found among them, that said to Ismahel: Kill us not: for we have stores”** — namely, the hope of repentance.
41.9: **“And the pit into which Ismahel cast all the dead bodies of the men whom he slew because of Godolias, is the same that king Asa made, for fear of Baasa the king of Israel: the same did Ismahel the son of Nathanias fill with them that were slain.”** — whomever the devil deceitfully infects, he casts into the place of brimstone and eternal fire.
41.10:
**“and captives”** — and captives
**“Ismahel carried away captive all the remnant of the people that were in Masphath”** — namely the faithful, remaining in contemplation or meditation of the law, or on the watchtower of the virtues.
**“daughters”** — souls.
**“the king's”** — of the eternal.
**“and all the people that remained in Masphath: whom Nabuzardan the general of the army had committed to Godolias the son of Ahicam. And Ismahel the son of Nathanias took them, and he departed, to go over to the children of Ammon.”** — which means “people of mourning”; for he makes captives companions of the perdition of the damned, who stand in eternal mourning.
41.11:
**“But Johanan, heard”** — by the grace of God.
**“the son of Caree, and all the captains of the fighting men”** — namely holy teachers, strengthened by the grace and mercy of God, who by fighting against spiritual wickednesses lead captives back to the Church.
41.14: **“And all the people whom Ismahel had taken, went back to Masphath: and they returned and went to Johanan the son of Caree.”** — as to a leader.
41.15: **“But Ismahel the son of Nathanias fled”** — “Resist the devil, and he will fly from you.”
41.16: **“Then Johanan took”** — This flight of the remnant, and their passage into Egypt against the word of the Lord, which Jeremias here recounts at long length, Isaias foretold long before, a hundred and fifty years, which lay between Isaias and Jeremias, saying: “Woe to you, apostate children, saith the Lord, that you would take counsel, and not of me,” etc.

44.1:
**“The word that came to Jeremias, concerning all the Jews that dwelt in the land of Egypt, dwelling in Magdal”** — it is a city of Egypt beyond the Red Sea.
**“and in Taphnis”** — it is a city in Egypt.
**“and in Memphis, and in the land of Phatures”** — a region of Egypt.
44.4: **“And I sent to you all my servants the prophets”** — it shows the mercy of the Lord and the watchfulness and diligence of the prophets.
44.15:
**“answered Jeremias”** — A foolish answer: they confess that he speaks in the name of the Lord, nor do they yield, but follow the counsel of their own perversity.
**“Mystically.”** — All heretics, set in the Egypt of this world, that is, in the darkness of error, offer sacrifices not to the true God but to demons, when they write fictions and perverse doctrines to deceive men and subvert the faith. Therefore evils shall come upon them, and they shall be “a desolation, and an astonishment.”
44.17:
**“But we will certainly do every word that shall proceed out of our own mouth, to sacrifice to the queen of heaven”** — of the moon, or to Juno, or to Nerecinthia, who is called the wife of Saturn and mother of the gods.
**“and to pour out drink offerings to her, as we and our fathers have done, our kings, and our princes in the cities of Juda, and in the streets of Jerusalem: and we were filled with bread, and it was well with us, and we saw no evil.”** — as if they had received the abundance of good things not from God but from demons.
44.26: **“Therefore hear ye the word of the Lord, all Juda, you that dwell in the land of Egypt: Behold I have sworn by my great name, saith the Lord: that my name shall no more be named in the mouth of any man of Juda, in the land of Egypt, saying: The Lord God liveth.”** — The Lord liveth, etc. The prophet, from the word of the Lord, forbids that his name be named by the mouth of the Jews in the land of Egypt; because those who had gone over there against the command of God ought not to have the protection of the Lord in that place. Mystically, moreover, the name of the Lord is not named by the mouth of heretics in the land of Egypt, because neither their speech nor their prayer, while they are in error, is acceptable to God. For “praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner.” Those therefore who persevere in error shall perish by the sword of strict judgment. But those who, leaving error, return from Egypt into the land of Juda, doing penance and thereafter holding the catholic faith, shall be saved.

45.1:
**“The word that Jeremias the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Nerias, when he had written these words in a book, out of the mouth of Jeremias, in the fourth year of Joakim the son of Josias king of Juda, saying:”**
• The word which Jeremias spoke, etc. Baruch, still unpractised in bearing the sufferings he was to undergo, was afraid of the calamity of captivity which was hanging over them in the time of Joakim the son of Josias, king of Juda; whence he complains that sorrow has been added to his sorrow; and he is answered by the Lord that he seeks peace for himself to no purpose, when the whole people labours under the sickle of tribulations. He signifies, moreover, those who in the pressure of the tribulations or persecutions with which the Church is burdened in the present waver in faintheartedness, seeking the consolation which is promised in the future; whence: “You shall be made sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy.”
• Josephus. The king of the Egyptians, when he had returned from the battle, summoned Joachaz to him from a city of Syria called Emath, and suddenly bound him, and gave the kingdom to his elder brother by the same father, named Joakim, and laid upon the province a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and one of gold. Joakim paid this money. But Joachaz he led away into Egypt, where he died, having reigned three months and ten days. The mother of Joakim was called Zabum, of the city of Abima. He was by nature unjust and most wicked, neither holy toward God nor gentle toward men. And when he was in the fourth year of his reign, a certain man named Nabuchodonosor received the rule of Babylon; at the same time he came with great equipment to the city of Circha, which is by the Euphrates, to fight against the king of the Egyptians, Nichan, for all Syria was under him. And when the king of Babylon learned the purpose of Nichan, he was not at all afraid, but came with a strong arm to the Euphrates. When the encounter was made, he was defeated and lost many thousands. And the king of Babylon, crossing the Euphrates, took all Syria as far as Pelusium, except Judea. But in the fourth year of Nabuchodonosor, which was the eighth of Joakim, he encamped against the Jews with a great army, to exact tribute from Joakim or else to fight. But Joakim, fearing his threats and desiring peace, gave him the tribute which he had received for three years. But in the third year, hearing that the Egyptians would again fight against Babylon, he did not pay the tribute, but was deceived by the hope of the Egyptian war; for the Egyptians did not presume at all to fight against him.
45.5: **“And dost thou seek great things for thyself? Seek not: for behold I will bring evil upon all flesh, saith the Lord! but I will give thee thy life, and save thee in all places whithersoever thou shalt go.”** — as if you will not be endangered there.

46.1: **“The word of the Lord that came to Jeremias the prophet against the Gentiles”** — The word which was made, etc. Rabanus. Hitherto the prophet has dealt in mixed fashion, for the sake of the fitness of the narrative, with Juda and Israel, with the Chaldeans and Egyptians. From here he prophesies the word of the Lord against the nations and provinces, that is, to Egypt, the Palestines, the Moabites, the children of Ammon, Idumea, Cedar and Elam, and at last to Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans, that they may know that they have acted against the will of the Lord, and what vengeance they are to suffer. First, then, he turns his speech to Egypt, which was the greatest scandal to the Jews, marking when this utterance was made: namely in the fourth year of Joakim the son of Josias, when Pharao Nechao, king of Egypt, fought at Charchamis with Nabuchodonosor and was overcome.
46.5: **“What then? I have seen them dismayed”** — Egyptians.
46.7:
**“Who is this”** — Egyptian.
**“that cometh up as a flood”** — the abundance of peoples.
**“and his streams swell like those of rivers”** — against Jerusalem or the land of the Chaldeans.
46.8:
**“Egypt riseth up like a flood, and the waves thereof shall be moved as rivers”** — as if it boasted that it would cover and destroy Judea and the land of the Chaldeans.
**“and he shall say: I will go up and will cover the earth: I will destroy the city”** — Babylon and Jerusalem.
46.9:
**“Scale down”** — Ironically.
**“Get ye up on horses, and glory in chariots, and let the valiant men come forth, the Ethiopians, and the Libyans that hold the shield”** — the proud, who trust in their own power and in the neighbouring provinces, Egypt and Ethiopia
**“Get ye up on horses”** — Heretics and schismatics, sprung from diverse provinces, vainly plan wars against the city of God. For “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” But in the day of the Lord’s vengeance his sword shall devour flesh. Of which it is said: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh.” And there shall be a victim of the Lord in the land of the north, by the river Euphrates, that is, the flowing of worldly pleasure, when they are delivered into the hands of him who set his throne in the north, that he may cast them into “the pool of fire and brimstone.”
46.11:
**“Go up into Galaad, and take balm, O virgin daughter of Egypt: in vain dost thou multiply medicines, there shall be no cure for thee.”** — Go up into Galaad, etc. It is a mountain to which Jacob came on the seventh day, fleeing from Charran; it lies toward the back of Phenicia and Arabia, joined to the hills of Libanus, and extends through the desert as far as beyond the Jordan, where Sehon king of the Amorrhites dwelt. It fell by lot to the children of Ruben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasses.
**“take balm”** — The Greeks call it recina. For “reci” is said of whatever flows. It is a tear exhaled by the sweat of trees, as of the cherry and the mastic and the like. The first resin is the terebinth, the most excellent of all; Arabia produces it, Judea, Syria, Cyprus and Africa, and the islands of the Cyclades. The second is the mastic, which is called mirtrix; this is brought from the island of Chios. The third is that of the pine, of which one kind is pictines, another pictine, one liquid, another dry, and they are brought from Colophon; whence the resin took the name colophonia. Resin, moreover, is fit for wounded bodies and is used for medicine; whence: “Is there no balm in Galaad?” Resin, therefore, is put for penance and for the medicine of conversion to God. Hence the prophet exhorts Egypt and the neighbouring provinces to do penance; otherwise they vainly look for medicines from false gods, because they will receive from them not health but confusion.
46.12: **“The nations have heard of thy disgrace, and thy howling hath filled the land: for the strong hath stumbled against the strong, and both are fallen together.”** — The nations have heard, etc. As though the comfort of the idols had failed, she fell before her enemies, and in mutual slaughter the strong fell with the strong. So heretics, who are ever at discord and turn about in various error, tearing one another, receive not the victory of truth, but, captives of error, fall together into the pit of perdition.
46.14:
**“Declare ye to Egypt, and publish it in Magdal, and let it be known in Memphis”** — a city given over to magic arts
**“and in Taphnis”** — is the metropolis of Egypt
**“Declare ye to Egypt”** — As if to say: you who have heard my prophecy, announce to Pharaoh that the time is at hand, and the tumult of war.
46.15: **“Why are thy valiant men come to nothing?”** — the idol, or Pharao
46.16:
**“He hath multiplied them that fall”** — because his people was handed over into the hands of enemies
**“and one hath fallen upon another, and they shall say: Arise”** — as they ought to exhort one another to battle, so they exhort one another to flight
**“and let us return to our own people, and to the land of our nativity, from the sword of the dove.”** — Nabuchodonosor, who, foolish and without heart, ascribes the victory, which is to be ascribed to God, to his gods
46.17:
**“Call ye the name of Pharao king Egypt, a tumult”** — of war
**“time hath brought”** — against you
46.18:
**“As I live, (saith the King, whose name is the Lord of hosts,) as Thabor is among the mountains, and as Carmel by the sea, so shall he come.”**
• For as Thabor, etc. That is, from the comparison of fruitful places, as if sunk in the sea, understand the great ruin of the power of the Egyptians.
• Thabor is the boundary of Zabulon, a mountain in the midst of the plain of Galilee, lofty with a wonderful roundness, ten miles distant from Diocesarea toward the eastern region. It was also the border between the tribes of Issachar and Nephthali. Carmel is where Nabal the Carmelite lived, and now there is a village named Carmela at the tenth mile from the town of Hebron, lying toward the eastern region, where there is a Roman garrison. Mystically, however, since Thabor is interpreted “coming light,” or “let light come,” and Carmel “tender” or “soft,” or “knowledge of circumcision,” they signify heretics who are proud in the light of worldly knowledge and wisdom, or Jews, soft or delicate, glorying in the circumcision of the flesh, who live under the true pharao and refuse to serve Christ, sunk in the sea of this world and into perpetual damnation.
46.19: **“Furnish thyself to go into captivity”** — prepare your baggage for flight
46.20:
**“Egypt is like a fair and beautiful heifer: one that shall goad her.”** — Nabuchodonosor, who turns her to flight from the face of arms
**“A fair and beautiful heifer”** — Because the Egyptian people, brought up in luxury, refused the yoke of discipline in untamed wantonness.
46.21:
**“Her hirelings also that lived in the midst of her, like fatted calves”** — given over to carnal pleasures
**“are turned back, and are fled away together, and they could not stand, for the day of their slaughter is come upon them, the time of their visitation.”** — Her hirelings also, etc. The princes of the Egyptians he calls not shepherds but hirelings, who had no care of the flock but gave themselves to avarice and luxury. Therefore they were turned to flight before their enemies. Mystically, however, we can understand by the hirelings of Egypt the feigned shepherds of the Church, pilgrim in this world, who, seeking earthly gain, do not presume to defend the sheep committed to them against the ravagers; whence: “But the hireling, and he that is not the shepherd, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and flieth.”
46.22:
**“Her voice shall sound like brass, for they shall hasten with an army, and with axes they shall come against her, as hewers of wood.”**
• His voice, as of brass, etc. Vengeance has come upon the historical Egypt by the just judgment of God, but it is also to come upon the spiritual Egypt on the day of judgment, which Scripture now proclaims as future, clear in the whole world; whence his voice is fittingly compared to sounding brass, which rings more loudly than the other metals, and the day of judgment will sound more strongly than all the earlier rebukes. For then God “shall come manifestly, and shall not keep silence.”
• “A fire shall burn before him: and a mighty tempest shall be round about him.” Then the angels will hasten to “gather out of his kingdom all scandals,” and the unfruitful trees will be cut down by the axes of a strict examination. Then the useless wood will be cut down, because “every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire.” And the multitude of the lost, who like locusts raise themselves up in a short flight, will be plunged into hell, and then the thought of all carnal men, which rests on the pleasures of the world, will be made plain, and will be handed over to be punished with the devil; whence it follows: The daughter of Egypt is confounded, etc.
46.23: **“They have cut down her forest, saith the Lord, which cannot be counted: they are multiplied above locusts, and are without number.”** — because they have been multiplied beyond number
46.24:
**“The daughter of Egypt is confounded, and delivered into the hand of the people of the north.”**
• that is, of demons
• Nabuchodonosor and the Chaldeans; for these destroyed everything and overthrew the state of the kingdom
46.26: **“And afterwards”** — Although it seems to intimate that the kingdom of the Egyptians was not destroyed beyond repair by Nabuchodonosor, since afterwards there were kings there down to Augustus, yet in a higher sense it designates the Christian times, when the worship of God was restored in the Egypt of this world, to practise which man was born; of which Isaias: “The Lord shall strike Egypt with a scourge, and shall heal it,” etc.
46.27: **“And thou my servant Jacob, fear not and be not thou dismayed, O Israel: for behold I will save thee from afar off, and thy seed out of the land of thy captivity: and Jacob shall return and be at rest, and prosper: and there shall be none to terrify him.”** — And thou, fear not, etc. This promise does not fit the Jews well, who are scattered over the whole world and wasted away, and have neither kingdom nor priesthood. But it fits the Christian people, which is gathered from all nations and returns from the captivity of error to the land of the Church, where it shall rest in hope and prosper by the success of virtues, and shall not fear the adversary, trusting in its God. It will not indeed be consumed, but like gold which passes through the fire it will be purified and proved. Yet we can say that that old generation will not be utterly consumed before the day of judgment, because “blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles should come in,” and then all Israel shall be saved.

47.1: **“The word of the Lord that came to Jeremias the prophet against the people of Palestine, before Pharao took Gaza.”** — The word of the Lord that came to Jeremias the prophet, etc. Jeremias, like Isaias and Ezechiel, foretells the coming plagues to the neighbouring nations, because they harassed the people of God and rejoiced in his adversity. So to the Palestines, as before to the Egyptians, he foretells the coming captivity.
47.2:
**“Thus saith the Lord: Behold there come up waters”** — the people of the Assyrians
**“come up out of the north, and they shall be as an overflowing torrent.”** — so that by multitude and violence it overwhelms everything
**“overflowing torrent, and they shall cover the land, and all that is therein, the city and the inhabitants thereof: then the men shall cry”** — with death hanging over each one
47.3:
**“At the noise”** — because the noise of the enemy will overcome the voice of those weeping
**“of the marching of arms, and of his soldiers, at the rushing of his chariots, and the multitude of his wheels. The fathers have not looked back to the children, for feebleness of hands,”** — that is, it was permitted to no one to take care of another, since the enemy raged against each one singly
47.4:
**“Because of the coming of the day, in which all the Philistines shall be laid waste, and Tyre and Sidon shall be destroyed, with all the rest of their helpers. For the Lord hath wasted the Philistines”** — because the Palestines came from Cappadocia
**“the remnant of the isle of Cappadocia.”** — their wealth and manly strength having been taken away
**“And Tyre and Sidon shall be destroyed”** — He shows that Tyre and Sidon belong to the Palestines, although Tyre fell to the lot of Nephthali, and Sidon, the boundary of the Chanaanites, to the lot of Aser; but he did not possess it, because he was not able to drive out the enemies.
**“The remnant of the isle”** — In which the Cappadocians dwelt, its former inhabitants having been slain; this is the boundary of the Chanaanites near Egypt, and it fell by lot to Juda, but he did not obtain it, because the Enachim, that is, the giants of the Philistines, resisted most strongly; and it is to this day a notable city of Palestine, although it was prophesied of it: Gaza shall be an everlasting mound; yet where it formerly stood hardly any traces remain. For it has been built in another place.
47.5:
**“Baldness is come upon Gaza”** — its strength
**“hath held her peace”** — from the voice of joy and gladness
**“Ascalon”** — a city of Palestine in the lot of Juda, but it did not have it, because it could not overcome its inhabitants
**“and the remnant of their valley: how long shalt thou cut thyself?”** — Baldness is come, etc. It signifies that a plague is coming upon heretics and schismatics and all enemies of the Church, because they have prepared snares for the confessors of Christ, have brought wars, and, the devil kindling them, many kinds of persecutions. In the end they themselves are handed over to the cruelest enemies and to everlasting punishments. For Philistines is interpreted “falling by drink”; Tyre, “distress”; Sidon, “hunting”; Ascalon, “infamous fire”; Gaza, “her strength”; all of which fit well Antichrist and his members, who, falling into apostasy through pride, burning with distress of mind, practise hunting in the world, seizing and killing those whom he can from the Church, whose strength is an infamous fire, that is, the concupiscence of the flesh; whence: “his strength is in his loins,” etc. For through lust he burns up the minds of carnal men, but in the end he will be cast down headlong.
47.6:
**“O thou sword of the Lord”** — It signifies the devil, to whom sinners are delivered for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved.
**“how long wilt thou not be quiet?”** — Nabuchodonosor, who exercised the vengeance of the Lord among diverse nations
**“Go into thy scabbard”** — Babylon.
**“rest”** — from the heat of slaying
**“and be still.”** — be quiet
47.7: **“How shall it be quiet”** — As if the sword cannot be quiet unless the Lord commands, to whom it exercises vengeance. Or as if he had spoken in the person of the afflicted to the sword of the Lord, but here he answers in his own person.

48.1:
**“Against Moab”** — against Moab
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts the God of Israel: Woe to Nabo”** — a seat, or prophecy
**“for it is laid waste, and confounded: Cariathaim is taken”** — a city, or a village of the woods
**“Against Moab thus”** — As there is a carnal and a spiritual circumcision, so there is a carnal and a spiritual Moab. Moab is interpreted “from the father” or “paternal water,” as one conceived of incest and drunkenness, as if the father were absent and unknowing. The king of the Moabites invited the soothsayer Balaam to curse, who prophesied this among other things against Moab: “A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise up out of Israel: and shall strike the chiefs of Moab.” Moab signifies secular wisdom, of which it is said: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise”; which, having as its author a sense that is generated from the knowledge of God, seems indeed to be born of the father, but because it is an adulterer and an adversary to the people of God, it is begotten of incest and a cave and night; whence according to Isaias it perished in the night, that is, in everlasting error, as the Egyptians were overwhelmed by the waves “from the morning watch,” that is, by night. And Lot, when Sodom was perishing by night, came to Segor, and the sun rose upon him. Hence Isaias: “Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste, Moab is silent.” It is to be noted that Nabo is interpreted “sitting” or “prophecy”; Chariathiarim, “city” or “village of woods”; Hesebon, “thoughts”; Luith, “of the cheeks”; Oronaim, “hole of sorrow.” Since therefore every doctrine contrary to the truth, without the inspiration of God, is born of human sense in the darkness of error, it is laid waste by night, and its arguments, that is, its walls, are destroyed by ecclesiastical discourse, that they may fall silent in everlasting silence, and their making may be turned to penance and tears, over Nabo, that is, prophecy or sitting, namely their teachers, and over Chariathiarim, where there are no fruitful trees but a barren wood; there will be wailing and lamentation, and all the ornaments of eloquence will be taken away, that they may remain naked and deformed. And if they seemed to have any manliness in the beard, it is shaved off, and by the ecclesiastical man it is proved effeminate and weak. They are girded with the sackcloth of penance, and on the housetops and doctrines in which they believed themselves lofty, and in the streets of the spacious way that leads to death, there will be wailing; and they will not go up through pride, but will go down into weeping. Then they will understand all their vain thoughts, which Hesebon means, and the fall and the ascent of pride, so that their voice will be heard even to the evil works they have done and the command which they thought to be God’s, condemning themselves by their own confession. And when they have done penance, which is meant by Luith, that is, the tears of the cheeks, they will come up to the altar, and as from a hole of sorrow at the entrance raise the cry of contrition to the Lord, saying: “A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit.”
**“Woe to Nabo”** — He foretells the devastation by the Babylonians that is to come upon Nabo and upon its famous cities, so that those who were enemies of the people of God and derided it will be turned into derision among the other nations; whence in what follows: “For Israel hath been a derision unto thee: as though thou hadst found him amongst thieves.” Hence Isaias: “All Moab,” etc. Moab is a province of the Arabs; Nabo a noble city in which was Chamos, the idol, who is also Beelphegor.
48.2:
**“There is no more rejoicing in Moab”** — from the father, or water, paternal
**“over Hesebon”** — a city of Seon, king of the Amorrites; whence: “there came a fire out of Hesebon, and a flame out of the midst of Seon”
**“they have devised evil. Come, and let us cut it off from being a nation. Therefore shalt thou in silence hold thy peace”** — thoughts
48.3: **“A voice of crying from Oronaim”** — a hole of sorrow
48.4: **“Moab is destroyed”** — a province of the Arabs
48.5:
**“For by the ascent of Luith”** — Gene is interpreted
**“shall the mourner go up with weeping: for in the descent”** — of the slope, namely of the road that leads to the Assyrians
48.6:
**“Flee, save your lives”** — Moab perishing
**“and be as heath in the wilderness.”** — the myrice is a lowly tree
**“Save your lives”** — Let those who wish to save their soul flee the crafty teaching of the philosophers and heretics, where destruction is certain, and by the humility of confession let them do penance for error in the desert of strict abstinence, and let them remain in the simplicity and truth of catholic doctrine.
48.7:
**“For because thou hast trusted in thy bulwarks”** — by dialectical disputations
**“and in thy treasures”** — of worldly wisdom or memory
**“thou also shalt be taken”** — by churchmen, who are armed with the shield of faith and fight with the shield of truth
**“and Chamos shall go”** — the fictions of heretics or philosophers, which they worship as idols
**“into captivity, his priests”** — worshippers
**“his princes together”** — ministers
48.8:
**“And the spoiler shall come”** — ecclesiastical
**“upon every city”** — the fortress of worldly knowledge
**“and no city shall escape”** — because every perverse understanding will be taken captive
**“and the valleys shall perish”** — false humilities
**“and the plains shall be destroyed”** — feigned virtues
48.9:
**“Give a flower to Moab”** — as if it has flourished until now
**“for in its flower it shall go out: and the cities thereof shall be desolate, and uninhabited.”** — Give a flower, etc. He who seemed to flourish by human invention and in secular learning will be reduced to desert and solitude, because every hypocrisy truly displeases God, as the following sentence shows: “Cursed be he that doth the work of the Lord deceitfully.” For it is necessary that we look not only at what we do, but also with what discretion we do it.
48.10:
**“Cursed be he that doth the work of the Lord deceitfully”**
• or slothfully
• either for the reward of a bodily thing, or for a word of praise, or for the favour of human judgment
• Sloth is born of torpor, fraud of private affection; the lesser love of God heightens the former, and self-love in its own right stirs up the latter. For he commits fraud in the work of God who, loving himself inordinately, hastens by what he does rightly to the goods of a passing reward. But this fraud is committed in three ways, because either the silent favour of the human heart, or the breath of applause, or some external thing is desired. Against which it is said through the prophet: “that shaketh his hands from all bribes”; for fraud is not only in the receiving of money, nor is a gift only one thing. There are three receivings of gifts for which men hasten by fraud. For a gift is favour won from the heart, from thought; a gift from the mouth is glory through applause; a gift from the hand is a reward through giving. But the just man shakes his hands from every gift, because in what he does rightly he seeks to receive neither empty glory from the human heart, nor praise from the mouth, nor a giving from the hand. He alone does not commit fraud in the work of God who, while he is watchful in zeal for good action, longs neither for the rewards of a bodily thing, nor for words of praise, nor for human favour. Therefore, since our good deeds themselves cannot escape the sword of lurking guilt unless they are fortified daily by anxious fear, it is rightly said through Job: I feared all my works, as though I had done them rightly in God’s sight, but what I have secretly endured in them I do not know. For often our good deeds perish by the robbery of fraud, because earthly desires thrust themselves into right actions; often they fail when sloth intervenes, and waste away as love grows cold.
**“and cursed be he that withholdeth his sword”** — the word of God
**“from blood”**
• the killing of carnal life
• And cursed be he that withholdeth, etc. This curse can fit all who follow the luxury of the world and neglect to chastise their bodies and bring them into servitude, according to that: “And they that are Christ’s, have crucified their flesh,” etc. For without shedding of blood there is no remission of sins; for “flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.” Cursed, therefore, is he who withholds the sword, that is, the word of God, from blood, by which, namely, the matter of sins is quickened: whatever carnal and earthly has grown in our members must be poured out, and cut off by the sword of the word of God.
*Gregory:* To withhold the sword from blood is to hold back the word of preaching from the slaying of carnal life, of which it is said: “my sword shall devour flesh.” Hence Paul says: “I take you to witness this day, that I am clear from the blood of all men. For I have not spared to declare unto you all the counsel of God.”
48.11:
**“Moab hath been fruitful from his youth, and hath rested upon his lees: and hath not been poured out from vessel to vessel, nor hath gone into captivity”** — of captivity
**“nor hath gone into captivity: therefore his taste hath remained”** — ancient happiness
**“remained in him, and his scent”** — fame
**“Hath been fruitful”** — It is shown that Moab came from abundance into ease and pride, and despised the afflicted people of God, because it suffered no affliction or captivity.
48.12:
**“Therefore behold the days come, saith the Lord, and I will send him men that shall order”** — that is, I will hand him over to enemies to be plundered, who will search through all his household goods
**“and overturn his bottles, and they shall cast him down, and shall empty his vessels, and break their bottles one against another”** — I will send him, etc. Mystically. Whoever trust in human philosophy, despising the faith of the Church and its simple teaching, there will come to them those who order and overturn their doctrines, and who plunder the treasures of false knowledge which the malignant spirits had in books as in vessels; and then they will be confounded at the end of life, proving that their study and the worship of their false gods profited them nothing. For the gods of the Gentiles are demons; then they will go with the devil and his angels into everlasting fire, but the just into life everlasting.
48.13:
**“And Moab shall be ashamed of Chamos”** — who will not be able to help
**“as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel”** — where he worshipped the golden calves
**“in which they trusted”** — of deliverance
48.15:
**“Moab is laid waste”** — under the name of Moab, the folly of the world and pride are refuted
**“and they have cast down her cities”** — enemies
**“and her choice young men”** — who trusted in their own strength or knowledge
**“are gone down to the slaughter”** — everlasting damnation
48.16:
**“The destruction of Moab is near to come”** — eternal
**“The destruction of Moab is near to come: the calamity thereof shall come”** — what is subject to a certain end is not lasting
48.17:
**“Comfort him”** — Ironically.
**“him, all you that are round about him, and all you that know his name, say: How is the strong staff broken, the beautiful rod?”** — Comfort him, all, etc. Ironically, or he calls them to penance, so that by fitting satisfaction they may escape misery.
**“Mystically.”** — The wise of this world and the heretics, whom Moab signifies, if they do not correct their foolishness and turn to the catholic faith, ruin and devastation will come upon them, upon all their cities, that is, their various sects. For those that stand far or near from the truth will be overthrown when the gospel shines.
48.19: **“Stand in the way, and look out, O habitation of Aroer”** — Aroer signifies amazement at the sudden fall
48.20: **“Moab is confounded”** — the answer of the one fleeing
48.25:
**“The horn of Moab is cut off”** — whatever there is of perverse doctrines in the world
**“and his arm is broken, saith the Lord”**
• The horn of Moab is cut off, etc. As he prophesied against Babylon and the Philistines because they oppressed the people of the Jews, so the devastation of the Moabites, that is, of Arabia, is foretold, by the Assyrians and Babylonians; for they were laid waste by both, when Sennacherib took Israel captive and Nabuchodonosor overthrew Jerusalem.
• The horn of Moab: whatever, namely, of perverse doctrines there is in this world, and whatever pertains to earthly knowledge and is thought strong, is overturned, so that nothing that was thought most strong is spared.
48.26:
**“Make him drunk”** — the cup of God’s wrath
