**“Because he lifted up himself against the Lord: and Moab shall dash”** — that is, in his punishment he will cease to punish others
**“his hand in his own vomit, and he also shall be in derision”** — who mocked others; thus the foolish wisdom of the world, mocking Christian simplicity, will recognise its folly at the end of its error
48.27: **“For Israel hath been a derision unto thee: as though thou hadst found him amongst thieves: for thy words therefore, which thou hast spoken against him, thou shalt be led away captive”** — like the daughter of Babylon
48.28:
**“Leave”** — O wise men
**“the cities, and dwell”**
• the counsel of the prophet
• dwelling-places of errors
**“in the rock”** — To Christ, according to that: “My dove, in the clefts of the rock, and in the hollow places of the wall.”
**“you that dwell in Moab: and be ye like the dove that maketh her nest”** — doing well; that is, preparing an eternal dwelling.
**“in the mouth of the hole in the highest place”** — that is, in the perfect confession of the passion and resurrection of Christ.
48.29:
**“We have heard”** — Isaias says almost the same.
**“the pride of Moab, he is exceeding proud”** — Heretics are proud and despise the simplicity of the Church.
**“his haughtiness, and his arrogancy, and his pride, and the loftiness of his heart”** — We have heard the pride, etc. In the preceding section he was calling those who err to penance, and was urging them to be converted to Christ so as to remain forever in his faith; now, recognizing that very many are incorrigible and obstinate, he says, in the person of those of Moab who have been saved and have learned his pride by their own experience: “We have heard the pride of Moab,” etc. And he accuses Moab of pride because he is puffed up more than his strength can bear or demands.
48.30:
**“I know”** — to whom nothing is hidden.
**“saith the Lord, his boasting, and that the strength thereof is not according to it”** — but beyond.
48.31:
**“Therefore will I lament for Moab”** — grieving over its misery and sadness, or folly.
**“and I will cry out to all Moab”** — the province or the metropolis.
**“I will cry out to all Moab, for the men”** — the synagogue of heretics.
**“wall”** — of sophistical fortification.
**“brick”** — frail and dissoluble.
**“that mourn”** — Therefore, over, etc. He shows the power of their former prosperity and the blow of their sudden overthrow.
**“The brick wall”** — Which is interpreted their strength, and it signifies the strongest doctrines of the heretics, built up by dialectic, in which the strength of error seemed to lie.
48.32:
**“with the mourning of Jazer”** — which exalts itself against the knowledge of God.
**“I will weep for thee, O vineyard of Sabama, thy branches”** — some wishing to be converted.
**“thy branches are gone over the sea, they are come even to the sea of Jazer: upon thy harvest”** — lest from it bread be made which is turned into the gall of asps.
**“and thy vintage”** — lest from it wine be made which is the gall of dragons.
**“the robber hath rushed in”**
• that he may trample and destroy, lest those eating and drinking from it die.
• evangelical.
**“I will weep for thee”** — The storm of this world. For it seems to signify that some of Moab wish to be converted to the Lord; for Sabama is interpreted as some conversion.
**“O vineyard of Sabama”** — Lifting up the height, because it tries to raise a tower of pride to heaven.
48.33:
**“Joy and gladness is taken away”**
• to heretics who have been converted.
• “Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted.”
**“from Carmel, and from the land of Moab”** — the knowledge of a false name; that is, of those who boast that they have the knowledge of circumcision.
**“and I have taken away the wine out of the presses”** — of dragons.
**“the treader of the grapes shall not sing the accustomed cheerful tune”** — because they will be overwhelmed by eternal silence.
48.34:
**“From the cry of Hesebon”** — thought.
**“even to Eleale, and to Jasa, they have uttered their voice: from Segor to Oronaim, as a heifer of three years old: the waters also of Nemrim shall be very bad”** — bitter, false, therefore barren.
**“from Segor”** — A city which overlooks the Dead Sea, where the boundary of the Moabites is. It indicates, therefore, that the wailing will resound to the farthest parts of the province. Of which Isaias: “his bars unto Segor, a heifer of three years old,” that is, of perfect age; for as in men the thirtieth year, so in cattle and beasts of burden the third year is the most vigorous.
**“the waters also”** — Isaias. “For the waters of Nemrim shall be desolate,” etc. And what is said here more briefly is set out fully in Isaias. For Nemrim is a town above the Dead Sea.
48.35:
**“And I will take away from Moab”**
• because when the kingdom failed, the use of sacrifices ceased
• When the sect of human wisdom perishes, the pomp and clamour of words cease, so that neither philosophers nor heretics who have gone out from the Church may find in their teaching anything useful for human life.
48.36:
**“Therefore my heart”** — affection
**“shall sound for Moab like pipes”** — singing a mournful song
**“and my heart”** — affection
**“for the men of the brick wall”** — of a fragile fortress
**“a sound like pipes, because he hath done more than he could”** — by being proud
48.37: **“For every head shall be bald, and every beard shall be shaven: all hands shall be tied together, and upon every back there shall be haircloth.”** — For every head, etc. Among the ancients the shaving of the beard and head was a sign of mourning; by these, therefore, the greatness of grief is shown: as if tears will not be private, public lamentations will resound; neither matrons nor virgins, nor childhood nor old age will be exempt; extreme captivity knows neither modesty nor weakness. Hence Isaias: “baldness upon all their heads, every beard shall be shaven.”
48.38: **“Because I have broken”** — Every teaching of philosophers and heretics, because it is fragile and useless, is crushed and scattered by the truth.
48.39:
**“How is it overthrown”** — the region of Moab
**“and they have howled”** — its inhabitants
**“How hath bowed down the neck”** — of pride
**“and is confounded! And Moab shall be a derision”** — of pride cast down: so human wisdom, the more it raises itself against God, the more, with truth prevailing, it is put to shame before all
48.40:
**“Thus saith the Lord: Behold he shall fly as an eagle”** — Nabuchodonosor, that is, rapacious and swift
**“shall fly, and shall stretch forth his wings”** — passing, that is, to Moab
48.41:
**“Carioth is taken”** — a famous city
**“and the heart of the valiant men of Moab shall be”** — Rightly he compares the heart of Moab to the heart of a woman in labour, because from great luxury one comes to great sorrow.
48.43:
**“Fear”** — of mind
**“and the pit”** — of deception
**“and the snare”** — of captivity
48.44:
**“He that shall flee from the fear, shall fall into the pit”** — of siege
**“and he that shall get up out of the pit”** — trying to escape
**“shall be taken in the snare”** — of captivity
**“for I will bring upon Moab the year of their visitation”** — of just retribution
48.45:
**“They that fled from the snare stood in the shadow of Hesebon”** — from their iniquity, that is
**“in the shadow”** — Because they hoped for comfort in its stronghold, but in vain: the fire of vengeance, the just judge repaying, overwhelmed the crown of the tumult of the sons of Moab.
48.46:
**“Woe to thee, Moab, thou hast perished, O people of Chamos: for thy sons, and thy daughters are taken captives.”** — that is, the disciples together with their masters are delivered to eternal captivity
**“taken captives”** — Woe to thee, etc. Because neither the fortification of cities nor the power of idols could defend you, so it will be everlasting woe to those who trust in human wisdom and serve diverse errors.
48.47: **“And I will bring back the captivity of Moab in the last days, saith the Lord. Hitherto the judgments of Moab.”** — And I will bring back, etc. It seems to signify the time of grace, in which “whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved.”

49.1:
**“Against the children of Ammon. Thus saith the Lord: Hath Israel no sons? or hath he no heir? Why then hath Melchom inherited Gad”** — is the idol of the Ammonites, and it means ‘my king’
**“Against the children of Ammon”** — After Moab the words turn to the sons of Ammon, and they are rebuked because they dared to invade the border of Israel; whence a worthy vengeance is foretold for them, and it is foretold that Israel will possess its possessors, having destroyed them.
49.2: **“Therefore behold the days come, saith the Lord, and I will cause the noise of war to be heard in Rabbath of the children of Ammon”** — a metropolis, which was afterwards called Philadelphia by Ptolemy Philadelphus, who held Arabia along with Idea.
49.3:
**“Howl, O Hesebon, for Hai is wasted. Cry, ye daughters of Rabbath, gird yourselves with haircloth: mourn and go about by the hedges: for Melchom”** — in which you trusted.
**“shall be carried into captivity, his priests”** — as the people, so the priests.
**“Ye daughters of Rabbath”** — The metropolis of the Moabites, which is now called Ariopolis, a compound name from Hebrew and Greek, not that it be called the city of Ares, that is, of Mars.
49.4:
**“Why gloriest thou in the valleys?”** — the abundance of crops in which the Ammonites trusted.
**“thy valley hath flowed away, O delicate daughter”** — the abundance of pride and of the people acquired.
**“that hast trusted in thy treasures”** — of knowledge.
**“and hast said: Who shall come to me?”** — a corrector or conqueror.
49.5:
**“Behold I will bring a fear upon thee”** — of churchmen.
**“saith the Lord God of hosts, from all that are round about thee”** — the catholic Church spread throughout the whole world.
49.6:
**“And afterwards I will cause the captives of the children of Ammon to return, saith the Lord.”** — And afterwards I will cause the captives to return, etc. That after the conversion of heretics to the faith, the captivity of sin will be dissolved, and they will be received into the communion of the Church from which they had gone out.
**“the captives of the children of”** — We can understand by the children of Ammon, who were born of Lot in a cave, in drunkenness and in incest, heretics, according to that: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.”
49.7:
**“Against Edom. Thus saith the Lord of hosts: Is wisdom no more in Theman?”** — It is foretold of Idumea that wisdom in Theman is no longer known.
**“counsel is perished from her children: their wisdom is become unprofitable.”** — Against Idumea, etc. Tropologically. Idumea is earthly and fleshly delight, which rises up against the spirit, that we may not do the things that are of the spirit; and it hastens to draw to itself the soul set in the midst, rebelling against the sons of Juda, to whom it was formerly subject, and it remembers its ancient grief against those who, departing from the flesh, follow the spirit. Therefore the Lord stretches out his hand over Idumea, to reduce it to desolation, and Theman, which is interpreted failing, and Dedan, that is, kinship, that they may serve the house of Juda. For “Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated.” The Lord loves Jacob because he supplants the fleshly and earthly, and receives its blessing. For first we live according to the flesh, afterwards according to the spirit. For vices come first, then the virtues by which the vices are overwhelmed. For the heart of man is inclined to evil from youth; but mature age condemns the errors of youth; whence: “The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember.” It is to be known, however, that Jacob received the first blessing, Esau the second, and at the end it is said to him: you shall be your brother’s servant. For when the flesh has been made subject to the spirit, Idumea will pass into Judea, and the flesh will serve reason.
49.8: **“Flee and turn your backs, go down into the deep hole, ye inhabitants of Dedan”** — it is a city of Idumea, and it is interpreted as kinship.
49.9:
**“If grapegatherers had come”** — plunderers who lay waste openly and utterly.
**“to thee”** — or to you.
**“would they not have left a bunch? if thieves in the night”** — who dig into houses by night.
**“they would have taken what was enough for them”** — they would have left something, either because they were sated or because they did not know.
**“if thieves”** — Heretics, who steal what suffices for themselves and daily seize some from the Church; entering the vineyard of the Lord, which he transplanted out of Egypt, they desire to lay waste everything so that they scarcely leave a cluster in it; but the Lord on the contrary brings into the open all their secrets, and those of the patriarchs of Esau, who were the first to invent heresies, through churchmen and teachers. And his first victory is to make plain what was covered.
**“Tropologically.”** — The word was spoken against the Jews, who envy Christians and persecute Jacob their brother, who seized or snatched away the birthright of the father. Or against heresies and opposing doctrines, which seem to us to be neighbours, but strive to drive out of the paternal inheritance the simple Jacob, the dweller in the house. For Idumea is interpreted earthly, and on account of the red colour it can be understood as bloody; whence: “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bosra?” So those who refer Idumea to the flesh think the soul is stirred up against it, that by mortifying our members, that is, fornication, uncleanness and the like, we may obtain an eternal victory in Christ.
49.10:
**“But I have made Esau bare, I have revealed his secrets”**
• equal to the Babylonians.
• namely all secrets: the caves and holes of the grottoes, because that region dwells in caves on account of excessive heat.
49.11:
**“Leave thy fatherless children”** — the poor man is left to you as an orphan; you were the helper.
**“I will make them live: and thy widows”** — blessing her widow, I will bless her.
49.12: **“For thus saith the Lord: Behold they whose judgment was not to drink of the cup”** — as the just man is scarcely saved, where will the wicked and sinners appear?
49.13: **“For I have sworn by myself, saith the Lord, that Bosra shall become a desolation, and a reproach, and a desert, and a curse”** — a city in Moab, which is interpreted as firm or strong or fortified.
49.14:
**“a rumour”** — spiritual.
**“I have heard”** — with spiritual ear.
**“from the Lord, and an ambassador”** — Christ, desired by all nations; for he himself is the angel of great counsel.
**“an ambassador is sent to the nations: Gather yourselves together”**
• with me.
• the exhortation of the envoy.
**“and come against her”** — Edom.
**“and let us rise up”** — and I will be the leader and first in the battle line
**“I have heard a rumour”** — This sentence is contained in Abdias in almost the same words, and so are many things of this chapter.
49.15:
**“For behold I have made thee a little one”** — in comparison with the other nations
**“I have made thee among the nations, despicable among men”**
• the rational, wise ones
• Behold, for a little one, etc. As if to say: O Edom, who are the least among all the nations round about, and in comparison with the other nations a little one, both in merit and in number, yet you are lifted up in pride beyond your strength. And though you dwell in the caves and caverns of the rock, humble and poor, you are exalted like an eagle, and swell so much in thought that you believe you dwell among the stars; but if beyond nature you could pierce the height of heaven, I would drag you down from there and bring you back to the earth of the other nations.
**“a little one”** — O heretic, though you seem great to yourself and despise the littleness of the Church, you are nevertheless small and despicable.
49.16:
**“Thy arrogancy”** — every arrogant heretic, because pride makes a heretic
**“hath deceived thee, and the pride”** — not ignorance
**“of thy heart: O thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock”** — in the clefts, that is, of schism and heresy, which are cut off from the rock, Christ, and from the unity of faith
**“and endeavourest to lay hold on the height of the hill”** — swelling in thought
**“though thou shouldst make thy nest as high”** — that is, if you could raise yourself beyond nature
**“as an eagle”** — which flies higher than all birds
**“thy nest”** — promising you the kingdom of heaven
**“Though thou shouldst make thy nest as high”** — Because heretics promise themselves the height and likeness of eagles, which gather to the Lord’s carcass. These things are also said against the flesh: because its strength was diminished at the coming of Christ, and it was made contemptible, subject to the rule of the soul, and it is raised up in vain, though it dwells in the caverns of the rock, whether in the senses or in the thoughts, and wishes to lord it over the soul, exalting its throne, and does not believe its works can be overcome. To it it is said that although it lifts itself up and imitates the heights of the eagle and deceives many of the saints, yet it will be overcome by the Lord. But what was said against heretics and the flesh can also be understood against the Jews.
49.17:
**“And Edom shall be desolate”** — the synagogue of heretics or of the Jews
**“every one that shall pass by”** — by looking
**“by it, shall be astonished, and shall hiss at all its plagues”** — by the greatness of the torments
49.18:
**“As Sodom was overthrown and Gomorrha”** — He shall rain snares upon sinners: fire and brimstone
**“and the neighbours thereof, saith the Lord: there shall not a man dwell there”** — acting manfully
**“and there shall no son of man inhabit it”** — of the rational, wise one
49.19:
**“Behold one shall come up as a lion”**
• the devil
• As the Lord chastised the pride of the Jews, whom he signifies by the Jordan, so he will fully chastise through the ministers of his wrath the obstinacy of the Idumeans and the envy which they had exercised against their brothers; and no one will resist his counsel and will. Heretics also and enemies of the Church will not escape torments fitting for them, but the most savage lion will thrust them down into Tartarus to be tormented for ever.
**“shall come up from the swelling of the Jordan”** — of the Jews
**“against the strong and beautiful”** — against Edom, that is, which seems to itself fair and strong
**“for I will make him run suddenly upon her: and who shall be the chosen one whom I may appoint over her? for who is like to me? and who shall abide me?”** — as if who would resist my voice
49.20:
**“Therefore hear ye the counsel of the Lord, which he hath taken concerning Edom: and his thoughts which he hath thought concerning the inhabitants of Theman: surely”** — with right faith and true doctrine
**“the little ones shall cast them down”** — the humble
**“of the flock”** — ecclesiastical
**“they shall destroy them”** — aposiopesis
**“with their habitation”** — perverse doctrines
49.21: **“at the noise of their fall”** — When the destroyer comes, the noise of their ruin will resound far and wide, striking terror into the neighbouring provinces.
49.22:
**“Behold he shall come up as an eagle, and fly: and he shall spread”** — to seize
**“his wings over Bosra”** — that is, the pride of heretics will be crushed
49.23:
**“Against Damascus. Emath is confounded and Arphad”** — the cities of Damascus and Arabia.
**“for they have heard very bad tidings, they are troubled as in the sea: through care they could not rest”**
• Emath is confounded, etc. After the Philistines, the Moabites, the Ammonites also and the Idumeans, he turns his words to Damascus, that is, Arabia. Damascus was once a royal city and held the primacy in all Syria, when Antioch, Laodicea and Apamea, which we know were enlarged after Alexander, were not yet flourishing; because therefore it afforded help to the ten tribes against Juda, he signifies that devastation from the Babylonians threatens it.
• The evil report, etc. Namely the captivity that threatens from the Babylonians, or, according to others, from the Romans; for when the people of the Jews was taken captive, Damascus, over which Aretha ruled, was likewise taken.
49.24:
**“Damascus is undone, she is put to flight, trembling hath seized on her”** — for sins, penitent.
**“anguish and sorrows have taken her as a woman in labour”**
• that she may bring forth the spirit of salvation and bear the fruit of good works.
• Damascus is undone, etc. Damascus is interpreted cup of blood or blood of sackcloth; all of which suit the heathens, who before the faith of Christ were friends of blood and cruelty and did works worthy of mourning and sackcloth. In the book of Days the history tells that when the year was completed the army of Syria went up against Joas king of the Jews, and came to Jerusalem and killed all its princes and sent all the spoil to the king of Damascus, though it had come with a few men; and God delivered into their hands a very great multitude, because they had forsaken the Lord God their Father. For after the end of the acceptable year, in which the gospel of Christ was preached, an army of the Gentiles went up from Damascus, with few men, against Juda and Jerusalem, who had forsaken the Lord; and the churchmen took away all their laws and the riches of the prophets and sent them to the king of Damascus; for in comparison with the whole world the faithful were still few, and yet the Lord delivered Jerusalem into their hands, because they forsook the Son of God, who was foretold through the prophets. Therefore by Damascus is signified the calling of the Gentiles, who, first lovers of blood, after they believed in Christ ceased to be a city of their former way of life; whence Isaias: “and shall be as a ruinous heap of stones.” For as a heap of stones is piled up from scattered stones, so from all nations a heap of believers is gathered in the ruin of the Jews who are falling, while the Gentiles rise.
49.28:
**“Against Cedar”** — These are the Agarenes, but under an assumed name they are called Saracens; they dwell throughout the whole wilderness, of whom the poet says: the Arabs, wandering far and wide.
**“Mystically.”** — Mystically: Cedar, which is interpreted as darkness, and Asor, that is, the arrow of light, signify heretics, darkened in mind, who, feigning arrows of light in the sayings of their doctrine, pretend to be sons of the east, when they are sons of darkness.
49.29:
**“their tents”** — synagogues.
**“and their flocks”** — disciples.
**“They shall take their curtains”** — the carcasses of sinners.
**“and all their vessels”** — the wickedness of anger.
**“and their camels”** — brutish, made deformed by the hump of sins.
**“shall carry off for themselves, and they shall call fear upon them round about”** — Their tents, etc. All these things properly signify the nation of the Saracens, who live in tents and have their seats where night compels them, and have many herds and flocks and droves of camels; but they had no doors nor bars, for they do not dwell in cities but in the wilderness; these were all destroyed by the Babylonians.
49.30:
**“Flee ye”** — by the spiritual Chaldeans rushing in.
**“get away speedily, sit in deep holes”** — of sinners.
**“sit”** — lying hidden.
**“you that inhabit Asor”**
• the metropolis of that nation.
• the arrow of that light.
**“saith the Lord: for Nabuchodonosor”** — the devil.
**“king of Babylon”** — of eternal confusion.
**“taken counsel”** — of guile and cunning.
**“and hath conceived designs”** — the devil or Nabuchodonosor.
49.31:
**“Arise, and go up to a nation that is at ease, and that dwelleth securely, saith the Lord: they have neither gates”** — of continence.
**“nor bars”** — of true defence.
**“they dwell alone”** — apart from God.
49.32:
**“And their camels shall be for a spoil”** — to demons.
**“and the multitude of their cattle”** — of the foolish.
**“for a booty, and I will scatter into every wind”** — of doctrine.
**“Who have their hair cut round”** — although, namely, they think themselves stripped of the hair of vices.
**“And I will bring destruction upon them from all their confines”** — because demons are near us and fly in this nearby air.
**“destruction”** — eternal.
49.33:
**“And Asor shall be a habitation for dragons”** — of demons.
**“desolate”** — from God
**“no man shall abide there”** — ecclesiastic
**“nor son of man inhabit it”** — truly rational
49.35: **“Thus saith the Lord of hosts: Behold I will break the bow of Elam, and their chief strength”** — Behold, I will break, etc. Elam is a region of Persia, whence the Elamites. For the prophet foretells that the Persians and Medes, although they laid waste Babylon and destroyed the kingdom of the Chaldeans, are themselves to be destroyed by the Macedonians. For he who rebuked the other kingdoms for their iniquities did not leave this kingdom unpunished. The Elamites also are interpreted as despising or tempting, and they signify the persecutors of the Church.
49.36: **“And I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven: and I will scatter them into all these winds: and there shall be no nation, to which the fugitives of Elam shall not come”** — And I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, etc. For the Son of man sends his angels from the four winds of heaven to gather all offences out of his kingdom.
49.37:
**“And I will cause Elam to be afraid before their enemies”** — by demons
**“and in the sight of them that seek their life: and I will bring evil upon them, my fierce wrath”** — of whom it is said: “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation, nor chastise me in thy wrath.”
49.39:
**“But in the latter days”** — because, the persecutors being dead, many will be converted to the faith
**“I will cause the captives of Elam to return”** — to the Lord
**“I will cause the captives”** — from sins

50.1: **“The word that the Lord hath spoken against Babylon, and against the land of the Chaldeans in the hand of Jeremias the prophet”** — The word that the Lord hath spoken, etc. The prophecy against Egypt, the Philistines, Moab, the children of Ammon, Damascus also and Cedar being ended, the discourse is directed against Babylon and the Chaldeans, so that those whom he before accused secretly, he now openly, by making their crimes manifest, plainly declares that devastation and desolation will follow. Isaias also and Ezechiel prophesied likewise against the Babylonians and Chaldeans.
50.2:
**“Declare ye among the nations, and publish it, lift up a standard: proclaim, and conceal it not: say: Babylon is taken, Bel is confounded, Merodach is overthrown, their graven things are confounded, their idols are overthrown”** — that is, the idols which they worshipped as gods
**“Their graven things are confounded”** — Their graven things are confounded. Isaias said similar things: “Behold I will stir up the Medes against them, who shall not seek silver, nor desire gold.”
50.3: **“For a nation is come up against her out of the north”** — of the Persians and Medes
50.4:
**“In those days, and at that time, saith the Lord, the children of Israel shall come”**
• to the Church
• seeing God
**“the children of Israel, they and the children of Juda together”** — men, that is, confessors
**“going”** — from virtue to virtue
**“and weeping”** — for their sins
**“The children of Israel shall come”** — This promise signifies the return of the people of God from the captivity which it endured under the Assyrians or Chaldeans; or rather the Christian times, when the sons of God from diverse nations came together to the catholic Church, where they might seek their God, asking and learning the way of truth, and turning the face of their heart to do the will of God, that they may be joined to him in an everlasting covenant.
50.5:
**“in Sion”** — the Church
**“They shall ask the way”** — of truth
**“their faces are hitherward”** — of hearts
**“They shall come, and shall be joined to the Lord by an everlasting covenant”** — because neither death nor life will be able to separate
50.6:
**“My people have been a lost flock, their shepherds”** — scribes and Pharisees, or heretics
**“have caused them to go astray”** — from the worship of God
**“and have made them wander”** — by the various sects of heretics
**“in the mountains”** — of pride
**“from mountain”** — of the law
**“to hill”** — the humility of heresy, which however is thought to have some height
**“they have gone, they have forgotten their resting place”** — of the Church, where the bride delights with the bridegroom
**“A lost flock”** — My people have been a lost flock. By this sentence are noted the kings of Israel who made the people err and turn aside to idolatry, of whom the first was Jeroboam the son of Nabat, who made the golden calves to be adored; then the other transgressors of the law.
50.7:
**“All that found them”** — visible and invisible enemies
**“have devoured them”** — Wandering.
**“and their enemies said: We have not sinned”** — they reckoned as nothing the sin of tearing the flock.
**“because they have sinned against the Lord the beauty of justice”** — against the command, namely of justice, and the hope of future reward, delivering Christ’s sheep to the bites of wolves.
50.8:
**“Remove”**
• captive in sins.
• by doing penance.
**“out of the midst of Babylon”** — of confusion.
**“and go forth out of the land of the Chaldeans”** — of those who take captive, that is, of demons, once the destruction of Babylon is heard.
**“and be ye”** — in Jerusalem, which is the place of vision and peace.
**“as kids”** — doing penance.
**“at the head of the flock”** — of the catholic Church.
**“Remove out of the midst of Babylon”** — Historically he warns the Israelites who were to be taken captive into Babylon not to suppose that they would have a lasting possession there, but to have hope of returning, and when the captivity was loosened, to flee from there, because it was to come that it would be laid waste by the Medes and Persians.
*Origen:* As our body stands in some place of the earth, so the soul, according to its state, is said to be in some place of the earth. Our body is either in Egypt or in Babylon or in Palestine or in Syria or wherever; and likewise the soul, and the diversity of places is distinguished according to the quality of life. For it is in Babylon when it is confounded and troubled, and, peace having been forsaken, endures the wars of the passions. To such souls it is said: “Flee ye from the midst of Babylon, and let every one save his own life”; for while it is in Babylon it cannot be saved. But he who there remembers Jerusalem groans and says: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?” For it is impossible for one set in Babylon to sing to God with instruments; the instruments of God’s hymns are idle there; whence: “On the willows in the midst thereof we hung up our instruments.” Our instruments are hung up while we are in Babylon, on the willows of its rivers. But if we come to Jerusalem, to the place of vision and peace, we shall play instruments, sing psalms, play the harp, and always praise God. And as the soul of the sinner is in Babylon, so the soul of the just is in Judea; but according to the measure of faith and life, they are separated in Judea itself into places differing among themselves. For one is in Dan, which is in the farthest part of Judea, or in the higher places, somewhat better, or in the middle borders of Judea, or around Jerusalem. But the most blessed of all is he who stands in the midst of Jerusalem. But he who is a sinner and weighed down by exceeding crimes is in Babylon; he who has not yet climbed to the summit of sins is in Egypt and dwells in its parts. And as those who are in Judea do not possess equal places (for one is in Dan, another in Nephthali, another in the borders of Gad), so in Egypt one dwells in Taphnis, another in Memphis, another in Syene, another in Bubastis.
50.9:
**“For behold I raise up, and will bring against Babylon an assembly of great nations”** — of demons.
**“from the land of the north”** — for every evil comes from the north.
**“and they shall be prepared against her, and from thence”** — openly, because then the hidden things of hearts will be made manifest.
**“she shall be taken: their arrows”** — punishment imposed and unexpected.
50.11:
**“Because”** — the cause why they suffer these things.
**“you rejoice”** — in the destruction of the Jews.
**“and speak great things, pillaging my inheritance”** — Israel.
**“because you are spread abroad as calves”** — frisking, namely in devouring it, like a calf upon the grass, mocking the captives with bellowing like bulls.
50.12:
**“Your mother is confounded”** — as if you will not rejoice for long.
**“Behold she shall be the last”** — Tropologically. At the end of the world, or at each one’s death, all the glory and pride of the Chaldeans and the confusion of the world will depart from us, and so all things will be overturned as God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrha, and there will be no further state of pleasure or of the world.
**“and she that bore you is made even with the dust: behold she shall be the last among the nations, a wilderness unpassable, and dry”** — Confounded is, etc. Isaias says similar things: “And that Babylon, glorious among kingdoms, the famous pride of the Chaldeans, shall be overthrown, as the Lord overthrew Sodom,” etc.
50.13:
**“Because of the wrath of the Lord it shall not be inhabited”** — because for her the famous cities of the Persians, Seleucia and Ctesiphon, were made.
**“but shall be wholly desolate: every one that shall pass by Babylon, shall be astonished”** — because so great a power has been reduced to nothing.
50.15:
**“Shout against her, she hath everywhere given her hand”** — to kill her.
**“As she hath done, so do to her”** — That is: as she through Nabuchodonosor laid waste the nations round about, so render to her the recompense.
50.16:
**“Destroy the sower out of Babylon, and him that holdeth the sickle in the time of harvest: for fear of the sword of the dove every man”**
• that is, a helper.
• Isaias, the same, and in the same words.
**“shall return to his people”** — Babylon having been taken.
**“For fear of the sword”** — The dove is called foolish because it feeds other people’s young; so Nabuchodonosor, by oppressing and cherishing others. Also he calls Nabuchodonosor a dove, not for simplicity but for the folly of pride.
50.17:
**“Israel is a scattered flock, the lions have driven him away: first the king of Assyria devoured him”** — who overthrew Jerusalem and set fire to the temple
**“and last this Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon hath broken his bones”** — The lions have driven him away, etc. Tiglath-pileser, who carried a great part of the Jews over to the Assyrians, and Sennacherib, who led the ten tribes into the mountains of the Medes, are called these lions.
50.18:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts the God of Israel: Behold I will visit”** — through Cyrus and Darius
**“the king of Babylon”** — Belshazzar, who reigned last in Babylon
**“and his land, as I have visited the king of Assyria”** — Sennacherib, when, that is, the angel of the Lord struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrians
**“Behold I will visit”** — The Lord visited the king of Babylon, that is, of confusion, as he visited the king of Assur, which is interpreted walking or directing, when he destroyed the devil, the king of confusion and ruler of these darknesses, namely antichrist, and all the persecutors of the Church who direct the arms of wickedness against the saints of God and shed innocent blood, and the heretics who direct the darts of wrong doctrine to kill the souls of the simple. For at the end of the world the devil, who seduced the nations, will be cast into the pool of fire and brimstone, and the beast, that is antichrist, and the false prophets, that is the heretics. But the saints will reign with Christ for ever, and their soul will be filled with all good things. Then “the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and there shall be none: and the sin of Juda, and there shall none be found.” For then the Lord will bind up the wound of his people and heal their bruises, and “God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes: and death shall be no more, nor mourning,” but a new people in the new city will rejoice for ever.
50.19:
**“And I will bring Israel again to his habitation”** — with Cyrus permitting it, nearly fifty thousand went out into Judea
**“he shall feed on Carmel, and Bason, and his soul shall be satisfied in mount Ephraim, and Galaad”** — so that there would be no more death or mourning, but a new people
50.20:
**“In those days, and at that time, saith the Lord, the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and there shall be none: and the sin of Juda, and there shall none be found: for I will be merciful to them”** — Whence: “But the grace of God, life everlasting.”
**“whom I shall leave”** — the others being cast off
50.21:
**“against the land”** — Babylon
**“of the rulers”** — of the Chaldeans
**“Go up”** — the army of the Medes and Persians
**“and punish the inhabitants thereof, waste, and destroy”** — so that the posterity of Babylon may perish utterly
**“and destroy all behind them, saith the Lord: and do according to all that I have commanded thee”** — Go up against the land of the rulers, etc. Mystically the preachers of Christ are commanded to strive to overthrow the kingdom of the devil and his wicked works and worst counsels, that they may put to death all the sinners of the land, and cut off from the city of the Lord all the workers of iniquity.
50.22: **“A noise of war in the land, and a great destruction.”** — at the destruction of Babylon, joy and exultation of many
50.23:
**“How is the hammer of the whole earth broken, and destroyed!”** — Babylon and her kings, who had crushed many nations
**“how is Babylon turned into a desert among the nations!”** — How is the hammer broken, etc. The hammer of the whole earth is the devil; but there is one who cares nothing for the hammer of the whole earth, namely a man standing upon walls of adamant, and in his hand is adamant. The story relates that adamant is stronger than every striking hammer, unbruised and unconquered, persevering, although the devil the hammer stands over it and the dragon is set upon it, as though it were untameable within; nothing so much does the perfect adamant suffer, standing in the hand of the Lord and in his sight. So there are two things contrary to the just adamant, the hammer and the anvil; whence it is said in the Proverb of those who are pressed by anxieties: they are between the hammer and the anvil. But the just man cares nothing for the hammer and the anvil, whose virtue shines the more the more he is struck. But Moses could not break the hammer of the whole earth, nor Abraham before him, nor Josue after him, nor any of the prophets; but Christ broke it, and the prophet, wondering at this, says: “How is the hammer of the whole earth broken!” First broken, then destroyed. When the devil said, “All these will I give thee, if falling down thou wilt adore me,” etc., he did not destroy it but only broke it, when he departed from him for a time; and afterwards he came, and then he was also destroyed. It is broken by each one of us when we are brought by the Lord into the Church and advance in faith. But it is destroyed and ground small when we come to perfection.
**“How is Babylon turned”** — The captivity of Babylon is understood when no confusion remains in us. “Thou art found and caught, because thou hast stood against the Lord.” But did Babylon alone resist, and not rather all nations, when, having forsaken the Creator, they worshipped idols? Or he says figuratively that every soul contrary to Jerusalem, that is, to the vision of peace, is Babylon; whence the saints were in Jerusalem, sinners in Babylon, and if the inhabitants of Jerusalem sinned they were sent into Babylon, and repenting they returned into Jerusalem. Babylon, then, is taken and does not know it; for “it is not subject to the law of God, neither can it be”; and Babylon is found and caught, because it hath stood against the Lord.
50.25:
**“The Lord hath opened his armoury”** — the Church
**“and hath brought forth the weapons of his wrath”** — sinners
**“for the Lord the God of hosts hath a work to be done in the land of the Chaldeans”**
• that is, of those who ascribe to the stars what happens on earth
• The Lord hath opened, etc. Origen. Another edition: Open ye her storehouses, and search her as a cave, and destroy her, that there be no remains of her; dry up all her fruits, that they may go down to the slaughter. Woe to them, for their day is come, the time of their vengeance; as the apostle says, he endured “with much patience vessels of wrath, fitted for destruction, that he might shew the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy,” etc.
• The same: He hath opened the treasure, etc. In the treasures of the Lord are vessels of wrath; outside the treasure are sinning vessels, which are not vessels of wrath but lesser ones. For they are servants who know not the will of the Lord and do it not. But he who enters the Church is either a vessel of wrath or of mercy; he who is outside is neither of mercy nor of wrath. I therefore seek another name for it: “The Lord of hosts,” it says, “hath a work to be done in the land of the Chaldeans.” According to different understandings, an earthly place is spoken of or named in many ways; and as Christ, by a different reckoning, has many names, though in the underlying subject he is one, yet various in his powers, so, by reason of the malice of the human race, earthly business, though one in the underlying subject, is yet very many by the diversity of understanding. For Christ is one underlying subject, but in one sense a physician, whence: “They that are well have no need of a physician,” etc.; in another a shepherd, because he is over the irrational; in another a king, because he rules the rational; in another the true vine, because men grafted into him bear abundant fruit; and the like. Since, then, in Christ there are very many understandings of different names and the underlying subject is one, so earthly business is one in the underlying subject but, according to understanding, very many. Often, too, in allegorizing, we have said that Babylon is earthly business, which is always confused with vices, afflicting Egypt; and Chaldea, because many consecrate to the stars what is done on earth and assert that it happens by their nod. Everyone, then, who thinks that the stars make men lustful, adulterers, chaste, or the like, is in the land of the Chaldeans. God therefore threatens especially those who are in the land of the Chaldeans; but advancing Abraham to better things, he says: I am he who brings thee out from the land of the Chaldeans. God is able to bring us out of the land of the Chaldeans, and let us believe that no other dispenses our life according to the qualities of merits. The work of the Lord of hosts, then, is in the land of the Chaldeans, because his times are come: open her storehouses, that is, the teachings of nativities; search her as a cave, and destroy her. He who rejects the reckonings of birthdays, who uses the word of truth against them, who shows that what the astrologers owe is false, who teaches that the judgments of God are unsearchable and cannot be comprehended by all, who asserts that the stars are not the cause of what happens upon earth, especially of what befalls Christians, carries out the command of the Lord.
50.26:
**“Come ye against her from the uttermost borders”** — the destroyers of spiritual Babylon
**“open that they may go forth”** — preachers
**“that shall tread her down: take the stones out of the way”** — of Babylon
**“the stones, and make heaps, and destroy her”** — that is, the vices of confusion
**“and let nothing of her be left”** — of vices
50.27: **“Destroy all her valiant men”** — the subtler and stronger vices
50.28:
**“The voice of them that flee”**
• he prophesies of those who have left their ancestral customs and the laws of the Gentiles
• Origen. Would that this were our voice, O catechumens, the voice of those who flee out of Babylon, that is, who flee vices and sins. For the voice of those who flee and are saved again: it is not enough to flee from the land of Babylon, but to be saved again from the land of Babylon, to declare in Sion the revenge of the Lord our God; that fleeing from the land of Babylon you may come from Sion of the watchers to the Church of God, to declare in Sion, that is, in the Church, the revenge from the Lord our God. Declare the revenge of his people against Babylon, to many, to everyone that bendeth the bow. For many are in Babylon, few in Jerusalem. For he did not say: Your father loved you because you were many; for you are few among all nations. Declare against Babylon, to many, to everyone that bendeth the bow, that none of her may be saved. Destroy, kill all things, that there be none saved of the Babylonian seed. According to all that she hath done, do ye to her. While you have in you wicked thoughts that resist piety and faith, you have Babylonians in you; but take revenge: kill all the sinners of the earth who are in you, and all the Babylonians, that being cleansed you may be able to pass over into Jerusalem, the city of God.
**“and of them”** — of the saved
50.30:
**“Therefore shall her young men fall”** — the strong
**“in her streets: and all her men”** — the robust
**“her men of war”**
• fighting against the Church
• which lead to death, for they will not seize the narrow way which leads to life
**“shall hold their peace in that day”** — of the visitation of the Lord, because after the judgment it will have no power to fight and to harm.
50.31:
**“Behold I come against thee, O proud one”** — king of Babylon.
**“saith the Lord the God of hosts: for thy day is come, the time of thy visitation.”** — that is, of your captivity and of your people.
**“Behold I come against thee”** — Mystically he proclaims to Antichrist, who shall be lifted up above all that is called God, and to his members, that is, all the wicked, the coming damnation; and that all the fortifications of worldly wisdom and the counsels of the malignant, by which he deceived men, are to be burned up in the fire to come, so that all his machinations and the weapons with which he assailed the Church throughout the world may be devoured by eternal destruction, because they were not afraid to bring false accusation and captivity upon the people of God; whence it follows: The children of Israel suffer false accusation.
50.32:
**“And the proud one shall fall”** — Antichrist.
**“he shall fall down, and there shall be none to lift him up: and I will kindle a fire in his cities”** — in the fortifications of worldly wisdom.
50.35: **“A sword”** — of the Lord, of which it is said: “If I shall whet my sword as the lightning”.
50.37: **“A sword upon their horses, and upon their chariots, and upon all the people that are in the midst of her: and they shall become as women: a sword upon her treasures, and they shall be made a spoil.”** — And they shall become as women, etc. Unwarlike as women, he destroyed them through the Medes and Persians; and all also who dwell in the confusion of the world, and who, relying on worldly wisdom, worship the idols of error instead of the truth, he will condemn in judgment together with the treasures of their teachings and works; and the doctrine of heretics will wither and be dried up, because their synagogue is a land of idols, and they glory in monstrous things, that is, in false fictions.
50.39:
**“Therefore shall dragons dwell there”** — These things are fully explained here in Isaias, historically and tropologically, according to Jerome.
**“with the fig fauns”** — wild men of the woods.
50.41:
**“Behold a people”** — The Persians and Medes.
**“cometh from the north”** — where he dwells.
**“and a great nation, and many kings”** — with Cyrus and Darius.
**“shall rise from the ends of the earth”** — Behold, a people shall come, etc. The history is plain: that an innumerable nation of the Medes and Persians, and many kings, came together with Cyrus and Darius for the destruction of Babylon, where Baltasar, having prepared a banquet, made public for his concubines to drink from the vessels of the temple which Nabuchodonosor had brought from Jerusalem. Therefore he saw a hand writing on the wall his own destruction and that of his kingdom; and when Daniel had explained it, worn out with grief and sadness, he made no preparation to resist, because that same night he was slain, and Darius succeeded to the kingdom.
50.42: **“They shall take the bow and the shield: they are cruel and unmerciful: their voice shall roar like the sea”** — with much noise and crashing.
50.43:
**“The king of Babylon hath heard”** — Belshazzar.
**“the report of them, and his hands are grown feeble”** — with sorrow and sadness.
**“his hands are grown feeble: anguish hath taken hold of him”** — of fear.
50.44:
**“Behold he shall come up like a lion”** — Nabuchodonosor.
**“from the swelling of the Jordan to the strong and beautiful: for I will make him run suddenly upon her: and who shall be the chosen one whom I may appoint over her?”** — as though this was done by my power and my judgment.
**“Behold one shall come up as a lion”** — Rabanus. He seems to signify that Nabuchodonosor, after he had overthrown the kingdom of the Jews like a lion, laid waste Judea and burned Jerusalem and the temple, returned victorious and secure to his own seat in Babylon, and left to his descendants the kingdom in Egypt, safe and whole. But by the dispensation and vengeance of the Lord it was transferred to Cyrus, of whom he says: “who shall be the chosen one whom I may appoint over her?” And to show that this was done not by the power of Cyrus but by the judgment of the Lord, he adds: “for who is like to me?” etc.
50.45:
**“Therefore”** — Hence Isaias: “Thus saith the Lord to my anointed Cyrus, whose right hand I have taken hold of”, etc.
**“Hear ye the counsel of the Lord, which he hath taken against Babylon: and his thoughts which he hath thought against the land of the Chaldeans: surely the little ones of the flocks shall pull them down”** — the Babylonians.
**“the little ones”** — the Medes and Persians, who seemed little and contemptible.
**“of the flocks shall pull them down”** — with the inhabitants.
**“their habitation”**
• Babylon.
• a breaking off, as if he said: do not believe me.

51.2: **“And I will send to Babylon fanners”** — the Medes and Persians.
51.3:
**“Let not him that bendeth”** — and because the bowmen or the mailed men of Babylon will not be able to resist.
**“bend his bow, and let not him go up that is armed with a coat of mail: spare not her young men”** — O Medes and Persians; they will spare neither age nor sex.
51.5:
**“For Israel and Juda have not been forsaken by their God the Lord of hosts: but their land”** — carnal life.
**“For Israel and Juda have not been forsaken”** — Because the Lord sent them for the vengeance of his people, whom he did not chastise by correcting but crushed by raging; whence: “Woe to the Assyrian, the rod of my anger.”
51.6:
**“Flee ye from the midst of Babylon, and let every one save his own life”**
• not yet, that is, the punishment is worthy.
• For he who by keeping silent assents becomes a sharer in the punishment and the guilt, while he still commits crimes and does not atone.
**“upon her iniquity: for it is the time of revenge from the Lord, he will I render unto her”**
• not through ministers but through himself
• Flee from the midst of Babylon, etc. After the plagues of Babylon he turns the exhortation to the Jews historically and to the faithful mystically, that they may flee from the midst of Babylon, that is, of worldly confusion.
*Origen:* Not by degrees, that is, not step by step, but swiftly go out, whoever of you have a soul confused by the passion of various vices; the word is directed to you. It can happen that one is in Babylon, but when he is on the farthest borders he seems in a manner to be outside Babylon. But it is another thing to be in the middle of Babylon, so that the space is equal on every side, and to dwell in its navel, as it were in the middle of the heart of a living creature. As the middle of a living creature is the heart, and Luke calls the heart of the earth the middle of the earth. As it seems to be said in Ezechiel: Tyre set in the heart of the sea; and now sinners ought to flee from the midst of Babylon, that is, from its heart. Flee therefore from the midst of Babylon, that leaving the middle you may begin to be on the borders, not in the middle. For he who is deeply sunk in vices is a dweller in the middle of Babylon; he who little by little leaves evil and turns his nature to better things, and begins not so much to possess virtues as to desire them, flees from the midst of Babylon, yet does not depart. By expounding in this way we must believe that the sacred writings have not even one tittle empty of the wisdom of God. For he who says: “thou shalt not appear empty before me,” much more does he himself speak nothing empty. The prophets, receiving of his fullness, sang what had been taken from the fullness. Therefore the sacred volumes always breathe the spirit of fullness. And there is nothing that does not descend from the fullness of majesty. And they breathe to those who have eyes to see heavenly things, and ears to hear divine things, and nostrils to smell those things which belong to the fullness. First, therefore, one must flee from the midst of Babylon, then each one save his soul. Nor did he say only “save,” but according to another edition, “save again.” Because having once tasted salvation, and falling from it by sin, we came into Babylon. Therefore each one must save his soul again, that he may begin to recover what he lost; whence Peter: “receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls,” etc. But it is in us to flee from Babylon, and in our power, if we will, to raise up again what has fallen.
**“Be not silent”** — Origen. Another edition: “be not cast away in her iniquities,” etc. He who is in the injustice of Babylon and has not done penance, it follows that he be cast out; whence it is said elsewhere: “I have chosen to be an abject in the house of my God,” not cast out. Here, however, he did not put “be not made abject” but “be not cast out.” For to be cast out is one thing, to be made abject another. What is despised is made abject; what is utterly alien to salvation is cast out. Whence: The leaders of my people shall be cast out of the house of their delights, because of their wicked wills. Their portions shall not profit them, because it is the time of his revenge from the Lord. In a wonderful sense he says that punishments are inflicted for the vengeance of him who suffers them. For when one is not avenged, he is left unpunished; whence: “I will not visit upon your daughters when they shall commit fornication.” God therefore does not punish sinners in anger, but it is expedient so to speak. It is a great anger of God not to endure torments. For he who is punished is punished for this, that he may be amended, even if he is corrected by that which is called the wrath of God. Punishment is promised also to the sinning sons of Christ, lest pardon be denied: “If his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments,” etc. See therefore how he is not yet worthy of punishment who still commits criminal wickedness and does not pay for it. For the visitation of God is shown by the usual torments. But as for him who sins and is corrected, I do not know what of punishment may run to him.
**“He will I render”** — The same, etc. God himself does not repay all; there are those to whom he repays through others, either punishing or healing by sorrow; whence: “he sent upon them the fury of his wrath.” Fury and wrath, distress, a sending in through the worst angels; to others perhaps he repays through good angels, as to those who are punished for their crimes. There are times when, the service of ministers set aside, he himself repays, as now to Babylon. When the wounds are slight and the cure ready, the physician sends a servant, sends a disciple, and heals by him. Sometimes he who is healed needs cutting and the knife; yet he does not come himself, but uses as minister one of the disciples who is able to cure. But when the wounds are incurable and there is deep rot in the dead flesh, when he needs neither servants nor disciples but the hands of the master himself, then he himself, with his loins girded, is roused to cut the wound with his hands. Likewise when the sins are lesser, God uses ministers; but when they are graver, then he himself hastens to the repayment.
51.7:
**“a golden cup”** — the adornment of speech
**“Babylon ... in the hand”** — by power
**“of the Lord, that made ... drunk”** — by vices
**“all the earth”** — that is, all who are of the earth
**“of her wine”** — in which is luxury
**“the nations have drunk”** — holding nothing certain
**“and therefore they have staggered”**
• Babylon a golden cup, etc. Babylon is not always a golden cup, nor always in the hand of the Lord. For when she has come to vengeance and been placed in the hand of the Lord, she will be made the earth which is touched upon in Job. Nor is she continually held in the hand of the Lord, but only then when the Lord shall restore to her what she deserves.
• Making all the earth drunk, etc. See all men drunk: we are made drunk by anger and sadness, we are made drunk and go out of our mind by love, concupiscence, vainglory. Observe that all the earth is full of sins, and you will not ask how Babylon made all the earth drunk. For the just man is not in the earth but above the earth, having his conversation in heaven; nor will it be fitting to say to him, “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt go”, but, You are heaven and into heaven you shall go; for he bears the image of the heavenly. The golden cup therefore makes all the earth drunk, that is, we are all made drunk by it as long as we are earth.
*Origen:* A golden cup of Babylon, etc. Nabuchodonosor, wishing to deceive men by the cup of Babylon, did not mix it in a vessel of clay, of iron, of bronze, of tin, or of silver, which surpasses these. He tempered the draught in a golden vessel, so that seeing the beauty of the shining gold you might cling with all your eyes to its appearance, and not consider what it holds within, but seize it and drink unknowing. Understand by the cup of Nabuchodonosor the pestilent words of wicked doctrines: what composition of speech they have, what beauty of eloquence, and you will know how each poet tempered a golden cup and cast in the poison of idolatry and foul speaking, and of those doctrines which kill the soul, and of knowledge falsely so called. But Jesus did the contrary. For knowing the golden cup of the devil, lest anyone coming to the faith should think that the cup of Christ also was such as he had left, and for the likeness of the material should fear error, he took care that this treasure should be held in earthen vessels. Often I have seen a golden cup in the fair adornment of speech, and considering the poisons of its doctrines, I have detected the cup of Babylon.
**“of her wine the nations have drunk”** — The same, etc. As in those who drink bodily wine beyond measure we see the motion of the drunken body, the feet staggering, the head and temples heavy, the mouth loose, and the words broken off with clinging lips, so those who have drunk of the golden cup of Babylon are unsteady in step, weakened in mind, with wavering effort; they hold nothing firm, but are always driven about in confusion, uncertain. The nations have drunk, and therefore they have staggered.
51.8:
**“suddenly”**
• not gradually, not by parts
• because “the day of the Lord shall so come, as a thief in the night.”
**“is fallen, and destroyed”** — in the heart of him to whom Christ has come
**“howl”** — lament
**“for her, take balm”** — that is, the angels, physicians of souls
**“for her pain”** — because no soul is incurable to God
**“if so she may be healed”**
• as if she can be healed if she wills
• as if the fault lies not in the art of the resin
**“Babylon is suddenly fallen”** — Jerome, etc. Because no soul is incurable with God, he gives counsel to those who can have, from the transmigration into Jerusalem and from the testimony, balm for making plasters, that they may take medicines and with all the zeal they can restore Babylon to health. Let us therefore ask the Lord to give us a rational balm, of which we may say: there is a plaster to apply, and oil, and bandages, and applying them let us bind up the wounds of Babylon, that she may be healed and, cured, cease to be what she had been. This is what he says: take balm for her correction, if so she may be healed. Where are the heretics, who introducing certain natures assert that there is a matter past hope which does not receive salvation at all? But God does not despise Babylon; for he commands the physicians to take balm, if so she may be healed. Some of them therefore, taking the balm of Babylon’s correction, did what had been unprepared, hearing that she could receive health; but because she would not be cured, the good physicians make their excuse and say: We have cured Babylon, and she is not healed.
51.9:
**“We would have cured Babylon”** — the voice of physicians answering the Lord
**“but she is not healed”** — because she does not want to obey us
**“let us forsake her”**
• because, that is, the work and expense are lost
• despaired of in her infirmity
**“and let us go every man to his own land”** — one’s own business
**“because her judgment hath reached even to the heavens”** — as fault grows, condemnation grows too
**“and is lifted up to the clouds”** — We have cured Babylon, etc. See lest at some time God command the angels to prepare medicines for your languishing soul, if so it may be healed, and they answer him: We have cured Babylon, showing that your soul is confounded by passion and is not healed. They do not blame the knowledge of the art nor the power of the balm, but you, who would not obey them. The angels of God are physicians under the great Physician, willing to cure our souls of their vices; these we ourselves drive away when we do not acquiesce in their counsels; seeing that they are losing their labour, they say to one another: Let us forsake her, etc., as if to say: a medicine was handed to us by God that we might cure the human soul; we have applied helps and medicines; she is stubborn, she will not observe what we say; our zeal is not followed by effect; let us go every man to his own land, that is, to his own domestic and nearer business. Beware when a physician or an angel of God, or he to whom the care of the word is entrusted for the medicines of salvation, forsakes you; for if they forsake you and say, Let us go every man to his own land, because “her judgment hath reached even to the heavens,” it is plain that the departure of the physician is your condemnation, beyond remedy, since you are unwilling to be cured. So it will befall you as it befalls those who are despaired of by physicians, and, indulging the pleasure of the disease, are plunged into worse. Often a prudent physician comes to the sick man and, as far as the art allows, does not cease his diligence of medicine; but if the sickness is so great that it resists the cure, or the sick man through impatience of pain does the contrary of what is ordered, the physician despairing leaves him, lest he expire under his hands and he seem guilty of his death. Let us not therefore die in the hands of the holy angels, lest they forsake us in despair and say: there is no plaster to apply, neither oil nor bandage, because her judgment has reached to heaven, is lifted up even to the stars. He who has a small sin does not carry his judgment up to heaven and the stars, for it is small and lowly. But he who grows in wickedness grows also in judgment, and together with the vices the punishment is increased. And because he sins so much that his judgment is lifted up to heaven, and through his impiety, resisting God, he ascends to the heights, God brings forth his judgment to humble what has been exalted.
51.10:
**“The Lord hath brought forth”** — against Babylon
**“our justices: Come, and let us declare”** — the voice of angels or of preachers, who, seeing the wound of Babylon incurable, exhort themselves, saying: “Come, and let us declare.”
**“in Sion”** — The Church, which alone attains to the contemplation of God with the angels
**“the work”** — that is, virtues and miracles
51.11:
**“Sharpen the arrows, fill the quivers, the Lord hath raised up the spirit of the kings of the Medes: and his mind is against Babylon to destroy it, because it is the vengeance of the Lord”** — for his people
**“the vengeance of his temple”** — that the Babylonians set it on fire
51.12:
**“Upon the walls of Babylon set up the standard, strengthen the watch”** — that no one may escape
**“set up the watchmen, prepare the ambushes: for the Lord hath both purposed, and done all that he spoke”** — through the prophets
51.13:
**“that”** — O Babylon.
**“dwellest upon many waters”** — because the Euphrates flows through its midst, or it typically signifies the multitude of peoples.
51.14:
**“hath sworn”** — firmly decided.
**“The Lord of hosts hath sworn by himself”** — with all his affection.
**“I will fill thee with men as with locusts”** — because countless nations gathered for its destruction.
**“and they shall lift up a joyful shout against thee”** — a triumphal song.
**“a joyful shout”** — by the enemies, for the victory obtained.
51.15:
**“He that made the earth by his power”** — the Son, who is the power and wisdom of the Father; for all things were made through him, etc.
**“that hath prepared the world by his wisdom, and stretched out the heavens by his understanding”** — because he made all heavenly things.
51.16:
**“When he uttereth his voice the waters are multiplied”** — of the preaching of doctrine.
**“in the air”** — heavenly.
**“he lifteth up the clouds”** — to the heights of preaching.
**“from the ends of the earth”** — from a humble purpose.
**“he hath turned lightning into rain: and hath brought forth the wind out of his treasures”**
• namely, whence spiritual riches can come forth.
• Lightnings into rain, etc. Preachers of the prophets are lightnings when they strike the enemies, and rains when they wash the devout from sins and pour forth the rain of salvation; whence spiritual fruits sprout and grow together into a ripe harvest.
• And he bringeth forth the winds, etc. The winds are the apostles, whose preaching runs through the world like a most swift wind; of whom it is said elsewhere: he made his arrows for them that burn. For wings are attributed to the winds themselves because of the swiftness of their running about; whence, he flew upon the wings of the winds.
**“He lifteth up the clouds”** — That is, preachers who defend us from the heat of the coming judgment with the rain of their eloquence when they set forth the things to come.
51.17:
**“Every man is become foolish”** — an idolater or a heretic or a schismatic.
**“by his knowledge”** — of the figment.
**“every founder is confounded by his idol”** — of idolaters, or of errors and of perverse doctrines.
**“because”** — that is, Israel is not such a worshipper of the one God; for although very many have erred, many nevertheless remained in the faith and therefore were freed.
**“what he hath cast is a lie”** — of the figment.
**“and there is no breath in them”**
• Every man is become foolish, etc. Rightly after the overthrow of Babylon he rebukes the makers of idols, who through the folly of the human mind make vain works, worthy of laughter, because there is neither breath in them nor voice nor any efficacy; whence they can deliver neither themselves nor their worshippers in the day of visitation.
• Confounded, etc. Rabanus. Having shown the overthrow of Babylon, the prophet returns to the author of so great a judgment, because there is no power except from God, who rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he wills.
51.18: **“They are vain works, and worthy to be laughed at, in the time of their visitation”** — of the general judgment.
51.19:
**“The portion of Jacob is not like them”** — doctrine, either prophetic or apostolic.
**“for he that made all things he it is”** — alone the unchangeable creator of all.
**“and Israel”** — the Church.
51.20:
**“Thou dashest together for me the weapons of war”** — warlike weapons or warriors.
**“and with thee I will dash nations together”** — by a just judge repaying each according to what he has done; as in the future each one will receive according to his works.
51.22:
**“and with thee I will break in pieces man and woman”** — both sexes.
**“and with thee I will break in pieces the old man and the child, and with thee I will break in pieces the young man and the virgin”** — any age.
51.25:
**“Behold I come against thee, thou destroying mountain”** — of pride
**“saith the Lord, which corruptest the whole earth”** — earthly men given over to all vices
**“and I will stretch out my hand”** — of vengeance
**“upon thee, and will roll thee”** — I will separate
**“down from the rocks”** — firm in faith
**“and will make thee a burnt mountain”**
• eternal, where you will pay the penalties of pride
• Behold I come against thee, etc. The destroying mountain is Nabuchodonosor and the kingdom of the Chaldeans, or the devil, who elsewhere is called a mountain of darkness because of the darkness of error.
• And I will make thee a burnt mountain, etc. To this mountain belong the Jews, heretics, blasphemers, and all the impious who persist in malice and are not converted, so that they become living stones in the building of God.
51.26: **“And they shall not take of thee a stone for the corner”** — the corner, that is, the foundation of the heavenly building
51.27:
**“Set ye up”** — the voice of the prophet
**“a standard”** — banners, warlike arms
**“Set ye up a standard in the land: sound with the trumpet among the nations: prepare the nations against her: call together against her the kings of Ararat”** — of Armenia
51.28: **“Prepare ye”** — because they will fill up the knowledge of God, the just will of him who repays retribution
51.30:
**“The valiant men of Babylon have forborne to fight, they have dwelt in holds: their strength hath failed, and they are become as women”** — unwarlike
**“her dwelling places are burnt, her bars are broken”**
• fortifications
• They have forborne, etc. When Cyrus and Darius came, the strength of Babylon and of its princes failed.
51.31:
**“One running post shall meet another”** — to the captured city
**“and messenger shall meet messenger: to tell the king of Babylon”** — Balthasar
51.32:
**“And that the fords”** — of the Euphrates
**“are taken”** — by the enemies
**“and the marshes are burnt with fire, and the men”** — the Babylonians
**“of war are affrighted”** — stupefied
51.33: **“The daughter of Babylon is like a threshingfloor”** — The daughter of Babylon is like a threshingfloor. The people of Babylon was so when, through the power of its kingdom and abundance of riches, it threshed and ground down the nations; but the time of its harvest comes, when it is forced to receive what it has done; of which it is said consequently in the person of the Jewish people: The king of Babylon hath eaten me up and devoured me, etc.
51.36:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord: Behold I will judge thy cause, and will take vengeance for thee, and I will make her sea desolate”** — the multitude of inhabitants; for above, the multitude of Egypt was compared to the sea
**“and will dry up her spring”** — that is, luxury
**“And I will make her sea desolate”** — And I will make her sea desolate, etc. Mystically. The sea of this world signifies turbulence, which the Lord makes desolate. For he will make its luxury cease, and the wicked will be scattered, who served the confusion of errors and vices.
51.37:
**“And Babylon shall be reduced to heaps”** — of sand
**“a dwelling place for dragons”** — of demons
**“an astonishment”** — of those wondering at and seeing its destruction
51.38:
**“They shall roar together like lions”** — greater demons
**“They shall roar”** — the leaders of the Chaldeans
**“they shall shake their manes like young lions”** — the lesser ones
51.39:
**“In their heat”** — the heat of tribulations
**“I will set them drink: and I will make them drunk”** — the cup of wrath
**“that they may slumber, and sleep an everlasting sleep”** — the sleep of eternal death
51.40:
**“I will bring them down”** — to be slain by the sword of the Lord
**“like lambs to the slaughter, and like rams”** — the leaders of Babylon
**“with kids”** — to sinful peoples
51.41:
**“How is Sesach taken”**
• Babylon
• Sesach is interpreted “the linen of a sack” or “the hand of a sack,” as Babylon is interpreted “confusion.” Sesach, then, is taken, and Babylon is made an astonishment, because idolaters and those who serve various vices will be overwhelmed by the waves of the future judgment, and, repenting too late, with Bel, which is interpreted “age,” that is, with the ancient enemy, will suffer perpetual confusion in hell; whence the faithful are warned to go out from their company, lest they perish with them: “Go out,” etc.
51.45:
**“Go out of the midst of her, my people”** — the faithful
**“that every man may save his life from the fierce wrath”** — that is to come
**“Go out of the midst of her”** — Let him who wishes to save his soul flee the fellowship of the lost, and fear the word of the Lord foretelling the vengeance of sinners, which is preached daily in the Church and heard in the holy scriptures, year after year bearing witness that the judge will say to those who shall be on his left hand: “Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire,” etc. For we ought not to grow soft in the desires of the flesh and be slothful in good, but be diligent in meditation on his law and in the exercise of virtues.
51.46:
**“And lest your hearts faint”** — by carnal desires
**“and ye fear for the rumour”** — Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire
**“that shall be heard in the land: and a rumour shall come in one year”** — from year to year
**“and after this year another rumour: and iniquity in the land”** — because iniquity will be repaid in the land of the dead
**“and ruler upon ruler”** — that those who were more powerful in sins may suffer greater torments
51.47:
**“Therefore behold the days come”** — of retribution; for he shall judge the world with justice and the people with equity
**“and I will visit”** — the images of error that heretics fashion
**“Babylon and all the land”** — earthly way of life
**“his”** — sending
**“shall be confounded”** — everlasting
**“and all”** — wandering and into error
**“her slain shall fall”** — by the sword of the Lord
**“in the midst of her”** — Therefore behold the days come, etc. He enumerates the plagues that are to come upon Babylon, and upon her nobles, her leaders and magistrates, and all the people, because, slain by various punishments, they will sleep the sleep of eternal death. Mystically he here announces the ruin of the faithless city, which the devil built from the beginning, and through which he has diligently fought against the city of God, because, when the elect of God are delivered, the wicked city will be plunged into eternal punishment; whence John in the Apocalypse: “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen,” etc.; and after a few words: “Go out from her, my people; that you be not partakers of her sins, and that you receive not of her plagues,” etc.
51.48:
**“and shall give praise over Babylon”** — because the plunderer of all nations has been laid waste
**“the heavens and the earth, and all things that are in them, for from the north”** — from which evils blaze up over the earth
51.50:
**“He that”**
• Israelites
• the voice of the prophet
**“have escaped the sword, come away”** — if you wish to be saved
**“stay not”** — in Babylon
**“remember the Lord afar off”** — in a distant land
**“and Jerusalem”** — the city of the great king
**“come into your mind”** — not Babylon, whose destruction is foretold
51.51:
**“We are confounded”**
• the voice of the people
• to the neighbours insulting them as if they were captives
**“because we have heard reproach”** — of the neighbours
**“shame hath covered our faces, because strangers have come upon the sanctuary of the house of the Lord”** — of the temple
51.53: **“If he should mount up”** — by growing proud
51.55: **“because the Lord has laid Babylon waste”** — the city of confusion
51.56: **“because the spoiler is come upon her, that is, upon Babylon”** — the devil
51.57: **“And I will fill”** — the cup of wrath
51.58:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the wall of Babylon”** — any fortification
**“that broad wall shall be utterly broken down, and her high gates shall be burnt with fire, and the labours of the people to nothing, and of the nations in the fire”** — eternal
51.64: **“And thou shalt say: Thus shall Babylon sink, and shall not rise up from the affliction; thus far are the words of Jeremias”** — Thus shall Babylon sink, etc. Historically, Babylon was not sunk in the Euphrates, although it was reduced to a wilderness; but he foretells the eternal destruction of the spiritual Babylon, which will be plunged into the depth of hell with its prince the devil; whence John in the Apocalypse: “A mighty angel took up a stone, as it were a great millstone, and cast it into the sea, saying: With such violence as this shall Babylon be thrown down.”

52.1: **“Sedecias was one and twenty years old”** — The history which relates that Sedechias was taken and Jerusalem laid waste by the Chaldeans is fully contained in the Book of Kings.
52.4: **“And it came to pass in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, the tenth day of the month, that Nabuchodonosor the king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem, and they besieged it, and built forts against it round about”** — And it came to pass in the ninth year, etc. The number nine, less than ten, signifies the imperfection of the law, as eleven signifies transgression. Rightly, then, Nabuchodonosor besieged the city in the ninth year of the reign of Sedecias, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, because when evil pastors know the decalogue and neglect to fulfil it, it must be that the ancient enemy, with his army, surrounds the people committed to them, hemming them in with a fortification of errors and vices. And the famine of the word of God prevails in the city, when the bread of doctrine is not freely dispensed, and the city is broken into, and the men of war flee by night. For when the temptation of the devil has broken through, the guardians of the peoples, who ought to have defended the city with the sword of the word of God, hemmed in by the darkness of ignorance and of sins, flee by night; and seeing the wolf coming, they leave the sheep.
