For this vision is seen in the fifth year of the captivity of Joachim king of Juda, which was also the fifth of Sedecias reigning in Jerusalem; after six years, that is, in the eleventh year of his reign, the city being taken, he was led away to Babylon. To those, then, who dwelt by the river Chobar and had of their own will given themselves up, it is revealed that they did well in obeying God’s decree. For in a short time both the province of Judea and Jerusalem are to be taken. The great cloud, which carries showers and rains over Judea, the fire infolding it shows the punishments to come and the evils of captivity; the brightness round about, God’s judgments laid open.
• Gregory. The whirlwind is the temptation of the mind which shook the Jewish people on every side; it comes from the north, from him who says: “I will sit in the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north.” For he held the mountain of the covenant when he subjected to himself the people who had received the law, and the hearts of the teachers, as the mountain of the covenant, and the great cloud. For the more he blazed against the Lord, the more he deserved to be blinded. For him whom they awaited in the law and the prophets, they denied when they saw him present. And a fire infolding: that is, by fire sometimes the Holy Spirit, sometimes malice is signified. Whence: “I am come to cast fire on the earth.” Of evil it is said: “and now fire devoureth thy adversaries.” Judea, however, wrapped itself in the fire of its own malice. All this from the north, because, led by the cold of its torpor to the darkness of ignorance, it broke out even to the malice of persecution. Whence: “I see a boiling caldron, and the face thereof from the face of the north.” But this fire burned in one place and shone in another. Whence: “brightness was about it.” While persecution is carried on in Judea, the preaching of the apostles is spread abroad in the world, according to that: “because you judge yourselves unworthy, behold we turn to the Gentiles.” Thus from the cruelty of malice that burned the mind of Judea, almighty God scattered light to the Gentiles. The fire that scattered the apostles first exercised itself in the very Redeemer of the human race. Whence it follows: “and out of the midst thereof, as it were the resemblance of amber.” By the resemblance of amber Christ, the mediator of God and men, is signified, because amber is of gold and silver. But when they are mixed, the silver grows in brightness, the gold grows pale from its own shining. So when humanity grew into the glory of majesty, the divinity tempered itself to human eyes from the power of its own brightness. Thus in Christ, as it were, while the gold grows pale the silver shines. Amber, therefore, in the fire: God and man in persecution. In the midst of it, the resemblance of amber, or of fire; for the four living creatures, that is, the evangelists, were made firm in faith by the incarnation of the Lord and afflicted by the fire of persecution.
• Jerome. The Septuagint: a spirit carrying off, or lifting up. Symmachus and Theodotion: a blast and spirit of tempest. Some understand the spirit carrying off or lifting up to be the Holy Spirit, who takes vices away from men, lifts up those who lie fallen, and makes the north wind, the coldest, from which evils blaze forth upon the earth, to withdraw; from whose face in Jeremias a terrible caldron is kindled. The cloud is the person of Christ, who came into Egypt of this world, upon a light cloud, which is more properly said by comparison with the lesser ones, namely the prophets, apostles, and all the saints. Of whom: “thy truth reacheth even to the clouds.” And: “I will command my clouds to rain no rain upon Israel.” And elsewhere: “the cloud is the dust of his feet,” and “clouds and darkness are round about him.” The fire flashing and the brightness round about it, according to that: “our God is a consuming fire.” Whence: “I am come to cast fire on the earth; and what will I, but that it be kindled?” Which, though it brings terror to sinners and punishments to the soul, yet glows with brightness and is full of light and splendour, therefore refining us, that it may bestow happier things on those who are pure and purged.
1.5:
**“And in the midst thereof”** — otherwise: his
**“the likeness”**
• Gregory. It is the fire which is light to believers and punishment to unbelievers
• not by nature
**“four”** — after the fourfold forms
**“living creatures”** — of the evangelists
**“and this was their appearance: there was the likeness of a man”** — of Christ
**“the likeness of a man in them”** — For these holy living creatures would not be holy unless they had the likeness of Christ. Whence the apostle: “Be ye followers of me, as I also am of Christ.”
1.6:
**“Every one had four faces”**
• the knowledge of faith by which they are known by God
• Gregory. For what Matthew thinks of the incarnation of the Lord, Mark, Luke and John think the same. So of all of them. Therefore this whole is in one, which is at once in four.
**“and every one four wings”** — because all together, on the wings of contemplation, raise their eyes to the divinity of Christ
1.7:
**“their feet”**
• the steps of actions
• Gregory. Because faith and contemplation are of no avail without works
**“Their feet were straight feet”** — not bent to crooked things
**“and the sole of their foot was like the sole of”** — that is, strength and discernment are in them; for by oxen are meant preachers. Whence: “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn.”
**“a calf's foot”** — Gregory. because they advance maturely and are strong and discerning, which is signified by the cloven foot
**“and they sparkled”** — Gregory. burning words which go out to the hearers and kindle them, and are subtle and fine, because they burn more with desire than they utter in word
**“like the appearance of glowing brass”**
• Gregory. which is very resonant: “Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth.”
• because preachers burn with desire and heal with the word
1.8:
**“And they had the hands of a man”**
• the active life
• the power of work under the flight of contemplation
**“under their wings”** — contemplative
**“on their four sides: and they had faces, and wings on the four sides”**
• Gregory. Justice, temperance, fortitude, prudence.
• Because in all parts of the world they show what they think of the humanity and of the divinity of the Lord; and while they proclaim that he is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, they fly everywhere on the wing of contemplation.
**“on their four sides”** — Jerome. Because preaching has gone out to the east, west, south and north.
1.9:
**“And the wings of one were joined to the wings of another”** — Gregory. because the power and wisdom of preachers are joined by the peace of charity and concord
**“And were joined”** — Jerome. The gospels are joined to one another, and flying through the whole world they run hither and thither; they are neither separated nor withdraw, but always go forward. The same we can say of the virtues of the soul, and of the flight of the times and the mingling of the elements, which leave the past behind and hasten to what is before. That the times slip away is shown in this short verse: “But meanwhile it flies, irreparable time flies.” And in a lyric poem: “Alas, the fleeting years glide away after me.”
**“They turned not”** — to earthly animals, that is. Whence: “No man putting his hand to the plough”
**“when they went”**
• the way of the mind
• Gregory. To the heavenly things.
**“but every one went straight forward”** — Before us are the eternal things, behind us the temporal. Whence: forgetting those things which are behind, and stretching forth myself to those which are before.
1.10:
**“And as for the likeness of their faces”** — of the first, or principal.
**“the face of a man”** — Matthew, namely, who says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ.”
**“and the face of a lion on the right side of all the four: and the face of an ox”** — Luke, who was a certain priest.
**“on the left side of all the four: and the face of an eagle”** — John, who says: “In the beginning was the Word.”
**“of all the four”**
• For what is said of the four living creatures is referred to all the perfect.
• The likeness of their faces. Some think that the four gospels are signified by the names of these living creatures: Matthew’s, who described the man, saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham”; the face of the lion is Mark’s, who says: “The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare ye the way of the Lord”; that of the calf refers to the gospel of Luke, who begins from the priesthood of Zacharias; that of the eagle to John, who, flying to the heights, says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God,” etc. Others, who follow the foolish wisdom of the philosophers, suspect that the two hemispheres are in the two cherubim of the temple, and that we and the antipodes are men as it were lying on our backs and falling. Many, following Plato, refer the rationality of the soul, the irascibility and the concupiscence, which he calls the logikon, the thymikon and the epithymetikon, to the man, the lion and the calf: reason, thought, mind and counsel, and the same power and wisdom, they place in the citadel of the brain; but fierceness, wrath and violence in the lion, which consists in the gall; lust, wantonness and desire of all pleasures in the liver, that is, in the calf, which clings to the works of the earth. Above these and apart from these three they place a fourth, which the Greeks call synderesis, the spark of conscience, which was not extinguished even in Cain, when, as if overcome by pleasures or by fury, and deceived at times by the very semblance of reason, we feel that we sin; this they properly assign to the eagle, which does not mix itself with the three but corrects their very errors; this is the spirit that “asketh for us with unspeakable groanings.” “For what man knoweth the things of a man, but the spirit of a man that is in him?” Whence Paul: “Your whole spirit, and soul, and body, [may be preserved] blameless,” etc. Yet this conscience, as is said in Proverbs: “The wicked man, when he is come into the depth of sins, contemneth,” we often see cast down headlong and lose its place, when some sin without shame, to whom it is deservedly said: “Thou hast had a harlot’s forehead, thou wouldst not blush.” This four-horse chariot God rules as a charioteer, and compels it, running in ordered steps, to obey his command.
*Jerome:* There are some who think that by this the four elements are shown in one man, who is called the lesser world according to the opinion of Hippocrates: namely fire, water, air, earth; how these are mingled with one another, and, though each is joined to the others, seem to touch one another, and in one person have four kinds and shapes of living and lifeless things, is not the business of this work. The four wheels also, rising from earthly things to the heights, joined to each of the four-formed living creatures, they reckon to be either the mixture of the same elements, or the circle of the four seasons, which is made up of three months each; and the year, “turning,” is so called from the fact that it is always turning and returns into itself; whence spring, summer, autumn, winter, and month and year. And what is said, “there was a wheel in the midst of a wheel,” they think signifies year within year. Whence another poet: “and the year turns upon itself by its own tracks.” They say also that the likeness of the firmament, which is compared to crystal, is the heaven we look upon, beneath which the four living creatures revolve and pass. The throne of sapphire colour, and the man sitting above it, in human likeness, of him who by his command rules all things and has all things under his feet. Whence at the end also it is said: “This was the vision like to the glory of God”; by which, as by a kind of picture and image, they say the wisdom of God is shown. The feet straight, and the sole of the foot like the sole of a calf’s foot, or round, which signifies that all earthly things fly up to the heavenly, and, all angles being cut off, follow roundness, which is the most beautiful of all figures; the sparks glowing show that all things are full of light; the hands of a man under the wings, of the man himself as also of the lion and the calf and the eagle, so that reason, namely, sustains all things and lifts them from the ground to heaven; this we can refer both to the gospels and to all that we have set above. Others say that the four passions of joy, sickness, desire and fear, of which two are present and two future, are signified by the four living creatures. Whence Virgil: “Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice.” These ought to be ruled by reason and the power of God; over these passions are set four virtues, prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, by whose judgment they are governed. Others think that the order of the camp of the twelve tribes in the wilderness is described, to the east and west and north and south, bound to one another both by charity and by blood; and that this is the wheel in the midst of a wheel, that they are led by the spirit, covered by the cloud in the desert, and lighted by the pillar of fire in the night, and do not return into Egypt but always hasten to go to the promised land. They say that the likeness of electrum is the holy of holies, and refer the face of a man to all Israel, that of the lion to the royal tribe of Juda, that of the calf to the priestly tribe, that is, Levi; outside is the eagle, namely the vengeance of God, looking on all things from heaven, which is ready to tear the sinner. Whence Osee: “As an eagle upon the house of the Lord,” that is, the temple. Over a chariot of this kind the Lord sits like a charioteer; he commands what is to be done, forbids what is to be avoided. This, as they think, is said to the people that is in Babylon, who, if it shall bow its neck to God and obey his reins, will by his help recover the land it lost.
**“The face of a man and the face of a lion”** — Gregory. Matthew, who says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ”; Mark, who begins thus: “The voice of one crying in the desert.” Christ himself also, whose members these are, was born as a man, suffered as a calf, rose again as a lion, ascended as an eagle. Each perfect man also is a man in reason, a calf in sacrifice, a lion in fortitude, an eagle in contemplation. For what is said of the four living creatures is referred back to all the perfect.
*Jerome:* The faces: he means the beginnings of the gospels, of which the man and the lion, that is, the birth of Christ and prophecy, hold the right side. But the ox, that is, of the victims and the priesthood of the Jews, is on the left, which, abolished, passes into the spiritual priesthood, of which: “Thou art a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedech.” So that all things cling to one another and are reckoned as one body. But the eagle, which is above both the birth and prophecy (which is fulfilled by the Lord’s coming) and above the priesthood that has passed away, and is outside all these, tells of the spiritual birth, how the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Whence: “Who shall declare his generation?” These are, according to the Apocalypse, the four living creatures full of eyes before and behind: the first like a lion, the second like a calf, the third like a man, the fourth like a flying eagle.
*Gregory:* The man and the lion on the right, because Christ’s birth and resurrection are a joy common to all; the ox on the left, because Christ’s death was sad for the apostles. Whence: “you shall be made sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy.” For on the right we have joyful things, on the left sad things; for we call the left what we reckon adverse. Rightly the eagle is described not as alongside but as above, because it signifies the ascension, and proclaims the Word of the Father, the Lord, with the Father. And since there are four living creatures, the eagle is over all, because John, by what he saw in the beginning, passed beyond even himself.
1.11:
**“And their faces, and their wings were stretched upward”** — Gregory. Because the intention and contemplation of the saints stretches above itself, that it may attain the heavenly good.
**“two wings of every one were joined”** — namely, stretched out.
**“and two covered their bodies”**
• Gregory. Fear and penitence, which hide past evils from the eyes of almighty God.
• Whence the Apostle: “We know in part and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away.”
**“Stretched upward”** — Jerome. We have said above that the gospels, the times, all rational creatures and the four virtues are joined to one another, so that whoever lacks one lacks all. That two wings are stretched out and raise themselves on high signifies the heavenly preaching and that all things tend to the majesty of God; two cover the bodies, because human knowledge is shut out and no perfect sight is given.
**“Two wings”** — Two wings. Namely love and hope of the saints, which lift every winged creature to God; which are well joined, for they love what they hope for, and they hope for what they love.
1.12:
**“And every one of them went straight forward”** — always present to itself, always judging what is good and what is evil, in which it grows and in which it decreases.
**“whither the impulse was to go”** — Gregory. In evils is the impulse of the flesh.
**“spirit”** — which is toward charity and the other virtues.
**“thither they went”** — following the spirit.
**“and they turned not”** — toward evils. But he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved.
**“when they went”** — toward the good.
**“And every one”** — Jerome. He who holds the plough-handle should not look back; let him not imitate Lot’s wife, lest he perish like Heli, who offended God by the vice of his sons. How much more then the living creatures, which are full of light and winged, which follow the Holy Spirit going before them, which so fly through the world and lift themselves to the heights that they protect their bodies with the wings of history and do not give us a fuller sight. That it is said a second time, “they turned not when they went,” signifies the mystery of both testaments: that in the four living creatures both the law and the gospel hasten to things to come and never move backward.
1.13:
**“And as for the likeness of the living creatures, their appearance was like that of burning coals of fire”** — If you touch a coal, you will be kindled; and with the holy you will be holy.
**“and like the appearance of lamps”** — Gregory. They spread a good reputation far and wide for the light of others.
**“This was the vision running to and fro in the midst of the living creatures”** — that is, if you strike the Gospels together in the midst of the letter and the lowly history, you will see the sacraments of the Holy Spirit.
**“a bright fire”** — Of which: “I am come to cast fire on the earth.”
**“and lightning going forth from the fire”** — the brightness of the saints.
**“fire”** — Of which: “He will sanctify them in the burning fire”; and elsewhere: “Coals of fire shall fall upon them”; and elsewhere: “with coals that destroy”; and in another place, having coals of fire: “You shall sit upon them; these shall be to you for a help.”
**“And lightning going forth from the fire”** — Whatever creature we look upon, it flashes forth the knowledge of God, while the Creator manifests himself in creatures.
1.14:
**“And the living creatures ran”**
• Gregory. Into contemplation.
• As the sky flashes with frequent fires, and lightnings in the blink of an eye and a moment run to and fro and return, and do not lose their source and, as it were, the fountain and matter of fire, so these living creatures, when they go on with unhindered foot, hasten to their own; but if they see anything set against their effort, they do not so much return as draw themselves together by stretching upward, about to give the light which they had hidden a little, so as to give food to their fellow servants in due time, lest they give the holy to dogs, nor pearls to swine. Whence: “I gave you milk to drink, not meat.”
**“and returned”**
• not being able to stay there long.
• to action.
**“like flashes of lightning”** — because through them, as they come down from contemplation, the heavenly light is sprinkled upon us.
1.15:
**“Now as I beheld the living creatures, there appeared upon the earth by the living creatures one wheel with four faces.”** — And as I beheld, etc. Jerome. Thus far the four living creatures, which have four faces, have been described, which follow the spirit and the cloud that was in the midst of the spirit; now a wheel is set by each of the living creatures, not joined to the living creatures that followed them; or one wheel appeared upon the earth, which, divided into four, had as many faces as there were living creatures following, and so great was the likeness of the four wheels following the four living creatures that it would most truly be believed to be one wheel.
**“There appeared one wheel”** — Gregory. Holy Scripture, which is turned toward its hearers on every side amid prosperity and adversity, is one; because only the Old Testament was given to the ancient people, which was turned as a wheel to instruct their ignorance.
**“upon the earth”** — Gregory. To him, namely, it was said: “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt go”; for almighty God has set his law over the hearts of sinners.
1.16:
**“And the appearance of the wheels, and the work of them was like the appearance of the sea”** — because in the Scriptures there are great volumes of meanings, and they are confirmed by the sacrament of baptism
**“and the four had all one likeness: and their appearance and their work was as it were a wheel in the midst of a wheel”**
• that you might not believe one wheel but another joined to another
• The Old Testament did not remain without change while the spiritual understanding lay hidden; when the Redeemer came, he made it be understood spiritually. But the New Testament, even through the pages of the Old Testament, is called eternal, because its meaning is never changed.
**“appearance”** — Septuagint. Tharsis, the eagle of jacinth, which has the likeness of heaven.
**“and the four had all one likeness”** — What the law preaches, the prophets also announce; this the gospel sets forth; this the apostles also preach throughout the world; for divine utterances, even if separated in time, are united in meaning.
**“a wheel in the midst of a wheel”** — Jerome. Because all things heavenly and earthly, and whatever falls under human understanding, are turned on their own wheels: the moon runs through in single months the yearly circle of the sun; the morning star, which is also the evening star, while it shines ruddy toward east and west and tempers the darkness of night with pure light, completes the same course in two years; the other stars also, which are called wandering, and whatever shines in heaven; also the varieties of crops, trees and herbs run on their own wheels through the four seasons; we see nothing that was not before. “Going round about, the spirit goeth forward,” and returns to its circuits; “all the rivers run into the sea,” and it is not filled, because they return to their fountains from the mother abyss. But in the course of the gospels, that is, of the four living creatures, which breathe, live, understand, the world was filled by the apostolic word in a short time. And the wheel in the wheel is the joining of the two testaments, which the ladder of Jacob and the tongs of Isaias and the two-edged sword show; or the gospels cohering with one another, whose course and stature reach to heaven.
*Gregory:* Wheel in wheel. The New Testament in the Old. For what is it that Eve is formed while Adam sleeps, except that the Church is formed while Christ dies; and many things of this kind.
1.17:
**“they went by their four parts”** — through preaching
**“they went”** — Gregory. To the minds of men
**“and they turned not when they went”** — because they follow the living creatures, which always tend toward what is before. Gregory. Because in the New Testament the Old is always held spiritually.
1.18:
**“The wheels had also a size”** — Scripture, namely, which fits one working well. Whence, he who stands, let him see lest he fall.
**“and a height”** — the promise of the heavenly kingdom
**“and a dreadful appearance”**
• on account of its greatness
• the terror of hell
**“and the whole body was full of eyes round about all the four”** — or of the living creatures themselves, through whom the perfect are designated
**“Size also”** — Stature is in the rectitude of command; height is in the loftiness of promise; excessive horror is in the terror of punishment.
**“And the whole body was full of eyes”**
• That the action of the saints is watched on every side.
• Like the Argus that the fables of the poets describe, whom Juno turned into a peacock because of his negligent guarding, so that what is the miracle of the Creator God would be the condemnation of unpunished adultery.
*Gregory:* For there is nothing in the Gospels that does not shine, and with its splendor illumine the world, so that things thought small and vile may gleam with the majesty of the Holy Spirit.
1.19:
**“And when”** — in Scripture
**“went”** — understanding, that is, the saints, so that they may live morally
**“the living creatures went”** — Gregory. To these, of whom one was preaching, one was also rest, and course, and elevation.
**“the wheels also went together by them; and when the living creatures were lifted up”**
• Gregory. Into contemplation.
• because as much as each man advances from Scripture, so much also it advances with him
**“from the earth”** — all together and in agreement
**“were lifted up with them”** — Gregory. With the one understanding.
**“the wheels also”** — of Scripture
1.20:
**“Whithersoever the spirit went”** — of the reader
**“thither as the spirit went the wheels also”** — whom the wheels followed, the intermediate things being passed over; following the living creatures, they tend to the Holy Spirit
**“were lifted up withal”** — with the one ascending
**“and followed it”** — living creatures
**“for the spirit of life was in the wheels”**
• by his own will; for the spirit of life was in the wheels
• whether one seeks the moral sense of the history or the spiritual sense
**“For the spirit of life”**
• Because through the holy words and the gifts of the Spirit we are made alive, so that we may drive away from ourselves works that bring death.
• He says this a second time, lest we think the wheels to be some vessel such as we see in the carts, wagons, chariots and cars; but living creatures, indeed above living creatures, because “the sensual man perceiveth not these things that are of the Spirit of God.”
1.21: **“When those went these went, and when those stood these stood, and when those were lifted up from the earth, the wheels also were lifted up together, and followed them”** — living creatures
1.22:
**“And over the heads of the living creatures was the likeness of the firmament”** — of heaven
**“as the appearance of crystal terrible to behold”** — Gregory. We, placed in this corruption
**“and stretched out”** — because whoever is perfect, weighed down by mortal flesh, cannot understand the blessedness of the angels
**“Firmament”** — Gregory. Of the heavenly powers, who at first, by free will, could slip like water in whichever direction, but others falling because they persevered, are like crystal made from water, because they are now wholly confirmed and cannot be changed.
**“Crystal”** — Which is most pure, and is said to harden from clean and shining waters by exceeding cold, so that water bound by frost is even named by the Greek name crystal. For in the heights above there is an exceptional purity which protects all things, that is, the rational and wise virtues, and the course of the four seasons, and the regions of the world, and the order of all things, and the gospel preaching, which is in part understood and in part veiled.
1.23:
**“And under the firmament were their wings straight, the one toward the other”** — so that the good which one has he bestows on the other; otherwise the wings are not straight
**“every one with two wings”** — by the charity of God and of neighbour
**“covered his body”** — by the wings the virtues, by the body the actions are signified
**“and the other”** — Gregory. For there are two kinds of men: one of the perfect, the other of the little ones.
**“The one toward the other”** — Jerome. In Hebrew, “of woman to sister”: a man covered his body with two wings, and a man covered likewise. Therefore he put the man after the woman in the same person, lest we think there is sex among the heavenly ones.
**“was covered in like manner”** — Each one, etc. Gregory. Here it is shown that they stretched their wings one toward the other and with two wings veiled their own body, because we ought so to bestow on others the virtues we have received that we do not cease to think of our sins with caution and daily to lament them with fear and penance; for with these wings the body is veiled.
1.24:
**“And I heard”** — Gregory. What first, with preaching advancing among few, is done among many.
**“the noise of their wings, like the noise”** — a similar thing in the Apocalypse
**“of many waters”**
• many waters: many peoples
• it proceeds, advancing
**“as it were the voice of the most high God”** — because in the saints he does this
**“when they went”** — by preaching
**“it was like the voice of a multitude, like the noise of an army”** — because, converted, they at once break out into the praise of God
**“and when they stood, their wings were let down”** — by contemplating those things that are of God
**“their wings”** — their virtues grow cheap
**“as it were the voice of the most high”** — Septuagint. The voice of the Word: that all things preached in the world are believed to be through the voice of the Son of God.
**“like the noise of an army”** — Because evil spirits and persecutors rise up against preachers.
**“And when they stood”** — For they could not bear the voice of the Almighty sounding in the heavens. So they stood, and in silence wondered at the power of God, who sat above the firmament, which to those below is like crystal, and to those above like the likeness of a sapphire stone, because all things are shown in likeness, not in truth.
*Gregory:* We who were believed in some way to fly by knowledge, let us lower our wings at the voice coming from above, while we weigh the nature invisible above us and his unsearchable judgments.
*Gregory:* Note the order. Above the living creatures the firmament; above the firmament the throne; above the throne man, because above the saints still living in this flesh are the angels; above them the greater angels; above them Christ.
1.25:
**“For when a voice came”** — sound of understanding
**“from above the firmament”** — transcending the height of the blessedness of the angels, thinking of the very nature of the Creator
**“that was over their heads”** — of the living creatures
**“they stood”** — in contemplation
**“and let down their wings”** — counting their own powers as nothing
1.26:
**“And above the firmament that was over their heads, was the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of the sapphire stone”** — Gregory. In which he sat as a man
**“and upon the likeness of the throne, was a likeness as of the appearance of a man above upon it”** — Gregory. The glory of God the Redeemer
**“as the appearance of the sapphire stone”**
• Gregory. The powers of heaven are compared to this, which has the colour of air, because the spirits over whom almighty God presides on high hold the dignity of a higher place in the heavens.
• Jerome. As in the crystal all the purest and brightest things in the heavens are shown, which illuminate our darkened body, so in the sapphire, that is, the throne of God, and above the firmament, which is heaven, the hidden and secret things of the incomprehensible God are shown, who “made darkness his covert,” and is seen in a cloud and darkness. Whence in Exodus: “And under his feet, as it were a work of sapphire stone.”
**“the likeness of a throne”** — Gregory. Thrones are the angelic powers, which surpass the angels themselves in the dignity of their place. For since angels are called messengers, and angels often come to men to announce certain things, thrones sent as messengers for a mystery are nowhere read of.
**“of a man”** — Jerome. That is, of God the Father. Whence: “A certain man planted a vineyard,” etc.; and elsewhere: “A certain man made a marriage for his son”; not that the Son is excluded from the kingdom, of which Isaias says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and elevated.” Whence John says of this: “These things said Isaias, when he saw his glory, and spoke of him”; but the Son reigns in the Father, for all things of the Father are the Son’s, who is the invisible image of God the Father.
1.27:
**“And I saw as it were the resemblance of amber as the appearance of fire”** — which is the burning of the Holy Spirit
**“within it round about”** — only
**“from his loins and upward”** — Gregory. That is, before the incarnation
**“and from his loins downward”** — Gregory. After the incarnation
**“I saw as it were the resemblance of fire”**
• the brightness of the Holy Spirit, as it were in the whole world
• Gregory. The likeness of fire and of the bow is one. In the fire is the ardour of the Holy Spirit, who is also signified in the bow, in which water and fire appear; and after the coming of the mediator the power of the Holy Spirit shone forth in the human race in this: that the water of baptism washed the elect of God and the fire of divine love kindled them. For as from a mixed colour, like water and fire, a bow is set in the cloud for propitiation, when it is said: “Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.”
**“shining”** — not only inwardly
**“round about”** — of the world
**“as it were the resemblance of amber”** — Gregory. In amber gold and silver are mixed, and through the silver the brightness of the gold is tempered, and through the brightness of the gold the appearance of the silver grows bright; so in our Redeemer the divinity is tempered to our eyes through the humanity, and through the divinity the human nature grows bright.
**“fire within it”** — Gregory. Before the incarnation the fire is within, in Judea only, and does not shine, because the Holy Spirit had filled Judea in many fathers, but it did not come to the knowledge of the Gentiles. But from the loins and downward the fire shines round about, because after the incarnation the grace of the Holy Spirit has been spread far and wide.
*Jerome:* He who sat on the throne is likened, from the loins upward, to amber, which within and without had the look of fire; from the loins downward, a fire shining round about in the circuit of morals. For the things above the loins, where sense and reason dwell, need no fire or flames, but the most precious and purest metal; but the things from the loins downward, where are intercourse and generation, where the incentives of vices are, need the purging of flames, that being purged they may have the likeness of the bow, which is commonly called the rainbow.
**“from his loins”** — Gregory. Through the loins the line of mortality is signified; from the loins of Abraham came the Virgin Mary, in whose womb the Son of God was incarnate. Whence: God was made known in the whole world.
*Gregory:* It is one man who, burning inwardly above the loins, held the angels to his love by his divinity; and below the loins, sending out the brightness of his fire round about, he called men back by his humanity to the desire of his holy ardour.
1.28:
**“As”** — that is, after the terror, a sign of mercy
**“the appearance of the rainbow”** — in which is God’s covenant with men, that the world may not again be lost by a flood
**“when it is in a cloud”** — by the incarnation
**“on a rainy day: this was the appearance of the brightness”** — according to the things the Spirit does in the world, which can be seen
**“round about”**
• Gregory. Of the world
• As the appearance of the bow, etc. The bow is a witness of both judgments: the blue, indeed, in the colour of water, signifies the judgment that was made; the red, in the colour of fire, signifies the judgment yet to be made, because the world, which was first judged by the flood, will be burned by the fire of judgment.
*Jerome:* For it cannot be otherwise. Whence the poet: it draws a thousand various colours from the opposing light. This bow is a sign of clemency and of the covenant of God which he made with men, that when it appears in the cloud we may know that we shall no more perish by a flood. Whence it is clear that after punishments and tortures and the purging of sins there will be the mercy of God, but for those who have deserved to see God reigning. Whence it follows: “this was the appearance of the brightness round about,” that is, round about the throne, either of God or of all the things that were seen.
**“On a rainy day”** — Gregory. When preaching, namely, is poured out, so that believers may come and, the Lord sparing, be called back.
**“of the likeness of the glory of the Lord”**
• not of the glory itself
• For what the glory of the spirit is within, it cannot behold; Isaias is said to have seen the glory of God, but according to what it does in the world.
**“I fell upon my face”** — the awareness of human frailty

2.1:
**“This was the vision”**
• is
• all that has been said before
**“And I saw”** — the likeness
**“And”** — therefore
**“and I heard the voice of one that spoke, and he said to me: Son of man, stand upon thy feet”**
• after penitence, through good works
• because, having fallen from humility, he is raised up by the Lord
**“and I will speak to thee”**
• other than to one lying prostrate, namely, that he may preach, and that one who has already corrected himself may correct others; which he cannot do who still lies in confusion
• And I saw, etc. What then if he had seen the very essence? But note to what misery we have fallen, who cannot bear the good itself, for seeing which we were created.
• Son of man, etc. Gregory. Note the order of speech and of work: first the likeness of glory is seen, that he may cast him down; afterwards he is addressed, that he may raise him up; then he sends the spirit of abundant grace, and lifts him and sets him upon his feet.
• For unless we see something of eternity with the mind, we do not fall down in repentance. But to those lying down the voice of the Lord brings comfort, that we may rise to work; but we do not rise by our own strength, but the spirit fills us and lifts us and sets us upon our feet, that we who lay prone in penance for our fault may afterwards stand upright in good work.
**“And I fell”** — Jerome. Not lifted up by the greatness of the visions. So Paul was buffeted, lest he be exalted by the greatness of the revelations. Abraham also fell on his face after he heard the words of God.
**“upon my face”** — Gregory. The saints are read to fall on their faces, where, that is, they see that in these visible things they humble themselves willingly, that they may be raised up in things invisible. But the wicked fall backward, where, that is, they do not see, because they fall there where they do not know what will follow them.
*Jerome:* To fall on the face is one thing, to fall backward another. Abraham, on hearing of the birth of Isaac, fell on his face and laughed; Heli fell backward; and in the gospel those who had come to seize Jesus “went backward, and fell to the ground.”
*Gregory:* When we behold something of God we fall on our faces, because we blush for the evils we remember having done. For a man falls there where he is put to shame.
**“Stand upon thy feet”** — Gregory. Like to which is: “He brought me out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs, and set my feet upon a rock, and directed my steps, and he put a new canticle into my mouth.”
2.2:
**“and the spirit entered into me”**
• holy
• without whom I could not stand
**“after that he spoke to me, and he set me upon my feet”** — Like: he set my feet upon a rock. We read of no sinner standing; of him it is said, “The step of thy foot shall not be firm.”
**“and I heard him speaking to me”** — Stand upon thy feet, etc. As one lying you cannot hear. It is also said to Moses: “But thou shalt stand with me”; and Daniel says: “And the spirit entered into me after that he spoke to me, and he set me upon my feet.”
*Gregory:* Paul, who was to be a preacher, is first cast down, lies, and hears: “Arise and go into the city, and there it shall be told thee what thou must do.”
**“And the spirit entered into”** — Gregory. He could not otherwise have risen when it was said to him “stand upon thy feet,” because by the grace of almighty God we can indeed strive toward good works, but we cannot fulfil them unless he helps who commands. For it is God, says the apostle, “who worketh in us both to will and to accomplish”; whence: “Without me you can do nothing.” For it must be known that our evils are ours alone, but our good things are both almighty God’s and ours. For by inspiring he goes before us that we may will, by helping he follows after that we may not will in vain. Grace therefore goes before and good will follows, and so the gift of the Almighty becomes our merit; whence Paul: “yet not I, but the grace of God with me,” as if to say: in that I was preceded by the gift of God alone, it is not I; but in that I followed the gift with my will, it is I also. And this I say against Pelagius and Celestinus.
2.3:
**“And saying: Son of man”** — Often to Ezechiel and to David it is said “Son of man”; to each, in the person of him who said “The Son of man hath not where to lay his head,” he comforts the captive people and exhorts them to penance.
**“I send thee to the children of Israel, to the nations”** — as though not the people of God
**“that revolt”** — who have turned back to a wicked work
**“that have revolted from me”** — not only the fathers; as if the impiety of both is equal
**“their fathers have transgressed”** — The Septuagint: provoking me, or turning into bitterness; for God is by nature kind and sweet, and is made bitter by vices
**“my covenant”** — one fault of pride
**“even unto this day”** — continually
**“this”** — the other of obstinacy
**“to the rebellious nations”** — Gregory. As he who withdraws from God in faith is an apostate, so he who returns to a perverse work, even if he has kept the faith. For one cannot profit without the other, unless perhaps works are done in order to receive faith, as Cornelius did.
2.4:
**“and the children”** — the great mercy of God, who sends to such, that no one should despair
**“are children of a hard face, and of an obstinate heart, to whom I send thee”** — the great confidence of the prophet, who does not fear to go to such
**“and thou shalt say”** — authority is given to the person, lest the prophet be despised by such perverse people
**“to them: Thus saith the Lord God”** — not I
**“And the children of a hard”**
• Gregory. The shamelessness of the sons is a grave fault: they do evil and do not blush, nor after the fault return to penance, because they have an untamed heart.
• Whence: “Thy neck is as an iron sinew, and thy forehead brass.” These also are rebuked in what follows for a heart of stone, which the Lord says he will tear out, and will give in its place a heart of flesh, that softened it may receive God’s precepts.
2.5:
**“If so be”** — like in Jeremias: “Perhaps they will hear”; and in the gospel, “Perhaps they will reverence my son”
**“or they”** — sons
**“will hear”** — me
**“and if so be they will forbear”** — from sin
**“for they are a house”** — because God had begun to dwell there through faith
**“a provoking”**
• by vices; me, namely, by nature meek
• through action
**“and they shall know”**
• a gentle guest
• without excuse, or profiting by the preaching heard
**“that there hath been a prophet in the midst of them”** — If so be they at least will hear, etc. Gregory. As if few will hear, or they themselves will perish, since the fathers, namely, were unwilling to repent and died in their guilt.
*Jerome:* God speaks with the feeling of one in doubt, to show man’s free will, lest foreknowledge of good or evil make unchangeable what God knows will be. For it is not because he knows things to come that we must do what he foreknew; but what we shall do by our own will, he, as God, knows beforehand.
2.6:
**“And thou, O son of man”** — as if you should feign humility out of fear, since you have to speak not only to the people but also to the elders
**“fear not”** — although perverse
**“them”**
• namely, bringing evils
• the freedom of the preacher
**“neither be thou afraid of their words”**
• Septuagint: nor be afraid of their face, for they will rage and be gathered together against you round about; though they be of a hard neck and an untamable heart, my commands are stronger; lest you say it was not foretold. They will rage and be gathered together against you round about, leaving, that is, no refuge.
• threats or slanders
**“for”** — therefore not to be feared; as if you should seek to please those who displease God. Whence: “Have not I hated them, O Lord, that hated thee?”
**“unbelievers”**
• in themselves
• toward God
**“and destroyers”**
• of the commandments
• to the weak
**“are with thee”** — of others, lest they die alone
**“and thou dwellest with scorpions”** — because the flattering and malicious cannot overthrow
**“thou dwellest; fear not their words, neither be thou dismayed at their looks”** — fear not their words
**“neither be thou dismayed”** — as if they were to be feared, had they not provoked me by their deeds
**“for they are a provoking house”** — Neither their words, etc. Whence: “But to me it is a very small thing to be judged by you, or by man’s day.”
**“With scorpions”** — Gregory. Whence: “They surrounded me like bees,” which have honey in the mouth and a sting in the tail. To be with the wicked in body does not harm the good, but in mind; if the spirit is lacking, the place does not help. Lot was holy in Sodom, sinned on the mountain; and in paradise the prince of our race fell; Abel cannot be made one whom Cain’s malice does not try. But let the weak avoid the company of the wicked, lest they take delight in imitating the evils which they often see and cannot correct.
**“Scorpions”** — Jerome. They strike with a curved wound and a hollow sting, so that the same blow both opens the skin and spreads the poison; each one receives his name according to his ways. Whence it is said to the Pharisees: “generation of vipers”; and of Herod, who was crafty: “Go and tell that fox”; and false prophets are compared to foxes, and now those of untamable heart are called scorpions; and in the Gospel it is said: “the sheep heard them not.” Those, therefore, who heard thieves and robbers lost the name of sheep, and they perished not as sheep but as vipers, foxes, scorpions.
2.7:
**“And thou shalt speak my words to them, if perhaps they will hear, and forbear: for they provoke me to anger”** — they provoke God by sinning
**“If perhaps they will hear”** — Jerome. Although those to whom we speak are evil, let us not cease, but preach in season and out of season, so that the hard man may be softened and hear, and the obedient man, his will changed, may not grow deaf.
2.8:
**“But thou, O son of man, hear all that I say to thee: and do not thou provoke me, as that house provoketh me”** — lest a like sin deserve a like punishment
**“open thy mouth”** — by speaking rightly
**“Hear all that I say”** — Gregory. Do not do what you forbid, lest in that in which you judge another you condemn yourself. Whence Balaam, filled with the Spirit of God for speaking, but held back by his own spirit in his carnal life, says of himself: “The hearer of the words of God hath said, who knoweth the doctrine of the Highest, and seeth the visions of the Almighty, who falling hath his eyes opened”; who saw what was right to say; but he despised living rightly.
**“Do not provoke”** — Gregory. Lest by keeping silent about what has been committed to you, and not rebuking evil deeds, you provoke God, as they do by doing evil.
**“Open thy mouth”** — That is: show yourself worthy of my words, and receive spiritual food; whence: “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.” And he answered: I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit. As it is said: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear,” so here: he that hath an open mouth to eat, let him eat. The Apostle also, who had the treasure of wisdom, says: “My mouth is open to you.” And of the Lord it is said: “Opening his mouth he taught them.”
**“and eat what I give thee”** — And eat, etc. Gregory. After opening the mouth we eat, because the food of life is increased in our senses when we begin to preach. Whence: “I opened my mouth and panted.”
2.9:
**“And I looked, and behold, a hand was sent to me”** — The Son of God, who opened the Scripture to his saints.
**“sent to me”** — The Seventy: outstretched.
**“in which was rolled up”** — obscure.
**“a book”** — holy Scripture.
**“and he spread”**
• that I might understand.
• Gregory. He spread it out when he expounded the riddles. Whence: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures.”
**“within”** — by the spiritual sense, to the elders.
**“and without”** — by the historical sense, to the weak.
**“and canticles”** — on those who are worthy of God’s witness, to whom it is said: “Sing ye to the Lord a new canticle.”
**“and woe”**
• on those who utterly despair, and when they have come into the depth of sins, despise.
• Within, because it promises invisible and heavenly things; without, because by the rightness of its precepts it arranges visible things; it commands how earthly and contemptible things are to be used or, by desire, avoided; it enjoins some things in outward actions, and what it commands outwardly is plain; other things concern hidden heavenly matters, which cannot be fully comprehended. Whence: “Stretching out the heaven like a skin, who coverest the higher rooms thereof with water.” For heaven is the Scripture, from which there shine for us both the sun of wisdom and the moon of knowledge, and from the ancient fathers the stars of examples and virtues; it is stretched out like a skin because, through its writers, what was formed by the tongue of flesh is unfolded before our eyes by the words of the teachers in exposition. By the waters, that is, the angels, of whom it is said: “Praise him, ye heavens of heavens: and let all the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.” He rules the higher parts of heaven who has disclosed to the angels alone the heights of the sacred word, which are said of the nature of the divinity or of the eternal joys, while we are still ignorant of them.
**“And behold a hand”** — The hand of the Lord is stretched out to those who obtain a benefit; it is drawn back from others. Whence: “All the day long have I spread my hands to a people that believeth not,” that is, that he might gather the children of Jerusalem, “as the hen doth gather her chickens under her wings,” and by the stretching out of his hands Israel overcame Amalec.
**“In which was rolled up”** — The Septuagint. The head of the book, of which it is said in the psalm: “In the head of the book it is written of me.” In the beginning, that is, this is rolled up, which no one can read, no one open, but the lion of the tribe of Juda, the root of David; nor is it devoured whole, but in the head. For it cannot be that human nature should devour all the treasures of this book.
*Gregory:* Through Ezechiel the order of preachers is signified; through the book, Scripture.
**“Within”** — that is, by spiritual understanding. Whence: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.” Whence: “The high hills are a refuge for the harts, the rock for the irchins.”
**“Lamentations”**
• Of those who are called to penance: as Samuel and Paul mourned and lamented over Saul and the Corinthians, whom they desired to save.
• Gregory. That you may punish sins. Read what is written in this volume: “And rend your hearts, and not your garments”; and again: “Be wretched and mourn,” and the like.
**“And canticles”** — Gregory. As if to say: that you may be glad at the promise of the joy to come, learn what is written in this volume. “Blessed are they that dwell in thy house, O Lord: they shall praise thee for ever and ever,” and all its streets shall be paved with precious and clean stone, and through all its lanes Alleluia shall be sung; and woe, as if you still cling in mind to the present age, if you delight in earthly pleasures and cannot love the eternal joys which you hear of: learn woe, that you may drive from your mind what you love; whence: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” and “their worm shall not die.”
2.10:
**“it before me, which was written”** — which in Isaias is said to be sealed to the unbelieving people, just as even today a veil is placed over the hearts of the Jews in the Old Testament.
**“and there were written in it lamentations”** — both within and without.
**“Within and without”** — Others: before and behind, that is, of the future and the past.

3.1:
**“And he said to me: Son of man, eat all that thou shalt find”** — in this book.
**“eat”**
• he does not say drink; for you are about to hear obscure and hard things.
• first.
**“this book, and”** — afterwards.
**“go speak”** — as if to be sated and to belch forth.
**“Eat”** — Gregory. Consider and understand, that is, first chew, and afterwards you can swallow and teach others.
**“Eat this book”** — Unless we have first eaten the open book, we cannot teach the children of Israel. Whence David, having obtained mercy: “I will teach the unjust thy ways, and the wicked shall be converted to thee.”
3.2:
**“And I opened”**
• as was commanded.
• Septuagint. God opened, that is, because he himself opened the prophet’s mouth and fed him.
**“my mouth”** — of the heart.
**“and he caused me to eat that book”** — otherwise I could not eat.
*Gregory:* We open the mouth when we prepare the sense for understanding the sacred word.
*Jerome:* With the mouth opened, the Lord bestows food, so that the beginnings of the will in us may be; from the Lord we obtain the perfection of blessedness; for it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. Yet to will and to run is of our free choice.
**“he caused me to eat”** — Gregory. He who so often holds it out to the mouth of our heart, as if it were an apple, as often as he opens understanding to us.
3.3:
**“And he said to me: Son of man, thy belly”**
• Septuagint: your mouth
• mind
**“shall eat”** — by reading the simple history
**“and thy bowels”**
• Septuagint: your belly
• the inner parts of the mind
**“shall be filled”** — a pious promise; for many read and depart empty; and even if they grasp with the mind the meaning of the sacred word, they do not store it up, keeping it in the bowels of the heart.
**“with this book, which I give thee. And I did eat it, and it was”** — because he had filled my bowels
**“in my mouth”**
• by preaching
• because I dipped the pen of the tongue in the heart
**“as honey sweet”** — The awareness of holy love profits more for preaching than the practiced knowledge of speech.
**“Thy belly shall eat”** — Gregory. The mind, that is, according to that: “I am pained in my belly,” that is, I feel the affliction of the mind. And elsewhere: “Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.” From the mind, that is, holy preachings; and the inward bowels of the mind, that is, right intention, holy desire, humility toward God, pious will toward the neighbour.
**“Shall be filled”** — Jerome. By constant meditation, storing it up in the treasury of memory, so that with the apostle we may have “bowels of mercy,” and the belly be filled, of which Jeremias says: “My bowels, my bowels are grieved.”
**“As honey”** — Whence: “How sweet are thy words to my palate! more than honey to my mouth.” And elsewhere: “The judgments of the Lord are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.” And Samson: He found honeycomb of honey in the mouth of the lion.
**“Over honey sweet”** — Gregory. Because those who have first learned to love the Lord in the bowels of their heart know how to speak sweetly of him; speech has no sweetness when life gnaws at it.
**“As honey sweet”** — The Lord after the resurrection ate a honeycomb. And in Proverbs it is said of the bee, although this is not found in the Hebrew: Go to the bee and learn how industrious she is, and how chaste she makes her work, by whose labours kings and the unskilled make use of for health. Moses and the prophets and the evangelists and other saints did this, so that whoever is a king, whose heart is in the hand of God, may use the guiding foods. But he who is simple and without the serpent’s cunning, having the innocence of doves, let him believe with simple faith and be saved, because snares are everywhere, and the devil “transformeth himself into an angel of light.” Honey of those which drops from the lips of a harlot, promising sweet things and inserting poisons.
3.4:
**“And he said to me: Son of man, go to the house of Israel”** — as if they themselves are unwilling to come to you
**“and thou shalt speak”** — it imposes the bridle of restraint
**“my words”** — only
**“my”** — not yours
**“to them”** — Go to the house; for although he was not with them in body, he was in mind, whose holiness was offended by their iniquity. Moses did the same, pitching the tabernacle far from the camp of the multitude; and when he had entered it, the pillar of the cloud came down and stood at the door of the tabernacle.
**“Thou shalt speak my words”** — He who in expounding the sacred word invents something to please his hearers speaks his own words, not God’s. But he who understands otherwise than the one who uttered it, and in another sense for the edification of charity, the words he speaks are the Lord’s, because God speaks to us through all of sacred Scripture only to draw us to love of him and of our neighbour.
3.5:
**“For thou art not sent to a people of a profound speech”** — Those who are sound do not need a physician, but those who are ill do.
**“and of an unknown tongue”** — as if there were no excuse for you: they are not foreigners to you; you know their language well enough to speak to them
**“thou art sent”** — but
**“to the house of Israel”** — one house is yours with them
3.6:
**“Nor to many nations of a strange speech, and of an unknown tongue”** — which is foreign to the speech of the law
**“whose words thou canst not understand; and if thou wert sent to them, they would hearken to thee”** — “A people, which I knew not, hath served me: at the hearing of the ear they have obeyed me.”
**“Nor to many nations”** — As if he said: why do I speak of one people? If I sent you to diverse nations, my authority and power would overcome every difficulty; and would that it were the time when I am about to send to all nations and give the grace of tongues, that my apostles may preach and subject the whole world and the diversity of tongues by one faith to my rule. They would hear more readily who are deep and of lofty speech, having nothing of Jewish levity, but walk with a grave and solid step; and though their tongues are unknown, they are known in faith. Whence it follows: “And if thou wert sent to them, they would hearken to thee,” etc. Finally he afterwards sent, and all alike believed. Whence: “Behold, we turn to the Gentiles”; and elsewhere: “I have not found so great faith in Israel.”
3.7:
**“But the house of Israel will not hearken to thee: because they will not hearken to me”**
• as if you should not be grieved, because they are unwilling to hear even me; to which is like: “He that despiseth you, despiseth me.”
• free choice is shown when it says they are unwilling to hear me; and two causes are given, namely that the forehead is worn down and the heart is hard
**“for all the house of Israel are”** — without reverence
**“of a hard forehead”**
• through shamelessness
• namely of the heart
**“and an obstinate heart”**
• Septuagint: of contention; often, that is, called to salvation, they were unwilling to hear.
• Those are of worn forehead who not only do not shrink from labouring for these worldly things, but in their labours are not ashamed to seem importunate for what is denied them. For to certain depraved minds nothing is more laborious than to be commanded not to labour in the labours of this world.
*Gregory:* The more often a fault is committed, the less the mind of the one committing it is ashamed. Whence: “Thou hadst a harlot’s forehead; now thou blushest.”
3.8:
**“Behold I have made thy face stronger than their faces”** — Yet be thou seemly, because behold I have given
**“stronger than their faces”** — who shall shame me before men
**“and thy forehead”** — against their forehead
**“harder than their foreheads”**
• that thou mayest dare to speak with the purpose thou hast undertaken
• Stronger, so that he may be overcome by no shame. Hence we learn that sometimes it is a grace to resist impudence, and when the occasion arises to grind forehead against forehead, lest our modesty and human shame fear the snares of rivals.
**“Behold I have made thy face”** — Gregory. Shame is praiseworthy in evil, and conversely, to blush at evil is a good of wisdom and of contrition. Whence: “There is a shame that bringeth glory, and there is a shame that bringeth sin.”
3.9:
**“like an adamant”** — who is in honour
**“and like flint”** — who, base, is trampled
**“I have made thy face”** — therefore
**“fear them not”** — who fear not the author
**“neither be thou dismayed at their presence”** — impudence
**“at their presence: for”** — that is, therefore
**“they are a provoking house”** — is exceedingly provoking, whose harshness is so often repeated
**“Like an adamant”** — That is, lest the tongue be restrained by shame through the honour shown by the hearers; and as flint, lest through contempt he keep silent from weakness.
3.10:
**“And he said to me: Son of man, receive in thy heart, and hear with thy ears, all the words”** — This is the food of the book, and these are the words in which, according to the diversity of the hearers, he speaks either lamentations, or a song, or woe to men. But it must be noted that the words of God are first to be stored up in our heart, and carefully attended to by us, and so to be brought forth to the people.
**“receive in thy heart, and hear with thy ears, all the words that I speak to thee”** — before
**“Hear with thy ears”** — We hear the words of the Lord when we do them, and so we rightly preach to our neighbours. Whence: “And immediately his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke right.”
3.11:
**“And”** — after
**“And go get thee in”** — Jerome. The Lord also came to the people of the Jews, the Father sending him, that he might preach release to the captives; in which is fulfilled: “Leading captivity captive, he gave gifts to men.”
**“to them of the captivity”**
• to the captivity; others: into captivity
• as much in mind as in body
• that is
**“To them of the captivity”** — Gregory. Allegorically. He who falls from good works into perverse ones comes from Jerusalem to Babylon; whence: “I will not remove, my helper.” Yet we must not despair of such men. For the prophet is sent to the captivity; whence: “Thou shalt come even to Babylon: there thou shalt be delivered.”
**“to the children of thy people”** — not of mine, whom they have offended
**“and thou shalt speak to them, and shalt say to them: Thus saith the Lord: If so be they will hear”** — in heart
**“and will forbear”** — When this is often repeated, the hardness of the transmigrated people is signified, and consolation is given to prelates, lest, perhaps despised by their subjects in their admonitions, they be saddened.
**“If perhaps they will hear”** — Gregory. Often, when we correct subjects, some are corrected and others neglect it; whence: “I rained upon one city, and upon another city I rained not.” Often, too, one and the same city is rained upon in part and dries up in part, when the same man, hearing the correction, amends some vices and, as if rained upon in part, bears fruit, but keeps others, and as if in part not rained upon is barren and dry.
3.12:
**“took me up”** — because I was not in the flesh, and walking in the spirit I did not fulfil the works of the flesh
**“spirit”** — who takes up the meek
**“and I heard behind me the voice”**
• of affliction, of penance
• turned to the Babylonian sinners, he heard as if behind his back the voice of the glory of the Lord, whose place is Jerusalem, that is, vision of peace
**“of a great commotion”** — of the anger of God upon Israel
**“great”** — Gregory. Often in holy speech something is said obscurely, so that, God dispensing it wondrously, it may be expounded in many ways.
**“Blessed be the glory of the Lord, from his place”**
• The soul of the just is the place of God, the lodging of God; or the Son, who says: “I am in the Father, and the Father in me.”
• in inaccessible light
**“And the spirit took me up”** — Gregory. The Spirit takes up the mind of the preacher; raised by the fear of God, he makes it a stranger to earthly desires, so that it pleases him to do only spiritual things. Whence: “Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that which endureth unto life everlasting.”
**“From his place”**
• The place of the glory of God is either a holy soul or an angelic spirit; and the glory of the Lord is blessed from its place when eternal praise is sung to the author of all things either by chosen men or by holy angels. In that the just think about the conversion of sinners, then, since in considering their vices they turn the eye to carnal acts, they are as if tending toward Babylon; yet according to the state of their uprightness, since in the praise of God they never cease to consider the good things of the saints, although by thought they are intent on something else, they hear as if behind them the voice of the glory of the Lord from Jerusalem, that is, from his place.
• Whence Micheas: “Behold the Lord will come forth out of his place, and he will come down upon the high places of the earth: and the mountains shall be moved under him, and the valleys shall melt like wax before the fire, and like waters that run down a steep place.” For when the Saviour came down from the Father, the high places of the earth and the mountains were moved, and the lower parts of the valleys were melted.
**“And I heard”**
• And I heard. Gregory. The voice of a great commotion follows the prophet, because after the word of preaching the mourning of the penitent is heard, who before lay, as if silent, secure in their sins; whence: “He hath rested on his lees.” The psalmist begs this, saying: “Thou that sittest upon the cherubims, let the earth be moved,” and elsewhere: “Thou hast moved the earth, and hast troubled it: heal thou the breaches thereof, for it has been moved.”
• When we turn over in mind the past judgments of the Lord, we hear behind us the voice of a great commotion; when we meditate on future things, we are moved by those that are before.
*Jerome:* Because the Spirit of God was in him, despising earthly things he is caught up by the Spirit and hears behind him the voice of a great commotion, forgetting the things that are past and stretching himself forward to the future, so as to leave the snares of enemies behind his back. In Exodus also, when Pharao and all his army pursued Israel, the angel in the pillar of cloud left the front of the camp, and coming behind stood all night between Israel and the Egyptians, that, the adversaries being past, Israel might hear: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.
**“Blessed be the glory”** — Blessed be the glory. Gregory. The hearts of sinners were the place of the evil spirit, but through penance they become the place of the glory of the Lord, and from there the blessing of the glory is heard in praise of God. Whence: first, from the injury done to the Creator through love of the world, they advance to high things even by wonderful works, that they may become living creatures of God, and by signs and by virtues and by desire fly to high things.
3.13:
**“And the noise of the wings of the living creatures”**
• explained above
• because from the very mourning of penitents the virtues of the saints arise, so that they advance all the more in good, the more wickedly they remember they have acted
• Or each living creature struck its own wings, or those of another in turn. For one of our virtues drives another to perfection, as the knowledge of the Word of God and the bowels of mercy; and all the saints in turn stir one another by their virtues to progress, by mutual examples, while each admires in another what he does not have in himself; whence: “esteeming others better than themselves.” God therefore does this in the hearts of men, as in the regions of the earth: he does not give all things to one, but one thing to one, another to another. For unless they needed one another in turn for mutual fruits, they would not have communion with one another. Thus therefore all are joined in one charity.
**“striking one against another, and”** — after
**“the noise of the wheels”**
• of the testaments
• because after the life of the saints came to honour, the words of the testaments appeared to men as venerable
**“following the living creatures, and the noise of a great commotion”** — After the preaching, the first commotion is to lament the evils we have done; but after the voice of the wings and wheels, the second is with great weeping to seek the heavenly goods which we have heard.
**“following the living creatures”** — Gregory. Because in the life of the holy fathers we learn what we ought to understand in Scripture, whose action opens to us what the page of the Testament says in their preachings: “He lifted me up and took me.” Balaam was raised up by the spirit of prophecy, by which he knew future things far off, but he was not taken up, because he did not separate his mind from earthly desires. “And I went away bitter.” The more sweet to the preacher is what he sees within, the more what he endures outwardly is turned into bitterness; whence: “In much wisdom is much indignation.” And: “He that addeth knowledge, addeth also sorrow.”
3.14:
**“spirit”** — again
**“also lifted me”** — to greater things, namely to those things in which the preacher advances while he carries the minds of the hearers on to the desire of God. Whence: “Fill up plentifully the streams thereof, multiply its fruits; it shall spring up and rejoice in its showers.”
**“took me up”** — held steadfastly
**“And I went away”** — lifted up and taken up
**“in bitterness in the indignation”** — having understood the indignation of God and turning over in mind the meaning of the vision
**“of my spirit”** — of man, namely; whence Isaias: “My spirit rises from the night to thee, O God.”
**“the hand”**
• the Son, through whom all things
• the prophet is not carried away in spirit but in body, which is read of Habacuc
**“for the hand of the Lord was with me”** — who says: “for without me you can do nothing”, of whom it is said through Moses: “I will lift up my hand to heaven.”
**“strengthening me”** — And I went away, etc. Whither I was carried, or was borne on high by the impulse of his spirit, desiring to go where the Lord commanded.
**“In bitterness in the indignation”**
• Gregory. Of Achab also it is said to the prophet: “Hast thou not seen Achab humbled before me? therefore I will not bring the evil in his days.” From this it is gathered how such bitterness in the saints, who fear to lose God, pleases God, if penance so pleased him even in a reprobate who feared to lose the present world; and how pleasing is voluntary affliction for faults in those who are pleasing, if this pleased for a time even in one who was displeasing.
• In bitterness, in indignation, etc. Gregory. For the book, sweet in the mouth, makes the heart’s mind bitter against itself, so that it displeases itself and pleases the Creator.
**“For the hand”** — that I might receive the name, namely of watchman, and teach what I have learned
**“The hand”** — Gregory. For no one prevails to do this with his whole heart for love of God unless the Holy Spirit has taken up his soul. Indeed we cannot rise perfectly to good things unless the Spirit both lifts us by coming to us and strengthens us by following after.
3.15:
**“And I came to them of the captivity”**
• namely
• Gregory. In the prophets, as things are explained by words, so sometimes words are explained by things, so that of them not only the words but also the deeds are prophecy; whence: “I came to the captivity, to the heap of new corn,” namely the sons of Israel, whose fathers many were already dead, but of the sons more were to believe and come to the fruitfulness of good work; whence they are called a heap of corn; for good souls are the fruits of God; whence: “Israel is holy to the Lord, the first-fruits of his corn.” For the Israelites believed first; the Gentiles followed.
**“to the heap of new corn”**
• of the sons
• Thesabib in Hebrew signifies the time when the new grain or barley is gathered, and after famine and want, before they are threshed on the floor, they promise some hope of food; so Israel, small and slender, as if reviving and sprung from the land of the Jewish people, promised a sowing.
**“of new corn”** — of holy souls
**“to them”** — namely
**“that dwelt by”** — as above
**“the river Chobar, and I sat where they sat”** — About to preach to them, he sympathizes, because speech is gladly received when it comes from one who sympathizes.
**“and I remained there”**
• seeing their wickedness and God’s just sentence against sinners
• that I may see first before I correct
• He who is to be a watchman, and is to speak God’s words to the people, ought to rest for a long time, and to grieve over what he sees, and to have none of those things in his conscience which he ought to correct in others.
**“seven days”** — during which I kept silent, understand
**“mourning”** — Jerome. Theodotion: wondering, to express the prophet’s amazement at seeing their iniquities. Aquila: resting, to show that although he was in the midst of them, he was separated in mind.
*Gregory:* Grieving, sympathizing with the wretched, as iron is first melted so that it may be joined with iron; or because the house of Israel is exasperated and does not acknowledge its fault through scourges, he sits grieving among the rejoicing, so that by his silence he shows that he had come to speak.
3.16: **“And at the end of seven days”** — Gregory. He had been sent to preach, and yet for seven days he kept silence in mourning, because he knows how to speak truly who has learned to be silent. For the discipline of silence is a kind of nourishment of the word. Whence: “A time to keep silence, and a time to speak”; silence first, speaking afterwards. If the holy prophet, who is sent to speak, keeps silent that he may speak rightly, how great a fault it is not to keep silent, for one whom no necessity compels to speak. By keeping silence, then, let us learn to speak.
3.17:
**“Son of man, I have made thee a watchman to the house of Israel, and”** — first
**“thou shalt hear”** — as if he should not presume to speak what he has not heard. Whence: “I will incline my ear to a parable; I will open my proposition on the psaltery.”
**“out of my mouth”** — To the Son
**“the word”** — of doctrine
**“Son of man”** — Jerome. A watchman is one who always stands on high, so that he sees far ahead whatever is coming; whose life ought to be high and circumspect.
*Gregory:* He calls the preacher a watchman. For he to whom the care of others is committed is called a watchman, that he may sit on the height of the mind, and draw the meaning of his name from the virtue of his action. The watchman ought to stand on high by his life, that he may be able to profit by foresight; whence: “Get thee up upon a high mountain, thou that bringest good tidings to Sion”; that he may rise above the life of those under him, and not subject his mind to earthly things, and so see their deeds the more keenly.
*Gregory:* To speak of God is of a mind quiet, strong, and free; whence: the land up to the windows, that is, earthly care reaching even to the priests, so that, like closed windows, they cannot pour out light on their subjects, but fall silent from the office of preaching.
3.18:
**“If, when I say to the wicked, Thou shalt surely die: thou declare it not to him, nor speak to him, that he may be converted from his wicked way, and live: the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity”** — by which he deserved it
**“his”** — not yours
**“shall die”** — not by death of the body, but of the soul, which by your admonition could always have lived
**“If, when I say”**
• Neither does the subject die by the fault of his superior, nor is the superior without fault, when the subject, not hearing the words of life, dies by his own fault. For death is due to the wicked man, but the way of life must be announced to him by the watchman, and his wickedness rebuked. But if he is silent, the wicked man will die in his iniquity, because the desert of his wickedness was that he was not worthy to have the watchman’s word spoken to him; yet he kills him who by keeping silence betrayed him to death.
• Jerome. There are two wicked men, or unjust, as the Septuagint translated: one who hears nothing from the watchman and dies in his wickedness, whose blood is required at the hands of the watchman. The other, to whom the watchman announces, and he despises it and dies by his own vice, and the watchman is free from fault. Whence we understand that the Lord therefore threatens the wicked man and says: “Thou shalt surely die,” that he may turn him from his wicked way and he may live. For the threat is not against men but against sins, nor against those who are converted from vices but those who remain in them. And it is a great danger to keep silent the words of God, whether from fear or sloth or flattery; whence Isaias: “Woe is me, because I have held my peace.”
**“his blood”** — Gregory. By blood sin is signified, which is imputed to the prelate’s fault if he has been silent; whence: “Deliver me from bloods,” that is, from the sins of the flesh.
3.19:
**“But if thou give warning to the wicked, and he be not converted from his wickedness, and from his evil way: he indeed shall die in his iniquity”** — He will die without you, because in the cause of death he is opposed by you; but you are joined to the death which you do not oppose.
**“But if thou give warning”** — The preacher ought to announce two things: faith and conduct. Impiety pertains to unbelief, the wicked way to action. He ought therefore to strive to draw men first to the piety of faith, and afterwards to the way of action.
