**“but thou hast delivered thy soul”** — “If any man’s work burn, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as by fire,” so that it may be tested, namely whether the watchman is free of guilt for the death of him who perished, or is guilty. For the master’s work is the disciple’s salvation.
3.20:
**“Moreover if the just man shall turn away from his justice, and shall commit iniquity: I will lay”** — as if he would not die at once
**“a stumblingblock”** — lest he find a level way and say, “I am turned in my anguish, whilst the thorn is broken”
**“before him, he shall die, because thou hast not given him warning”** — your fault, as if he could have lived if the teacher had taught
**“he shall die in his sin”** — before the fall; for one had to be watchful lest he fall
**“and his justices shall not be remembered”** — of recompense
**“his justices which he hath done”** — first
**“but I will require his blood”** — because you were silent, and because you were unwilling to be careful in preaching, you will be a partaker in the damnation
**“at thy hand”** — whom you ought to have guarded
**“Moreover if”** — As we read of two wicked men, one who did not hear and perished, the other who heard and persevered in his wickedness, so there are two just men: one who did not hear and perished, the other who heard and, being converted, saved his soul. It is also to be noted that a just man can fall, and, if he has had a teacher, be converted to better things. Good works therefore need a constant instructor, lest, having slipped, he draw back his foot from the best course.
**“I will lay a stumblingblock”** — Gregory. That is, because he would not repent of that in which he had offended, God puts before the one who despises him a place where he may fall the more heavily. For a sin which is not quickly blotted out by penance is either a sin and the cause of a sin, or a sin and the punishment of a sin, or a sin at once both cause and punishment of a sin; whence Moses: “The sins of the Amorrhites are not yet at the full.” And David says: “Add thou iniquity upon their iniquity”; and another prophet: blood touched blood, that is, sin is added to sin. Paul also says: “that they may fill up their sins always.” And to John also it is said by the angel: “He that is filthy, let him be filthy still.” And here also: If he shall commit iniquity, “I will lay a stumblingblock before him.” As if, because by repenting he would not see where he has already stumbled, I, forsaking him by a just judgment, will lay before him a place where he may fall the more heavily. But this is not to drive him to sin, but not to free him from sin; as in that: “I will harden the heart of Pharao.” God is said to harden when he does not free from hardening. For he does not harden the heart of the sinner.
**“shall not be remembered”** — Gregory. This is especially to be considered by us: when we commit evils, we recall past good deeds without cause, since in the committing of evils there ought to be no confidence in past good deeds.
3.21:
**“But if thou warn”** — before sin
**“the just man”** — even the just man needs a teacher; whence: “to the wise and to the unwise, I am a debtor”
**“that the just may not sin, and he doth not sin: living”** — well in the world
**“he shall live”** — in heaven
**“because thou hast warned him”** — as by your teaching
**“and thou hast delivered thy soul”** — by proclaiming it
3.22:
**“And the hand of the Lord was upon me, and he said to me: Rise”** — because he sat where they sat
**“go forth”**
• because you had gone in to the transmigration
• from Judea
**“into the plain, and there I will speak to thee”** — because there, that is, in the midst of the captives, you cannot see the glory of God
**“Rise and go forth into”** — Gregory. The truth of the history being preserved, the divine utterances sometimes indicate causes from the place; as when Moses came down from the mountain, the law was given to the people of the Jews in the plains. And Ezechiel is commanded to go forth into the plain. Sometimes from the time, as when the Lord was preaching to the Jews it is said, “It was winter.” The Lord therefore, in the midst of the Israelites, speaking to the prophet, says: “Go forth into the plain, and there I will speak to thee”; for he first deigned to pour the grace of prophecy into Judea, and afterwards to show it in the breadth of the Gentiles.
**“go forth into the plain”** — Jerome. Not into rough valleys, not into steep rocks, but into the breadth of the plain, which can receive the glory of the Lord. Whence the apostle to the Corinthians: “Be you also enlarged.” When he goes in to the captives, of whom it has been said that they are mad and persecute him, he needs a strong hand that he may be able to resist; but when he goes into the plain, the hand of the Lord is made upon him, without whose help he could not go out; but “strong” is not added, because he goes out to see the glory of the Lord, not to fight.
*Gregory:* Morally. Go forth into the plain: correct those placed outside yourself, and restrain them from iniquity. There the preacher sees the glory of God, because he perceives the glory of doctrine the more abundantly, the more he extends himself into the labor of preaching out of love of his neighbors. But from the plain he returns to the house, that in what he says he may also recognize what he himself is. For if he speaks well and does not do well, he goes out to the plain indeed by speaking, but by knowing himself he scorns to return to the house. He is shut up in the midst of the house when by the grace of the Spirit he is recalled to examine the secrets of his own mind, that his soul may rest within itself in God, and not run about through outward desires; whence: “Arise, take up thy bed, and go into thy house.” In the house, after the plain, the preacher is commanded to be shut up, that after the grace of doctrine which he ministers to his neighbors he may return to conscience and examine it more subtly, lest for what he preaches outwardly he seek praise inwardly; whence: let not strangers be partakers with thee, of whom it is said: “strangers have risen up against me, and the mighty have sought after my soul.” Bands are put upon him, because the more he examines himself, the more he recognizes with how many infirmities of his mortality he is bound; whence: “having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ”; and David says: “that he might hear the groans of the prisoners”; and Jeremias: “he hath built round about me that I may not get out, he hath made my fetters heavy.” “He shall not go forth from the midst of them”: because on account of the hard minds of the hearers he is silent even from good things. Whence it follows: “And I will make thy tongue stick fast to the roof of thy mouth.” But sometimes the Lord, with the zeal of his love, kindles the hearts of preachers even against the tongues of those who resist, that they may not be silent; whence it is added: “But when I shall speak to thee, I will open thy mouth,” etc.
3.23:
**“And I rose up”** — at the Lord’s command he goes in and goes out, and sits with those who sit, because the captives could not hear one who stood
**“and went forth into the plain”** — the nations, where they were spread far and wide
**“and behold there”** — among the nations
**“the glory of the Lord”** — the very majesty appeared to the nations, which before had declared itself to the chosen of the Jews, the Spirit revealing it
**“stood there, like the glory which I saw by the river Chobar: and I fell upon my face”**
• not bearing to endure the standing glory
• the glory having been seen
**“And behold the glory of the Lord stood there”** — which he saw before, walking and lifting itself up and at times standing; for beside the river of this world, Chobar, which is interpreted “very heavy,” the glory was seen, which signifies that all the glory of this world flows past and has no stable footing. But the glory of God is seen standing and persevering when the prophet stands in the plain; it could neither stand nor be seen in the midst of the captives.
**“and I fell upon my face”** — Gregory. Because although man is raised by contemplation to understand sublime things, yet from the contemplation of God’s majesty he understands the weakness of his condition, and he, as it were, has no standing who sees himself to be ash and dust before the eyes of God.
3.24:
**“And”** — therefore
**“the spirit entered into me”** — that he might raise up the one falling
**“and set”** — he raised him up
**“me”** — who humbly kept silent
**“upon my feet”** — that in a good work I might stand, as it were upon my feet, from uprightness
**“and set me upon my feet”** — Here it is treated of the prophet in the plain, because the Holy Spirit was to be given even to the chosen of the Gentiles, who would take them up and first cast them down from the state of pride, and afterward establish them upon their feet, that is, in good works; whence: “And make straight steps with your feet.”
**“and he spoke to me”** — Gregory. Historically, he gives us through the prophet an example of obedience, who now runs here, now there, and always breaks the judgement of his own will before the command of God.
**“Go in”** — Gregory. The prophet goes out from the midst of the people into the plain, and from the plain returns to the house, so that the preaching which was made to Judea may go forth to the Gentiles; and when these are filled with faith, spiritual Judea may receive the gifts of spiritual doctrine which she lost before. And “shut thyself up in the midst of thy house”: because in the time of Antichrist the converted Jews will be afflicted with harsh persecutions by those Gentiles who have remained in unbelief; whence: “because it is given unto the Gentiles, and the holy city they shall tread under foot two and forty months.”
**“and he spoke to me, and said to me: Go in; and shut thyself up in the midst of thy house”** — Go in, etc. As if to say: because you have been strengthened by the sight of the Lord’s majesty, fear nothing, but return to your house, either for the necessities of the body, as some think, or as a sign of the siege to come; and as Isaias, barefoot and naked, announced the three years' captivity and the nakedness of the people, so you also, shut up in the house, by the very deed are a prophet of the nearby siege of Jerusalem.
3.25:
**“And thou, O son of man, behold they shall put bands upon thee”** — the darts that are foreseen wound less
**“and they shall bind thee with them”** — the evils are foretold that he is to suffer; yet in all things he is obedient
**“and thou shalt not go forth from the midst of them”** — And thou, O son of man. That he is shut up in the house, that he is bound, that he does not go forth, but among the multitude of captives suffers the solitude of a prison, is the judgment of the siege: Jerusalem, shut up and surrounded by the army of the Chaldeans, will allow no one to go out. This is the pot of which Jeremias speaks, and Ezechiel in what follows, in which the flesh of the people is consumed.
**“Behold they shall put”** — Gregory. The prophet is bound in the house, because faithful Judea will endure the tribulation of persecution from her own kindred, pressed by the bands of sorrow; “and thou shalt not go forth from the midst of them,” because the preaching will not reach the hearts of the wicked; “and I will make thy tongue stick fast to the roof of thy mouth,” because then, the reprobate pressing upon them, the knowledge of the preachers is compelled to be silent. “But when I shall speak to thee,” etc.: because when Enoch and Elias preach, many of the Jews who had remained in unbelief will return to the knowledge of the truth. For then, as at the end, the mouth of the prophet is opened, when through the preaching of Elias and Enoch, the Jews returning to the faith, it is recognized that the prophecy was of Christ.
3.26:
**“And I will make thy tongue stick fast to the roof of thy mouth, and thou shalt be dumb, and not as a man that reproveth”** — because they are unworthy of rebuke
**“And I will make thy tongue”** — Sometimes on account of the fault of the preacher, sometimes on account of the fault of the hearer, the word of preaching is withdrawn; sometimes on account of good hearers the word is given even to evil teachers; sometimes it is withdrawn for the sake of justifying both, sometimes for the sake of condemning both.
**“for they are a provoking house”** — Because the house is, as it were, of such bitterness and of such contention against God that they do not deserve to hear one rebuking them. From this it is plain that where there is a multitude of sinners, the sinners are unworthy to be corrected by the Lord.
3.27:
**“But when I shall speak to thee, I will open thy mouth, and thou shalt say to them: Thus saith the Lord God”** — “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak”
**“He that heareth”**
• with the ear
• Jerome. The second edition of Aquila: he that hears shall be heard, and he that forsakes shall be forsaken. As if to say: to him who has, it shall be given; and from him who has not, even what he seems to have shall be taken away.
**“let him hear”**
• Septuagint: he who is unbelieving, let him be unbelieving
• with the mind
**“and he that forbeareth”**
• in body
• from the tumult of the world
**“let him forbear”**
• in heart
• is not recalled by the example of the wicked
**“for they are a provoking house”** — He that heareth, let him hear. Jerome. It belongs to the same wisdom both to be silent and to speak according to the time, and to give food to fellow servants in due season; whence Isaias: “I have held my peace to a people not believing. Shall I always be silent, saith the Lord?” He therefore who was silent because of the multitude of sins, since he saw that some could be converted, of whom it is said: “he that heareth, let him hear,” etc.—with his mouth opened, speaks to the people not by his own will but by the command of the Lord.

4.1:
**“And thou, O son of man, take thee a tile”** — an earthly hearer
**“and lay it”** — with attentive mind, considering its quality, both life and understanding
**“before thee”** — to be taught
**“and draw upon it”** — in heart
**“the city of Jerusalem”** — the joys of the heavenly homeland
**“And thou, O son of man”**
• Gregory. As if to say, know what you are, even if, raised above yourself, you behold divine secrets.
• Jerome. The wicked, though they are tolerated, suddenly fall; and the weak behold their punishments, lest they imitate their faults; whence here the desolation of Judea is added.
*Jerome:* This also is a sign of the siege. Symmachus renders “tile” more plainly as a little brick, or abacus, in whose dust they are accustomed to write grammas, that is, the lines of geometry, with a rod; whence some approve the science of geometry, observing that Jesus sent spies to describe the land, which is proper to geometry. In Zacharias also the angel has a geometer’s reed to measure Jerusalem.
4.2:
**“And”** — after
**“lay siege against it”** — that is, make known to the advancing soul what temptations follow
**“and build”** — by preaching
**“forts”** — by which the city is shut in, so that no one may go out
**“and cast up”** — Gregory. You will bring together, that is, earthly thoughts
**“a mount”** — by which the ditches are filled
**“and set a camp against it”** — showing the gathered ambushes of evil spirits. For there are certain vices akin to one another.
**“a camp”** — the guards of soldiers
**“and place battering rams”** — single vices rushing in
**“round about it”** — And lay siege against it, etc. Gregory: The preacher lays siege when, by the words of holy admonition, he shows to each one the virtues, or in what ways vices lie in ambush.
*Gregory:* For when Jerusalem is described in an earthly heart, presuming on the love of heavenly peace, a sharper temptation rises up; whence: “Son, when thou comest to the service of God, prepare thy soul for temptation.”
*Jerome:* The fortifications are the evils fortified coming against the mind, so that vices hide under the appearance of virtues and show themselves on high in image, though they are low in action.
**“And place battering rams”**
• Gregory. By which the foundations of walls are shaken and stones are loosened. By this description is signified the city’s near captivity under King Sedecias, in whose eleventh year both he himself was taken and the city. We may, however, say that the tile is set down in mockery of Israel, because it served Pharao in clay and brick. Or the city which they thought most firm and impregnable is compared to a most fragile brick, which at the touch of water is at once dissolved; of which it is said: “Shall the hardest rock, like the mountain of the desert of the daughter of Sion, be turned into a brick,” corrupted by the Babylonian flood; whence: “therefore the Lord will bring upon them the waters of the river, strong and many, the king of the Assyrians.”
• For sometimes single vices strike the mind from here and there, which the preacher sets around in a circle, while he shows how smoothly lust strikes, how harshly impatience kills, and so on.
4.3:
**“And take unto thee an iron pan”** — the wrath of the Lord, untameable, bent by no prayers; for nothing is harder than iron; this is set up as an iron wall, so that the city is shown to be broken in a short time
**“set it for a wall of iron”** — if the hearer will not be corrected
**“between thee and the city: and set thy face resolutely against it”** — sometimes by acting more severely
**“thy face resolutely against it”** — the judgment of severity, according to that: “But the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things, to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth.”
**“and it shall be besieged, and thou shalt lay siege against it”** — you show it surrounded by snares of temptations, so that the more fearful he is, the more watchful he may live
**“a sign”** — of the siege
**“is”** — that is, this
**“to the house of Israel”** — And thou take, etc. Gregory. Iron is a strong metal. In a pan food is fried; by the iron pan, therefore, is signified the strong frying of spiritual zeal, which fries the soul of the teacher, because he is greatly tormented when he sees the weak forsake eternal things and seek temporal; whence: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” So Paul burned against vices, but prepared the nourishment of virtues from his own affliction.
**“set it”** — Gregory. that if he who is taught will not hear, the teacher nevertheless, because of the zeal he shows, is not guilty, and is secure on the day of judgment. No sacrifice is greater to God than zeal for souls; whence: “The zeal of thy house hath eaten me up.” Hence it is commanded that fine flour sprinkled with oil be fried in a pan, that is, that the clean mind be burned by the ardour of holy zeal, and be mingled with the charity of mercy, which burns and shines in the sight of God.
**“and set thy face resolutely”** — Gregory. Sometimes by acting more severely. Whence: “Hast thou daughters? have a care of their body, and shew not thy countenance gay towards them.”
4.4:
**“And thou shalt sleep upon thy left side, and shalt lay the iniquities of the house of Israel upon it, according to the number of the days that thou shalt sleep upon it, and thou shalt take upon thee their iniquity”**
• that is, you shall signify their captivity
• The left parts are assigned to Israel, which was in Samaria without the temple and the knowledge of God; the right to Juda, which was in the worship and religion of God. And it is to be noted that in the one is the punishment of sinners, in the other the exercise of virtue. That the prophet’s days are here a year is for those who suffer; and the years which the sons of Laban thought of for Jacob were as a few days. Nor is there variety only in punishments according to the diversity of merits, but also in the reward of the good: the lambs on the right, the kids on the left; whence: “The heart of the wise man is in his right hand: and the heart of the fool in his left hand.”
**“And thou shalt sleep”** — Jerome. Under Phacee the son of Romelia, who reigned in Israel twenty years, Phaceia the son of Manahem his lord having been struck down, Theglathphalasar king of the Assyrians took Aion and Abel, the house of Maacha, and Janoe, and Cedes and Asor and Galaad and Galilee and all the land of Nephtali, and carried them over into Assyria. After him reigned in Israel Osee the son of Ela nine years, and he was taken with all Samaria by Salmanasar king of the Assyrians, and Israel was carried away into Elam and Aher beside the river Gozan, into the cities of the Medes. In the sixth year of king Ezechias, as the history of Kings relates, Osee was taken; from which, if we reckon how many years Israel was in the distress of captivity, from the sixth year to the twenty-ninth (for Ezechias reigned the whole time, twenty-four years). Manasses succeeded him, fifty-five years. Afterwards Ammon reigned two years, then Josias thirty-two years, after him Joakim, who is also Eliakim, eleven years. Then Joachin, who is also Jechonias, who was at once led into captivity. In his place reigned Sedecias eleven years, under whom Jerusalem was taken and the temple destroyed. So from the first captivity of Israel, which was made under Phacee, to the eleventh year of Sedecias, in which the temple was laid desolate, there are one hundred and sixty-four years. From the second, when Osee was taken and all Samaria overthrown, one hundred and thirty-five years. And the years of the desolation of the temple were seventy. These added to the first captivity make two hundred and thirty-four years. For in the second year of Darius the temple was built under Zorobabel and Jesus the high priest, Aggeus and Zacharias prophesying; he reigned thirty-six years, and one being taken away, his thirty-five years are added. After him reigned Xerxes the son of Darius thirty years. After him Artabanus seven months, and Xerxes, who is also Macroceir, forty years; after him Xerxes two months and Sogdianus seven months. Darius surnamed Nothus succeeded him, who reigned nineteen years. After him reigned Artaxerxes, who is also Mennon, the son of Darius and Parysatis, forty years, who is called Assuerus by the Hebrews. Under him is told the history of Mardochai and Esther, when all the people of Israel, delivered from the danger of death, received their former liberty. And from the hundred and fifty-second year of Darius to the last year of Assuerus there are one hundred and fifty-five years and four months, which added to the former years, two hundred and thirty-four, make three hundred and eighty-nine years and four months.
*Jerome:* But he who wishes to reckon from the first captivity, which was made under Manahem the son of Gaddi, king of Israel, who reigned in Samaria ten years, when Phul king of the Assyrians received from Israel a thousand talents of silver as tribute, and after him the other two years of Phacee, which he reigned in Israel, will find that in the twenty-ninth year of Assuerus three hundred and ninety years are completed, when the history of Esther was; which is more credible. For it was not when the empire of Assuerus was ended, but while he still reigned, that Israel cast off the yoke of servitude.
**“Thou shalt sleep upon”** — Jerome. The sleeping on the right side, namely of forty years, is easily reckoned. For after Eliakim, who is also Joakim, his son Joachin, who is also Jechonias, reigned three months. While he reigned the servants of Nabuchodonosor went up to Jerusalem and besieged it. Meanwhile Nabuchodonosor came, and Joachin king of Juda went out to him, and his mother, and his servants, and his princes, and his eunuchs, and the king of Babylon received him in the eighth year of his reign, and took away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the king’s house; and a little after he carried over all Jerusalem and all the princes and all the strong men of the army, ten thousand, and every artificer and engraver, only the poor being left. He being taken, Sedecias reigned eleven years, under whom the city was taken and the temple destroyed, whose desolation remained until the second year of Darius, that is, seventy years. In the thirtieth year of the desolation of the temple Cyrus reigned in Persia, Astyages king of the Medes having been overthrown; he, according to Isaias, sent back to Jerusalem nearly fifty thousand of the tribe of Juda, and the vessels of the temple which Nabuchodonosor had carried off, and the other things which Esdras relates. As therefore for the ten tribes we reckon three hundred and ninety years from Phacee, under whom Theglathphalasar laid waste the multitude of the Israelites, to the fortieth year of Assuerus, when the persecution of all the Jewish people was lessened; so from the first year of Jechonias, when a great part of Jerusalem was carried over into Babylon, to the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, which is the thirtieth of the desolation of the temple, forty years are reckoned, under whom the captivity of the Jews was relaxed and liberty restored to the people.
4.6:
**“And when thou hast accomplished this”** — or, you have fulfilled
**“thou shalt sleep again upon thy right side, and thou shalt take upon thee”** — that is, you shall signify their captivity
4.7:
**“thou shalt turn thy face to the siege of Jerusalem”** — as if not only by words but also by gesture and bearing you were to show the siege of the city, prophesying
**“and thy arm shall be stretched out”** — bare or stretched out
**“And”** — thus
4.8:
**“Behold I have encompassed thee with bands: and thou shalt not turn thyself from one side”** — so that no rest from torments be hoped for
**“to the other, till thou hast ended the days of thy siege”**
• others: of confinement
• Behold I have encompassed, etc. Jerome. The bonds of the Lord, by which we are bound unto salvation, are one thing; those of the devil, by which the woman of the gospel was bound eighteen years, another; whence each one is held fast by the cords of his own sins, and the Lord looses him, in the type of Lazarus raised, who lay in the tomb bound with bands and winding cloths.
4.9:
**“And take to thee wheat and barley, and beans, and lentils, and millet, and fitches”** — others: oats
**“And take to thee”** — Jerome. As in time of famine delicacies are not sought, but only how the belly may somehow be filled, so the prophet mixes everything into one, and makes three hundred and ninety loaves to eat on each day, which have twenty sicles each, that is, staters. Now a sicle, that is, a stater, has four drachmas, and eight drachmas make a Latin ounce; so that one loaf is said to have ten ounces, by which the soul is rather dragged along than sustained.
**“and make thee bread”** — Jerome. But it is to be noted that according to the number of the days of the left side, three hundred and ninety loaves baked under the ashes are made, to be eaten on each day, and about the loaves of the right side nothing at all is said. In this it is secretly signified that the punishment is not the same for the peculiar people, or for the sinner who has knowledge of God, and for him who departs altogether from the religion of the truth.
4.10:
**“And thy meat that thou shalt eat”** — as one who keeps off death rather than provides strength
**“shall be in weight twenty staters a day: from time to time”** — from evening, that is, until evening; others wrongly think it is to be understood from year to year
4.11:
**“And thou shalt drink water”** — Jerome. The scarcity of water increases the scarcity of food. For he is commanded to drink each day the sixth part of a measure, namely the Hebrew hin. Now the hin makes two Attic choruses, that is, two Italian sextarii, so that the hin is the measure of the Jewish sextarius and of our military one, the sixth part of which makes the third part of the Italian sextarius.
**“Allegorically.”** — The Jews, since the offence against God, eat to this day loaves baked under the ashes, mixed of wheat, barley, bean, lentil, millet and oats. Of these, one is the food of men, the other of beasts of burden. For because they believe in one God, they have something of wheat; but because they deny the Son, they are fed with the barley of beasts of burden, and with beans, by which the belly is swollen and the mind is said to be oppressed, whence it is a detestable food to the Pythagoreans. For a lentil Esau lost his birthright. Millet is the food of rustics and country folk and fattened fowl. Fitches, or oats, and herbs feed the brute animals. That Elias, fleeing Jezabel, is said, according to the Septuagint, to have found bread baked under the ashes, is a sign of want; whence also he is fed by ravens, so that he who found no food in Israel might be fed with the nourishment of unclean nations. The law also, which they read and do not understand, is bread baked under the ashes and covered with human dung; whence Paul: he counts the gains of the law and the observance of ceremonies as dung, that he may gain Christ.
4.12:
**“as barley bread baked under the ashes”** — so, that is, they are to be made just as barley bread baked under ashes
**“thou shalt eat it, and with the dung that cometh out of a man thou shalt cover it, in their sight”** — lest they be ignorant, for ignorance is not wont to temper miseries
4.13: **“So shall the children of Israel eat”** — The prophets prophesy not only by words but also by deeds. As Ezechiel eats bread in dung, so the children of Israel, or the whole people of the Jews, or, as others think, the ten tribes, shall eat polluted bread among the nations. Although he does not threaten those who have already been cast out, but those who are to be cast out of the land of promise.
4.14:
**“And I said: Ah, ah, ah, O Lord God, behold my soul hath not been defiled, and I have not eaten any thing that died of itself”** — which dies without effusion of blood
**“or was torn by beasts”** — by demons
**“Ah, ah, ah”** — Jerome. He does not contradict the Lord’s command, but gives reasons, rather he prays, why he cannot do this; and he obtains what he asks, and the severity of the sentence is tempered. It is asked why Ezechiel refuses lesser things, while Osee at once joins himself to a harlot, and does not say that he has a chaste body or that he ought not to be defiled by union with a harlot, though, as the apostle testifies, he who cleaveth to a harlot is made one body. Whence it is shown that it was not so in fact according to the letter, but was a figure of the synagogue or of the church.
4.15: **“Neat's dung”** — Lighter evils, namely. For the dung of oxen is far removed from the uncleanness of human dung. To this day this sentence is kept among the Jews, that they do not eat their bread in human dung. For they neither serve idols nor worship the monstrous things of demons, but in buffalo dung, while they do everything for the flesh and the belly and earthly goods; whence: “he that doth those things, shall live in them.” But we eat the bread that came down from heaven. Of which: man ate the bread of angels, living not on the flesh of Egypt but on the thinness of manna.
4.16:
**“And he said to me”** — what he showed would be done in deed, he shows by speech
**“Son of man: Behold, I will break in pieces the staff of bread”** — others: support
**“Behold, I will break in pieces”** — All the sleeping on the left and right side, and the mixing of the bread baked under ashes with a variety of six kinds, foreshadows the incredible want, which he here makes plain: “Behold, I will break in pieces,” etc.
**“in Jerusalem: and they shall eat bread by weight, and with care: and they shall drink water by measure, and in distress”** — In the church also the Lord, being angry, judges us unworthy of his bread; and would that we might at least deserve to receive it by weight and with care, and that the tip of Lazarus’s finger might moisten the parched tongue, “so that when bread and water fail, every man may fall against his brother”, and there be discord everywhere, and the tunic of Christ is rent, which not even the soldiers dared to rend in the passion. And we pine away in our iniquities while we have not the bread of God; whence Jeremias: “the little ones”, that is, the common people of the church, “have asked for bread, and there was none to break it unto them.” But Paul, who was a man and knew that Christ broke the legal loaves and gave them to the disciples to be distributed, says confidently: “The bread which we break, is it not the partaking of the body of Christ?” But they cannot eat the staff, that is, the firmness, of bread, who still need the milk of infancy and are not able to take solid food. And nothing so strengthens the mind of the one who eats as the bread of life, which indeed strengthens the heart of man.
4.17:
**“So that when bread fail”** — of the word of God
**“and water”** — of doctrine
**“every man may fall”** — hoping for help; for it is of human nature in the greatest straits to trust more in a neighbour than in oneself
**“against his brother, and they may pine away in their iniquities.”** — for which they suffer

5.1:
**“And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife that shaveth the hair: and cause it to pass over thy head, and over thy beard: and take thee a balance to weigh in, and divide the hair.”** — signifies famine and pestilence
**“And cause it to pass over thy head”** — Jerome. The hair and the beard are a sign of beauty and manliness; when they are shaved off, foul nakedness appears, and the better part of the head is as if dead. So Jerusalem and her people, dead and separated from the living body of God, is handed over to famine, pestilence, slaughter by the sword, captivity and dispersion.
5.2:
**“A third part thou shalt burn with fire in the midst of the city, according to the fulfilling”** — or reckoning
**“of the days of the siege: and thou shalt take a third part, and cut it in pieces with the knife”** — outside: the slaughter; it is wars
**“was about it”** — of the city
**“and I will draw out the sword”** — moreover
**“after them”** — lest captivity be the sum of evils
5.3: **“And thou shalt take thereof a small number”** — that is, those who are to return from captivity
5.4:
**“And thou shalt take of them again, and shalt cast them in the midst of the fire”** — It signifies the Macedonians, under whom the inhabitants of Judea, and especially Jerusalem, suffered many things.
**“and shalt burn them with fire”** — that is, to the people of the Jews
**“out of it shall come forth a fire into all the house of Israel”** — Out of it, etc. Jerome. As the history of the Machabees tells that a certain part of the Jews gave themselves up to Antiochus Epiphanes and stirred him up to persecute the people, and many other things that are written in that history and in the books of Josephus, and especially the dissension of Hyrcanus and Alexander, on occasion of which Pompey came to Jerusalem and subjected it to the Romans. Afterwards under Titus and Vespasian the city was taken and the temple overthrown, and fifty years later under Aelius Hadrian the city was destroyed to the ground and lost also its former name.
5.5:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: This is Jerusalem, in the midst of the nations”** — as the navel of the world. Whence: “he hath wrought salvation in the midst of the earth.”
**“I have set her”** — as an example of good
**“I have set her in the midst of the nations”** — Jerome. On the east it is encircled by Asia, on the west by Europe, on the south by Libya and Africa, and on the north by Scythia and Armenia and Persia and all the nations of Pontus. She is therefore set in the midst of the nations, so that, since “his name was great in Israel,” known in Judea, all the nations round about might follow her examples; but she herself followed the impiety of the nations placed around her.
5.6:
**“And”** — on the contrary
**“she hath despised my judgments”** — following the example of the Gentiles
**“so as to be more wicked than the Gentiles; and my commandments, more than the countries that are round about her: for they have cast off my judgments”** — backwards
**“and have not walked in my commandments”** — by making progress
5.7:
**“Because you have surpassed”** — Jerome. As if to say, what ground have I to complain, that you do not walk in my commandments and do not do my judgments, when you have even surpassed in wickedness the Gentiles that are round about you, and have not done those things which the Gentiles, with the natural law written in their hearts, have often done.
**“Because you have surpassed the Gentiles”** — Jerome. To this he referred three times, therefore first: “Therefore thus saith the Lord God: Behold I come against thee,” etc.; second: “therefore the fathers shall eat their children in the midst of thee”; third: “therefore as I live, saith the Lord.” And it is to be noted that he professes to do the honourable and fitting things according to the merit of those who endure, but the sad things and those unworthy of God he says he does not do, but only that they are done, as here: “therefore the fathers shall eat their children in the midst of thee.”
5.8:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord God: Behold I”** — not another
**“come against thee, and I myself”** — not through an angel, not through any minister
**“will execute judgments in the midst of thee in the sight of the Gentiles”** — although angry, I will not exceed the measure of punishments
5.9:
**“And I will do in thee that which I have not done”**
• before
• Because: “the servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes”, and: “the mighty shall suffer mighty torments.”
**“the like to which I will do no more”** — Jerome. He is about to do much harsher things after the death of the Son. For it is one thing to have worshipped idols at some time, and another to have slain the Son of God.
5.10:
**“Therefore the fathers shall eat the sons”** — in the Roman siege, not only in Babylon
**“in the midst of thee, and the sons shall eat their fathers: and I will execute judgments in thee, and I will scatter thy whole remnant into every wind.”** — because by the Roman captivity they were scattered throughout the whole world; and this is “into every wind”: the scattering of the hair and beard
**“Therefore the fathers”** — Jerome. We read that mothers have devoured their sons, but not fathers their sons nor sons their fathers.
*Jerome:* In the Church masters are often stirred up against disciples, that is, fathers against sons, and disciples against masters, that is, sons against fathers, by mutual sedition; whence the apostle: “But if you bite and devour one another, take heed you be not consumed one of another.” Hence the prophet: “that they may eat my flesh.” And Job: “Who will grant that we may be filled with his flesh?” Moreover it is said to masters who seek the gains of the world and not the salvation of those subject to them: “who devour my people as they eat bread.” Of whom the apostle: “and they shall eat up the houses of widows.”
5.11:
**“Therefore as I live, saith the Lord God”** — this properly refers to Jerusalem
**“Because thou hast violated my sanctuary with all thy offences”** — that is, deserting me, you worshipped idols in my temple
**“and with all thy abominations: I will also break thee in pieces”** — your idols
**“and my eye shall not spare”** — when I shall see your affliction
**“and I will not have any pity”**
• aposiopesis
• And I will not have pity on your affliction, because you would not have pity. For “blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.”
**“Therefore as I live”** — Jerome. The Lord says the same to priests and masters: “you have violated his sanctuary,” etc. I also will bruise you and break you in pieces, and will repay what you have unjustly done to my people, with whose wool you clothe yourselves and on whose milk and cheese you feed, and the broken and sick you do not seek out.
5.12:
**“A third part of thee”** — this has been said above in this chapter
**“shall die with the pestilence, and shall be consumed with famine in the midst of thee”** — The Septuagint says this differently; but Aristeas, Josephus, and the whole school of the Jews assert that only the five books of Moses were translated by seventy
5.13:
**“And I will accomplish my fury”** — He speaks in human fashion: not that he is angry, but we feel him as angry through punishments and torments.
**“and will cause my indignation to rest upon them, and I will be comforted”** — vengeance having been taken
**“and they shall know that I the Lord have spoken it in my zeal, when I shall have accomplished my indignation in them.”** — under the metaphor of husband and wife; for while he loves his wife he is jealous, and if he neglects her he says: “My zeal shall depart from thee; I will no longer be angry with thee.”
**“and they shall know that I the Lord”** — Jerome. Not consumed by famine and pestilence and sword, but scattered into every wind, by the deaths of others and by their own miseries they will feel God angry, whom they were unwilling to know as merciful.
5.14: **“And I will make thee desolate”** — Jerome. It profits Jerusalem to be made desolate in its vices and reduced to a desert, and to know its sins, so that she who ought to have been an example of virtues to the other nations may be an example of miseries; as he who says: “I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner as all my fathers were”; whence elsewhere: “And they that have passed by have not said: The blessing of the Lord be upon you,” that they may see her reproach and grieve.
5.15:
**“And thou shalt be a reproach, and a scoff, an example, and an astonishment amongst the nations that are round about thee, when I shall have executed judgments in thee in anger, and in indignation”** — Whence Paul: “We were by nature the children of wrath.”
**“and in wrathful rebukes”** — We too, with Jerusalem, weighed down in this tabernacle, groan, bearing the wrath of the Lord, because we have sinned against him.
5.16:
**“I the Lord have spoken it: When I shall send upon them the grievous arrows of famine, which shall bring death, and which I will send to destroy you”** — Of these things, in our times the memory is stirred up more by the thing itself than by the letter, since we see captives.
**“and I will gather together famine against you: and I will break among you the staff of bread”** — or support.
**“bread”** — The arrows of famine, etc. Jerome. It is manifest that whatever evil we suffer comes upon us for our sins; whence the famine too, in the book of Kings, and in Ruth, and under Elias when for three years and six months the heaven was shut, and under Eliseus, whose incredible want was made up by a sudden abundance, was sent by the judgment of God.
*Jerome:* Upon us, for whose sins famine is sent: first of the word of God, then death; so that we who do not hear, “Taste, and see that the Lord is sweet,” may perceive the Lord; the death of sinners is most evil.
5.17:
**“And I will send in upon you famine”** — The bread of the word of God, that came down from heaven.
**“and evil beasts”** — all harmful animals.
**“unto utter destruction, and pestilence”** — disease.
**“and blood”** — the sword.
**“And evil beasts”** — Jerome. The evil beasts are sent upon us when we are given up to the passions of ignominy, to a reprobate sense, and to the conscience of sins, which torment and tear our soul: dissensions, heresies, schisms, emulation, envy, detraction, many desires, and avarice, which is the root of all evils, are the worst beasts; whence: “Thy prevarication shall reprove thee”; and elsewhere: “Deliver not up to beasts the souls that confess to thee.”

6.2: **“Son of man, set thy face”** — or harden.
6.3:
**“And say: Ye mountains of Israel”** — who are occupied with idols.
**“hear”** — not with ears but by the command and power of the Creator, to whom is like: “The sea saw and fled: Jordan was turned back.” It is also said to the sea: be silent and be dumb; and of the earth it is said: “He looketh upon the earth, and maketh it tremble.”
**“the word of the Lord God: Thus saith the Lord God to the mountains”** — to the proud.
**“and to the hills”** — puffed up with knowledge.
**“and to the rocks, and the valleys: Behold, I will bring upon you the sword, and I will destroy your high places”** — in which they worshipped idols.
**“Ye mountains of Israel, hear”** — Jerome. Tropologically. It signifies that idols are to be overthrown, and altars and ceremonies; by the mountains of Israel we can understand princes, and those who were strong in wisdom and power and knowledge and riches; and note that the face is set against their minds, and he speaks not to the mountains alone but also to the hills, rocks, and valleys, in which a lower dignity and the degrees of knowledge and prudence are recognized.
*Jerome:* Tropologically. The mountains are those who have attained perfect knowledge; the hills, those a little lower; the rocks, those having no knowledge, and trusting only in their way of life, who presume certain things for themselves from the Scriptures, “having a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” The valleys are the last in the Church, who, though lower in life and knowledge, yet do not depart from the assembly of the Lord’s household. All are bidden to hear the word of the Lord, that each according to his measure may understand what the Lord commands.
**“Thus saith”** — Jerome. In this prophet it is often said “Adonai Lord”; Adonai is one of the ten names of God and signifies Lord, which we also often use of men. Sara called Abraham her lord by this name, and where it is said, “My lord the king,” Adonai is written. When therefore two names of Lord are joined, the first is common, the second proper to God; the proper name is called “appneon,” that is, ineffable, which was written on the golden plate that was on the priest’s forehead.
6.4:
**“And I will throw down”** — not.
**“your altars, and your idols shall be broken in pieces”** — by which they are fashioned in the heart.
**“your idols”** — fashioned gods.
**“and I will cast down”** — so that there the bodies of the dead are cast, where before the sacrifices were.
**“your slain”** — so that, namely, they may feel that they themselves are dead and that their fashioned things profit them nothing.
6.5:
**“I will lay the dead carcasses of the children of Israel before your idols: and I will scatter your bones round about your altars”** — not only of the mountains but of those who lay around the altars.
**“And I will scatter”** — In saying that he scatters the bones of the mountains, he shows that the strongest of them are to be separated from one another. For it profits the perverse in knowledge that the wicked be divided from the wicked, as those who built the tower were scattered for their own good and their tongues were divided, lest the worst agreement make them worse; so the bones of the mountains are scattered that they may understand their efforts to be vain.
6.6:
**“In all your dwelling places”** — to cities, villages.
**“The cities”** — assemblies of heretics.
**“shall be laid waste, and the high places”**
• of pride.
• the cause by which the cities of the mountains are destroyed, namely that they demolish the high places.
**“shall be thrown down, and destroyed, and your altars shall be abolished”** — of perverse doctrines.
**“and shall be broken in pieces: and your idols shall be no more”** — which they feigned in their heart.
**“and your temples shall be destroyed”**
• not temples.
• the shrines that they built against the temple of the Lord
**“and your works shall be defaced”**
• not of God
• of the mountains, that is, of teachers and of false knowledge
6.7:
**“And the slain shall fall in the midst of you: and you shall know that”** — or because
**“The slain”** — Jerome. He whom the mountains have slain, or the churchmen who by living badly have killed their own salvation; then there will be the end of the proud mountains, that they may know that he is the Lord. But it can also happen that, of one people of the mountains, when some are slain, others know; for when the pestilent one is scourged, the fool will be wiser.
6.8:
**“And I will leave in you some that shall escape the sword among the nations, when I shall have scattered you, through the countries”** — Whence: I have left me seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal; and Paul says: “There is a remnant saved according to the election of grace.”
**“That shall escape”** — Jerome. The apostles, namely, were kept from the seed of Israel, that scattered through the world they might preach the gospel. But it can also be said that some were preserved from the Jewish captivity so that among the nations they might remember his name and preach his power; and the heretics who shall be able to escape the sword of their perdition and the fictions that had been stirred up against God, scattered hither and thither, will remember the name of the Lord, doing penance and rejoicing that they have been taken captive by the Catholics.
6.9:
**“And they that are saved of you shall remember me amongst the nations to which they are carried captives: because I have broken their heart that was faithless”**
• with idols
• Whence Osee: the spirit of fornication hath deceived them
**“and revolted from me: and their eyes”** — full of adultery
**“that went a fornicating after their idols: and they shall be displeased”** — repenting
**“Because I have broken”** — Of the heretics, whose heart is profitably broken, that is, the treasure of perverse doctrines, because it departed from the Lord; and their eyes that go a fornicating after their own inventions, because when they remember the Lord they will be displeased with themselves in their abominations; and understanding the truth of the true faith they will know that he is the Lord, who therefore strikes that he may heal.
**“And their eyes”** — And their eyes: through whose windows death enters. Whence the two elders in Daniel had Susanna stripped, so that at least they might enjoy the beauty of her uncovered body.
6.10: **“And they shall know that I the Lord have not spoken in vain that I would do this evil to them”** — I have not spoken in vain, because they have repented. It is said to the unrepentant: I have struck your sons in vain, for they did not receive correction, or were unwilling to receive it.
6.11:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: Strike with thy hand”** — separating from evil works
**“and stamp with thy foot”** — lest the sinner walk on the way
**“and say: Alas, for all the abominations of the evils”** — that you may lament and weep over the things that displease you
**“of the house of Israel: for they shall fall by the sword, by the famine and by the pestilence”** — this is the cause why the inhabitants, namely of the mountains and of the altars and the worshippers of idols, are to fall by sword, famine and pestilence
**“Strike with thy hand”** — that you may signify, not only by voice but also by gesture and bearing, astonishment and wonder over their sins; for as, when we behold something new and marvelous, we shudder in body as well as in mind, clap our hands, strike the foot against the ground, and incline the voice to weeping, so the prophet does, seeing with the eyes of the mind the punishments to come and the abominations of the house of Israel.
*Jerome:* He who is given over to one or several vices and cannot be parted from them falls, as if by a kind of lethargy of pestilence, into sickness.
*Jerome:* He who departs from the Church will straightway die by the pestilence; he who seems to himself learned and careful, unless he be on his guard, will be struck by the sword of the enemy; he who, content with simple faith, lives like a brute animal, is indeed in the Church but profits by no work, and does not, like the ant, prepare food for himself in the harvest, will die of famine.
6.12:
**“He that is far off”** — fleeing the siege in the deserts
**“of the pestilence”** — famine
**“shall die: and he that is near”** — carried about by every wind of doctrine
**“by the sword”** — of enemies
**“shall fall”** — divided from the unity of faith
**“and he that remaineth, and is besieged”** — in the city
**“by the famine”** — of the word of God
**“shall die”** — not knowing him who says: “I am the life”
**“and I will accomplish my indignation upon them”** — in all these
6.13:
**“And you shall know”** — those who survive
**“that I am the Lord, when your slain shall be”** — by enemies
**“amongst your idols”** — which they worshipped
**“round about your altars, in every high hill, and on all the tops of mountains, and under every woody tree”** — that is, groves
**“and under every thick oak”** — that where they had sinned there they might be punished
**“the place where they burnt sweet smelling frankincense”** — not to God, who is able to deliver
**“to all their idols”**
• which did not profit them
• And you shall know, etc. Jerome. When the masters of the heretics have been crushed and overcome by churchmen who are instructed in the teaching of the Scriptures, we see them lying slain among the idols of perverse doctrines, which they had fashioned from their own heart; and those who exalted themselves against the knowledge of God laid low on the mountains and hills, under every woody tree, who had pompous words and the shade of leaves but not the fruits of good works; who were under every leafy oak, which bears not the fruit of men but of cattle; where they burnt sweet-smelling frankincense to all their idols. For as the saint delights God by his odor, so does the sinner, in whose person it is said: “My sores are putrified and corrupted, because of my foolishness”; he burns foul-smelling incense to his idols.
6.14:
**“And”** — then
**“stretch forth”** — for vengeance
**“my hand”** — until now restrained
**“upon them”** — heretics
**“And I will make the land”** — their church
**“desolate, and abandoned from the desert of Deblatha”** — which is in the land of Emath, which is now called Epiphania
**“in all their dwelling places”** — so that there is nothing between the desert and the great sea that the hostile sword has not consumed
**“From the desert of Deblatha”** — Jerome. Deblatha means a mass of figs, and of dried figs pressed together; so that, namely, after the heretics have found bitterness in a feigned sweetness, which belonged not to cultivated land but to the wilderness, they may know that the Lord is ruler. For honey drops from the lips of a harlot, which for a time makes the throat of those who eat it fat, and afterwards is found more bitter than gall. This is also signified by the two baskets of figs in Jeremias before the face of the temple, one of very good figs, the other of very bad, of which the one is referred to the Church, the other to the congregation of the malicious.
*Jerome:* Many think Deblatha and Reblatha are the same, because of the resemblance of daleth and resh in the Hebrew letters, which differ by a small stroke.

7.1:
**“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying”** — that is, or to the twelve tribes
**“End”** — The end
**“an end is come upon”** — captivity
**“An end is come”** — Jerome. Now already in the present. For in the fifth year of Sedecias, Ezechiel began to prophesy among the captives in Babylon, and in the ninth year of Nabuchodonosor he besieged Jerusalem, and in the twenty-first year of Sedecias he took it.
7.2:
**“the four quarters of the land”**
• not only upon the mountains and hills
• Upon the four quarters. Jerome. Others read wings; whence Isaias: “From the ends of the earth we have heard praises”, which, namely, were being done by the apostles in the whole world; and elsewhere: “If you sleep among the midst of lots, you shall be as the wings of a dove covered with silver”; and elsewhere: “how often would I have gathered together thy children, as the hen doth gather her chickens under her wings”; and elsewhere: “He spread his wings and took them”. And certain spiritual men, taking the wings of the earth by which we are called to heavenly things, set down four kinds of believers: the house of Aaron, the house of Levi, the house of Israel, and those that fear the Lord; whence: “Bless the Lord, house of Israel; bless the Lord, house of Aaron; bless the Lord, house of Levi; you that fear the Lord, bless the Lord.” In Aaron they understand the priesthood; in Levi, the keepers of the temple and the ministers; in Israel, the whole people; in those that fear the Lord, the proselytes.
7.3:
**“Now is an end come upon thee, and I will send my wrath”** — anthropopathos
**“upon thee, and I will judge thee according to thy ways”** — as if not unjustly, and yet from indignation
**“and I will set all thy abominations against thee”** — that you may understand what you have done
7.4:
**“And my eye shall not spare thee, and I will shew thee no pity: but I will lay thy ways upon thee”** — that you may see
**“and thy abominations shall be in the midst of thee”** — that you may know
**“And you shall know”** — thus
**“that I am the Lord”**
• alone
• Thy ways, etc. Like to this is that: “I will revenge Jacob my servant according to his ways, and will repay him according to his inventions.”
**“And my eye shall not spare thee”** — Jerome. As a physician cuts and burns in order to spare, he does not spare. An incurable wound must be cut away with the knife, lest the sound part be drawn in. God scourges every son whom he receives; whence: “I will strike and I will heal.” Every medicine has bitterness for a time, but the fruit of the pain is shown in health; whence Amos: “You only have I known of all the tribes of the earth; therefore I will visit upon you all your iniquities.”
7.5:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: One affliction, behold an affliction is come”** — unique
**“One affliction”** — the vengeance of God
**“behold it is come”** — as if it is before your eyes; you will no longer escape
7.6:
**“An end is come, the end is come”** — your iniquity is complete
**“it hath awaked”** — it has slept until now
**“against thee, behold it is come”** — as if, lest you think I threaten future things, I show with my finger
**“An end is come”** — Jerome. That is, the extreme of your sins, according to that: “Fill ye up the measure of your fathers,” and that: “the iniquities of the Amorrhites are not yet at the full”; while this was being fulfilled, the punishment was put off.
*Jerome:* We can interpret this spiritually against the people of the Jews, upon whom came the end and the consummation, “from the blood of Abel the just, even unto the blood of Zacharias the son of Barachias”. For as long as they had not laid hands on the Son of God, the sentence of the Lord slept for them; but after they killed the heir, that the inheritance might perish, there awoke against them the whole order of miseries and perplexity, because they sought not heavenly things but desired to cleave to the earth.
*Jerome:* These things can be said of the last captivity, when after the killing of Christ the end came upon them. And sin awoke against them, and that saying of the apostle was fulfilled: “Now the wrath of God is come upon them to the end.” Then they were judged according to their ways, when the indignation of God was poured out upon them, and they received according to their crimes, that the desolation might remain until the consummation.
7.7:
**“Destruction is come upon thee that dwellest in the land: the time is come”** — is upon all who dwell in the land. But the holy one says: I am a stranger with thee and a sojourner, as all my fathers were.
**“the day of slaughter is near”** — as today also we argue by our eyes.
**“and not of the joy of mountains”** — of the masters, whence: Thou enlightenest wonderfully from the everlasting hills.
7.8:
**“Now very shortly”** — I do not foretell things to come.
**“I will pour out my wrath upon thee, and”** — now.
**“I will accomplish my anger in thee”** — as if there is no wrath without judgment.
**“and I will judge thee according to thy ways”** — works.
**“thy ways”** — not mine.
**“and I will lay upon thee”** — upon thy head, that thou mayest feel it.
**“Now very shortly I will pour out my wrath”** — From the fifth year of the transmigration of king Jechonias to the ninth year of the reign of Sedechias, when Nabuchodonosor besieged Jerusalem, there are three years in between; whence it is rightly said: Now very shortly.
7.9:
**“And my eye shall not spare”** — He who alone beholds all things, through whom the world sees all things.
**“neither will I shew mercy: but I will lay thy ways upon thee”** — the cause why he does not spare.
**“I will lay upon thee. And thy abominations”** — that thou mayest know, and by repentance amend.
**“shall be in the midst of thee: and you shall know that I am the Lord that strike”** — who strike whom I love.
7.10:
**“Behold the day, behold it is come: destruction is gone forth”**
• now from the counsel of God.
• that is, the near captivity is shortened and threatens.
**“the rod hath blossomed”**
• with which he threatened, and from the blossom has brought forth the fruit of plagues.
• which you have deserved.
**“pride hath budded”** — The rod hath blossomed, etc. Jerome. Of which: “I will not take my rod from thy son.” And the apostle: “What will you? shall I come to you with a rod?” etc. David also says: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod: and their sins with stripes. But my mercy I will not take away from him.” The end of the blossoming rod is health and correction, which does not come by the merit of those who are corrupted.
7.11:
**“Iniquity is risen up into a rod of impiety”** — with which you beat your subjects impiously.
**“nothing of them”** — not of them, who indeed are dragged by their masters like dumb animals.
**“nor of their people, nor of the noise of them”** — by which, led astray by their masters, they cried: Crucify, crucify him.
**“And”** — and therefore.
**“there shall be no rest among them”** — but eternal captivity.
7.12:
**“The time is come, the day is at hand”** — of captivity.
**“who”** — therefore who.
**“The time is come”** — Jerome. Not only for Jerusalem but also for him to whom it is said: “Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee: and whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?” And the apostle says, “The time is short”; and elsewhere: “the fashion of this world passeth away”; and he put the present time, for it slips away daily and never continues in the same state; and the Lord says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away.” What then can be perpetual in human affairs?
**“Let not the buyer”** — Jerome. It is natural to rejoice in buying possessions and to mourn in selling, but with captivity impending both are vain; whence: The time is short; those who have, let them be as if they had not; and those who weep, as if they did not weep; and those who buy, as if they did not possess.
7.13:
**“For the seller shall not return”** — by the manner of the jubilee, because before the jubilee captivity will come.
**“although their life be yet among the living”** — as those who now live will see captivity, and it will not be deferred for long.
**“For the vision”**
• the threat foreseen.
• by which it comes about.
**“which regardeth all the multitude thereof, shall not go back”** — void
**“neither shall man be strengthened in the iniquity of his life”**
• his iniquity will not profit him
• He that selleth, etc. Jerome. We can say that after the prophetic vision departed from the Jews (for “the law and the prophets were until John”), after the killing of the Saviour it will not return to them, nor will they henceforth have prophets; and it is significantly said: for the vision that regardeth all the multitude thereof shall not go back.
• For it shall return to those who believe: namely to the apostles and to the remnants who are made safe.
7.14:
**“Blow the trumpet”**
• you who serve this office
• which having been heard
• Jerome. We read of trumpets in many places, as: “lift up thy voice like a trumpet”; and elsewhere: “Blow up the trumpet on the new moon, on the noted day of your solemnity”; and in the apostle: “with the command, and with the trumpet of God, shall come down from heaven”; and in the Gospel: “Sound not a trumpet before thee.” And in Numbers we find trumpets of beaten work and of silver, which are compared to prophetic and apostolic teaching; and it is commanded that all be made ready for battle at the sign of the clangor and the trumpet.
**“let all be made ready”**
• Ironically.
• to battle against the Babylonians
**“And”** — yet
**“there is none to go to the battle”** — because it did not profit to be warned
**“for my wrath”** — with God angered, human strength is nothing
**“shall be upon all the people thereof”** — Jerusalem, or the land of the Jews
*Jerome:* In our land also, that is, Jerusalem, when either public persecution or the incentives of vices strive to overcome us, the teachers in vain call us back with the trumpet and hasten to prepare us for battles, since there is no strength in us, because our present sins have deserved the wrath of God.
7.15:
**“The sword without: and the pestilence, and the famine within”** — as above
**“he that is in the field”** — outside the Lord’s city, that is, the church
**“by the sword”** — of the devil
**“shall die; and they that are in the city”**
• negligent
• not preparing foods, by which the one who works his land will be filled with loaves
7.16:
**“And such of them as shall flee shall escape”** — that is, the few who have avoided the sword of heretics, or the famine and death of sloth
**“they shall be in the mountains”** — you will not be saved elsewhere
**“like doves”** — Whence: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly and be at rest?”
**“of the valleys”** — then
**“all of them trembling, every one for his”** — for
**“Like doves”** — Jerome. These doves, as long as they are in the valleys, tremble at every little thing; we are bidden to imitate their innocence, of which it is said: “If you sleep among the midst of lots, you shall be as the wings of a dove covered with silver,” etc. In the likeness of this the Holy Spirit descended and remained upon the Saviour.
7.17:
**“All hands”** — no one will dare to rebel
**“shall be made feeble”** — by fear
**“and all knees shall run with water”**
• from the greatness of terror the bladder will not be able to hold back the flowing waters
• All hands shall be made feeble. Jerome. In our land, that is Judea, the Church, in which is the confession of God, when iniquity abounds and charity grows cold, all the hands of good works are made feeble, and the knees run with water: of those, namely, who seek unclean embraces, suffering a flow of seed. Such ought to gird themselves with the haircloth of penance and fear the judge to come; whence: “Strengthen ye the feeble hands, and confirm the weak knees.”
7.18:
**“And they shall gird themselves with haircloth”** — of penance
**“and fear shall cover them”** — this was done to that people not only under the Babylonians but under the Romans
**“and shame shall be upon every face”** — The redness of the face is a sign of shame; the consciousness of sins shines in the face, which is the hope of salvation. Whence, to one glorying in his sins it is said: “Thou hast the forehead of a harlot; thou knowest not how to blush.”
**“and baldness upon all their heads”**
• which is a sign of mourning
• The saints of God, that is, the Nazarites, and those who have deserved to come to the priesthood, do not shave their heads, for they have no works of death, nor are they made unclean, because they are holy, that is, Nazarites of the Lord; and if anyone should die near them, all their former days are not reckoned as of their sanctification. Samuel, because he was a saint of God, possessed the everlasting ornaments of the head; whence in the Canticles: “thy locks are black as a raven.” Samson, who lost his hair, lost his strength, and when his hair grew again he recovered his former strength, so that dying he slew many more than he had slain living. Eliseus, although he had baldness of the body, yet because he was a Nazarite of the Lord, enjoyed the locks of the head; whence the little boys, because they were little and had not yet come to manly age, mocking his baldness and saying: “Go up, thou bald head; go up, thou bald head,” were torn by the bites of wild beasts, whose dwelling is the forests and woods.
**“Upon all”** — Which signifies mourning, namely, when the hair loses its beauty and we lose the comeliness of our locks; whence: “Instead of a well set hair, baldness” on account of your works; and another prophet says: “all heads in every place shall be shorn, and every beard shaved”; and Micheas: “Make thee bald, and be polled for thy delicate children: enlarge thy baldness as the eagle”; and baldness is commanded to be made over the dead.
7.19:
**“Their silver”**
• and then, with captivity pressing, let those things not be a burden to the fleeing which a little before were pleasures
• Speech.
**“shall be cast forth, and their gold shall become a dunghill”**
• because he who is outside the church cannot have cleanness
• teeth dashed against the most precious metal are hurt no less than by a hard stone
**“and their gold”** — Sense.
**“their”** — who are outside the Church
**“shall not be able to deliver them”**
• from famine or siege
• from eternal hunger
**“in the day of the wrath of the Lord”**
• sensuality
• the eyes of the wicked are insatiable
**“They shall not satisfy their soul, and their bellies shall not be filled”** — because from it idols are made, condemning their worshippers
**“because it hath been the stumblingblock of their iniquity”** — silver and gold
**“Their silver shall be cast forth”** — Jerome. Those who flee from Jerusalem cast away their gold and silver on the broad and spacious way that leads to death, because they have left the narrow way of salvation.
**“Their silver and their gold”** — Jerome. Silver is eloquence, gold the sense of the Scriptures; these, which are the choice things of the world and were given to us for ornament, heretics have set for fuel and matter of pride, and out of them they have made images of their diverse doctrines, and of their abominations and stumblingblocks, so that from whence they could have worshipped and adored God, from thence they give offence.
7.20:
**“and the ornament”** — as those things which I had given for ornament
**“they have turned into pride; and have made of it the images of their abominations, and idols; therefore I have made it”** — gold and silver
**“into uncleanness”** — Symmachus rendered it as loathing, showing the filth of idols.
7.21:
**“And I will give it into the hands of strangers”** — of enemies
**“for spoil, and to the wicked of the earth for a prey, and they shall defile it”** — therefore
**“And I will give it”** — Jerome. We too are handed over into the hands of enemies, and of those alien to God, when we make our ornaments the images of demons; and all our glory is possessed by the wicked, so that they may subject us to their power.
7.22:
**“And I will turn away my face”** — that I may not see these abominations
**“from them”** — who are unworthy of my face
**“And”** — then
**“they shall violate”** — Turned away, he does it.
**“my secret place”** — the Holy of Holies, which lay open only to the priests and to the high priest alone
**“And robbers shall enter into it”** — Jerome. We know that this was done both by the Babylonians, and by Antiochus and Pompey, and finally under Vespasian and Titus, when the temple was overthrown and all was fulfilled that the prophetic word records. Allegorically: in our case, because of our evil works God turns away his face, and so the secret place of God is violated, so that in place of priests and saints robbers enter in and everything is defiled, so that the place which ought to have been of holiness becomes a place of uncleanness; whence: “My house shall be called the house of prayer; but you have made it a den of thieves.”
7.23:
**“Make a shutting up”** — The Lord to the prophet
**“for the land is full of the judgment of blood, and the city is full of iniquity”** — The same also happens to us if our land is full of bloodshed and our dwelling full of iniquity.
*Jerome:* Make a shutting up, that is, shut up my wrath in a brief word; so that, since the land is full of the judgment of blood (for all judge in blood, shedding innocent blood, which Scripture records the Jews also did in the case of Naboth), so their blood may be shed, and the city be shown full of iniquity. For under Manasses also Jerusalem was filled from gate to gate with the blood of the prophets; and a shutting up shall come upon them, so that no one can escape.
7.24:
**“And I will bring”** — in place of the prophets and priests
**“the worst”** — Babylonians or demons
**“of the nations, and they shall possess their houses”** — souls; the temple of God; the seed; and what you yourselves are
**“And”** — so
**“I will make the pride of the mighty to cease”** — by which it deserved this
**“and they shall possess their sanctuary”** — which a pig entering has defiled, and therefore they are not mine.
**“their”** — not mine
7.25:
**“When distress cometh upon them, they will seek for peace and there shall be none.”** — which surpasses all understanding; whence: “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you.”
**“Distress”** — Jerome. He who has heard “Peace be to this house” and has neither kept it nor retained it in his heart, but has driven it away by evil works, will seek it and will not find it.
7.26:
**“Trouble shall come upon trouble, and rumour upon rumour”** — heaping evils upon evils
**“and they shall seek a vision of the prophet, and the law shall perish from the priest, and counsel from the ancients.”** — the prophet’s own words foresee the future things; the priests interpret the law; the elders examine counsel; whence: “in the council of the just and in the congregation, the works of the Lord.”
**“Trouble”** — On the contrary, it is said to the saints: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice”; and: “They shall go from virtue to virtue,” so that present goods may add to future goods.
**“and they shall seek”** — Jerome. Daily these things are sought in the churches, which, having lost vision, law and counsel, vainly boast that they have prophets, priests and elders.
7.27:
**“The king”**
• therefore
• Sedecias
**“shall mourn, and the prince”** — all of the Jews
**“shall be clothed with sorrow, and the hands of the people”** — when these things have happened
**“of the land”** — not of God; whence: “They that depart from thee shall be written in the earth, but the names of the saints are written in heaven.”
**“shall be troubled.”** — losing their order
**“I will do to them according to their way, and will judge them according to their judgments”** — according to that: “With what judgment you judge, you shall be judged”; and that: “Wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself.”
**“will judge them, and”** — thus
**“they shall know”** — at last
**“that I am the Lord.”** — namely, that they may feel through torments whom they did not perceive through benefits
**“The king shall mourn”** — Jerome. Allegorically. The king mourning for our sins is Christ, who says: “What profit is there in my blood, whilst I go down to corruption?” and weeping over the city he says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered together thy children,” etc. The princes are either good, that is, the apostles, who mourn for sinners, or evil, to whom it is said: “Hear the word of the Lord, ye princes of Sodom”; who, according to the Septuagint, are clothed with sorrow, because they have not the armor of God and are not clothed with Christ. For as many as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ.
**“According to their way”** — Jerome. God repays sinners according to their ways, but toward the saints his mercy exceeds measure. For “the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, that shall be revealed in us.” “The wages of sin is death,” according to their works. But the virtue of the just shall enjoy the bounty of the Lord; whence: “But the grace of God, life everlasting.”
**“and they shall know that I the Lord”** — Jerome. This verse is often put in this book, because the knowledge of God follows torments and sufferings, so that they may come to know through torments whom they did not understand through benefits.

8.1:
**“And it came to pass in the sixth year, in the sixth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I sat in my house”** — fleeing the crowd of the multitude
**“and the ancients of Juda sat before me”** — either wishing to hear the words of the prophet, or lying in wait
**“And”** — then
**“fell”** — suddenly
**“there upon me”** — “Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above.”
**“the hand of the Lord God”** — an operation, so that I might know the mysteries of the vision
**“And it came to pass in the year”** — In the fifth year of the captivity of Jechonias, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, the previous vision was made to the prophet; but this one in the sixth year of the same king, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month, that is, from the former a year and two months later; for either the prophecy was interrupted for so long a space, or the things were done which the foregoing discourse contains.
**“In the sixth year”** — Jerome. The number six belongs to the making of the world, which was made in six days; the fifth day of the month, the number five, to the five senses of the flesh, which look upon earthly things and do not yet contemplate heavenly ones; because the word is directed to the elders of Juda, of whom seventy held censers and twenty-five in the temple adored the sun.
**“and the ancients of Juda”** — The elders of Juda, not of Israel, that is, of the ten tribes who were carried away earlier; for the speech is to those who were led into captivity from the tribe of Juda with Jechonias.
8.2:
**“And”** — thus
**“And I saw, and behold a likeness”** — a likeness of a thing, not the thing itself
**“as the appearance of fire: from the appearance of his loins, and downward, fire”** — by fire are purged the works of coition, which are signified in the loins, down to the lower parts
**“and from his loins, and upward, as the appearance of brightness, as the appearance of amber”** — the works of virtues, which rise from the loins to what is higher, have brightness and splendour
**“From the appearance of his loins”** — Jerome. But note that the fire is not carried all the way to the feet, nor the brightness of the amber up to the head, but downward and upward; so that both in sinners and in saints, according to the diversity of merits, one reaches to this or that member, another to that or that; and as those who hold to the perfection of holiness reach even to the crown of the head, so those who lie in the depth of sin have the soles of fiery feet.
8.3:
**“And the likeness of a hand was put forth”** — not the hand itself; for in God nothing is corporeal
**“took me by a lock of my head”** — For the whole head cannot be grasped by the hand.
