**“and the spirit lifted me up between the earth and the heaven, and brought me in the vision of God into Jerusalem”** — in spirit, not in body, as we can behold the heavens and the depths of the sea and the lower regions, that is, grasp the reasons of each thing by thought.
**“near the inner gate”** — whence he could see other things.
**“that looked toward the north”**
• of the outer court.
• from which evils flare up; from which the pot is kindled.
**“where was set the idol”** — Baal.
**“of jealousy to provoke to jealousy”**
• of God.
• The idol, namely, which provokes the Lord to jealousy and zeal; whence: “They have provoked me with that which was no god, and I will provoke them with that which is no people.”
**“The likeness of a hand”** — Of a human body, of course, so that he who is taken may not be frightened. For if it had seized him in the likeness of a serpent or other beast, it would not undeservedly have terrified him.
**“and lifted me up”** — Jerome. First he is seized by the likeness of a hand, then lifted up by the spirit, not at once to heaven but between earth and heaven, that leaving earthly things for the time he may hasten to heaven. And we can say that the prophet was seized by the likeness of God’s hand on account of good works, and is lifted up by the Spirit on account of knowledge of spiritual things.
8.4: **“And behold the glory of the God of Israel was there, according to the vision which I had seen in the plain.”** — And behold the glory was there, that is, that by its presence it might destroy the idol and the temple; whence the overthrow of the temple quickly follows. Whence Isaias says that a narrow bed cannot hold two, and a short cloak cannot cover both. As if to say: “What agreement hath Christ with Belial?” and “What agreement hath the temple of God with idols?”
8.5:
**“And”** — after this.
**“he said to me”** — or the Spirit who lifted me up.
**“Son of man, lift up thy eyes towards the way of the north.”** — for there is the statue of Baal.
8.6:
**“the great abominations that the house of Israel committeth here, that I should depart far off from my sanctuary? and turn thee yet again and thou shalt see greater abominations.”**
• which lie hidden within.
• This too can be understood of our city Jerusalem and of our temple, since like Ophni and Phinees we work the wickedness of idols in the tabernacle of God, and fornicate with those who have vowed themselves to the warfare and service of God, and we pluck the first-fruits of the sacrifices, giving them for the use of dependents and servants, and we do everything for the sake of gain. But if what we see is so great, how much greater are the things that escape our sight!
**“Son of man, dost thou see, thinkest thou”** — Jerome. As if you should not think that I destroy the temple undeservedly and abandon my city, look at what they do here, and do not think there is an end of wickedness in these things; you will see still greater ones.
8.7: **“And he brought me in to the door of the court: and I saw”** — in vision.
8.8: **“And he said to me: Son of man, dig in the wall. And when I had digged in the wall, behold a door.”** — Dig in the wall, that is, that you may enlarge the hole which you saw, and when it is opened may see what you did not see while standing outside. In this it is shown that both in churches and in each of us, greater things are shown through small vices, and as if through holes one comes to the greatest abominations. For the tree is known by its fruits, as “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh”; the words bursting forth are a sign of the inner man. Whence: foul speech sometimes reveals the lustful man; the desire for a trifling thing marks hidden avarice. For greater things are shown by lesser; and conscience cannot be disguised in the face and eyes, when a luxurious and wanton mind shines in the countenance, and the secrets of the heart are made known by the movement of the body and by gestures. Whence: alas, it is hard not to betray a crime by the face.
8.10:
**“And I went in and saw”** — in vision.
**“and behold every form of creeping things, and of living creatures, the abomination, and all the idols of the house of Israel, were painted on the wall all round about.”** — And behold every likeness: not only was there the idol of jealousy at the entrance of the gate, but all the walls of the temple were painted with various images of idols, so that there was no beast which the painting of the wall did not show. This we see to this day in the temples of the Gentiles, where a foolish religion adores all kinds of beasts; whence Virgil: “and monsters of gods of every kind.”
**“And behold every form”** — We too paint idols on the walls of our temple when we lie under vices, and paint in our heart the consciousness of sins and various images, of which it is said: “O Lord, in thy city thou shalt bring their image to nothing,” and elsewhere: “Nevertheless man passeth as an image.” For there is no man who does not at some time have the image either of holiness or of sin; whence of fury it is said: “Their madness is according to the likeness of a serpent: like the deaf asp,” etc.; and of wicked men: “Ye offspring of vipers, who hath shewed you to flee from the wrath to come?”; and of the crafty man: “Go and tell that fox”; and of lovers of women: “horses mad after women.” Of brutes also and the senseless: “Do not become like the horse and the mule,” and many things of this kind.
8.11:
**“And seventy men of the ancients of the house of Israel, and Jezonias”** — He is named as if the chief priest, who, having lost religion, worshipped idols in the temple of God.
**“the son of Saaphan”** — that is, of judgment and condemnation.
**“stood in the midst of them”** — firm in wickedness.
**“that stood”** — in the evil of the obstinate.
**“before the pictures”** — which they worshipped.
**“every one had a censer”** — for sacrificing.
**“in his hand: and a cloud of smoke went up from the incense”** — rising from the incense, it showed the sacrileges of those offering.
**“And seventy men”**
• Jerome. We must pray that the elders of the house of Israel, multiplying the sacred number seven by seven tens, do not stand in their errors and worship pictures of idols, and the smoke of sacrilege not rise up resisting God.
• It signifies that not all the priests did these things, but perhaps were subject to other sins.
*Jerome:* When we have seen the wicked people gathered together, of which it is said: “I have hated the assembly of the malignant,” and rulers worse than the people, and a prince more wicked still, who is perfect for the people and the priests, let us say that Jechonias stands before the pictures, and that each one holds censers, adoring not the majesty of God but their own opinions, and that no good odor reaches God but a stench reaches the idols.
8.12:
**“And he said to me: Surely thou seest”** — or you have heard.
**“O son of man, what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every one in private in his chamber”** — as if from these it is shown what each does in his chamber.
**“for they say: The Lord seeth us not”** — many think that the Lord does not care for such things and that our sins do not reach him.
**“Thou seest, O son”** — Jerome. According to the anagogical sense we can understand the leaders of the churches doing in darkness what it is shameful even to say: this is the hidden man, of whom it is said: “enter into thy chamber ... thy Father who seeth in secret will repay thee.”
**“Seeth not”** — If we thought of the Lord as present, seeing all things and avenging, we would sin scarcely or never.
**“the Lord hath forsaken”** — Jerome. This also belongs to the philosophers, who from the course and constancy of the stars suppose that the heavenly things are providently ruled, and that earthly things are despised, as if nothing right is done on earth according to order.
8.13: **“And he said to me”** — Jerome. After the vices of the princes and the elders, women are brought in mourning for a lover, deprived of his company, and rejoicing if they can obtain it. Those who subtly interpret the fables of the Gentiles follow the killing and rising again of Adonis with lament and joy, one of which they think is shown in seeds that die in the earth, the other in crops by which the dead seeds are born again. We too call those women who either grieve or rejoice at the goods or evils of the world with a soft and effeminate mind, and who mourn Thamuth, that is, what they in the world call most beautiful.
8.14:
**“And he brought me in by the door of the gate of the Lord's house, which looked to the north: and behold women sat there mourning for Adonis”**
• Others: Thamuth.
• And behold women sat there mourning for Adonis, whom the Hebrews and Syrians call Thamuth; whence, because according to the Gentile fable the lover of Venus, a most beautiful young man, is told to have been killed and to have come to life again in the month of July, they call that same month of July by the same name, and celebrate for him a yearly solemnity, in which he is mourned by women as if dead, and sung and praised as if coming to life again.
8.15:
**“And he said to me: Surely thou hast seen, O son of man: but turn thee again and thou shalt see greater abominations than these”** — aforesaid
**“greater abominations”** — He will know that all heretics are worse than the former ones, that is, than the idol of jealousy, and the figures of animals painted on the wall, and the women mourning Adonis, through whom idolatry and pleasure are shown, who understands the prophet saying: “Seeing thou hast hated discipline: and hast cast my words behind thee,” and elsewhere: “they have turned their backs to me.” We are not ignorant that Marcion and other heretics, who tear the Old Testament to pieces, despise the Creator, that is God, and worship and adore some other new god whom they have fashioned from their own heart. And all the heretics of our time, who preach the Son of God a creature and yet adore him, having left the temple of divinity and holding it behind their back, confess that they adore a creature. But we so adore the sun of justice that we adore God in the temple of the Old Testament, where is the law and the prophets, where the cherubim and the propitiatory.
8.16:
**“And he brought me into the inner court of the house of the Lord: and behold at the door of the temple of the Lord, between the porch and the altar, were about five and twenty men having their backs”** — despising the Creator
**“towards the temple of the Lord, and their faces to the east”** — against which the Lord taught to pray wherever men may be, lest they worship toward the east after the manner of the Gentiles
**“and they adored towards the rising of the sun”** — that is, worshipping the creature
**“were about five and twenty men”** — It signifies twenty-five men, who are set in a square on a solid footing, and from the five senses make by five times five the figure of a quadrangle, not only having the temple behind their back but, after the manner of idols, putting to their nostrils a branch of palms, which in Greek are called Bacce, that by this he may signify that they adore idols.
8.17: **“because they have filled the land with iniquity”** — Heretics, who have filled the land with iniquity and “have turned to” the knowledge of a falsely so-called name, to provoke the Lord to anger; they do not fear to worship the idols which they have fashioned.
8.18:
**“Therefore”** — for all these things
**“Therefore I also will deal with them in my wrath”** — Not that he acts cruelly, as the heretics falsely claim. For Paul, whom they call a worshipper of the good God, says something similar: “If I come again, I will not spare.” For those who do not understand what profits them, and often pray, it is expedient that they not be heard; whence in praying we say: “Thy will be done,” not ours. It is a mark of great happiness not to deserve mercy in the present. So to these who are of the house of Juda and have departed from the confession of the Church, the Lord will not spare when they cry with a loud voice; whence: “Their cry has come to me,” etc. He will not hear them, that being forced by evils they may understand what they have done.

9.1:
**“And he cried in my ears with a loud voice, saying”** — The Seventy: “To me vengeance, and I will repay, saith the Lord.”
**“The visitations of the city are at hand”** — the captivity being near
**“and every one hath a destroying weapon in his hand”** — he had not, as the Seventy translated; for he narrates present and future things, not past.
**“The visitations are at hand”** — Every vengeance is a visitation, as of a sick man awaiting the physician. Whence: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with stripes. But my mercy I will not take away from him.”
*Jerome:* He who strikes the wicked because they are wicked, and has the instruments of slaughter to kill the worst, is a minister of God.
9.2:
**“And behold six men”** — angels of God, obedient to the will
**“came”** — for taking away the sins of men, who were made on the sixth day
**“from the way of the upper gate”** — that is, the third gate
**“which looketh to the north: and each one had his weapon of destruction in his hand”** — the seventh, namely
**“and there was one man”** — Christ
**“in the midst of them clothed”** — in the habit of a high priest
**“with linen”** — in Hebrew, baddim
**“and had a writer's inkhorn”** — that he might write down the sins of all and separate the number of the saints from the sinners
**“at his reins: and they went in, and stood by the brazen altar”**
• there were two altars: one of incense, inside, golden; the other of burnt offerings before the temple, bronze
• And they stood, ready at the command of him who bids, so that they might know that whoever they saw there whose sins had not been forgiven is subject to the Lord’s sentence and to slaughter.
**“weapon of destruction”** — The Seventy: the axe, of which: “Behold the axe is laid to the root of the tree.”
**“There was also one man”** — Of whom John says: in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks, “one like the Son of man.”
*Jerome:* For “linen,” which we have rendered according to Symmachus, the Septuagint have “podere,” Theodotion has the Hebrew word itself, “baddim,” and Aquila has translated it as something chief; where we put “inkhorn,” the Septuagint put “a sapphire girdle about his reins.” Aquila: “the scribe’s rasti in his hands”; Aquila: “melanodochion,” that is, the scribe’s inkhorn, “at his loins”; Symmachus: “he had the writer’s tablets at his reins.” “Atramentarium” in Greek is “calamarium,” because the reeds are laid up in it; others more expressively call it “thecae,” because they cover the writers’ reeds.
9.3:
**“And the glory of the Lord of Israel went up from the cherub”** — Singular number, masculine gender; cherubim, plural number, neuter gender.
**“upon which he was, to the threshold of the house: and he called to the man”** — Christ, who is “a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedech,” and the angel of great counsel.
**“to the threshold of the house”** — Others: the open court of the house, which, namely, is not pressed down by a roof but enjoys the freedom of the air.
**“clothed with linen”** — The Seventy: a podere, which because it reaches down to the feet is so called; it is one of the eight vestments of the high priest, which in Latin is called talaris, about which Jerome composed a splendid work.
9.4:
**“And the Lord said to him”** — the man clothed with linen
**“Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem: and mark Thau upon the foreheads of the men that sigh, and mourn for all the abominations”** — according to that: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?”
**“that are committed in the midst thereof”**
• Publicly.
• The letter Thau, the last in the ancient letters of the Hebrews, which the Samaritans use to this day, has the likeness of the cross, which is often signed on the foreheads of Christians, and by whose protection we are signed. There are those who think that, because this letter is the last in the Hebrew alphabet, it is shown that in the multitude of sinners the remnants of the saints remain. But those who sigh and mourn are saved, because they neither sinned nor consented to sinners, and lamented the sins of others, as Samuel for Saul, and Paul for those who did not do penance; whence: “We who are in this tabernacle do groan,” and elsewhere: “I have great sadness, and continual sorrow in my heart.”
**“and mark Thau”** — Thau, which is of course the last of the twenty-two letters among the Hebrews, shows perfect knowledge in the men who sigh and mourn. But the Hebrews maintain that, since among them the law is called Thora and this letter is written at the beginning of its name, they receive this mark who have fulfilled the precepts of the law.
9.5:
**“And to the others”** — six men.
**“he said in my hearing: Go ye after him through the city”** — who left us an example that we should follow his steps.
9.6:
**“old”** — according to that: “The understanding of man is grey hair.”
**“young”** — who is most ready for the wars of faith.
**“and maidens”** — who keeps chastity with her whole mind.
**“children”** — who is nourished with the milk of infancy and cannot yet take solid food.
**“and women”** — who by weakness of soul bear witness to the frailty of their sex.
**“Utterly destroy”** — who can say: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us.”
**“but upon whomsoever you shall see Thau, kill him not, and begin ye at my sanctuary”** — The Seventy: begin at my saints.
**“So they began at the ancient men”**
• who held censers and offered sacrifice.
• whence sin began, there judgment begins.
**“who were before the house”** — there is no sanctity of place when God is offended.
**“old and young”** — All these perish if they believe themselves to be anything without the seal of Christ.
**“begin ye at my sanctuary”** — Or it signifies the priests who moved about in the temple and worshipped idols, or those who, for the merit of the priesthood, were called holy among the people, and who, having been among the peoples the cause of sin, were the first to deserve punishment.
9.7:
**“And he said to them: Defile the house, and fill the courts with the slain”** — The angels would not dare to defile the temple with blood unless the Lord had commanded it, the glory departing.
**“Defile the house”** — Everyone who has died in sin defiles the courts of the temple, in which lives he who rises with Christ.
9.8:
**“And the slaughter being ended”** — on those who did not have the seal.
**“And the slaughter being ended I was left”** — Jerome. Some think that this can be understood as from the person of the Lord, of whom Ezechiel went before as a type, concerning the people of the Jews, who “have all gone aside, they are become unprofitable together”; whence: “Save me, O Lord, for there is now no saint.” For the Lord alone was found who “did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.”
**“I was left”** — Jerome. Thinking that of so great a slaughter no one had been left except me. It should be noted, however, that he does not say “I alone remained” but “I remained.” For it is to be understood along with the others who were marked.
**“pouring out thy fury”** — It signifies the greatness of the punishment, as there: “Contempt is poured out upon princes”; and elsewhere: “my steps were well nigh poured out.” And in a good sense: “The charity of God is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost,” and “Grace is poured abroad in thy lips.”
9.9:
**“And he said to me: The iniquity of the house of Israel”** — of the ten tribes.
**“and of Juda”** — of the two.
**“is exceeding great”**
• It is a repetition.
• Jerome. As if the greatness of the punishment answered to the greatness of the iniquity; for, as the Stoics think, either all sins are equal or all punishments.
**“And”** — therefore.
**“the land is filled with blood”** — of the slain.
**“and the city is filled”** — this is because the city is filled with aversion.
**“perverseness”** — from the worship of God.
**“for they have said”** — The cause of so great crimes is revealed: namely, that they did not think God had providence.
**“hath forsaken”** — as they say.
**“The Lord hath forsaken the earth, and the Lord”** — does not care for earthly things; whence here there is toil for the upper ones; that care disquiets the quiet ones
**“seeth not”** — now, and if he has seen before
**“And he said to me”** — Jerome. He consoles the weeping prophet, as if I were not doing this unjustly; they themselves did this to themselves.
9.10: **“Therefore neither shall my eye spare, nor will I have pity: I will requite their way upon their head”** — that is, the hearts, or the princes who are the heads of the people
9.11:
**“And”** — obedience fulfilled
**“And behold the man”** — Christ
**“that was clothed with linen”** — worn down in many ways by human flesh
**“that had the inkhorn at his back, returned the word, saying: I have done as thou hast commanded me”** — as with the seal of thau I have armed the foreheads of those who mourn
**“And behold the man that was clothed with linen”** — The six men to whom it was commanded to pass through the city, following him, etc., report nothing of the kind, because they carried out the sentence not in joy but in mourning, which is proved not by speech but by deed.

10.1:
**“And I saw and behold in the firmament”** — as above
**“that was over the heads of the cherubims”** — of the living creatures
**“as it were the sapphire stone, as the appearance of the likeness of a throne”** — of a throne
**“there appeared over them”** — the cherubim
**“And I saw and behold”** — Jerome. Note in what ways the former vision and this one disagree or agree, or from comparing both you may perceive the divine mysteries without our prompting; and what I advised before, that of the firmament and the throne and the hand of a man, not truth but likeness is spoken. For we do not behold the glory of the Lord face to face, with unveiled countenance, but we see all things in a likeness and image, while we are encompassed with a frail body.
10.2:
**“And fill thy hand”** — Jerome. That after the slaughter and the corpses of the dead he may cleanse Jerusalem, according to that of Isaias: “He will sanctify it in burning fire, and will devour it like the substance of hay.” These are the coals which the prophet, when asked, desires as a remedy for the tongue and for those who lay waste vices with lies: “What shall be given to thee, or what shall be added to thee, to a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals that lay waste.”
**“And he spoke to the man, that was clothed with linen, and said: Go in between the wheels that are under the cherubims and fill thy hand with the coals of fire that are between the cherubims, and pour them out upon the city. And he went in, in my sight”** — It is to be noted that in Isaias, who had sinned only in speech and said that he had unclean lips, one coal is taken with tongs for cleansing. But here, because the city is full of iniquity, and after the punishments many coals are taken for the corpses of the dead, and not with one hand but with both, although this too is understood, that the coals are taken and scattered not for purification but for punishments and torments.
10.3:
**“And the cherubims stood on the right side of the house, when the man went in, and a cloud filled the inner court”**
• from which they had withdrawn
• The cherubim, as holy and heavenly powers, seem to hold the right side of the house of God. But the left parts belong to those that are sent to punishments, of whom it is said: a sending in by evil angels.
10.4:
**“And the glory of the Lord was lifted up from above the cherub to the threshold of the house”**
• recapitulation
• because while the majesty of the Lord is present, punishments are not carried out
**“and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the Lord”** — which was in the court
10.5: **“And”** — therefore
10.6: **“And when he had commanded the man that was clothed with linen, saying: Take fire from the midst of the wheels that are between the cherubims: he went in and stood beside the wheel”** — He went in and stood, stunned either by grief for the city to be punished or by the greatness of the glory; nor does he put his hand to the fire.
10.7:
**“And”** — therefore
**“who took it”** — He does not say what he did when he came out, because he preferred to leave the account of the sad matter for us to understand rather than set it before our eyes.
10.9:
**“And I saw, and behold there were four wheels”** — as above
**“by the cherubims”** — the living creatures
10.12:
**“And their whole body, and their necks, and their hands, and their wings”** — in these he signifies the images of the working of things, not of the members
**“and the circles”** — that is, with iron, by which the roundness of the wood is shaped
10.14:
**“And every one had four faces”** — one living creature
**“one face”** — the first face
**“one face was the face of a cherub”** — the same as above, the face of a calf; whence it is given to understand that the face of the cherub is that of a calf
**“and the second face, the face of a man: and in the third was the face of a lion: and in the fourth the face of an eagle”** — One face, etc. The exposition of the past vision contains the sense of all these; and it must be known that what was said above, the face of an ox on the left of the four, is not to be taken as though one were on the right and another on the left, but the equal order of all is described. For each had four faces, so that they are described not by a difference of places, right and left, but in one order by degrees.
**“and the second face”** — Here they are not described, some on the right and some on the left, but the order of all is equal, because each had four faces.
10.15: **“And the cherubims were lifted up. This”** — Note that we should understand the same in the explanation of the living creature as above.
10.16: **“And when the cherubims went”** — living creatures
10.17:
**“When they stood, these stood: and when they were lifted up, these were lifted up”** — or lifting up
**“for the spirit of life was in them”** — Jerome. All things live for God and perceive their Creator; “he is not the God of the dead, but of the living”; whence also all the bodies of the wheels are full of eyes, and in the psalm it is said: “The heavens shew forth the glory of God, and the firmament declareth the work of his hands. Day to day uttereth speech, and night to night sheweth knowledge.” The sun, moon, sea, rivers, mountains and hills praise the Lord, and the elements revolve in their circuit year by year, and we perceive on earth the order of the heavens, that, keeping the ancient order of the law, they may revolve and run, and we see nothing new upon the earth.
10.18:
**“And the glory of the Lord went forth from the threshold of the temple”**
• where it stood
• of the inner court
**“and stood over”** — Jerome. Thus little by little God’s protection left Israel: first it was in the temple, afterwards it stood in the court or on the threshold; and when it withdrew from the temple, a cloud and darkness filled its inner places; and again the glory itself sat upon the cherubims, and as they at once departed to the outer parts, the wheels followed.
10.19:
**“And the cherubims lifting up their wings, were raised from the earth before me. And as they went out”** — the inner court
**“the wheels also followed. And it stood in the entry of the east gate of the house of the Lord”** — not now in the door of the temple but after the court and after the threshold, at the entrance of the gate
10.20:
**“This is the living creature”** — over which the throne; over which the glory
**“which I saw under the God of Israel by the river Chobar: and I understood that”** — or: because
**“cherubims”** — fullness
**“And I understood that they were cherubims”** — Multitude of knowledge: the knowledge of the mysteries of God, and his throne and rest; whence: “Thou that sittest upon the cherubims, shine forth.” The glory of the Lord always sits in the multitude of knowledge, and it is then made manifest when all things are shown to be ruled by providence, that nothing happens by chance, and that it ought not to be said: “The Lord hath forsaken the earth, and the Lord seeth not”; whence: the gaze of the cherubims and their desire is to forget the things that are past and to stretch themselves forward to the future.
10.22:
**“And as to the likeness of their faces”** — or: faces
**“they were the same faces which I had seen by the river Chobar, and their looks, and the impulse of every one to go straight forward”** — to forget the past and advance to the future

11.1:
**“And the spirit lifted me up, and brought me into”** — Christ, who leads us to the Father
**“to the gate”** — where the glory was
**“the house of the Lord”** — of the Church
**“the east gate, which looketh towards the rising of the sun”** — of righteousness, namely of whom: “Behold a man, the Orient is his name”
**“and lifted me up”** — Jerome. I could not follow the glory as it flew away, that is, so that I might not remain in the temple confused by the cloud of ignorance, but standing in the east gate of the house of the Lord, which looks toward the rising of the sun, might know the mysteries that follow.
*Jerome:* Twenty-five men, referring all things to the five senses. But this number is found in a good sense hardly or never, although in Leviticus they are chosen for the priestly ministry from twenty-five years old. For this is not in the Hebrew but in the Septuagint; for there it is thirty, which is both at the beginning of this prophecy and in the age of the Lord when he was baptized by John. We speak, however, of five wise virgins and five foolish. But here the number five is set in the midst, and according to the quality of those who use it can be referred either to good or to evil.
**“Jezonias the son of Azur, and Pheltias the son of Banaias”** — The number two, namely, which divides unity; and in the number of the second day, according to the Hebrew truth, it is not seen to be approved by the Lord; whence into the ark the unclean are brought in “two and two.” But the Lord, drawing both into one, made both one, and broke down the middle wall of partition, the enmities, in his flesh, condemning them; whence: “I and the Father are one,” that is, that he might call them back from the Jewish duality into one by the priesthood of the Christian faith. Of these Jews, when they were lost, the Lord suffers not under one prince but under two, Anna and Caiphas, that he might show the torn error of their religion.
11.2:
**“And he said to me: Son of man, these are the men that study iniquity, and frame a wicked counsel”** — despairing because of the consciousness of their crimes, and unwilling to repent
**“in this city”** — ready for destruction
11.3:
**“Saying: Were not houses lately built? This city is the caldron, and we the flesh.”** — by the Babylonian, by the burning heat of consumption, whose fiery missiles
**“Were not houses lately built”** — As if, although houses that had fallen before were lately built after the first captivity, we nevertheless know that this city is like a cauldron, and we like flesh to be consumed and burned in it.
11.4: **“Therefore prophesy against them, prophesy, thou son of man.”** — they saying this
11.5:
**“And the spirit of the Lord fell upon me, and said to me:”** — a second time
**“said to me: Speak: Thus saith the Lord”** — because
**“Thus have you spoken, O house of Israel”** — as if you are not the flesh of the lost city, but those whom you have scandalized
**“for I know the thoughts of your heart.”** — testing hearts and reins
11.6: **“You have killed a great many”** — Jerome. As if to say, I will explain how the city is the cauldron and you the flesh, not according to the sense in which you said it, but the one you do not fear. The city indeed will be filled with flesh like a cauldron, yet not with yours but with that of those whom you have slain.
11.7:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord God: Your slain, whom you have laid”** — by scandalizing
**“in the midst thereof, they are the flesh, and this is the caldron: and”** — or as
**“I will bring you forth out of the midst thereof.”** — who think that you are to die in this city
11.8:
**“the sword”** — of the enemies
**“You have feared the sword, and”** — of the enemies
11.9:
**“And I will cast you out of the midst thereof,”** — of the city
**“I will deliver you into the hand of the enemies, and I will execute judgments upon you.”** — as not undeservedly
11.10:
**“You shall fall by the sword”** — although outside the city
**“in the borders of Israel”** — in the bounds of your province
**“I will judge you and you shall know”** — vexation alone will give understanding to hearing
**“that I am”** — not another
11.11:
**“This”** — the city as you think
**“shall not be as a caldron to you, and you shall not be as flesh in the midst thereof: I will judge you in the borders of Israel.”** — because, namely, not among the nations but among Christians
11.12:
**“And you shall know that I am the Lord: because you”** — therefore these things to you
**“in my commandments, you have not walked”** — by advancing
**“and have not done my judgments, but you have done”** — on the contrary
**“according to the judgments of the nations that are round about you.”** — that you should be an example to them
**“And you shall know”** — According to that: “When he slew them, then they sought him”; namely, that they might come to know through torments him whom they did not perceive through benefits.
11.13:
**“And it came to pass, when I prophesied, that Pheltias”** — bending toward ruin
**“the son of Banaias died: and I fell down upon my face”** — with the feeling of one who suffers with them
**“and cried with a loud voice”** — with the ardour of faith
**“and said: Alas, alas, alas”** — for the third time
**“O Lord God: wilt thou make an end of all the remnant of Israel?”** — as though, you being indignant, even the remnant that seemed to remain will perish
**“And it came to pass”**
• Jerome. When Pharao was dead the children of Israel groaned and cried to the Lord; for while he lived they could not. Isaias also, when king Ozias the leper was dead, saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and elevated, and the seraphim standing about him. And understanding that he had unclean lips, he deserves to take a coal from the altar to cleanse his lips. But here, while the strength of God prophesies, the prince who had turned away from the Lord’s service falls, that he may be raised up by Christ. For the Lord is the resurrection, the devil is the fall; whence: “Behold this child is set for the fall,” namely of those who stood in the worst way, “and for the resurrection” of those who had fallen.
• From these we learn that one must not mock those who are delivered to punishments by the judgment of God, nor say to those who have turned from sin, or repent, or have gone out of the church: “Get ye far from the Lord.”
**“Pheltias”** — The other of the princes is kept safe: Jechonias, namely, who is interpreted “his ears resound”, of the soul, namely; son of Azur, which is interpreted “supported” or “help”.
**“of Banaias”** — of a builder or mason, who by falling turned away from the Lord; the son of a very bad building; by merit he falls, prophesying through the one whom the Lord strengthened, who formerly obeyed God and was upheld by his help; he rightly remains in the kingdom.
11.14: **“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:”** — thus complaining
11.15:
**“Son of man”** — as if: these are not those remnants who are in Jerusalem, as you suppose, but those who are captive in Babylon
**“thy brethren”** — of your own stock
**“thy brethren, thy kinsmen, and all the house of Israel, all”** — are
**“to whom ... have said”** — by reproaching
**“the inhabitants of Jerusalem have said: Get ye far from the Lord”** — as if he said: you have gone far from the Lord, because you are captives, and you delivered yourselves up with Jechonias
11.16:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord God:”** — say to them
**“Because far off”**
• from the land of Israel
• a little, that is, from the church
**“I have removed them”** — to be
**“among the Gentiles, and because I have scattered them among the countries”** — strange
**“I will be”**
• therefore
• that, mindful of their sins, those who had withdrawn through vices may return through penance
**“to them a little sanctuary”** — because they obeyed me
**“a little sanctuary”** — Because some of them would not submit to idolatry but were mindful of God’s commandments, like Daniel and the three boys and those like them.
11.17:
**“Therefore speak”** — to his fellow captives, namely those who are in Babylon, the kinsmen of the prophet Ezechiel
**“I will gather you from among the peoples”** — Jerome. Many suppose that these things happened under Zorobabel and Jesus the son of Josedech, and Esdras and Nehemias, to the tribe of Juda and those who returned with them; but the inhabitants of Jerusalem who were taken captive under Sedecias king of Juda, or who fled with Jeremias into Egypt, they say were scattered into all lands and did not return to the city of Jerusalem. But the full conversion of those who were captives, and of the remnants of Israel, is understood in Christ, when the remnants were saved, and three thousand believed in one day. But even daily the proud inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem, “whose heart walketh after their scandals and abominations,” deserve the offence of God. But those who receive a soft heart instead of a stony one return to the Church through penance, and walk in the precepts of the Lord and keep his judgments.
11.18:
**“And they shall go in thither, and”** — having entered
**“shall take away all the scandals, and all the abominations thereof”** — the idols for which you offended God
**“from thence”** — from that ground
11.19:
**“And I will give them one heart”** — of fear and service of God, so that you do not serve different idols
**“and will put a new spirit”** — to which is like: “Create a clean heart in me, O God”
**“will put a new spirit in their bowels: and I will take away the stony heart”** — hard, according to that: “stiff-necked and uncircumcised of heart”; and: “Pharao’s heart was hardened”
**“out of their flesh, and will give them a heart of flesh”** — soft, in which the commandments of God are written on the fleshly tablets of the heart
11.20:
**“That they may walk in my commandments”** — converted
**“and keep my judgments, and do them: and that they may be my people, and I may be their God.”** — who now, against
11.21:
**“whose heart walketh after their scandals”** — the sins by which God is offended
**“and abominations”** — idols
**“walketh after their way”** — life
**“I will lay upon their head, saith the Lord God.”** — for whom to say is to do
11.23:
**“And the glory of the Lord went up from the midst of the city, and stood over the mount that is on the east side of the city.”**
• Wondrously, even to this day, the glory of the Lord, which forsook the temple, stands upon the Mount of Olives, and shining in the sign of the cross looks upon the temple dissolved into ashes.
• And the glory went up. Whence: “Arise, let us go hence.” And: “Your house shall be left to you desolate.” And Josephus says that a voice of angels was heard in the temple: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”
**“And the glory went up”** — Little by little the glory of the Lord withdraws from Jerusalem: first leaving the temple, it stands in the court or on the threshold of the house; afterwards in the entry of the east gate; last of all, the wings being lifted up and the wheels following, it stands over the mount that is on the east of the city, the mount namely of Olivet, whence the Lord ascended to the Father.
**“mount”** — Of Olives, namely as a sign of cutting off and of light, so that from there it might see Jerusalem about to perish and burn.
11.24:
**“And the spirit lifted me up, and brought me into Chaldea, to them of the captivity, in vision, by the spirit of God: and the vision which I had seen was taken up”** — He signifies that he was carried from Babylon to Jerusalem not in body but in spirit
**“the vision which I had seen was taken up from me”** — which had led me in spirit to Jerusalem and had shown me all things
**“To them of the captivity, Jerome.”** — To those, namely, of whom above: “And the ancients of Juda sat before me,” etc., to whom the prophet, present in body, saw visions, all of which happened so that the captives might receive consolation, namely that they should return to Jerusalem and walk in God’s commandments.
11.25: **“And I spoke to them of the captivity all the words of the Lord”** — namely the things

12.2:
**“Son of man, thou dwellest in the midst of a provoking house: who have eyes to see, and see not”** — obstinacy, deprived of the eyes of the heart
**“and ears to hear, and hear not”** — Not by fault of the senses. Whence: “If you were blind, you would not have sin.”
**“for they are a provoking house”** — Of the provoking one: that is, of him who turns me to bitterness, though I am sweet by nature. Whence: “O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet.”
12.3:
**“And thou, O son of man”** — In this chapter he signifies the captivity of Sedechias.
**“prepare thee all necessaries for removing”** — so that by the images they may know the captivity not only by hearing but also by the sight of the eyes
**“and remove by day in their sight: and thou shalt remove out of thy place to another place”** — from heavenly things to earthly things
**“Thou, therefore, O son of man”** — Some will have it that the captivity of Sedecias, whose name is interpreted “the Lord just,” went before as a type of the Saviour, who coming down from heavenly to earthly things took a human body as the vessels of captivity; which we do not approve. For an impious king cannot go before in figure of him who is the example of all piety.
**“And remove”** — Literally, the history of the Kings and the prophet Jeremias tells of Sedechias taken by the Babylonians and Chaldeans, and led from place to place, from Jerusalem, that is, to Babylon, and the rest that Ezechiel says in what follows.
*Jerome:* Those who will have Christ understood by Sedecias take the vessels of captivity as the human body, and the dug-through wall because he broke through the bars of hell, and rising again appeared only to believers; carried on the shoulders, when he ascended with the angelic powers into heaven; he goes out hidden, and veils his face, that the divinity may not be seen in mortal flesh; he does not see the earth, lest it be lit by his eyes, since it does not deserve his sight. For “the eyes of the Lord are upon the just.” But all this he did that by the likeness of a man he might turn the hard hearts of Israel to the faith. He was also given for a portent; whence: “Behold this child is set for the fall and for the resurrection of many in,” etc.
12.4:
**“And thou shalt bring forth”** — He is commanded to do this in figure, which Sedechias did in fact.
**“thy furniture”** — that is, baggage
**“as the furniture of one that is removing by day in their sight”** — these things having been done
**“thou shalt go forth”** — or walk
12.5:
**“Dig thee a way through the wall”** — For by night Sedechias, the wall having been dug through, fled to the deserts of the Jordan, and there was seized by the Babylonians and led to Reblatha, and there his sons were slain before him.
**“Dig thee a way through the wall before their eyes: and thou shalt go forth through it.”** — This is to be noted, that at the same time Jeremias prophesied in Jerusalem and Ezechiel in Babylon, and the prophecy of the former was sent to the captives, and that of the latter to those who dwelt in Jerusalem, that the providence of the one God might be proved in different regions, and that those who heard might understand that what befalls the people comes to pass not by the power of idols but by the command of the Lord.
12.6:
**“In their sight thou shalt be carried out upon men’s shoulders”**
• The Seventy: you will carry.
• that is, little packs, and which fugitives are accustomed to carry for comfort
**“thou shalt be carried out in the dark”** — so that you may not be seen by anyone
**“thou shalt cover thy face”** — or as a sign of blindness. For he was blinded by Nabuchodonosor; or that he may not be recognized and be kept with greater care.
**“and shalt not see the ground”** — For he was led blind into Babylon and did not see it.
**“for I have set thee for a sign of things to come to the house of Israel.”** — For in figure the words of the prophets, as well as the deeds, went before.
12.7:
**“I did therefore as he had commanded me”** — that is
**“I brought forth my goods by day, as the goods of one that removeth: and in the evening I digged through the wall with my hand: and I went forth in the dark, and was carried on men’s shoulders”** — or carrying
12.9:
**“Son of man, hath not the house of Israel, the provoking house, said to thee”** — that is
**“the provoking”** — my sweetness
**“What art thou doing?”** — this
12.10:
**“Say to them: Thus saith the Lord God”** — not man
**“concerneth my prince”**
• Christ
• Sedechias
**“This burden”**
• which I bear
• is
**“that is in Jerusalem, and all the house of Israel”** — or who
12.11:
**“Say: I am a sign of things to come to you”** — that is, I foretell to you the things that are to come
**“as I have done, so shall it be done to them”**
• Led away, and his own.
• because
**“they shall be removed”** — Christ also, and his own, taken captive in this world.
**“and go into captivity”** — Babylon.
12.12:
**“And the prince that is in the midst of them, shall be carried on shoulders”**
• of angels.
• or of beasts, or of his companions.
**“shall be carried”** — into heaven.
**“in the dark”** — unknown to the unbelievers.
**“he shall go forth through the wall”** — the middle wall of enmity, breaking down.
**“they shall dig through”** — his companions.
**“to bring him out: his face”** — of Christ.
**“shall be covered”** — either by fear or by the veil of blindness.
**“That he may not see”**
• of the Jews; for a veil is placed over their hearts.
• Babylon.
12.13:
**“And I will spread my net”**
• taken, with the Lord permitting and dispensing.
• For “him who knew no sin he hath made sin for us”; and elsewhere: “The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, is taken in our sins.”
**“over him, and he shall be taken in my net, and I will bring him”** — The power is mine, not the enemies’.
**“into Babylon”** — namely the confusion of the world.
**“into the land of the Chaldeans”** — who are interpreted as if demons, that he might draw back to salvation those enslaved to demons, and “lead captivity captive.”
**“and he”** — unworthy of his sight.
**“shall not see”** — made blind.
**“and there he shall die”**
• that he might give life to all by his death.
• Indeed it is dangerous to compare the captivity and death of an impious king with the sacrament of the Lord.
12.14:
**“And all that are about him”** — the apostles and apostolic men.
**“his guards”**
• namely
• namely helpers.
**“and his troops I will scatter into every wind”** — “Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth.”
**“And”** — also
**“I will draw out the sword”** — by the hands of enemies.
**“after them”** — that they may be crowned with various martyrdoms.
12.15:
**“And”** — so at last
**“they shall know”** — either themselves or converted through them
**“that I am”** — not another
**“the Lord”** — by whose will all things are done
**“when I shall have dispersed them among the nations, and scattered them in the countries”** — that they may bring forth fruit, and that their fruit may remain
12.16:
**“And”** — yet
**“I will leave a few men of them”** — like John the apostle
**“from the sword, and from the famine, and from the pestilence”** — freed
**“that”** — left behind
**“they may declare”** — by word or by example
**“all their wicked deeds”** — for which they endured such great things
**“their”** — of the Jews and of the Gentiles to whom they shall go
**“among the nations whither they shall go, and”** — then
**“they shall know”** — namely, that having received penance, they may know that I am the Lord
12.19:
**“And say to the people of the land: Thus saith the Lord God to them that dwell in Jerusalem in the land of Israel”** — that is, the inhabitants of the Church, who, if they offend God, will eat their bread in anxiety
**“their bread in care”**
• or: in care
• by hunger for the word of God
• of hunger
**“They shall eat”** — besieged by Nabuchodonosor and by the Chaldeans
**“and drink their water”** — of teaching
**“in desolation”** — thirst
**“that the land may become desolate”** — the inhabitants of the land be destroyed
**“from the multitude”** — of the faithful
**“for the iniquity”** — as if not without cause
**“Their bread in care”** — Jerome. After the prince and his companions he comes to the people. It is said to the inhabitants of Jerusalem that in the evil of the siege they will eat their bread in want and distress, and drink their water not in abundance but in torment and tribulation.
**“of all that dwell therein”** — For the iniquity: or by the vice, namely of the princes who are to be seized and handed over to the Babylonians; or through our hardness we lose the word of God.
12.20:
**“And the cities”** — of the whole world, of the Church
**“that are now inhabited shall be laid waste, and the land shall be desolate”** — from all cultivation
**“And you shall know”** — as if you will know him raging whom you were unwilling to know merciful
**“And you shall know that I am”** — That God may be known as offended, which indeed we can see in a time of persecution.
12.21: **“And the word of the Lord came”** — He had prophesied above against the prince, then against the people. But the multitude, not believing, took up a worn-out proverb, namely: the threat of the prophets will be put off to a long time. Therefore the word of the Lord came to him.
12.22:
**“Son of man, what is this proverb that you have in the land of Israel, saying: The days shall be prolonged”** — of the threat
**“and every vision shall fail”** — of the prophets
**“The days shall be prolonged”** — Even today the unbelieving crowd and the hard hearts of mortals do not receive God’s prophecy, but think that all that the prophets threaten, and what the gospel says, is to be deferred to another time.
12.23:
**“Say to them therefore: Thus saith the Lord God”** — who knows not how to lie
**“I will make this proverb to cease”** — that it be no more said
**“this proverb, neither shall it be any more a common saying in Israel, and”** — therefore
**“tell them that the days are at hand”** — of the captivity
**“and the effect”** — the thing
12.24: **“For there shall be no more any vain visions, nor doubtful divination in the midst of the children of Israel”** — which has an uncertain end, so that at one time it is said and at another it is fulfilled
12.25: **“For I the Lord will speak; and what word soever I shall speak, it shall come to pass, and shall not be prolonged any more; but in your days”** — It signifies the nearby captivity, and Sedecias with the people, and Iamia about to be taken
12.27: **“Son of man, behold the house of Israel, they that say: The vision that this man seeth, is for many days to come”** — is deferred
12.28: **“Therefore say to them: Thus saith the Lord God: Not one word of mine shall be prolonged any more: the word that I shall speak shall be accomplished”** — soon

13.2:
**“Son of man, prophesy thou against the prophets of Israel”** — heretics
**“that prophesy, and thou shalt say to them that prophesy out of their own heart”** — in which heresies have been fashioned
**“Against the prophets of Israel”** — The idiom of Scripture calls each one the prophet of his own prediction and speech; whence they are called prophets of Baal and of idols, and prophets of confusion; and Paul: “One of themselves, a prophet of their own, said: The Cretans are always liars,” etc.; and in Osee: “They know the prophet is mad,” etc. In the Church the good prophets are the apostles and apostolic men; the false prophets are heretics.
13.3:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: Woe to the foolish prophets”** — for there are others who are wise
**“That follow their own spirit”**
• Septuagint: who prophesy out of their own heart
• not of God
**“and nothing”** — of truth
**“see”** — because they have lost the sun of justice
**“And see nothing”** — Whence prophets are called seers. Whence it is said: “The vision of Isaias,” and “The vision of Abdias”; and that: “Lift up your eyes, and see”; and elsewhere: “Open thou my eyes: and I will consider the wondrous things of thy law.”
13.4:
**“Thy prophets, O Israel, were like foxes in the deserts”** — lying in wait for domestic birds
**“Like foxes”**
• Jerome. Of whom it is said: “Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vines”; and elsewhere: “They shall be the portions of foxes.”
• Heretics. Whence: “The foxes have holes: but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.”
13.5:
**“You have not gone up to face the enemy”** — fighting with prayers and resisting God’s sentence
**“You have not gone up”** — As Aaron, who first stood in the midst like a wall and stopped the fire that was devouring the people of Israel. Of Jeremias it is said that he should not meet the Lord nor stand against the wrath of the Lord, namely by perseverance in prayer. For the sentence of the Lord is broken by the prayers of the saints; whence it is said to Moses: “Let me alone, and I will destroy this people.”
13.6: **“See vain things, and foretell lies, saying: The Lord saith, whereas the Lord hath not sent them: and they have persisted to confirm what they have said”** — they do not correct themselves as true prophets do if ever they err
13.7:
**“Have you not seen a vain vision and spoken a lying divination”** — a second time
**“And”** — yet
**“You say: The Lord saith, whereas I have not spoken”** — laying a lie upon me
13.8:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord God: Because you have spoken vain things”** — O heretics
**“Therefore thus”** — Jerome. All these things we can say of the heretic, for all their fictions are dissolved by the wrath of God.
13.9:
**“And my hand shall be upon the prophets that see vain things, and that divine lies”** — therefore
**“They shall not be in the council of my people”** — in the church but in the synagogue of Satan
**“Nor shall they be written in the writing of the house of Israel”** — Whence elsewhere: “they that depart from thee, shall be written in the earth.”
**“Neither shall they enter into the land”**
• of the living
• of the promise, namely
**“Of Israel shall they enter”** — but into the land of the dead
**“And you shall know that I am the Lord God”** — separated from the people of God
13.10:
**“Because they have deceived my people”** — as if they would suffer these things because they deceived
**“Saying”** — namely, announcing prosperous things in place of the rigour of penance
**“Peace, peace”** — namely, not once
**“And there is no peace, and”** — Metaphorically.
**“The people built up a wall”** — through the commands of the law and the threats of the prophets, so that he would ward off every assault, so that those converted to God might be surrounded by this as by a wall.
**“And they daubed it with dirt without straw”** — pure, namely without mixing, and of no strength.
13.11:
**“Say to them that daub without tempering”** — namely, those who promise vain things.
**“That it shall fall: for there shall be an overflowing shower”** — namely, the most savage enemies, the Babylonians and Chaldeans.
**“And I will cause great hailstones”** — hailstones
**“Falling violently from above, and a stormy wind throwing it down”** — so that a sudden whirlwind overturns the unstable wall.
13.12: **“Behold, when the wall is fallen: shall it not be said to you: Where is the daubing”** — the help that you promised.
13.14:
**“And I will break down the wall”** — namely, the defence.
**“That you have daubed with untempered mortar: and I will make it even with the ground, and the foundation thereof shall be laid bare, and it shall fall, and shall be consumed in the midst thereof, and you shall know”** — by the work itself.
13.16:
**“Prophets of Israel”** — who daub.
**“That prophesy to Jerusalem”** — namely, are the cause of evils.
**“And that see visions of peace for her”** — yet
**“And there is no peace”** — which they proclaim.
13.17:
**“And thou, son of man, set thy face against the daughters of thy people”** — so that you signify my wrath.
**“And thou, son of man, set thy face”** — Above, to the false prophets; now he is commanded to prophesy to the false prophetesses, for it is read that prophets of each sex, both true and false, existed.
**“Set thy face”** — Septuagint: harden your face. Like this: “the face of the Lord is upon them that do evil”, and elsewhere: “so let sinners perish at the presence of God.”
**“Against the daughters”** — Heretics, namely, who like women preach pleasure and lust, as Epicurus and the like. For others, like men, praise abstinence, as Pythagoras, and the sophists, who as it were daub the wall and promise some strength. But their building perishes. For “unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.”
**“That prophesy out of their own heart: and do thou prophesy against them”** — False prophets against true prophets, and false prophetesses against the true prophetesses of God, the prophetesses Olda and Debbora, and the four daughters of Philip the evangelist; the false prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla. These, the Hebrews say, were instructed in magic arts and divined by necromancy and a pythonic spirit, such as she was who was seen to raise up the soul of Samuel.
13.18:
**“And say: Thus saith the Lord God: Woe to them”**
• sweet flattery
• Metaphor.
• as Epicurus, Jovinian and Eunomius, whose cry is: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.”
**“That sew cushions under every elbow, and make pillows”** — promising rest, namely.
13.19:
**“And they violated me among my people”** — persuading them to love pleasure.
**“For a handful of barley”** — on which brute animals feed.
**“And a piece of bread, to kill souls”** — calling them dead if nothing is put into their mouth.
**“Which should not die, and to save souls alive”** — in word.
**“Which should not live”** — in deed.
**“To kill”** — They cut short the testimonies of the Scriptures, so as to drag the just to death, and to give life to sinners with empty promises.
13.20:
**“Therefore”** — to be destroyed.
**“Thus saith the Lord God: Behold I declare against your cushions, wherewith you catch”** — free.
**“Flying, and I will tear them off from your arms”** — the cushions, namely, not the prophetesses. For I do not wish the death of a sinner.
**“And I will let go the souls”** — and I will let go the souls
**“That you catch, the souls”** — which you catch; free souls.
13.21:
**“And I will tear your pillows”** — with which the heads of the deceived were veiled, when a man ought to behold the glory of the Lord with unveiled face.
**“And will deliver my people out of your hand, neither shall they be any more in your hands to be a prey”** — that is, prey.
**“And”** — then.
13.22:
**“Because with lies you have made”** — with false fear.
**“The heart of the just to mourn, whom I have not made sorrowful”** — to whom you have imposed fear.
**“And you have strengthened the hands”** — with false promises.
**“that he should not return”** — penitent.
13.23:
**“Therefore you shall not see vain things”** — false visions.
**“nor divine divinations any more”** — For I do not call prophecies those of which there is “no soothsaying in Jacob, nor divination in Israel.”
**“And”** — thus.
**“I will deliver my people out of your hand, and you shall know”** — in the very work.
**“that I am the Lord”** — I who have freed the lost.

14.1:
**“And”** — after these things.
**“some of the ancients of Israel came to me”** — not all, lest all seem to err.
14.2:
**“And”** — that he might show why they had come.
**“the word of the Lord came to me, saying”** — For it is not in the nature of man, even of a holy heart, to know the secrets. Whence: of the Saviour alone it is said, “seeing their thoughts.”
14.3:
**“Son of man, these men have placed”** — The Seventy: thoughts. Symmachus and Theodotion: idol.
**“their uncleannesses in their hearts, and have set up the stumblingblock of their iniquity”** — leaving nothing of their former ways
**“before their face”** — despairing of better things
**“shall I answer when they inquire of me”** — who come in this way
14.4:
**“Therefore”** — Because, that is, they came with a perverse heart.
**“speak to them, and say to them: Thus saith the Lord God”** — as if not from your own person, lest the authority seem slight
**“Man, man of the house of Israel”** — Man, man of the house of Israel: not of other nations, whose error can have pardon.
**“that shall place his uncleannesses in his heart, and set up the stumblingblock of his iniquity before his face, and”** — Thus.
**“shall come”** — with such a heart
**“to the prophet inquiring of me by him: I the Lord will answer him according to the multitude of his uncleannesses”** — In the multitude: that is, according as he wills and believes, he shall hear. For he does not deserve correction who asks with the mind not of learning but of testing.
14.5:
**“That”** — That is, be deceived.
**“the house of Israel may be caught in their own heart, with which they have departed from me through all their idols”** — trusting
**“That the house of Israel may be caught”** — That the house of Israel may be caught. As if they do not leave off their former crimes, they do not deserve to hear the truth, but are to be deceived with a deceitful heart. Whence: “Why do you tempt me, ye hypocrites?” And elsewhere: “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things.”
14.7: **“For every man, man of”** — Secondly, “man, man” is said so that the inner and the outer may be signified. For many, having a bodily face, take on the images of various beasts; whence: “O Lord, in thy city thou shalt bring their image to nothing”; and “Man when he was in honour did not understand: he hath been compared to senseless beasts, and made like to them.” These are not man-men but man-beasts; and in the gospel: “generation of vipers,” etc.—they are not man-men but man-vipers; and elsewhere: “The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests”; and of Herod: “Tell that fox”—they are not man-men but man-foxes. But those who are truly man-men, if they have erred, are corrected by punishments, that they may know that he is the Lord.
14.8:
**“And I will set my face against that man”** — so that by the severity of the countenance the hardness of the brow may be softened
**“and will make him an example, and a proverb”** — so that, he being destroyed, others may know that I am the Lord who know the secrets of the heart
**“and will cut him off from the midst of my people, and”** — Thus.
**“you shall know that I am the Lord”** — you shall know that I am the Lord, proving the hearts and reins
14.9:
**“And the prophet”** — false
**“when the prophet shall err, and speak a word, I the Lord”**
• Not another.
• as sins demand
**“have deceived”** — Or: I deceived.
**“that prophet, and will stretch forth my hand upon him”** — the prophet
**“and will cut him off”** — Like punishment for like sin, so that he who inquires and he who is inquired of bear their iniquity.
**“I the Lord have deceived that prophet”** — As Achab king of Israel, going to battle, would not hear Micheas the prophet, yielding to the false prophets; and Micheas said that he saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and the spirit of error freely offering himself to deceive the king. The devil, who stands in the sight of the Lord, receives power from the Lord first over the substance of Job, then over his body. Balaam the soothsayer is sent by the Lord to deceive Balach the son of Sephor. But all this is said lest it be put down to the strength of the false prophets that the people is deceived and prefers to hear a lie rather than lend its ear to the truth, but rather to the wrath of God.
**“I will deceive the prophet”** — I will deceive the prophet. Whence: “he himself shall scorn the scorners”; and that: “If they walk toward me perversely, I too will walk against them in perverse wrath”; and “with the perverse thou shalt be perverted.”
14.11:
**“that he may go no more astray”** — through their occasion
**“That the house of Israel from me”** — who, that is, was unwilling to hear the words of the Lord
**“nor be polluted with all their transgressions”** — by divinations of this kind
**“but may be my people, and I may be their God”** — or I will be
14.13:
**“Son of man, when a land”** — Son of man, land: the Church.
**“shall sin against me, so as to transgress grievously”** — when it sins against me, so as to transgress the commandments of the Lord
**“I will stretch forth my hand upon it”** — Aggravating the vengeance.
**“and will break”** — He brings four plagues upon the sinful land: famine, sword, pestilence, beasts.
**“the staff of the bread thereof”** — The support of bread.
**“and I will send famine upon it”** — Of the word of God.
**“and will destroy man out of it”** — Rational.
**“and beast”**
• The unlearned man.
• Against men and beasts thou wilt preserve, O Lord.
**“I will stretch forth my hand”** — Jerome. The hand of the Lord is stretched out over the sinful land so that the staff, or strength, of bread may be broken; the outstretched hand threatens blows, though he who lifts it is unwilling to strike sinners, but to frighten them by the stretching and to keep the frightened ones safe.
14.14:
**“And if these three men be in the midst of it”** — The church.
**“Noe”** — The rulers of the church.
**“Daniel”** — The continent.
**“and Job”** — Good married people.
**“they themselves”** — Whose justice is proclaimed.
**“shall deliver their own souls by their justice”** — Only.
**“And if these three”** — Jerome. Though Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses and the other patriarchs were just, only these are mentioned. For when the flood was threatening the earth, Noe could not put it off, but he had his sons, who perhaps were of his virtue, preserved as the seedbed of the human race. Daniel did not mitigate by any tears the imminent captivity of the Jews. Job, who was struck not on account of sins but for a trial, delivered neither house nor sons. Others say that these three men are named together because they saw prosperity and adversity and again prosperity, and so it is secretly signified that Israel, which first abounded in good things and afterwards endured captivity, could return to its former happiness if it does penance.
14.15:
**“And if I shall bring mischievous beasts also”**
• Demons.
• “Deliver not up to beasts the souls that confess to thee.”
14.16:
**“these three men”** — The teachers of the church.
**“who shall be in it, as I live, saith the Lord God, they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters”** — Unlike good fathers.
**“shall deliver”** — The justice of the just shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.
**“neither sons”** — Jerome. If these three gathered together cannot protect a sinful land from the wrath of God, what do some think, that by the virtues of parents sinful sons can be freed from the fires of hell? Neither father nor mother will be able to free a sinful son, nor will the sons' vices harm them, but “the soul that sinneth, the same shall die.” Lot could not free his wife, because she looked back, but only his daughters, who perhaps had not sinned. Josias, a holy man, not only did not free the sinning people, but himself died in their sins. Sometimes, however, for the sake of Abraham and David the Lord promises his mercy to their posterity, but only to those whose way of life the merits of the fathers assist.
14.17: **“Or if I bring the sword upon that land”** — Of whom it is said: They shall be given into the hands of the sword; and to Mary: “And thy own soul a sword shall pierce.”
14.19: **“Or if I also send the pestilence upon that land”** — Septuagint: death. Of which: “The death of sinners is most evil”; and “the soul that sinneth, the same shall die.”
14.20: **“son nor”** — Unless they have their works and faith. In vain, then, do the Jews say: “Our father is Abraham,” since they do not have his works. “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man.” Be they saints, be they prophets, we read nevertheless: do not trust in men; and again: “It is good to confide in the Lord, rather than to have confidence in man; it is good to trust in princes”—not of the world only but of the churches; who, if they are just, will free only their own souls, not the sons or daughters whom they have begotten in the church.
14.21:
**“For thus saith the Lord: Although”** — As if the prayer of so great men could not deliver from these plagues one by one; what if I should bring all of them together?
**“my four grievous judgments, the sword”** — Of enemies, by which they are slaughtered.
**“and the famine”** — In siege.
**“and the mischievous beasts”** — By which those fleeing in the deserts and mountains are devoured.
**“and the pestilence”**
• The Vulgate edition: death.
• Which always follows famine.
**“I shall send in upon Jerusalem”** — Upon Jerusalem, so that by these plagues together.
14.22:
**“Yet there shall be left”** — By my mercy.
**“in it some that shall be saved”** — Into captivity.
**“who shall bring away their sons and daughters: behold”** — for
**“they shall come among you”** — into Babylon, namely
**“and you shall see their way, and their doings: and you shall be comforted concerning the evil that I have brought upon Jerusalem, in all things that I have brought upon it.”** — And you shall be comforted. You, namely, when you see that I have delivered them from these scourges, so that by their perversity you may learn that Jerusalem was justly overthrown, the temple burned, the people made captive. This is said of Jerusalem, to which, while Ezechiel prophesied among the Chaldeans, captivity was impending.

15.2:
**“Son of man, what shall be made of the wood of the vine”** — The overthrow of the city is foreshadowed by various likenesses.
**“what shall be made of the wood of the vine”** — The vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth is the house of Israel, of which in Isaias: “I planted a vineyard, Soreth,” that is, beautiful and chosen. While this vine bears fruit, nothing among all woods is more precious; otherwise it is handed over to the fire with root and branches. But other woods, even when cut down, have some usefulness.
*Jerome:* Similar in the gospel: “If the salt have lost its savour,” etc.; and the eye, which enlightens the whole body, if it be blinded, hears from the Lord: “If then the light that is in thee, be darkness: the darkness itself how great shall it be!” For compared with the transgressor, and with him who denies God after having confessed him, the punishment of those who never knew God is lighter. But the woods of the forests, according to the variety of believers, have some usefulness in the house of God, in which “there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earth.”
*Jerome:* We can take the vineyard and Jerusalem as the multitude of believers, which, if it has lost the cultivation of its former religion, and has produced no fruits of virtues, and has not brought forth the wine that gladdeneth the heart of man, will be handed over to eternal fires and be reckoned as nothing. For “that servant who knew the will of his lord, and did not according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes.” Similarly it is said in the gospel: “I am the true vine; and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me, that beareth not fruit, he will take away: and every one that beareth fruit, he will purge it, that it may bring forth more fruit.” If the Saviour is the vine and we the branches and the Father the husbandman, while we keep the precepts of God we are always raised up, and our cultivation is a purging. “For it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that showeth mercy.” For if, bearing fruit, we are purged by the Father that we may bear more, it is shown that by the help of God we shall come to the end and the fruit of fullness. The branch that beareth not fruit is taken away by the Father, but what is afterwards done to it by God the scripture does not say. For perhaps separation from the body of Christ is perpetual destruction.
15.3: **“Shall wood be taken of it”** — of the vine
15.4:
**“Behold it is cast into the fire for fuel: the fire hath consumed both ends thereof”** — when the shoots are cut off, both parts of them
**“and the midst thereof is reduced to ashes: shall it be useful for any work?”** — burned
15.5: **“Even when it was whole it was not fit for work: how much less, when the fire hath devoured and consumed it”** — or consumed
15.7:
**“And I will set my face against them”** — Septuagint: I will set firm.
**“they shall go out from fire”** — the city being burned
**“and a fire”** — the hostile sword
**“shall consume them”** — those who escaped
**“and you shall know that I am the Lord”** — you who have escaped from the weight of miseries
15.8:
**“I shall have made their land a wilderness, and desolate”** — into eternal solitude, namely
**“because they have been transgressors, saith the Lord God”** — for it is one thing to despise what you do not know, another to neglect what you have worshipped.

16.1: **“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:”** — Jerome. Where the compass of each prophecy is short, we set down the whole chapters, immediately adding what seems right to us. But here, because a long discourse is directed to Jerusalem, as far as this: “when I shall be pacified towards thee,” etc., while she is reproached with how she sinned, we find it necessary to set down the whole prophecy in parts and to fit due explanations to each.
16.2:
**“Son of man, make known to Jerusalem her abominations.”** — which you have dissembled
**“Son of man”** — Jerome. It profits sinners much to know what they have done, whence the penitent says: “I know my iniquity,” etc. Jerusalem is taken in four ways: either that which was set on fire by the Babylonian and Roman fire; or the heavenly city of the firstborn; or the church, which is interpreted “vision of peace”; or the souls of individuals, who by faith behold God. But what most interpret of the heavenly Jerusalem the church does not accept, lest we be compelled to understand all that is said in the present prophecy of the ruin and torments of the heavenly powers and their restoration to their former state.
**“make known to Jerusalem her abominations”** — Under the figure of a harlot is set out first Jerusalem’s joining in partnership with her husband, and her birth and upbringing, puberty and marriage, adultery and repudiation, and then recall; so that the husband’s mercy and judgment, and the crimes of the adulteress and harlot, may be known.
16.3:
**“And thou shalt say: Thus saith the Lord God to Jerusalem”** — dative or vocative case
**“Thy root, and thy nativity is of the land of Chanaan, thy father was an Amorrhite”**
• that is, celebrated in much speech
• that is, talkative
**“and thy mother a Cethite.”** — that is, one who rages, or sends others into madness
**“Thy root, and”** — Jerome. Great is the faith, great the boldness of the prophets. Great is Daniel, who dared to say to the elder joining murder to adultery, “O thou seed of Chanaan, and not of Juda,” while still a boy. And Isaias, who cries out to the people and the princes of the Jews: “Hear the word of the Lord, ye rulers of Sodom,” etc. Great also is Ezechiel, who, charging the whole city with ignobility, says: Thy root, etc.
**“Chanaan”** — Jerome. Because the people was called out of Egypt and was there for a long time. For Cham, father of Canaan, was prince of the Egyptians; or, according to the likeness of crimes too, we say that the root of Jerusalem is the land of Egypt.
**“thy father was an Amorrhite”** — Jerome. If this is said to Jerusalem, which is of the race of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and has God for father, what will become of us, who, called from the filth of the Gentiles, lost every stain in the laver of the Saviour, if we defile the garment of Christ and have not a wedding garment at the feast? Then, with feet and hands bound, we shall be cast into the exterior darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
**“thy mother a Cethite”** — Jerome. That is, one who is mad or drives others into madness. For everyone who commits sin is born of the devil; whence the name of this ancient father is famous in the whole world, and he turns many into madness. Whence it is said to Jerusalem: “Hearken, O daughter, and see, and incline thy ear: and forget thy people and thy father’s house. And the king shall greatly desire thy beauty”; and it is promised her that if she is willing to return to her true father, she will be restored as she was born.
16.4:
**“And when thou wast born”**
• from such parents
• It signifies that she did not at once receive the law, nor were the beginnings of her shameful birth cut off, because she had lived first as a Gentile.
**“in the day of thy nativity”**
• the female genitals are in the navel as the seed of men is in the loins. Whence: “His strength is in his loins, and his force in the navel of his belly.”
• Jerome. It is natural for newborn infants first to have the navel cut, then to be washed with water to wash away the blood, thirdly to have the moisture of the little ones dried with salt, fourthly to have the tender bodies bound with swaddling clothes, lest they become misshapen or deformed; whence the bodies of barbarians are straighter than those of the Romans, for until the second and third year they are always wrapped in swaddling clothes. But Jerusalem had none of these.
**“thy navel was not cut”**
• the navel, by which, namely, the fetus is nourished in the womb, as trees and shoots are nourished unseen by the moisture of the earth through their roots
• Jerome. Septuagint: They did not bind thy breasts. A careful mother, as soon as the little girl is born, binds her breasts, that they may cease to swell from tenderness and may preserve virginal beauty; when she comes to puberty it is said to her: “Will a bride forget her ornament, her breastband?”
**“was not cut”** — Septuagint: They did not bind thy breasts. Scripture has this custom, that for the heart it puts the breast, the chest, and the breasts, according to the fitness of the places. The priest, from whose mouth they seek doctrine and the law, receives the breast. John reclines upon the breast of the Lord, to draw wisdom.
**“neither wast thou washed with water”** — Jerome. The bloody bodies of newborn infants are washed at once. Spiritual generation also needs a spiritual washing. For no one is clean, not even an infant of one day; whence: “I was conceived in iniquities; and in sins did my mother conceive me.” The second birth looses the first; whence: “Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost,” etc.
