**“for thy health”** — For there are washings of Gentile heretics, but they do not wash unto salvation. In the church too, those who receive baptism without full faith receive water, not the Spirit.
**“nor salted with salt, nor swaddled with clouts.”** — even the Saviour was wrapped in the swaddling clothes of infancy, and everyone who is born needs God’s protection
**“nor salted with salt”** — The tender bodies of infants, while they still retain the warmth of the womb, are usually touched with salt, that they may be dried and made firm. But Jerusalem, born of wicked parents, obtained no savour, no care. But to those born again in Christ it is said: You are the salt of the earth. And the apostle: let your speech be seasoned with the salt of grace; whence also in common speech the wise are called savoury, the foolish unsavoury. Every sacrifice also is seasoned with salt. He who is seasoned with this salt will no longer say: “My sores are putrified and corrupted.” He himself is called salt, by whom things earthly and infernal and heavenly are salted; whence: “Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will.”
16.5:
**“No eye had pity on thee”**
• God being offended
• Septuagint: thy
**“to do any of these things for thee”** — at least
**“of these things”** — four
**“out of compassion to thee: but thou wast cast out”** — for your iniquity
**“upon the face of the earth”** — let us pray that we be not cast out for iniquity upon the face of the earth, where the way is broad and spacious that leads to death
16.6:
**“passing by”**
• yet
• It must be noted that no one, when he is born, can commit any actual sin, except in the time of the washing, when the wise generation is taken up by the faith of the believer
**“And passing by thee, I saw that thou wast trodden under foot”** — guilty, that is, of mortal crimes
**“I said to thee when thou wast in thy blood”** — I called, that is, granting repentance
**“when”** — although
**“thou wast in thy blood: Live”** — converted
**“I have said to thee”** — although
16.7:
**“to multiply”** — the abundance of all things
**“as the bud of the field: I caused thee”** — as by the blessing of Jacob, of whom: “Behold the smell of my son is as the smell of a plentiful field, which the Lord hath blessed”
**“thou didst increase and grow great, and advancedst”** — so that you could say: “The king hath brought me into his chamber”
**“and camest to woman's ornament”** — the time of puberty
**“woman's”** — adornment
**“thy breasts were fashioned, and thy hair grew”** — the maturity of young girls is shown honorably
**“and thou wast naked”** — although marriageable
**“Thou wast naked”** — Jerome. That is, not protected by God’s help. If anyone has not the garment of Christ, he is naked, who is not clothed with the bowels of mercy, goodness, humility, modesty, meekness, patience; he lies upon the face of the earth, and his beauty is disfigured by confusion and nakedness.
16.8:
**“And passing by thee”** — in great mercy he again visits the sinner
**“and saw thee: and behold thy time was the time”** — when you could be joined to a husband
**“of lovers”** — of God, that is
**“The time of lovers”** — Jerome. The time of lovers may be understood as the time of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, when the Lord promised them that after Egyptian servitude he would free his people
**“Of lovers”** — What is said of Jerusalem let us refer to our soul, which, as long as it is set in infancy, is without sin. But when the time of its age comes, many are the lovers: of demons, of heretics, and of perverse doctrines, who desire to turn aside to it; they are driven back by the protection of the Lord, that it may receive not the attendants of the devil but the ministers of the Saviour.
**“and I spread my garment”** — having had mercy on you
**“over thee”** — naked
**“and covered thy ignominy. And”** — therefore
**“I swore to thee, and I entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord God”** — that you might be joined to me rather than to other lovers
**“and thou becamest mine”**
• joined in my marriage
• Shame, that is, of the genitals. For we surround our shameful parts with greater honor; whence: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered”; which Cham did not cover in his father, and is condemned to eternal curse
**“I spread my garment”** — The Seventy. “I spread my wings,” whence: “He spread his wings, and hath taken them and carried them on his shoulders”; and elsewhere: “How often would I gather together thy children,” etc.
**“I swore to thee”** — Jerome. According to that: “The Lord hath sworn, and he will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech.” And the end of every controversy among men is an oath. At the time of the wedding, therefore, Israel received God’s oath as a dowry gift.
16.9:
**“And”** — therefore
**“I washed thee”** — Whence Isaias: “If the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Sion, and shall wash away the blood of Jerusalem”
**“with water”** — of baptism.
**“and cleansed away thy blood from thee”** — as he washed the woman with an issue of blood.
**“and I anointed thee with oil”** — water is not enough to wash and cleanse the blood.
**“And I anointed thee with oil”** — Jerome. As the Samaritan, that is, the keeper, who poured oil and wine into their wounds in the seed. Our Lord was anointed with oil, not to soothe the pain of wounds but to bestow gladness; whence: “God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.” The demons also have the feigned lightness of oil, promising through heretics sweet things which are turned into bitterness; whence: “But let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head.” From the anointing, the anointed one, that is, christ, is named. See, therefore, how far Jerusalem had advanced, which, anointed with spiritual oil, had received the name of christ; whence of Abraham: “Touch ye not my anointed.”
16.10:
**“And I clothed thee with embroidery”**
• Septuagint: various.
• which befits a woman, not a man.
• Jerome. With the various ceremonies of the law, according to the Septuagint, by which, intent upon them, she might flee idols; these are the various garments of Joseph, whom his brothers would not have sold unless they had first stripped him; of which: “The queen stood on thy right hand, in gilded clothing; surrounded with variety”; whence: “Put on the new man,” etc.; and elsewhere: “Put ye on therefore, as the elect of God, the bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, meekness, patience”: what is more beautiful than this variety? The high priest also, when about to enter the holy of holies once a year, wore various garments. For riches do not make this variety of garments, but holiness and the diversity of virtues; otherwise Pharao and Nabuchodonosor would be written of as having had these garments, and not Joseph, a stranger and the son of a shepherd.
**“and shod thee with violet coloured shoes”** — Whence: “And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace.”
**“And shod thee with violet coloured shoes”** — Jerome. Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, compares the violet in the high priest’s garments to the air, in which he thinks heavenly things are signified; and one is not shod until he is washed with water; whence also the apostles, who are commanded to shake the dust from their feet, have their feet washed. And in the Canticles: “I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?” Moses also and Jesus Nave are commanded to loose their shoes, because the place on which they stand is holy; so that when the feet have been washed and they themselves purged of all filth, shod with violet, which is the colour of the air, they may walk to meet the Lord in the air, and hasten to the heavenly kingdoms.
**“I girded thee about with fine linen”** — Jerome. Of which the finest threads are woven in the high priest’s garment. Of which in Proverbs: the woman makes two cloaks, namely of the present age and of the future. With fine linen the loins are girt whenever the fat incentives of lust are to be made lean; whence the apostle: “Stand therefore, having your loins girt about,” etc.; and the Lord in the gospel: “Let your loins be girt, and lamps burning in your hands.” For unless we restrain the floods of the loins we cannot have lamps in our hands. And the Lord to Job: “Gird up thy loins like a man.” Those about to eat the lamb, shod, holding a staff, standing in the truth of the gospel, and prepared for the blood of Christ, are said to have their loins girt. With this girdle mortifying the loins, Elias, and John the Baptist also, were girded; of whom: “My loins are filled with illusions.”
**“and clothed thee with fine garments”** — Septuagint: tricapti, a name which they too coined, as new names are often coined for new things, namely because they are believed to have the fineness of hairs.
**“And clothed thee with fine garments”** — Namely, most fine. And rightly, because the people’s heart was thickened; whence in the book of Wisdom the spirit of wisdom is called subtle and unchangeable, and the bread of angels, that is, manna, is recorded to have been most fine.
16.11:
**“I decked thee also with ornaments”** — a general term, under which it places, as it were, the species.
**“and put bracelets”** — good works.
**“And a chain about thy neck”** — Jerome. I think the necklace here is called from various gems, hanging down upon the breast of women; which is the most beautiful ornament of women.
16.12:
**“And I put a jewel upon thy forehead”** — over thy nostrils.
**“and earrings in thy ears”** — lest you hear the judgment of blood; lest you be mingled with the envious or detractors.
**“and a beautiful crown”** — name of almighty God; whence: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us.” Of this crown the apostle says: “there is laid up for me a crown of justice.”
**“beautiful”** — or comely.
**“And I put a jewel”** — Circles, namely like earrings, which are wont to hang from the woman’s forehead and to hover over her nostrils or mouth. He calls them earrings by way of likeness, so that he may say securely: “For we are the good odour of Christ unto God.”
**“And a beautiful crown”** — Jerome. Namely the name of almighty God, which is written with four letters and is called ineffable among the Jews, which was on a golden plate upon the priest’s head, because his name cannot be spoken, whose majesty even the heathen world does not ignore; whence on the altar of the Athenians was written: To the unknown God.
16.13:
**“And thou wast adorned with gold”** — wisdom.
**“and silver”** — eloquence.
**“and wast clothed with fine linen”** — lest the spouse’s beauty be weighed down by a heavy mantle.
**“and embroidered work”** — according to Symmachus, what above is subtle, here is polymitum.
**“and many colours: thou didst eat fine flour”**
• after clothing he provides food.
• Of which: “Unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die,”
**“and honey”** — The sweet gifts of the Holy Spirit.
**“and oil”** — The grace of the Father, which sustains and refreshes the weary and nourishes the light. Whence: “lamps are lit in the tabernacle of God.”
**“thou didst eat”** — thus.
**“wast made exceeding beautiful”** — with such food.
**“exceeding”** — weightily.
**“exceedingly”** — so that nothing can be added.
**“And”** — after.
**“wast advanced”** — by these gifts.
**“to be a queen”** — because the city of the great king, of whom: “Give to the king thy judgment, O God, and to the king’s son thy justice”; and elsewhere: “The queen stood on thy right hand, in gilded clothing; surrounded with variety.”
**“Fine flour, and honey, and oil”** — Jerome. That Jerusalem may eat, either by parts, as most think, or by the mixture of the three, the sweeter bread which came down from heaven; and under three names, as some think, it signifies the sacrament of the Trinity: not that the substance is one and another, but that by the different names, fine flour, honey and oil, the one sweetness of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit is shown.
**“And wast advanced to be a queen.”** — This is not found in the Septuagint, because at Alexandria, translating the scriptures into the Greek tongue from the Hebrew truth, they feared to publish it, lest they should seem to offend the king of Egypt if they said that the kingdom of Israel was owed by God. The more learned think that only the books of Moses were translated by them.
*Jerome:* What we say of Jerusalem, lest we have it in individual cases and cause tedium to readers, let us refer once to the church. For if according to the apostle Jerusalem is our mother, and our mother is the church, and Jerusalem is the church.
16.14:
**“And thy renown went forth among the nations”** — that all the nations should speak of you.
**“for thy beauty”** — which I gave.
**“for thou wast perfect through”** — by my bounty. For “unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it. Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it.”
**“my”** — not yours.
**“Thou wast perfect through my beauty”** — “So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.” When we have done all things, let us say that we are unprofitable servants; what we ought to do we have done, not so that we take away free will from God’s benefit, but that freedom itself ought to have the Lord as helper.
16.15:
**“trusting in thy beauty”**
• a great danger: not to trust in God’s mercy but in one’s own comeliness; the higher each one is, the more he should fear.
• therefore
**“thou playedst the harlot because of thy renown, and thou hast prostituted thyself to every passenger, to be his”** — not of God’s
**“In thy beauty”**
• Jerome. Demons usually despise common foods; they desire foreign nourishment, whence: “his chosen food.” He does not wish to deceive just anyone. They hasten to supplant Saul, the king chosen by the Lord, and Judas the apostle; therefore let us not trust in our beauty.
• We should not think that the bounty of God is our virtue. Whence: “Glory not thyself of to morrow: for thou knowest not what the day to come may bring forth.”
**“thou playedst”** — That thou mightest be his: not God’s, but his by whom you are defiled, who receives all vices and takes into his bosom the passing spirit of diverse sins, and spreads his feet to every passer-by; here he pours out his fornication, and begins to bear the lordship of him whose guest he has become.
16.16:
**“And taking of thy garments”** — from Jerusalem. So it can be understood: all things, namely the precepts of the law and the riches and abundance of all things, she assigned to idols.
**“thou hast made thee”** — which I gave you.
**“high places”** — others: idols.
**“sewed together on each side: and hast played the harlot upon them, as hath not been done before, nor shall be hereafter”** — by other nations. For those who from the beginning served idols are less guilty.
**“Sewed together on each side”** — Jerome. Our Jerusalem also, which is called the vision of peace, is rent by heretics, when, plucking one testimony and another from their proper places, they try to sew them to things to which they cannot be fitted; whence above: woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand; which the Lord forbids, saying: “No man putteth a piece of raw cloth,” etc. Nor does he put “new wine into old bottles”; this the Nazarenes do, who have fitted the observance of the old law to the grace of the gospel.
16.17:
**“And thou tookest thy beautiful vessels, of my gold, and my silver, which I gave thee, and thou madest thee images of men”** — we have one husband and worship one image, namely of the invisible and almighty God.
**“And thou tookest thy beautiful vessels”** — The Lord commanded that censers, bowls, candelabra and the ark of the covenant be made, all either of gold or gilded, and others of silver; all of which Jerusalem melted down and turned into idols of Bel or Baal, Chamos, Astaroth, Melchon.
*Jerome:* Spiritually, we make idols of the gold and silver of the holy scriptures when we corrupt the grace of understanding and eloquence by heretical perversity, and “set our mouth against heaven.” And thou hast made thee male images, in which all heretics fornicate, while each thinks that what he fashions is most strong, and can be overthrown by no assault; of which it is said: “O Lord, in thy city thou shalt bring their image to nothing”; and elsewhere: “Surely man passeth as an image.”
**“images of men, and hast committed fornication with them”** — Images, namely, that she might turn all the worship she had received for use into blasphemy.
16.18:
**“thou tookest thy garments of divers colours, and coveredst them”** — or covered them.
**“my oil”**
• not yours.
• as above.
**“my sweet incense”** — others: incense, of which: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight.”
**“And thou tookest thy garments”** — We too do the same whenever we surround heretical perversity with temperance, prudence, fortitude, justice and other virtues, and so deceive the simple, so that, seeing the honeys of virtues, they do not beware the poisons of vices.
16.19:
**“And my bread”** — The Septuagint: the showbread, namely which we are commanded to offer to God.
**“which I gave thee, the fine flour”** — the purest sense of the Scriptures.
**“and oil, and honey, wherewith I fed thee”** — which Jonathan tasted, and “his eyes were enlightened,” and he was strengthened.
**“thou hast set before them”** — of idols.
**“for a sweet odour”** — to idols.
**“And”** — that other.
**“it was done, saith the Lord God”** — Fine flour, and oil, and honey. Wretched Jerusalem set these before the sight of her idols, which are sweet and most pleasant by nature; but when they are offered to idols and false doctrines, they become bitter.
16.20:
**“And thou hast taken thy sons, and thy daughters, whom thou hast borne to me”** — Of whom it is said: “I have brought up children, and exalted them: but they have despised me.”
**“And thou hast taken thy sons”** — Jerome. Our Jerusalem also, supplanted by heretical perversity, takes her sons, who are stronger in faith, and her daughters, namely those still weak in faith; or the sons who know the mystical things, the daughters who follow the simple history; and hands them over to demons to be devoured, and when she kills them she believes she gives life and appeases the idols, which are glutted by their slaughter.
**“and hast sacrificed the same to them to be devoured. Is thy fornication small?”** — Whence: “They sacrificed their sons, and their daughters to devils.” And elsewhere: “They shed the blood of their sons and of their daughters, whom they sacrificed,” etc.
16.21:
**“Thou hast sacrificed and given my children”** — Septuagint: your own, namely those whom you bore from fornication. Whence: “My firstborn son is Israel.”
**“and given my children to them”** — And thou hast given them. Symmachus and Theodotion: “thou hast transferred”; for the heathen either pass their little children through fire, or compel the grown to pass through it.
16.22:
**“And after all thy abominations, and fornications, thou hast not remembered the days of thy youth, when thou wast naked”** — And I covered thee.
**“and full of confusion, trodden under foot in thy own blood”** — And I washed and joined thee to me.
16.23: **“And it came to pass after all thy wickedness (woe, woe to thee”** — A double curse. Whence John: “Woe upon all the inhabitants of the earth.”
16.24:
**“That thou didst also build thee a common stew”** — As a harlot.
**“A common stew”** — A common stew. Sinning with a bold brow. Whence: when the sinner has come into the depths, he scorns.
**“and madest thee a brothel house”** — All these things can be understood of individuals, if they obey vices.
**“in every street”**
• Common to all.
• For it is the broad and spacious way which leads to death.
**“That thou didst also build thee”** — And thou hast built thee. It describes Jerusalem under the person of a woman, who, after many benefits from her husband, commits fornication and withdraws from her husband. For thus withdrawing from God, she clings to idols.
16.25:
**“At every head of the way”** — At every head of the way: so that she leaves out no kind of sin.
**“thou hast set up a sign of thy prostitution”** — By which is signified the place of fornication.
**“and hast made thy beauty to be abominable”** — That is, the soul, which she has received from God.
**“and hast prostituted thyself”** — Or, thou hast spread wide.
**“thy feet”** — By yielding to the temptations of vices.
16.26:
**“And thou hast committed fornication with the Egyptians”** — To the Gentiles.
**“thy neighbours, men of large bodies, and hast multiplied thy fornications”** — Surpassing them in baseness.
**“to provoke me”**
• As if for this reason you did it.
• The Egyptians are called large of flesh, either because of the greatness of their baseness or because of the deformity of their sins.
**“The Egyptians thy neighbours”** — Jerome. Whence the saint is called one of small flesh, which daily wastes away in him, and, made thin by virtues, is called not flesh but spirit; whence: “For thee my soul hath thirsted; for thee my flesh, O how many ways!” Hence the Corinthian fornicator is delivered to the destruction of the flesh that the spirit may be saved. Of this flesh it is said: “All flesh is grass, and all the glory thereof as the flower of the field,” etc. Of this the apostle says: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.” In Genesis also it is said: “My spirit shall not remain in man, because he is flesh.” “They who are in the flesh cannot please God.” The flesh of the saints is another, of which it is said: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God.”
16.27:
**“Behold, I will stretch out”** — Or, I have stretched.
**“my hand upon thee”** — To be corrected.
**“and will take away”** — Hence it is clear that the Jews lost the observance of the law.
**“thy justification”**
• Or: thy right.
• Not mine.
**“And”** — “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you.”
**“I will deliver thee up”** — “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you,” etc.
**“to the will of the daughters of the Philistines that hate thee”** — the cities or towns of Palestine
**“the daughters of the Philistines”** — or of the Palestinians
**“that are ashamed of thy wicked way”** — I will stretch out my hand, that I may visit your sins by punishing them. Whence: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod.” And note that the hand of God is sent out for trial and stretched out for the punishment of sinners. Whence in Job: “Put forth thy hand,” etc.
*Jerome:* Our Jerusalem also, if she passes over the ceremonies of God, and his hand is stretched out over her, with the observance of the law taken away, is handed over to the daughters of Palestine, not the sons. For we are not handed over first to the heavier punishments, but according to the quality of our sins to lighter ones, that, corrected in the lesser, we may avoid the greater torments of suffering. Philistiim, that is Palestini, with the first part of the letters changed, is interpreted as falling by the cup, or by making; by which is signified that we are to be handed over to adverse powers, who have drunk of the cup of Babylon and fallen, whose works are perverse; and so great will be the correction and ignominy of wretched Jerusalem that even the demons will blush at the greatness of our sins.
16.28:
**“Thou hast also committed fornication”**
• as with the Egyptians, who were also your neighbours
• According to the tropological sense, we often pass from some sins to others, and not even so are we satisfied, but as with a long rope and the strap of a heifer we draw sins along and multiply our fornication in the land of Chanaan, which is interpreted “fluctuation,” with the Chaldeans, who also sound with us like demons; and we have our feet in the brine, and can never say: “He hath set my feet upon a rock,” etc. We are also subjected to the perversities of heretics, who have the likeness of demons, or of the demons themselves. Of whom the apostle says: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood,” etc.
**“with the Assyrians”** — therefore they were handed over to both, because they worshipped the images of both
**“because thou wast not yet satisfied: and after thou hadst played the harlot with them, even so thou wast not contented”** — or satisfied
**“Thou hast also committed fornication with the Assyrians”** — Palestine is near Egypt; whence the Lord to Abraham: “To thee will I give all the land from the river of Egypt even to the great river Euphrates”; so that on one side it has the Egyptians and on the other the Assyrians, with whom she is said in what follows to have committed fornication.
*Jerome:* Morally. This can be referred to every soul that, having left the worship of God, gives itself up to vices and lust, and neither does it fare happily in the worldly life which it follows, but loses both the riches of the world and of religion, and of its own accord thrusts itself upon lovers. There is also another, spiritual, fornication, when, deserting the Church, we are joined to heretics and build our brothel “at the head of every way”; to whom it is said: “Stand ye on the ways, and see and ask for the old paths, which is the good way, and walk ye in it.” That is, in the books of Moses, Jesus, the Judges and the Kings, and also of Isaias and Jeremias and the other prophets, at all the beginnings of the ways he builds his brothel, who ill uses the testimonies of doctrine, saying: This says Isaias, this Osee, this Moses, this Daniel. And well does he set the brothel not in the middle of the ways nor at the ends of the ways, but at the beginning. For if he should come to the knowledge and depths of the books, he could not err. He makes his high place, or its base, in every street, mingling himself with the lasciviousness and vices of the heathens and the impious, even among the heretics themselves; when she has been defiled by them, she lies open, having no favour but exposed to contempt, because in easy faith she has lost chastity.
16.29: **“Thou hast also multiplied thy fornications in the land of Chanaan with the Chaldeans”** — for entering Chaldea, which is the land of Chanaan, they imitated the errors of those under whose rule they lay
16.30:
**“Wherein shall I cleanse thy heart”** — with the remedy. As if: what more ought I to have done for you? Whence Osee: “What shall I do to thee, Ephraim? What shall I do to thee, Juda?”
**“saith the Lord God: seeing thou dost all these the works”** — aforesaid
**“of a shameless prostitute”** — that is
16.31:
**“Because thou hast built thy brothel house at the head of every way”** — as if you worshipped idols not in secret but in complete freedom
**“and thou hast made thy high place”** — The Septuagint: the base, that is, the altars
**“in every street: and wast not”** — or you make other faces
**“as a harlot”** — crafty
**“by disdain enhanceth her price”** — hard to be asked, that is, so that she might give more readily
**“wast not”** — The Septuagint: you were not like a harlot gathering wages. As if: you gave what you ought to have received. For you are not protected by the help of the demons you worship, oppressed by various calamities.
16.32:
**“But as an adulteress, that bringeth in strangers over her husband”** — freely
**“strangers”** — to herself
16.33:
**“Gifts are given to all harlots: but thou hast given hire”** — the goods which I had given you
**“to all thy lovers”** — to demons, idols; whence in Osee: “She did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil, and multiplied her silver.”
**“to all harlots”** — Jerome. These things are to be referred to the Church and to the souls of the faithful, who give the marriage gifts, namely gold in understanding, silver in eloquence, and garments by which our shame and foulness are covered, to their lovers, that is, to demons, or to teachers of perverse doctrines, when they assert that lust does no harm, and that the genital members of the body naturally demand intercourse, and that all foods may be used without distinction, and the like.
**“thou hast given them gifts to come to thee from every side, to commit fornication with thee”** — Jerome. It signifies every kind of sin, so that she is not thought to be content with one but always endures a hunger for sinning, and, against the laws of nature, is defiled in every member and polluted even to the crown of the head.
16.34:
**“And it hath happened in thee contrary to the custom of women in thy fornications, and after thee there shall be no such fornication”** — which is compared with you
**“for in that thou gavest rewards”** — which other women do not do
**“and didst not take rewards”** — which other women do
16.35:
**“Therefore”** — because, that is, you did the aforesaid things
**“O harlot, hear the word of the Lord”** — what you did and what you are to suffer
16.36:
**“Thus saith the Lord God”** — first let us lay the foundations of the history
**“Because thy money hath been poured out”**
• by you
• that you gave what you ought to have received
• Jerome. According to the tropological sense, every soul receives spiritual money from the Lord, whence: “To one he gave five talents, and to another two, and to another one.” But if it has acted negligently, the shame of Jerusalem is uncovered to her lovers, namely the demons, on the day of judgment or in the time of penance when they are rebuked; and first God alone sees hidden things, whence: “And thy Father who seeth in secret will repay thee.” And elsewhere: “God searching the hearts and reins.” But when it shall be fulfilled that there is nothing hidden that shall not be revealed, and that: “Judge not before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness,” etc. And when the time of correction has come, then that of Osee will be fulfilled: “Their own devices have surrounded them,” and that: “their thoughts between themselves accusing, or also defending one another, in the day when the Lord shall judge the secrets of men,” and that: “Behold the man, and his works before his face.”
**“thy money”** — which you had received from me
**“and thy shame discovered through thy fornications with thy lovers, and with the idols of thy abominations, by the blood”** — which you sacrificed to demons
**“of thy children”** — of good thoughts, which are slain by one who inclines to evil works
*Jerome:* All these things are said by metaphor of an adulteress and murderess, who not only committed fornication against her husband but also slew her children, against Jerusalem; and that all the nations whose idols she adored are to be gathered against her, and she turned all the gifts of God to their worship; and the temple of Baal will be destroyed, and all the altars of the city will be overthrown by fire, and nothing will remain in it.
**“whom thou gavest them”** — If Jerusalem, which committed fornication with idols, suffered these things, what do we think she will suffer, who is guilty of the blood of Christ?
16.37:
**“Behold, I will gather together all thy lovers with whom thou hast taken pleasure, and all whom thou hast loved, with all whom thou hast hated: and I will gather them together against thee on every side, and will discover thy shame”** — by the law of adulteresses
**“in their sight, and they shall see all thy nakedness”** — genitals
16.38: **“And I will judge thee as adulteresses, and they that shed blood are judged: and I will give thee blood in fury and jealousy”** — great is the fury of a husband against an adulteress, and it cannot be redeemed by any price
16.39: **“And I will deliver thee into their hands, and they shall destroy thy brothel house”** — seedbed of fornication
16.40: **“And they shall bring upon thee a multitude, and they shall stone thee with stones”** — so all commonly are wont to stone an adulteress
16.41:
**“And they shall burn thy houses with fire, and shall execute judgments upon thee in the sight of many women”** — that they may fear like things
**“many”** — of cities
**“And”** — thus
**“thou shalt cease from fornication”** — as though, even angry and avenging, I have mercy. By this very punishment I provide for you, because thus you will cease to commit fornication.
**“and shalt give no hire any more”** — to lovers
16.42:
**“And my indignation shall rest in thee”** — when I long to love you
**“and my jealousy shall depart from thee, and I will cease and be angry no more”** — when I have delivered you eternally into captivity, after you have departed from me
**“and my jealousy shall depart”** — Because I shall now be secure about your chastity; that is, according to those who take this in a good sense. For others take it in the contrary sense, as is proper to the great anger of God: not to be angry once he has despised the fornicator and given up hope for his salvation.
*Jerome:* If the heretics who do not receive the Old Testament find fault with what is said according to the Septuagint: “and thou didst grieve me,” etc., on the ground that God not only receives anger but is subject to sorrow and sadness, let us ask them how they receive what is surely the command of the good God: “Grieve not the Holy Spirit of God, whereby you are sealed.” For whatever they say to us on this, we also will turn back against them in defence of the present saying.
16.43:
**“Because”** — namely, this you did
**“thou hast not remembered the days of thy youth”** — of the benefits which I gave you in youth
**“but hast provoked me in all these things”**
• The Seventy: you were grieving
• to sadness, whereas by good works you ought to have provoked to joys
**“wherefore I also have turned thy ways”** — your works
**“upon thy head, saith the Lord God, and”** — yet
**“I have not done according to thy wicked deeds”** — when you ought to have been overthrown. For the fault is greater than the punishment.
**“and I have not done according to”** — Divine mercy is shown, in that the punishments are less, while the sins are said to be greater.
16.44:
**“Behold every one that useth”** — After the catalogue of vices and the correction by which he is drawn back to salvation, there is fitted to him a proverb common among people: “As the mother was, so also is her daughter.”
**“As the mother was”** — Namely Cethea, who, raging or turning into madness, is interpreted as incitements, namely of this world, which lead the captive soul to destruction and divide her from her husband, that is, the Word of God.
16.45:
**“thy mother's daughter”** — likeness
**“Thou art, that cast off her husband”** — the Word of God
**“sisters”** — Jerome. Of Sodom and Samaria: the one signifies the Gentile life and lust, the other the snares of heretics.
**“who cast off their husbands”** — The word and teaching of God. For the feet of those who err always wander, running hither and thither. For they are carried about by every wind of doctrine, from one falsehood to another; and when they find they have sweated in vain over the first, they pass on to the second and the third.
**“your mother was a Cethite”** — Jerome. Above he said: your father an Amorrhite and your mother a Cethite. Here, with the order and number changed: Your mother a Cethite and your father an Amorrhite. For when crimes have advanced, they are split into parts, and, unity forsaken, they grow into a multitude and into a crowd that cannot go up with Jesus to the mountains. The sisters of Jerusalem are Samaria and Sodom, of whom one is at the right hand, the other at the left, even according to the bodily understanding, if you look east from the temple of Jerusalem you will find it so.
16.46:
**“And thy elder sister”** — because she sinned first, and was first led captive by the Assyrians
**“elder sister is Samaria, she and her daughters that dwell at thy left hand: and thy younger sister that dwelleth at thy right hand is Sodom”** — the Gentiles
**“Thy elder sister is Samaria”** — Jerome. Jerusalem, which is also called Judah, lies between the two sisters; she was led into Babylon by the Chaldeans, and she sinned much more wickedly than Samaria and Sodom, worshipping an idol in the temple and killing the Son of God afterwards.
**“Sodom”** — which is referred to the Gentiles. For Sodom at that time was not, since it had earlier been destroyed by divine fire together with Gomorrah, Adama and Seboim.
*Jerome:* According to the tropological sense, Samaria and Sodom, that is, heretics and heathens, often commit lighter sins than those who are thought to be Jerusalem, namely the churchmen; whence to the Corinthians: “It is absolutely heard that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as the like is not among the heathens,” etc. The heretics who receive only the Old Testament are wont to understand three natures in man: spiritual, animal, earthly; and they refer the spiritual to Jerusalem, the animal to Samaria, and the earthly to Sodom. We briefly ask them: how can the three natures, spiritual, animal, earthly, which are different from one another, have one mother and one father, which does not agree with their fiction; and how are the animal and earthly natures, according to this prophet, restored to their ancient state, that is, the spiritual, for this is contrary to their reasoning. That Samaria signifies heretics is proved both in Osee and in many other places, and especially in this testimony: “Woe to you that despise Sion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, and have gathered the grapes of the first fruits of the nations.” For all heretics despise Sion, which is interpreted “watchtower,” that is, the Church, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, that is, in the pride of perverse doctrines, which they think to be sublime, by which they gather the grapes and plunder the chiefs of the nations, that is, they draw the powerful into error.
16.47:
**“But neither hast thou walked in their ways, nor hast thou done according to their wickednesses”** — because
**“a little”** — or: a little
**“less ... almost more wicked things”** — or: more wicked
**“thou hast done almost more wicked things than they in all thy ways”** — by deeds, by thoughts
16.48:
**“As I live, saith the Lord God, thy sister Sodom herself, and her daughters, have not done as thou hast done, and thy daughters.”** — As I live: absolutely, pre-eminently. In the Old Testament this is an oath. In the New: “Amen, amen, I say to you”; whence: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” And elsewhere: “I will please the Lord in the land of the living.” As no one is called good absolutely but God alone, although we speak of a good tree, a good man, a good shepherd, a good servant, whence: none is good but God alone; so the angels and the other powers, the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, although living, are called dead in comparison with almighty God. For who is the man that liveth and shall not see death? Whence the Apostle says of God: “Who only hath immortality, and inhabiteth light inaccessible.”
*Jerome:* Describing by an oath the crimes of Sodom and her daughters, he places first the pride of the devil, his own and first sin. Whence the Apostle: “Lest being puffed up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil,” on account of which, namely, he fell from heaven. For “God resisteth the proud, but to the humble he giveth grace.”
16.49:
**“fulness of bread, and abundance, and idleness”** — Jerome. The seedbed of pride is fulness of bread, abundance of goods, and idleness; or, according to the Septuagint, abundance of delicacies and luxury. The rich man of the Gospel is not recorded to have sinned in anything else than that, abounding in wealth and riches, he broke out into such great pride that he did not stretch out his hand to the needy Lazarus, forgetful of his own condition, so that he gave the wretched man not even what was to be thrown away; whence elsewhere: “He that exalteth himself shall be humbled, and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.”
**“Behold this was the iniquity of Sodom thy sister, pride, fulness of bread, and abundance, and the idleness of her, and of her daughters: and they did not put forth their hand to the needy, and to the poor.”** — Of pride, fulness of bread, and abundance, and idleness: this is the sin of Sodom, and on account of it forgetfulness of God follows, which thinks present goods to be perpetual and that it will never be in need; whence in the law: take heed, lest when thou hast eaten and drunk and art filled, and hast built excellent houses, and hast sheep and oxen, silver and gold, thou forget the Lord thy God; whence Solomon: give me neither riches nor poverty, but only give me the necessaries of life.
**“and the idleness”** — Jerome. Others read “delights,” according to that sense: “the soul of every idler is in desires.” For something must always be done, lest the field of our heart, with the hand idle, be taken over by the thorns of evil thoughts.
16.51:
**“And Samaria committed not half thy sins: but thou hast surpassed them with thy crimes, and hast justified thy sisters by all thy abominations which thou hast done.”** — not absolutely, but by comparison with you. As that is said: “This man went down justified rather than the other.”
**“And Samaria committed not half thy sins”** — Jerome. For the servant who knew his lord’s will and did not do it “shall be beaten with many stripes”; and the mighty shall suffer mighty torments.
16.52:
**“Therefore do thou also bear thy confusion, thou that hast surpassed thy sisters with thy sins, doing more wickedly than they: for they are justified above thee”** — not that they are absolutely just, but by comparison with a worse one
**“bear thy confusion”**
• The second plank after shipwreck is, when you have sinned, to blush, lest you hear: “Thou hadst a harlot’s forehead, thou wouldst not blush.”
• Jerome. That is, that you be tormented by your own conscience, and now, by your own will, endure the torment, lest you endure it forever.
**“thou that hast surpassed thy sisters”** — Jerome. The Septuagint: you who corrupt others have corrupted your sisters, namely by your example, proving them to greater sins; as if a priest living badly and disgracing his dignity by his deed should corrupt laymen by his example; whence: he that shall scandalize one of these little ones, etc.
**“be thou also confounded”** — Jerome. Confusion is followed by disgrace, disgrace by correction, correction by consolation, and consolation by salvation. According to that: tribulation worketh patience, patience trial, trial hope; and hope confoundeth not, in the future, namely because in the present they have destroyed their sins by confusion; whence: there is a confusion that leadeth to death, and there is a confusion that leadeth to life. And the Holy Spirit exhorts sinners thus: let all my enemies be ashamed and troubled; let them be turned back, and be ashamed very speedily; and in another place: tell thou first thy iniquities, that thou mayest be justified. And: the just man is the first accuser of himself. What wonder then if Jerusalem is provoked to confusion and disgrace, she who justified her sisters by sinning?
16.53: **“And I will bring back”** — And I will bring back. A great advance after confusion and disgrace, which she willingly accepted as brought upon her by the judgment of God. As if she said: I will bear the wrath of God, because I have sinned against him. Restoration to her ancient state is promised her. But because Sodom and Samaria were justified by comparison with her crimes, first the conversion, or captivity, of Sodom is restored, according to Aquila; second, the captivity of Samaria, according to the same; last, Jerusalem is restored. For who doubts that among the three, the Gentile, the heretic, and the churchman, he is worthy of much greater punishments who is of greater dignity? Whence Peter: the time is that judgment should begin at the house of God. And in this the prophet: begin ye at my saints; that is, that Jerusalem, last of all, her sisters having been converted and restored before, may bear her disgrace and be confounded for her sins, and console her sisters while she is more severely punished. Or let her be confounded for this reason, that she has provoked God to wrath; whence it is clear that the wrath of God is not natural to him, but that he, merciful and gentle, is provoked to wrath by our vices; whence: according to thy hardness and impenitent heart thou treasurest up to thyself wrath. And elsewhere: thou sentest thy wrath, and it consumed them. For what is joined and united in one body cannot be sent, but what is outside, as a spear, a dart, and the like.
16.55: **“And thy sister Sodom”** — Jerome. The Jews, among other fables, say that at the coming of their christ, that is, of antichrist, and in the kingdom of a thousand years, Sodom will be restored, so as to be like the paradise of God and like the land of Egypt, and Samaria to its former happiness, namely that they will return from the Assyrians into the land of Judea. For we read that the ten tribes were taken captive by Phul and Salmanassar and Teglaphalassar, kings of the Assyrians, and are there captive to this day. Jerusalem, they say, will then be rebuilt, and all her daughters, namely the cities and villages and castles that had been under her power, will flourish as before, and she herself will be built up with gold and silver and precious stones; whence Isaias: “And I will restore thy judges as they were before, and thy counsellors as of old,” etc. And David: “Deal favourably, O Lord, in thy good will with Sion; that the walls of Jerusalem may be built up”; and elsewhere: the cities of Juda shall be built. So they. But we say that Sodom returns to its ancient state when the Gentile soul, once impious, restored to its nature, understands its Creator. Samaria also receives its ancient blessedness, the error of heretics being despised, when it is joined to Christian doctrine and faith; and then Jerusalem, that is the Church, will return to her state. Of which it is said: “His place is in peace.” And elsewhere: Jerusalem, which is built as a city, etc.
16.56:
**“And Sodom thy sister was not heard of”** — that you might bring her overthrow back to memory and fear
**“heard of in thy mouth, in the day of thy pride”** — when you were sinning proudly
16.57:
**“Before”** — namely
**“thy malice was laid open: as it is at this time, making thee a reproach of the daughters of Syria”** — Palestine
**“and of all the daughters of Palestine round about thee, that encompass thee on all sides”** — revealed, namely, so that you become a reproach to the daughters through all the cities of Syria and Palestine
**“making thee a reproach of the daughters of Syria”** — Jerome. Syria is called Aram in Hebrew, which is interpreted loftiness; and according to the explanation of that place of Isaias where Aram and Ephraim agree against Juda and Jerusalem, it is the shrewd wisdom of the heathen, which seeks for itself a loftiness of knowledge, as the heretic assails Juda, in whom, namely, he cannot prevail against the true confession. Here too is the same arrogance of Syria, that is, of the philosophers, with the daughters of the foreigners, in whom the manifold error of the various doctrines among the nations is shown. Jerusalem holds this also as a reproach, by whose fault she is overcome.
16.58:
**“thy wickedness”**
• therefore
• by which you surpassed the others in wickedness
16.59:
**“For thus saith the Lord God: I will deal with thee”** — therefore, that you may bear your wickedness
**“as thou hast despised the oath”** — that you may receive what you deserve
**“in breaking the covenant”** — you would bring to nothing
16.60:
**“And I will remember”** — namely, when it has been fulfilled: “I will kill and I will make to live: I will strike, and I will heal.”
**“my covenant with thee”** — which I once had with you
**“in the days of thy youth”** — or: mine
**“and I will establish with thee an everlasting covenant”** — not of the law, which has passed away, but of the gospel, which is everlasting
16.61:
**“And”** — thus
**“thou shalt remember thy ways”** — of deeds and thoughts
**“and be ashamed”** — namely, having remembered
**“when thou shalt receive thy sisters”** — Samaria and Sodom and their companions
**“thy elder and thy younger: and I will give them to thee for daughters”** — others for the testing. For there must be heresies, that they who are approved may be made manifest.
**“but not by thy covenant”** — namely by merit, but from my mercy
16.62:
**“And I will establish my covenant with thee”** — that is, when you have undergone punishments for sacrilege, you may obtain pardon not from your covenant but from my clemency
**“And”** — then
**“thou shalt know that I am the Lord”** — having remembered my benefits
16.63:
**“That thou mayest remember, and be confounded”** — as he who says: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.”
**“and mayest no more open thy mouth”** — Jerome. This belongs to the saints; whence: “Our mouth is open to you, O ye Corinthians.” And of the Saviour: “And opening his mouth, he taught them.” And in the psalm: “I will open my mouth in parables.” To the sinner it is said: “Thou hast sinned, be still.” And to the sinner God said: “Why dost thou declare my justices, and take my covenant in thy mouth?” and: “Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner.” To the holy man it is said: “Open thy mouth,” etc. Whence we ought, even when by the mercy of God we have received our former glory and the everlasting covenant of the gospel, and when the Lord has been pacified toward us for all that we have done, to keep the memory of our sin and always keep our mouth shut, we who are saved not by our works but by the grace of God.

17.2: **“Son of man, put forth a riddle”** — It signifies that what is said is obscure. For a parable presents one thing in words and holds another in meaning.
17.3:
**“and speak a parable to the house of Israel, and say: Thus saith the Lord God: A large eagle with great wings, long-limbed”** — having commanded many nations and surrounded by an innumerable army
**“full of feathers”** — The Septuagint: of nails
**“and of variety”** — of diverse nations
**“came to Libanus”**
• the temple
• Jerome. Whence Zacharias: “Open thy gates, O Libanus, etc.” For in the holy Scriptures the temple, which was famous and lofty, is often called Libanus.
**“and took away the marrow of the cedar.”** — namely Jechonias, king of Juda, with his mother and the princes of the people, and all the works of Jerusalem and the vessels of the temple
**“A large eagle with great wings”** — Jerome. According to the anagogical sense, though the interpretation may seem forced: as other living creatures are referred both to a good and to a bad sense, so also the eagle, as the lion, and it is said in a good sense: “a lion’s whelp, Juda.” In the contrary sense: “your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about.” Of the eagle in a good sense: that the just man made rich makes himself wings like an eagle, that he may be able to return to the house of his predecessor; and in Isaias: “they that hope in the Lord shall take wings as eagles.” Fittingly, then, he who had said, “I will make strength, and by the wisdom of understanding I will take away the bounds of the nations, and will plunder their strength,” etc., now under the person of the eagle comes to Libanus, which is interpreted “whiteness” and is referred to incense; he will not touch small and lowly shrubs, but the tops of the cedars, and the princes and the royal stock. Whence Habacuc: “his meats are choice.” He makes a covenant with those whom he has taken, that they bow their necks to the king of Babylon; and let the apostles fulfil that: “whom I have delivered up to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme”; and elsewhere: “whom I have delivered up to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved.” We ought not, therefore, if for some sin we are cast out of the congregation of the brethren and from the house of God, to resist, but with an even mind to bear the sentence passed upon us, and to say with the prophet of the Lord: “I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justify my cause,” etc. It often happens that, subject to one, we pass over to another, who promises us his help and does not allow us to remain in our former judgment. But this is by every means to be avoided, lest our branches be dried up and our shoots wither, and we be thought to act against the covenant.
**“Eagle”** — Two eagles are set forth in this prophet; of the first it is now spoken, of the other in what follows.
17.4:
**“He cropped off the top of the twigs thereof: and carried it away into the land of Chanaan”** — namely into Babylon, which is in the land of Chanaan
**“in a city of merchants”** — The Septuagint: walled
**“he set it”** — Chanaan, that is, into Babylon, where Jechonias grew old, from whose later family, as Matthew bears witness, the Lord was born through Salathiel and Zorobabel.
17.5:
**“And he took of the seed of the land, and put it in the ground for seed”** — Nathania, uncle of Jechonias, whom under a changed name he called Sedecias, and set over Jerusalem as king
**“that it might take a firm root”** — of the kingdom
**“over many waters”** — peoples
**“on the surface”** — because he did not establish the kingdom with a deep root
**“he planted it”** — his uncle
17.6:
**“And it sprung up and grew into a spreading vine of low stature”** — because it was under another
**“the branches thereof looked towards him”** — that it might rule over the peoples of the Jews, but look toward the empire of Babylon
**“towards him”** — understand: the eagle
**“and the roots thereof were under him. So it became a vine”** — from Nathania, who is also Sedecias
17.7:
**“And there was another large eagle”** — Pharao, king of Egypt
**“large, with great wings, and many feathers”** — Septuagint: with talons, on account of the rapacity, that is, the laying waste of many nations.
**“and behold this vine”** — Sedecias, king in Jerusalem, appointed by Nabuchodonosor.
**“bending as it were her roots”** — namely, ambassadors.
**“towards him”** — the eagle, namely the king of Egypt, asking for help against Nabuchodonosor.
17.8: **“It was planted in a good ground upon many waters”** — by Nabuchodonosor.
17.9:
**“Say thou”** — Say these things to him, O prophet.
**“Thus saith the Lord God: Shall it prosper then?”** — such a vine, an unfaithful vine.
**“shall he not pull up the roots thereof”** — the first eagle.
**“and this without a strong arm”** — Jerome. For Sedecias, fleeing, was left without the help of the king of Egypt, and was seized by the commanders of Nabuchodonosor in the plains of Jericho, and his companions were scattered here and there, as the Book of Kings and Paralipomenon and Jeremias attest.
17.10: **“Behold, it is planted”** — by Nabuchodonosor, or trusting in the help of Pharao.
17.12:
**“Say to the provoking house: Know you not what these things mean?”** — this parable set forth above.
**“Tell them: Behold the king of Babylon cometh”** — or will come.
**“the king of Babylon”** — the first eagle.
**“to Jerusalem: and he shall take away the king”** — namely Jechonias.
17.13:
**“And he shall take one of the king's seed”** — Sedecias.
**“and make a covenant with him”** — of peace.
**“and take an oath of him”** — of keeping the covenant.
**“Yea, and he shall take away the mighty men of the land”** — into Babylon.
17.14:
**“That it may be a low kingdom”** — of the Jews.
**“and not lift itself up”** — against Nabuchodonosor.
17.15:
**“who”** — who, Sedecias.
**“revolted from him”** — revolting from him, Nabuchodonosor.
**“sent ambassadors to Egypt”** — asking for help.
**“that it might give him horses, and much people”**
• against Nabuchodonosor.
• but.
**“shall he that hath done thus prosper, or be saved?”** — breaks the covenant.
**“And”** — that is.
**“and shall he escape that hath broken the covenant?”**
• punishment.
• Shall he escape? Jerome. From this we learn that faith is to be kept even among enemies, and that one must consider not to whom but by whom you have sworn. For he who believed you for the name of God’s sake and was deceived was found much more faithful than you, who by means of the divine majesty contrived plots against your enemy, nay, one already your friend.
17.16:
**“As I live, saith the Lord God: In the place where the king”** — in Babylon.
**“who”** — Nabuchodonosor.
**“made him king”** — in Juda
**“In the place where the king”** — For Sedecias was taken and led to Reblatha. And there, his sons having first been slain, he was blinded, and shut up like a wild beast in a cage, and carried over to Babylon; whence, though the Scripture seems contradictory, in both statements it is nevertheless most true. For it was said to Sedecias: “and thou shalt enter Babylon, and shalt not see it.” He entered, for he was led; and he did not see it, for he was blinded.
17.17:
**“And not with a great army, nor with much people shall Pharao fight against him”** — Nabuchodonosor or Sedecias
**“And not with a great army”** — Jerome. It is understood in two ways. Either the king of Egypt, coming against Nabuchodonosor, will not be able to fight, nor with a small army to resist so great a multitude; or Sedecias himself will be overcome by Pharao, in whom he hoped for help, not that he overcame him, but that he was the cause of his being overcome, because Sedecias hoped in him.
17.18: **“For he had despised the oath, breaking his covenant, and behold he hath given his hand”** — giving himself up to the king of Egypt, committing sacrilege against God
17.19: **“the oath he hath despised”** — It is a worldly saying: who asks whether deceit or valour is to be sought in an enemy? Yet Sedecias did worse, who deceived not an enemy but a friend to whom he had been joined by the covenant of the Lord.
17.20:
**“And I will spread my net over him, and he shall be taken in my net: and I will bring him into Babylon”** — whatever Nabuchodonosor did against Sedecias he did not do by his own strength but by the wrath of God, in whose name he had been forsworn.
**“and will judge him there for the transgression by which he hath despised me”** — By which he hath despised me. For he who despises an oath despises him by whom he swore, and does injury to him in whose name the adversary had put his faith.
17.22:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: I myself will take of the marrow of the high cedar”** — namely Christ, who says, “But I am appointed king by him.”
**“and will set it: I will crop off a tender twig from the top”** — or sprout
**“I will crop off a tender twig from the top of the branches thereof”** — the prince had failed from Juda, and he came for whom it was reserved, who is the expectation of the nations
**“I myself will take of the marrow of the high cedar”** — Jerome. The true Nabuchodonosor takes from the marrow of the high cedar and from the top of its branches, so that the kingdom may be low and not lifted up. But God the Father, who speaks to Ezechiel, plants on the high mountain one of royal stock and of the family of David.
17.23:
**“On the high mountains of Israel will I plant it, and it shall shoot forth into branches, and shall bear fruit”** — Whence: I will raise up to David a just sprout
**“and it shall become a great cedar”** — this mountain filled the face of the earth
**“and all birds shall dwell under it”**
• of heaven
• holy ones
• of which Habacuc says: “Horns are in his hands: there is his strength hid,” he who desires to gather as a hen gathers her chickens under her wings
17.24:
**“and they shall know”** — Figuratively.
**“all the trees”** — the faithful
**“of the country, that I the Lord have brought down the high tree”** — the Jews
**“high”** — formerly
**“and have exalted the low tree”** — the Gentiles
**“low tree: and have dried up the green tree”** — that is, the Jews flourishing and sprouting in the law and the prophets
**“and have caused the dry tree to flourish”** — the people of the nations, so that he might fulfil in deed what he has always spoken
**“Have brought down the high tree”** — Jerome. Whence Simeon: “Behold this child is set for the fall, and for the resurrection of many.” Also the grain of mustard, the smallest of all seeds, once it has grown high, is a dwelling of birds.
**“I the Lord have spoken and have done it.”** — Some, interpreting otherwise, refer the high tree humbled and the low tree exalted to the passion of the Saviour, who, “being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” and after the resurrection that very tree was exalted, which, before green, was dried up by death, and afterwards, coming to life again, received its former vigour. Others refer it to Israel, that humbled and withered at the first coming, it will at the second be restored to its former state; whence Paul: “when the fulness of the Gentiles shall come in, then all Israel shall be saved.”

18.2:
**“What is that you use among you this parable as a proverb”** — I am he who repays the sins of the fathers upon the sons
**“in the land of Israel, saying”** — mockingly
**“The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge.”**
• As if to say: as it is absurd for the fathers to eat sour grapes and the children’s teeth to be set on edge, so it is unjust for the fathers to sin and the sons and grandsons to be tormented
• In Exodus it is read: “I am he who visit the sins of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation.” But here, say the heretics who do not receive the Old Testament, how great is the cruelty of the God of the law and the prophets, who extends his anger to the third and fourth generation. But these must be answered that in this too the clemency of God the Creator is shown. For it is mercy not to punish at once, but to hold back the sentence and defer vengeance. There are those who explain it thus. They say the father in us is the slight prick of the senses and the incentives of vices; the son, if the thought has conceived the sin; the grandson, if what you have thought and conceived you have completed in deed; the great-grandson, that is, the fourth generation, if you have not only done it but glory in the sin, according to that: “The wicked man, when he is come into the depth of sins, contemneth.” God therefore does not punish the first and second stings of thoughts, which the Greeks call propatheiai, without which no man can be, but only if one has resolved to do what he has thought, and refuses to correct by penance what he has done. Whence: “No man is without sin, not even if his life be but of one day.” And elsewhere: “Who shall glory that he hath a chaste heart?” And “the stars also are not pure in his sight,” and against his angels he devised something perverse. But if that sublime nature is not without sin, how much more frail man, who says with the apostle: “Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” He, when he has done all good things, ought to say: “I am an unprofitable servant; I have done that which I ought to do.” And that: “Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it. Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it.” To prove that the first impulse of thought, indeed the slight prompting of the mind, is not punished by God, but only if what you have conceived in the mind you carry out in deed, this from Genesis must be brought forward: Cham sinned by mocking his father’s nakedness, and the sentence was received not by himself but by Chanaan his son. “Cursed,” he says, “be Chanaan, he shall be a servant to his brethren.” For what justice is it that the father should sin and the son be punished? And that which the apostle sets on the other side, that the woman will be saved if her children continue in faith and holiness and chastity, seems not to be just, namely that if the children and grandchildren are good the parents should be saved. For many holy parents have wicked children, and many sinners have holy children. According to this sense, therefore, which we have given, it is to be understood that the sins of the fathers are punished in the branches, not in the root; let it suffice to have said this of the proverb or parable, so that the law and the prophets, that is, Exodus and Ezechiel, indeed God himself, who spoke both here and there, may not seem to differ in his sentences, or to correct here what he cursed there.
**“What is that you use among you”** — For that is a parable which is said in Exodus: “I am the Lord, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me.” And elsewhere: “visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and the children’s children, unto the third and fourth generation.” For this sounds one thing in the words and holds another in the sense. We until now think that the two testimonies set above are not a parable but set forth a plain sentence; and although we do not dare to say anything, as neither does the earthen vessel against the potter, “Why hast thou made me thus?”, yet we suffer a hidden scandal, that it seems an injustice of God that one should sin and another mourn the sins. For if he repays sins unto the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one should sin and another be punished. But he adds: “to them that hate me.” For the children are not punished because their fathers sinned, but because, like them, by a kind of inherited evil, they hate God.
18.3:
**“As I live, saith the Lord God”** — Aposiopesis.
**“this parable shall be no more to you a proverb in Israel.”** — although among others who do not have knowledge of God
18.4:
**“Behold all souls are mine”** — by nature, not by merit, as Moses and Elias are called men of God; a man of sin and son of iniquity is not called a man of God
**“as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, the same shall die.”** — because it is not with him who is life
**“The soul that sinneth”**
• Jerome. Not by the abolition of substance, but by being removed from him who says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” And elsewhere: “Every one that liveth, and believeth in me, shall not die for ever”; and: “He that keepeth my word shall not see death for ever.” But what Balaam says, “Let our soul die the death of the just,” is to be taken thus: let it die to the world and to sin, and live with the souls of the just, whose life is Christ. They can say: “I will please the Lord in the land of the living.” “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” Balaam also, which is interpreted “vain people,” that is, the Gentiles, who desire to have fellowship with the souls of the just, Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, who are called eutheis, that is, upright and just; whence the book of Genesis took its name from their title.
• As if: as the sins of sons do not harm fathers, so the sins of fathers do not overflow onto sons, but the soul that sins itself shall die.
18.5:
**“And a man”**
• father
• As if: by this you may know that what was said, “I will repay the sins of the fathers,” etc., does not sound as many think, nor is it like that saying, “The fathers have eaten a sour grape,” and the like.
**“if a man be just”** — a list of the father’s virtues, which are divided into seventeen parts
**“and do judgment”** — first
**“and justice”**
• second, like the first
• Jerome. Whoever has this has Christ, who was made for us justice and sanctification, so that he may do true justice and not accept persons in judgment.
**“And if a man be just”** — In Proverbs it is said: “The thoughts of the just are judgments.” He who has this virtue, that he does nothing without judgment and reason, sings securely that word of the prophet: “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves,” and “in judgment he shall not accept person”; he will advance to such blessedness that he understands the judgments of God, which are “a great deep.”
18.6:
**“upon the mountains”** — third
**“hath not eaten”** — by worshipping idols
**“And”**
• fourth
• sixth
• also keep in your own manner
**“nor lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel: and”** — fifth
**“hath not defiled his neighbour's wife”** — forbids adultery
**“nor come near to a menstruous woman”**
• through the flow of unclean blood each month, women’s heavy and sluggish bodies are relieved
• Every man is a neighbour. Otherwise you might freely defile the wife of your enemy or of a stranger; but every man is your neighbour, for nothing is nearer to man than man. Besides, according to this parable: “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho,” etc. For everyone who does good is a neighbour.
**“Upon the mountains hath not eaten”** — Like the one who said: “I give thee thanks, O God, that I am not as this publican.” Heretics too, who seek higher things, eat on the mountains of pride.
**“to the idols”** — The images that heretics fashion from their own heart, toward which they lift the eyes of the heart, while they think falsehood and lies to be truth.
**“the house of Israel”** — Because they are found in the Church, and through the pretext of the false name of knowledge they seduce the simple, so as to introduce the doctrines of philosophers into the house of Israel, that is, of those who behold God with the mind.
**“and his neighbour's wife”** — Jerome. The wife of a holy man is wisdom; whence Solomon: “Love her, and she shall embrace thee; love her, and she shall keep thee.” He defiles her who finds fault with the blessings of others, and, kindled with the torches of envy, violates the holy and corrupts the chaste.
**“come near to a menstruous woman”** — Jerome. If anyone has approached, the fetuses conceived are said to contract a taint of the seed, so that lepers and those with elephantiasis are born of this corruption, and bodies foul in both sexes, through smallness or deformity of limbs. For corrupt matter degenerates. It is therefore commanded that men observe measure and times, not only with other women but also with their own wives, to whom they seem joined by law, according to that: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth”; whence: “A time to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces.” Let the wife therefore beware lest she conceal it out of desire for intercourse, and the husband lest he use force on her, thinking her subject to him at all times for the pleasure of marriage; whence: “That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour”; whence in the sayings of Sextus the Pythagorean: He is an adulterer who loves his own wife too ardently.
18.7:
**“And”** — seventh
**“hath not wronged any man”**
• Grieve not the Spirit, that is, the one who dwells in you
• The Septuagint: “hath oppressed.” Whence Habacuc: “the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself”
• eighth
**“hath restored the pledge to the debtor”**
• not to everyone, otherwise it would become an occasion and matter for many of taking pledges and riches; but if he is manifestly poor
• That is, to him who is poor and has pledged his own garment, and ought to receive it back before sunset, lest, oppressed by the cold, he cry to the Lord, who is the avenger of injury. We also restore the pledge to the debtor when, to him to whom we are joined by love, and who owes us mutual charity, we return his pledge, keeping back nothing of his debt with us.
**“by violence”** — ninth
**“hath taken nothing away”** — The apostle says of robbers: with such a one, not so much as to eat
**“his bread”**
• bread
• tenth; whatever food
• Jerome. Here we are taught that alms are not to be given to the sated, nor to those who belch from fullness, but to those who are tormented with emptiness. In bread all food is understood. His own: let us turn into mercy bread not acquired from robberies or usuries and another’s harm. “The redemption of a man’s soul are his riches.” Many oppress poor clients and farmers (not to mention the violence of soldiers and judges) by power, or commit thefts, so as to give a little out of much to the poor and glory in their crimes; and the deacon publicly in the churches recites the names of the offerers: so much this one offers, so much that one has promised; and they please themselves at the applause of the people, though conscience torments them; and we give the wretched occasion to rejoice in what they are given and not to mourn what is seized from them. But it is better to say that the bread of the just man is he who says: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven.” Of whom we say in prayer: give us our supersubstantial or coming bread, that what we are to receive always afterwards, we may deserve to receive daily in the present age. The just man gives this bread to the hungry, namely those who hunger and thirst after justice. This bread is not to be given to those who have eaten and drunk and been filled and, grown fat, have kicked, lest they vomit it up. Whence Solomon: he will vomit it up and will defile your good words; whence the Saviour: “give not that which is holy to dogs.”
**“his”** — not from robbery
**“hath given to the hungry”** — not to one who is full, not to one who belches from plenty, but to one who is tormented by emptiness
**“and the naked”** — eleventh
**“hath covered with a garment”**
• with a garment, or with faith and virtues
• of which: “Naked, and you covered me.”
• as many of you as have been baptized have put on Christ
**“Hath not wronged any man”** — Let him not hear. “Why is earth and ashes proud?” That is, forgetting his condition, he sets his mouth against heaven and says with the true Nabuchodonosor: “I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my throne.”
**“by violence hath taken nothing away”** — Jerome. All plunder is mixed with violence. There is also a holy violence and a desirable plunder; whence: “From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent bear it away.” But the adverse powers hasten to the plunder of souls. Whence Jacob: “A wicked beast hath devoured him, a beast hath seized Joseph”; whence also the sheep that follow the Lord are not snatched out of his hands.
**“covered the naked”** — Lacking this garment, the naked man was cast out of the wedding feast. Whence, to Jerusalem: “But thou wast naked and full of confusion.”
18.8:
**“upon usury”** — twelfth
**“Hath not lent”** — to anyone, whatever
**“And”** — thirteenth
**“taken any increase”** — of whatever thing, any excess whatever
**“from iniquity”**
• fourteenth
• that in every work he flees iniquity
**“hath withdrawn his hand, and hath executed true judgment”**
• fifteenth
• it seems the same as in the first, but here “true” is added
• similar to the first, but divided into parts
**“Hath not lent upon usury”** — Jerome. In the Hebrew, usury of every kind is forbidden. The Septuagint: he has not given his money upon usury, as in the Psalm: “He that hath not put out his money to usury.” In which only usury of money is forbidden. In the law it is said: to your brother you shall not lend upon usury; to strangers you shall lend upon usury. Note the progress. At the beginning of the law interest is taken away only from brethren; in the prophet, from all; in the gospel there is increase: you shall lend to those from whom you hope not to receive.
**“nor taken any increase”** — Some think usury is only in money, but the divine Scripture takes away the surplus of every thing, so that you receive no more than you gave. In the fields they are accustomed to exact usuries of grain, wine, oil and other kinds, as though the divine word did not call this surplus; as if in winter we give ten measures that in harvest we may receive fifteen, that is, more by half. He who thinks himself most just takes a fourth part more. They are accustomed to argue and say: I gave one measure, which sown yielded ten measures; is it not just that I receive half a measure more from what is mine, when by my liberality he has nine and a half? “Be not deceived,” says Paul, “God is not mocked.” Let the merciful lender answer whether he gave to one who had or to one who had not. To one who had he ought not to have given; but he gave as to one who had not. Why then does he exact more, as from one who has? Others, when money is lent, are accustomed to receive little gifts of various kinds; but let them understand that usury is called surplus, whatever it is, if it is more than what they gave.
**“From iniquity hath withdrawn his hand”** — Jerome. That is, that in every work he flee iniquity, which is committed not only by the hand but by the other members; whence Solomon: “let wicked lips be far from thee,” and elsewhere: “they have spoken iniquity on high.” Whose foot runs to iniquity, and the eye, if it has seen another’s wife to lust after her, is not an imitator of him of whom it is said: “who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.”
**“hath executed true judgment between man and man”** — Jerome. Or his neighbour. This seems to be the same as if he be just and do judgment; but with truth of judgment added, an intensification of virtues is seen; whence also in Proverbs: after many precepts the correction of judgment is brought in, and after all, to correct judgment. Therefore the apostle rebukes those who have lawsuits among themselves, because the least and the despised is chosen, who according to the gospel is first, to judge between man and man; he who has destroyed the things that are of a little child and has come to the perfect man, and then needs a greater judgment that he may be able to come to the truth of judgment.
18.9:
**“Hath walked in my commandments”**
• sixteenth
• “The commandment of the Lord is lightsome, enlightening the eyes.”
**“And”**
• seventeenth
• “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves.”
**“kept my judgments, to do truth: he is just”** — he who has done these things and not those will not die for the sins of his father
**“he shall surely live”** — by his own virtues
**“saith the Lord God”** — In my precepts he hath walked. Jerome. If he keep my judgments or my justifications, that is, so as to do them and keep what is done; whence: “The justices of the Lord are right, rejoicing hearts: the commandment of the Lord is lightsome, enlightening the eyes.” But it is asked how in this same prophet God says: I gave them statutes that were not good, in which they shall not live. But the Jews do not live, following the killing letter, and Christians live, understanding the life-giving Spirit.
**“He is just”** — Jerome. The just man is the churchman who preaches the catholic faith; his son is the disciple, who if he is deceived by the error of heretics will be called pestilent; whence: “he hath not sat in the chair of pestilence.” This one sheds the blood of the deceived and doubles all sins upon himself, eating on the mountains of pride and defiling the church of his neighbour, grieving, oppressing and supplanting the needy and poor in the knowledge of the Scriptures, seizing those whom he has led astray from the church, not restoring the pledge which he received from his master, not fulfilling that: freely you have received, freely give.
18.10:
**“that”** — but
