**“if he beget a son that is a robber”** — The Septuagint and Theodotion: pestilent. For as pestilence produces diseases and lays waste regions, so a pestilent man ravages everything.
**“a shedder of blood, and that hath done”** — Septuagint: sins
**“And if he beget a son”** — This too can be understood in us, to whom it is said: “Hearken, O daughter, and see, and incline thy ear: and forget thy people and thy father’s house,” and the king shall desire thy beauty; so that we who are born of the stock of the Gentiles may leave the crimes of our parents, and do judgment and justice, and live in it.
18.11: **“Though he doth not all these things”** — but defiling the virtues of the father
18.12:
**“That grieveth the needy and the poor, that taketh away by violence, that restoreth not the pledge, and that lifteth up his eyes to idols”** — which he fashioned from his own heart
**“that lifteth up his eyes to idols, that committeth abomination”** — so that the diligence of the disciple increases the error of the master, and he demands back from those to whom he gave more than he gave
18.13:
**“That giveth upon usury, and that taketh an increase: shall such a one live? he shall not live.”** — because
**“Seeing he hath done all these detestable things”** — but
**“he shall surely die”** — eternal
**“his blood shall be upon him”** — condemnation
**“shall be upon him”** — not in another, not in the father
18.14: **“But if he beget a son, who, seeing all his father's sins, which he hath done, is afraid, and shall not do the like to them”** — as if: do not wonder if the son of a truly just man, turning aside to sins, dies; for on the contrary, if a sinner begets a son who, seeing all the sins
18.17: **“That hath turned away his hand from injuring the poor, hath not taken usury and increase, but hath executed my judgments, and hath walked in my commandments: this man shall not die for the iniquity of his father”** — to whom he is unlike
18.18: **“As for his father, because he oppressed and offered violence to his brother, and wrought evil in the midst of his people, behold he is dead in his own iniquity.”** — not another’s
18.19:
**“And you say”** — he poses the question
**“Why hath not the son borne the iniquity of his father?”** — he answers
**“Verily, because the son hath wrought judgment and justice”** — as one who is just and has not followed the father’s works
**“hath kept all my commandments, and done them, living, he shall live”**
• as the wicked father will die by death
• because he did the works of life
18.21:
**“But if the wicked do penance for all his sins”** — turn aside from evil
**“which he hath committed, and keep all my commandments, and do”** — do good
**“But if the wicked”** — As if: the son is not weighed down by the father’s sins, nor is another involved in others' sins, so that the very same man who was before wicked and a sinner, if he does penance, is not condemned for his earlier sins.
18.22:
**“all his iniquities”** — if he repented of all
**“that he hath done: I will not remember”** — because he remembers
**“in his justice”** — by which he kept all the precepts
**“which he hath wrought”** — by free will
**“he shall live”** — In his justice, which he hath wrought. Jerome. Not so much mine, that is, as his; although it is part of my justice to repay good to the good and evil to the evil.
18.23:
**“Is it my will”** — God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; where the sentence of God appears stern and harsh, yet it condemns not men but sins.
**“that a sinner should die, saith the Lord God, and not that he should be converted from his ways”** — namely, let sins perish; let the man be saved
18.24:
**“But if the just man turn himself away from his justice, and do iniquity according to all the abominations which the wicked man useth to work, shall he live?”** — who is a son of death
**“all his justices which he hath done, shall not be remembered”**
• to his salvation
• but
**“in the prevarication, by which he hath prevaricated, and in his sin, which he hath committed, in them”** — not in others'
**“But if the just man turn himself away”** — But if the just man turn himself away. As if: as old sins do not weigh down the just man before the sinner, so old righteousnesses do not help the sinner before the just man. For each man is judged in whatever he is found in.
18.25:
**“And”** — yet
**“Is it my way”** — As if: you think I punish undeservedly the sins of the fathers in the sons; but every one dies in his own sin and lives in his own justice. In both, not past things but present are punished. But your opinion is unjust, who think it is not a parable but history, that the crimes of some are punished in others.
18.26: **“For when the just turneth himself away”** — The people of Israel, just before, turned away from their justice, because they left the author of justice, and did iniquity by denying the Son of God. Therefore in the sin and in the crime which they have wrought they shall die, not in many but in one, killing the heir that they might lose the inheritance.
18.27:
**“And when the wicked turneth himself away”** — Gentile
**“from his wickedness”** — idolatry
**“which he hath wrought, and doeth judgment, and justice”** — which were commanded to the Jews by the law
**“he shall save his soul alive”** — formerly dead
18.28:
**“Because he considereth”** — that is, that he had perished in iniquities
**“and turneth away himself from all his iniquities which he hath wrought, he shall surely live”** — believing in him who says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
18.29: **“And the children of Israel say”** — To this day Israel blasphemes God, because he has forsaken his people and taken up a multitude of the Gentiles; the Lord reproves them, because their ways are perverse. But the Lord’s sentence is just, that, the wicked husbandmen being destroyed, he let his vineyard to others; which the Jews, understanding it in the parable of the gospel, said: it shall not be so.
18.30:
**“Therefore will I judge every man”** — whether Jew or Gentile; “there is no respect of persons with God.” Each shall be crowned in his faith or condemned in unbelief.
**“according to his ways, O house of Israel, saith the Lord God. Be converted”** — Jews and Gentiles, namely to him who can heal your bruises
**“Be converted”** — Properly this word is directed to Israel, that they may do penance and leave their iniquities.
**“and do penance for all your iniquities: and iniquity shall not be your ruin”** — It is better to take this exhortation, “be converted and do penance,” in the person of the Jews.
18.31:
**“Cast away from you all your transgressions, by which you have transgressed, and make to yourselves a new heart”** — leaving behind the oldness of the letter
**“and will put a new spirit”** — in the newness of the spirit
**“and why will you die, O house of Israel?”**
• who are the sons of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Of whom it is said: “God of the living, and not of the dead.”
• And make to yourselves a new heart. The new heart of Israel is to believe in him whom it had earlier denied; the new heart of the Gentiles is to leave idols, and, with the worship of the dead scorned, to believe in him who is the God of the living.
18.32:
**“For I desire not the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord God, return ye”** — who have departed
**“Turn ye, and live.”**
• by penance; dead through sins
• As if to say: why will you die, who ought to live by the merit of your fathers and by my mercy? Because “I desire not the death of the sinner.”
**“For I desire not the death”** — I do not wish you to die, whom I begot unto salvation; “I have brought up children, and exalted them: but they have despised me.”

19.1:
**“Moreover take thou up a lamentation for the princes of Israel”** — namely all who were born of the stock of Josias
**“Take up a lamentation”** — With captivity near, the prophet does not so much foretell future things as narrate past ones. For after the sixth year of King Sedechias we read directly in what follows: “And it came to pass in the seventh year.”
19.2:
**“And say: Why did thy mother”** — Jerusalem.
**“the lioness lie down among the lions”** — Metaphorically, all.
19.3:
**“One of her whelps”** — Namely, Joachaz son of Josias, whom Nechao the pharao led into Egypt, and put Joachim in his place; to him succeeded his son Jechonias, who with his mother and the nobles of the city was led by Nabuchodonosor into Babylon, of whom was born Salathiel, father of Zorobabel.
**“He became a lion”** — Jerome. These things had already happened when the prophet spoke. For after Jerusalem had led out Joachaz, son of Josias, from the royal stock and made him king, he proved so cruel in a short time that he is remembered, morally, as having seized prey and devoured men.
19.4:
**“And the nations heard”** — his fame
**“of him the nations”** — Egyptians
**“and not without his wounds”** — the victory was bloody
19.5:
**“But she seeing”** — the mother Jerusalem, who had borne and nourished him and made him king
**“that she was weakened”** — the kingdom failing
**“and her hope was lost; took one”** — Jechonias, son of Joachim
**“of her young lions”** — of other kings
**“a lion”** — king
19.6:
**“who went up and down among the lions”** — having entered the way of his predecessor
**“and became a lion; he learned to catch the prey and to devour men”** — with excessive cruelty
19.7:
**“He learned to make widows and to lay waste their cities”** — to be laid waste
**“and the land became desolate, and the fulness thereof by the noise of his roaring”** — terrified
19.8:
**“And”** — therefore
**“And they spread”** — Jerome. Not that this was done to Jechonias, who gave himself up to the king of Babylon and was carried off into Chaldea, but that the figure of the lion may be kept, who is taken in pits, bound with chains, and kept in cages.
**“The nations came together against him on every side out of the provinces, and they spread their net over him; in their wounds he was taken”** — Otherwise, according to the history, we read this of Sedecias, who was raised to the kingdom after Jechonias; and the occasion for this is that, because the chains are called a cage and a prison, many understand it of Sedecias rather than Jechonias. But Jechonias was kept in prison, and was not put to death, only deprived of his kingdom. Sedecias, however, the history tells only that he was led blind to Babylon and immediately killed.
19.10:
**“Thy mother”** — one thing is said in many words
**“is like a vine”** — The Seventy: a flower on pomegranate trees
**“in thy blood”** — by the redness of the flowers
**“planted by the water”** — where it is nourished by moisture
**“Thy mother is like”** — Jerusalem, who above was compared to a beautiful woman and then to a lioness nursing whelps, is now compared to a most beautiful vine.
**“her fruit and her branches have grown out of many waters”**
• A vine, however beautiful, however far extended by long shoots, if you take away the stakes and canes, lying on the ground withers by the heat, especially if a burning wind, which the Greeks call elisona, elsewhere kaysona, has dried its fruit, so that it withers and is as it were burned by fire with its heats.
• It signifies Babylon or Egypt, to which they fled; or Judea itself, in which a few poor remained, over whom Godolias was set, to gather and rule the remnants of the people, whom Ismael of the royal stock slew in Maspha; and this is what is said: fire hath eaten her.
*Jerome:* According to the anagogical sense we refer this to the Church, because in the last time, iniquity being multiplied, “the charity of many shall grow cold,” that even the elect, if it be possible, may be tried, and her princes be taken in the nets of the devil, who, not content with the capture of one king, hastens daily to take kings and princes; whence: his choice food. The branches of which churches, which a while ago were equal to flowers and the red of blood, are dried up by the burning wind; whence in the gospel, those who had sprung up, when the sun was risen, were scorched, and withered away; so that scarcely one of the branches remains to rise up into a rod and become a worthy prince of the people; whence Isaias: I will send forth a famine and a thirst upon the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst of water, etc. Whence we ought to weep and lament over the princes of Israel, by whose vice and pride Judea was taken, and Jerusalem.
19.11:
**“and she hath strong rods to make sceptres for them that bear rule”** — The Seventy: into the tribe of leaders, so that of course kings would come from there
**“and her stature was exalted”** — God resists the proud
**“her stature among the branches; and she saw her height in the multitude of her branches”** — so that she was proud: we see the goods of others and do not know our own
19.12:
**“and was plucked up”** — in the wrath of the Lord
**“in wrath and cast on the ground; and the burning wind dried up her fruit”** — by an elegant figure he shows the ruins of Jerusalem
**“are withered and dried up; her strong rods; the fire”** — Ismael
19.13:
**“And”** — yet
**“Now she is transplanted into the desert”** — so beautiful, so fruitful
19.14:
**“And a fire is gone out”** — Ismael
**“from a rod”** — the royal tribe
**“of her branches, which hath devoured her fruit, and she hath no”** — from then on
**“a strong rod”** — any king who would govern the people; but with Johanan son of Carea they fled into Egypt
**“a sceptre of rulers”** — of royal stock, which ceased in Judea thereafter until he should come for whom it is reserved, who will be the expectation of the nations
**“This is a lamentation, and it shall be for a lamentation”** — Jerome. From this it is clear that what was said above: Why is thy mother a lioness, etc., and here: thy mother is like a vine, etc., pertain to Jerusalem, which lost her lions and her branches, and there remained in her no rod that might rise up into a royal tribe; for it began with lamentation and ends in lamentation. Take up a lamentation, etc.; this is lamentation in the beginning and in the end. For the royal stock is to be followed with weeping and lamentation.

20.1: **“And it came to pass”** — eleven months and five days after the earlier vision
20.2:
**“And”** — after
**“the word of the Lord came to me, saying”** — before they speak he knows what they seek
20.3:
**“Are you come to inquire”** — Many examples bear witness that it was the custom of the people of Israel to ask of the Lord through the prophets whatever they doubted. Saul, seeking the asses, goes to Samuel. When the son of Jeroboam was sick, his wife is sent to them in Silo to the prophet Achias. David also, a prophet, asks another prophet, Nathan, whether he ought to build a house for the Lord. In the New Testament also Agabus foretells to Paul what is to come. It is written in Deuteronomy: the nations which the Lord is about to destroy before thee hear dreams and divinations, but to thee the Lord hath not so given.
**“As I live”** — A fitting answer is given to those who ask. To the holy it is said: “While thou art yet speaking, I will say, Here I am.” To sinners, such as the elders of Israel, rebuke for their sins is given, and an oath is added so that the sentence may be firmer: they are refused.
20.4:
**“If thou judgest them, if thou judgest, son of man”** — as if: they came to ask about things they doubt; but you, son of man, judge them
**“If thou judgest them”** — It is not the answer of a prophet but the sentence of a judge, for their iniquities, because they followed the iniquities of their fathers.
**“the abominations”** — Not that the sins of the fathers overflow onto the sons, but it is shown that they did similar things, and by hereditary evil drew out a long rope of sins, so that those whose sins they imitate may fear the punishments.
20.5:
**“And say to them: Thus saith the Lord God: In the day when I chose Israel, and lifted up my hand for the race of the house of Jacob, and appeared”** — known
**“to them in the land of Egypt, and lifted up”** — against the Egyptians
**“my hand”** — as about to strike
**“In the day when I chose”** — Israel, while it was in Egypt, knew God so little that Moses, sent to them, said: “If they ask me, Who sent you? what shall I say to them?” And the Lord said: “He who is hath sent me.” There, then, he was made known to them, how he lifted up his hand for them against the Egyptians.
20.6:
**“In that day I lifted up my hand for them, to bring them out of the land of Egypt, into a land which I had provided for them, flowing with milk and honey”** — for they were not yet perfect but to be nourished with the milk of infancy
**“Into a land which”** — Jerome. Literally, no one can doubt that Judea was given to them and is more fertile than all lands, for whoever has surveyed the whole land from Rinocorula to Mount Taurus and the river Euphrates, and the power of its cities and the pleasantness of its regions.
**“which excelleth amongst all lands”**
• Namely Palestine and Phenicia, Arabia, Syria, Coele, Cilicia, and the other regions which the Lord promised again to Israel if he kept the precepts. But if he did not receive them, it was the fault of unbelief; for even in Palestine and the province of Judea many nations remained which were not subjected to them. Yet the one who promises is not guilty of falsehood or of crime, but he who made himself unworthy of the promise. Moreover this is the condition of the one promising: “If you be willing, and will hearken to me, you shall eat the good things of the land.” But if you will not, the sword shall devour you. Therefore men are chosen, sometimes according to the present, sometimes according to foreknowledge; and he who is chosen cannot at once not be tempted or perish. For Saul, chosen for the kingdom, and Judas, for the apostleship, afterwards perished by their own fault.
• Jerome. Aquila, firmament. Symmachus, religion. Theodotion, strength; because this land is, as it were, the foundation of all lands, because in it are God’s religion and temple and ceremonies and knowledge of God.
20.7:
**“And I said to them”** — first going out of Egypt
**“Let every man cast away the scandals of his eyes”** — namely the idols which they had served for a long time, so that they would not deign even to look at them
**“and defile not yourselves with the idols of Egypt”** — by worshipping
**“I am the Lord your God”**
• not the Egyptians, not the various monsters
• Let us turn our eyes away from the spectacles, or rather the offences, of Egypt, the sand of the circus, the theatres, and from all things that defile the purity of the soul and enter into the mind through the senses; whence: “Death is come up through our windows.”
**“Every man”** — Jerome. To us, who are coming out of Egypt, it is commanded that we cast away the scandals of our eyes, lest the things that formerly delighted us now take hold of us, lest the idols of Egypt defile us, namely the inventions of the heretical philosophers, which are rightly called idols.
20.8:
**“they provoked me”**
• because
• by free will
**“would not hearken”** — namely doing forbidden things and murmuring against Moses
**“every man cast away the abominations of his eyes, neither did they forsake the idols of Egypt, and”** — therefore
**“I said”** — I decreed
**“I would pour out my indignation”** — with the mind with which I had conceived it
**“upon them, and accomplish my wrath against them in the midst of the land of Egypt”** — because they had not yet gone out when he wished to pour out wrath
20.9:
**“And”** — as if I spared my name, lest the nations have occasion to blaspheme, among whom I was made known to them
**“I did otherwise for my name's sake”** — What I was thinking of doing on account of justice I did not do, on account of mercy, lest my name be polluted and I seem unable to fulfil what I had promised Israel.
20.10:
**“Therefore I brought them out”** — Jerome. Up to here the prophet has described what he promised them in the land of Egypt, and how they at once offended, and what he had planned against them and yet did not do; what follows he spoke to those who had gone out of Egypt.
**“Therefore I brought them out from the land of Egypt, and brought them into the desert”** — These things are said to those who were led out of Egypt into the desert, so that, freed from the vices of the Egyptians, they might more easily keep God’s precepts in the solitude.
20.11: **“And I gave them my statutes, and I shewed them my judgments, which if a man do, he shall live in them”** — also adding nothing, as in the gospel
20.12: **“Moreover I gave them also my sabbaths, to be a sign between me and them”** — of the true sabbath; and circumcision is the sign of true circumcision, so that, cleansed from all vices, we may live to him through the whole week, day and night, that we may rest in the eternal sabbath
20.13:
**“But the house of Israel provoked me”** — also
**“in the desert: they walked not in my statutes, and they cast away my judgments, which if a man do he shall live in them”** — also adding nothing, as in the gospel
**“and they grievously violated my sabbaths”**
• not once
• not a little
**“I said therefore”** — when he said to Moses: “Let me alone”
20.14:
**“But I spared them for the sake of my name”** — sparing the Egyptians and the other nations, lest they be scandalized; and those also on whom he had mercy, waiting for their repentance
**“before the nations, from”** — Jerome. Now indeed they had been cast out of Egypt. But above he says: before the nations, in whose midst they were, because they had not yet gone out.
20.15: **“So I lifted up my hand over them”** — by the Amalekites and others who fought against them in the desert
20.16: **“Because they cast off my judgments, and walked not in my statutes, and violated my sabbaths: for their heart went after idols”** — the Egyptians
20.17:
**“Yet my eye spared them, so that I destroyed them not”**
• altogether
• that is, the sons together with the fathers. For he brought the sons into the land of promise.
**“My eye spared”** — Jerome. How did he spare, since besides Jesus Nave and Caleb the son of Jephone none entered the land of promise? Whence we understand that they live, neither reserved for eternal punishments nor blotted out of the book of the living nor consumed before the face of the Lord. For if, because they did not enter the land of promise, they are to be believed to have perished, then Moses also perished, who only saw it and did not enter. We believe also that the prayers of Moses were heard, who, interceding for the people, said: if thou forgive them this sin, forgive it; but if thou do not, strike me out of thy book. Let us hear, moreover, that the sentence of the Lord upon his sons and servants is not destruction but amendment. “Whom the Lord loveth he chastiseth,” etc., and elsewhere: when he slew them, they sought him. And in another place: I will kill and I will make to live.
20.18:
**“And I said”** — after the slaying of the fathers he gives precepts to the sons, in which he spares the fathers also
**“to their children in the wilderness: Walk not in the statutes of your fathers”** — that they not imitate their sins, whose torments you have seen
20.19: **“I am the Lord your God”** — he says the same things to the sons as before to the fathers
20.20:
**“And sanctify my sabbaths”** — show them holy, by reverencing them
**“that they may be a sign”** — as above
**“between me and you: and that you may know”** — thus
**“that I am”** — not another
20.21:
**“And”**
• yet
• therefore
**“But their children provoked me”**
• imitating the wickedness of their fathers
• because
**“they walked not in my commandments, nor observed my judgments”** — in heart
**“to do them”** — in deed
**“which if a man do, he shall live in them: and they violated my sabbaths”** — to set out the plain things is idle
**“and I threatened”** — Because they sinned as their fathers did, they deserved a similar sentence, but they were spared by the same clemency and for the same causes. The same author softens wrath with the same patience for both.
20.22: **“But I turned away my hand”** — vengeance
20.23: **“Again I lifted up my hand”** — Where in the Old Testament the Lord lifted up his hand against the sons of those who fell in the desert, wishing to scatter them, Scripture does not say; but from what is said here it is to be believed that it was done; or it signifies this: that after they came into the land of promise, their sins demanding it, they were delivered to various nations and kings, and then the precepts, good in their own nature, were made to them not good.
20.25:
**“Therefore I also gave them statutes that were not good”** — to them: namely, although they were made good in nature, they were not good to them, since in captivity they are not able to keep the precepts of the law
**“and judgments, in which they shall not live”** — yet believing that they live in them
**“Therefore I also gave them”** — Jerome. He does not say evil but not good. For it does not at once follow that what is not good is evil. For the Apostle says: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman”; which if he do, it is neither good nor evil. He gave them therefore, scattered among the nations, precepts not good, because he let them go according to the desires of their heart, that they might do what is not fitting.
*Jerome:* We can say that before the offence they received only the decalogue, but after idolatry and blasphemy the manifold ceremonies of the law, that they might offer sacrifices to God rather than to demons, and that by comparison with sacrilege it might be made lighter; which was not in itself good, yet not evil, because it was offered to God; and not good, because they had offended the author of good.
20.26:
**“And I polluted them”** — that is, I showed them polluted, as a priest separates lepers from the people
**“in their own gifts”** — with idols they offered what is due to God
**“when they offered”**
• namely the firstborn
• passing through fire to Baal
**“all that opened the womb, for their offences: and they shall know”** — deserted by God and given over to idols
**“that I am the Lord”** — whom by their fault they provoked to anger
20.27:
**“Wherefore speak to the house of Israel, O son of man, and say”** — to the elders who came to you to inquire
**“to them: Thus saith the Lord God”** — Septuagint: Adonai, the Lord
**“Moreover in this also”** — often and much
**“your fathers blasphemed me”** — from whose stock you are descended
20.28:
**“And I had brought them into the land, for which I lifted up my hand to give it them: they saw”** — for
**“every high hill, and every shady tree, and there they sacrificed”** — to idols
**“their victims: and there they presented”** — Others: and there they gave the provocation of their offering
**“the provocation”** — to provoke me
20.29:
**“And I said to them: What meaneth the high place to which you go? and the name thereof was called High-place”** — ancient error keeps the former name
**“high place”** — in Hebrew bama is high place; bamoth, the plural, high places
20.30:
**“Wherefore say to the house of Israel: Thus saith the Lord God: Verily, you are defiled in the way”** — with crimes
**“you are defiled in the way of your fathers”** — deserving a like punishment
20.31:
**“in the offering of your gifts, when you make your children pass”** — you have broken out into such wickedness
**“you defile yourselves with all your idols unto this day”** — it was not enough to have done it once
**“shall I answer you, O house of Israel”** — bound by such great crimes
**“As I live, saith the Lord God, I will not answer you”** — unworthy of my answer
**“when you make your children pass”** — Not that the elders, placed in captivity, did this, but those who were in Jerusalem, on whom captivity was impending, did not cease to do this.
20.32:
**“Neither shall the thought of your mind come to pass”** — as if you think I could not fulfil it
**“come to pass, by which you say”** — namely this
**“We will be”** — living by our own judgment
**“as the Gentiles, and”** — not under the Lord
**“as the families of the earth”** — so that we too may be one of the many nations
20.33:
**“As I live, saith the Lord God, I will reign over you with a strong hand, and with a stretched out arm”** — as though I would not despise you like runaway servants who neglect God
**“and with fury poured out, I will reign over you”** — I will call back to my kingdom
**“As I live, saith”** — As if: I will do all this so that you have me as king, not so that I scatter you, although you have chosen to serve demons.
20.34:
**“And I will bring you out from the people”** — I will not suffer you to be in eternal captivity
**“I will gather you out of the countries, in which you are scattered”** — by hostile necessity
**“with a strong hand, and with a stretched out arm”** — striking
**“and with fury poured out, I will reign over you”** — whether you will or no
20.35:
**“And I will bring you into the wilderness of people”** — I will call you back into former servitude, so that you may feel as angry one whom you neglected as merciful
**“and there will I plead with you face to face”** — there, namely
20.36: **“even so will I judge you”** — As if: I will do to you, who worship idols in Babylon, what I did to your fathers in Egypt, so that I may bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will be judged with you face to face, as I contended against them when they went out of Egypt.
20.37:
**“And I will make you subject”** — afterwards
**“to my sceptre, and will bring you into the bands of the covenant”** — bound by which you may not depart from my love
20.38:
**“And I will pick out from among you”** — to cast out
**“the transgressors, and the wicked”** — who persevere in evil
**“And”** — yet
**“out of the land where they sojourn”** — of exile
**“will bring them out of the land, and they shall not enter into the land of Israel”** — because they will perish in various regions
**“And you shall know”** — by the distinction of the wicked and the good
**“that I am the Lord”** — who do all things by judgment
20.39:
**“And as for you, O house of Israel: thus saith the Lord God: Walk ye every one”** — you are unworthy of my command, nor does your worship delight me
**“Walk ye every one after your idols, and serve them. But if in this also you hear me not, but defile my holy name”** — while you pretend to offer to me what you offer to idols, and do such great blasphemy against my name that, being worshippers of idols, you nevertheless say you are mine
**“any more with your gifts, and with your idols”** — know this
20.40:
**“In my holy mountain”** — Christ or the church
**“in the high mountain of Israel, saith the Lord God, there”** — not elsewhere
**“there shall all the house of Israel serve me; all of them”** — they will serve me
**“I say, in the land in which they shall please me, and there will I require your firstfruits”** — for through Christ or the church the firstfruits and tithes and all worship are turned into a sweet-smelling odour
**“and the chief of your tithes with all your sanctifications”**
• In my holy mountain. Of which: The mountain shall be made manifest on the top of the mountains, etc.; and elsewhere Isaias: Get thee up upon a high mountain, thou that bringest good tidings to Sion.
• Whatever is said of the people of Israel, who, delivered from Egypt, committed many sins in the wilderness and offended the Lord, and, brought into the land of promise, worshipped idols, and yet afterwards was delivered by the clemency of God, let us refer to those who have been delivered by the hand of God from the Egypt of this world, and in the wilderness of vices sigh after Egypt and do things worthy of punishment, but nevertheless are preserved through penance by the clemency of God alone.
20.41:
**“I will accept of you for an odour of sweetness, when I shall have brought you out from the people, and shall have gathered”** — or: when I shall have gathered
**“out of the lands into which you are scattered, and I will be sanctified in you”** — because they will see that people, namely the saved, glorify me
20.42:
**“And you shall know”** — you being saved
**“that I am the Lord, when I shall have brought you into the land of Israel, into the land for which I lifted up my hand to give it to your fathers”** — which they lost by their fault; you received it not so much by your merit as by my mercy
20.43:
**“And there you shall remember”** — Jerome. We cannot remember our crimes and vices unless we have been brought into the land of Israel, where, placed there, we say with the apostle: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.”
**“and you shall be displeased”** — Symmachus: you shall seem little ones to yourselves; that is, that when they have been exalted they may believe themselves humble, because the Lord gives grace to the humble, and elsewhere it is written: “Before destruction the heart is exalted, and before it is humbled” [the Latin: before tribulation the heart is exalted, and before loftiness it is humbled]. For contrition follows pride, and loftiness follows humility.
20.44:
**“And”** — for certain
**“you shall know”** — you saved
**“that I am the Lord”** — suffered for your sins
**“when I shall have done well by you for my own name’s sake”** — not your merit, namely, whose crimes deserved not mercy but punishment
20.46:
**“Son of man, set thy face against the way of the south, and drop towards the south, and prophesy against the forest of the south field”** — metaphorically, Jerusalem, where is the dwelling of beasts and fierce men
**“Set thy face”** — Set thy face. It needs a hardening of countenance and a hardness of brow, so that this prophet may speak fearlessly, especially when sad tidings are announced to the whole multitude of the people.
**“drop towards the south”** — Jerome. That is, so that the wrath of God may not be seen as wholly poured out. But if it is so great a drop, what do you judge of the whole showers?
*Jerome:* Allegorically. He calls this world a forest, one not having fruit-bearing trees but the dwelling of beasts; whence: “The voice of the Lord prepareth the stags: and he will discover the thick woods.” These are the forests and woods that devoured more in the battle of the army of Absalom than the sword slew. The green tree, that is, those who live in evil. The dry, those who are dead to justice. “Every face shall be burned in it from the south even to the north”: from those, that is, who seemed fervent in spirit, even to those who, as impiety increases and the charity of many grows cold, have lost their former heat; so that “all flesh” may see that “the flame of the Lord is not quenched.” “Ah, ah,” etc. The prophet prays that the Lord may not do what he threatens, that is, that the forest be not set on fire, that not all the trees be burned up, but that they may either receive a place of penance, or that the necessity of announcing it be not laid upon himself, especially since the people do not understand, and by the obscurity of the words are provoked the more to madness.
20.47:
**“And say to the south forest: Hear the word of the Lord: Thus saith the Lord God: Behold I will kindle a fire in thee, and will burn in thee”** — according to that: begin from my saints
**“every green tree”** — not trees indeed, but wood prepared for burning
**“and every dry tree”** — which can have nothing living
**“the flame of the fire shall not be quenched: and every face shall be burned in it, from the south even to the north”**
• Babylon
• so that indeed every route through the nations into captivity is fulfilled by sword, famine, and pestilence
**“and will burn in thee”** — Saints indeed, and sinners, so that some may escape the evils of captivity by death, others be given over to eternal punishments.
**“from the south”** — Jerusalem indeed, which for those who are in Babylon lies to the south; just as, on the contrary, the pot of Jeremias, which signifies Jerusalem, is set on fire from the face of the north, that is, of Babylon.
20.48:
**“And shall see”** — he will know
**“all flesh”** — for which the salvation of God is to be seen
**“that I am”** — not another
**“the Lord have kindled it”** — by the burning of a forest, or a flame that can be quenched by no one’s help
20.49:
**“And I said”** — understanding this
**“Ah, ah, ah, O Lord God: they say of me: Doth not this man speak by parables?”** — as if: speak more plainly; we do not understand your parable

21.1: **“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:”** — because they were seeking a plain sentence, which was said figuratively above, is made plain clearly
21.2:
**“Son of man, set thy face toward Jerusalem”** — this he called a forest above
**“and let thy speech flow towards the holy places”** — that is
21.3:
**“And say to the land of Israel: Thus saith the Lord God: Behold I come against thee”** — this he called a flame above
**“out of its sheath, and will cut off in thee the just, and the wicked.”** — green wood and dry wood. Whence: “For if in the green wood they do these things, what shall be done in the dry?”
21.5:
**“That all flesh may know”** — above: “And all flesh shall see that I the Lord have kindled it, and it shall not be quenched”: the flame or forest
**“that I the Lord have drawn my sword out of its sheath”** — because after a short interval Jerusalem with its temple was set on fire by the Babylonians
21.6:
**“And thou, son of man, mourn”** — as if not with a moderate grief
**“with the breaking of thy loins, and with bitterness”** — so that your groaning is brought forth from the depths of your bowels and the bitterness of your soul
**“And thou, O son of man”** — The prophet is commanded that, when they are silent and do not ask why he prophesied these things, he should act, so that he may be asked why, and answer what the Lord has spoken.
21.7:
**“And when they shall say to thee: Why mournest thou?”** — as if: why do you groan with such grief? What evil has befallen you?
**“thou shalt say: For that which I hear: because it cometh, and”** — then
**“every heart shall melt”** — so that the minds of men that pass by may not dare to resist
**“and all hands shall be made feeble, and every spirit shall faint”** — of warriors
**“and water shall run down every knee”** — of urine
**“behold it is come”** — what I often foretold
**“and it shall be done”** — in deed
**“saith the Lord God”** — not I
**“For that which I hear: because”** — The thing, namely, which I had heard before is now fulfilled in deed: the raging army of the Babylonians, which is now at hand.
**“And every knee”** — It is natural that, fear compelling, the bladder of the urine is loosened, which also usually happens from the greatness of diseases.
21.9:
**“Son of man, prophesy, and say: Thus saith the Lord God:”** — to the sword
**“Say: The sword”**
• Nabuchodonosor
• the devil
**“the sword is sharpened, and furbished”** — Sword: the devil. Whence: to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. And in the psalm: “He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation: indignation and wrath and trouble, which he sent by evil angels.” Some think this sword was in the hand of an angel under David when he struck Jerusalem.
21.10:
**“to kill victims”** — that is, may kill many
**“It is sharpened, that it may glitter”** — you are Nabuchodonosor
**“thou removest the sceptre of my son”** — Israel
**“thou hast cut down every tree”** — namely the multitude of the people
21.11:
**“And I have given it”** — the sword
**“to be furbished, that it may be handled”** — Nabuchodonosor
**“this sword is sharpened, and it is furbished, that it may be in the hand of the slayer.”** — therefore
21.12:
**“Cry”** — O prophet
**“and howl”** — bear witness to impending evils with lamentation
**“O son of man”** — because this sword spared no one
**“for this sword is upon my people”** — namely in the church
**“it is upon all the princes of Israel, that are fled”** — others, strangers
**“they are delivered up to the sword with my people, strike therefore upon thy thigh”** — that is, assume the posture of one mourning
21.13:
**“Because”** — because to me
**“it is tried”** — the sword is tried
**“and that when it shall overthrow the sceptre”** — the kingdom, namely that will be no more, and will end in King Sedecias
**“It is tried”** — It is proved by the Lord when he overthrows Juda and those like him, into whom, after he had eaten the morsel, Satan entered.
21.14:
**“Thou therefore, O son of man, prophesy, and strike thy hands together”** — as before: the thigh, for astonishment and wonder
**“and let the sword be doubled”**
• that the sins of Jerusalem may be paid off, because she “received of the hand of the Lord double for all her sins”
• that the sword may come to kill not once only but a second and a third time
**“let the sword of the slain be tripled”** — First, Nabuchodonosor came while Joakim reigned. Second, when he carried off Jechonias. Third, when Sedecias was reigning. This is the sword tripled of great slaughter, etc.
21.15: **“And languish in heart, and that multiplieth ruins. In all their gates I have set the dread of the sharp sword, the sword that is furbished to glitter, that is made ready for slaughter.”** — in others: clothed
21.16:
**“Be thou sharpened”** — O sword.
**“go”** — Boldly, with me as leader, me as helper.
**“to the right hand, or to the left, which way soever thou hast a mind to set thy face”** — Onslaught.
**“Be thou sharpened, go”** — But the Lord rejoices and exults, and is an exhorter of the raging sword, that it may go to the right or to the left, so that with the wicked slain the good may remain, that this may be fulfilled: “What hath the chaff to do with the wheat? saith the Lord.”
21.17: **“And I will clap my hands together”** — That is, that I, as a supporter, may urge you on as you rage against my adversaries. Do not fear what Sennacherib suffered; you are the minister of my will; fulfil my sentence.
21.18:
**“And”**
• After these things.
• A second time.
21.19:
**“And thou son of man”** — You who wish to know what this sword is.
**“set thee two ways, for the sword of the king of Babylon to come”** — Through them.
**“both shall come forth out of one land: and with his hand he shall draw lots, he shall consult at the head of the way of the city”** — Crossroads.
**“Set thee two ways”** — Who goes out indeed by one road from the land of the Chaldeans, but when he has come through the desert and the wilderness to the fork of the roads of the land of Arabia, which is called that of the children of Ammon, of which roads one leads to Jerusalem on the right hand, the left one to Rabbath of the children of Ammon, which is the metropolis and is now called Philadelphia; mindful of the slaughter that befell the king of the Assyrians, when a hundred and eighty-five thousand were slain in one night, he will fear to turn aside to the right, and will stand, consulting the oracle in the disordered rite of his nation.
*Jerome:* The devil stands at the fork of the road, desiring to keep his own and burning to win others; he always desires to go to the right, that is, to overthrow those who are to be set on the right, that he may exult in slaughter there, where with rams and the heaping up of earthly works he may seize wretched Jerusalem. And at first indeed he seems to do nothing and to strive in vain. But when he recalls the iniquities of those who are in the Church, and by evil works they bring the demons back to the memory of their crimes, all the sins of the people and their thoughts are laid open, and therefore they are taken, because they have heaped up new sins. Let another say this to us; the truth of the history we have begun must be pursued.
21.20:
**“Thou shalt make a way that the sword may come to Rabbath”** — Nations.
**“of the children of Ammon, and to Juda unto Jerusalem”** — Who are gathered under the name of Christ.
21.21:
**“For the king of Babylon stood”** — The devil, who lies in ambush in secret at every head of the ways. Whence: “They have laid for me a stumblingblock by the wayside.”
**“in the highway, at the head of two ways, seeking divination, shuffling”** — In the quiver.
**“arrows”** — Inscribed with the names of each, so that he may see whose arrow comes out and which city he ought to attack first.
21.22:
**“On his right hand”** — That he might go against Jerusalem and attack it.
**“was the divination for Jerusalem, to set battering rams, to open the mouth”** — Encouraging his army.
**“in slaughter, to lift up the voice”** — Of the exulting army.
**“in howling, to set engines against the gates, to cast up a mount, to build forts”** — By which he might shut in the city.
21.23:
**“And he shall be”** — Doing this.
**“in their eyes as one consulting the oracle in vain”** — In the opinion of the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
**“And”** — As if.
**“imitating the leisure of sabbaths”** — That is, playing and accomplishing no work.
**“but he”** — Nabuchodonosor.
**“will call to remembrance the iniquity”** — Trusting not in his own strength but in their iniquity, because he will know that they have offended the Lord and heaped the sins of their fathers with new crimes, and that their transgressions were open to all.
21.24:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord God: Because you have remembered your iniquity, and”** — That is.
**“have discovered”** — To all.
**“your prevarications, and your sins have appeared in all your devices: because, I say, you have remembered, you shall be taken with the hand”** — Nabuchodonosor.
21.25:
**“But thou”** — Sedecias, in whom the kingdom of the kings of the stock of David ended, up to Christ.
**“profane wicked prince of Israel, whose day is come that hath been appointed in the time of iniquity”** — Long before.
**“But thou profane”** — After the overthrow of the city and the captivity of the people, the word is addressed to the leader of Israel.
21.26:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: Remove the diadem, take off the crown: is it not this”** — and this therefore because this is
**“that hath exalted the low one, and brought down him that was high”** — that is, he did nothing by judgment, but as the king of Babylon humbled whom he wished and exalted whom he wished.
**“Remove the diadem”** — As if the priesthood and the kingdom of the Jews perished because of you. For cidaris is the crown of the priest, the crown of the king.
**“is it not this”** — Jerome. Symmachus says it well: neither this nor that ceased, that is, the priesthood or the kingdom; both continued, whence those who came afterwards, down to Christ, were at once kings and priests; of whom the high priest Hyrcanus put the diadem on his head, and in vain wished to claim both this and that for himself, since the kingdom was not due to him after Sedecias, but to him for whom it was laid up. Of these Malachias speaks: “You priests have defiled my name.” And a little after: “My will is not in you, and I will not receive a gift of your hand”; and a little after: “in every place there is sacrifice, and there is offered to my name a clean oblation”; which is done, that is, at the coming of Christ, when the desired of all nations comes.
21.27:
**“iniquity, iniquity, iniquity”**
• not once, not twice, but a third time will I set iniquity.
• three times, that is, for ever.
**“I will shew it”** — it was not reckoned to you at once.
**“till he came”** — Christ.
**“to whom”** — The Father judges no one, but “hath given all judgment to the Son.”
**“judgment belongeth, and I will give it him”**
• The Father will deliver the kingdom to Christ, that is, the priesthood or the church gathered from the Gentiles.
• Whose is the judgment. “Give to the king thy judgment, O God, and to the king’s son thy justice”: this is he for whom the kingdom and the priesthood are laid up; whence Jacob: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda, nor a ruler from his thigh, till he come that is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of nations.”
21.28:
**“And thou son of man, prophesy, and say: Thus saith the Lord God concerning the children of Ammon, and concerning their reproach”** — because they too are to be taken.
**“And thou, O son of man”** — It was said above that the sword of the king of Babylon stood at the fork of the right and the left, of which the right led to Jerusalem, the left to Rabbath of the children of Ammon, and that the lot went out that he should go to Jerusalem; because, when it is stormed and taken, he foretells that its kingdom and priesthood have perished. It remains, therefore, and the order of the division demands, to show what was done about the left. The prophet is therefore commanded to speak to the children of Ammon.
**“and thou shalt say: O sword, O sword, come out of the scabbard”** — The word is addressed to the same sword.
21.29:
**“when”** — although, that is.
**“they see vain things in thy regard”** — they were answered by demons, all of whose things are vain.
**“and they divine lies: to bring thee upon the necks of the wicked that are wounded”** — of the sons of Ammon.
**“whose appointed day is come”** — that is, through you.
**“in the time of iniquity”** — appointed by God.
21.30:
**“Return”** — with the work completed.
**“into thy sheath”** — into Babylon.
**“in the place wherein thou wast created, in the land of thy nativity. I will judge thee”** — that is, that I may judge you in the land of your nativity.
21.31:
**“And I will pour out upon thee”** — because you are taken by the power of the Medes and Persians. Whence Isaias: “Behold I will stir up the Medes against them.”
**“my indignation: in the fire of my rage will I blow upon thee”** — that I may cause you, that is, to be consumed.
**“In the fire of my rage”** — Jerome. Because he was speaking under the person of the sword, indeed of the king and of the kingdom of Babylon, he keeps the metaphor.
**“of men that are brutish”** — Who do not know how to forge swords and sharpen them; that is, that you may not be sharpened and polished and shine to kill, but may be food for the fire, and the blood which you have shed may rather flow back upon you in sight of all, and you may be given over to eternal oblivion and perish for ever; because I the Lord have spoken this, with whom to have said is to have done.

22.2:
**“And thou son of man, dost thou not judge”** — otherwise, does not.
**“dost thou not judge”** — As if to show her that she is justly judged, and deservedly endures the impending captivity, and by many bloods has brought on the time of her ruin.
22.3:
**“And thou shalt shew her all her abominations, and shalt say: Thus saith the Lord God”** — that is, this is she.
**“This is the city that sheddeth blood in the midst of her”** — publicly.
**“that”** — therefore.
**“her time may come”** — of captivity.
**“and that hath made idols against herself”** — idolatry, as the greatest, is first reproached.
22.4:
**“in thy blood”** — which thou hast shed
**“Thou art become guilty in thy blood which thou hast shed: and thou art defiled in thy idols which thou hast made”** — because of the works of thy hands
**“and thou hast made thy days to draw near, and hast brought on”** — through all these things
**“the time of thy years: therefore have I made thee a reproach to the Gentiles, and a mockery to all countries”** — or to the Gentiles
**“hast brought on the time”** — Which, namely, was foretold long before and was deferred so that you might do penance. But you, according to your hardness and impenitent heart, treasure up to yourself wrath against the day, that is, therefore, etc.
22.5:
**“Those that are near, and those that are far from thee, shall triumph over thee: thou filthy”** — because you have ceased to be clean
**“infamous”** — noble in evil, as once in good you surpassed the other cities
**“great in destruction”** — the higher you are raised, the more heavily you fall
22.6:
**“Behold the princes of Israel, every one”** — as though, to pass over the others, few in number
**“his arm in thee”** — judging not in justice but in the strength of might
**“in thee to shed blood”** — innocent
22.7:
**“father and mother”**
• others
• since it is written: “He that shall curse father or mother, let him die the death.”
**“have abused ... in thee”** — others cursed
**“have oppressed the stranger in the midst of thee”** — as if sojourning and exile were not enough affliction
**“fatherless and widow”** — whose whole protection lies in the laws
**“have grieved ... in thee”** — others: oppressed, which is worse
22.8: **“Thou hast despised my sanctuaries”** — that you did not discern between the holy and the profane, and between days consecrated to religion and days permitted for works and the needs of the flesh
22.9:
**“Slanderers”** — Theodotion and Symmachus, deceitful, who did everything deceitfully and violently
**“in thee to shed blood”** — the innocent, since it is written: “The innocent and the just thou shalt not kill.”
**“upon the mountains”** — wise in high things, lifted up against God
**“have eaten ... in thee”** — or incest
**“have committed wickedness in the midst of thee”**
• openly
• that it should be rare even in corners, since those who do it fear being caught
22.10:
**“nakedness”** — namely, joined with stepmothers against law and right
**“discovered the nakedness of their father in thee; the uncleanness of the menstruous woman”** — not sparing nature nor granting respite to shame
22.11:
**“And every one with his neighbour's wife”** — neighing after the wife of a neighbour, or entering her
**“hath committed abomination”** — which is worse
**“the father in law hath wickedly defiled his daughter in law, the brother hath oppressed his sister”** — not knowing the rights of a sister, so as to violate not a full sister but one of the same father
22.12:
**“They have taken gifts”** — they turned the need of the poor into gain, so that they might take usury
**“in thee to shed blood”** — the innocent
**“usury and”** — that is
**“thou hast taken increase, and hast covetously”** — for the sake of gain
**“thy neighbours”** — friends
**“and thou hast forgotten me”** — as if: you did all these things because you forgot me. The memory of God excludes all crimes.
22.13: **“Behold, I have clapped my hands”** — I have assumed the appearance of one who is angry, so that you may understand and know in your mind whether you can bear my wrath, either in spirit or in your hands.
22.15:
**“And I will disperse thee”**
• when you have been taken
• O Jerusalem
**“in the nations and will scatter thee among the countries”** — as useless chaff to be snatched hither and thither
**“I will put an end to thy uncleanness in thee”** — as if my severity will be turned into mercy. For I will do this so that your uncleanness fails and you receive your former purity, and so I will possess you.
22.16:
**“And I will possess thee in the sight of the Gentiles, and thou shalt know”** — possessed by me
**“that I am the Lord”** — by which I render to each according to his works
22.18:
**“Son of man, the house of Israel is become dross to me”** — the dirt and refuse of metal
**“all these are brass”** — which feigns gold
**“and tin”** — which is like silver
**“and iron”** — which all violate the silver
**“and lead”** — the weight of iniquity
**“in the midst of the furnace: they are become the dross of silver”** — Son of man. Following the captivity, with the destruction of the city at hand, fire is applied, so that, under the figure of smelting, pure silver may remain, which had been mixed with brass, tin, iron and lead and made impure; of which three, brass, tin and lead, are materials that fuse together and are melted by fire. But iron softens between anvil and hammer, is drawn thin, and takes various forms according to the will of the craftsman. As therefore the silver which the above-mentioned metals defile is sent into the furnace, so “I will gather you,” etc.
22.20:
**“As they gather silver, and brass, and tin, and iron, and lead in the midst of the furnace: that I may kindle a fire in it”** — of famine, of pestilence
**“to melt it: so will I gather you together”** — you
**“in my fury”** — so that with the dross removed, pure silver may remain
**“and in my wrath, and will take my rest”** — content with the grief of your punishments, I will restrain vengeance
**“and I will melt you down”** — And I will melt you down. Whence Malachias: “like a refiner’s fire, and like the fuller’s herb, and he shall sit refining and cleansing the silver”; “and he shall refine them as gold, and as silver,” and “he shall purify the sons of Levi.” And Isaias: “The Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Sion,” etc. Like it: “Prove me, O Lord, and try me”; and afterwards it is added: “burn my reins and my heart”; that is, that all the phlegm of the harmful humour of our loins may be dried up.
22.22: **“As silver is melted in the midst of the furnace, so shall you be in the midst thereof: and you shall know”** — as if I will do all these things so that you may know in this way that I am the Lord, and judge of all, and rewarder
22.23: **“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:”** — Because the hearer would ask what the dross is which has violated the purity of silver and has mixed with bronze, lead, tin and iron; what is said there under the figure of the city and the furnace is here said under the appearance of a land neither watered nor rained upon.
22.24:
**“not rained upon”** — Whence: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon her.” We look for this rain when the early and the latter rain is given to us. Whence: “Thou shalt set aside for thy inheritance a free rain, O God.”
**“in the day of wrath”** — Jerome. By which each one plans for himself a multitude of sins.
22.25:
**“There is a conspiracy of prophets in the midst thereof”** — The Seventy: of the leaders in the midst of her having the likeness of a lion. Of which: “your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion”
**“like a lion that roareth and catcheth the prey, they have devoured souls”** — the devil and his companions desire to devour souls, not bodies
**“they have taken riches and hire, they have made many widows in the midst thereof”** — by slaying men
**“There is a conspiracy of prophets in”** — Jerome. This, that is, is the dross of the city, and of the very hard land, and the squalor full of briars.
**“they have devoured souls”** — That these things then befell the people of the Jews is doubtful to no one. For because of the priests and princes and prophets the Lord brought evil upon them. In our Jerusalem also there are many who devour souls and take a price and make many widows, who have lost the Lord their spouse. The faction and conspiracy of these prophets is that they favour one another, and do everything for the sake of base gain.
22.26:
**“Her priests have despised my law”** — since the rulers of the temple ought to be those from whose mouth knowledge of the law is sought
**“have defiled my sanctuaries: they have put no difference between holy and profane”** — mixing right and wrong
**“they have put no difference”** — except for money
**“nor have distinguished between the polluted and the clean”**
• distinction
• thoughtless
**“they have turned away their eyes from my sabbaths, and I was profaned”** — as far as in them lies
**“in the midst of them”** — of whom: “there hath stood one in the midst of you, whom you know not”
**“and from my sabbaths”** — The rest of the day, which is in the knowledge of the scriptures, they do not reflect upon, nor say with the prophet: “Open thou my eyes, and I will consider the wondrous things of thy law.” Nor with the apostle: “But we all, with open face beholding the glory of the Lord.”
**“and I was profaned”** — Jerome. Of whom: “there hath stood one in the midst of you, whom you know not.”
22.27:
**“Her princes”** — The prophets and priests are compared to lions; the princes, as lesser, are compared to wolves.
**“in the midst of her, are like wolves ravening the prey”** — of their subjects
**“to shed blood”** — not of bodies but of souls
**“And to run after gains through covetousness”** — Not content with that. Those who serve the altar live from the altar, but after they have come to the ministry of the altar, they gather the riches of Croesus and the luxuries of Alcinous.
22.28:
**“And her prophets have daubed them”** — because they daubed the wall without mixing in straw, which is scattered by rains
**“without tempering the mortar, seeing vain things, and divining lies”** — not prophesying
**“unto them”** — to the wretched land
22.29:
**“The people”** — as the master, so also the disciple
**“of the land”** — not of God but of earthly works
**“have used oppression, and committed robbery”** — not the rich. For a man’s ransom is properly his riches
**“the needy and poor”** — of whom it is written: “But the poor man suffers no threatening or exchange”
**“The stranger”** — Who is not yet a citizen of the church but only a hearer, having the beginnings of faith; as when “they go round about the sea and the land to make one proselyte, you make him the child of hell.”
22.30:
**“And I sought among them for a man”** — among so many and so great vices
**“that might set up a hedge”** — intercession
**“and stand in the gap before me in favour of the land, that I might not destroy it: and I found none”** — To interpose: one who could resist my anger, as Moses and Aaron and Samuel; whence also it is said to Moses, as one resisting and striving: “Let me alone, and I will destroy this people.”
22.31:
**“And”** — therefore
**“And I poured out my indignation upon them, in the fire of my wrath I consumed them: I have rendered their way upon their own head, saith the Lord God”** — as if not without judgment and without measure
**“Their way”** — Jerome. Assigning their own sins to the authors, or on the head of the people, namely the leaders, princes and prophets, none of whom dared to resist the angry Lord; because of them the squalid and desert land did not deserve to receive the rain of the Lord.

23.2:
**“Son of man, there were two women”** — Samaria and Jerusalem
**“daughters of one mother”** — of the stock of Israel
**“Son of man”** — Jerome. The twelve tribes of Israel, which had been joined together in Egypt, were afterwards divided into two and ten tribes; the two are called Juda, the ten Israel. Thereafter Roboam the son of Solomon, of the tribe of David, reigned in Jerusalem, where were the temple and the priests and a great part of the tribe of Levi. Over the ten tribes in Samaria reigned Jeroboam the son of Nabath, of the tribe of Ephraim and Joseph; of these Samaria is now called Oolla, which in our tongue sounds “tabernacle”; but Jerusalem Ooliba, that is, “my tabernacle in her.” For the ten tribes also were a tabernacle, not of God but of idols. For Jeroboam (to turn the people away from the worship of God) had set golden calves in Dan and Bethel; whence: Son of man, there were two women.
**“of one mother”** — Jerome. Of Cethe, namely of whom above: “Thy father an Amorrhite, and thy mother a Cethite.”
23.3:
**“And they committed fornication in Egypt”** — for they would not have received the law on Mount Sinai forbidding the worship of idols, once led out of Egypt, unless they had worshipped idols in Egypt
**“There were their breasts pressed down”** — When it is said, let every man cast away the abominations of Egypt from before his eyes, it signifies that Israel served idols in Egypt, and there the breasts of her youth were broken.
23.4:
**“And their names”**
• that is, these, namely
• Jerome. What Joseph, Ephraim, Samaria, Jezrael and Israel signify, and how they are opposed to the house of David and Jerusalem, that is, to the church, has been fully said in the exposition of Osee. Of whom it is said: “The sons of Ephraim who bend and shoot with the bow: they have turned back in the day of battle,” and elsewhere: “And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and chose the tribe of Juda”; for God chose the house of confession, that is, the church, and rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, which is “increase,” namely those who, having abandoned the law of God, went after the golden calves. And they are called Oolla, that is, a tabernacle not of God but of error and of demons; and she is the elder and older sister, on account of her multitude and the captivity by the Assyrians, and committed fornication against God.
**“Oolla”**
• Samaria
• a tabernacle of error and of demons
**“the elder”** — the elder
**“and Ooliba her younger sister: and I took them”** — when they groaned from the works of Egypt, serving in mortar and brick
**“and they bore sons and daughters”** — in the wilderness or in the land of promise
**“Now for their names, Samaria”** — Heretics.
**“The elder”** — because of the multitude of the ten tribes, or because after the death of Moses Joshua the son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim, ruled the people; whence also Jeroboam, who tore them from the house of David.
23.5:
**“And Oolla committed fornication”** — leaving the chastity of faith and truth, against God
**“against me, and doted on her lovers, on the Assyrians”** — namely
**“that came to her”** — to her
23.6:
**“Who were clothed with blue”** — promising themselves lofty and heavenly things
**“princes”** — not any of the people
**“and rulers”** — of heretics
**“beautiful youths”** — not worn out by age
**“all horsemen”** — whose idols she followed
**“mounted upon horses”** — Of whom: “some in chariots, and some in horses.”
23.7:
**“And she committed her fornications”** — from whom, against God’s command, she sought help
**“with those chosen men”** — that is, leaders and magistrates, who promise themselves knowledge and eloquence
**“all sons of the Assyrians, and in all of them on whom she doted, in uncleannesses”** — idols
23.8:
**“Moreover also her fornications which she had committed”** — that is, before she believed
**“in Egypt”** — in youth
**“she did not forsake”** — because she also practised in heresy
**“for they also”** — The Egyptians
**“lay with her in her youth”** — they lay with her shamefully, whose images she worshipped
**“and they bruised the breasts of her virginity”** — deflowering her and losing the virginity she had in the church
**“and poured out their fornication upon her”** — they not only committed fornication but also poured out fornication
23.9:
**“Therefore have I delivered her”** — Whence: Paul, “I have delivered them to Satan.”
**“into the hands of her lovers”** — namely Phul, Thelgathphalasar and Salmanasar
23.10:
**“They discovered”** — Morally: the uncovering of the city is captivity.
**“her disgrace”** — as of a harlot.
**“her sons”** — endowed with knowledge.
**“and her daughters”** — simple and unskilled.
**“took away”** — into captivity of body or of soul.
**“and slew her with the sword”** — spiritual or bodily.
**“And they became”** — because above he had said sons in the plural.
**“infamous women”** — as an example for all women, and that they might be celebrated in the talk of all for evil.
**“And they became infamous”** — Heretics become infamous among all the doctrines of the world, so that their shame is punished as an example for all women.
**“and they executed judgments”** — So that they left nothing of safety in her. For even today they are held captive in the mountains and cities of the Medes.
23.11:
**“And when her sister saw this”** — namely her sister’s plagues.
**“her sister”** — the church.
**“Ooliba”** — Jerusalem, in which she did not fear the temple of God, by her example.
**“she was mad with lust more than she, and she carried her fornication beyond the fornication of her sister”** — namely of heretics.
**“she was mad with lust more than she”** — Because she made idols once and outside, in Dan and Bethel, but this one often, even in the high places and in the temple of God, adored the statue of Baal and committed fornication with the Assyrians; for the idol Baal, or Bel, or more plainly Belus, was consecrated by the kingdom of the Assyrians in honour of his father, by Ninus the son of Belus.
**“beyond the fornication”** — Jerome. Allegorically. The church surpasses heretical lust, because “that servant who knew the will of his lord, and did not according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes.” Heretics also commit unspeakable things outside, and perish in shipwreck outside the ark of Noe. But churchmen, though following the true faith, imitate the vices of Assyria and Chaldea, and follow the many-coloured images of sins, and therefore are worthy of greater torments.
23.13: **“And I saw that she was defiled, and that they both took one way”** — so that the fornication of both would be one.
23.14:
**“And she increased her fornications: and when she had seen men painted”** — in this, namely, she increased her fornications.
**“on the wall, the images of the Chaldeans”** — who are interpreted as demons.
23.16:
**“She doted”** — namely with lust.
**“upon them with the lust of her eyes”** — deceived by their form and dress.
**“and she sent messengers to them”** — asking for help.
**“she sent messengers”** — Jerome. We send messengers to the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as demons, when we lay open to them and offer our breasts to be struck, where the lodging of the mind is, and, sated with pleasures, pass from some to others, and desire not so much fornication as a number of harlots, and come to such madness that after serving God for a long time we return to Egypt and do what we did not do in the world before we received the name of faith.
23.17:
**“And when the sons of Babylon were come to her”** — demons, heretics.
**“to the bed of love, they defiled her with their fornications, and she was polluted by them”** — therefore she withdrew from their covenant.
**“and her soul was glutted with them”** — all pleasure, being brief, quickly brings satiety.
23.18:
**“And she discovered her fornications”** — like a public harlot.
**“and discovered her disgrace: and my soul was alienated from her”** — because I saw her shames made public, as one who had surpassed her sister’s crimes, and by the greatness of her punishments would also surpass her sister.
23.19:
**“For she multiplied her fornications”** — even in her more advanced age.
**“remembering the days of her youth”** — when she wantoned in lust for the Chaldeans.
23.20:
**“And she was mad with lust after lying with them”** — of the Egyptians.
**“whose flesh is as the flesh of asses, and whose issue as the issue of horses”** — namely of the seed, or the members so large that they surpass the deformity of horses.
23.21: **“And thou hast renewed the wickedness”** — Namely, the wickedness of your youth did not cease after you became mine; but in the desert and in the land of promise you sighed after your old lust, in which you were deflowered, and the breasts of your puberty were broken.
23.22:
**“Therefore, Ooliba”** — because, that is, you remembered the flesh of the Egyptians and imitated the shameful deeds of the unclean nation, which worships the images of all beasts
**“thus saith the Lord God: Behold I will raise up against thee all thy lovers with whom thy soul hath been glutted”** — from whose satiated embrace, that is, from whose covenant you withdrew, so that however great the love had been before, you would be turned into such great loathing
**“Behold I will raise up against thee all thy lovers”** — Jerome. Tropologically. This is said of Jerusalem, but refers to the soul, which, joined to the embraces of God by virtues, afterwards committed adultery in vices and withdrew from him; and with its crimes laid bare it is stripped and disgraced and shown to all, that it may desist from its crime, and not glory in the dignity of its name, but for the conscience of evil and the remembrance of Egypt dare no longer lift its eyes to heaven. Hence its nose is cut off and its ears are cut away, because it had turned the odour of good fragrance into stench, and had heard the judgment of blood; and this we understand not only of smell and hearing but of sight also, of which, because they abused it badly, Samson and Sedecias were deprived. God also makes it deaf and dumb, lest the tongue pass on even to the earth, and all touch is taken away in those who have utterly lost life. And these things will happen that all may be purged by fire, and that the fornication of Egypt may perish, and they may no longer lift their eyes to evil things.
23.23: **“The children of Babylon, and all the Chaldeans, the nobles, and the kings”** — Or the tristatae, of whom in Exodus: chosen riders, tristatae; for which Latin simplicity translated “three-fold stratores”; but tristates is among the Hebrews a name meaning to sit after royal dignity; of whom, however, he did not reach three, who were the leaders of the horse and foot and of the tribunes, whom we call masters of both services and prefects of the title of the supplies.
23.24: **“And they shall come upon thee well appointed with chariot and wheel, a multitude of people: they shall be armed against thee on every side with breastplate, and buckler, and helmet: and I will set judgment before them”** — so that you may be judged by those whom you had abandoned and whose covenant you had made void
23.25:
**“And I will set my jealousy against thee”** — the zeal of God is not kept even among the enemies of the faith
**“which they shall execute upon thee with fury: thy nose and thy ears”** — As adulteresses and women caught in lewdness, that, being disfigured, you may cease to please. For as in the face all the beauty of the countenance consists in the comeliness of the nose, and from the ears of women pearls and jewels hang, so the dignity of kings and judges, which is marked in the face and ears, is cut off by their sword.
**“and what remains shall fall by the sword: they shall cut off”** — not mine
**“and thy daughters”** — not mine, whom you bore from adultery
**“and thy residue shall be devoured by fire”** — the rest, that is
23.26:
**“And they shall strip thee of thy garments”** — with which I had adorned you
**“instruments of thy glory”** — Golden and silver ones, that is, which I gave you for the ceremonies of the temple; of which: “I gave them gold and silver, and they made them into Baal.”
23.27:
**“And I will put an end to thy wickedness in thee, and thy fornication”** — which you learned, that is, in Egypt
**“brought out of the land of Egypt; nor shalt thou lift up thy eyes”**
• with ears and ears cut off
• a shameful thing added
**“to them”** — your lovers
**“nor remember Egypt any more”** — of the Egyptians’ lust, that is, by whose great fleshliness you took delight
**“And I will put an end”** — As if to say: I have done all these things so that, her beauty lost and her face, poisoned and disfigured, I may make your wickedness rest.
*Jerome:* All these things are said under the figure of an adulteress, and punishment is given on account of adultery, so that she no longer glories in her beauty but blushes at the foulness she has earned by the greatness of her pleasures.
23.28:
**“For thus saith the Lord God”** — It profits Jerusalem to have enmity against the Assyrians, and not to remember Egypt; but behold, I will deliver you
**“Behold, I will deliver thee into the hands of them”** — to be punished
**“Behold, I will deliver”** — For she is not handed over before she repents, that, after being purged of her old sins by punishments, she may lose all the labours which she gained by the harlot’s art, and see her nakedness and shame, and know that the Lord did not do all this to her, but her own fornications, by which she committed fornication after the nations, which he enumerated above, that she might worship their images.
23.29: **“And they shall deal with thee in hatred, and they shall take away all thy labours, and shall let thee go naked, and full of disgrace, and the disgrace of thy fornication shall be discovered, thy wickedness, and thy fornications”** — not the Lord
23.30:
**“They have done these things to thee, because thou hast played the harlot with the nations”** — whom you worshipped
**“among which”** — images
23.31:
**“Thou hast walked in the way of thy sister”** — that is, of Samaria
**“Thou hast walked, and I will give her cup”** — whose sins you followed
**“I will give her cup”**
• The punishment, that is; whence: “a cup in the hand of the Lord of strong wine,” etc. Which in Isaias is called “the cup of ruin and the cup of fury”; and to Jeremias the Lord says: “Take the cup of wine unmixed from my hand, and thou shalt make all nations drink,” etc.
• Jerome. For just as some purgatives are given so that the harmful humour in the body is expelled, so also the Lord gives the most unmixed cup of torments, so that whatever gall and bitterness was in sinners may be taken away and they be restored to their former health.
23.32:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: Thou shalt drink thy sister's cup, deep, and wide”** — by the greatness of the punishments
**“thou shalt be”** — then
**“had in derision”** — at the time of captivity
23.34:
**“And thou shalt drink it, and shalt drink it up”** — otherwise: you will drink off
**“even to the dregs, and the fragments thereof”** — that is, you will devour to such an extent that even the fragments
**“and thou shalt devour”** — then, as it were: you will be wearied of your fornication
**“thou shalt rend thy breasts”** — broken by the Egyptian fire, and subdued by lovers, and torn
**“And thou shalt drink it”** — This can be understood significantly of Jerusalem, which drank the last of the cup of her sister Samaria, and, as it were, drained to the bottom the dregs of her torments.
**“Thou shalt rend thy breasts”** — Septuagint. I will take away her feasts and new moons, so that instead of solemnity and joy you may have eternal lamentation and mourning.
**“because I have spoken it, saith the Lord God”** — Because he had described the adulteries of Samaria and Jerusalem separately, it followed that he should announce their punishments together.
