24.1:
**“And the word of the Lord came to me in the ninth year, in the tenth month, the tenth day of the month, saying”** — of the captivity of Joachim. For in the fifth year he began to prophesy; and in the tenth month of the same ninth year, on the tenth day of the tenth month, the word of the Lord came to him, he being settled in the regions of Babylon
**“And it came to pass”**
• Jerome. But note how captivity came in order from the beginning of the prophecy to the present day, on which the city began to be besieged: first the sword is called for; then two ways are set, Ammon and Jerusalem, of which the lot falls to the right on Nabuchodonosor. Silver, brass, tin, lead and iron are melted in the city. The land also is not rained upon but is overgrown with thorns. Afterwards, under the name of two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, their sins are told, how the one has been taken and the other is to be taken. Last of all, in the ninth year, the tenth month, the tenth day of the month, it is shown to Ezechiel, placed in captivity, and to those who were with him and had given themselves up with king Jechonias, on what day the city began to be besieged; and the likeness of the caldron is set forth, that as flesh and bones are burned up in a caldron by the fire, so the whole city with its citizens may perish, and none of the besieged remain who is not consumed by famine, sword and pestilence, and the rest be led captive into Babylon.
• Jerome. There are some who according to the tropological sense transfer this place to the consummation of the world; sometimes the number which in the divine Scriptures is the number of punishments and sorrows, and which always follows justice, they temper by the mercy of the tenth month and the tenth day. For punishments are applied to the sick so that health may follow the pain. The world therefore, which “is seated in wickedness,” is set on fire with divine fire on the day of judgment, and the city of bloods is set upon the coals of fire, that what is in Isaias may be fulfilled: “Thou hast coals of fire, sit upon them, these shall be thy help.” But this is hard: how, when the flesh and bones are consumed, with which even the Pharisees are full (whence: “Woe to you scribes and Pharisees, who are like to whited sepulchres, which are full of the bones of the dead”), it should now be said that the rust and filth of the world are not consumed, but that even after the severity of the judgment wickedness remains. This is easily solved according to that of the apostle: “God hath concluded all under sin, that he may have mercy on all.” For the creature “was made subject to vanity.” And the blood that was shed is set in the open before the whole creation, that the crimes of all may lie open. But the most smooth rock is Christ, who followed the people of Israel in the wilderness, of which “they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ,” because in him all things are revealed, and that is fulfilled: “Nothing is hid that shall not be revealed.” But the Lord says that he will not have mercy, nor pass over the sins of the world, nor spare the wicked, nor be appeased, so that the ways of the wicked may perish; whence: “and the way of the wicked shall perish.”

This prophecy can pertain to the time of the Lord’s passion, on account of which Jerusalem was surrounded by an army and her children slain; and when Titus, the son of Vespasian, besieged her, no one escaped to safety; and the temple under Titus, and fifty years later under Adrian the city, was consumed by eternal fire. But it signifies the present captivity, when Ezechiel saw these things in Babylon; and Jeremias at the beginning of his book puts it thus: “I see a boiling caldron, and the face thereof from the face of the north.”

**“For her blood”** — the murders of the sons, the slaughters.
**“is in the midst of her; she hath shed it upon the smooth rock; she hath not shed it upon the ground, that it might be covered with dust”** — Upon the smooth rock, so that it might lie open to all, and not be covered with earth or dust. It is the nature of things that if blood is poured out on the earth, the ground drinks up the moisture of the blood, and it is covered little by little with earth or dust. But if it is poured out upon a flat rock, it runs down and takes up a broad place. In this it is clear that she committed murders not hidden but public and open, according to that: “the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth to me from the earth.”

• as often.

• make no mourning for the dead; let your crown be bound about you; which is shorn in mourning; and you shall have shoes on your feet, which mourners are accustomed to cast off; whence David, fleeing from Absalom and repenting over the death of Uriah, walked with bare feet
• And if your wife dies (who, if she was good, is nothing more lovable to a man, and is provided to man by God), and is joined by law and becomes one body.

**“let the tire of thy head be upon thee”** — Jerome. The Hebrews say that the Babylonian masters of the law, keeping the precepts, even to this day bind the decalogue written on small parchments around their head, and that these are what is commanded to hang before the eyes and on the forehead, that they may always see what has been commanded; and that since Ezechiel was a priest, he ought not to lay aside the crown of glory but keep it bound on his head. But we, following the Septuagint, understand a crown of hair.
*Jerome:* Allegorically. Let us come to the anagogical sense, if it does not seem forced to the watchfulness of the reader. The Son of man, Christ, who in the evening of this world lost his former wife, neither wept for her, nor covered his face with a garment, nor received any consolation of men; and he foretold these things to come in the morning, which were fulfilled in the evening; and again in the morning, at the second coming, he proved done what he had foretold would come. The sanctuary of the Jews, and what they had held desirable in their eyes, and for which their souls trembled, was polluted; and their sons also and daughters fell by the Roman sword.

**“and the thing that your eyes desire”** — in which the desire of your salvation

• offered by those who console
• You shall not cover your faces. When custom is kept in mourning, the grief is moderate; but when such great necessity of evils falls upon them that the grief is greater than any weeping, and each man, anxious about his own death, does not groan over the miseries of others, though they be near.

**“You shall have crowns on your heads”** — For they ought not to mourn and take up the signs of mourning, because through the shadow they have received the truth, and some of them became Nazarites; and every one shall be comforted by his brother. 24.25:
**“And thou, O son of man”** — still more openly
**“behold in the day wherein I will take away from them their strength”** — the confidence of the temple

**“With him that hath escaped”** — Not to himself, for what he had foretold would come, that man now announces as accomplished; and you shall not be silent any more, but shall rebuke them, and say that all things have befallen them deservedly, that you may be a sign to them, according to that of Zacharias, where the prophets are called men portending; and the Lord says elsewhere: “by the hands of the prophets I was likened.”

25.1: **“And the word of the Lord came”** — Jerome. When Jerusalem was taken or besieged, after he who could escape came to Babylon and announced that the city was taken, or already about to be taken, and the temple, according to the custom of all the prophets, the word is turned against the other nations round about who insulted the ruin of the city and the burning of the temple; and first against the children of Ammon.
25.2:
**“Son of man, set”** — others: harden
**“thy face against the children of Ammon”** — who are of Lot
25.3:
**“And thou shalt say to the children of Ammon: Hear ye the word of the Lord God: Thus saith the Lord God”** — not I
**“Because thou hast said: Ha, ha, upon my sanctuary”** — you insulted, namely rejoicing in the ruin of the temple
**“because it was profaned”** — by the entry of enemies
**“and upon the land of Israel, because it was laid waste”** — specially
**“and upon the house of Juda”** — two tribes
**“Son of man”** — Jerome. Now he adds the rebuke of the sons of Ammon and of the other nations, and the prophecy of things to come.
*Jerome:* Allegorically. By the sons of Ammon, who sprang from the seed of Lot, begotten in a cave and in drunkenness by incest, we can understand all heretics, of whom John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would no doubt have remained with us.” These are sprung from declension. For this is what Lot signifies, because “they are all gone aside, they are become unprofitable together, there is none that doth good.” Against them the face of the prophet is set, or hardened, that he may crush them with his authority; and he says to them: Because you have mocked the church in persecution and in the oppression of vices, saying that the sanctuary was profaned, either by the vice of those who serve vice or by the cruelty of enemies; and the land of Israel, that is, the senses seeing God, laid waste by the choir of virtues; and the sons of Juda, that is, the true believers and those who confess rightly, led into captivity, have ceased to serve the Lord. Therefore, O every one that mocks, you shall be delivered to the children of the east, who have fallen from the light, that you also may learn to confess the Lord. But by a figure it is said that the children of the east set their folds upon them, and pitch their tents, and drink milk, and eat the fruits; and the once proud city becomes a dwelling of camels, who, having laid down the burden of sins, can enter through the eye of a needle; and the children of Ammon a fold of flocks, which are ruled by a good shepherd; that when they have been delivered to the shepherds of the east they may know that he is the Lord. And again he reproaches them that they mocked, with excess of feeling of heart, at the ruin of the people, and thought the land of Israel wholly deserted; for which they deserve the hand of an avenging God; that they who went beyond measure in mockery and joy over the ruin of the house of Juda are not delivered to the children of the east, but are for the plunder of all nations, and are slain out of the peoples, and perish, and are crushed; and they are to be believed to be not of the stock of Abraham but of all the nations; and then let them know, by the greatness of their evils, the crushing of the people, and the slaying, that he is the Lord.
*Jerome:* What we understand generally of the church we can understand of each one of the saints, at whose fall the men of this world and the demons rejoice, if they have lost long-kept chastity, thinking it a consolation to themselves if they have more partners in crime and punishment. But no one does this except a son of Ammon, that is, a son of the people that was begotten in declension.
**“because they are led into captivity”**
• The Madianites and the whole waste of the desert lie next to the land of Arabia; they have herds of camels and multitudes of sheep and goats, and live on these riches. History tells that this also happened to the land of Israel in the Book of Judges, when the Madianites came and wasted all their regions as far as Gaza.
• Metaphorically, then, through the Madianites, Ishmaelites and Agarenes, who are now called Saracens, taking to themselves the false name of Sarah, so that they may seem to be born of the free-born mistress, the Scripture signifies.
*Jerome:* Rabbath is the metropolis of the sons of Ammon, which was afterwards called Philadelphia by Ptolemy Philadelphus, who held Arabia.
*Jerome:* Let us not doubt that Nabuchodonosor overthrew Arabia after Jerusalem was taken, as Scripture above attests: “And thou, son of man, set thee two ways, of Ammon and of Jerusalem, and the sword of the king of Babylon come.”
25.4:
**“Therefore will I deliver thee to the men of the east”** — Nabuchodonosor and his army
**“for an inheritance, and they shall place”** — metaphorically
**“their sheepcotes”** — as shepherds
**“in thee, and shall set up their tents in thee; they shall eat thy fruits”** — with flocks of camels and of all peoples sent in
**“and they shall drink thy milk”** — the fertility of the land
25.5:
**“And I will make Rabbath”** — a proper name; or it is interpreted because of its greatness, for it means greatest
**“a stable for camels, and the children of Ammon a couching place for flocks, and you shall know”** — by the necessity of evils
**“that I am the Lord”** — who foretold the future and fulfilled it
25.6:
**“For thus saith the Lord God: Because thou hast clapped thy hands”** — not only did you insult, or say Euge, euge, etc.
**“and stamped with thy foot, and hast rejoiced with all thy heart against the land of Israel”** — desolate
25.7:
**“Therefore behold I”** — not through an angel, not through any minister
**“will stretch forth my hand”** — to strike
**“upon thee, and will deliver thee to be the spoil of nations”** — not of camels, or of all
**“and will cut thee off”** — by uprooting
**“from among the people”** — from the number of peoples
**“and destroy thee out of the lands, and break thee in pieces; and thou shalt know that I am the Lord”** — who judge all things, in that I have power over all nations
25.8:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: Because Moab and Seir have said”** — insulting the house of Juda because it was taken by the Chaldeans
**“Behold, Moab and Seir, behold, as all the nations”** — without the help of God
**“the house of Juda”** — exposed to the power of Babylon
**“Because they have said”** — Jerome. The Jews fable that when the city was taken and the temple opened, the sons of Ammon and Moab and Seir, seeing the cherubim overshadowing the propitiatory, said: As all nations worship idols, so Juda also has the idols of its own religion; and therefore the Lord, being angry, delivered them to captivity.
*Jerome:* Allegorically. Moab, from his father Seir, hairy and rough, to this day despises the house of Juda, in which is the true confession, and thinks it as easily overthrown as the fortifications of the other cities; whence the Lord threatens that he will open or dissolve all the strength of the Moabites, so that they cease to have cities and put no trust in the art of dialectic, but all those borders, which for the dashing of the waves they call headlands, shall be destroyed; and the famous and chosen lands, Bethiesimoth, that is, house of solitude, and deserted, and Beelmeon, that is, having a fountain or above a fountain, and Cariathaim, which the Septuagint translated a maritime city, shall perish, though they have the strength of fighters, and the famous go to battle with the art of fighting and fortified on every side. Yet the famous part of their land is not a house of habitation but of solitude; but those who think they have the fountain of knowledge and a maritime city that can bear all the storms of the world, promising themselves patience and strength, shall then be turned thither, that they may be delivered to the children of the east, of the true light in Christ, as the children of Ammon, who trusted in the heretical multitude. But let us trust in the progress and in the very threat the clemency of God, that they be delivered with the children of Ammon to the children of the east for an inheritance, so that no heresy may be named among the nations, but, judgments and vengeances having been wrought on Moab for the arrogance of their doings, they may know at the end that it is the Lord who disposes all things. That by Moab is meant the pride of the philosophers, of whom: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise,” etc., Amos shows thus: “For three wickednesses of Moab,” etc., as far as “because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into ashes.” For whatever there is in the world of perverse doctrines, whatever belongs to earthly knowledge and is thought to be strong, this is overthrown by the art of dialectic, and like a fire is dissolved into ashes and embers, that what was thought the strongest may be proved to be nothing; whence Isaias: “We have heard of the pride of Moab, he is exceeding proud.”
25.9:
**“Therefore behold I will open”** — at present
**“the shoulder of Moab”** — the strength of Moab, so that the Babylonian may enter even to them
**“from the cities, from the cities”** — that they may cease to be
**“I say, of his, and from his borders, the noble”** — cities
**“cities of the land of Bethiesimoth”** — a deserted village
**“and Beelmeon”** — a very large village
**“and Cariathaim”** — a maritime city
25.10:
**“to the people of the east”** — to the Babylonians
**“with the children of Ammon”** — Moab will be given up, namely
**“and I will give it”** — Moab
**“for an inheritance, that there may be no more any remembrance of the children of Ammon among the nations”** — just as there is no longer memory of the sons of Ammon among the nations, so in Moab I will execute judgments
25.11:
**“And”** — thus
**“I will execute judgments in Moab; and they shall know that I am the Lord”** — who gave up Juda for sin; and I will avenge myself on the sons of Ammon and Moab
25.12:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: Because Edom hath taken vengeance”** — the flesh that rises up against the spirit
**“to revenge herself”**
• because he was supplanted in the womb by Jacob, from whom Juda came
• formerly ruling, now subjected
**“of the children of Juda”** — who follow the spirit
**“Because Edom hath taken vengeance”** — Jerome. Whereas above he put two together, Moab and Seir, afterwards, keeping silence about Seir, he spoke against Moab; then he returns to Seir. But it must be known that the same Edom is called Seir and Esau, and the one nation is Idumea and Duma and Edom and Esau and Seir. Seir, because hairy, took the name of the hairy one; Edom, bloody, who for the cooking of the red lentil lost his birthright and from the dish got this name; Esau, which is interpreted made.
25.13:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord God”** — therefore
**“will stretch forth my hand”** — I myself, not through others
**“upon Edom, and will take away out of it man”** — who seems rational
**“and beast”** — of simple faith
**“and will make it desolate from the south”** — others: of Theman, which is interpreted 'failing'
**“and they that are in Dedan”** — the city, which sounds like kinship
**“by the sword”** — spiritual
**“I will stretch forth my hand”** — my hand upon Idumea. But it should be known that in Hebrew Idumea is never written, but always Edom, which the Greek translation rendered as Idumea.
25.14:
**“And I will lay my vengeance”**
• when they had taken vengeance on Juda
• Jerome. He puts the sword in the hand of Israel, that Edom may be overthrown and feel the wrath and fury of the Lord, and understand that his vengeance has availed to this, that he serve the house of Juda; whence: “Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated.” He loves Jacob because he supplants the carnal and earthly, and deserves to receive his blessings. For first we live according to the flesh and afterwards according to the spirit; first are the vices, then the virtues by which the vices are overthrown. For the heart of man is inclined to evil from youth, and mature age condemns the errors of adolescence; whence: “The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember.” And it is to be noted that Jacob received the first blessing, Esau the second, and at the last it is said of him: “Thou shalt serve thy brother”; that after the flesh has been made subject to the spirit and joined to it, it may cease to be flesh, and Idumea pass over into Judea.
**“upon Edom by the hand”** — not through another
**“of my people Israel”** — upon whom they exercised vengeance
**“and they shall do”** — my people
**“in Edom”** — the hostile nation
**“according to my wrath”** — fulfilling my indignation
**“and my fury: and they shall know my vengeance”** — that it was, of course, just
25.15:
**“Thus saith the Lord God”** — Septuagint: Adonai the Lord
**“Because the Philistines have taken vengeance”** — After the sons of Ammon and Moab and Seir, who are themselves Idumeans, being joined by kinship to the people of Israel and the house of Juda through Lot and Esau, he comes to the Philistines, who are on the shore and the line of the sea.
**“Because the Philistines have taken vengeance, and have revenged themselves with all their mind, destroying and satisfying old enmities”** — The Philistines, falling by drink, who, drunk from the golden cup of Babylon, rage and with all their mind insult, remembering the old enmities against Israel, by which they were divided from the people of God; and though the Lord says, “Revenge is mine, and I will repay,” they avenge themselves, fulfilling the old enmities.
25.16:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord God: Behold I will stretch forth my hand”** — that I may kill the killers
**“upon the Philistines, and will kill the killers, and will destroy the remnant of the sea coast”** — which is beaten by the salt waves
**“the Philistines”** — Jerome. The Septuagint translated “allophylos,” that is, foreigners, not by the general name of the nations who are not of the race of the Jews, but by the special name of their own nation, which is now called Palestine, the letter phe being changed into pi according to the custom of the Greeks, as among us for the Hebrew “phasca” the Greek and Latin “pascha” is celebrated.
25.17:
**“And I will execute great vengeance upon them, rebuking them in fury”** — which yet has an end of mercy, because thus they will know, etc.
**“and they shall know”** — the Philistines
**“that I am the Lord, when I shall lay my vengeance upon them”** — he who strikes is himself healed

26.1:
**“And it came to pass”** — After the Philistines comes the region of Phoenicia, whose metropolis is Tyre, which in Hebrew and Syriac is called Sor.
*Jerome:* Tyre is interpreted “distress,” and signifies the soul which is occupied with disturbances; which, when it has seen Jerusalem overthrown by its vices, Jerusalem in which was the temple and the vision of peace, exults, and thinks that the rule of the once renowned city is transferred to itself. This is understood also of contrary doctrines, and of the men of the world, who, when they have seen some just man fallen through negligence, rejoice and insult him, as though the ruin of others were their own resurrection; whence it follows: “Therefore thus saith,” etc.
26.2:
**“Son of man, because Tyre hath said”** — mocking and rejoicing
**“of Jerusalem”** — taken
**“Aha, the gates of the people are broken”** — as if I had a most secure harbor
**“she is turned to me”**
• she taken
• the multitude, namely, that was ruled by her will
**“I shall be filled”** — she deserted
**“now she is laid waste”** — who before was full
26.3:
**“Therefore”** — because you, namely, said these things
**“Thus saith the Lord God: Behold”** — as if he were present
**“I”** — not through others but I myself
**“against thee, O Tyre, and I will cause many nations to come up to thee”** — the Babylonians with many nations
26.4:
**“And they shall break down the walls of Tyre”** — the fortifications by the assault of siege engines
**“and destroy the towers thereof”** — sophisms
**“and I will scrape her dust from her”** — down to the ground, that is, so that even the dust is scraped away
**“and make her like a smooth rock”** — as if she will be so humbled that she is compared to the most polished rock, made empty
26.5:
**“A drying place”** — so that nets are spread out in the city once most crowded
**“for nets in the midst of the sea, because I have spoken it, saith the Lord God”** — whose words cannot be made void
**“for nets”** — with which they caught the deceived multitude. He will make the nets dry, so that other fishermen whom the Lord sent to fish may come in.
26.6:
**“Her daughters also”**
• cities, towns, villages
• Jerome. The daughters, who were kept as if in a bridal chamber and, for their more secret teachings, were not easily entrusted to anyone, will be brought out into public, to be cut down by the ecclesiastical sword.
**“thereof”** — of Phoenicia
**“that are in the field”** — of Phoenicia
**“shall be slain by the sword”** — Metaphorically, because he called them daughters, he puts the sword for the slaying.
**“and they shall know”** — at the end of things
**“that I am the Lord”** — who commanded these things to be done
**“and they shall know that I am the Lord”** — Jerome. I who left Jerusalem to be destroyed for the sins of the fathers, and destroyed the defenses of Tyre for its insulting and joy.
26.7:
**“For thus saith the Lord God: Behold”** — for
**“I will bring against Tyre Nabuchodonosor”** — the devil
**“king of Babylon”** — of confusion
**“from the north, the king of kings”**
• not only of peoples
• that is, of kingdoms, of which he says: “All these will I give thee, if falling down thou wilt adore me.”
**“with horses, and chariots, and horsemen, and companies, and much people”** — souls in the straits of sin
**“from the north”** — the wind which is very hard and sinister, called by name dexter, presuming on the dignity of the name.
**“with horses, and”** — Of which: “A horse is a vain thing for safety”; and: “They have slept that mounted on horses”; and elsewhere: “He hath cast the horse and his rider into the sea.”
26.8:
**“Thy daughters”** — that is, the cities subject to you and the castles
**“that are in the field”**
• in the field of the world
• on the shore
**“he shall kill with the sword: and”** — after
**“he shall compass thee with forts”** — so that you do not escape the rule of the devil
26.9:
**“And he shall set engines of war and battering rams against thy walls”** — whatever he may have in doctrines
**“and shall destroy thy towers with his arms.”** — by the multitude of his armed men
26.10:
**“By reason of the multitude of his horses, their dust shall cover thee: thy walls shall shake at the noise”** — that is, the multitude will be so great
**“of the horsemen, and wheels, and chariots shall shake”** — by repute
**“thy walls shall shake at the noise of the horsemen, and wheels, and chariots, when they shall go in at thy gates, as by the entrance of a city that is destroyed.”** — secure, as in the open field
26.11:
**“With the hoofs of his horses”** — Such will be the security of the victors.
**“he shall tread down all thy streets”** — broad and wide is the way that leads to death
**“thy people he shall kill with the sword, and thy famous statues shall fall to the ground.”** — that is, the idols that are fashioned in the heart. Whence: “thou shalt bring their image to nothing.”
26.12:
**“They shall waste thy riches, they shall make a spoil of thy merchandise: and they shall destroy thy walls, and pull down thy fine houses”** — in which you exulted
**“pull down thy fine houses: and they shall lay thy stones”** — you will come to such desolation indeed
26.13:
**“And I will make to cease”** — I the Lord
**“the multitude of thy songs”**
• in which you trusted in worldly wisdom
• another reading: of your canticles
26.14:
**“And I will make thee like a naked rock, thou shalt be a drying place”** — that is, fishing will cease, and you will be made low so that you are a drying place for nets
**“for nets, neither shalt thou be built any more: for I have spoken it, saith the Lord God.”** — because, delivered up by the Lord, she was utterly overthrown by Nabuchodonosor; whence: “whom I have delivered up to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.”
**“neither shalt thou be built”** — into the kingdom, namely of the peoples, so that you might have your own rule as under Hiram; but the rest were to serve kings, whether Chaldeans or Macedonians or Ptolemies or Roman kings.
26.15:
**“Thus saith the Lord God to Tyre: Shall not the islands shake at the sound of thy fall, and the groans”**
• Of virtues, that is.
• while the soul, long given to chastity and other virtues, falls
• in the assault of Nebuchadnezzar
**“of thy slain when they shall be killed in the midst of thee, the islands shall shake”** — who are tossed by the false waves of this world
26.16:
**“shall come down from their thrones”** — from the throne of pride
**“all the princes”**
• by repute
• who rule over various islands
**“of the sea, and take off their robes”** — all the glory of ruling
**“and their broidered garments”** — shining with variety
**“cast away”** — from themselves
**“and be clothed with astonishment”** — and
**“they shall sit on the ground”** — cast down by humility
**“and with amazement shall wonder at thy sudden fall”** — thinking nothing in the world lasting, from your fall
**“robes”** — Jerome. The Seventy: crowns, which namely they seemed to possess by good works.
**“broidered garments”** — the variety of virtues, namely.
26.17:
**“And taking up a lamentation over thee”**
• a mournful song
• and
**“they shall say to thee: How art thou fallen”** — who wast safe before
**“that dwellest in the sea”** — of this world
**“renowned city”** — in reputation
**“that wast strong in the sea”** — against the fiery darts of the devil
**“with thy inhabitants”** — thoughts
**“whom all did dread”** — adversaries
**“that dwellest”** — Tyre, as they report, was formerly an island; but with mounds thrown up, either by Nabuchodonosor or by Alexander, from an island it was made almost not an island.
26.18:
**“Now”** — otherwise, then
**“shall be astonished”** — in thy fall
**“the ships in the day of thy terror”** — through which the waves of this world pass
**“and the islands in the sea shall be troubled because no one”** — almost
**“shall be troubled”** — Lest they endure similar ruins, the ruins of others are examples for others. For “my own affair is at stake when the neighbouring wall is on fire,” while in this sea of life victory is never certain and secure.
**“because no one cometh out of thee”** — Jerome. The Seventy: in thy going out. For we are judged not by what is past but by what is present. And one must be wary and always fear lest the storm of one hour overturn ancient glory and solid firmness.
26.19:
**“For thus saith the Lord God: When I shall make thee a desolate city like the cities that are not inhabited: and shall bring the deep upon thee”** — metaphorically, because the speech is about an island
**“And”** — of the multitude of enemies
**“and many waters shall cover thee”** — many peoples
**“When I shall make thee”** — Jerome. This can be referred to those who, set in the distresses of the world, are led down to hell and covered with the waves of the abyss, that is, of punishments, and are dragged to the lower parts of the earth and joined with those who are in the ancient desolation, so that they are not inhabited by the Holy Spirit; of whom: “The wicked man, when he is come into the depth of sins, contemneth.” Nor hereafter shall they be in the land of the living, but shall perish and be brought to nothing, and therefore shall cease to be. Those abuse these testimonies who say that the punishments of the impious, and not of sinners, are everlasting; who, sought by God, were not found, and have ceased to be forever, because by their own fault they lost him who says, “I am the life.”
26.20:
**“And when I shall bring thee down with those that”** — concerning whom: they will go into the lower parts of the earth
**“descend into the pit”**
• of hell
• where, namely, there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth
**“to the everlasting people, and shall set thee in the lowest parts of the earth”** — in which the ancient dragon is
**“as places desolate of old”** — where no remembrance of the saints is
**“with them that are brought down”** — concerning whom: they will go into the lower parts of the earth
**“into the pit”** — of hell
**“that thou be not inhabited”** — on the contrary
**“in the land of the living”** — Concerning which: “I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living”; and elsewhere: “Blessed are the meek: for they shall possess the land.”
26.21:
**“I will bring thee to nothing”** — you will perish for ever
**“and thou shalt not be, and if thou be sought for, thou shalt not be found any more for ever”** — and you will not be sought and not found again for eternity, that is, the age
**“and thou shalt not be”** — Whence: “O forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I go hence, and be no more.” For that which is not in God, who alone truly is, is said not to be.
**“saith the Lord God”**
• And sought: by him who came to seek what had perished. It is not therefore the fault of the seeker, but of him who fled the hand of the good shepherd.
• For ever, that is, the age, namely seventy years, which is the span of a man’s life. Whence: “The days of our years in them are threescore and ten years.” For Isaias says that after seventy years Tyre was to be restored whole.

27.2:
**“Thou therefore, O son of man, take up a lamentation for Tyre”** — Take up a lamentation over Tyre. He who strikes is the one who has care for the one lamenting; whence Samuel lamented Saul, and the apostle those who did not do penance, and Jeremias lamented the overthrow of Jerusalem in a fourfold alphabet.
**“Allegorically.”** — Whatever is said of Tyre is referred to the distresses of the world, which is “seated in the wicked one,” and is hemmed in and shaken by various waves, that is, disturbances; whence: “They that go down to the sea in ships, doing business in the great waters, these have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep.”
27.3:
**“And say to Tyre that dwelleth at the entry of the sea, being the mart of the people for many islands”** — for it was an island; or because it is a most secure harbour and takes in ships coming from the open sea.
**“Thus saith the Lord God”** — ascribing to yourself the good you have, and the beauty that comes to you from various regions.
**“to the trading of the peoples”** — For even today the trade of almost all nations is carried on there.
**“of perfect beauty”** — Jerome. Perfect beauty is found only in the body of Christ, which is the church; whence: “Thou art all fair, my love, etc.”
27.4:
**“and situate in the heart of the sea, thy neighbours”** — but these were bestowed on you by the bounty of God.
**“that built thee”** — as if to say: you think that to be yours which belongs to another.
**“have perfected thy beauty”** — And in the heart (that is, in the middle), according to that: “the mountains shall be removed into the heart of the sea.” The Lord also is said to have been in the heart of the earth and to have descended into hell.
**“Thy neighbours, that”** — Before he comes to those who dwell far away, he describes the help of the neighbouring peoples.
27.5:
**“with fir trees of Sanir”** — who is also Hermon, which mountain others call Samor.
**“have built thee with all sea planks; they have taken cedars from Libanus”** — Lebanon means whiteness or whitening, which pertains to grace coming from elsewhere.
**“to make thee masts”** — the excessive beauty of the ship.
**“With fir trees of”** — Figuratively: speaking as if to a ship, he signifies the beauty and abundance of the city, and as if to a shipwreck, he afterwards declares its overthrow.
*Jerome:* Allegorically. From fir trees or cedars of Sanir the planks are cut with which the ship is built, and from cedar or cypress of Libanus the mast is raised. Fir trees, for their lightness and the joints of the planks holding one another more softly and gripping each other; or cedars, for their incorruptibility. Sanir: the way of the lamp; or more truly, the God of watchings, because all the ship’s prosperity and illumination comes from the true light.
27.6:
**“they have cut thy oars out of the oaks of Basan”** — the craftsmen of the Lord.
**“thy benches they have made for thee”** — mortifying their bodies, or turning the use of their teeth to the praise of God.
**“of Indian ivory, and cabins”** — Others: storerooms.
**“out of the oaks of”** — Whence: “The Lord said: I will turn them from Basan, I will turn them into the depth of the sea.” Basan is interpreted as shame. Therefore the Lord turns those who were in the depth of the sea and in the shame of sins into oars, so that, sailing with the apostles, they may reach the shore of the homeland.
**“from the islands of Italy”** — The Seventy: “from the islands of Cethim,” which we have rendered “of Italy,” understanding by that region, which is nearer to Greece, all the western parts of the islands.
**“Septuagint”** — Cethim, which is interpreted “struck,” so that by the blows of the devil she is not so much destroyed as tested.
27.7:
**“Fine broidered linen”**
• which is of the land.
• It is described what each province gave.
**“from Egypt”** — in which it is produced in greatest abundance.
**“was woven for thy sail, to be spread on thy mast: blue and purple”** — by which, namely, they are brought.
**“from the islands of Elisa”** — He calls the islands of the Ionian sea thus.
**“were made thy covering”**
• a shade for sailors in the heat.
• Hyacinth is referred to the air, whose colour it has; purple, to the sea, from which it comes; as is fine linen to the earth, from which it springs; to these, with scarlet twice dyed added, the priest’s garments are woven, which signify the four elements, earth, air, fire and water; and of these are all the things which Tyre, ungrateful to the Creator, takes to herself, saying: “I am of perfect beauty.”
**“Fine broidered linen from Egypt”** — As if to say: “What hast thou that thou hast not received? And if thou hast received, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received?”
27.8:
**“The inhabitants of Sidon”**
• which is a neighbouring island.
• Jerome. Sidonians, hunters; Aradians, those who bring down. We say that Tyre, the proudest city, which afterwards is to be ground down when the wind blows, has citizens or princes who are hunters, of whom: “Our soul hath been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers.” For where we read “of the fowlers,” in the Hebrew it is “of the Sidonians”; these hunt unwary souls and are made rowers, that they may lead them to shipwreck.
**“and the Arabians were thy rowers; thy wise men”** — Of whom: “the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light.”
**“O Tyre, were thy pilots”** — for the rudders pertain to wisdom.
27.9:
**“the ancients of Gebal, and the wise men thereof”** — grown old in evil days.
**“furnished mariners”** — drawing them to shipwreck
**“The ancients of Gebal”** — Jerome. In type of the synagogue the elders are rejected, as Cain and Ismael; in type of the church the younger is chosen, Abel, and Isaac receives the inheritance. Of the sons of Isaac also, Jacob the younger dwells at home in simplicity; Esau the elder is a hunter and wanders in the woods; whence: “Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated.” These in the womb had done neither good nor evil, that the one should be chosen and the other cast out, but in type of the synagogue and the church the elder is repelled and the younger taken up.
**“all the ships of the sea”** — Jerome. “All the ships of the sea and their mariners were made” into the west of the west. As it is said: song of songs, work of works, age of ages, meaning greater and more prolonged than other ages; but in this place it signifies the greatness of the western parts. For ships and rowers of this kind do not go to the east, nor to the rising of the light where the sun of justice is born, but to the west of the west, where the light goes down, where is the beginning of darkness.
27.10:
**“The Persians, and Lydians, and the Libyans were thy soldiers in thy army”** — because in battle most brave, most famous
**“they hung up the buckler and the helmet”** — to terrify the enemies
**“The Persians”** — Most brave, whose king Cyrus was foretold by the prophecy of Isaias, who, when Astyages king of the Medes was overthrown, took Babylon. The Lydians also at that time were most brave, whose king Croesus was taken by the same Cyrus.
**“in thee for thy ornament”** — We read in Paralipomenon that the Libyans came against Jerusalem together with the Troglodytes and Ethiopians.
*Jerome:* Persians, tempting; or Lydians, tempted, begotten. Libyans, who in Hebrew are interpreted “Phut”: these strive in vain to defend Tyre, since they are overcome by temptation and serve generation and lust, and multiply empty words, having neither the helmet of salvation nor the shield of faith, but put forward only glory and the noise of speeches for her ornament.
27.11:
**“the men of Arad were with thy army”** — otherwise, with his
**“upon thy walls round about; the Pygmeans also”** — most ready for war
**“that were in thy towers”** — Pygmies, which is turned into a contest
**“their quivers”** — because archers
**“hung up on thy walls”** — on the battlements of the walls
**“The men of Arad”** — Aradus, an island which is itself a whole city and has opposite it the town Antaradus, near Tyre.
*Jerome:* Aradians, those who bring down, who put forward knowledge falsely so called and have in the quiver of their breast the fiery darts of the devil, with which they wound and inflame the hearts of the deceived. These strive to bring down those who strive to ascend to high things, and they fulfil the beauty of Tyre, of which in Proverbs: “Let not the desire of beauty deceive thee.”
27.12:
**“The Carthaginians”**
• which is a colony of the Tyrians
• The Seventy: Tharsis, which means a search for joy, not in a good sense, like the spies Moses sent to search the land of promise, but those who slip in to search out our liberty.
**“thy merchants, with a multitude of all kinds of riches, with silver”** — with the charm of eloquence
**“iron”** — with arms for fighting
**“and lead”** — with the most grievous wickedness, which in Zacharias sits upon the talent of lead
**“supplied thy fairs”** — from the parts of the west
**“tin”** — by the likeness of eloquence. For tin deceives by resembling silver.
27.13:
**“Greece”**
• Ionians, who in Hebrew are Javan
• Jerome. Greece, that is Javan, which is interpreted “is and is not,” and signifies the wisdom of the world; which, if it finds anything rightly, “is” is said; if the contrary, “is not.”
**“Thubal and Mosoch, they were thy merchants”** — who made a precious trade
**“they brought slaves and vessels of brass”** — from Corinth
**“to thy people”**
• For many discourse well of the good of nature, of duties, of continence, of despising riches, which the Stoics claim properly for themselves; and they seem to gain the souls of men whom they have deceived, and they have vessels of brass with which they feign the likeness of gold, which they bring in upon the peoples of Tyre, that they may supplant them by the opinion of false doctrine.
• Moloch, that is, the Cappadocians, whose metropolis, which after Augustus Caesar was called Caesarea, is to this day called Mazaca in their language.
• Stranger and sojourner is interpreted as one who indeed does not eat the flesh of the lamb, of which: the sojourner and hireling shall not eat of it.
**“Thubal”** — Iberians, that is either the Orientals or, from the parts of the west, the Spaniards, named from the river Iberus.
27.14:
**“From the house of Thogorma”** — Phrygia, which formerly abounded most in these
**“horses and horsemen”** — Of which: “a horse is a vain thing for safety”; and elsewhere: “they have slept that mounted on horses.” And: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, who have no understanding”; whence Doeg, accuser and slayer of the priests, was prefect of the mules.
27.15:
**“The men of Dedan were thy merchants”** — where they are beaten by the waves of the sea
**“many islands were the traffic of thy hand, they exchanged for thy price teeth of ivory and ebony”** — precious woods of black color
**“they exchanged for thy price”**
• with other wares
• Ivory: promising from India the whiteness, that is, of eloquence; but they are of ebony and black colour, according to that: “if the Ethiopian change his skin.”
**“Dedan”** — The proper name of a place, which is interpreted as kinship, so that we may recognize in heretics the likeness of divine doctrines. Dedan is a region of India, or of the Idumeans.
27.16:
**“The Syrian was thy merchant”** — to whom the zeal of trade is inborn
**“stacte”** — of the best odour
**“purple”** — of royal dignity
**“broidered works”** — by dialectical art
**“fine linen”** — given over to earthly works
**“and silk, and chodchod, they set forth in thy market”** — the Hebrews say that all precious wares are signified by this name, or a kind of wares which our speech does not express
**“Syrian”** — Aram, that is, which is interpreted “high”: one who swells with pride, promising himself the knowledge of a false name.
**“silk”** — Jerome. For which in Hebrew is Ramoth, which is interpreted the vision of death; for all earthly works hasten to perish.
27.17:
**“Juda and the land of Israel”**
• which is now called Palestine
• Jerome. That is, the church, which both confesses and discerns God, ought not to bring to Tyre the first corn, that is, the word of God, of which: “Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God.”
**“they were thy merchants with the best corn: they set forth balm, and honey, and oil, and rosin”** — in which the land of Juda, now called Palestine, abounds
**“balm”** — That which grows in the vineyards of Engaddi, or the ointment of which it is said: “Like the precious ointment on the head, that ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron.”
**“and honey”** — Of which: “Hast thou found honey? Eat what is sufficient for thee.”
**“oil”** — Of which the lamp of the tabernacle of the Lord is lit, lest it be said to us: “You sold oil in Egypt.” Of which: “The oil of the sinner shall not fatten my head.”
**“rosin”** — Suited to wounded bodies, it is taken for medicine. Whence: “Is there no balm in Galaad? or is no physician there?”
**“they set forth in thy fairs”** — That we may know more plainly what it is to carry all these things to the market of Tyre, let us hear: “Give not that which is holy to dogs,” etc. And that: “It is not good to take the bread of the children, and to cast it to the dogs.” Yet the Chanaanite woman, because she was coming out of the borders of Tyre and Sidon and drawing near to the land of Jerusalem, obtained what she asked.
27.18:
**“The men of Damascus were thy merchants in the multitude of thy works, in the multitude of divers riches, in rich wine”** — for from Damascus was brought very rich wine, and especially wool
**“in wool of the best colour”** — for Tyre has no clothing of its own
**“Damascus”** — Drinking blood, because according to the Hebrews there is a field there where Abel was slain by Cain; of such things the markets of Tyre are gathered.
27.19:
**“Dan, and Greece, and Mosel”** — from these regions these things are brought to the markets of Tyre
**“have set forth in thy marts wrought iron”** — wrought by dialectical art
**“Dan”** — It took its name from the patriarch Dan and his tribe, and the place where he dwelt, where today is Paneas, which was once called Caesarea Philippi; whence the Jordan, that is, the river Dan, which flows from Lebanon.
**“wrought iron”** — Jerome. Greece boasts that it brings forth everything by judgment and reason, and the vocal sound which is signified in the reed, and stacte of the best odour.
27.20:
**“The men of Dedan were thy merchants in tapestry for seats”**
• by which they are carried and rest
• by the beauty of words
27.21:
**“Arabia, and all the princes of Cedar”** — the region of the Saracens, which abounds in these animals
**“they were the merchants of thy hand: thy merchants came to thee with lambs”**
• which were sacrificed
• who lie about the lamb of God
**“and rams”** — who trouble the waters; they strike the sheep with their horns, they fight
**“and kids”** — who will stand on the left
**“Arabia, and all”** — Jerome. Arabia, evening; Cedar, darkness, who carry to Tyre rams and lambs and kids, which they offer on the altars, which they have feigned from a wicked and rebellious heart.
27.22:
**“The sellers of Saba, and Reema”** — conversion, but here in a bad sense
**“they were thy merchants”** — Arabia
**“with all the best spices, and precious stones”** — by which they falsely claim the best fragrance; with the precious stone with which they build churches of perversity
**“and gold”** — by sense
**“which they set forth in thy market”**
• for the sake of shameful gain
• for they do nothing freely, whereas the kings of Arabia and Saba freely offer gifts to Christ
27.23:
**“Haran, and Chene”** — preparation
**“and Eden”** — delights
**“thy merchants”** — sellers
**“Saba, Assur”** — directing
**“Chelmad”**
• or Cherma
• which means ‘vines’ of the Sodomites, that is, those who come to the market of Tyre to direct wicked things; nay, rather to rebuke with punishments and correct what is depraved. Whence: “that thou mayst destroy the enemy and the avenger,” etc.
**“Haran”** — The Septuagint. Charan, that is, holes, which signify fleshly senses, through which is all the preparation of men of the world, who think only of delights if they increase the trade of Tyre.
27.24:
**“They were thy merchants in divers manners”**
• bound
• having, that is, household goods
**“with bales of blue cloth, and of embroidered work, and of precious riches”** — with cords; the powers of the air, who bestow their treasures at the fairs of the world
**“which were wrapped up and bound with cords”** — of sinners
**“cedars”** — Septuagint: cypresses
**“they had cedars also”** — Nothing, that is, was lacking to thee that pertained to the riches of the isles; but this glorification is a burden to thee, because thou canst not bear riches with moderation; poverty also is a temptation; whence Solomon: “Give me neither riches nor beggary.” For in the one pride, in the other impatience and lying steals in.
27.25:
**“The ships of the sea”** — in Hebrew, Tharsis
**“were thy chief in thy merchandise: and thou wast replenished, and glorified exceedingly in the heart of the sea”** — because it cannot bear your delights
27.26:
**“the south wind”**
• in Hebrew, cadi; in Greek, kaicon, which we call the burning wind, of which: “The sun shall not burn thee by day, nor the moon by night.”
• Jerome. By this wind Jacob was scorched, yet not broken, who said: “In the day I was parched with heat, and by night with frost.” Those also who were hired from the first hour bore the heat and burning of the whole day, and yet receive the penny, because scorched, not broken; whence: “I am black but beautiful, because the sun hath altered my colour.”
**“Thy rowers”** — Jerome. Those above, the Sidonians and Aradians, that is, hunters and layers-down; for they hunt in the waves of this world souls unto death, which they lay down in the depths.
**“hath broken thee in the heart of the sea”** — In the heart of the sea, your riches, that is, the waves of the world, where nothing is stable, nothing perpetual. Whence: “Fool, this night thy soul will be taken from thee.” And that of the apostle: “For they that will become rich fall into temptation,” etc.
*Jerome:* The history is clear; therefore to almost every verse we attach brief little maxims.
*Jerome:* The prophecy is mixed between the city and the ship, so that you may understand each by the other, and both pertain to the end of the age and to shipwreck.
27.27:
**“Thy riches, and thy treasures, and thy manifold furniture, thy mariners”** — Sidonians and Aradians
**“and thy pilots”** — according to the Septuagint, counsellors of Byblos, which in Hebrew is called Gebal
**“who kept thy goods, and were chief over thy people: thy men of war also, that were in thee”** — Persians, Lydians, Libyans
**“Who were in thee, with all thy multitude”**
• the common people
• Septuagint: by mingling
**“that is in the midst of thee shall fall”** — as of nothing
**“in the heart”** — midst
**“of the sea”** — of the world
**“in the day”** — of judgment
**“of thy ruin”** — of evils
27.28:
**“at the sound of the cry”** — in your fall
**“of thy pilots”** — These are bishops of heretics.
**“shall be troubled, the fleets”** — of the deceivers
27.29:
**“and shall come down from their ships”** — in which they gloried
**“all that handled”** — supposedly
**“the oar. Mariners, and all the pilots of the sea”** — tossed by the waves
**“shall stand upon the land”** — in a stable place
27.30:
**“and shall mourn over thee with a loud voice”** — which they enriched with merchandise
**“and shall cry bitterly”** — showing the bitterness of mind by outcry
**“And they shall cast up dust”** — Doing penance for earthly works, they are either sprinkled with the ashes of the heifer, according to the law, that they may be purified, or they will lay ashes under themselves; whence: “Strew ashes under thee, and make lamentation.” And that: “If in Tyre and Sidon had been wrought, etc., they had long ago done penance in sackcloth and ashes.” And: “I did eat ashes like bread,” etc.
27.31:
**“And they shall shave themselves bald for thee, and shall be girded with haircloth and they shall weep for thee with bitterness of soul”** — “It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to the house of feasting.”
**“with most bitter weeping”** — that they may lament Tyre and redouble the mournful song
**“They shall shave themselves bald for thee”** — This is what is usually done in mourning when all joy has been shut out. The hairs of the apostles were numbered, because they consecrated their hair to the Lord like the Nazarites. While Samson had his hair he had strength; when his locks were taken away he was captured by the Philistines.
**“and shall be girded”** — Jerome. The old lust is condemned, so that those who lived in luxury, doing penance, live in austerity and hardness. The Ninevites do penance in sackcloth. And it is said to Jerusalem: “Weep to me, like a virgin girded with haircloth.”
*Jerome:* All these things we refer to the heretics, who in the breaking and shipwreck of Tyre will perceive their error, and, set in the midst of the sea, will long to free their souls, and will bewail the wrongly gathered riches with which they enriched many kings, that is, their heresiarchs, and the ignoble crowd, whose wealth will fall in the midst of the sea.
27.32:
**“and shall take up a mournful song for thee, and shall lament”** — saying
**“What city is like Tyre, which is become silent in the midst of the sea”** — “Be dumb and be silent”; and according to that: “But to the sinner God hath said: Why dost thou declare my justices, and take my covenant in thy mouth?”
27.33:
**“Which by thy merchandise that went from thee”** — as if to say: what have you gained by so great labour?
**“by sea didst fill many people; by the multitude of thy riches and of thy people didst enrich the kings of the earth”** — Of whom: “The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes met together, against the Lord,” etc.
27.34:
**“Now”** — but
**“thou art destroyed by the sea”** — according to that: “Pharao’s chariots and his army he hath cast into the sea.” And elsewhere: “they sunk as lead in the mighty waters.”
**“thy riches are in the bottom of the waters”** — that is, you say: “I am come into the depth of the sea: and a tempest hath overwhelmed me.”
27.35:
**“All the inhabitants of the islands are astonished at thee”** — who are beaten by the waves of this world
**“and their kings”** — otherwise, oarsmen
**“all their kings being struck with the storm have changed their countenance”** — knowing their own destruction, showing heart’s grief by weeping and tears
27.36:
**“The merchants of people have hissed at thee”** — Imitating the voice of a serpent, or by astonishment and hissing bearing witness to the greatness of the amazement.
**“thou art brought to nothing, and thou shalt never be any more”**
• Others: the age of one man, that is, seventy years.
• To God, who calls those things that are not as those that are. Whence Isaias: “All his adversaries shall be as if they were not.”
**“Thou shalt never be”** — Jerome. Whence: “Give not thy sceptre to them that are not.” And elsewhere: “Before I go hence, and be no more.”
**“any more”** — That is, for eternity. In this place the Hebrew can signify both: a single age, that is, and eternity.

28.2:
**“Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre: Thus saith the Lord God: Because”** — into heaven
**“thy heart is lifted up, and thou hast said: I am God, and I sit in the chair of God in the heart of the sea”** — that is, when you are held in the narrow confines of an island.
**“whereas thou art a man”** — frail.
**“and not God”** — Christ is man and God.
**“and hast set thy heart as if it were the heart of God”** — so that even the men of your kingdom might provoke Solomon with riddles.
**“Son of man”** — As above, under the figure of a ship, first the riches and then the ruin and mourning of Tyre are described, so for the prince of Tyre both his pride and his ruin are set in order.
**“Thus saith the Lord”** — Jerome. Nabuchodonosor in Isaias was so lifted up that he dared to say: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds, I will be like the most High”; and cast down from his throne he deserves to hear: “How art thou fallen, O Lucifer, who didst rise in the morning?” And in the prophet Pharao says this: “The rivers are mine, and I made them.” And the prince of Tyre: “I am God,” etc. All of which, although they are not of men but of raving demons, we must nevertheless take as hyperbole, in that they swelled so much with prosperity that they did not know themselves to be men and presumed to themselves an eternal empire; although under the type of kings and princes and single cities and provinces, the opposing powers are shown, of whom: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood,” etc. and elsewhere: “not the wisdom of the princes of this world.” And again: “Which none of the princes of this world knew.” In Daniel, of whom it is read: Michael, prince of the Jews, and the prince of Greece, and the prince of the Persians. And in Deuteronomy: “When the most High divided the nations,” etc. Nor is it a wonder that the worst princes went before in the figure of demons, as the best went before in the figure of Christ.
28.3:
**“Behold thou art wiser than Daniel”** — as if we were to posit this.
**“no secret is hid from thee”** — Thou art wiser than Daniel, who overcame all the wisdom of Egypt. Or even if you are wiser than he, and desire to make yourself equal to the greatness of God, yet you will be taken by your enemies, and will no longer say, “I am God,” taught by destruction that you are a man and not God.
28.6:
**“Therefore thus”** — Jerome. Wherever, according to the Septuagint, Lord is placed second, the first name is the tetragrammaton, which properly pertains to God and is called ineffable; the second is according to the common name, which is often found also in men.
*Jerome:* If we wish to say that the prince of Tyre is the same power to which the city itself or province was entrusted by God, let us take this testimony: “I have said: You are gods and all of you the sons of the most High. But you like men shall die, and shall fall like one of the princes.” For the provinces were handed over to them to rule, as to judges by the emperor; who, forgetful of their honour, rise up against their Lord, so that, dispersed through the whole world, under the names of the idolatry of gods they took the names of gods to themselves, and, puffed up with pride, fell into the judgment and snare of the devil; of whom: “I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven.”
28.7:
**“Therefore behold, I will bring upon thee strangers the strongest of the nations”** — when its city is taken.
**“they shall draw their swords against the beauty of thy wisdom”** — in which you trust.
28.8: **“They shall kill”** — pierced with many wounds.
28.10:
**“he shall surely die”** — that is, most shameful.
**“of the uncircumcised”** — of the unclean.
**“Thou shalt die by the hand”** — by power.
28.12:
**“Take up a lamentation”** — Because we have learned who the prince of Tyre is and how he fell through pride, that we may know the lamentation over his former glory, he first reminds him what he was, so that he may grieve that he has lost what he had.
**“And say to him: Thus saith the Lord God: Thou wast the seal”** — expressed
**“of resemblance, full of wisdom, and perfect in beauty”** — where there is the likeness of God, there is the fullness of wisdom and perfect beauty.
**“Thou wast the seal of resemblance”** — Which is said of the Saviour: “Him hath God the Father sealed.” And in the Psalm: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us.” And elsewhere: “Dearly beloved, we know that when he shall appear, we shall be like to him.” And elsewhere: “Who is like to thee?” For likeness is one thing, equality another; whence the most savage heresy, which confesses in Christ only a likeness of the Father, takes away his nature.
**“Thou wast the seal”** — Jerome. Others read resignaculum, because the king of Tyre sealed back the image of God to which he was made, that is, destroyed it. And it is to be noted that the image becomes a likeness only when it is completed in the baptism of Christ.
28.13:
**“in the pleasures of the paradise”** — in Hebrew, Eden.
**“of God: every precious stone was thy covering”** — it is shown to him whatever he has lost.
**“the sardius”** — purple, in which is the blood of the cross.
**“topaz and jasper”** — the greenness of faith.
**“the chrysolite, and the onyx, and the beryl, the sapphire”** — whose conversation is in heaven.
**“and the carbuncle”** — burning in spirit.
**“and the emerald: gold”** — wisdom
**“the work of thy beauty and thy pipes”** — signifies the capacity of the mind
**“were prepared in the day that thou wast created”**
• for receiving the divine sacraments
• Sardius, topaz, etc. Jerome. These are the stones which the high priest, who is a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech, bears engraved on the breastplate upon his breast. These are the living stones, of whom in the Apocalypse of John the city is built; these are the pearls of the prophets and apostles, all of which are sold that the precious pearl may be bought, which has seven eyes, that is, the seven graces of the Holy Spirit.
• Topaz, burning: the contemplation of the saints.
• Chrysolite shines like gold and has burning sparks, in which the saints are signified, who shine with wisdom and give to others the words of preaching and the signs of virtues.
• Onyx: black signifies humility, white purity, red passion.
• Beryl: green and pale. The saints indeed are green by faith, pale by humility.
• Emerald, very green, which, staining the herbs and air around it with its greenness, signifies the faithful who ascend in hope to the unfading inheritance and spread to their neighbours by words and examples.
• Pliny treats these stones fully in the thirty-seventh book of the Natural History.
**“of the paradise of God”** — For it is “not of God” among those who change the truth into a lie and boast that they have paradise; here he shows that it is not a man but a contrary power which dwelt in paradise, although the Jews by a figure called hyperbole think it is prophesied of Hiram, king of Tyre.
**“every precious stone”** — It is not said that the king of Tyre was surrounded by every precious stone, but that every stone he had was precious. For there are many precious stones which he does not mention here: chalcedony, sardonyx, chrysoprase, crystal, and others.
28.14:
**“Thou a cherub stretched out, and protecting, and I set thee in the holy mountain of God, thou hast walked in the midst of the stones of fire”**
• signifies the heavenly Jerusalem
• in paradise, the third heaven, namely, the heaven to which Paul was caught up
**“Thou a cherub stretched out, and protecting”** — the ark, namely, and the mercy seat; or the city of Tyre, to which once holy and special power was given.
**“in the midst of the stones”** — Concerning these: “He that maketh his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire,” so that not only God, who is called a consuming fire, consumes hay, stubble and wood, but also the angels, who are called burning stones; whence: “I am come to cast fire on the earth,” etc.
28.15:
**“Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day of thy creation”** — as if: your wickedness is of the will, not of nature. Every creature was created good and perfect.
**“until”** — by God
**“iniquity was found in thee”** — in the treasure of your heart, through pride and abuse of power
28.16:
**“By the multitude of thy merchandise”** — that is, while you seek many things, not content with the benefit of your Creator
**“thy inner parts were filled with iniquity”** — of heart, namely, so that being sated and fattened you might kick back and abandon God
**“and thou hast sinned”** — because evil thoughts proceed from your heart
**“and I cast thee out from the mountain of God”** — paradise
**“and destroyed thee, O covering cherub, out of the midst of the stones of fire”** — much more therefore must we fear, if that great one was cast out
**“And destroyed thee, O covering cherub”** — Jerome. Cherub is of masculine gender, singular number; cherubim is the plural, which is interpreted “multitude of knowledge,” in whom God rests and sits; whence: “Thou that sittest upon the cherubims, shine forth before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasses”; and elsewhere: “He ascended upon the cherubims, and flew.”
28.17:
**“And thy heart was lifted up with thy beauty”** — while you think what is God’s is yours
**“thou hast lost thy wisdom in thy beauty”** — while you want to be more than you were created
**“to the ground”** — so that in place of beauty and wisdom, deformity and folly may possess you
**“I have cast thee”** — from the mountain of God; whence: “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer”
**“before the face of kings”**
• Jerome. So that they may be terrified by your example, either of good kings, whose heart is in the hand of God, or of evil ones, whose kingdoms the devil showed to the Saviour, who met the king of Babylon, saying: “You too are taken, as we are,” etc.
• Whence: “I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven”; whence Jeremias: “How hath the Lord covered with obscurity the daughter of Sion in his wrath! how hath he cast down from heaven to the earth the glorious one of Israel.”
28.18:
**“Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries by the multitude of thy iniquities, and by the iniquity of thy traffic”** — which you had on the mountain of God
**“therefore I will bring forth a fire from the midst of thee”** — kindled with the devil’s fiery darts; of which: “They are all adulterers, their hearts like an oven”; of which Isaias: “walk in the light of your fire,” etc.
**“to devour thee”** — going forth outside
**“to devour”** — Jerome. Whence Isaias: “it shall devour as stubble the matter in that day,” etc. This fire, which is called strange, Nadab and Abiu offered at the altar of the Lord, and therefore they were consumed by divine fire; whence Moses: “This is what the Lord hath spoken: In them that approach to me I will be sanctified.” For the sanctification of the Lord is the punishment of sinners.
**“and I will make thee as ashes”** — That the fire may consume all that you have built up with your evil conscience. You, who ought to have done nothing servile in rest and on the sabbath, gathered wood on the sabbath, that the fire might have something to devour in your breast. But it profits that all evil works be turned into ashes, that the harmful fire may be altogether extinguished.
*Jerome:* The Hebrews are wont, among their other fables, to understand these things as said against Hiram, king of Tyre, although there were very many years from Solomon to Ezechiel, which men at that time clearly could not have outlived; and to pronounce them as if the prophet spoke to him in irony: “Art thou the seal of likeness,” etc., whereas on the contrary you have sinned and are to be dissolved into ashes. And their fables add a miracle, that without the authority of Scripture they say Hiram lived a thousand years.
28.19:
**“All that shall see thee among the nations, shall be astonished at thee: thou art brought to nothing”** — because
**“and thou shalt never be any more”** — according to that: I will not spare thee, and I will not have mercy
28.20: **“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying”** — after Tyre the word is made to Sidon, because they are of one province
28.21: **“Son of man, set thy face against Sidon”** — Jerome. Allegorically. The Sidonians are hunters. Of whom: “Our soul hath been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers.” And elsewhere: “from the snare of the hunters, and from the sharp word.” In Proverbs also: The eye of the harlot is the snare of the sinner. But there are also good hunters. Whence Jeremias: “Behold I will send many fishers, and they shall fish them: and after this I will send many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain.” These, from fishers of fishes, were made fishers of souls; whence the village of Peter and Andrew, Bethsaida, is said to mean the house of hunters. The prophet is therefore commanded to set his face against Sidon, that standing firm he may slay such hunters. “Behold I come against thee,” namely, and I will be glorified in thee when I have slain thee, “and all who shall live shall know that I am the Lord,” who render to thee what thou deservest. I will send pestilence and blood into thy streets. For wide and spacious is the way that leadeth to death.
28.22:
**“And shalt say: Thus saith the Lord God: Behold I come against thee, Sidon”** — I will come
**“and I will be glorified in the midst of thee”** — when you have been taken by the Babylonians
**“and they shall know that I am the Lord”** — convicted by the weight of evils
**“when I shall execute judgments in her, and shall be sanctified in her”** — by punishing her
28.23:
**“And I will send into her pestilence, and blood in her streets”** — who had stood badly
**“by the sword on all sides in the midst thereof”** — which the Lord came to send on earth, that he might separate things ill joined
**“And”** — thus
**“they shall know”** — by which they remained
28.24:
**“And the house of Israel shall have no more”** — when they have ceased
**“a stumblingblock of bitterness”** — as before, when they attacked them
**“nor a thorn causing pain”** — to the people of God
28.25:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: When I shall have gathered together”** — that is, when this has been done
**“the house of Israel”** — before it was scattered
**“out of the people among whom they are scattered: I will be sanctified in them before the Gentiles”** — not as with the Sidonians in evil but in good, that is, when he has had mercy on them and they have dwelt in the land which he gave to their father Jacob
**“and they shall dwell in their own land”** — Of which: “I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living”; which he gave to Jacob, who supplanted his elder brother and deserved to receive his firstfruits.
**“When I shall have gathered together”** — Jerome. But all these things are said against the adversary powers, that at the end of time they shall be destroyed and there shall be eternal security, when the Lord shall have gathered together the house of Israel, namely those who discern God by understanding, and shall be sanctified in them, that which is written being fulfilled: “Be holy, because I am holy.”
*Jerome:* Many refer these things to the time of Zorobabel, Esdras and Nehemias, when the people of Israel returned and dwelt in its own land; others hope they will be fulfilled at the last time, and within a thousand years.
28.26:
**“And they shall dwell therein secure, and they shall build houses”** — upon a firm rock. Whence: “Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.”
**“and shall plant vineyards, and shall dwell with confidence”** — secure
**“when I shall have executed judgments upon all that are their enemies round about”** — then
**“and they shall know that I am the Lord their God”** — whose promises are firm, whose judgments are true

29.1:
**“In the tenth”** — In the year of the captivity of Joachim
**“in the tenth month, the eleventh day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying”** — after Sidon, which also is situated on the shore of Phoenicia
**“In the tenth year”** — What place does it hold among the ten days? One. Whence in the beginning of Genesis it is not said the first day but one, to teach that the same day ever returns. The same ten reaches to the hundred, by which the lamb is taken for the victim, to be sacrificed on the fourteenth day; and so the order of numbers proceeds by its tens up to a thousand, and ten thousand, and a hundred thousand, and beyond. After the tenth year the twelfth month is put, that the perfect number of the twelve apostles and prophets, who are contained in one volume, may be shown.
29.2:
**“Son of man, set thy face against Pharao king of Egypt”** — any king of Egypt
**“king of Egypt”** — because from the other side of Judea it is situated on the same shore
**“and thou shalt prophesy of him”** — because things were to come to him
**“Against Pharao”** — Among the Egyptians royal dignity is signified by this name, as among the Romans their kings are called Caesars and Augusti, and among the Syrians Antiochi, among the Persians Arsacidae, among the Philistines Abimelech, and after Alexander in Egypt Ptolemy, down to Cleopatra, by whose defeat at Actium Egypt became a Roman province.
*Jerome:* These things are said by metaphor, as if to the king of Egypt, because that king was not an adversary of Israel, but by promising great things separated them from God. According to the anagogical sense, he calls the devil a dragon, who is also called Pharao, because he separates and divides from God. Egypt, that is Mesraim, signifies those who trouble and afflict, namely those whom he can subject to himself. Job speaks most fully of this dragon. And David: “Thou hast broken the heads of the dragons.” This dragon is called great in comparison with the lesser dragons. Of whom: “Thou hast broken the heads of the dragons in the waters.” And elsewhere: “There are creeping things without number: creatures little and great”; this dragon is the king of all that are in the waters. But he sits and lies in the midst of the rivers, that is, of the heresies, through which he has flowed into the Egypt of this world and watered the souls of the seduced, not with rains from heaven but with turbid waters from the earth. Whence Jeremias: “And now what hast thou to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the troubled water?” for which in the Hebrew is Sior, which signifies turbid and muddy waters. Opposed to these are the waters of which it is said: “Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water,” and elsewhere: he that shall drink of the water that I shall give him shall not thirst for ever, but “it shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into life everlasting.” These rivers come from heaven. Whence: “The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful: the most High hath sanctified his own tabernacle.”

It is of divine mercy that the abundance of this world perish, and the streams of Egypt be dried up, and the land be made desolate, and the sentence of God be scattered, from the tower of Syene, which is interpreted a circle, that it may have nothing right in itself, even to the land of the Ethiopians, who are called humble; that is, that all pride which had raised itself against the knowledge of God may be both destroyed and humbled unto salvation.
**“From the tower”** — Septuagint. Magdalo is the name of a place, namely the tower of Syene, which to this day remains a fortress subject to the Romans, where are the cataracts of the Nile, up to which place the Nile is navigable from our sea. He therefore says that all Egypt is to be laid waste, as far as the borders of Ethiopia, with which the farthest region of Egypt is joined.
29.11:
**“The foot of man shall not pass through it”** — Jerome. That is, any rational creature; nor the foot of a beast of burden, so that not even the simple should remain in it, whom Pharao, the men having been sent away, wished to retain in Egypt, while Moses contradicted and wished to free the beasts also from the captivity of Egypt. And it shall not be inhabited forty years: which number is one of affliction and punishment; whence Moses and Elias and Christ himself fasted forty days and forty nights, and the people was in the wilderness forty years, that afterwards, circumcised in Galgal, it might be freed from the reproach and disgrace of Egypt. By the mystery of this number Ezechiel slept forty days on his right side, and the people who were to serve in Egypt four hundred years are signified, which make forty decades or four hecatontads. The rains of the flood for forty days bring shipwreck upon the world. For it was just that he who had offended God through the four elements of the world, of which all things consist, should be punished by that very number; and that Israel, which had sinned against the sabbath, should bear the punishment of seven decades, that is, of seventy years.
**“nor shall it be inhabited during forty years”** — The Egyptians are spared, and because they were once guests of Israel, they were condemned for a shorter time. Tyre kept its sabbaths for seventy years, and at last was restored. The captivity of Juda and the overthrow of the temple fulfilled seventy years, until Cyrus the king. For the mighty shall mightily suffer torments.
