29.17:
**“And it came to pass in the seven and twentieth year, in the first”** — in the month
**“in the first month”** — otherwise: in the twentieth
**“And it came to pass in the seven and twentieth”** — It is asked how, after the tenth year of the preceding discourse, the twenty-seventh year is at once set down, and in what follows the tenth and the twelfth, and in the last description of the temple the twenty-fifth. But the solution is easy. Because both the earlier prophecy and this one concern Egypt, although they were made at different times, yet those which concern one province are joined to one another; which we often read in Jeremias, namely that the times are described in a preposterous order: for in some places the deeds of Sedechias are related first, and afterwards those of Joachim, who was before him. In the psalms, since the song is lyric, the order of history is not sought.
**“And it came to pass in”** — In Genesis we read that on the twenty-seventh day of the second month the waters of the flood overflowed the face of the earth, and on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month they ceased, and the ark of Noe rested upon the mountains of Ararath, that is, of Armenia; whence we have it that this number is referred both to good and to evil, since in it both the wrath of God begins through the flood and clemency returns. And because among the Hebrews the month, which with us runs by kalends, nones and ides, is reckoned by the course of the moon, whence the Greek mene, that is, moon, took its name from the month. By this number it is said that on the twenty-seventh day of the moon a little light remains, lest the wrath of God be wholly without mercy. But when the whole orb of the moon is filled, then the pasch and all the chief solemnities are celebrated. In this number therefore both good and evil are contained alike: good for Nabuchodonosor, evil for the Egyptians, whose devastation is announced.
29.18:
**“Son of man, Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon hath made his army to undergo hard service against Tyre”** — to me in the assault on Tyre, so that he might fulfil my will
**“every head was made bald, and every shoulder was peeled”** — carrying baskets of earth and stones
**“and there hath been no reward given him, nor his army for Tyre, for the service that he rendered me against it”** — to him or to his army, because he found nothing precious in Tyre
**“Son of man”** — Jerome. When Nabuchodonosor was besieging Tyre, since it was girt by the sea and its walls could not be reached with rams and engines and mantelets, he ordered the endless multitude of his army to bring stones and earth, and, the middle of the sea, or rather the very narrow strait, being filled up, to make the neighbouring shore continuous with the island. When the Tyrians saw this, and the work already finished, and the foundations of the walls shaken by the battering of the rams, they carried off in ships to the islands whatever precious things they had, so that, the city being taken, Nabuchodonosor should find nothing worthy of so great a labour. And because in this part he obeyed the will of God, after some years Egypt was given to him. And Tyre was much more cruel than Egypt. For the former was attacking Jerusalem; the latter promised vain help. But it is one thing to deceive weakness with hope, another to fight against the people of God; and this is what is said: Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon made his army to serve.
*Jerome:* When Nabuchodonosor received the reward of a good work, we understand that a reward is paid to the heathen if they have done any good; whence in Jeremias Nabuchodonosor is called the dove of God, because he served the will of God against a sinful people; whence: “I will bring my servant Nabuchodonosor.” We are therefore condemned by comparison with the Gentiles, who do the law by nature, while we neglect even the written law; on which Paul disputes most fully in his epistle to the Romans.
29.19: **“Behold, I will set”** — Some say that this was fulfilled under Nabuchodonosor. Others, under Cambyses son of Cyrus, who laid Egypt waste as far as Ethiopia, so that he even killed Apis and destroyed all their idols. For which cause they think he was turned to madness by the fall of his horse and was pierced by his own dagger. Herodotus relates this history most fully, where all Egypt is described by its districts and villages and forts, and the source of the Nile, and the peoples, and the measure of the land round about as far as the desert of Ethiopia, and the shores of the great sea, and the borders of Libya and Arabia are shown. The cause of God’s wrath, however, is against the Egyptians, who deceived the people of God with their help, so that it did not hope in God and provoked him to anger.

**“And for the service that he hath done me against it”** — Tyre
**“I have given him the land of Egypt, because he hath laboured”** — otherwise: he labored

**“And in Taphnis”**
• which is the royal city
• Jerome. Taphnis: supply “of the devil”; those yielding to his mouth will lose the light of truth and turn day into night, and will feel the sceptres of Egypt and all its rule broken in Taphnis.
**“the day shall be darkened”**
• with a cloud of sorrow and mourning
• all things are filled with darkness and gloom
**“when I shall break there the sceptres of Egypt”** — that is, the royal line
**“and the pride of her power shall cease in her: a cloud shall cover her”** — so that the rays of the sun of justice may not shine in it
**“and her daughters”**
• not only women
• towns
30.19:
**“And I will execute judgments in Egypt: and they shall know that I am the Lord.”** — then, that is, when I shall have shown myself as judge
**“judgments”** — Many, not one. For as in the house of God there are many mansions, so Egypt has various punishments, so that when all these things have been done the Egyptians may know that he is the Lord, whose judgments are true and justified in themselves.
30.20: **“And it came to pass in the eleventh”** — Jerome. He returns to the order of the prophecy: after the twenty-seventh year he now sets down the eleventh, a question which is also contained in the earlier passages. For when the word of the Lord against Tyre was spoken in the eleventh year, which was set down first, in what follows he speaks to Pharao in the tenth year. And again he sets down the twenty-seventh, as we said, and now the eleventh. But, to omit other matters which are contained in the order of the psalms, such as those psalms in which David changed his countenance before Abimelech, and concerning Doeg the Edomite, and when he was found in the cave, and the fiftieth psalm of penitence, in whose title it is shown that he went in to Bethsabee the wife of Urias, these are earlier than the third psalm, in which he is noted as fleeing from the face of Absalom his son. But in the psalms the answer is easy. For it is a lyric song, in which the order of history is not sought but the songs of single deeds. In history, however, this must be said: that things said about one matter at different times ought not to be divided by reason of time but gathered together in the narration of one place; for example, that what was said of Egypt at one time and another may be known in one order of reading. When we have said this, the question still remains why in this same place the word of the Lord came first to Pharao in the tenth year, and afterwards in the twenty-seventh, and then the eleventh, when according to order the tenth should have been marked first, the eleventh second, the twentieth third, for the single prophecies. But we can answer: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God,” etc.; and elsewhere: “Who shall search out the abyss and wisdom?” We can say of them this, that in the prophets the order of history is not kept except in some places. For they do not narrate things past but foretell things to come, as the will of the Holy Spirit may be. In history, however, the narration is not put out of order.
30.21:
**“Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharao king of Egypt”** — metaphorically
**“and behold it is not bound up, to be healed, to be tied up with clothes”** — according to that: “Neither plaster to apply, nor oil, nor bandages.”
**“and swathed”** — or that it might receive a plaster
**“with linen, that it might recover strength”** — if this had been done, that is. For therefore the merciful and compassionate Lord again breaks his arm, so that the sword may fall utterly from his hand, and Egypt be scattered among the nations or destroyed
**“and hold the sword”** — to go forth to war
**“arm”** — The strength of power; whence: “Break thou the arm of the sinner and of the malignant.” This arm is broken in our adversaries when, persecuting us, they cannot oppress us; and for the salvation of the servants of God the king of Babylon often rises against Pharao, that the more powerful may oppress the powerful, and the wicked be handed over to worse ones, the Lord strengthening the arms of the worst, that he who is delivered may know that he is the Lord.
*Jerome:* Of the king of Babylon no mention is made in this chapter, lest he seem to provoke the wrath of the lords against the captive people set in Chaldea. But it is said of the king of the Assyrians, who by that time had been taken by the Chaldeans, and all the strength of the Assyrians lay under the Babylonian empire; whence also the Assyrians take the ten tribes, that is, Israel, but the Chaldeans overcome the two, that is, Juda and Benjamin, and overthrow Jerusalem.
30.22:
**“Therefore, thus saith the Lord God: Behold, I come against Pharao king of Egypt, and I will break into pieces his strong arm”** — before
**“but”** — already
30.25:
**“And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and the arms of Pharao shall fall”** — or thus
**“and they shall know”** — It is the progress of virtue to know that he is the Lord; whence by contrast the sons of Heli were pestilent, not knowing the Lord. But of the kings who did right in the sight of God it is written that they knew the Lord.

31.1:
**“And it came to pass”** — He here inveighs against the same Pharaoh, who is compared to the Assyrian king; and after a very long prophecy a lament over the same man is taken up, and from then on against all Egypt.
**“in the eleventh year”** — Allegorically. For they had not yet come to the twelfth, which is the number of full and perfect virtue; whence there are twelve sons of Jacob, from whom afterwards the twelve tribes are named, and the twelve names of the prophets are contained in one volume, and the apostles are twelve, of whom one, Judas, was the traitor, in whose place Matthias is chosen, and the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, twelve years old, is raised up by the Lord. The woman with the issue of blood also receives health in the twelfth year. But because Pharao is rebuked and afterwards lamented, the third month and one day are heaped up to the number of eleven years; whence in what follows, in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the first of the month, the word of the Lord came to Ezechiel, saying: “Son of man, take up a lamentation for Pharao the king of Egypt, and say to him.” For he who is lamented is lamented that he may understand how great goods he has lost; and yet, because he was Pharao, and his arm had not yet been bound up nor had recovered its former strength, therefore in the twelfth year and the twelfth month the twenty-ninth day still remains, that the number of twelve years may be completed; so on the first day of the month the word of the Lord comes to the prophet.
31.2:
**“Son of man, speak to Pharao king of Egypt”** — to the antichrist; when he falls, the other rulers of this darkness and princes of the world will fall more easily
**“and to his people”** — to another, to the multitude. “For many are called, but few are chosen.”
**“To whom art thou like in thy greatness?”** — to another, to the height: “Everyone that exalteth himself shall be humbled.”
**“To whom art thou like”** — As if: do not wonder if the Babylonians conquer you and overthrow your empire and destroy the Egyptian wealth, since Assur, far stronger than you, was wiped out by them.
31.3:
**“Behold, the Assyrian was like a cedar in Libanus, with fair branches”** — under the figure of a tree he describes the power of the Assyrian king
**“Behold, the Assyrian was like a cedar”** — Jerome. His beauty is proclaimed, which was changed into foulness by a perverse will; whence: “The Lord will break the cedars of Libanus,” that is, one lofty, set on Libanus, the highest of the mountains; the more sublime he was, the harder he would fall; whence he is called “a great sense.”
**“with fair branches, and full of leaves, of a high stature, and his top was elevated among the thick boughs”** — But it must be known that whatever is said of the king of the Assyrians in future time is recorded by the Septuagint as though already past; and so he speaks either to the tree or to the prince of the Assyrians, so as to use both the masculine and the feminine gender in one person, since both the tree is referred to the Assyrian and the Assyrian is named in the tree.
31.4:
**“The waters nourished him”**
• as if he grew great only because the waters nourished him
• not of Siloe, which flows with silence, but the waters of Rasim and of Egypt
• The waters, that is, most abundant. For abyss is a multitude of the sound of waters.
**“the deep set him up on high”**
• upon which darkness was borne in the beginning of the world
• The deep. Jerome: to which the demons beg, in the gospel, not to be sent.
**“the streams thereof ran round about his roots, and it sent forth its rivulets to all the trees of the country”** — namely his companions.
**“the streams”** — The rivers. Of which: “What have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, that you should drink the water of rivers?” And elsewhere: “Behold, the Lord will bring upon you the waters of the river, strong and many, the king of the Assyrians, and all his glory.”
31.5:
**“Therefore was his height exalted above all the trees of the country”** — Whence all these things were delivered to me.
**“and his branches were multiplied, and his boughs were elevated because of many waters”** — watered, namely by the waters of the deep.
31.6:
**“And when he had spread forth his shadow”** — so that he might subject all to his dominion.
**“all the fowls of the air made their nests in his boughs”** — everyone who commits sin is born of the devil and is counted among the number of his branches.
**“and all the beasts of the forest brought forth their young under his branches”** — who have lost the gentleness of Christ.
**“and the assembly of many nations dwelt under his shadow”** — these are the birds, these the beasts, namely.
**“in his boughs”** — Jerome. Note that in the dwelling itself there is a different condition. Some dwell in the branches like fowls, promising themselves knowledge in philosophy and in the doctrines of heretics. Others dwell like wild beasts, savage and cruel. Others like a multitude of very many nations, that is, mingled together with diverse vices.
**“the fowls of the air”** — The birds of the air. Those that eat the seed by the wayside, or because all have sinned and need the glory of God. Whence: “They are all gone aside, they are become unprofitable together”; therefore they made nests in his branches.
31.7: **“And he was most beautiful for his greatness, and for the spreading of his branches”** — so that there was no one who was not sheltered by his shade, except him who said: “For the prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not any thing.”
31.8:
**“The cedars”** — Or cypresses.
**“in the paradise of God were not higher than he, the fir trees”** — Or pines.
**“did not equal his top, neither were the plane trees to be compared with him for branches: no tree in the paradise of God”** — so that I may gather the individual trees.
**“no tree”** — By this many understand that this is not said of the king of the Assyrians, but of the opposing power which is said in the discourse on Tyre to have been created among the cherubim, adorned with precious stones, and afterwards to have fallen by its own fault to earthly things; which, falling, is called Lucifer; whence: “I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven.” But we, to follow the history, understand all these things as said in hyperbole: that the Assyrian was of such great power, and so oppressed all nations, that he compared himself to the height of the angels.
*Jerome:* Therefore no tree in paradise is equal to him, because every tree was not like him and his beauty, because they were not lifted up in pride but knew their humility, nor did they with sacrilegious daring aspire to the likeness of God.
31.9:
**“For I made him beautiful”** — Or her.
**“envied him”** — And they envied him. For as many as Assur desires to have unto destruction, so many they desire unto salvation.
31.10:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord God: Because he was exalted in height”** — Metaphorically.
**“and shot up his top green and thick, and his heart was lifted up”** — namely of Antichrist.
**“in his height”** — so that he might say: “I will be like the Most High.”
31.11:
**“I have delivered him”** — Or her.
**“into the hands of the mighty one of the nations”** — namely of the king of Babylon, so that what he conquered the Assyrian is understood to be by the power of God.
**“he shall deal with him”** — according to the Lord’s commands.
**“I have cast him out according to his wickedness”** — Secretly he warns the Babylonian not to cruelly oppress the people of God, who was delivered to him, lest he suffer things like the Assyrian, who was cruel and impious.
**“The mighty one of the nations”** — Jerome. Namely, to another, a detestable power, to which he is handed over for punishment, that of Antichrist, that is, of Satan.
31.12:
**“And shall cut him down”**
• Or her.
• They will kill.
• The axe is laid to the root of the tree.
**“Strangers, and the most cruel of the nations; and cast him away”** — so that he may fall in his pride.
**“Him”** — Otherwise, her.
**“Upon the mountains, and his boughs shall fall in every valley, and his branches shall be broken on every rock of the country”** — that all may be led down to hell who were in his company, sharing in the punishment as in the fault
**“And shall depart from his shadow”** — by which they were covered, so that they might not see the sun
**“All the people of the earth”** — compared to the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth
**“And shall leave him”** — or her
31.14:
**“For which cause”** — your ruin having been seen
**“None of the trees by the waters shall exalt themselves for their height”** — into pride; nor will they think anything of themselves, nor reckon their riches their own because of the watering of their waters
**“Nor”** — confounded with fear
**“Shoot up their tops among the thick branches and leaves, neither shall stand up in their height”** — others: their own
**“All that are watered”** — which were under the rule of Assur
**“For they are all”**
• which he speaks of by metaphor, he makes clear
• kings
**“Delivered”** — Whence: “all they that go down to the earth shall fall”
**“Unto death to the lowest parts of the earth”** — hell. Whence: “they shall enter into the lowest parts of the earth”
**“In the midst of the children of men”**
• not of trees
• not with the angels of God
**“With them that go down into the pit”**
• of hell
• others: into the everlasting pit
31.15:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: In the day when he went down to hell, I brought in mourning”** — his companions, or the holy powers, who will mourn that he went down to hell
**“I covered him”** — by metaphor, according to that: “I am come into the depth of the sea: and a tempest hath overwhelmed me”
**“With the deep”** — of which waters it was watered before
**“And I withheld its rivers”** — nations
**“thereof”** — of the deep
**“And restrained the many waters”** — so that they would not raise him up but would press him down
**“Grieved for him”** — the Assyrian, or that tree, namely
**“Libanus”** — in which he had been exalted
**“And all the trees of the field trembled”** — themselves fearing the same
31.16:
**“With the sound of his fall”** — He openly shows that he is speaking metaphorically of the Assyrian. For the fall of what tree would shake all nations?
**“I shook the nations”** — so that all might know his ruin
**“When I brought him down to hell”** — this also does not suit a tree
**“With them”** — with these his companions
**“That descend into the pit”** — of hell
**“Were comforted”** — while they see evil things repaid to the evil and good things to the good
**“Of the earth”** — in the heart of the earth
**“All the trees of pleasure”**
• in Hebrew, Eden
• of paradise
**“The choice and best in Libanus, all that were moistened”** — just as he
**“With waters”**
• of God
• All the trees of pleasure, etc. Or: all the trees that were once good, and were watered with waters, and dwelt in the height of Libanus, shall receive comfort when they see their prince suffer like torments.
31.17:
**“For they also shall go down with him”** — for they also with it, namely with the tree, or with him, the Assyrian
**“Shall go down with him to hell to them that are slain by the sword”** — trees are not slain by the sword
**“And the arm of every one shall sit down”** — will rest
**“Under his shadow”** — punishment
**“In the midst of the nations”**
• not of the forests but of the nations
• who will be in hell
31.18:
**“To whom art thou like, O thou that art famous and lofty among the trees of pleasure?”**
• Finally, the address turns to the Assyrian himself.
• as if no one is like you; you have surpassed all kings
**“Behold”** — yet
**“Thou art brought down with the trees of pleasure”** — the kings who were in your retinue
**“To the lowest parts of the earth”** — the lower world, namely; whence: “They shall go down into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be the portions of foxes,” etc.
**“In the midst of the uncircumcised”**
• of the unclean
• these are the trees which he called cedars or cypresses
**“Thou shalt sleep”** — not in rest
**“With them that are slain by the sword”** — of the Lord
**“This is Pharao”**
• It is Pharao, to whom it is said: To whom art thou like, O famous, etc.
• The Seventy. Thus is Pharao, and all his multitude: just as the Assyrian above was cut down and fell, so also the Egyptian.
• He joins the last things to the former, who had said above: “To whom art thou like in thy greatness?” “Behold, the Assyrian was like a cedar in Libanus,” etc. Now he adds: “this is Pharao, and all his multitude,” as if to say: just as the Assyrian, the cedar and cypress, was cut down and cast down by the Babylonian, so also Pharao and his people, that is, the tree itself and its branches, will be cut down by the Babylonian.
**“To whom art thou like, O thou that art famous”** — O Pharao, namely, to whom it was said at the beginning: To whom art thou like in thy greatness, etc.; namely, to the Assyrian, who fell.

32.1:
**“And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, in the first day of the month”** — First.
**“And it came to pass in”** — In many copies, according to the Septuagint, the twelfth year and the tenth month are given. But according to other interpreters, the tenth year and the twelfth month; so that either Jerusalem has already been taken and Pharao’s joy is taken away by the evils hanging over him, or else, about to be taken, he may grieve more over his own miseries than rejoice over the captivity of others.
32.2:
**“Son of man, take up a lamentation for Pharao the king of Egypt”** — the power to which Egypt was entrusted, either one province or Egypt of the whole world
**“And say to him: Thou art like the lion”** — who goes about seeking whom he may devour
**“Of the nations”** — of the nations, not of one, namely
**“Thou art like”** — Not made by your own fault from the beginning. Whence: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he hath been compared to senseless beasts, and made like to them.”
**“And the dragon”** — To the devil, who said: the rivers are mine, and I made them.
**“That is in the sea: and thou didst push with the horn in thy rivers”**
• Raised up into pride by the watering of rivers.
• That is, that you might possess the land and the water.
**“horn”** — As if.
**“in thy rivers, and didst trouble the waters”** — By the multitude of the army.
**“with thy feet, and didst trample upon their streams”** — Whence the Apostle: “But he that troubleth you, shall bear the judgment, whosoever he be.”
**“the lion”** — Of whom: “He lieth in wait in secret like a lion in his den.” And Jeremias: “A lion out of the wood hath slain them.”
**“in thy rivers”** — To the princes of heresy, who imitate churchmen, saying to the Lord: “Through thee we will push down our enemies with the horn”; but they do not push with the horn for salvation, so as to lift up from earth to heaven, but to cast down into the depths.
**“and didst trouble”** — Jerome. He does not wish to drink the waters of Siloe, which go with silence, but the troubled and muddy waters of Egypt, which before they were trampled by the feet of the dragon were pure and flowing in their own order, but after they were troubled lost the order of their course. For heretics do not use testimonies of Scripture that cohere, but trouble everything. But since he is an enemy and an avenger, he not only troubles other waters but also tramples his own rivers, nor does he spare even his own; whence: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for man hath trodden me under foot”; and where: “let not man be magnified upon the earth.”
32.3:
**“Therefore, thus saith the Lord God: I will spread out my net”** — That is, the Old and the New Testament.
**“with the multitude of many people”** — The devil always delights in multitude and crowds.
**“and I will draw thee up in my net”**
• Who, like a serpent, wast wrapped in many coils.
• In the net. Of which: “The kingdom of heaven is like to a net cast into the sea, and gathering together of all kind of fishes”; the good of which they chose into their vessels, but the bad they cast out.
32.4:
**“And I will throw thee out”** — Who didst set thy mouth against heaven and didst boast thyself like the Most High.
**“I will cast thee away into the open field”** — Whose snares lay hidden in the sea of this world.
**“and I will cause ... to dwell upon thee”** — To be devoured.
**“all the fowls of the air”**
• According to that: “Thou hast given him to be meat for the people of the Ethiopians.”
• In which they eat the seed by the way.
**“and I will fill the beasts of all the earth with thee”**
• Not only the fowls.
• Beasts, which are made savage by vices; but by beasts and fowls heretics also can be signified.
• Or by the fowls of the air and beasts of the earth we may understand the peoples of the deceived and the cruelty of the nations.
32.5:
**“And I will lay thy flesh”** — That is, the remains.
**“upon the mountains and will fill thy hills”**
• The lesser, that is.
• Others: valleys.
**“with thy corruption”**
• Of heretics.
• All these things are said figuratively: that is, when the fowls of the air and beasts shall have been sated with his flesh, that is, his army and all the multitude, the rest of the part is turned into worms and corruption; then the heavens will be wrapped in darkness.
**“Mountains”** — The mountains: that is, the princes of heretics, or the contrary powers that run about through the air; and the valleys, penetrating to hell, bound with threefold chains.
32.6:
**“And I will water the earth with thy stinking blood”** — When all things shall swarm with worms.
**“upon the mountains and the valleys shall be filled with thee”** — The lower faithful.
**“And I will water the earth”** — Jerome. For the pride and arrogant swelling of heretics is filled not so much with living and pure blood as with putrid and stinking blood; whence: “Make them as dung of the earth.” And elsewhere: “raising the poor out of the dung.” The valleys are minds too much cast down, either the lower regions or the lowly sense of heretics, who do everything for earthly things.
32.7:
**“And I will cover the heavens, when thou shalt be put out”** — Who transformed thyself into an angel of light.
**“and I will make ... dark”** — over thee; and no joy shall be yours; and at your ruin all peoples and kings shall dread with excessive horror.
**“the stars thereof”** — of heaven, or of the dragon.
**“And I will cover”** — Whence: the light of the wicked shall be put out.
**“The heavens”** — Of which: against the spirits of wickedness in the high places.
**“And I will make dark”** — Jerome. It cannot be understood literally. For this has never been done, or is to be done.
**“The stars”** — Of which James: the wandering stars, to whom the darkness of gloom is reserved for ever.
**“I will cover the sun with a cloud”**
• To which, namely, the sun of justice is opposed.
• The Lord, namely, who came down into Egypt upon a light cloud, weighed down by no burden of sin; or the prophets or the apostles, of whom: “I will command my clouds that they rain no rain upon it.” And in the psalm: “Thy truth reacheth even to the clouds.”
**“The moon”** — That is, the church of heretics will not give its light, nor deceive those who believe in the knowledge of a false name.
32.8:
**“I will make all the lights of heaven to mourn over thee: and I will cause darkness upon thy land”** — that is, I will send the inhabitants of the land into darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
**“All the lights”** — Whatever seems to be doctrine in heretics will be killed when the dragon is put out; and the Lord himself will cover the land of heretics with the darkness of ignorance, so that the blind lead the blind into the pit.
32.9:
**“And I shall provoke to anger the heart of many people”** — so that those who formerly served Pharao may be angry against him, seeing his captivity led into another land, to which the dragon did not know it had been brought.
**“Upon the lands”** — Good ones, namely, which Pharao does not know; when, namely, the captivity of Pharao is changed into another captivity, of which: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive.”
32.10:
**“And I will make ... to be amazed at thee”** — namely, at your fall.
**“many people”** — who formerly admired your power.
**“and their kings”** — whose kingdoms the devil showed to the Lord. And of whom: “The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes met together.”
**“shall be horribly afraid for thee”** — namely, this will happen.
**“when my sword shall begin to fly”** — striking here and there, sparing no one.
**“upon their faces”** — namely, of the kings.
**“and they shall be astonished on a sudden”** — fearing a ruin like their own.
**“My sword”**
• Of which: “For the word of God is living and effectual,” etc. It flies about, dazzles the eyes of those who see and terrifies their faces, so that, astonished at the ruin of Pharao, they see themselves in him cast down.
• The Son, of whom: “Behold this child is set for the fall, and for the resurrection of many in Israel,” namely, that he may raise those who lie low and humble those wrongly lifted up.
32.12:
**“By the swords of the mighty”** — others: of giants.
**“I will overthrow thy multitude”** — which followed you.
**“all these nations are invincible”** — giants who were held in the army of the king of Babylon.
**“and they shall waste the pride of Egypt, and”** — by such ministers.
**“Invincible”** — All these will be handed over to be punished by worse ones. Of which: the sending in through evil angels. And the apostle: “whom I have delivered to Satan.”
32.13:
**“I will destroy also all the beasts thereof”**
• not only men.
• who are compared to senseless beasts.
**“that were beside the great waters”** — or many.
**“and the foot of man shall trouble them no more, neither shall the hoof of beasts trouble them”**
• Such will be the solitude that it makes clear waters turbid and muddy.
• Such will be the solitude that it makes clear waters turbid and muddy.
**“Beside the waters”** — If he is blessed who sows upon waters, where the ox and the ass tread, then on the contrary he is unhappy who cannot even hold the simple any longer by his error, so that the foot of man does not tread in them, so that the waters of Egypt do not seem to have in themselves even a sign of wisdom and reason.
32.14:
**“Then will I make their waters clear”** — I, not another.
**“their waters”** — troubled by the damnation of the dragon.
**“and cause their rivers to run like oil”**
• that is, most pure and shining, with none troubling them.
• so that they may be, that is, the nourishment of the true light.
32.15:
**“When I shall have made the land of Egypt desolate”** — as if these things will happen because of the desolation of Egypt.
**“and the land shall be destitute of her fulness, when I shall have struck all the inhabitants thereof”** — or thus.
**“they shall know”** — those who remained.
**“that I am the Lord”** — alone.
32.16:
**“This is the lamentation, and they shall lament therewith”** — not in hope of salvation, but because he, cast down from such great power by the vice of his pride, has been sent into eternal punishments.
**“the daughters of the nations”** — souls oppressed by him, or also others who no longer dwelt in Egypt but in the land of the living.
**“they shall lament therewith”** — the dragon.
**“for Egypt, and for the multitude thereof”** — destroyed by the Lord.
32.17:
**“And it came to pass in the twelfth year”** — in the same year and month, that is.
**“in the fifteenth day of the month”** — not on one day, as above.
**“And it came to pass in”** — Jerome. Above, on the first day of the month; here, the fifteenth day. On the first day, that is, on the kalends of the month, is the beginning. On the fifteenth, that is, when the whole orb of the moon is full; and if it was the first month, it is the first day of the unleavened bread; but if the seventh, of the feast of tabernacles, when the tents are pitched, which are the greatest solemnities among the Hebrews. But the lamentation is made over the strength of Egypt, that it may cease to be strong in evil and receive weakness; for the weaker, the stronger. 33.1: **“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying”** — Again the word of the Lord comes to the prophet, who had been silent for some time, because a prophet, or human nature, cannot sustain continuous prophecy; and he speaks the same things as above: “Son of man, I have made thee a watchman to the house of Israel,” etc.; which, if you look at them carefully, are similar indeed but not the same, since in very many points they differ. And this we ought to observe in all the holy Scriptures: where there seems to be some similarity of sense, not everything is said the same in all, but very much is either taken away or added, and one must take account of the differing words of each among themselves.

The office is to be feared above all, lest we approach unworthy, lest, taken up by the people, we be negligent and serve the belly and idleness, lest we think we have received an honour and not a burden. *Jerome:* From these things we learn that a man, however wicked and impious, if he hears the words of his teacher and repents, can be saved from his impiety; and that the teacher is no less condemned if he has not taught, whether through fear of danger or through despair of the sinner, since he is guilty also of the blood of him who could have been set free; and that in both free will is preserved, since it is in the teacher’s will either to speak or to be silent, and in the hearer’s either to hear and act and be saved, or to despise and perish by contempt; nor does it follow at once that because a prophet foretells, what he foretold comes to pass. For he does not foretell that it may come, but threatens that it may not come; nor, because God speaks, is it necessary that what he threatens be done, but he threatens so that he to whom he threatens may repent, and what was to be may not happen if the words of the Lord are despised.

33.21:
**“And it came to pass”** — Jerome. By comparing the two, one can show in what respects the present prophecy differs from the past one, and in what respects it says similar things.
**“And it came to pass in the twelfth”** — In the eleventh year of the reign of Sedecias, in the fifth month, Jerusalem was taken. But this prophecy was made in the twelfth year, in the tenth month, on the fifth day of the month, of the captivity or transmigration, when Jechonias was taken. From this it is shown that one year and four months and five days after Jerusalem was taken, there came one citizen of Jerusalem who announced that the city had been taken and laid waste, and had come to Babylon. But one day before he came, in the evening, the hand of the Lord was upon Ezechiel, which opened his mouth, that had long been shut; and whatever he was to say, he repeated what had been done before, and was silent no longer, seeing his prophecy fulfilled in deed, and that the people who were in Babylon, or those who were captives, doubted no more of the prophetic prediction. For then the prophet’s mouth is opened when he shows by the deed what he foretold, and he cries out with full freedom when he declares things not future but present or past.
*Jerome:* Allegorically. Ezechiel is interpreted “strength of God.” But Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. It is understood, therefore, that when Jerusalem was taken and overthrown, whoever could escape the unbelief of the Jews, such as the apostles were and the remnants that were saved, he announces to Christ himself that all the ceremonies of the Jews have been overthrown, which they to this day think must be kept, not hearing that saying of the apostle: “You who are justified in the law, you are fallen from grace.” Therefore, when Jerusalem was taken and overthrown, the mouth of the Lord is opened through the apostles and those who can say: “My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians,” and “Do you seek a proof of Christ that speaketh in me?” and that: “I opened my mouth and panted,” which, that is, can never be silent, nor hear with Israel: “Hear, O Israel, and be silent”; but “into all the earth their sound hath gone forth.” Whence, according to this sense, the eleventh year is referred to the twelve tribes, the tenth month to the time of the Jewish propitiation, and the fifth day of the month to the five senses; all of which are shown to have been taken and blotted out with Jerusalem when the Gospel succeeded; and in the evening, that is, at the consummation of the world, the hand of God was upon Ezechiel, who had sung through the prophets of the future ruins of the city, and in the morning showed that they had been fulfilled.

34.1:
**“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying”** — After the capture of Jerusalem, which he who had fled announced in Babylon, he spoke of those who dwell in the ruins of Jerusalem; then to those who, placed in captivity, nevertheless persevered in wickedness, unwilling to hear the words of the prophet; now he directs his speech to the shepherds, that is, the princes, by whose fault the sheep, that is, the peoples, were scattered.
**“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:”**
• And it is to be noted that from the twelfth year, the fifth day of the tenth month of the captivity of Jechonias and of those who had been taken captive with him, up to the twenty-fifth year, when the temple is built upon the mountain of the city that was built, and the incredible mysteries of the Church are unfolded, no year in between and no time is set down, but it is said simply: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying.”
• Speak to them, or to them: that we may understand that all things which are read through thirteen years were spoken at different times, and yet have no fixed spaces of time between them. But the word of the Lord came to the pastors of Israel, that is, the kings and princes, or the scribes and Pharisees and masters of the Jewish people, and in the gospel to bishops, priests, deacons. Or allegorically, to the angels of the several churches to whom John writes in the Apocalypse.

35.1:
**“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:”** — The whole prophecy of this chapter is against mount Seir, that is, of the sons of Esau and Edom, who in the Greek tongue and in ours are called Idumeans; because in the time of necessity and distress, when Juda was being taken by the Babylonians, they insulted them and the whole people of the Jews, and thought the land had been handed over to themselves to possess; and not only did they not receive their sons, that is, of Jacob their brother, but pursuing them they shut them up in the hands of the sword; which Symmachus says more openly: you hated blood, and your blood shall pursue you.
*Jerome:* If the word of the Lord were always in the prophets, and had a continual lodging in their breast, Ezechiel would not so often say: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying”; but because of human frailty and the necessities of this life it often departs; whence: “He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending, and remaining upon him, he it is,” etc. For this would not be proper to Christ if it always remained in others. To Moses also it is said: “I will take away of the spirit that is in thee,” which he would certainly not have had unless it had descended to him from the Lord.
*Jerome:* Allegory. Mount Seir: it is no wonder if in this place Seir, that is, rough and hairy, is understood in a bad sense, since Elias also is called a hairy man. For Esau was red and, as it were, rough with a skin; Elias is described only as hairy. In Esau, who is bloody and blood-stained, the rough skin is compared to mortal works and is a sign of death itself. In Elias it is an increase of manliness, whose dwelling in the wilderness and austerity of life shows him not only a man but a most strong one. Moreover Jacob, who supplanted Esau and received his firstborn rights, because he dwelt simply at home and was not a hunter, while the giant Nemroth is called smooth and sleek

**“their way was before me like the uncleanness of a menstruous woman”**
• To whom all things are open.
• Son of man. The Lord gives a clearer account of why he handed over the people of Israel to captivity, and promises that, out of his mercy, he will bring them back and bestow far greater gifts.
**“Son of man”** — Jerome. Allegorically. Whoever is of the house of Israel and discerns the peace of Christ, which surpasseth all understanding, dwells in his own land, that is, the Church, or in the lodging of the flesh, which was handed over to him by God. But if he defiles both, and is compared to menstruous uncleanness, God will pour out his indignation upon him, for the blood either his own or of those whom he has scandalized.
36.18:
**“And I poured out my indignation upon them for the blood which they had shed upon the land”** — Moreover.
**“with their idols”** — With perverse thoughts.
**“for the blood”** — For the blood: of the prophets and other just men. Whence: “Jerusalem, that killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent to thee”; and: the blood that was shed shall be required of this generation, from the blood of Abel the just even to the blood of Zacharias.
*Jerome:* Others of the Jews refer these things to the time of Zorobabel, when under king Cyrus many of Juda and Benjamin were brought back into Judea. Others to the kingdom of a thousand years, when under Christ, whom they think will come, the city of Jerusalem is to be built, and the temple, of which the last part of this prophecy treats.
36.19:
**“And I scattered them among the nations”**
• That they might be compared to unbelieving nations.
• By the Babylonian captivity, or the Roman, because they shed the blood of Christ.
**“and they are dispersed through the countries”** — As chaff from the wheat of the church.
36.20:
**“And when they entered among the nations”** — As if: they did not thus perceive their sin, but profaned the name of the Lord when it was said of them: “This is the people of the Lord, etc.”
**“whither they went”** — Captives.
**“they profaned my holy name, when it was said of them”** — By mockery.
**“This is the people of the Lord”** — Who boasted that he alone knew the worship of God.
**“and they are come forth out of his land”** — The church.
36.21: **“And I have regarded my own holy name”** — Not for their sake; for I am the creator of all.
36.22: **“Therefore thou shalt say to the house of Israel: Thus saith the Lord God: It is not for your sake that I will do this, O house of Israel”** — “Not to us, O Lord, not to us; but to thy name give glory.”
36.23:
**“And I will sanctify my great name”** — I will show to be holy.
**“which was profaned among the Gentiles, which you have profaned in the midst of them”** — Before all.
**“that the Gentiles may know that I am the Lord, saith the Lord of hosts, when I shall be sanctified in you before their eyes”**
• By bringing you back to your former glory.
• Namely, if they do penance, then the whole crowd of the nations will know that I will take them away, etc.
36.24: **“For I will take you from among the Gentiles, and will gather you together out of all the countries, and will bring you into your own land”** — That is, the church.
36.25:
**“And I will pour upon you clean water”**
• namely, those who believe and have turned from error
• the teaching of God’s word
• of saving baptism
**“and you shall be cleansed from all your filthiness”** — from sins
**“and I will cleanse you from all your idols”** — which you have feigned in your heart
36.26:
**“And I will give you a new heart”**
• which you lost through sin
• of believing in the Son of God
**“and put a new spirit within you”** — Whence David: “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me,” etc.
**“And”** — then
**“I will take away the stony heart”**
• all hardness
• of unbelief
**“out of your flesh, and will give you a heart of flesh”**
• which receives the commandments of God
• soft and tender, which can receive in itself the Holy Spirit, inscribed with saving letters
• A new spirit. Jerome. Note that he gives a new spirit and a new heart after the pouring out of water.
36.27:
**“And I will put my spirit in the midst of you”** — then
**“I will cause you to walk in my commandments”** — from virtue to virtue
**“and to keep my judgments”** — which you formerly neglected
**“and do them”** — with the heart
36.28:
**“And you shall dwell in the land”** — of confession
**“which I gave to your fathers”**
• the teachers
• Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the saints and prophets
**“And”** — thus
**“you shall be”** — again
**“my people, and I will be”** — whom you offended
**“your God”** — this is proved in the present time
36.29:
**“And I will save you from all your uncleannesses: and I will call for corn”** — from which heavenly bread is made
**“and will multiply it”** — “unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die”, it alone will remain
**“and will lay no famine upon you”** — the famine of the word of God, which the prodigal son underwent, who squandered his substance and, under compelling hunger, fed on the husks of swine
36.30:
**“And I will multiply the fruit of the tree”** — of wisdom, of which it is said: “She is a tree of life to them that embrace her”
**“and the increase of the field”** — in the likeness of Jacob, whose smell was as the smell of a plentiful field, which the Lord hath blessed
**“that you bear no more the reproach of famine among the nations”** — which the unbelief of the Jews suffers until today; but after they have attained blessedness they will say with the apostle: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.”
36.31:
**“And you shall remember”** — knowing where you have been scattered.
**“your wicked ways, and your doings that were not good, and your iniquities, and your wicked deeds shall displease you”** — by which they formerly pleased.
36.32:
**“It is not for your sakes”** — who perished by their own error.
**“I will do this”** — the things mentioned above.
**“saith the Lord God, be it known to you”**
• but for my mercy, understood.
• therefore.
**“be confounded, and ashamed at your own ways, O house of Israel”** — over your former vices, and understand your Creator.
**“Be confounded”** — He exhorts the wandering that they be confounded in their ways and be restored into the cities of the church.
36.33:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: In the day that I shall cleanse you from all your iniquities, and shall cause the cities to be inhabited”** — churches.
**“and shall repair the ruinous places”**
• which, namely, fell in you.
• which had fallen in the synagogues.
36.34:
**“And the desolate land”** — of confession.
**“shall be tilled”**
• with former ceremonies.
• with the ceremonies of God.
**“which before was waste”** — it was seen, namely, by all the saints who pass by the works of earthly conduct.
**“in the sight of all that passed by”** — of the saints passing by worldly things.
36.35:
**“They shall say”**
• marveling.
• as if: how has this come about?
**“This land that was untilled”**
• formerly.
• once, in which all virtues perished.
**“is become”** — now.
**“as a garden of pleasure”** — like the paradise of God.
**“And the cities”** — of Judea.
**“abandoned”** — which did not have God as guest.
**“and desolate”** — by the Holy Spirit.
**“and destroyed”** — by their unbelief.
**“fenced”** — by the faith of Christ.
**“are peopled”** — by confession and the name of the Saviour.
36.36:
**“And”** — thus.
**“the nations, that shall be left round about you, shall know”** — every creature, namely the angels too, who surround the land of Israel
**“that I the Lord have built up”** — in them
**“what was destroyed, and planted what was desolate”** — with the trees of all virtues
**“I the Lord have spoken”** — as if I had fulfilled what I foretold through the prophets
**“and done it”** — what I promised by word
36.37:
**“Thus saith the Lord God”** — Penitents are admonished that even when they have returned to the churches they should always seek the Lord and find him, so that the flocks of the Lord may be multiplied by the crowds of those returning.
**“Moreover in this shall the house of Israel find me”** — sought for a long time and not found
**“that I will do it for them”** — then
**“I will multiply them as a flock”** — not only in the aforesaid things will they feel my generosity
**“of men”**
• that is, those full of reason and confession, and of faith
• not of brute animals
36.38:
**“As a holy flock, as the flock of Jerusalem”** — in which properly is the worship of God and the vision of peace
**“in her solemn feasts”** — which the mercy of the Lord has received
**“so shall the waste cities be full of flocks of men, and”** — then
**“they shall know that I”** — alone
**“the Lord”**
• not willing the death of a sinner
• In the solemnities. In which is eaten the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, and the flesh and blood of the lamb; and in the seven weeks and in the tabernacles of this world we celebrate the feasts of the Lord, that the cities once desert may be made full of flocks of men, and may know by reason that he is the Lord who has provided all things.
**“and they shall know that I am the Lord”** — overlooking the sins of men on account of penance.

37.1:
**“The hand of the Lord was upon me”** — The Son, through whom the Father works. For “All things were made by him: and without him was made nothing that was made.”
**“and brought me forth in the spirit of the Lord”** — not in the body but outside it
**“was upon”** — Jerome. By the parable of the resurrection the restoration of Israel is treated. For as it seems incredible that dry bones, worn away by great age, should rise again, so does the restoration of the people of Israel, led into captivity and scattered over the whole world, seem incredible to those who do not know the power of God; yet it will come, because “I the Lord have spoken, and will do it.” Finally the earlier prophecy too, in which the ancient state is promised to the mountains of Israel, to whom it is said: “I will turn to you, and you shall be ploughed,” etc., pertains to this which is now said under a parable to the dry bones, in fulfilment of what is said in the gospel: what is impossible with men is possible with God. They were led out, moreover, from the sepulchres of captivity and from the bonds with which they were held bound in the Babylonian servitude. The Jews falsely claim that these things were fulfilled under Zorobabel, when a great commotion was made and the kingdom of the Chaldeans was transferred to the Medes and Persians, or in the presence of their Christ whom they await. But we understand it spiritually, after the cross of the Saviour, and as happening daily in those who, like Lazarus, bound with the bands of their sins, are raised at the voice of the Lord; and they are truly the house of Israel, once dry and having no hope of salvation, but, the spirit of grace entering into them and the Lord stretching out his hand from the depth of hell, they are freed; and those who had first said: Lord God, thou knowest, afterwards, being freed, will hear: O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?
37.2:
**“And he led me about”** — not allowed to rest
**“through them on every side: now they were very many upon the face of the plain”** — not covered by earth
**“and they were exceeding dry”** — dried up by the long age of time
37.3:
**“And he said to me: Son of man, dost thou think these bones shall live?”** — they could live
**“And I answered: O Lord God, thou knowest.”** — who has full knowledge of future things
37.4: **“And he said to me: Prophesy concerning these bones; and say to them”** — It is remarkable that he speaks to dry bones, which before sinews, flesh and skin and the life-giving spirit of God cannot hear the word.
37.6:
**“And I will lay sinews upon you”** — so that you may be joined
**“and will cause flesh to grow over you, and will cover you with skin”** — for beauty, namely that flesh may cover the foulness of nakedness
**“And”** — then
**“I will give you spirit and”** — in it
**“you shall live, and”** — after these things
37.8: **“And I saw, and behold the sinews, and the flesh came up upon them: and the skin was stretched out over them, but there was no spirit in them.”** — only human bodies lay, not having spirit
37.9:
**“And he said to me: Prophesy to the spirit, prophesy, O son of man, and say to the spirit: Thus saith the Lord God: Come, spirit, from the four winds”** — namely, the quarters of the world
**“and blow upon”** — as in the first creation of man God breathed into his face, and man became a living soul, so also the second creation, that is the resurrection of the dead, is quickened by the breathing of the Spirit.
37.10:
**“And I prophesied as he had commanded me: and the spirit came into them, and”** — so
**“they lived”** — Whence: “Thou shalt send forth thy spirit, and they shall be created: and thou shalt renew the face of the earth.”
**“and they stood up upon their feet, an exceeding great army.”** — the assembly of the dead
37.11: **“Son of man: All these bones”** — He seems to raise a question, since these things are said not of the general resurrection but of the resurrection of the house of Israel, who say: Our bones are dried up, etc. For what need was there to say it specially? But those who read this chapter of the general resurrection refer it to the resurrection of the saints. Of which: “Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection. In these the second death hath no power”; because the resurrection of the saints is one, that of sinners another; whence also in the Psalm: the wicked shall not rise again in judgment, etc.
37.12:
**“Therefore prophesy”** — a third time
**“and say to them”** — as if compelled by those who say this
**“Thus saith the Lord God: Behold I will open your graves, and will bring you out of your sepulchres, O my people: and will bring you into the land of Israel.”** — As if: they do not rise throughout the whole world. But they say that land of Israel of which it is said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land.” And again: “I will please the Lord in the land of the living.”
**“Behold I”** — Here too it is asked: if the graves are opened, how were the bones upon the face of the field and very dry?
**“and will bring you out”** — According to that: “the hour cometh, wherein all that are in the graves shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and they that have done good shall come forth unto the resurrection of life.” And elsewhere: “they that hear shall live.”
37.13:
**“And”**
• then
• brought out of the graves
37.14:
**“And shall have put my spirit in you, and you shall live, and I shall make you rest upon your own land: and you shall know”** — through all these things
**“that I am the Lord”** — that is, who fulfil what was promised by working
37.16:
**“And thou son of man, take thee a stick: and write upon it”**
• the name
• that is
**“Of Juda”** — of two tribes
**“and of the children of Israel”**
• the name
• with
**“his associates: and take another stick”** — for there were two kingdoms long opposed to each other
**“and write upon it”** — the prophet is ordered to do this as a figure of the Lord, who says: “I have been likened, by the hand of the prophets.”
**“For Joseph the stick”** — others: a rod
**“of Ephraim”** — who is of Joseph, that is, of the ten tribes
**“And thou son of man, take thee a stick”** — The ten tribes, which are called Israel, to this day serve in captivity in the mountains and cities of the Medes; but the two, which are called Juda, taken captive by the Chaldeans, returned to their own land after seventy years; and the Lord here promises that he will subject both to his rule.
*Jerome:* That the Lord rejected the tribe of Ephraim and chose the tribe of Juda, David says thus: “And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph: and chose not the tribe of Ephraim,” but he chose the tribe of Juda. Of whom it is said: the sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda, etc. At the coming of the Saviour the two rods, and according to the Hebrew the two sticks, were joined into one sceptre of empire, and in the baptism of Christ those long separated are united into one new man and one nation, that they may no more be polluted with idols and abominations, but, cleansed by the laver, may be the people of God; and Christ may rule over them, and they may dwell upon the land of the meek and of the living, which he gave to his servant Jacob, who supplanted the people of Israel in his mother’s womb. But if we wish, according to the prophecy of Osee, which is almost all directed to the ten tribes, that is, to Joseph and Ephraim and Samaria and Israel, to understand the knowledge falsely so called and the various crowds of heretics, we say this: that in the last time, when the fulness of the Gentiles shall have come in and all Israel shall be saved, we shall say that the adversaries of the people of God, who fought against the house of Juda and the confession of the church, give themselves up to the faith of the church, all errors being abandoned, and the princes of this world, who are destroyed, and their patriarchs, who plunged them into the pit, being abandoned; and that they rise up and leave their idols and their abominations, which they fashioned from the heart, and from all their seats in which they had sinned pass over to the faith of the church, and are cleansed, and are the people of Christ, and he their God.
37.17: **“And join them one to the other into one stick, and they shall become one in thy hand.”** — so that they are not two but one, nor are they called Judah and Israel but by one name, Jews; and they are not held in two hands but in one hand of the Saviour
37.19:
**“Say to them: Thus saith the Lord God: Behold, I will take the stick of Joseph”** — the ten tribes
**“which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel”** — of whom was Jeroboam the son of Nabat
**“that are associated with him, and I will put them together with the stick of Juda”** — the two tribes
**“and will make them one stick: and they shall be one in his hand.”** — metaplasm
37.21:
**“And thou shalt say to them: Thus saith the Lord God”** — explanation of the above
**“Behold, I will take the children of Israel”** — Jerome. If the Jews and Judaizing Christians wish to refer these things to the kingdom of a thousand years, they will be compelled by necessity to accept that all who shall be saved will dwell in the land of Israel, that Jerusalem is to be built, the temple raised, all the ceremonies of the law observed, and the sabbath, and the injury of circumcision, and eating and drinking, and abundance of riches to be reckoned as the highest blessedness and all wealth; whereas the apostle says: “Meat for the belly, and the belly for the meats; but God shall destroy both it and them.” But as the former discourse of the prophet, in the type of the resurrection, showed the restoration of the Jewish people to be not carnal but spiritual, so here too it pertains not to the happiness of the flesh but of the soul, and to the faith of Christ by which we are cleansed in baptism, whose kingdom is everlasting.
37.22:
**“And I will make them one nation”** — under the rule of one king
**“in the land on the mountains of Israel”** — of whom it was said above
**“and one king”** — Christ. Of whom: “And of his kingdom there shall be no end.”
**“shall be king over them all: and they shall no more be two nations”** — but one fold and one shepherd
37.23:
**“Nor shall they be defiled any more”** — as if: I will cleanse them from all vices
**“with their idols, nor with their abominations, nor with all their iniquities: and I will save them out of all the places in which they have sinned”** — while still captives
**“and I will cleanse them: and”** — cleansed
37.24:
**“And my servant David shall be king over them, and they shall have one shepherd”** — that is, not only king but also shepherd; great condescension softens the proud name of empire by the name of shepherd
**“they shall walk in my judgments”** — united in their own land
**“and shall keep my commandments”** — in heart
**“and shall do them”** — in deed
**“And my servant”** — David. Of whom: “The Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father,” etc. Who, being in the form of God, “thought it not robbery to be equal with God,” but “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” becoming obedient “unto death.”
37.25:
**“And they shall dwell in the land which I gave to my servant Jacob, wherein your fathers dwelt, and they shall dwell in it, they and their children”** — not only they, that is
**“and their children's children, for ever”** — as if: and the children of their children, and those who shall be born of them
**“And David”** — Christ
**“my servant shall be their prince for ever”** — not for a short time
37.26:
**“And I will make”** — when they shall have been under such a king
**“a covenant of peace with them, it shall be an everlasting covenant with them: and I will establish them”** — in the church, so that they may say: I have set my feet upon a rock
**“and will multiply them”** — by the number of the faithful or of virtues
**“and will set my sanctuary in the midst of them for ever”** — According to the Jews, the temple which was built under Zorobabel; but that was burnt by Roman fire. Therefore all things are to be referred to the church and to the times of the Saviour, when his tabernacle was set in the church, where he became our God, and we his people.
**“A covenant of peace”** — not of contest or war, as in the Old Testament, but of peace, which surpasses all understanding. Of which: “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you”; and elsewhere: “And his place is in peace.”
37.28:
**“And the nations shall know”** — this is the advancement of all
**“that I am the Lord the sanctifier of Israel”** — in the Spirit
**“when my sanctuary shall be in the midst of them”** — of the faithful

38.1: **“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:”** — It must be known that this is the last discourse made to Ezechiel. For after this we can find nothing like it, except that which is written in the twenty-fifth year: of the captivity of Jechonias, the hand of the Lord was upon me, and he brought me thither, that is, into the land of Israel, when the building of the temple is described and the order of its ceremonies is related.
38.2:
**“Son of man, set thy face against mount Seir, and prophesy concerning it, and say to it”** — Others: make firm.
**“thy face against Gog, the land of Magog”** — In Greek doma, in Latin a roof.
**“the chief prince of Mosoch”** — Madness.
**“and Thubal”** — the whole; or all
**“Set thy face”** — There is need of much consideration, or of a firm setting of the countenance, that we may be able to recognize with unveiled face what is said when it is revealed.
**“and prophesy of him”** — Against Gog and Magog, etc. Gog and Magog are opposing nations, namely enemies of the saints, which go forth from the corners of the earth, leaving the straight line; these are the head of proud madness and of all evils, according to that: “The whole world is seated in wickedness.”
*Jerome:* Gog: roof. Magog: of the roof. The roof: the princes of heretics. Of the roof: those who receive their doctrines. And fittingly, after many mystical prophecies in this volume, he directs the last against Magog and Gog. For if the time of judgment is, according to Peter, that it begin at the house of God, and Ezechiel who says: begin at my sanctuary, and the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death; in Isaias also the first discourse is against Judea, in which is the confession of the Lord, and the last against the four-footed beasts that are in the desert; and here rightly the last discourse is made against Gog and Magog, who fight against the city of God, that is, the church, of which: “The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful.” And: a city seated on a mountain cannot be hid. And: Jerusalem, which is built as a city.
**“Gog, the land of Magog”** — Every pride, and the knowledge falsely so called, which “is lifted up against the knowledge of the truth,” is shown by these names. Of such housetops Isaias says: “In the vision against the valley of Sion, thou hast gone up to the housetops.”
38.3:
**“And say to him: Thus saith the Lord God: Behold, I come against thee, O Gog, the chief prince”** — of the prince
**“Mosoch”** — of madness
**“and Thubal”** — of all
**“Behold, I come against thee”** — Jerome. The Jews and our judaizers think that Magog and Gog are Scythian nations, innumerable and savage, which stretch beyond Mount Caucasus and the Maeotian marsh, and along the Caspian Sea as far as India; and that after the thousand years' reign they are to be stirred up by the devil, to come into the land of Israel to fight against the saints, with many nations joined with them: first Mosoch, whom Josephus calls the Cappadocians; then Thubal, whom he likewise calls Iberians or Spaniards, but the Hebrews suspect to be Italians; having with them the Persians and Ethiopians and Libyans. Gomer also and Thogorma, whom they call Galatians and Phrygians; the Sabeans also and Dedan, and the Carthaginians or Tharsis. And this is what John says: “And when the thousand years shall be finished, Satan shall be loosed out of his prison, and shall go forth, and seduce the nations which are over the four quarters of the earth, Gog and Magog,” etc.; not understanding that the whole book of John, which is headed with the title of revelation, is mystical. Others, however, leaving the earthly sense and the Jewish and old wives' fables, which are harmful, and acquiescing in themselves, drag themselves down too far into the depths, ascend to the heights, and invent far worse nonsense, describing the wars of the devil and his army in the heavenly Jerusalem, and under the etymologies of the individual nations interpreting the spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places.
38.4:
**“And I will turn thee about, and I will put a bit in thy jaws”** — first I will make you waver from your opinion
**“and I will bring thee forth”** — to salvation
**“thee”** — scattered
**“and all thy army, horses and horsemen all clothed with coats of mail”** — who imitate the armour of God and boast that they have the breastplates of justice
**“a great multitude, armed with spears”** — with which they may strike
**“and shields”** — with which they may cover themselves
**“that take hold of”** — of those who seize against the church
**“in thy jaws”** — Bind their jaws with bit and bridle, so that the unbroken and wanton horse, which would fall headlong over cliffs, may be held by the bridle of the Lord. Whence: “Thou shalt ride upon thy horses, and thy riding is salvation.” John saw such horses and riders in heaven.
*Jerome:* This also is briefly to be noted: that in Ezechiel Gog is called the prince of the land of Magog; but in the Apocalypse Gog and Magog are the nations that come out from the four quarters of the earth. And as from Jacob, who was first called Israel, the whole people of the Hebrews was called Israel; from Aram, Syria; from Mesraim, Egypt, whose names are written in Genesis; so also from the prince Gog all who are subject to him are called Magog.
38.5: **“The Persians, Ethiopians, and Libyans with them, all with shields and helmets.”** — that is, the most savage nations and enemies of Israel, against whom wars against the people of God are read of
38.6:
**“Gomer, and all his bands, the house of Thogorma, the northern parts”** — that is, coming from the north, which is the coldest and is called by the name right
**“and all his strength”** — Magog
**“and many peoples with thee”** — subject peoples
38.7:
**“Prepare”** — Ironically.
**“and make thyself ready, and all thy multitude that is assembled about thee”** — subject to your rule
**“and be thou commander over them”** — a commander
38.8:
**“After many days thou shalt be visited”** — I will visit their iniquities with a rod, etc.
**“at the end of years”** — Whence John: “It is the last hour,” and the people of the Gentiles is led in the eleventh hour to tend the vineyard
**“thou shalt come to the land”**
• to be assaulted
• of the saints, which bears fruit a hundredfold and sixtyfold and thirtyfold
**“that is returned from the sword”** — that it may stand in peace
**“is gathered”** — with the error of the Gentiles despised
**“out of many nations, to the mountains of Israel”** — the patriarchs and prophets
**“which have been continually waste”** — without the law and commandments of God; whence afterwards it is said: “More are the children of the desolate than of her that hath a husband.”
**“This”** — land
**“brought forth out of the nations, and they shall all of them dwell”** — is led out of the peoples, and they dwelt; otherwise, they will dwell
**“That is returned from the sword”** — Scatter thou the nations that delight in wars.
**“waste”** — These are the deserts and waterless places in which the devil cannot find a place, because they are called to salvation.
38.9:
**“And thou shalt go up”** — Gog, the devil, prince of heretics
**“and come like a storm”** — that he may confound all things with darkness and error. For he does not have the early and the late rain.
**“and like a cloud”** — of words
**“to cover”** — as far as in you lies
**“the land”** — of believers
38.10:

38.11:

**“I will come to them that are at rest, and dwell securely”** — our king, the peaceful one, because his place is made in peace
**“all these dwell”** — he says

38.12:
**“To take spoils”** — of the church

38.13:

39.1:
**“And thou, son of man, prophesy against Gog, and say: Thus saith the Lord God: Behold, I come against thee, O Gog, the chief prince”** — Others: ros
**“And thou, son of man”** — The Jews say that what is said in this chapter will come to pass after the thousand years' reign: that Gog, prince of Mosoch, Ros and Thubal, will be slain on the borders of Israel and devoured by all the birds and beasts; and that the inhabitants of the cities of Israel will for seven years have the use of wood not from the forests but from the arms of Gog; and that he himself is to be buried in the valley which in Hebrew is called Gen, and the name of that sepulchre is to be called Polyandrum, that is, where a multitude of men is buried. And that he is to be buried for seven months by the house of Israel, that the land may be cleansed; and that a day is to be appointed on which Gog is to be slain, and men set to search diligently for the bones and bury them, that nothing remain unburied.
**“of Mosoch and Thubal”**
• But after seven months the land is to be traversed, as they say, and if a human bone is found, it is to be marked with a superscribed title, so that afterward it may be buried by those who have been appointed to such an office.
• The name of the city is to be called Amona, which in Greek is called polyandrion, that is, a multitude of buried men; and so the land is to be cleansed.
• But we, keeping to the sense of the exposition we have begun, will defer the individual points we have set out.
**“against thee, O Gog”** — Gog too has his own trinity: Ros, Mosoch and Tubal, the head, that is, and madness, and all things; so that there is no vice that he does not possess.
39.2:
**“And I will turn thee round, and I will lead thee out”** — with empty hope, namely, I will allure him; by which, led astray, he will hasten to battle to be slain, disappointed of the hope of victory
**“and will make thee go up from the northern parts”**
• the last things

**“And”** — then
**“I will break thy bow”** — which is

39.4:
**“upon the mountains of Israel”** — of which: the mountains round about it

**“to the birds, and to every fowl, and to the beasts of the earth to be devoured”** — bloodthirsty ones. For as it is said: “Thou hast given him to be meat for the people of the Ethiopians,” of the dragon, that is, so those deceived by heretics are food of demons.

**“Thou shalt fall upon the face of the field”** — which is tilled by the husbandmen of God

39.6:
**“And”** — that he may receive the teaching

**“they shall burn with fire, and shall make a prey of them to whom they had been a prey, and they shall rob those that robbed them, saith the Lord God”** — by the Holy Spirit, that is, by ecclesiastical discourse, which whoever has it can speak: “Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he spoke in this way, and opened to us the scriptures?”

• in clear light
• For the sepulchre of Gog was not in the mountains but in low valleys and rough places, which in Hebrew are called Gen; which the heretics, though they are in the west, pretend to be in the east, that they may deceive the travellers, that is, those who pass through this world, not as inhabitants but as pilgrims, like him who said: “I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner as all my fathers were.” For which of those who pass by, of whom it is said, “And they that have passed by have not said: The blessing of the Lord be upon you,” etc., is not amazed and astonished when he sees a valley of travellers, which to the inhabitants seems a mountain?

**“and all his multitude”** — in which they always rejoice

40.1:
**“In the five and twentieth year of our captivity”** — Jerome. Ezechiel was handed over to Babylon in the first captivity, with King Joachim.
**“in the beginning of the year”** — He states the time simply, so that it may fix the root of the history in the hearts of listeners, whence it may bring forth spiritual fruits.
**“the tenth day of the month, the fourteenth year after the city was destroyed”** — Second.
**“in the selfsame day”** — For by the same light of justice he strikes the proud, and the same light gives life to the afflicted and penitent.
**“the hand of the Lord was upon me”** — who in body was in Babylon.
**“the hand of the Lord”** — The power of authority.
**“and he brought”** — in spirit.
**“me”** — who in body was in Babylon.
**“thither”**
• In the twentieth and, etc. Jerome. In the beginning of the year, the tenth day of the month, etc. Theodotion: in the new year. The new year among the Hebrews is called the seventh month, which among them is called Theri, so that on the calends of the seventh month there is the sounding of trumpets, and on the tenth day of the same the day of fasting and atonement, and on the fifteenth, when the whole orb of the moon is full, the day of tabernacles; it is given to be understood that on the tenth day, of the atonement of the Lord, the building of the city was shown to Ezechiel.
• The fourteenth year. Gregory. For Sedecias reigned eleven years in Jerusalem after the first captivity; after whose captivity, which is the second, in the fourteenth year the prophet saw the last vision; and eleven and fourteen are twenty-five. He saw the first vision in the fifth year of the former captivity, this last in the twenty-fifth year. It is plain, therefore, that twenty years intervened up to the last vision. Above he made mention of the twenty-seventh year, but he describes the time of the king about whom he began to prophesy.
• As he showed the restoration of the people, indeed the quickening of the bones of the field, under the image of the resurrection, so the Lord promises the rebuilding of the city, which fourteen years before had been destroyed by the Babylonian fire, under a description of it; so that, as he marked out the captivity and overthrow by the pot set on the fire from the north, and the prophecy was shown true in the deed, so by faith in the things past the truth of the future building may be prepared by the prophecy.
• This is not said of that time, in which the temple was built under Zorobabel and Jesus, as the Jews rave. For this is far more worthy than that of Solomon, which is as nothing in comparison with it.
**“In the five and twentieth year”**
• Jerome. If in the fifth year of the captivity of Joachim, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, the heavens were opened to Ezechiel by the river Chobar and he saw the visions of God; and now it is said that in the twenty-fifth year of the same captivity, in the beginning of the year, the tenth day of the month, the hand of the Lord was upon him, etc.: it is plain that when nineteen years, nine months and five days of the twentieth year were completed, all his prophecy was woven together.
• Jerome. We judge it better to keep silent about these things, and what follows to the end of the volume, than to say little about them.
*Gregory:* About to speak of mystical matters, he first sets out the history, so that it may be known from the time what is to be believed in the revelation. At the beginning of the book he indicated in what year he began to prophesy; at the end, in what year he saw the last vision.
*Jerome:* Allegory. It signifies fourteen generations, when these are completed, up to David, and from him to the transmigration, and from there to the birth of Christ, the restoration of the city is promised. Whence: “He shall build my city,” etc. And elsewhere: “to preach to the captives release,” etc.
40.2:
**“In the visions of God”**
• not in vision
• in contemplation. For nothing about this city is said literally.
• that is
**“he brought me into the land of Israel, and set me upon a very high mountain”**
• that is, Christ
