• of whom: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.” Of whom Isaias: “Get thee up upon a high mountain, thou that bringest good tidings to Sion.”
• in comparison with the other mountains. Of which: “I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me”; and elsewhere: “mountains round about him.”
**“very high mountain: upon which there was as”** — for it is a likeness, not the thing itself.
**“the building of a city”** — of the church. Of which: “Glorious things are said of thee, O city of God.” And elsewhere: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city.” And elsewhere: “The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful.” And: “A city seated on a mountain cannot be hid.”
**“bending towards the south”**
• that is, of the Holy Spirit’s breath humbling itself toward the south
• not toward the north, as the synagogue
• To the south? Where the light is full and the sun of justice is set at the highest point of heaven. Whence: “Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind: blow through my garden, and let the aromatical spices thereof flow.”
**“upon which there was”** — Gregory. Because he alone bears the morals and faults of all. Whence: “I labour, bearing.”
**“towards the south”** — Jerome. Whence: “Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind, etc.” For the north wind, a very harsh wind, is driven away, so that love may not be chilled in God’s garden and the flowers wither.
40.3:
**“And he brought me in thither”** — that he might show him all that was within
**“and behold a man”**
• of whom: “Behold a man, the Orient is his name.”
• the same as the mountain
**“whose appearance was like”** — not of amber, as is said at the beginning of the book, nor was he girt with a golden girdle, as is said in the Apocalypse
**“the appearance of brass, with a line of flax”** — the line by which all things are set in order
**“in his hand”**
• which he did, he taught
• Gregory. That is, in the power of Christ; or, in the work he did, what he taught.
**“and a measuring reed in his hand”** — the measuring reed in his hand: the writers, in the dispensation of God’s hidden judgment
**“thither”** — that is, he enters the building of the city who considers the ways of the saints which he may imitate.
**“the appearance of brass”** — Jerome. For this material is more sonorous than all metals and resounds far with its ring; whence in the statue of Daniel the kingdom of the Greeks, for the eloquence proper to them, is shown in the likeness of brass; by which it is manifest that those still need teaching who have not yet learned the full mysteries of the temple to be built spiritually.
**“and he stood in the gate”** — Of brass, because it is durable and sonorous; and Christ, “rising again from the dead, dieth now no more,” etc.; through whose assumption of humanity the glory of majesty resounded.
**“a line”** — Jerome. Of whom Zacharias says that he had a geometric line in his hand, to measure the breadth and length of the city.
**“a line of flax”**
• a fine, that is, spiritual preaching, which does not suit the synagogue
• Others: of the stonemasons, namely the angels, who minister at God’s command; or of Moses and all the prophets and apostles, who build the city of God.
**“a measuring reed”** — Gregory. That is, holy Scripture, by which we measure every action of our life.
**“reed”** — The prophetic grace. Of which: “My tongue is the pen of a scrivener that writeth swiftly.” And of John it is said: “What went you out into the desert to see? a reed shaken with the wind?” This reed they desire to imitate who, writing, write iniquity, against whom David prays: “Rebuke the wild beasts of the reed.”
**“he stood in the gate”** — Jerome. Because through him we go in to the Father, without whom we cannot enter into the city, that he may receive the worthy and take in the unworthy. In the gate also is judgment. Whence: “They hated him that rebuked in the gate.” And elsewhere: “he shall not be confounded when he shall speak to his enemies in the gate.”
*Gregory:* He who stands in the gate is partly outside and partly inside; he is partly seen and partly hidden, and Christ is visible through his humanity, invisible through his divinity.
40.4:
**“And this man said to me: Son of man, see with thy eyes”** — first
**“and hear with thy ears”** — after
**“and set thy heart”**
• consider
• moreover, nothing profits to have seen and come unless you commit it to memory.
**“upon all that I shall shew thee”** — he makes the author attentive, so that he may hold it in memory.
**“for thou art brought hither that they may be shewn to thee”** — Gregory. As if you were therefore brought that you might see, and therefore see that you might announce.
**“declare all that thou seest”** — so that those who cannot see for themselves may learn through you.
**“to the house of Israel”**
• to those, namely, who behold God in the mind, of whom was Nathanael, who most eagerly sought Christ, and heard: “Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile.”
• And in Zacharias he is called a foolish shepherd.
• He shows that nothing is sweeter than contemplation and knowledge. Whence: “One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may see the delight of the Lord.” And he adds: “I have loved, O Lord, the beauty of thy house.”
**“this man”** — Jerome. The true architect, namely, whom Paul imitates, saying: “As a wise architect, I have laid the foundation,” namely in distinction from him who is foolish.
*Gregory:* The man who had brought the prophet into the building speaks standing in the gate; he stood with his face inward and his back outward, but the prophet held his face toward the gate, whence he heard the words of the speaker. For the eyes of the Lord always look upon his building; and he who unceasingly hears the words of God ought always to behold with the eyes of the heart when he shall depart from this life; whence: “having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.”
**“Son of man”** — Gregory. As if to say: look at spiritual things spiritually, but remember your carnal weakness. For it often happens that he who is lifted up in contemplation is the more wearied by temptation.
**“with thy eyes”** — Spiritual things. Like this: “Lift up your eyes and see the countries, for they are white already to harvest.” And: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.” The building of the city is seen; the order of ceremonies and of the priesthood is heard, and the description of the land.
**“declare all”** — Gregory. Whence elsewhere: “And he that heareth, let him say: Come.”
40.5:
**“And behold there was a wall on the outside of the house round about”** — according to the humanity; for within is the divinity.
**“and in the man’s hand”** — who is, namely.
**“a measuring reed”**
• not only the geometer’s cord.
• Gregory. Namely, holy Scripture, by which we measure every action of our life.
**“of six cubits”**
• in which is the active life.
• which more correctly in Greek is palestes, that is, the sixth part of a cubit.
**“and a handbreadth: and he measured the breadth of the building”** — also the height and breadth of one reed, that is, of six cubits and a handbreadth.
**“one reed”**
• one measure.
• Gregory. Because the ancient fathers, who preached our Redeemer both by prophesying and by living well, had as it were six cubits in the perfection of the work, and a palm in the beginning of contemplation.
**“the height one reed”**
• one measure, because each soul, as far as it is widened in love of neighbour, so far is it raised up in the knowledge of God.
• In the hand of the man: namely, in the power of Christ, or in the deeds he did and the things he taught.
• It must be known that all the Hebrew words and names, properly speaking, which have been set down in the Greek and Latin translation, have been corrupted by excessive age and depraved by the faults of the copyists.
**“And behold there was a wall”** — Symmachus and the Seventy: a wall-enclosure, which, namely, on every side surrounded the house, that is, the temple of the Lord.
*Gregory:* The wall itself is the Saviour, whence: “a saviour, a wall and a bulwark shall be set therein”; and before the wall are the prophets, namely those who were sent, prophesying to build up faith before the Lord appeared in the flesh.
**“on the outside”** — The true architect proves that living stones are placed: some fit for the foundation, some for the middle wall, some for the upper places, some for the lower, and some outside the temple in the circuit of the enclosure.
**“of the house round about”** — Gregory. Namely of men and of angels.
*Gregory:* This building cannot be taken according to the letter, since it is said first to be measured with a reed of six cubits and a palm, then with fourteen cubits, whose gate-fronts are sixty cubits. For what is contained is less than what contains.
**“reed”** — This signifies that our manner of life is known, which is in six days, in which the world was made, and the account of each of the works; namely, that one thing pertains to works, another to the mind; whence the breadth is equal to the height, the breadth being for works, the height for the soul, which hastens to high things.
**“handbreadth”** — Which is now of the seven but is not a cubit. For the active life we accomplish in work; of the contemplative we scarcely touch anything, and little, even when we stretch the heart. Whence: “Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known.” And rightly the six cubits are placed first, the handbreadth after, because the active life goes before, the contemplative follows.
**“and he measured the breadth”** — Gregory. Almighty God, who is not stretched out in great things nor narrowed in small things, thus speaks of the whole Church together as if of one soul, and conversely, as in this place: “and he measured the breadth of the building.”
**“the breadth of the building”** — Gregory. Namely, love of neighbour. For breadth lies in equality. Whence: “Thy commandment is exceeding broad.” And elsewhere: “Love your enemies.” The height, which stretches upward in loftiness, looks to the contemplation of the contemplative.
40.6:
**“And he came”**
• in the limbs
• namely the man whose name is East, that he may enlighten those whom he finds in the first part of the vestibule, or in the very entrance of the gate: “This is the gate of the Lord, the just shall enter into it.”
**“to the gate”** — Scripture, faith.
**“that looked toward the east”** — I am the way, the truth, and the life.
**“and he went up”** — as we advance.
**“the steps thereof”**
• because the place was not level, and the building itself was on higher ground.
• of the gate.
**“and he measured the breadth of the threshold”** — that you may know that all things lie open to the knowledge of God. The threshold is said to be one reed in breadth, and its height and length are passed over in silence. For it is both a way and an entrance, and through it one must proceed into the interior.
**“of the gate”**
• that is, of holy Scripture.
• that is.
**“one reed the breadth, that is, one threshold”** — for there is also another.
**“And he came to the gate”** — Gregory. The man himself is the gate. He enters through himself, while the members enter through him; and whoever opens to us the gate of heaven.
**“to the gate that looked toward the east”** — He would not enter through the others, though there were very many.
**“the steps”**
• Steps are the merits of virtues. For no one becomes highest at once.
• Namely several, whose number is passed over in silence, so that the difficulty of the ascent may appear; and however many steps you set before yourself, know that they are fewer than what is left in doubt.
**“the gate”** — Gregory. That is, of holy Scripture: two thresholds, namely the inner allegory and the outer letter. From the outer, that is the letter, we arrive at the inner allegory, for each builds in its own way.
**“one threshold”** — Gregory. The gate rises from the threshold so that it may be a gate. Therefore the fathers are the threshold of the gate, from whom Christ according to the flesh.
40.7:
**“And every little chamber”**
• or chamber.
• The hearts of them, namely those in which the soul is joined by love to the invisible Bridegroom. One reed in length, etc. For as much as one loves, so much does one bear with one’s neighbour with patience; if one ceases to bear, one ceases to love.
**“one reed long, and one reed broad”** — so that the inner parts of the chambers may have the full measure of a reed, that is, six cubits and a palm, while the work and the reckoning agree.
**“and between the little chambers were five cubits”**
• He placed the chamber above, but many make it one, as many churches are one church.
• And between the little chambers five, etc. Gregory. For there are in such chambers some who are not yet able to penetrate subtle things, being still weighed down by the five senses. These are not chambers but between the chambers, because through those who love God perfectly they are led to the perfection of the mind.
**“and between the little chambers”** — That is, they are on the outside; for they have not yet penetrated the secrets of Christ, nor can they say: “The king hath brought me into his chamber.” Whence elsewhere: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.” But while the disciples dwell at home with Christ, others who cannot hear his mysteries desire that the word of God go out to them outside. Therefore the measure of five cubits is put in them, that they may be taught to refer all things to the five senses.
**“And the threshold of the gate by the porch”** — Gregory. By the outer threshold we understand the fathers of the Old Testament, through whose preaching perverse works were punished; by the inner threshold, the teachers of the New Testament, by whose preaching the mind is restrained from unlawful thoughts. Those were outside because they did not see Christ in the flesh, but they were not divided from holy Church, because in mind, work and preaching they held these sacraments of the faith. For as we are saved by faith in the passion of Christ now past, so they were saved by faith in the same passion to come. They therefore were outside, not outside the mystery but outside the time.
40.8:
**“and the threshold”**
• another.
• Through the threshold each one enters the gate. But there are two thresholds: the fathers of the Old and of the New Testament.
**“of the gate”**
• of the other.
• he who believes enters this gate of Christ.
**“by the porch”** — of which before.
**“within”** — because the one is outside and the other inside.
**“one reed”** — Because in holy Scripture both the teaching of perfect work and the beginning of heavenly contemplation are found; the preacher is understood by the gate. The outer threshold is the active life, the inner the contemplative; for through the one we walk in faith, through the other we hasten toward hope.
40.9:
**“And”** — third
**“he measured the porch of the gate”** — the courts of eternal blessedness
**“eight cubits”** — which pertain to the sacrament of the resurrection and of the Lord’s day
**“and the front thereof”** — the merit of the present life
**“two cubits”**
• the love of God and of neighbour
• because of both testaments, or the letter and the spirit, or the mystery of the tongs with which in Isaias the coal is taken from the altar, whence the lips of the prophet are cleansed
**“the porch”** — through which we come to the temple of God
**“the porch of the gate was inward”**
• not outside
• The porch, not that which is above; whence it is added: “the porch of the gate was inward.”
**“The porch of the gate eight cubits”** — Gregory. The inner porch is the breadth of eternal life, which now, within the narrow limits of the present life, is already beheld by the mind through hope; whence: “Go ye into his gates with praise, into his courts with hymns: and give glory to him.” For when we confess our sins with tears we enter the gate of the narrow life, but when we are brought to eternal life we enter the courts of our gate; whence: “Enter ye in at the narrow gate.” The porch, therefore, is measured with eight cubits. For there all are to be received who so order the things that revolve in seven days that through them they may reach the kingdom of heaven. For while we now act cautiously, we hasten intent upon the day of judgment, which is the eighth. Whence: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight.” But because no one comes to that day except him who has devoutly held the love of God and neighbour, there follows: “and the front thereof two cubits.” For as through the porch within is eternal rest, so through the front of the gate the quality of the visible life must be signified, whose measure is the love of God and neighbour, which is the scarlet twice dyed.
40.10:
**“And the little chambers”**
• the little chambers which were built in the porches beyond the eastern gate, looking toward the eastern way
• the hearts of those burning with the love of God, who were kindled with the love of the Trinity both in the Old and in the New Testament
• Lest we should think there were only two chambers, he set three on each side, to show the number six, which is shown in the gospel water-pots, in which the waters were changed into wine, and daily the Jewish waters are turned into wine, which maketh glad the heart of man, and becomes sweeter by the blood of Christ.
**“of the gate that looked eastward were three on this side, and three on that side: all three were of one measure”** — namely looking toward the north and the south, toward the eastern way
**“and the fronts of one measure”** — the same is repeated
**“on both parts”**
• of the Old and New Testament
• Or the three chambers are the three virtues, faith, hope, charity, without which those who can do any work cannot be saved; and these same were as much in the new teachers as in the old. Or because there were three distinctions of the old fathers, and three of the new. For the fathers were before the law, and in the law, and afterwards the prophets. In the new people, first the firstfruits of the Hebrews believed, and the fullness of the Gentiles followed, and at the end the remnant of the Jews will come. In each testament also there are three orders of preachers: the continent, the married, and the preachers; whence the same prophet saw three men delivered, Noe, Daniel and Job.
*Gregory:* Gregory. The eastern way between the three chambers on this side and the three on that is the Son of God, who appeared in the flesh among the old and new fathers.
**“three on this side, and three on that side”** — Whence: “his pavilion round about him.”
**“all three were of one measure”** — The faith is the same, though the merits and the quality of life differ, and though the dignity is not the same for all; yet for all there will be one life of blessedness. Whence: “In my Father’s house there are many mansions”; and of this also, that all receive one penny in the vineyard, though they come at different hours; because even if one has more and another less, yet one joy gladdens all from the vision of their Maker.
**“the fronts”** — namely of the fathers of the Old and New Testament, who are rightly called fronts because their good deeds are made known to us, while what lies hidden within is the porch. Whence: “Thy cheeks are as the bark of a pomegranate, beside what is hidden within thee.”
40.11:
**“And he measured the breadth”** — under the law
**“of the threshold of the gate ten cubits”** — which perfect number contains the sacraments of the decalogue and of the four gospels, which, beginning from one, reaches four so as to fill up the denary
**“and the length”** — namely the height
**“of the gate”** — under grace
**“thirteen cubits”**
• for he fulfils the precepts of the law by that very thing by which he believes the Trinity to be almighty God
• Of thirteen cubits. Rabanus. Thirteen cubits, after the eight, contain the sacrament of the books of Moses, which is also shown in the five loaves, and in the Samaritan woman, who is reproved because she had had five husbands, and the sixth, whom she thought she had, she had not. Yet the eight and the five are completed in one cubit, that is, the fourteenth, because in Christ all things are recapitulated; whence: “and one cubit was the end on both sides.”
**“and he measured the breadth”** — Gregory. First he measured the threshold of the gate with one reed, then the breadth with ten cubits, the length thirteen; because the holy fathers, whom we know from holy Scripture to have been before the law, knew indeed that the one almighty God, that is, the holy Trinity, exists, but did not openly preach it; keeping purity of life, they had, as it were, in the six cubits of the reed, the perfection of works, and, often seeing angels, the palm of contemplation. But when the law was given, the people of the Hebrews kept the commandments of the decalogue.
**“And he measured the breadth of the threshold of the gate ten cubits”** — Because that ancient people, ignorant of the subtlety of faith, served the commandments of the decalogue; and the length of the gate is thirteen cubits, because through the New Testament, in the heart of the faithful people, knowledge of the Trinity grew above the commandments of the decalogue.
**“And he measured the breadth of the threshold of the gate”** — Gregory. Moses was more instructed than Abraham, and the prophets than Moses, and the apostles than the prophets, in the knowledge of God.
**“of the threshold of the gate”** — The threshold of the gate is Christ, who says: “I am the door,” in whom is the sacred number of the Old and New Testament. Or the saints, through whom we enter to the knowledge of God.
40.12:
**“and the border”** — faith, which goes before charity
**“before the little chambers one cubit”** — lest it be divided into errors and schisms
**“and one cubit”**
• the extremes were joined into one cubit
• while the Old and New Testament are embraced by one measure of Christ, and one cubit encloses the breadth of thirty cubits in the ark of Noe
**“the border”** — Christ, in whom both testaments are fulfilled; whence: “Christ is the end of the law.”
**“on both sides”** — that is, of both.
**“and the little chambers were six cubits on this side”**
• namely of the Jews and of the Gentiles
• for all the elect, both in the synagogue and in the church, believed in Christ
**“and that side”**
• on each side
• The chambers: the thoughts of the faithful, in which chaste souls are joined to their Maker by love. But above he says the chamber was measured with one reed, which has six cubits and a palm, because there are those who, loving God, are exercised only in good works, which is signified by the six, and there are those who possess the palm of contemplation.
**“And one cubit was the border on both sides”** — Namely of the gate and of the threshold, or of the border and the chambers; because when the majesty of the Lord shall appear, faith will end, that it may no longer be; charity, that it may be perfect.
**“The little chambers were six cubits”** — Rabanus. They did not have a palm, nor any added rule above which would call the present way of life to future blessedness, but only six cubits. Whence it follows: and he measured the gate.
40.13:
**“And he measured the gate”** — the scripture
**“from the roof”**
• because the fervour of love is still in secret
• or wall
**“of one little chamber”** — of love
**“to the roof of another”** — or the wall
**“in breadth”**
• because good work is the witness between knowledge and love, which, if it is lacking, it is certain that there is neither the gate of holy speech nor the chamber
• because scripture is partly hidden. Whence: “Who stretchest out the heaven like a skin: who coverest the higher rooms thereof with water”; namely the higher things of it, that is, to the multitude of the angels
**“five and twenty cubits”** — namely, so much was the space between door and door, or gate and gate
**“door”** — of faith
**“door against door”** — of the thing
**“From the roof of one little chamber”** — Gregory. Because our humility is proved by the hidden things of Scripture, but by what we say of our charity we are more truly approved in the sight of God.
**“In breadth five and twenty cubits”** — Gregory. Five extended into itself makes twenty-five, and the five senses are multiplied in themselves, when what is done through them is increased in good.
**“Five and twenty”** — This number, although square, is nevertheless referred to the five senses. For five times five makes twenty-five, which lies between the roof of the chambers and the roof; and yet, being placed on both sides opposite each other, from the upper parts it has door against door.
40.14:
**“He made also fronts”** — namely works which are seen and are perfect. For the number six is perfect.
**“of sixty cubits”** — Gregory. The perfection of works is expressed according to the decalogue.
**“and to”** — beside
**“the front the court”** — from the broadening of works through love. Whence: “Thy commandment is exceeding broad.”
**“of the gate”** — of heaven
**“on every side”**
• that love be everywhere
• And he made fronts, etc. I think that between the outer wall of the temple, through the circuit, and the temple building itself in the court, that is, in the middle, there were certain things placed for ornament, which Symmachus calls circumstances, that is, certain standing things raised up from the ground on high.
**“He made also fronts of sixty cubits”** — That is, by this it is shown that at the entrance of the gate, to those entering at once, a wall of sixty cubits presents itself, with various ornaments, which refer to the constitution of the world, that from creatures the Creator may be understood. And all things running in order and reason show the variety of the world, which among the Greeks, cosmos, took its name from ornament, and was made in six days, so that for each day ten are reckoned, which number we said above to be perfect. After this, as we enter the inner court, before the porch itself of the inner gate there meet us chambers with slanting windows, which hold a space of fifty cubits, which number also is itself sacred. And after seven full weeks of feast and joy, the first day of the eighth begins, which is the day of the resurrection, and it brings us in to the nearness of the temple. For when we have done all things, doing penance for the former error, then we are made near and close to God, so that in the outer court the order of creatures may teach us the knowledge of the Creator, and constancy; and in the inner, the true jubilee, in which all our debts are forgiven us, may instruct us in true theology and bring us in to the holy of holies. It must also be noted that the inner court has many windows, not straight and equal but slanting and narrow outwardly and widening within, so that through certain small openings we may penetrate to the inner things and reach the fullness of the brightest light that dwells in the temple.
40.15:
**“And before the face”** — and before the face of; the inner place before the gate is described
**“of the gate”** — of the gate, namely of the inner
**“which reached even to the face of the porch”** — which reached to the face of the porch; that is, which faced the inner gate
**“of the inner gate, fifty cubits”**
• of the inner gate, fifty cubits of space
• fifty cubits, namely.
• Gregory. The court of the gate, etc. And before the face, etc. By the gate faith is signified; by the court, charity; by the place that lies near the face of the porch of the inner gate, hope; without these, whoever can now use reason cannot enter the heavenly building.
**“fifty cubits”** — Gregory. By fifty eternal rest is signified; for the seven has its perfection, since in it the number of days is completed. And through the law the sabbath is given for rest. This, multiplied by itself, rises to forty-nine, to which if the one is added, it comes to fifty, because all our perfection will be in the vision of that One, in whose vision will be the perfection of salvation and joy. To this the jubilee also, that is, the fiftieth year, is given for rest; because whoever comes to eternal joys will have no more labor and groaning.
40.16:
**“And”** — there
**“slanting windows”** — Septuagint: hidden.
**“in the little chambers”**
• to each chamber, namely
• where the bridegroom delights.
**“and in their fronts”**
• in the larger ones
• porches that are before the chambers.
**“which were within the gate on every side round about”** — Gregory. Because he who has the light of contemplation within his heart sees.
**“and in like manner there were”** — Gregory. For the grace of contemplation is given to the greatest and the least, which even a married man often has.
**“also in the porches windows”** — which are below, that is, in the smaller ones.
**“round about within”** — for the mind goes round so that it may find what it seeks.
**“and before the fronts”** — namely of the porches.
**“the representation”** — or carving.
**“of palm trees”**
• of victory.
• because in the world there is not substance but shadow.
• Slanting windows, without coziche, received their name from arrows, because like arrows a narrow light is let into the building and widens within; and everything round about was full of windows of this kind.
• Slanting windows, through which light can enter, a thief cannot.
**“Slanting windows”** — Gregory. Of which the outer part is narrow and the inner part wide; for although the saints see something faintly of the true light, they are nevertheless enlarged within themselves.
**“And in their fronts”** — Gregory. The fronts are the highest men, who are set forth for others to see.
**“And before the fronts the representation of palm trees”** — After the sixty and fifty cubits, the chambers, the porches, the fronts of the porches, and the many windows round about, a picture of palm trees is shown to us, so that, possessing victory over the world, we may be made worthy to see the palms of virtues.
40.17:
**“And”** — after these things.
**“he brought me into the outward court”** — the aforesaid man
**“and behold there were chambers”**
• Gregory. Of which “a desirable treasure resteth in the mouth of the wise.”
• Septuagint: chambers. Aquila: storerooms. Symmachus: exedrae, which had been prepared for the dwelling of the Levites and priests.
**“and a pavement of stone”** — the humility of the hearers.
**“of stone”** — the strength of faith.
**“in the court”** — the breadth of charity, by which they are subject one to another.
**“on every side”** — of the treasure-chambers.
**“thirty”** — where the denary is multiplied by three, so that the life and tongue of the teacher may be made firm in the Trinity.
**“chambers encompassed the pavement”**
• That teachers may guard those subject to them, and be kindled by them to better things. For there are chambers round about the pavement, and conversely.
• The treasury chambers, full of spiritual riches (of which it is said: “The redemption of a man’s soul are his own riches.” And the apostle rejoices that his disciples are filled “with all utterance, and all knowledge.” Gaza in the Persian tongue means riches, or chambers, which in Greek are pastophoria), show to the bridegroom the prepared bedchambers, which are thirty, to show the perfect age of those dwelling in them.
• A pavement of stone, etc. That is, lest the footsteps of the inhabitants be defiled with the mud and earth and dust of sins, but may walk upon living stones, of which the temple of God is built. Or the spaces between the columns were before the doors of the chambers, to support the building placed above. Of which: “They gave me and Barnabas the right hands,” Peter and John, “who seemed to be pillars.” And elsewhere: “the pillar and ground of the truth.” John in the Apocalypse: “He that shall overcome, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God.”
**“Chambers”** — Gregory. The hearts of teachers, full of the riches of wisdom and knowledge. But the prophet, led to the outer court, saw the treasury chambers outside, because one thing is contemplation, which cannot tell how much it sees; another is knowledge and teaching, which sees only as much as it can express by the tongue. Phylax in Greek means to keep. Gaza in Persian means riches.
**“And a pavement of stone”** — Either the spaces between the columns, to show that the court has before the doors a row of columns and a pavement in front of the gates; or porches behind the back of the gates, in which porches I think the columns were arranged in order, so that before the treasury chamber there were porches, and in the fronts of the porches columns supporting the porches.
**“Thirty”** — Gregory. The number ten is taken for perfection, because the keeping of the law is contained in the ten precepts; for the active life and the contemplative are joined together in the decalogue, in which both the love of God and of neighbour is commanded to be kept; that the teacher may have these, let him advance in the faith of the holy Trinity.
40.18:
**“And the pavement”** — or a porch behind the backs of the gates, which defended the dwellers of the chambers from the rains.
**“in the front”** — in the ascent of the porch.
**“of the gates”** — of teachers.
**“according to the length”**
• longsuffering.
• because hearers ought to have the same hope and faith that teachers have.
**“of the gates was lower”** — because the merits of those subject are not equal to those of the teachers.
**“Was lower”** — For what is lower is always placed among higher things, that is, so that by an ascent and by steps we may come to things mystical and secret and full of spiritual riches. And the full and perfect number is in the number of ten tens, which also multiplies the seed of Isaac a hundredfold. But because he was on the earth, and could still say, “I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner as all my fathers were,” he is said to have sown barley and reaped a hundredfold. For not yet was the grain of wheat dead in the earth, that it might bring forth much fruit, and satisfy the hunger of the Jewish people, that is, of hearing the word of God, with the bread that came down from heaven.
40.19:
**“And”** — through the masters of the Church.
**“he measured the breadth”** — the breadth of charity which they showed to their neighbours by their work.
**“from the face of the gate”** — namely of faith, which, while we are still placed on earth, opens the knowledge of God to us.
**“lower”** — of the active life.
**“to the front of the inner court”** — signs by which he shows how much he sees within.
**“inner”** — of contemplation.
**“without”** — because it is known by its outward fruits.
**“a hundred cubits”** — ten times ten make a hundred; whence great perfection is signified by a hundred; whence he shall receive a hundredfold, that is, perfection, so that he wills nothing in the world.
**“to the east, and to the north”**
• Thirty chambers. A hundred cubits to the east. To this prophecy that saying of the Gospel agrees: “The seed fell upon good ground, and brought forth fruit, some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, some a hundredfold.” For here thirty and sixty and a hundred are set down, that by these as by steps we may come to perfect knowledge; so, however, that the number fifty may lead us to the inner house, which, the sabbath of the seven weeks being finished, comes out into the day of the resurrection.
• He measured the breadth from the face of the lower gate, etc. Because our Redeemer daily measures the life of the faithful by the measure of perfection, either in the hope of good work through faith, or in holy desires through contemplation.
**“To the east”** — To the east. On account of the Jews, from whom the sun of justice arose.
**“To the north”** — On account of the nations numbed by the cold of unbelief, among whom he reigned who said: “I will place my seat to the north.” Or by the east are signified the just, who, as they were born in the light of faith, have continued in innocence; but by the north, sinners, who, fallen into the cold of the mind, have grown numb under the shadow of their sin. But these also come to perfection through penance.
40.20:
**“the gate”**
• namely the preacher.
• Septuagint: and he brought me to the north, and behold a gate looking toward the outer court.
**“also, which looked”** — by knowing, by announcing.
**“the way”** — life.
**“northward”** — of the sinner.
**“He measured also both the length and the breadth of the gate of the outward court”** — The gate also that looked toward the way, etc. First. In this it is to be considered what is brought in first through the north gate; second, through the south gate; third, through the east gate. For from the north evils break out upon the inhabitants of the earth. For he who is an inhabitant of the earth, not a stranger and a sojourner, lies open to the darts of him who comes from the north, whose fiery darts are quenched by the shield of faith; and the outer court is named to the north, the inner to the south. For he says: “and he brought me into the inner court, to the south gate,” which is found written likewise of the eastern court. For the first entrance to virtue is to tread the north underfoot, and by fifty and twenty-five to reach the summit of the hundred; then to be brought in to the southern quarter and drive out the cold of the north; then to come to perfect virtue, that is, to the eastern gate, in which the sun of justice rises, through which the high priest alone enters. But it is to be noted that, though there are four quarters, of the western gate nothing is said, of which it is written: “Make a way for him who ascendeth upon the west: the Lord is his name,” that, preparing the way for the Lord alone, according to that: “Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God,” we may be able to hear what is said at the end of the psalm: “Who mounteth above the heaven of heavens, to the east.”
**“Of the outward court”** — Gregory. Of the present life, in which everything that is seen bodily is measured both in length and in breadth; because when a sinner is led to the faith, it is necessary that his teacher consider how much, in the length of hope and the breadth of charity, he advances by his admonition. These things belong to the preacher, because through him they are in those under his charge.
40.21:
**“And the little chambers thereof three on this side, and three on that side”** — because both the letter and the spirit, both history and tropology, pertain to the sacraments of the Trinity.
**“and the front thereof”** — visible works.
**“and the porch thereof”** — faith, which is rather suggested, through which one comes to works.
**“according to the measure of the gate”** — namely the eastern.
**“former”** — by merit, not by order.
**“fifty cubits long”**
• as above.
• in which eternal rest is signified after seven weeks; for it extends through the day of resurrection to the kingdoms of heaven, in which is true rest.
**“the length thereof and the breadth”**
• the love of neighbour.
• for all good things that are done bodily are shown through the five senses
**“five and twenty cubits broad”** — And the little chambers thereof, etc. Gregory. The three gates here and three there, that is, the holy souls of the hearers, God’s brides, advancing in faith in the Trinity through the admonition of the preacher, the preaching of the Old and New Testament having been heard.
**“Fifty cubits long, the length thereof”** — Because no one can come to eternal rest unless he can now stretch his hope toward it patiently.
**“And the breadth, five and twenty cubits”** — The number five, taken by itself, comes to twenty-five, because good works, when they begin to be done through fervour, rouse the soul to increase and are multiplied of themselves; whence they also make breadth in the mind, so that they are not narrow through fear but spread wide through charity.
**“Five and twenty cubits”** — Which are referred to the five senses: through five rows of squares, one of which is fitted to the length and the other to the breadth. In the length is shown rest and the love of the more sacred knowledge. In the breadth, the reasoning pertaining to the senses is demonstrated.
40.22:
**“windows”** — of contemplation
**“thereof”**
• Gregory. All things as above.
• of the gate, namely, through which the entrance of life is opened
**“The windows thereof”** — Gregory. The gate that is to the north has windows and a porch and gravings, because when a sinner is brought back to life he often receives the light of contemplation, and from the memory of his iniquity the grace of humility and the efficacy of good working, so that everything that is perceived to be done may be seen graven in his life.
**“and the porch”** — of humility
**“and the gravings”**
• The Seventy: palms.
• of good work
• were
**“And the porch”** — Because whoever, placed at the entrance of the virtues, has entered the three and three chambers and has recognized the front and porch by the measure of the former gate, will also arrive at those things and will behold those things which he is to receive most fully in the eastern gate.
**“And a porch was before it”** — Gregory. The porch is before the steps, because he who first believes afterward ascends by the steps of the virtues to the approach of the gate. Cornelius came to works through faith, but was made firm in faith through works.
**“according to the measure”** — because as it receives the just, so also penitents after sin. Whence: “For I did eat ashes as bread.”
**“of the gate”** — namely, was
**“that looked to the east, and they went up to it by seven steps”** — that is, through the sevenfold Spirit; for from the fear which is the beginning of wisdom we climb to piety, then to the rest. But Isaias, because he was speaking of heavenly things, in descending set down “the spirit of wisdom and of understanding,” etc.
**“by seven steps”** — Because through the seven steps of the week, and the pot that is kindled from the face of the north, and the ceremonies of the Jews, to whom God gave “precepts that are not good, and judgments in which they shall not live,” we climb to higher things and to the porch of the gate.
**“and a porch was before it”** — the gate
*Gregory:* And a porch before it. Because unless one has first had humility, he does not ascend to these steps of spiritual gifts. Whence: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, but upon the humble and quiet?” And: “In his heart he hath disposed to ascend by steps, in the vale of tears,” etc. And elsewhere: “Who sendest forth springs in the vales.”
*Gregory:* And a porch before it. Faith, that is; for by faith one comes to works. Cornelius also came to works by faith; for he believed in one God, but did not know that his Son was incarnate. By faith his works pleased God. For “without faith it is impossible to please God.”
40.23:
**“and the gate of the inner court”** — the approach to eternal blessedness
**“inner”** — or inner
**“over against the gate”** — in a straight line
**“of the north, and that of the east”** — because it receives sinners and the just
**“and he measured from gate”**
• of beginning
• namely of the outer north gate
**“to gate”**
• the inner of the same north gate
• Gregory. The entrance of perfection and completion, to which one runs by the way of perfection, which is signified by a hundred
**“a hundred”** — so that, as if by these steps, withdrawing from the outer gate, we may arrive at the inner
**“cubits”**
• as above
• And he measured from gate to gate a hundred cubits, etc. Gregory. Therefore from gate to gate there are a hundred cubits, so that the very delay of living, through which we grow daily in virtues, may be as it were a certain pause in going, so that the approach to the inner gate may be reached more perfectly.
• Gregory. And he measured from gate to gate a hundred cubits. The inner court is measured, which extends from the outer gates to the inner gate by a hundred cubits, so that he who has begun to enter by loving may have the breadth of perfection in his mind, and run through the court of perfection until he comes to the secret joys.
**“And the gate of the inner court”** — There is not only one gate of the north, which above is called the outer gate, but another, which has a likeness to the eastern gate, as the Septuagint said more plainly: “And the gate of the inner court, looking to the north gate, as was the gate that looked to the east.”
*Gregory:* The gate of the inner court is said to be set over against the gate of the east and of the north, which is not said of the south. Because by the east we understand those who are beginning, and by the north the fallen. It was fitting, therefore, that strength to enter the inner court should be given to beginners and to the fallen. But of those who by fervour of spirit remain in virtues no one doubts; for it is certain that the entrance of heaven lies open to them.
40.24:
**“And he brought me out to the way of the south, and behold the gate that looked to the south: and he measured”** — by the same measure
**“he measured the front thereof”** — These things, in the gate of the east and of the north, have been explained above.
**“And he brought me out to the way”** — Through each entrance Ezechiel (whom God strengthened, for this is the meaning of his name) is led, and from the gate of the north he passes to the southern gate.
*Gregory:* It is to be noted that in the spiritual building there is an entrance to the east, and to the north, and to the south. The way lies open to the east, so that those who have well begun the sacraments of faith and have been sunk in no depth may come to eternal joys. The gate lies open to the north, so that those who, after the beginning of warmth and light, have fallen into the cold and darkness of sins may return through penance to pardon, and know what is the true joy of the inner reward. The way lies open to the south, so that those who burn with holy desire in the virtues may daily penetrate by spiritual understanding the mysteries of inner joy.
*Gregory:* Although there are four quarters of the world, only three gates are set in the outer building, which is spiritual, that is, the holy Church, by which one comes to eternal joys: faith, hope, charity. In the east is faith, by which the true light is born in the mind. To the north, hope, because a sinner, if he despairs of God’s mercy, perishes altogether; whence it is necessary that he who has been put out by his iniquity should live again through the hope of mercy. To the south, charity, because it burns with the fire of love. For at the southern gate the sun is carried up on high, because through charity the light of faith is lifted up in the love of God and neighbour. Through these three gates one comes to the inner court, that is, to the secret joys.
40.25:
**“And the windows thereof”**
• all things, that is, were full of light, to be referred to the parts.
• Through which, namely, the light enters to the soul of the one who sees, especially if the length of his life has been prolonged by the mystery of the fiftieth year, that is, the jubilee, and he has been able to attain to the breadth of a more divine sense. In which breadth and in the streets wisdom acts confidently and cries aloud with a lofty voice, and enters by seven steps that she may come to the porch, and through the palms of her purpose and effort may hold everlasting victory.
40.26:
**“and there were seven steps to go up to it: and a porch before the doors thereof: and there were graven palm trees, one on this side”** — on the right, lest he be lifted up in prosperity, which is done through fear.
**“and another on that side in the front thereof”**
• on the left, lest he be broken in adversity, which is done through hope.
• And graven palms, etc. Of which it was said at the gate of the northern quarter, let it suffice to have admonished this much: that what is said there according to the letter, we understand spiritually in the southern; for history and tropology run on the same lines. But the one is lowlier, the other more sublime; the one cleaves to the earth, the other flies up to heavenly things.
**“And there were graven palm trees”** — Gregory. Above he said: the picture of palms, which is the showing of signs; now they are called graven palms, in which the demonstration of good works is signified. Whence: “That they may see your good works, and glorify your Father,” etc. Those who show that holy works are impressed upon their life bear palms graven on the forehead, because they show how great a victory will follow them hereafter in their works. Or in the gate of the east there is a picture, in the gate of the north and south a carving, because the sign of victory which is shown to beginners is held more firmly and strongly in those who return and are fervent.
40.27:
**“And there was a gate of the inner court towards the south”** — lest we think there is only one court.
**“and he measured”** — that after the sacrament of the week and of the Old Testament he might come to the good land and the grace of the gospel.
40.28:
**“And he brought me”** — not only the court is at the southern gate.
**“into the inner court”** — the third, that is.
**“to the gate”** — Judea.
**“south gate: and he measured the gate according to the former measures”**
• all these things have been said and explained above.
• And he brought me in, etc. Gregory. These things are repeated in the three inner gates, which have already been said of the outer gates for a second or third time.
*Gregory:* Here again three gates are described, by which, as above, we understand preachers. But there is one Church in the preachers of the Old and New Testament. The gates above have seven steps, here eight, because they preach in concord the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit and announce the joys of eternal reward. Whence: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight.” The outer gates are the ancient fathers, who by the precepts of the law kept the works of the people rather than their hearts. The inner are the preachers of the Church, who by spiritual admonitions keep the hearts of the hearers. Those gates have seven steps, these eight, because in the veneration of the law the seventh day, and in the New Testament the eighth, is in the sacrament, which is the third from the passion, the eighth from the creation, which follows the seventh. But if by the name of gates we take only the apostles, who were the first preachers of the Church, who taught us to hold faith, hope and charity above all: they are the gates in these virtues, who lead us through those same virtues to the inner understanding of eternal wisdom. They are the outer gates, they are the inner: for to beginners they speak outer things, to the perfect mystical things. Whence: “I gave you milk to drink, not meat.” And elsewhere: “We speak wisdom among the perfect.” And: “I could not speak to you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal.” They establish us in the first entrance of faith, hope and charity. They preach the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom to those who are advancing, and lead us by a more subtle sense to inner things; whence first their seven steps, afterwards eight, are spoken of.
**“Into the inner court”** — Each court has its own measures and orders, and there is a different grace in the same measures, while we recognize the same things in one way at the beginning, another at progress, and another at the end.
**“At the south gate”** — Gregory. In the first description the eastern gate is before the gate of the north and of the south. In the second, between the gate of the south and the north, because Christ by his divinity preceded all things, and by his humanity came among all things, who became the end of departing Judea and the beginning of the Gentiles that followed. Above he put the gate of the north before the southern gate, because the Gentile world was before the synagogue; for Heber, from whom the Hebrews, was a Gentile.
40.30:
**“And the porch round about”** — this has not yet been said.
**“five and twenty cubits long, and five cubits broad”**
• because through the simple life, which is led by the five senses, they are enlarged in love of neighbor.
• And the porch round about, twenty-five cubits in length, etc. For if we triple eight we make twenty-four, to which one is added so that twenty-five is filled up. For good hearers, who are the porches of the gates of eternal hope, hold longanimity, and the eighth day, in the faith of the Trinity, which is one God. Eight, therefore, is multiplied by three, but is made firm by the confession of one God. The porches are level, because the hearts of such are humble. They have length, because they persevere long-sufferingly in hope. The length is measured by twenty-five cubits, because they believe in the resurrection of the flesh on the eighth day through the Trinity, and that same Trinity to be one God. By the porch which is inner, the faith of the perfect can be understood; by that which looks outward, the faith of beginners. Or by the inner porch the higher precepts, by that which looks outward the least. For through the porch one goes to the steps and the gate, and through the precepts to the virtues and the entrance of heavenly grace.
**“Five and twenty cubits long”** — So that the length may take in the breadth of the former court, that is, twenty-five cubits of the outer court, and the breadth may hold five cubits; these measures, that is, twenty-five and five, we refer to the five senses, which, if we ascend to higher things, we multiply five times, and make spiritual out of carnal. Whence: “Lift up your eyes, and see the countries; for they are white already to harvest.” And: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.” And: “O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet.” And: “We are the good odour of Christ unto God.” And: “Our hands have handled, of the Word of life.” And finally, not as on the north side, where they make only seven steps, but after the number seven the number eight is present, that we may pass from the synagogue to the church, from the Old Testament to the new, from earthly things to heavenly.
40.31:
**“And the porch thereof to the outward court”** — They are within through love. But because some still live according to the bodily senses, they look outward through simplicity.
**“and the palm trees thereof”** — this has been explained above.
**“in the front: and there were eight steps”** — this too remains to be said.
40.32:
**“And he brought me into the inner court by the way of the east”** — what is said here of the eastern gate was said above of the southern.
**“And he measured the gate”** — the Lord.
**“according to the former measures”** — And he brought me in, etc. Jerome. From the north side, to whose court one ascends by only seven steps, he passes to the south gate and to the court of the same gate. To this one ascends not by seven only but by eight steps, namely that we may pass through the old things to the new, that is, come through the patriarchs and prophets to the apostles, so that in the one there is a hebdomad, in the other an ogdoad. But now he comes to the highest, and brought the prophet in by the way of the inner gate, or through the court to which one goes by the eastern way. The word “way,” according to the Septuagint, is found only in this place; in the north and south side it is wholly passed over, that we may understand that only on the eastern side is that way which says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”; for through him we come to the Father; of which: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way,” who, namely, think nothing sinister about Christ, but their faith is pure, defiled by no heresy.
40.34: **“And the porch thereof, that is, of the outward court”** — Jerome. So that all things may be seen enclosed by the eastern light, according to that: “and there is no one that can hide himself from his heat.” But if we take the court as outer and inner, we understand thus: that God is both poured around and poured within. Whence: “who holdeth the heavens in his palm, and the earth in his fist.” And: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth my footstool,” that is, that he may be believed to be within all things. Whence: “and the mind, poured through the limbs, moves the whole mass,” etc. But when we have passed over, by the arms of justice on the right hand and on the left, through glory and ignominy, through good and evil report, through praises and reproaches, and have taken victory from this world, then palms are given us on both sides, whom neither joys have changed, nor sorrow, nor prosperity nor adversity broken. And not by seven steps as on the north side, nor by seven and eight as in the south, but by eight steps only we ascend to the heights, because the sacrament of the number eight, that is, the gospel, suffices for us, that we may say: “And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, but now we know him so no longer,” but according to the spirit.
40.35:
**“And he brought me”** — Again, but not as above to the outer court, but the inner; whence in what follows, the porch looked to the outer court; in which the progress of one entering is shown, while in each place the names and measures are proper, and the windows round about, showing all things full of the light of knowledge.
**“into the gate that looked to the north”** — the Gentiles.
**“and he measured according to the former measures”** — And he brought me to the gate that looked to the north, etc. Gregory. What was said above of the southern and eastern gates is repeated here in the same words of the northern gate.
40.36:
**“The little chamber thereof, and the front thereof, and the porch thereof, and the windows thereof round about it was fifty cubits long”** — in which are the sacraments of forgiveness.
**“and five and twenty cubits broad”**
• in which are the divine senses.
• What are we to say of the mystical senses of the prophet Ezechiel, we who scarcely grasp the very words of his history?
**“The porch thereof”** — The porch of the gate is the words of preaching, which we first receive humbly, that we may come to the understanding of the sacred discourse. Let the inner gate, then, be for us the New Testament, the old the outer, because the former opens the spiritual understanding, the latter keeps the history of the sacred discourse for the unlearned. And the inner gate has two sides: the love of God and of neighbour.
*Gregory:* What the outer court, the chamber, the fronts, the porch, the windows, the length, the breadth, and the carving of the palms signify has been said above.
40.37:
**“The porch thereof looked”** — that by this, namely, in the porch of the inner court, we may see outward things, and, contemplating the knowledge of things past and present, by which we may come to the double palms and victories, and know the mysteries of the eight steps; and having entered the treasuries, in which the riches of the temple are kept, and our ... are washed from every stain of sin.
**“by eight steps”** — Gregory. The gates of the spiritual building have seven steps, because they preach to their hearers fear, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom. But when they command that all things now be left, and that the mind be set on the contemplation of the heavenly country and delight in its mysteries, they add the eighth step and carry them over to the inner things; whence to him who said he had kept the commandments of the law from his youth it was added: “One thing is yet wanting to thee. If thou wilt be perfect, go, sell all,” etc. By the number eight also are signified the day of the eternal judgment and the resurrection of the flesh; whence the psalm which is inscribed for the eighth begins from the dread of judgment: “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation,” etc. In it all this time is ended which revolves in seven days, and that which follows after seven days is rightly called the eighth, on which our flesh also shall rise from the dust; whence by the law too circumcision is done on the eighth day, for through the member which is circumcised mortal propagation is begotten and the number of the departing and the succeeding is increased, which after the resurrection will not be, because “they shall neither marry, nor be married, but are as the angels of God in heaven”; and on the eighth day the foreskin is cut off, because there propagation of the flesh has no place, where the flesh, rising again, has the perseverance of eternity.
40.38:
**“And at every chamber”** — the hearts of teachers, which keep the riches of knowledge.
**“a door in the forefronts of the gates: there”** — in the doorway, that is, which is in the front of the gates; admonished by the words and works of the fathers.
**“they washed”** — with tears of compunction.
**“the holocaust”**
• themselves, whom they have consecrated to the Lord; but because they offend in many things, they wash with tears so that the holocaust may be made fat and full of marrow.
• In the forefronts of the gates. Gregory. By the words and works of the preachers, by which we recognize outwardly how they live within themselves. And there is a door at each treasury in the forefronts of the gates, because each of the teachers opens understanding in the heart of the hearer in the sayings and works of the fathers; otherwise he has no door in the forefronts of the gates, and ought not to be called a treasury of the spiritual building.
40.39:
**“And in the porch”** — namely the people.
**“of the gate”** — that is, of the preacher, who is the inner gate.
**“two tables”** — while the people with humble mind receive the words of preaching; in that table the sacrifice is constructed from virtues.
**“two tables on this side, and two tables on that side: that the holocaust might be slain thereon”**
• that the holy fire consume it all.
• when the whole man is vowed to God and gives up all earthly things.
**“and the sin offering”**
• what we have committed knowingly.
• that is, to do evil.
• in deed.
**“and the trespass offering”**
• in ignorance.
• in thought.
• That the holocaust may be slain upon them, etc. Gregory. Rightly on the four tables of the inner gate the holocaust is sacrificed, both for sin and for trespass. For he who wholly despises the world and gives himself to God as a holocaust, here also knows perfectly how to bewail the sins of deed and of thought, either the evil that he did, or the good that he ought to have done and did not do.
**“And in the porch of the gate were two tables on this side”** — Gregory. While the tables are described as four on each side, and the sum of the conclusion is stated, that there were eight tables on which they sacrificed, it is clear that this is not said of each of the six gates that were spoken of; for in like manner all would have not eight but forty-eight tables. Nor can it be said of one only; for after the porch of the gate is described, where two tables on this side and two tables on that side are told of, still at the outer side, which goes up to the door of the gate that goes toward the north, two tables are mentioned, and it is added: and at the other side before the porch of the gate two tables, between which the gate that looks toward the way of the north is also said to be; whence it is clear that there is one porch inside and another outside, because the inner and the outer gate of the north are both described afterwards. For when he had described three gates above, he also recorded three others of the inner court, and the outermost gate of the north. Now therefore, when two tables on this side are described in the porch of the gate, and two tables, the discourse is still woven of the same inner gate, because it is added: at the outer side which goes up to the door of the gate, and at the side before the porch of the gate two tables. The inner gate, then, is described as having two tables at the sides in the porch, and the outer gate likewise two; and four on this side and four on that are produced alike, while at each side two are described in the porch of the inner gate, and two on this side and that outside in the porch of the north gate, which together are all eight, on which sacrifice is made.
*Gregory:* And in the porch of the gate two tables. Allegorically. Our gate in the inner porch has four tables, because holy Church received four orders of rulers for the instruction of the faithful; whence he himself gave some apostles, and some prophets, other some evangelists, other some pastors and doctors, who are one order; for he truly feeds who teaches. The outer gate also has four tables: the synagogue, namely the chief priests, the ancients of the people, the scribes and the Pharisees, who were called teachers of the law. In each gate there are two tables on this side, two on that, because in the beginning holy Church had apostles and prophets, namely those who arose after the apostles; but now it has evangelists and doctors. Evangelists are those who announce the joys of the heavenly country; but the apostles and prophets have been taken away. And so these two tables were as it were on the other side.
40.40:
**“And”** — that is, to omit doing good.
**“On the outward side”** — because the law was given and kept in the outer guard of the letter.
**“which goeth up to the entry of the gate”** — the historical understanding of the law.
**“that looketh toward the north, were two tables”** — because under fear of threats it has crushed the cold hearts of the Jews.
**“and at the other side before the porch of the gate were two tables”** — And at the outer side which goeth up to the door, etc. The gate also that goes toward the north has two tables on this side and two tables on that: namely the chief priests and the ancients of the people, in the greater authority of rule, and the scribes and Pharisees, who presided over the people in a lesser place. But these tables are beside the gate that goes toward the north, because, though they presided over the people, the synagogue, raging in the persecution of our Redeemer, broke out into the torpor of unbelief; yet these tables had a sacrifice, which they held according to the letter; whence they fell into torpor, who were not set on fire by the flame of the Spirit. But the tables of the inner gate have a holocaust, those in whose hearts the fire of the Spirit has blazed and burns, whether of apostles and prophets or in the mind of evangelists and doctors; which fire, because it consumes every thought in good work, kindles with the flame of the love of God all that it finds, like a holocaust, all at once. And these tables are made of square stones, because while they daily meditate the words of the sacred utterance, to offer to the Lord the holocaust of prayer, they are built as of square stones; for the words of holy Scripture are square stones, which everywhere stand firm and are nowhere reproved. For in all that they narrate of the past, in all that they preach of the future, in all that they sound spiritually, in all that they announce morally, they have a standing as on a different side, because they have no reproof. The hearts of the saints therefore are tables of God for the holocaust, built of square stones, because those who always think on the words of God slay themselves to the carnal life. Whence: “The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps shall not be supplanted.” And elsewhere: “Thy words have I hidden in my heart, that I may not sin against thee.”
**“Two tables on this side and on that side”** — Gregory. Two tables on this side and on that, because in the love of God faith and life are necessary; whence: “Without faith it is impossible to please God.” And elsewhere: “Faith without works is dead.” In love of neighbor, patience and kindness; whence: “Charity is patient, is kind”; that is, that it may bear evils inflicted with equanimity, and bestow its own goods kindly. The outer gate also, that is the law, has two sides, that is the spiritual fathers and the carnal people, in which there are tables: in the spiritual, doctrine and prophecy; in the carnal, circumcision and sacrifice.
40.41:
**“Four tables”**
• faith, life, teaching and prophecy in the minds of the good.
• four on each side.
**“on this side”** — when the peoples are advancing, holy preaching keeps patience and kindness, which previously among the carnal kept circumcision and sacrifice.
**“and four tables on that side: at the sides of the gate were eight tables”** — all together.
**“upon which they slew the victims”** — Jerome. Namely the others, and together there are sixteen tables, by which number the mysteries of the prophets are shown, so that whatever we offer in the New Testament we may approve as foretold by their prophecy.
**“Eight tables were”** — Gregory. Because whatever faith believes, whatever life shows by example in good works, whatever patience humbly bears, whatever kindness bestows and ministers, whatever doctrine teaches wholesomely, whatever prophecy foretells, whatever circumcision outwardly left by commandment, whatever sacrifice did from the devotion of the offerer, this shows to be a victim in the eyes of almighty God. For in the law, which is the outer gate, the people also by carnal sacrifice sacrificed the devotion of their heart.
40.42:
**“And the four tables”** — of the inner porch.
**“for the holocausts”** — because the other four are for the outer sacrifice, namely.
**“of stones”** — these are living stones which roll over the earth and have with them the corner stone by which the walls of the Old and New Testaments are held together; the four, however, show the evangelical sacraments.
**“made of square”** — so that they stand equally on every side.
**“long”** — of hope.
**“one cubit”**
• for in themselves they are perfect as far as they can be in this world.
• because one God, one faith, one baptism.
**“and a half, and in breadth one cubit”**
• of charity as far as concerns the neighbour.
• because certain divine mysteries cannot be fully grasped by man in this life. For “we know in part, and we prophesy in part.”
**“and a half”** — because they can neither fully know nor love God.
**“and high”** — of faith, which is of invisible things.
**“to lay the vessels upon”** — who take in the words of piety, so that from them a holocaust of life and of prayer is offered up.
**“in which the holocaust”**
• the martyrs, of whom: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”
• who wholly leave the world and set themselves on fire with the fire of love for the Lord, for an odour of sweetness.
**“and the victim”**
• who still make lawful use of the world, retaining it as a part of themselves.
• In length one cubit and in breadth one cubit, etc. Jerome. In length and breadth of one cubit and a half, that is, square; which, alike and joined together, make three cubits; and these three cubits have in height one cubit, that it may preserve the mysteries of the Trinity in the measure of one cubit, that is, of the divine majesty. Whence: “baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.” And the name of God is as it were a cubit of one height, which embraces three properties and always consumes the holocausts of our offerings.
**“The four tables for the holocausts”** — Gregory. Because both those who in holy Church keep faith, life, patience and kindness already abound in the highest virtues, and those who in the synagogue knew doctrine and prophecy, circumcision and sacrifice, by offering some things and keeping back others, offer the victim of their devotion.
**“Of square stones”** — Gregory. That is, to the saints, whose life stands firm in prosperity and in adversity: in prosperity it is not lifted up, in adversity it is not broken; by persuasions it is not drawn to evil; by reproaches it is not called back from good.
*Gregory:* Of the square stones. Of these square stones it is said: the bricks are fallen, that is the Jews, but we will build with square stones, that is with the apostles, martyrs and doctors of the Church; of these the porch, that is the people, has four tables built, because they take faith, life, patience and kindness from the life of the saints as an example.
**“To lay the vessels upon”** — The souls, namely, of the faithful; whence: “He is to me a vessel of election.” And elsewhere: “Be you cleansed, you that carry the vessels of the Lord”: the vessels, namely, being pastors and teachers.
**“Holocaust”** — Gregory. The whole burnt offering. And the law indeed bids us love God and neighbour, commanded the divine commands to be kept, restrained from the coveting of other men’s goods, yet does not order all things to be given up. In the New Testament it is said: “Every one of you that doth not renounce all that he possesseth, cannot be my disciple.” And: “whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself,” etc. The tables of the inner gate therefore have the holocaust, because in the virtues of the New Testament we burn all things as it were for a holocaust when we altogether renounce worldly goods. But the tables of the outer gate have the sacrifice, not the holocaust, because the precepts of the law order tithes to be offered, not all things to be given up.
40.43:
**“and the borders of them”** — that is, of those who offer up their souls to the Lord by continence and holiness of body.
**“of one handbreadth, turned inwards round about; and upon the tables the flesh of the offering”**
• because for those converted from the flesh by their preaching they offer prayers to the Lord.
• And their borders of one handbreadth. Because through the preaching of the teachers the works of the hearers are stretched out. For in the palm the hand is stretched out, in which works are signified. In the palm the greatest finger and the least are stretched out, so that by the teacher’s admonition the hearer may so do great things as not to omit small ones.
• But upon the tables, etc. R. The names of these tables, I think, are contained in Matthew and Mark and Luke and John; their turned-back border above, inward round about the edge, surrounded them, that it might hold the holocausts within and not let them flow out anywhere, and might hold the flesh of the offering. Pardon, reader, the difficulty of the places; or if you can find something better, teach it; we gladly learn what we do not know.
**“of one handbreadth”** — Gregory. That, from the teaching of the learned, as unity is kept in faith, so it may be kept in work, lest through the good one does, the other break out into evil of discord.
**“turned inwards”** — Gregory. That is, that what they say with the mouth they may fulfil in deed, looking round on their conscience on every side, lest the hungry man eat their harvest; whence Solomon: “The slothful hideth his hand under his armpit, and will not so much as bring it to his mouth.” For the table of God is the preacher; he carries the holocaust and the victim, as a chariot he rules, as a charioteer. Whence: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and the driver thereof.”
*Gregory:* The synagogue had spiritual fathers in doctrine and prophecy, from whom it might draw an example of life in virtues; but the rude people, serving more by fear than by love, would not imitate the virtues which it saw, and therefore the outer gate, which goes toward the north, has no tables for the holocaust.
40.44:
**“and without the inner gate the chambers of the singing men”** — to whom is said: “Sing ye to the Lord a new canticle”, who with the angels cry: Glory to God in the highest.
**“in the inner court, which was on the side of the gate”** — in which hope is signified.
**“that looketh to the north. And their prospect”** — one of the two, however, looked as it were towards the south and the north.
**“towards the south”** — in which charity.
**“one at the side of the east gate”** — which is faith.
**“which looketh toward the north”**
• where the sluggishness of sin.
• In the inner court, etc. Rabanus. Namely, it looked to the north and to the south and to the east, that the singers of the Lord, and those who are engaged in the office of angels, may always remember by what steps they have come to the heights, and diligently recognize the mysteries of the several places.
• Against the way, that is, there is one way for all, which says: “I am the way.”
**“Without the gate”** — Namely, behind the wall, which the Septuagint translated peribolus, which surrounded the whole temple in a square round about. The prophet was brought into the inner court, and to the north and to the south and to the east gate, and again to the north, of which it was said above. Their sense the Saviour’s testimony briefly shows: “In my Father’s house there are many mansions”; these being completed, he enters the temple, that is, the holy of holies.
*Gregory:* Without the inner gate, the chambers of the singing men. Because there are still some elect who are outside the secret joys of the inner life, who sing their desire to almighty God through the ardour of great love, and so they are both within and without. For they walk by faith, not by sight. These are the singers who do God’s commands by singing, that is, by love, not fear. Whence: “Thy justifications were the subject of my song, in the place of my pilgrimage.” And elsewhere: “Mercy and judgment I will sing to thee, O Lord.” He sings judgment who does not tremble to come to it.
*Gregory:* Without the inner gate the chambers of the singing men in the court. That is, the inner gate is holy Church. Outside this is the inner court, with regard to the following gates, namely of the north and of the south and the east. But outer with respect to the inner gate. For holy Church has two lives, one in which she labours on earth, the other in which she is rewarded in heaven. In both she offers a sacrifice: here the sacrifice of compunction, of which: “A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit.” There the sacrifice of praise, of which: “Then shalt thou accept the sacrifice of justice, oblations and whole burnt offerings,” etc. In both sacrifices flesh is offered: here while bodies are mortified, there while they rise in glory. The inner gate therefore has its inner parts, namely that life which none of us has yet seen. It has outside the court, that is, the present life, in which every good is done that we may come to good without end.
**“of the gate that looketh to the north”** — Gregory. Moreover the treasuries are within the gate of the north and of the east, and they look toward the southern way, because the hearts of the saints, placed between faith and hope, look toward the southern way, who burn with the fires of holy charity.
*Gregory:* Of the gate that looketh to the north. By the gate of the north the Gentile world is signified, through which he possessed in the cold of torpor, who said: “I will sit in the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north.” By the way of the south, Judea, in which the spiritual fathers burned with heavenly love. By the gate of the east, the Lord himself, of whom it is said: “Behold a man, the Orient is his name.” And: “the Orient from on high hath visited us.” The chambers of the singing men are therefore at the side of the north gate, because not only in Judea were the hearts of the saints spiritually kindled, but also among the Gentiles converted to the faith.
