But they received examples of this ardor from the spiritual fathers of the synagogue; whence: the chambers placed on the side of the north look toward the way of the south. It is to be noted, moreover, that the chambers are between the gate of the north and of the east, because after the incarnation of the Lord a multitude of the Gentiles came to the faith, and the hearts of the loving rise up among the faithful themselves and the sacraments of the Lord’s incarnation, which they love to the very marrow. The holy chambers therefore have on this side the gate of the north, on that side of the east, because among the very mysteries of their redemption which follow, and the carnal men whom they tolerate within holy Church, many of the Jews advance by strong love; and among those things which they love and those which they tolerate, like certain chambers they keep the riches of the spirit in the mind, and do not fail among these things, but stretch the eyes of the mind toward the southern way. For what do we suffer that our fathers did not endure for the love of God? The eastern gate is described as between the gate of the south and of the north, because the Lord, born of Judea, soon drew the Church from the Gentiles into his faith. The eastern gate also looks to the gate of the north, because the Lord forsook the synagogue and gathered the multitude of the Gentiles.
**“of the east gate”** — Gregory. Because after sins forgiven in baptism, and after faith received, we all offend in many things; therefore let us lift the eyes of the mind to the way of the south, so that, burning with holy charity, the heat of love may free us from the fault of sluggishness and coldness.
40.45:
**“And he said to me”** — the man, that is, who led me in.
**“this is the chamber which looketh towards the way”** — only.
**“southern”** — in which is the fullest light.
**“of the priests”** — that is, of the greater ones.
**“that watch”** — by praying, preaching, doing good, resisting evils, and defending the Church.
**“in the wards of the temple”** — which we are.
**“Of the priests”** — For these look only toward the southern way, who, occupied only with spiritual things, are always anxious about those things that belong to the love of God.
40.46:
**“But”** — but.
**“the chamber which looketh”** — because they desire to receive and save those who come from the north, who offer victims for sins.
**“to the way of the north”** — and the southern, understand.
**“shall be for the priests who watch”** — that is, of the lesser ones, who, while the greater attend to the greater, by correcting the lives of the carnal make them fit for sacrifice, so that in the sight of almighty God they set their flesh on fire for an odour of sweetness.
**“over the ministry of the altar”**
• of the outer.
• in which victims are offered for sin
**“these are the sons of Sadoc”** — both serving the Lord in their office
**“who come near”** — chosen
**“Levi”** — that is, of the faithful people taken up through the sacraments of faith and set apart from the faithless
**“to the Lord, that they may minister”** — the man that walked in the perfect way, he served me
**“to him”**
• not to himself
• Of the sons of Levi: Of these sons it is said: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to be made the sons of God.”
**“The priests who watch shall be”** — Those who preside over the correcting and examining of sins, and who turn their eyes back to the way of the north, that they may see in the minds of sinners what the chills of sloth are, and yet be warmed by the flame of charity.
**“The sons of Sadoc”** — Of the just, or of the justifying, that is, of almighty God, of whom: “The Lord is just, and hath loved justice: his countenance hath beheld righteousness.”
**“who come near of the sons of Levi”** — Jerome. Levi is interpreted “taken up”; and they are taken up by the Lord that they may come near to him, lest it be said of Moses alone: “Moses drew near to the Lord,” but that all who minister to God may be said to draw near.
40.47:
**“And”** — the same who brought me in, that is, into the inner court, that is, the holy of holies
**“he measured the court”** — the breadth of the faithful peoples
**“long”** — of hope
**“a hundred cubits”**
• because perfect
• that the priests of the Lord, serving in ministry, who had entered by the narrow and strait way, may have the broadest walking places, and may dwell in the perfect and complete number of virtues
**“and in breadth”** — of charity
**“foursquare”** — that the life of the faithful may be equally perfected in the four virtues: namely justice, fortitude, temperance and prudence
**“and the altar”** — the greater: a living victim, holy and pleasing to God
**“that was before the face”** — to be looked upon as an example
**“of the temple”**
• of the lesser, who nonetheless are the temple of God
• A hundred cubits in length and in breadth, etc. Gregory. The length of hope and the breadth of charity are not void in the hearts of the faithful, for through faith they work whatever they can. For “in Christ Jesus only faith availeth, which worketh by charity.” If therefore in the life of the faithful, each according to his measure, the longanimity of hope and the breadth of charity and the certainty of faith and the zeal of work are perfect, the court of the temple has a hundred cubits foursquare, in which all the sides are equal; for while we live in this life we find all these virtues equal in us. For as much as we love, so much we presume from hope, and as much as we believe, so much we love. But of faith and work John says: “He who saith that he knoweth God, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar.” For the knowledge of God pertains to faith, the keeping of the commandments to work. Yet charity is called greater than faith and hope, because when in the future those shall cease, this shall be perfected.
**“The court”** — The court itself, in which were two exedrae or treasuries, assigned as dwellings for the guardians of the temple or of the altar.
**“altar”** — That is, it was in the court itself, so that the prayer of the saints to the Lord may never cease.
40.48:
**“And he brought me into the porch of the temple: and he measured the porch five cubits”** — because he who had entered was instructed in divine senses, and went in neither to the right nor to the left, but by the royal way
**“on this side, and five cubits on that side: and the breadth”** — by which one enters into the porch of the temple
**“of the gate three cubits on this side”** — the mystery of the Trinity, which is the gate to the Lord, since the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both. This number is the one gate of those who, after baptism, come to salvation through the Trinity
**“On this side, and on that side”** — Jerome. It is elegantly said, not on the right nor on the left, lest there should seem to be anything left-handed in the holy of holies.
40.49:
**“And the length of the porch was twenty cubits, and the breadth eleven cubits, and there were eight”** — that is, by the sacred number
**“steps to go up to it”** — that is, the inner gate
**“And there were pillars in the fronts”**
• Whence: “He that shall overcome, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God.”
• Peter and John are called pillars of the Church
**“one on this side, and another on that side”**
• He does not say two, lest a dual number occur, but one and one, which is a perfect number.
• This number is taken for the unity of God.
**“twenty cubits”** — The number twenty, like the dual, because of the two tens, is wont to be taken in a bad sense, as is eleven, which lacks one to fill the sacred number, namely twelve; and yet they are said to be in the porch of the temple, because although the priests are holy and placed in the ministries of the temple and offer victims daily to Christ, yet because they dwell in a frail body subject to vices, they have twenty and eleven. Whence: “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?”
**“And there were pillars”** — The holy pillars of the Church: Peter and John, two pillars through whom we enter into the holy of holies, and by whose teaching our entrance is to Christ.

41.1:
**“And he brought me into the temple”** — At length, after many mysteries and various entrances, and in individual places their properties.
**“six cubits”** — Isidore. The sacrament of all creatures. For the world was made in six days; through knowledge of these, and of the causes and reason of their making, we enter into the temple of God, and from the order and constancy of creatures we know the Creator.
41.2:
**“And the breadth of the gate was ten cubits”** — Which is a sacred and perfect number, in which, in the seventh month on the tenth day of the month, is the fast of atonement.
**“and the sides of the gate five cubits on this side”** — Or shoulders. Whence: “I put my shoulder to work.” Also in the high priest’s vestment the shoulder-piece is bound with the breastplate, so that works may be completed by reason. Whence: “By thy commandments I have had understanding.”
**“and five cubits on that side: and he measured the length thereof forty cubits”** — Of the gate, of whose breadth and shoulders he has spoken only above.
**“and the breadth twenty cubits”** — Of ten cubits. Jerome. On the tenth day of the first month, which is called Nisan, the lamb is taken for the immolation and preparation of the pasch. In the seventh month, then, the tenths are offered into the barns of God, or, as Scripture is wont to say, the winepresses. Whence: be enlarged you also; so that when anyone has entered the temple through the ten cubits of the gate, the sides on both parts of it, or, as is properly said in the Hebrew, the shoulders, which refer to works, are measured. These shoulders of the gate on both sides have five cubits each, so that through the earthly and divine senses, of whose difference it was said above, they may enter the approaches of the temple.
**“The length thereof forty cubits, and the breadth twenty”** — Twenty times forty makes eight hundred, which number is near to eight. Whence: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight.” Or because through the tribulations and straits of this world we enter into the sanctuary of God. For forty is the number of labor. Whence: Moses and Elias fast by this number, and Israel is vexed and tried in the wilderness, and after many labors enters the land of promise. And our Lord, according to the frailty of the body he assumed, is tempted forty days in the wilderness, that after the victory the angels may come and minister to him.
*Jerome:* And twenty cubits in breadth. When after tribulations and straits we shall say with the apostles: “in all things we suffer tribulation, but are not distressed.” And with the prophet: “in tribulation thou hast enlarged me.” Then may the widest entrance be opened to us, which has a breadth of twenty cubits. This too is a dual number, that having overcome the struggles of the world and of earthly things they may enter the inmost parts of the temple, and we may hear with the disciples: “Have confidence, I have overcome the world.”
41.3:
**“Then going inward”** — Although we always advance, a greater progress is opened to us; whence, after entering the temple, he enters again inwardly.
**“two cubits”** — According to the higher sense, through the dual number we enter to the place where the holy of holies is. Whence: “and the gate six cubits”, through which, having entered, we possess eternal rest, which is shown in the sevenfold number.
41.4:
**“The length thereof twenty cubits”** — Because before the face of the temple, and at its very entrance, the measure of our past labour and struggle always meets us; for whatever reason the double holds in the single numbers, two tens have the same.
**“This is the holy of holies.”** — Jerome. Note that in the description of the tabernacle the holies of holies are spoken of in the plural, but here the holy of holies in the singular, that after the holies we may come to the holy, as after many songs to the Song of Songs, which is the song of all songs, which singing we are joined to the bridegroom and embrace him.
**“And he measured the length thereof twenty cubits, and the breadth twenty cubits, before the face of the temple: and he said to me: This is the holy of holies.”** — If the holy of holies is before the face of the temple, how great a blessedness must we judge to be in the inner parts of the temple? Whence: “This labour is before me, until I go into the sanctuary of God, and understand concerning their last ends.”
41.5:
**“And he measured the wall of the house”** — The holy of holies.
**“of six cubits”** — For the structure of the world and every visible creature that was made in six days.
**“and the breadth of every side chamber four cubits round about the house on every side”** — Not on one side only.
**“four cubits”** — Isidore. These four show the elements from which all things are compacted, and especially human bodies; fighting against these, and subjecting them to the power of the soul, the holy deserve to enter the inner parts and to know the secrets of the Lord.
41.6:
**“And the side chambers one by another, were twice thirty-three”** — Others: of three.
**“and they bore outwards, that they might enter in through the wall of the house in the sides round about, to hold in, and not to touch the wall of the temple”**
• And the side chambers, etc. Rabanus. The side chambers themselves, which were round about the house and were separated by four cubits from the wall of the temple, were joined to one another, so that one side chamber touched another, and had in length not thirty-three cubits but twice thirty-three, that is, sixty-six. In Leviticus it is said: at the birth of a male, after one week, both the woman who bore and the one who was born are to fulfil thirty-three days, that they may come to purification. But if she bear a female, they are to observe a double number, that is, sixty-six. And because to come to the holies of holies we need not only the first birth but also the second, that born in the flesh we may be born again in the spirit, therefore not sixty-six but twice thirty-three are set down, that each birth may be owed to God the author and to his elements, and that the side chambers which support the structure of the temple may go round the house in a double circuit.
• And there were projections, etc. For holy men break forth through the wall of the temple in the multitude of believers: namely through all the sides round about; and they hold up the foundations of the church, and yet they do not touch the wall of the temple, content only to have seen, and from afar to have adored the unspeakable mysteries; for we see now through a glass in a dark manner, and we cannot touch and comprehend in the fullest truth.
41.7:
**“round about”** — Isidore. This most beautiful figure is found even among the philosophers: the heaven, the sun, the moon and the other stars, and the point of the earth; and in human bodies the eyes, like other stars, and the shape of the head, which is the receptacle of all the senses; the rounded fingers and thighs and arms are marked by this roundness.
**“by winding stairs and into the upper loft”** — The things that are below are always narrower, in fasting and in the restraint of a single diet; and little by little, as we climb to the heights, a broader way opens to us; whence: “Thou hast enlarged me when I was in distress.”
**“into the upper loft”** — Rabanus. In the book of Kings, Eliseus and Elias had this upper room. And in the Acts of the Apostles: Tabitha, that is, Dorcas, and our Damula, who by good works had ascended to the heights. Peter also, upon whom the Lord set the foundations of the church, went up beyond the upper room and came to the roof, which in Greek is doma, that is, the sun-terrace of the roof, and learned the sacraments of the Church, unknown before to the world. The Saviour also, in a large and broad upper room, cleansed of all filth, furnished and prepared for a spiritual banquet, made the pasch, delivered to his disciples the mystery of his body and blood, and left us the eternal festival of the spotless Lamb.
41.10:
**“And between the chambers”** — Symmachus: exedras.
**“Six cubits, five cubits, twenty cubits”** — By these it is signified that from this world and from earthly senses, and from the dual number of two decades, which amounts to twenty, we deserve to ascend not only into the holy of holies but also into their upper rooms, and always to keep in memory that through the six days of our creation, and through the five senses, and through the twenty cubits of breadth, we have ascended to the upper room of the temple, and leaving earthly lowliness and the sense of the letter, we have passed over to the summit of the church, and rejoice in the fellowship of the Spirit.
41.11:
**“And the door of the side chambers was turned towards the place of prayer: one door was toward the north”** — From which evils blaze out upon the earth.
**“And the door of the side chambers”** — Fittingly the place of prayer is at the door toward the north, that according to the apostle we may pray without ceasing and say with Jeremias: let not the apple of my eye cease, whether desiring to avoid present evils or giving thanks for things past. For in the tabernacle of this body we always groan and say: “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?”
**“one door was toward the north”** — Jerome. For after the cold of the north we pass to the heat of the south; and yet again the place of prayer is within: at the door of the north, that we may escape dangers; in the south, that we may give thanks for things past, and the possession of victory may be secure for us. The five cubits also in this place indicate the divine senses, by which we ascend from earthly things to higher.
41.12:
**“And the building that was separate, and turned to the way that looked toward the sea, was seventy cubits broad: and the wall of the building, five cubits thick round about: and ninety cubits long.”** — That is, was.
**“And the building that was separate”** — That is, that after labours and dangers, and the waves and shipwrecks of this world, of which Jeremias writes, and Daniel and Zacharias, we may attain the true and lawful sabbath of seven decades, and eternal rest may be ours. And through the breadth of five cubits we come to the length of ninety cubits. At which age Sara, by the promise, bore a son, who at ninety years, that is, nine decades, brought forth Isaac, joined to Abraham, a hundred years old, that is, ten decades, who has the mystery. What this number signifies the following Scripture will show.
41.13:
**“And he measured the length of the house, a hundred cubits: and the separate building”** — From the holy of holies.
**“a hundred cubits”** — Jerome. This number is perfect, ten tens, that we may serve the Lord in mind, word and deeds, remembering that saying of the apostle: “that you may be able to comprehend what is the breadth, and length, and height, and depth.”
41.15:
**“And he measured the length of the building over against it, which was separated at the back of it”** — Others: behind the back.
**“the galleries on both sides a hundred cubits: and the inner temple, and the porches of the court.”** — Ecthetae, which they call solaria at Rome, projections from the walls of upper rooms, or maeniana from their inventor, which some of the Greeks call exostrae.
41.16:
**“The thresholds, and the oblique windows, and the galleries round about on three sides, over against the threshold of every one”** — The temple itself.
**“and floored with wood all round about.”** — Of wisdom and life, which is in paradise.
**“And the ground was up to the windows”** — Until that which is perfect comes.
**“And the oblique windows”** — Jerome. Pardon, reader, the difficulty, and grant forgiveness to one who confesses it; for we look through oblique windows, made in the manner of a net, and always closed, and we can scarcely send the eye as far as the inner house of our heart, so that all things we perceive we see in shadow and image, that we may cry out with the apostle: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God!” etc. Who has known the mind of the Lord, except the angel of great counsel, who, being worthy, can open his mysteries?
**“Galleries”** — Which they call solaria at Rome, projections from the walls of upper rooms, or maeniana from their inventor, which some of the Greeks call exostrae.
41.17: **“And even to the inner house, and without all the wall round about within and without, by measure.”** — For nothing in the temple of God is without measure and reason.
41.18:
**“And there were cherubims and palm trees wrought”**
• that is, in the wood, which reached from the pavement up to the windows
• the multitude of knowledge
**“and palm trees”**
• a sign of victory
• after the multitude of knowledge
**“so that a palm tree was between a cherub and a cherub”** — so that one was fenced in by the sides of two palm trees
**“and every cherub had two faces”** — not four, as above, namely of man, lion, calf and eagle
41.19:
**“The face of a man”** — in which is reason
**“was toward the palm tree on one side, and the face of a lion”** — in which is anger, which in Greek is more significantly called thymos; not that which is disturbance and next to vice, but that which strengthens the softness of the mind and makes the spirit of one fighting braver
**“was toward the palm tree on the other side: set forth through all the house round about.”** — The face of a man by the palm tree, etc. Rabanus. In the beginning we are subject to concupiscence, which is referred to the calf because of earthly works. And some things are carnal, others spiritual, the last of which is assigned to the eagle. But when we have entered the holy of holies and possessed the inner parts of the temple, we need nothing but reason and fortitude, of which the one is referred to understanding and foresight, the other to perseverance of soul. Every wall, therefore, round about the temple, from the pavement up to the ceilings, had cherubim and palm trees wrought with wonderful art. After these the sanctuary was opened through four corners, facing the face of the holy things. For first we have a multitude of knowledge, through which we win victory over the enemy, and afterwards the sanctuary is opened to us, and the temple, which has four corners, that is, a most firm standing that inclines to no side. For a square is made firm on a stable base, and in the mystical number four signifies the four elements, of which all solid and lasting things consist. And all things looked toward the face of the sanctuary, before which sanctuary was the appearance of an altar of wood.
41.22:
**“The altar of wood was three cubits high: and the length thereof was two cubits: and the corners thereof, and the length thereof, and the walls thereof were of wood. And he said to me”** — that is, the man who had brought me into the secret parts of the temple
**“This is the table before the Lord.”** — the wooden altar, which has corners and horns; which, namely, in the likeness of the bush burns and is not consumed; of which: “Thou hast prepared a table before me against them that afflict me.”
**“The altar of wood”** — On which fire is kindled, that is, the table of incense, which suffers nothing from the fire but in the fire becomes purer, like the works of the saints, of which the apostle says: “The fire shall try every man’s work, of what sort it is.” They do not perish, but are made purer and brighter by the fire. So the woods of the altar, which are of the trees of paradise, are not burnt by the fire of vices but are made purer. It is no wonder that this is believed of the sanctuary and the inner parts of the temple and the altar of incense, since even the acanthon, a kind of wood or like wood, becomes cleaner the more it burns.
41.23: **“and two doors”** — the sacraments of both testaments
41.24:
**“And in the two doors”** — so that in the history we may have the spiritual understanding, and in the tropology the truth of the history; for the one needs the other
**“on both sides were two little doors, which were folded within each other: for there were two wickets on both sides of the doors”** — In the two doors, etc. For in larger dining halls two doors are wont to cling together and be joined, so that the larger entrance is closed or opened not by two huge doors but by four smaller ones.
41.25:
**“And there were cherubims also wrought in the doors of the temple”** — of which it was said above
**“and the figures of palm trees”** — so that victory is given to those entering after the fullness of knowledge
**“like as were made on the walls: for which cause also the planks were thicker in the front of the porch without”** — Thicker planks, etc. That they might have firmness and be able to receive carving. According to the spiritual understanding, the doors are both firmer and carved, that they may have firmness and beauty, lest anyone like Ozias should be able to burst into the holy of holies and claim the priesthood for himself.
41.26:
**“Upon which were the oblique windows, and the representation of palm trees on this side, and on that side in the sides”** — the posts above the threshold
**“of the porch, according to the sides of the house”** — for nothing in God’s temple is without measure and wisdom
**“and the breadth of the walls”**
• Upon which were oblique windows, etc. Jerome. Or hidden, so that even the light itself which was given within might not have perfect knowledge, nor be a clear light open to all, but be hidden from many in part, because “we see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face.” And we do not yet know as we ought to know. “But when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away.”
• On this side and on that, in the little shoulders of the porch, etc. He beautifully did not put right and left, lest he seem to say anything sinister in these things which are great and hidden, but “on this side and on that”; whence: “If one strike thee on thy right cheek, turn to him also the other.” For in a holy man both are perfect.

42.1:
**“And he brought me forth”** — after I had contemplated the inner parts more diligently
**“into the outward court by the way that leadeth”** — otherwise, leaning
**“to the north, and he brought me”** — or brought in
**“into the chamber”** — The Seventy: an exedra; Theodotion: a pastophorion, that is, a chamber
**“that was over against the separate building”** — that is, receiving those who came from the north
**“and over against the house toward the north”**
• And he brought me forth. Out of despair and the greatness of the matter I had been resolving to pass over this present testimony in secret; but I judged it better to say something than to say nothing at all, taking up that saying of Socrates: I know that I know not. For part of knowledge is to know what you do not know.
• Leading to the north. Looking, that is, toward the parts of the north, but not set in the north, that the passage might be easier for those who were leaving the colds of the north, from which evils break forth upon the earth. We read in the Books of Numbers that Dan and Nephthali and Aser, the tribes of the sons of the handmaids of Rachel and Lia, kept their camp on the northern side. Now also in the front of the length there were a hundred cubits of the north door, and fifty of the side, so that from ten tens the square and perfect number, and from seven weeks, which is the number of remission, and into the beginning of the ogdoad, as of union, it bursts forth, the priestly spaces in the temple of God might be shown.
**“The way that leadeth to the north”** — This too he had seen above, before he penetrated the inner parts; but we see differently when we have perfect knowledge, and differently at the beginning of discipline. And it is necessary that he who has beheld the inner things should, according to the same form and measures, see both the hidden mysteries and the things that are outward.
42.2: **“was the length of a hundred cubits”** — has
42.3:
**“Over against the twenty cubits of the inner court, and over against the pavement of the outward court that was paved with stone”** — protecting the priests from rain and heat
**“Over against the twenty cubits of the inner court”** — It signifies that the hundred and the fifty of the outward court have the same force as the twenty of the inner court. For if you reckon four times five in the twenty, you will find both testaments, that the law may be held in the gospel, and the gospel not depart from the root of the law.
**“and over against the pavement of the outward court that was paved with stone”** — Rabanus. It signifies that the pavement of the outward court was laid with living stone, so that the steps of the priests might be defiled neither by the dust of summer nor the mud of winter; whence also the Lord, about to ascend to the Father, washed the feet of the apostles, that they might ascend to the kingdoms of heaven with clean and purified steps. He also said: “Shake off the dust from your feet,” that is, that they should suffer nothing of earthly gifts to remain with them from those people.
**“where there was a gallery joined to a triple gallery”** — Where there was a portico joined to a triple portico, etc. Rabanus. In which the mystery of the Trinity is shown: which, though it is divided into the names of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, is nevertheless joined together in one divinity.
42.4:
**“And before the chambers”** — some say exedras, others chambers
**“a walk ten cubits broad, looking to the inner parts of a way of one cubit. And their doors were toward the north”** — of the exedras or storerooms which were in the upper parts, lower ones. Whence: “The greater thou art, the more humble thyself in all things”; as Paul says: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle.”
**“ten cubits broad”** — Of ten cubits in breadth: the perfect number, that is, either on account of the decalogue of the law or the mystery of the gospel. For if from one you come through two and three to the fourth, the ten is made, and the number of the gospels, in whose breadth the priests walk, going before each of the treasuries.
**“looking to the inner parts of a way of one cubit”** — Rabanus. For priests ought always to look to the inner parts of his way, which leads to one cubit, that is, the worship of one Godhead. Whence: “I have manifested thy name to men.” For this is the way looking to the inner parts, which says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No man cometh to the Father, but by me.” For no one comes to the Father except through the Son.
42.5:
**“Where were the store chambers”** — the treasure-houses of the Lord’s treasures
**“lower above: because they bore up the galleries, which appeared above out of them”** — namely, which enjoyed free air
**“lower above”** — Upper chambers. Whence in the Psalm: “Who waterest the mountains from thy upper rooms.” For unless one has been a mountain and has risen to higher things, he is not watered by the rains of the Lord. They are watered, according to the diversity of their merits, from the first, second and third upper chamber.
**“from the lower parts, and from the midst of the building”** — They appeared above from the lower parts, etc. So that the second upper room might be higher than the pavement of the lower house, and the third higher than the second; and the higher one went up, the loftier the upper room he used, which grew from humility. Whence: “He that will be greater among you, let him be the least of all.”
42.6:
**“For they were of three stories, and had not pillars, as the pillars of the courts”** — of the building
**“fifty cubits from the ground”** — the number of the remission of all debts
**“of three stories”** — Of which: “Describe them to thyself threefold, by counsel and knowledge, that thou mayest answer words of truth.” The lower and outer parts need columns; the higher and inner parts do not have the use of columns, that is, of foreign help.
42.7:
**“And the outward wall”** — the outer wall which surrounds the store chambers
**“that went about by the chambers, which were towards the outward court on the forepart of the chambers, was fifty cubits long”** — as above
**“Chambers”** — Of the singers who guard the altar; their breadth was as great as their length, fifty cubits.
42.8:
**“For the length of the chambers of the outward court was fifty cubits: and the length”** — which was between the temple and the northern house
**“before the face of the temple”** — of the inner court
**“a hundred cubits”** — Not fifty, as of the store chambers; so that after the remission of all sins we may await the perfect rewards in the hundredfold number.
42.9: **“And there was under these chambers, an entrance”** — For it behooves us to possess the riches of God, and from the outward court to find an entrance under the treasury of the east, and through the height of the enclosure that looks to the way of the east to come to the building set apart for the holy, before which are the treasuries; and in the very way there is a likeness of the treasuries that were in the way of the north. For although we come to the entrance of the east, yet the likeness of the greater is in the lesser, and we cannot come to the light of the east except by the way of the north, that is, by the lesser and the humbler we aspire to the greater and the higher.
42.11: **“And the way before them was like the chambers which were toward the north: they were as long as they, and as broad as they: and all the going in to them, and their fashions”** — that is, the length was like the breadth, that is, the same measure, by the square
42.12:
**“According to the doors of the chambers”** — they had the same measure and likeness as the store chambers which were on the way facing the south
**“that were towards the south”** — or south
**“towards the south”** — Jerome. For leaving the cold of the north behind by the east, we come to the south, in which the bridegroom rests at noon, that is, dwells in full light.
**“there was a door in the head of the way”** — Unless it has been opened by him who says, “I am the door,” and “hath the key of David,” we cannot reach the vestibule of the saints, set apart by virtues, and which receives those coming from the north.
42.13:
**“And he said to me”** — my guide, that is, he who led me into the outer court, and showed me the aforesaid store chambers or exedrae, of which much has been said
**“The chambers of the north, and the chambers of the south”**
• that is, which are to the north and to the south
• Rabanus. I think there are things that contain either the simplicity of history or spiritual understanding, so that through the north we may come to the south; for the letter is not to be read so, and the foundations of history laid so, that we do not come to the heights, nor is the roof to be set upon the most beautiful building from above in such a way that there are no solid foundations.
**“which are before the separate building: they are holy chambers, in which the priests shall eat, that approach to the Lord into the holy of holies: there they shall lay the most holy things, and the offering”** — the victim of the burnt offering
**“for sin, and for trespass”** — of ignorance
**“in which the priests shall eat”** — Hence we learn that there are many kinds of food, of which it is lawful or not lawful for priests to eat, and which may be taken as food not in all places, nor by all, nor at all times.
**“The priests that approach”** — Rabanus. The priests who eat in the storerooms, in which there are many riches, are the very ones who approach to the Lord, of whom it is written that Moses approached to the Lord, the others could not. In the building of the mystical temple and the sacrament of the Church there are many priests and apostolic men who draw near to the Lord, and not to any place whatever but into the holy of holies: “there they shall lay the most holy things,” etc.
**“for it is a holy place”** — And the offerings, etc. So that they may not only offer a continual sacrifice, but, according to the diversity of times and the quality of sin and of ignorance, may know how to appease the Lord; for the place is holy, and in it the dignity of the priesthood dwells.
42.14:
**“And when the priests shall have entered in, they shall not go out of the holy places into the outward court: but there”** — within
**“they shall lay their vestments”** — in the innermost parts of the temple
**“wherein they minister, for they are holy”** — therefore they should not be declared to those who lack perfect holiness
**“they shall not go out”** — To those, namely, who cannot penetrate the inner parts of the temple nor know the secrets of divine knowledge, with the garments in which they had been clothed within, the bowels of mercy and the Lord the Saviour; whence: “Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ”; nor shall they use those words of which God speaks: my mystery is for me and mine, lest they give that which is holy to dogs, and pearls to swine.
**“they shall put on other garments, and so they shall go forth to the people”** — And so they shall go forth to, etc. They will so speak to the people as the people can hear; whence that saying: “I gave you milk to drink,” not, that is, solid food, “for you were not able as yet.” And that: “My little children, of whom I am in labour again, until Christ be formed in you.” For to little ones and sucklings solid food is not only of no profit, but kills them; which suits men of perfect age.
42.15:
**“Now when he had made an end”** — the aforesaid man
**“of measuring the inner house, he brought me out by the way of the gate”** — not the outer court but by way of the gate, etc.
**“that looked toward the east: and”** — first
**“He measured it on every side round about.”**
• otherwise, the likeness of the house round about, in order
• And when he had made an end, etc. He shows that all the things said above, in the outer and inner parts of the temple, that is, the holy of holies, belong properly to the building of the temple, and of the inner temple. Whence it follows: “he brought me out by the way of the gate that looked toward the east: and he measured it,” etc.
**“Round about”** — Others take it to be a likeness, not the house itself, because “we see now through a glass in a dark manner.” “But when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away.” Whence Moses in the tabernacle and Solomon in the building of the temple made not the truth of the tent and of the temple but a likeness and figure, that through lesser and earthly things we may understand heavenly and spiritual things.
*Rabanus:* First he measured toward the eastern quarter five hundred reeds round about. Secondly toward the north, thirdly toward the south, fourthly toward the sea, that is, the west: through the four winds, that is, the wall round about, as much in length as in breadth, foursquare. This wall had together two thousand reeds. But if a reed was of six cubits and of the sixth part of a cubit, it is plain that the outer wall had round about two thousand reeds, which make twelve thousand three hundred thirty-three cubits and a third, from the two thousand reeds. In the Book of Jesus Nave, in the suburbs, this measure is carefully kept. The legion of devils also chose this number for the drowning of the swine, so that what was separated by the precept of the Lord from those who serve God might be referred to the opposite side, to the perdition of those who lead a life worthy of filth and foulness. Every wall that is outer and has a spacious length and breadth foursquare contains the number of the apostles, that is, twelve thousand, so that a thousand is reckoned to each apostle, and yet it does not come to the measure of the fulness of Christ and of the perfect man unless there be joined to it also the palm-breadth, which makes three hundred thirty-three cubits and a third part of a cubit, through which the mystery of the Trinity is shown, which girds and fortifies all things and renders the dwellers in its temple most safe. Whence the ark of Noe has a length of three hundred cubits and a height of thirty cubits, which is finished in one cubit. But that fifty cubits are added there in breadth is a sacrament of remission. Whence also the Lord came at thirty years to baptism, and Ezechiel at the beginning of the volume sets the thirtieth year, and the three hundred thirty-third number is completed by three added and a third part. But as for what the Septuagint have, and the Latin translation, while in the speed of dictating we look less carefully, namely “the wall of it round about, a length of five hundred cubits,” the Hebrew truth does not have this, but simply a length of five hundred, and the Latin of five hundred, so that “reeds” is understood.
42.16: **“And he measured toward the east, with the measuring reed, five hundred reeds with the measuring reed round about.”** — that is, the quarter
42.20:
**“Five hundred cubits long”** — The five-hundredth, which is near the fiftieth, pertains to the remission of all sins. Whence: “the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty.”
**“making a separation between the sanctuary”** — From this we have the whole description above of the temple, which was entrusted to the priests who are the sons of Sadoc for their ministry. This wall, however, was spread out over so great a space that, containing the whole, it separates the sanctuary and the place of the common people.

43.2:
**“And behold the glory of the God of Israel came in by the way of the east, and his voice was like the noise of many waters, and the earth shone with his majesty.”** — God
**“like the noise of many waters”** — many waters: many peoples
**“By the way of the east”** — By which it had gone out when the city of the Lord was struck with fury. But it enters, or rather returns to it, because he had shown the temple of the Lord on the mountain; and yet what is said in what follows is much more: “The Spirit lifted me up,” etc. For here only the glory of the God of Israel enters; there it is said that the fulness of the glory of the Lord was in the temple. Whence also Isaias: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and elevated: and his train filled the temple,” which is when, “with open face beholding the glory of the Lord,” we are reformed into the image of the Creator.
**“And his voice was”** — One voice, on account of the one consent in the praise of God, though of many waters. But the voice of those singing is doubled, to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts,” etc.
*Rabanus:* And the earth shone with his majesty. Which was done properly at the coming of Christ, when “their sound hath gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the whole world.” And it is fulfilled daily in believers, and will be perfectly fulfilled when “this corruptible shall put on incorruption.”
43.3: **“Chobar”** — Which signifies burden and weight. For what is heavier than the rivers of Babylon? Of which: “Upon the rivers of Babylon there we sat and wept, when we remembered thee, O Sion.” Of which it is written: “for the fashion of this world passeth away.” For nothing in the confusion of this age is lasting, but all things pass away and flow. But whoever considers this falls upon his face, understanding how far he is from the majesty of God, and bends his knees to the Father in the name of Jesus Christ.
43.4: **“And the majesty of the Lord”** — when I had fallen
43.5:
**“And the spirit lifted me up”** — because, lying down, I could not proceed
**“and brought me into the inner court”** — because I had fallen outside
**“and behold the house was filled with the glory of the Lord”** — as one who had earlier seen the glory of the Lord of Israel coming by the east way; I saw the house filled with the glory of the Lord
43.6:
**“and I heard him speaking to me”** — it is not said what, unless perhaps that saying of the apostle: “I heard secret words, which it is not granted to man to utter.”
**“out of the house”** — inner
**“And a man”** — that is, the Lord, to whom alone belongs what follows: the place of my throne, etc.
43.7:
**“Said to me: Son of man, the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet”**
• the Church
• His place is in peace, which surpasses all understanding
**“where I dwell in the midst of the children of Israel”** — of those who see the Lord
**“for ever”** — not for a time, as in the temple of Solomon
**“and they shall not profane”** — These are those who live holily and purely in the Church.
**“the house of Israel shall no more profane my holy name, they and their kings”**
• both the people and their kings
• they defiled, namely
**“by their fornications”** — by which they committed fornication against God
**“and by the carcasses”** — who vainly claimed the royal name for themselves
**“of their kings”** — for the arrogant offends God; the humble one calls forth mercy
**“and the place of the soles of my feet”** — We will adore in the place where his feet stood. And rightly it is said, the apostles stood. In the Church, indeed, the feet of the Lord stand. In the synagogue they walk about and pass by.
43.8:
**“who have set”** — through pride
**“their threshold by my threshold”** — so that there would be nothing between the holy and the profane
**“and their posts by my posts”** — which before
**“and there was but a wall between me and them, and they profaned my holy name by the abominations which they committed, for which reason”** — namely the higher causes
**“I consumed them in my wrath”**
• They who have set, etc. Rabanus. Let them hear this, according to the letter, the silly women laden with sins, who are carried about with every wind of doctrine, “ever learning, and never attaining to the knowledge of the truth”: that it is a mind joined to God, not the nearness of churches and a dwelling close to God, that provokes his mercy in itself, but rather that God’s indignation is stirred when the unworthy dwell in consecrated places.
• And they profaned my holy name, etc. Rabanus. What does nearness of dwelling profit, and a wall between our cell and the altar of the Lord, when with the things which we do in secret, and which it is shameful even to say, the name of the Lord is defiled and polluted? I think that none pollutes the name of the Lord except one who is seen to believe in his name and to be reckoned by his title. And as he takes away the members of Christ to make them the members of a harlot who first believed in Christ, so he pollutes the name of the Lord who first received the faith of his name. Otherwise the heathen and the Jew, since they are themselves polluted, and the very defilement and pollution, cannot pollute and defile the name of the Lord; it is those to whom it is said who pollute it: “By you my name is blasphemed among the Gentiles.”
**“And their posts”** — So that there would be one entrance for priests and laity. Whence the apostle: “But let a man prove himself, and so let him approach the body and blood of the Lord.”
**“And there was but a wall between me and them”** — So that a short wall would separate the priestly sacrifices and the places of the sacraments of the body and blood of the Lord.
43.9:
**“Now therefore let them put away”** — as if the Lord said to the prophet: nevertheless command that they put away their fornication, etc.
**“their fornication far from me, and the carcasses of their kings”** — because I abhor such things
**“and I will dwell in the midst of them for ever”** — not for a time, as in the synagogue
**“And I will dwell in the midst of them”** — He promises at once the reward of good work: “and I will dwell in the midst of them.” Whence: “there hath stood one in the midst of you, whom you know not.” Not for a short time, as in the synagogue, but always, which is proved in the Church of Christ.
43.10:
**“But thou, son of man, shew to the house of Israel”** — of them, that is, of those who behold God with the mind
**“the temple and”**
• the temple having been seen
• in the mind
• the great reward of the temple seen
**“let them be ashamed of their iniquities, and let them measure the building”** — “Show to the house,” etc. Rabanus. It is no small work to show to hearers what you have seen with the eyes of the flesh or in the mind, so that they themselves seem to have seen it with you.
**“The temple”** — Jerome. That it is on a mountain, indeed on the summit of the mountain, so that we may not think it that house which is told to have been built by Solomon in the books of Kings and Paralipomenon. For that one was of another order and measure, and had great difference in each particular, being so much inferior to the temple which is now shown to Ezechiel that not only its worshippers and keepers but even its builder Solomon sinned and offended God, though afterwards he did penance, writing Proverbs, in which he says: “Last of all I did penance, I looked back that I might choose instruction.” But this house, which is shown to the house of Israel through Ezechiel, is such that whoever has beheld it in his mind ceases from his iniquities for desire of it. Whence: “O Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house; and the place where thy glory dwelleth.” And: “One thing I have asked of the Lord, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life,” when, that is, I shall begin to live and be with Christ, who is the life of believers.
43.11:
**“And”** — the measures and proportions of the building having been seen
**“be ashamed of all that they have done, the form of the house and its fashion”** — of them, that is, of those who go out to those who are outside
**“and the goings out”** — of them, that is, of those who through the teaching of masters penetrate to the high and inner things
**“and the whole plan thereof”** — The Seventy: substance, that is, furnishings, namely riches
**“and all its ordinances, and all its order, and all its laws, shew them”** — who are confounded for their iniquities
**“and thou shalt write it in their sight, that they may keep all its forms”** — therefore you will show it, that they may keep it; otherwise it profits nothing to know the description
**“and its ordinances, and do them”** — in work
**“The descriptions”** — “In my Father’s house there are many mansions.” And elsewhere: he has set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the sons of Israel or of the sons of God.
43.12:
**“This is the law of the house”** — which is, namely
**“upon the top”** — “A city seated on a mountain cannot be hid”; of which: the rush of the river makes glad the city of the Lord, that is, the church
**“of the mountain”** — the summit of the mountains, from which the prince of Tyre was wounded
**“All its border”** — the boundaries
**“thereof”** — of the house
**“round about is most holy; this then is the law of the house”** — that is, said or to be said
**“Is most holy”** — Rabanus. In the tabernacle which was made by Moses and in the temple built by Solomon, only the inner parts, where were the cherubim and the propitiatory and the ark of the testament and the table of incense, were called the holy of holies; but in this house all the borders are reckoned as holy of holies.
43.13:
**“And these are the measures of the altar by the truest cubit”** — perfect
**“which is a cubit and a handbreadth”** — of the altar
**“was a cubit”** — that is, which receives those things consumed by fire
**“and a cubit”** — another
**“the breadth; and the border”** — otherwise, a boundary
**“unto its edge”** — in place of which Jerome has put “above the crown”
**“round about, one handbreadth”** — the height of the hollow
**“and this was the trench of the altar”**
• But these are the measures, etc. Rabanus. Who shall search out the abyss and wisdom? “O the depth of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God,” etc. In Exodus the altar was of five cubits in length and five in breadth; here, withdrawing from the five senses, it tends to unity, in which is the truest cubit, to which is joined a handbreadth, that is, a palm, having the sixth part of a cubit.
• This is briefly shown: that around the circuit of the altar itself, on its edge and in the circle of the altar itself, the lip was turned back and like a crown, graceful to look at in the manner of a lily.
**“And a cubit in the breadth”** — Rabanus. So that the inner parts, that is, the secret parts, and the spaces of the altar, which are shown in the breadth, might be ended in one cubit. And the border thereof unto its edge. Round about the altar, that is, at the margin and circle, there was a spreading lip, like a crown in the manner of a lily, most beautiful to see.
**“This also was the trench”** — For the lower and deep parts, which cling to the earth, are contained in the number two, which suits unclean animals. But the upper parts, reaching to the ledge or to the propitiatory, have the breadth of one cubit, so that the number two may pass over to the solitary and to the good of marriage, and what is lower may come to the blessedness of union.
43.14:
**“And from the bottom of the ground to the lowest brim”** — the greatest propitiatory
**“two cubits, and the breadth of one cubit: and from the greater brim to the lesser brim”** — Septuagint: to the lesser mercy-seat, unto the greater mercy-seat
**“From the lesser brim unto”** — Rabanus. From the lesser propitiatory, etc. The lesser propitiatory is the stone cut out of the mountain without hands. The great propitiatory is the same stone which grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth. Or the lesser propitiatory is when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; the great propitiatory, when he received the glory which he had with the Father before the world was made; for we first acknowledge the lowly things of Christ, and so come to the height of the divinity. And the propitiatory of both natures belongs only to the sacrament of the one altar. Between the two propitiatories are four cubits, signifying the four elements of the world, which themselves also come to the breadth of one cubit. And it is to be noted that in the measure of the altar the first cubit in breadth is joined to none, but is perfect by its own unity. But the second cubit of breadth, after two cubits, grows to the top. And the third, after the lesser and the greater propitiatory, through the four elements tends to the mystery of one cubit, so that the first and second and third cubit in the altar of the Lord are said to be not first, second and third, but one and one and one.
43.15: **“And the Ariel itself”** — My light is God, according to some; according to Jerome, lion or strength of God. Which is properly referred to the altar, in which is either the illumination of God or the lion and his strength. Whence: “A lion’s whelp, my son Juda,” etc. It is of four cubits and has four horns; or the upper parts of the four horns are ended in one cubit, so that the measure of the gospels, and their strength running through the whole world, may be shown under the illumination of God and the strength of the lion, and they may come to one cubit of divine confession.
43.16:
**“And the Ariel”** — he reveals gradually
**“twelve”** — on account of the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles
**“Foursquare, with equal sides”** — Through the four sides, on every side twelve cubits make likewise forty-eight cubits of the priestly cities, so that, as it were by these foundations divided through the whole world, the strength of the Church may be made firm.
43.17:
**“And the brim”** — Septuagint: mercy-seat. Symmachus: circuit
**“fourteen cubits long, and fourteen cubits broad in the four corners thereof, and the crown”** — Septuagint: Sion
**“was about it”** — of the mercy-seat
**“half a cubit, and the bottom of it”** — Symmachus: completion
**“one cubit round about: and its steps”** — of the mercy-seat
**“And the brim fourteen cubits”** — It signifies that our Lord, who is truly the propitiation, not only for our sins but for the whole world, came through fourteen generations from Abraham to David, and again through another fourteen to the captivity of Jechonias, and by the sacrament of the same number descended to earthly things, so that in the third fourteen, by the sacrament of the divine number, he might save the four corners of the world, of which it is said: “Many shall come from the east and the west, and the north and the south, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.”
**“Half a cubit”** — For sinners, who are saved only by the mercy of the Creator. Whence: “For nothing shalt thou save them.”
**“One cubit”** — In which the just are saved, by the number, namely the single and perfect one that imitates the one divinity. Whence the Apostle: “For God indeed was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself”; by whose propitiation both sinners and the just are reconciled.
**“turned toward the east”** — And the steps thereof, etc. Rabanus. These are the twenty-four books of the Old Testament, which in the Apocalypse of John have harps and crowns on their heads. Or the sacraments of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, in which true propitiation is given to us. And on this account the number of the steps is left uncertain, so that however great the zeal with which we have climbed to higher things, we may think ourselves to be among the lower, reflecting on that: “They shall go from virtue to virtue.”
43.18:
**“And he said to me”** — With these things shown, the aforesaid man teaches how, the work being finished, the altar ought to be cleansed and consecrated: first, namely, the victim is offered and given to the priests.
**“Holocaust”** — Rabanus. Note that the calf is offered whole as a holocaust, and the fatness of its body is consumed by divine fire. “And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, but now we know him so no longer.” But the he-goat is offered on the second day indeed as a victim, but the holocaust is reserved for the excellence of the Lord. It is also to be noted that, according to the Hebrew, Ezechiel himself, as a priest, is commanded to take the calf and make the holocaust and sprinkle its blood round about, both on the altar and on the corners and on the crown or base. But the Septuagint show other priests doing this. But Ezechiel himself too is of the number of the priests.
43.19:
**“And thou shalt give to the priests, and the Levites, that are of the race of Sadoc”** — the just
**“who approach to me, saith the Lord God, to offer to me a calf”** — who was sacrificed for us
43.20:
**“And thou shalt take of his blood”** — by which we were redeemed
**“and shalt put it upon the four horns thereof”**
• of the altar
• because by this blood the four quarters of the world are purified
**“And”** — that all things may be cleansed and the propitiation may be firm
**“upon the four corners of the brim”** — others: of the mercy-seat
**“and upon the crown”** — others: the base
**“round about”** — of the mercy-seat
**“and thou shalt cleanse, and expiate it”** — the altar of Christ is cleansed by blood, so that the prayers of the saints may come pure to God
43.22:
**“And in the second day thou shalt offer a he goat without blemish for sin: and they shall expiate”** — in the goat
**“a he goat”** — Because it is an animal always hastening to high places, and suffering no danger on the cliffs, and there finds a way where other animals find ruin; whence in Greek the flock of goats is called the way of life of the lofty.
**“the altar, as they expiated it with the calf”** — Those about to keep the Passover take from the flock a lamb and a kid. And those who could not keep the Passover at first, keep it in the second month; one of which belongs to penitents, the other to the just.
43.23:
**“And when thou shalt have made an end of the expiation thereof, thou shalt offer a calf”** — Moses, the meekest
**“of the herd without blemish, and a ram”** — Elias, like Moses; whence he dares to say, I alone am left
**“of the flock without blemish”**
• A calf of the herd without blemish, etc. Rabanus. Moses and Elias appear on the mountain with the Lord, that is, the law and the prophets, who announced that he was to suffer in Jerusalem.
• After the altar and its measures were shown on the top of the mountain, and the consecration and expiation through one calf without blemish and a he-goat, or, according to the Septuagint, two kids, of which the calf pertains to Christ, and the others to the apostles and ministers, lest in the consecration of the spiritual altar, which properly pertains to the Church, the law and the prophets should seem to be excluded. Therefore, the altar being consecrated, a calf without blemish and a ram are taken up and are offered in the sight of the Lord. And the sons of Sadoch, that is, the priests of the just, sprinkle salt upon their heads, that the law, namely, and the prophets may be seasoned with the savour of the gospel; nor is there any sacrifice, according to the command of the law and the apostle (who says: “let your speech be seasoned with salt”), that lacks salt. And each is offered as a holocaust to the Lord, that the body, which is signified in the law, and the cloudiness of prophecy, may be converted by the fire of the Lord, that is, the Holy Spirit (of whom it is said, “fervent in spirit”), into a spiritual and subtle substance.
43.25:
**“seven days”** — the altar having been cleansed
**“thou shalt offer a he goat”** — the word
**“for sin daily: they shall offer also a calf”** — the work
**“of the herd, and a ram”** — thought
**“A he goat for sin”** — That by these sacrifices the altar is cleansed to perfection over seven days. In the seven is signified the sabbath rest that is kept for the people of God, in which we hope for true rest, and do not do the servile work of sin.
*Rabanus:* In the he-goat and the calf and the ram are shown the three general sins to which the human race is subject. For we sin either by thought, or by word, or by deed. Thought pertains to the ram; it is the first of all sins, and from it two kinds are born. The kid and the he-goat pertain to speech, which disputes about higher things. Works are signified in the calf, which is made subject to the plough and to labour and to earthly works. These, therefore, we ought to offer to God without blemish through the seven days of the true and perfect sabbath, and to expiate the altar, that our prayer may come clean to God.
43.26:
**“Seven days shall they expiate the altar, and shall cleanse it: and they shall consecrate it”** — Septuagint: their hands
**“And they shall consecrate it”** — By the gifts of the sacrifice, namely for the high priest, for the priests, and for the people, so that no one stands empty before the Lord.
43.27:
**“And the days being expired, on the eighth day and thenceforward, the priests shall offer your holocausts upon the altar, and the peace offerings: and I will be pacified towards you”** — pleased with these
**“On the eighth day”** — That they may say with the apostle: “we are risen with Christ,” and may reach beyond the eighth day to heavenly things, and offer for us a holocaust, or the things that are for the peace of our sins and our salvation, that through the fire of the Holy Spirit all that we think, speak and do may be converted into spiritual substance.

44.1:
**“And he brought me back to the way of the gate of the outward sanctuary, which looked towards the east: and it was shut”** — virgin Mary; virgin before childbirth; virgin in childbirth; virgin after childbirth
**“And he brought me back”** — There are many gates in the description of the temple, both within and outside the altar, whose figure and consecration and sacrifices the preceding discourse runs through; this finished, it comes to the outer gate of the sanctuary, which looked toward the east, and was shut. Whence also “he brought me back to the way.”
**“The gate of the sanctuary”** — Of which: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites; and woe to you, doctors of the law, who take away the key of knowledge. You yourselves do not enter, etc. This is the book sealed in Isaias; this is the book whose seals no one can loose and open except the lion of the tribe of Juda.
44.2:
**“And the Lord said to me: This gate”** — knowledge of the Scriptures
**“shall be shut, it shall not be opened”** — fully
**“And a man”** — although perfect in comparison with others
**“shall pass through it: because the Lord the God of Israel”** — alone
**“hath entered in by it”**
• whence: “The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the most High shall overshadow thee.”
• who entered with the doors closed
**“and it shall be shut”**
• THIS GATE WAS SHUT, etc. Rabanus. Before the Saviour took on a human body and, taking the form of a servant, humbled himself, the law and the prophecy and all knowledge of the Scriptures were shut; paradise was closed.
• But after he hung on the cross and said to the thief, “this day thou shalt be with me in paradise,” at once the veil of the temple was rent and all things were opened, and the veil being taken away we say: “but we all beholding the glory of the Lord with open face,” etc. If all things have been revealed in Christ, how will the gate be shut and not be opened? But although we have come to the highest knowledge, in comparison with divine knowledge “we know in part,” “we know in part”; “but when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away.” Whence Paul too calls himself now perfect, now imperfect. For he is perfect in comparison with others, imperfect in comparison with divine knowledge.
• But that the eastern gate beyond the bounds of the world is always shut, John makes known when he says: “No man hath seen God at any time: the only begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.” As if he had said in other words: “And it shall be shut for the prince, and the prince himself shall sit in it” to eat bread of perfect and consummate knowledge. “But no one knoweth the Son but the Father, and no one knoweth the Father but the Son, and he to whom it shall please the Son to reveal him.”
**“it shall be shut”** — Rabanus. For no one can know the sacraments of the Lord’s passion and body and blood, in keeping with the majesty of the thing; but so great is the goodness and clemency of our prince that, although he sits alone in the gate which is shut and eats bread before the Lord, yet he wishes to have many companions at his table, and says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock: if any man open to me, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.” But he eats bread alone before the Lord, because his substance and divine nature is separated from all.
44.3:
**“For the prince”**
• of the Word of God
• Septuagint: or leader
• at whose coming it will be unlocked
• for his use
**“The prince himself”** — Christ, namely, who is a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech, himself the victim
**“shall sit in it, to eat”** — with us
**“his bread”** — heavenly bread and wine, of which: “I will not drink from henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I shall drink it with you new in the kingdom of my Father”; namely, that kingdom of which it is said: “The kingdom of God is within you.”
**“before the Lord: by the way of the porch of the gate”** — because he is poured into all within
**“shall enter in”** — so that he may lead in those who cannot enter by themselves
**“and by the same way”** — because he is poured around all outside
**“shall go out”** — so that he may lead others out and speak to those who cannot grasp harder things
44.4:
**“And he brought me”** — the aforesaid man
**“by the way of the north gate, in the sight of the house”** — of the temple, namely
**“And I saw, and behold the glory of the Lord filled the house”** — the temple, namely
**“of the Lord: and I fell on my face”**
• not able to bear the majesty
• And I fell on my face, etc. Lest, desiring to see more than human frailty can bear, he lose the very light of his eyes. Whence: the Lord calls him more familiarly son of man.
**“and behold the glory filled”** — Rabanus. At the completion of the tabernacle and in the building of Solomon’s temple the glory of the Lord appeared, which afterwards was destroyed in comparison with the glory of the gospel. Whence Paul: “For even that which was glorious in this part was not glorified, by reason of the glory that excelleth.” But let us not think the destruction of the former glory an abolition; rather, “when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away,” as if you compared a lamp or a lantern with the rays of the sun. Whence: “He was a burning and a shining light,” etc. But after the sun of justice came, the light of the lantern was hidden; whence: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”
44.5:
**“And the Lord said to me”** — because, having fallen humbly, he deserved to be strengthened
**“Son of man, set thy face against mount Seir, and prophesy concerning it, and say to it”** — first
**“thy heart”** — the mind
**“and behold”** — second
**“with thy eyes”** — the inner ones, of which it is said to Abraham: “Lift up thy eyes, and see the stars of heaven”
**“And”**
• and
• “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.”
**“with thy ears, hear all”** — the ceremonies of the temple and the statutes
**“that I say to thee concerning all the ceremonies of the house of the Lord, and concerning all the laws thereof: and”** — finally
**“attend with thy heart”** — because the many entrances signify the order of the ceremonies
**“mark well the ways of the temple, with all the goings out of the sanctuary”** — that is, it is a preface and a preparation of the prophet for understanding those things which he is afterwards to learn concerning the order of the temple
**“ceremonies”** — Rabanus. Note that in this quarter of the world, which lies in the wicked one and is set in the cold of the north, the order of the heavenly ceremonies is shown to us.
44.6:
**“And thou shalt say to the house of Israel that provoketh me: Thus saith the Lord God: Let all your wicked doings suffice you, O house of Israel”** — that is, the first sin
**“suffice you”** — He exhorts to repentance for earlier sins, lest by adding sins to sins we prepare fuel for the future fire.
44.7:
**“In that you have brought in strangers uncircumcised in heart, and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in my sanctuary, and to defile my house: and you offer my bread”** — namely, of the showbread, sprouting in all churches from the one bread
**“the fat”** — from which fat of wheat he satisfied them
**“and the blood”** — which was poured out by the passion of Christ
**“and you have broken my covenant by all your wicked doings”** — as if, since you bring such men into the sanctuary and defile my house, how do you dare to offer the bread, etc.? namely, the mystical sacraments; and you do not understand that you have broken my covenant, etc.
**“In that you have brought in”** — “A little leaven corrupteth the whole lump.” In some copies it reads: Bring not the wicked into the tabernacle of the just.
**“strangers”** — Rabanus. Strangers, unless circumcised in heart, flesh, ears, lips, eyes, taste, and smell, ought not to be brought into the sanctuary. Let bishops and priests hear this, lest they bring in such men. Whence: “Impose not hands lightly upon any man.”
**“uncircumcised”** — We circumcise our heart with the knife of God, and take away the foreskin, when shameful thoughts do not go out of our heart, lest it be said of us: “The heart of this people is grown gross.” The flesh likewise is circumcised if men are given over not to luxury but only to necessity in food, in clothing, and the rest, that it may hear: “This day have I taken away the reproach of Egypt from you”; for the Egyptians are of great flesh.
44.8:
**“And you have not kept the ordinances of my sanctuary: but you have set keepers of my charge in my sanctuary for yourselves”**
• namely, not for me
• who might serve you, and for your comforts you have defiled my sanctuary
44.9:
**“Thus saith the Lord God: No stranger uncircumcised in heart, and uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter”** — although he seems to be among the people of Israel
**“into my sanctuary, no stranger”** — from God
**“that is in the midst”** — bodies
**“of the children of Israel”** — No stranger, etc. Though he be a son, though a kinsman, though bound by old custom or close tie, if he is uncircumcised in heart or flesh, let us not bring him into the sanctuary of the Lord, nor make the ministers of Christ our own ministers, and for carnal comforts defile the altar of the Lord.
44.10:
**“Moreover the Levites”** — the priestly rank
**“that went away far from me, when the children of Israel went astray, and have wandered from me after their idols, and have borne”** — or they will bear
**“their iniquity”** — But the Levites also who went far away, etc. Jerome. According to the Septuagint it means that the Levites of the priestly rank who went astray, after they have received their iniquities, shall stand in the sanctuary and slay the holocausts, and these shall stand to minister to them, etc. But if so, how can it stand that Levites who departed after idols should themselves minister in the house and slay the holocausts? For what more will the priests, the sons of Sadoch, do, who kept the ceremonies of God? The Hebrew has this sense: the wicked Levites shall bear their iniquities, because they were ministering in my sanctuary in the office of the gates. For they themselves offered the holocausts and victims and stood in the sight of the Lord, etc. Symmachus, considering the order of the reading and the sense, interprets more rightly, saying: I had set them as keepers of the doors of the house, and of all its ministry, and of all that is done in it, so that it does not pertain to those who are to be in the temple but to those who were.
**“and have wandered”** — If any in the time of error or persecution followed idols which they had fashioned from their own heart, and not only by voice but by the subscription of the hand affirmed the Son of God to be a creature, how do they retain the pontifical or priestly eminence, who, reduced to laymen, ought to have bewailed their former crimes? But whatever is sinned by many is great.
44.11: **“shall be”** — The Septuagint: they will be ministering in my holy places
44.14:
**“And I will make them doorkeepers of the house”** — to everlasting shame, so that they may be seen degraded by everyone entering and leaving
**“for all the service thereof, and for all that shall be done therein”** — And I will make them doorkeepers, etc. As if for the priestly office by which they were accustomed to offer the holocaust, the victims, and every sacrifice, they will be turned to the lowest rank.
44.15:
**“But the priests”** — Namely.
**“and Levites, the sons of Sadoc”** — That is, of the just, or of the just man of God.
**“who kept the ceremonies of my sanctuary, when the children of Israel went astray from me, they shall come near to me, to minister to me: and they shall stand before me, to offer me the fat, and the blood, saith the Lord God”** — The fattest living victim, namely, and pleasing to God.
44.16:
**“They shall enter into my sanctuary, and they shall come near to my table, to minister unto me”** — They should kindle, namely, incense.
**“and to keep my ceremonies”** — Every rite, namely, of sacrifice.
44.17:
**“And when they shall enter in at the gates of the inner court, they shall be clothed with linen garments”** — Not of wool.
**“they shall be clothed”** — Whence: “Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ.” And elsewhere: “Put on the bowels of mercy, of goodness, of humility, of meekness and of patience.” And again: “And put on the new man, who according to God is created in justice and holiness of truth.”
**“neither shall any woollen come upon them, when they minister in the gates of the inner court and within”** — That is, in the inner parts and in the holy of holies.
**“with linen garments”** — Jerome. The Egyptian priests use linen not only within but also outside. But divine religion has one dress for ministry and another for ordinary use.
*Rabanus:* With linen garments, that is, when this mortal shall put on immortality, and this corruptible, incorruption. These garments we make for ourselves by our own labour; those that are woven from above, such as the tunic the Lord had, which could not be torn, we put on when we know the secret and hidden things of the Lord, and have the Spirit, who searcheth even the deep and profound things, which are not to be shown to the people who are not sanctified nor prepared for the holiness of the Lord, lest, if they should hear things greater than themselves, they be unable to bear the majesty of knowledge, and be choked as it were by solid food, who must still be nourished with milk. There are also the worst garments. Whence: “He put on cursing, like a garment.” And a little after: “May it be unto him like a garment which covereth him; and like a girdle with which he is girded continually.” Whence also the Lord, who bore our sins, is said in Zacharias to have filthy garments.
44.18:
**“linen mitres”** — Others, cidares.
**“on their heads”** — The crown of grace. Whence: “The crown of graces shall receive thy head.”
**“and linen breeches on their loins”** — So that decency and propriety may be kept; that is, lest those climbing the steps of the altar and running about in their ministry should expose their shame.
**“they shall not be girded with any thing that causeth sweat”** — Tightly bound, lest in priestly and Levitical ministries they become unfit, and be unable to hold and yield the victims, drag them, and run about.
**“Linen mitres on their heads”** — In holy things the priests cover their heads, because “in thy sight no man living shall be justified.” And: “the imagination and thought of man’s heart are prone to evil from his youth.” And: the linen breeches shall be on their loins, lest in the sight of the Lord any shame of a defiled conscience and of the nuptial act appear. Whence: “Let your loins be girt.” And the apostle says: “Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth,” and let the imitators of Christ hear: “Justice shall be the girdle of his loins: and faith the girdle of his reins.”
**“And they shall not be girded”** — Lest they seem to observe the good of continence unwillingly, and to eat bread in the sweat of their face; but to fulfil the Lord’s command willingly.
44.19:
**“And when they shall go forth to the outward court to the people, they shall put off their garments wherein they ministered, and lay them up in the store chamber of the sanctuary”** — Where riches are kept at home.
**“and they shall clothe themselves with other garments: and they shall not sanctify the people with their vestments”**
• let another teaching go forth to the common, ignoble crowd, lest the people be sanctified in their stoles
• And when they shall go forth to the outward court to the people, etc. Rabanus. It is a grave thing to take on the burden of a multitude beyond one’s strength, as Solomon says: “It is a snare for a man quickly to sanctify something of his own”; for when he has made a vow, repentance creeps in. The Nazarites offer themselves of their own will, and whoever has vowed anything and not fulfilled it is guilty of the vow.
