*Rabanus:* It is to be noted that the names of the forty-eight cities which in the book of Numbers are given to the Levitical tribe to dwell in, with their suburbs, are here passed over in silence; as also the cities of the fugitives, of which three are beyond the Jordan, namely Bosor and Ramoth and Gaulon, in the two tribes and the half tribe, and three on this side of the Jordan, namely Cedes and Sichem and Cariatharbe. For in the mystical description, and the dwelling of the saints, and their perfect conversation, there was no need to describe the helps of fugitives, which Israel needed while still placed on earth; and Israel, coming in haste to this city through many labours and dangers, says in each of the saints: “I am a stranger and a sojourner.” And: “I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar; my soul hath been long a sojourner.”
48.3: **“And by the border of Aser, from the east side even to the side of the sea, one portion for Nephthali.”** — And by the border of Aser, etc. After the borders of the seven tribes, the firstfruits are described from east to west.
48.8:
**“And by the border of Juda, from the east side even to the side of the sea, shall be the firstfruits which you shall set apart”** — to the Lord
**“five and twenty thousand in breadth, and in length”** — whose number is uncertain; for in the description of the individual tribes the measure is not fixed, but the length is always greater than the breadth
**“as every one of the portions”** — of the tribes
**“from the east side even to the side of the sea”** — from the east even to the sea
48.9:
**“The firstfruits which you shall set apart for the Lord: shall be the length of five and twenty thousand”**
• of reeds
• which is referred to the five senses. Whence: you will possess the divine sense
**“and the breadth of ten thousand”** — that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, and length, that is, and depth, etc.
**“The breadth”** — It signifies consummate and perfect virtue, which through the decalogue of the Old Testament comes to the evangelical sacrament. For if, starting from one, you add the following number up to four, you will complete ten; and the Old Testament is bound together in the New, and the New will be opened out in the Old.
*Jerome:* Reading these things over, I can only say: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God!”
48.10:
**“thousand, and toward the sea”** — the west
**“ten thousand in breadth, and toward the east also ten thousand in breadth, and toward the south five and twenty thousand in length: and the sanctuary of the Lord shall be”** — the temple of the Lord
**“in the midst thereof”** — of the priestly firstfruits
**“And these shall be”** — Beside the border of the Levites are described the four quarters of the firstfruits of the sanctuary, which belong not to the people, nor to the base common crowd, nor to the Levites of lower rank, but properly belong to the worship of the priests.
**“To the north”** — Isidore. That leaving the colds of the north we may come to the west, where our vices may set and perish. From there let us pass to the east, and the sun of justice having risen upon us, let us come to the south, in which the light of justice is for us most bright and perfect. And both from the north to the sea and from the east to the south, twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth, so that everywhere the same measure of length and breadth may be kept.
48.11:
**“The sanctuary shall be for the priests”** — not to the common people
**“shall be”** — not indiscriminately
**“of the sons”** — only, not to others
**“Sadoc”** — The Seventy: Sadue
**“who kept my ceremonies, and went not astray when the children of Israel went astray, as the Levites also went astray.”** — that is, the just. Of whom: “The Lord is just, and hath loved justice”; here he says: “For neither doth the Father judge any man, but hath given all judgment to the Son”; of whom: “Give to the king thy judgment, O God: and to the king’s son thy justice.”
**“The children of Israel”** — Of whom above; who, that is, do not offer victims, but, content with the privilege of the name and the humility of their error, always say in the heart: “I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.” For it suffices the Arians and such as they, if they are not driven out of the temple, if they keep some shadow and image of their former name.
48.12:
**“And for them shall be the firstfruits of the firstfruits of the land”** — as the tithes of tithes.
**“holy of holies, by the border of the Levites.”** — that the Levites may have the border of the priests, but not its navel, that is, its middle, nor be able to hold that very possession.
48.13: **“And the Levites in like manner shall have by the borders of the priests five and twenty thousand in length, and ten thousand in breadth. All the length shall be five and twenty thousand, and the breadth ten thousand.”** — But the Levites also, etc. Isidore. The possession of the Levites is described, which is indeed next to the borders of the priests, and has the same space in length and breadth, on account of the multitude of the Levites, which the fewness of the priests has; yet it uses its own boundaries and understands that it is separated from the priestly rank, to repress the pride of the ministers, who, ignorant of the humility of their station, swell up above the priests.
48.14:
**“And they shall not sell thereof, nor exchange, neither shall the firstfruits of the land be alienated, because they are sanctified to the Lord.”** — not to a man.
**“And they shall not sell thereof”** — That the eternal possession of the Levitical distribution may remain, and the merit of their dignity not be overcome by price, nor be transferred from one to another, because what is sanctified to the Lord is not theirs to whom it is given, but his in whose name it is held.
48.15:
**“But the five thousand that remain in the breadth over against the five and twenty thousand”** — understand: in length.
**“shall be a profane place”** — that is, secular.
**“for the city for dwelling, and for suburbs: and the city shall be”** — Of which: “The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful”; and “A city seated on a mountain cannot be hid.”
**“in the midst thereof”** — of the land.
**“profane”** — Lay, that is, where the people may dwell anywhere; not that they are unclean, or that he thinks anything in the dwelling of the holy land is defiled, but because it is permitted to all except the priests to dwell there. By which we understand that all things which we refer to the senses, that is, to the pleasures of the body, which we take in by sight and hearing, touch, smell and taste, are profane, and do not have the sanctity of the temple, nor belong to the priestly privilege, but to lay vileness.
48.16:
**“And these are the measures thereof”** — and these are its measures; of the city.
**“And these are the measures”** — Isidore. When we have departed from the north wind, the coldest, we pass to the south; and after the light of knowledge has risen in us, we dread the setting of fortitude, considering not the past but the future, and not having a sure possession of virtue, but daily saying in prayer: “Lead us not into temptation”, one, that is, which we cannot bear.
**“on the north side”** — Each side of the city has four thousand five hundred reeds, which make eleven thousand and seventy-five paces, or, according to others, eight hundred and five, so that every city alike, as is written at the end of this volume, may have in its circuit eighteen thousand reeds, which make forty-four thousand and three hundred and forty paces. And the forty-fourth psalm is inscribed: “Unto the end, for them that shall be changed,” and it pertains to the beloved, namely the lovable one of the Lord. Or, according to Aquila, “for the lilies”; Symmachus, “for the flowers” of the Church, which is the city of the Lord and contains the sacraments; of which: “The queen stood on thy right hand, in gilded clothing; surrounded with variety.” And: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within,” that is, inwardly, that it may not be like sepulchres whitened outwardly, but that she may wash everything of the dish, within and without.
48.17:
**“And the suburbs of the city shall be to the north two hundred and fifty, and to the south two hundred and fifty, and to the east two hundred and fifty, and to the sea two hundred and fifty.”** — And the suburbs shall be, etc. These spaces go round the walls of the city in a circuit, to divide between the city and the rest. From which it is shown that no one has leave to work these spaces of the city or to gather their fruits, but that they are free from the use and work of men, so that around the walls the other parts of the city may have the pleasantness of shrubs and herbs growing of their own accord, and of the other things the earth brings forth.
**“Two hundred and fifty”** — Reeds, namely, which have six cubits and one palm, and each side makes six hundred and seventeen paces, or nearly so; and in common, a thousand reeds, having two thousand four hundred and sixty-eight paces.
48.18:
**“And the residue in length by the firstfruits of the sanctuary”** — of reeds.
**“ten thousand toward the east, and ten thousand”** — of reeds.
**“toward the west, shall be as the firstfruits of the sanctuary: and the fruits thereof shall be for bread to them that serve the city.”** — who with words build the walls and mend what is broken and ruinous.
**“And the residue”** — After the description of the holy city and its suburbs, he says the rest is to be assigned to the workers of the city, namely the remaining part of the firstfruits of the sanctuary.
48.19:
**“And they that serve the city, shall serve it out of all the tribes of Israel.”**
• let no one think himself exempt from the works of the city; let all eagerly build up the city.
• Out of all the tribes, etc. This was also done in the tabernacle: according to the variety of their means, one gives gold, another silver, scarlet, fine linen, purple, etc. And though the gifts differ in the quality of their substance, the reward of the givers is one; indeed it is greater for those who offer greater things according to their means, though small, like the poor widow in the Gospel.
48.20:
**“All the firstfruits, of five and twenty thousand”** — all the firstfruits of the twenty-five thousand; of the sanctuary.
**“All the firstfruits”** — We briefly touch on this: that all the firstfruits of the sanctuary and the possession of the city, reckoned together by the square, contain two hundred and forty-six thousand and a third part. For if twenty-five thousand reeds, which have six cubits and one palm each, make by number, that is, by Roman reckoning, sixty-one thousand six hundred and sixty-seven paces, there is no doubt that these reckoned fourfold make the higher number. From which we perceive that all things are to be understood spiritually, and that the possession of the Church is much wider than that of the Levites once was in Judea, who did not even receive parts of the holy land, but from each tribe received, from forty-eight cities, not a possession in full but a dwelling and lodging; so that those too who seem to be laymen and have not come to the priestly and levitical rank, yet if they work in the city of the Lord, may feed on the holy land, the land of the meek and of the living; whence: “I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”
48.21:
**“And the residue shall be for the prince on every side of the firstfruits of the sanctuary, and of the possession of the city over against the five and twenty thousand of the firstfruits unto the east border: toward the sea also over against the five and twenty thousand, unto the border of the sea, shall likewise be the portion of the prince: and the firstfruits of the sanctuary, and the sanctuary of the temple shall be in the midst thereof.”** — of the city.
**“shall be for the prince”** — Of whom above: he who receives as much as one tribe. But here we say that whatever remains out of all the tribes, he alone receives, so that there is no tribe that does not offer gifts to the prince, not from elsewhere but from the firstfruits which serve the temple and the sanctuary and the parts assigned to the city; and this is: “over against the five and twenty,” etc., so that the firstfruits may be between the seven and the five tribes, and in the firstfruits of the city and its suburbs, and in the midst of the city the sanctuary of the temple. But also of the possession of the city, whatever is left will be assigned to the prince; and the farthest part of the seven tribes, neighbouring the firstfruits and the city and the temple, in the tribe of Juda, and the farthest part of the five tribes, by the same right as above, in the tribe of Benjamin, and that farthest part itself will belong to the prince.
48.22:
**“And from the possession of the Levites, and from the possession of the city which are in the midst of the prince's portions”** — But of the possession of the Levites and of the possession of the city, in the middle of the portions: whatever remains is assigned to the prince.
**“what shall be to the border of Juda, and to the border of Benjamin, shall also belong to the prince.”** — And it shall belong to the prince, etc. By the same right that farthest part itself will belong to the prince; from which the sacraments of Holy Scripture are to be wondered at and thought on rather than spoken of. For in the former division, beyond the Jordan, the land was divided by Moses to two tribes, Ruben and Gad, and to the half tribe of Manasses. But on this side of the Jordan, by Josue the son of Nun and Eleazar the son of Aaron. Juda possessed on the south, and Ephraim and the half tribe of Manasses on the north. Afterwards, however, when spies had been sent from Silo, and a description of the land by each tribe had been brought to Josue and to Eleazar, Benjamin received a possession beside Juda on the south, and beside Ephraim and the half tribe of Manasses. The second, the tribe of Simeon, received an inheritance in the tribe of Juda, that what was said might be fulfilled: “From Levi and Simeon I will divide them in Jacob, and will scatter them in Israel.” The third, Zabulon, received Galilee, in which is mount Thabor. The fourth, Issachar, where Jezrahel is, as far as the Jordan. The fifth, Aser, as far as mount Carmel, which overhangs the great sea, and Tyre and Sidon. The sixth, Nephthali, in Galilee as far as the Jordan, where is Tiberias, which was formerly called Chenereth. The seventh, Dan, as far as Joppe, where are the cities Ajalon and Selebi and Emmaus, which is Nicopolis. Although, as is read, they afterwards took for themselves, the other tribes having crossed over, the city Lesem, of the tribe of Dan, which is Paneas. Since these things are so, and there is so great a difference between the former description of the tribes and that which is now in our hands, it must be considered here how in the past too the city and temple were placed between the tribe of Juda and Benjamin. And in the former description indeed Juda was on the south and Benjamin on the north. But here the reverse, so that Juda is on the north and Benjamin on the south. After which the second is Simeon, the third Issachar, the fourth Zabulon, the fifth Gad, five tribes namely; whence also for the remaining tribes from the east side, etc.
48.23: **“And for the rest of the tribes: from the east side to the west side, one portion for Benjamin.”** — portion or possession.
48.25: **“And by the border of Simeon, from the east side to the west side”** — or: western.
48.28:
**“And by the border of Gad, the south side southward”** — note: which Juda held before.
**“southward: and the border shall be from Thamar, even to the waters of contradiction”** — it signifies not a place but the waters in which the people contradicted the Lord and Moses offended.
**“From Thamar”** — Which is now Palmyra, built by Solomon; for palm in Hebrew is called thamar, and it is now called Palmyra, perhaps because there are palm groves there.
**“Contradiction of Cades”** — Isidore. The whole inheritance of the holy land is bounded on the south side by the borders of Egypt and the torrent of Rhinocorura. And because Gad is interpreted “temptation,” in the possession we pass from the palm-grove to the waters of contradiction, as far as Cades, which is interpreted “holy,” that we may understand that even after the victory over the world we ought always to be anxious in fear, mindful of that verse: temptation is the life of man upon earth; and that we come to holiness with adversaries resisting, and so obtain the victory; and from near by let us contemplate the torrent full of rains.
**“Cades, the inheritance over against the great sea”** — Cades, etc. The same word in Hebrew sounds both torrent and inheritance, but here rather torrent, which enters the great sea, Rinocorule. Cades, however, is Batine in the desert, which extends as far as the city Petra.
48.30:
**“And these are the goings out”**
• And these are the goings out; the exits of the gate.
• Concerning the circuit of the city, which on each side in the square had four thousand five hundred reeds, the preceding discourse foretold, which make eighteen thousand reeds, as is also set down in the present chapter, that is, forty-four thousand paces and three hundred and forty paces. Now it is written that on each side, that is, eleven thousand paces and eighty-five paces, there were three gates.
48.31:
**“And the gates of the city according to the names of the tribes of Israel, three gates on the north side, the gate of Ruben”** — who was the firstborn.
**“the gate of Juda one”** — who was the author of the royal line.
**“the gate of Levi one”** — from whom the priests.
48.32:
**“And at the east side, four thousand and five hundred: and three gates, the gate of Joseph one, the gate of Benjamin”** — the two sons of Rachel.
**“the gate of Dan one”**
• son of Bala, the handmaid
• And at the side. “Who is wise, and he shall understand these things? for the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them: but the transgressors shall fall in them.”
• And the gates of the city, etc. Isidore. These twelve gates or exits, according to the quality of merits and virtues, I judge to be joined to the single tribes, under the names of the apostles and the patriarchs. Of these it is written more openly in the Apocalypse of John. And within the mysteries of the divine Scriptures it is attested, and it is necessary, that such a city hold eighteen thousand reeds in circumference, under which number, in two from the twentieth psalm, the natural law and the grace of the gospel are described, by which the Church, that is, the city of the Saviour, is built up.
*Jerome:* This is briefly to be noted: that the same tribes encamped around the tabernacle in such a way that to the east were Juda, Issachar and Zabulon, sons of Lia; to the south Ruben, Simeon and Gad, two sons of Lia and a third, the son of Zelpha, Lia’s handmaid; to the west Ephraim, Manasses and Benjamin, two of them sons of Rachel, because Joseph, in place of the tribe of Levi, which was assigned to the sacrifices, was divided into two tribes, Ephraim and Manasses; to the north Dan, Nephthali and Aser, of whom the first and third are sons of Bala, Rachel’s handmaid, and the second the son of Zelpha, Lia’s handmaid, ignoble and placed to the north, being born indeed of handmaids at variance with one another. But this is according to the Book of Numbers and the description of the tabernacle, which was spoken by the mouth of Moses at God’s command. But our city, which is the city of the great king, whose builder and maker is God, of which it is said: “the most High himself hath founded her,” has another description and measure of the tribes in the holy land, and another order of possession and sides of the single tribes. First, three gates are set against the northern side, etc., of whom the firstborn is Ruben, Juda the author of the royal stock, and Levi. Concerning whose name nothing is said in the description of the tabernacle and the camp, so that, possessing the birthright as a royal and priestly race, we may despise the cold of the north.
48.33: **“And at the south side, thou shalt measure four thousand and five hundred: and three gates, the gate of Simeon one, the gate of Issachar one, the gate of Zabulon one.”** — three sons of Lia
48.34:
**“And at the west side, four thousand and five hundred, and their three gates, the gate of Gad one, the gate of Aser one”** — these two sons of Zelpha, Lia’s handmaid
**“the gate of Nephthali one”** — son of Bala, Rachel’s handmaid
48.35:
**“Its circumference was eighteen thousand: and the name of the city from that day, The Lord is there.”** — now Jerusalem, that is, vision of peace
**“there”** — We shall never depart from it, as from the former. Whence: “Arise, let us go hence.” “And your house shall be left to you desolate”; but it has an eternal possession, and he himself becomes its possession, according to that: “Behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world.”

1.1:
**“And they walked in the midst of the flame,”** — Loosed, the bonds having been burned away. The fire rendered the service of a benefactor; it did no harm.

**“praising God”** — their deliverer
1.2:
**“Then Azarias standing up”** — strong in adversity, for to stand is the part of the strong
**“prayed in this manner, and opening his mouth”** — as if of a treasure of wisdom; as also the world, opening its mouth, a hidden treasure.
**“in the midst of the fire”** — where others die of fear
1.3:
**“Blessed art thou”** — There are two blessings: one from us to God, which is to praise him; and the other from God to us, which is to give forgiveness of sins and an increase of good things. And this is the morning dew.
**“Blessed art thou, O Lord”** — Whatever distresses press upon us, let us say these things with the whole affection of the heart, and let us not doubt that whatever adversity befalls us, we justly endure it. Whence: “And the daughters of Juda rejoiced, because of thy judgments, O Lord.”
1.4:
**“For thou art just in all that thou hast done to us, and all thy works are true, and thy ways right,”** — humility and justice
**“and all thy judgments true.”** — There are two judgments: one hidden in this life, but the other open on the day of the great judgment.
1.6:
**“For we have sinned”**
• in us
• another reading: against us
• They had not sinned, nor were they of that age when they were led away, so that they should be punished thus for a past life; these words are therefore said in the person of the people, as that saying of the Apostle: “For that which I work, I understand not. For I do not that good which I will; but the evil which I hate, that I do,” etc.
• It seems that this cannot be said even of the adults themselves, because they fulfilled the commandments revealed to them through the Holy Spirit.

**“And we have not hearkened to thy commandments,”**

**“nor have we observed nor done”** — and if in some way we did
**“as thou hadst commanded us, that it might go well”** — in body and soul
**“with us.”** — doing

1.9:
**“And”** — so

**“and most wicked,”** — in themselves

**“And now we cannot open our mouths”** — against thy justice, or against the enemies.

• but

**“And take not away thy mercy from us for the sake of Abraham thy beloved”** — he offers a man on behalf of a man

**“as the stars of heaven”** — in good things

**“it may please thee”** — Christ.

1.1:
**“In the third year of the reign”** — from when he began to pay tribute; in the eleventh year he was taken captive by Nabuchodonosor
**“Joakim king of Juda”**
• son of Josias, in whose thirteenth year Jeremias began to prophesy, under whom also the woman Olda prophesied.
• The father of Joakim, spelled with an “m”, who is also called Jechonias, succeeded his father Joachin in the kingdom.
• In the third year of the reign of Joakim, etc. When Josias was slain by Pharao Nechao, the people set up his son Joachaz as king; Pharao led him away bound into Egypt, after laying a fine upon the land, and in his place advanced his brother Eliakim to the kingdom, having changed his name to Joakim, as the history of Kings and Paralipomenon testifies. In the third year of this king Nabuchodonosor came and took him away, and in his place set Sedecias, of whom it was said: “Thou shalt be brought to Babylon, and thou shalt not see it.” For he was bereft of his eyes by Nabuchodonosor.
1.2:
**“And the Lord delivered into his hands Joakim the king of Juda”** — by whose will it came to pass, not by the strength of enemies, namely Nabuchodonosor and others.
**“and part of the vessels”** — And part of the vessels. For though you turn over all the books of the philosophers, you will find only part of the vessels, that is, of the doctrines of truth. But because they join falsehood to truth, they are said to have not all the vessels but a part. For many heretics, knowing some authorities and expounding them by their own measures, carry off from the house of God a part of the vessels, as in Boethius, On Philosophy, who was seizing the garments of philosophy. For the books of the holy fathers are called the vessels of God.
**“the house of God”** — The Church.
**“and he carried them away”** — the devil, or the philosopher, or the soul.
**“into the land of Sennaar”**
• the stench of teeth, or lying.
• Duran is said to be a certain river beside which the giants built the tower of Babel.
• Sennaar. Where the plain of Duran is, where the tower that those who had moved from the east tried to build up to heaven; whence the place is called Babylon, that is, confusion, from the confusion of tongues.
• For the giants were striving to make the tower, setting mountain upon mountain, which God destroyed; whence it was called Babylon, that is, confusion.
**“to the house of his god”** — of Mercury, or of another god.
**“and the vessels”** — other true sentences.
**“brought”** — the devil, or a philosopher, or a heretic.
**“into the treasure house”** — the world; the conventicles of heretics.
**“of his god”**
• of the idol.
• heresy.
• And he carried away the vessels, etc. He showed some reverence to God, in whose place of worship he set some of the vessels, and did not carry away all of them.
1.3:
**“And the king spoke to Asphenez”**
• Nabuchodonosor.
• Jerome. That is, tamer of horses.
**“the master of the eunuchs, that he should bring in some of the children of Israel, and”** — that is.
**“of the king's seed”**
• David.
• And of the seed. From this the Hebrews think that Daniel and his companions were eunuchs, according to what Isaias says to Ezechias: “Of thy sons that shall issue from thee, they shall take away, and make eunuchs in the palace of the king.” But if they were of the royal seed, it is certain that they were of the seed of David; but perhaps what follows does not cohere: and the children of the tyrants, in whom there is no blemish; for if they had been made eunuchs, no nations would say there was no blemish in them.
**“and of the princes”** — of nobles.
1.4:
**“Children in whom there was no blemish,”**
• not a bond
• of mind or body.
• In whom there was no blemish, etc. Those who are without blemish do not seem to be cut off. For some are made eunuchs either by force or by infirmity, but some castrate themselves for the heavenly court or country, and these are not cut off except by will alone, and these are without blemish.
**“well favoured”** — He uses the proper words.
**“and”** — what is more.
**“skillful in all wisdom, acute in knowledge, and instructed in science,”** — “Discipline is the ordered correction of morals.”
**“and such as might stand in the king's palace”** — Distinguished by these, they are worthy of the king’s sight.
**“that he might teach them the learning”** — Letters, namely the liberal arts and the Chaldean tongue, which differs from the Hebrew by a certain peculiarity, although Abraham came to Juda.
**“and the tongue of the Chaldeans.”**
• Syriac, because it is one with the Chaldean tongue
• Philo thinks the Hebrew tongue is Chaldean, because Abraham was from the Chaldeans. But how could the boys teach a tongue they knew? Perhaps, according to the opinion of some, Abraham had both the Chaldean and the Hebrew tongue.
• And he held them so dear that he commanded the same food and the same drink to be prepared for them as for himself.
1.5:
**“And the king appointed them a daily provision”** — provision
**“daily, of his own meat”** — his own
**“and”** — not of just any kind, but
**“of the wine of which he drank himself, that being nourished three years”** — anticipation, because he now says they were nourished, and is about to say how they were nourished
**“afterwards they might stand before the king.”** — and because he commanded, therefore it was done
1.6:
**“Now there were among them”** — boys
**“of the children of Juda”** — for there were many others
**“Daniel”** — judgment, or God judges me
**“to Daniel, Balthasar,”** — Jerome. That is, the hair of the head
**“Ananias”** — that is, grace of the Lord
**“Sidrach”** — my beauty
**“Misael”** — my people
**“Misach”** — that is, he who knows laughter, or of joy
**“and Azarias”** — help of the Lord
**“Abdenago.”** — serving; I am silent
1.7:
**“And gave them names”** — Those whom the devil captures he calls by another name: he calls the just unjust, the chaste incestuous, and so on.
**“And the prince of the eunuchs gave them names”** — As Pharao did to Joseph. For he would not have them keep the names of Judea in the land of captivity. Whence: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?” But the Lord changed the old names for the good, and gives names of virtues from things, as to Abraham and Sara; and in the Gospel the Lord gave Simon the name of Peter. For Simon means obedient, but afterwards he was confirmed in the faith of Christ, and for enduring sufferings; and he called the sons of Zebedee not Boanerges, as some think, but Boanercercen, that is, sons of thunder.
1.8:
**“But Daniel purposed”**
• The king appointed them a daily provision, etc. But Daniel purposed, etc.
• But Daniel purposed. He who will not eat of the king’s table lest he be defiled, if he knew the wisdom and learning of the Egyptians to be sin, would never have learned it; but he learned it not to follow it but to judge and refute it. For if one unskilled in this art were to write against the astrologers, or one ignorant of philosophy were to argue against the philosophers, who, though laughable, would not laugh, or by laughing be unlaughed at? With this intent, then, the boys learn the Chaldean learning, with which Moses learned the wisdom of the Egyptians.
**“in his heart”** — not in words: for intention prevails over words
**“that he would not be defiled”** — against the law
**“with the king's table”**
• food
• as if meat offered to idols, or gluttony
**“nor with the wine”** — drunkenness
**“which he drank: and”** — therefore
**“he requested the master of the eunuchs that he might not be defiled.”** — so that he would not compel him to be defiled with the food of foreigners
1.9:
**“And God gave to Daniel grace”** — to Daniel, I mean, as also Joseph, who were taken captive, that is, made captives, rather for the sins of others: Joseph for the sins of his brothers, Daniel for the sins of the people of Jerusalem
**“And God gave”** — But God gave. He who for the sin of his elders was led into captivity receives the reward of his virtues; for he purposed in his heart not to be defiled with the king’s table, and had preferred poor food to the royal feasts. Therefore he deserved from God favour in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs; whence it is given to understand that, if the saints are ever loved by unbelievers, it is not from their own goodness but from God’s mercy.
1.10:
**“And”** — therefore
**“And the prince of the eunuchs said to Daniel:”** — as if I would do what you ask, but I fear
**“I fear my lord the king”** — Similarly, because Pilate feared Caesar more than God, he earned the punishments of hell; first he washed his hands, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this just man; look you to it.” And again: “Knowest thou not that I have power to release thee?”
**“who if he should see your faces leaner than those of the other youths”** — eating the royal food
**“your equals”**
• with whom you ought to be compared, in age as in body and beauty
• Therefore he put “of your own age.” For younger men are wont to be more beautiful than their elders.
**“you shall endanger my head to the king.”** — you will make me liable for my head
1.11:
**“And Daniel said to Malasar”** — because the prince of the eunuchs did not consent, yet he does not lose heart; he assails another with prayers, and knocks so that it may be opened to him
**“whom the prince of the eunuchs had appointed”** — from this he can do what is asked
**“over Daniel, Ananias, Misael, and Azarias:”** — therefore he could do what was asked
1.12:
**“Try, I beseech thee, thy servants for ten days”**
• he approaches cautiously, seeks goodwill
• A period suited to the trial, neither too short nor too long, which could quickly be obtained.
**“Try us”** — The greatness of his faith is admirable: he promises not only bodily fullness for himself on a meaner diet, namely by pulse, but also fixes a time, not from rashness but from the greatness of faith by which he despised the royal feasts.
**“and let pulse be given us to eat, and water to drink”** — which our law does not forbid
1.13:
**“and”** — after these things
**“look upon our faces, and the faces of the children that eat of the king's meat: and as thou shalt see, deal with thy servants”** — a comparison having been made: if you see us not equally full-bodied and fair, grant us pulse
1.15:
**“After ten days, however, their faces appeared better”** — whom the bread which came down from heaven satisfied
**“and fatter”** — in beauty
**“than all the children that ate of the king's meat.”** — in fatness
1.16:
**“So Malasar took away”** — for himself
**“their portions and the wine of their drink”** — lest anyone perceive this
1.17:
**“But to these children God gave”** — concerning heavenly things
**“and learning”** — concerning earthly things
**“in every book”** — by teaching
**“and wisdom,”** — to be learned
**“But to Daniel understanding”** — beyond the others, because what others saw in a vision, he saw with the eyes of the mind
**“of all visions and dreams.”** — of riddles by which future things are shown
1.18:
**“And when the days were ended”** — for three years according to the king’s command
**“after which the king had ordered that they should be brought in,”** — the youths
**“the prince of the eunuchs brought them in”**
• Arphanaz
• otherwise: Arphaxat
1.19:
**“And when the king had spoken to them”** — testing their wisdom
**“there were not found such”** — in wisdom
**“among all”** — boys
**“as Daniel, Ananias, Misael and Azarias.”** — whom the bread of life and the fountain of wisdom had fed and taught
**“And”** — therefore
**“they stood in the king's presence.”** — as about to serve
1.20:
**“And in every matter”** — as if they rightly stand in the king’s presence, because every word of wisdom, etc.
**“of wisdom”** — of divine things
**“and understanding”** — of worldly things
**“that the king inquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the diviners”** — from the altars
**“and magicians”** — magicians who philosophize about individual things
**“Diviners and magicians”** — Others take them as sophists and philosophers, not according to this philosophy and sophistic discipline which the Greeks profess, but the teaching of a barbarian people, by which the Chaldeans philosophize even to this day.
1.21:
**“And Daniel continued even to the first year of king Cyrus.”** — In honour; for in what follows it is said that he saw a vision in the third year of King Cyrus; for Darius having died, he was with Cyrus.
**“And Daniel continued”** — It is to be said in what follows how he is said to have been there until the first year of Cyrus, and afterwards it is read that he was there in the third year of the same and the first of Darius.

2.1:
**“In the second year of the reign of Nabuchodonosor”**
• But in the year of Sedechias, etc.
• after he subjected foreign nations to himself
**“In the second year”** — If the boys went in before the king after three years, how is it now said that he dreamed this in the second year? The Hebrews solve it thus: the second year is here said to be that in which he ruled over all the barbarian nations, the Assyrians, Egyptians, Moabites, and the remaining peoples, not only the Jews and Chaldeans. Whence Josephus: “After the second year of the Egyptian captivity Nabuchodonosor saw a wonderful dream, and it fled from him.”
**“Nabuchodonosor had a dream”** — not for himself, but for Daniel and the captives of God
**“A dream”** — The impious king saw a dream so that God might be glorified through Daniel’s interpreting, and the captives serving God might have comfort from it. So too Pharaoh: not because they deserved it, but Joseph and Daniel were worthy to be preferred to all by interpretation.
**“and his spirit was terrified”** — Morally: because the carnal man cannot bear spiritual things.
**“and his dream went out of his mind.”** — so that through his inquiry the power of God might be shown, and his saints somewhat refreshed.
2.2:
**“Then the king commanded that the diviners be called together”**
• from the altars
• others, enchanters who work with words
**“The magicians”** — But common custom and speech take magi for sorcerers.
**“and the magicians”**
• Magi who philosophize about individual things.
• And sorcerers, etc. Who use victims and blood, and often touch dead bodies.
**“and the Chaldeans”** — mathematicians, astrologers
**“The Chaldeans”** — Chaldeans: philosophers of the Chaldeans, mathematicians; namely, because according to this art even the kings and princes of that people do everything. Whence also at the Lord’s nativity they first noted his rising, and coming to Bethlehem, they adored the child.
**“to declare to the king his dreams. And when they had come, they stood before the king”** — they did not sit, because ready to hear
2.3: **“And the king said to them: I saw a dream”** — a shadow and as it were a breeze; and he retained the traces of the dream, so that, others reporting, he could recall what he had seen and not be deceived by liars.
2.4: **“And the Chaldeans answered”** — Up to here in Hebrew; from here on, up to the vision of the third year of King Balthasar which Daniel saw, he wrote in Hebrew letters indeed, but in the Chaldean language, which he calls Syriac.
2.5:
**“And the king answered and said to the Chaldeans: The thing”** — dream or vision
**“is gone from me. Unless you tell me”** — before
**“the dream and”** — after
**“its interpretation”** — the interpretation, namely what it portends
**“you shall be put to death”** — He threatens punishment and sets forth rewards, so that if they can tell the dream, which he could not recall, he may also believe the explanation of the dream; otherwise their interpretation would have no credit.
**“and your houses shall be confiscated.”** — confiscated; that is, they will be of the fisc, that is, of the king’s community. For the fiscus is the king’s purse.
2.6:
**“But if you tell the dream and its interpretation”** — If punishment does not frighten, let rewards entice.
**“rewards”** — in the present
**“and gifts”** — in the future
**“and great honour you shall receive from me.”** — among neighbours and friends
2.7: **“They answered a second time and said: Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will declare its interpretation.”** — again they entice him with kindness
2.8:
**“The king answered and said: I know for certain that you seek to gain time”**
• the span of life
• by circumlocution of words
2.9:
**“If therefore you tell me not the dream”** — for some trace of the dream remained in him, so that if anyone told it he would recognise it at once
**“there is one”** — firm, alone
**“concerning you”** — to me
**“sentence,”**
• no one will intercede for you
• namely this
**“that you have also framed a lying interpretation, and full of deceit,”** — by feigning
**“to speak before me till the time pass away. Tell me therefore the dream, that I may know that you also give a true interpretation thereof.”** — he clings to his purpose, stands by his sentence, repeats the same
2.10:
**“Then the Chaldeans answered before the king, and said: There is no man upon earth”** — for it is one above the heaven who can do this
**“that can accomplish thy word, O king;”** — at last, compelled, they acknowledge God the Creator of all
**“neither doth any king, though great and mighty”** — much less can the servants of kings resolve it
2.11: **“For the thing that thou askest, O king, is difficult; nor can any one be found that can shew it before the king, except the gods, whose conversation is not with men.”** — The soothsayers and all worldly learning confess that foreknowledge of the future belongs to God alone, not to men; whence it is proved that the prophets spoke by the Spirit of God, who foretold the future things.
2.12:
**“Upon hearing this, the king in fury, and in great wrath, commanded that all the wise men should be put to death.”** — he did not command concerning only one
**“wise men”** — not concerning the foolish and the flatterers
**“of Babylon”** — not concerning those of a foreign country
2.13:
**“And the decree being gone forth”** — by the king
**“the wise men were slain.”**
• they were being prepared to be killed; whence after 'the wise men': 'do not destroy'
• The wise men were slain. The Hebrews ask why Daniel and the three boys did not go in to the king with the other wise men, and yet are ordered to perish with them; and they solve it thus: when the king promised very great gifts and the highest honour, they would not go, lest they seem to seek dignity and riches. Or perhaps the Chaldeans, envying their wisdom and glory, went in alone, as if they alone were to receive the rewards, but afterwards wished almost to have partners in the penalty. But Daniel and his companions did not come, lest they seem to seek rewards, or because of envy, lest the Chaldeans perhaps envy their wisdom.
2.14:
**“Then Daniel inquired concerning the law and the sentence”** — not knowing the cause of his danger; for the Chaldeans had concealed the king’s question, lest Daniel and the three boys should be preferred to them in the explanation of the vision
**“of Arioch”** — Arioch, that is, reducing to solitude
2.15:
**“And he asked him that had received the orders of the king”** — namely this
**“why so cruel a sentence was gone forth from the face of the king”** — from the secret
2.16: **“that he would give him time”** — Not that he might search out hidden things beforehand by sagacity of mind, but that he might entreat the Lord of hidden things. He joins others with himself in prayer, lest he seem to presume on the privilege of his own merit; and that those whose danger is common may make a common prayer.
2.17: **“And he went into his house, and told the matter to Ananias, and Misael, and Azarias his companions”** — Morally. Do not be wise to yourself alone; you ought to profit all, and to teach others with you.
2.18:
**“To the end that they should ask”** — with himself
**“mercy at the face of the God of heaven concerning this secret”** — the hidden dream by which future holy things are signified
**“and”** — which having been found
**“that Daniel and his companions might not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.”** — “He loves his enemies, does good to them that hate him, and prays for them that persecute him.”
2.19:
**“Then was the mystery revealed to Daniel by a vision in the night”**
• by God
• Then to Daniel, etc. He learns the king’s dream by his own dream; rather, he knows both the dream and its interpretation by the revelation of God, which the demons did not know and the wisdom of the world could not know. Daniel knows what had been unknown to all the generations gone before, God revealing the mystery.
**“And”** — therefore
**“Daniel blessed the God of heaven”**
• he is not ungrateful; he ascribes it to God, not to himself
• in contrast to those gods who dwell on earth and deceive earthly men with demonic arts and tricks
• The God of heaven, etc. “The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth shall perish.”
2.20:
**“And speaking he said: Blessed be the name of the Lord from eternity and for evermore: for wisdom”** — by which mysteries are known
**“and fortitude”** — of kingdoms
**“are his.”** — are his, not of men, not of demons, not of kings
2.21:
**“And he”** — and he himself, not another
**“changeth times and ages”** — note that by a general discourse he prepares the hearer, already hinting that the dream is about the change of kingdoms
**“And he changeth”** — Let us not wonder, then, if at times we see kings succeed kings and kingdoms succeed kingdoms, all of which happen by the decision of God, who knows the causes of all things, who strikes down all things, and permits evil kings to be raised up, so that they punish the wicked and reform the good.
**“taketh away kingdoms and establisheth them, giveth wisdom to the wise”** — Whence: “A wise man shall hear and shall be wiser”; and: “For to every one that hath shall be given, and he shall abound: but from him that hath not, that also which he seemeth to have shall be taken away.”
**“and knowledge to them that have understanding.”** — to those who love the correction of conduct
**“giveth wisdom”** — Wisdom is of heavenly things, knowledge of earthly things, discipline the ordered correction of conduct. First we are corrected through discipline, then we know, and afterwards we are wise.
2.22:
**“He revealeth”** — He to whom God reveals the deep things wonders and says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God!” This man, the Holy Spirit dwelling in him, “searcheth the deep things of God,” and in the depth of his soul digs very deep wells, and casts out the earth that covers the waters; “he drinketh water out of his own vessels, and of the fountain of his own wells.”
**“and knoweth what is in darkness”**
• ignorance
• He knew that the patriarchs dug wells, and the Philistines at night heaped earth into them, and the patriarchs dug again until they found water. So every faithful soul ought to watch because of the snares of the devil, that it may come to the living water, that is, Christ. The prophet David rebukes the drowsiness of those souls, saying: “O ye sons of men, how long will you be dull of heart?” For we ought to be mindful of the divine spark, and of the image impressed upon us, of which the same David says: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us.”
**“knoweth what is in darkness”** — Darkness: ignorance; light: knowledge and doctrine. For perverse things are not hidden from God; right things surround and cleave to him. Or darkness: mystical and deep things. Whence in Proverbs: “He shall understand a parable and the interpretation, the words of the wise and their riddles.” And in the Psalm: “Dark water in the clouds of the air, at the brightness in his sight.” For he who forsakes earthly things and climbs to the heights, like a bird desires the thinnest air and the ether, and becomes a cloud to which the truth of God comes, which is wont to rain through the saints; such a one, filled with a multitude of knowledge, has many dark waters, wrapped in mist, which only Moses and those like him enter, and he speaks to God face to face; of whom: “He made darkness his covert.”
**“and light is with him.”** — wisdom and knowledge
2.23:
**“To thee”** — therefore
**“O God of our fathers, I give thanks”** — lest it seem to be of his own merit, he refers these things to the justice of the fathers and the truth of God, who has mercy on their seed even in captivity
**“and I praise thee: because thou hast given me wisdom”** — of explaining
**“and strength”** — of enduring
**“thou hast given me, and now thou hast shewn me”** — to me alone
**“what we desired of thee”** — us four. He avoids arrogance, lest he seem to have obtained it alone, and gives thanks because he alone understands the mystery of the dream
2.24:
**“The wise men”** — He imitates the Lord’s mercy in praying for his persecutors. Nor does he wish those to perish for whom he himself would have perished had they been killed.
**“bring me in”** — He avoids arrogance, since he could have gone by the straight road himself, and therefore wishes to be brought in.
2.25:
**“Then Arioch in haste brought in”** — as far as the praise (goes)
**“Daniel”** — to whom nothing
**“to the king, and said to him: I have found a man”** — “I have found a man,” etc. He refers God’s grace to his own diligence and says he has found him, though Daniel offered himself readily; and he shows the manner of messengers, who want their good news to seem their own.
**“of the children of the captivity”** — “Of the children of the captivity”: not that Daniel is of the sons of Juda, that is, of royal stock, but he is not a priest, as the fable of Bel says at its end.
2.26:
**“The king answered, and said to Daniel, whose name was Baltassar: Thinkest thou indeed that thou canst tell me the dream that I saw, and the interpretation thereof?”** — he keeps the order of the dream
**“Thinkest thou indeed”** — He keeps the order of the question: he first asks about the dream, which the magi did not know, and after that about the interpretation of the dream; so that when he has recognized what he saw, he may believe the interpretation, which admits varied conjecture.
2.27:
**“And Daniel made answer before the king, and said: The secret”** — note that anything hidden can be called a mystery
**“The secret that the king”** — He removes from the king a wrongful suspicion, lest he think human skill can find what belongs only to God’s knowledge.
**“desireth to know, none of the wise men, or the philosophers, or the diviners, or the soothsayers can declare to the king.”**
• admirable simplicity; he shows innocent those who sought his death, for one must not do harm to those who do harm
• who look outward and from these foretell the future
2.28:
**“But there is a God in heaven that revealeth mysteries”**
• as if to say: you vainly ask of men on earth what God alone knows in heaven
• “But there is God.” Not gods; he watchfully draws him back from the opinion of many gods.
**“who hath shewn to thee, O king Nabuchodonosor”** — without flattery, with truth joined to it, he flatters him as king
**“what is to come to pass in the latter times”** — things to be fulfilled, now begun; and of all these there will be a general fulfillment at the end
**“what is to come to pass”** — Either from the time the dream was revealed to Daniel until the consummation of the world, or surely the whole interpretation of the dream tends to the end, in which the image and statue that is seen is to be ground to pieces.
**“Thy dream, and the visions”** — here he takes dreams and visions for the same thing
**“Thy dream”** — There are six kinds of dreams. Two are those which not even any saint can avoid: from excessive emptiness of the belly, and from excessive gorging. The third is from the nocturnal illusions of the enemy. The fourth is from a thought entertained beforehand, the illusion following. The fifth is by revelation of the Holy Spirit, which happens in many ways. The sixth is from thoughts entertained beforehand, or from cares pertaining to our head, Christ, or to the Church, or to the members, a revelation following.
**“of thy head”** — Of the mind, namely, from which the thought arises; or the head is Christ and we the members, this shepherd and we the flock. Whence: “Let the weakness of the flock reach where the firmness of the shepherd has gone before.”
**“thy head”** — Of thy head, etc. He does not say of the eyes, lest we should think anything corporeal, but of the head. Whence in Proverbs: “The eyes of a wise man are in his head,” that is, in the principal part of the heart. Whence: “Blessed are the clean of heart,” etc., and “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” Others on this occasion, following Plato, suspect that wisdom is in the brain.
**“upon thy bed”** — he names the place so that it may be more believed
2.29:
**“Thou, O king, didst begin to think in thy bed, what should come to pass hereafter”** — another reading: after these things
**“Thou, O king”**
• He indicates the cause of the dream, namely that God revealed future mysteries to the king, because he wished to know the future; and, that he may marvel at the grace of divine inspiration, he sets out not only what he saw in the dream but what he had thought beforehand.
• It must be considered that dreams, by which the future is signified and truth is shown as if through a cloud, are not open to diviners and the wise of the world, but are reserved to the knowledge of God alone.
**“and he that revealeth mysteries shewed thee what shall come to pass”** — “And he that revealeth mysteries sheweth thee.” “Who maketh his sun to rise upon the good and the bad”: his clemency is so great that he revealed through Daniel even to Nabuchodonosor the mystery of his dispensation, which governs the world.
*Jerome:* Let us question those who assert that there are different natures: of which nature do they understand Nabuchodonosor to be, good or evil? If good, why is he called impious? If evil (which is true), according to those who say there are good and evil natures, but all are good inasmuch as they are creatures of God, why did God reveal his mysteries to one evil and earthly?
2.30:
**“To me also”**
• As if you should not think that knowledge of the future can be grasped by human skill.
• He excuses the wise men of Babylon and avoids envy, lest the king think that he who is about to speak had it from his own wisdom.
**“this secret is revealed, not by any wisdom that I have more than all men alive: but that the interpretation might be made manifest to the king, and thou mightest know the thoughts of thy mind”** — he honors the king, as if to say: your desire is the cause of this revelation, because you wished to know the future
2.31:
**“Thou, O king, sawest”**
• behold the dream of Nabuchodonosor
• as if an imagining
**“and behold there was as it were a great statue”**
• this pertains to the whole
• others, an image, as a likeness of things to come
• Great. All refers to the great and the lofty, etc.
**“this statue, which was great and high, tall of stature, stood before thee”** — in your sight
**“and the look”** — his face
**“thereof was terrible”** — or, to see it was terrible
2.32:
**“The head of this statue”** — the kingdom of the Chaldeans
**“of this statue”** — It divides the kingdoms as they were ruled by kings.
**“was of fine gold”** — because of their riches
**“but the breast and the arms of silver”** — of the Medes and Persians
**“of brass”** — Of the Macedonians, who were most famous for the valour of Alexander; and it is compared to bronze, which resounds more than the other metals.
2.33:
**“And the legs of iron”** — the kingdom of the Romans
**“the feet part of iron and part of clay”** — because the kingdom was divided
2.34:
**“was cut out of”** — Christ: “the stone which the builders rejected”, that is, the Jews: “the same is made the head of the corner.”
**“it struck the statue upon the feet thereof that were of iron and of clay, and broke them in pieces”**
• rightly in the feet first, because when the Lord was born the Romans were ruling, and in them he broke all earthly empire
• and so
2.35:
**“Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold broken to pieces together, and became like the chaff of a summer’s threshingfloor, and they were carried away by the wind: and there was no place found for them: but the stone that struck the statue, became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.”**
• “For of his fulness we have all received.”
• and filled the whole earth, as through Constantine, who gave permission to the whole world to serve God.
2.36: **“This is the dream: we will also tell the interpretation thereof before thee, O king.”** — the wise king, silent, hears everything, recognising the truth
2.37:
**“Thou art a king of kings: and the God of heaven”** — to whom you owe everything, not to vain and deaf idols
**“a kingdom, and strength”** — against enemies
**“and power”** — over subjects
**“and glory”** — among foreigners
**“hath given thee”** — in this land
2.38:
**“And all places wherein the children of men, and the beasts of the field do dwell”** — so that I may briefly comprehend all things
**“the children of men, and the beasts of the field, and the birds of the air”** — of the air
**“he hath also given”** — not by your merits, but freely
**“into thy hand”** — by power
**“and hath put all things under thy power”** — because they do not contradict
**“hath put all things under thy power: thou therefore art the head of gold”** — He established all things. Thou therefore, O king, art the head of gold: the first kingdom, namely that of the Babylonians, is compared to the most precious gold.
2.39:
**“And after thee shall rise up another kingdom, inferior to thee, of silver”** — and after you there shall arise another kingdom, less than you, of silver, of the Medes and Persians, which is compared to silver: less than the former, but following greater
**“And another third kingdom of brass”** — It signifies Alexander and the kingdom of the Macedonians and of his successors, which is rightly called brazen, because among all metals brass is the more sonorous and rings more clearly, and its sound is spread far and wide; which shows not only the power of the kingdom, but also the eloquence of the Greek speech.
2.40:
**“And the fourth kingdom shall be as iron”** — Of the Romans; which breaks in pieces and subdues all things, is at last subdued.
**“As iron breaketh into pieces, and subdueth all things, so shall that break and destroy all these”** — the aforesaid kingdoms
2.41:
**“And whereas thou sawest the feet, and the toes, part of potter’s clay, and part of iron: the kingdom shall be divided”** — which has been fulfilled today; for just as at the beginning nothing was stronger or harder than the Roman empire, so at the end nothing is weaker
**“but yet it shall take its origin from the iron”** — because from the beginning strong and hard
**“according as”** — according to which
**“thou sawest the iron mixed”** — weaker
**“with the miry clay”** — otherwise: of potsherd and mud
2.43:
**“And whereas thou sawest the iron mixed with miry clay”** — otherwise: of potsherd and of clay
**“they shall be mingled indeed together with the seed of man”** — that is, they were men descending from the former seed, like potsherd and clay
**“but they shall not stick fast one to another, as iron cannot be mixed with clay”** — because they are discordant, nor of so great strength as the former, and degenerate from them
2.44:
**“But in the days of those kingdoms”** — These kingdoms having gone before, the kingdom of Christ both was foretold and has come.
**“the God of heaven will set up”** — the Father
**“a kingdom”** — of his Son and of the Church
**“that shall never be destroyed”** — “And of his kingdom there shall be no end.”
**“and his kingdom shall not be delivered up to another people”** — Whence: “And my glory I will not give to another.”
**“it shall break in pieces, and shall consume all these kingdoms”**
• in comparison with his own kingdom
• When Moses had come down from the mountain and had found the Jews who had made the molten calf, he obtained by prayers from them that it should be destroyed, and he burned it so far that it was made dust, and afterwards he gave water to all to drink; which signifies baptism and penance. For in baptism we are washed with water; by the fire of conscience, or by material fire, we are purged; or by the Holy Spirit, who is called the ancient fire.
**“break in pieces”** — Christ will therefore break the kingdom of the world, so that he may build his own there. Whence it was said to Peter: “Kill and eat,” that is, incorporate into yourself, namely make all conform to you.
**“these”** — that
**“and it shall stand for ever.”** — the others being transitory
2.45:
**“According as thou sawest”** — as if this was signified to you in a vision
**“that out of the mountain”** — from the proud people of the Jews
**“was cut out”** — by material flesh
**“the stone”** — Christ, of whom: “The stone which the builders rejected; the same is become the head of the corner.”
**“without hands”**
• begotten without the seed of man, of a virgin, who, when all kingdoms are broken, became a great mountain and filled the whole earth, of whom: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob.”
• The stone without hands. The impious Porphyry and the Jews refer these things to the people of the Jews, whom they wish to be the strongest at the end of the ages, and to break all kingdoms, and to reign for ever.
**“and broke in pieces, the clay, and the iron”** — the first Roman empire, under which Christ was born
**“and the brass, and the silver, and the gold, the great God hath shewn the king what shall come to pass hereafter, and the dream is true, and the interpretation thereof is faithful.”** — Likewise he says the revelation of the dream was not due to his own merit, but that it might be made manifest to the king, that God alone is to be worshipped.
2.46:
**“Then king Nabuchodonosor”** — Porphyry proudly slanders this: that a most proud king adored a captive; as also the Lycaonians, because of the greatness of the signs, wished to sacrifice victims to Paul and Barnabas. Therefore the error of the Gentiles, who think gods whatever is above themselves, ought not to be imputed to Scripture, which simply relates all that was done.
**“fell on his face”** — It may have happened that, struck by the newness of the thing, he fell without knowing it.
**“Fell on his face”** — He who falls on his face sees where he falls; but he who falls backward does not know where he falls. Whence it is believed that Heli the priest of the Lord perished, who fell backward.
**“and worshipped Daniel, and commanded that they should offer in sacrifice to him victims and incense.”** — to be prepared or carried
**“Then the king spoke to Daniel: Truly your God”** — not ours
**“Truly your God”** — We can say that the king himself reveals why he adores Daniel and commands victims to be sacrificed, and whom and to whom he speaks, saying: “Indeed your God,” etc. He adores not so much Daniel as God in Daniel, who reveals mysteries; which we read that Alexander the Great also did in the high priest Jaddus; or perhaps, confounded by the greatness of the matter, he is stunned and does not know what he does, and he who does not understand the true God adores his servant.
**“is the God of gods”** — of all
**“revealing mysteries, for thou couldst disclose this secret.”** — this is proved in you
2.47:
**“and the Lord of kings”**
• as of heaven and earth
• because
2.48:
**“Then the king advanced Daniel to a high station”** — this is the cause of the dream
**“Then the king advanced Daniel”** — This also Porphyry reproves: that Daniel did not refuse the gifts and received Babylonian honour; and he does not consider that the king saw the dream, and the interpretation was revealed to Daniel, so that on this occasion Daniel might grow, and for the consolation of the captives become prince over all the Chaldeans, and the power of God be made manifest. So Joseph was exalted with Pharao, Mardochai with Assuerus, so that the captives might have some solace, seeing a man of their own nation prince of the Egyptians or of the Chaldeans.
2.49:
**“And Daniel requested of the king, and he appointed”**
• the king
• Daniel however asked: He does not forget in his reward who his companions were in prayer and in the anxiety of danger.
**“over the works of the province of Babylon Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago: but Daniel himself was in the king's palace.”** — not withdrawing from the king’s side, an honoured familiar

3.1:
**“King Nabuchodonosor made”**
• as if to say: he was not mindful of the benefit received from God
• Headlong forgetfulness of the truth: he who adored the servant of God as God, that he himself might be adored, ordered a golden statue to be made for himself, of infinite weight, that it might strike the beholders with amazement and be adored more easily. An occasion of salvation is given even to the barbarians: that they who in the revelation of the dream through Daniel had known the power of the one God, might learn in the fortitude of the three children to despise death and not to worship idols.
• Whoever worships his own covetousness, which is the service of idols, because this man worshipped silver and gold, and that was covetousness, and the service of idols.
**“a statue of gold”** — memory of a benefit is fleeting, memory of an injury clings like a burr
**“of sixty cubits high, and six cubits broad, and he set it up in the plain of Dura”** — Theodotion. Dorcas; Symmachus: Duran; the Seventy: peribolon, in Latin: a vineyard or enclosure
3.2:
**“Then Nabuchodonosor the king”** — High things stand more dangerously and fall more quickly. The princes are gathered to adore the statue, so that afterwards the subjects may not refuse; and the rich and powerful, lest they lose riches or power, are not slow to obey, and their example the subjects do not hesitate to follow.
**“sent to call together the nobles”** — princes: the language of the Philistines or Alophyles.
**“the magistrates, and the judges, the captains, the rulers, and governors, and all the chief men of the provinces”** — with whose consent the people readily agree
**“to come to the dedication”** — to prayer
3.3:
**“Then they were gathered together”** — as it was commanded
**“the nobles, the magistrates, and the judges, the captains, and rulers, and the great men that were placed in authority, and all the princes of the provinces, to come to the dedication”** — to prayer
**“the statue which king Nabuchodonosor had set up. And they stood before the statue”** — gathered, marvelling
3.4:
**“and the herald cried with a strong voice”** — with a loud voice
**“To you it is commanded, O nations, tribes, and languages”** — not that all peoples of all nations could have been gathered in the plain of Dura, but it is believed that all adored through their princes of all nations.
3.5: **“ye fall down and adore”** — No one adores God falling down. But demons and idols are adored by men falling down, as here and in the Gospel: “All these will I give thee, if falling down thou wilt adore me.” It must also be known that heretics, who compose false doctrines with the brilliance of worldly eloquence, make a golden statue, and as far as in them lies, by persuasion compel others to adore the idol of falsehood.
3.6: **“But if any man shall not fall down and adore, he shall the same hour be cast into a furnace of burning fire.”** — he adds a penalty for whoever does not obey the command
3.7:
**“Upon this therefore”** — because he commanded, and added threats
**“at the time when all the people heard”** — among the princes
**“the sound of the trumpet, the flute, the harp, the sackbut, the psaltery, the symphony, and all kind of music; all the peoples fell down”** — both in mind and in body; but those who in the Apocalypse adore God fall on their faces.
3.8:
**“And presently at that very time some Chaldeans came and accused the Jews”**
• Jews, whom they envied as set over them, and were offended by their religion and their turning from idols; seizing therefore the occasion, they accuse them before the king.
• They do not at once say that he should kill them, but first they draw them into hatred against the king.
3.10:
**“Thou, O king, hast made a decree”** — which it is not lawful to violate
**“that every man”** — you excepted no one
**“who shall hear the sound of the trumpet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, symphony, and every kind of music”** — all these things were done so that they might honour the statue, and the people might be more quickly seduced.
3.11: **“And if any man shall not fall down and adore, he shall be cast into a furnace of burning fire.”** — as if they were not moved even by the aforesaid punishment
3.12:
**“Now there are certain Jews whom thou hast set”** — whom you set over us
**“Now there are certain”** — Enviously, as if you had made captives and slaves princes, that is, set over us; lifted up in pride, they have despised your commands.
**“over the works of the province of Babylon, Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago, these men”** — whom you honored, they dishonor you; ungrateful, forgetful of the kindness.
**“have slighted thy decree, O king; they worship not thy gods”**
• as if the injury also rebounds on the gods.
• They worship not thy gods. It is plain that the gods of Nabuchodonosor are one thing, and the statue which he ordered to be erected for his worship another. Others say it is the custom of Sacred Scripture to call one idol in the plural. Whence: “These are thy gods, O Israel, that have brought thee out of the land of Egypt”; and in the book of Kings Jeroboam, setting up the golden calf in Bethel, is recorded to have made idols; conversely, many demons are called by the singular, as in the Gospel, Legion.
3.13:
**“Then Nabuchodonosor in fury, and in wrath”** — by the worst counselors
**“Sidrach, Misach”** — Daniel is not mentioned, because he stood by the king, who did not adore his own statue.
3.14:
**“And Nabuchodonosor the king spoke to them and said: Is it true”** — as is said
**“O Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago, that you do not worship my gods”** — as above
3.15:
**“Now therefore if you be ready”** — to obey
**“at what hour soever you shall hear”** — although he commanded them to be brought in fury, he nevertheless gives time for amendment, and shows that he holds them dear.
**“the sound of the trumpet, flute, harp, sackbut, and psaltery, and symphony, and all kind of music, prostrate yourselves and adore the statue which I have made; but if you do not adore, you shall be cast the same hour into the furnace of burning fire. And who is the God that shall deliver you out of my hand?”** — Wondrous forgetfulness. He can deliver, whose servant you adored a little before, whom you proclaimed the true God and Lord of the kingdom.
3.16: **“We have no occasion”** — As if it is not necessary to hear words; for by the very deeds you will test our steadfastness and constancy, and in us the power of God.
3.17:
**“For behold our God”**
• who is true, not yours who are false
• What was thought to be a matter of terror becomes a matter of strength. They do not put it off to a distant time; they promise themselves help at once: For behold, God, etc.
**“is able to save us”** — As if: if he does not deliver, it is of justice in his promise, not of his weakness. As if they said: He can well make us be delivered; but if he does not wish to deliver, we did not merit to be freed, and by our preceding merits he permits us to be scourged.
**“from the furnace of burning fire, and to deliver us out of thy hands, O king.”** — whatever torments you may inflict
**“O king, to deliver”** — In the Hebrew ‘king’ is not found, lest they be thought to flatter the impious man or to call him king who compels to iniquity; or lest they seem to provoke the king boldly to the shedding of their own blood. Thus they render him the honor due, so that the worship of God is not harmed.
3.18:
**“But if he will not,”** — carefully; they do not put the contrary, namely ‘if he cannot,’ but ‘if he will not,’ so that it is of the will of God and not of impossibility, if they perish
**“be it known to thee, O king, that we will not worship thy gods”** — gods are worshipped, statues are adored
**“That thy gods”** — In reversed order, what they answer last: ‘It is not necessary,’ etc. As if: It is certain that we have a God who can deliver; finally they answered thus to the first and second: We do not worship your gods, and we do not adore your statue.
**“nor adore the golden statue which thou hast set up.”** — who are worshippers and adorers of the true God; whence these princes and judges of the world therefore please Nabuchodonosor. But those who adore the statues of emperors displease God.
3.19:
**“Then was Nabuchodonosor filled with fury: and”** — therefore
**“the countenance of his face was changed”** — A changed countenance is said of evil, and change is said of good. Whence some Psalms are titled: “For those who shall be changed.” Yet some take this as evil. Of Anna also it is read: “and her countenance was no more changed.”
**“against Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago, and”** — kindled with fury
**“he commanded that the furnace should be heated seven times more”** — so that he may terrify more
**“And he commanded that the furnace should be heated”** — As if plain fire were not enough; but fury and wrath, close to madness, cannot keep measure, and he thinks to terrify with the threat of manifold punishment those whom he sees resisting steadfastly.
3.21:
**“And immediately these men were bound, with their coats”** — Theodotion said ‘saraballis,’ which is Chaldean and signifies coverings of the thighs and shins, that is, breeches.
**“and their caps”** — it is Greek; a kind of little cloak or cap.
**“and their shoes, and their garments”** — bound and clothed, for the king’s command pressed, nor was it allowed to strip them.
**“were cast into the furnace of burning fire.”** — of the furnace
3.22:
**“For the king's commandment was urgent, and the furnace was heated exceedingly. And the flame of the fire slew those men that had cast in Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago.”** — It is an anticipation, because this will be said more fully in what follows.
**“Those men”** — Of whom it was said before: “And the strongest men that were in his army,” etc. He did not destroy just anyone by chance, but the most valiant and the most ready for war, so that he would fear not only the miracle but would also feel the disaster of his army.
3.23: **“But these three men, that is, Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago, fell down bound in the midst of the furnace of burning fire.”** — falling headlong because they were bound; but the bonds burn, and the flame does not touch the bound men
3.24:
**“Then Nabuchodonosor the king”** — the vision by so great a miracle.
**“was astonished”** — the king is rebuked by the princes being punished, that living he may glorify God.
**“and rose up in haste, and said to his nobles”**
• by whose suggestion he had done this.
• the strongest of the army, of whom it was said above.
**“Did we not cast three men”** — only.
3.25:
**“He answered, and said”** — he asked so as to infer this.
**“Behold I see four men loose, and walking”** — since he had sent only three, and bound.
**“in the midst of the fire, and there is no hurt in them”** — that the fire, though wise, burned the bonds and preserved the bodies.
**“and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God”**
• an angel according to the Seventy, or as others think, of Christ; although it is asked how the impious king could have seen the Son of God.
• According to Symmachus: “The form of the fourth is like the sons of God,” in which angels are signified, who are called both gods and sons of God; this angel, or Son of God, is Christ, who went down to the furnace of hell, in which the souls of the saints were held and yet were not burned, that he might deliver them from hell; he who is “the angel of great counsel.”
3.26:
**“Then Nabuchodonosor came”** — he does not send messengers ahead.
**“to the door of the burning fiery furnace, and said: Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago”** — he humbly begs them to come out, whom he had proudly thrust in: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High.”
**“ye servants of the most high God”** — servants of the living God most high, not of deaf and dumb idols.
**“go ye forth, and come”** — Loosed, who were bound, sent.
**“And immediately Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago went out from the midst of the fire”** — They do not resist being sent, nor contradict those about to come out.
3.27:
**“And the nobles, and the magistrates, and the judges, and the great men of the king being gathered together, considered”** — Marvelling.
**“these men, that the fire had no power on their bodies, and that not a hair of their head had been singed, nor their garments altered”** — Breeches.
**“nor their garments altered”** — Much less burnt.
**“and”** — And also.
3.28:
**“And”** — And also.
**“Then Nabuchodonosor breaking forth”**
• In praise of God.
• Again he confesses God, condemns idols, and praises the boys who worship the true God and serve him alone.
**“Blessed be the God of them, to wit, of Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago, who hath sent his angel”** — He calls the angel the one he said above was like the Son of God.
**“and delivered his servants that believed in him, and they changed the king's word, and delivered up their bodies”** — To torments.
**“that they might not serve, nor adore any god, except their own God”** — In other copies: alone.
3.29: **“By me therefore this decree is made”** — Some most wrongly refer this to the devil, asserting that at the consummation of the world even he will receive the true knowledge of God, and will exhort all to penance; and they will have him to be the king of Ninive, who last of all comes down from the throne of his pride, and obtains the rewards of humility and does penance.
3.30: **“Then the king promoted Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago”** — Those who say above that the three boys were not judges of the provinces but prefects of individual works, hold that here they were first appointed judges of the provinces.

4.1:
**“Nabuchodonosor the king, to all peoples, nations, and tongues, that dwell in all the earth, peace be multiplied unto you”**
• The letter of Nabuchodonosor is placed in the prophet’s book, so that it may be believed not to be a book invented afterwards by another, as a sycophant lies, but to be Daniel’s own.
• This letter seems to have been sent after the vision of the tree and the change of seven years.
4.4:
**“I, Nabuchodonosor”**
• All this is from the letter.
• Jerome. The history is plain and needs no great exposition. For it is said that, for offence against God, Nabuchodonosor was turned to madness and for seven years lived among the beasts, on herbs and roots, and afterwards, restored to his kingdom, praised and glorified the King of heaven, because “all his works are true, and his ways judgments, and them that walk in pride he is able to abase.” But because some wish to understand by Nabuchodonosor the opposing power, of which it is said: “I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven.” And in the Apocalypse: “The dragon, falling to the earth, draws with him the third part of the stars.” And Isaias: “How art thou fallen, Lucifer, who didst rise in the morning?” They assert that it could not have happened that a man nourished in delights should live seven years on hay, and be so long among the beasts without the tearing of his body.
