And they ask by way of objection: if another succeeded him, whose folly was it, if he yielded to him the empire which he held so greatly; or how the empire was kept for him for so long a time, and he was without a king, especially since the histories of the Chaldeans contain nothing of the kind, nor could those who wrote of lesser things have passed over these in silence. All these things they urge so that, since the history does not stand, the devil may be signified by Nabuchodonosor; which we do not accept, lest all that we read seem shadow and fables. For who does not know that madmen live like brute beasts in the fields and wooded places? And histories, Greek and Roman, relate that far more incredible things have happened to men, since fables also tell of Scylla and the chimera, the hydra and the centaurs, and many things of the kind; what wonder if, to show the power of God and to humble the pride of kings, Nabuchodonosor endured these things?
**“was at rest in my house, and flourishing in my palace”** — In the world, according to those who understand by Nabuchodonosor the devil, who says: “All these will I give thee, if falling down thou wilt adore me.” And elsewhere it is said: “The whole world is seated in wickedness.”
4.5:
**“I saw a dream that affrighted me”** — Let it be answered that the devil saw the dream, unless perhaps whatever is in the world is seen as shadow and dream.
**“and the visions of my head troubled me”** — Of the mind, not of the eyes; for mysteries are revealed to him for the glory of the servants of God.
4.7: **“Then came in the diviners, the wise men, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers”** — Because this belongs to God alone.
4.8:
**“Till their colleague Daniel came in before me”** — Familiar.
**“Daniel, whose name is Baltassar, according to the name of my god”** — For so was the god of Nabuchodonosor called.
**“Till their colleague came in”** — The Seventy. I know not for what reason they passed these things over; therefore for this cause and like ones their translation was rejected, and that of Theodotion, commonly celebrated, which agrees both with the Hebrew truth and with the other translators.
**“who hath in him the spirit of the holy gods: and I told the dream before him.”** — No wonder Nabuchodonosor errs, in the manner of the Gentiles, and thinks whatever he sees above him to be not God but gods.
4.9:
**“Baltassar, prince of the diviners”** — Others: of enchanters. No wonder he was made chief of all the soothsayers, who had learned the wisdom of the Chaldeans at the king’s command, and was found ten times wiser.
**“because I know that thou hast in thee the spirit of the holy gods, and that no secret”** — Secret.
**“no secret is impossible to thee: tell me the visions of my dreams that I have seen, and”** — That is.
4.10:
**“This was the vision of my head in my bed: I saw, and behold a tree”** — Nabuchodonosor.
**“and the height thereof”** — Of such a one the prophet says: “I have seen the wicked highly exalted, and lifted up like the cedars of Libanus.” Those who are raised up not by greatness of virtues but by pride are therefore cut down and fall.
**“in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof was exceeding great.”** — Let us ask those who do not accept the history in this vision: who is this Nabuchodonosor who saw the dream, who is Daniel who expounded the dream and foretold things to come, and how Daniel, who according to them is understood as holy strength, is made by Nabuchodonosor chief of the soothsayers and is called his colleague.
4.11:
**“The tree was great, and strong: and the height thereof”** — The excellence of the king.
**“The sight thereof”** — Theodotion. Dominion. The despisers of the history cavil at this, that Nabuchodonosor by no means possessed the whole world, who held only the provinces of the east; but we take all these things as said by hyperbole, and on account of the pride of the impious king, who in Isaias boasts so much as to claim that he rules heaven and the globe of the earth like a nest and the eggs of birds.
4.12:
**“Its leaves”** — The glory of the kingdom.
**“were most beautiful, and its fruit”** — Riches.
**“exceeding much, and in it was food”** — Whom it fed.
**“for all: under it dwelt cattle”** — The simple.
**“and beasts,”** — The fierce.
**“and in the branches thereof the fowls of the air had their abode”** — The light, the lying.
4.13: **“A watcher”** — Theodotion. Angel. For angels are ever watchful, ready for the service of God. We too ought to imitate them by frequent night watches. Of him also it is said: “He shall neither slumber nor sleep, that keepeth Israel.” In what follows also it is said: “By the sentence of the watchers,” that is, of the angels.
4.15:
**“Nevertheless leave the stump of its roots in the earth”** — It signifies that the king is to be deposed, but the kingdom is to be preserved for him.
**“and let it be tied with a band of iron, and of brass, among the grass, that is without”** — By the hardest temptation, or as a madman.
4.16:
**“Let his heart be changed from man's, and let a beast's heart be given him; and let seven times”** — Years.
**“and seven times”** — Some lie that the seven years were changed into seven months by the prayer of Daniel.
**“pass over him.”**
• By the yearly course.
• Because it must be so done.
4.17:
**“By the sentence of the watchers”** — Of the angels, whose nations he was oppressing, whose word and petition was that he should be deposed.
**“This is the decree, and the word and demand of the holy ones”** — Of them before God.
**“till the living know”** — In him.
4.19:
**“and his thoughts”** — Because he understood the dream to be contrary to the king, and showed the fear of his heart by the paleness of his face. For he, who had greatly honoured him, grieved for the king and was not ungrateful; and lest he seem to insult him he says: My lord, etc.
**“Baltassar, the dream”** — Seeing him terrified, and that he did not wish to say anything unfavourable against himself, he exhorts him to speak truly and simply what he understands.
4.20:
**“The tree which thou sawest which was high and strong”** — He sets out the truth without injury to the king, and so that he may not seem to rebuke proudly, he explains the height of power.
**“whose height reached to the skies”** — By your presumption.
4.21: **“And the branches thereof”** — Princes.
4.22: **“It is thou, O king, who art grown great and become mighty: for thy greatness hath grown, and hath reached to heaven”** — Hyperbole.
4.23:
**“let it be bound with iron and”** — Those who contradict the history ask us how he was bound with iron and brass, or who bound him, since it is clear that all madmen are tied with chains lest they kill someone.
**“let it be sprinkled with the dew of heaven, and let his feeding be with the wild beasts, till seven times pass over him.”** — Otherwise: over her.
4.24:
**“This is the interpretation of the sentence of the most High”**
• Not mine.
• Who can do all things.
**“This is the interpretation”** — He softens the severity of the sentence with gentle words, and lightens the evils with promises. Whence: “Thy kingdom shall remain to thee.”
4.25:
**“They shall cast”** — Men.
**“thee”** — Mad.
**“from among men, and thy dwelling shall be with cattle and with wild beasts, and thou shalt eat grass as an ox, and shalt be wet with the dew of heaven: and seven times”** — Years.
**“shall pass over thee”** — Completed.
4.26: **“thy kingdom shall remain to thee”** — This too the cavillers accuse, wondering that after his savagery, after such torments, after the food of hay and herbs, he confesses God, and is what he had been. But let them answer how it is fitting that angels, who never fell, should have as their prince one who has been restored through penance.
4.27:
**“Wherefore, O king, let my counsel”**
• foreknowledge.
• Nabuchodonosor did works of mercy to the poor according to Daniel’s counsel, and therefore the sentence was deferred until the twelfth month; but because he boasted, saying, “Is not this the great Babylon?” etc., he lost the good of mercy through the evil of pride.
• Because of his humility he remained in the kingdom for another year, and because he had done good to the poor according to Daniel’s counsel; but, lifted up in pride, he was at once cast out and turned into madness.
• In Jeremiah the people of the Jews are commanded to pray for the peace of the Babylonians, because in their peace is the peace of the captives.
**“Wherefore”** — Although God had foretold it, and his foreknowledge cannot be changed, yet he exhorts to almsgiving and mercy to the poor, because he did not know whether it was a threat of God; for the sentence was changed also in the case of Ezechias and of the Ninivites, not by any vanity of judgment, but by the change of those who, being converted, deserved pardon. Also in Jeremias the Lord says that he will bring evils upon a nation, and if it does good, he will change his threats into clemency, and moreover promises that he will give good things; but if it does evil, he says that he changes his sentence, not in regard to the men but to the works, which have been changed. For God is not angry with men but with vices, and when these are no longer in the man, he does not punish what has been changed. For he intends to punish sins, and to save men.
**“perhaps he will forgive”** — Daniel, foreknowing the future, doubted God’s sentence; in this appears the intolerable rashness of those who boldly promise pardon to sinners. Yet no one is to despair, because pardon is promised even to Nabuchodonosor, if he does good.
4.30: **“And the king answered, and said: Is not this the great Babylon, which I have built to be the seat of the kingdom, by the strength of my power, and in the glory of my excellence?”** — those things which he was turning over in his mind, on account of those things which had been said to him by Daniel.
4.31:
**“And while the word was yet in the king's mouth”** — who wish to reign by themselves.
**“while the word was yet”** — Arrogant boasting is punished at once. Nor is the sentence delayed, lest mercy to the poor should seem to have profited the soul; in his pride he at once lost the kingdom, which he had held for some time through mercy; because he swelled above men over the greatness of his work, he was made lower than men.
**“a voice came down from heaven:”** — as a weight.
**“To thee”** — not to another.
**“O king Nabuchodonosor, it is said: Thy kingdom shall pass from thee”** — an open voice is sent before, so that it may be known that vengeance was sent from the Lord.
4.32:
**“And they shall cast thee out from among men”** — as a madman.
**“with cattle and wild beasts”** — with tame beasts.
**“and wild beasts”** — by nature.
**“thy dwelling shall be with cattle and wild beasts: thou shalt eat grass like an ox”** — not truly.
**“and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know”** — a great consolation in misery.
**“that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men”** — over all nations, “without whose nod not even a leaf of a tree falls.”
**“and giveth it to whomsoever he will.”** — “All power is from God.”
4.33:
**“The same hour”** — so that he might know that it is the punishment of pride.
**“the word”** — of God.
**“was fulfilled upon Nabuchodonosor, and he was driven away from among men”** — out of his mind.
**“and did eat grass like an ox, and ... with the dew of heaven”** — because he was covered only by the sky.
**“his body was wet with the dew of heaven: till his hairs grew like the feathers of eagles”** — of wings.
4.34:
**“Now at the end”** — of seven years.
**“of the days”** — of the days foretold by the Lord.
**“I Nabuchodonosor lifted up my eyes”** — of mind and body.
**“lifted up my eyes to heaven”** — I lifted up to heaven, where God is. Whence: “Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.”
**“And my sense was restored to me”** — He shows that he lost his reason, not his human form, which some think from what follows: “My figure was restored to me.”
**“and”** — therefore.
**“I blessed the most High”** — who rules in the kingdom of men.
**“and I praised and glorified him that liveth for ever: for his power”** — Believe from experience.
**“is an everlasting power, and his kingdom is to all generations”** — In all times, whether of the law or of the gospel. For Nabuchodonosor, once his sense had first been restored, could not be ignorant of this either.
4.35:
**“According to his will”** — In this he speaks as a man does, as if God acted not according to justice but according to will; and while he proclaims God’s power, he seems to accuse his justice, as if he had undeservedly suffered punishments.
**“doth according to his will, as well with the powers of heaven, as among the inhabitants of the earth: and there is none that can resist his hand”** — of his power
4.36:
**“At the same time”** — at that very time, when I knew him, that is
**“my sense”** — which I had lost
**“returned to me, and I came to the honour and glory of my kingdom, and my shape”**
• the restoration of sense
• the human form which, being mad, he seemed to have lost
**“My nobles”** — According to those who contradict the history, all the angels will seek the devil to be restored to the kingdom, and his glory will be greater than that of those who obeyed him, he who was proud against the Lord; and he did evil so that he might have good.
**“returned to me: and my nobles”** — So great was the wickedness of Evilmerodach that all sought him. Whence he was also afterwards put in prison by his father.
4.37: **“Therefore I Nabuchodonosor do now praise, and magnify, and glorify the King of heaven: because all his works are true, and his ways judgments, and them that walk in pride he is able to abase.”** — He understood that he had been punished for pride and justly humbled.

5.1:
**“Baltasar the king”** — Not the son of Nabuchodonosor, as is commonly believed, but, as Berosus says, who writes the history of Chaldea, and Josephus who follows him, after Nabuchodonosor, who reigned forty-four years, his son Evilmerodach succeeded. Of him Jeremias writes that in the first year of his reign he lifted up the head of Joachim king of Juda, and brought him out of the house of prison. To him succeeded his son Regusar, who had a son Laborsordech, the father of this Balthasar, by whom, when he was slain by the Medes and Persians, the kingdom of the Chaldeans was destroyed, and Darius succeeded; Xenophon writes this in the childhood of Cyrus the elder, and Pompeius Trogus; some think this Darius to be Astyages, others the son of Astyages.
**“made a great feast for a thousand of his nobles”** — Others: the king himself drank wine before all the princes whom he had summoned.
**“and every one drank according to his age”** — because they were seated at the feast according to age, or no one was compelled to drink beyond his strength.
5.2:
**“he commanded”** — He commanded, etc. The Hebrews relate that, thinking vain the promise of God by which Jeremias had said that the captivity of the Jews would be relaxed, which Zacharias also mentions at the beginning, as though mocking a vain hope of the captives he made a great feast and brought the vessels into the midst; at which the divine judgment at once appeared.
**“Drunk”** — And so, forgetful of what had happened to Nabuchodonosor.
**“being now drunk”** — Tropologically. Whoever, a heretic or another, takes up the words of the prophets and abuses the testimonies of sacred Scripture to his own sense, and gives to drink to those whom he deceives, and with whom he fornicates, departing from God, takes the vessels of the temple and is made drunk in them, and praises not God, whose vessels they are, but gods of gold, that is, those composed of secular learning, and of silver, those built up by the charm of eloquence and the art of rhetoric, of brass and iron, which, namely, the fables relate, and the songs of the poets, having much difference of elegance or of folly. Of these, because they are handed down as utterly foolish, they are deservedly called gods of stone or of fire. All these Deuteronomy divides into two parts: “Cursed be the man that maketh a graven and molten thing,” namely “the work of the hands of artificers, and shall put it in a secret place”; for all heretics hide the doctrines of their lies, “to shoot in the dark the upright of heart.”
**“that they should bring the vessels of gold and silver which Nabuchodonosor his father had brought away”** — great-grandfather
5.4:
**“They drank wine”** — of error
**“and praised”** — insulting the God of the Jews
**“their gods”** — to whom, granting victory, they drank in the vessels of the Lord
**“of gold”** — philosophical senses
**“and of silver”** — by the elegance of eloquence
**“and of brass”** — the songs of poets
**“of iron, and of wood, and of stone”** — the empty inventions of the Gentiles
5.5:
**“In the same hour”**
• So it was said above of Nabuchodonosor: “As the word was yet in the mouth of the king Nabuchodonosor,” that they may see the punishments inflicted for another cause.
• While the vessels were in the idol-house of Babylon, the Lord was not angry, because they seemed, in their own opinion, to have been consecrated to divine worship. But once divine things are defiled by human uses, punishment soon follows the sacrilege.
**“there appeared fingers, as it were of the hand of a man, writing over against the candlestick”** — so that both the hand and what is written may appear better
**“upon the surface of the wall of the king's palace”** — so that it may be understood to pertain to the king
5.6:
**“Then was the king's countenance changed”** — the word “changed” is also taken in a bad sense
**“and his thoughts troubled him: and the joints of his loins were loosed”** — from excessive terror
5.7:
**“the king cried out aloud to bring in the wise men, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers”** — Forgetful of what had happened to Nabuchodonosor, he follows the ancient error of his people: he calls magi, Chaldeans and soothsayers, not God’s prophet.
**“And the king spoke, and said to the wise men of Babylon: Whosoever shall read this writing, and shall make known to me the interpretation thereof, shall be clothed with purple”** — Shall be clothed with purple. Among the Jews anointing makes kings; among the Gentiles there are four insignia, namely purple, the clasp, the ring and the diadem. Granted without the others, one of these did not give the fullness of honour but only a share of it.
**“and shall have a golden chain on his neck”** — which was of the highest dignity
**“and shall be the third man in my kingdom”**
• after me, or one of the three princes
• having the third part of the kingdom
5.10:
**“Then the queen”** — Josephus. Grandmother. Origen: the mother of Balthasar. Whence she can know past things that the king did not know, let Porphyry therefore blush, who dreamed she was the king’s wife and mocks her for knowing more than her husband.
**“Then the queen, on occasion of what had happened to the king, and his nobles, came into the banquet house: and she spoke and said: O king, live for ever: let not thy thoughts trouble thee, neither let thy countenance be changed.”** — because
5.11:
**“There is a man in thy kingdom that hath the spirit of the holy gods in him”** — except Symmachus, who followed the Chaldean truth; the others translated it as the spirit of God
**“and in the days of thy father knowledge and wisdom were found in him”** — Everywhere rewards are given to virtue; whence a barbarian woman praises Daniel with such great praise.
**“for king Nabuchodonosor”** — grace to this king
**“thy father”** — great-grandfather, by the custom of Scripture, which calls grandfathers and their successors fathers
5.13:
**“Then Daniel was brought in before the king. And the king spoke, and said to him: Art thou Daniel of the children of the captivity of Juda”** — an argument from nature, as if: you are one of those who were accustomed to foretell the future
**“whom my father the king brought out of Judea?”** — to whom you have said true things
5.14:
**“I have heard of thee, that thou hast the spirit of the gods”** — by which you can
**“and excellent knowledge”** — of worldly things
**“and understanding”** — of hidden things
**“and wisdom”** — of divine things
**“are found in thee”** — than in others
5.17:
**“To which Daniel made answer, and said before the king: Thy rewards be to thyself”** — Thy rewards. Let us imitate Daniel, who despised the king’s dignity and gifts, already then following that gospel word: “Freely have you received, freely give”; for he announced sad things, and so had judged it right to accept gifts from that.
**“and the gifts of thy house give to another: but the writing I will read to thee, O king”**
• freely
• he had received freely, and gave freely
5.18: **“O king, the most high God”** — He sets forth the example of his great-grandfather, to teach the justice of God, and to show that the great-grandson, on account of similar pride, also endures similar things.
5.19: **“whom he would”** — If kings do what they will, where is the providence of God, where the precept, where that: “The heart of the king is in the hand of God,” etc.? But we call every saint a king, in whose mortal body sin does not reign, and whose heart is kept, because it is in the hand of God. And what is in the hand of the Father no one shall snatch out of it; what is snatched away is understood not to have been in it.
5.22:
**“Thou also his son, O Baltasar, hast not humbled thy heart, whereas thou knewest all these things”** — about Nabuchodonosor, by whose example you ought to have been corrected, knowing that “God resisteth the proud, but to the humble he giveth grace.”
**“Thou also his son”** — Some refer these things to Antichrist, saying that, imitating the pride of his father the devil, he is lifted up against God. But we ask of them who is the Daniel who interpreted to him the writing of God, who are the Medes and Persians who slew him and succeeded to the kingdom. For there is no doubt to anyone that after Antichrist the saints are to reign.
5.23:
**“But hast lifted thyself up against the Lord of heaven”** — which Nabuchodonosor had reverently placed in the temple of his God
**“the vessels of his house have been brought before thee: and thou, and thy nobles”** — not you alone
**“and thy wives”** — which is worse
**“and thy concubines have drunk wine in them”** — consecrated to divine uses
**“and thou hast praised the gods of silver, and of gold, and of brass, of iron, and of wood, and of stone, that neither see, nor hear, nor feel”** — drinking in the vessels of the true God
**“but the God who hath thy breath”** — breath
**“in his hand”** — power
**“and all thy ways”** — works, thoughts
5.24: **“Wherefore he hath sent the part of the hand which hath written this that is set down”** — on the wall
5.25:
**“And this is the writing that is written: MANE”** — Number.
**“Thecel”** — Weighing.
**“Phares”**
• Division.
• Mane, thecel: the first pertains to the ending of the kingdom, the second to the ending of the king’s life, the third to the transfer of the kingdom.
5.26:
**“And this is the interpretation of the word. MANE: God hath numbered thy kingdom”** — Since mane sounded number, thecel weighing, and phares division, it was a task not only of reading but also of interpretation.
**“and hath finished it”** — He finished it.
5.27:
**“Thecel: thou art weighed in the balance”** — Of God’s judgment or justice.
**“and art found wanting”**
• Having less than you thought.
• So that the sword kills before nature dissolves, whence: “Wicked men shall not live out half their days.”
5.28: **“Phares: thy kingdom is divided, and is given to the Medes and Persians”** — Into the Medes and Persians. For Cyrus, king of the Persians, with Darius his uncle joined to him, overthrew the empire of the Chaldeans.
5.29:
**“Then by the king’s command”**
• He received the insignia so that he might become known to Darius, who was to succeed, and be honored by him, and so be able to help the people of God.
• No wonder if, although hearing sad things, he paid the reward, since he had not at once believed the things to come which he had heard. For by honoring the prophet of God he thought he earned pardon, yet he did not obtain it, because the sacrilege was greater than the reverence due to a man of God.
5.30:
**“The same night”**
• Josephus says that when Babylon was besieged by the Medes and Persians, Balthasar king of Babylon fell into such forgetfulness of himself that he held a most celebrated feast, and drank from the vessels of the temple, and, though besieged, gave himself to banquets. Whence the history can stand that the same night he was taken and slain, while all were either terrified by the miracle of the vision and its interpretation, or occupied by the festivity or the drunkenness of the feast.
• Hence Isaias: “Behold I will stir up the Medes against them,” etc.; and Jeremias: “The daughter of Babylon is like a threshingfloor, this is the time of her thrashing: yet a little while, and the time of her harvest shall come.” And that she was taken at a feast Isaias makes plain thus: “Babylon, my beloved, is become a wonder to me. Prepare the table, behold in the watchtower them that eat and drink: arise, ye princes, take up the shield.”
5.31:
**“And Darius the Mede”** — By reverence for age and nearness of kinship to the kingdom.
**“succeeded to the kingdom, being threescore and two years old”** — The hand of the Medes rather than the kingdom of the Persians; and Cyrus’s uncle, who was earlier, ought by right of nature to have been the successor.

6.1:
**“It seemed good to Darius”** — But as to the order being reversed, so that the history is told under Darius before it is under Balthasar, which is made plain in what follows, since Balthasar was slain by Darius, this is the reason why he joined history at once to history. For at the end of the preceding vision he said: “And Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom, being threescore and two years old.” Under this Darius, therefore, these things were done.
**“It seemed good to Darius, and he appointed over the kingdom a hundred and twenty governors to be over his whole kingdom”** — Josephus says of this kind: “Darius, who destroyed the empire of the Babylonians, with the help and joint fighting of his kinsman Cyrus, was in the sixty-second year of his life when he took Babylon, and was the son of Astyages, who among the Greeks is called by another name, Assuerus. And he took with him Daniel the prophet and made him one of the three princes who were over his kingdom.” From which it is clear that Darius led Daniel with him into Media, and held him in the honour in which Balthasar had set him, and there is no doubt that he had heard of the sign that befell Balthasar, and the interpretation of Daniel, and how he foretold the kingdom of the Medes and Persians.
6.3: **“And the king thought to set him over all the kingdom”** — Two, with whom the third was set over them as prefect.
6.4:
**“and the governors”** — A hundred and twenty.
**“sought to find occasion”** — Envy goading them on.
**“against Daniel”**
• That they might find for Daniel from the king’s side.
• From the king’s side: namely, the one who had made him a close friend and colleague.
**“With regard to the king”** — The Hebrews suspect that the side of the king is the queen, or the concubines who sleep at his side; so, they say, they sought occasion in speech, in touch, in a nod, in a go-between. And they could find no cause or suspicion, because he was a eunuch. This is said by those who are accustomed to weave long tales on the occasion of a single word.
**“they could find no cause, nor suspicion, because he was faithful”** — In all things.
6.5: **“Then these men said: We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, unless perhaps concerning the law of his God.”** — A happy way of life, in which enemies find no fault except in the law which he keeps.
6.6:
**“Then the princes, and the governors”** — What they could not do by truth, they attempt by lying.
**“craftily suggested to the king”**
• They secretly suggested false things.
• For concealing their thoughts, as if honoring the king, they plot snares for Daniel.
6.8:
**“Now, therefore, O king, confirm the sentence, and sign the decree”** — Or: edict.
**“By the Medes and Persians”** — It is clear that there was one kingdom under Darius and Cyrus of the Medes and Persians, because Cyrus was Darius’s nephew through a daughter. Hence Daniel is said to have served now under this one, now under that one.
6.10:
**“Now when Daniel knew this”** — From this we learn not to offer ourselves rashly to dangers, but as far as lies in us to avoid snares. For Daniel did not act openly against the king’s command, but in his house and in secret obeyed the command of the true king.
**“into his house”** — In Latin, walls or roofs or upper rooms are called domata, and also auleta or cenacula (upper chambers). The Lord celebrates the Pasch in an upper chamber; the Spirit descended in an upper chamber upon a hundred and twenty souls. Daniel also, despising the king’s commands, prays not in a lowly place but in a high one, both according to the precept of God and the counsel of Solomon, who says that prayer is to be made toward the temple.
**“and opening the windows in his upper chamber towards Jerusalem”** — Where there is a vision of peace.
**“three times a day”** — Third, sixth, ninth.
**“Three times a day”** — The Holy Spirit came down upon the apostles at the third hour; at the sixth, Peter, wishing to eat, went up into the upper room to pray; and “Now Peter and John went up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer.” At these three times Daniel prayed.
6.12:
**“O king, hast thou not decreed, that every man that should make a request to any of the gods, or men, for thirty days, but to thyself, O king, should be cast into the den of the lions?”** — They bring it in generally, so that the king is held by his own concession not to decree concerning Daniel otherwise than he had spoken before.
**“The word is true according to the decree of the Medes and Persians, which it is not lawful to violate.”** — It must often be noted that the kingdom of the Medes and Persians is one, so that we may save the fact that Daniel is recorded as having been under Darius at one time and under Cyrus at another.
6.13:
**“Then they answered, and said before the king: Daniel, who is of the children of the captivity of Juda”** — as though it were the more intolerable thing
**“hath not regarded”** — a captive
**“thy law”**
• which is to be revered by all
• even of the king
**“nor the decree that thou hast made: but three times a day he maketh his prayer”** — his God
6.14:
**“Now when the king had heard these words, he was very much grieved”** — he saw himself caught by his own voice, and envy the cause of the plots
**“in behalf of Daniel he set his heart”** — his whole intention
**“to deliver him”** — not by authority, lest he seem to act against the law, but by reason and counsel he wishes to free Daniel
**“And even till sunset”** — The king had such eagerness to free him that, though most powerful, he took no food until sunset; and they had such obstinacy in evil that they were moved neither by the king’s will nor by the injury.
6.15:
**“But those men perceiving the king’s design”** — that he wished to rescue him
**“said to him: Know thou, O king, that the law of the Medes and Persians is, that no decree which the king hath made”** — As if to say: Do not labour in vain; what you have decreed you cannot change; a universal law cannot be overturned.
**“may be altered”** — to anyone
6.16:
**“Then the king commanded”** — to his servants
**“Thy God, whom thou always servest”** — He yields to the multitude and to his adversaries who agree together; he does not dare to deny the death of his friend, and what he himself cannot obtain he commits to the power of God. He speaks without doubt, he affirms boldly: “Thy God, whom thou always servest, he will deliver thee.” He had heard that the three children, though lesser, had overcome the Babylonian flames, and that many mysteries had been revealed to Daniel.
6.17:
**“And a stone was brought, and laid upon the mouth of the den: which the king sealed with his own ring”** — he entrusts him to the power of God
**“and with the ring of his nobles, that nothing should be done against Daniel”** — that he might not seem to hold any suspicion against them, and as if not trusting in the power of God, to contrive something for a friend; and that the power of the deliverer might shine more clearly
**“that nothing should be done”** — He who is secure from the lions fears men, lest the enemies devise anything against Daniel.
6.18:
**“And the king went away to his house”** — Such is his goodwill that neither by night nor by day does he take food, nor does he sleep, since with the prophet in danger he hangs, as it were, on a single feeling. How much more, then, ought we, for our own sins, to bend God to mercy by vigils and fasts, when a king who knows not God does this for the one whom he wishes to deliver from danger.
**“And the king went away to his house and laid himself down without taking supper, and meat was not set before him, and even sleep departed from him.”** — A lake, in Latin, is a gathering of sweet waters, as the lake Benacus and others; which the Greeks call limne, that is, a pool.
6.19:
**“Then the king rising very early in the morning, went in haste”** — because he believed that he would live whom he had entrusted to the living God
**“went in haste to the lions’ den”** — a pit sunk deep, or an arched cistern
6.20:
**“And coming near to the den”** — forgetting royal pride, the victor comes to the captive; the Lord runs to his servant
**“cried with a lamentable voice to Daniel”** — he shows the affection of his heart both by voice and by tears
**“and said to him”** — with tears
**“Daniel, servant of the living God”** — to distinguish him from the gods of the Gentiles, who are images of dead men
**“Thinkest thou”** — He who said above, “Thy God will deliver thee,” does not doubt, but tempers his sentence in ambiguity, so that when Daniel appeared unharmed, the more incredible the thing, the more just the indignation against the princes.
6.21: **“And Daniel answering the king, said: O king, live for ever”** — he honours the one who honours him, and prays for him eternal life
6.22:
**“My God hath sent”** — Let him say the same who is rescued from the jaws of the invisible lions, that is, from the pit of the lions of hell.
**“and hath shut up the mouths”** — The fierceness or rage of the lions was not changed, but shut up by the angel, because the prophet had gone before with good works, so that in this deliverance the repayment of justice rather than grace is noted.
6.23: **“Then was the king exceeding glad for him, and he commanded that Daniel should be taken out of the den: and Daniel was taken out of the den, and no hurt was found in him, because he believed in his God.”** — “Faith overcomes the world.”
6.24:
**“And by the king’s commandment, those men were brought that had accused Daniel: and they were cast into the lions’ den, they and their children, and their wives”** — For no law is fairer than that the makers of death should perish by their own art.
**“and they did not reach the bottom of the den”** — Perhaps there were steps of ascent there.
**“before the lions caught them, and broke all their bones in pieces”** — Where it is plain that Daniel was preserved by the power of God, not by the will or sluggishness of the lions.
6.25: **“Then king Darius”** — As through Nabuchodonosor, so in this place some understand through Darius an opposing power, which calls all to penance; and it is asked whether this will be in this world or in another, or after other worlds. But charging this to raving, we say that among barbarian nations signs are done through the servants of God, so that the worship and religion of the one God may be proclaimed.
6.26:
**“It is decreed by me”** — That peace may be multiplied to you.
**“that in all my empire and my kingdom all men dread and fear the God of Daniel”** — This is the fruit of miracles, that the name of God may be exalted.
**“For he is the living and eternal God”** — Others: dead.
**“and eternal for ever”** — Others: transitory.
**“and his kingdom shall not be destroyed, and his power”** — Honour.
6.27:
**“He is the deliverer, and saviour, doing signs and wonders in heaven, and in earth”** — In which the true God is proved.
**“who hath delivered Daniel out of”** — Otherwise: from the pit.
6.28:
**“Now Daniel continued unto the reign of Darius”** — In Chaldea, in the highest honour.
**“and the reign of Cyrus the Persian”** — But Daniel. What is read above at the end of the first vision: “And Daniel continued even to the first year of king Cyrus,” is not to be taken as the time of his life, since in the last vision we read: “In the third year of Cyrus king of the Persians, a word was revealed to Daniel surnamed Baltassar.” But this is signified: that until the first year of Cyrus the king, who destroyed the empire of the Chaldeans, Daniel was powerful in Chaldea; afterwards he was transferred by Darius to the Medes.

7.1: **“In the first year”** — This section and the following are earlier according to the history than the two above. For this one and the next are recorded to have happened in the first and third year of king Balthasar; but the one read before the one above happened on the last day of his reign. And this we read not only in Daniel but also in Jeremias and Ezechiel. But in the earlier chapters the order of the history is followed, what wonders and signs happened under Nabuchodonosor and Balthasar and Darius or Cyrus. In these, however, dreams are told, which were seen at various times, of which the prophet alone was aware, and therefore they have among the barbarians no wonder of sign or revelation. But they are written so that their memory may last among posterity.
7.2:
**“I saw in my vision by night, and behold the four winds of the heaven”**
• Because each angel prays or acts for the kingdom committed to him.
• Four: the angelic powers of man’s angels, who also admonish the wicked to do well, to whom the principal kingdoms are entrusted. Whence: “When the Most High divided the nations: when he separated the sons of Adam, he appointed the bounds of people according to the number of the children of Israel. But the Lord’s portion is his people: Jacob the lot of his inheritance.”
**“the four winds”** — The four angelic powers that preside over the kingdoms set in the fourfold world, that is, opposing powers, because according to the merit of each nation a power, either good or evil, is set over it; as in Daniel, Michael is called prince of the Hebrews. In Isaias, of the prince of Babylon: “How art thou fallen from heaven.” In Ezechiel, of the prince of Cyrus: “Thou a cherub stretched out, and protecting.” Of the prince of the Egyptians: “Thou great dragon that liest in the midst of thy rivers.” Generally, of the evil powers: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood; but against principalities and powers,” etc. They fought among themselves because they make the kingdoms promised to them fight. He calls the kingdoms beasts, differing in cruelty, because they differ in places, customs, and power.
**“strove upon the great sea”** — They strove upon the sea. That is, in the world, false and overflowing with the waves of the sea. Whence: “The kingdom of heaven is like to a net cast into the sea.” Whence also the dragon “is called king over all that are in the waters.” And David says: “Thou hast broken the heads of the dragons in the waters.” And the prophet Amos: “If he go down into the depth of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and he shall bite him.”
7.3:
**“And four great beasts”**
• We reserve what these beasts signify to be explained by the angel.
• The fierceness and cruelty of kingdoms is signified by the names of beasts.
**“great”** — For royal cruelty.
7.4:
**“The first was like a lioness, and had the wings”** — The subject kingdoms over which it ruled and flew.
**“The first was like a lioness”** — Note the order: in the image the head is said to be of gold; this lioness is that. The kingdom of the Babylonians, because of its cruelty or luxury, is called not a lioness but a lion. For those who have written on the natures of beasts say that lionesses are fiercer, especially if they are nursing cubs, and that they are always eager for mating.
**“had the wings of an eagle”** — As the lion holds the kingdom among beasts, so the eagle among birds; and the kingdom of the Assyrians lasted long, as the eagle lives a long time among birds.
**“and had the wings of an eagle”** — On account of the pride of the most powerful kingdom, whose prince says in Isaias: “I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven, and I will be like the Most High.” Whence it is said to him: “If thou be lifted up on high like an eagle, thence will I bring thee down into the abyss.”
**“I beheld till her wings were plucked off”** — Of the lioness or of the eagle.
**“and she was lifted up from the earth”** — The empire of the Chaldeans being overthrown; whence follows: And stood upon her feet as a man, etc.
**“and stood upon her feet”** — If it is read of Nabuchodonosor, it is clear that after he lost the kingdom and his power was taken from him, he was restored again to his former state, but not as a lioness; he learned that he was a man, and recovered the heart that he had lost.
**“and stood upon her feet as a man, and the heart of a man was given to her”** — If it is to be understood generally of the kingdom of the Chaldeans: after Balthasar was slain and the Medes and Persians succeeded, the Babylonians felt themselves to be men, humble and of frail nature.
7.5:
**“And behold another beast like a bear”**
• Who is most sparing in diet, strong, severe.
• And behold another beast, that is, the kingdom of the Persians, which for its hardness and fierceness is compared to a bear. For it was rigid and sparing in diet after the manner of the Lacedemonians, so that in its pottage it used salt and cardamom. The beast like a bear, in the vision of the statue, has the breast and arms of silver.
**“stood up on one side”** — Stood up on one side, because, as the Hebrews say, it did nothing cruel against Israel. Whence in Zacharias white horses are spoken of.
**“and there were three”** — Three kingdoms united: of the Medes, of the Persians, of the Chaldeans.
**“rows”** — Others: verses.
**“and three rows”** — Three princes, as Balthasar and Darius had three princes, who presided over a hundred and twenty satraps. Others think there were three kings of the Persians after Cyrus, but they do not name them; we, however, know that after Cyrus, who reigned thirty years, there reigned Cambyses his son, and the magi brothers, then Darius, in whose second year the rebuilding of the temple was begun; the fifth, Xerxes the son of Darius; the sixth, Arthabanus; the seventh, Artaxerxes, who was surnamed Longimanus; the eighth, Xerxes; the ninth, Sogdianus; the tenth, Darius surnamed Nothus; the eleventh, Artaxerxes, who is also Memnon; the twelfth, Ochus; the thirteenth, Arses the son of Nothus; the fourteenth, Darius, son of Sarsames, who was overcome by Alexander king of the Macedonians. How then do we say there were three kings of the Persians, unless perhaps we choose some of these as the most cruel, whom we do not have from the histories? Therefore let us take the three rows in the mouth of the kingdom of the Persians, and in the teeth the three kingdoms of the Babylonians, Medes, and Persians, which were brought into one. As to what follows: “And thus they said to it: Arise, devour much flesh.” That signifies the time when by Assuerus, whom the Septuagint call Artaxerxes, at the suggestion of Aman the Agagite, all the Jews were ordered to be slain in one day; and well put: he does not say he will devour them, but thus they say to it: “Arise, devour much flesh,” so that there was only the attempt, but the issue of the matter did not follow.
**“were in the mouth thereof, and in the teeth thereof, and thus they said to it”** — Aman and his friends.
**“Arise”** — Assuerus.
**“devour much flesh”** — The Jews.
7.6:
**“After this I beheld, and lo, another like a leopard”** — Who is carried headlong into blood and rushes by a leap into death.
**“like a leopard”** — The kingdom of the Macedonians, of which in the statue: “its belly and thighs of brass.”
**“and it had upon it four wings”** — For nothing was swifter than the victory of Alexander, who ran from the Illyrian and Adriatic sea to the Indian ocean and the river Phison, not so much by wars as by victories, and in seven years subdued to himself a part of Europe and the whole of Asia. The leopard also, of varied colour, signifies the diverse kingdoms subject to Alexander.
**“and the beast had four heads”** — It signifies his successors: Ptolemy, Seleucus, Philip and Antigonus.
**“and power”** — as if it were not the strength of Alexander but the will of God that did this.
**“was given to it”** — by God
7.7:
**“and lo, a fourth beast, terrible”** — The Roman empire, namely, of which in the statue: “its legs of iron, its feet part of iron and part of clay.” But now it mentions iron: it had great teeth of iron, etc.
**“After this I beheld in the vision of the night, and lo, a fourth beast, terrible”** — And behold a fourth beast, terrible. It is strange that above he set the lioness, the bear and the leopard for three kingdoms, and compared the Roman to no beast; unless perhaps he kept silent the name that he might make the beast fearful, and that whatever fiercer we think of in beasts we may understand of the Romans. The Hebrews maintain that what is passed over in silence here is said in the Psalm: “The boar out of the wood hath laid it waste, and a singular wild beast hath devoured it.” For which in the Hebrew is found: “All the beasts have torn it,” because in the empire of the Romans all the kingdoms that were before separate were together.
**“and wonderful, and exceeding strong, it had great iron teeth”** — most strong princes
**“eating and breaking in pieces”** — because all nations were by them either slain, or subjected to tribute or to servitude.
**“and treading down the rest with its feet”** — by the exaction of tributes
**“and it was unlike to the other beasts which I had seen before it”** — In the earlier beasts there were single signs of strength; in this one all were.
**“and had ten horns”**
• they say that at the coming of Antichrist ten kings will divide the Roman world.
• because he himself is the author of transgression.
**“And it had horns”** — And it had horns. Porphyry mixes the two latter beasts, of the Macedonians and of the Romans, into one kingdom of the Macedonians, and divides it: wishing the leopard to be understood as Alexander himself, and the beast unlike the others as the four successors of Alexander; and thereafter, down to Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes, he enumerates ten most cruel kings, whom he does not place of one kingdom, for example Macedonia, Syria, Egypt, Asia, but out of diverse kingdoms makes one kingdom in order, so that what is written, “a mouth speaking great things,” may be taken not of Antichrist but of Antiochus.
7.8:
**“I considered the horns, and behold”** — Antichrist, ignoble, born in an obscure place.
**“And behold, a horn”** — And behold a horn. In vain does Porphyry suspect this to be Antiochus Epiphanes, because it rose after the ten horns, and three of the ten were plucked up: the sixth, Ptolemy Philometor, and the seventh, Ptolemy Evergetes, and Artaxias king of Armenia; of whom the former Ptolemy died long before Antiochus was born. Against Artaxias indeed Antiochus fought, but he remained in his former kingdom. Let us say therefore that at the consummation of the world, when the kingdom of the Romans shall be destroyed, there will be ten kings who shall divide the Roman world among themselves, and that an eleventh, a little king, will arise, and will overcome three kings of the ten, that is, Egypt, Africa and Ethiopia, as will appear more clearly in what follows; and when these are slain, the other seven will bow their necks to the conqueror.
**“And three of the first horns were plucked up”** — three kings: first, Antichrist will humble the king of Egypt, of Africa, of Ethiopia.
**“at the presence thereof.”** — by the presence of his power
**“And behold eyes like the eyes”** — Lest we think, according to the opinion of some, that he is either the devil or a demon, but one of men in whom all Satan is to dwell bodily.
**“And behold eyes like the eyes of a man were in this horn, and a mouth speaking great things.”** — For he is a man, son of perdition, who is lifted up above every thing that is called God or that is worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as if he were God.
7.9:
**“I beheld till thrones were placed”**
• Like John in the Apocalypse: “After these things, immediately I was in the spirit,” etc., as far as: “which are the seven spirits of God.”
• Thrones. Whom John calls twenty-four thrones; of which Paul: “whether thrones, or dominations”; and in the Gospel: “you also shall sit on twelve seats judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”
**“Thrones were placed”** — The angelic powers, or the twenty-four elders whom John describes, or as the Lord says to the apostles: “You shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” For the angels of the Lord and all the elect will accompany the Lord in the judgment, and will be thrones of God, because he will sit in them.
**“and the Ancient of days sat.”**
• a stern and true judge
• The Ancient of days: the Father, namely. For although the person of the Son appears in judgment, yet the Father or the Holy Spirit will not be absent. And the Father is from himself, the Son from the Father, and whatever he has is ascribed to him from whom he is.
• God is said to be sitting and ancient of days, so that the bearing of the eternal judge may be shown. He is also described as an old man, so that the maturity of the sentence may be proved.
**“The Ancient of days”** — who alone sits on the throne in John.
**“His garment”**
• the excellence of the deity
• The Saviour is transfigured on the mountain, “and taking on the glory of the divine majesty, is seen in white garments.”
**“was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool.”** — a pure and sincere judgment is shown, receiving no person in judging.
**“His throne”**
• So that sinners may fear through the greatness of the torments, and the just be saved, “yet so as by fire.”
• The throne of God, morally, as Gregory says, are monks and hermits, who dwelling in one place strive to serve God, and do not run about from place to place; in their quiet hearts God sits; and they are rightly called a flame of fire, because they are inflamed with the love of God and neighbour and with desire for the heavenly country.
**“like flames of fire,”** — that he may punish the wicked and purge the good.
**“the wheels of it like a burning fire,”**
• the swiftness of judgment against sinners
• Its wheels: preachers, namely the apostles and their successors, who with great renown traversed the world preaching, who are rightly called a kindled fire, of which it is said: “I am come to cast fire on the earth; and what will I, but that it be kindled?”
**“The wheels of it”** — Others: chariot. Ezechiel also brings in the Lord seated on a four-horse chariot, and all things of God are flame, of whom elsewhere: “Our God is a consuming fire,” that we may know that he will burn wood, hay and stubble on the day of judgment; and in the Psalm: “A fire shall go before him, and shall inflame round about him.”
7.10:
**“A swift stream of fire”** — the severity of judgment
**“issued forth from before him.”** — so that he might drag sinners into hell
**“Thousands of thousands”**
• Not that the number of the servants of God is so great, but because human speech could not express a greater.
• These are the thousands and these the ten thousands, of which in the Psalm: “The chariot of God is attended by ten thousands,” etc. And elsewhere: “Who maketh his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire.” The office of the angels is twofold: some repay rewards to the just, others preside over the several torments.
• Gregory. The number of the heavenly citizens is both infinite and defined: countable to God, and innumerable to us. Though to stand by is one thing, to minister another. For there stand by, without doubt, other powers who do not go out to seek and announce peace to men. But those minister who come to fulfil the offices of messengers, yet even so they do not withdraw in contemplation from the inmost things. And because those who minister are more than those who principally stand by, the number of those who stand by is shown as, so to say, defined, but that of those who minister as indefinite.
**“and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him. The judgment sat”**
• the order of the judges
• Judgment, namely true, for the humbling of pride. Therefore the Roman kingdom will be destroyed, because that horn spoke great things.
**“and the books were opened.”** — the order of judgment
**“And the books were opened”** — And the books were opened. The consciences and works of each, in either part, whether good or evil, are revealed to all. The good book is that of the living; the evil is that which is in the hand of the accuser, who is the enemy and avenger, of whom: “The accuser of our brethren.” This book is earthly, of which the prophet: “They shall be written in the earth.”
7.11:
**“I beheld because of the voice of the great words”** — of Antichrist
**“which that horn spoke,”** — against God
**“and I saw that the beast was slain, and its body destroyed”**
• all the wicked
• As Christ is the head of all the good, so Antichrist is of all the wicked.
**“And I saw”** — And I saw. In one empire, because of Antichrist blaspheming, all kingdoms are destroyed together, and there will be no earthly empire, but the dwelling of the saints and the coming of the Son of God triumphing, of whom it is said: “And behold, one like the son of man came with the clouds of heaven”; who in the dream of Nabuchodonosor is written as the stone: “Cut out of the mountain without hands,” etc., which broke the clay, iron, brass, silver and gold. Now he is introduced under the person of the son of man, that the assumption of human flesh in the Son of God may be signified; whence: “Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven? This Jesus,” etc.
**“and given to the fire to be burnt,”**
• of hell
• for then all kingdoms will end
7.12:
**“and that the power of the other beasts was taken away, and times of life”** — in which they live under Antichrist
**“were appointed”** — by God
**“them”** — to the elect
**“for a time, and a time.”** — as long as the persecution will last; for those days are shortened for the sake of the elect
7.13:
**“I beheld therefore in the vision of the night, and lo, one like the son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven,”**
• who in John: “The lion of the tribe of Juda, the root of David,” is called
• Let Porphyry answer, to which of men this can apply, or who this is so powerful that “all nations serve him,” who has broken and ground down the little horn, which is interpreted as Antiochus. If he says that he was overcome by Judas Machabeus, let him show how he comes with the clouds of heaven as the son of man, and reaches the Ancient of days, and power and honour and a kingdom are given; and how “all peoples, tribes and tongues shall serve him,” and “his power is an everlasting power” which is closed by no end.
**“I beheld therefore”** — Whence the Apostle: “Who being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God,” etc. Made in the likeness of men, and found in habit as a man, “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even to the death of the cross.”
**“and he came even to the Ancient of days,”**
• “His going out is from the end of heaven, and his circuit even to the end thereof.”
• equal to the Father in all things
**“and they presented him before him.”** — on the cross
7.14:
**“And he gave him”** — The Father
**“power”**
• “All power is given to me.”
• “A name which is above all names.”
**“and honour and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes and tongues shall serve him.”** — “All nations shall serve him.”
**“His power is an everlasting power”** — “Who resists his power?”
**“and his kingdom that shall not be destroyed.”** — “And of his kingdom there shall be no end.”
7.15:
**“My spirit trembled”** — these things having been seen
**“my spirit trembled.”**
• of the man
• because
**“I Daniel was affrighted at these things, and the visions of my head troubled me.”** — of the mind
7.16:
**“I went near”** — therefore
**“to one of them that stood by,”** — whose image I had seen
**“and the truth”** — of understanding
**“asked the truth of him concerning all these things.”** — of the visions
**“He told me the interpretation”** — the exposition
7.17:
**“These four great beasts are four kingdoms, which shall arise out of the earth.”**
• because earthly
• Of the earth, because earthly: “All that is earthly shall return to the earth.” The saints will not receive the earthly but the heavenly. Let the fable of a thousand years therefore cease.
7.18:
**“But the saints of the most high God shall take the kingdom,”** — after the kingdoms of the world are ended, after the death of Antichrist
**“and they shall possess the kingdom for ever and ever.”** — The Machabees did not obtain the kingdom forever
7.19: **“After this I would diligently learn concerning the fourth beast, which was very different from all, and exceeding terrible: his teeth and claws were of iron: he devoured”** — therefore
7.21:
**“I beheld, and lo, that horn”** — Antichrist
**“made war against the saints, and prevailed over them,”** — by harassing their bodies
7.22:
**“till the Ancient of days came”** — the venerable judge
**“and judgment”** — the victory of judgment
**“gave judgment to the saints of the most High, and the time came”** — of judgment
**“Came, and the saints obtained the kingdom.”** — for eternity
7.23:
**“And thus he said: The fourth beast”** — Roman
**“shall be the fourth kingdom upon earth, which shall be greater than all the kingdoms,”** — preceding
**“and shall devour”** — with the sword
**“the whole earth, and shall tread”** — by tribute
**“and shall break it in pieces.”** — by power
7.24:
**“And the ten horns of the same kingdom shall be ten kings,”** — in the time of Antichrist
**“and another”** — Antichrist
**“shall rise up after them, and he shall be mightier than the former, and he shall bring down three kings”** — of Egypt, Ethiopia, Libya
**“bring down.”** — to himself
7.25:
**“And he shall speak words against”** — And words against. Symmachus. He will speak as God would. As one who takes to himself the power of God, so he takes also the words of divine majesty.
**“and shall crush the saints of the most High”** — And the saints of the Most High. For he will surpass the saints, puffed up with such pride that he will try to change laws and ceremonies, “lifted up above all that is called God, or that is worshipped.”
**“think himself able to change times”** — To change times. That is, temporal things, namely the order and course of times.
**“they shall be delivered”**
• by God
• for punishing
• the saints
**“into his hand”** — in power
**“until a time”** — a year
**“and times”** — Two years, according to Hebrew idiom; for they have a dual number.
**“and half a time.”** — six months
**“Half a time.”** — Whence: “And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh should be saved.”
7.26:
**“And judgment”** — judging
**“shall sit, that his power may be taken away,”** — the Antichrist, that is, the little horn
**“and be broken in pieces”** — the kingdom having been lost
**“and perish even to the end.”** — for ever
7.27:
**“The kingdom”** — Christ’s
**“and power, and the greatness of the kingdom, under the whole heaven,”** — or: over
**“under the whole heaven”** — as a heavenly kingdom
**“may be given to the people of the saints”** — a common good
**“of the most High,”** — Christ
**“whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all kings shall serve him, and shall obey him.”** — the saints, or kings, whether they wish or not: “for all power is from God”.
7.28:
**“Hitherto is the end of the word. I Daniel”** — I Daniel. Up to here the book of Daniel was written in the Chaldean and Syriac language; what follows to the end of the volume is in Hebrew.
**“was much troubled with my thoughts, and my countenance”** — of body and of mind
**“was changed in me: but I kept the word in my heart.”** — Like: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.”

8.1:
**“In the third year of the reign”** — The preceding vision was earlier, because it was in the first year of the reign of Balthasar, this one in the third; whence: “After what I had seen in the beginning.”
**“I Daniel, after what I had seen”** — that is, the earlier vision
**“in the beginning”** — the first year of the reign of Balthasar
8.2:
**“saw in my vision when”** — that is
**“I was in the castle”** — that is, riding or returning
**“When I was in Susa”** — Susa is the capital of the region of the Elamites, in which Daniel, according to Josephus, “built a lofty tower, constructed of square stone, and of such size and beauty that to this day it seems new; and in it the remains of the kings of the Persians and Medes are laid, and the keeper or warden and priest is a Jew.”
**“in the castle”** — because the metropolis is of such strength that it seems to be a castle
**“which is in the province of Elam,”**
• that is, worldly or everlasting
• In Elam, or as Symmachus says: in the city from which the region took its name; and from Elam, Elamite, as from Babylon, Babylonia, for which the Seventy translated the region as Elamais. But in the city of Elam all the places that belong to it are said to be.
**“and I saw in the vision that I was”** — I saw, however, in the vision that I was over the gate of the same castle
**“of Ulai,”** — that is, a marsh, from a swamp, or pain of the thigh, or of a little shade
**“over the gate of Ulai”** — For which Aquila: over Ubal Ulai. Theodotion: over Ubal. Symmachus: over the marsh of Ulai. The Seventy: beside the gate of Ulai. Now Ulai is the name of a gate or place, as the Trojan gate, the Carmental gate of Rome.
8.3:
**“And I lifted up my eyes”** — Although in the vision these things are seen in shadow, that is, in image, yet we could not see even these unless our eyes were raised.
**“And behold a ram stood”** — the kingdom of the Medes and Persians
**“And behold a ram”** — that is, Darius, uncle of Cyrus, who after Astyages his father reigned over the Medes.
**“before the water,”** — Ulai, or the gate, which in Hebrew is ubal
**“having two high horns,”** — Darius and Cyrus
**“and one higher than the other, and growing up.”** — Cyrus, who extended the kingdom on every side
**“And one higher than the other”** — Cyrus, that is, who after Astyages his maternal grandfather ruled the Medes and the Persians along with his uncle Darius.
8.4:
**“I saw the ram pushing with his horns”** — shaking his head and stirring the wind
**“Afterward I saw the ram”** — Not the ram itself, Cyrus or Darius, but the ram of the same kingdom, that is, the other Darius, who was the last king of Persian power, whom Alexander, son of Philip, overcame; that this Darius was most powerful, both Greek and Latin and barbarian histories testify.
**“against the west, and against the north, and against the south, and no beasts could withstand him,”** — to Alexander
**“nor be delivered out of his hand”** — power
8.5:
**“And I”** — Daniel
**“understood.”** — the change of kingdoms, provoked by the earlier vision
**“I understood”** — From the earlier visions, in which the second kingdom was signified by silver, it is also understood that the empire of the Medes and Persians will fall.
**“And behold a he goat of goats”** — the kingdom of the Greeks
**“And behold a he goat”** — Alexander, king of the Greeks, who, after Thebes was overthrown, took up arms against the Persians, and having joined battle at the river Granicus, overcame Darius’s commanders, and at length struck the ram himself, and broke his two horns, that is, the Medes and Persians, and cast him under his feet, and subjected both horns to his empire.
**“came from the west”** — Macedonia
**“upon the face of the whole earth”** — because, given the position of that land, the western region is the quarter
**“and he touched not the ground”** — with great speed, because he ran more by victories than by wars
**“And the he goat had a notable horn between his eyes”** — Alexander, who destroyed the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, in Darius the very wealthy, son of Sarsames, by a certain assault.
8.6:
**“And he went up to the ram that had the horns”** — Darius, son of Sarsames, in whom the kingdom of the Medes and Persians was destroyed.
**“which I had seen standing before the gate”** — as if immovable
8.7:
**“And when he was come near the ram”** — Darius, that is
**“he was enraged against him, and struck the ram, and broke his two horns”** — the Medes and Persians
**“and the ram could not withstand him”** — Alexander
**“And when he had cast him”** — bound
**“down on the ground, he stamped upon him, and none”** — of his friends
8.8:
**“And the he goat became exceeding great”** — the world having been subdued
**“exceeding”** — suddenly
**“And when he was grown, the great horn was broken”** — by death
**“the great horn”** — Alexander himself
**“and there came up four horns under it towards the four winds of heaven”** — through the four quarters of the world
**“And there came up four horns”** — When he had died in Babylon in the thirty-second year of his age, four of his commanders rose up in his place: Ptolemy the son of Lagus held Egypt; Philip, who was also Arideus, the brother of Alexander, held the Macedonians; Seleucus Nicanor held Syria and Babylon and all the kingdoms of the East; Antigonus reigned in Asia.
8.9:
**“And out of one of them”** — Seleucus
**“came forth a little horn”** — Antiochus Epiphanes, son of Seleucus, who was also called Philometor, who without the knowledge of the senate seized the empire by guile, when he had been a hostage at Rome, and fought against Ptolemy Philometor and against the Egyptians, that is, against the south.
**“and it became great against the south”** — the Egyptians
**“and against the east”** — them, namely those who were plotting revolution in Persia, at last fighting against the Jews
**“and against the strength”**
• of God
• the people of God, who is strong in him
8.10:
**“And it was magnified”** — when, having taken Judea, he entered Jerusalem and set up an image of Jupiter Olympius in the temple.
**“even unto the strength of heaven”** — that is, the sons of Israel, who were guarded by the custody of angels
**“and it threw down of the strength, and of the stars, and trod upon them”**
• For he subjected many of the saints to idolatry, and trod them under his feet like a star of heaven, and laid waste the people and the city too.
• In the one hundred and forty-third year from Seleucus, who first reigned in Syria after Alexander, Antiochus entered Jerusalem and laid waste all of it; and three years later, returning, he set up a statue in the temple of Jupiter.
**“And it threw down of the strength”** — Under the form of Antiochus it is said of the prince of darkness: he threw down of the strength and of the stars; this happens when he breaks some who shine with the light of justice and are strong in the power of their works; he is magnified even to the prince of the strength, because he is lifted up against the very author of virtue; he takes away the continual sacrifice, that is, because he interrupts, in those whom he has taken, the zeal of the Church’s way of life.
8.11:
**“And even to the prince of the strength”** — God himself, whose saints he persecuted, or Judas Machabeus
**“it was magnified”** — by his own judgment and that of men
**“and it took away from him the continual sacrifice”** — which was offered in the morning and in the evening
**“and cast down the place of his sanctuary”** — Jerusalem and the temple, placing in the temple an image of Jupiter Olympius
8.12:
**“And strength”**
• as though not by his own power but by God’s
• Because unless the deserts of those who perish demanded it, the adversary could in no way get possession of those who believed rightly. Truth is cast down on the ground, because then the faith in heavenly things is bent down to the desire of temporal life, being overcome. And he shall prosper and shall do, because then he rages with immeasurable cruelty without any objection, not only in the minds of the reprobate, but also in the bodies of the elect.
**“was given”** — by God
**“him”** — to him, Antiochus
**“against the continual sacrifice”** — God makes a man reign against the continual sacrifice, on account of sins, and he shall be overthrown.
**“because of sins”** — of the people
**“and”** — thus
**“truth shall be cast down on the ground”** — with the worship of idols growing, the religion of God decreed
**“and he shall prosper”**
• by his own judgment
• so that he even sought that the law of God should be burned and forbade circumcision
**“and shall do”** — according to his own heart
8.13:
**“And I heard one of the saints speaking”** — some angel, his name left unspoken
**“and one saint said to another”** — to the angel
**“I know not to whom that was speaking: How long”** — namely these things will be fulfilled, that is, over what span of time they will be fulfilled, from when they began to be fulfilled
**“How long”** — Some refer this to Antichrist, and say that what was done in type under Antiochus is to be fulfilled under him.
**“shall be the vision, concerning the continual sacrifice, and the sin of the desolation”** — of the temple in which images
**“that is made”** — under King Antiochus of Syria, by the judgment of God
**“and the sanctuary”** — of God
**“and fortitude”** — of the saints
8.14:
**“And he said to him: Unto evening and morning”** — It signifies the succession of night and day, that is, continually.
**“two thousand three hundred days”**
• that is, six years, and three months, and twenty days.
• Two thousand three hundred days. From the entry of Antiochus into Jerusalem, in the hundred and sixty-third year of the kingdom of the Greeks, until the cleansing and restoration of the temple done by Judas Machabeus in the hundred and sixty-ninth year, when the number of those days was completed according to the prophetic truth.
**“and”** — then
**“shall be cleansed”** — by Judas Machabeus, who overcame the commanders of Antiochus.
**“the sanctuary”** — the temple
8.15:
**“And it came to pass when I Daniel saw the vision”** — as a picture and an image
**“and sought the meaning”** — For not everyone who sees understands; as we often see Holy Scripture with our eyes and do not understand it in our heart.
**“that behold there stood before me as it were the appearance of a man”** — Of Michael.
**“the appearance of a man”** — For angels are not men, but they are seen as men, as Abraham at the oak of Mambre saw three men who were certainly not men, of whom one is adored as God and Lord. Whence: “Abraham saw my day, and was glad.”
8.16:
**“And I heard the voice of a man”**
• Of Michael.
• The Jews suppose this man to be Michael; and because the vision was about wars and the contests of kings, indeed about the successors of kings, Gabriel is fittingly assigned to this office, because he is set over wars. Now Gabriel is interpreted “strength” or “the strong one of God”; whence at the time when the Lord was about to be born, and to declare war on the demons, and to triumph over the world, Gabriel came to Zachary and to Mary. And afterwards it is read of the triumphant one: “Who is this King of Glory? the Lord who is strong and mighty: the Lord mighty in battle. He is the King of Glory.” But wherever healing and cure are necessary, as for Tobias, Raphael is sent, who is interpreted “healing” or “medicine of God.” But where propitiation or expiation is necessary, Michael is sent, who is interpreted “Who is like God?”, who by his name signifies that in God is true medicine. The angels have received their names from their offices.
**“between Ulai: and he called, and said: Gabriel”** — to whom it belongs
**“make this man to understand”** — Daniel, namely.
**“that man”** — Otherwise: this man.
8.17:
**“trembling, I fell”** — Because he had been standing, he fell, lest he should seem to himself to be lifted up in pride of angelic nature or dignity; he is reminded of frailty.
**“on my face, and he said to me: Understand, O son of man”** — remember that you are as a man.
**“for in the time”** — not immediately
**“the end shall be fulfilled”** — the end of completion
**“where I stood”** — as one fallen, and lay on the ground on all fours.
8.18: **“And when he spoke to me I fell flat on the ground: and he touched me, and set me upright”** — so that he might see and understand what is said without fear.
8.19:
**“And he said to me: I will shew thee what things are to come to pass in the end of the malediction”** — At the time when this curse will be fulfilled upon the people of the Jews and upon Antiochus himself, or at the end of the world under Antichrist and upon him.
**“for the time hath”** — of the vision
**“its end”** — of completion
8.20: **“The ram, which thou sawest with horns, is the king of the Medes and Persians”** — Darius, namely the son of Sarsame.
8.21: **“And the he goat, is the king of the Greeks, and the great horn that was between his eyes, the same is the first king”** — Alexander
8.22:
**“But whereas when that was broken”** — dead
**“there arose up four for it: four kings shall rise up of his nation, but not with his strength”** — because no one could be equal to Alexander.
8.23:
**“And after their reign, when iniquities shall be grown up, there shall arise a king of a shameless face”** — Antiochus, headlong in all things.
**“and understanding”**
• fulfilling in deed, or doing
• making to understand, and by open act showing what is now set forth
**“dark sentences”** — these visions
8.24:
**“And his power shall be strengthened”** — Gregory. That man’s strength is not strengthened by his own powers, because he is lifted up in the glory of perdition by the power of Satan.
**“but not by his own force”** — rather of God, from whom every power is.
**“and he shall lay all things waste, and shall prosper, and do more than can be believed”** — Antichrist, of whom it is said, and the fourth, which will proceed happily.
**“And he shall destroy the mighty”** — Gregory. He shall destroy the mighty when he conquers in body those who are unconquered in mind. Or when he draws to the nod of his will those who were believed holy and strong, in whose hand deceit is directed, because in that hand fraud is aided by deed; for what he says deceitfully, this he asserts by working wonders. For whatever the lying tongue feigns, this the hand of the deed displays as if it were true.
8.25:
**“According to his will”** — wicked
**“and craft shall be successful”** — at his nod
**“craft in his hand”** — in deed
**“and his heart shall be puffed up”** — great in pride in his own eyes
**“and in the abundance of all things he shall kill many”** — of the saints
**“And he shall rise up against the prince of princes”** — God, who says: “By me princes reign.”
**“shall rise up”** — so that he sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself as if he were God.
**“and shall be broken without hand”**
• “With the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked.”
• In Elymais, desiring to plunder the temple of Diana, where, his army lost, he was broken without hands; that is, he perished by sorrow and disease.
**“without hand”** — Not by the war of angels, not by the contest of saints, but at the coming of the judge he will be struck with eternal death by the breath of his mouth alone.
8.26:
**“And the vision of the evening and the morning”** — by the succession of times
**“which was told”** — fulfilled
**“is true”** — when the devastation is finished and the cleansing comes
**“thou therefore seal up the vision”** — in the heart or in the letter
**“thou therefore seal up”** — Gabriel, having explained the vision, adds: “Thou therefore seal up the vision,” marking its obscurity, that it is not to be open to many, and cannot be understood unless it is fulfilled in deed.
**“because it shall come to pass after many days”** — in the heart or in the earth
8.27:
**“And I Daniel languished, and was sick for some days”** — Having seen these things, he says something similar to Abraham when he saw the Lord: “I will speak to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes,” etc.
**“and when I was risen up, I did the king's business”** — I am become all things to all men, now fulfilling that gospel saying: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s; and to God the things that are God’s.”
**“and”** — yet
**“I was astonished at the vision, and there was none that could interpret it”** — the names of the kings and all the times of the kingdoms, because he had not heard these
**“could interpret”** — as an angel would, or because he had heard of kings but did not know their names; he had known future things but did not know at what time they would be. He therefore marvelled at what alone he could do, and committed all things to the knowledge of God.

9.1:
**“In the first year of Darius”** — He who is said above to have succeeded Balthasar, who first freed captive Israel, then Cyrus.
**“In the first year”** — Lest we think him to be the son of Hystaspes, in whose second year the temple was built, which Porphyry suspects in order to stretch out the years of Daniel; or him who was overcome by Alexander, king of the Macedonians. Both the father’s name and the victory he added, because he was the first of the seed of the Medes to overthrow the kingdom of the Chaldeans, so as to remove the error arising from the likeness of the name.
**“the son of Assuerus”**
• who is also Astyages
• not the one who is read of in Esther
**“of the seed of the Medes, who reigned”** — first
9.2:
**“The first year of his reign, I Daniel understood by books”** — Jeremias
**“I Daniel”** — Jeremias foretold seventy years of the desolation of the temple, after which the people would return into Judea, and the temple would be built; which fact does not make Daniel negligent but moves him to prayer, that what God promised by his mercy, he might fulfil by his prayer, lest pride cause negligence, and negligence beget offence. We read in Genesis that a hundred and twenty years of penance were appointed before the flood. But because for a hundred years the sons of men neglected to do penance, God does not wait for the twenty to be completed, but brings on beforehand what he had afterwards threatened. Whence also it is said to Jeremias, because of the hardness of the Jews: “Pray not for this people, for I will not hear thee.” And to Samuel: “How long wilt thou mourn for Saul, whom I have rejected?” Therefore in sackcloth and ashes he asks that what God promised be fulfilled, not because he is incredulous of things to come.
**“the number of the years, concerning which”** — number
