**“the word of the Lord came to Jeremias the prophet, that seventy years should be accomplished of the desolation”** — of the temple
9.3:
**“And I set my face”** — not ungrateful for God’s promise
**“my face”** — of the mind
**“to the Lord my God, to pray”** — by the privilege of charity
**“and make supplication with fasting, and sackcloth, and ashes”** — these are the weapons of penitents
9.4:
**“And I prayed to the Lord my God, and I made my confession, and said: I beseech thee”** — whose servants we are
**“O Lord God”** — whose creatures we are
**“great”** — we the least
**“and terrible”** — to despisers
**“who keepest the covenant”** — Therefore God does not at once do what he promises, but fulfils his promises to those who keep his commandments.
**“and mercy to them that love thee, and keep thy commandments”** — “If you love me, keep my commandments.”
9.5:
**“We have sinned”** — he recounts the sins of the people in his own person, because he is one of them, as Paul in his epistle to the Romans.
**“we have committed iniquity”** — in others
**“we have done wickedly”** — against ourselves
**“have done wickedly, and have revolted: and we have gone aside from thy commandments, and thy judgments”** — because
9.6:
**“We have not hearkened to thy servants the prophets”** — “He that despiseth you, despiseth me.”
**“that have spoken in thy name”** — not their own
**“to our kings, to our princes, to our fathers, and to all the people of the land”**
• no one therefore is excusable
• that is, to us
9.7:
**“To thee, O Lord, justice”** — because we justly suffer what we deserve
**“but to us confusion of face”** — “The confusion of my face hath covered me.”
**“as”** — “According to thy justice.”
**“at this day”** — is evident
**“to the men of Juda, and to the inhabitants”** — to the leaders, because the leaders are from Juda. Whence: “The prince shall not fail from Juda,” etc.
**“of Jerusalem, and to all Israel”** — alike in punishment as in fault
**“to them that are near”** — those who were leaders and inhabitants of Jerusalem, for now there are none such
**“and to them that are far off”** — scattered
**“in all the countries whither thou hast driven them”**
• from thee
• from your land
**“for their iniquities by which they have sinned”** — as if I do not accuse you, but accuse myself and mine
**“against”** — against
**“thee.”** — Wonderful, that servants should be against the Lord.
9.8: **“O Lord, to us belongeth confusion”** — therefore
9.9:
**“But to thee, the Lord our God, mercy”**
• confusion to himself
• because above he had said: To thee, O Lord, justice; lest he be thought merely just, he adds: But to thee, the Lord our God, etc., so that he turns the judge’s sentence toward mercy.
9.10:
**“And we have not hearkened to the voice of the Lord our God”** — who says: “Attend, O my people, to my law.”
**“to walk”** — advancing
**“in his law, which he set before us”** — not in others
**“by his servants the prophets”** — to whom we must give credence
9.11:
**“and”** — yet
**“all Israel”** — “All have gone aside, they are become unprofitable together.”
**“have transgressed thy law”** — which is wonderful
**“and have turned away”** — turned aside from thee inclining them
**“from hearing thy voice, and the malediction, and the curse, is fallen upon us”** — not the whole wrath is poured out upon us, which we could not bear
**“which is written in the book of Moses the servant of God, because we have sinned against him.”** — In Deuteronomy we read the curses and blessings, which were afterwards spoken on Mount Garizim and Hebal, over the just and the sinners.
9.12:
**“And he hath confirmed his words”** — fulfilled, namely
**“which he spoke against us”** — to be crushed
**“and against our princes that judged us,”** — not according to God
**“that he would bring in upon us a great evil, such as never was under all the heaven”** — hyperbole
9.13:
**“As it is written in the law of Moses, all this evil is come upon us: and”** — yet
**“we entreated not thy face, O Lord our God”** — great hardness: even when scourged they do not give way, or if they pray, they are not turned from iniquity
**“that we might turn”** — to thee
**“from our iniquities, and”** — that is
9.14:
**“And the Lord hath watched upon the evil”**
• our wickedness
• And he hath watched, etc. When we are chastised for our sins, God watches over us; when he does not do this, he is said to sleep for us. Whence in the Psalm: “The Lord was awaked as one out of sleep, and like a mighty man that hath been surfeited with wine.” For our malice and wickedness make him drunk, and when it is chastised in us he is said to “awake” and to rise from drunkenness, that he may make us, who are drunk, awake to justice.
9.15:
**“And now, O Lord our God, who hast brought forth thy people”** — he recalls the ancient benefit, so as to provoke God to a like deed
**“out of the land of Egypt with a strong hand, and hast made thee a name”** — glory
**“as at this day”** — as on this day
**“we have sinned”** — upon us
**“we have committed iniquity”** — against our neighbours
9.16:
**“O Lord, against all thy justice”** — but
**“let thy wrath and thy indignation be turned away, I beseech thee, from thy city Jerusalem”** — in place of the person he brings in the thing, rhetorically
**“and from thy holy mountain.”** — Sion
**“For by reason of our sins, and the iniquities of our fathers”** — “I will visit the sins of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation”
**“Jerusalem, and thy people are a reproach to all”** — to the Gentiles
9.17:
**“Now therefore, O our God, hear the supplication of thy servant, and his prayers: and shew”** — fulfil what you have promised
**“thy face upon thy sanctuary”** — temple
**“which is desolate, for thy own sake.”** — not us, who are unworthy
9.18:
**“Incline, O my God, thy ear, and hear”** — Anthropopathically: when we are heard, God seems to incline his ear; when he looks upon us, he seems to deign to regard us with his eyes; when he turns away his face, we seem, both to his eyes and ears, unworthy.
**“open thy eyes, and see”** — make us worthy of your sight and hearing
**“our desolation, and the city”** — if not us, at least the city
**“upon which thy name is called.”** — “Give glory to thy name.”
**“for it is not for our justifications”** — because unworthy
**“that we present”** — humbly
**“our prayers before thy face,”** — on which we presume
**“but for the multitude of thy tender mercies.”** — “According to the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out our iniquity.”
9.19:
**“O Lord, hear”** — that is, your servants
**“O Lord, be appeased”** — even though angry
**“hearken”** — even though set against us
**“and do”** — what we ask
**“delay not”** — quickly hear us
**“for thy own sake, O my God”**
• affectionately
• than which nothing is greater; what then, when asked for his own sake, can he deny?
**“because”** — therefore
**“thy name is invocated”** — “Give not thy honour to strangers.”
**“upon thy city”** — for protection
**“and upon thy people”** — protect what is yours
9.20:
**“Now while I was yet”** — While you are still speaking, I will say: Here I am.
**“speaking, and praying”** — A hendiadys.
**“and confessing my sins,”** — because it is a confession of praise; he defines it.
**“and the sins of my people of Israel,”** — not only of the people, because “in many things we all offend”; or, out of humility, although he did not sin, he joins himself to the people that he may obtain pardon.
9.21:
**“As I was yet speaking in prayer,”** — Whence, while he was still speaking, I say: Behold, I am here.
**“behold the man Gabriel”** — It signifies not sex but strength, in the more honorable sex.
**“whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, flying swiftly”** — in the past vision, which he here carries out.
**“touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice.”** — because the prayer lasted from the morning sacrifice until the evening one, and so bent God to mercy. Whence: “The continual prayer of a just man availeth much.”
9.22:
**“And he instructed me”** — So obscure is the vision that even the prophet needs to be taught.
**“and spoke to me, and said: O Daniel, I am now come forth”** — not from the face of God, as if I withdrew from him who is everywhere, but to teach you, having been made visible to you from invisibility.
9.23:
**“From the beginning of thy prayers”** — from the time you began to ask, you obtained.
**“the word came forth”** — From God.
**“the word”** — The meaning.
**“I am come to shew it to thee”** — which you do not know.
**“because thou art a man of desires”** — or beloved of God and worthy of God’s love, as Solomon is called Edida; or a man of desires, so that, in answer to your desire, you hear secrets, knowing things to come.
**“therefore do thou mark the word”** — If this is said to Daniel, what ought we to do, whose eyes are blinded by the darkness of ignorance and the mist of vices?
**“and understand the vision.”** — O Daniel. Here he speaks in the person of God: Seventy, etc.
9.24:
**“Seventy weeks”** — of years, that is, four hundred and ninety, from the going forth of the word, so that Jerusalem may be built again.
**“are shortened”** — Not in number, that is, so that they are not four hundred and ninety years, but in quantity. For, as they say, they are not reckoned by the solar year, which has three hundred and sixty-five days, but by the lunar year, which has three hundred and fifty-four days; the solar exceeds the lunar by eleven days.
**“upon thy people”**
• not mine, as you said. God speaks similarly in Exodus to Moses: “Go down, for thy people has sinned,” as if not his, whom he deserted.
• As if: God will soon look upon your people, for whom you asked, who nevertheless is not his as far as you said there, because your name is invocated upon the city and upon your people; but it is yours, for whom you made supplication.
**“and upon thy holy city”** — not mine.
**“that may be finished”** — In the passion of Christ, who took away the sins of the world.
**“transgression,”** — blotted out.
**“and sin may have an end, and ... may be abolished”** — Explanation.
**“iniquity”** — In the time of grace.
**“and justice may be brought”** — Of the gospel.
**“everlasting”** — which surpasses the justice of the law.
**“and vision and prophecy may be fulfilled; and the saint of saints may be anointed.”**
• “The law and the prophets were until John”; because before the coming of Christ all these things were hoped for rather than possessed.
• Seventy weeks are shortened upon the people. The Hebrews explain it thus, as if to say: O Daniel, know that from this day on which I now speak to you (it was the first year of Darius, who slew Balthasar and transferred the kingdom of the Chaldeans to the Persians and Medes) until the seventieth year of weeks, that is, four hundred and ninety years, these things will come upon your people in parts. First God will be propitiated to you as you pray, and sin will be blotted out, and transgression will receive its end. For now, with the city and the temple destroyed, the people is in mourning, but in a short time it will be restored; and not only this will be done in these seventy weeks, but Christ will be born, that is, everlasting justice, and vision and prophecy will be sealed, so that no prophet may be found in Israel, and the saint of saints will be anointed, of whom therefore it is said: “God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness,” etc.; who says: “Be ye holy, because I am holy.” Know therefore that from this day on which I now speak to you, and promise the word of God that the people will return and Jerusalem be rebuilt, until Christ and the desolation of the temple, weeks are counted: sixty-two, and another seven, in which, in their own order, two things will be done of which I spoke before: that the people will return and the street be rebuilt by Nehemias and Esdras under Artaxerxes, in the twentieth year of his reign. At the end of the weeks, therefore, the sentence of God will be fulfilled in the straitness of the times, when the temple will again be destroyed and the city taken. For after sixty-two weeks Christ will be slain, and his people will not be, who are to deny him; or, as they say, the dominion of that people will not be, which it thought it would retain. And why do I speak of Christ to be slain and of the people to be utterly forsaken, when a people with a leader to come, that is, Vespasian, will destroy both the city and the sanctuary? After his death, when seven weeks had passed, that is forty-nine years, Aelius Hadrian (by whom afterwards the city Aelia was founded from the ruins of Jerusalem) overcame the rebelling Jews, Tinius Rufus the master of the army fighting; and then the victim and sacrifice failed, and until the consummation of the world the desolation will continue.
• Tertullian, in his book Against the Jews, says this word for word: “Whence then do we show that Christ came within sixty-two weeks? The number is from the first year of Darius, since at that time this vision is shown to Daniel. For he says: ‘Know thou and take notice that from the prophesying of the word I answer you these things which follow in the text, concerning the building of the wall,’ etc. Whence we must reckon from the first year of Darius. For then Daniel saw this vision. Let us see therefore how many years are fulfilled until the coming of Christ. Darius reigned nineteen years, Artaxerxes forty-one, Ochus, who is also Cyrus, twenty-four years, Argus one year, another Darius, who is also Melas, twenty-one, Alexander the Macedonian twelve years; after him Sother reigned in Alexandria thirty-five years, and Philadelphus succeeding him reigned thirty-nine years. After him Evergetes twenty-five years, then Philopator seventeen, after him Epiphanes twenty-four. Likewise another Evergetes thirty-seven years, Sother thirty-eight years, Ptolemy thirty-seven, Cleopatra twenty years and six months. Likewise Cleopatra reigned together with Augustus thirteen years. After Cleopatra, Augustus ruled another forty-three. For all the years of Augustus were fifty-six in number. We know moreover that in the forty-first year of the rule of Augustus, who ruled after the death of Cleopatra, Christ was born, and Augustus lived on fifteen years after Christ was born; and the remaining time of years, from the day of Christ’s birth to the forty-first year of Augustus after the death of Cleopatra, will be four hundred and thirty-seven years and six months. Whence sixty-two weeks and a half are fulfilled, which make four hundred and thirty-seven years and six months, on the day of Christ’s birth; and everlasting justice was manifested, and the saint of saints, that is Christ, was anointed, and vision and prophecy were sealed, and sins were forgiven through faith in the name of Christ. But what is it that he says, to seal vision and prophecy, since all the prophets announced that he was to come and to suffer? Because therefore the prophecy was fulfilled, he said that by his coming vision and prophecy are sealed, since he is the seal of all the prophets, fulfilling all that the prophets of old announced of him; because after his coming and his passion there is now no vision nor prophecy that announces that Christ is to come. And a little after he says: Let us see what the other seven and a half weeks, which remain, divided off in the cutting off of the former weeks, in what year or act they were fulfilled. For after Augustus, who lived on fifteen years after the birth of Christ, Tiberius Caesar succeeded, twenty-two years, seven months and twenty-eight days. In the fifteenth year of his rule Christ was baptized, being about thirty years old. Likewise Caius Caligula, three years, eight months, thirteen days. Nero, fourteen years, seven months, thirteen days. Galba, seven months, twenty-eight days. Otho the emperor, eight months, three days. Vitellius, eight months, twenty-eight days. Vespasian in the first year of his rule conquered the Jews, and the years make fifty-two in number and six months. For he reigned eleven years; and so on the day of the capture the Jews fulfilled the seventy weeks foretold by Daniel.”
• Africanus: In the twentieth year of Artaxerxes king of the Persians the word went forth, when Nehemias his cupbearer, as is read in Esdras, asked and obtained that Jerusalem be rebuilt; and this is the word that went forth, which gave leave to build the city, which until that time lay open to the inroads of the neighboring nations. For under the rule of king Cyrus, who had given power to those who wished to return to Jerusalem, Jesus and Zorobabel and Esdras the priest, and those who wished to set out with them, tried to build the temple and the city and its walls, but the nations round about forbade it, that the work might not be completed, as though this were done without the king’s order. So the work hung interrupted until Nehemias and the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, at which time of the kingdom of the Persians one hundred and fifteen years had run, and of the captivity of Jerusalem one hundred and eighty-five. Then first Artaxerxes ordered the walls to be built, and Nehemias had charge of the work. Then the street was built and the walls set round. From that time, if you wish to count the weeks of seventy years, you will be able to find them as far as Christ. But if we take the beginning of these weeks from another time, the times do not agree and we run into many contradictions. For even if we count the seventy weeks from Cyrus, and from his first indulgence, by which the captivity of the Jews was relaxed, we shall find a hundred years and more that exceed this number of weeks; and many more if from the time when the angel spoke to Daniel; and a greater number is added if you take the beginning of the captivity as the start of the weeks. For the kingdom of the Persians lasted until the beginning of the Macedonians two hundred and thirty years, and the Macedonians reigned three hundred years, and from then until the fifteenth year of Tiberius Cesar, when Christ suffered, there are sixty years; all of which make five hundred and ninety, so that a hundred years are left over. But from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes to Christ seventy weeks are completed, according to the lunar reckoning of the Hebrews, who count the months not by the course of the sun but of the moon. For from the hundred and fifteenth year of the kingdom of the Persians, when Artaxerxes was passing the twentieth year of his reign, and it was the fourth year of the eighty-third Olympiad, to the two hundred and second Olympiad and the second year of the same Olympiad, and the fifteenth year of Tiberius Cesar, four hundred and seventy-five years are gathered, which make four hundred and ninety years of the Hebrews.
• Note that Africanus and Bede agree in sum, and differ in this alone: that Africanus says the Roman kingdom had been sixty years until the fifteenth year of Tiberius Cesar, when he says Christ suffered, but Bede fifty-seven years until the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Cesar, when he says Christ suffered. Although therefore he says there were fifty-seven years until the eighteenth year of Tiberius Cesar, in which he intimates that there were only fifty-seven years until the eighteenth year of Tiberius Cesar, yet he agrees with Africanus in sum, because what Africanus puts less in the kingdom of the Persians, he puts more in the kingdom of the Romans. But let us follow Bede, who says that Christ suffered in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, because according to Luke Christ was baptized right after the thirtieth year, which was the fifteenth year of Tiberius Cesar. Then he suffered after three years, not in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Cesar.
• Africanus does not define from what beginning he starts his Olympiads, whether from the beginning at which they began to be, or whether he looks to another beginning. But this is to be known: that from that beginning which he takes, two hundred and two had passed, according to him, in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Cesar; but in the twentieth year of king Artaxerxes, who had gone long before, eighty-three Olympiads had already passed, yet so that the fourth year of the eighty-third was then beginning. Therefore of the two hundred and two aforesaid, or rather, to speak more truly, of two hundred and one and a half, because in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Cesar only two years of the last had flowed by, of those, I say, take away the eighty-three which had passed, as was said, in the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes, and then there will remain to you a hundred and eighteen Olympiads and a half, which make four hundred and seventy-four solar years. For an Olympiad contains a space of four years; add to these years the fourth year of the eighty-third Olympiad, which was beginning at the aforesaid time of Artaxerxes, and there will be four hundred and seventy-five years. Therefore count carefully from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, according to the aforesaid number of Olympiads, up to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Cesar, and you will find four hundred and seventy-five solar years, which make four hundred and ninety years of the Hebrews; and this is what Africanus says obscurely.
**“Seventy”** — Bede in the book On the Nature of Things. These words designate the incarnation of Christ, who fulfilled the law and the prophets, and was anointed “with the oil of gladness above his fellows”; the seventy weeks, divided by sevens of years, signify four hundred and ninety lunar years. But it must be noted that he declares these same weeks to be not simply reckoned but shortened, secretly warning us to know that the years are indicated as shorter than usual. Know therefore, he says, and take notice: “from the going forth of the word, to build up Jerusalem again, unto Christ the prince, there shall be seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks: and the street shall be built again, and the walls in straitness of times.” From Esdras’s narrative we have learned that Nehemias, cupbearer of King Artaxerxes, in the twentieth year of his reign, in the month of Nisan, obtained from him leave to restore the walls of Jerusalem, the temple having been built long before with Cyrus permitting. And that he completed this work also, as was said, in straitness of time, being so attacked by the neighboring nations that the builders, each with a sword girded at his side, are said to have fought with one hand and recovered the wall with the other. From this time, therefore, to Christ the prince seventy weeks are reckoned, that is, four hundred and ninety years of twelve lunar months, which are four hundred and seventy-five solar years. For the Persians reigned from the aforesaid twentieth year of King Artaxerxes to the death of Darius one hundred and eighteen years. From then the Macedonians, to the death of Cleopatra, three hundred years. Then the Romans held the monarchy until the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, fifty-seven years; which together, as we said, are four hundred and seventy-five solar years. And they are contained in twenty-five nineteen-year cycles. For nineteen times twenty-five makes four hundred and seventy-five. And because in each cycle seven embolismic months are added, multiply twenty-five by seven and it makes one hundred and seventy-five, which are the embolismic months of four hundred and seventy-five years. If therefore you wish to know how many lunar years these months make, divide the one hundred and seventy-five months by twelve, and they make fourteen years and seven months. Join these to the aforesaid four hundred and seventy-five years: there will be four hundred and eighty-nine years and seven months. And add these surplus months to part of the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, under whom the Lord suffered, and you will find the weeks fixed beforehand, or the term fixed beforehand, that is, from the going forth of the word by which it was commanded that the walls of Jerusalem be rebuilt, to his passion, seventy shortened weeks, that is, four hundred and ninety lunar years. And that by his baptism, when the saint of saints was anointed, the Holy Spirit descending upon him like a dove, not only the seven and sixty-two weeks had been completed, but also a part of the seventieth week was already begun. And after sixty-two weeks, he says, Christ shall be slain, and the people that shall deny him shall not be his. Christ was slain not immediately after the sixty-two and seven weeks, but at the end of the seventieth week, which, as far as we can judge, he set apart from the other weeks because he was to relate more about it. For in that week Christ was crucified, and was denied by the faithless people not only in the passion but continually from the time he began to be preached by John. But what follows: “And a people with their leader that shall come, shall destroy the city and the sanctuary: and the end thereof shall be waste, and after the end of the war the appointed desolation,” does not belong to the seventy weeks. For it had been foretold that the weeks themselves would reach to the leadership of Christ, but Scripture, having foretold his coming and passion, shows what would also happen after this to the people who would not receive him. For it says the leader to come is Titus, who in the forty-second year after the Lord’s passion, with the Roman people, so destroyed the city and the sanctuary that there did not remain “a stone upon a stone.” Whence, having touched on these things by anticipation, it soon returns to expounding the event of the week which it had passed over. “And he shall confirm the covenant,” that is, of faith, “with many, in one week,” that is, the last one itself, in which either John the Baptist, or the Lord, or the apostles by preaching converted many to the faith. “And in the half of the week the victim and the sacrifice shall fail”: the half of this week was the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when, Christ’s baptism having begun, the purification by victims gradually began to grow cheap to the faithful. Again, what follows: “And there shall be in the temple the abomination of desolation: and the desolation shall continue even to the consummation, and to the end,” looks to later times, the truth of which prophecy is attested by the history of the ancients and the events of our own times. We have therefore set out the whole testimony of the prophet and expounded it as far as ability allowed, because we know that this is unknown to most readers and demands a special kind of week. For those are mistaken who think the Hebrews used such years; otherwise the whole series of the Old Testament wavers, and no one’s age ought to be understood as great as it is written, but is to be restricted to the course of the moon. It must be known that Africanus, the course of weeks which we have carried down, according to the chronicle of Eusebius, to the seventeenth or eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, in which we believe the Lord suffered, begins from the same starting point as we do, and thinks it was completed in the fifteenth year of the same emperor, in which he believed him to have suffered, setting the years of the Persian kingdom at one hundred and fifteen, of the Macedonians three hundred, of the Romans sixty. But let the diligent reader choose what he thinks better to follow.
9.25:
**“Know thou therefore”**
• It makes attentive.
• Let not the Hebrews move us if seven weeks are counted first, and afterwards sixty-two, and again one is divided into two parts. For this is an idiom of the Hebrew speech and of ancient Latinity, that they reckon the lesser number before the greater. For example, we, according to the property of our language, now say: Abraham lived a hundred and seventy-five years. They on the contrary: He lived five seventy and a hundred. Therefore it is not fulfilled as it is read, but as the whole is reckoned together, so it received its end. Nor is it to be ignored that some of them say that the one week, of which it is said: “And he shall confirm the covenant with many, in one week,” is divided between Vespasian and Hadrian, so that according to the history of Josephus Vespasian and Titus made peace with the Jews for three years and seven months, while three years and six months are reckoned under Hadrian, when Jerusalem was utterly overthrown, and the Jews were slain in throngs, so that they were driven even from the borders of Judea. This the Hebrews say, not greatly caring that from the first year of Darius king of the Persians to the final overthrow of Jerusalem, which happened under Hadrian, a hundred and seventy-four Olympiads are counted, that is, six hundred and ninety-six years, which make ninety-nine Hebrew weeks and three years, when Chochebas the leader of the Hebrews was crushed and Jerusalem was razed to the ground.
**“and take notice: that from the going forth of the word,”** — of years, that is, four hundred and ninety from the going forth of the word, so that it may be answered by Artaxerxes and Jerusalem be built.
**“to build up Jerusalem again, unto Christ the prince”** — Of princes.
**“there shall be seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks”** — He seems to set apart the last, as if about to say more of it, of which he adds: “And he shall confirm the covenant with many, in one week.”
**“and shall be built again”** — From Nehemias.
**“the street”** — Jerusalem.
**“and the walls in straitness of times.”** — in a short time.
9.26:
**“And after sixty-two weeks”** — Understand: and seven.
**“Christ shall be slain”** — not immediately fulfilled for them, but afterwards at the end: the Seventy.
**“the people ... shall not be his”** — but of Caesar or of the devil. Whence: “They shall be the portions of foxes.”
**“that shall deny him”** — “We have no king but Caesar.” And elsewhere: “We know not from whence he is.”
**“And”** — Therefore.
**“the city and the sanctuary”** — The temple.
**“a people shall destroy”** — Roman.
**“with their leader that shall come,”** — Vespasian.
**“and the end thereof shall be waste, and after the end of the war”** — under Vespasian.
**“the appointed desolation.”** — by God for eternity.
9.27:
**“He shall confirm the covenant”** — That is, while John and Christ and the apostles were preaching, many were saved, and the true victim began to be held cheap in the hearts of the faithful or of the elect.
**“And he shall confirm the covenant with many, in one week:”** — And he shall confirm the covenant, etc. This is to be understood of the three and a half years in which Christ preached, and he confirmed what he had promised to the fathers.
**“and in the half of the week the victim and the sacrifice shall fail.”** — for three years of the last week had already passed when the Lord was baptized, that is, in the four hundred and eighty-sixth, to which are added three years and six months, and part of the eighteenth year of Tiberius; and they are four hundred and ninety.
**“And in the temple shall be the abomination of desolation”**
• the abominated desolation.
• abominable sacrifices after the death of Christ.
**“even to the consummation”** — of the world.
**“and to the end the desolation shall continue”** — of the Jews.

10.1:
**“In the third year”** — At the end of the first vision we read that Daniel was there until the first year of king Cyrus; which is to be understood thus: that he was among the Chaldeans in his former dignity until the first year of king Cyrus, and afterwards was transferred to the Medes, where in the first year of king Cyrus he learned the mysteries of the seventy weeks. Now, in the third year of king Cyrus, he is related to have seen these things.
**“a word was revealed to Daniel surnamed Baltassar, and a true word, and great strength”** — of God, who is going to do this, and of the prophet, who is going to understand.
**“and he understood the word”** — We too see or read letters in vain unless we understand them.
10.2:
**“In those days I Daniel mourned”** — “Be converted to me with all your heart, in fasting, and in weeping, and in mourning.”
**“In those days”** — Anagogically. He who is in mourning and grieves for the absence of the bridegroom eats not the desirable bread “that came down from heaven,” nor takes solid food, which is understood of the flesh, nor drinks the wine that “maketh glad the heart of man,” nor “maketh the face cheerful with oil.” And this fast makes the tears of the bride availing, “when the bridegroom shall be taken away from” her; nor does Daniel dare to entreat the Lord otherwise.
**“three”** — for the mystery of the Trinity.
**“weeks days”** — so that the prayer may not seem fleeting and accidental.
10.3:
**“bread”** — heavenly.
**“desirable”** — as if I abstained from more delicate foods, which we ought to do much more in time of fasting; for those who use unlawful things ought to abstain even from lawful ones.
**“I ate no”** — completely.
**“and flesh”** — the body of Christ.
**“and wine”** — Blood.
**“entered into my mouth. Neither was I anointed with ointment”** — After the manner of the Persians and Medes, who to this day use ointments in place of baths.
**“till were accomplished”** — The end crowns, not the fight.
**“the days of three weeks”** — For the mystery of the Trinity.
10.4:
**“By the great river”** — Ezechiel saw a vision by the river Chobar; to John the Baptist the heavens were opened over the waters of the Jordan. Let the ravings of those be silent, therefore, who, seeking shadows and images in the truth, try to overturn it itself, so that they falsify rivers and trees and paradise by the laws of allegory.
**“which is the Tigris”** — The river Tigris took its name from the tiger, a very swift beast, by reason of its excessive speed.
10.5:
**“And I lifted up”** — There is need of lifting up the eyes, that we may see mystical things.
**“my eyes”** — Of the mind.
**“and I saw”** — Thus.
**“And behold a man”**
• Symmachus: As a man. For he was not a man but had the likeness of a man.
• His angel, who was also the angel of the whole captive people; for Michael was over the people who had remained in Judea.
**“clothed in linen”** — Theodotion. Belts; the Septuagint: fine linen; Aquila: caip, that is, chief.
**“and his loins”** — In Jerome’s commentary on Ezechiel you will find these things fully explained.
**“girded with the finest gold”** — Others: ophat. Aquila: in the colour ophat.
10.6:
**“And his body”** — Was.
**“like the chrysolite”** — Others: tarshish, because that stone is of sea colour.
10.7:
**“And I Daniel alone saw the vision”** — Likewise Paul in the Acts of the Apostles: while the others did not see, he alone beheld the vision; the others heard the sound, but did not understand the force of the voice.
**“for the men that were with me saw it not”** — “The sensual man perceiveth not these things that are of the Spirit of God.”
**“but an exceeding great terror fell upon them”** — If a beast touch the mountain, it shall be stoned.
**“and they fled away, and hid themselves”**
• “For every one that doth evil hateth the light.”
• “I heard thy voice in paradise, O Lord, and I hid myself.”
10.8:
**“And I being left alone saw this great vision: and there remained no strength in me”** — The strength of God having been seen.
**“and the appearance of my countenance was changed in me, and I fainted away, and retained no strength”** — Likewise Moses said: “And I am terrified and trembling”; and Abraham: “I will speak to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes.”
10.9:
**“And I heard the voice of his words: and when I heard”**
• Or: saddened.
• In mind.
**“I lay in a consternation, upon my face, and my face was close to the ground”** — Knowing that “he is ashes, and will return into ashes.”
10.10: **“And behold a hand touched me”** — The angel appears in the figure of a man and sends a human hand to the prophet, so that, looking on a body of his own kind, he may not be afraid. For like seeks like.
10.11:
**“Thou man of desires”** — Symmachus: Desirable, because every holy man having in himself the beauty of the soul is loved by God.
**“understand the words that I speak to thee, and stand upright”** — Because by the urgency of prayers, and affliction of the body, and hardness of fasts, he desires to know things to come and the secrets of God.
10.12:
**“And he said to me: Fear not, Daniel”**
• On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, that is Nisan, with the three weeks, namely twenty-one days, completed, he sees this vision and hears it from the angel, because from when he began to pray and afflict himself in the sight of the Lord, his words were heard.
• But that he said, “I am come for thy words,” means this: after you began with tears, and fasting, and prayers, to call upon mercy, I took the occasion to enter before God to pray for you.
**“for from the first day”** — He was heard at once, but the angel was not sent at once; delay is given as an opportunity of praying and desiring more, so that he might be able to merit more.
**“that thou didst set thy heart to understand, to afflict thyself in the sight of thy God, thy words have been heard”** — that the captive people under Darius might be released.
**“and I am come for thy words”** — who was offering your prayers to God.
**“I am come”** — Gregory. As if he said: The merits of your prayers demand that the people of Israel be freed from the yoke of their servitude; but as yet the people of the Persians, to whom Darius the first gave leave to return to the Lord, are still under the same yoke, to be more fully purged. Whence the prince of the Persians rightly opposes me concerning the deliverance of that people, although your prayers and the tears of those who were left in Judea help. Whence: And behold Michael, one.
10.13:
**“The prince”** — angel.
**“But the prince of the kingdom”** — Jerome. It seems to me that this is the angel to whom Persia was entrusted, according to that: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he appointed the bounds of people according to the number of the angels of God.” These are the princes of whom Paul says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect, which none of the princes of this world knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”
**“resisted me one and twenty days: and behold Michael”** — who is over the Jews.
**“resisted me”** — Acting on behalf of the province committed to him, that the captive people of God might not be sent away; and perhaps, although the prophet was heard from the time he began to pray, an angel was not at once sent to him to announce God’s indulgence, because for twenty-one days the prince of the Persians resisted him, enumerating the sins of the Jews, for which they were justly held captive and not released.
*Gregory:* We rightly call the angelic spirits soldiers of God, since we are not ignorant that they fight against the powers of the air; yet they carry on these conflicts not by toil but by command, because whatever they seek to do in acting against unclean spirits they can do from the help of him who can do all things.
**“one of the chief princes”** — angels.
**“came to help me”** — the prince of the Persians resisting your prayers and my embassy, who was offering your prayers to God.
**“and I remained there by the king of the Persians”**
• the angel.
• beside Michael, who was speaking against the prince of the Persians.
10.14:
**“But I am come to teach thee what things shall befall”** — which you were asking for.
**“thy people in the latter days”** — not in the near future, but at the end of the age.
**“for as yet the vision is for days”** — will be deferred.
10.16:
**“And behold, as it were the likeness of a son of man touched my lips, and”** — therefore.
**“O my Lord”** — Others: Lord, in thy vision my inward parts are turned within me. Whence: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and let all that is within me bless his holy name.” For before we deserve the vision of God, our inward parts are outside and look outward; but afterwards they are turned within, and we are safe in them. Whence elsewhere: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.”
10.19:
**“And he said: Fear not, O man of desires, peace be to thee: take courage and be strong. And when he spoke to me, I grew strong”** — Other reading: I was strengthened.
**“And I said: Speak, O my lord, for thou hast strengthened me.”** — Otherwise he could not hear the mysteries of God. As if to say: You have made it so that I can hear and perceive what you speak.
10.20:
**“And he said: Dost thou know wherefore I am come to thee?”** — As if to say: I have come therefore to teach you that your prayers have been heard.
**“and now I will return, to fight”** — before God.
**“Prince of the Persians”**
• the angel.
• who does not want your people to be released from captivity.
**“When I went forth”**
• Ancient histories are to be turned over and considered, lest perhaps that time is signified when the Persians were overcome by the Greeks.
• As if he said: I was going forth from the sight of God to announce to you what is to come upon your people, though I am not secure, since the prince of the Persians stands there and contradicts your prayers and my mission; “and behold the prince of the Greeks,” that is, the angel of the Macedonians, “was coming,” and entered into the sight of God, to accuse the prince of the Persians and Medes, that in their places the kingdom of the Macedonians might succeed. Wonderful are the mysteries of God: for when the people of the Jews had been released from captivity, Alexander king of the Macedonians overthrew the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, Darius having been slain, and the prince of the Greeks overcame the prince of the Persians. He desired to transfer both the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, and the Jews with them, into his own kingdom. For he wishes the power of his own to increase in earthly things.
**“of the Persians. For when I went forth, there appeared the prince of the Greeks coming.”** — Because Alexander, having overthrown Greece and subjected it to his power, took up arms against the Persians; and therefore it is no wonder if the prince of the Macedonians is called the prince of the Greeks.
10.21:
**“But I will tell thee”** — As if to say: The matter is still in doubt. For while you pray to the Lord and I offer your prayers, the prince of the Persians stands opposite, who does not wish your people to be released from captivity; yet because the prince of the Greeks attacks the prince of the Persians, having Michael as a help: I will tell you what is set down in the scripture of truth.
**“what is set down in the scripture of truth”** — the foreknowledge of God.
**“and none is my helper”**
• in prayers for you to God.
• I who am that angel who offers your prayers to God.
**“And none is my helper”** — Gregory. What peace can there be in the heights, if even among the angelic spirits themselves a contest is waged by fighting, who always stand in the sight of truth? But because all the ministries of the angels have been set over the several nations for dispensing, when the conduct of the subjects deserves, each against the other, the help of the spirits set over them, the very spirits who preside are reported to come against one another. For that angel who spoke to Daniel is recognized as set over the captive peoples of Israel placed in Persia; but Michael is found to be set over those of the same people who had remained in Judea. Whence there the same angel says to Daniel: None is my helper, etc. And above: Behold Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me; as if: he was held back by others, but is said to come to help. And when he goes forth to fight against the prince of the Persians, the prince of the Greeks appears to him; for Judea had committed some offence also against the Greeks, and on that account he resisted its deliverance. So the angel hears the prayers of the prophet, but the prince of the Persians resists, because although the life of the just man praying now demands the deliverance of that people, yet the life of the same people contradicts it. Michael helps, but the prince of the Greeks comes to battle, because so long a captivity of the oppressed could have merited pardon, but what they had done wrongly against the Greeks stood in the way of their deliverance. The lofty spirits ruling nations by no means contend on behalf of those who act unjustly, but justly judge and examine their deeds; and the justice or guilt of each nation is the consistory of the heavenly court, the will of its Maker over itself, the highest will, which, while they always behold it, they never wish for what they cannot obtain.
**“in all these things, but Michael your prince.”** — To whom the people of the Jews was entrusted; and I and the prince of the Greeks now fight with common labor against the prince of the Persians.

11.1:
**“I”** — Daniel.
**“But from the first year of Darius the Mede”**
• He who overthrew the Chaldeans and freed me from the hand of my enemies as far as lay in him, and sealed the den of lions with his ring so that my adversaries might not kill me.
• But I, from, etc. The prophets are accustomed to introduce persons suddenly, without any preface of words, as here: “Thou art my refuge from the trouble which hath encompassed me: my joy, deliver me from them that surround me,” and suddenly the person of the Lord is introduced answering: “I will give thee understanding, and I will instruct thee in this way, in which thou shalt go: I will fix my eyes upon thee.” So here too, when the prophet says: From the first year of Darius the Mede, etc., the Lord suddenly answers: and now I will shew thee the truth. As if to say: because you wish to know what is to be concerning the kings of the Persians, hear the order of events and listen to what you seek.
**“But I from the year”** — According to the Vulgate edition, up to the end of the book, the vision that went before and that which appeared to Daniel in the third year of the king of the Persians are thought to be one; but according to the Hebrew truth, what follows is separate, and written in inverted order. The reason for this was stated above. For what is written is not narrated as under the third year of Cyrus, but under the first of Darius, who slew Baltassar.
**“stood up”** — Before the Lord, that is, asking his mercy for him who loved me, that he might be strengthened and confirmed, either he himself or his kingdom; and while I persisted in prayer, I learned this from the Lord answering: and behold, three kings will yet stand in Persia.
11.2:
**“And now I will shew thee the truth.”** — I, the Lord.
**“Behold there shall stand yet three kings in Persia,”**
• And behold there shall stand yet three kings in Persia, that is, Cambyses the son of Cyrus, and Esmenides the Magian, who took to wife Pathapta the daughter of Cambyses. When he had been slain by the seven Magi, the same Pathaptis married Darius, who succeeded in his place, and by him bore a son Xerxes, who, a most powerful and very wealthy king, led an innumerable army against Greece, and did those things which the histories of the Greeks relate. For he burned Athens under the prince Galla, and the war was waged at that time in Monophilis, and the naval battle at Salamis, when Sophocles and Euripides were held famous, and Themistocles, fleeing to the Persians, died by drinking the blood of a bull. In vain, therefore, do some write of Darius, who was overcome by Alexander, as the fourth king; he was not the fourth but the fourteenth king of the Persians after Cyrus, whom Alexander both overcame and slew in the seventh year of his reign.
• And it is to be noted that, after the four kings of the Persians after Cyrus had been enumerated, he passed over nine and went on to Alexander. For the prophetic spirit did not care to follow the order of history, but to touch on whatever is notable.
11.3: **“A strong king shall rise up, and shall rule”** — Alexander, who, having overcome the Illyrians and Thracians, Greece being conquered and Thebes overthrown, passed over into Asia, and, Darius’s generals being put to flight, took the city of Sardis; and afterwards, India being taken and the city of Alexandria founded, when he was thirty-two years of age and in the twelfth year of his reign, he died of poison in Babylon.
11.4:
**“And when he shall come to his height, his kingdom shall be broken, and shall be divided”** — his kingdom
**“towards the four winds”** — Namely, the east and the west, the south and the north. For in Egypt, which is to the south, Ptolemy the son of Lagus reigned first; in Macedonia, which is to the west, Philip, who is also Arideus, the brother of Alexander. Seleucus Nicanor held Syria and Babylon and the upper places which are to the east. Antigonus ruled Asia and Pontus and the other provinces in the same region, that is, to the north; and this we say according to the regions of the whole world; but he who is in Judea has Syria to the north and Egypt to the south.
**“but not to his posterity,”** — because he had no children
**“nor according to his power with which he ruled.”** — Because the divided kingdom became weaker, while the successors also rage against one another with internal fury.
**“For his kingdom shall be rent in pieces”** — For it shall be torn. For Cappadocia and Armenia, Bithynia, the Bosphorus and Erachaia, and other provinces, withdrawing from the power of the Macedonians, set up different kings for themselves.
**“even for strangers, beside these.”**
• the more obscure and lesser, namely Perdicas, Craterus, Lysimachus
• to four successors, namely
11.5:
**“And the king of the south shall be strengthened”** — Ptolemy son of Lagus
**“The king of the south”** — Ptolemy the son of Lagus, who first reigned in Egypt, a most prudent, most valiant and most wealthy man, so much so that he restored Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes, when expelled, to his kingdom, and obtained Cyprus and Phenicia; and, Demetrius the son of Antigonus having been conquered, he restored to Seleucus Nicanor the part of his kingdom which Antigonus had taken away; Caria also and Phenicia, many islands and cities and regions he subjected to himself.
**“and of his princes”**
• Ptolemy Philadelphus
• Ptolemy Philadelphus, the second king of Egypt, son of the former Ptolemy, under whom the Seventy at Alexandria are said to have turned the holy Scripture into the Greek tongue, who also sent many gifts to Eleazar the high priest and to the temple; over his library presided Demetrius Phalerius, an orator and philosopher among the Greeks. He is said to have been of such power that he surpassed his father Ptolemy.
• The histories relate that Ptolemy Philadelphus had three hundred thousand foot, twenty thousand horse, two thousand chariots, four hundred elephants, which he first brought from Ethiopia, fifteen hundred long ships, which they call liburnians, another thousand for carrying the soldiers' provisions, and also a great weight of gold and silver, so that from Egypt every year he received fourteen thousand and eighty talents of silver, and fifteen hundred thousand artabas of grain, a measure which holds three modii and a third part of a modius.
11.6:
**“And after the end of years”** — of many, against whom they fought
**“they shall be in league together.”**
• will become friends
• Ptolemy Philadelphus and, third, in Syria Antiochus, who was also called Theos, that is, God
**“And the daughter”** — Berenice
**“of the king of the south”** — of Ptolemy Philadelphus
**“the daughter of the king”**
• Therefore, leaving aside the other kingdoms, namely of Macedonia and Asia, he tells only of the kings of Syria and Egypt, because Judea, lying in the middle, was held now by these kings, now by those; and it is the purpose of holy Scripture not to weave a foreign history but that which is joined to the Jews.
• Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy Philadelphus, will come to be married to Antiochus after long wars.
**“shall come”**
• after long wars
• about to be married
**“to the king of the north”** — Antiochus
**“to make friendship,”** — between father and husband
**“but she shall not obtain”** — Berenice
**“the strength of the arm, nor shall stand”** — in the kingdom of Syria
**“her seed”** — the son who was born to him from Antiochus
**“and she shall be given up,”**
• by the princes of Antioch, Eacleon and Genues, to be killed with the son
• and she will be given up by Laodice, the former wife of Antiochus, whom she afterwards killed with poison, although he, overcome by love of her, had restored her to honor, when before, Berenice having been set over her, he had held her as a concubine; but she feared the husband’s wavering mind.
**“and they that brought her, and they that strengthened her in these times.”**
• by whom she could prevail
• Antiochus himself, killed by poison, who indeed reigned third in Syria. For Seleucus, also called Nicanor, reigned first; second, Antiochus Soter.
11.7:
**“And a plant of the bud of her roots shall stand up”** — in the kingdom
**“a plant of the bud of her roots. And he shall come”**
• of Ptolemy Philadelphus
• Ptolemy Euergetes, brother of Berenice, who took the kingdom of Syria from Callinicus, whom Laodice had substituted for Antiochus his father.
**“with an army, and shall enter into the province”** — Syria
**“of the king of the north, and shall abuse”** — He shall overthrow.
**“them”** — the mother and the son
**“and shall prevail.”** — by the right of the victor, so far as to take Syria and Cilicia, and the upper parts beyond the Euphrates, and almost all Asia
**“shall prevail”** — Because he heard that a sedition was being stirred up in Egypt, he carried off from the kingdom of Seleucus forty thousand talents of silver and precious vessels, and two thousand five hundred images, among which were also those which Cambyses had taken from Egypt and carried into Persia; and he himself obtained Syria, handed over Cilicia to his friend Antiochus, and to Exantipus, another leader, the provinces and lands of the Euphrates.
11.8:
**“Moreover, their gods and graven things, the precious vessels also of gold and silver, he shall carry away captive into Egypt. He”** — that is, Evergetes
**“shall prevail against the king of the north.”** — that is, Callinicus
11.10:
**“But his sons”** — Seleucus Cereanus, and Antiochus the Great.
**“of him”** — Of Callinicus, Seleucus.
**“shall be provoked”** — in hope of victory, to avenge their parent
**“and they shall assemble”** — both brothers
**“a multitude”**
• the kingdoms of the east
• against Ptolemy Philopator
**“of many armies. And he shall come hastening”** — Antiochus the Great
**“And he shall come hastening”**
• Seleucus the elder brother having been killed in Phrygia, in the third year of his reign, by the treachery of Nicanor and Eupator, Antiochus the Great came from Babylon into Syria, which Ptolemy Philopator, son of Evergetes, who reigned fourth in Egypt, then held.
• For when, against the generals of Ptolemy, by the treachery of Theodotus he had obtained Syria, which by succession was now held by the kings of Egypt, he came to such boldness, despising the luxury of Philopator and the magic arts which he was said to serve, that he attempted of his own accord to make war on the Egyptians.
11.11:
**“And being provoked”** — Syria having been lost through the treachery of Theodotus
**“the king of the south”** — Philopator
**“shall go forth”** — with a multitude gathered
**“and shall fight against the king of the north”** — Antiochus the Great, whom he calls now king of the north, now king of the south, according to the position of Egypt and Judea. For the same place, according to the nature of the place, is to the south for one, to the north for another. For example, if we speak of Judea, it is to the north for the Egyptians, to the south for the Syrians.
**“and shall prepare an exceeding great multitude, and a multitude shall be given into his hand”** — the battle having been joined near the town of Raphia, which is at the gates of Egypt, where Antiochus lost his whole army and, fleeing through the desert, was nearly captured
11.12:
**“and he shall take a multitude, and his heart shall be lifted up”** — power
**“his heart”** — of Philopator
**“and he shall cast down many thousands”** — of Antiochus
**“but he shall not prevail”** — to take the adversary, because the battle was at last ended on certain terms
11.13:
**“For the king of the north shall return”**
• Antiochus
• For the king shall return, etc. Antiochus the Great, having heard of the luxury or death of Philopator, with Philip of Macedon attacks his kingdom with joint force, peace having been made with Agathocles and Ptolemy Epiphanes, with whom he had formerly fought, on this condition, that he should join the neighbouring cities from the kingdom of Ptolemy to his own kingdom; and this is: many shall rise up, etc.
**“and shall prepare a multitude much greater”** — than usual
**“than before: and in the end of times and years, he shall come in haste”** — the treaty having been broken
11.14:
**“And in those times many shall rise up against the king of the south”** — Ptolemy, that is Epiphanes, Philopator his father being dead, who was then four years old
**“also the children of prevaricators of thy people”** — leaving the law, wishing against the command to sacrifice to the Lord in another place
**“Also the children of prevaricators”** — While Antiochus the Great and the generals of Ptolemy were fighting against each other, Judea, set in the middle, was torn into opposing parties, some consenting to or favouring Antiochus, others Ptolemy. At length Onias, priest of the Lord, taking very many of the Jews, fled into Egypt, and being honourably received by Ptolemy, received the region which was called Heliopolis, and, with the king’s consent, built in Egypt a temple like that of the Jews, which remained until the reign of Vespasian, two hundred and fifty years. But the city itself, which was called Onias’s, when the Jews afterwards fought against the Romans, was destroyed to the ground, so that no trace of either city or temple remained. Under the occasion, then, of Onias the high priest, countless bands of Jews fled into Egypt. At that time Cyrene also was filled with their multitude. For Onias asserted that he was fulfilling the prophecy of Isaias, who writes: “There shall be an altar of the Lord in Egypt, and his monument at the borders thereof,” and this is: “The children of the prevaricators of the people,” etc.
**“shall lift up themselves”** — into pride, boasting that they fulfil the command of the Lord
**“to fulfill the vision”** — of Isaias
**“and”** — but
**“and they shall fall”** — both the city and the temple having been destroyed
11.15:
**“And the king of the north shall come”** — Antiochus the Great, wishing to recover Judea.
**“And shall come”** — When Antiochus held Judea, Scopas, the general of Ptolemy, was sent; fighting bravely against him, he took Judea and returned to Egypt. Therefore: the king of the north will come, etc.
**“and shall cast up a mount, and shall take the best fenced cities”**
• to attack the garrison of Scopas in the citadel of Jerusalem, which he also took.
• as Ptolemy previously held it.
**“and the arms”** — strength.
**“of the south”** — of Egypt.
**“shall not withstand”** — him.
**“and his chosen ones shall rise up”** — the generals of Ptolemy.
**“And shall rise up”** — Antiochus the Great, wishing to recover Judea and Syria and very many cities, put to flight Scopas, the general of Ptolemy, near the Jordan, where Paneas is now built, and besieged Sidon with ten thousand armed men; for its relief Ptolemy sent famous generals. But they could not raise the siege, and Scopas, overcome by famine, surrendered, and was sent away naked with his companions.
**“to resist, and they shall not have strength”** — so that Scopas may be freed from the siege.
11.16: **“And he shall come upon him and do according to his pleasure, and there shall be none to stand against his face: and he shall stand in the glorious land, and it shall be consumed by his hand”** — Judea, properly Jerusalem, in which, having been received with honour, he pursued the party of Scopas.
11.17:
**“And he shall set his face to come to possess all his kingdom”** — not only Syria and Cilicia and the other provinces which were Ptolemy’s.
**“and he shall make upright conditions with him. And”** — therefore.
**“a daughter”** — Cleopatra.
**“of women”** — a pleonasm, as in that: “so she spoke with her mouth,” and “I have drunk in this voice with my ears.”
**“And a daughter of women”** — In the seventh year of his reign he betrothed his daughter to the young Ptolemy, and in the thirteenth he handed her over; and as her dowry Syria and Judea were given to him.
**“he shall give him, to overthrow it”** — Ptolemy, or that kingdom, namely.
**“and she shall not stand, neither shall she be for him”** — his treachery; namely, because Ptolemy and his generals, perceiving the deceit, acted more cautiously, and Cleopatra favoured the part of a husband rather than of a parent.
11.18:
**“And he shall turn”** — into Asia.
**“his face to the islands”** — by a naval battle.
**“and shall take many”** — Rhodes, Samos, Colophon, and many others; but Scipio Nasica met him, with his brother Publius Scipio Africanus, who had conquered Hannibal. Antiochus therefore, being defeated, was ordered to reign within the Taurus, and thence he fled to Apamea and Susa, and will penetrate to the cities at the farthest bounds of his kingdom; and when he fought against the Elymeans, he was destroyed with his whole army.
**“he shall cause the prince to cease”** — Epiphanes, whom he had attacked by invading the Roman empire, he allowed to rest.
**“of his reproach, and his reproach shall be turned upon him”** — defeated and driven out by the Romans.
11.19:
**“And he shall turn”** — fleeing from Asia.
**“his face to the empire of his own land, and he shall stumble, and fall, and shall not be found”** — his place.
11.20:
**“And there shall stand up in his place, one most vile, and unworthy of kingly honour”** — Seleucus Philopator, son of Antiochus the Great, who in Syria did nothing worthy of his father’s rule, and perished inglorious and without any rewards.
**“and in a few days he shall be destroyed, not in rage nor in battle”** — the strength of the Roman people shall be crushed by him, that is, by Antichrist.
11.21:
**“And a plant of the bud of her roots shall stand up”** — Antiochus Epiphanes.
**“in his place”** — of Seleucus his brother.
**“one despised”**
• And there shall stand up in his place one despised. Antiochus Epiphanes, namely his brother, before this worthless and despised by all, but, as if gentle and mild, got possession of the kingdom by fraud. This passage and what follows some refer only to Antiochus; ours refer some things to him, some to Antichrist, whose type he bore, some to both, as in the seventieth Psalm, which is entitled with the name of Solomon; some are referred to him, some to Christ, some suit both.
• Antiochus is the type of Antichrist, and what in part goes before in Antiochus must be wholly fulfilled in Antichrist. As Solomon is the type of Christ. For it is the custom of holy Scripture to send ahead the truth of future things in types, as in the Psalm which is entitled with the name of Solomon, not all things fit him, such as this: “And he shall continue with the sun, and before the moon,” etc.; “And he shall rule from sea to sea,” and the like. And as here: “In him shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed: all nations shall magnify him.” But in part, and as in a shadow and image of the truth, they were foretold in Solomon, which are perfectly fulfilled in the Saviour.
**“And there shall stand up in his place one despised”**
• Thus far, as to the order of the history, there is no dispute between Porphyry and ours. What follows to the end of the book, he interprets of Antiochus Epiphanes, the brother of Seleucus, son of Antiochus the Great, who after Seleucus reigned eleven years in Syria and held Judea, under whom came the persecution of the law of God and the wars of the Machabees. Ours say that all these things are prophesied of Antichrist.
• Antichrist, namely, who at the end of the world will rise up out of a small nation, that is, of the people of the Jews, so humble and despised that kingly honour is not given him, but he obtains the princedom by fraud; and the arms of the fighting Roman people will be overcome by him and broken; and he will do this because he will pretend to be the prince of the covenant, that is, of the law and testament of God. “And he shall enter into rich cities, and shall do that which his fathers never did,” etc. For none of the Jews but he ever reigned in the whole world; he, against the strongest thoughts of the saints, namely, will enter into counsel.
**“and the kingly honour shall not be given him”** — by those who in Syria served Ptolemy.
**“And he shall come privately”** — pretending clemency.
11.22:
**“And the arms”** — strength, whence also the hand is called the army; greatness.
**“of the fighter”** — Ptolemy, that is, Philometor.
**“shall be overcome”** — The commanders of Philometor.
**“before his face”**
• Of Antichrist.
• By the deceits of Antichrist.
**“and shall be broken”** — Ptolemy Philopator.
**“yea also the prince of the covenant”** — He will be afflicted, namely.
**“The prince of the covenant”** — Judas Machabeus, whom he overcame by fraud; or the prince of the covenant himself, who offered peace to Ptolemy, and was prince of the covenant not of Epiphanes, who reigned as the fifth in Egypt, but of Philometor, son of Cleopatra, the sister of Antiochus, whose uncle this Antiochus was. And when after the death of Cleopatra, the eunuch Eulaeus, the nurse of Philometor, and Lenaeus ruled Egypt and demanded back Syria, which Antiochus had seized by fraud, battle arose between the uncle, namely Antiochus, and the boy Ptolemy. And when they met between Pelusium and Mount Cassius, the generals of Ptolemy were defeated. But Antiochus, sparing the boy and feigning friendship, went up to Memphis and, receiving the kingdom of Egypt and saying that he was providing for the boy’s affairs, with a small force subdued all Egypt: “what his fathers did not do,” etc. For none of the kings of Syria so laid waste Egypt.
11.23:
**“And after friendships with him”** — Antichrist, pretending to be the leader of the covenant, will first invade the kingdom of Egypt.
**“he will deal deceitfully”** — invading his kingdom.
**“and he shall go up”** — Memphis.
**“and shall overcome”**
• Egypt.
• little by little.
11.24:
**“And he shall enter into rich and plentiful cities: and he shall do”** — Antiochus or Antichrist.
**“that his fathers never did, nor his fathers’ fathers”** — any of the people of the Jews.
**“spoils”** — Of Egypt.
**“and their prey, and their riches, and against the best fenced”** — because he is most crafty.
**“devices”**
• of the saints.
• the servants of the commanders.
**“shall forecast”**
• a more cunning plan.
• he will do, namely.
**“and this until a time.”**
• until God’s will permits.
• not always, not whatever he wishes.
11.25:
**“And his strength shall be stirred up”** — According to Porphyry: of Antiochus.
**“And shall be stirred up”** — Our writers interpret all these things according to the higher sense as being about Antichrist, who is to lay waste the people of the Jews and come from Babylon. Whence he will first overcome the cities and the king of Egypt, who is one of the three horns of which it was said above.
**“and his heart shall be stirred up against the king of the south”** — Ptolemy, the son of his sister.
**“with a great army: and the king of the south”** — the commanders of Ptolemy or the king of Egypt.
**“shall be stirred up to battle with many and very strong succours”** — against Antiochus or Antichrist.
**“and they shall not stand, for they shall form designs against him.”** — they will not be able to resist the deceit of Antiochus, who will feign peace with Ptolemy and eat bread with him, and afterwards will seize Egypt.
11.26:
**“And they that eat bread with him”** — Philometor.
**“shall destroy him”** — Ptolemy.
**“and his army shall be overthrown”** — of the king of the south or of Egypt.
11.27:
**“And the heart of the two kings shall be to do evil”** — each lying in wait for the other; so art is deceived by art
**“Of the two kings”** — No one doubts that Antiochus made peace with Ptolemy and entered into a banquet with him and plotted deceits that did not succeed, because he could not obtain his kingdom but was driven out by the soldiers of Ptolemy. But that there were said to be two kings whose heart was crafty, so as to do evil to each other, cannot stand according to the history: for Ptolemy was young in age and deceived by the fraud of Antiochus; what evil could he think? Whence ours refer all this to Antichrist and to the king of Egypt, whom he will overcome first.
**“and they shall speak lies at one table, and they shall not prosper”** — Antiochus and his princes
**“because as yet the end is unto another time.”** — the battle; because they will not complete their designs
**“And they shall not prosper”** — Because he was driven out of Egypt by the captains of Ptolemy, and afterwards was shut out by the siege of his two nephews and by the command of the Romans, who were friends to them.
11.28:
**“And he shall return into his land”** — driven back by the captains of Egypt
**“holy covenant”** — Concerning Antichrist no one doubts that he will fight against the holy covenant, and, fighting first against the king of Egypt, will be terrified by the help of the Romans. These things went before, imaged under Antiochus Epiphanes, that the most wicked king who persecuted the people of God might prefigure Antichrist, who will persecute the people of Christ. Many of ours think that, because of the greatness of his cruelty and baseness, Nero will be Antichrist.
**“with much riches: and his heart shall be against the holy covenant”** — Both Greek and Roman history relate that Antiochus, driven out by the Egyptians, came into Judea, that is, the holy land, and despoiled the temple, and carried off very much gold; and having placed a garrison of Macedonians in the citadel, he returned into his own land; and when two years had passed he again gathered an army against Ptolemy and came to the south. And when the two brothers of Ptolemy, sons of Cleopatra, whose uncle Antiochus was, were besieged in Alexandria, two legates of the Romans came, one of whom was Marcus Publius Lenas; when he had found him standing on the shore, and had said on behalf of the senate that he was commanded to withdraw from the friends of the Roman people and be content with his own dominion, and he had put off his answer to the counsel of his friends, he made a circle on the sand with the staff he held in his hand, and, drawing it round the king, said: The senate and people of Rome command that you answer in this place what counsel you take. Whence he, terrified, said: If this pleases the senate and people of Rome, we must withdraw. And at once he moved his army.
**“and he shall succeed and shall return”** — by command of the Romans
**“into his own land.”** — Judea, which observes the covenant of God
11.29:
**“At the time appointed he shall return, and he shall come to the south”** — Because he again, having gathered his forces, came into Egypt and besieged his two nephews, Ptolemy Philometor with his brother, when he was removed by the command of the Romans. Antichrist also will feel the arms of the Romans.
**“but the latter time shall not be like the former.”** — he will not succeed as he did before, when he came into Egypt
11.30:
**“And the galleys and the Romans shall come upon him”** — The Italians.
**“and he shall be struck”** — not by death, but by the humbling of his pride
**“and shall return.”** — others will threaten him
**“and shall have indignation against the covenant of the sanctuary”** — For he did worse when he came the second time to Jerusalem; and this is: “and they shall have indignation against the covenant of the sanctuary.”
**“And shall have indignation”** — This is more fully in the book of Machabees, because after the Romans drove him out of Egypt, that is, Antiochus, he came in indignation against the holy covenant, and was invited by those who had forsaken the law of God and had mingled themselves with the ceremonies of the heathens. Which is to be fulfilled more fully under Antichrist, who will be indignant against the covenant of God, and will devise against those whom he wishes to forsake the law of God. Whence Aquila: And he will devise that the covenant of the sanctuary be forsaken.
**“and he shall succeed: and he shall return and shall devise against them that have forsaken the covenant of the sanctuary.”** — namely, how he would repay those who had turned to idols
11.31:
**“And arms”** — The Jews understand these things neither of Antiochus Epiphanes nor of Antichrist, but of the Romans, of whom it is said: “and galleys shall come, or Italians and Romans, and they shall be humbled.” After many times, they say, concerning those same Romans who came to the help of Ptolemy and threatened Antiochus, king Vespasian will arise. And his arms shall rise up, and seeds from seed, that is, Titus his son with the army, and they shall defile the sanctuary, and take away the continual sacrifice, and deliver the temple to eternal desolation. For Siim and Cethim, whom we call Romans and galleys, the Hebrews hold to be Italians and Romans.
**“And arms shall stand on his part, and they shall defile the sanctuary of strength”**
• Others take “seed” as progeny; they wish, however, those to be signified who were sent by Antiochus two years after he had despoiled the temple, to exact tribute from the Jews, and who would take away the worship of God and set up in the temple an image of Jupiter Olympius and statues of Antiochus, which he now calls the abomination of desolation, when the holocaust and the continual sacrifice were taken away; all of which they contend went before as a type of our Antichrist, who is to sit in the temple of God as if he were God.
• Antichrist will sit in the temple as God, that he may take away the law of God. Some of the Jews pretended to keep the law of God and afterwards were with the Gentiles. Others remained in religion, which will be so in the time of Antichrist, when “the charity of many shall grow cold.” Whence: “But yet the Son of man, when he cometh, shall he find, think you, faith on earth?”
**“and shall take away the continual sacrifice, and they shall place there the abomination”** — of the temple
11.32:
**“And such as deal wickedly against the covenant shall deceitfully dissemble.”** — this also in the book of Maccabees
**“but the people”** — Mathathias with his sons and such like
**“that know their God shall prevail and succeed.”** — namely the law
11.33:
**“And they that are learned among the people”**
• in the law
• How much the Jews suffered under Antiochus the books of Machabees report, and their triumphs are a witness to it, who for the keeping of the law of God endured flames and swords and slavery and plunderings and the utmost penalties. These things will certainly come to pass under Antichrist, many resisting his power and fleeing from it. The Hebrews interpret these things of the last overthrow of the temple, which happened under Vespasian and Titus, saying that there were very many who knew their God and died for the keeping of his law.
**“shall teach many”** — to resist and to keep the law of God
**“and they shall fall”** — the saints
**“by the sword, and by fire”** — of Antiochus or of Antichrist
**“And they shall fall by the sword”** — Mathathias of the village of Modin, who rebelled against the captains of Antiochus, striving to keep the law of God, but was killed; and his sons, some of them deceived by the treachery of the enemy, as the book of the Maccabees bears witness.
11.34:
**“And when they shall have fallen”**
• under Antichrist
• Some of the Jews understand this also of the emperors Severus and Antoninus, who loved the Jews in pretence. Others understand it of the emperor Julian, that when they had been oppressed by Gallus Caesar and had suffered much in captivity, he will rise up, pretending to love the Jews and pretending to sacrifice in their temple, in which they will have a small hope of help. And very many of the Gentiles will be joined to them, but deceitfully; for they will pretend to be friends for the sake of the worship of idols, and this so that those who are approved may be made manifest. For the time of their true salvation is under Christ, whom they falsely think is yet to come, when they are about to receive Antichrist.
**“they shall be relieved”** — saints resisting Antichrist
**“with a small help”** — by divine strengthening against Antichrist
**“and many shall be joined to them deceitfully.”** — the ministers of Antiochus or of Antichrist
11.35:
**“And some of the learned shall fall”** — That they may be deceived, “insomuch as to deceive (if possible) even the elect.”
**“that they may be tried”**
• As if all these things will therefore happen so that they may be tried and chosen.
• The saints, as in a furnace: “as the furnace tries the vessels of the potter,” etc.
**“and may be chosen”**
• made proven
• from the number of men
**“and made white”** — according to that: “And I shall be made whiter than snow.”
**“even to the appointed time”** — not always
**“appointed”**
• by God
• “there is no power but from God”; and “all things have their time.”
**“because yet there shall be another time.”**
• of rest after tribulation
• of true victory at the coming of Christ
11.36:
**“And the king shall do according to his will”** — Porphyry and those who follow him think these things are said of Antiochus Epiphanes.
**“And the king shall do according to”** — From this place the Jews think it is said of Antichrist, that he will rise after the little help of Julian, just as we also understand these things of him.
**“And he shall be lifted up”** — against the worship of God
**“And he shall magnify himself”** — in pride, so that he even orders his own image to be placed in the temple
**“against every god”** — Whence: “Who opposeth, and is lifted up above all that is called God, or that is worshipped, so that he sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself as if he were God.”
**“And he shall speak great things against the God of gods”** — blasphemies
**“and shall prosper”** — each shall prosper
**“till be accomplished”**
• upon him
• is finished, that is, their fury
**“the wrath”**
• of God
• Till the wrath be accomplished, that is, till God be angry with him so that he perish. For Polybius and Diodorus, who write the histories of the libraries, relate that he acted not only against the God of the Jews, but, inflamed by the torches of avarice, tried to plunder the very rich temple of Diana, which was in Elymais, and was overpowered by the guardians of the temple and the neighbours who gathered round, and, turned to madness by certain phantoms and terrors, at last died of disease; and they record that this befell him because he tried to plunder the very rich temple of Diana. But we say that it befell him, if anything did, because he exercised excessive cruelty against the saints of God and defiled his temple. For he was not punished because he tried to do it and left off, repenting, from carrying it out, but for what he did.
**“For is made”** — in God’s foreknowledge
**“the determination”**
• others: in him will be the consummation
