For among the proud, as Scripture witnesses, there are always quarrels, and, according to the sentence of the Truth: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be brought to desolation, and house upon house shall fall.” The books and letters of Antiochus are sent into Jerusalem and to the cities of Juda, that they should follow the laws of the nations of the earth, and forbid holocausts and sacrifices and atonements to be made in the temple of God. For it is the greatest care and the greatest zeal of heretics and pagans either to confound divine worship in the Church of Christ or utterly to extinguish it, lest the sincerity of right faith, which worketh by charity, be offered to God as an acceptable holocaust on the altar of the believing heart, and lest the mystical sacrifices of the body and blood of the Lord, with the holy prayer of the faithful and the atonement of good works, be worthily presented in the true temple of God, the creator of all and giver of good things; they forbid the keeping of the sabbath, because they deny that there will be a rest of holy souls in the heavenly kingdom. They command altars and temples and idols to be built, because they desire to make the minds of the faithful vessels of malignant spirits; and swine’s flesh and common cattle to be immolated, that is, to lead an unclean life, and after the manner of brute animals to wallow in luxury and the lusts of the flesh; and to leave their children uncircumcised. That is, to temper thoughts, words, and deeds with no guard, no continence, and no discretion, so that they forget the divine law, and change the justifications of God into the making of diverse crimes. And all these things they compel to be done not only by the persuasion of words but also by the torment of diverse punishments. Whence it follows:
1.53: **“And they drove away the people of Israel into lurking holes, and into the secret places of fugitives.”** — And whosoever, etc. Cruelty is lacking in a cause when impiety is in control; savagery rages when cupidity burns. Antiochus through writings ordains torments throughout his whole kingdom, and to inflict death on the worshippers of God. So too Antichrist through his most wicked ministers seeks out various kinds of punishments, to tear away, crush and destroy the Christians from the state of the most holy religion.
1.58: **“Thus by their power did they deal with the people of Israel, that were found in the cities month after month.”** — On the fifth day, etc. The month Casleu is the same among the Greeks that is called December among the Latins. On the fifteenth day of this month, in the hundred and forty-fifth year of the kingdom of the Greeks, which they begin to reckon from the first year of Seleucus, Antiochus Epiphanes set up the abominable idol of desolation in the temple of God, that is, the image of Jupiter Olympius, in the eighth year of his rule. In which year, namely, in Samaria on the top of mount Garizim he built a shrine of Jupiter the Stranger, or the Hospitable, the Samaritans themselves begging him by letter to do so, as Josephus is witness. But we read in the Gospel according to Matthew that the Saviour, when the disciples asked about the sign of his coming and the consummation of the world, answered among other things: “When therefore you shall see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place: he that readeth let him understand.” When we are called to understanding, it shows that what is said is mystical. Now it is written in Daniel in this manner: “And in the half of the week my sacrifice and libations shall be taken away, and in the temple shall be the abomination of desolations, even until the consummation of the time, and the consummation shall be given upon the desolation.” Of this the Apostle speaks, that the man of iniquity, the adversary, is to be lifted up against all that is called God or is worshipped, so that he dares to stand in the temple of God and show that he himself is the Lord. His coming, according to the working of Satan, will destroy those who receive him, and bring them to desolation. But it can be taken simply either of Antichrist, or of the image of Caesar which Pilate set up in the temple, or of the equestrian statue of Hadrian, which stood in the very holy of holies up to the present day. According to the truth of the Scriptures an idol is also called an abomination, and the word desolation is added for this reason, that the idol was set up in a desolated and abandoned temple. Now when the idol of zeal was set up in the temple of God, throughout all the cities of Juda the ministers of the most wicked king build altars round about, and before the doors of the houses and in the streets they burn incense and sacrifice; because when the unclean Antichrist reigns, his supporters and all the wicked, having cast aside the true worship of the one God and despised the house of God, which is the holy Church, in confusion and with order disturbed, in various places of various errors and manifold crimes, will bring deadly sacrifices to demons. And it is well said that they built altars round about, because, having left the simplicity of truth, they follow the erring sects of impiety; for “round about,” as the Psalmist testifies, all “the wicked walk.” And they burn incense and sacrifice before the doors of the little houses and in the streets, who are not worthy to enter to the altar of God and there offer to God the incense of pure prayer, but on the broad and spacious way that leads to death carry their deeds and words with them to the wicked enemy. “And the books of the law of God,” it says, “they burnt with fire, cutting them in pieces.” They cut in pieces and burn with fire the books of God, who through the fire of cupidity, by heretical perversity, desire to tear apart the sincerity of the law of God from the state of its rectitude, and are eager to slay with the sword of their malice the holy preachers, to whom the treasure of the testaments of God is entrusted. What is signified by the number twenty and five, if not those who, entangled by the five senses of the body in carnal desires, do and savour things contrary to the law of God, which consists in two testaments and in two precepts, namely the love of God and of neighbour? Twenty-five, then, is made by the number five multiplied in itself, and this number is rightly compared to the deserters of the law of God, who through each single sense of the body, that is, through sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch, oppose the divine precepts which are written in the Pentateuch. And therefore it is said that they sacrificed upon the altar that was over against the altar, because on the altar of impiety, which pride had raised up against the altar of the catholic faith, all the wicked offer to the devil the unhappy sacrifices of their deeds and words.
1.61: **“And they hanged the children about their necks in all their houses: and those that had circumcised them, they put to death.”** — And the women, etc. The sense of the history is plain, which sets forth the torments that the wicked persecutors inflicted on the worshippers of God, both then in the Old Testament and now likewise in the new. Nor is it easy for anyone to count up all the kinds of punishments that the most wicked tormentors inflicted on the martyrs of Christ. But according to allegory, what are shown by the women who circumcised their sons, if not the honourable persons of the faithful, who, looking about their deeds and words and thoughts with the utmost discretion, hasten to cut off with the sword of the spirit whatever superfluous thing they find in them? The spiritual Antiochus desires to slay these, because he strives either to strike them bodily by torments, or to kill them in soul spiritually by denial. Now Antiochus is interpreted “the silence of poverty,” and he is rightly judged by this name, who, devoid of spiritual knowledge and destitute of holy virtues, persecutes through envy in others that which he himself has least in himself. Whence it is well added: “And they hung,” it says, “the children about their necks in their houses.” Because they are not slow to put to death, on account of the confession of the faith, those who are little ones not in understanding but in malice, and humble in spirit. Likewise “those who had circumcised them they put to death,” because the holy preachers, who restrain and chastise their subjects with the knife of piety and the word of evangelical doctrine, are most of all harassed by the troubles of persecutions.
1.64: **“And there was very great wrath upon the people.”** — And many, etc. No persecution and no tribulation could ever tear from the faith of Christ the saints of God, who are predestinated and called according to the foreknowledge of God the Father; but persisting in the truth, they neither ate in idolatry nor consented to be defiled by the uncleanness of sins, nor did they suffer the holy law of God to be broken and corrupted by heretical perversity, but rather chose to die for the name of Christ than to consent to impiety. Whence one of them, relying on this confidence, writing to the disciples, thus bore witness, saying: “For I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor angel, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor might, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” But let us see what consolation was sent to the laboring servants of God.

2.13: **“To what end then should we live any longer?”** — In those days, etc. In the book of Daniel, where mention of this place is made under a riddle, it is found written thus: “And the wicked shall dissemble in covenant deceitfully; but the people that know their God shall prevail and shall do. And they that are learned among the people shall teach many: and they shall fall by the sword, and by fire, and by captivity, and by spoil for many days. And when they shall have fallen, they shall be relieved with a small succour; and many shall come to them deceitfully. And some of the learned shall fall, that they may be tried, and may be chosen, and made white even to the appointed time, because yet there shall be another time.” How much the Jews suffered from Antiochus, the present history of the Machabees relates, and their triumphs are a testimony of it; for the keeping of the law of God they endured flames and swords, and servitude and plunderings and the last penalties; that these things will be under Antichrist, there is no one who doubts, many resisting his power and fleeing in various directions. The Hebrews interpret these things, in the last overthrow of the temple, which happened under Vespasian and Titus, as having been of the many of the people who knew their God and were slain for the keeping of the law. “And when they shall have fallen,” he says, “they shall be relieved with a small succour; and many shall come to them deceitfully. And some of the learned shall fall, that they may be tried, and may be chosen, and made white even to the appointed time, because yet there shall be another time.” The small help signifies historically Mathathias of the village of Modin, who rebelled against the captains of Antiochus and strove to preserve the worship of the true God. But he calls it a small counsel because he did not live long after the defence was begun, but died when one year had run its course. And afterwards Judas his son, who was called Machabeus, fell fighting, and his other brothers were deceived by the fraud of their adversaries. Mystically, however, Mathathias signifies the Lord the Saviour, who is the prince of the people of God and defender of his elect, whose sons fight for the house of Israel, and defend the sanctuary of God and the divine law. Mathathias is interpreted “gift of God,” the hidden meaning of which name has laid open to us the sacrament of his incarnation. Whence he himself also says in the Gospel: “For God so loved the world, as to give his only begotten Son; that whosoever believeth in him, may not perish, but may have life everlasting.” For he who is given by God is surely the gift of God. But these things are said only of his incarnation. As for his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, it must be believed that he makes this dispensation itself together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. As also the Holy Spirit is read to be the gift of God, yet with the Father and the Son is believed and adored as one God. Whence in the Gospel he is read both as sent and as having come of his own will, as in that word of the Lord: “I will ask the Father, and he shall give you another Paraclete.” And again: “But when the Paraclete cometh,” he says, “whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceedeth from the Father, he shall give testimony of me.” And elsewhere the Truth itself says to Nicodemus: “The Spirit breatheth where he will; and thou hearest his voice, but thou knowest not whence he cometh and whither he goeth.” This Mathathias, then, is told to be the son of John, son of Simeon, a priest of the sons of Joarib. John is interpreted “grace of God,” Simeon “hearing,” Joarib “the Lord exalting.” Rightly, then, these interpretations fit this mystery, because the mediator of God and men can be called the grace of God, as in that word of the apostle: “By the grace of God he tasted death for all”; and hearing, because he himself says in the Gospel: “The things I have heard from the Father, these I speak in the world”; and the Lord exalting, of whom the prophet says: “Be thou exalted, O Lord, in thy own strength.” For he is deservedly named priest, of whom it is written: “The Lord hath sworn, and he will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech.” The sons of this Mathathias are all the saints, who are also called his body and members. But how they can be designated by the number five is not unfittingly asked. For so many sons of Mathathias are read to have been historically, that is, John who was surnamed Gaddis, and Simon, who was surnamed Thasi, and Judas who was surnamed Machabeus, and Eleazar, who was surnamed Abaron, and Jonathan, who was surnamed Apphus. Let us see, then, whether anywhere this number is found in the New Testament to express the same thing. We read also the apostle Paul saying to the Ephesians of Christ thus: “He that descended is the same also that ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. And he gave some apostles, and some prophets, and other some evangelists, and other some pastors and doctors, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ.” Behold, here five kinds are marked out in those persons whom the divine calling has appointed to the teaching office of the Church. But let us consider how the sons of Mathathias themselves, with the interpretations of their names, can be fitted to these kinds. The first of his sons, then, is named John, who was surnamed Gaddis. John means the Lord his grace. Gaddis means a kid, or my temptation. Well, then, these names suit the order of the apostles, unless I am mistaken, who by the Lord’s grace were chosen to the height of this honour. Yet they suffered many temptations and injuries from sinners; which the Saviour himself seems to foretell to them when he says in the Gospel: “I have chosen you out of the world, that you should go and bring forth fruit, and your fruit should remain.” And again: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves. Be ye therefore wise as serpents and simple as doves,” and the rest. Behold, those who are filled with the grace of the Lord are shown to be afflicted in no small measure by the insults of all the wicked. The second of the sons of Mathathias was Simon, who was surnamed Thasi, who in most of the following places is called Simon. Simon, or Simeon, is interpreted hearing, or he heard sadness; Thasi, the searching out of joy. Not unfittingly do these suit the order of the prophets, who, enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, both foresee the future punishments of the wicked, and by tasting the consolation within foreknow the coming rewards of the saints; and they persuade others to guard against future evils and to seek future goods. The third son in order was Judas Machabeus. For Judas is interpreted confessing or glorifying, and Machabeus a warrior. And this name fits the evangelists very well, who preach the Gospel of peace and of the glory of Christ throughout the whole world, and overthrow the wicked errors of pagans and heretics. The fourth son, that is, Eleazar who was surnamed Abaron, in the former name sounds the help of God, in the latter a lofty generation; not undeservedly is he likened by figure to pastors, who, strengthened enough by the help of God and lofty in faith and virtues, are set in place as rulers in the Church, that by feeding them rightly with sound faith and good provisions they may lead the sheep of God to the greenness of the heavenly fatherland. The last of the sons was called Jonathan, having the surname Apphus, a name which, according to the interpretation, fits the holy doctors best. For Jonathan is interpreted the gift of a dove, or the Lord’s own willing one. Apphus means fugitive or thousandth. And well are the doctors of Christ expressed by these names, who, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, subject themselves to the Lord with a willing mind, that, discharging an embassy in his stead, they may preach the law of God in the world, and teach men to flee earthly desires and to seek eternal joys, so that there, according to the signification of the number a thousand, God rewarding, they may receive both the fullness of the reward and possess true blessedness with Christ and his angels. And as to what follows here: These saw the evils that were done in the people of Juda and Jerusalem, etc. Because these, indeed, recognise with compassion the various scandals which are committed by the wicked in the Church of God, and are eager to avenge them with the spiritual sword, they fear not to offer themselves as a victim and to hand themselves over to death for the salvation of their own. Whence it follows:
2.14: **“And Mathathias and his sons rent their garments, and they covered themselves with haircloth, and made great lamentation.”** — And Mathathias rent, etc. What then is it to rend garments, but to deliver bodies to torments? And what is it to be covered with haircloth, but to punish the just, as though sinners, with torment? Haircloth too is made of goats, a rough and bristly covering. For goats are rightly referred to sins, since in the judgment of the Lord they are set on the side of sinners. Therefore the Lord, because he took on the flesh of sin, is recorded to have put on haircloth. For if we take it historically, we nowhere read that he used haircloth. So while the Jews were troublesome to him by insults and plots, he hid his divinity under the veil of the flesh from darkened minds; because they did not deserve to know him whom with such impiety they were seeking to kill. For on account of the sins of the peoples the redeemer of the human race delivered his flesh to death, and had compassion on our weakness; of whom the Lord himself says through Isaias: “for the wickedness of my people have I struck him”; and: “he shall bear their iniquities.” “Therefore will I distribute to him very many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong, because he hath delivered his soul unto death, and was reputed with the wicked: and he hath borne the sins of many, and hath prayed for the transgressors.” Likewise his sons also, that is, the apostles and martyrs, taught by his example, did not hesitate to die in time for the laws of God and the salvation of their brethren, that for this they might merit the joys of the heavenly kingdom with the holy angels. Whence the apostle John says: “In this we have known the charity of God, because he hath laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.”
2.16: **“And many of the people of Israel consented, and came to them: but Mathathias and his sons stood firm.”** — And they came, etc. For the spiritual Antiochus sends into the city of Modin, which is interpreted judgment, that is, into the holy Church, where the judgments of the law of God are most diligently kept; that those who had fled there, seeking a remedy for their souls, he may compel to depart from the law of God, and to pay to the devil the victim of sins and the worship of impiety. But what is added we cannot read without groaning, that many of the people of Israel consenting came to them, when we see some compelled by torments to apostatize from the religion of piety; others, enticed by desire of this world, to slide backward; others, led astray by the cunning of heretics, to be deceived; others also, by their own luxury and lust, to return to the former filth of vices. Yet what follows greatly rejoices: that Mathathias and his sons stood firm, since without doubt they stand firm in truth and justice who have merited to be sons of the true Mathathias, that is, Jesus Christ, and, keeping his faith and commandments, with steadfast mind desire by his grace to obtain the rewards of eternal life.
2.17: **“And they that were sent from Antiochus, answering, said to Mathathias: Thou art a ruler, and an honourable, and great man in this city, and adorned with sons, and brethren.”** — And they that were sent, answering, etc. Whether by guile or by force, the ancient enemy always plots how he may overthrow the worship of piety in the Church of Christ. For he it is who came to tempt our redeemer in the desert, saying: “If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread.” And after he set him upon the pinnacle of the temple in the holy city he said: “If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down. For it is written that he hath given his angels charge over thee, and in their hands shall they bear thee up, lest perhaps thou dash thy foot against a stone.” And thence, carrying him to a high mountain, he showed him all the kingdoms of the world and the glory of them, and said to him: “All these will I give thee, if falling down thou wilt adore me.” The same daily, by his ministers, deceitfully suggests to his members that for worldly ambition they should forsake the way of justice, and do the bidding of the most wicked king who reigns over all the children of pride.
2.19: **“Then Mathathias answered, and said with a loud voice: Although all nations obey king Antiochus, so as to depart every man from the service of the law of his fathers, and consent to his commandments:”** — And Mathathias answered, etc. The constancy of Mathathias strengthened the minds of his sons; so too the patience and longanimity of our Lord Jesus Christ strengthens the faith of all believers. Whence he says to his disciples: “Wonder not if the world hate you. Know ye that it hath hated me before you,” “and fear ye not them that kill the body, and are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him that can destroy both soul and body in hell. In your patience you shall possess your souls,” and your reward shall be great in heaven. “But he that shall persevere to the end, he shall be saved.”
2.26: **“And shewed zeal for the law, as Phinees did by Zamri the son of Salomi.”** — And as he left off, etc. This Jew who sacrificed to idols before the eyes of all signifies wicked Catholics, who by evil works and the mark of sins scandalize their neighbours. For in this they are shown to sacrifice to idols, that they are manifestly captive to the principal vices. Whence the apostle Paul calls avarice the service of idols. But the sword of Mathathias slays these upon the altar, because the vengeance of the most just judge exacts just punishment on such. And he also killed at that very time the man whom Antiochus had sent, who compelled to sacrifice; because on the day of the last judgment not only sinful men, but the instigators of sins, that is, the malignant spirits, will receive the deserved punishment of eternal damnation. At the same time the altar of impiety will be destroyed, because after the judgment is finished no further power of sinning will be granted to the wicked. But what follows: “He shewed zeal for the law, as Phinees did by Zamri the son of Salomi,” shows that the brave deeds of the holy fathers prefigured the most noble act of our redeemer in the last times.
2.28: **“So he, and his sons fled into the mountains, and left all that they had in the city.”** — And he cried out. These words of Mathathias prefigured the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which he exhorts us daily to forsake the vanity of this world and to seek the joys of the heavenly kingdom. For he himself says in the Gospel: “Whosoever doth not renounce all that he possesseth, cannot be my disciple. He that loveth father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me”; and “he that taketh not up his cross daily and followeth me, is not worthy of me. For he that will save his life, shall lose it: and he that shall lose his life for my sake, shall find it. For what doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his own soul? Or what exchange shall a man give for his soul? For the Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels: and then will he render to every man according to his works.” For our Redeemer flees, and his sons, into the mountains, and they leave all that they have in the city, when under the guidance of the truth itself we desire to ascend to the height of the virtues, and cast away, as superfluous, despising them, the things that belong to the luxury of the world. Hence it is that we read in the Gospel that the same Lord led his disciples into the mountains, and sat there, and there taught them; there he prayed, and there he fed the multitudes, that by his examples he might always call us to higher and more perfect things.
2.39: **“And Mathathias and his friends heard of it, and they mourned for them exceedingly.”** — Then they went down, etc. Those who did not go up into the mountains with Mathathias and his sons, but went down into the desert, that sitting there they might seek judgment and justice, we can better understand by allegory as the Jews who, after receiving the grace of the baptism of Christ, thought that circumcision and the old law were to be observed. And well are these remembered as having gone into the desert, who, when the truth of the Gospel was dawning, regarded the deserted shadow of the law as still necessary for themselves, and preached that the legal sabbath must be observed, although all these things went before in figure in the times of the law, and are to be observed spiritually in the New Testament. Against them the apostle argues most copiously in his epistles, asserting that Christ is the end of the law, unto justice to every one that believeth. These, therefore, are deservedly struck by the sword of the spiritual enemies, who do not think that the grace of Christ suffices them for salvation. According to tropology, too, in those who seek the desert may be understood all the slothful, who reckon it enough for themselves that they have received the divine gifts of the Christian religion and the flood of baptism, and after the washing away of filth do not wish to practise works of virtue, nor do they remember that parable of the Gospel in which the Saviour, speaking in the Gospel of the unclean spirit, said that the unclean spirit went out of the man, and walked through dry places, seeking rest, and found none. Again, that with seven other spirits more wicked than himself he returned to his former house, empty, swept with brooms, and adorned. Such men are easily overwhelmed by the spiritual enemies, because they did not take care to be armed with the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, the breastplate of justice, and the sword of the spirit, with which they ought to have resisted their enemies. Whence it is added that Mathathias and his friends mourned for the death of these, because the Church is afflicted with great sorrow when she sees that some of the number of her own have fallen, through the snares and persecutions of malignant enemies, into the precipice of sins.
2.40: **“And every man said to his neighbour: If we shall all do as our brethren have done, and not fight against the heathens for our lives, and our justifications: they will now quickly root us out of the earth.”** — And every man said, etc. The good, therefore, greatly detest idleness, which is the enemy of the soul, and so they choose rather to fight daily against their spiritual enemies with virtues than to grow numb in sluggish, idle sloth; above all since they presume to have the hope of victory not from themselves but through the divine help, and promise themselves security not in the present but in the future, when, all adversities being destroyed, at last death itself “shall be destroyed”; “nor shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor sorrow any more, for the former things are passed away”; when the saints shall be made joyful in the joy of God’s countenance, and shall enjoy most wholesome delight at his right hand even to the end.
2.44: **“And they gathered an army, and slew the sinners in their wrath, and the wicked men in their indignation: and the rest fled to the nations for safety.”** — Then was gathered together, etc. As the Scripture tells, it is plain that when the Saviour and his apostles were preaching the Gospel, many of the Jewish people came to the faith, believing the law and the prophets which bore witness of the coming of Christ; and also very many of the proselytes and strangers, forsaking their idols and the superstition of heathenism, flocked together from all sides to hear the word of God, and were added to the number of believers. And they slew the sinners in their wrath, and the wicked men in their indignation. Stirred up by zeal of faith, they cast out and drove away the malignant spirits from men possessed through error, and laid bare to them the poisons of their deceit. Driven thence also, they fled to the nations, according to that of the Gospel in which, men being healed, the devils were permitted by the Saviour to go into the swine, that the unclean possessors might possess the vessels of uncleanness.
2.48: **“And they recovered the law out of the hands of the nations, and out of the hands of the kings: and they yielded not the horn to the sinner.”** — And they recovered, etc. The soldiers of Christ recovered the law out of the hands of kings when, persisting in the truth of the Gospel, they yielded to no error, but rather by their preaching subjected the erring to the truth. Hence it came about that very many of those who, puffed up with worldly pride, had before been persecutors of the Christian religion, the same, afterwards converted, became most firm defenders of the truth, and “they yielded not the horn to the sinner,” because they did not consent to iniquity; according to that of Esther, who said in her prayer: “Give not, O Lord, thy sceptre to them that are not.”
2.49: **“Now the days drew near that Mathathias should die, and he said to his sons: Now hath pride and chastisement gotten strength, and the time of destruction, and the wrath of indignation:”** — And the days drew near, etc. This exhortation of Mathathias, by which he exhorted his sons to be zealous for the law of God and to give their lives for the covenant of their fathers, agrees well with the teaching of the Gospel, by which the truth itself instructed his disciples by words and examples how they should resist all the errors of the Jews, and of the pagans and heretics, and convert the world by their preaching to the faith. And he confirmed this same teaching of his by the testimony of the law and the prophets, showing that the same is the author of the New and the Old Testament.
2.64: **“You therefore, my sons, take courage, and behave manfully in the law: for by it you shall be glorious.”** — You therefore, etc. We read in the Gospel of John that the Saviour, hastening to his passion, on the same night in which he was betrayed, after the mystic supper and the washing of the feet, which he performed for his disciples girded with a towel, gave very many proofs of his exhortation; among which he also foretold the passion that was to be theirs in the world, and promised the glory of the kingdom to come and the joy of the heavenly country. But since the death of Mathathias prefigures the passion of the Redeemer, let us hear how, on the other hand, he ordained the teaching for the whole time of this present life.
2.65: **“And behold, I know that your brother Simon is a man of counsel: give ear to him always, and he shall be a father to you.”** — And behold, Simeon. We said above that Simeon means “hearing,” and he rightly said that Simeon was a man of counsel, because those who, by the teaching of the grace of the Holy Spirit, are instructed by inward hearing, are useful in all things and fit for counsel. Whence the Psalmist says: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me: for he will speak peace unto his people,” etc. And in the Apocalypse: He that heareth, he says, let him say: Come. The heavenly master exhorts us to hear those whom he himself, teaching within, has made wholesome masters for us. And Judas, he says, Machabeus, strong in might, shall be the prince of the army for you; he shall conduct the war of the people. What is signified by Judas Machabeus, if not the first preachers of the Gospel, who, instructed by the Saviour himself, were fit to conduct the war of the Christian people? But since Judas means “confession,” and in very many places holds the type of the Saviour himself, let us know that our war is then conducted in order, when he himself deigns to direct our counsel and our action. Whence the Truth himself says to the disciples: “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, unless it abide in the vine, so neither can you, unless you abide in me, for without me you can do nothing.” “And behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world.”
2.69: **“And he blessed them, and was joined to his fathers.”** — And he blessed them, etc. It is found written in the Gospel how the Saviour, after he finished the supper which he had with his disciples before his passion, ended the last preaching by which he instructed the disciples that same night, and at the end a prayer directed to the Father, and commended his disciples to him to be kept, saying: “Holy Father, keep them in thy name whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we also are.” And a little after: Sanctify them, he says, in truth. “Thy word is truth. As thou hast sent me into the world, I also have sent them into the world,” and for them I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth, and the rest. For with such speeches our Mathathias instructed and blessed his disciples. And so he was laid with his fathers, because in all things, as it was written of him, he confirmed by fulfilling them the sayings of the holy fathers, by his passion and resurrection and ascension.
2.70: **“And he died in the hundred and forty-sixth year: and he was buried by his sons in the sepulchres of his fathers in Modin, and all Israel mourned for him with great mourning.”** — And he died. It was said above that Mathathias rose up in the hundred and forty-fifth year, when the Gentiles were profaning the temple of God, and his sons with him, to be zealous for the law of God and to avenge the deeds. Now also the Scripture relates that the same Mathathias died in the hundred and forty-sixth year. Whence it appears that he lived no more than one year together with his sons after the vengeance was begun, and so he died. For this number of years fits well with the mystery of the Lord’s passion, because after the fulness of time in which God decreed to send his Son, according to the testimony of the law and the Gospel, in the sixth age of the world he suffered on the sixth day for man, who was created on the sixth day, and by the price of his blood perfectly redeemed and restored him. But that he is said to be buried by his sons in the sepulchre of his fathers signifies that the memory of his passion is fittingly venerated daily by the faithful in the holy Church, where is the place of judgment and equity, and that a wholesome mourning is celebrated there, because holy men, kindled with desire of eternal life, strive for the attaining of it to be pricked with saving tears in the chambers of their hearts.

3.5: **“And he pursued the wicked and sought them out, and them that troubled his people he burnt with fire:”** — And he rose up, etc. Mathathias dying, Judas Machabeus his son succeeded in his place, and all his brethren helped him, and all who had joined themselves to his father. What then is signified to us in this deed, if not that our Redeemer, after he had fulfilled his passion and resurrection and ascended into heaven, first appointed the apostles as his successors in the preaching of the Gospel, the Holy Spirit having been sent from heaven; who are rightly reckoned under the name of Judas, that is, confessing, because Luke says of them in the Gospel: “And they were always in the temple, praising and blessing God.” These, then, all his brethren and all who had joined themselves to his father helped, because men of the lesser order, and all believers who came together to his faith by the teaching of Christ, laboured with the choir of the apostles to the best of their strength in bearing witness to the Gospel. And they fought the battle of Israel with joy, and he enlarged the glory of his people. Because that apostolic company itself, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, preached the word of God earnestly everywhere, rejoicing in tribulations, in necessities and in distresses, increasing and multiplying everywhere the number of those who believe in the Lord. He put on a breastplate as a giant. Because he fortified himself on every side with the strength of faith. He girded himself with warlike arms. According to that of the apostle Paul, by which he taught, saying: “Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of justice, and your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace; in all things taking the shield of faith, wherewith you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one; and take unto you the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God.” And so he fought against the enemies and protected the camp of the Church. And he was like a lion in his works, and like a lion’s whelp roaring for his prey. Like, that is, in manner to that lion of whom it is written: “Behold the lion of the tribe of Juda, the root of David, hath prevailed,” and of whom Jacob the patriarch, in figure, in the mystical blessing of his sons says among other things: “Juda is a lion’s whelp: to the prey, my son, thou art gone up: resting thou hast couched as a lion, and as a lioness, who shall rouse him?” That hunting, therefore, was spiritual, when spiritual hunters with the nets of the Gospel drew men to the faith. Thus, then, the mystical Judas pursued the wicked, and burnt with fire those that troubled his people, because by pursuing, whether persecuting men or even malignant spirits, with such zeal and such action, he brought upon them no small disturbance, the flames of envy being kindled.
3.6: **“And his enemies were driven away for fear of him, and all the workers of iniquity were troubled: and salvation prospered in his hand.”** — And they were driven away, etc. And he grieved many kings. Those, that is, who strove to resist the Gospel of Christ. And made Jacob glad with his works. When he strengthened the people of believers by word and example. And his mercy for ever in blessing. According to that of the Wise Man: “All peoples,” he says, “will declare the wisdom of the saints, and the whole church of the saints will shew forth their praise.” And he went through the cities of Juda, and destroyed the ungodly out of them. Because in examining the faith of the Churches, he struck with anathema the heretics who held opinions contrary to the right faith. And he was renowned even to the utmost parts of the earth. Because “their sound hath gone forth into all the earth: and their words unto the ends of the world.”
3.12: **“And he took their spoils, and Judas took the sword of Apollonius, and fought with it all his lifetime.”** — And he gathered together, etc. What is expressed by Apollonius, if not the cruelty of the Jews, who had gathered together from Samaria a great army against Israel, because by observance of the letter of the law they strove to overthrow the faith of Christ, as though contrary to the precepts of God. But Judas went out to meet Apollonius, and struck him and killed him. Because Christ in his apostles overthrew and crushed the error of the Jews by the testimony of the law itself and the prophets, showing that the shadow of the law and the prophets prefigured the truth of the Gospel. And many of them fell down wounded. Because many of the Jews, wounded by envy, fell. But the rest fled. That is, they sought salvation for themselves from the teaching of the Church. Of whom Judas took the spoils, when the disciples of Christ turned all the ceremonies of the law, which they had held carnally, to spiritual use. And Judas took the sword of Apollonius, and fought with it all his lifetime. By the sword of Apollonius we understand nothing other than the word of the law and the prophets, which the holy preachers take up and fight with it all their days, when, taking from the carnal people the history of the divine law, interpreted in a spiritual sense by apostolic tradition, they overthrow the errors of all nations; and in all the days of this age the power of the joy of holy Church brings forth a most glorious victory.
3.13: **“And Seron captain of the army of Syria heard that Judas had assembled a company of the faithful, and a congregation with him,”** — And he heard, etc. By Seron, captain of the army of Syria, is signified the power of this world, which is rightly reckoned under the name of Syria. For Syria is interpreted lofty, or moistening, because this world is lifted up with pride and weighed down with luxury. Seron therefore resolves to overthrow Judas and those who are with him, when worldly arrogance plots snares against the holy teachers and the people of the faithful, and gathers the camps of the wicked for this, that by the aid of very many it may oppress the innocent, trusting more in the power of its kingdom than in the power of God. But it happens to him contrary to his expectation, because the stone cut out of the mountain without hands will crush the proud statue, and will break in pieces the gold, the silver, the brass and the iron, and the kingdom will be given to the people of the saints. The lion of the tribe of Juda, the root of David, hath prevailed, to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth.
3.16: **“And they approached even as far as Bethoron: and Judas went forth to meet him, with a small company.”** — And they approached even as far as Bethoron, and Judas went forth to meet him, with a small company. It is well said that the army of Seron approached Bethoron, because it brings forth its whole action with tumult. For Bethoron is interpreted house of wrath. Judas met him with a small company, because the company of the saints answers enemies not by wrath but by patience and humility, being commanded by the Lord, who says: “Be at agreement with thy adversary betimes, whilst thou art in the way with him.” “But I say to you not to resist evil: but if one strike thee on thy right cheek, turn to him also the other; and if a man will contend with thee in judgment, and take away thy coat, let go thy cloak also unto him.”
3.17: **“But when they saw the army coming to meet them, they said to Judas: How shall we, being few, be able to fight against so great a multitude and so strong, and we are ready to faint with fasting today?”** — When they saw, etc. The words of the fearful express the frailty of certain subjects, who, considering their own weakness rather, fear a fall more than they have confidence in God through the strength of faith. But the skill of the teachers, restraining the fear of such with pious exhortations, gives them sure hope of the future help of God, who is the protector of all who hope faithfully in him.
3.24: **“And he pursued him by the descent of Bethoron even to the plain, and there fell of them eight hundred men, and the rest fled into the land of the Philistines.”** — And there fell. Well is the sum of those who fall to their salvation enclosed in the number eight, because those who willingly yield to the truth, by spiritual circumcision cut off from themselves all pleasures spiritually, and strive to gather into themselves the virtues of the eight beatitudes. But the rest who fled came into the land of the Philistines. Because, although some of the persecutors can in no way resist the truth, yet they choose rather to flee to the hiding places of their errors than to yield and obey the useful counsel of spiritual masters. And well is it said that they fled into the land of the Philistines. For Philistim is interpreted double ruin; for he has a double ruin who first falls by sin, and then, despairing by himself, perseveres in evil.
3.26: **“And his fame came to the king, and all nations told of the battles of Judas.”** — And fear fell. The fear of Judas and his brethren fell upon all nations, when the power of Christ shone forth in his members through mighty works and miracles. And his name came to the king. Because the preaching of his Gospel became known to the power of this world; and all nations told of the battles of Judas, when the nations of the whole world proclaim the victory of our Redeemer over death and the author of death.
3.27: **“Now when king Antiochus heard these words, he was angry in his mind: and he sent and gathered the forces of all his kingdom, an exceeding strong army.”** — Now when he heard, etc. The passions of this historical Antiochus, with which he raged immoderately, that is, anger, covetousness, pride, well express the ways of the spiritual Antiochus, with which he most violently troubles the whole world: but now through his members, and near the end of the world by himself, when there will be such tribulation as was not before, nor shall be after. He is angry when he hears the glory of the saints and their virtue and constancy; he gathers an army, giving it pay for a year, when through the comforts of the present life and honours he incites all the ambitious to persecute the faithful; and, intent on worldly pride and covetousness, he chooses his nobles to provide for the affairs of the kingdom, when he appoints his ministers and followers to this: to suggest the allurements of present things, and by provoking to earthly pleasures to draw to themselves those who consent. For by the name of sons are reckoned those who are imitators of antichrist. These he nourishes through his nobles, when through the most wicked he corrupts with various vices and makes food for the eternal fire. This he chiefly commands his officers: to root out the strength of Israel and the remnant of Jerusalem, and to set strangers in their place, because no intention, no zeal, is more the devil’s than to overthrow the Church of Christ, to soften the strength of faith in the elect, and to bring in vices in the place of virtues.
3.39: **“And he sent with them forty thousand men, and seven thousand horsemen: to go into the land of Juda, and to destroy it according to the king’s orders.”** — And Lysias chose. What is signified by Lysias, but worldly pride, which through three men, that is, through three orders of persecutors, brings war upon the Church of Christ, that is, through pagans, through heretics, and through false Christians; to whom are added forty thousand men and seven thousand horsemen, to destroy Juda according to the king’s word. What is signified by the number forty but the whole of the time in which the Church endures persecution in the world. For there are four principal parts of the world, that is, east, west, north and south, in which the Church stands spread abroad. To gather her the Son of God came down into the world; and where he fasted for his passion forty days and forty nights, to show our temptation in his flesh, which he deigned to share from our mortality. Whence from the hour of his death to the dawn of the resurrection there are forty hours, if that hour itself is not counted. After the resurrection also he willed to be with his disciples on this earth no more than forty days; still mingled with their life in human conversation, and taking with them the food of mortals, though now not to die; that through those very forty days he might signify that by a hidden presence he would fulfil what he promised, when he said: “Behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world.” But by the number seven, by which the thousands of horsemen are described, nothing else is shown than the fullness of persecutions; because as by the number seven the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is shown, so on the contrary it is read in the Gospel that the wicked spirit brought into the man with him seven spirits more wicked than himself, and elsewhere it is read that the Lord cast out seven devils from the sinful woman; therefore all the persecutors are rightly gathered together, the devil instigating, for this: to destroy the Church of Christ and to force the confessors of almighty God to blaspheme; and this they do not sluggishly, but accomplish with all their strength.
3.40: **“So they went forth with all their power, and came, and pitched near Emmaus in the plain country.”** — And they went forth, etc. What is expressed by Emmaus but the lovers of the world, who through the covetousness of the age neglect to have the friendship of God. Whence it is written: “Whosoever therefore will be a friend of this world, becomes an enemy of God.” And John says: “If any man love the world, the charity of God is not in him.” And deservedly such are called by this name. For Emmaus is interpreted a people cast away; and indeed they are worthy of being cast away who prefer the love of the present age to the love of God. Whence the Truth itself says in the Gospel: “He that loveth father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me.” Nor is it unfitting that Emmaus is said to be in the plain country, because “broad and spacious is the way that leadeth to death, and many there are who enter in thereby.”
3.41: **“And the merchants of the countries heard the fame of them: and they took silver and gold in abundance, and servants: and they came into the camp, to buy the children of Israel for slaves: and there were joined to them the forces of Syria, and of the land of the strangers.”** — And they heard. I judge that these merchants, who seek the servitude of the Hebrews, signify none better than the wicked spirits, who desire the destruction of the faithful, and rejoice in this: that through earthly cupidity they may take from us heavenly glory, and turn the liberty which we have in the glory of Christ into the worship and servitude of the devil. Whence it is read in the Gospel that the devil himself, leading our head, the mediator namely of God and men, up into an exceeding high mountain, showed him all the kingdoms of the world and the glory of them, and tempting him said: “All these will I give thee, if falling down thou wilt adore me.” And it is well said that “there were joined to them the forces of Syria, and of the land of the strangers,” because all the luxurious and those estranged from the true worship of God are joined to our enemies, and by working our destruction are fellow-workers of the unclean spirits.
3.42: **“And Judas and his brethren saw that evils were multiplied, and that the armies approached to their borders: and they knew the orders the king had given to destroy the people and utterly abolish them.”** — And Judas saw. While the persecutors rage and prepare battle against the faithful, the faithful themselves are the more stirred up, after the example of Judas and his brethren, to increase of faith and progress in virtues, according to that of the Psalmist who says: “Whilst the wicked man is proud, the poor is set on fire.” Such then ought to be the intention of the servants of God: that they fight for the people and their saints, because for the state of the faith of the Christian religion and for the salvation of the brethren they ought to contend earnestly against the spiritual wickednesses and against wicked men, and to implore the help of God by constant prayer, for it is he of whom it is written: “A helper in due time in tribulation; to thee the poor man is left; thou wilt be a helper to the orphan,” because with fatherly kindness he considers the labour and sorrow of his own, he breaks the arm of the sinner and the malignant, he judges for the fatherless and the humble, “that man may no more presume to magnify himself upon earth.”
3.54: **“Then they sounded with trumpets, and cried out with a loud voice.”** — And they were gathered together, etc. Those who had been gathered together to fight against the enemies came to Maspha, over against Jerusalem. And what is signified by Maspha, which is interpreted judgment, but the Old Testament? The place of prayer was in Maspha, which always looks forward to the New Testament and gives testimony to the Gospel of Christ. For thither it is necessary that the spiritual soldiers of God turn the intention of their heart, that they may be instructed by divine reading how they ought to fight against spiritual enemies. For the place of prayer was in Maspha, formerly in Israel, who first made known to us the divine oracles through the books of the law and the prophets, and then through the Gospel. They fasted that day. Because they gave attention to continence. They put on sackcloths and ashes on their heads. Because they decree to do penance worthily for God for their sins, which they contracted through the frailty of the flesh. And they rent their garments. When they chastise the body and mortify the carnal desires in themselves. As to what follows, that “they laid open the books of the law, in which the Gentiles searched for the likeness of their idols,” it shows that those who are proved to serve worthily show their remembrance of the divine precepts by good deeds. For the law of the Lord is undefiled, converting the souls of the elect, it reproaches the evil deeds of the faithless, and detests the worship of idols, and contradicts every work of impiety. They bring out the priestly ornaments, who worthily perform the offices of the ecclesiastical priesthood; they give the firstfruits and tithes, who ascribe to God the beginning and the perfection of a good work; they stir up the Nazarites who had fulfilled their days, who through purity of chastity strive to present to God a pleasing life at all times; and they cry with a loud voice to heaven, who by pious prayers and good deeds move the divinity to mercy. For as the cry of the wicked, which they utter by blasphemy and evil works, provokes God, so the confession and faith of the saints, which works by love, appeases the divine majesty at all times.
3.55: **“And after this Judas appointed captains over the people, over thousands, and over hundreds, and over fifties, and over tens.”** — And after this, etc. He calls tribunes those who were over a thousand soldiers, whom the Greeks call chiliarchs; centurions, those over a hundred; pentecontarchs, those over fifty; and decurions, those over ten. For holy preachers set their subjects in order, that nothing disorderly may be found in them, but the warfare of Christ may be carried out reasonably. Whence Paul says to his hearers: “Let all things be done decently, and according to order.” And again: No one, he says, “shall be crowned, unless he strive lawfully.”
3.56: **“And he said to them that were building houses, or had betrothed wives, or were planting vineyards, or were fearful, that they should return every man to his house, according to the law.”** — And he said to them, etc. For it is written in Deuteronomy: “What man is there that is fearful, and faint hearted? let him go, and return to his house, lest he make the hearts of his brethren to fear, as he himself is possessed with fear.” By these words he teaches that no one can take up the profession of contemplation, or the exercise of spiritual warfare, who still fears to be stripped of earthly works, lest again through weakness of mind he return to his former filth, and by his example call others back from evangelical perfection and weaken the vigour of the faithful. Such are therefore commanded to depart from the fight and return to their house, because they cannot fight the wars of the Lord with a double heart. For “a double minded man is inconstant in all his ways.” For such it is needful that they do not even take up the beginning of renewal. It is better for them to remain in the active life than, following contemplation lukewarmly, to involve themselves in greater danger. For it is better not to vow than to vow and not to pay. In like manner he also is kept back from such warfare who has taken a wife, who has planted a vineyard, as it were the offspring of children. For the servant of a wife cannot serve in divine warfare, nor can he attain the pursuit of contemplation who is still fixed in the delight of the flesh. “No man,” says the apostle, “being a soldier to God, entangleth himself with secular businesses; that he may please him to whom he hath engaged himself.”
3.57: **“So they removed the camp, and pitched on the south side of Emmaus.”** — And they removed the camp, etc. Rightly is the army of Judas said to pitch camp on the south side of Emmaus, because the soldiers of Christ, when they prepare to fight against their enemies, choose rather to be kindled by the warmth of faith than to grow numb with the cold of unbelief.
3.58: **“And Judas said: Gird yourselves, and be valiant men, and be ready against the morning, that you may fight with these nations that are assembled against us to destroy us and our sanctuary.”** — And Judas said: Gird yourselves, etc. Such ought to be the teaching of holy preachers, and such the exhortation, that they stir up the minds of their hearers and strengthen their hearts to resist the devil and his army, while committing the hope of victory to God alone.

4.1: **“Then Gorgias took five thousand men, and a thousand of the best horsemen: and they removed out of the camp by night.”** — And Gorgias took, etc. Gorgias takes five thousand into his army, as the devil strives to gather to himself carnal men, given over to the five senses of the body by the allurement of pleasures. He takes a thousand horsemen with him, as he arranges to wage his whole war in pride and contempt of the commandments of God, so that in this he may overcome the ranks of the opposing party, when he persuades them to transgress the precepts of God. For the beginning of all sin is pride, where the author of death finds ruin for himself and his followers. And it is well said that he moved the camp by night, because he desires to accomplish all his wickedness, through blindness of mind, in those subject to him, so that they may in no way foresee what ruin threatens them from consent to sin.
4.2: **“That they might come upon the camp of the Jews, and strike them suddenly: and the men that were of the castle were their guides.”** — And the sons, etc. The castle here signifies not the height of virtues but the exalting of vain glory. For those give leadership to sinners who dare to lift themselves up in pride. The malignant spirits too can be noticed in these guides, who belong to the part of him who said: “I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne in the sides of the north, and I will be like the most High.” For these leaders of iniquity never cease to draw those who consent to them into the pit and the whirlpool of crimes.
4.3: **“And Judas heard of it, and rose up, he and the valiant men, to attack the king’s forces that were in Emmaus.”** — And Judas heard, etc. Note, reader, that the adverse party which was joined to Gorgias makes the whole arrangement of its war by night; and Judas and his followers by day, because the workers of wickedness and the executors of errors are always committed to it, ruling in darkness, hating the light of the divine precepts and loving the obscurity of worldly pleasures. Whence it is said through Paul: “They that sleep, sleep in the night; and they that are drunk, are drunk in the night.” But we, who are of the day, are not children of night nor of darkness. But Judas, that is, the confessor of God, orders his whole preparation for war in the light of faith and in meditation on the law of God. Whence he appears in the field with only three thousand men, with those, that is, who, acting confidently not in worldly power but in the faith of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, strive with simplicity of mind to lead an honest life in this world.
4.14: **“And they joined battle: and the Gentiles were routed, and fled into the plain.”** — And they raised, etc. As the enemies come against them into battle, the companions of Judas sound the trumpet, and the Gentiles are crushed, because by the sound of the trumpet the voice of preaching is expressed. The soldiers of Judas sound the trumpet when the preachers of Christ proclaim the Gospel in the whole world. Whence the enemies are crushed, because the Gentiles are subjected to this faith of Christ, and the spiritual enemies too are crushed by the power of Christ, and, slain by the sword of the Holy Spirit, are sunk into the depth of the abyss.
4.15: **“But all the hindmost of them fell by the sword, and they pursued them as far as Gezeron, and even to the plains of Idumea, and of Azotus, and of Jamnia: and there fell of them to the number of three thousand men.”** — And they pursued them, etc. The names of the places to which Judas pursued his enemies show the efficacy of his valor. For Gazeron is interpreted “near my light”; Idumea, “red” or “earthly”; Azotus, “paternal fire”; Jamnia, “sea” or “his right hand.” And what is shown by Gazeron, but the light of faith, and by Idumea but the heathen state? And by the paternal fire, what but the ardor of charity? And by Jamnia, what but depth of knowledge and the effect of good work? So long, then, does the choir of holy doctors pursue the heathen people, until it leads them from the error of heathenism to the light of faith, and kindles in them the fire of charity, and provokes them to meditation on the divine law and zeal for good work. For this pursuit is saving and the slaying wholesome. Whence it is added: “And there fell of them to the number of three thousand men.” For as there were three thousand companions of Judas who pursued, so too three thousand fell on the enemies' side. They fell, not to perish utterly, but that after the fall they might be raised up and stand the better, because, imbued with faith in the holy Trinity, they strove to reach the fellowship of those whom they acknowledged they had pursued with a pious mind.
4.18: **“And Gorgias and his army are near us in the mountain: but stand ye now against our enemies, and overthrow them, and you shall take the spoils afterwards with safety.”** — And Judas returned, etc. The soldiers of Christ also ought never to be quickly secure of victory while war threatens, but ought to fight until they are certain of the conversion of their spiritual enemies. For when, by pursuing sinful men or unbelievers, they have converted them to penance for sins and to the faith of Christ, which works good works through love, then it is fitting that they gather their spoils, that is, make use of their knowledge and share in the industry of their pious labor. For in gold we can take wisdom; in silver, eloquence; in blue silk, heavenly conversation; in purple, the shedding of blood through martyrdom. For then we fruitfully gather these riches, when we find them acceptable in right faith, if we transfer this victory to the spiritual enemies. Then we ought to be secure, when after the end of the present life there is no need to fear the snares of enemies. For then we gather the spoils wholesomely, when we shall receive from Christ the worthy rewards of our labor. Whence it is well said that Judas exhorted his men not to covet the spoils while the cruel wars of the enemies were threatening; when the enemies had been utterly overcome, then he returned with his men to gather the spoils of the camp, because it is necessary that every preacher admonish his hearers to guard against the darts of enemies as long as it is the time of war. But when the time of peace itself has come, namely the peace which the Saviour promised his disciples, saying: “My peace I give unto you,” then prelates and subjects alike will have eternal joy from the promised reward, because they will no longer fear the sorrow that follows of labors and tears, for then it is the time to sing praises to God their helper. Whence it is written:
4.25: **“So Israel had a great deliverance that day.”** — And turning they sang a hymn, etc. Salvation is greater in Israel when the number of believers is multiplied in the Lord from the peoples; who acknowledge the Saviour by faith, confess him with the mouth, and glorify him in good work. Or otherwise, then there will be greater salvation in Israel, when there will be no adversity in the Church of Christ. And it is significantly added, “in that day”: namely the day of the resurrection, when the most noble bride will be joined in the heavenly kingdom above to the bridegroom, when all the saints in the sight of God will rejoice not only in the rest of their souls but also in the immortality of their bodies.
4.27: **“And when he heard these things, he was amazed and discouraged: because things had not succeeded in Israel according to his mind, and as the king had commanded.”** — Whosoever of the aliens, etc. Finally the aliens, escaping, announce the victory of Judas to Lysias; for those who are not taken as most saving prey of Christ through the ministry of the holy doctors announce the glory of Christ, though unwilling, being constrained by the truth, to their masters, by whom they are nourished unto death. For Lysias, which is interpreted “generating,” signifies the powerful of the world, who, though they have been begotten, have not yet deserved to be begotten by the baptism of Christ. These therefore, hearing the victory of the soldiers of Christ, are amazed and discouraged in mind, because things did not succeed in Israel such as they wished, and as the king commanded. For their will was this: that the preaching of the Gospel through the holy doctors should not prevail, nor the multitude of those believing in the Lord be increased. And they knew that such things pleased their rulers also, that is, the unclean spirits; for, venerated by men with divine worship in the profane images of idols, they persuaded them of this, that they should not receive the faith of Christ; but they did not prevail, because the Father made manifest the glory of his Son far and wide among all nations.
4.28: **“So the year following Lysias gathered together threescore thousand chosen men, and five thousand horsemen, that he might subdue them.”** — And the year following, etc. And Lysias chose sixty thousand men and five thousand horsemen to fight against Israel; so with all the time of this world, which is divided into six ages, through the five bodily senses the prince of this world, the rulers of these darkness urging him on, strives to overcome the soldiers of Christ by tearing them with various vices, and through wicked men he plots the death of the good. But Judas meets them with ten thousand men, because the army of our king is in this stronger than the rest: that in all things it is eager to obey the divine precepts, and sending constant prayers to the Lord it is strengthened by the hand of him in whose power it chiefly trusts, and it keeps on in the battle until its enemies and the adverse band are utterly slain by the spiritual sword; whence it is added in the prayer of Judas.
4.33: **“Cast them down with the sword of them that love thee: and let all that know thy name, praise thee with hymns.”** — Cast them down, etc. There are five books of the law of God, and there are five senses, as we said before, the bodily ones. For he who according to the teaching of the law restrains the concupiscence of the flesh, “turning away his eyes that they may not behold vanity,” “stopping his ears that they may not” hear the detracting tongue, and obscene songs for worldly uses, by hearing which frequently the inner man is defiled; he who holds back his smell and taste, lest he make use of the allurement of pleasures; “who refrains his tongue from evil, and his lips that they speak no guile, turns away from evil and does good, seeks peace and pursues it”—this man, overcoming his enemies, shall take a most saving victory, and shall rejoice in the most abundant triumph. But the spiritual Lysias, though once, twice and thrice crushed he has taken to flight, yet does not desist from the wickedness begun, but again raises up renewed battles. Whence it is written:
4.35: **“And when Lysias saw that his men were put to flight, and how bold the Jews were, and that they were ready either to live, or to die manfully, he went to Antioch, and chose soldiers, that they might come again into Judea with greater numbers.”** — And Lysias seeing, etc. It is well said that Judas, the enemies being crushed and the wars lulled for a time, exhorts his men to cleanse; for the holy doctors have the greatest zeal that, in whatever respects the Church of those subject to them has been hurt by enemies, it may again be restored to its former state of holy conversation. According to the tropological sense, moreover, it is necessary that each of the faithful, if anything in his mind has been defiled by the fraud of the enemy—and that mind we can well take as designated by the name of mount Sion, because Sion is interpreted a watch-tower; and “blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God”—should purge what has been done with an urgent gaze, until it is renewed to the full. For there we can understand the sanctification deserted, and the altar profaned, and the gates burnt; for there the sacrifice of praise was offered to God on the altar of faith, and the entrance of the heavenly life was meditated. In the courts, moreover, shrubs grow up when in human hearts the growth of superfluous thoughts is generated. “The chambers,” it says, “they saw thrown down.” The pastophoria are called in Greek thalami, or bedchambers, in which the Levites kept watch in the courts of the house of the Lord, of which mention is made in the last vision of the prophet Ezechiel. The chambers therefore are thrown down when the secrets of the mind are torn to pieces by unlawful desires. But all these things most of all need to be purified most earnestly by penance for sins, and amendment of morals, and pious prayers to the Lord. Whence it is rightly written of the army of Judas that when they saw the sanctuary desolate, “they rent their garments, and made great lamentation,” etc.
4.41: **“Then Judas appointed men to fight against them that were in the castle, till they had cleansed the holy places.”** — Then Judas appointed men, etc. It is aptly said that Judas appointed men to fight against them that were in the castle, till they had cleansed the holy places; for this our Redeemer appoints through his preachers, that his soldiers may earnestly fight against those who dwell in the castle of pride, that is, men puffed up with the spirit of conceit, or also the malignant spirits swelling with pride, until they purge the hearts of the elect from every stain of iniquity. “And he chose priests without blemish, whose will was set upon the law of God, and they cleansed the holy places”; for, having cast out from ecclesiastical office those who had in themselves the leprosy of error or the stain of crimes, he chose as ministers of the word men willing and approved in morals in the faith of God, that he might make the assemblies of the holy Church free from all contagion of error. Therefore it is added that he “took away the stones that had been defiled into an unclean place”; because heretics, who wished through the conversation of right faith and sound doctrine to become precious stones, he anathematized, smitten and cast out from the communion of the Church, and made it plain to all that they were reprobate.
4.44: **“And he considered about the altar of holocausts that had been profaned, what he should do with it.”** — And he considered, etc. The altar of holocausts is the pure faith, right doctrine, and clean conduct of Christ’s ministers. But if this altar has been profaned by heretical perversity or by the enormity of crimes, it will now have to be destroyed, that is, to be deposed from the dignity of the priesthood, lest perhaps it be a reproach to holy Church that she has perverse and wicked teachers, who have been led astray by the cunning of the devil. Whence the Lord says in the Gospel to his disciples: “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt lose its savour, wherewith shall it be salted? It is good for nothing any more but to be cast out, and to be trodden on by men.” Of this Paul also, writing to Titus, says: “A man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid: knowing that he, that is such an one, is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned by his own judgment.” Hence he also says to certain offenders: “By you the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles.” So, then, when the mystical altar has been put down, these stones ought to be laid up in the mountain of the house in a fitting place, until the prophet comes and gives answer, saying: that sinners ought to be brought under penance, until by holy teachers it is judged what fitting satisfaction has been made for the crime committed. But in their place whole stones ought to be put, according to the law, that a new altar may be made like the former one: because men sound in the catholic faith, instructed in the knowledge of the holy scriptures, and religious in good morals, ought to be put in the place of government from which the transgressors have fallen, according to the authorities of the divine law, so that without reproach, in newness of life and by the rule of justice, service may be rendered to God in the holy Church, which Christ acquired for himself by the price of his blood as a bride “not having spot or wrinkle.”
4.51: **“And they set the loaves upon the table, and hung up the veils, and finished all the works that they had begun to make.”** — And they built the holy places, etc. Holy preachers build the holy places within the house, inside, and the temple, when they adorn the people subject to them within by the knowledge of the sound faith, and without by honest conduct. They sanctify the courts when they dedicate those newly coming to the faith by instructing them in the divine sacraments. They make new holy vessels when they make the hearts of men fit for receiving the word of God. They bring in the candlestick, and the altar of incense, and the table into the temple, when they raise up in the Church of God the light of spiritual doctrine, the purity of holy working, and the meditation of the holy scriptures. In the candlestick, then, on which the lamps ought to shine, we can rightly see the discourse of evangelical doctrine, on which holy teachers, kindled with the fire of the Holy Spirit, ought to shine, that those who enter may see the light. Whence the Truth himself says in the Gospel: “Neither do men light a candle and put it under a bushel, but upon a candlestick, that it may shine to all that are in the house.” By the altar of incense we can understand nothing better than the perfect life of the saints, whence daily the odour of virtues and of holy prayer is fragrant in the sight of the Most High. The table of the Lord, then, we understand to be none other than the sacred scripture, in which the refreshment of souls consists. But as to what is said, that they hung up the veils and finished all the works that they had made: in the hanging of the veils the hiding of the mysteries is expressed. For the mysteries of the divine law are not all to be laid open to all, but according to the capacity of each one’s mind and the progress of knowledge and of virtues. Whence the Lord commands the apostles, saying: “Give not that which is holy to dogs; neither cast ye your pearls before swine.” And Paul says to untaught disciples: “I gave you milk to drink, not meat; for you were not able as yet; but neither indeed are you now able.” Of the knowledge of the perfect, then, he says elsewhere: “But we all, beholding the glory of the Lord with open face, are transformed into the same image, as by the Spirit of the Lord,” etc. They finish, then, all the works that are to be done in the house of God, who strive in faith, speech and work to fulfil in order all the commandments of the Lord; and nothing is lacking in perfection where the human will in all things obeys the divine will.
4.58: **“And there was exceeding great joy among the people, and the reproach of the Gentiles was turned away.”** — And before morning, etc. Of this renewal Josephus thus tells, saying: On the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu, which the Macedonians call Appelleon, they lighted the lamps upon the candlestick, and burned the holocausts which they offered on the new altar. These things were done after three years, on the same day on which their religion had been changed to the profane custom of idols. For the temple, destroyed by Antiochus, so remained for three years. For in the hundred and forty-fifth year these things were done in the temple, on the twenty-fifth day of the month Appelleus, in the hundred and fifty-third Olympiad. But it was renewed on the same day, the twenty-fifth of the month Appelleus, in the hundred and forty-eighth year, in the hundred and fifty-fourth Olympiad. The desolation of the temple happened according to the foretelling of Daniel, which he had foretold four hundred and eight years before, by which he signified that the Macedonians would destroy it. And Judas with his citizens celebrated sacrifices for the renewal of the temple for eight days, leaving out no kind of delight, but feeding them with the most costly feasts; and he glorified God with praises and psalms, and they delighted one another with songs. For the renewal of the solemnities, after a mutual interval, religion being inspired, the receivers of the law decreed that their posterity should celebrate this renewal of the temple for eight days. Whence from that time until now we celebrate this feast, calling it Lights, because beyond hope this splendid light of the religion to be cherished appeared to us. Mystically, however, the renewal of the temple is the conversion of men to penance for sins, who had been defiled by some errors and crimes.
