For such a victory is well fitting to those who from heavenly teaching have learned to love their enemies and to do good to them that hate them; to pray for those who persecute and slander them, to bless those who curse, and not to curse back. They receive the spoils of the slain when they turn all their efforts to ecclesiastical use. Whence it is fittingly added: “And the marriage was turned into mourning, and the noise of their musical instruments into lamentation.” Because the holy preachers teach those whom they seize as a saving prey, and utterly slay as to carnal life and the acts of the old man, to change the vain joy of the world into the mourning of penance, and vain jests and useless songs into divine psalmody, with the compunction of tears. And so they return to the bank of the Jordan when they bring them to the state of the Christian religion and to the precept of holy baptism, that there the gospel rite may be fulfilled, for which all the labour was spent.
9.53: **“And he took the sons of the chief men of the country for hostages, and put them in the castle in Jerusalem in custody.”** — And Bacchides heard, etc. When the persecutors of the faithful, stirred up by envy, strive to disturb them on the spiritual sabbath, on which the worshippers of Christ themselves are free from earthly desires to hear the word of God and to sing praise to the Lord, and endeavour to defile the sacrament of baptism by secular power, the mystical Jonathan stirs up his own to spiritual battle, that is, that by constancy of mind and strength of faith they may fight on the opposite side against their enemies; not that they should hurt them by fighting or striking them, but that they may conquer better by enduring with patience and meekness and repaying with benefits, according to that saying of the Saviour, in which he says to his disciples: “You have heard that it hath been said to them of old: An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth. But I say to you not to resist evil: but if one strike thee on thy right cheek, turn to him also the other. And if a man will contend with thee in judgment, and take away thy coat, let go thy cloak also unto him.” And again: “In your patience you shall possess your souls.” Hence Paul also says: “If thy enemy be hungry, give him to eat; if he thirst, give him to drink. For, doing this, thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head. Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good.” For God, who gives victory to his servants and lays their enemies under their feet, is won by such sacrifices. Whence in the later part it is written that Jonathan made peace with Bacchides, and that Bacchides swore that he would do him no harm all the days of his life, and he restored to him the captivity which he had before taken as plunder from the land of Juda.
9.54: **“Now in the year one hundred and fifty-three, the second month, Alcimus commanded the walls of the inner court of the sanctuary to be thrown down, and the works of the prophets to be destroyed: and he began to be destroyed: and he began to destroy.”** — And in the year one hundred, etc. We said above that Alcimus, the defiler of the law and betrayer of his country, signified heretics, who fear not to profane the testament of God with wicked sects and to disturb the Church of the Lord. Here he now destroys the walls of the inner holy house, and is recorded as demolishing the works of the prophets. Which can fittingly be applied to the heretics themselves, who strive not only to corrupt the oracles of the prophets by various traditions, but also, in whatever way they can, to violate and scatter the bulwark of the faith, which is attentively guarded in the hearts of believers for the practice of the justice of the law of God. But let us see what follows:
9.55: **“At that time Alcimus was struck: and his works were hindered, and his mouth was stopped, and he was taken with a palsy, so that he could no more speak a word, nor give order concerning his house.”** — At that time. Because although heretics are proud with excessive arrogance, although for a time they seem to prevail over the faithful through the aid of the powerful of this world, yet by the judgment of almighty God they will be overthrown at the end, and the vigour of their wicked will shall be dissolved, when what they wish they cannot bring to effect. Nor is it allowed them to give order concerning their house, that is, concerning their future conduct, the sentence of the judgment on high now hanging over them; but that will come to pass which is said through the Psalmist: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things. Who have said: We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is Lord over us?”
9.57: **“And Bacchides saw that Alcimus was dead: and he returned to the king, and the land was quiet for two years.”** — And he was dead. Because, for heretics who persist in their wickedness to the end of this present life, the second death will follow, and they will be cast, according to the sentence of the Apocalypse of John, into the pool of eternal fire, and will be tormented with fire and brimstone in the sight of the holy angels and in the sight of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torments will ascend up for ever and ever, nor will they have rest day or night, because they adored the beast and his image, and they gnawed their tongues for pain, and blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and wounds, and did not fruitful penance for their works, because while it was allowed they would not purge themselves beforehand of their errors. And Bacchides saw that Alcimus was dead: and he returned to the king, and the land was quiet for two years. For two years the land was quiet, when the Church had peace for a time from the persecution of unbelievers and the troubling of heretics, according to that which is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Now the church had peace throughout all Judea, and Galilee, and Samaria; and was edified, walking in the fear of the Lord, and was filled with the consolation of the Holy Ghost.” But that peace and security will not be lasting and enduring in the present life, the following sentence makes manifest, where it is written:
9.61: **“And he apprehended of the men of the country, that were the principal authors of the mischief, fifty men, and slew them.”** — And they thought. All enemies envy the peace and quiet of the Church of God. Whence, tormented by the happy success of the good, they seek the help of the wicked to do harm. This the letter of Bacchides signifies, secretly sent to his associates who were in Judea, to seize Jonathan and those who were with him in Judea; because when cruel persecutors do not prevail outwardly by torments to overthrow the confessors of Christ, they build up snares inwardly through false brethren, who seem to remain in the Church, so that those whom they could not overcome with the sword, these they may deceive by guile. Whence the apostle Paul often in his epistles complains of the deceit of false brethren, who crept in to pervert the truth of the Gospel. But they could not, because their design was made known to them. For it is the work of a good teacher’s diligence that the people subject to him know how to foresee and beware of the craftiness of the perverse. And he seized, it says, of the men of the country, who were the princes of the wickedness, fifty men, and slew them. Who are those fifty of the men of the country who were the princes of the wickedness and were slain by Bacchides, if not those who, content with the surface of the royal letter, wish to observe the Pentateuch of the law not spiritually but carnally, in circumcision and superfluous ceremonies? These the teacher of the Gentiles rebukes, writing to the Galatians, where he says: O senseless Galatians, who hath bewitched you? How turn you again to the weak and needy elements, which you desire to serve again? You observe days, and months, and times, and years. I fear for you, lest perhaps I have laboured in vain among you. You did run well; who hath hindered you that you should not obey the truth? This persuasion is not from him that calleth you. A little leaven corrupteth the whole lump. I have confidence in you in the Lord that you will not be of another mind: but he that troubleth you shall bear the judgment, whosoever he be. Now that such have been slain unto death of the soul by the deceit of the ancient enemy, let us see what follows:
9.64: **“And he came, and camped above Bethbessen, and fought against it many days, and made engines.”** — And Jonathan withdrew. What is the meaning that Jonathan, when Bacchides made a tumult, gathered himself with his men in Bethbessen, which is in the desert, and built up its ruins, strengthening it, if not that holy preachers, when they see the hand of the persecutors prevailing, so that they cannot go forth in public with the word of preaching, withdraw for a time into secret places, that there they may give themselves to fasting and prayers, and whatever of the uprightness of their life slipped away through carelessness among the people while it was being kept, this may be renewed again in full, apart from them, by the earnestness of good zeal. For Bethbessen is interpreted house of the flowering mouth. For the mouth flowers when it resounds with prayers and psalmody and hymns made up in the praises of God. This the Lord also seems to command his disciples in the Gospel, where he says: When they persecute you in one city, flee into another. Whence the Truth himself, when the Jews thought to kill him, “walked no more openly among the Jews; but he went into a country near the desert, unto a city that is called Ephrem, and there he abode with his disciples.” And elsewhere it is read that he went out into a mountain to pray, and spent the night in the prayer of God. So also Paul and Barnabas, when they were preaching the word of God in Iconium, and an assault was made by the Gentiles and the Jews with their rulers, to use them contumeliously and to stone them, “understanding it, fled to Lystra, and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the whole country round about, and were there preaching the gospel.” But the wickedness of the ancient enemy allows no place in the world to be safe from snares. Hence Bacchides also leads his army against Bethbessen, to fight against it and not allow the worshippers of God to live in quiet.
9.72: **“And he restored to him the prisoners which he before had taken out of the land of Juda”** — And Jonathan left. What is the meaning that Jonathan left his brother Simon in the city and himself went out into the country to pursue the adversaries, if not that holy teachers give themselves within to the virtues, and yet without, with the shield of faith and the sword of the spirit, do not cease to fight against the enemies. But the enemies of the Church themselves are not uniform; rather they are manifold in various kinds of persecution, since Jews, pagans, heretics and schismatics, and also false Christians, build up calamities to harm the good, as was shown above. This the very names set forth, not unfittingly, by their interpretations. For Odaren is interpreted his generation, and Phaseron, a cutting off. Whence by Odaren and his brethren can be denoted those who, through the unity of the Catholic confession, pretend to be of the same generations as the good and simple, but show themselves strangers to their society by wicked deeds. Of whom the Apostle says: “They profess that they know God: but in their works they deny him.” By Phaseron, however, are designated the rest, who differ from the unity of the Church not only in religion but also in the profession of faith; such never cease to prepare schisms, and quarrels and calamities for true Christians, but the spiritual leaders turn their contrivances and snares back upon them, and do not allow them to harm the soldiers of Christ by their frauds.
9.73: **“So the sword ceased from Israel: and Jonathan dwelt in Machmas, and Jonathan began there to judge the people, and he destroyed the wicked out of Israel.”** — And he was turned. The storms of war ceasing, Jonathan goes into Machmas, and dwelling there he judges the people and destroys the wicked out of Israel; because, the wars of the wicked having been quieted, the holy preachers strive to restore what had before been diminished of the morals of their subjects on account of the threatening tempests of battles, and strive in every way to render to their Creator, with good morals, the due burden of just service. For Machmas, historically, is a large village, which is shown even to this day in the territory of Helia, keeping its ancient name, and distant nine miles from it, near the town of Rama. For Machmas is interpreted tribute of the town, or decree; by which, clearly, the holy Church is signified, where God is served earnestly every day, and where, according to the decrees of the law of God, just judgments are diligently exercised by the learned among the faithful, and the wickedness of the wicked is driven far away from the true Israel.

10.1: **“Now in the hundred and sixtieth year Alexander the son of Antiochus, surnamed the Illustrious, came up and took Ptolemais, and they received him, and he reigned there.”** — And in the hundred and sixtieth year, etc. He calls him the Illustrious Antiochus, whom the Greeks call Epiphanes, the son of Antiochus the Great, of whom more is related above.
10.6: **“And he gave him authority to gather together an army, and to make arms, and that he should be his confederate: and the hostages that were in the castle, he commanded to be delivered to him.”** — And Demetrius heard, etc. Concerning this war of Demetrius and Alexander, it seems not out of place to consider what Pompeius Trogus and his abridger Justin report. For thus it is written in the Epitome of the same Pompeius Trogus, in the thirty-fifth book: Demetrius, having seized the kingdom of Syria, thinking the idleness of his new reign dangerous, resolved to enlarge the strength of the kingdom and increase its resources by wars with his neighbours. And so, hostile to Ariarectes, king of Cappadocia, because he had scorned marriage with his sister, he received as a suppliant his brother Holofernes, who had been wrongfully driven from the kingdom; and rejoicing that an honourable pretext for war had been given him, he resolved to restore him to the kingdom. But Holofernes, with an ungrateful mind, having made a pact with the Antiochians, who were then offended with Demetrius, formed a plan to drive from the kingdom the man by whom he was being restored. When Demetrius learned this, he spared his life, lest Ariarectes be freed from fear of war with his brother, but ordered him seized and kept in custody at Seleucia; and the Antiochians, not terrified by the judgment, did not cease from their revolt. And so, with Ptolemy king of Egypt, Attalus king of Asia, and Ariarectes king of Cappadocia helping, being provoked to war by Demetrius, they openly set up a youth of the lowest condition, to reclaim by arms the kingdom of Syria as his father’s; and that no insult might be lacking, the name of Alexander is given him, and he is said to be the son of Antiochus the king. Such was the hatred of Demetrius among all that to his rival not only royal strength but also nobility of birth was granted by the consent of all. Then Alexander, by a wonderful change of fortune forgetful of his former baseness, girded with the strength of almost the whole East, makes war on Demetrius, and having conquered him deprives him of life and kingdom alike. Yet Demetrius did not lack courage in repelling the war. For he first put the enemy to flight, and when the kings renewed the war he slew many thousands in the battle line. But at last, with unconquered spirit, fighting most bravely among the bravest, he fell. At the beginning of the war Demetrius had entrusted two sons, with a great weight of gold, to Guidius his host, that they might be removed from the dangers of war and, if fortune so fell out, be kept for avenging their father. And the elder Demetrius, having passed the years of boyhood, hearing of the luxury of Alexander, whom unexpected wealth and the ornaments of another’s good fortune held idle in the palace, as if captured among troops of harlots, with the Cretans helping, attacks him as he was secure and fearing nothing hostile. The Antiochians also, to correct their old offence against the father by new services, surrender to him. But the soldiers too, kindled by favour for the father toward the youth, preferring the sanctity of their former oath to the pride of the new king, transfer their standards to Demetrius; and so Alexander, brought down by fortune with no less force than he had been raised up, is defeated in the first battle and killed, and paid the penalty to Demetrius, whom he had slain, and to Antiochus, whose origin he had falsely claimed.
10.14: **“Only in Bethsura there remained some of them, that had forsaken the law, and the commandments of God: for this was a place of refuge for them.”** — And Jonathan came. While Demetrius was offering peace by letters, Jonathan, dwelling in Jerusalem, began to renew the city. For although persecutors sometimes terrify the faithful with threats, and sometimes cherish them with blandishments, yet the holy teachers press on constantly with spiritual building and renew the city of the Church, so that her enemies can neither break in by force nor surround her by fraud. Hence it is that Jonathan ordered the workmen to fortify Mount Sion on every side with square stones, because the preachers of the Gospel especially study to surround the camp of the Church with holy and strong men, whom the square stones signify, lest the place be easily open to enemies to invade the holy city. For every square thing, however it is turned, is accustomed to stand firm. To this figure the hearts of the elect are likened, who have learned to stand so in firmness of faith that by no adversity of things that befall, not even by death itself, can they be bent from the uprightness of their state. By Bethsura, which is interpreted house of the strong, sometimes the Church, sometimes the sacred scripture is signified, in which the strong, that is, the holy teachers and apostolic men, are seen to dwell together. But as in the present Church good and evil exist together, until the net of the Lord, drawing good and bad fishes to the shore, that is, to the end of the world and to the judgment of the final separation, brings them, so holy scripture has both pious readers, who search it with a catholic sense, and wicked ones, because they try to pervert it by dragging it by force to their own sense. Whence the apostle Paul, writing to Timothy, says: “All scripture, inspired of God, is profitable to teach, to reprove, to correct, to instruct in justice, that the man of God may be perfect, furnished to every good work.” But “evil men and seducers shall grow worse and worse: erring, and driving into error.” Hence also the prince of the apostles says that the unlearned and unstable pervert the sacred scriptures to their own destruction. Therefore, when the persecutions of the Gentiles from without have ceased, because they have forsaken the law of the Lord and would not keep the way of truth, for this reason Bethsura is said to become a refuge to them, because whatever they have wickedly devised in their mind or uttered in perverse speech, all this they strive to confirm by testimonies of holy scripture wrongly understood.
10.22: **“And Demetrius heard these words, and was exceeding sorry, and said:”** — And he was grieved. Because the patience of the saints often softens the fury of persecutors, and the meekness of the humble lays low the boldness of the proud. Hence it is that Paul teaches, saying: “If thy enemy be hungry, give him to eat; if he thirst, give him to drink. For, doing this, thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head. Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good.”
10.25: **“And he wrote to them in these words: King Demetrius to the nation of the Jews, greeting.”** — And he was grieved. Because the patience of the saints often softens the fury of persecutors, and the meekness of the humble lays low the boldness of the proud. Hence it is that Paul teaches, saying: “If thy enemy be hungry, give him to eat; if he thirst, give him to drink. For, doing this, thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head. Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good.”
10.66: **“And Jonathan returned into Jerusalem with peace and joy.”** — And he heard, etc. Because the kings of Syria and of Egypt, contending about the kingdom, each sought the help and friendship of Jonathan, I think nothing else is signified than this: that all the carnal, proud, avaricious and voluptuous, although they always disagree among themselves and can never firmly keep the covenant of true peace, nevertheless sometimes, seeing the unanimity and concord of sacred Scripture or of holy Church, themselves pay her honour. For the gift which they do not see themselves to have, they revere as possessed in her, and some on this account seek her aid and desire to have her friendship, so that, helped thence by opportune comforts, they too may be made better by the imitation of virtues.
10.67: **“In the year one hundred and sixty-five Demetrius the son of Demetrius came from Crete into the land of his fathers.”** — In the year one hundred and sixty-five Demetrius came, etc. What is signified by Apollonius, prefect of Celesyria, whom Demetrius sent with an army into Judea, if not the officers and ministers of earthly power, to whom it has been committed by their lords to overthrow the faith of Christ and to compel its confessors to blaspheme? These, trusting in the number of their horsemen, that is, exalting themselves in the support of the proud, insult Jonathan because he exercises power in the mountains with the holy doctors; they mock at the hope which they have of help from above, and challenge them into the plain, that is, to earthly desires and the delights of the world, that they may more easily overwhelm them while they dwell in the lowest things. “For broad is the way that leadeth to death, and many there are who go in thereat.” But Jonathan and Simon with ten thousand fight against Apollonius and his camp, and overcome and lay him low, when the holy preachers of Christ, having joined to themselves a number of the faithful who duly keep the commandments of the Decalogue, fight steadfastly against the persecutors of the faith, and, relying on divine help, conquer and overcome all their enemies who devise evils against them. For Joppe, which is interpreted beauty, fitly signifies the world, whose appearance seems beautiful to the carnal, because in it they desire to fulfil the desires of their flesh. There indeed Jonathan overthrows the garrison of Apollonius, when the band of doctors, by warring against it, tramples down the vain philosophy of the world and its followers through the truth of the Gospel. The same company of holy preachers also fights against Azotus, which is interpreted fire of the father’s brother, when it desires to extinguish in men the desire of earthly things. But the armies of Apollonius flee into Azotus to Dagon, their idol, to free themselves, when unbelievers seek protection from the demons whom they superstitiously worship. For Dagon is interpreted fish of sadness, signifying the devil, who, lurking in the sea of this world, strives to deceive those he can. But Jonathan set fire to Azotus, and the temple of Dagon, and slew with the sword those who fled into it, because the holy doctors, with the fire of the strict anathema, condemn the devil together with the desire of the world for ever, and strike the idolaters with the sword of the divine word, because they preach the punishment which will follow them into Gehenna.
10.85: **“So they that were slain by the sword, with them that were burnt, were almost eight thousand men.”** — And there were those who fell, etc. By the number eight both spiritual circumcision and the day of resurrection are shown, as we have often said. Where all who are not circumcised in the spirit of the living God are handed over to the punishment of everlasting fire.
10.86: **“And Jonathan removed his army from thence, and camped against Ascalon: and they went out of the city to meet him with great honour.”** — And he removed from thence. Jonathan moved the camp forward and camped against Ascalon, when the holy preachers dispose the equipment of a pious contest, to overthrow the errors of the Gentiles and to convert them to the faith of Christ. These receive them with devotion, when they gladly render obedience to them in the Gospel. Whence it is rightly added:
10.87: **“And Jonathan returned into Jerusalem with his people, having many spoils.”** — And Jonathan returned into Jerusalem with his people, having many spoils. Because when the doctors of the New Testament, preaching the word of God to the Gentiles, see themselves enriched by the faith of believers, they soon return into the Church of Christ to give thanks to God, that they may render worthy praises to him by whose grace they received this gift, over which they exult with great rejoicing.
10.88: **“And it came to pass: When Alexander the king heard these words, that he honoured Jonathan yet more.”** — And it came to pass, etc. What is it that Alexander, hearing the deed of Jonathan, added to honouring him, giving him royal ornament, if not that the princes of the Gentiles, recognizing the magnanimity and fortitude of the Church, render her the honour of royal dignity, because they acknowledge her truly to be the spouse of the heavenly king, and give her cities for possessions, since they hand over to her the dwelling of their territories.

11.8: **“And king Ptolemee got the dominion of the cities by the sea side, even to Seleucia, and he devised evil designs against Alexander.”** — But king Ptolemee. Ptolemee Evergetes, who reigned in Alexandria after Ptolemee Philometor, as the books of the Chronicles testify, gave his daughter as wife to Alexander Balas, king of Syria; her afterwards, enmity having arisen between himself and his son-in-law, he took away and gave in marriage to Demetrius the son of Demetrius, with the kingdom which he had taken from Alexander; which Scripture now seems to recall.
11.22: **“And when he heard it, he was angry: and forthwith he came to Ptolemais, and wrote to Jonathan, that he should not besiege the castle, but should come to him in haste, and speak to him.”** — In those days. What is it that Jonathan attacks those who were in the citadel of Jerusalem by means of those who are in Judea, if not that the holy doctors pursue the contumacy of those who, relying on exaltation of heart and pride, prepare to resist the divine precepts; against whom he makes many engines, because by manifold discipline and the varied teaching of the Scriptures they strive to assail them and to provoke them to humility. But as then some of those who hated their own nation, wicked men, went to the king accusing Jonathan, so also now those who refuse to receive ecclesiastical discipline abominate those who strive to take their iniquity from them, accusing them before the powers of the world, that they may turn them to hatred of them and stir up persecution against them. But they do not prevail, since God is the helper and protector of his own, and “delivered them out of all their troubles.”
11.28: **“And Jonathan requested of the king that he would make Judea free from tribute, and the three governments, and Samaria, and the confines thereof: and he promised him three hundred talents.”** — And he requested. By “toparchies,” that is, the lordship of villages or towns, he names those places which Demetrius added to Judea from the kingdom of Samaria, of which he tells in what follows, that is, Lidda and Ramatha. For Lidda is a city of Palestine on the shore of the great sea, and Ramatha is the city of Samuel, of which it is told in the book of Kings. Rightly therefore king Demetrius, granting Jonathan immunity out of friendship, added the aforesaid cities to Judea, remitting the tax of tithes and tribute, and the salt pits, in which the making of salt was owed to the state; and also all the other debts, which were rendered to him with royal pride, he forgave, according to the agreement made with Jonathan.
11.40: **“And he pressed him much to deliver him to him, that he might be king in his father's place: and he told him all that Demetrius had done, and how his soldiers hated him. And he remained there many days.”** — But Tryphon. How Demetrius came into the hatred of his army Pompeius Trogus shows, saying: Demetrius, having recovered his father’s kingdom, and himself corrupted by success, slipped through the vices of youth into sloth, and drew upon himself as much contempt among all by his idleness as his father had drawn hatred by pride. And so, when the cities were falling away from his rule everywhere, to wipe out the stain of sloth he resolved to make war on the Parthians; and the peoples of the East saw his coming not unwillingly, both because of the cruelty of Arsaces, king of the Parthians, and because, accustomed to the old rule of the Macedonians, they bore the pride of the new people with indignation. And so, since he was helped by the auxiliaries of the Persians, the Elymaeans and the Bactrians, he routed and laid waste the Parthians in many battles; yet at last, deceived by a feigned peace, he was captured, and led through the faces of the cities to the peoples that had raged, and shown for a mockery of favor. Then, sent into Hyrcania, he was kindly treated and kept according to the dignity of his former fortune.
11.41: **“And Jonathan sent to king Demetrius, desiring that he would cast out them that were in the castle in Jerusalem, and those that were in the strong holds: because they fought against Israel.”** — And Jonathan sent, etc. Why is it that Jonathan asks king Demetrius to cast out those who were in the castle in Jerusalem and in the strong holds, who also fought against Israel, while Demetrius on the contrary asks help from him against his enemies, unless it is that holy teachers seek from the princes of the nations and from all the people the overthrow of error and pride, and they themselves likewise ask of the holy teachers the support of doctrine and prayer to overcome spiritual enemies? For neither order can duly perform the effect of its ministry without the help of the other, because neither can holy teachers gain the merit of winning souls without the conversion and obedience of their subjects, nor can the subjects themselves merit salvation without the teaching and instruction of their masters. For each order, as was said before, is supported by the one and helped by the other. Whence Paul says to the Thessalonians: Then “we live, if you stand in the Lord,” because “we rejoice for you before our God.” And to the Corinthians: “Our glory,” he says, “we are yours, as you also are ours, in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
11.51: **“And they threw down their arms, and made peace, and the Jews were glorified in the sight of the king, and in the sight of all that were in his realm, and were renowned throughout the kingdom, and returned to Jerusalem with many spoils.”** — And they saw, etc. That the Jews, taking victory over their enemies, compelled them to ask for peace and to give them their right hands, signifies that the strength of holy Church stands above all enemies, and either makes them yield wholesomely through confession, or justly punishes the scorners persisting in their obstinacy, because she received from her Saviour our Lord Jesus Christ the power of treading upon serpents and scorpions, and upon all the power of the enemy. Of her, speaking elsewhere in the Gospel to his apostle Peter, he says: “Thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” And the Jews, he says, were renowned in the kingdom. Because the confessors of Christ appear glorious in the whole world, but holy men do not ascribe this glory to themselves, but to their King, namely God, the giver of all good things. Whence it is added: And returned to Jerusalem with many spoils. The Psalmist also testifies that he gives thanks of this kind to God, saying: I have declared thy justice in a great church, lo, I will not restrain my lips. In the Church therefore the faithful, each having the spoils of virtues, return to give praise to God, since they attribute the victory they have gained not to their own strength but to divine grace, saying with the Prophet: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us; but to thy name give glory, for thy mercy and thy truth.”
11.53: **“And he falsified all whatsoever he had said, and alienated himself from Jonathan, and did not reward him according to the benefits he had received from him, but gave him great trouble.”** — And Demetrius sat. That Demetrius repaid Jonathan evil for his benefits signifies that carnal fools, when they are counseled to salvation, do not answer their benefactors according to the benefits owed, but according to the wicked counsels of their heart. For whatever is done for their advantage, they reckon all of it as harm, and, roused by the goad of envy, they choose to serve their most wicked will.
11.62: **“And the men of Gaza made supplication to Jonathan, and he gave them the right hand: and he took their sons for hostages, and sent them to Jerusalem: and he went through the country as far as Damascus.”** — And Jonathan went out, etc. By Jonathan’s crossing beyond the river we can understand the preaching of the word to those who have not yet been washed in the baptism of Christ, because holy preachers sometimes call the Gentiles to holy baptism, and sometimes rouse the faithful to progress in virtues. When therefore Jonathan returns across the river, the army of Syria comes to him as a help, because when the apostles had passed from the Jews to the preaching to the Gentiles, soon very many of the Gentiles came together to the faith and baptism of Christ, and these were helpers to the holy preachers in the Gospel of God, that they might bring the pagans to belief. He went to Ascalon, which is interpreted weighed or infamous fire, and they came out of the city to meet him with honour. With the holy preachers, those who served the ambition of the world, hearing the word of God, at once, leaving behind the greed of the world, ran together to obedience to the Gospel. And he went to Gaza, and besieged it, and “they that were in Gaza shut him out”. By Gaza, which is interpreted strength, is expressed the obstinacy of unbelievers, in which the hard minds of the wicked shut themselves in, because they will not consent to yield to the truth. Jonathan besieged it, and “burnt all the suburbs round about”, when the teachers of Christ on every side press the faithless with the testimonies of the holy scriptures, and lay waste, by overcoming them, the contrivances of their errors. Whence the men of Gaza asked Jonathan to give them right hands, whose sons he took as hostages, sending them to Jerusalem: when, the wickedness of the proud having been overcome, and being no longer able to resist the truth any longer, they beg the masters of the Church to give them the covenants of peace, and hand over their sons to them as hostages, that is, they allow into the Church the pledges of faith in exchange for error, namely renunciation and the submission of obedience, so that sure hope of their conversion to the faith may be given.
11.64: **“And he went against them: but left his brother Simon in the country.”** — And Jonathan heard, etc. The princes of Demetrius, who transgressed in Cades of Galilee, can not unfittingly be understood as the secular powers, who, although they are numbered among the faithful on account of the catholic confession (for Cades, which is interpreted holy, or changed, and Galilee, that is, a migration made, express this by a figure), yet often such men contrive deceit against the business of the heavenly kingdom. Jonathan went against them, because it is necessary that the skill of the holy teachers meet these, lest they carry out in deed the deceit they plan in mind. Yet he left his brother Simon in the country to guard it within against the wantonness of the insolent. For so holy preachers, although they sometimes reach out to regulate the acts of the world and to restrain the attacks of the undisciplined, nevertheless in no way cease to order the ministry of their own right within the Church. But they always have there those who preserve regular discipline in all things, so that as they are useful in outward matters, so in inward matters they may be found wholesome everywhere.
11.66: **“And they desired him to make peace, and he granted it them: and he cast them out from thence, and took the city, and placed a garrison in it.”** — And Simon came near. What is signified by Bethsura, but the reading of the holy scriptures, because Bethsura is interpreted house of the strong; and well can holy scripture be called the house of the strong, because there all the strong and valiant men dwell, ever speaking and doing well, because with the Psalmist they meditate on the law of the Lord day and night. In this house heretics sometimes seem falsely to dwell, since they are proved to read the scriptures, but not at all to understand them. Whence it is said that Simon fought against Bethsura for many days, and took the city, and cast out the wicked inhabitants from there, and placed a garrison there, because holy teachers have this chiefly as their endeavour, they do this with their whole effort, to overcome heretics by destroying their false opinion, and to snatch the scripture of the law of God from their hands. Placing a garrison in it. That is, pious searchers and meditators of divine wisdom, who strive to understand rightly and to utter duly the divine word.
11.70: **“And all that were on Jonathan's side fled, and none was left of them, but Mathathias the son of Absalom, and Judas the son of Calphi, chief captain of the army.”** — And Jonathan, etc. What is it that Jonathan pitched camp at the water of Genesar, unless that the company of holy preachers, kindled by the Spirit of God, prepares to meet the waves of the world and the persecutions of unbelievers? They say the lake of Genesareth is the same as the sea of Galilee or the sea of Tiberias. But it is called the sea of Galilee from the adjoining province, and the sea of Tiberias from the nearest city, which was once called Cenereth, but rebuilt by Herod the Tetrarch in honour of Tiberius Caesar was named Tiberias. Further, Genesar is so called from the nature of the lake itself, which is said to raise a breeze for itself from itself with its rippling waters; in the Greek word it is said as if “generating a breeze for itself.” For its water is not spread out in the manner of a pool, but is stirred by frequent blowing breezes, sweet to the taste and fit for drinking. But by the custom of the Hebrew tongue every gathering of waters, whether sweet or salt, is called a sea. This lake, with the Jordan flowing into it, extends a hundred and sixty stadia in length and sixty in breadth. Therefore, since the pool or sea signifies the present world, our Jonathan with his men hastens to resist the worldly tumult and strives to keep watch before daylight in the plain of Asor. That is, he takes care to watch zealously against the snares of the devil who is on the watch. For Asor is interpreted “arrow of light.” And the apostle, writing of the same apostate angel, says: “For Satan himself transformeth himself into an angel of light.” Whence it is no wonder if his ministers “be transformed as the ministers of justice.” There the foreigners, meeting them in the plain, set ambushes in the mountains, because either malignant spirits, or even perverse men, strive to seduce whomever they can by luxury, or pride of the present life, or worldly desires. Against these it is necessary that the soldiers of Christ run to meet them and fight bravely with them, lest perhaps they consent to their persuasions and be dissolved by pleasures and enticements. But when battle was joined, “all that were on Jonathan’s side fled, and none was left of them, but Mathathias the son of Absalom, and Judas the son of Calphi, chief captain of the army,” because, alas, many of the churchmen are overthrown by ambition and the pleasure of the world itself. Whence in the gospel parable the Lord says that the thorns sprung up and choked the crop, that is, riches and a life of pleasure choke the word, so that it bears no fruit. Yet Mathathias, who is interpreted “gift of God,” and Judas, that is, “confessing,” remain with Jonathan, because those who are enlightened and strengthened by the gift of God, and by believing rightly and working well are truly confessors of God, these persevere in the camp of the Church, and press the enemy bravely, until they crush him and restore to their former camp his own who had fled by yielding to the enemy. But let us see what Jonathan did when his soldiers were turned to flight.
11.73: **“And they of his part that fled saw this, and they turned again to him, and they all with him pursued the enemies even to Cades to their own camp, and they came even thither.”** — And Jonathan rent, etc. For so the superiors and teachers of the Church ought to act when they see their own faltering in battle and turning their backs to the enemy: to rend their garments, that is, to afflict the body with fasts and tears; and to put earth upon their head, that is, to turn over in their mind the frailty of the body; and to pray to God for their own sins or those of the people, that he, who is almighty, may work salvation for the weak and bring them back to their former health. And so it is fitting to exhort each one, who had been captive to the devil’s will, to come to his senses again out of the devil’s snares, and to return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is bountiful to forgive.
11.74: **“And there fell of the aliens in that day three thousand men: and Jonathan returned to Jerusalem.”** — And there fell, etc. Note that the aliens are laid low by the number three, because by faith in the holy Trinity all the enemies of the Church are crushed, overcome and laid low. And the throng of believers returns with its leader to the mystical Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all, that there they may give thanks and praise to our God for ever and ever.

12.23: **“And we also have written back to you: That our cattle, and our possessions are yours: and yours, ours. We therefore have commanded that these things should be told you.”** — And Jonathan saw, etc. That Jonathan sends letters to the Romans and to the Spartans and to other places, to renew the pact and friendship with them which his brother Judas before him had entered upon with them of his own accord, shows that holy preachers ought to have great concern to strive with all zeal to renew and preserve everywhere the peace which Christ offered in the world. For the Son of God himself, who came on earth to make peace in his flesh between heavenly and earthly things, wished at once at the rising of his birth to have it sung by angels: “Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will”; which peace indeed the same mediator of God and men, now made man, commended to his disciples, saying: “Have salt in you, and have peace among you”; “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you”; for by peace and concord the whole body of Christ is united, ruled and made firm. But whoever does not wish to have peace with his neighbours has no fellowship in the body of Christ, nor can he now come to eternal rest, from which he has separated himself by contention. And this is an example, etc. How the Spartans were of the race of Abraham is not easily found; yet it could have happened that Abraham, besides Isaac, whom Sara bore to him, had more sons, by Agar, and also by Zechura, as Scripture makes plain, so that the origin of the Spartans proceeded from one of them. But Josephus, making mention of this place, seems to wish to express not only a kinship of the Spartans with the Jews but also some fellowship, and reports the letter of the Lacedemonians written thus: Arvis, king of the Lacedemonians, to Onias, greeting. Reading a certain writing we found that the Jews and the Lacedemonians were of one race, and had a family bond with Abraham. It is just therefore, since you are brothers, both to send to us and to ask what you judge necessary for yourselves; and we will do the same, and we reckon your own things and ours together as common. The bearer of the letters, Demotiles, brings you letters written in square form, having as a seal an eagle carrying off a dragon in its claws. The letter, then, sent by the king of the Lacedemonians contained a text of this kind.
12.24: **“Now Jonathan heard that the generals of Demetrius were come again with a greater army than before to fight against him.”** — And Jonathan heard. But what does it signify that Jonathan went out from Jerusalem against the generals of Demetrius, who had come out to fight against him, and met them in the land of Amath, if not that the sacred order of teachers is always ready to fight against the persecutors of the Church, that is, Jews, pagans and heretics, and to resist their perfidy? Going out from Jerusalem, he met them in the land of Amath, because, although for a time they leave the quiet of inner contemplation, by which they behold with the eye of the soul the loftiness of the Creator and the greatness of the heavenly rewards, in order to do battle with the enemies, yet they in no way turn aside from the straightness of truth. For Amath means “my truth.” But whether they contend in the conflict of disputations against their errors, or patiently bear their scourges when they come, they in no way abandon the truth of justice, nor do they give them the power to enter by any fraud into the region of the Church; they strive with all their might to crush the wickedness of their guile at the very beginning, and to keep the camp of the Church unharmed.
12.34: **“(For he heard that they designed to deliver the hold to them that took part with Demetrius,) and he put a garrison there to keep it.”** — And Jonathan sent. Having sent out scouts, Jonathan explores the camp of the enemies, as the holy preachers through industrious men search out the fraud of their enemies, so that, having discovered their wicked counsels, they may more easily guard against their guile. Who reported to them that they intended to come upon them by night. For they prepare to come by night who with blind heart plan to do the works of darkness. And on the other side Jonathan commanded his men to watch and to be in arms ready for battle, and all the night; because it is the mark of chosen teachers to teach their subjects to be watchful and wary at every time of this life, in which, living in uncertainty, they press on to a certain end. And the adversaries hearing that Jonathan was ready with his men for battle, “were struck with fear,” and “they kindled fires in their camp,” and planned flight. Jonathan followed them, but did not overtake them, because he found them already across the river. The adversaries fear that the men of the Church are preparing for spiritual battle; and kindling fires in their camp, that is, they feign the strength of war in their squadrons. But in the morning of the dawning faith the spiritual Jonathan pursues his enemies, whom nevertheless he does not overtake, that is, did not bring to belief, because, seeing them seething in love of the fluctuating world, he judged them to be irrecoverable.
12.36: **“And to build up walls in Jerusalem, and raise a mount between the castle and the city, to separate it from the city, that so it might have no communication, and that they might neither buy nor sell.”** — And he returned. That Jonathan, having returned, resolved to build the walls of Jerusalem, and, a counsel having been held with the elders of the people, built fortresses, and a great height between the citadel and the city, to separate it from the city, signifies the holy teachers, after they have been occupied for a time with outward wars, treating within with spiritual men about the fortification of the Church, lest perhaps it be harmed by internal enemies. Those, therefore, who were in the citadel of the city and lay in wait for the citizens of Jerusalem, signify the heretics, who, set in the citadel of their pride, never cease to contrive wiles against the Church. Mystical Jonathan shuts them off with a spiritual guard, that they may be alone and “neither buy nor sell,” because by the most powerful excommunication they have been cut off from the unity of the Church, and neither is their sect received, nor is ecclesiastical doctrine in any way entrusted to them for defilement, as to the foulest swine, most shameful in all filth, the Lord the Saviour himself speaking against this and forbidding it in the Gospel, where he says: “Give not that which is holy to dogs; neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest perhaps they trample them under their feet, and turning upon you, they tear you.” The wall, therefore, which fell upon the brook toward the east, which Jonathan also repaired, signifies those who seemed in the Church to exercise some guardianship over the flock committed to them. But leaning on transitory things and serving the ambition of the world, they have slipped into the pleasures of this life and have fallen from their own state; these the skill of the saints must strive to restore, and to bring back to their former firmness by strengthening them with ecclesiastical doctrine.
12.41: **“And Jonathan went out to meet him with forty thousand men chosen for battle, and came to Bethsan.”** — And when Tryphon had thought. This Tryphon holds the figure of hypocrites and heretics, who act one way and speak another, and contrive something else in intention. Against him Jonathan comes with forty thousand, because against such men evangelical doctrine and the keeping of the commandments of God are necessary. For he who has kept the precepts of the law according to the teachings of the gospel will safely break through the ranks of enemies. But that Tryphon by guile persuaded Jonathan to send his army away from him and go peaceably with him, and so having deceived him took him captive and slew those who went with him, signifies the ruin of those who do not observe themselves lawfully, and have no caution in circumspection of heart and conduct of body. For these, because they do not heed that doctrine of the Gospel where the Saviour commanded his disciples, saying: “Watch ye, and pray that ye enter not into temptation.” And again: “Beware,” he says, “of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.” Deservedly the army of enemies overcomes and destroys them, because the doctrine of the heavenly Master is not worthily kept by them. Furthermore, in place of Jonathan his brother Simon discharges the priesthood and holds the leadership of the people, since in the present Church, as some depart, others are put in their place, to hold the place of government and diligently exercise the soldiers of Christ in the spiritual camp, that by fighting they may be able to resist all enemies in due season. But Tryphon, as a type, in like manner tries to deceive Simon with false pretences, as he had deceived his brother, because the ancient enemy never ceases, through himself and his ministers, to lay snares for the worshippers of Christ. But he who worthily bears the office of Simon, that is, of the obedient one who duly submits to the divine precepts, aided by help from above can avoid the scandal of all enemies. Tryphon also slew together with Jonathan his sons, whom he had received as hostages, although he had promised that they should be kept safe together with their father, because the ancient enemy drives whomever he seduces into the death of sin. Their sons, that is, their works, although before he feigned peace by flattering, in the end he will show worthy of eternal torment. Jonathan too can bear the type of the simple who are in the Church, whom the cunning of the crafty seems for a time to take captive when it afflicts them with bodily losses, whose souls nevertheless, persisting in the truth of faith, will freely after the death of the flesh escape into perpetual light. Whence very many of them, after the departure of this present life, have deserved to have victorious signs beside their tombs, as Simon is read in what follows to have set up a memorial for his father and mother and brothers on their tombs. Furthermore, the saints, whom the Saviour comforts as they abide in their simplicity and innocence, saying: “Fear ye not them that kill the body.” And after this: “They have not what they can do to you, but rather fear him who, after he hath killed, hath power to cast into the hell of fire.” And again: “Blessed are ye,” he says, “when they shall revile you, and persecute you, and speak all that is evil against you, untruly, for my sake: be glad in that day and rejoice, for your reward is very great in heaven.” And again: “Rejoice,” he says, “and be glad, because your names are written in heaven”; of whom the Psalmist also says: “The just shall be in everlasting remembrance: he shall not fear the evil hearing.” These, namely, are believed after death to be stronger and to live more happily, since their King and Lord himself, namely Jesus Christ, is known to declare their triumphs in the whole world with shining signs and miracles, so that beside the memorial of their relics sight is given to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, and speech to the dumb, and healing cure is granted for various sicknesses through their prayers. And on the contrary, in the same place perjurers and the malicious are seized by demons, the wicked and unbelieving are punished, and the demons themselves are tormented with strong torments, according to what they are forced openly to confess by roaring.

13.27: **“And Simon built over the sepulchre of his father and of his brethren, a building lofty to the sight, of polished stone behind and before:”** — And Simon built. Simon makes a memorial of polished stone over the tombs for his father and mother and brothers, when holy preachers, by recalling the deeds of the fathers who went before and their glorious end, as an example to those present, show them with great authority; for this is to place polished stone before and behind: that they may strive to declare plainly to their hearers, in a clear narration, how before the end of life they lived by pious doctrine and holy conduct, and what example of patience and longsuffering they left to posterity after their death. That holy men are called by the name of father and mother and brothers, the Saviour shows in the Gospel, saying: “Whosoever shall do the will of my Father that is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.” Hence also the apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: “For if you have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet not many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, by the gospel, I have begotten you.” And of Timothy to the Philippians he says: “But know ye the proof of him, that as a son with the father, he hath served with me in the gospel.” Simon also set up seven pyramids, one against another, for his father and mother and four brothers, when any teacher shows how to each person of the fathers before, the light of wisdom, which is given to the faithful through the sevenfold Spirit, was bestowed. “And round about these he set great pillars: and upon the pillars arms for a perpetual memory,” when he intimates the firmness and uprightness of their faith, and how in that faith they fought with spiritual arms against the enemies. “And by the arms ships carved, which might be seen by all that sailed on the sea.” Because they make known by teaching how the just who went before crossed the sea of this present life in the ship of the cross of Christ, for the hope of consolation of all who labour in the waves of this world, that they may know that as the aforesaid ship brought those safely to the shore of rest, so also belief in the passion of Christ and in our redemption, if they wish to have works worthy of that belief, may bring them to the harbour of eternal salvation.
13.31: **“But Tryphon when he was upon a journey with the young king Antiochus, treacherously slew him.”** — But Tryphon. Pompeius reports thus of him: while these things were being done meanwhile in the parts of Syria, Tryphon, who had labored to be appointed by the people as guardian to Antiochus, the stepson of Demetrius, slew his ward and seized the kingdom of Syria; having held it for a long time, at length, the favor of the new rule fading, he was conquered in war by the boy Antiochus, brother of Demetrius in the same manner, who was being brought up in Asia, and the kingdom of Syria returned again to the offspring of Demetrius.
13.34: **“And Simon chose men and sent to king Demetrius, to the end that he should grant an immunity to the land: for all that Tryphon did was to spoil.”** — And Simon chose, etc. That Simon sent men to king Demetrius to grant an immunity to the land, this, if I am not mistaken, signifies that holy Church sends her preachers to the princes of this world, that she may win them to herself by the word of faith, and bring to nothing the deeds of the figurative Tryphon, that is, of heretics and schismatics, and that by the rigor of external powers they may crush their pride, on account of which they were unwilling to yield to ecclesiastical meekness. To these the legates themselves also bring a crown of gold and a baen, which they report to be an ornament of the neck made of golden rings according to the custom of the province; as they promise them in return the crown of eternal life for the good fight, and heavenly rewards for the timely comfort by which they help the Church with their edicts and defenses.
13.43: **“In those days Simon besieged Gaza, and camped round about it, and he made engines, and set them to the city, and he struck one tower, and took it.”** — In those days. What is it that Simon undertakes to assault Gaza, but that the holy preachers strive to overcome the errors of the world? Gaza, which is interpreted “his strength,” signifies the hardness and obduracy of the Gentiles. Simon therefore builds many engines against Gaza, when the holy teachers build various kinds of doctrines to take the strongholds of the Gentiles, that they may bring them as a saving prey under the dominion of their king, namely Jesus Christ; in which “he struck one tower, and took it,” when he laid low the pride of the Gentiles and brought their hearts into obedience to the Gospel. But those who had broken out were taken within the engine in the city. Because the insolence of the barbarians, although it may have ceased to escape the net of the Gospel, was nevertheless bound round and pressed down by the truthful testimonies of the law of God. “And there was a great uproar in the city.” When the whole world was shaken by the preaching of the Gospel. For a great uproar was made in the city when the fierceness of the Gentiles was stirred up to persecute the confessors of Christ, so that they might become true martyrs who were faithful asserters of the faith and doctrine of Christ.
13.45: **“And they that were in the city went up with their wives and children upon the wall, with their garments rent, and they cried with a loud voice, beseeching Simon to grant them peace.”** — And they went up. Who are those who went up upon the wall with wives and children, with their garments rent, and asked that right hands be given them by Simon, but those who, long entangled in the cares and desires of this world, afterwards converted, rending not their garments but their hearts by penance, seek that right hands of reconciliation and fellowship be given them by the ecclesiastics; to whose petition the spiritual Simon, consenting in mercy, does not strike them with the sword of anathema, but, leading them out of the superstition of paganism, removes their errors by cutting them away, that he may prepare a worthy dwelling in their breasts for the Lord Christ.
13.48: **“And having cast out of it all uncleanness, he placed in it men that should observe the law: and he fortified it, and made it his habitation.”** — And then he entered. Then also, when the errors of the Gentiles have been cast out, the holy teachers will enter with praises of God into the assemblies of the Gentiles. Then also they place there men who keep the law, because by their pious preaching they cause true worshippers of Christ to be there. And they fortify it and make there a habitation for themselves. When through the Gospel they strengthen the Church on every side with the fortification of faith, the teachers themselves, dwelling in her house, await from the judge of the living and the dead, at the end, the eternal rewards to be repaid them for the pious labor which they spent for their confession.
13.49: **“But they that were in the castle of Jerusalem were hindered from going out and coming into the country, and from buying and selling: and they were straitened with hunger, and many of them perished through famine.”** — But they that were. These who were in the castle of Jerusalem and often harassed the Jews signify heretics and schismatics, who, setting themselves in the castle of their pride, stir up quarrels and wars against Catholics. Simon forbids them to go out and come into the country, and to buy and sell, because the holy teachers with the Catholics forbid them to have any communion of fellowship; “and many of them perished through famine,” because many of these, when they have been anathematized and cut off from the communion of the Church, perish by hunger for the word of God and want of spiritual knowledge. But because, driven by extreme necessity, they have asked that right hands of communion be given them by the Church, this covenant is laid upon them by her: that they abandon their errors and anathematize the wicked sects to which they formerly adhered, and cleanse their conscience from all the wickedness of heresies, and so be restored to the communion of the Church; whence it is fittingly added.
13.52: **“And he fortified the mountain of the temple that was near the castle, and he dwelt there himself, and they that were with him.”** — And they entered, etc. These numbers, that is, the hundred and seventy-first and the twenty-third, are full of sacred mysteries. For the hundredth, in which Abraham begot Isaac, the son of promise, signifies the perfection of life. The seventieth, in which the captivity of Jerusalem was loosed, signifies perfection. The seventieth, in which the captivity of Jerusalem was loosed, signifies the remission of sins. But because this consists only in the unity of the Church, therefore the one was added above the number seventy. Furthermore, the twenty-third number designates the faith of the holy Trinity with the two precepts of charity, in which the whole fullness of the law consists. But the second month, in which those who were unclean on account of the soul of a man seemed to keep the Pasch, shows the time of grace and of the calling of the Gentiles. When therefore, according to this distinction and signification of the mystical numbers, the victory is taken by the faithful, that is, that they may fervently keep whole the faith of the holy Trinity with the two precepts of charity according to the gospel doctrine, and having the perfection of life according to their measure, by abiding in the unity of the Church in understanding and faith, they may come to the fullness of remission. So then rightly, with a song and branches of palms, that is, with true praise and certain victory, they will enter the heavenly Jerusalem, where they may render forever manifold thanks and praises to their Creator for the salvation and security obtained, because the great enemy of Israel is crushed, and death with its author stands condemned forever. Nor does the sense of what follows shrink from this exposition, where it is written that Simon ordained that the joy of this day should be kept every year, and that he fortified the mountain of the temple that was near the castle, and dwelt there himself and they that were with him; because at every time of this life the memory of that day is to be kept in hope, on which, triumphing over death, we shall be restored to eternal life by the grace of our Redeemer. For therefore every year we celebrate the solemnities of the Lord’s resurrection, to show that we hope through his resurrection and victory over death, and that the resurrection of our bodies will be at the end of the world, and life everlasting in the heavenly kingdom. Wherefore we ought to fortify the mountain of the temple, which is near the castle, that is, to hold in the heart with firm faith the incarnation of Christ, which by its own perfection surpasses all the height of the perfection of the saints, and in this at every time of our life, both by ourselves and also by those committed to us or joined to us by fellowship, to labor piously, that, joined and united to his body, we may become heirs of the heavenly kingdom together with the Head himself. The joy and memory of which day the blessed apostle Peter commends to us in his epistle, saying: “But of this one thing be not ignorant, my beloved, that one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord delayeth not his promise, but dealeth patiently for your sake, not willing that any should perish, but that all should return to penance. But the day of the Lord shall come as a thief, in which the heavens shall pass away with great violence, and the elements shall be melted with heat. Seeing then that all these things are to be dissolved, what manner of people ought you to be in holy conversation and godliness, looking for and hasting unto the coming of the day of the Lord, by which the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with the burning heat? But we look for new heavens and a new earth according to his promises, in which justice dwelleth. Wherefore, dearly beloved, seeing that you look for these things, be diligent that you may be found before him unspotted and blameless in peace; and account the longsuffering of our Lord, salvation.”
13.53: **“And Simon saw that John his son was a valiant man for war: and he made him captain of all the forces: and he dwelt in Gazara.”** — And Simon saw. Simon, seeing that John his son was a valiant man, committed to him the command of all the forces, to show that no master ought to commit to his son or disciple the power and order of ecclesiastical government unless he first sees him to be a man, that is, proved in judgment and zealous in works of virtue. But because we said above that Simon bears the figure of the holy teachers, in this place he can express by signification the prince of shepherds, who gave to the catholic people the ministry of sacred government and the knowledge and effect of all the virtues; and what is written in what follows suits him very well.

14.11: **“He made peace in the land, and Israel rejoiced with great joy.”** — And all was quiet. It is written in the prophet Isaias of the Lord the Saviour himself: “His empire shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace: he shall sit upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom; to establish it and strengthen it with judgment and with justice, from henceforth and for ever.” His principality and empire will be over the throne and kingdom of David, which had been scattered after the Babylonian captivity, that he might establish it and strengthen it and teach that it is everlasting, lest God’s promise be judged void; and in the psalm the prophet says: “In his days shall justice spring up, and abundance of peace, till the moon be taken away.” For this promise suits no one else but the only mediator of God and men, Christ Jesus, who was incarnate for us and, through the obedience of the cross, was made possessor of heaven and earth. To him the Father says in the psalm through the prophet: “Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance, and the utmost parts of the earth for thy possession.” The whole land of Juda was quiet all the days of Simon, because the land of the Church, from the time of Christ’s incarnation for ever, although outwardly it endures persecutions from enemies, yet enjoys true peace within. To her the same Saviour says in the Gospel: “My peace I give unto you, my peace I leave with you.” He sought the good of his nation. And his power and his glory pleased them all his days. That is, all good things were conferred on the Church by him, in the remission of sins and the dominion of virtues. Whence his power and his glory please them, because she chose to serve him alone at all times. He took Joppe for a haven, and made an entrance to the isles of the sea. When from the people of the Gentiles he founded the Church for himself, whence he might open the entrance of faith through the Gospel to the nations of the whole world. Joppe is interpreted “beauty”; and what is more beautiful than the holy Church, to whom the bridegroom says in the Canticle of Canticles: “How beautiful art thou, my love, how beautiful art thou! thy eyes are doves' eyes, besides what is hid within.” Whence he enlarged the bounds of his nation, that is, of the Church, and obtained the dominion of the whole world. And he gathered together a great number of captives. Of whom it is written in the psalm: “Ascending on high he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men.” And he took Gazara and Bethsura and the castle. Because, having subdued her, he brought her, made clean through the Gospel, under his own dominion, and took away the uncleannesses of sins and vices, cleansing her with the laver of regeneration. And there was no one to resist him. Of which it is written: “In thy will, O Lord, all things are set, and there is none that can resist thy will. For thou hast made heaven and earth, and all things that are under the cope of heaven; thou art Lord of all.” And every man tilled his land in peace. That is, exercising his body with virtues, or the land of the Church with good works. Each of the saints tills according to his strength. And the land yielded its fruits. Our flesh, that is, likewise brings forth the fruit of good works. And the trees of the fields. That is, men, ever flourishing with the greenness of faith, put forth the shoots of virtues. The ancients sat all in the streets, and treated of the good things of the land, and the young men put on glory and the apparel of war. By the ancients we can understand the prophets, apostles and teachers of the holy Church, who help their hearers with counsels and strengthen them with sermons. The young men are the assembly of the faithful, because, relying on the glory of the confession of Christ, they put on the arms of virtues, that they may more easily crush the host of the enemies. He provided victuals for the cities. That is, he supplied the Churches with words of doctrine. And he appointed them to be places of defence. That is, that they might guard the treasure of spiritual wisdom, in a pure conscience and faith unfeigned. This he did until the name of his glory was named even to the ends of the earth, because “their sound hath gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world,” the sound of the apostles' preaching. Whence it is said through Isaias: “The Lord shall make the glory of his voice to be heard, and shall show the terror of his arm.” He made peace in the land. Because he is our peace, who hath made both one. And Israel rejoiced with great joy. Because “the just shall rejoice in the Lord, and shall hope in him, and all the upright in heart shall be praised.” And every man sat under his vine and under his fig tree, and there was none to make them afraid. According to what is said in Micheas: “Every man shall sit under his vine, and under his fig tree, and there shall be none to make him afraid.” This is the vine of which he spoke in the Gospel: “I am the vine, and you the branches; and my Father is the husbandman.” “Every one that doth not bring forth good fruit shall be cut down, and cast into the fire.” Its fruits are drunk and eaten, and make glad the heart of man, and make the friends of the bride drunk, and in the kingdom of God are drunk new every day. And he rests under the fig tree and fears no snares, who enjoys the sweetness of the Holy Spirit and is filled with its fruits: charity, joy, peace, continency, patience. Of such a one it is said that he is the planter who planted a fig tree and ate its fruit, who built such houses and planted vineyards; of which the apostle speaks: “I have planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase.” He shall eat the labors of his hands, and sowing in the spirit, “of the spirit shall reap life everlasting,” and shall not be supplanted by the frauds of the devil and his attendants. And he strengthened all the humble of his people, and sought the law. The humble of the people are the saints, whom in the Gospel he calls poor in spirit. The works also of the people of God shall not grow old, but shall be renewed and completed or strengthened every day, that they may not walk in the oldness of the letter, but in the newness of the spirit. Such a law our Simon sought. And he took away every unjust and wicked man. As now through holy teachers he excommunicates heretics and schismatics and all the impious, and at the end of the world will cast them out. “And they shall gather out of his kingdom all scandals.” He glorified the sanctuary and multiplied the vessels of the holy places. When he causes the religion of the New Testament to be kept in order and rightly in his Church. And he multiplies the number of those who believe and do well, because they themselves are the vessels of the saints, fit for the ministry of God, to receive the divine gifts and the gifts of the Holy Spirit.
14.16: **“And it was heard”** — That, when Simon received the priesthood, various nations sent ambassadors to him, asking for the things that are of peace, signifies that, when the apostles and teachers of the New Testament preached the Gospel in the world after the passion of Christ, his resurrection, and his ascension into heaven, a multitude of the nations flocked to the faith and earnestly asked to have peace with the Church. Sending letters, that is, laying open to them the secrets of their heart by confession, so that by receiving the word of truth they might be built up by them in the rule of justice, a perpetual memorial on tablets of brass. For it is written: “The just shall be in everlasting remembrance: he shall not fear the evil hearing.” For brass is a metal that lasts long, and the company of the saints has a most firm and most bright state of its dwelling.
14.24: **“And after this Simon sent Numenius to Rome, with a great shield of gold the weight of a thousand pounds, to confirm the league with them. And when the people of Rome had heard”** — And after this. That Simon sent to the Romans a golden shield having the weight of a thousand pounds, to confirm a league with them, signifies that the holy teachers in the preaching of the Gospel promise the heavenly kingdom and eternal blessedness to the nations, if they will receive the faith of Christ and keep the Gospel teaching to the end of life. For the roundness of the shield, the splendour of the gold, and also the perfection of the number a thousand signify, by a figure, the crown of eternal rest.
14.26: **“For he hath restored his brethren, and hath driven away in fight the enemies of Israel from them: and they decreed him liberty, and registered it in tables of brass, and set it upon pillars in mount Sion.”** — And they decreed, etc. Ebul is the sixth month among the Hebrews, which among the Greeks is called Gorpieus, and among the Latins September, but the order of the numbers is scattered because of the different beginnings of the years that exist among the several nations. For the Hebrews, who have Nisan, that is, April, as their first month, have the aforementioned Ebul in the sixth place. But the Greeks, who begin their year from their first month Apileus, that is, from the kalends of December, have Gorpieus as the tenth month. But the Latins, who had the more ancient beginning of their year from the kalends of March, reckoned September the seventh month.
14.47: **“And Simon accepted thereof, and was well pleased to execute the office of the high priesthood, and to be captain, and prince of the nation of the Jews, and of the priests, and to be chief over all.”** — And Simon accepted. Peribolus in Greek is the name of the wall of the court of the house of the Lord, which surrounded the whole temple in a square round about, as blessed Jerome shows in his exposition of the prophet Ezechiel, book thirteen. In the famous place, then, of the inner court of the house of the Lord were set the tables of brass, on which the priesthood of Simon and of his sons had been confirmed by writing. Mystically, however, the priesthood of Christ and of his sons, that is, of the Christian people, is confirmed in the court of the house of the Lord, that is, in the present Church, the Scripture bearing witness, and is declared to be firm and perpetual among all nations. Whence it is that is written in the Psalm: “The Lord hath sworn, and he will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech.” And again: “Once, he says, have I sworn by my holy one, if I lie unto David. His seed shall endure for ever, and his throne as the sun before me: and as the moon perfect for ever, and a faithful witness in heaven.” It is the custom of men to swear often, so that someone may be able to believe them. But God swears once, because he is changed by no variation of time. We have said, however, that his swearing is promising things to come. For he binds himself by the oath of him who has none stronger. He says also in his holy one, that is, in Christ, who said: “Preserve my soul, for I am holy”; he adds also: “If I lie unto David.” “If” is put negatively, which common usage also has. The seed of Christ are all who shall believe in him with faithful mind, because in them the kingdom to come is sown, which the coming harvest shows. As also in the twenty-first Psalm he himself says: “My seed shall serve him.” The saints, therefore, will remain for ever, who dwell in an excellent and blessed manner of life. Whence we do not properly say that those remain, since they are driven away from the kingdom of the Lord. The throne of God, moreover, is here to be understood as the faithful soul, in which he truly sits, when he has filled it with the illumination of his majesty. For so it is written: “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom.” He added: “as the sun before me.” That soul of the just, which we have called the seat of the Saviour, was indeed bright. But in saying “as the sun,” he makes a comparison with visible things. For it is great to shine from a creature, much better to shine from the creator.
