The perfect moon signifies the change of the body from corruption to incorruption. For then the nature of our bodies will be perfect, when that mortality or corruption will be no more. For that the moon itself, which waxes and wanes, signifies the changeable nature of human flesh can be shown in many places of the Scriptures. These testimonies from the Psalms we have set down to show that the priesthood of the true Simon is most firm and everlasting.

15.1: **“And king Antiochus the son of Demetrius sent letters from the isles of the sea to Simon the priest, and prince of the nation of the Jews, and to all the people:”** — And king Antiochus sent, etc. This Antiochus, who was surnamed Sidetes, was the son of Demetrius Soter, and brother of the younger Demetrius, who reigned in Syria after Alexander Balas. Now Demetrius Soter reigned twelve years after Antiochus Eupator, the son of Antiochus Epiphanes, as the chronicle of Eusebius and Jerome testifies. After him Alexander Philopator reigned ten years. After him Demetrius, the son of Demetrius, three years; who, taken by the Parthians, was thrust back into Hyrcania by king Arsaces. After him Antiochus Sidetes, brother of the same Demetrius, held the kingdom fourteen years. After his death it was restored again to Demetrius, who afterwards held it four years. But how the succession of the kingdom came about for the brothers Demetrius and Antiochus: it ought not to seem burdensome to the reader if I bring in something here from the History of Pompeius Trogus, who in the thirty-sixth book reports of this as follows. Antiochus, therefore, mindful that his father had been hated for pride, and his brother despised for sloth, lest he fall into the same vices, took Cleopatra, his brother’s wife, in marriage; he pursued with the greatest diligence the cities which had revolted at the beginning of his brother’s rule, and having subdued them added them again to the bounds of the kingdom; and he subdued the Jews, who under the Macedonian rule, in the time of Demetrius his father, had by arms claimed their liberty; and their strength was so great that after this they suffered no Macedonian king, and using their own rulers they harassed Syria with great wars. Likewise, in the thirty-eighth book, and the thirtieth, he joins these things to his former narrative. For Demetrius, as was said above, when he had made war on the Parthians, and had been victor in many engagements, was suddenly encircled by ambushes, lost his army, and was taken; Arsaces in Hyrcania not only gave him royal honor, but also gave him his daughter in marriage, and promised that the kingdom of Syria, which Tryphon had seized in his absence, should be restored. After the death of this man, his return despaired of, Demetrius, not bearing captivity, weary of a private life though wealthy, silently planned flight to his kingdom. His exhorter and companion was his friend Callimander, who after his captivity had come from Syria through the deserts of Arabia, guides having been bought with money, in Parthian dress, to Babylon. But as he fled, Phraates, who had succeeded Arsaces, by the swiftness of his horsemen along short cuts overtook and drew him back; and when he was brought to the king, Callimander was given not only pardon but also a reward for his fidelity; Demetrius, however, was severely chastised, and was sent back with his wife into Hyrcania, and ordered to be kept under closer guard. After an interval, when the children also that had been born gave a pledge of his loyalty, flight was attempted again with the same friend as companion. But with equal ill fortune he was caught near the end of his kingdom, and brought again to the king, that as one hated he might be removed from his sight. Then too, given back to his wife and children, he was sent back to Hyrcania, a city for him a punishment. And he was presented with golden dice in reproach of his boyish levity. But this so mild clemency of the Parthians toward Demetrius was caused not by the mercy of the nation, nor regard for kinship, but because they desired the kingdom of Syria, intending to use Demetrius against his brother Antiochus, as the matter, or the time, or the fortune of war should require. When he heard this, Antiochus, thinking he should seize the war first, led against the Parthians the army which he had hardened in many wars. But through luxury the equipage was no less than the soldiery; for eighty thousand armed men were followed by three hundred thousand camp-followers, of whom cooks and bakers were the greater number; and of silver and gold so much that even common soldiers fixed their boots with gold, and spurned the very material for love of which peoples fight with the sword. The kitchen utensils too were of silver, quite as if they were going to a banquet and not to war. When Antiochus came, many eastern kings met him, handing over themselves and their kingdoms with execration of Parthian pride. There was no delay in the engagement; Antiochus, victor in three battles, when he had seized Babylonia, began to be held great. And so, all peoples flocking to him, nothing was left to the Parthians but their ancestral borders. Then Phraates sent Demetrius into Syria with a Parthian guard to seize the kingdom, that by this arrangement Antiochus might be recalled to defend his own country; meanwhile, since he could not do so by force, he tried Antiochus everywhere with ambushes. Because of the multitude of men, Antiochus’s army was divided among the cities for winter quarters, and this was the cause of destruction. For when the cities saw themselves burdened by the exactions of supplies and the injuries of the soldiers, they revolted to the Parthians, and on the appointed day they attacked the army divided among them, by ambush, so that none could bring aid. When this was announced to Antiochus, he set out to bring help to the nearest, with the band which wintered with him. On the way he met the king of the Parthians, against whom he fought more bravely than his army did. But at last, though by valor he overcame the enemy, deserted through the fear of his own men, he was slain. For him Phraates held funeral rites in royal fashion, and the daughter of Demetrius, whom Antiochus had brought with him, he took as wife, captured by love of the maiden. Then he began to repent of having let Demetrius go, and to bring him back he had hurriedly sent squadrons of horse; but they found Demetrius, fearing this very thing, already in his kingdom, and having tried everything in vain they returned to their king. Antiochus’s army having been destroyed in Parthia, his brother Demetrius, freed from the Parthian siege and restored to the kingdom, when all Syria was in mourning because of the lost army, as if the wars in which one brother was captured and the other slain had been successfully waged by himself and his brother, resolved to make war on Egypt, Cleopatra his mother-in-law promising the kingdom of Egypt as the price of help against her brother. But, while he desired what was another’s, as usually happens, he lost his own through the revolt of Syria. For the Antiochenes first, under the leadership of Tryphon, execrating the pride of the king, which had become intolerable through the conversation of Parthian cruelty, then Apamea and the other cities, following the example, revolted from Demetrius in the king’s absence. Ptolemy also, king of Egypt, attacked by him in war, when he learned that his sister Cleopatra, with the wealth of Egypt put on ships, had fled to Syria to her daughter and to Demetrius her son-in-law, sent in a certain young Egyptian, son of the merchant Protarchus, to seek the kingdom of Syria even by arms, a story having been composed as if he had been received into the royal family by adoption of king Antiochus, and was not a Syrian, since they spurned any king whatever lest they suffer the pride of Demetrius. The name Alexander was put upon the young man, and great aid was sent from Egypt. Meanwhile the body of the slain Antiochus, sent back by the king of the Parthians in a silver coffin for burial in Syria, arrived. When it was received with great zeal by the cities and by king Alexander to confirm belief in the story, this won him great favor of the people, all thinking that tears not feigned were shed for them. But Demetrius, defeated by Alexander, when he was pressed by evils on every side, was at last deserted even by his wife and children. Left, therefore, with a few slaves, when he sought Tyre, intending to defend himself by the sanctity of its temple, he was killed as he disembarked from the ship by the governor’s command; for the causes aforesaid, etc. That Antiochus demands from Simon the cities possessed through battles signifies that the ancient enemy always envies the virtues of the saints and wishes to subject them to himself in unjust servitude; but Simon, the spiritual one, claiming them for himself, said they were his own right, and the inheritance of his fathers, and that the enemy ought to have no communion there, because the possession of virtues belongs properly to the elect, not to the reprobate. Whence the lands of the Chanaanites, into which the children of Israel are led, the sons of Sem had once obtained by lot in the division of the world; these afterwards the posterity of Cham possessed by force and power, through the iniquity of persuasion, in which too the most just judgment of God is proved. He both expelled those from the foreign places which they had wickedly occupied, and restored to these saints, as the possession of their fathers, that which had been assigned to their stock in the division of the world. This figure is known to stand in us also by the most certain reason. For the will of the Lord naturally assigned the possession of our heart not to vices but to virtues. After the prevarication of Adam, when the vices grew insolent, that is, the Chanaanite peoples were driven from their proper region, when by the grace of God they have again been restored to them by our diligence and labor, we are to believe that we have not so much occupied foreign lands as received back our own.
15.38: **“And the king appointed Cendebeus captain of the sea coast, and gave him an army of footmen and horsemen.”** — And the king appointed. What is signified by Cendebeus, the captain of the sea coast, whom Antiochus sends to wage war on the Jews, if not the powers of this world and the persecutors of the Christian religion? Whom the mystical Antiochus, Antichrist, sends with an army of lictors and executioners to the destruction of the Christian people, that they may trample down the true Judea, that is, the Church, and take captive by error, or slay by blasphemy, the people of the faithful. Moreover Cendebeus is ordered to build Cedron. For Cedron is a torrent, or a valley near Jerusalem on the eastern side, which John the evangelist also mentions in the passion of the Lord. And Cedron was ordered to be built for this reason, that the gates of the city might be blocked and the people hemmed in. Cedron is interpreted sorrow, or grief, or pain. And fittingly he was ordered to build Cedron, to whom it was committed to inflict the pain of punishments on the confessors of Christ.

16.1: **“Then John came up from Gazara, and told Simon his father what Cendebeus had done against their people.”** — And John went up, etc. We said above that Simon, the high priest, signified the prince of priests, namely him who by the obedience of the cross offered himself to the Father for us, whose two sons are the peoples of believers from the Jews and from the Gentiles. To these he commends the strength of war against all enemies and foes of the truth, that is, against Jews, pagans and heretics, and also against malignant spirits, that they may defend the Christian faith and protect the true confessors of God. Be you, he says, in my place, and my brethren, and go out and fight for our nation; and let the help from heaven be with you. Who are these brethren but those of whom the Truth itself, rising from the dead, says in the Gospel to the women visiting his sepulchre: “Go, tell my brethren that they go into Galilee, there they shall see me.” In the place, then, of Christ and the apostles are the saints, who, doing the will of the heavenly Father, seek the victory of the truth and the salvation of souls. Theirs is the help from heaven, from him assuredly of whom it is written in the Psalm: “God is wonderful in his saints: the God of Israel is he who will give power and strength to his people.” These chose twenty thousand fighting men, because they appoint only those as fit for spiritual warfare who become executors and doers of God’s commandments in the two precepts of charity.
16.6: **“And he and his people pitched their camp over against them, and he saw that the people were afraid to go over the river, so he went over first: then the men seeing him, passed over after him.”** — And he pitched his camp, etc. That this captain, when he saw the people afraid to go over the river, went over first, shows that those who act in the Church in the place of masters and in the office of teacher ought to strengthen by the example of their own faith and constancy the timidity of those subject to them, and to whet them for the battle line against the enemies with sacred trumpets, that is, with divine teachings; and so the spiritual Cendebeus and his camp are put to flight, and many of them fall wounded, because shaken with fear they at length feel the power of the divine majesty.
16.9: **“At that time Judas John's brother was wounded: but John pursued after them, till he came to Cedron, which he had built:”** — Then was wounded, etc. That Judas was wounded in the battle and John pursued the enemies, signifies, unless I am mistaken, what Paul says: “Blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel should be saved,” because while the Jewish people delays in the faith of Christ, the Church of the Gentiles strongly presses the enemies, until she either converts the blind to repentance by saving compunction, or punishes those who persevere in wickedness by preaching to them with threats the future punishment. But when the times of the nations shall be fulfilled and their fullness shall have come in to the faith, then all Israel, that is, the whole Church from both peoples, will be saved by the gift of Christ through saving confession by faith, hope and charity.
16.11: **“And Ptolemee”** — And Ptolemee. What is figured by Ptolemee, if not hypocritical and crafty men? These, then, attaching themselves to good masters with feigned discipline and pretending a piety whose power they utterly do not know, for the most part come to the honor of ecclesiastical dignity, the masters themselves bestowing it; for to be sons-in-law of the high priest is this: that those very persons whom the good masters regenerated with water and the word should receive a share in the power of their government. But when, having received the rank of their own power, they have begun each to be slaves to their desires, they strive by the circumventions of guile to supplant and overthrow the very honors of their benefactor, and they kill his sons and servants alike, since they spare no person living with them. But through money and flattery they gain the secular powers, and harass the Church with hidden snares or open persecutions. Nor is it a wonder that such wickedness can at times prevail in the Church, since we read that the head of the Church was handed over and taken captive to the Jews by the guile of the traitor Judas. Simon Magus was baptized by Philip, but was not purged from the wickedness of his mind. Julian the Apostate, raised up by the Church as a reader, persevered to the end of his life a savage enemy in the malice he had begun. Even the age of this time has not a few such, who, though they do not kill their masters with the sword, yet do not cease to persecute them with envy and hatred.
16.22: **“But when he heard it he was exceedingly afraid: and he apprehended the men that came to kill him, and he put them to death: for he knew that they sought to take him away.”** — And running before, etc. John indeed, his father having been slain by guile, guards himself more cautiously against the enemy and kills the men who had come to destroy him; so anyone, even of the number of the faithful saved by the grace of God, being provident and careful to preserve his own salvation, having heard of the deception practised by other enemies, strives to guard against their snares and to crush their perverse machinations. For simplicity alone does not suffice anyone for preserving his salvation, but with simplicity there ought equally to be prudence. Whence the Saviour says in the Gospel to the disciples: “Be ye therefore wise as serpents and simple as doves.” And the Apostle says: “Do not become children in sense: but in malice be children.” Simplicity, then, ought to be had by us, that we may harm no one; prudence also, that we be not despised by others; nor is there much difference between deceiving anyone and being able to be deceived by another.
16.23:
**“And as concerning the rest of the acts of John, and his wars, and the worthy deeds, which he bravely achieved, and the building of the walls, which he made, and the things that he did:”**
• And the rest of the acts of John. This John, leader of the Jews and at once high priest, was a man of valour, and accomplished many wondrous works. He also, waging war against the Hyrcanians and conquering them, received the name of Hyrcanus; and asking of the Romans the right of friendship, by decree of the senate he was reckoned among their friends. But how Josephus tells of this same Hyrcanus, to make clear what is briefly said at the end of the book of Machabees, seems to us not unfitting to be set down here. For after he had at some point recalled the victory of Simon, he reports of his end thus: And he also dies at a banquet, taken by the treachery of Ptolemy his son-in-law, who, having shut up Simon’s wife and two sons in custody, sent trusted friends to kill John, the third, whose name was also Hyrcanus. But the young man, learning of the attack that was being prepared, hastened to the city, relying on the great multitude of the people, both for the memory of his father’s valour and because the wickedness of Ptolemy was hateful to all. Ptolemy wished to enter by another gate of the city, but was cast out by the people, who had received Hyrcanus sooner. And he indeed at once withdrew to a certain fortress beyond Jericho, which is called Dagon.
• Hyrcanus, however, obtained his father’s honour of the pontificate. After he had offered sacrifices to God, he quickly sought Ptolemy, intending to bring help to his mother and his brothers together; and having attacked the stronghold, he was superior in other matters, but yielded to a just grief. For whenever Ptolemy was pressed, he scourged his mother and brothers, led up onto the wall openly, so that they could be seen, and threatened to throw them down headlong unless he withdrew at once. Whence fear and pity moved Hyrcanus more than anger. But his mother, in no way terrified by the blows, but by the threatened death, stretching out her hands, begged her son that he should not, broken by the wrongs done to his own, let the wicked man escape; for she herself would count the death set before her by Ptolemy better than immortality, provided that he paid the penalty for the things he had done against right to her house. John, however, now considering his mother’s obstinacy and hearing her prayers, was impelled to rush upon him; then seeing her scourged and torn, he was made weak, and was wholly full of grief. Because of this, when the siege had been long drawn out, the sabbatical year came, which among the Jews it is the custom to keep as a rest in every seventh cycle, after the example of the seventh days. And in this Ptolemy, having got respite from the siege, killed the brothers of John together with their mother and fled to Zeno, who was surnamed Cotylas, tyrant of Philadelphia. But Antiochus, angry at what he had suffered through Simon, led an army into Judea, and sitting down there at Jerusalem, besieged Hyrcanus. But he, having opened the sepulchre of David, who had been the richest of kings, and taking from it more than three thousand talents of money, persuaded Antiochus, by the gift of three hundred talents, to depart from the siege; and he was the first of the Jews to begin to support foreign auxiliaries from private wealth. And again, when Antiochus, having undertaken war against the Medes, gave him time for vengeance, he at once advanced against the cities of Syria, thinking them empty of defenders, which was true. He took Medeba indeed and Samega with their neighbours, and also Shechem and Garizim, and besides these the race of the Cutheans, who dwell in the places adjoining the temple, built after the example of that which is at Jerusalem. He took also not a few other cities of Idumea, and besides Adora and Marisa. He advanced as far as Samaria, where the city Sebaste now is, founded by king Herod, and shut it in on every side, and set his sons Aristobulus and Antigonus over the siege. They, resisting not at all, came by the necessity of famine to the point that those who were within the city were forced to touch even unaccustomed flesh. So they called to their aid Antiochus, surnamed Spondius, who, when he had obeyed them with ready will, was overcome by Aristobulus and Antigonus, and he indeed fled as far as Scythopolis, the brothers, mentioned above, pursuing. But these, returning to Samaria, drove the multitude again within the wall, and having taken the city by storm they demolished it, and led away its inhabitants captive. But things being prosperously done in this way, they did not allow their eagerness to cool. But advancing quickly with the army as far as Scythopolis, they struck it also, and all the fields within Carmel were laid waste. In the second place, envy of the affairs of John and his sons stirred up a sedition of the nations, and many gathered against them and did not rest until they were conquered in open war. The remaining time of John, when he lived most fortunately, and administered affairs excellently for thirty years, he dies, three years having been administered, leaving five children, a man plainly most blessed, who had given no occasion for anyone to complain of his lot. In short, he alone had three things, and those the chief. For he was both prince of the nation, and high priest, and besides a prophet, with whom God conversed, so that he was altogether ignorant of nothing of things to come; for he also foresaw and foretold concerning his two elder sons that they would not remain in the Lord’s affairs. He held the pontificate itself after his father’s death, according to the faith of the chronicles, for twenty-six years. But his father Simon had been pontiff before him for eight years. Before him Jonathan, his brother, for eighteen years. Judas also, brother of Jonathan and Simon, held the pontificate for three years, although he had waged many wars before with the generals of the kings of Syria. After John, indeed, Aristobulus his son received the pontificate among the Jews, who, wishing also to become king at the same time, took the badge of the diadem, after four hundred and eighty-four years of the Babylonian captivity. He killed his brother Antigonus by treachery, and having completed one year in the kingdom, ended his life by the wretched death of a fratricide. His brother Anneus, who was also Alexander, succeeded him in the kingdom, which he held twenty-seven years so cruelly that, the people being provoked, he asked them what he could do to reconcile the people’s minds to himself. The answer was: if he were to die. For perhaps, having suffered such grave things at the hands of a dead man, they would return to favour, so as to lay aside their hatred against the departed. Roused by these things, and by the habit of rebelling, having killed many he drove the rest into a city whose name is Bethsel, and its capture brought a bitterer plague than usual, with so savage a course of cruelty that of that number he crucified eight hundred in the midst of the city. In their sight he ordered their wives and sons to be slaughtered. He looked on at this reclining in the midst of his concubines, merry among wine and cups, but drunk more with blood than with wine.
• By this deed alone he terrified the people more than by war, so that the next night eight thousand of the Jews went down beyond Judea, for whom the end of flight would be the death of Alexander. When he was dead, Alexandra his wife, who was also surnamed Salma, reigned in Jerusalem nine years. Thereafter, when the two brothers, sons of Alexander, Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, were fighting over the rule, the Romans had occasion to invade Judea. So Pompey, at Hyrcanus' invitation, came to Jerusalem; the city taken and the temple opened, he went in as far as the holy of holies; he led with him Aristobulus, his younger brother, but confirmed the pontificate to Hyrcanus, and made Antipater, the father of Herod of Ascalon, procurator of Palestine. And so Hyrcanus, slothful in spirit, with the aid of the aforesaid procurator Antipater, held the pontificate thirty-four years. Afterwards, Antipater having been killed by poison at a banquet, Herod his son succeeded to the kingdom, who also killed Hyrcanus. Hence also Herod, son of the aforesaid Antipater of Ascalon and of his mother Cypris, an Arab, received the rule of the Jews from the Romans; in his time, the nativity of Christ being near, the kingdom and priesthood of Judea, which before had been held by succession of the lesser, was destroyed, the prophecy being fulfilled in which he speaks thus through Moses: “There shall not fail a prince out of Juda, nor a ruler from his thighs, till he come to whom it is laid up, and he shall be the expectation of the nations.”
• In this place also Christ, whom the scripture of Daniel mentions beforehand, receives his end. For up to Herod the christs, that is, the priests, were kings of the Jews, who began to rule from the sixty-fifth Olympiad and from the restoration of the temple under Darius, down to Hyrcanus and the hundred and eighty-sixth Olympiad, four hundred and eighty-three years having passed in between; which years Daniel also marks, saying: “And thou shalt know and understand, from the beginning of the word to answer and to build Jerusalem, unto the princedom of Christ, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks.” These sixty-nine weeks make four hundred and eighty-three years, in which the christs, that is, the priests consecrated by anointing, reigned down to Hyrcanus; he, last of all, having been taken by the Parthians, Herod the son of Antipater, who had no claim to Judea, received it from Augustus and the senate, and his sons reigned after him until the last captivity of Jerusalem, no pontiffs being appointed by succession of the priestly line, nor serving God for the duration of life according to the law of Moses. Certain ignoble men, and at another time others, and some for one year or a little more, bought the priesthood from the Romans. All which things the prophet Daniel also foretells, saying thus: “And after seven and sixty-two weeks” the chrism shall perish, “and judgment shall not be in him, and the people shall corrupt the holy temple with the leader that shall come, and they shall be cut down in the flood of war.” And in what follows: “And upon the temple,” he says, “shall be the abomination of desolations, and even to the consummation of the time, consummation shall be given upon the desolation.” Herod appointed a certain Ananelus, summoned from Babylon, high priest of the Jews, and after a short time gave Aristobulus, brother of his wife and grandson of Hyrcanus, as successor. When he had been killed after a year, he gave the priesthood back again to Ananelus. And now there was no lawful succession in the priesthood, but, the end of the law itself and of the priesthood drawing near, all things were in confusion. This Herod, moreover, was vigorous in the acts of war, in the government of the kingdom, and in the restoration of buildings, but of most unhappy and most cruel character. At Jerusalem he built many great houses. Samaria, long sitting in ashes, he raised up from the foundations in honor of Augustus; he called it Augusta, that is, Sebaste, and in Pamis he built the temple which is called Pamon. He founded Caesarea in the name of Caesar, which was formerly called the Tower of Strato. He founded besides Antidana and Antipatris, and built Herodium, in honor of his father Antipater and of himself. Countless works also he built with great skill in the several cities which he ruled. But amid these things he killed Hyrcanus, who had once been priest of the Jews, on his return from the Parthian captivity, and his son, who had succeeded his father in the priesthood. He also most cruelly killed the sister of the latter, his own wife, with two sons of his own, already youths, and the mother of the wife he had slain, his mother-in-law. Indeed Herod himself, lest he be thought ignoble and perhaps be charged as a stranger to the seed of the Jews, burned all the books in which the nobility of the Jewish nation was kept written in the temple, so that, the proofs failing, he too might be thought to belong to it. Moreover, to mingle his offspring with their royal race, having cast off Doris, a woman of Jerusalem, whom he had taken as wife while a private man, and Antipater, the son born of her, he joined to himself Mariamne, daughter of Alexander, granddaughter of Aristobulus the brother of Hyrcanus, who before him was king of the Jews. She bore him five sons, of whom two, Alexander and Aristobulus, he himself killed in Samaria, and without delay afterwards he destroyed with a like crime their mother also, than whom he had known nothing dearer. Of these, Aristobulus had begotten as his son Herod, by Berenice, whom we read in the Acts of the Apostles was struck by an angel. He also added to what he had cruelly done above this: that he killed the husband of his sister Salome. And when he had given her to another, he killed this man also, as her husband. He also slew the scribes, interpreters of the divine law, with a like crime.
• But when he had learned, from the information of the magi, of the birth of Christ our Lord, who was born in Bethlehem in the thirty-second year of his reign, he ordered all the little ones to be killed. But after he had completed the thirty-seventh year of his reign, he died a death marvelously fitting, of a dropsy under the skin, with worms bursting forth over his whole body. How Josephus tells of the end of Herod does not seem unfitting to bring into this little work of ours; he relates it in this way. For he had a fever, not a moderate one, and an intolerable itching held the whole surface of his body. He was vexed with continual torments of the colon, and his feet had swollen as from the fault of water under the skin; moreover the swelling of the belly, and the rotting of the testicles breeding little worms, and besides frequent panting, and broken sighs, and a contraction of all his limbs wearied him, so that those who referred these things to the divinity said that they were the punishments of the sophists. But he, although he struggled with the torments of so many ills, was nevertheless desirous of life, and hoped for health by remedies he had devised. At last, having crossed the Jordan, at Callirrhoe he used hot waters, which flowing into a lake rich in bitumen, called Asphaltites, were drunk for their sweetness. There his body, which the physicians had decided to foment with warmer oil, was plunged into a vessel full of it, and was so dissolved that he rolled his eyes loose like a dead man. Then those who were attending him were thrown into confusion, and he seemed to look toward their outcry. But despairing of health, he ordered fifty drachmas to be divided to each of the soldiers, and much money among the officers and friends. And when, returning, they had come to Jericho, seized with black bile, and himself nearly changed to death, he devised a necessary deed; for he commanded that the nobler men of every city of all Judea be gathered and shut up in a place called the Hippodrome. Then, having called to him his sister Salome and Alexander her husband, he said: I know that the Jews will celebrate that death of mine with festal joys; but I can be mourned by others, and gain most illustrious honors of burial, if you do what I command. These men, who are held in custody, when I have breathed out my soul, surround with soldiers and kill at once, so that all Judea, hateful to me, and every house may weep for me. And at the same time, with these commands given, letters were brought from the envoys whom he had sent to Rome, in which it was reported that Acme the handmaid had been put to death by command of Caesar, and that Antipater was condemned to death. Yet it was also written that if the father preferred to send him into exile, Caesar had permitted it. But Herod, a little revived by this news and again overcome by pains, for he was racked by hunger and cough alike with violence, tried to reach his breath. And having taken an apple, he also asked for a knife, for he was accustomed to eat it cut. Then, looking around lest anyone should hinder him, he raised his right hand as if to strike himself. But when Achiabus his cousin had run up and held back his hand, a very great wailing was raised in the palace at once, as if the king were dead. And Antipater, having quickly heard this, regained confidence, and now glad, with money also sent ahead, begged the guards to release and dismiss him. Their chief not only prevented this from being done, but even quickly told the king. He, crying out more strongly than the strength of a sick man could manage, at once sent guards and killed Antipater, and commanded that he be buried, dead, in Hyrcania. Then he again corrected his will, and wrote as successor Archelaus, the eldest brother of Antipater, and Antipas as tetrarch. And after the death of his son, five days having passed, he died, in the thirty-fourth year from when he killed Antigonus and gained the kingdom, and the thirty-seventh after he was declared king by the Romans. He died therefore in the forty-seventh year of the empire of Augustus; in his place his son Archelaus, appointed by Augustus, reigned nine years until the end of Augustus himself.
• For then, the Jews no longer enduring his ferocity but accusing him before Augustus, he was banished to Vienne, a city of Gaul; and to lessen the power of the Jewish kingdom and tame its insolence, four brothers were appointed tetrarchs in his place: Herod, Antipater, Lysias and Philip. Of these, Philip and Herod, who was formerly called Antipas, had been ordained tetrarchs even while Archelaus was alive. But after Archelaus, Herod, tetrarch of the Jewish nation, held the principality twenty-four years, when the emperor Tiberius had given him this power; in the twelfth year of Tiberius, Pilate was sent by the same emperor as procurator of Judea, and he continued there ten years together, almost to the very end of Tiberius. But in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, and likewise the fifteenth of the reign of Herod, as the histories tell, John, the son of Zachary, preaching in the desert near the river Jordan, bears witness that Christ the Son of God is present in the midst of them; and the aforesaid Herod, at the urging of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, ordered him beheaded at a banquet at the request of a dancing girl, as the holy Gospel plainly shows. The Lord Jesus Christ himself also announces the way of salvation here among the people, proving by signs and miracles that what he said was true. Likewise, in the eighteenth year of both principalities, Jesus Christ, according to the prophecies that had been spoken beforehand of him, came to the Passion. There, presented to this Herod by Pilate’s envoys, not received with faith but scorned through worldly pride, clothed in a white garment, he was sent back again to Pilate, by whom, through the service of the soldiers, he was crucified, and on the third day rose again from the dead. Now divine Scripture relates that the beginning of the preaching of the gospel was made in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, and he maintained that Jesus himself spent the whole time of his teaching under the high priests Annas and Caiphas. In these spaces scarcely four whole years are contained. The legal precepts were by then ceasing, and through ambition; for the honor of the priesthood was given to no one for merit of life or of birth. But by Roman power the highest priesthood was now granted to some, now to others, so that they were changed in yearly successions. Finally, the same Josephus relates that four in order, after Annas, discharged the office of the pontificate up to Caiphas, writing in these words: Valerius Gracchus, having removed Annas from the priesthood, appointed Ismael, the son of Bassus, high priest. But rejecting him also not long after, he put Eleazar, the son of the high priest Ananias, in the pontificate in his place. After a year he also removes him from the office and handed over the ministry of the pontificate to one Simon, the son of Canisus. He too having discharged it no longer than the space of one year, received as successor Joseph, otherwise Josippus, who was also named Caiphas. And by this the whole time in which our Lord and Saviour is described as having taught on earth is confined within the space of four years, in which these four successions of high priests, which Josephus records, are described as scarcely serving one year each. But how Herod the tetrarch lost his kingdom Josephus tells, saying: The accuser of Herod the tetrarch, Agrippa, son of Aristobulus, whom Herod’s father killed, came to Tiberius. But he not receiving the accusation, and staying at Rome, he sought the notice of some powerful men. But he cultivated with the greatest services Gaius, the son of Germanicus, while he was still a private man; and one day, amid a plentiful provision of feasts at which he was being entertained by him, at the end, with hands stretched out, he openly began to pray to God that he might quickly see him lord of all, Tiberius being dead. When one of his intimates had reported this to Tiberius, he at once ordered Agrippa to be shut up. He was kept in prison under great hardship for six months, until the death of Tiberius. But when he was dead, after a reign of twenty-two years and three days, Gaius Caesar, succeeding to the empire, released Agrippa from his chains and gave him the tetrarchy of Philip, for the latter had by then died, and called him king. And when he had come to his kingdom, Agrippa stirred up through envy the desires of Herod the tetrarch. Herodias his wife chiefly provoked him to hope for the kingdom, reproaching him with his concord and saying: That through not having been willing to sail to Caesar he lacked greater power; for since he had made Agrippa a king from a private man, how could he hesitate to give him, a tetrarch, the same honor? Led on by these things, Herod came to Gaius, by whom, for his avarice, he was sharply rebuked, and fled to Spain. For the accuser Agrippa had followed, and Gaius also added Herod’s tetrarchy to him. And so Herod, living abroad in Spain, died with his wife Herodias also with him. But Pontius Pilate, the governor, in the same year in which the Saviour suffered, secretly by night set up the images of Caesar in the temple, as Josephus tells. And this was the cause of the first sedition and troubles for the Jews.
• But afterwards, spending the sacred treasure, which the Jews call Corban, on an aqueduct of Jerusalem, he gave the seeds of a second sedition. But when the same Pilate reported to Tiberius concerning the teaching of the Christians, and recalled some things of the deeds of the Redeemer himself, his passion and resurrection, Tiberius referred it to the senate, that he might be received among the other sacred things. But when, by the decree of the fathers, Tiberius had decided that the Christians be removed from the city, he threatened death by edict to the accusers of the Christians. Tertullian writes in the Apologeticus that many of the Roman senators and knights were put to death by the same. Therefore divine vengeance condemned the Jews for the crime committed. But Pilate himself also, who performed the office of an unjust judge against the Saviour, in the same times of Gaius was tormented with such and so great disasters of evils that he is reported to have pierced himself through with his own hand and by violence cast away his wicked life. For he could not escape unpunished for so great a crime, as we find in the histories of the Greeks, of those at least who write the Olympiads and compose annual books of things done for the memory of posterity. But Agrippa, who also was Herod, son of Aristobulus, after the killing of James the son of Zebedee, sent the apostle Peter into prison and stirred up persecution against those believing in Christ, but did not escape unpunished, as Luke makes plain in the Acts of the Apostles, and Josephus recalls in the eighteenth book of the Antiquities, who relates of him in this manner: He had completed, he says, the third year of his rule over all Judea, when by chance he came to Caesarea, which was formerly called Strato’s Tower. There he put on spectacles for the citizens in honour of Caesar, on a day of vows, as it seemed, for Caesar’s safety. And when the men of the whole province, endowed with honour and means, had assembled there, on the second day of the spectacles, clothed in a shining robe wonderfully woven of gold and silver, at the beginning of the day he proceeds to the theatre, where, when the silver garment had first received the rays of the sun in its bosom, the brilliance of the quivering metal poured forth a light doubled for the spectators by the reflected splendour, so that the terror of the sight dazzled the eyes of those looking, and through this their arrogance, the artificer, feigned something more of him than is of human nature. At once the voices of the flattering crowd ring out, sounding honour but bringing destruction, and from this side and that the crowds cry out from the benches that he be called God, and he is humbly entreated to be gracious, the peoples saying: Until now we have held you as a man, but from this time we confess that you are above human nature. But the king did not check the acclamation held against what is right, nor shrank from the impiety of the unlawful flattery, until, looking up a little after, he saw an angel hanging over and standing above his head, and he perceived him at once to be the minister of his destruction, whom before he had not known as the provider of honours. And behold, suddenly a torment seized him, from an incredible pain of the belly, and a swelling. And looking to his friends he said: Behold, I, your God, am at once driven forth and thrown down from life, since a certain divine power has convicted the false voices lately bestowed on me, and I, who was just now called immortal by you, am now hurried headlong into death. But the sentence which God has appointed must be accepted, and we have lived either to be despised, or have fulfilled the length of life which was thought blessed. And when he had said this, being more violently tossed by the force of the pain, he was at once carried back to the palace. And when it was spread abroad that he would die within a few days, a huge multitude of every age and sex, assembling according to the custom of the fathers, besought almighty God for the king’s safety, lying prostrate at the edge of his couch. And the whole royal house resounded with lamentations and groans. Meanwhile the king himself, lying in an upper chamber, and looking down, and seeing all prostrate and bowed down with weeping, did not himself refrain from tears; but, tormented for five continuous days by pains of the belly, he violently broke off his life, in the fifty-fourth year of his age and the seventh of his reign; for he had reigned four years under Gaius Caesar, holding the tetrarchy of Philip for three years, and in the fourth adding also that of Herod, and the other three years having passed under Claudius Caesar. After Agrippa the father, who held the kingdom of Judea for seven years, his son Agrippa was put in the kingdom by Claudius, which he held for twenty-six years, that is, up to the second year of Vespasian, when the destruction of the city took place. But how Josephus tells of this, we think should be set down in this place: Claudius, he says, appointed Agrippa, son of Agrippa, king of the Jews, but sent Felix as procurator of the whole province, of Samaria also and Galilee and the region called Transjordan. And after a few words he added this also: A most bitter sedition is also kindled by the high priests against the priests and the chief men of the people of Jerusalem, each of whom, complaining to themselves, set themselves up as leaders of their own faction, with bands of ruined young men rejoicing in revolutions. These, clashing with one another, first provoked each other with abuses, then afterwards struck each other down with stones, and there was no one to restrain them, but all things were done as in a city having no ruler. So the high priests came to such want that they sent their servants to the threshing-floors and seized the tithes which were owed to the priests; and it happened that some of the lesser priests, whose food had been taken by force, perished of hunger. So the violence of the seditions had confounded right and wrong. Likewise after a few words he adds this also: Sometimes also in the midst of the city they slew those who met them, especially on feast days, the assassins mingling with the crowds and going about with daggers hidden, so that whoever was marked out by them, if he came close, they killed him; and by wicked art, when he had fallen whom they had struck down with a secret wound, the murderers themselves proudly pretended to be indignant against those who committed such things in the midst of the city, and in this way their hidden crimes remained concealed; and first of all by them Jonathan the high priest was killed. After him very many were butchered, so that the fear of death was now heavier than the deaths themselves, while each one, as if always set in readiness, hoped at every moment to be killed.
• When Claudius, having completed fourteen years in the empire, with seven months and twenty-eight days, had died, Nero received the empire, which he held fourteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. In his second year Festus, procurator of Judea, succeeded Felix; by him Paul is sent bound to Rome, and remaining two years in free custody, after this is released to preach, Nero not yet breaking out into such crimes as the histories relate of him. James, the brother of the Lord, when he had ruled the Church of Jerusalem for thirty years, was stoned in the seventh year of Nero by the Jews, who were avenging on him that they had been unable to kill Paul. Albinus succeeded Festus as governor of Judea; Florus succeeded Albinus, whose luxury and avarice and other shameful deeds the Jews could not bear, and they rebelled against the Romans. Against them Vespasian, the master of the soldiery, was sent and took very many cities of Judea. Nero first, above all his crimes, also persecuted the Christians. Of them he killed the most eminent at Rome, Peter by the cross, Paul by the sword. He, venturing nothing at all by the right of war, almost lost Britain; for two most noble towns were taken and overthrown there under him. Finally Nero, when he was being sought by the senate for punishment, fleeing from the palace, killed himself at the fourth milestone from the city, in the suburban house of his freedman, between the Salarian and Numentan roads, in the thirty-second year of his age; and in him the whole family of Augustus was ended.
• After Nero, Galba in Spain, Vitellius in Germany, and Otho at Rome seized the empire. Galba, in the seventh month of his reign, was beheaded in the middle of the forum of the city of Rome. Vespasian drove the Jews, overcome in two battles, back to their walls. Otho, in the third month of his reign, at Vitriacum, otherwise Venatrum, fell by his own hand. Vitellius, the seventh of the Romans, is cast into the Tiber by the generals of Vespasian. Vespasian reigned eight years, eleven months, twenty-two days; he was called emperor by the army among the Jews, and committing the war to his son Titus, he set out for Rome by way of Alexandria. In his second year Titus, Judea being taken and Jerusalem overthrown, killed six hundred thousand men. Josephus, however, who knew it, affirms that six hundred thousand men perished by the sword and famine, and another hundred thousand captives were publicly sold. He relates that the cause of so great a multitude being found at Jerusalem was the feast of unleavened bread. For this reason the Jews, flocking to the temple from every nation, were shut up in the city as in a prison. For it was fitting that they should be put to death in the same days of the Pasch in which they had crucified the Saviour. Now the whole time is reckoned to the second year of Vespasian; and the last overthrow of Jerusalem is forty-two years from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar and from the beginning of the preaching of the gospel; two hundred and thirty-eight years from the captivity which they suffered under Antiochus; five hundred and ninety years from the second year of Darius, under whom the temple was built again; and from the first building of the temple under Solomon to its last ruin, which was made under Vespasian, one thousand one hundred and two years. Here ends the first book of Machabees.

1.1:
The second book of the history of the Machabees, though it is shorter, yet in a certain way retraces the times of the earlier book of the same work, being more ancient in historical narration, except that the former makes at its beginning a brief mention of Alexander the Great of Macedon. For this book also recalls the benefits of King Seleucus, surnamed Nicanor, toward the Jews; the history of the Antiquities of Josephus and the Chronicle of Eusebius testify that he made the Jews worthy of their own commonwealth, and assigned them equal honour with the Macedonian and Greek inhabitants. Likewise Antiochus the Great, as the above-mentioned authorities testify, praises them in frequent letters and endows them with manifold gifts. The same book also has a narration different from the former, yet it does not destroy the truth of the history; for although it contains many testimonies of the former book, nevertheless it interposes many things which are not found in that. For it seems to have been written by those who stayed in the land, to those who were in foreign regions. Whence it begins thus.
**“To the brethren the Jews that are throughout Egypt, the brethren, the Jews that are in Jerusalem, and in the land of Judea, send health, and good peace.”** — To the brethren that are throughout Egypt. This Demetrius, under whom the men of Jerusalem recall that they prayed for the Jews established in Egypt, is he who after Antiochus Eupator reigned over Asia and Syria, and who was himself surnamed Soter, that is, Saviour. For up to him the number of years that has been reckoned, that is, the hundred and sixty-ninth, runs. For Antiochus Epiphanes, who began to reign after the hundred and thirty-seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks, reigned eleven years, Antiochus Eupator two years, and Demetrius Soter twelve years; these are, from the beginning of the reign of Seleucus Nicanor, king of Syria, from whom the times of the kingdom of the Greeks are reckoned, to the end of Demetrius, a hundred and sixty-two years. If to these are added the seven years of the reign of Alexander, who is described by Pompeius Trogus as ignoble and vicious and unworthy of royal dignity, but who nevertheless is said to have held the kingdom ten years, they make a hundred and sixty-nine. Let us say it another way. After Alexander, Antigonus first reigned over Asia, eighteen years, and after him Demetrius, who was also called Poliorcetes, reigned seventeen years. This Demetrius, then, in the seventeenth year of his reign gave himself up to Seleucus, and Asia was joined to the kingdom of Syria in the twenty-eighth year of Seleucus Nicanor. If, then, we begin now to reckon the series of years from the first year of the reign of Antigonus, who reigned in Asia seven years before Seleucus began to reign in Syria, placing those same seven years before the reign of Seleucus, and in that way bring the reckoning of the years of the kings of Syria down to the last year of Demetrius Soter, the whole sum of the former number is found there. But it is a wonder how in what follows Judas is said, in the hundred and eighty-eighth year, to have sent greeting with the senate to Aristobulus, the teacher of King Ptolemy, and to have sent word about the purification of the temple, which they were about to perform on the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu, when Judas is read in the former book to have died long before the above-mentioned Demetrius. Indeed, in the sixth year of Demetrius, according to the credit of the chronicles, he is found to have been slain. But since the authors of those books themselves are uncertain, they seem not absurdly to differ in the reckoning of times, especially since in the books of the law the edition of the Seventy interpreters differs much from the Hebrew truth in the reckoning of years.
1.7: **“When Demetrius reigned, in the year one hundred and sixty-nine, we Jews wrote to you, in the trouble, and violence, that came upon us in those years, after Jason withdrew himself from the holy land, and from the kingdom.”** — We Jews, etc. But this Jason is the brother of the high priest Onias, whom the following part of this book shows to have flown to Antiochus Epiphanes, that is, a noble man who, out of ambition for the high priesthood, went to him and persuaded him to establish the Gentile rite at Jerusalem.
1.10: **“The people that”** — Aristobulus was by birth a Jew, but is recognized as a Peripatetic philosopher, who wrote commentaries explaining Moses to Ptolemy Philometor, as the chronographers report, at the same time that Antiochus Epiphanes was reigning over Syria and Asia.
1.11: **“Having been delivered by God out of great dangers, we give him great thanks, forasmuch as we have been in war with such a king.”** — From great dangers, etc. How Antiochus Epiphanes, who inflicted evils on the Jews beyond all the kings who were before him in Syria, lost his kingdom and ended his life, the former book of this history recounts, and Josephus testifies in the twelfth book of the Antiquities of the Jews, saying: King Antiochus, going through the upper province, heard of a city of the Persians excelling in riches, and in it a most precious temple of Diana, full of every kind of ornament; moreover he had heard that Alexander, son of Philip, king of the Macedonians, had left arms and breastplates there. Moved, therefore, he went out against Elymais and besieged it. But those who were in it, not at all terrified by his assault or by the siege, but resisting stubbornly, he departed almost deceived. For going out of the city they put him to flight and pursued him as far as Babylonia, where, when he had come after the loss of many of his soldiers, one of the Jews announced to him both the destruction of the generals whom he had left to fight against the Jews, and that the strength of the Jews had grown. Therefore, upon his former anxiety, this evil increasing, he fell into sickness, and while it lasted and the sufferings grew, he understood that he was to die. And calling together his friends he told them that his disease was grievous, confessing that he suffered these things because, afflicting the nation of the Jews, he had despoiled the temple and had despised God. When he had said this, he immediately expired. Whence I wonder at Polybius of Megalopolis, who, being a good man, says that Antiochus perished because he wished to lay waste the temple of Diana in Persia. For he who committed no sin at all, but only thought of it, is held to no guilt. But if it seems to Polybius that Antiochus ended his life for this reason, it is much more truly believed that the king perished on account of the sacrilege against the temple at Jerusalem.
1.18: **“Therefore whereas we purpose”** — Indeed these things, which the Jews of Jerusalem write to the Jews who were throughout Egypt, about the fire found in the well, turned into the likeness of thick water, we have been able to find nowhere, neither in the writings or sayings of Esdras nor of Nehemias; just as that also which they affirm in what follows about the ark and the hiding of the tabernacle by Jeremias can in no way be found written in the book of Jeremias himself. Whence it is clear that they either learned these things by the tradition of their elders, or found them written in their apocryphal books. Let us therefore leave what is uncertain, and turn the pen to those things which are manifest by the sure attestation of the canonical books.

3.1: **“Therefore when the holy city was inhabited with all peace, and the laws as yet were very well kept, because of the godliness of Onias the high priest, and the hatred his soul had of evil,”** — Therefore when the holy city, etc. Therefore, because the high priests were various under various kings, we have judged it necessary, following the account of the historians, to recite the names of those priests who held the priesthood in the times of the kings, and also of those who were in the Jewish nation after the captivity of Babylon, that the truth of the history may appear the more clearly. First, then, Sadoch was priest of the temple which Solomon built. After him his son Achimaas succeeded to his honour. After him Joram, and after him Auxidramus. Then Nideas. After Nideas, Sudeas. After him Hylus. To Hylus succeeded Jonathan, and to him in turn Urias. To Urias, Nerias. After Nerias there was Odeas. After him Sellum. Then Elchias. After him Zara. And after him was Josedech, who was led captive into Babylon. All these, then, succeeded to the priesthood, sons after fathers, in order. After Josedech his son Jesus received the priesthood; under him the temple was rebuilt. And after him Joachim his son. When he also was dead, John his son received the honour. When John ended his life, his son Jaddus succeeded to the primacy of the priests; under him Alexander, king of Macedon, came to Jerusalem. After him Onias his son is held illustrious. After him Simon his son, whose surname was the Just, on account of his careful religion toward God and his ready kindness toward his citizens. Then Eleazar, brother of Simon, high priest of the Jews, took up the ministry of the temple, Simon’s son Onias being left very young. This Eleazar, at the request of Ptolemy Philadelphus, sent the seventy interpreters to interpret the divine law. After Eleazar his uncle Manasses received the priesthood. After Manasses Onias, son of Simon the Just, high priest of the Jews, is held illustrious; he, by not paying the customary tribute to king Ptolemy, drove him to anger. But Joseph, a man noble among his own, sent as ambassador by the Jews to Ptolemy, when he had deserved the king’s friendship by his many services to him, was made governor of Judea and of the neighbouring regions. After Onias, Simon, son of Onias, is held illustrious as high priest of the Jews. Under him Jesus the son of Sirach composed the book of Wisdom, which he called Panaretos, that is, capable of all virtues; and he made mention of Simon in it. After Simon his son Onias is held distinguished, to whom Arius king of the Lacedemonians sent ambassadors. He held the priesthood while Antiochus the Great reigned over Syria and Asia, and Seleucus Philopator his son, until Antiochus Epiphanes. Under this high priest Onias these things were done which are told of Simon, the overseer of the temple, while Seleucus Philopator reigned over Syria and Asia, to whom Antiochus Epiphanes succeeded in the kingdom. But Simon, overseer of the temple of Jerusalem, fleeing to Apollonius, the leader of Phenicia, and promising him many gifts, began to claim the priesthood for himself. When Seleucus heard this, he sent Heliodorus to look to the matter; who, when he had come into Judea, judging unjustly and doing many things wrongly, was frightened by divine signs against him, and returned to Seleucus. But the priest Onias had taken care that Simon should become a fugitive, etc. Finally, this history, according to the rule of tropology, hints that all who, urged on by pride and avarice, presume to defile the sanctification of the Lord and to handle it unworthily with polluted hands, are to be punished by heavenly judgment; for, as the truth attests, the house of God is a house of prayer for all nations, nor is it lawful for anyone to make it a den of thieves. Hence the Psalmist also says: “Holiness becometh thy house, O Lord, unto length of days.” Nor is it lawful to do or store anything there, except to be free for the praises and prayers of God alone. Whence the Lord himself in the Gospel cast out of the temple those who sold and bought in it, and poured out the money of the moneychangers, and overthrew the chairs of them that sold doves. And after this was done he was daily teaching in the temple. According to allegory, however, Onias, the great priest of God and keeper of the figurative temple, signifies the Lord the Saviour, who was made by God the Father a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedech, and is keeper and inhabitant of the temple of the true God, which is the Church; which the name of Onias seems sufficiently to express. For Onias is interpreted the sorrow of the Lord, or the Lord of sorrow; and who can be better called the sorrowing Lord than our redeemer, of whom it is said through Isaias: “We have seen him, and there was no sightliness, that we should be desirous of him: despised, and the most abject of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity. Surely he hath borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows.” Heliodorus, however, the invader or plunderer of the treasury of the Lord, signifies pagans, or Jews, or even heretics, who without reverence for God wish to abuse his gifts and turn them to a wicked act. For pagans invade the treasure of the temple of God when they strive to destroy the faith and worship of Christ. The Jews invade when they desire to confound the Christian religion with the ceremonies of the old law. Heretics also invade when they long to corrupt the truth of the gospel and the sincerity of the law of God with false doctrines. But when Onias prayed, there came down a terrible horseman, having golden armour: he, namely, of whom John wrote in his Apocalypse, saying: “I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse; and he that sat upon him was called faithful and true, and with justice doth he judge. And his eyes were as a flame of fire, and on his head were many diadems, and he had a name written, which no man knoweth but himself. And he was clothed with a garment sprinkled with blood; and his name is called the Word of God.” To the members of Christ who pray, he himself brings help, “who is the way, the truth, and the life”; both to overcome enemies and to terrify the presumptions of the wicked: his horse was white, because his Nativity was incorrupt; and his garment bloody, because the death of his flesh was innocent; and he himself terrible, because exceedingly wonderful, and a most just judge. He was adorned with the best coverings, because he shines most brightly with the beauty of all virtues; his armour was golden, because his works are wonderful. For by his gift his Church has “the shield of faith,” the breastplate of justice, “the helmet of salvation, the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God.” With these arms he himself daily fights in his members against his enemies. This horseman, namely, with violence struck Heliodorus with his front hooves, because the sacrament of the incarnation overthrows all enemies, that is, pagans, Jews, and heretics, so that, confounded, they may at some time desist from the savagery of their crimes.
3.26: **“Moreover there appeared two other young men beautiful and strong, bright and glorious, and in comely apparel: who stood by him, on either side, and scourged him without ceasing with many stripes.”** — Those two young men, then, who appeared with the horseman himself, “beautiful and strong, bright and glorious, and in comely apparel, who stood by Onias on either side, and scourged Heliodorus without ceasing with many stripes,” signify the teachers of both testaments, who, standing around the incarnation of Christ, comely in the strength of faith and good works, best in the glory of miracles, and most beautiful in the apparel of holy knowledge and wisdom, existing at various times, scourge by their preachings the insensibility of the wicked, and compel them to fall to the ground. And so it will come about that he who proudly attacked before the temple appears powerless by the correction of discipline, “for there is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord,” because “whatsoever the Lord hath pleased he hath done, in heaven, in earth, in the sea, and in all the deeps,” and there is none who can resist his will; he is the Lord of all. But that Onias, offering a saving victim for the man’s health, saved Heliodorus himself, wrapped round with great darkness, signifies that the mercy of our Redeemer often confers the benefit of conversion on the ungrateful and undeserving, so that by the grace of him who offered himself a saving victim for the sins of the world they may be rescued from their errors, and willingly, from the power of Satan, in whose wickedness they were once captives, they may according to his will give thanks to their Redeemer, and proclaim his praise in all the earth.

4.7:
**“But after the death of Seleucus, when Antiochus, who was called the Illustrious, had taken possession of the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias ambitiously sought the high priesthood:”**
• But after Seleucus, etc. Of this Josephus relates thus. About the same time, Onias the chief of the priests having died, Antiochus conferred the chief priesthood on his brother. For the son whom Onias had left was still an infant. But we shall show in its proper place the particulars which seem to belong to this boy. But from Jesus, for he was the brother of Onias, the king in anger took away the chief priesthood, and gave it to his younger brother, named Onias. For Simon had these three sons, to whom the chief priesthood, as we said before, came. And Jesus indeed named himself Jason, but Onias was named Menelaus. Therefore Jesus, the chief of the priests, first stirred up sedition against Menelaus, and the multitude of the people being divided into two, they stood on the side of Menelaus the son of Tobias, but the greater part of the people helped Jason. Whence Menelaus and the sons of Thobias, in distress, went away to Antiochus, making known to him that they wished to abandon the laws of their fathers and their way of life, and to observe the customs of the Greeks. They asked him therefore to permit them to build a gymnasium at Jerusalem. And when he had granted it, they concealed their circumcision, so that in nakedness they might not appear unlike the Greeks. And leaving all the other things which their ancestral custom imposed on them, they followed the deeds and rites of other nations. So far Josephus.
• But I wonder how, Onias being dead, Antiochus is said to have given the priesthood to the brother of Jason, since this History does not agree with this narration, as will be shown in what follows. Finally, Antiochus Epiphanes, when he had withdrawn by order of the senate from the region of the Ptolemies, which he had suddenly invaded, came to Judea, and there handed over the pontificate to Jesus, who is also Jason, the brother of Onias; and when he had afterwards been expelled, he gave him as successor Onias, surnamed Menelaus. And so, sedition having arisen among the chiefs on account of the dignity of the priesthood, the seeds of great miseries sprang up. This faction, then, of the proud and of transgressors of the law of God brings us no allegory useful for edification. But, alas, in this time Jason has found many imitators of his crime: those who are set forth in the Church of the people of God, and by the blood of his only-begotten Son the Redeemer, having abandoned the teaching of the Gospel and true religion, fly from the worship of the one God, which is commended and made known there, to secret idolatry by depraved morals; while through ambition for money and the riches of the present life, leading a luxurious life, detestable to God, and heeding the favour of flatterers, they draw many with them to perdition. These indeed, according to the Apostle, “profess that they know God, but in their works they deny him.” For they are not content with moderate food and clothing. But “they that will become rich, fall into temptation, and into the snare of the devil, and into many unprofitable and hurtful desires, which drown men into destruction and perdition. For the desire of money is the root of all evils; which some coveting have erred from the faith, and have entangled themselves in many sorrows.”
4.18: **“Now when the game that was used every fifth year was kept at Tyre, the king being present,”** — Now when the game that was used every fifth year, etc. While Ozias, who is also Azarias, the leprous king, reigned in Judea, and Phacea in Jerusalem, and Eschylus among the Athenians, and Aemulius among the Latins, in the second year of Eschylus, judge of the Athenians, the first Olympiad was held, in which Choreb of Elis was victor. The men of Elis hold the contest every fifth year, four years having been completed in between, in which four yearly rulers are appointed; this Olympiad Iphitus, son of Praxonides, or of Aemon, first instituted. From this time the Greek history of times is believed true; for before this they brought forth differing opinions, as each one thought good. For it is described that Antiochus then celebrated this game of the fifth year at Tyre, and the things that are afterwards recorded of Jason and Menelaus were done later. Jason indeed had taken captive his own brother, that is, Onias the elder, son of Simon. By Menelaus, that is, the younger Onias, who had two names, he was accused before the king, and deceived, and driven out a fugitive into the country of the Ammonites. Menelaus however obtained the principality, but did nothing about the money promised to the king for the priesthood; for which cause he too was likewise removed from the priesthood, Lysimachus succeeding him. While he held the priesthood, Menelaus, Antiochus being absent, thinking he had got a convenient time on account of quelling the Tarsians and Mallotes, stole certain vessels of gold from the temple and gave them to Andronicus the officer, whom the king had left to guard the region. Whence Onias the elder, his brother, whom Jason had taken captive, moved, rebuked Menelaus for the impiety committed, keeping himself in a safe place at Antioch beside Daphne. Whence Menelaus, going to Andronicus, asked him to kill Onias. And when he had come to Onias, and given his right hand with an oath, although Onias was suspicious of him, and had persuaded him to come forth from the sanctuary, he at once slew him, not fearing justice; for which cause not only the Jews but other nations also were indignant, and took it grievously, at the unjust death of so great a man. Hence the Jews likewise, and the Greeks, went to the king when he returned from the places of Cilicia, revealing what had been done. Antiochus, moved by this even to the shedding of tears, remembering the sobriety and modesty of the dead man, and inflamed in mind, ordered Andronicus, stripped of his purple, to be led about through the whole city, and in the same place where he had committed the impiety against Onias, the sacrilegious man to be deprived of life, the Lord repaying him a fitting punishment. For many sacrileges having been committed in the temple by Lysimachus at the counsel of Menelaus, and the rumour spread abroad, a multitude was gathered against Lysimachus. Some seized stones, others strong clubs, and some threw ashes at Lysimachus; and many indeed were wounded, some also struck down, and all were turned to flight; and the sacrilegious man himself they killed beside the treasury. Concerning these things, therefore, judgment began to be agitated against Menelaus. And when the king had come to Tyre, three men sent by the elders brought the matter before him. And when Menelaus was being overcome, he promised Ptolemy much money to persuade the king. And so Ptolemy, going to the king, who was placed in a certain court as if to take the air, brought him off his opinion; and Menelaus, guilty of all malice, he acquitted of the charges, but the wretched men, who even if they had pleaded their cause before the Scythians would have been judged innocent, he condemned to death.

5.1: **“At the same time”** — Portents, therefore, sometimes portend prosperity, and sometimes prefigure adversity; but always according to what the supreme judge decides is fitting for each thing and time. Nor is it a wonder that in the times of the Machabees horsemen in golden robes, and cohorts armed with spears, were seen running through the air, and the gleaming splendour of golden arms foretold adversity to come and a disaster about to fall on the Jews; since before the overthrow of Jerusalem, under Vespasian and Titus, as Josephus testifies, we have learned that a star shining like a sword in every respect hung over the city from above, and moreover a comet burning with deadly flames was seen throughout the whole year. But before the time of the destruction and of the war, when the people were gathering for the feast of unleavened bread, on the eighth day of the month Antiochus, which is April, at the ninth hour of the night, so great a brightness of light surrounded the altar and the temple that all thought it had become the brightest day; and it lasted for half an hour. This seemed favourable to the unskilled and ignorant; but the deadly portent did not escape those learned in the law and all the upright teachers. At the same feast also a heifer, brought to the sacrifices and standing at the altars, gave birth to a lamb in the very hands of the ministers. Moreover the door of the inner temple, which faced east, though it was covered with bronze as usual, and so of immense weight that it was scarcely closed by twenty men pushing with utmost effort, and was held fast, secured with iron bars and bolts and with bars sunk deep, suddenly at the sixth hour of the night appeared opened of its own accord. Moreover, when the feast day had passed, some days after, on the twenty-first day of the month Artemisius, which is called May among us, a prodigious sight appeared, almost beyond belief, which would truly have been thought false, had not the destruction that followed their evils confirmed the faith of hidden things. For near sunset chariots and four-horse teams were seen carried through the air over the whole region, and cohorts of armed men mingling with the clouds, and cities encircled by unexpected armies. Likewise on another feast day, which is called Pentecost, when the priests entered the temple by night to fulfil the ministries as usual, they first perceived certain movements and noises, then heard voices beneath them saying: Let us depart hence. Another still more terrible thing is added. For a certain Jesus, son of Ananias, a plebeian and a rustic, four years before the war, when the city was still in peace and abundance, at the feast of tabernacles suddenly began to cry out: A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice over Jerusalem and over the temple, a voice over bridegrooms and over brides, a voice over the people. And ceaselessly, day and night, going about through all the streets, he cried this, until some of the chief men of the people, moved with indignation as at an ill omen, seized the man and afflicted him with many blows. But he, saying nothing at all for himself, and not even entreating those who stood about, repeated the same words with equal obstinacy and cry. Then the princes, understanding, as was the case, that there was something more than human in the man, brought him to the Roman judge, before whom, torn with scourges to the very bones, he shed neither prayers nor tears; but uttering the same voice piteously and with a kind of wailing, he pronounced it at nearly every word, adding also this: Woe, woe to Jerusalem. The wretched city therefore endured all these prodigies because always, according to the testimony of the lawgiver, it acted in sedition against the Lord, and, ungrateful for his benefits, treated insultingly and killed the servants of the supreme father of the family who were sent to it by him. And last of all, killing the heir himself, they cast him out of the camp. Whence the Lord himself in the Gospel, rebuking the unbelieving city, says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered together thy children, as the hen doth gather her chickens under her wings, and thou wouldest not? Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate.” For this was foretold of old, and this was fulfilled in later times, that the most savage murderers should receive the fitting reward of their guilt, so that some were killed by famine, some slain, and the captives were led by the enemies into all parts of the world. And so was fulfilled that word of Jeremias, who prophesied of the same nation and city, saying: “Juda hath removed her dwelling place because of her affliction, and the greatness of her bondage: she hath dwelt among the nations, and she hath found no rest: all her persecutors have taken her in the midst of straits. The ways of Sion mourn, because there are none that come to the solemn feast: all her gates are broken down: her priests sigh: her virgins are in affliction, and she is oppressed with bitterness.”
5.5: **“Now when there was gone forth a false rumour, as though Antiochus had been dead, Jason taking with him no fewer than a thousand men, suddenly assaulted the city: and though the citizens ran together to the wall, the city at length was taken, and Menelaus fled into the castle.”** — But when a false rumour had gone forth that Antiochus had departed this life, Jason, taking with him no fewer than a thousand men, suddenly assaulted the city; and as the citizens ran together to the wall, at last, the city being seized, Menelaus fled into the castle.
