After these he appeared again for forty days; because he had been dead forty hours, he confirms for forty days that he lives; and by forty can be understood a type of the present age, in which Christ dwells in the Church; or because man, made up of four elements, is instructed against transgression of the decalogue.
**“appearing to them”** — to appear is said of that which is unusual.
**“appearing”** — Bede. To build up faith in his resurrection, appearing alive to the apostles more often after the resurrection, he also takes food and offers his flesh to be touched. But through the mystery of this dwelling with them he signifies that he will fulfil what he had promised: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world.” This number signifies temporal life, because after we have been “buried together with Christ by baptism into death,” as if the Red Sea had been crossed, we have need of a guide in this wilderness who may lead us to the heavens; and, rewarding with the denarius of his image, he would reward with the presence of the Holy Spirit as with the true rest of the jubilee.
**“and speaking”** — which was a sign of truth, namely, the things he had been accustomed to say to them before.
**“of the kingdom of God.”** — namely, of the gospel, the Church, and the heavenly kingdom, which are all one kingdom.
1.4:
**“eating together”** — He announces signs of a true body, because it is proved not by one bodily sense, but by sight, hearing, touch, by appearing, speaking, and eating together.
**“he commanded them, that they should not depart from Jerusalem”**
• “But you, sit you here in the city, until you be endued with power from on high.”
• The Church does not depart from the vision of eternal peace.
**“but should wait for the promise of the Father”** — for the testing of faith, obedience and patience
**“the promise”** — Which he promised through Joel, as is had in what follows; and although promised by Christ, it will nevertheless be fulfilled by the Father. Or it is said to be of the Father, because it is promised in his Word, that is, in Christ.
**“which you have heard (saith he) by my mouth.”** — not of the apostles or of others, or not of the Father, who was not incarnate
1.5:
**“For John”**
• therefore you need the promise of the Spirit, because in the baptism of John the Spirit was not given
• Bede. When the Lord said that John baptized with water, he did not add “but you will baptize,” but “you shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost,” because neither the apostles nor their followers in the Church to this day are able to baptize otherwise than in water; but when the name of Christ is invoked, the inward power of the Holy Spirit purifies the souls and bodies of the baptized, which did not happen in John’s baptism.
• Bede. Baptism is given in two natures, bodily namely and spiritual, because the man who is baptized consists of two, namely body and soul; yet it is one baptism, as there is one man.
• Bede. Baptism is an anointing; whence in some books it is found thus: John anointed you with water; you shall be anointed with the Holy Spirit. But the baptism of the Lord, which is in the Holy Spirit, looks not only to that time at which the apostles and the other believers of that time were baptized with water for remission, the grace of the Spirit having been commanded by the Lord; but also to that in which, the Lord sending the Spirit, they received him more fully. Whoever even now has received baptism for remission is baptized in the Spirit, by whose gift, his sins being loosed, he is helped to advance even in good.
**“indeed baptized”** — many or you
**“with water,”** — alone, without the Spirit
**“But you shall be baptized”** — Augustine. When Peter denied, the apostles had not been baptized, not with water but with the Spirit; for after the resurrection it was said: “You shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost,” for they were not yet confirmed by the resurrection of Christ and the sending of the Spirit. As circumcision was not necessary for the just before it was commanded to Abraham and his posterity, so after the sacrament of the New Testament, that is, baptism, was given in place of circumcision by the Lord saying: “Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost,” etc. It is certain that no one belongs to the body of Christ unless baptized, except those to whom martyrdom is reckoned for baptism. Likewise it is written when Paul was baptized, and it is not written when the other apostles were baptized; but we must understand that they were baptized because of that: “Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost,” etc.
**“but you shall be baptized”**
• Bede. They had not yet been baptized, either with John’s baptism, or with the baptism not of water but of the Holy Spirit, whom we understand to be baptized; or, what is more credible, with Christ’s baptism. For it was fitting that they should be baptized who were to baptize others.
• Rabanus. Here it is promised that the baptism of the apostles would surpass the baptism of John. Those who were baptized by John were baptized only with water, as is clear in Andrew and in the other disciple. To Peter also it was said: “He that is washed needeth not but to wash his feet”; afterwards their faith was confirmed by Christ, whose feet he also washed at the supper, and to whom he gave his body; after the resurrection he breathed the Spirit on them; on the day of the ascension he blessed them; afterwards he sent the Spirit.
**“with the Holy Ghost, not many days hence.”** — A time is interposed to prove their obedience. The days were not many, because of the speed of salvation for the believers to whom they were to preach.
1.6:
**“They therefore”** — Continuing from 'he commanded them, etc.': those who had come together
**“who were come together”** — they were present at his ascension
**“asked him, saying:”** — A servant utters this.
**“Lord, wilt thou at this time”** — after your resurrection, the Spirit coming upon them
**“Lord, wilt thou”** — Bede. Because appearing to them he had spoken of the kingdom of God and had promised the coming of the Holy Spirit, therefore they now ask about the kingdom of God, whether it is to be restored at the present coming of the Spirit or reserved for the saints in the future. For the carnal, the resurrection of Christ being fulfilled, believed that the kingdom of Israel would come quickly, according to that: “But we hoped that it was he that should have redeemed Israel.”
**“restore again the kingdom”**
• you bring in the day of judgment and the kingdom of the true Israel
• temporal or spiritual, which is clear in the Greek
**“to Israel?”**
• because both were possessed earlier and afterwards lost
• not of this but to this Israel
• it hints that the spiritual kingdom had been promised by the prophets
1.7:
**“But he said to them: It is not for you to know”**
• that is, it is not for men to know the day of judgment, so that, as if held in suspense, they always await judgment
• But when he says, 'It is not yours to know the times,' he shows that he himself knows, to whom belong all the things that are the Father’s; but it is not expedient for them to know, so they should live as though to be judged every day.
**“It is not for you to know”** — He does not say 'it will not be', but 'it is not', noting that they are still weak and therefore not yet fit for the secret.
**“the times or moments”** — the number of times or moments, up to the end of the age
**“which the Father”** — Bede. He says: the time of that kingdom is so secret that it lies open only to the knowledge of the Father; but you shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit, so that what you cannot do because of the weakness of the flesh, you may be able to do by the power of the Holy Spirit.
**“hath put in his own power:”** — he will not put; because God sees as past whatever he wills to be future
**“in his own power”** — Bede. He said this excusably, as true man; yet the power of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit is one; the Son’s power is also the Father’s power.
1.8:
**“But you shall receive the power”**
• because they are weak
• in place of knowledge of signs, confidence
**“But you shall receive”** — The knowledge of times is taken away, but the divine help they need is applied; in this way, when something is taken from children, something else is given so that they are not utterly saddened.
**“the Holy Ghost coming”**
• The Holy Ghost comes upon you, because the higher is poured into the lower nature, according to that: “The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee.”
• You need not know that, because the power of the Spirit, which is more necessary, will come upon you.
• who will teach you
• Of the Holy Ghost coming upon you, etc. Bede. When the Spirit comes upon you, he will bring not the kingdom of Israel, or the kingdom of God in Israel, as you suppose, but will grant you the power of bearing witness of me; and the time of that kingdom is so far off that first the fame of the gospel will run through not only Jerusalem but all the borders of Judea and Samaria, and even the ends of the world round about.
**“upon you”** — inwardly
**“and you shall be witnesses unto me”**
• by word and example, or by signs
• of the resurrection
**“in Jerusalem”**
• by the vision of peace
• In Jerusalem, and in all Judea, etc. Rabanus. The order of the places’ names is kept in sequence. Jerusalem is followed by the neighbouring province of Judea, to which Samaria is joined by position; from there the whole earth’s fellowship is introduced.
**“In Jerusalem”** — Rabanus. Mystically: he foretold that they would preach in the vision of peace, in the confession of true faith, in the keeping of God’s commandments, and among those who have made themselves strangers to the land; through whom, like the spokes of wheels from the middle of the earth, where he wrought salvation, spiritual grace and saving doctrine flowed down through the whole world.
**“and in all Judea”** — by confession
**“and Samaria”** — by keeping the commandments of God
**“even to the uttermost part of the earth.”**
• to those who are estranged from earthly things
• from this, he commanded that they should not leave Jerusalem
1.9:
**“And when he had said these things”**
• Otherwise Mark relates, saying: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven.” But because Luke added it more significantly, “when he had said these things, he was raised up,” he shows that the Lord ascended into heaven when those discourses which he had recounted were finished.
• Bede. In the Greek it is thus: “And when they were beholding him going up to heaven,” that is, they gazed toward heaven whither he was going; whence the angels say to them: “Why stand you looking up to heaven?” And that they beheld him going into heaven is shown there: “shall so come, as you have seen him going into heaven.”
• Rabanus. Because they were to announce good things and to signify the joy of the angels at the Saviour’s ascension, who rejoice in the fellowship of human nature.
• Rabanus. Creation everywhere obeys its Creator: the stars announce him being born, suffer with him suffering, the clouds received him ascending, and will accompany him returning to judgment.
• Bede. The angels appear for two reasons: namely, to console the sadness of the ascension by recalling his return, and to show that he truly went into heaven, and not as if into heaven, as with Elijah.
**“he was raised up”** — Rabanus. He was raised up, and received: they look to the weakness of the flesh; or this is to be referred to the power of the divinity; likewise also what follows, as he goes into heaven, according to what he says: “No man hath ascended into heaven, but he that descended from heaven.”
1.10:
**“while they looked on”** — so that those who are witnesses of the one rising may also be witnesses of the one ascending
**“And while they were beholding him going up to heaven”** — by his divinity, or by the cloud; for before this the earthly body had not received heaven
**“him going up, behold two men”** — chiefly the sex and number of the witnesses is shown
**“stood by them in white garments”** — The angels are said to stand in white because they are free from weakness, fault and death.
**“in white garments”** — Bede. White garments suit exaltation, and therefore at the ascension the angels appear in white garments. For he who appeared at the nativity as a lowly God is shown at the ascension as a man exalted. The places also agree: since the man was born in a lowly city, he returned to the heavens from a lofty mountain.
1.11:
**“Who also said: Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven?”** — Earlier it had been said to sit in the city; but here they stand looking up to heaven, as though hoping he would return suddenly.
**“shall so come”** — Bede. He will come to judge in the same nature in which he came to be judged. For if he received immortality, he did not lose his nature, whose eternal glory, shown beforehand to three disciples on the mountain, will be seen by all the saints after the judgment, when the impious man shall be taken away that he may not see the glory of God.
**“Sulpicius”** — That place in which the feet of Christ ascending stood could not be joined to the pavement with the rest of the paved part, rejecting whatever was applied to it, the marbles being thrown out into the faces of those who set them in. This is a proof of the dust trodden by him, that the footprints are seen impressed, and the earth still keeps the same appearance, as if the footprints were pressed in.
**“as you have seen him going into heaven.”**
• in the same form and substance of flesh
• the same himself, in the same body, with angels and men present
• You will see him coming as you have seen him going; for he will come openly.
1.12:
**“Then”** — Having heard this, which the two men said
**“they returned to Jerusalem”**
• because they had gone out of Jerusalem to the Mount of Olives; but they returned, so as to sit in Jerusalem, after that rebuke: “Why stand you looking up to heaven?”
• Then they returned, etc. Rabanus. The return of the apostles from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem signifies the Church, which, ascending from the active life to the contemplative, descends again into the active way of life. For the Mount of Olives was called by the ancients the mount of three lights: namely, of the lamp shining forth from the temple, and of the sun rising on the other side, and of the oil, the natural light on the mountain itself; which three agree with perfection: on account of the light of the divine Word shining from the Church, on account of the splendor of the sun of justice, on account of the brightness of a pure conscience.
**“Mystically.”** — Bede. He who beholds the glory of Christ ascending, enriched by the promise of the Holy Spirit, enters the city of peace on a sabbath journey; and there will be a sabbath in place of a sabbath, because having ceased from evil, he will rest in heaven.
**“from the mount that is called Olivet”** — Olivet is said to mean a multitude of olive trees
**“which is nigh Jerusalem, within a sabbath day's journey.”**
• it is distant from Jerusalem by the space of a mile
• a thousand paces; whose authority this is, is unknown
1.13:
**“And when they were come in”** — In the Greek it is put thus: When they had entered the city, they went up into the upper room where Peter etc. were staying. In the Greek the order of the names is this: Peter and Andrew, James and John, Simon Zelotes and Jude of James.
**“they went up into an upper room”**
• the city they went up into the upper room, that is, the high house, as if to meet the Holy Spirit. The upper room is a type of perfection, in which the Spirit is to be awaited.
• Rabanus. The upper room is called the third storey, a figure of charity built upon faith and hope: “For the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost.”
**“upper room”** — Bede. It is a place upstairs, signifying that those lifted from the earth ascend to the heights of knowledge and virtue.
**“where abode”** — perseverance of perfection, which earns the Spirit
**“Peter”** — acknowledging
**“and John”**
• the grace of God
• Rabanus. The list of the apostles is given so that no false men be received beyond these, and the places of each are arranged by the distinct degrees of merit.
• Rabanus. These are the twelve sons of Jacob, the twelve fountains of the desert which Israel found in Elim, the twelve loaves of proposition, the twelve stones on the pontiff’s garment, the twelve loaves of proposition, the twelve stones of the altar, the twelve stones he raises from the Jordan, the twelve oxen under the molten sea, the twelve stars in the crown of the spouse, the twelve foundations, the twelve gates, the twelve months of the year, the twelve hours, the twelve fruits of the tree of life.
**“Peter and John”** — Peter is put first, because he is prince and shepherd. Peter and John are rightly put first, who ran together to the tomb, because they loved more than the others: the first, if it is lawful to say so, loved more than the rest; Jesus loved the other very much.
**“James”**
• supplanter
• this one, called the Lord’s brother, is the son of Mary, his mother’s sister, who is called Mary of Cleophas, from his father or family
**“and Andrew”** — manly, a Greek name
**“Philip”** — mouth of a lamp or of lamps
**“and Thomas”** — abyss, or twin; in Greek Didymus, either because he was born a twin or because he was a twin, bearing the likeness of the Saviour’s image
**“Bartholomew”**
• a Syrian name
• son of one suspending the waters, that is, the clouds, which pertains to the flesh of the Saviour
**“and Matthew”** — given
**“of Alpheus”** — Alpheus: learned, a fugitive, or a thousandth
**“and Simon Zelotes”**
• Simon Zelotes, cousin of the Saviour, because Hegesippus testifies that Cleophas, his father, was the brother of Joseph
• Rabanus. When the son of perdition perished, the number of the apostles remained incomplete; for according to the likeness of the moon the Church waxes and wanes, but the old things pass away and new things come.
**“Zelotes”** — Bede. Zelotes is called Cananaean in Hebrew. Cana is interpreted as ‘zeal’; it is a village where the Lord turned water into wine. He afterwards, after James his brother, governed the Church of Jerusalem.
**“and Jude the brother of James.”** — Jude, brother of James, son of Alpheus, who is also called Thaddeus and Lebbeus, and a little heart, a worshipper of his own heart and of others
1.14:
**“All these were persevering”** — to have begun is not virtue but to have finished
**“with one mind”** — they dwell in the house with one manner of life
**“in prayer”** — Bede. Those who await the Spirit persevere of one mind: “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful”; and therefore whoever wishes to receive him should persevere in prayers and in brotherly charity, because prayer earns the help of God.
**“with the women”** — whom they had in their company, as Jesus also had them
**“and Mary the mother of Jesus”**
• she is designated by her proper name as more worthy than the others, because she is a virgin and a mother
• Of Mary or Jesus. Bede. This is set down distinctly in Greek. For Luke took care to show that the brethren of the Lord at that time were sharers in the faith, of whom it was said before the passion: “For neither did his brethren believe in him.”
**“Mary the mother”** — Rabanus. The virgin is distinguished from the women, though sometimes the word woman is used not of corruption but of sex. Behold, the beginning of the newborn Church is adorned with the flower of virginity.
1.15:
**“In those days”** — when the apostles were in the upper room
**“rising up”** — in the flesh, because of the crowd; in spirit, for the advancement of merit; or he is said to rise up who first fell by denying.
**“Peter in the midst of the brethren, said:”**
• The shepherd speaks for the sheep.
• a parenthesis, that is, between.
• Rabanus. Jesus is said to have stood in the midst, as if condescending in common compassion; this example is to be taken by the pastors of the Church.
**“in the midst of the brethren”** — Of the brethren, that is, of the sons of God, of whom one is the Father in heaven; although that company also had the four ways in which men are called brethren: by nature, Peter the brother of Andrew, and John of James, and Jude of the other James; by nation, all were Israelites and were called Jews; by kinship, those also who were called brethren of the Lord or of Mary were brethren to one another; by carnal affection also, all are born of one Adam. But most of all, brethren according to the grace of regeneration.
*Rabanus:* This number, one hundred and twenty, agrees with the age of Moses, so that as under this number, Moses having died, Josue succeeded, who led the people into the promised land, so in the Church the headship of Christ succeeded the old law, leading the true Israel to the kingdom of heaven. This number also grows from one up to fifteen, having seven and eight, the type of the new and the old law. For it was fitting that the mystery which the lawgiver showed in years, the preachers of grace should signify by number.
**“now the number of persons together was about an hundred and twenty:”**
• the reckoning is set down of those not yet made gods, because the Spirit, who makes men gods, had not yet come.
• in place and in will.
• he gives this according to the custom of those who count, not because the Spirit doubted the number.
1.16:
**“Men, brethren,”** — whose office is to examine the causes of individuals.
**“Men, brethren”** — Bede. Peter feared to remain at the number eleven. For every sin pertains to eleven; for he who acts perversely transgresses the precepts of the decalogue; and therefore the number of the apostles was restored to twelve, so that through the two parts of seven (for three times four are twelve) the grace which they preached might be kept even in the number.
**“must needs”** — it is necessary, or fitting.
**“the scripture ... be fulfilled”** — because it has already begun, it ought not to remain half-finished.
**“which the Holy Ghost spoke before”** — that the complete number of the apostles be prepared by the Holy Spirit.
**“by the mouth of David”** — speaking in the prophet; for the sentence was not of man but of the Holy Spirit.
**“concerning Judas, who was the leader of them that apprehended Jesus:”** — the guide of them to the taking, or of the kiss to betraying.
1.17:
**“Who was numbered with us”** — made equal in number only, not in merit.
**“and had obtained”** — God judging not according to foreknowledge.
**“part”** — the apostleship.
**“of this ministry.”** — of teaching and of signs; or he calls the ministry the leadership of those who seized Jesus.
1.18:
**“And he indeed hath possessed a field”**
• he caused it to be possessed by others.
• Rabanus. Some ridiculously explain the field possessed by Judas as hell. Others think he possessed that field because he was buried in it with strangers.
• Bede. The betrayer found a punishment worthy of himself when he killed with a noose the throat from which the traitor’s voice had gone out. He also sought a fitting place of destruction, so that he who had betrayed the Lord of men and angels, hating heaven and earth, as if to be joined with the spirits of the air, after the example of Achitophel and Absalom, should perish in the midst of the air. A fitting end also followed his death, that the bowels which had conceived the betrayal should fall burst and be poured out into the air; death being a punishment like to the fraud, or betrayal, or fault.
**“hath possessed a field”** — Rabanus. Not that he possessed a field, but that the price of the field had been his, who sold the Lord of life. Having lost the land of the living, he possesses the field of blood and of death, the eternal memory of his crime and of his name; for Judas did not possess the potter’s field bought with the price of blood, since he at once punished the crime of betrayal in himself; but “possessed” is said, that is, he caused it to be possessed.
**“of the reward of iniquity”** — of his own.
**“bowels”** — Rabanus. The seat of deceit, burst asunder by so great a crime, could not hold itself together. Fittingly, moreover, the bowels are poured out through the seat of guile, not through the place of the kiss, that is, the mouth with which he kissed Jesus, though with a false exterior, but through the other, in which the poison of hidden malice lay.
1.19:
**“And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem”** — he possessed it, so that it was called; or it became known, so that it was called.
**“So that ... was called”** — Rabanus. This, as some say, Luke inserts into Peter’s speech, because, writing in Greek, he gives the name of the field among the Hebrews and sets down the interpretation of that name in the Greek tongue. Or Peter, in the course of his speech, mentioned the name of that field in the speech of Jerusalem, and transferred it into the Galilean way of speaking. For although the Jews and the Galileans were of the same language, yet they differ not a little in speech. Or many think that the Latin interpreter added this. Above he had said that the Scripture must be fulfilled, but the sentence hangs, not yet ended up to this point: “It is written in the book of Psalms,” etc.
**“the same field ... in their tongue”** — of the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
**“their”** — Rabanus. Of those dwelling in Jerusalem, because even if both spoke Hebrew, yet the peculiarity of the language of the Jerusalemites differed from that of the Galileans, of whom the apostles also were; which is shown in the passion of the Lord, where Peter too, unwilling, was betrayed by his speech as being a Galilean.
**“Haceldama”** — It is Syriac.
1.20:
**“For it is written in the book of Psalms”** — By this it is shown that there is one book of Psalms, not five.
**“Let their habitation become”** — These verses are clear, because Judas, having received the penalty of his betrayal and gone away into hell, forsook the dwelling of human fellowship; and with Matthias taking his place, the full number of the apostles was restored.
**“desolate”** — Bede. Until the chosen one, Matthias, is taken in his place, or let it not be Judas himself who dwells in it, but another be taken in his place, because he was judged unworthy of penance.
**“and let there be none to dwell therein”**
• that is, let his name be blotted out from the number of the twelve apostles, both in the present and in the future.
• dwelling.
• Psalm 68.
**“And his bishopric”**
• an observation, or over-watching; for a bishop is a watcher or overseer.
• Psalm 108.
**“let another take”** — That is, another from the multitude of disciples; or another in comparison with Judas; the other of the two for whom lots were cast.
1.21:
**“must”** — because the prophetic Spirit foretold it.
**“of these men”** — not women: because the sex is weaker for travelling, the person more modest for preaching, and the authority lower for bearing witness.
**“who have companied with us”** — of these men, not of others who did not see; for a witness is not fit who was not present at what is to be witnessed.
**“all the time”** — not from half the span of time.
**“came in and went out”**
• that is, of his humanity.
• he was always in the entering and going out of places, he who preached to many cities, not having where to lay his head; or he entered, beginning from the baptism of John, and went out on the day he was taken up.
**“among us”** — with us present; or among men.
**“the Lord Jesus”**
• that is, our Lord.
• a good and faithful servant, who, as before, as he was accustomed, now also after the ascension professes Christ his Lord.
1.22:
**“Beginning from the baptism of John”** — because after the baptism of John he began to work and to teach.
**“until the day wherein he was taken up from us”** — this is of power.
**“a witness with us of his resurrection”** — because he had said of the resurrection: “and you shall be witnesses unto me.”
1.23:
**“And they appointed two”**
• for the love that is twofold.
• from equal examples they knew the two to be equals, so that they did not doubt they were to be preferred to the rest; but to prefer one to the other was not of men but of God.
• Bede. Clement reports that these two, who were appointed to the lot of the apostleship, were of the number of the seventy disciples.
**“Joseph, called Barsabas”**
• son of rest.
• or ‘Barnabas’; this is said by anticipation, because the reason for the name is shown in what follows.
**“who was surnamed”** — Bede. He lingers on the praise of Barnabas: because Matthias has for his praise that he is chosen by lot, Barnabas’s praise is heaped up, lest he should seem to be rejected as unworthy; which was made clear afterwards, because he was ordained apostle of the Gentiles with Paul, reserved for that office.
**“Justus”**
• he was of such virtue that even the Romans who knew him called him just.
• Bede. It is either Latin or Hebrew, and it means sparing or lifted up.
**“and Matthias”**
• given, or gift of God.
• Bede. Show whom you have chosen to take the place of this ministry, that he may go to his own place, that is, the apostolic lot.
**“And Matthias”** — Bede. Matthias means given, or gift of God, to whom the gift of the apostleship was conferred by the Lord; or it is interpreted little of God, because by merit he who was just by the praise of men is surpassed by the little one.
1.24:
**“And praying, they said”** — an example of prayer is given to those casting lots, because, as Solomon says: “The lots are cast into the lap, but they are disposed by the Lord.”
**“Thou, Lord, who knowest the hearts of all men”**
• which lie hidden from us, who see only outward works.
• they do not doubt about the knowledge of God, and therefore they seek its showing, so that they too may know what he knows.
**“shew whether of these two thou hast chosen”** — he puts the past tense because he was already chosen in foreknowledge.
**“of these two”** — they know that one of the two is to be chosen, but not which one.
1.25:
**“to take”** — that there may be one of the witnesses
**“the place of this ministry”**
• that is, the ministry and apostleship itself
• apostleship
**“and apostleship, from which Judas hath by transgression fallen”** — he cast himself down by his own impiety
**“that he might go to his own place”**
• to that to which he was condemned beforehand
• hell
1.26:
**“And they gave them lots”** — Bede. Not by this example, or because Jonas was caught out by lot, is lot to be trusted indiscriminately, since, according to Jerome, the privileges of individuals cannot establish the common law.
*Jerome:* On Jonas. From this example we ought not to trust in lots, since privileges cannot make a common law. For as the ass speaks to the condemnation of Balaam, and Caiphas also prophesies without knowing it, so here too the fugitive is caught by lot, not by the power of lots, but by the will of him who rules uncertain things by lot.
*Bede:* it is said to fall from above, because the lot is governed by God
**“And the lot fell”** — Bede. Here he is chosen by lot, lest it differ from the law, in which the high priest was sought by lot, as is said of Zacharias: by lot he rose to put on the incense, because the true priest was to be sought, until he should come who by his own blood entered into the holy of holies, whose sacrifice is offered at the Pasch, but was consummated on the day of Pentecost by the appearing of the Spirit; until the truth should come, it was lawful to practise the figure. Therefore Matthias is ordained before Pentecost, he is sought by lot. The seven deacons, who afterwards were ordained not by lot but by the choice of the disciples, and by the prayer and imposition of hands of the apostles.
**“upon Matthias”** — so that with the number of the twelve apostles made complete, the Spirit might be given perfect; behold, the moon after its loss has received an increase

2.1:
**“And when the days of the Pentecost were accomplished”**
• Genitive.
• The days of Pentecost. Bede. According to the history, the day of Pentecost, that is the fiftieth, was reckoned from the slaying of the lamb, on which the law was given; here, however, it is reckoned not from the Lord’s supper or the day on which he was crucified, but, according to Augustine, from his resurrection, the fiftieth day on which the Spirit was sent, who by his coming consecrated the Lord’s day and showed that the Pasch was to be celebrated on the same day. The Spirit came on a solemn day, that so great a power might have many to approve it and to know the various tongues. And therefore on the fiftieth, because pardon was granted in the jubilee, and through the Spirit sins are remitted, charity is poured out, which covereth a multitude of sins; in the spiritual jubilee the guilty are released, debts are forgiven, exiles return to their country, the lost inheritance is restored, slaves, that is men sold under sin, are freed from the yoke of servitude.
• Rabanus. Pentecost is Greek; in Latin, fifty. And the ancient people kept Pentecost, that is the fiftieth day; for from the day of the slaying of the lamb, by which the children of Israel went out of Egypt, on the fiftieth day the law was given in fire. In the New Testament also, on the fiftieth day from the Pasch of Christ, the Spirit descended upon the apostles, appearing in fire. The law on Mount Sina, the Spirit on Mount Sion. The law on the high place of the mountain, the Spirit is given in the upper room. As the forty days in which after the resurrection he conversed with the disciples signify the present Church, so the fiftieth, on which the Spirit is given, expresses the tenfold number of eternal reward. Fifty is seven times seven, and eight: and the seven belong to the Old Testament, because on the seventh day God rested from his works, and on the seventh day the rest of the sabbath was appointed, and for seven days Israel made unleavened bread. The eight to the new, because Christ rose on the eighth day, or because the precepts of the new law are given in the eight beatitudes, or because the resurrection to come is hoped for on the eighth day. The Holy Spirit therefore, teaching the fulfilment of the two laws, descended on the fiftieth day, which number consists of seven and eight.
**“they were all”** — no one was absent, or because the number of twelve was complete
**“together”** — having one heart and soul
**“in one place”** — not bodily in different places
**“In one place”** — That is, in the upper room, which they had gone up into; for he who desires the Spirit, passing beyond the dwelling of the flesh by contemplation of the mind, tramples it underfoot.
2.2:
**“And suddenly there came”** — the grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow effort, according to that: “The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful”
**“from heaven”** — to signify that the Spirit is heavenly
**“From heaven”** — The Spirit is given that God may be loved. On earth he is given that the neighbour may be loved; for he was given twice after the resurrection, to commend the two precepts of charity.
**“a sound”** — he came with a sound, who had come to teach sounds
**“A sound”** — The sudden event can be called the speaking of tongues, sounding from the mouth of the apostles.
**“as of a mighty wind coming”**
• it is a likeness or confirmation
• At Pentecost the Spirit was sent from heaven, that those who were soon to be divided might receive the knowledge of tongues, lest, going through the world, they should need interpreters; and because God is simple in nature, the Spirit is given once from heaven. But for men, who consist of a twofold substance, namely body and soul, he is to be loved in two ways. On earth he is given twice: first in the efficacy of signs for the healing of bodies, afterwards in the forgiveness of sins for the remedy of souls.
**“Wind”** — Rabanus. Before the passion the Spirit was given to the apostles for the grace of teaching and of healings; after the resurrection Jesus breathed the Spirit on them and said: “Receive ye the Holy Ghost: whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them,” etc. This gift he had before given to Peter alone, but, as is believed, then by anticipation; now it is bestowed on Peter also with the rest, by fulfilment, and power was given of forgiving to those whom he sent to the office of preaching.
**“mighty”** — yet it did not terrify anyone, as in the law
**“Mighty”** — By comparison with what went before, the grace of the apostles is called mighty; or the Spirit came in the likeness of a mighty wind.
**“and it filled the whole house”**
• or the mighty sound filled the house; or the Spirit filled its inhabitants, for the Spirit of the Lord is rich
• Bede. At the giving of the law the people stood far off for fear; here, with the Spirit coming, they were gathered together in one in love.
**“the whole house”** — The Spirit is poured out on those sitting in one house, so that the unity of the Church may be commended, in the upper room, with the third law beginning.
**“where they were sitting”** — in the lofty upper room, signifying perfection
**“sitting”** — That what was said to them might be fulfilled: “Sit you here in the city.” Sitting is a sign of humility and steadiness, by which a seat is prepared for the Holy Spirit, who rests upon the humble.
*Gregory:* The Spirit appeared in fire, but by himself he spoke inwardly, and neither was the fire God nor that sound, but by what he showed outwardly he expressed what he bore within. For he who made the disciples inwardly inflamed with zeal and instructed by the word showed fiery tongues outwardly. In the sign, therefore, their bodies felt fire with a sound; but by invisible fire and a voice without sound their hearts were taught.
2.3:
**“And there appeared”** — outwardly by fiery colour, inwardly by spiritual inspiration
**“AND THERE APPEARED”** — Bede. The Spirit appeared in fire and tongues, because all whom he fills he makes burn, and makes them speak, burning from themselves and speaking of him; it was also shown that the Church, spread everywhere, was to speak with the voice of all nations.
*Gregory:* The Holy Spirit appeared over the disciples in fiery tongues, and gave them knowledge of all tongues, signifying that the Church, filled with the Holy Spirit, was to speak in all tongues; here, therefore, humility merited power, pride incurred confusion. The Holy Spirit is shown in fire, because our God is “a consuming fire,” and by him the rust of sin is consumed and the cold of sluggishness is driven out. Teachers have fiery tongues, because by preaching they inflame the hearts of their hearers, and they burn with zeal whom the fervor of the Spirit kindles and punishes by penance.
**“parted tongues”** — the tongues were divided, in the appearance of fire
**“Parted tongues”** — Rabanus. The dispersion of tongues was made at the tower; but what pride scattered, humility gathers again: in pride there is dispersion, in humility there is concord. Behold, the saying of the Lord is fulfilled, who said: “I will not leave you orphans,” but: “I will send the Spirit, the Paraclete,” who, as their advocate, spoke for them in all tongues; he who came in place of the word brought tongues, for the tongue has kinship with the word, so that they cannot be separated from each other; so the Word of the Father, that is, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are inseparable, nay, of one nature.
**“as it were of fire”** — It may be the genitive.
**“As it were of fire”** — The same. The Spirit came in fire, because the Spirit purges, enlightens, kindles, and burns sinners. For fire has four natures: it burns, purges, warms, and enlightens. Likewise the Spirit burns up sins, purges hearts, shakes off sluggishness, and lights up ignorance. Fire also is incorporeal and invisible in its own nature, but is seen when it has taken some body, appearing of different colour because of the materials in which it burns; so the Spirit cannot be seen except through the creatures in which he works.
**“and it sat”** — to the steadfast, a steadfast judge, not to be driven away from them by any distinction. That it sits is royal power, or because it rests in the saints.
**“upon”** — because it was higher.
**“every one of them”** — in each, whole, yet not divided or diverse among many.
2.4:
**“and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost”** — so that it does not receive another spirit, because full vessels do not receive increase.
**“And they began”** — Behold the sign of fullness: the full vessel bursts; fire cannot be hidden in the bosom.
**“to speak with”** — This is to be referred to one or to several.
**“With divers tongues”** — Bede. Because they spoke in all tongues; or, speaking in their own tongue, that is, Hebrew, they were understood by all, as if they were speaking in the proper tongue of each. The same. In Greek, “in others,” according to that of the prophet: “In other tongues and other lips I will speak to this people,” etc.
**“According as the Holy Ghost”** — Bede. The Spirit, dividing to every one according as he will, breathes as much as he wills, where he wills, how he wills, when he wills, and to whom he wills.
**“according as the Holy Ghost”**
• Bede. The apostles could understand and speak all peoples’ tongues in the Holy Spirit, and their words too, by a greater miracle, uttered in whatever language, were equally understood by all who heard.
• Bede. The variety of tongues signifies the gifts of graces. Therefore the Spirit first gave tongues to men, by which human wisdom is taught and learned outside, so as to show that the wisdom of God easily makes men wise.
**“gave them to speak”** — who was the channel of tongues.
2.5:
**“Now there were dwelling at Jerusalem”** — that is, the inhabitants of the city.
**“dwelling Jews, devout men”** — gathered for the festival day.
**“out of every nation”** — Rabanus. As if it were said: wherever born. For the captivity, which took place under Antiochus not many years before, caused Jews to be born among all nations.
2.6:
**“And when this was noised abroad”** — that is, by the sudden sound, or by which the apostles began to speak.
**“were confounded”** — This confusion is set against the confusion of tongues, from which Babel received its name. So the humility of the apostles answers human pride.
2.7:
**“And they were all amazed”** — in heart.
**“all and wondered”** — in face.
**“saying: Behold, are not all these, that speak, Galileans?”** — they are Galileans in speech, dull, distant from the Hebrews.
2.8:
**“And how have we heard, every man our own tongue wherein we were born”**
• that is, of course, their own.
• Bede. The question is whether those who spoke used the different speech of each one’s tongue, that is, so that each of them, speaking now in this tongue, now in another, ran through them all in this way; or rather whether their speech, uttered in any tongue whatever, was understood by each hearer according to his own tongue; so that, when one of the apostles was teaching in the Church and the others were silent, one speech reached the hearing of all, having in itself this power: that, though the hearers were of different nations, each according to his own tongue received the hearing of the one speech uttered by the apostle and grasped its meaning.
**“every man our own tongue”** — Rabanus. All tongues are said to be seventy-two, whence also the disciples of the second order were chosen under this number, so that the number of preachers might agree with the number of tongues.
**“have we heard every man”** — In this was signified that one Church of all nations would speak in tongues.
2.9:
**“Parthians”** — perfectly dividing, or the perfection of dividers.
**“and Medes”** — equal, or measurers.
**“and Elamites”** — The same as Persians.
**“and inhabitants of Mesopotamia”** — Mesopotamia is interpreted surrounding, because it is surrounded by two rivers, Tigris and Euphrates.
**“and Judea”** — confession or glorification.
**“Judea”** — Bede. Judea signifies not the whole nation but a part of it, that is, the tribe of Juda and Benjamin, in distinction, namely, from Samaria, Galilee, Decapolis, and the other regions in that province; all of which, although they speak the Hebrew language, yet each has its own distinct manner of speaking.
**“and Cappadocia”** — hand of the executioner, or of the scout, or hand redeeming for the Lord.
**“Pontus”**
• inclining, or inclination.
• Cappadocia, Pontus, etc. Bede. These five provinces, which are placed after Judea, speak Greek indeed, but from the custom of their country there is a difference in sound; whence the grace in the apostles is wonderful, which not only taught them the difference, but also made in their speech the distinction of the peculiarities in each of the tongues, according to the number of the provinces.
**“and Asia”**
• Lesser.
• lifting up the Lord, or the formation of the Lord, or walking, or raising up or offering, or elation
2.10:
**“Phrygia, and Pamphylia”** — conversion from ruin, or division of those falling
**“Egypt”** — darkness, distress, or tribulation
**“and the parts of Libya”** — coming or entering
**“about Cyrene”** — inheritance or heritage
**“strangers of Rome”** — Bede. In Greek: Romans sojourning, that is, Jews who led a sojourning life at Rome.
**“Jews also”** — of the tribe of Juda
2.11:
**“proselytes”** — Bede. Those were called strangers who, born of the Gentiles, had taken up circumcision and Judaism. Therefore not only those who were Jews by nature had come together from the different parts of the world, but also those who, born of the uncircumcision, had adhered to their rite.
**“Cretes”** — called, or completed by calling
**“and Arabians”** — humble, or western, crafty or deceivers
2.12: **“And they were all astonished, and wondered”** — religious
2.13:
**“But others”** — differing from the religious
**“mocking”** — a manifest error, for it does not produce the eloquence of many tongues but of one tongue
**“full of new wine”** — Bede. Although they were mocking, yet mystically they spoke the truth, because they were filled not with old wine, which failed at the wedding of the Church, but with the new wine of spiritual grace; for now the new wine had come into new bottles, since the apostles were sounding forth the great works of God not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit.
2.14:
**“Standing”** — in the purpose of good
**“But Peter”** — speaks as a shepherd for the sheep
**“standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice”**
• with his height, or with his own quality fitted to this
• as one filled with new wine
**“and spoke to them”** — after the voice, or this is the voice of a Jewish man, etc.
**“Ye men of Judea”** — Men of Judea, etc. That is, there are two causes of prudence: that they are Jews, and that they dwell in Jerusalem, which sobriety befits.
**“and all you that dwell in Jerusalem”** — that is, both peoples
**“be this known to you”** — not what the mockers said, or this new wine
**“and with your ears”** — full of spiritual new wine
**“receive my words”** — full of spiritual new wine
2.15:
**“For these are not drunk, as you suppose”** — Isaias: “Woe to them that rise up early in the morning to follow drunkenness”
**“seeing it is but the third hour of the day”**
• the third hour, the third law
• we know the hour, or the hour of drinking has not come
• At three hours. Daniel, kneeling, prayed at the third, sixth, and ninth hours. And because the Lord sent the Spirit at the third hour, ascended the cross at the sixth, and laid down his soul at the ninth, he deigned to make these same hours known and sanctified to us more excellently than the rest.
**“The third hour of the day”** — Bede. The Holy Spirit, about to preach the glory of the Trinity to the world, fittingly descended at the third hour, because it was said above: “they were persevering in prayer.” Rightly they receive the Spirit at the hour of prayer, to show that the grace of the Spirit is not received unless the mind is lifted up from the pursuit of the flesh.
2.17:
**“And it shall come to pass, in the last days, (saith the Lord,)”** — this is inserted so that honour may be paid to the word of the Lord
**“I will pour out”**
• in the manner of a fountain, according to measure
• By this word he shows the abundance of the gift, because the Spirit was to be given not only, as formerly, to prophets and priests, but to all persons everywhere, of both sexes.
**“of my Spirit”** — to me coeternal
**“Of my Spirit”** — Rabanus. He looks to the diverse gifts, not to the diminution of substance.
**“upon all flesh”** — a fleshly heart, not a stony one; whence it also follows: upon servants and prophets
**“Upon all flesh”** — He explains consequently what all flesh is, there: “and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy,” etc.
*Rabanus:* Upon all flesh, of male and female, or of the circumcised and the Gentile, according to that: “There is neither male nor female, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian nor Scythian, bond nor free.”
**“and they shall prophesy”** — hence inexcusable, because their sons and their daughters prophesy
**“Shall prophesy”** — “The law and the prophets were until John”; from that time “the kingdom of God is preached.” But it is one thing to prophesy of Christ, another to foretell what is to come and to teach.
**“your sons”** — as Agabus and Simon the Black
**“and your daughters”** — the daughters of Philip
**“and your young men”**
• the faithful of the New Testament
• as John and Paul
**“shall see visions”** — they will see clear mysteries
**“and your old men”**
• clinging to the old law
• as Peter and James
**“shall dream dreams”** — they will see shadows and figures
2.18:
**“And indeed”** — behold, what he said before: upon all flesh
**“upon my servants and upon my handmaids”** — before from fear, now from obedience
2.19:
**“And I will shew”**
• Up to here about the coming of the Spirit; now about the signs and wonders of judgment
• Rabanus. Mystically: the wonders in heaven are labours in the Church. The signs upon the earth are vengeance upon earthly men. Blood is in martyrdom. Fire is the gospel or the Holy Spirit. Vapour of smoke is the soul, or compunction of heart.
**“wonders in the heaven above”**
• with Christ born a new star shone out, and with him crucified the sun was darkened
• Beda. The prodigy which he says further, that is, signifies something. A prodigy, which is shown to the eyes; a sign, by which another is signified.
**“Wonders in the heaven”** — With Christ being born a new star appeared; with him mounting the cross the sun was darkened, and the heaven covered with darkness.
**“and signs on the earth beneath”** — which trembled when Christ gave up the Spirit; it opened the tombs, the rocks were split, the bodies of the saints who had slept rose up
**“blood”** — of the Lord’s side
**“Blood”** — Bede. Not only of the wound, but also of the sweat, when in prayer “his sweat became as drops of blood”; which is placed among the signs of the Godhead, because it is not found in human nature. Therefore it signifies that the whole world was to be washed in the blood of Christ, so that, as the tabernacle had been consecrated with the blood of victims, so the faithful people would be dedicated with his blood; and that the place of prayer would not be at Jerusalem alone, but “in every place of his dominion” the elect would lift up hands to the Lord through prayers.
**“and fire”** — of the Holy Spirit
**“smoke”** — Bede. Of compunction and weeping: as smoke from fire, so compunction from the ardor of the Holy Spirit. The blood flowing from the side of the dead man, against the nature of our bodies, was in place of a sign, namely of our salvation and life, which proceeded from his death. In the fire can also be understood the enlightenment of the faithful, and in the vapour of smoke the blindness of the Jews; whence the Lord, when about to give the law, came down in fire and smoke, because he enlightens the humble with his brightness, and darkens the proud with the mist of error.
2.20:
**“The sun”**
• Christ; the gospel
• the gospel
**“shall be turned into darkness”**
• that is, heresy
• the cross
**“and the moon”** — the Church
**“into blood”**
• Of martyrs.
• The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, etc. This is believed to have been fulfilled partly in the passion of Christ, and partly to come before the day of judgment; for then the sun was darkened, but the moon turned into blood could not appear to men, because then, being at the fourteenth day, as at the Pasch, it had been hidden from human sight by day through the interposition of the earth.
**“before the great and manifest day of the Lord come”** — Not of men.
**“great”** — As prepared in space, in work, in brightness.
**“and manifest”** — Not hidden; for God will come manifestly.
2.21:
**“And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord”**
• As if to those who fear, he sets forth counsel.
• Before the day, not in the day.
• By faith, by mouth, by work.
**“Whosoever shall call upon”** — This is what Peter says: “God is not a respecter of persons”; but in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh justice, is acceptable to him.
**“shall be saved”** — With endless salvation of soul and body.
2.22:
**“Ye men of Israel”**
• To whom it was prophesied.
• Bede. Like a learned master he first admonishes the unbelievers, so that, once they are pricked with fear, he may afterwards give counsel of salvation; and because he speaks to those who know the law, he shows that he is the Christ who was promised by the prophets; yet he does not first name him the Son of God on his own authority, but a man approved, just, raised from the dead.
**“hear”** — From me, not from scoffers.
**“these words”**
• That the prophecy is fulfilled.
• Whether spoken or to be spoken.
**“Jesus of Nazareth”** — Jesus, whom you slew, that he was a man approved, etc.
**“a man”** — Manly, or a true man.
**“approved of God among you”** — Before you, or in your bodies.
**“by miracles, and wonders”** — By resurrections of the dead.
**“and signs, which God did”** — The Father, or divinity.
**“in the midst of you”** — Hence inexcusable.
2.23:
**“This same being delivered up, by the determinate counsel”** — Of the Holy Spirit.
**“By the determinate counsel”** — Rabanus. Notable only in this, that they did it with a mind not obedient.
**“and foreknowledge”** — Of the Father, not ours.
**“And foreknowledge”** — Rabanus. In the Greek it is thus: receiving him thus delivered by foreknowledge; for he was delivered by the governor into their power, that they might choose either him or a robber; but the robber being granted life, they slew Jesus by the hands of soldiers.
**“of God”** — Of Christ.
**“being delivered up”** — By the Jews; by the Father, or by himself; or delivered to the soldiers by the Jews.
**“by the hands of wicked men”** — Of soldiers.
**“have crucified”** — By various mockings.
**“have slain”** — By word; for he who commands also does the deed.
2.24:
**“Whom God raised up”**
• Freedom was given by the Spirit.
• Rabanus. He raised him up according to the humanity, which they most hated.
**“Raised up”** — Bede. Not the common resurrection which is deferred to the end, but one that was celebrated on the third day, so that the assertion of this resurrection might be a testimony of divinity.
**“having loosed the sorrows of hell”** — either by his resurrection or by the loosing of the dead
**“Having loosed the sorrows”** — Bede. The sense of this sentence seems to be that, the Lord descending to hell, the sorrows of the punishments were loosed, because they could not touch him; but according to the Greek, in which it is written: loosing through him the sorrows of death, inasmuch as it was impossible that he should be holden by it. It is plain that by his descent the saints were freed from the places of hell; who, although they were in the bosom of Abraham, that is, in the consolation of rest, yet were not wholly loosed from the sorrow of death, or of hell, because they had not merited to enter the joys of heaven until that of the prophet was fulfilled: “Thou also by the blood of thy testament hast sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit,” etc., “wherein is no water.” For they were prisoners before they were led out.
**“as”** — the prophecy of David, unchangeable
**“it was impossible that he should be holden by it”** — or from that death; for he who was free from death could snatch from the dominion of death whom he willed
2.25:
**“For David saith concerning him”** — not in his own person but in the person of Christ
**“I foresaw”** — the voice of the assumed man
**“the Lord”** — the Godhead or the Father
**“before my face”**
• he felt the help as present
• I foresaw the Lord before my face, etc. Allegorically. Rabanus. Bede. Coming among the things that pass away, I did not take my eye from him who always remains, foreseeing this, that after temporal things I might run back to him; and this, “I have not done sin, neither was guile found in me,” I shall ascribe not to man but to God; for this reason also there is joy in thought, and exultation in words, namely on account of the resurrection, by which the world is set free.
**“I foresaw the Lord”** — The voice of Christ after the resurrection, rejoicing at the right hand. The left is the present life, the right the eternal. That I may not be moved. After the resurrection all things will be immovable. And my tongue rejoiced. Because rest is given after labour; for he laboured in the hope of eternal life. Thou wilt not leave: that I may not be moved again by the corruption of a repeated cross and death. Thou hast made known to me. I know that I am to come always. Thou shalt make me full. With full joy, that is, I shall not die again.
**“always”**
• as inseparable
• Before me, etc. Bede. In explaining what he himself did, he gives us, mere men, counsel to avoid sins. For the devil by no means turns to sin him who continually beholds the presence of God with the eye of the mind.
**“because he is at my right hand”**
• prosperous things
• by the manner of a guardian
• Bede. What is the reason he is not moved? Because the Lord helps from the right, the left not prevailing. For if he is not on the right, the devil occupies that part, as is said of Judas: “And may the devil stand at his right hand.”
**“that I may not be moved”** — in the hope of rising again
2.26:
**“For this”** — because the flesh will rise on the third day, or because the Lord stands at the right hand
**“hath been glad”** — with joy
**“my heart”**
• thought
• of the patriarch
**“and my tongue hath rejoiced”** — in the words of the prophet
**“and rejoiced”** — Bede. In the passion he said, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death,” and began to fear and to be heavy, to show himself a true man in soul and body, and truly capable of suffering. But the soul and the tongue rejoiced, because by his passion the human race was to be saved.
**“moreover my flesh also”**
• will not fail in destruction, but in the hope of resurrection it will fall asleep
• that is, the apostles
**“shall rest”** — in the sepulchre
**“in hope”** — of resurrection
2.27:
**“Because thou wilt not leave my soul”** — human
**“my soul”**
• to be possessed in hell
• which descended into hell
**“in hell”**
• to which he descended but did not remain, so that he might help those who needed it; but he was not left there, because he quickly rose
• Bede. It is evident that the soul was not left in hell, which, once those for whom it had descended were taken away, at once returned to the heights; nor was the flesh corrupted, but glorified by swift resurrection.
**“nor wilt thou suffer”** — by this he proves that he was free from human frailty and had surpassed the human condition
**“thy Holy One”** — my body, sanctified, through which others also are to be sanctified; thou wilt not suffer it to be corrupted, because thou hast made known, etc.
**“to see corruption”** — of putrefaction and worms
2.28:
**“Thou hast made known to me the ways of life”**
• I know that I am to rise again, because: “Thou hast made known to me the ways of life”
• by which one goes to eternity, in which after the passion thou shalt fill me with gladness
• which are in the joy of holiness
• Thou hast made known to me, etc. Bede. This is understood not only of him who, having once received the fullness of divine power and wisdom, destroyed death by himself, rising again to life, but also of the just, who through him, having found the way of truth, return to life, and will be made joyful seeing his face, because that sight is above all things and perfect blessedness.
**“thou shalt make me full”** — to him ascending to heaven thou wilt give the delights of the right hand even to the end
**“with joy”** — at the ascension the joy was not half-full
**“with thy countenance”** — I shall see face to face, or with Christ God, who is the face of the Father
2.29:
**“Ye men”** — He addresses the principal sex.
**“brethren”** — by calling them brothers, in body and in faith, he flatters them
**“let me freely speak to you of the patriarch David”** — He says this lest they take offence
**“that he died, and was buried; and his sepulchre is with us to this present day”** — Whence it appears that he did not say this of himself: “Nor wilt thou give thy holy one to see corruption.”
2.30:
**“Whereas therefore he was a prophet”** — David
**“and knew that God hath sworn to him with an oath, that of the fruit of his loins”**
• of the lust of the man in his loins
• Of the fruit of his loins. Bede. In the Greek it is found: “of the fruit of his belly, to raise up Christ and to sit upon his throne.”
**“one should sit upon his throne”** — because Christ sat upon spiritual Israel
2.31:
**“Foreseeing”** — from afar
**“he spoke of the resurrection of Christ; for neither was he left in hell”** — according to the soul
2.32:
**“This Jesus hath God raised again”** — not two or three
**“whereof all we”** — who saw him after the resurrection
**“are witnesses”** — of the resurrection
2.33:
**“Being exalted therefore by the right hand of God”**
• by prosperity; or he himself was exalted, who is the right hand of the Father
• because the psalmist said: “He is at my right hand, that I be not moved.”
**“and having received the promise”**
• Joel
• or received from Christ in the Gospel
**“of the Holy Ghost, received of the Father”** — he received as man
**“having received”** — As true man, that he might pour out the Spirit, as Joel says: “I will pour out,” etc. Or the apostles receive from him the promise of the Spirit in the Gospel, that the Spirit will be sent by the Father.
**“he hath poured forth”**
• the gift of tongues, or the Spirit
• as God
• he does not depart from the word of the prophet Joel saying: “I will pour out,” etc.
• Bede. In Greek: he poured forth this gift which you now see and hear.
**“he hath poured forth this”** — Bede. He who before said that Jesus was raised up by God, now lifting the faith of his hearers higher, declares that this is the true Lord, who he affirms has poured forth the Spirit; for this is a sign of deity. And he rightly used the word “pouring forth,” which he recalled above that the prophet Joel had set down, that from this it might also be clear that he is the Lord Jesus, who before the taking of flesh was wont to speak in the prophets, who gives signs and wonders in heaven and on earth, who saves all that call upon him, and fulfils the other things that the prophet describes, as true God.
**“this which you see”** — in mind
**“and hear”**
• in fiery tongues
• in sound
• in our speech
2.34:
**“For”** — whence it is clear that he foretold not of his own ascension but of Christ’s
**“David ascended not into heaven”** — as in these last things David prophesied not of himself but of Christ, because he was to be sent from Sion, that is, to come from the stock of David, and to rule in the midst of enemies, so also what was set before does not pertain to David but to the death and resurrection of Christ
**“but he himself said: The Lord said”** — by the inner reasoning of the coeternal Word
**“The Lord”** — the Father
**“to my Lord”** — to the man Christ
**“sit thou”** — rest, or judge
**“on my right hand”**
• in eternity, or in the unity of person with the Son, who is the right hand of the Father
• Bede. If Arius objects from this difference that the Son is less and the Father greater, we answer him: the lower name belongs to him to whom it is commanded to sit, as Peter also afterwards expounds, that “God hath made both Lord and Christ, this same Jesus, whom you have crucified.”
• Rabanus. Peter plainly shows from this psalm that the kingdom of Christ is not earthly but heavenly, and evidently establishes both his natures: the human, which is of David, and the divine, according to which he is at the right hand of the Father. In the one he is the son of David, in the other he is the Lord of the same; whence he also adds: “Most certainly, therefore.”
**“Sit thou on my right hand”** — Bede. This is what Peter says of the Lord, whom heaven indeed must receive until the times of the resurrection of all; for then, when the times of refreshment shall come from the presence of the Lord, he is to send him, who has been preached, from the royal seats, Jesus Christ, to judge the living and the dead.
2.35:
**“Until I make”** — always, because he is always putting them down in the present and in the future
**“thy enemies”** — demons or men
**“footstool”** — the humble or the subjects
**“thy footstool”** — of the flesh or of the apostles
2.36:
**“most certainly”** — because the prophet said these things
**“Therefore let all know”** — of man
**“the house of Israel”** — bodily and spiritual
**“that both Lord”** — David
**“this same”** — of whom he says: “To my Lord.”
**“Lord, this same”** — Bede. Showing that “Lord” is the name of majesty and power, to which every creature ought to be subject; Christ is the name of royal or priestly dignity. In the law kings and priests were anointed in figure of him.
**“and Christ”**
• that is, king, when he said: Sit, etc.
• or “God has anointed you,” etc.
• or “I have been appointed,” etc.
**“And Christ”** — Bede. He is truly Christ, anointed with the full abundance of the Holy Spirit, who from the same Spirit by his power gives to whom he will.
**“hath made”** — he made according to the flesh, in his nativity or in his resurrection
**“God”** — the Father or the Godhead
**“this”** — namely
**“Jesus”** — Jesus is his proper name
**“whom you have crucified”**
• whom you thought worthless
• according to the flesh; for the divinity could not suffer or be crucified
• This same Jesus, whom you have crucified, etc. Bede. Jesus is Lord and Christ, one person existing in two natures: because in his divinity he was born eternally of the Father, and in his humanity was made temporally, when, with the Holy Spirit working, he was incarnate in the womb of the virgin.
2.37:
**“Now when they had heard these things, they had compunction in their heart”**
• from the moment he said, men of Judea
• Solomon: the words of the wise are as goads, according to that: “And in your beds be sorry.”
**“had compunction”** — Bede. The prophecy of Joel is fulfilled, for after the fire of the Holy Spirit follows the vapour of compunction; smoke is wont to draw out tears. Those who had mocked begin to weep, they beat the breast, they offer prayer to God as a sacrifice, that they may be able to taste that blood, by him to be saved, which they had before called down upon themselves and upon their children.
**“and said to Peter”** — as to physicians and guides; the blind and the sick speak
**“and to the rest of the apostles: What shall we do”**
• show us
• behold the fruit of compunction
**“men and brethren?”** — because they too are Israelites
2.38:
**“Peter”** — forestalled the fervour of faith
**“But Peter said to them: Do penance”**
• of the heart
• Do penance, etc. Bede. About to speak of baptism, he first set forth the lamentations of penance, so that they might first drench themselves in the water of their affliction, and afterwards be washed by the sacrament of baptism.
**“said, Do”** — fulfil by deed
**“and be baptized”** — let him be dipped
**“every one of you”** — no one for another
**“in the name of Jesus Christ”** — of whom we have spoken: and the Lord made him Lord and Christ; this is said because they did not believe him the Son of God
**“In the name”** — Rabanus. In the honour, or in this form, or in one of the three, the faith is contained.
**“for the remission of your sins”** — especially of the cross, of which he had said, whom you have crucified
**“and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.”** — which you marvel at in us
2.39:
**“to you”**
• to the Jews
• or to you standing here, and to all the Jews placed far away
**“For the promise is”** — that is, I will pour out upon you of my Spirit
**“and to your children, and to all”** — even to the Gentiles, who are not repelled from the gift of spiritual things
**“that are far off, whomsoever”**
• by place or by knowledge of God
• And to all that are far off, etc. Rabanus. This looks back to that testimony of the prophet which he put last, namely: “Whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved”; which pertains specially to the calling of the Gentiles, who, made far off from the sons of Israel, were to be saved by the invocation of the name of the Lord.
**“shall call”** — by grace, not by merits
2.40:
**“other”** — those things are passed over, because they were of the same kind
**“And with very many other words did he testify”** — concerning Christ
**“and exhort”** — he adjured
**“did he testify and exhort”** — The testifying and the exhorting are the same.
**“them, saying:”** — showing them to be sick and himself the physician
**“Save yourselves from this perverse generation.”**
• Save yourselves from the generation of the Jews, who do not do penance
• This is the manner of testifying and exhorting; but Luke summed up Peter’s many words in a brief sentence.
**“from this perverse generation”** — There are two generations: one of the good, the other of the wicked.
**“this perverse”** — which is perverse and provoking
2.41:
**“They therefore that received his word”** — that is, that word: Do penance, etc.
**“about”** — It is said of number as “about” is of place.
**“three thousand”**
• a number fitting for faith, which is threefold and yet one
• Bede. Where the baptism of the Church was first celebrated, divine mercy gathered three thousand souls to the confession of the Trinity; and Moses indeed commanded the solemnity of the firstfruits to be begun on the fiftieth day after the Pasch, on which the law was given, but now, the Holy Spirit coming, not sheaves of ears of corn but the firstfruits of souls are consecrated to the Lord.
2.42:
**“And they were persevering”** — not for one day only
**“in the doctrine”** — of faith
**“of the apostles”** — not of Peter alone, because it was the same for all
**“and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers.”** — either of communion or of the holy
2.43:
**“And fear came upon every soul”**
• except believers
• imperfectly, for “perfect charity casteth out fear”
**“fear”** — on account of the preaching, or on account of the wonders that follow
**“many”** — the account of the power draws near
**“many wonders also and signs”** — joined to the preaching
**“were done by the apostles in Jerusalem, and there was great fear in all.”** — besides the hundred and twenty of whom it was said
2.44:
**“And all”** — All also. There is joined an account also of the sharing and of the selling, and of the equal division, in which the virtue appears.
**“Were together”** — Bede. Charity poured out in hearts quickly begets love of God and of neighbour; whence, on account of the twofold heat of charity, the Spirit was given twice to the apostles.
**“and had all things common.”** — the sign of brotherly love is to possess all things and to have nothing of one’s own
2.45:
**“Their possessions”** — fields
**“and goods”** — flocks
**“they sold, and divided them to all, according as every one had need.”** — not according to rank but according to need, as with the manna
2.46:
**“And continuing daily”** — as the apostles
**“with one accord”** — God makes those of one custom dwell in a house
**“in the temple,”** — in prayer, behold contemplation
**“and breaking”** — here the active life is signified
**“from house to house”** — not in the temple, so that the holy place would be for prayer and the common table for food
**“bread”** — holy or bodily (bread)
**“they took their meat”** — in honour of their master
**“with gladness and simplicity”** — asking nothing
**“of heart,”** — with the unity of charity
2.47:
**“Praising”** — joining in praise
**“God”** — giving thanks for the precepts, according to that: “And a hymn being said, they went out unto mount Olivet”
**“and having favour with all the people.”** — giving thanks before the people, or giving thanks to the people themselves, or finding favour in the sight of the people
**“The Lord”** — not only did the former persevere, but the Lord
**“And the Lord increased”** — In the Greek: The Lord increased daily those who should be saved. Behold, after this another narrative begins thus: “Peter and John, etc., into the same.” This can be explained thus: since the Lord daily gathered believers into his Church as the apostles preached, the first of the apostles went up into the temple to pray to God for the same thing, that is, that he might always increase the Church.
**“daily such as should be saved”** — not only at Pentecost
**“together”** — the unity of the apostolic rule

3.1:
**“Now Peter and John”**
• he begins with the principal ones
• He follows up the aforesaid virtue. They are linked to one another in turn, so that discourses succeed virtues, and virtues succeed discourses.
**“went up”** — he who prays goes up
**“into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer.”** — not of the prayer but of the day
**“At the ninth hour”** — Bede. The apostles, about to enter the temple at the ninth hour, first heal a man long lame; afterwards, labouring until evening, they imbue many thousands of men with the word of faith, because the teachers of the Church preach first to the Jews, afterwards to the Gentiles; these are the labourers whom the father of the family leads into the vineyard at the ninth and the eleventh hour.
3.2:
**“And a certain man who was lame from his mother's womb”** — whose health is hard to obtain
**“Lame from his mother's womb”** — Bede. The people of Israel, rebellious not only from the incarnation but even from the time of the law, was as it were lame from its mother’s womb; which was prefigured in Jacob wrestling with the angel and limping, because that people, prevailing over Christ in the passion, is blessed in some through faithlessness...
**“was carried,”** — in this is shown a long and grave infirmity
**“whom they laid every day at the gate of the temple, which is called Beautiful,”**
• from a certain special ornament
• Ozias king of Jerusalem wished to usurp the priestly office, and was struck with leprosy in the forehead; and his son Joas reigned in his place, and this man built the beautiful gate.
**“at the gate of the temple, which is called Beautiful”** — Bede. Allegorically: the beautiful gate of the temple is the Lord, through whom whoever enters is saved; to this gate Israel, weak and unable to walk, is carried by the voices of the law and the prophets, that it may ask of those entering the help of faith and wisdom, because the prophecies of things to come set their hearers as it were at the gate. But Peter leads into the temple one to whom, through his confession, and perhaps also through the surname Peter, the keys of heaven were given.
**“that he might ask alms”** — mercy
**“of them that went into the temple.”** — he believed that those who frequented the temple would be merciful
3.3: **“He, when he had seen Peter and John about to go into the temple, asked to receive an alms.”** — from them
3.4:
**“But Peter with John fastening his eyes upon him, said: Look”** — as if showing their poverty by their dress
**“upon us.”** — whom you know to be poor
3.5: **“But he looked earnestly”** — he looked upon
3.6:
**“But Peter said: Silver and gold I have none;”**
• I have not; or, I have not at present; or, it is not at present at hand
• Silver and gold, etc. Mindful of that precept, “Do not possess gold nor silver,” the money that was laid at the apostles' feet they did not store up for themselves, but kept for the uses of the poor who had left their patrimonies.
• Bede. Allegorically. Silver, etc. The first tabernacle had indeed the ordinances of worship, the holy of holies adorned with gold and silver; but the blood of the gospel shines more precious than the metals of the law, because the people who had lain weak before the gilded doorposts enters the heavenly temple in the name of Jesus Christ crucified.
**“but what I have, I give thee:”** — he shows that he has other things
**“In the name”** — a grateful servant glorifies not himself but the Lord, so that he may be believed in, whom they resisted
**“of Jesus Christ”** — Holy
**“of Nazareth”** — from the place
**“arise, and walk.”** — walking gives full health in these two; for walking is proof of health
3.7:
**“And taking”** — Bede. He raises him by word, and strengthens him by the right hand, because the teacher’s word has little force in the hearer if it is not commended by the example of his own action.
**“by the right hand”** — the right hand is the prosperity of salvation
**“he lifted him up, and forthwith”**
• not with medicinal slowness
• no delay intervenes, lest the healing be thought to come from elsewhere
**“his feet and soles received strength”** — his steps were strengthened
**“and soles.”**
• which are weakened in paralytics
• the sole is so called from flatness
3.8:
**“And he leaping up”**
• not rising
• according to the prophet saying: “Then shall the lame man leap as a hart”
**“And he leaping up, stood”** — Bede. The order of perfection: he who had lain first rises, then takes up the way of virtues, and so enters with the apostles the gate of the kingdom.
**“stood, and walked, and went in with them”** — it is an example of giving thanks to the Lord
**“into the temple”** — heavenly
**“walking, and leaping, and praising God.”** — he was fulfilling two precepts
3.9:
**“And saw”** — his health
**“all the people”** — behold the fullness of witnesses
3.10:
**“And they knew him,”** — they did not doubt about the person
**“that it was he who sat begging alms at the Beautiful gate of the temple: and they were filled with wonder and amazement”** — not in faith
**“with wonder and amazement”** — Bede. Ecstasy is also said of fear and a departure of the mind, when the mind is not estranged by fear but is taken up by the inspiration of a revelation.
**“at that which had happened to him.”** — good things befall
3.11:
**“as he held Peter and John, all the people ran”** — not the priests
**“All the people ran”** — Bede. Allegorically. Israel being saved through the apostles, the whole world ran to the threshold of the true peacemaker, of whom it is said: “His empire shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace.” He is the stone cut out of the mountain, who, while the earthly kingdom falls, alone holds a peaceful empire throughout the world.
**“to them”** — to be worshipped
3.12:
