**“But Peter seeing, made answer to the people:”** — to the running and the amazement, or to the city being amazed
**“Ye men of Israel, why wonder you at this? or why look you upon us, as if by our”** — it shows why the people were running
**“strength or power”** — these two are necessary for salvation
**“we had made”** — we ourselves, not God
3.13:
**“The God of Abraham”**
• because Abraham believed him even in the time of uncircumcision
• Rabanus. Three are named, with no wicked man interceding: either on account of the primacy of justice, or on account of the continuous succession of the just, or on account of the number of witnesses.
• By recalling the fathers he urges faith, lest he seem to be introducing something new.
• Rabanus. In these three the whole mystery of the Church is completed: for either good from good, as Isaac from Abraham; or evil from evil, as Ismael from the handmaid Agar; or evil from good, as Esau from Isaac and Rebecca; or good from evil, as the sons of Jacob born of handmaids; which is likewise observed in spiritual generation.
**“The God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”** — He notes the Trinity; the God of the fathers here, unity.
**“and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers”**
• of the three, or of all
• “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.”
**“hath glorified”** — in the healing of the paralytic
**“his Son Jesus”**
• not us, whom you behold
• consubstantial
**“whom you indeed delivered up”** — the Saviour of the world had come to save, and you delivered him to death
**“Delivered up”** — etc. You killed, etc. Bede. The wise teacher, speaking of the Lord to those who would kill him, first recalls the humanity by which he could be delivered up and killed; then, the resurrection gradually being made plain, he declares him to be God and the Son of God, and preaches him also as the author of life.
**“and denied before the face of Pilate”** — asking that not him but Barabbas be released
**“when he judged he should be released”** — although a Gentile, in whom the Jews are condemned
3.14:
**“But you denied the Holy One”**
• in himself
• without sin
**“and the Just”**
• toward his neighbour
• without iniquity
**“denied, and desired a murderer to be granted unto you”** — Barabbas, the author of sedition and murder
3.15:
**“But the author of life”**
• of Lazarus and of the others
• of the present and of the future
**“you killed”** — in that he delivered him up, he killed him
**“You killed”** — By will and by word; and this is against the law, which says: “He that killeth a man willfully shall be put to death.”
**“whom God”** — the Father
**“hath raised from the dead”** — far off, lest he die again
**“of which”** — of Christ
**“we are witnesses”** — or made
3.16:
**“And in the faith of his name, this man, whom you have seen”** — healthy
**“and known”** — paralysed
**“hath strengthened”** — in health
**“his name”** — knowledge
**“and the faith”** — invocation of his name
**“which is by him”** — Christ, man and God
**“hath given perfect”** — in body and soul
**“Perfect soundness”** — in the two things that are commanded
**“this soundness”** — bodily health
3.17:
**“And now, brethren, I know”** — gently rebukes their crime
**“through ignorance”** — Two things worked together: your ignorance and the foreknowledge of God.
3.18:
**“But those things which God before had shewed by the mouth of all”** — they all spoke with one mouth
**“by the mouth of all”** — Therefore it had to be fulfilled, because not one but all prophesied.
**“the prophets”** — to distinguish them from the false
**“that his Christ should suffer”** — whence also above: God made Christ
3.19:
**“Be penitent, therefore”**
• because you did so, therefore repent
• of evils
**“and be converted”** — to good. Whence: “Decline from evil, and do good.”
**“that your sins may be blotted out”** — although done through ignorance
**“your sins may be blotted out”** — Bede. Then sins will be wholly blotted out, when by the power of the resurrection the last death will be destroyed.
**“That when the times shall come”** — because it is past in the incarnation, or future in judgment
**“the times of refreshment”** — the separation of the universal judgment and the redemption of the just
3.20:
**“That when”** — Continuing from what precedes, namely: that when the times of refreshment have come from the presence of the Lord, then your sins will be blotted out.
**“from the presence”** — from the face
**“of the Lord”** — of Christ in the flesh
3.21:
**“Whom indeed must”** — ambiguity of the word
**“Whom heaven indeed must receive”** — Etc. The Church sits by faith, or in heaven at the right hand of the Father.
**“must”** — etc. Bede. This is what the prophet testifies was said to the same Christ by the Father: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thy enemies thy footstool.” For taken up into heaven he sits at the right hand of God on the throne of majesty, remains always God, and was never absent from there; but in his humanity he is to come from heaven to judge and to restore all things which God has spoken by all the prophets from the beginning of the world, because the saints entering with the Lord into joy, the reprobate will be subject to punishments with the devil; which being completed, nothing will remain of the things promised by the prophets.
**“heaven indeed”** — the Church
**“receive, until the times”** — in judgment
**“of the restitution”** — of fulfilment or renewal
**“of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth”** — not by men, that is, spoken through men
**“of his holy prophets, from the beginning of the world”** — not recently invented but written long ago
3.22:
**“For Moses said”**
• Peter set down the sense of Moses, not the words
• he puts first, before the others, the first writer of the divine law
**“For Moses”** — He gives examples, not of all who spoke, or of all that was said.
**“That”** — not Josue the son of Nun, but the Lord Jesus
**“That a prophet”** — Bede. The Son of God took flesh from the people of Israel, appearing in the likeness of Moses, that as he led carnal Israel, instructed and purified by legal ceremonies and rites, into the promised land, so also Jesus by the grace of the gospel led spiritual Israel to heaven. And as the despisers of the law of Moses were cast out of the promised land by enemies, so those who despise the teaching of the gospel will be driven out of the company of the saints by the avengers of the spirit; and this is what follows: “And every soul,” etc.
**“shall raise up”** — by being born or by rising again
**“unto you”** — for your advancement
**“the Lord your God”** — to distinguish from false gods
**“of your brethren”** — Rabanus. Josue from Ephraim, Jesus from Juda.
**“like unto me”** — as me, by obeying as to me
**“him”** — the true man, or one foreshadowed by me
**“you shall hear”** — placed for the imperative.
**“according to all things”** — diminishing nothing, adding nothing.
3.23:
**“And it shall be”**
• this, that every soul, etc.
• It shall be, etc. Bede. Briefly and clearly, by the testimony of the prophets and the law, he teaches that Christ is to be heard by all nations; he will condemn the unbelievers and grant the faithful eternal blessing.
**“every soul”** — the principal part for the whole man.
**“which will not hear”** — obeys.
**“that prophet shall be destroyed”**
• by men.
• or by God.
• according to the law.
• or from the lot of the saints.
• shall be slain.
• Rabanus. Those of the carnal people who resist Josue, and those of the spiritual people who resist Christ, are cut off; in disobedience to either, death follows, whether carnal or spiritual.
**“shall be destroyed”** — He shall be cut off from the lot of the saints and from the land, or he shall be cast outside the bounds of blessedness.
**“from among the people”** — spiritual.
3.24:
**“And all the prophets”**
• after Moses.
• Bede. Although the patriarchs and the saints of earlier time prophesied much of Christ by words and deeds, yet properly the time of the prophets, namely of those who wrote openly of the mystery of Christ and the Church, took its beginning from Samuel and lasted until the captivity of Babylon.
**“from Samuel”**
• as from the prince of the prophets.
• Under Samuel the times of the kings began in Judea.
**“and afterwards”** — down to John the Baptist.
**“who have spoken”** — prophetically.
**“have told of these days”**
• times of refreshment, that is, of both advents of the Lord.
• by this you are inexcusable.
3.25:
**“You are the children of the prophets”** — either by ancient custom or by nature.
**“and of the testament”**
• as follows, namely: In thy seed, etc.
• Of the covenant. What follows below, saying: In thy seed all nations shall be blessed.
**“of the testament”** — Bede. From that covenant which was made to Moses, and from this which was spoken to Abraham, the severity and the goodness of God are plain. Goodness is in those who have merited to be blessed through faith in Christ; severity is in those who have been cut off for contempt and disobedience.
**“our fathers”** — Because it was promised not only to Abraham but also to Isaac and Jacob.
**“saying to Abraham”** — to whom the promise was first made.
**“And in thy seed”** — not in seeds but in one seed, who is Christ.
**“in thy seed”** — All families. Bede. The seed of Abraham is Christ, in whose faith the blessing was promised to all families, namely Jews and Gentiles.
**“shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed”** — not one nation.
**“all the kindreds”** — Bede. Not that all are blessed, but because none is blessed except in him, as also that: “which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world.”
**“shall be blessed”** — Bede. In Adam cursed by sin, in Christ blessed; in whom those too are blessed who preceded the incarnation, because the same man God opened the gate of heaven, and at the end he will say to all the elect: “Come, ye blessed of my Father,” etc.
3.26:
**“to you”** — indeed
**“first”** — before the Gentiles
**“God raising up”** — according to the flesh
**“his Son”** — Bede. It must be observed that he called the same Son of God the seed of Abraham on account of his two natures, lest they should believe Christ to be only man, or the Son to be one of man and another of God, by which snare Nestorius and many others were deceived.
**“hath sent him”** — made to be incarnate
**“to bless”** — preaching, or making them blessed
**“to you, that every one may convert himself”** — shows the freedom of the will
**“from his wickedness”** — by which he is assailed

4.1:
**“And as they were speaking to the people”** — Peter spoke for himself and John; or the two speak to the crowd.
**“the priests came upon them”** — Priests, etc. Who seemed to be the teachers and judges of the people.
**“and the officer of the temple, and the Sadducees”** — Just, or justified, is the meaning.
**“the Sadducees”** — Who denied the resurrection, and therefore were grieved at their teaching.
4.2:
**“Being grieved”** — Grieved, that a crowd flocked to hear the apostles.
**“that they taught the people”** — this is common to all
**“the resurrection from the dead”** — This especially against the Sadducees; but both were grieved, because the apostles affirm that Jesus, whom they had killed as a man, was glorified by God the Father.
4.3:
**“And they laid hands upon them, and put them in hold”** — of the prison
**“till the next day; for it was now evening”** — this is the cause of keeping them in custody
4.4:
**“But many”** — not all
**“of them who had heard the word, believed; and the number of the men was made five thousand”** — of the sheep that hear or know the voice of the shepherd
**“and the number of the men was made”** — If in the five thousand men whom the Lord fed in the desert the people of the law, set free by Christ, is understood, the five thousand here also, instructed by the apostles, can signify the people of the Gentiles, who will spiritually follow the mysteries of the same law. And well are both given a heavenly gift at evening, because: “When the fulness of the time was come, God sent his Son” on earth, etc.
4.5: **“And it came to pass on the morrow, that their princes, and ancients, and scribes, were gathered together”** — there were three assemblies of the people
4.6:
**“And Annas”** — is set apart
**“and Caiphas, and John, and Alexander”** — priests who held the chief rank from the stock of Aaron
**“and as many as were of the kindred of the high priest”** — with the chief priests listed, others are mentioned without number
4.7:
**“And setting them in the midst”** — of the council
**“By what power, or by what name, have you done this”** — whether they say the deed was done by divine power, because of its brilliance, and not by some other power
4.8:
**“Then Peter, filled with the Holy Ghost”** — in the midst of the council, or of the council
**“Holy Ghost”** — at Pentecost
**“Peter”** — as prince of the apostles
4.9:
**“If”**
• for: whether
• it can be an interrogation
**“we this day are examined”** — we are brought before the judges
**“concerning the good deed done to the infirm man”** — in the healing of the paralytic
4.10:
**“Be it known to you all”** — to the rulers and elders
**“and to all the people of Israel, that by the name”** — was saved by the Saviour
**“of our Lord Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God hath raised from the dead, even by him this man standeth”** — he stands here present, who could not stand before
4.11:
**“This”** — whom you crucified
**“is the stone”** — This is the stone. Rabanus. Answering the questions put to him, he preaches about Christ, and above all about David, to whom, as to their patriarch, they had given faith above others.
**“rejected”** — Augustine. Of the rejected stone, there is no history.
**“was rejected by you the builders”** — according to the law
**“the builders”** — Bede. There were Jews who alone read the law and the prophets for building up; these, while they built, came to the corner stone that embraced two walls, that is, they found in the Scriptures that Christ would come in the flesh, who would establish two peoples in himself; and because the Jews preferred to stand on one wall, that is, to be saved alone, they rejected the stone which was fitted not for one but for two; but, they being unwilling, God set him as the head of the corner, that from two peoples and two testaments there might arise the building of one and the same faith.
**“which is become”** — God raised from the dead
**“the head of the corner.”** — that he may be the prince of both testaments and peoples
4.12:
**“Neither is there salvation in any other”**
• except in the Saviour
• Bede. If the salvation of the world is in Christ alone, then our fathers also were saved by his incarnation and passion, by which we also believe we are saved; for though the sacraments differ according to the reckoning of the times, yet one and the same faith agrees, because the dispensation which we learned as accomplished through the apostles, they learned through the prophets as to come. For there is no redemption except in the blood of him who gave himself a redemption for all.
**“salvation”** — of the world
**“nor”** — of this man
4.13:
**“Now seeing the constancy of Peter”** — boldness
**“illiterate”** — Not because they were wholly ignorant of letters, but because they did not have skill in the art of grammar.
**“and ignorant men”**
• unskilled
• Bede. Those were called idiots who, content only with their own tongue and natural knowledge, did not know the study of letters.
• Bede. The unlettered are sent to preach, lest the faith of believers be thought to come about not by the power of God but by eloquence, according to that: “not in wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ should be made void.”
**“ignorant men”** — Bede. Idiots are those who had not trained their own natural ability through teaching; idioma is Greek, in Latin “proprietas.”
**“they wondered”** — not knowing the cause of their steadfastness and strength
**“and they knew them that they had been with Jesus”** — unlettered
4.14:
**“Seeing the man also who had been healed standing with them”** — the apostles
**“who had been healed, they could say nothing against it.”** — because he was not, or had not been, healed
4.15: **“But they commanded them to go aside out of the council”** — they will make you outside the synagogue
4.16:
**“Saying: What”** — that their deed be no longer spread abroad
**“shall we do to these men?”** — to the unlearned
4.17:
**“But that it may be no farther spread among the people, let us threaten them”** — only this counsel remains
**“that they speak no more in this name to any man.”** — a Jew or a Gentile
4.18:
**“And calling them, they charged them not to”**
• by any occasion or in any place
• And calling them, etc. That not at all, etc. Then was fulfilled: “You shall be hated by all men for my name’s sake.”
**“speak at all, nor teach”** — preach
4.19:
**“But Peter and John answering, said to them: If it be just in the sight of God”**
• while he looks upon us
• before God, whom truth pleases
**“you”** — forbidding
**“to hear you rather than God”** — commanding to preach
**“judge ye.”** — But Peter and John, etc. Judge. Rabanus. You who are judges, do your duty, not by uttering a perverse word but by judging justly. Behold, full grain is found in the ear, which before was bent over as in the grass.
4.20:
**“For we cannot but”** — For we cannot, etc. That is, we are unwilling; or it has been turned into nature, as with the confirmed angels not to sin.
**“the things which”** — signs
**“we have seen and heard.”** — preaching
4.21:
**“But they threatening”** — lest they be thought to have believed
**“sent them away”** — because of the people
**“not finding”** — not finding a cause that would please the people, not their conscience
**“how they might punish them, because of the people”** — not God
**“for all men glorified”**
• God in whose name they did this
• Bede. Deeds or words are glorified when, spread abroad by report, they are carried to the knowledge of very many. But God is glorified in the deeds of men, which is proper to Christian piety and humility, as he himself says: “That they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”
**“glorified”** — In the Greek: all glorified in that which was done, and “in that which had happened” is not found.
**“in that which had come to pass.”** — the paralytic being healed
4.22:
**“For the man was above forty years old”**
• the cause of the glorifying is the long time of the infirmity
• Bede. Of forty years. According to the history, the perfect age of the man is shown to those who slandered. Allegorically: the people of Israel not only for forty years in the wilderness, despising the manna, sought the filth of Egypt, but even in the land of promise limped between the rites of God and of idols. Or this number signifies the fullness of the twofold law. For four times ten make forty; the transgressor of both, lying disabled, passes beyond as it were the perfection of forty.
**“above forty years old”** — Whence a greater glory or grace of the power; and therefore he speaks not of the man’s age but of the time of the infirmity.
4.23: **“And being let go”** — Peter and John
4.24:
**“Who having heard it”** — Bede. Having heard the threats of the persecutors, they ask for themselves confidence to resist through signs of power.
**“with one accord lifted up”** — in the usual manner
**“With one accord lifted up”** — Rabanus. Without noise, or in the perfection of unanimity, according to that: “If two or three shall be gathered together in my name, of everything whatsoever they shall ask, it shall be done to them.”
**“their voice to God”** — not to a man, so that they may give an example to the rest
**“and said: Lord, thou art he that didst make heaven and earth, the sea, and all things that are in them.”** — great power is shown
4.25:
**“Who, by the Holy Ghost”** — not by human sense
**“by the mouth of”** — as through a trumpet, so that the word of man is not spoken back
**“our father”** — Our father was David, but yours was a boy.
**“David, thy servant, hast said:”** — out of envy
**“Why did the Gentiles rage”**
• lest the kingdom pass to the Jews
• Bede. Not as one ignorant does the prophet ask, but wondering at the madness of the impious, he rebukes those who rose up against the Saviour, not harmed by him but helped by him in many ways.
• A roar is the voice of a lion. Whence Jeremias: “My inheritance is become to me as a lion in the wood: it hath cried out against me.”
**“and the people”** — The Jews
**“meditate”**
• stirred by an unskilled and unreasoning motion
• they made a plan, diligently considering how they might kill him
**“vain things”** — that Christ would not rise again
**“Vain things”** — Concerning Christ who was to come, or that he would be held in death.
4.26:
**“The kings of the earth stood up”** — Herod and Pilate
**“of the earth”** — not of heaven
**“and the princes”** — of the priests
**“assembled together”** — into the court of Caiphas
**“Assembled together”** — Herod and Pilate came together into friendship.
**“against the Lord”** — the Father. Whence do you prove this? Because it was against Christ, who is the Son of his Father
**“and”** — for: because
**“against”** — who contradicts the Son and the Father
**“his Christ”** — of whom it will be said later: “But I am appointed king by him over Sion, his holy mountain,” etc.
4.27:
**“For of a truth there assembled together in this city”** — wicked
**“against thy holy child Jesus”** — “Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth,” etc.
**“whom thou hast anointed”**
• by the Holy Ghost
• you made him Christ
**“Anointed”** — They explain the name Christ as from chrism, that is, from anointing, according to that: “Thy God, O God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.”
**“Herod, and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel”** — the two peoples were reconciled on the cross
4.28:
**“To do what thy hand”**
• power
• Christ
• not his own
• foreknowledge
**“and thy counsel”** — the Spirit
**“decreed to be done”** — as you foreknew concerning Christ
4.29:
**“And now, Lord”** — Therefore, in persecution, they commend to God what they suffer.
**“behold their threatenings, and grant unto thy servants”** — They ask for that which they need.
**“that with all confidence they may speak thy word”** — even among persecutors
**“With all confidence to speak”** — They ask God this, that they may be able to speak the word of God with all confidence.
4.30:
**“By stretching forth thy hand”**
• Christ
• your power
**“to cures, and signs, and wonders to be done”** — for the strengthening of preaching
**“By the name of thy holy Son Jesus”** — Bede. In Greek: through the name of your servant Jesus, which agrees more with the wishes of the apostles, who were striving that the man crucified by the Jews, with miracles shining forth through his name, might be taken up into heaven and the Son of God be made known.
4.31:
**“The place was moved”** — The great power of the prayer of the faithful; but this was done to stir up minds.
**“And when they had prayed, the place was moved”**
• In this moved place the fear of those can be understood who by believing were to be made subject to the apostles, who, their terror dispelled, learned to rise again with Christ and to savour heavenly things.
• Bede. Because they were seeking strength and courage against the deceit of enemies, they ordered, as a sign that their prayer was heard, that the earth should move, so that they might know that earthly hearts would yield to them, under whose feet the earth was shaken with fear when the Spirit came.
**“wherein they were assembled; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost”** — They had asked for this gift, that they might be able to speak with confidence.
4.32:
**“And the multitude of believers”**
• Because it is said: “But the Lord added daily,” and “they were multiplied.”
• The multitude, etc. Bede. The difference of things and places is to be noted: for in the building of the proud tower, the tongue and mind of the human race, though one, were by the merit of iniquity divided, so that though men there spoke with all tongues, yet no one understood the will or words of his neighbour; but in Jerusalem tongues were united by the merit of humility, and there was one tongue for all and the same and one will; which is done even to this day, when the elect, in manifold speech, with united heart and harmonious purpose serve the Lord, while the reprobate, serving the devil, are driven about with different mind and with contentious zeal and strife among themselves.
**“had but one heart and one soul”**
• one feeling; one soul; and there was one will of all
• Had one heart and one soul, etc. Bede. Those who had left the world, not glorying in nobility of birth so as to prefer themselves to others, but born as from the bosom of one and the same mother, the Church, rejoiced in the same love of brotherhood.
• Bede. This place agrees with what was said above, that those who had received the Spirit spoke with the tongues of all. The union of tongues was a presage that the Church through the Spirit would have one heart and soul among diverse nations and tongues; for not all believers spoke with all tongues, but the union of diverse tongues in the faith of Christ showed that there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism.”
**“neither did any one say that aught of the things which he possessed”** — not of men, but of the things which they possessed
**“Neither did any one”** — Mystically. The virtues which the just possess they judge not to be their own, but of those for whose benefit they dispense them.
**“all things were common”** — Bede. In Greek ‘cena’, whence cenobites, that is, those living in common. Cenobia are their dwellings.
**“was his own; but all things were common unto them”** — Bede. Those who so live that all things are common in the Lord are called “cenobites”; which life is the happier the more it imitates the future age, where all things are common, because “God is all in all,” and because there is the highest peace and security. The city in which the type of this life went before was called Jerusalem, that is, vision of peace.
4.33:
**“And with great power”** — of confidence or of signs
**“did the apostles give testimony”** — This properly belonged to those to whom it was said: “You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem.”
**“Did the apostles give”** — Bede. He distinguishes the order of teachers and hearers. For the multitude of believers, with temporal things despised, were joined to one another by the bond of charity. The apostles, shining with virtue, laid open the mysteries of Christ.
**“of the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord”** — which they most hated, and which is the principal sign of faith
**“and great grace”** — of the Holy Spirit, or of the sharing of which it follows: Selling, etc.
4.35:
**“And laid it down before the feet of the apostles”** — at their feet, or as if falling down at their knees
**“And distribution was made to every one, according as he had need”** — not according to persons and gifts, but according to need
4.36:
**“Joseph”**
• Rabanus. Barnabas, increased, is interpreted ‘son of consolation’: increased by growth and advance in spiritual good.
• Bede. I think this is Barnabas who was ordained with Paul as apostle to the Gentiles.
**“who”**
• Joseph
• selling, they brought the prices; and Joseph
**“Barnabas”** — Bede. Some think he was rather the colleague of Paul, he concerning whom the lot was cast with Matthias, paying too little attention to the fact that this one is called Barnabas and that one Barsabas, and that this one is interpreted ‘son of consolation’, that one ‘son of rest’.
**“which is, by interpretation, The son of consolation”** — Wherever Scripture puts the names of things or persons with an interpretation, it signifies that a more sacred meaning is in them. Rightly is he called son of consolation who, having despised present things, consoles himself with the hope of future ones. For the Holy Spirit too is called Paraclete for this reason, because by his infusion he gives paraclisis, that is, consolation, to those who have tribulation in the world; as also Peter, on account of the grace of the Spirit, was called Bar Jona, that is, son of a dove.
**“The son of consolation”** — Rabanus. Or because of the alms by which he comforted the poor. Or for the consolation of the reward he deserved to receive from God. Or because he was deemed worthy to comfort the apostles in place of Judas.
**“a Levite, a Cyprian born”** — by birth
4.37:
**“Having land”** — wherever or on whatever occasion
**“sold it”** — the cause of the scattering
**“this same”** — or: ‘that one’
**“and brought the price”** — not some part but the whole price of the field
**“and laid it at the feet of the apostles”**
• that it might become common to all
• He proves that what he avoids touching is to be forsaken, and teaches that the gold which he lays beneath the steps of the apostles is to be trodden underfoot.

5.1: **“But a certain man named Ananias”** — His name is not placed first, as with Joseph, because his fault made him ignoble.
5.2:
**“And by fraud kept back”** — The fraud was because he had vowed the whole, as the others did.
**“of the price of the land, his wife being privy thereunto”** — she, because she was a partner in the crime, was rightly also a partner in the death
5.3:
**“But Peter said:”** — although he had placed it before the apostles’ feet, yet Peter speaks as the prince of the apostles
**“Ananias, why hath Satan tempted”**
• a rebuke
• Rabanus. He uses the past tense, because the temptation was complete. Temptation is carried out in three ways: by persuasion, by delight, by consent; all of which was fulfilled in Ananias.
**“Why hath Satan tempted”** — Bede. Another translation: Why hath Satan filled thy heart? Where it is to be noted that nothing can fill the mind of man according to substance except the creating Trinity, since the soul is filled with created things only according to operation and the impulse of the will. But Satan fills the heart of someone not indeed by entering into him and into his understanding, nor by entering the access of the heart, since this power belongs to God alone; but by a cunning and fraudulent deception drawing the soul into affections of malice, with the forethoughts and incentives of vices with which he is full. Satan therefore filled the heart of Ananias not by entering but by inserting the poison of his malice.
**“Satan”** — opposed to the Holy Spirit
**“and by fraud keep part of”** — Rabanus. In this there seems to have been a lie, because he had vowed the whole; but it is better not to vow than after a vow not to perform to the Holy Spirit.
5.4:
**“Did it not”** — you could have acted otherwise, because did it not remain, etc.
**“Whilst it remained, did it not remain to thee?”** — it was yours; it could profit you
**“and after it was sold”** — what now
**“was it not in thy power.”** — before it was sold, because we are not compelled but urged to be perfect, the Lord saying: “If thou wilt be perfect, go, sell what thou hast,” etc.
**“Why hast thou conceived this thing in thy heart”**
• with the plan settled, you fixed it
• what you ought to have kept
**“this thing?”** — this thing: of lying or defrauding
**“Thou hast not lied”** — what he thinks secret is made plain by unbelief
**“to men, but to God.”**
• “He who searches hearts”
• “Thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie.”
**“but to God”** — Above he had said to the Holy Spirit. It is plain, therefore, that the Spirit is God.
5.5:
**“fell down”** — Rabanus. The beginnings of laws are always commended by acts of vengeance: the two sons of Aaron offering fire are consumed by fire; Oza, supporting the ark, died; he fell, so that the other transgressors may be terrified by his example.
**“and gave up the ghost,”**
• he breathed out his spirit
• Rabanus. That transgressors of the law of Christ, though not punished with temporal death, may know that eternal death hangs over them.
**“fell down, and gave up the ghost”** — Bede. Not for the sake of gain did he give so severe a sentence on the transgression, but foreseeing the future, and the tares that would corrupt the simplicity of the Church with evil ways. For from these the race of the Sarabaites is said to have arisen, who, by no means having forsaken their own goods, pretend to keep the strictness of the apostles. He suffered the guilty to be cured by no penance, but for the fear of those after them cut off the harmful shoot at the root.
**“And there came great fear”**
• This swift vengeance struck great fear.
• And there came great fear, etc. Bede. An anticipation, since few had heard of the husband’s death alone before the wife’s departure, although it could be said of those few that they feared.
**“upon all that heard it.”** — the hearts of all the faithful
5.7:
**“Of three hours”** — Rabanus. A little time of repentance is given to the wife, whose fault is more venial than her husband’s, since she consented to the head.
**“the space of three hours after, when his wife, not knowing what had happened, came in.”** — not knowing that her husband was dead
5.8:
**“And Peter said to her:”** — to the thing, not the word; to the wife’s coming in, not to the speech
**“Tell me, woman, whether you sold the land for so much?”**
• if it appears that so much of the price was that part, which indeed agrees, etc.
• it appears that part of the price was present
• Tell me, etc. Rabanus. By questioning the wife he shows her fault from her own confession, which her husband had revealed in the deed.
5.9:
**“And Peter said unto her: Why have you agreed together”**
• in the way said before
• Why, etc. Rabanus. Said reproachfully; or it is to be punctuated thus: Why? As if he said: What is this? Then he answers himself and says: Surely it was agreed among you to tempt the Spirit of the Lord.
**“to tempt the Spirit of the Lord?”**
• not us men, as you thought
• To tempt, etc. Rabanus. The temptation of the Spirit was in this, that they tested how great his knowledge is.
**“Behold the feet of them who have buried”** — in a brief account he sums up everything, for whoever is buried is dead
**“thy husband are at the door, and they shall carry thee out.”**
• to the sepulchre
• by this brevity he also shows that she is about to die
5.10:
**“Immediately she fell down before his feet, and gave up the ghost.”** — because not only those who do but also those who consent to the doers are worthy of death
**“And the young men coming in”** — who stood at the door
**“found her dead: and carried her out”** — as he had said before: and they shall carry thee out
**“buried her by her husband”** — Rabanus. From this many take an example, that wives should be buried beside their husbands. Others think it unworthy to take examples from transgressors, whom partnership had made equal in merit in crime, and likewise in death and burial.
5.11:
**“And there came great fear upon the whole church”** — the assembly of the faithful believers
**“and upon all that heard these things.”** — even the unbelievers
5.12:
**“And by the hands of the apostles”**
• not only by words or by shadow, as is said of Peter
• the greater cause of fear is described, and the zeal of the rulers is stirred up, which is mentioned below
**“of the apostles”** — Not of Peter alone; although for his honour the others are passed over, their deeds are not passed over.
**“were many signs and wonders wrought among the people.”** — whence the zeal of the priests is kindled
**“And they were all with one accord”** — the wise
**“all with one accord”** — Rabanus. As said above: they are to be admired in this, that the greatness of grace had not made their minds diverse.
**“in Solomon's porch.”** — in the house of the wise man, where they together persevered in prayer and teaching
5.13:
**“But of the rest”**
• of the unbelievers
• But of the rest, etc. By the example of Ananias and his wife: for the punishment of the two who had fraudulently joined themselves to them gave an example to the rest.
**“no man durst join himself unto them;”** — feignedly
**“but the people magnified them.”** — standing afar off and amazed
5.14:
**“was more increased”** — was increasing
**“the multitude of men and women who believed in the Lord, was more increased”** — Rabanus. So great was the multitude of believers that, as the strength of faith grew, the shadow alone sufficed; or so many sick were then brought by believers that he could not touch them all.
**“of men and women”** — no sex is excluded from the kingdom of God, for there is no respect of persons with God
5.15:
**“Insomuch that they brought forth the sick into the streets”** — that were broad
**“brought forth the sick, and laid them on beds and couches”** — of whatever kind, according to the different couches
**“that when Peter came”** — as if he were the prince
**“his shadow at the least”**
• Bede. Then Peter with the shadow of his body invisibly relieved the sick, who now with the invisible shelter of his intercession strengthens the sick faithful; and because Peter too is a figure of the Church, he himself walks upright, but with his shadow raises those lying down; because the Church, intent on heavenly things, passes through the earth as in a shadow, and here with the sacraments and figures of heavenly things renews those whom there she rewards with everlasting gifts.
• Rabanus. The saying of the Lord is fulfilled: “He that believeth in me, the works that I do, he also shall do; and greater than these shall he do.”
5.16:
**“And there came also together to Jerusalem a multitude”** — besides the inhabitants of Jerusalem
**“out of the neighbouring cities, bringing sick persons”** — with diseases and pains
**“and such as were troubled with unclean spirits”** — to distinguish them from good spirits
**“who were all healed.”** — to keep hold of the apostles
5.17:
**“Then the high priest rising up, and all they that were with him,”** — this heresy was one of the seven heresies of the Jews
**“the heresy”** — Bede. Rabanus. Heresy is interpreted as division; or heresy from choice, because, having disregarded the sayings of others, it chooses what it thinks is to be followed.
**“of the Sadducees”** — Bede. Sadducees are interpreted “the just.” They were named from Sadoc the priest, either on account of race or on account of morals; but justifying themselves, they claimed for themselves what they were not. Denying the resurrection of the bodies, they said that souls perish with the flesh; but they believed that there was neither angel nor any spirit; they rejected all the Scriptures except the books of Moses; and therefore they most of all agreed with the princes in the persecution of the apostles, who by power and signs gave testimony to the resurrection of Christ.
**“were filled with envy.”**
• zeal produced this fruit
• which not only began but in that hour reached the fullness of malice
5.18: **“And they laid hands on the apostles, and put them in the common prison.”** — either on account of the strength of the prison, or on account of the fame of the power displayed in public
5.19:
**“But an angel of the Lord”** — to distinguish him from the evil one
**“An angel of the Lord leading them out”** — Bede. Thomas does not doubt that Christ had flesh and bones, whom he saw enter with the doors shut; behold, he himself with his companions, still clothed in mortal flesh, goes out with the doors shut.
5.20:
**“Go, and standing”** — firm and steady, or open
**“speak in the temple”** — in a crowded place which the priests frequented
**“to the people”** — not to priests
**“all the words of this life”** — concealing nothing for fear
**“of this life”** — Rabanus. Christian or eternal, which is not added because the sect of Christ was notorious, for which they were given over to prison.
5.21:
**“Who having heard this, entered”** — according to the angel’s command, obedience was ready
**“early in the morning, entered into the temple, and taught”** — as it had been commanded: speak to the people
**“the high priest coming, and they that were with him, called together the council”**
• because they had been placed in custody for this purpose, that they might be brought to judgment
• of priests and scribes
**“and all the ancients”** — by age
**“of the children of Israel; and they sent to the prison to have them brought”** — the apostles
5.22: **“But when the ministers came, and opening the prison”** — which they had found shut
5.23:
**“Saying: The prison indeed we found shut”**
• so that the miracle may be greater
• The prison indeed, etc. Bede. The mad Jews, who goaded by envy say that Jesus was stolen from the tomb by the apostles, will by that same theft say that the apostles were taken out of the shut prison.
**“with all diligence, and the keepers”**
• not negligent
• so that there may be less opportunity of escaping
**“standing before the doors”** — not from the side or from behind
5.24:
**“The officer of the temple”** — Bede. According to the Greek, the word officer should be read in the singular, as also in what follows, where it says: Then the officer went away with the ministers.
**“and the chief priests”** — powerful and wise
**“they were in doubt”** — whether it had been done by fraud or by power
**“They were in doubt”** — Bede. Nor do they believe even so; for inner malice hardens a faithless heart, even against manifest signs.
5.25:
**“But one came and told them: Behold, the men whom you put in prison are in the temple”** — it is clear there was no fraud, since after the escape they are not hidden
**“standing, and teaching the people”** — which you forbade
5.26:
**“Then went the officer with the ministers, and brought them without violence”** — behold the greatness of faith: not to fear those who had bound themselves
**“for they feared the people”** — not God
5.27: **“And when they had brought them, they set them before the council”** — for the Lord had said: “they will deliver you up in councils”
5.28:
**“Saying: Commanding”** — Commanding. Bede. In Greek: “Did we not strictly command you?” For such speech suits one who is rather asking.
**“we commanded you”** — we did not speak lightly but commanded with pontifical authority
**“that you should not teach in this name”** — Jesus; which they are silent about because of renown or hatred
**“and behold, you have filled Jerusalem”** — not only did you teach against our prohibition, but you also filled
**“You have filled Jerusalem”** — new and culpable
**“and you have a mind to bring the blood upon us”**
• by proclaiming that he was just, and Christ, the vengeance of blood
• Rabanus. It is plain that it is said by antiphrasis: “His blood upon us,” etc.
• Bede. In Greek it is read as a question, and the rash question of the high priest is refuted by a prudent answer.
• Rabanus. They speak by questioning, for there is usually doubt in words when the settled judgment is held firm in the heart.
**“the blood upon us”** — Bede. The chief priest has forgotten the debt which he himself and his people invoked, saying: “His blood be upon us and our children.”
**“of this man”** — not of God
**“this”** — Jesus; which they do not add, as said above, for two reasons
5.29:
**“But Peter ... answering”** — as the leader
**“and the apostles”** — Out of fervour and zeal they do not allow one to speak for all.
**“said: We ought to obey God, rather than men”** — By speaking briefly they give an example of not using a roundabout of words.
5.30:
**“The God of our fathers”**
• Above he had said: “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”; therefore now he says briefly: the God of the fathers.
• Rabanus. Not new, nor recently invented by us, so that their disobedience may be inexcusable.
**“hath raised up”** — In the resurrection; this they hated most.
**“Jesus, whom you put to death”** — Here they plainly bring the blood upon them.
**“hanging him upon a tree”** — As one guilty and cursed.
5.31:
**“Him hath God ... to be Prince”** — Of the whole Church that is in heaven and on earth.
**“and Saviour”** — Of men.
**“hath exalted”** — By miracles, or by ascension into heaven.
**“with his right hand”** — By the prosperity of eternity, or by the Son.
**“to give repentance to Israel”** — Therefore miracles were done; therefore he ascended into heaven.
**“and remission of sins”** — Which is the fruit of penance.
5.32:
**“And we are witnesses of these things”** — Of the miracles, of the ascension, of the sending of the Spirit.
**“and the Holy Ghost”**
• Lest the human word be worthless.
• He is a witness.
**“The Holy Ghost”** — Bede. He strengthened us so that, even while you resist, we may firmly preach the great works of God; he himself, speaking in us, forms the words you hear.
**“whom hath given”** — He will not give.
**“God ... to all”** — Now before you.
**“to all”** — Rabanus. Not to us alone, but to all who obey, even to you if you are willing to receive. In this he calls them to repentance.
5.33:
**“When they had heard these things, they were cut to the heart”** — In their hearts.
**“and they thought to put them to death”** — Because they could not stop them with words.
5.34:
**“But one in the council rising up, a Pharisee”** — Not a Sadducee, who denied the resurrection.
**“named Gamaliel”**
• Gamaliel. A disciple of the apostles, as was supposed, remaining among the Jews by the counsel of the apostles, so that he might destroy their worst counsels and soften their fury.
• Bede. As Clement says, Gamaliel was a fellow of the apostles in the faith, but he remained with the Jews by the apostles' counsel, so that in such a storm he might be able to calm their fury.
**“a doctor of the law”** — Not an unskilled man, who would not be heard.
**“respected by all the people, commanded the men to be put forth a little while”** — He judged that the apostles should withdraw, as if they were to be shut out.
5.35:
**“And he said to them: Ye men of Israel”** — Who ought to be sober and prudent.
**“take heed to yourselves”** — Not judging with fury.
5.36:
**“Theodas”** — Bede. Josephus says that Theodas persuaded many, having taken their possessions out of the city, to besiege the banks of the Jordan; and being a magician he called himself a prophet, and promised that by dividing the river he would give them passage. By order of Fadus the procurator a troop of horsemen came upon them, and, many being killed or taken, carried his head back to Jerusalem.
**“affirming himself to be somebody”** — A great prophet, or Christ.
5.37:
**“Judas”** — Of this man Josephus says that he compelled the people, lest by paying tribute to the Romans they should lose their liberty, putting forward from the law that God alone is to be served, and that those who gave tithes ought not to give tribute; which heresy grew so much that the Pharisees and a great part of the people asked Christ whether it was lawful to give tribute to Caesar.
**“in the days of the enrolling”** — when the decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled
**“and drew away”** — from the truth
**“the people after him”** — much, so that we should not wonder at the multitude of believers
**“he also perished; and all, even as many as consented to him, were dispersed”** — those consenting with those doing; the same punishment seizes them
5.38: **“And now, therefore, I say to you, refrain”** — do not kill
5.39:
**“But if it be of God, you cannot overthrow it”** — The council presses more heavily, so that it is not despised.
**“lest perhaps you be found even to fight against God. And they consented to him”** — To consent is to join sense to sense.
5.40:
**“And calling in the apostles”** — by common consent
**“after they had scourged them”** — Rabanus. Behold, the strength of faith is plain, which could not be restrained by words; nor were they first forbidden by speech and now scourged, but only now scourged with rods.
**“they charged them”** — “In their synagogues they will scourge you.”
**“that they should not speak at all in the name of Jesus”** — “And you shall be hated by all men for my name’s sake.”
5.41:
**“And they indeed went from the presence of the council, rejoicing”** — “Be glad in that day and rejoice, for behold, your reward is great in heaven.”
**“that they were accounted worthy”** — That they were accounted worthy, etc. They did not think they were labouring but receiving the greatest gift, because blessed are those who suffer persecution for my sake.
**“to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus”** — not for any crime; where Christ is the cause, there a curse is to be desired
5.42:
**“And every day”** — Often such things are placed between chapters, briefly gathering many things, so that an end is set to the preceding discourse and a foundation to the following one.
**“in the temple, and from house to house”** — the neighbouring houses of the temple, or of the whole city
**“they ceased not”** — those things that pertain to morals
**“to teach and preach Christ Jesus”** — faith concerning Jesus, who was the Christ

6.1:
**“And in those days”** — previously he had said “every day”
**“the number of the disciples increasing”** — by the zeal of the preachers
**“the number of the disciples”** — of Christians, by which at that time they were called disciples
**“a murmuring”** — Bede. The cause of the murmuring was that the Hebrews, as more learned in the ministry, preferred their own widows to the widows of the Greeks.
**“of the Greeks”** — Rabanus. Either of foreign Gentiles dwelling in the city, or of Jews by race who had been born and brought up among the Greeks. They murmured because they were despised, or because their widows were not admitted to the ministry, or because they were burdened with the daily ministration beyond the others.
**“were neglected”** — Rabanus. They were more burdened by the contempt.
6.2:
**“Then the twelve calling together”** — by common consent
**“the twelve calling together the multitude”** — they seek the consent of the multitude, which ought to be taken as an example
**“It is not reason”** — Bede. The apostles show that bishops and teachers of the Church ought not to be entangled in bodily affairs.
**“that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables”** — the dishes of the mind are better than the feasts of the body
6.3:
**“Wherefore, brethren, look ye out”**
• not women
• Consider, etc. Seven, etc. Bede. Here the apostles were already making distinctions, and through the churches their successors appointed seven deacons who would be of higher rank than the rest and stand near the altar like pillars, not without the mystery of the number seven.
**“among you”** — let them be chosen from all among you
**“men of good reputation”** — to whom all bear witness.
**“seven men”** — this number is fitting to the Holy Ghost.
**“full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom”** — which is evident in signs and tongues.
**“whom we may appoint”** — you choose, that we may appoint.
**“over this business”** — that they themselves may serve, or preside over those who serve.
6.4:
**“But we will give ourselves continually to prayer”**
• we shall adhere to this active life, to contemplation.
• pray without ceasing.
**“But we will give ourselves”** — They do not ask about themselves, but judge.
**“and to the ministry of the word”**
• of preaching.
• for yourselves and others.
**“continually”** — that others may be instructed.
6.5:
**“And the saying was liked”** — lest a stumbling block be made to the gospel, they calm the murmurs, they aim at the agreement of all.
**“the saying was liked by all the multitude. And they chose”**
• the multitude of the people.
• They chose, etc. And praying, etc. Rabanus. This order is to be kept: in the case of those to be ordained, the people choose, the bishop ordains.
**“Stephen”** — Rabanus. Here he is placed first and alone is praised, so that in one all may be praised, or honor may be given to the first martyr.
**“a man full of faith”** — in God, or whom, as the outcome proved, men were to believe in both respects.
**“and of the Holy Ghost, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas, a proselyte of Antioch”** — here he alone is called a proselyte, either because the others were not proselytes, or because he was to be notable; therefore he is called a proselyte as if a stranger.
6.6:
**“These they set”** — those who chose.
**“before the apostles; and they praying”**
• the apostles.
• And praying, etc. Bede. The common dispensation required that ministers be chosen; and when these were found worthy, as the providence of saving counsel gradually increased, it pleased them that these same men be ordained ministers of the holy altar and of the Lord’s blood, as well as of the refection and the common table. This is proved from this, that it is said: “praying, they imposed hands upon them”; this is proper to those who are advanced to the office of the most holy altar.
• By this example prayers are made in ordinations, although the prayer of the apostles is not written.
**“imposed hands upon them”** — by this authority hands are laid on deacons.
6.7:
**“And the word of the Lord”**
• he had said, with the number of disciples increasing, etc.
• And the word of the Lord, etc. Rabanus. It seems like a recapitulation, because he had said, “every day they ceased not teaching,” etc., and he returns to this very thing, saying, “And the word of the Lord increased.”
• Rabanus. Often in this book and also in the Gospel such chapters are inserted, lest sentences ending suddenly or introduced suddenly become cheap. Whence, to adorn the end of the past narrative and the beginning of the following, and for the praise of the Gospel and of the apostles, these words are inserted: “And the word of the Lord increased, and the number of the disciples was multiplied.”
• A greater cause of persecution arises from this, because zeal had previously been stirred up when the people believed.
**“increased”** — in the faith and work of believers.
**“and the number of the disciples was multiplied in Jerusalem exceedingly”** — for it had not yet been preached in other cities.
6.8:
**“And Stephen”** — crowned, or a pattern of martyrdom for believers.
**“Stephen”** — In Greek; in Latin, “crown”: what he was to receive in fact, he anticipated by the presage of his name, for after Christ’s cross he was the first crowned with martyrdom, who was stoned in humility, yet exalted. In Hebrew Stephen is interpreted “our rule,” who, first to suffer, became for the martyrs who followed the pattern of dying for Christ.
**“full”** — thus it is to be punctuated: full of the Holy Spirit, supply grace and fortitude; he did signs and wonders.
**“of grace”** — of the Holy Spirit.
**“and fortitude”** — of faith.
6.9:
**“There arose some”** — assembly or gathering
**“which is called”**
• from a region
• these three places are near to one another
**“of the Libertines”** — Bede. Libertines are called the sons of freedmen, that is, of those who were released from slavery and given liberty. It is plain, then, that those who first resisted the faith of Christ were of servile stock; and though freed by men, they were nevertheless slaves of sin, figuring heretics and persecutors of faith and holiness.
**“and of the Cyrenians”** — Cyrene is a city
**“and of the Alexandrians”** — Alexandria is the metropolis of Egypt
**“and of them that were of Cilicia and Asia”** — Cilicia and Lesser Asia are next to each other
6.10:
**“And they were not able to resist”**
• they indeed wished and tried
• Rabanus. “Take no thought how or what to speak; for it is not you that speak, but the Spirit of your Father that speaketh in you.” That also is fulfilled: “I will not leave you orphans,” but “I will send you the Paraclete,” etc.
**“They were not able to resist”** — Bede. It was fitting that in the first martyr he should confirm what he had promised in delivering martyrs for his name, saying: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which your adversaries shall not be able to resist.”
**“the wisdom”** — of the Scriptures
**“and the spirit that spoke”** — with all confidence and without fear
6.11:
**“Then they suborned men”** — the cunning of deceit
**“to say, they had heard him speak”** — because he preferred the new law to the old
**“words of blasphemy against Moses and against God”**
• the Father
• to whom he said Christ was equal
6.12:
**“They stirred up”** — to the council
**“the people, and the ancients, and the scribes”** — excelling in authority
**“and running together, they took him”**
• because they could not resist, they prepare to inflict death
• behold, violence
6.13:
**“And they set up false witnesses”** — he imitates the passion of Christ, against whom false witnesses rose up
**“who said”** — accusing out of envy
**“This man”**
• they add to this what they were ordered to say
• From contempt they call him not by his proper name, but “this man,” as if he were carnal and weak.
**“ceaseth not to speak words against the holy place and the law”** — Jerusalem, because he preferred the Church and the new law to the temple and the old law
6.14:
**“For we have heard him say, that this Jesus of Nazareth”** — from Nazareth, which is a lowly and inferior place
**“shall destroy this place”** — holy and to be revered by all
**“and shall change the traditions”** — that the new law may succeed the old
6.15:
**“And all that sat in the council, looking on him, saw his face as if”** — by terrible brightness or the beauty of whiteness
**“the face of an angel”** — he was truly an angel, that is, a messenger of God’s will

7.1:
**“Then the high priest said”** — to Stephen
**“Are these things so”** — that you have blasphemed God, the law, and the holy place
7.2:
**“Who said”**
• prudent
• contemporaries
• because they were of one kind
• Ye men, etc. The God of glory, etc. Stephen, mindful of that precept, “Love your enemies,” etc., announces salvation to his persecutors.
**“Men, brethren”** — Bede. Because Stephen was accused of having blasphemed against Moses and God, at the beginning of his speech he meets their slander, saying that the God who spoke to the fathers and prophets is the God of majesty and glory. He also praises Moses, but proves them rebellious and ever disobedient; yet he used skill in speaking to the rebellious, beginning as if he feared them: “Ye men, brethren, and fathers.” A gentle and mild speech wins the hearer, that it may commend the speaker. He began winningly that he might be heard for long; and he who was accused of speaking against God and the law preaches the true God at the beginning of his speech. He also so expounded the law that he was the preacher of him whose destroyer he was accused of being; and in the course of the speech, refuting their errors, he fully showed the vigor of his mind and that he was free from fear of the enemy.
**“and fathers”** — elders
**“hear”** — with the inner ear
**“The God of glory”**
• whose glory is for ever
• first he shows that he does not blaspheme God
**“appeared”** — by an angel
**“to our father Abraham”** — both by faith and by flesh
**“When he was in Mesopotamia”** — Bede. Mesopotamia is situated at the head of Syria, to the north.
**“when he was in Mesopotamia”** — Rabanus. Mesopotamia and Charran are in Chaldea; he migrated from Mesopotamia to Charran.
7.3:
**“And said to him”** — And he said, etc. In Genesis it seems to be contained that the Lord spoke to Abram after the death of his father, who died in Charran, where his son dwelt with him; but before he dwelt in that city, when he was in Mesopotamia, it was said to him: “Go forth out of thy country,” etc.
**“Go forth out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and come into the land which I shall shew thee”**
• that obedience and patience may be greater
• Go forth out of thy country and from thy kindred, etc. By the country and kindred of Abram he means the fatherland and race of the Chaldeans, from which he had already gone out, living now in Mesopotamia, but he was still held by hope and desire of returning; and therefore he hears: “Go forth out of thy country and from thy kindred,” not that he should draw his body out, which he had already done, but that he should tear out the love of his heart. And therefore what follows: “Then he went out of the land,” etc., is to be understood not of the body but of the love, by which he was torn away forever from the Chaldeans in place and in desire. According to the faith of the chronicles, in the same year he left Chaldea, entered Mesopotamia, stayed in Charran, and was led into the land of promise.
• Rabanus. Stephen omitted the third item, that is, “and from thy father’s house,” which was done on account of the people’s excessive skill or unskillfulness.
• Bede. From Chaldea, in which is Charran.
• Rabanus. Abraham went out from Ur of the Chaldeans. Ur is interpreted “fire.” The Chaldeans worship fire, to which they even sacrifice men. The Hebrews relate that Aram, the brother of Abram, was offered to the fire of the Chaldeans and burned, but that Abram’s fire was put out by God; wherefore he fled from there with his father and Lot, the son of Aram, and the whole household, to Charran, where, after his father died, it was said to him: “Go forth out of thy country,” etc.
7.4:
**“Then he went out”** — willingly
**“of the land of the Chaldeans”** — Mesopotamia
**“and dwelt in Charan, and from thence, after his father was dead”**
• Thare
• His father, etc. But he promised, etc. Rabanus. He returns to the origin of the race of Israel and the beginning of divine friendship, so that he omits nothing in which he might seem to blaspheme.
**“he removed him into this land, wherein you now dwell”** — You dwell, etc. Not the apostles, who had left the land, nor Stephen, who was already as if at the point of death.
7.5:
**“And he gave him no inheritance”** — although he possessed many fields there, yet he had no field of his own
**“in it, no, not the pace of a foot”** — the least part: for he possessed the cave with the field not by inheritance but bought it for a price from Ephron the son of Seor the Hittite
**“but he promised”** — wherefore it is given to his seed by his merit
**“to give it him in possession”** — inheritance
**“and to his seed after him, when as yet he had no child”** — this is said so that the knowledge of God promising may appear more clearly
7.6:
**“And God said”** — by an angel, as is supposed
**“That his seed should sojourn”** — a stranger who does not cultivate his own land
**“in a strange country”** — Canaan or Egypt, namely
**“and that they should bring them under bondage”** — Egyptians
**“and treat them evil”** — afflicting them with hard labours
**“four hundred years”**
• Because thy seed shall be a sojourner, etc. Bede. It is not to be understood as if it said that this seed was to be ill treated and subjected to bondage for four hundred and thirty years; but it is to be read by hyperbaton: that his seed will be a stranger for four hundred and thirty years, in part of which time bondage also occurred, because it is written: “In Isaac shall thy seed be called.” From the year of Isaac’s birth to the year of the departure from Egypt, four hundred and thirty-five years are counted, in which that seed was to be a stranger, whether in the land of Chanaan or in Egypt.
• Rabanus. It is to be joined thus: sojourner, four hundred and thirty years. For from when God promised Abraham until Jacob’s going down into Egypt there were two hundred and fifteen years; from Jacob’s going down into Egypt until Israel’s departure out of Egypt there were two hundred and fifteen years. The Hebrews served in Egypt a hundred and forty-four years. In Genesis, however, only four hundred years are counted; in Exodus and in Stephen’s preaching thirty are added. For sometimes in the Scriptures, where a great number is set down, the smaller number is passed over for the sake of brevity, where not the care of counting but only the greatness is shown, which Genesis followed. But Exodus, the time of the sojourning being ended, carefully describes the whole space of the pilgrimage. In the Acts of the Apostles also Paul assigns four hundred and thirty years to this number, saying, as it were, after four hundred and thirty years; which number is completed not from the first promise, but from the birth of Isaac until the distribution of the land of promise.
7.7:
**“And the nation which they shall serve”** — the Egyptians
**“will I judge”**
• with ten plagues and the drowning of Pharao with all the people in the Red Sea
• Rabanus. Judgment sometimes signifies discernment, as there: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause”; sometimes punishment, as: “Judge them, O God.”
**“said the Lord; and after these things they shall go out”** — out of Egypt
**“and shall serve”**
• they shall begin to serve
• freed from human servitude
**“to me in this place”**
• the land of promise, namely
• he shows that he does not blaspheme the holy place
7.8:
**“The covenant of circumcision”** — Rabanus. The covenant or sign was made so that the people of Israel might be divided from the Gentiles not only by morals but also by a bodily sign. It is placed in the genital member so that the diminishing of the flesh would be in that part which is covered by the secrecy of modesty, and because it was to be kept through all generations it was placed in the genital member.
**“and he gave him the covenant of circumcision”** — Mystically: circumcision signifies the mortification of the flesh. It is done on that member by which the pleasure of the flesh is fulfilled. Also in that by which it was covered, carnal circumcision signifies that boasting of glory in spiritual circumcision is to be avoided.
**“and so he begot Isaac”** — that is, circumcised, not in the foreskin
**“the eighth day”** — Rabanus. By the eight days the mystery of our circumcision is shown, which is contained in the eighth day of the New Testament, which is in the Lord’s resurrection, and in the eight beatitudes; on the eighth day we are circumcised from vices.
**“And Isaac begot Jacob”** — circumcised; the word circumcised is repeated, and Jacob circumcised, the twelve patriarchs circumcised, so that he praises them rather than blames them
7.9:
**“And the patriarchs, through envy, sold Joseph”** — because he was loved more than the others by the father
**“sold into Egypt”** — on account of the dreams that promised him great things
**“Sold into Egypt”** — Telling it briefly, he passes to the end. For he was sold first not to the Egyptians but to the Ishmaelite merchants and the Madianites, and they sold him into Egypt to Putiphar, a priest.
7.10:
**“and delivered him”** — from the hand of his brothers, from the pit, from the hand of the merchants, and from the lady of Egypt, from danger of death, and at last from the prison itself
**“out of all his tribulations”** — adversities and dangers
**“and he gave him favour”** — before the priest, and the prince of the prison, and Pharao
**“and wisdom”** — of interpreting dreams and of foreseeing counsel
7.11:
**“Now there came a famine”** — Rabanus. It is doubted whether the famine came over the whole world.
**“upon all Egypt and Chanaan”** — with all the inhabitants in all Egypt and Chanaan
**“and great tribulation”** — the same, tribulation and famine
**“and found no”** — even if they sought; from this it is thought that there was famine everywhere
**“food, our fathers.”** — that they are patriarchs is plain, because he does not blaspheme the fathers, whom he even calls his own
7.12:
**“But when Jacob had heard that there was corn in Egypt, he sent our fathers”** — except Benjamin
**“first,”** — at the first time Joseph recognized them, and they him at the second
7.13: **“And at the second time, Joseph was known by his brethren, and his kindred was made known”** — for he had hidden it before, because the Egyptians, worshipping the sheep, hated the eating of sheep, which Israel offered
7.14:
**“And Joseph sending, called thither”** — called out
**“Jacob, his father, and all his kindred”** — Joseph’s brothers, namely the sons of the brothers as well, because Jacob was not kindred but offspring
**“seventy-five souls.”**
• a part for the whole.
• Rabanus. If Jacob and Joseph with the two sons are not counted, there will be only sixty-six; when they are added, they make seventy. Luke adds five more, according to the edition of the Seventy, which he knew to be the Vulgate and confirmed by the authority of the Greeks. If then he had opposed the accustomed authority, he who seemed to detract from an edition long believed would not have been trusted. He preferred therefore to confirm the faith of Christ with the interpreters agreeing, rather than to make his speech suspect for the sake of the Hebrew truth.
**“Seventy-five souls”** — Bede. This is said according to the edition of the Seventy interpreters. In the Hebrew only seventy are found; but if the series of souls is reckoned according to Genesis, with Jacob and Joseph added, together with the two sons who were in Egypt, only seventy are found.
7.15:
**“So Jacob went down”** — Allegorically: he who goes down into Egypt, that is, clings to the world, truly goes down.
**“Went down”** — According to the position of the places, the descent was from the land of promise into Egypt; but since slavery had followed liberty, it is said that Jacob went down into Egypt with his family.
**“Jacob into Egypt, and he died himself”** — in Egypt.
**“and our fathers,”** — each patriarch in his own age.
7.16:
**“Translated”** — Rabanus. By synecdoche they are said to have been translated, for Joseph alone, to whom Jacob said: “I have given thee Sichem, a portion above thy brethren.” Therefore in the book of Josue his bones are read to have been buried in it, which the children of Israel carried over from Egypt at his command. For in Exodus it is read: “Moses took Joseph’s bones with him,” because Joseph had said to the children of Israel: “Carry out my bones from hence with you.”
**“and they were translated”** — Bede. Of Joseph alone the Scripture testifies that his bones, translated from Egypt, were buried in Sichem; but from the words of Stephen and the writings of Jerome, who dwelt in those places, it is clear that the other patriarchs also were buried there, although the memory of Joseph is more famous, who gave this command concerning his bones, to whose tribe that city belonged. Jerome, in the history of Paula, says thus: He passed over to Sichem and saw the sepulchres of the twelve patriarchs. The same: the twelve patriarchs are not buried in Arboc but in Sichem.
**“into Sichem, and were laid in the sepulchre”**
• And were laid in the sepulchre, etc. Rabanus. Genesis teaches that Abraham bought a sepulchre from Ephron the son of Seor the Hethite in Chariatharbe, in which he himself and Isaac, Jacob and Adam were buried. Likewise it teaches that Jacob received, near Sichem, a part of a field where he might pitch his tents, from Emor the father of Sichem, a hundred pieces of silver being given. Abraham therefore did not buy the sepulchre from Emor the father of Sichem but from Ephron the Hethite, in which the twelve patriarchs are not buried but in Sichem, as we have said. But Stephen, speaking in the popular way, follows the opinion of the people; for, joining two narratives, he aims not so much at the order of the history as at the cause with which he was dealing. For being accused of having taught against the holy place and the law, he shows that Christ was promised from the law, and that they then wished to serve neither Moses nor the Lord.
• Bede. He confuses two histories and entangles the one with the other. For Abraham did not buy from the sons of Emor the son of Sichem, but Jacob bought Sichem from them. Therefore it is to be joined thus: they were translated into Sichem, by the sons of Emor the son of Sichem, as if it were said: into that Sichem which Jacob bought, from the sons of Emor the son of Sichem. In Genesis Sichem is read to have been the son of Emor, whence some think there were two Sichems, of whom the one is called by Luke the father of Emor, the other by Genesis his son. Some join the beginning and the end of the sentence, saying, from the sons of Sichem, and afterwards bring in Emor son, so that this place agrees with Genesis.
**“In the sepulchre that Abraham bought”** — Bede. This is of Jacob alone, whose body his sons took out of Egypt and buried in the double cave, where Abraham was buried with Sara, and Isaac with Rebecca, and there Lia was laid. Whence that city is called Hebron, that is, marriage, because the fathers were buried there with their wives.
**“that Abraham bought”** — he bought that cave for four hundred shekels from Ephron the son of Seor the Hethite.
**“for a sum of money of the sons”**
• to the sons of Sichem, so that it is an explanation of the preceding.
• From the sons, etc. He returns to the order of the narrative; for he had said before, by way of anticipation, that they were carried over into Sichem by the sons of Emor, the son of Sichem.
**“Hemor, the son of Sichem.”** — who was the son of Emor.
7.17:
**“And when the time drew near”** — four hundred and thirty years.
**“of the promise”** — of that promise of which it was said: “They shall come out and serve me in this place.”
**“which God had promised”** — in Greek: ‘promised’.
**“to Abraham, the people increased”**
• Israel, Christ having been crucified and the apostles having suffered.
• Joseph and his brothers having died.
7.18:
**“Another king”** — This king is the devil, who loves the effeminate and hates the manly.
**“arose in Egypt, who knew not Joseph.”** — he did not know, or did not repay the kindness.
7.19:
**“This same dealing craftily with our race”**
• by commanding the midwives to kill the males.
• Our race, etc. Our fathers, etc. He says “our fathers” and “our race” lest it seem that he blasphemes the fathers.
**“afflicted our fathers”** — clearly by commanding that the infants be exposed; that is, or afflicted them with the pain of servitude.
**“that they should expose”** — into the river.
**“their children, to the end they might not be kept alive.”** — that is, that they might be kept alive.
7.20:
**“At the same time”** — when the new king arose over Egypt.
**“was Moses born, and he was acceptable to God”**
• from whom he had favour.
• Rabanus. Moses is a type of the Saviour, who, the devil being struck down, freed his own race. He was hidden for three times in Israel: from Abraham, namely, to David; from David to the transmigration of Babylon; from then to the nativity of Christ. Cast out by the Jews, he was taken up and nourished by the Church of the Gentiles coming to baptism, which was before the daughter of the devil; he who was “mighty in work and word before God and all the people,” who in the fulness of times “hath visited us, and wrought the redemption of his people.”
**“Acceptable to God”** — He shows that he did not blaspheme Moses.
**“Moses”** — Rabanus. Aquaticus, because he was taken from the water. Or Liniens, because he was found in a basket smeared with pitch.
**“who was nourished”** — because he had a beautiful face.
**“three months in his father's house.”** — secretly.
7.21:
**“And when he was exposed”** — in the river Nile.
**“Pharao's daughter took him up”** — from the river.
**“Pharao's daughter”** — who had come to the river to wash.
7.22:
**“And Moses was instructed”** — so that he would surpass others
**“in all the wisdom of the Egyptians; and he was mighty in his words”** — eloquent
**“and in his deeds.”** — mighty
7.23:
**“And when he was full forty years old”** — It is usual to say of a good thought that it rises into the heart.
**“it came into his heart to visit”** — who were weakened by the burden of servitude
**“Her brethren, the children of Israel.”** — by race
7.24:
**“And when he had seen one of them suffer wrong, he defended him”** — his brother
**“striking the Egyptian, he avenged him”** — He shows that the one who did the wrong was not of his own kin.
7.25:
**“And he thought”** — that is, he thought they would understand that what he had done in one case he would do in all.
**“that his brethren understood that God by his hand would save them”** — the deed by which he deserved to be their deliverer
**“But they understood it not.”** — the figure of the Jews is plain
7.26: **“And the day following, he shewed himself to them when they were at strife; and would have reconciled them in peace, saying:”** — Christ through the apostles preached peace
7.27:
**“But he that did the injury to his neighbour thrust him away”** — by word, as the Jews did to Christ
**“saying: Who”** — unknowing, he prophesies that Moses was given to Israel as prince and judge
**“hath appointed thee prince and judge over us?”**
• Who appointed thee, etc. God alone: “There is no power but from God.” From this, they had received such an answer from Christ: “Man, who hath appointed me judge, or divider, over you?”
• Who appointed thee prince and judge over us? In his contention he already rebukes them, who at that time were opposed to the law and to Moses.
7.28: **“What, wilt thou kill me, as thou didst yesterday kill the Egyptian?”** — Wilt thou kill me, etc.? Some think that he who was defended brought up the matter out of anger.
7.29:
**“And Moses fled”** — Moses, fearing the Egyptians on account of the one he had killed
**“Fled”** — Moses fled into Madian, that is, Christ into the Gentiles.
**“upon this word”** — because he wished to be hidden
**“and was a stranger in the land of Madian, where he begot”** — by Sephora, daughter of the priest of Madian, whom he had taken as wife
**“two sons.”** — Gersam and Eliezer
7.30:
**“And when forty years were expired,”** — Behold, he does not blaspheme but praises.
**“There appeared”** — Rabanus. So Christ after his ascension appeared through the apostles to the Jews and unbelievers who were quarrelling and who resisted the apostles.
**“in the desert of mount Sina”** — while he was driving the flock into the inner parts of the desert
**“an angel”** — Michael in the person of the Lord, or he himself “angel of great counsel”
**“in a flame of fire in a bush.”**
• which was made so that they might fear and know that “our God is a consuming fire”
• Rabanus. Therefore the form of the fire, which cannot be imitated, was shown to them, so that they would not make any likeness.
• Rabanus. In the flame of the bush was a sign of deliverance, because that people, although inflamed by temptation, was nevertheless not to perish in tribulation. The same is signified in the loosing of the shoe, because it is as easy for God to free anyone from slavery as it is ready for a man to take off a shoe.
**“In a flame of fire”** — In the flame of fire. The fire in the bramble is the Holy Spirit, and the sins of the people are like thorns, because the heat of the Holy Spirit did not consume the sins of that people, who set dense thorns of wickedness against the benefits of God.
**“in a bush”** — Rabanus. The bramble burns but is not consumed, and the name of bramble suits the mountain; for Sinai is interpreted “bramble.” The bramble is a kind of thorn, signifying the Church, which is inflamed by persecution but does not perish, because Christ speaks in it.
7.31:
**“And Moses seeing it, wondered at the sight”** — that the burning bush was not consumed, contrary to custom.
**“And as he drew near to view it, the voice of the Lord came unto him, saying:”** — now he is called the Lord, whereas before he was called the angel.
7.32:
**“I am the God”**
