• always present.
• Serpents are not to be feared where God is present and speaking.
**“I am”** — “I am” is the proper word of God, according to that: “I am who am”; and: “He who is hath sent me to you.”
**“of thy fathers”** — by saying this he shows that he is their true son, not yet to be called yours.
**“The God of Abraham”** — not recent and new.
**“and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.”** — these three are mentioned, to whom the promise was made, which is fulfilled.
**“And Moses being terrified”** — hearing the name of the Lord.
7.33:
**“And the Lord said to him:”** — lest you think you are the lord of the Church.
**“Loose the shoes from thy feet,”** — Loose the shoes from thy feet, etc. Bede. Morally, he admonishes us that, standing in the Church, which is holy ground, we renounce dead works.
**“for the place wherein thou standest, is holy ground.”** — holy feet ought to touch a holy place.
7.34:
**“Seeing”** — Rabanus. God is wholly sight, wholly hearing. He sees all things, hears all things. But he is said to see and to hear when he has mercy.
**“I have seen the affliction of my people”** — by saying “my” he shows that he has mercy on them.
**“I have seen and I have heard”** — Rabanus. Although I permit someone to be tempted, it is not therefore to be thought that I do not know.
**“which is in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and am come down to deliver them.”** — to descend is to have compassion mercifully.
7.35:
**“This Moses”** — behold, praise, not blasphemy.
**“whom they refused”** — Synecdoche: many are said to have denied when one had spoken, or perhaps several agreed.
**“Who hath appointed thee prince and judge over us? This”** — what the proud man had asked is answered by the humble one.
**“God sent to be prince and redeemer”**
• from the slavery of Egypt.
• A prince and redeemer, etc. Great praise, since he is called prince and redeemer and leader of the people.
**“by the hand of the angel”** — by work or power, because he struck the firstborn and inflicted the other plagues.
7.36: **“He brought them out, doing wonders and signs”** — here, with God and Aaron, he struck Egypt with ten plagues, and in the desert he worked signs with the manna and the rock and countless others.
7.37:
**“This is that Moses who said:”** — to you.
**“This is that Moses”** — He turns back on them the blame which they themselves, disobedient and unbelieving, were heaping on Moses.
**“Moses who said”** — Bede. So that the teaching of Christ may not seem new, Moses, whom your fathers would not obey, foretold that he would come in the form of a man and give the precepts of life.
**“to the children of Israel, a prophet”** — visible in flesh, but with a terrible majesty above me.
**“unto you”** — not to others besides you.
7.38:
**“This is he that was in the church”** — in the assembly of the people, not alone as before, when he was speaking with the angel.
**“in the wilderness”** — in the desert of mount Sina.
**“with the angel who spoke to him on mount Sina”** — both to him and to all the people
**“and with our fathers”** — to the children of Israel
**“our fathers.”** — not only to your own
**“who received the words of life to give unto us.”** — not only to them
**“The words of life”** — Rabanus. The two tablets with the Decalogue, and the other commandments, of which it is said: “He that shall do them, shall live in them.”
7.39:
**“Whom our fathers would not obey”** — they are accused twice over: because they were unwilling, and because they did not obey
**“but thrust him away, and in their hearts turned back”** — although not in their bodies
**“into Egypt”** — to which they desired to return; or they turned back into the manner of the Egyptians, adoring the calf
7.40:
**“Saying to Aaron:”** — To Aaron. Rabanus. As to a leader, as though they spoke ignorant of the godhead. For the true God was not made, but made all things; nor is he a creature, but the creator of all.
**“Make us gods”**
• they say gods in the plural, not one God
• by the error of the nations
• Rabanus. They say gods because of the two pillars that went before them out of Egypt, in honour of which one image was made, but both pillars were adored; and therefore they say, “that may go before us,” because the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night went before the people.
**“to go before us”** — in providence and power
**“For as for this Moses”** — they say this by disparaging and dishonouring him
**“who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we know not what is become of him.”** — death or life, because he had sat forty days and nights with the Lord on the mountain
7.41:
**“And a calf”** — from the custom of the Egyptians, who worship the ox; the people is also shown by this to be wanton and dull
**“made in those days”** — so that they might worship
**“and offered sacrifices to the idol”** — they are accused more than if they had done this with a living animal
**“and rejoiced in the works of their own hands.”** — they worshipped not their creator but works made by themselves
7.42:
**“And God turned, and gave them up”**
• permitted
• But God turned, etc. Augustine. It is manifest that God works in the hearts of men to incline their wills, whether to good or to evil, etc.
**“them up to serve the host of heaven”** — that they should serve the host of heaven: the sun, moon, and stars, because they serve God by carrying out their courses
**“The host of heaven”** — Host of heaven. Bede. The host of heaven is sometimes called the army of angels, but in this place he names the stars as the host of heaven, since he at once adds: faithful to his God, etc.
**“In the books of the prophets”** — In the book of the prophets. Although there are many prophets, yet it is called one book; and among the Hebrews the twelve prophets are one book. Augustine, however, names twelve books.
**“Did you offer victims and sacrifices to me for forty years, in the desert, O house of Israel?”**
• Did you offer victims, etc. Rabanus. Although out of the necessity of serving God they poured out libations, yet, turned away in mind, they truly served idols; from the time when they transformed gold into the head of a calf. But if afterwards they are read to have offered to God, it was done not out of good will but out of fear, because of the slaughter of those who fell for the idols. For wherever there was occasion, they always returned in heart to Egypt.
• “Did you offer victims and sacrifices to me for forty years in the desert, O house of Israel?” Bede. It is asked how they did not offer to God, since it is read that some of them offered to God, not willingly but from fear of punishments. But does God not accept what is offered? He accepts the will of those who offer.
7.43:
**“And you took unto you”** — instead of the tabernacle of God
**“the tabernacle”**
• a tabernacle made
• And you took unto you the tabernacle, etc. Bede. Although you seemed to bring victims and sacrifices to the tabernacle, yet with your whole mind you embraced the shrine of Moloch, or Melchon. Now Moloch, or Melchon, is the idol of the Ammonites, which is often found, and is interpreted “our king.”
**“of Moloch”** — as to the true God
**“and the star of your god”** — of Lucifer, whom you worship as God
**“Rempham, figures”**
• understand: you took up to worship
• Rabanus. The star of your god is Lucifer, to whom they assigned images; the same gods were adored in images and stars.
• Rabanus. Some say it thus: “the star of your god,” so that the word pertains to God, because they took up not the Lord himself but his star.
**“The star of your god Rempham”** — Bede. You indeed forsook the true and living God, and you took up the star Rempham, that is, your own handiwork, for God; it signifies Lucifer, to whose worship the Saracens were enslaved; and because Rempham is interpreted your handiwork or your rest, he consequently adds: “figures which you made to adore them.”
**“which you made to adore them. And I will carry you away beyond Babylon.”**
• and into the farther parts of it
• And I will carry you away, etc. For these sacrileges you will be led captive beyond Babylon. The first martyr is not to be thought to have erred, because where it is written in the prophet “they were led beyond Damascus,” he said “beyond Babylon”; for he put the meaning rather than the word, because beyond Damascus they were led into Babylon, or beyond Babylon.
7.44:
**“The tabernacle of the testimony”**
• because in it was the ark in which the testimony was
• Since they were saying that he acted against the holy place, he shows that he did not speak blasphemy against the holy place.
**“was with our fathers”** — he always calls them common fathers
**“The tabernacle of the testimony was with our fathers”** — Bede. Because they said he was against the holy place, he shows that God does not value the adornment of stones but the splendour of souls; whence it is understood that as the tabernacle was abandoned when the temple was made, so the temple itself, when a better succeeds, is to be destroyed; whence Jeremias: “Trust not in lying words, saying: The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord.” And afterwards: “I will do to this house, in which my name is called upon, and in which you trust, as I did to Silo,” “where my name dwelt from the beginning.” “And I will cast you away from my face.”
**“in the desert, as God ordained for them”** — who was the author and disposer of the whole craft
**“according to the form”** — Rabanus. Which he had shown him on Sinai, because it is also shown that the tabernacle itself was made according to the form.
**“speaking to Moses, that he should make it according to the form which he had seen.”** — Rabanus. Historically it is said with Jesus, because Moses had died.
7.45:
**“Which also our fathers receiving, brought in”** — to be venerated and carried on the shoulders
**“our fathers with Jesus”** — in the figure of Jesus Christ
**“into the possession of the Gentiles”** — of the Chanaanites
**“whom God drove out”** — by whose power they were blotted out from Israel, as demons were driven out from Christians along with paganism
**“before the face of our fathers, unto the days of David.”** — join it thus: the tabernacle was until the days of David, and in the days of Solomon the temple succeeded the tabernacle
7.46:
**“Who”** — David
**“found grace before God,”** — pleasing to God, and he received freely from him what he asked
**“and desired”** — knowing that that tabernacle did not always suffice and was a shadow of the Church
**“to find a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.”** — the true temple, of which that was the figure, namely the Church
**“to find a tabernacle”** — The true temple, of which that was the figure, which would not be changed in place, that is, the Church, which he foresaw would be firm and unchangeable, of which the Apostle says, “The sure foundation of God standeth firm,” and elsewhere: “For other foundation no man can lay, but that which is laid; which is Christ Jesus.”
7.47: **“But Solomon built him a house.”** — David, a man of blood, was forbidden; but Solomon, a figure of the true peaceful one, that is, of the Son of God, the Peace, built a house for the Lord
7.48:
**“Yet the most High dwelleth not in houses made by hands”**
• the Lord does not dwell in things made by hands
• But the most High, etc. Rabanus. From the sentence of Solomon he convicts the Jews; who, when the temple was built, said: “If heaven, and the heavens of heavens cannot contain thee, how much less this house which I have built?” And to the word of Solomon he adds the testimony of the prophet: “Heaven is my seat,” etc., that it may be more manifest that he does not dwell in the temple of the Jews alone.
**“as the prophet saith:”** — As the prophet saith, etc. Bede. He first spoke of the first tabernacle, which was a shadow and not the truth; afterwards he set down the testimony of one speaking of the tabernacle that was more truly so: “If I shall enter into the tabernacle of my house,” etc. Last he set down the sentence of Isaias, so that: “In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand.”
7.49:
**“Heaven”** — the saints, in whom God presides by dwelling
**“is my throne,”**
• he is as it were a throne and not a house
• Heaven is my throne, etc. Thus he shows that he encompasses all things; whence elsewhere: he asserts that he measures heaven with a span and encloses the earth with a handful.
**“and the earth my footstool.”**
• sinners, whom he casts down by condemnation
• And the earth, etc. By the example of the earth he designates every creature of the Creator.
**“What house”** — He says this therefore, lest they trust in the temple so as to think God is only its inhabitant
**“will you build me?”** — to whom heaven is the throne and earth the footstool
**“saith the Lord; or what is the place of my resting?”** — Or what is the place of my rest, etc. Bede. Not a golden or marble place of earthly habitation, but that which the prophet adds: “upon whom shall my Spirit rest? but upon the humble and quiet, and him that trembleth at my words?”
7.51:
**“You stiffnecked”**
• you are
• not enduring the yoke of the law
• Stiffnecked, etc. Rabanus. Purged of the crime for which the false witnesses accused him, he begins to accuse the Jews, because one who is without crime is worthy of the office of teacher.
**“and uncircumcised”** — not bearing the light yoke of Christ, with a circumcised heart
**“in heart”**
• and though circumcised in the flesh, yet not in heart, from unbelief
• Uncircumcised in heart and ears, etc. Bede. He showed them that the circumcision in which they boasted against the grace of the gospel does not avail for salvation, for they had an unclean thought and hearing.
**“and with your ears”** — which are deaf and not purged of vices
**“you”** — not I, whom you accuse
**“you always resist the Holy Ghost”**
• not to me but to the Holy Spirit
• because you never do penance
**“as your fathers did”**
• of whom he had foretold: to whom your fathers would not obey
• nor is this begun just now
**“your fathers”** — Rabanus. Above he said “our fathers,” speaking persuasively; now, rebuking, he calls them “your fathers,” yet they are those to whom they are alike in malice.
**“so do you also”** — equal to them in wickedness
7.52:
**“Which of the prophets”** — there is none whom they have not persecuted
**“have not your fathers persecuted?”** — not ours
**“And they have slain them who foretold of the coming of the Just One;”**
• this is for the accusation of those who betrayed the just one and killed him
• And they have slain them, etc. Rabanus. He lays down three degrees of their malice: first, that they resisted the Spirit; second, that they persecuted the prophets; third, that, with malice growing, they slew them.
7.53:
**“Who have received the law”** — by this he shows them inexcusable
**“into the disposition”** — by the ministry
**“of angels”**
• ordained through angels: the law was given into the hand
• not of other ministers who were inferior
**“and have not kept it”** — by deed, sinning knowingly
7.54:
**“Now hearing these things”** — because they were jealous of the praise of God
**“they were cut to the heart”** — from the excess of their rage
**“and they gnashed with their teeth at him”** — in bestial fashion
7.55:
**“But he, being full”** — as he was grieving, or in that hour grace overflowed especially
**“of the Holy Ghost”** — who was speaking in him: “For it is not you that speak, but the Spirit of your Father that speaketh in you.”
**“looking up steadfastly to heaven”** — whence he hoped for help
**“saw the glory of God”**
• that, troubled in the flesh, he might be comforted by the Spirit
• Bede. Some of the elect, still held in this life, have merited with the cleansed eye of the heart to see the glory of God, as Stephen here and Paul, caught up to the third heaven.
**“Saw the glory of God”** — He saw the glory of God. Bede. To strengthen the martyr’s patience, heaven is opened, and lest the man to be stoned stagger on the earth, God made man, crucified, appears in glory.
**“and Jesus”** — the true man who rose again truly and ascended.
**“Standing”** — Immovably, because he was not to fall again; or the bearing of one who helps, and judges wrongs, and fights for his servant is thus shown.
**“on the right hand of God”** — where after labor he rests and judges, sitting on a throne.
**“I see the heavens”** — Rabanus. About to depart from earth, he saw the heavens opened, so that he who despised earthly life for Christ may deserve the inheritance of heaven. And therefore in the very passion he sees the reward.
**“and the Son of man”**
• not by the unfolding of the elements but by spiritual revelation, which was happening in the heart of the just.
• whom you thus esteem, or he shows the truth of the resurrection.
**“Son of man”** — Bede. Although he is the Son of God, he preferred to call himself Son of man, so that the unbelief of the Jews may be confounded, who crucified him as a mere man, whom they refused to believe to be God.
**“standing”**
• because to stand is of one fighting or helping; rightly he saw standing at the right hand him whom he had as helper among persecutors.
• the truth of the resurrection is shown.
**“on the right hand”** — where he judges all invisibly, who as judge of all will come visibly.
**“of the power of God”** — whom Stephen was invoking.
7.57:
**“And they crying out with a loud voice, stopped their ears”** — so that they might not hear him blaspheming.
**“and with one accord ran violently”** — the whole crowd is blamed, because unanimous in evil.
**“upon him”** — as an abominable one.
7.58:
**“And casting him forth”** — Rabanus. In this they were glorifying that they fulfilled the law; for Moses said of the blasphemer: “Lead him out beyond the camp and let the people stone him.”
**“without the city”** — Bede. The Lord also suffered outside the gate, who chose us out of the world for heaven; and Stephen, as a stranger to the world, is stoned outside the city; for not having here a lasting city, he sought the future one with his whole mind; and while the martyr of the world directs his gaze to the heavens, the persecutor of hard neck sends his hand to stones.
**“they stoned him”** — and Christ suffered outside the city.
**“And the witnesses laid down”**
• the false witnesses who stoned him according to the law which says: the hand of the witnesses shall first stone him.
• either from excessive fury, or lest they touch with their clothes something defiled.
7.59:
**“And they stoned Stephen”** — Here a proper name is put, that the cause of the name may be opened; for here he was truly crowned.
**“invoking, and saying: Lord Jesus”** — he prays as if present.
**“receive”**
• into heaven.
• Lord, receive, etc. To heaven, which I saw opened, Christ said to the Father: “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.” Stephen, as a servant to the Lord: Lord, receive my spirit.
**“my spirit”** — giving the body to stoning, he prays that the spirit be kept.
7.60:
**“And falling on his knees”** — secure, he did not bend his knees for himself.
**“Falling on his knees”** — Bede. He prayed standing for himself; for his enemies he bends the knee. Their greater iniquity demanded a greater remedy of supplication; and wonderful is the martyr’s virtue, who, out of zeal reproaching with the guilt of unbelief those by whom he was held, in the ardour of charity prayed in death for his killers.
**“he cried with a loud voice, saying: Lord, lay not this sin to their charge”**
• he imitates Christ saying: “Father, forgive them.”
• that it may be unloosable, but forgive them to the penitent.
**“for they know not”** — Rabanus. Many of them, in killing Stephen, thought they fulfilled the law because they believed him a blasphemer; Christ had also foretold this: “The hour cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doth a service to God.”
**“he fell asleep”** — Beautifully it is said he fell asleep and was not dead, because he offered the sacrifice of love and fell asleep in hope of resurrection.
**“And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord”** — Saints do not die, because they are changed for the better, and temporal life is turned into eternal.

8.1:
**“And Saul was consenting to his death”** — He was consenting. Indeed he did not stone but consented to those stoning, whence he would perish, unless the grace of God and penitence came to his aid, because those who do and those who consent are worthy of death.
**“And at that time there was raised”** — on which Stephen was killed
**“At that time”** — Rabanus. On which Stephen was killed? Not because the persecution was then only made, but because from that day a great persecution began, one of the leaders of the Church having been killed.
**“the church”** — A gathering or congregation, or calling.
**“which was at Jerusalem”** — not elsewhere, according to that: “And you shall be witnesses unto me in Jerusalem,” etc.
**“were dispersed”** — This is what the Lord commanded: “When they shall persecute you in this city, flee into another.” For it was carried out at his bidding, so that by occasion of the tribulation it might become a seedbed of the gospel.
**“through the countries of Judea and Samaria”** — in the likeness of grains of seed, so that from them a great harvest of faith might be multiplied.
**“except the apostles”** — who, as shepherds of the flock, were steadier than the rest.
8.2:
**“And devout men took order for Stephen's funeral”**
• that is, they performed the custom of burial.
• curaverunt returns to what he had left off, saying he fell asleep, but had not added about the burial of the body, which he now does.
**“devout men”** — from fear of the persecutors.
**“devout”** — Fearing God; either Christians who were afterwards scattered, or Jews fearing God, even if not yet Christians.
8.3:
**“But Saul”** — Rabanus. From Saul the persecutor, who was king of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, from which also came Paul; but according to the custom of the ancients, descendants take their names from their ancestors.
**“made havock”** — Rabanus. Like a wolf among the flock, according to the prophecy of Jacob: “Benjamin a ravening wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey, and at night he shall divide the spoils.”
**“of the church”** — ran about tirelessly to ravage.
**“entering in from house to house, and dragging away men and women”** — in the manner of ravagers, he spared neither sex.
**“dragging”** — He dragged them, he did not kill them, because perhaps the Lord was guarding his hands so that they would not be polluted with the blood of the innocent.
**“committed them to prison”** — of the prison.
8.4:
**“were dispersed”** — Rabanus. Although scattered through fear, they were nonetheless steadfast in preaching the gospel.
**“went about preaching”** — from place to place.
8.5:
**“Philip”**
• Bede. He was of the number of those scattered, who first preached Christ in Samaria.
• A deacon, second after Stephen; he is recounted second after him as heir and of the same rank.
**“going down to the city of Samaria”** — according to the position of the place, or because that city was lower than Jerusalem.
**“preached Christ unto them”** — that he was man and true God.
8.6:
**“Intendebant”** — Rabanus. Two causes of faith: hearing the words and seeing the signs; they believed because of the words of preaching and the signs of powers.
**“Were attentive”** — From this chapter and the history of the Samaritan woman it is proved that the minds of this people were ready to believe.
**“the people with one accord, hearing those things which were said by Philip”** — the words.
**“and seeing”** — miracles.
8.7:
**“For many of them who had”** — demons.
**“crying”** — namely the demons.
**“with a loud voice, went out. Many also sick of the palsy”** — the enfeebled.
8.8: **“And there was great joy in that city.”** — Truth being known, they rejoiced that they had been set free from darkness.
8.9:
**“Man”** — As if of low birth.
**“Now there was a certain man named Simon”** — Not deservedly, because he was disobedient in his deeds.
**“who before had been”** — Good things are always opposed by their contraries.
**“a magician in that city”** — A trickster.
**“Magician”** — Rabanus. Magi philosophize about individual things: about the nature of the world, the course of the stars, and their movements.
**“Seducing”** — Leading away from the truth, or turning people into ecstasy or stupor and amazement by his tricks.
**“the people of Samaria, giving out that he was some great one”** — a prophet or an angel, or God or the Son of God.
**“which is called great”** — they did not know the name of Christ.
8.10:
**“to whom they all gave ear”** — a servant or a younger man.
**“from the least to the greatest”** — a king or a decrepit old man.
**“saying: This man”** — Simon.
**“is the power”** — Christ.
**“of God”** — not an angel.
8.11:
**“And they were attentive to him, because”** — namely, that.
**“for a long time, with his magical practices”** — by arts or false powers.
**“had bewitched them”** — by deceiving.
**“To bewitch”** — To take the rational mind away from men.
8.12:
**“Philip”** — Rabanus. Some say this Philip was an apostle and one of the twelve, but this does not seem true according to the sequence of this book.
**“preaching of the kingdom of God”** — as in that saying: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”
**“in the name of Jesus Christ”** — Of Jesus Christ, etc. Rabanus. Of whom they were ignorant; or, as has been said, in the name of Jesus I preached the Trinity. For whoever believes one person of the Trinity perfectly cannot lack belief in the other two.
**“they were baptized, both men and women”** — In Christ Jesus there is not male nor female, etc.
8.13:
**“Then Simon himself believed also”** — Feignedly and falsely, lest he be held in contempt by resisting believers.
**“Then also Simon himself”** — Bede. He believed the words of Philip, and, overcome by the miracle, truly believed; or, which is more credible, he pretended to believe until he should receive baptism, so that he who was so greedy of praise that he wished to be believed Christ might learn the art by which he could work miracles. Which his successors also are read to have done, who, instructed in evil arts, entered the Church fraudulently and steal baptism.
**“and being baptized, he adhered to Philip”** — In body, not in heart; for he wished to have power so that to whomever, etc., as follows below.
**“Seeing also the signs and exceeding great miracles which were done, being astonished, he wondered”** — desiring to be able to do such things.
8.14:
**“Now when the apostles”** — Of whom Philip, of whom it was spoken before, was not one.
**“who were in Jerusalem, that Samaria had received”** — Now it appears which city it was: Samaria, which was spoken of before, namely Samaria itself.
**“the word of God, they sent unto them Peter and John”**
• who were pillars.
• not one but two, just as Christ also sent two: “in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand.”
**“They sent Peter and John”** — They sent Peter and John. Peter joins John to himself, because the virginity of the Church is pleasing and acceptable.
8.15:
**“Who, when they were come, prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Ghost”**
• now indeed water alone baptizes the ones who are
• visibly
8.16:
**“For he was not as yet come upon any of them”** — the Holy Spirit
**“but they were only baptized”** — that is, they were dipped in water only, not in the Holy Spirit
**“In the name of Jesus”** — It is not to be read so, “in the name of Jesus” only, as to exclude the other persons.
**“in the name of the Lord Jesus”** — Jesus, etc. Because before they believed in the Father and the Holy Spirit; as the other Jews did; or the full faith of the one Person confirms the faith of the Trinity.
8.17:
**“They laid hands”** — Rabanus. Philip, who preached the gospel in Samaria, was one of the seven. For if he had been an apostle, he could lay on hands that they might receive the Spirit, which is lawful for bishops alone. For a priest, whether the bishop be present or absent, when he baptizes, anoints with chrism that has been consecrated by the bishop, yet does not sign the forehead with oil, which the bishop alone does when he gives the Spirit the Paraclete to the baptized.
**“upon them”** — behold the example of confirmation
**“and they received the Holy Ghost”** — which was shown because they spoke with tongues
8.19:
**“Power”** — Rabanus. Not only to baptize in water and to preach, or to work miracles, which Philip had, but that on whomever I shall lay my hands, etc.
**“Saying: Give me also this power”** — Bede. The apostles could not give that power for money, to whom it was said: “Freely have you received, freely give.”
**“that on whomsoever I shall lay my hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost. Peter”** — speaks as the chief, first
8.20:
**“Thy money”**
• Not ours, who do not desire it, but yours, which you compare to the Spirit, that you may sell it for him and buy him with it. Therefore he wished to buy the Spirit, that by selling it to others he might receive more.
• Rabanus. From this example is taken that the alms of the lost are not received.
• Bede. The apostles, not wanting the money, say “Let it be with you,” that is, keep what is yours, and this unto perdition, that for money unjustly gathered you may pay eternal punishment.
**“be with thee to perdition”** — as if it perish with you from your money
**“To perdition”** — Bede. When the just pronounce a sentence of malediction, they burst forth to it not from a wish for vengeance but from justice. For looking inwardly on the judgment of God, they know with what curse the wicked ought to be struck outwardly, and they do not sin in the curse, in which they do not differ from the judgment of God. For when both the innocence of the one cursing remains and the curse destroys the guilty, it is gathered from both sides that the sentence is pronounced by the supreme judge; whence Simon, cursed by Peter, perished eternally.
**“because thou hast thought that the gift of God”** — the Holy Spirit, who is God and the gift of God
8.21: **“Thou hast no part nor lot in this matter”** — in which it was said that the Spirit would be received through his hands
8.22:
**“Do penance therefore”**
• Do penance. For the covetousness and the wicked sense by which you thought the Spirit could be made a matter of trade.
• Do penance, etc. Rabanus. That all may see what you are. Not that Peter does not know that he will not do penance, but because he is commanded to preach to all, he does his office, so that the man may be inexcusable. He is also rebuked before all, lest they be further deceived by him.
**“for this thy wickedness”** — that is, by the double evil of covetousness, namely also of wicked faith
**“Pray to God”** — To whom the heart lies open, of whom the prophet says: “How good is God to Israel,” whom you cannot deceive, because the Holy Spirit will flee the feigned.
**“that perhaps”** — he speaks not affirmatively but doubtfully, lest we despair
8.23:
**“In the gall”** — of treachery
**“For in the gall of bitterness”** — Bede. The Spirit descended in a dove, that he might teach that he is received by the simple. For he who keeps bitterness in his heart, though he seem to be baptized, is not loosed from the bond of sin. But being cleansed, as it were, for a moment at the hour of baptizing, he is soon oppressed sevenfold by a fiercer demon. In vain, then, does he try to buy grace who does not strip himself of the raven mind.
**“and in the bonds”** — by the cords by which anyone is bound of sins
**“of iniquity”** — of sin
**“I see thou art”** — although you are silent, yet it is not hidden from me
8.24:
**“Then Simon answering, said: Pray you”** — Pray, etc. Because of despair he does not dare to pray himself but asks the apostles, so that they may pray for him; nor does he dare to pray for himself, who does not believe he is to be heard. He also speaks deceitfully to the apostles.
**“for me to the Lord, that none”** — fearing the present blows, he wishes to avoid them
**“which you have spoken”** — Not what I believed, but as an unbeliever he imputes to them what is to come.
8.25:
**“And they indeed”** — Peter and John
**“having testified”** — bearing witness more firmly, by words or by signs
**“and preached the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem”** — according to the manner of custom
**“and preached the gospel to many countries of the Samaritans”** — not only in Samaria
8.26:
**“But an angel of the Lord”** — to distinguish them from the angels of Satan
**“Now an angel”** — After the return of the apostles, the history turns to Philip.
**“spoke to Philip, saying: Arise”** — in both there is a sign of perfection
**“towards the south”** — Bede. Rightly is he sought, found, and washed at noon, who, burning with devotion, deserved to be consecrated to God as the firstfruits of the Gentiles. In him that was fulfilled: “Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands to God.” Mystically Philip goes out toward the south, that is, the apostles go to the Gentiles, where there is the heat of faith.
**“to the way that goeth down”**
• from the metropolis of the Jews into the cities of the Gentiles, which are desert
• The way does not go down, but one goes down by the way, from the nature of the place.
**“from Jerusalem into Gaza”**
• that is, Africa
• Gaza, metropolis of the Philistines
**“into Gaza”** — Bede. The old Gaza, which was once the border of the Chanaanites near Egypt, was utterly destroyed, and another was built in its place. Allegorically it signifies the Gentiles deserted by the worship of God; the way that goes down from Jerusalem, and opens the way of salvation, is Christ, who is the truth and the life. For he came down from the heavenly Jerusalem to the lowest things, and whitened with the water of baptism the blackness of sin.
**“this is desert”** — it is not the way but Gaza that is called desert
8.27:
**“And rising up, he went”** — in the one perfection, in the other obedience
**“And behold a man”** — because of his manly soul
**“of Ethiopia”** — By nature and by merit: for the Ethiopian is dark; whence: “Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands to God.”
**“of great authority”**
• by strength and integrity of mind
• Bede. He is rightly called so, who was so zealous in Scripture that he did not cease to read even on the way, and loved religion so much that he came from the farthest parts of the world to the temple of the Lord. Whence deservedly, while he sought an interpreter of what he read, he found Christ whom he sought; and, according to Jerome, he found more in the desert, at the fountain of the Church, than in the gilded temple of the Synagogue. This Ethiopian changed his skin, because he laid aside the filth of sin in the laver.
**“an eunuch”** — a type of the Gentiles who in Christ are circumcised from carnal desires
**“Candace the queen of the Ethiopians”**
• the queen of the south came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon
• Of great authority under Candace the queen, etc.; over all her treasures, etc. Bede. The queen of the Ethiopians, sending her treasure ahead to Jerusalem, is the Church of the Gentiles, about to bestow the gifts of faith and virtues; the interpretation of the name fits her. For Candace is interpreted “changed,” of whom it is written in the psalm: “For those who shall be changed,” and elsewhere: “Hearken, O daughter, and see, and incline thy ear: and forget thy people and thy father’s house.”
**“Candace the queen”** — It was the custom of that region for women to rule, and for them to be called Candace.
**“who”** — it is the custom of eunuchs to guard the treasures of the powerful
**“over all her treasures”** — riches
**“had come”** — before he spoke to Philip
**“to Jerusalem to adore”** — because of the renown of the city and the fame of the temple, it was the custom of the Gentiles to approach famous places dedicated to the worship of gods
8.28: **“he was returning, sitting in his chariot, and reading”** — He began to return, reading Isaias. Wherever in the New Testament the beginning of salvation is told, testimony is taken from Isaias, who is interpreted ‘the salvation of the Lord.’
8.29: **“And the Spirit said”** — the Holy Spirit or an angel
8.30: **“And Philip running thither, heard him reading the prophet Isaias. And he said: Thinkest thou that thou understandest what thou readest?”** — Thinkest thou that thou understandest, etc. And how, etc. Rabanus. They recognize each other’s language either by the teaching of the eunuch or by the Spirit of Philip.
8.31:
**“Who said: And how can I, unless some man shew me?”** — he who was reading the book was not ignorant of the language
**“unless some man shew me”**
• about what the prophet is treating
• How can I, unless some man shew me, etc. Here he reproves the boldness of those who think they can understand divine Scripture without a teacher.
**“And he desired Philip”** — in the figure of the teachers who are taken from the Gentiles
**“that he would come up and sit”** — advanced in this
**“with him”** — sitting with him; and the eunuch or Philip rolled back the book
8.32:
**“And the place of the scripture which he was reading was this”** — The place of Scripture, etc. Rabanus. The Lord preparing, it should be read thus: the place of Scripture was here. Or thus: Here, as a sheep to the slaughter, etc.
**“He was led as a sheep”**
• innocent
• Bede. A sheep, when it is led to the slaughter, does not resist, and Christ suffered of his own will. Or as the lamb was wont to be sacrificed at the Passover, so Christ our Passover was sacrificed; and as a lamb before the shearer, he not only redeemed us with his blood but covered us with wool, that he might warm with his garment those who were cold with unbelief. Whence the Apostle says: “As many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ.”
**“to the slaughter”** — the passion of the cross
**“was led”** — that he might be crucified
**“and like a lamb”** — “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world.”
**“before his shearer”** — Pilate and the Jews
**“without voice”** — He answered little to Pilate and the high priests, but to Herod nothing.
8.33:
**“In humility his judgment was taken away”**
• because in his passion, humbling himself, he did not judge, but allowed himself to be unjustly judged
• Bede. Because the judge of all found no truth of judgment without fault: he was condemned by the sedition of the Jews and the voice of Pilate.
**“In humility”** — Rabanus. By the passion, which humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death.
**“his judgment was taken away”** — in Barabbas the robber, whom they sought as though he were just
**“His generation”**
• his heavenly generation cannot be declared, which John spoke of in part
• who could explain even the carnal generation, how he was born of a virgin without seed?
• Bede. It is impossible for the divinity to be known, of which it is said: “Before the day star I begot thee.” The birth of the virgin also, how can it be explained? To Mary asking the reason of it, it was said: “The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the most High shall overshadow thee,” etc.
**“who shall declare, for his life shall be taken from the earth”** — that he might live in heaven, not on earth
**“shall be taken”** — “The second man, from heaven, heavenly,” set apart from earthly things by heavenly holiness. Or he passed from life into death.
8.34: **“And the eunuch answering Philip, said”** — the place of Scripture, if he himself was expounding it, or Philip, if he himself was reading
8.35:
**“Then Philip, opening his mouth”**
• which agrees with his name
• Bede. Who is interpreted “mouth of the lamp.” Beautifully he opens his mouth while bringing the obscurity of prophecy into the light of knowledge, or this circumlocution designates a longer discourse.
• Mystically. Philip opens the mouth of the Church, so that from this he is preached to the Gentiles, whom they had not known before.
**“opened”** — Rabanus. He opened the treasure of knowledge, or opened his mouth so that the Spirit speaks in him, according to that: “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.”
**“said”** — he was led as a sheep to the slaughter
**“preached unto him Jesus”** — He resolved the question of that one who asked about whom the prophecy spoke. He shows, however, that it was prophesied of Jesus.
8.36: **“to a certain water”** — For to this end the preaching had brought him, who had heard about baptism on the way, to need water.
8.37:
**“If thou believest”** — Rabanus. He did not fail to know his faith, but wanted a clear confession, so that an example of asking and confessing might be given to those who were to baptize and to those to be baptized.
**“with all thy heart, thou mayest”** — with all the heart, it is allowed to be baptized
**“And he answering, said: I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God”** — that is, to be the Son of man
8.38:
**“And he commanded the chariot to stand still; and they went down”** — the one to be baptized ought to be humbled, whence Jordan is interpreted “descent”
**“into the water, both Philip and the eunuch: and he baptized him”** — dipped
8.39:
**“And when they were come up”** — advancing
**“out of the water”** — which is as it were the foundation
**“the Spirit of the Lord”** — Jerome. He says that the angel did this in the Holy Spirit.
**“and the Spirit of the Lord”** — Rabanus. Or the Spirit rushed strongly upon the eunuch, as he also came upon the apostles. The stronger the faith, the greater the spiritual impulse. From the fact that the Spirit rushed upon the eunuch, Philip is said to have been an apostle; yet we do not read that a mission was made by him either by imposition of hands or by invocation of the Holy Spirit. Whence it appears that on the firstfruits of the Gentiles the Holy Spirit descended neither by imposition of hands nor by invocation but of his own accord, that the apostles might have an excuse against the Jews accusing them because they baptized the Gentiles. For who could forbid the Spirit of the Lord? Or who would keep from the water those upon whom the Spirit had descended?
**“took away Philip; and the eunuch saw him no more”** — because, having been made perfect, he had no need of teaching; because the Paraclete, whom the Father sends, himself teaches all things
**“And he went on his way rejoicing”** — to his homeland or to the kingdom of heaven
8.40:
**“But Philip was found in Azotus”** — one of the five cities of the Philistines
**“found”** — Rabanus. He was not found by men in the rapture, because he walked in solitude or with exceeding swiftness.
**“and passing through, he preached the gospel to all the cities”** — not distinguishing persons
**“to Caesarea”** — Bede. He means Caesarea of Palestine, where he is described as having had a house, which is shown to this day, and also the chamber of his four daughters, virgins who prophesied.

9.1:
**“Saul”** — He returns to what he said above: “Saul still made havoc of the church.”
**“as yet”** — not yet giving up ravaging and persecuting
**“breathing out threatenings”** — in words
**“and slaughter”** — in deed
**“threatenings and slaughter”** — By threats he terrified the absent; with slaughter he afflicted those present; it is doubted whether he killed, or scourged, or did both.
**“breathing out threatenings and slaughter”** — He breathes like fire, not stirred by another; he himself set others alight.
**“against the disciples of the Lord”** — because Christians were then called thus
**“went to the high priest”** — not called, but of his own accord, zeal stirring him
9.2:
**“and asked of him”** — they are not given to him, but he himself asked
**“letters”** — a letter of dispatch
**“to Damascus”** — a city of Syria, remote, because he had already carried on persecution in nearby places
**“to the synagogues”** — of the Jews
**“that if he found”** — because they were few
**“of this way”** — of this way, by which the disciples of the Lord lived
**“men and women”** — he persecutes both sexes
**“bring them bound to Jerusalem”** — he does not say that he should kill
9.3:
**“And as he went on his journey, it came to pass”** — to come to pass is said of good things
**“that he drew nigh to Damascus”** — he was to be stopped when he drew near the city
**“and suddenly”** — the grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow efforts
**“shined round about him”** — that he might be terrified
**“a light from heaven”** — as fire appeared to the apostles before, so light shone on Paul
9.4:
**“And falling on the ground”** — Terrified, he flees to the ground, or as one adoring he falls on his face.
**“he heard a voice saying to him: Saul”** — repeated in rebuke
**“Saul”** — he asks in rebuke, not from ignorance
**“why persecutest thou me?”**
• in the members
• Why persecutest thou me? Bede. He does not say “my members” but “me,” because he still suffers enemies in his members, and declares that the benefits bestowed on his members are done to himself, when he says: “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat,” and in explaining adds: “As long as you did it to one of these my least, you did it to me.”
9.5:
**“Who said: Who art thou, Lord?”**
• whether God or an angel
• You read that he sought God; he names the Lord, who gave the voice from heaven.
**“And he: I am”** — I, God, speak from heaven, whom you thought dead.
**“Jesus”** — Saviour
**“I am Jesus”** — Bede. He does not call himself God or the Son of God, but says: take up my weakness of humility, and lay down the scales of your pride.
**“whom thou persecutest”** — as a man
**“It is hard for thee to kick against the goad”** — the word and power of God
9.6:
**“And he trembling”** — by the lightning
**“and astonished”**
• he was astonished, not thinking Jesus to be in heaven
• because of the voice, which came with astonishment
**“said: Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?”** — show your will and I will obey; he understood that the goad was driving him to the work
**“and there it shall be told thee what thou must do”**
• And it shall be told thee, etc. An example of learning is given, and pride is rebuked, so that no one may think another unworthy to be taught by him what he does not know.
• Bede. He does not at once show what is to be done, but teaches beforehand in the city that he is to be heard, so that he might stand the more firmly in good afterwards, in proportion as he had first been overthrown and had fallen from his former error.
9.7:
**“Arise”** — Bede. Work unwearied like the ox, and be a teacher of the Church. In the law it is written: “Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn.”
**“go into the city”** — Rabanus. About to enter the city, he is terrified, lest he bring sorrow to the saints; therefore, subdued, he is commanded to enter, that he may learn the faith which he had attacked.
**“Now the men who went in company with him stood”** — they did not fall
**“amazed”** — by the light of brightness
**“hearing indeed a voice, but seeing no man”** — they had not seen the face of the speaker
**“hearing a voice”** — Rabanus. The voice of Paul, as is read below, Paul saying: “They that were with me saw indeed the light, but they heard not the voice of him that spoke with me.”
9.8:
**“And Saul arose”** — now of his own accord
**“And his eyes were opened”** — Rabanus. It is shown to him in the body what he suffered before in the soul. For as an open eye without sight, so the law is useless without faith in Christ.
**“And Saul arose from the ground”** — And his eyes being opened, he saw nothing, etc. Bede. He could not see well again with his eyes unless first blinded; having the wisdom by which he was troubled shut out, he committed himself to faith.
**“by the hands”** — holding him by the hands
9.9:
**“And he was there three days”** — And he was there, etc. Rabanus. Here is given a pattern for penitents, that they begin from three days; this three-day period also marks the stage of catechumens.
**“three days”** — Bede. It appears that during the three days in which, blinded, he awaited the light of grace, he was not sluggish in idleness, but, enlightened by God, searched into heavenly things. It is credible that even at that time he was taught the dispensation of the gospel, of which he glories to the Galatians, saying: “Neither did I receive it of man, nor did I learn it; but by the revelation of Jesus Christ,” and a little after: “To reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles,” etc.
**“without sight”**
• so that he may know how opportune it is for the soul to be freed from blindness
• Because he did not believe that God, rising on the third day, had conquered death, he is instructed by his own example, who changed the darkness of three days when the light returned.
**“he did neither eat nor drink”** — And did neither eat nor drink, etc. Rabanus. This happened to his soul, which had no inner food or drink; but by the bodily fasting and thirst it is shown that a hungry soul ought to be satisfied.
9.10:
**“Now there was a certain disciple”** — Of Christ.
**“at Damascus, named Ananias”** — He is rightly called “grace of God,” to whom the illumination of Paul was given by God.
**“Ananias”** — Rabanus. It is a sign of familiarity to be called by one’s own name.
**“And the Lord said to him in a vision: Ananias. And he said: Behold I am here, Lord”** — He confesses that he is a servant and ready to obey.
9.11:
**“And the Lord said to him: Arise, and go”** — let nothing else intervene, but go once you have risen.
**“into the street”** — Rabanus. Vici are called the fields of cities, or the neighbourhoods close to one another inside the city.
**“that is called Strait, and seek”** — in the tribe of Juda, that is, among the Jews who were there.
**“in the house of Judas, one named Saul of Tarsus”** — that is, from Tarsus of Cilicia, whence he had migrated with his parents.
**“For behold he prayeth”** — He has made him meek; he is to be feared by no one.
9.12:
**“And he saw a man named Ananias”**
• in a vision.
• of the tribe of Juda.
• each is shown to the other in a vision, and his name is indicated, so that they are known to each other before they see each other.
**“coming in, and putting his hands upon him, that he might receive his sight”** — inner and outer.
9.13:
**“But Ananias answered: Lord, I have heard by many of this man”** — the sheep fears the wolf.
**“how much evil he hath done to thy saints in Jerusalem”** — in the holy city he did evil to the saints, and therefore he is to be feared in other places.
9.14:
**“And here he hath authority”** — and the will is not lacking.
**“from the chief priests to bind”** — to persecute, not to kill.
9.15:
**“And the Lord said to him: Go thy way; for this man is to me a vessel of election”** — to be proved by the multitude of tribulations, or unharmed in the flesh.
**“Go thy way; for”** — Bede. He is not to be feared as a persecutor, but embraced as a brother, because he is ready to endure the evils that he inflicted on the saints.
**“to carry my name”** — he will bear that name whose invokers he came to bind.
**“before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel”** — to the Jews.
9.16:
**“For I will shew him”** — you will not teach him, but baptize him.
**“how great things he must suffer for my name's sake”** — the chosen vessel is tested in temptation; for the furnace tests the potter’s vessels.
9.17:
**“And Ananias went his way, and entered into the house”**
• to Saul.
• And entered into the house. The prophecy of Isaias is fulfilled, saying: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb,” that is, Saul with Ananias.
**“And laying his hands upon him”** — as catechumens are still seasoned with salt.
**“he said: Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus hath sent me”** — to whom you said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?
**“he that appeared to thee in the way as thou camest”** — he speaks of a sign, so that he may know that he was sent by the Lord.
**“that thou mayest receive thy sight”** — in both ways.
**“and be filled with the Holy Ghost”** — in baptism
9.18:
**“And immediately”** — lest it be thought to have happened by chance
**“there fell from his eyes as it were scales”**
• Bede. The body of a serpent is covered with scales; the Jews are serpents and a brood of vipers, whose unfaithfulness Saul followed, and as with the skin of a serpent had covered the eyes of his heart; but when the scales fell under the hand of Ananias, it was shown in his face that he had received light in his mind.
• Rabanus. That the scales fall is a likeness of the inner sight renewed from the veil of the law.
**“and he received his sight”** — because he had seen even before
9.19:
**“And when he had taken meat”** — double
**“he was strengthened”** — doubly
9.20:
**“And immediately he preached Jesus in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God”**
• that Jesus Christ is man
• Immediately entering into the synagogues, etc. He fulfils the word of the Lord saying: “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself,” etc.
9.21:
**“And they were all astonished, and wondered”** — unbelievers who did not know the mystery
**“Is not this he who persecuted in Jerusalem those that called upon this name”**
• of Jesus, that he now preaches
• Is not this he, etc. Rabanus. He gives an example of not blushing, where the truth is plain, to change one’s opinions.
**“And came hither”** — and hither: he did not come to do what he is doing
**“for that intent”** — he applied such diligence to persecution
9.22:
**“But Saul”**
• the proving of the chosen vessel had such a beginning
• Bede. Peter and Paul are Latin or Greek names and not Hebrew, because Hebrews have no ‘P’.
**“increased much more in strength, and confounded the Jews who dwelt at Damascus, affirming that this is the Christ”** — Jesus is man; Christ is God
9.23:
**“And when many days were passed”** — from baptism
**“the Jews consulted together”** — or: ‘counsel’
**“to kill him”** — whether it was in Damascus is doubted, but it seems more that it was done there
9.24:
**“But their laying in wait was made known to Saul”** — either through the information of men or through the Spirit
**“And they watched the gates”**
• they not only made a plan but etc.
• They watched. Not the Jews but the citizens with their king Aretas, as he himself writes to the Galatians; for the Gentiles agreed with the Jews in persecuting Christians.
9.25:
**“But the disciples taking him”**
• of Christ or of the Church
• Taking him, etc. Bede. Of Christ or of the Church. In Greek ‘his’ is not added, so that the disciples of Christ or of the Church are understood generally. For Paul did not yet have disciples.
**“by the wall”** — Bede. This kind of escape is kept in the Church, when someone surrounded by the snares of the devil or the traps of the world is saved by the defense of faith and hope. For the wall of Damascus, which is interpreted “drinking blood,” is the adversity of the world. King Aretha is the devil. The basket, which is made or woven of rushes and palms, is the joining of faith and hope. The rush is the greenness of faith, and the palm the hope of eternity. Let him, then, who sees himself girded by the wall of adversity go up into the basket of virtue, and he will escape.
*Gregory:* He did it in the manner of a soldier who, besieged in a narrow place, breaks out into the open field so as to kill many of the enemy; afterwards, having gained many, he underwent death for Christ, because he did not flee from fear of death who said: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”
9.26:
**“And when he was come into Jerusalem”** — He did not come to Jerusalem to the apostles as soon as he was baptized, but, as he writes to the Galatians, he first went into Arabia and returned from there to Damascus. Then after three years he came to Jerusalem to see Peter, etc. Then, as Luke testifies, he came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. But whether he endured the plots at Damascus on the first or the second occasion is not easily clear. For the second can be understood from what is said, that when many days were passed the Jews took counsel.
**“he essayed to join himself”** — He essayed, etc. This is what he himself says in the epistle: “And I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea, which were in Christ:” yet they had heard of me.
9.27:
**“Barnabas”**
• a Levite
• Barnabas. Bede. He was a Cypriot by birth, a Levite, who is recorded above to have brought the price of a field to the feet of the apostles.
**“took him”** — Bede. When this was done, and to which apostles he was led, he himself shows, writing to the Galatians: “When it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb,” etc. And afterwards: “Then, after three years, I went to Jerusalem, to see Peter, and I tarried with him fifteen days. But other of the apostles I saw none, saving James the brother of the Lord.” So what he says next, “and he was with them coming in and going out,” means during the fifteen days in which he stayed with Peter and James; and what he says in his epistle: “Then I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.” This is what Luke says: “he spoke”: and he disputed with the Greeks.
**“brought him to the apostles, and told them”** — Barnabas about Paul, or Paul about himself
**“how he had seen the Lord, and that he had spoken to him; and how in Damascus”** — when, as the history foretold, he preached Jesus
9.29:
**“He spoke also to the Gentiles, and disputed with the Greeks”**
• Born among the Greeks, Jews.
• Bede. He taught the Greeks in Jerusalem and the Jews in Damascus, a city of the Gentiles, because in the city of God the Gentiles are to be gathered, while the Jews are to remain in the unbelief of the Gentiles.
**“with the Greeks”** — Rabanus. Those are called Jews among the Greeks who were born in the dispersion among them.
9.30:
**“when the brethren had known”** — He himself did not fear, but agreed with the brethren.
**“they brought him down to Caesarea”**
• Palestine.
• Whence the Lord: “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another.”
**“to Caesarea”** — Caesarea Philippi is a city of Syria. Tarsus is a city of Cilicia.
**“and sent him away to Tarsus”** — as to friends of the Church.
9.31:
**“the church had peace throughout”**
• not only at Jerusalem.
• The church indeed, etc. Such passages, as said above, are often inserted at the end of narratives and at the beginning, to the praise of the apostles and of the faith of the Church.
**“Judea, and Galilee, and Samaria”** — Whence the Lord: “You shall be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria,” etc.
**“had peace”** — in itself.
**“was edified”** — into one holy temple of God.
**“walking”** — by conversing or growing by degrees of preaching.
**“in the fear of the Lord and the consolation of the Holy Ghost”** — because it is the Paraclete.
**“and the consolation”** — Consolation is given in labour. Whence it is clear that the Church was being tempted.
**“was filled”** — or was multiplied.
9.32: **“And it came to pass that Peter, as he passed through, visiting all”** — by running about and preaching.
9.33:
**“a certain man named Eneas”** — Rabanus. Eneas signifies the human race, languishing with love of earthly things, but healed by the work and the word of the apostles; for since the world is divided into four regions, and the course of the age is varied by four seasons, he who embraces present things is laid low on a bed as if for eight years. The bed is sloth, in which the sick mind rests, which is weakened by the pleasure of the flesh and the delight of the age.
**“who had kept his bed for eight years, who was ill of the palsy”** — not nine, so that the power may be more glorious.
9.34:
**“And Peter said to him: Eneas”**
• brother.
• Aeneas is interpreted as brother.
**“the Lord Jesus Christ healeth thee”** — not I; he seeks not his own glory but the Lord’s.
**“arise”** — this is fulfilled: he shall leap like a lame stag.
**“and make thy bed”** — let no one else make your bed for you.
**“arise and make thy bed”** — Arise and make your bed: he commanded him whom he had healed of paralysis to rise and make his own bed, showing that one who has received faith in the heart should not only shake off sluggishness but also prepare works in which he may rest.
**“And immediately”** — without delay.
**“he arose”** — because a part of the work is put for every work.
9.35:
**“Lydda and Saron”** — These cities were converted to God, for on that account miracles were done among them.
**“who were converted to the Lord”** — although before they had been turned away.
9.36:
**“And in Joppe there was a certain disciple”** — a Christian.
**“named Tabitha”** — Rabanus. Tabitha is rendered from Hebrew into Latin as Dorcas, or as a gazelle, as is found in the copies.
**“Dorcas”** — Allegorically: that is, a little doe or a wild goat; it signifies a soul lofty in zeal for virtue, but contemptible in the opinion of men. For Luke, in setting down the interpretation of the name, signifies that a mystery lies in it: these animals, dwelling on the mountains, see sharply. Whence from the keenness of sight they are called dorcades in Greek. So those who are lofty in merit of works look upward, and watch carefully over themselves; they live simply, they walk with a discreet step of action as with a cloven hoof, and they chew the cud of the word of God by constant meditation.
**“This woman was full of good works”** — having nothing imperfect
**“and almsdeeds which she did”** — not accepting persons
9.37:
**“And it came to pass in those days”**
• when Peter came to Lydda
• And it came to pass, etc. Bede. When the saints sin through the frailty of nature, they succumb, as it were in the days of good works, to a sudden sickness. But when they at once persist in tears, rise with hope of recovering virtue, call upon the helps of the saints, and think again on the good works they had left off, they do what follows: “whom when they had washed,” etc.; the things that are told of the calling of Peter and of the showing of the almsdeeds of Dorcas.
• Bede. If saints fall into death of the soul through ignorance or weakness, they deserve to be raised again for the integrity of their right intention, as happened to Peter, to whom what is written of Dorcas can rightly be applied.
**“that she was sick, and died”** — it was not a sudden death
**“Whom when they had washed”** — in some copies it is found: when they had washed with ointments
**“in an upper chamber”** — Rabanus. It is placed in an upper place, either on account of the height of her merit, or on account of the sublimity of the miracle that was to be done for her.
9.38:
**“And forasmuch as Lydda was nigh to Joppe”** — or: to
**“the disciples hearing that Peter was there, sent unto him two men”**
• the more prudent sex
• the number of witnesses whom the Lord sent
**“desiring him that he would not be slack to come unto them”** — they do not state the cause, lest he refuse to come, out of humility
9.39:
**“And Peter rising up, went with them”** — ready and humble, he used no excuse
**“And when he was come, they brought him into the upper chamber. And all the widows stood about him”** — holy women pray for a holy woman as holy
**“weeping”**
• they weep before him who was merciful to their misery, and they weep before him who was merciful
• They show the work of his mercy, so that it is clear that they rightly weep; and therefore Peter has compassion on them.
**“widows weeping”** — Bede. These are the pious thoughts of the penitent soul, which had for a time laid aside their former yoke, as it were the rule of a husband; they humbly pray for the sinning soul.
**“and shewing him the coats and garments which Dorcas made them”** — they pray not with their own voices for the dead woman but with her works, because almsgiving frees not only from the second death but also from the first death
9.40:
**“And they all being put forth”** — Rabanus. This was done after the example of Christ raising the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, to avoid pride, or lest the unworthy see the sign.
**“Peter kneeling down prayed”** — he prays as a servant, but Jesus fulfils it as God
**“and turning to the body, he said: Tabitha, arise”** — in the name of Jesus, not in my own
**“And she”** — the prayer having been made
**“she opened her eyes”** — Bede. The right order of those rising again: first she opens the eyes of the mind; afterwards, having recognized the voice of Peter, she sits up, and recovers the light of her circumspection that had been lost, so that they may live for the teaching of those who help.
**“she opened her eyes, sat up, arose”** — These are the three stages of resuscitation.
**“and seeing Peter, she sat up”** — she sat up from the sight of Peter
9.41:
**“And giving her his hand”**
• help
• Tabitha rises when Peter’s hand touches her, because a soul languishing in sins recovers its strength in no better way than by the examples of the saints.
**“he lifted her up”** — an example of good work
**“And when he had called the saints and the widows”** — to whom she had given benefits
9.42: **“And it was made known throughout all Joppe”** — this was the chief cause of the virtues
9.43:
**“And it came to pass, that he abode many days in Joppe”** — beautiful, or beauty
**“with one Simon”** — he stays in the house of the obedient man
**“a tanner”** — tanner from curia, or tanner from hides

10.1:
**“And there was a certain man in Caesarea”**
• from Caesar, so called in honour of the one in whose honour it was built
• And there was a certain man, etc. Rabanus. By the merit of perfection and manly work, according to that: “There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job,” etc.
**“Cornelius”** — Bede. He did not reach faith by virtues, but virtues by faith. Gregory says: Cornelius, whose alms before baptism are praised by the testimony of an angel, came to works not by works to faith but by faith to works. For if before baptism he did not believe in God, how did he pray, or how would God hear him, if he did not ask the progress of good from him? He knew, then, God the creator of all, but was ignorant of the Son incarnate; he had faith, and his alms and prayers pleased God; by good work he merited to know God, and, believing the mystery of the incarnation, to come to baptism. Therefore through faith he came to works, but in faith he is made firm through works.
**“a centurion”** — a leader having under him a perfect number, a hundred
**“band”** — of Roman soldiers
**“that which is called the Italian”** — sent from Rome, which is in Italy
10.2:
**“A religious man”** — above the degree of fear
**“and fearing God”** — below the degree of religion
**“with all his house”**
• of his house
• here grace appears, because his whole household was religious and God-fearing
• Religious and fearing God with all his house, etc. Rabanus. And all these things are believed to have been bestowed by the good of nature, by familiarity with the Jews, and by spiritual inspiration; for although the Jews, scattered, read the commandments of the law in the synagogue every sabbath, yet this is ascribed more to divine inspiration than to natural good, so that the first Church of the Gentiles is believed to have conceived, in the likeness of the Virgin Mary, of the Spirit without the seed of man, that is, by the teaching of a master.
**“giving much alms to the people”** — without distinction of persons
**“and always praying to God”** — according to the apostle saying: “Pray without intermission.”
10.3:
**“Saw”** — Rabanus. Not at night, not in dreams, because Gentiles of coarse sense were not accustomed to see spiritual and mystical visions. In this also is declared that the divine mystery was to be made manifest to the Gentiles without figure or riddle.
**“about the ninth hour of the day”** — Bede. Well did he receive the oracle of seeking baptism at the ninth hour, for he was to be baptized in the death of him who gave up the spirit at the ninth hour.
**“in a vision manifestly, about the ninth hour”** — Rabanus. Mystically, the Gentiles believing at the end of the age are the workers of the ninth hour; this hour is also dedicated to prayer, as was shown before in the example of Peter and John.
**“coming in unto him”** — Rabanus. Perhaps calling him to himself, and an occasion is given to Peter to excuse himself against the Jews who disputed with him and said: “Why didst thou go in to men having uncircumcision?” etc.
**“Cornelius”** — Familiarity is shown, by which the name of the Gentile man was inserted into the knowledge of the angels.
10.4:
**“beholding him”** — Good works and almsgiving tempered the angelic brightness so that he could bear it.
**“being seized with fear”**
• because he is a man inferior to an angel
• yet he did not fall on his face
**“said: What is it, Lord?”** — for what purpose have you come?
**“Thy prayers and thy alms”** — Bede. When alms and prayers were received, the teacher of salvation is at once ordered to be summoned; it is plainly hinted that by alms and prayers he sought from God full knowledge of his salvation.
**“are ascended”** — from the valley of heathenism, which God forgets
**“for a memorial in the sight of God”**
• that he may repay you in heaven
• because you have given benefits to all
10.5:
**“And now”** — do not delay to fulfil the orders
**“send men”** — the principal sex
**“And now send”** — Rabanus. Here begins the repayment, so that God, who is merciful, will have mercy on you, because: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy,” etc.
**“to Joppe”** — Bede. It is not Cornelius himself who is sent to Peter, because his whole household was to be baptized.
**“Joppe”** — Rabanus. It is a city in the land of promise, near the Tyrrhenian sea and situated on its eastern shore, into which Jonas, going down, entered a ship to flee.
**“and call hither one Simon”** — hitherto unknown to you
**“who is surnamed Peter”** — to distinguish him from the tanner in whose house he was lodging
10.6:
**“He lodgeth with one Simon”**
• to whose distinction the surname Peter was given
• He lodgeth with one Simon, etc. Bede. Peter lodges in the house of Simon, that is, of the obedient, who is a tanner; for the teacher of the Church willingly dwells where there are the obedient, who chastise the body and bring it into subjection, having passed beyond the waves of the age by freedom of mind; for by constancy of faith they despise the passing glory of the world and its terrors.
**“a tanner, whose house is by the sea side”** — Tyrrhenian
10.7:
**“And when ... was departed”** — Rabanus. He does not say “when Cornelius had woken,” to whom the angel was seen neither in a dream nor in an ecstasy, but openly.
**“the angel who spoke to him, he called”** — did not delay to obey
**“two of his household servants”** — he sends a larger number of witnesses, and fit witnesses
**“two of his household servants, and a soldier”** — Bede. Cornelius sent three to Peter, because the Gentile world, believing the apostolic faith, subdued Europe, Asia and Africa, partly by military pursuits, that is, by earnestness in preaching, partly by being occupied with household business. But it is to be noted that one soldier and two household servants are sent; for the stronger they are, the fewer in the members of the Church. You will find more who hear than who know how to speak the word.
**“a soldier who feared the Lord”** — Rabanus. He does not call them servants fearing the Lord, because he had said that he was religious and fearing the Lord with all his house.
**“of them that were under him”** — from the hundred soldiers subject to him
10.8: **“To whom when he had related all”** — which the angel had said to him
10.9:
**“And on the next day”** — after the vision of Cornelius
**“whilst they were going on their journey, and drawing nigh to the city”** — Joppe
**“drawing nigh”** — Bede. Another reading: “appearing to them,” that is, to those who were sent by Cornelius, that is, only drawing near so that they could be seen from the house of Simon the tanner.
**“Peter went up to the higher parts of the house”** — Peter goes up to the upper rooms, about to see the higher mysteries; he goes up as if to meet the vision
**“to the higher parts”**
• Rabanus. Another reading: “into the upper room” is also seen, because the Gentile people is as it were the upper house. The synagogue, however, is below, because it is immersed in the world.
• Bede. Signifying that the Church, having left the desire of earthly things, will have its conversation in heaven. At the sixth hour Peter, amid prayers, hungers: that is, for the salvation of the world, which Jesus came to seek and to save in the sixth age of the world, which he indicated when at the same hour he sat upon the well of Samaria.
**“to pray, about the sixth hour”** — an example is given of praying at that hour
10.10:
**“And being hungry”**
• examples of fasting and of prayer are given together
• “Being hungry,” etc. Rabanus. By compassion he hungers for the salvation of the Gentiles, which is now shown in the vision; which was seen at the sixth hour because it was made in the sixth age of the world.
**“he was desirous to taste”** — historically, or to preach to the Gentiles
**“they were preparing”** — the servants preparing the meal
**“there came upon”** — from heaven above, or from God
**“upon him”** — human nature
**“an ecstasy of mind”** — a lifting up from earthly things
10.11:
**“And he saw”** — hungering in body, he is satisfied in spirit with the salvation of the Gentiles, whom he is bidden to convert
**“the heaven opened”**
• not by the opening of the element but by divine revelation and spiritual
• It is signified here that heavens are open to the Gentiles and that an entrance is to be laid open.
**“The heaven opened”** — Bede. The opening of heaven is a revelation of heavenly mysteries, soon to be future for the Gentiles.
**“and a certain vessel descending”** — the body of Christ
**“a certain vessel”** — Bede. The Church, endowed with incorruptible truth and faith. Now the moth does not consume linen, which corrupts other garments. Therefore the faithful man shuts out of his heart the corruption of evil thought, so incorruptibly firm in faith that in his mind he is not gnawed, as by a moth, by wicked thought. Otherwise: the moth is the heretic, wishing to corrupt the garment of the Lord but not able, which was signified in that tunic of the Lord which the soldiers did not divide. The four corners by which the sheet was let down are the four regions of the world through which the Church is extended; or the four beginnings are the four evangelists, through whom the Church, imbued with the heavenly gift, is lifted up.
**“as it were a great linen sheet”**
• because she keeps the whiteness of chastity, conceived without seed
• because dead
• because he rose again
• because of fellowship in the Godhead
**“linen sheet”** — For the Church, for the whiteness of holiness and the mortification of the flesh.
**“four corners”**
• the gospels which were written about Christ
• that is, four angels
**“let down”** — because it descends from heaven
**“from heaven to the earth”** — because the Church is kept and increased by the grace of the Spirit coming upon her
**“From heaven to the earth”** — Rabanus. Hence we are warned that where our head is, and the root of which we are the branches, there the anchor of our hope should reach.
10.12:
**“Wherein were”**
• kinds of animals
• Bede. It is said of all the wicked: “Man when he was in honour did not understand: he hath been compared to senseless beasts, and made like to them.” But Solomon shows the man, that is, the uncorrupted man, saying: “Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is all man.”
**“All manner of fourfooted beasts”** — Bede. All nations are to believe and are to be taken into the unity of the body of Christ, that all may become its members.
**“All manner of fourfooted beasts, creeping things, and fowls”** — Bede. Those animals are the nations, unclean in their errors but cleansed by the threefold lowering, that is, by the mystery of the Trinity in baptism; who, having left behind the image of man, took on the forms of beasts and serpents.
**“creeping things of the earth”**
• clinging to earthly things
• venomous and deceitful
• three kinds of nations, which are brought into unity to become the Church
**“and fowls of the air”** — proud
10.13:
**“And there came a voice to him: Arise, Peter”**
• to preach the gospel
• “Go, baptize all,” etc.
**“Kill”** — Cleanse, mortify, and slay, that you may make a victim for God, so that those rescued from the old may pass into newness.
**“and eat”**
• what they had been among the Gentiles, and make what you are
• receive into the unity of the body of the Church, whose prince is Peter
**“Eat”** — Bede. He who eats food set outside transfers it into his own body. He therefore commanded the Gentiles, set outside through unbelief, to be grafted into the fellowship of the Church, which Peter signifies.
10.14:
**“But Peter said: Far be it from me, Lord”** — signifies the disdain to come against the Gentiles
**“for”** — signifies fear of going to the Gentiles because of the offence to the Jews, or because of the uncleanness and cruelty of the Gentiles
**“I never did eat any thing that is common”**
• among the Gentiles
• I did eat any thing that is common, etc. The Jews call those foods common which all men use. And those animals are unclean which do not divide the hoof, nor chew the cud, and, among fishes, those that are not scaly. But those foods are called unclean which are the flesh of beasts or reptiles, eaten by no men. He does not divide the hoof who does not distinguish the letter from the Spirit, or the persons of the Trinity. He does not chew the cud who does not call again to memory the word of God which he hears, nor keep it in deed.
• Bede. These things were fittingly shown to Peter when Cornelius the Gentile sent to him, so that he should not hesitate to hand the faith to the uncircumcised; for Cornelius himself was among the animals shown in the vessel, whence Peter is also confirmed by the Holy Ghost to do it.
• Bede. Peter thought the Gentiles unclean, but the providence of God already counts them among the clean. Common is put for unclean, because he who serves various allurements is not clean, according to that: “No man can serve two masters. You cannot serve God and mammon.” He who desires to be clean should not divide his mind, but bind it fast in the love of God alone.
• Bede. Because the mystery of the Trinity was to be preached by the twelve apostles through the four parts of the world, therefore the four lines were sent down from heaven a third time. Or, according to Ambrose, the figure repeated a third time expressed the working of the Trinity, and therefore in the ministries the questioning is put three times, and the confirmation is celebrated three times, and no one is cleansed except by a threefold confession. So also Peter, questioned a third time about the love of God, corrected with a threefold answer what he had sinned by denying three times.
**“and unclean”** — among the Jews
10.15:
**“And the voice spoke to him again”** — first in the Old, second in the New Testament, the command is given that salvation be preached among the Gentiles
**“the second time to him”** — It was made concerning the Gentiles, saying: Kill and eat.
**“That which God hath cleansed”** — By the cross of Christ the saved are cleansed from among the Gentiles.
10.16:
