**“And this was done thrice”** — that is, the vessel shown to commend the truth of the vision, or for the faith of the Trinity, in which the Gentiles are to be baptized.
**“and presently the vessel was taken up into heaven”** — Bede. After the threefold sending, the linen is received into heaven, because after the Church’s life on earth, cleansed by faith and baptism and journeying onward, it will be happily taken up into the heavenly dwelling.
**“the vessel was taken up into heaven”** — Bede. The body of Christ in the ascension? Or the Church is to ascend at the end, when the elect will be gathered from the four winds.
10.17:
**“Now, whilst Peter was doubting within himself, what the vision that he had seen should mean, behold the men”** — as if to the unlocking of a hidden mystery.
**“who were sent from Cornelius, inquiring for Simon's house”** — of a tanner.
10.18: **“And when they had called”** — a certain one.
10.19:
**“And as Peter was thinking of the vision, the Spirit said to him”**
• The Holy Spirit speaking inwardly, or the angel who had appeared to Cornelius.
• in the mind, not in the ear of the flesh.
**“Behold three men”**
• the vision had been shown to you in the figure of these three.
• the number of witnesses, and the principal sex.
10.20:
**“Arise, therefore”** — explains what was said: Arise, kill and eat.
**“get thee down”** — Bede. He is bidden to come down from the roof and go to preach, that the Church may not only behold the Lord by ascending to the heights, but also, to those who knock at the door of Simon, that is, of obedience, in the lowest places and as if still placed without, may preach by returning to the active life, as if rising from a couch. The house of Simon is said to be by the sea, that is, by the waves and furies of the world, where wicked men devour one another like fishes. But the conversation of the saints is in heaven.
**“and go with them, doubting nothing”** — this refers to what was said: Far be it, Lord.
**“for I have sent them”** — therefore it was said: That which God hath cleansed, etc.
10.21:
**“Then Peter, going down to the men”** — because the Spirit had said: Go down; he does not wait for a messenger to be sent to him by them.
**“Behold, I am he”** — Behold, I am he, etc. He shows that he knows their coming; he also gives an example of humility, dropping the roundabout of words.
**“whom you seek”** — He asks not because he does not know, but so that they may confess; and he leaves an example of avoiding boasting.
**“what is the cause for which you are come”** — What is the cause for which you have come? He said by the Spirit that the soldiers were present, and kept silent about the cause for which they had come, because to preserve humility the prophetic Spirit sometimes touches the mind in part and sometimes does not touch it.
10.22:
**“Cornelius, a centurion, a just man, and one that feareth God, and having good testimony from all the nation of the Jews”** — your, because you too are a Jew; this was added to persuade.
**“Received an answer”** — The Lord answered through the angel, for his almsdeeds and prayers.
**“of an holy angel”** — not from an unclean spirit.
**“into his house”** — By this they persuade, because the angel ordered him to enter his house, though he was a Gentile.
**“and to hear”** — to obey the one commanding.
**“words of thee”** — in these words it appears that Cornelius had told them the vision.
10.23:
**“Then bringing them in, he lodged them”**
• they stayed that night.
• Bringing them in, etc. Here begins the fellowship of the apostles with the Gentiles. Because he, who had heard from the angel the command that he should enter a Gentile’s house, had gone down to them, therefore he receives the Gentiles as guests.
**“And the day following he arose, and went with them: and some of the brethren from Joppe accompanied him”** — because the Spirit came down on Cornelius and his people before baptism.
10.24:
**“And the morrow after”** — they stayed that night on the road.
**“he entered into Caesarea. And Cornelius waited for them”** — he showed his desire and diligence.
**“having called together his kinsmen and special friends”**
• Necessary friends are called inseparable friends who do not leave even in necessity.
• Having called together his kinsmen, etc. There are two causes of the calling together: closeness of kinship and friendship.
**“And when Peter had entered”** — ready to obey.
**“came to meet him”** — Bede. The hearer comes to meet the teacher, who with a clean heart and attentive ear received the word of faith with desire. For he who is drawn to believe is as it were raised up from lying down by the teacher. If anyone, blushing for his stains, falls on his face and shows the signs of humility and shame, he rightly deserves to be raised up by his master.
**“at his feet”** — according to the custom of praying.
**“worshipped”** — as God. That was ignorance, not wickedness; for the angel did not teach him that he was God but showed him a teacher, as was said of Saul.
10.25: **“Cornelius, and falling down”** — by the gesture of his body he shows the devotion he had within.
10.26:
**“But Peter lifted him up, saying: Arise”** — as you.
**“I myself also am a man”** — a true one and not God.
10.27:
**“And talking with him, he went in”**
• the house.
• Speaking, he went in, etc. Bede: The holiness of the act merited communion of equality; as in the case of Ananias and Sapphira the fault, zeal for vengeance revealed the right of power.
**“and found many”** — his kinsmen and friends whom he had called together.
10.28:
**“And he said to them: You know”** — it is a question or an affirmation.
**“how abominable it is for a man that is a Jew, to keep company or to come unto one of another nation. But God hath shewed to me”**
• in a vessel.
• without doubt.
**“Hath shewed”** — Showed. Rabanus. Where he said: Go with them, doubting nothing; or there: what God has cleansed, you must not call common.
**“to call no man common or unclean”** — man.
**“common”**
• Peter understood it to have been said of all nations.
• because no man is to be distinguished.
**“or unclean, to call no man”** — because no man is to be distinguished, with: “For there is no respect of persons with God.”
10.29: **“For which cause, making no doubt, I came when I was sent for. I ask”** — he does not ask out of ignorance but on account of their confession.
10.30:
**“And Cornelius said: Four days ago, unto this hour”**
• fasting and prayer are works worthy of an angel’s vision.
• Rabanus. On the first day he saw the angel and sent messengers. On the second the messengers arrived at Joppa. On the third he set out with them. On the fourth they came to Caesarea.
**“Four days ago, unto this hour”** — Bede. In the Greek and in certain copies it is written thus: From the fourth day until this hour, fasting and praying, from the sixth hour until the ninth, and behold a man, etc. It was fitting that he be heard who for three continuous hours hastened, or prolonged, the earnestness of his prayer from the sixth to the ninth, at which time the Lord, who was being entreated for the salvation of the world, prayed with his hands stretched out on the cross.
**“I was praying in my house, at the ninth hour, and behold a man”** — in the form of a man: angels are almost always seen so, on account of the excellence of the male sex.
**“stood”** — for an angel to stand is not to fall.
**“before me in white apparel”** — because good things were being announced.
10.31:
**“Cornelius, thy prayer is heard”** — the persistence of so great fasting and prayer merited obtaining what he sought.
**“and thy alms are had in remembrance in the sight of God.”** — In the sight of God. Rabanus. In Greek: we are present in the sight of God; which is rightly said of one who was ready to obey God, believing him to be present everywhere.
10.32: **“Send therefore to Joppe, and call hither Simon”** — who will speak what is necessary to you.
10.33:
**“Immediately therefore”** — as one obedient.
**“I sent to thee: and thou hast done well in coming.”**
• as I also did by sending to you.
• not badly, as the Jews thought
**“Now therefore”** — in that you did well by coming
**“all we”** — I and my friends and kinsmen whom I gathered before your coming
**“are present in thy sight, to hear”** — to obey
**“all things”**
• we will add nothing
• we will leave nothing out
**“whatsoever are commanded thee by the Lord.”** — taught by Peter, he does not think him God but an apostle of God
10.34:
**“Then Philip, opening his mouth”** — to the Gentiles
**“And Peter, his mouth”** — who had listened patiently as with a closed mouth
**“said: In very deed”** — not only in a vision but by manifest signs, as Cornelius related what the angel had revealed to him
**“I perceive, that God is not a respecter of persons”** — he does not discern between Gentiles and Jews
**“God is not a respecter of persons”** — Bede. It is plain that God is not a respecter of persons, because he sent his only-begotten Son, who is the maker and Lord of all, to make peace for the human race, in whose name, the prophets bearing witness, not the Jews only but all believers should receive the remission of sins.
10.35:
**“But in every nation”** — both Jew and Gentile alike
**“he that feareth him”** — as you fear him
**“and worketh justice”** — the alms, prayers, and fasts which you have performed
**“is acceptable to him.”** — just as he has accepted you
10.36:
**“word”**
• of the gospel
• he made the Son, who is the Word of the Father, to be made flesh
**“God sent”** — “I was not sent but to the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel”
**“to the children of Israel, preaching peace”**
• God, through his Word Jesus Christ, announcing peace
• that is, reconciling
**“by Jesus Christ”**
• not through another messenger
• because
**“This”** — Jesus, who is the Word of the Father: “And the Word was made flesh”
**“is Lord of all”** — is of all, not of one nation
10.37:
**“You know the word which”**
• or that
• You know, etc. Bede. He briefly embraces all that is said in the Creed: that Jesus is the Christ; that he is the Lord of all, sent for the reconciliation of the world; proclaimed by the voice of John; anointed with the Holy Spirit; declared by miracles, God dwelling in him; crucified, dead, raised again, manifested to his own; the judge of all who is to come; one who will spread the Church through the whole world by faith.
• Rabanus. It is to be read thus: you know Jesus; and John preached Jesus of Nazareth, how he anointed him, etc. Or John preached this, that he anointed him, but not in an earthly manner, but by the Spirit and the power of signs.
• Bede. Another edition: as God anointed him, John therefore preached Jesus, as God anointed him with the Holy Ghost, saying: “He shall baptize in the Holy Ghost.” And again: “I saw the Spirit coming down as a dove,” etc.
**“hath been published through all Judea”** — Jesus had not preached elsewhere
**“word”** — the preaching of the gospel
**“for it began from Galilee”** — Of this Matthew says: “From that time Jesus began to preach”
**“after the baptism”** — after which Jesus was baptized
10.38:
**“Jesus of Nazareth: how God anointed him”** — Anointed him, etc. Bede. Not with visible oil but with the gift of grace, which the visible oil with which the baptized are anointed signifies; nor was he then anointed with the Holy Spirit when the dove descended upon him, for then he prefigured the Church, in which the baptized receive the Holy Spirit; but he was anointed with a mystical and invisible anointing when “the Word was made flesh,” that is, when human nature, joined to the Word of God in the womb of the virgin, became one person with him; and therefore we confess that he was born of the Spirit and the virgin Mary. For it is better to understand it so than to signify the divinity of the Son dwelling with the man whom he assumed, lest we make Christ’s person twofold, falling into the doctrine of Nestorius.
**“God, with the Holy Ghost, and with power, who”** — not having where to lay his head
**“went about”** — tireless and humble
**“doing good”** — by instructing in morals
**“and healing”** — that is, by signs
**“all that were oppressed by the devil,”**
• by bodily affliction, which Satan is often permitted to inflict
• who were troubled by an evil spirit
**“for God”**
• the Father with the Son
• the divinity with the true man
10.39:
**“And we are witnesses of all things”**
• as he himself says: “and you shall be witnesses unto me,” etc.
• we are witnesses in the region, etc., or of all that he did in the region
**“that he did in the land of the Jews and in Jerusalem, whom they killed”** — here it is plain that the Jews are rightly rejected and the Gentiles chosen
**“hanging him upon a tree”** — as a cursed and guilty man
10.40:
**“Him God”** — the Father, or the divinity
**“raised up the third day, and gave him to be made manifest”**
• he visited us after two days
• after the resurrection
10.41:
**“Not to all the people, but to witnesses preordained by God”** — whom God had chosen and had foreshadowed in many ways
**“who did eat”**
• Who did eat with him for forty days, etc. Bede. In the Greek is added: for forty days. Not that every day they ate and drank with him. For that would be contrary to John, who interposes eight days in which he was not seen by them, that he might be manifested the third time; and he fasted before his death, needing food, as many days as he ate after the resurrection, no longer needing food. He fasted before death, that we might abstain from the desires of this world; he ate, teaching in this that he is with us “even to the consummation of the world.” Fasting belongs to the contest, because he who is in the struggle abstains from everything; the food is in the hope of peace, which will be perfect when “this mortal hath put on immortality”; but we, while we walk the way of the Lord, fast from the vanity of the world and are refreshed by the promise of things to come.
• Rabanus. Through forty days, not continually but at certain times within that number of forty days.
**“and drink with him”** — fish, bread and honeycomb, which are true signs of the body
**“and drink”** — Bede. Here Peter explains what is passed over in the Gospel, that after the resurrection they drank with Christ, unless we believe it to be indicated there where he says: “Until I drink it with you in the kingdom of my Father.”
10.42:
**“And he commanded us to preach to the people”** — whom the remnants of foods foreshadowed
**“and to testify”** — not only to Jews but also to Gentiles
**“that it is he who was appointed by God”** — the Father, who gave all judgment to the Son
**“to be judge of the living”** — of the just, or of those who are found alive at the coming of Christ
**“and of the dead.”** — of sinners, or of those who died earlier and sleep
10.43:
**“To him all the prophets give testimony”** — we are not the only witnesses
**“give testimony, that by his name all receive remission of sins”** — “whoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved”
**“all”** — both Jews and Gentiles
**“who believe in him”** — by faith with works
10.44:
**“yet”** — not yet with the words finished
**“fell down”** — Bede. He came down suddenly. Or he fell from the mountain of the Jews into the valley of the Gentiles, according to that: “The valleys shall abound with corn.”
**“the Holy Ghost”**
• He falls on him, the Spirit, upon whom he rests humble.
• Bede. That he may not hesitate to give baptism to the Gentiles, it is confirmed by the testimony of the Holy Spirit. And this was done that Peter might not be blamed, and that his companions might be astonished, who were to be witnesses against the Jews; and therefore the Spirit descended before baptism, and not by the invocation of Peter; and in a new order the Spirit running before is found as a testimony of the faith of the Gentiles, but never to have happened among the Jews.
**“The Holy Ghost”** — Bede. The Spirit is the gift of God, insofar as he is given to those who through him love God; but in himself he is God even if he is given to no one, coeternal with the Father and the Son; nor is he less than they because they give and he is given. For he is so given as the gift of God that he gives himself as God: “For the Spirit breatheth where he will.”
**“upon all”** — Cornelius with his people.
10.45:
**“were astonished”** — not knowing that grace pertains to the Gentiles.
**“the faithful of the circumcision, who came with Peter, for that the Gentiles also”** — Gentiles.
**“of grace”** — gifts.
**“the grace of the Holy Ghost was poured out”** — according to Joel: “I will pour out of my Spirit,” etc.
10.46:
**“For they heard them speaking with tongues”** — It is a sign in the tongues that the Spirit has come down.
**“and magnifying God.”** — because they were speaking in tongues not vain things but the mighty works of God.
**“Then Peter answered:”** — for the astonishment of his companions.
10.47: **“Can any man forbid water”** — God gave first what is greater, and reversed the order; can he forbid what is less? You came for this, that you might be witnesses; therefore judge: Can any man forbid water, etc.
10.48:
**“And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.”**
• by his companions or by himself.
• In the name of Jesus, etc. Though it is the rule of the Church that baptism be given in the name of the Trinity, yet Luke testifies that it was given in the name of Jesus Christ. Ambrose, resolving this, says that the mystery is made full through the unity of the name, because he who says Christ designates also the Father, from whom the Son is, and the Holy Spirit; he who says Father shows forth the Son and the Spirit likewise; and he who names the Spirit names the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Son, whose Spirit he also is. Whence, that authority may be joined to reason, one is baptized also in the Spirit, according to that: “But you shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost,” and the Apostle: “In one Spirit we were baptized.”
• Bede. It is especially fitting for us to be baptized in the name of Christ, according to that: “Know you not that all we, who are baptized in Christ Jesus, are baptized in his death?”

11.1:
**“And the apostles and brethren, who were in Judea, heard”** — besides the apostles.
**“who were in Judea, that the Gentiles also had received the word of God.”** — on account of the eunuch and Cornelius.
11.2: **“And when Peter was come up to Jerusalem, they that were of the circumcision contended with him”** — not companions but believers from the Jews who were in Jerusalem.
11.3: **“Saying: Why didst thou go in to men uncircumcised, and didst eat with them?”** — You did two things against the law.
11.4: **“began”** — from the beginning of the vision; or beginning to announce salvation to the Gentiles.
11.5:
**“I was in the city of Joppe praying”** — in which hour God would not let me be deceived.
**“and I saw in an ecstasy of mind a vision, a certain vessel descending, as it were a great sheet let down from heaven by four corners, and it came even unto me.”** — it was not announced to me by another.
11.6:
**“Into which looking, I considered”** — carefully and without negligence.
**“fourfooted creatures of the earth, and beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air: kill and eat”** — Rabanus. I wonder that some interpret this as about certain foods forbidden by the law, since neither serpents nor creeping things can be eaten; nor did Peter so understand it, but that all men are equally called to the gospel, and that no one is unclean by nature; for he, rebuked not because he had eaten beasts but because he had communicated with the Gentiles, expounded the mystery of this vision.
11.7:
**“And I heard also a voice saying to me”** — I, and not another.
**“Arise, Peter”** — he is shown to be familiar from the name.
11.8:
**“And I said:”** — Behold the first excuse.
**“Not so, Lord;”** — as you also now reject it.
11.9:
**“And the voice answered”** — Behold the second excuse.
**“the voice answered again from heaven:”** — made.
**“What God”** — not another.
**“hath made clean,”** — that is, commanded to be cleansed.
**“do not thou call common.”** — do not refuse it not only by deed but also by word.
11.10:
**“And this was done three times”** — which is a sign of firmness, whence the third excuse arises
**“And all were taken up again into heaven.”**
• from this it is signified that the Gentiles are to be received into heaven
• behold the fourth excuse
11.11:
**“And behold, immediately there were three men”**
• lest the vision be thought to have been shown for another reason
• the fifth excuse: the number of witnesses coming, and of the principal sex
**“immediately there were three men come to the house wherein I was”** — I did not first approach them
11.12:
**“And the Spirit said to me”** — behold the sixth excuse
**“that I should go with them, nothing doubting.”** — he forbade me to do what you do, and ordered me to do what you find fault with
**“And these six brethren went with me also”** — the seventh excuse: testimony made
**“And these six brethren”** — Bede. Because the world was made in six days, through six brethren perfect works are shown, which accompany the teacher, when to the hearers among the words of exhortation an example of perfection is shown.
11.13:
**“And he told us how he had seen an angel in his house”** — the eighth excuse: namely the narration of the faithful man about the vision of the angel in his house, on whose coming Peter was summoned
**“standing”** — an angel is said to stand in the usual manner
11.14: **“Who shall speak to thee words, whereby thou shalt be saved”** — the tenth excuse: because the angel announces the salvation which you deny
11.15:
**“And when I had begun to speak, the Holy Ghost fell”** — the eleventh excuse: the descent of the Spirit
**“upon them, as upon us also in the beginning.”** — in the same way and not less
11.16: **“And I remembered the word of the Lord”** — the twelfth excuse: the word of the Lord about the Holy Spirit spoken to them, which was fulfilled among the Gentiles
11.17: **“If then God gave them the same grace, as to us also who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ; who was I, that could withstand God?”** — do not attempt it: for if I could not, neither will you be able
11.18:
**“Having heard these things, they held their peace”** — from the rebuke of Peter
**“and glorified God”** — they gave thanks to the Saviour
**“saying: God then hath also to the Gentiles”**
• as to us
• Then to the Gentiles also, etc. This is what is read in Job: “Out of the north gold will come, and to God a fearful praise,” because first in the cold breast of the Gentiles the splendour of faith arose, and for that same unexpected faith Judea glorifies God with trembling.
**“given repentance unto life.”** — which appears in the descent of the Spirit
11.19:
**“Now they who had been dispersed”** — He returns to what he had said. Therefore those who had been scattered went about preaching the word of God. For the narrative about Philip, Peter, John, and Paul has been inserted.
**“by the persecution that arose on occasion of Stephen”** — begun from his death
**“went about as far as Phenice”** — the western province of Syria
**“and Cyprus and Antioch”** — a city of Syria
**“speaking the word to none”** — on account of Antioch, in which they spoke; or they were not of those who spoke in Antioch
**“but to the Jews only.”** — after the example of Christ saying: “I was not sent but to the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel”
11.20: **“But some of them were”** — Rabanus. Not of those who had been scattered from Jerusalem, but they were of Cyprus and Cyrene. Or, Antioch excepted, they spoke to the Greeks in the other places, that is, in Cyprus and Cyrene. Otherwise: those Greeks to whom they spoke were Jews by race, but lived among the Greeks in the dispersion.
11.21: **“And the hand of the Lord was with them: and a great number believing, were converted to the Lord.”** — And the number of believers grew, etc. Bede. Now after the revelation of the sheet, in which the holy animals from above rest in heavenly hope, the Church began to grow, since the gospel is preached through foreign provinces, islands and cities, not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles.
11.22:
**“And the tidings came to the ears of the church that was at Jerusalem”** — that they also spoke to the Greeks
**“touching these things”** — concerning these Greeks who believed in Antioch
**“and they sent Barnabas”** — to test their faith
**“And they sent Barnabas”** — Rabanus. Barnabas was manly in goodness. Barnabas is often praised in this book, lest it be believed that he lacked the apostleship through the unworthiness of his merit, he who was afterwards ordained apostle of the Gentiles by the apostles.
11.23:
**“Who, when he was come, and had seen the grace of God”** — the power
**“of God, rejoiced”** — after a great number had been converted
**“and he exhorted them all with purpose of heart”** — as they had purposed and begun
**“And he exhorted them all with purpose of heart”** — He changed or added nothing, but taught perseverance, because the faith in them was true and full.
**“to continue in the Lord”** — in the faith of the Lord, or that they may be members of the Lord
11.24:
**“For he was a good man”** — the good man exhorts good things
**“and full of the Holy Ghost and of faith. And a great multitude was added”** — at the coming of Barnabas
**“a great multitude was added to the Lord”** — to the former number of believers
11.25:
**“Tarsus”** — For it was said above that the brethren led him by night to Caesarea and sent him away to Tarsus.
**“to seek Saul”** — To seek Saul. Behold the goodness of Barnabas, who does not presume to teach the people alone but seeks a partner in the apostleship.
11.26:
**“whom, when he had found, he brought to Antioch”** — to the faithful, from whom there was nothing to be feared
**“And they conversed there in the church a whole year”** — not idly
**“and they taught a great multitude”** — which he had previously said was added to the Lord, together with those who were increasing during the year
**“so that at Antioch the disciples were first named Christians”** — by this name the Christians were called before
**“so that the disciples were named Christians”** — Rabanus. Every sect took its name from its author. Therefore, when the faith was founded and had attained firmness, first in Antioch, where faith flourished above other places, the name Christian was taken from Christ.
11.27:
**“And in these days”** — in that year in which they lived there
**“there came from Jerusalem”** — as from a higher place, both in position and in merit
**“prophets”** — by grace
**“Prophets”** — Rabanus. Of whom it was said: “And your sons shall prophesy.” It is praise of Antioch that many perfect men gathered there.
11.28:
**“rising up”** — And rising up in body, since he spoke to the multitude
**“Agabus”** — Bede. ‘Messenger of tribulation’ is the meaning of his name; according to that name he here prophesies a general famine, and a little below, chains.
**“signified by the Spirit, that there should be a great famine”** — signified through the Spirit a great famine
**“over the whole world”** — grievous, or because through the whole world
**“which came to pass under Claudius”** — to come in the whole world, not across intervals of places
11.29:
**“And the disciples”** — Bede. The disciples seem in this not to have kept the command of God, who says: “Be not solicitous for tomorrow.” But it is plain that he does not disapprove if someone provides for these things in the human way, but that he should not serve God for them, so that in his work he looks not to the kingdom of God but to temporal things. To this rule, therefore, this precept is brought back: that in providing for these things we look to the kingdom of God, but in the service of God we do not think about them.
**“every man according to his ability”** — not according to will but according to the quality of their substance
**“purposed to send relief”** — by a collection of alms
**“to the brethren who dwelt in Judea”** — not to themselves
**“in Judea”** — Bede. They knew that in Judea, and most of all at Jerusalem, the famine would rage more sharply, where the poor of the saints were, who, having sold their goods, houses and lands, had brought the prices to the apostles, and had not much leisure afterwards for acquiring money. Some also were fined for the faith, their substance being taken away by the Jews, of whom the Apostle says: “And took with joy the being stripped of your own goods.”
11.30: **“Which also they did, sending it to the ancients, by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.”** — who were approved, or were faithful ministers

12.1:
**“And at the same time”**
• when Paul and Barnabas were sent into the ministry
• Bede. Not the time of famine, which histories report was made in the fourth year of Claudius; since Herod died in the third year of that same reign, but at the time when offerings were being carried to Jerusalem.
• Bede. It is not to be thought that the Herod who was tetrarch, afterwards made king, is the one designated in this chapter. Josephus relates that Caius, having taken the empire, at once gave the rule of the Jews to Herod, the son of Aristobulus (whom he, however, calls Agrippa), and in the fourth year, that is, the last of his reign, gave him a seat of rule as well. But the Herod who had killed John, or had been present at the passion of Christ, he condemned, after he had been grievously tormented, to perpetual exile. Moreover, this Herod or Agrippa, struck by an angel in the third year of Claudius, the seventh of his own reign, left the kingdom to his son Agrippa; the Aristobulus I mentioned had been killed, together with his brother Alexander, by their faithless father, that is, by the Herod under whom Christ was born.
**“stretched forth”** — by ministers; what someone orders, he himself does
**“Herod the king”** — who had been present at the passion of Christ, the son of Herod under whom Christ was born
**“his hands”** — to hold and bind some of the Church
**“to afflict”** — with torments
**“some of the church”** — as if they were of the inner circle of the Church
12.2:
**“he killed”** — he not only afflicted some but also killed
**“James”** — of Zebedee
**“And he killed James”** — Bede. Clement of Alexandria relates a history of this James, and says that he who had brought him, James that is, before the judge for martyrdom, himself also confessed that he was a Christian; and as they were being led away, he asked James on the road to grant him forgiveness. And he, deliberating a little, said, “Peace be to thee,” and kissed him, and so both were punished together by the sword.
12.3:
**“And seeing that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded”** — he added the affliction of some and the killing of James
**“to take up Peter also”** — because it would please more where the leader was killed
**“Now it was in the days of the Azymes.”** — therefore he was not killed but seized, as they also said of Christ: “It is not lawful to put anyone to death during the Pasch.”
12.4:
**“And when he had apprehended him, he cast him into prison”** — as long as it is not lawful to kill him, they think it lawful to torment him in confinement
**“four files”** — A quaternion is called the leader of four soldiers; for as a centurion has a hundred, so a quaternion has four soldiers under him.
**“of soldiers to be kept”** — the guarding of the prison alone was not enough
**“intending, after the pasch, to bring him forth to the people.”** — Rabanus. For it would be a greater favour if the Jews themselves killed him, since he was the leader, and not Herod himself, as with James.
12.5:
**“Peter therefore was kept in prison. But prayer was made without ceasing”**
• an example of praying for those in danger, and especially for the pastors of the Church
• for so one must pray, according to that: “The continual prayer of a just man availeth much.”
12.6:
**“And when Herod would have brought him forth, the same night”** — on which night a release was opportune
**“Peter was sleeping”** — not having hope of escaping at that hour
**“between two soldiers, bound with two chains”** — Rabanus. Four difficulties heap up the guarding: soldiers, chains, prison, keepers.
**“and the keepers before the door kept the prison.”** — these four magnify the guard: soldiers, chains, keepers, prison
12.7:
**“And behold an angel of the Lord stood by him”** — of the Lord; and stood by
**“a light”** — A sign of the presence of the angel of God, whose presence gave light to Peter alone, and shone for no others.
**“shined in the room”** — from the presence of the angel
**“striking Peter on the side”**
• by bodily touch
• Rabanus. The angel could have bodily touch, with a body taken from the air.
**“Striking on the side”** — Bede. The striking of the side is a remembrance of the passion of Christ, from whose side our salvation flowed; and to us also, held in the pressure of chains, Peter gives such comfort, saying: “Christ therefore having suffered in the flesh, be you also armed with the same thought.”
**“Peter, raised him up, saying: Arise quickly. And the chains fell off from his hands.”** — first the distress is loosed
12.8:
**“Gird thyself”** — Bede. We read that the prophets and apostles used girdles, but Peter, because of the severity of the prison, had loosened his bonds for the time, so that the tunic let down about his feet might somehow temper the cold of the night, giving an example to the weak that when they are tried by bodily discomfort or human injury, it is allowed to relax something of the strictness of their purpose; and because it is said: “Let your loins be girt, and your feet shod,” in the preparation of the gospel of peace, we are commanded to take up again the badges of spiritual virtues and of the preaching of the word.
**“and put on thy sandals”** — an example is given of not walking without sandals, the angel commanding and the apostle carrying it out
**“thy sandals”** — a caliga is a kind of footwear
**“And he did so. And he said to him: Cast thy garment about thee, and follow me.”** — let fear not hinder
12.9: **“And going out, he followed him, and he knew not that it was true which was done by the angel”** — he did not think it was happening but that it was shown in imagination
12.10:
**“And passing through the first”**
• two soldiers
• the first quaternion with its men
**“and the second ward”**
• the guards of the prison
• the second quaternion with its men
**“they came to the iron gate”** — which is thought to have been in the court of the prison
**“that leadeth to the city”** — it is clear the prison was outside the city, or in the outer part of the city
**“they came to the iron gate that leadeth to the city”** — Bede. Narrow, indeed iron, was the gate that leads to the heavenly Jerusalem, but by the footsteps of the apostles it has been made passable for us, who by their own blood overcame the iron door; for iron doors yield to Peter, the keeper of the heavenly hall, who, holding the summit of the Church, overcomes hell.
**“which of itself”** — of its own accord
**“opened to them. And going out, they passed on through one street: and immediately”** — so that he might know that what was happening was true and not a vision
12.11:
**“Coming to himself”** — He returned to this, which had been before in common understanding, from the height of contemplation.
**“said: Now I know in very deed”** — it shows that he did not know this before
12.12:
**“And considering”** — where he was
**“he came to the house of Mary the mother of John, who was surnamed Mark, where many were gathered together and praying.”** — the cause of the prayer: for Peter, or from the event
12.13:
**“And when he knocked at the door of the gate, a damsel came to hearken, whose name was Rhode.”**
• seeing, or strong, or the vision of strength, or the strength of vision
• The maid came out, but ran in, etc. Also the woman was the first of all to announce to the disciples the Lord come out of the tomb, as: “Where sin abounded, grace did more abound.”
12.14: **“And as soon as she knew Peter’s voice, she opened not the gate for joy”** — from impatience, namely to announce Peter’s arrival
12.15:
**“But they said to her: Thou art mad.”** — because they knew Peter had been imprisoned
**“But she affirmed that it was so.”** — the thing
**“It is his angel.”** — Jerome. Great is the dignity of souls, that each from the moment of birth has an angel assigned to it for its guard.
**“Tyconius”** — The angel of a man seems to be the inner man, who always contemplates God by faith.
**“Then said they: It is his angel.”** — Bede. That each has an angel, Scripture bears witness. Whence the Lord says: “Their angels always see the face of the Father.” And Jacob: “The angel that delivereth me from all evils.” And here the disciples believed that Peter’s angel was coming.
12.16: **“But Peter continued knocking. And when they had opened, they saw him, and were astonished.”** — because they were sure he would not be released by men
12.17:
**“But he beckoning to them with his hand”** — by enjoining silence
**“to hold their peace”** — Until he related the power, or he bids them be silent so that his arrival is not made known in the city by the shouting of the rejoicing people.
**“told how the Lord had brought him out of prison”** — not men, not his own cunning or strength
**“And he said: Tell these things”** — the power granted to their prayers
**“to James”** — James the just, namely the son of Alpheus; the other James had been beheaded
**“and to the brethren”** — praying for me
**“And going out, he went into another place.”** — the same night, to another place, for fear of Herod and the Jews
12.18:
**“Now when day was come”** — the next day after Peter’s leading out of prison
**“there was no small stir among the soldiers”** — the guards
**“what was become of Peter”** — It appears that Peter left the prison closed; had it been open, there would be no doubt that he had escaped.
12.19:
**“And when Herod had sought for him”** — in prison
**“and found him not; having examined”** — he inquired whether the guards knew what had become of him
**“the keepers, he commanded they should be put to death”** — to be brought to him, so that he might take vengeance on them
**“going down”** — Rabanus. That Peter’s release might harm no one, Herod is not permitted to take vengeance on the guards.
**“to Caesarea”** — Bede. Although, according to the situation of the places, he seems to mean Caesarea Philippi, because this also, like Tyre and Sidon, is a city of Phenicia, yet Josephus says these things were done in Caesarea of Palestine, which was formerly called Strato’s Tower, situated on the shore of the great sea on the border of Phenicia and Palestine.
**“he abode there.”** — therefore he drew near to their borders
12.20:
**“And he was angry with the Tyrians and the Sidonians.”** — Tyre and Sidon are cities of the province of Phoenicia
**“And they indeed”** — the Tyrians and Sidonians
**“with one accord came to him, and having gained”** — and they persuaded
**“Blastus, who was the king’s chamberlain”** — as it were keeper of the treasures
**“they desired peace, because their countries were nourished”** — for he was their friend and patron, and perhaps governor
**“were nourished”** — Bede. They had need of the friendship of the king’s neighbours, because their region was very narrow, hemmed in by the borders of Galilee and Damascus.
12.21:
**“And upon a day appointed, Herod”** — appointed beforehand by agreement
**“being arrayed in kingly apparel”** — his glory is described, so that his misery may afterwards be greater
**“sat in the judgment seat”** — in, or: 'upon'
**“judgment seat”** — where there was the place of judgment
**“and made an oration to them.”** — flattering and fawning
12.22: **“And the people made acclamation, saying: It is the voice of a god, and not of a man.”** — flattery and the perversity of faith is shown
12.23:
**“And forthwith an angel of the Lord struck him”** — Immediately, etc. Bede. Josephus: while he did not shrink from the impiety of unlawful flattery, looking up a little after, he saw an angel hanging over and standing above his head, and perceived at once to be the minister of his destruction him whom before he had known as the provider of good things; thereupon, tormented for seven continuous days with pain in the belly, he violently ended his life.
**“because he had not given the honour to God”** — by persecuting the apostles and rejecting the name of God
**“and being eaten up by worms, he gave up the ghost.”** — gradually, not suddenly
12.24:
**“But the word of the Lord”** — with the false lord dead, the word of God grows
**“increased”** — among the faithful
**“and multiplied”** — in those who were increased daily
12.25: **“And Barnabas and Saul returned”** — he returns to what he had said, sending to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul

13.1:
**“Now there were”** — besides those who came from Jerusalem
**“in the church which was at Antioch, prophets”** — concerning the future
**“and”** — that is
**“doctors”** — of things past
**“Prophets and doctors”** — They were the same, prophets and teachers. Or some of them were prophets, and others teachers.
**“among whom was Barnabas, and Simon”** — audible, hearing sorrow; or the name of a dwelling
**“Niger”** — Rabanus. From heat, if it is Latin. Or it is interpreted ascending, if it is Hebrew.
**“and Lucius”** — himself raising up or rising
**“of Cyrene”** — of the city of Cyrene mentioned above
**“and Manahen, who was the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch”** — one who is nourished by the same milk is called a foster brother
13.2:
**“And as they were ministering”** — those who have just been named
**“to the Lord, and fasting, the Holy Ghost said to them”** — to the prophets
**“the Holy Ghost said: Separate me”** — Separate, so that they serve the teaching alone
**“Saul and Barnabas”** — It is clear that they returned from Jerusalem to Antioch.
**“Separate me Barnabas and Saul”** — Bede. According to the order of the history, Saul seems to have received the apostleship with Barnabas, and the name of Paul, in the thirteenth year after the passion, and in the fourteenth year, according to the agreement of James, Cephas and John, to have set out for the teaching of the Gentiles. And the Ecclesiastical History agrees, saying that the apostles had been commanded to preach in Judea for twelve years.
**“for the work”**
• of the apostleship
• therefore Paul is called a vessel of election, and set apart for the gospel of God
**“whereunto I have taken them”** — I will take; for future things are to God as past things
13.3:
**“Then they, fasting and praying”** — so that preaching may be prepared for them
**“and imposing their hands upon them”** — in the manner of those being ordained
**“sent them away”** — for the work to which they were taken
13.4:
**“So they”** — Saul and Barnabas
**“being sent by the Holy Ghost”** — Rabanus. Sent away by men, they are at once sent by the Holy Spirit to Seleucia; the leader of their journey was the one who had set them apart from the rest.
**“went to Seleucia”** — so called from King Seleucus
**“Went to Seleucia”** — Rabanus. In some copies it is found: they went to Seleucia, which is Salamis; but there are two names for one city.
13.5:
**“And when they were come to Salamina”** — which is in Cyprus
**“they preached the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews”** — on account of the reverence or the hardness of the Jews
**“In the synagogues”** — Bede. For the sake of those ignorant of places, I thought it should be noted once: wherever you see the synagogue of the Jews, know that the things told were done in the city.
**“And they had John also”** — who was called Mark
**“in the ministry”** — of preaching
13.6:
**“And when they had gone through the whole island, as far as Paphos, they found a certain man, a magician”** — a sorcerer
**“Bar-jesu”** — Bede. It is read corruptly as Bariehu, or as others have it, Bariem.
**“a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Bar-jesu”**
• son in evil, or son of sorcery
• that is, a sorcerer
13.7:
**“Who was with the proconsul”** — proconsul: a name of dignity, second from the consul
**“Sergius Paulus”** — Sergius and Paulus are the names of one man.
**“a prudent man”** — who by the goodness of his nature desired the word of God
13.8:
**“But Elymas the magician withstood them”** — a sorcerer, which is common to others; it is proper to him
**“Elymas”** — Rabanus. Elymas, according to some, is interpreted “the measure of my God” or “magician”, and therefore he resisted.
**“for so his name is interpreted”** — that is, magician, which looks to transgression, who always resists God
**“seeking to turn away”** — Rabanus. He wished to turn to transgression him who had begun to turn from the faith, according to his name.
13.9:
**“Saul”** — Rabanus. It is interpreted “the temptation of one looking back”, or “security”, or “wonderful”.
**“otherwise Paul”** — Bede. From Sergius Paulus the proconsul, whom he brought under the faith, he received the name Paul.
**“Then Saul, otherwise Paul”**
• Bede. Fittingly, the apostle of the Gentiles receives his name from a Gentile.
• Rabanus. So called from Sergius Paulus; when merits change, names change also. Saul was a son of sorrow when he persecuted the Church, but Paul a son of the right hand when he called not only himself but many others to the right hand. For as the name of Barnabas was changed, so that instead of Joseph he was called Barnabas, that is, “son of consolation,” so Saul, after the rank of apostleship, received the name of Paul, who, made “from proud humble,” was called Paul instead of Saul. Saul is named from Saul the impious persecutor; Paul from a small and humble spirit. Whence, interpreting his own name, he said: “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.”
**“filled with the Holy Ghost”** — formerly, or now, more lively
**“looking upon”** — through the Spirit
**“him”** — Elymas
13.10:
**“Said: O full”** — full things do not receive increase
**“of all guile, and of all deceit, child of the devil”** — not by being born but by imitating
**“enemy of all justice”** — of God and of his laws
**“thou ceasest not to pervert the right ways of the Lord”**
• faith and repentance
• commandments
13.11:
**“And now behold, the hand of the Lord”** — that is, power
**“is upon thee, and thou shalt be blind”**
• outwardly as you are also inwardly
• And now, etc. You shall be blind. Bede. It was fitting that Paul work miracles for the completion of the apostleship, which the Lord had chosen him for, though he long kicked against the goad.
**“not seeing the sun”** — as you do not see the sun of justice
**“for a time”** — of penance or of death
**“And immediately there fell upon him”**
• not by chance but from above, from God
• And immediately there fell, etc. Rabanus. Here is fulfilled what is read in the Canticles: “Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vines,” because Paul caught the false prophet who was laying waste the tender vineyard, that is, the mind of the proconsul; the apostle, mindful of his own example, knew that the light of the mind can arise from the darkness of the eyes. For he did not deserve to have the eyes of the flesh who labored to take away the eyes of the mind from others.
**“a mist and darkness”**
• the beginning of blindness
• blindness itself
**“And going about”** — turning himself around in a circle, in the manner of the blind
**“he sought some one to lead him by the hand.”** — to lead him
13.12: **“Then the proconsul, when he had seen what was done,”** — that is, with the doctrine of Christ, the power of the miracle
13.13:
**“Now when Paul and they that were with him had sailed from Paphos,”** — those of whom Barnabas was one
**“that were with him, they came to Perge”** — the city
**“in Pamphylia.”** — of that region
**“And John departing”** — this is the cause of the future separation
**“from them, returned to Jerusalem.”** — whence he had come with them
13.14:
**“But they”** — Paul and Barnabas with their companions
**“passing through Perge”** — not sailing, but on foot
**“came to Antioch in Pisidia.”** — or of Syria
**“They came to Antioch”** — Bede. There are two Antiochs: one in Syria, founded by King Seleucus, which was formerly called Reblatha, where the disciples were first called Christians. The other is the one just mentioned, in the province of Pisidia.
**“Antioch in Pisidia”** — Rabanus. To distinguish it from the other Antioch, as is believed; but it is thought by many to be the same.
**“And entering into the synagogue on the sabbath day, they sat down.”** — where they were accustomed to assemble, and to read the law and the prophets, in the manner of the Lord’s day
**“They sat down”** — Rabanus. As if about to hear the law, not to preach; behold an example of humility.
13.15:
**“And after the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent”** — “A city seated on a mountain cannot be hid.”
**“the rulers of the synagogue sent to them, saying: Ye men, brethren”** — because you are Jews
**“if you have any word”**
• as if they said: this is the work of this day, in which they do nothing else; a thing said in doubt, which is a sign of unbelief
• said doubtingly, which is a sign of unbelief
**“of exhortation”** — not of preaching, not of choosing
**“to make to the people, speak.”** — not to us, who have no need
13.16:
**“Then Paul rising up”** — according to the custom of readers, because of the multitude of hearers
**“and with his hand bespeaking silence”** — namely by some customary sign of silence
**“said: Ye men of Israel”** — Jews
**“and you that fear God”**
• Gentiles
• he distinguishes the God-fearers, because not all feared God
**“hear”** — both
13.17:
**“The God of the people of Israel chose”**
• before all peoples who worshipped other gods
• he chose from every kind of men
**“fathers”**
• not “fathers” of him
• Abraham and the rest
**“our”** — not yours, which is said to persuade
**“and exalted the people”** — from servitude
**“when they were sojourners in the land of Egypt”** — serving in mud and brick
**“and with an high arm”**
• by the power by which he struck the Egyptians with many plagues
• Christ, who is the arm of the Father
13.18:
**“And for the space of forty years”** — signifies the long patience of God
**“endured their manners in the desert.”** — their heaviness is shown
13.19:
**“And destroying seven nations”** — seven vices or countless ones
**“In the land of Chanaan”** — Rabanus. Namely, the land of the repromission, which was given to Israel, as most think, for this reason: that in the first division after the flood the seed of Sem received this province by lot, but afterwards it was violently possessed by the Chanaanites. And therefore by right of war it is restored to its former inhabitants. And deservedly are the Chanaanites destroyed, of whose stock it is said: “Cursed be Chanaan, a servant of servants shall he be,” whose father Cham was impious toward his father, and therefore deserved to be cursed.
**“divided their land among them, by lot”** — signifies peace and the equality of division
13.20:
**“four hundred”** — Bede. God had said to Abraham: “Thy seed shall be a sojourner in a strange land four hundred years.” And again he said: “In Isaac shall thy seed be called.” From the rise of that seed, therefore, to the going out of Israel from Egypt there were, according to Exodus, four hundred and five years. Add to these forty years in the desert and five in the land of Chanaan, after which were completed the land seems to have rested from wars, and the lot to have been cast upon it, and you will find four hundred and fifty years.
**“and fifty years. And after these things,”** — that is, after four hundred and fifty years, and the division of the land
**“he gave unto them judges, until Samuel the prophet.”** — He gave judges until, etc. The time of the judges passes to prove the patience of God.
13.21:
**“And after that they desired a king”** — against the will of God
**“God gave them Saul the son of Cis”** — the patience of God is increased
**“a man of the tribe of Benjamin”** — evil from the last tribe, which is a kind of vengeance
**“forty years.”** — with the time of Samuel; for so it is in Chronicles: Samuel and Saul for forty years
**“forty years”** — Bede. The book of Kings does not openly set out for how many years Saul reigned, but the Apostle, speaking in the common way, said what the more frequent report held. The chronicles, however, testify that Samuel and Saul ruled over Israel forty years.
13.22:
**“And when he had removed him, he raised them up David to be king”** — because of the humility of the root and person, or raised up in the figure of Christ
**“to whom giving testimony”** — continual patience is shown
**“he said: I have found David”** — unless I sought, he would appear to no one
**“the son of Jesse”** — of a small stock
**“a man according to my own heart”** — this on account of him, or Christ born of David’s seed
**“who shall do all my wills.”** — this applies most of all to Christ
13.23:
**“Of this man's”** — the things foretold tended to this
**“Of this man's seed God according to his promise”**
• not suddenly but after many promises of the prophets this was done
• this: “who shall do all my wills”
• “Of the fruit of thy womb I will set upon thy throne.”
**“hath raised up to Israel a Saviour, Jesus”**
• he gives the translation along with the name, because Jesus is interpreted as “saviour.”
• Spiritually.
13.24:
**“preaching”** — not giving what was reserved for Christ
**“John”** — whose authority is great
**“before his coming”** — in the manner of a lamp. Whence: “I have prepared a lamp for my christ.”
**“the baptism of penance to all the people of Israel.”** — of forgiveness, because through penance sin is forgiven
13.25:
**“And when John was fulfilling his course, he said:”** — the office of the forerunner before the face of Christ
**“whom you think me to be”**
• behold what was prophesied of him
• by asking; or, I am not Christ, whom you think me to be
**“I am not he.”** — to be is proper to deity
**“but behold, there cometh one after me”** — because I am his forerunner
**“whose shoes I am not worthy”** — John was not that bridegroom of whom, as bridegroom, etc. The shoe, that is, the incarnation of Christ, by which it indeed befitted Christ, not needing others; he was not worthy.
**“to loose the shoes of his feet”** — to open the mystery of the incarnation
13.26:
**“Men, brethren”** — a sweet message
**“children of the stock of Abraham”** — Jews, namely
**“and whosoever among you fear God”**
• Jews, namely
• or it can be taken of the Gentiles
**“unto you”** — to Jews
**“to you”** — Rabanus. To the Jews: “I was not sent but to the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel.” Or to you who are dispersed, because, as follows, the inhabitants of Jerusalem rejected it.
**“the word of this salvation is sent”** — the gospel, or Christ, the Word of the Father
13.27:
**“For they that inhabited Jerusalem, and the rulers thereof, not knowing him”** — Jesus, not knowing him to be the Saviour
**“and the voices of the prophets, which are read every sabbath, judging”**
• because they were judges of the people
• Jesus.
**“judging”** — Rabanus. Judging that Jesus is guilty of death, or judging the voices of the prophets, that is, not believing; for “he that detracteth his brother, detracteth the law, and judgeth the law”; how much more those who detract from Christ.
**“have fulfilled them”** — not knowing the prophecy
13.28:
**“And finding no cause of death in him”** — although they sought
**“they desired”** — “Away with him, away with him, crucify him.”
**“of Pilate, that they might kill him”** — through the hands of soldiers
13.29:
**“And when they had fulfilled”** — he himself said on the cross: “It is consummated.”
**“all things”**
• because all things were done through them: an unarmed hand, an armed mouth
• which they fulfilled, as was said
**“that were written of him”** — which was prophesied about the passion
**“taking him down from the tree”**
• not the unbelieving Jews, but Joseph, who was a Jew by birth; and because of him the Jews are said to have done this
• allowing them to be taken down because of the sabbath, lest the bodies remain longer on the cross against the precept of the law
**“they laid him in a sepulchre”** — This is said of the Jews on account of Joseph, as before; or because the Jews guarded the tomb.
13.30:
**“But God”** — his divinity, which is one with the Father and the Spirit
**“hath raised up”** — according to the man
**“Who”** — by known and certain witnesses
13.31:
**“from the dead the third day, who was seen for many days”** — forty
**“who came up together with him”** — to the mountains near Jerusalem
**“with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who”** — not their successors
**“to this present are his witnesses”** — fit
13.32:
**“And we declare unto you”** — and to your children
**“declare it”** — that is, the promise
**“the promise which was made to our fathers”** — that he raised him up
13.33:
**“This same God hath fulfilled”**
• the prophecy in which it is said: “I have begotten thee,” as below
• This same God hath fulfilled, etc. Bede. In Greek: how God has fulfilled this to their children, to us.
**“to our children, raising up Jesus”** — he shows this to be the promise
*Bede:* In the second psalm: some copies have ‘in the first’, which is explained thus: the first and second psalms were composed among the Hebrews as one psalm, because it begins from blessedness and ends in the same.
**“as in the second psalm also is written: Thou art my Son”**
• not a servant as the others
• consubstantial
• My Son, etc. Bede. It is not to be thought that this example of the psalm pertains to the resurrection of Christ, which he mentioned just before, but to the incarnation, of which he had spoken above. For the following verse clearly bears witness of the resurrection, since above he had dealt with the incarnation, the passion, and the resurrection. He establishes both by the testimonies of the prophet; who therefore says: You are the eternal Son before the ages; now, born in time, you will appear.
**“Thou art”**
• this is proper to the deity
• in the divinity, where there is neither yesterday nor tomorrow
**“this day have I begotten thee”** — for that birth from God is of the Virgin
13.34:
**“And to shew that he raised him up from the dead, not to return now any more to corruption, he said thus”** — I will fulfil what I promised David, namely that Christ would be born of him
**“I will give you”** — because I will fulfil
**“the holy things of David”**
• that is, of Christ, who is the true David, strong of hand
• Rabanus. The holy things of David, that is, the holy temple born of the seed of David, that is, the body of Christ raised up into incorruption.
• Holy things of David, faithful, etc. Bede. Isaias, foretelling the mysteries of the New Testament, says: “I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the holy things of David, faithful.” In Hebrew: “And I will strike with you an everlasting pact, the faithful mercies of David.”
**“faithful”** — without lying
13.35:
**“And therefore, in another place also, he saith”** — Thou shalt not suffer, etc. Rabanus. After the resurrection he does not die: “death shall no more have dominion over him”; and therefore he says holy and faithful, that is, incorrupt and to remain eternally.
**“thy Holy One”** — the body of Christ
**“to see corruption”** — putrefaction
13.36:
**“For David”** — therefore these things were foretold of Christ and not of David
**“in his generation”** — in the fourteenth generation from Abraham
**“when he had served, according to the will of God”** — he had done the will of God; whence above: “who shall do all my wills.”
**“slept, and was laid unto his fathers”** — as one added to the number of the born, so too of the dying
**“and saw”** — by experience
**“corruption”** — of worms
13.38:
**“Be it known therefore to you, men, brethren”** — it answers to what he had said: But God raised him up
**“that through him”** — Jesus the Saviour
**“forgiveness of sins is preached to you”** — sins
**“from all the things”** — this is said so that they not trust in the law
13.39:
**“from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses”** — which was the power and increase of sin
**“In him every one that believeth is justified”** — because: “The just man liveth by faith.”
13.40:
**“Beware, therefore”** — while believing, he is justified
**“lest that come upon you”** — it happen that we be despisers
**“which is spoken in the prophets”** — in one book of many prophets
13.41:
**“Behold, ye despisers”**
• beware, unbelievers
• In Greek: hear, despisers, and wonder; regard, and perish.
**“and wonder”**
• the incarnation of Christ, in not believing whom you are despisers
• Rabanus. Wonder. Join it thus: wonder and be scattered by the Assyrians and Chaldeans, and last by the Romans, because I work the work of both vengeances.
**“and perish”** — denying the incarnation of the Word
**“if any man shall tell it you”** — Rabanus. You will not believe, if any man shall tell it you, etc. Or they are said not to believe, because of the greatness of both vengeances, until they are fulfilled.
13.42: **“And as they went out, they desired them, that on the next sabbath, they would speak unto them these words.”** — that which was said is fulfilled: you will not believe, if any man tell it to you
13.43:
**“And when the synagogue was broken up”** — by the apostles, or when they began to return to their homes
**“many of the Jews, followed”** — not the rulers
**“who served God”**
• God
• dwelling
• Rabanus. And of those worshipping. It is better read worshipping God, as it is in the Greek. It signifies, however, those who were Gentiles by nature but Jews in religion, called in Greek proselytes.
**“strangers”** — this is to be understood of Jews
**“Paul and Barnabas”** — who are thought to have been Gentiles, or Jews coming from the dispersion
**“who speaking to them, persuaded them to continue”**
• that they might be not only hearers but doers, both beginners and the perfect
• by persevering
**“in the grace of God”** — which they had received, but were still unskilled
13.44: **“the next sabbath day, the whole city almost came together”** — according to the custom of the Jews
13.45:
**“And the Jews seeing the multitudes”** — to come together to the apostles
**“were filled”** — not a little
**“with envy”** — of envy
**“and contradicted”** — he who envies the truth is a blasphemer
**“those things which were said by Paul, blaspheming”** — he who contradicts the truth is a blasphemer
13.46:
**“Then ... boldly”** — not fearing the princes of the Jews
**“Paul and Barnabas said”** — from zeal for God
**“To you it behoved us”**
• according to that: “I was not sent but to the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel”
• because it was promised
**“First”** — Rabanus. Jesus came first to heal the daughter of the ruler, but the woman suffering from an issue of blood snatched away the healing.
**“of eternal life”** — Rabanus. Not because they knew that there was an eternal life, which they rejected, but the apostles spoke from their own sense and their own faith.
**“behold we turn to the Gentiles”**
• that the woman with the issue of blood might be healed
• “The mountains are carried into the heart of the sea”
13.47:
**“For so the Lord hath commanded us”**
• foretold
• For so, etc. Rabanus. The prophecy is an unchangeable command to us; first it is said, then the testimony of the prophet is brought in, addressed to the person of the Father speaking to the Son.
**“The Lord: I have set thee”**
• Christ’s coming had already taken place
• after the darkness of unbelief
• Bede. The apostles think that what was said specially to Christ was said to themselves, because they are his members; just as, on account of the union of the same body, it was said: “Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” etc.
**“I have set thee”** — Rabanus. He does not say, I have set you, because what is said to Christ pertains to the apostles, who are his members.
**“to be the light”** — openly
**“of the Gentiles”** — not only in one, as before among the nation of the Jews
**“that thou mayest be for salvation”** — which is needed against the weakness of sin
**“unto the utmost part of the earth”** — through all the borders
13.48:
**“And the Gentiles hearing it, were glad”** — after darkness, of light; after sickness, of health
**“and glorified the word of the Lord”** — they confessed the gospel, or Christ, the Word of the Father, and gave thanks
**“and as many as were ordained to life everlasting, believed”** — by God
**“ordained”** — The order is that after present labours and the mortification of the flesh, life follows.
**“to life everlasting”** — by which the Jews judged themselves unworthy
13.49:
**“was published”** — because it is true seed
**“And the word of the Lord throughout the whole country”** — with the Jews rejected, it is sown among the Gentiles, but yet it was preached to both
13.50:
**“religious women”** — Rabanus. Either of the Jews who kept the religion of the law, or of the Gentiles who began to keep the religion.
**“and honourable, and the chief men”** — the chief and foremost men
**“of the city”** — of Antioch, that of which we spoke
**“raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas: and cast them out of their coasts”** — the chief men, because they did not believe
13.51:
**“But they, shaking off the dust”**
• Shaking off the dust, etc. According to the precept of the gospel the dust is shaken off, as a testimony that they have made their labour vain.
• Bede. The dust is shaken off as a testimony to their labour, who entered their city and preached to them; or the dust is shaken off so that they take nothing from those who despise the gospel, not even what is needful for food.
• Rabanus. Because at the judgment they will be cast out by Christ as “the dust which the wind driveth from the face of the earth.” But if they had received the apostles, they would have loosed their feet, that is, their senses, from the dust, that is, from vices.
13.52:
**“And the disciples”** — that is, the Christians, as has often been said
**“the disciples”** — Bede. While the Jews persecute the faith, the disciples on the contrary are enriched with spiritual joy.
**“were filled with joy and with the Holy Ghost”** — joy is of the fruits of the Holy Spirit

14.1:
**“And it came to pass in Iconium”** — is a city
**“that they entered together”** — Paul and Barnabas
**“entered into the synagogue of the Jews, and so spoke that a very great multitude both of the Jews and of the Greeks did believe”** — the Greeks are Gentiles, or dispersed Jews
14.2: **“But the unbelieving Jews stirred up and incensed the minds of the Gentiles against the brethren”** — who believed
14.3:
**“A long time therefore they abode there”** — at Iconium
**“dealing confidently”** — preaching with confidence
**“in the Lord, who gave testimony”** — in signs and wonders
**“to the word of his grace”** — of baptism, in which remission is given through the Spirit
14.5: **“And when there was an assault made by the Gentiles and the Jews with their rulers, to use them contumeliously”** — torments
14.6:
**“They understanding it, fled”** — According to that: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another.”
**“fled”** — Rabanus. The flight of the apostles was not so much from fear as from love of the word of God.
**“cities of Lycaonia”** — of the region
**“to Lystra, and Derbe”** — these are two cities
**“and to the whole country round about, and were there preaching the gospel”**
• they had fled in order to preach there
• And the whole country round about, etc. Bede. What follows in the Greek: But God made peace, some Latin copies have less. And “they were there preaching the gospel” is followed in the Greek by: and all the multitude was moved at their teaching; but Paul and Barnabas remained in Lystra. And these verses also are not found in some of our copies.
14.8:
**“And there sat a certain man at Lystra, impotent in his feet”** — because he could neither stand nor walk
**“Claudus”** — Bede. As that lame man whom Peter and John heal at the gate of the temple prefigures the salvation of the Jews, so this sick man of Lycaonia prefigures the Gentiles, far removed from the religion of the law and the temple, but gathered together by the preaching of Paul. “They gave,” he says, “to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship, that we should go unto the Gentiles, and they unto the circumcision.” But the times also agree with the exposition, because that man was healed in the first time of the faith, when the word was not yet entrusted to the Gentiles; but this man, when the Jews were rejected for their unbelief and sprinkled with the dust of damnation, is saved amid the new joys of the converted Gentile world.
**“from his mother's womb”** — a greater power in the healing of him who had been lame from the womb and had never walked
14.9:
**“This same heard Paul speaking”** — the Holy Spirit showing it, or the signs of infirmity and faith appearing
**“seeing that he had faith to be healed”** — his faith was so great that he could be saved by it, or he believed this, that he might be saved
14.10:
**“Said with a loud voice”**
• who have sat until now
• in the name of the Lord
• a good servant glorifies the Lord
• Said with a loud voice, etc. Bede. In Greek: Said with a loud voice: I say to thee, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, arise upon thy feet upright.
**“Stand upright on thy feet”** — not as before, among strangers
**“And he leaped up”**
• the speed of the healing is shown
• that he leaps as a lame servant
**“and walked”** — from long-standing habit, so that it is not thought that he had gone out only for an hour
14.11:
**“the multitudes”** — whose understanding was disturbed
**“they lifted up”** — Rabanus. In this is noted their wantonness. Or the thought was higher than their own barbarous tongue, ignorant of the one God.
**“they lifted up their voice in the Lycaonian tongue, saying: The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men”**
• they say this from the tradition of the Gentiles, among whom gods are reported often to have appeared in various forms
• the foolish error of the Gentiles, who think that everything above them that they see is gods
14.12:
**“And they called Barnabas”** — who seemed to be the first
**“Jupiter”** — the father of the gods and the king of men
**“but Paul”** — who was the leader of the word
**“Mercury”**
• is interpreted as speech or eloquence
• Bede. He is said to have been eloquent and learned, and is thought to furnish men with tongue and speech. Whence the Latins call him Mercury, as if running in the middle, that is, between the ears and tongues; but the Greeks call him Hermes, that is, interpreter.
14.13:
**“The priest also of Jupiter that was before the city”** — at Lystra
**“oxen”** — for sacrifice
**“and garlands”**
• he brought to adorn the head of the god, or by some mode of worship unknown to us
• Bede. It was the custom of the Gentiles that those sacrificing to the honour of their gods should take garlands, the victims being crowned at the same time.
**“garlands”** — Rabanus. That he might adorn the front of the temple according to the rite of the Gentiles, or place them upon them, as about to sacrifice to them as to gods.
**“bringing before the gate, would have offered sacrifice with the people”** — to Barnabas as to Jupiter
14.14:
**“Which”** — namely, that they wished to sacrifice
**“when the apostles Barnabas and Paul had heard”** — they do not wait, nor bear patiently that the honour of God is given to them
**“rending their clothes”** — a sign of great grief
**“rending”** — Bede. In fear they tear their garments, because they are honoured with worship of gods. The Jews did this as often as they heard anything blasphemous against God. Herod, who did not give honour to God but yielded to the immoderate favour of the people, was struck down by an angel.
**“they leaped out among the people, crying”** — stirred in spirit
14.15:
**“And saying: Ye men, why do ye these things?”** — to mortals
**“We also are mortals, men like unto you”** — not gods
**“preaching to you to be converted from these vain things”** — from Jupiter, Mercury and the other gods
**“to be converted”** — converted, because you have turned away
**“to the living God”** — not mortal, as we are, and your gods
**“who made the heaven, and the earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them”** — by the name of heaven, earth, and sea he comprehends all creatures
14.16:
**“Who in times past suffered all nations”** — of free choice
**“to walk in their own ways”** — not the way, because of the diversity of errors
**“in their own ways”** — not of God
14.17:
**“And indeed”** — but he bore witness to himself as God through creatures and benefits
**“he left not himself without testimony, doing good”** — he did not leave him wholly; but doing good, etc.
**“from heaven, giving rains and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness”**
• satisfying the belly and the pleasure of the flesh
• Filling our hearts with food, etc. Rabanus. He speaks of carnal things, because gladness comes from food and wine, which gladdens the heart of man.
14.18: **“And speaking these things, they scarce restrained the people from sacrificing to them”** — to show their weakness
14.19:
**“Now there came thither certain Jews from Antioch, and Iconium: and persuading the multitude”**
• for the killing of Paul
• Now there came thither, etc. Bede. In the Greek this narrative begins so: While they remained and taught, certain men came, etc.
**“drew”** — Rabanus. They dragged him to be stoned, like a corpse; of this he himself says to the Corinthians: “Once I was stoned.”
**“drew him out of the city”** — as an abominable man
14.20:
**“But as the disciples stood round about him”** — so that he might not be seen by the Jews, and so they wished to defend him
**“he rose up and entered into the city, and the next day he departed with Barnabas to Derbe”** — Rising, etc. He went on to Derbe. Bede. Earlier, by anticipation, he had said: “He fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe”; and afterwards he narrated part by part, first what was done at Lystra, then what at Derbe.
14.21:
**“And when they had preached the gospel to that city”** — the word of God
**“and had taught many”** — because not all received it
**“they returned again to Lystra, and to Iconium, and to Antioch”** — by the same footsteps by which they had come
14.22:
**“Confirming the souls of the disciples”** — not destroying the faith but confirming it, as founded
**“and exhorting them to continue in the faith”** — praying to the Lord for them, or exhorting the disciples themselves that they should persevere
**“to continue in the faith”** — Rabanus. Against many tribulations, because the multitude of tribulations calls for the perseverance of faith.
**“that through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God”** — Rabanus. Labour is put first, and then the entry into the kingdom is preached, because: “The hope of reward is the comfort of labour.”
**“and that through many tribulations”** — Rabanus. Although the way of tribulations is hard, yet the kingdom of heaven, by which one goes to life, is to be sought; they conclude this exhortation thus, as being uncertain whether they would return to them again. And this is “when they had appointed,” that is, ordained in their place those who were to depart. But at that time bishops and priests were of the same name.
14.23:
**“And when they had ordained to them priests in every church, and had prayed with fasting”** — with the disciples fasting; whence it is clear that they themselves also fasted
**“they commended”** — by prayer, that they might be stronger
**“them to the Lord, in whom they believed”** — the disciples
14.24:
**“And passing through Pisidia”** — in the region in which there was another Antioch
**“they came into Pamphylia”** — the region in which was the city of Perge
14.25: **“And having spoken the word of the Lord in Perge, they went down into Attalia”** — a city, as many say
14.26:
**“And thence they sailed to Antioch”** — that former one from which they had gone out, set apart by the Spirit for the work of the gospel
**“from whence they had been delivered”** — by the brethren
**“the grace of God”** — to the Holy Ghost saying: “Separate me Paul,” etc.
14.27:
**“And when they were come”** — to Antioch
**“and had assembled the church”** — they assigned the fruit of their labour
**“what great things God had done”** — in teaching and in signs
**“with them”** — he co-operated with their obedience
**“how he had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles”** — Christ, or faith, which is the door
14.28: **“And they abode no small time with the disciples”** — in Antioch

15.1:
**“And some”** — of the Jews: Christians indeed, but still Judaizing
**“coming down”** — according to the letter, by the situation of the place or the smallness of the sense
**“from Judea”**
• literally
• by true confession
**“taught the brethren”** — believing from among the Gentiles
**“That except you be circumcised after the manner of Moses”** — spiritual circumcision alone is not sufficient, and neither is faith in Christ
15.2:
**“when there had been contest”** — by the Jews
**“contest”** — By Paul and Barnabas against those who said these things.
**“no small”** — against Paul
**“Barnabas”** — against Barnabas
**“determined”** — Rabanus. Namely those who had come down from Judea, and the brethren whom they were teaching to be circumcised, and the apostles themselves.
**“that they should go up”** — by situation of place or height of sense
**“should go up”** — Bede. Paul writes of this going up of his to the Galatians: “Then, after fourteen years, I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also with me,” “and communicated to them the gospel, which I preach among the Gentiles,” where the number of years which he set down must be reckoned. Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom in the thirtieth year after the Lord’s passion, that is, the last of Nero. Peter sat in the episcopal chair at Rome twenty-five years. But twenty-five and fourteen make thirty-nine. Therefore Peter also is believed to have come to Rome in the same fourteenth year after the Lord’s passion in which Paul speaks with him at Jerusalem, that is, the fourth of Claudius Caesar; and at the same time from this reckoning it is proved that Paul came to the faith in the same year in which the Lord suffered and rose again.
**“Paul and Barnabas, and certain others”** — from both sides dissenting
**“of the other side, to the apostles and priests”** — by age or rank
**“to Jerusalem about this question”** — whether it was to be believed of the Gentiles
15.3:
**“They therefore”** — those who decided that they should go up
**“being brought on their way”** — led on at the beginning of the journey
**“by the church”** — of Antioch, which he said had been gathered
**“passed through Phenice, and Samaria, relating the conversion of the Gentiles; and they caused great joy to all the brethren”** — charity rejoices with truth
15.5:
**“But there arose”** — in body or in the incontinence of mind
**“some of the sect of the Pharisees”** — who formerly were Pharisees, now believing in Christ
**“that believed”** — who had believed in Christ
