**“saying: They must be circumcised”**
• you must, O judges
• That they must be circumcised, etc. Deceived by this error, the Galatians mingled circumcision and observance of the law with the grace of baptism.
**“especially”** — believing Gentiles
15.6:
**“And the apostles and ancients assembled”**
• to see the opinion of each side after their announcement
• Rabanus. Here is given an example of holding a gathering to decide the matters that are necessary for faith.
15.7:
**“And when there had been much disputing”** — the question between the judges of each side
**“Peter, rising up”** — rising is often said, and he speaks before all, as the prince
**“said to them: Men, brethren, you know, that in former days”** — since Cornelius was baptized
**“by my mouth”** — Rabanus. Not by another of the apostles: as if he said, I who first preached to the Gentiles will first cast off from them the yoke of the law; for no apostle preached to the eunuch, but Philip the deacon, and he was filled with a free gift.
15.8:
**“And God, who knoweth the hearts”** — their true faith
**“gave testimony”** — I would not have dared without his testimony
**“giving unto them the Holy Ghost”** — to speak in tongues
15.9:
**“And put no difference”** — because he gave the same Spirit and the same gifts
**“among us”** — the circumcised
**“and them”** — the uncircumcised
**“by faith”** — not by circumcision
**“purifying their hearts”** — by the Spirit
**“purifying their hearts by faith”** — Bede. Therefore it is not necessary that those be cleansed by the circumcision of the flesh whose faith so great purifies their hearts that even before baptism they deserve to receive the Spirit; but we believe that we are saved through the grace of Christ, as they also. If therefore they, that is, the fathers, being unable to bear the yoke of the law, believed that they would be saved by grace, then this grace made the ancient just to live by faith, and therefore the sacraments, though different in times, yet ran together in harmony to the unity of the same faith.
15.10:
**“Now therefore”** — because he bore witness
**“why tempt you”** — as if not believing the testimony
**“God”**
• not us
• who gave the Spirit to the uncircumcised
**“why tempt you God”** — Bede. It is agreed that what was said, “Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God,” is to be understood in many ways. He therefore tempts him who strives to do otherwise than he himself commands, who is confident that he can keep his precepts without grace; but Peter seeks to take the heavy yoke of the law from the neck of the disciples, that he may lay on them the sweet yoke of liberty.
**“to put a yoke”** — the burden of circumcision and of the law
**“upon the necks of the disciples”** — the strength of the faith of believers
**“which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear”** — because we could not by the law fulfil all things, or observe all that was in the law
**“have been able to bear”** — Rabanus. Or, we could not because of the intolerable burden; but we the circumcised also believe we are saved by the grace of God and not by circumcision.
15.11:
**“But by the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ”** — the free gift of God without the works of the law
**“we believe to be saved, in like manner as they also”** — the Gentiles believe
15.12:
**“And all the multitude held their peace”** — But all the multitude held their peace, etc. The order of speaking, or of speakers, is to be noted: because while each spoke they fell silent, first for Peter.
**“and they heard Barnabas and Paul telling what great signs and wonders God had wrought among the Gentiles by them”** — because uncircumcision does not hinder virtues
15.14:
**“Simon hath related how God first visited”** — because weak
**“to take of the Gentiles a people to his name”** — that a people may be called the people of God
15.15:
**“And to this”** — to Simon
**“agree the words of the prophets”** — treating of the salvation of the Gentiles
**“as it is written:”** — in the prophets
15.16:
**“After these things”** — because I was angry and turned away
**“I will return”** — Historically: after the transmigration
**“and will rebuild”**
• I will restore
• in the prophets
• I will return, and will rebuild, etc. Mystically: I will return to the Gentiles, whom he had earlier said would enter his ways, to confirm which sense James brought in the testimony. This plain testimony agrees with the words of Simon.
**“the tabernacle of David,”**
• Jerusalem, the city of David
• the Church, which is the strong hand, which fell in the valley of gentility
**“The tabernacle of David”** — The tabernacle of David. Rabanus. The shadow of the law, corrupted by the traditions of the Pharisees, is raised up by grace with the Lord revealing it, that is, the Lord appearing in the flesh, so that not only the Jews but also the Gentiles seek his name.
15.17:
**“That the residue of men may seek”** — those who are of the Gentiles
**“the residue of men”** — apart from Israel, that is, apart from the Jews who believe in Christ
**“the Lord”** — who has done good to Israel confiding in himself
**“and”** — that is
**“all nations upon whom my name is invoked”**
• by the priests in baptism
• Upon whom the name has been invoked, etc. Rabanus. According to that: “The priests invoked upon Israel.” And: “You shall invoke my name upon the children of Israel.” And elsewhere: “Moses and Aaron among his priests,” etc.
**“is invoked”** — For the future, in the prophetic manner.
**“my name, saith the Lord, who doth these things.”** — fulfilling what had been prophesied
15.18: **“To the Lord was his own work known from the beginning of the world.”** — he foreknew from eternity what he was going to do among the Gentiles
15.19:
**“For which cause I judge”** — agreeing with Peter
**“for which cause I judge”** — Rabanus. What was to be judged rightly was that which is confirmed by the testimony of three: of two apostles and of the prophets.
**“they are not to be disquieted”** — what the Lord builds, man will not disturb
15.20:
**“But that we write unto them”** — I judge
**“that they refrain themselves”** — let this be their circumcision
**“from the pollutions of idols”** — worship
**“and from fornication,”** — that they may be chaste
**“and from things strangled”**
• lest the weaker suffocate themselves
• that they not eat meat
**“From things strangled”** — Bede. A thing strangled is carrion, of which Ezechiel says: “The priests shall not eat of any thing that is dead of itself or caught by a beast, whether it be fowl or cattle.” It is fitting that this precept be kept by those who are anointed with spiritual oil, that they eat not that whose blood has not been poured out; which the letter of the apostles decreed to be kept.
**“and from blood.”** — that they drink not
**“From things strangled, and from blood”** — Bede. That is, from shedding blood or from eating with the blood. These things were indeed granted to those coming from the Gentiles for the rudiments of the faith and the inveterate custom of the Gentiles; but lest the same be thought sufficient for the more perfect also, he watchfully added: Moses, etc.
**“And from blood”** — Rabanus. From the shedding of human blood, and that he do not to another what he does not wish done to himself. This is the precept of love of neighbor, which is the lower; the other is the higher: “All things therefore whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you also to them.” By the one malice is restrained, by the other kindness is spread abroad. As to those still unlearned, the higher is not imposed, but that they be chaste and abstain, etc. And it follows:
15.21:
**“For Moses of old time”**
• therefore I judge to write, because the Scripture of Moses, in which circumcision is commanded, is read on every sabbath; so also the sentence of Scripture is to be carried, lest it be doubtful
• For Moses of old time, etc. Bede: that is, even if they are not burdened by us with the harshness of the precepts, yet as time goes on, when they come more frequently to the reading of the law and the prophets, they will little by little take up the rules of life and the duties of loving one another. For it is agreed that the primitive Church, still judaizing, kept the sabbaths here.
15.22:
**“Then it pleased”**
• to commend them to the faithful envoys and suitable witnesses
• Rabanus. Peter speaking, Barnabas and Paul relating, and James, bishop of Jerusalem, judging, the sentence rightly pleased
**“it pleased to send to Antioch”** — Rabanus. Those sent by Christ as envoys can send envoys of their own.
**“the apostles and ancients”** — Apostles and elders, etc. The common title of the apostles is put first, so that no occasion of dissension be left.
**“with the whole church, to choose men of their own company”** — besides the apostles and elders
**“and to send to Antioch, with Paul and Barnabas, namely, Judas, who was surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren.”** — who were not of the apostles
15.23:
**“Writing by their hands:”** — of Barnabas and Paul
**“The apostles and ancients, brethren,”** — from the Jews
**“to the brethren of the Gentiles”** — Rabanus. The first benefit of the style is that the apostles call the Gentiles brethren, that is, sons of the one God.
**“greeting”** — Rabanus. It is an ellipsis. Or: every word is too narrow for the breadth of charity. And therefore no word is put, so that they may be understood to wish them all good things together.
15.24:
**“Forasmuch as we have heard, that some from us”** — concerning whom above, and some coming down from Judea were teaching
**“going out”** — who also went out from our judgment
**“have troubled you with words”**
• not in the right sense
• vain
**“subverting your souls”**
• from the truth of the gospel
• Bede. In Greek: subverting your souls, saying it is necessary to be circumcised and to observe the law, which we did not command.
**“to whom we gave no commandment”**
• therefore it is said going out from us
• saying what we did not command
15.25:
**“It hath seemed good to us, being assembled together, to choose out men”**
• we were not compelled to write these things; namely, we decided of our own will
• so that the authority may be greater
15.26:
**“Men”** — they are commended, that they may be believed
**“that have given”** — into every temptation
**“their lives”** — lives
**“for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”** — for the proclamation of his name
15.27:
**“We have sent therefore”** — because it pleased us, we sent
**“Judas and Silas, who themselves also”** — with Barnabas and Paul
**“will, by word of mouth, tell you the same things.”**
• which are contained in the epistle
• which Barnabas and Paul
15.28:
**“It hath seemed good”** — That is, it pleased the Holy Spirit, who is the judge of his own power: “he breatheth where he will,” and speaks what he wills; and to us, not only by our own will but by the prompting of the same Spirit.
**“to the Holy Ghost and to us”** — to whom nothing seemed good without the Spirit
**“To the Holy Ghost”** — Rabanus. And to us, indeed in human sense, but sound.
**“than these necessary things”** — Rabanus. These are necessary things, without which there is no salvation; but circumcision is not necessary; and what you do not want done to you, do not do to others.
15.29:
**“That you abstain”** — Such instruction teaches sobriety and temperance.
**“from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication; from which things keeping yourselves, you shall do well. Fare ye well.”**
• It is justice to abstain from evils and to do good.
• “Decline from evil and do good.”
15.30:
**“They therefore being dismissed,”** — according as it was said above: It pleased the apostles and ancients, etc.
**“went down”** — Barnabas and Paul
15.31:
**“Which when they had read”** — the faithful of Antioch from the Gentiles
**“they rejoiced for the consolation”** — because it was said: It hath seemed good to us to lay no burden upon you
15.32:
**“But Judas and Silas, also themselves”** — except Paul and Barnabas
**“being prophets”** — by teaching and by foretelling of things to come
**“with many words”** — as they said in the letter; they report the same things to you
**“comforted the brethren”** — by that consolation which we spoke of
**“and confirmed”** — in the faith of the gospel apart from the law
15.33:
**“And after they had spent some time there”** — in Antioch
**“some time, they were let go”**
• Judas and Silas
• permitted to depart to Jerusalem
**“with peace by the brethren, unto them”** — the apostles
15.34: **“It seemed good to Silas”** — Rabanus. The subject is the discourse to come; but Judas alone went away to Jerusalem.
15.35:
**“They continued at Antioch, etc. After some days, etc.”** — about perfect morals
**“and preaching”** — Christ and the heavenly kingdom
**“with many others”** — with teachers
**“the word of the Lord”** — not their own
15.36: **“And after some days, Paul said to Barnabas”** — whether their faith is firm or not
15.37: **“And Barnabas would have taken with them”** — in his company
15.38:
**“But Paul desired”** — saying that he ought not to be taken or received
**“him”** — Barnabas
**“as having departed from them out of Pamphylia”** — John, departing from Pamphylia, returned to Jerusalem
**“and not gone with them to the work, might not be received”** — lest the still untrained be burdened
**“to the work, might not be received”** — Bede. Since he had stationed himself too lukewarmly at the front of the battle line, Paul rightly cast him off, lest the strength of the others be corrupted, as if by his contagion.
15.39:
**“there arose a dissension”** — They did not sin in this, because not every disturbance is sin, but the unreasonable one, and that which is not done justly.
**“so that they departed one from another”** — not moved by fault but stirred by the Spirit they separate, so that they may preach to more
**“taking Mark”** — Bede. He who was joined to him by kinship, for they are read to have been cousins. Barnabas, dismissed by Paul, returned to his native island, and nevertheless carried on the work of the gospel enjoined on him.
15.40:
**“Paul choosing Silas”** — Rabanus. The Lord made him remain for this, according to that: “But it seemed good unto Silas to remain there,” so that he might work with Paul, as Mark did with Barnabas; for in this there was a divine counsel.
**“departed, being delivered”** — dismissed or commended
**“the grace of God”** — to the Holy Spirit
15.41:
**“And he went through Syria and Cilicia”** — in shortening the narrative he does not give the names of the individual places
**“confirming the churches”** — which had already been founded

16.1:
**“And behold, there was a certain disciple there named Timothy”** — is interpreted as beneficent
**“the son of a Jewish woman that believed”** — Rabanus. Or “of a Jewess”; and that she was a Jewess appears from the fact that it says his father was a Gentile.
16.3:
**“he circumcised him”** — Not that the figures of the law brought any profit after the truth of the gospel, but lest through the occasion of the Gentiles the Jews should fall away from the faith, for whom the old shadow was to be taken away little by little, as idolatry was for the Gentiles. For the legal shadows, because they were instituted by the Lord, were at times made use of by the apostles in that time to avoid the unbelief of the Jews; but the Gentile institution, devised by Satan, was never received by the saints.
**“Him Paul would have to go along with him: and taking him he circumcised him”**
• Rabanus. He circumcised Timothy because of the scandal of the Jews, lest he should seem to condemn the law of Moses, but that he did not impose it on the Gentiles as not necessary for them. He did not circumcise Titus, lest the Gentiles take from him an occasion of being circumcised. And this is what he says: “But because of false brethren unawares brought in,” etc.
• Rabanus. Because of the Jews, lest they persecute him or Timothy, or lest, offended, they be estranged from the faith.
**“because of the Jews”** — Rabanus. “I became a Jew to the Jews, that I might gain them.”
**“who were in those places”** — at Lystra and Iconium
**“For they all knew that his father was a Gentile”** — and his son, uncircumcised, would not hand on the teaching of circumcision, and they had not wished to be circumcised
16.4:
**“And as they passed through the cities, they delivered unto them the decrees for to keep”** — ordinances
**“the decrees for to keep, that were decreed by the apostles”** — Rabanus. They did not preach what they themselves had done, but what the apostles had decreed because of the will of God. And it is an example of teaching rightly even what you yourself have not done.
**“that were decreed by the apostles”** — Rabanus. In a figure of this deed, priests were clothed in linen breeches, as those who would sow a work, not those who would do it.
16.5:
**“the churches”** — Rabanus. This concerns the often-repeated chapters which are inserted into the narratives.
**“were confirmed in faith”** — among those who had believed before
**“and increased in number daily”** — among those who, converted to the faith, were baptized
16.6:
**“And when they had passed through Phrygia, and the country of Galatia”** — in which are the Galatians, so named from the whiteness of body, and they are interpreted as milky
**“they were forbidden by the Holy Ghost”**
• who foreknew that the men of Asia would not only believe
• They were forbidden, etc. Bede. “God is terrible in his counsels over the sons of men.” One promises to follow the master in all things and is not permitted. Another, bidden to follow, is forbidden to bury his father. Saul is dragged unwilling and resisting. To Cornelius, persevering in prayers and almsgiving, the way of salvation is shown as if in return for a reward; and God, who knows hearts, out of the grace of a kindness removed the teacher from Asia, lest what is holy be given to dogs, and the wicked heart be more severely judged for contempt of the preaching.
**“to preach the word in Asia”** — in the lesser, because almost all the aforesaid cities and regions are in greater Asia
16.7:
**“And when they were come into Mysia”** — which is in Europe; for then they crossed from Asia into Europe
**“they attempted”** — that is, again into Asia
**“to go into Bythynia”** — in which the door of faith was not open
**“and the Spirit of Jesus suffered them not”** — of the Saviour, because they were not going to receive salvation
**“they attempted to go into Bythynia, and the Spirit of Jesus suffered them not”** — Rabanus. The apostles are permitted to wish but not to go, that human weakness may appear, and that it is subject to the divine counsel, saying: “Thy will be done.” The provinces too from which the apostles are forbidden are kept for others to preach in them, as John and Philip preached the gospel in Asia Minor, Luke in Bithynia, etc.
16.8: **“And when they had passed through Mysia”** — in which the door of faith was open
16.9:
**“a man of Macedonia”** — The angel of that nation, made like a Macedonian man by the peculiarity of his tongue, or by a special form, or by a sign of speech.
**“standing”** — Angels are always said to stand.
**“and beseeching him”** — in human form
**“and saying: Pass over into Macedonia, and help us”** — hence it is clear that the Macedonian was a man
**“help us”** — Rabanus. This is said in the person of a man, for angels do not need human help. Or the angel says this on behalf of those over whom he presides, that they may be baptized and be saved. By saying “Help us,” he shows that the Macedonians were either inspired by God through angels, or that some teachers had begun to be taught.
16.10:
**“And as soon as he had seen the vision, immediately”** — swift obedience is noted by “immediately”
**“we sought to go into Macedonia”** — here Luke shows that he was a companion of Paul
16.11: **“And sailing from Troas, we came with a straight course”** — with full sails
16.12:
**“to Philippi”** — Samothracia, Neapolis and Philippi are cities.
**“which is the chief city of part of Macedonia, a colony”**
• to those coming from the sea it presents itself first
• Colony. Bede. It is that which, through lack of natives, is filled with new cultivators; whence a colony is so called from the cultivation of a field.
**“And we were in this city some days conferring together”** — by deliberating or thinking
**“Some days conferring together”** — In some books it is found: “conferring the word of the Lord on the sabbath day.”
16.13:
**“upon the sabbath day, we went forth without the gate by a river side, where it seemed that there was prayer”** — that is, a place fit for the speaking of preachers or the preaching of those praying
**“and sitting down, we spoke to the women that were assembled”** — it shows that he called the prayer a speaking
16.14:
**“a seller of purple”** — Bede. A queen clothed in royal purple, or a weaver of purple, or a seller of purple, signifies the Church, which sells purple while she sheds blood for Christ, that she may be able to purchase life. Purple rightly designates blood by colour and by nature, because it is made from the blood of shellfish. Lydia compelled the apostle with his companions to enter her house, because the Church received with devout heart the preaching rejected by the Jews.
**“of the city of Thyatira”** — of the people of that city
**“worshipped”** — by nature or by law, heard from the Jews
**“God”** — true
**“did hear, whose heart the Lord opened”** — the door of faith
**“heart”** — the devil shuts hearts, but God opens
16.15:
**“And when she was baptized, and her household, she besought us, saying: If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord”** — that is, if I am worthy that God dwell and remain in me: enter and remain
**“come into my house”** — they had not been accustomed to enter the houses of the Gentiles, because of the Jews
**“and abide there”** — by staying for some interval
**“she constrained us”** — Rabanus. Here an example is given, or two examples are given: one of compelling guests, the other of entering to those lately converted.
16.16:
**“a certain girl, having a pythonical spirit”** — Rabanus. Python is the name of an evil spirit, through whom the soothsayers do this: that they raise the dead to speech and divination by incantation.
**“it came to pass, as we went to prayer, a certain girl, having a pythonical spirit”**
• Bede. Of pythonic divination it is found in the book of Kings, where at Saul’s request the pythoness called up from the dead either the soul of Samuel or rather, in its place, an unclean spirit. This kind of magic was invented by Pythian Apollo and is said to be so called from his surname; the Hebrew name also agrees with it, since “python” means mouth of the abyss.
• Bede. He who gathered the seller of purple into the Church himself, strictly punishing the python-woman who proclaimed the great works of God with an unclean mouth, deprived her of her art. For this is the power of the apostles: that “whatsoever they shall bind upon earth, shall be bound also in heaven”, and conversely.
**“met us, who brought to her masters much gain by divining”** — by the price of divination
16.17:
**“This same following Paul”** — Rabanus. Although she had met them, she cries out not in front but behind them, keeping feminine modesty.
**“and us, cried out, saying: These men”** — These men. Bede. This confession is not of will; but, the fear of the Holy Spirit compelling, the lying spirit speaks the truth, not daring, with the light present, to hide its darkness.
**“are the servants of the most high God”** — although they are humble, yet their God, whose servants they are, is high
**“who preach unto you the way of salvation”** — briefly praises the servants of God, and God, and his teaching
16.18:
**“And this she did”** — That is, she cried out either by a good nature, or with God compelling it, through the Python spirit.
**“many days. But Paul being grieved”** — that she was possessed by the devil.
**“turned”** — because she was crying out after him.
**“and said to the spirit: I command thee”** — I adjure not by power but by prayer.
**“in the name of Jesus Christ”** — not by my own.
16.19:
**“But her masters, seeing”** — of the girl.
**“that the hope of their gain was gone”** — or of the spirit.
**“apprehending Paul and Silas, brought them into the marketplace to the rulers”** — I command thee to go out, etc. Because he went out, etc. Bede. Barien, who attacked the faith by art, he blinded, depriving him of sight; and this perverse woman, although she spoke with a true mind, he deprived of her art only, because it was unworthy that an unclean spirit should proclaim the word of the gospel. He commanded her to go out and be silent, because demons ought to confess God with trembling, not to praise him with joy.
16.20: **“And presenting them to the magistrates, they said: These men disturb our city, being Jews”** — who are evil, or captives, or of another law.
16.21:
**“And preach a fashion”** — the faith of Jesus Christ, in whose name the Python spirit had gone out.
**“which it is not lawful for us to receive”** — by hearing.
**“nor observe”** — by deed.
**“being Romans”**
• who are better than Jews, or lords, or of a dissimilar law.
• Bede. It was already decreed by the Romans that no god should be received unless the senate approved.
16.22: **“And the people ran together against them; and the magistrates rending off their clothes, commanded them to be beaten with rods”** — the one pertains to abomination, the other to punishment.
16.23: **“they cast them into prison”** — Rabanus. And by this the power of the one who frees is greater. To the same point pertains what follows: “thrust them into the inner prison, and made their feet fast in the stocks.”
16.25:
**“And at midnight”** — “I rose at midnight to give praise to thee.”
**“And at midnight, Paul and Silas praying”** — One must pray at midnight, and in dangers the diligence of prayer must be kept.
**“Paul and Silas praying, praised God”** — or were singing a hymn.
**“And they that were in prison, heard them”** — Paul and Silas.
**“that were in prison”** — bound.
16.26:
**“And suddenly there was a great earthquake”**
• to strike fear and to open the doors of the prison.
• There was a great earthquake, etc. Bede. The devotion of those praying and the power of prayer are expressed, because while they sang hymns in prison, their praise moves the earth, shakes the foundations of the prison, opens the doors, and loosens the chains of the prisoners.
• Allegorically. He who counts it all joy when he falls into divers temptations, and gladly glories in his infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in him. Such a one praises God in prison with Paul and Silas, saying with the prophet: “Thou art my refuge from the trouble which hath encompassed me: my joy,” etc.
**“so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened”** — the great power of prayer by which all the doors are opened, namely inner and outer.
**“and the bands of all were loosed”** — not only of Paul and Silas but also of the other prisoners.
16.27: **“And the keeper of the prison, awaking out of his sleep”** — from the great earthquake.
16.28:
**“But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying: Do thyself no harm, for we all are here”**
• the prisoners whom you were guarding.
• He cried with a loud voice, “Do thyself no harm,” etc. Rabanus. It is a loud voice by which the knowledge of hidden things is made known. For he knew, even in the darkness, the one who wished to kill himself, and spared the guard, his enemy.
16.29:
**“Then calling for a light”** — by the servants.
**“he went in, and trembling, fell down at the feet of Paul and Silas”** — He fell down, etc. Rabanus. On account of power and knowledge: power, because the doors were opened by the earthquake; knowledge, because Paul knew why he wished to kill himself; therefore, before all others, he fell down at the feet of Paul and Silas.
16.30:
**“And bringing them out”** — out of the prison.
**“he said: Masters”** — he begins to honour them more than was fitting
**“what must I do, that I may be saved?”** — he perceives that he has hitherto acted badly
16.31:
**“But they said: Believe in the Lord Jesus”** — not in many lords, as you have said of us
**“and thou shalt be saved”** — they announce a saviour to him who was seeking salvation
**“and thy house”**
• not you alone but also
• believing in Jesus
16.32: **“And they preached the word of the Lord to him”** — not one only, but both, for joy, because the door of faith was opened in that hour of the night; or the fairness of doing good is shown
16.33:
**“And he, taking them the same hour of the night, washed their stripes”**
• of whom he had said, and when they had inflicted many stripes on them
• washing, he was washed
**“washed their stripes, and himself was baptized”** — Bede. A fine variety: those whose stripes of wound he washed, through them he lost the stripes of crime.
**“immediately”** — Rabanus. The swiftness of obedience is signified: the grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow delays.
16.34:
**“he laid the table for them, and rejoiced”**
• with baptism received, spiritual fruit follows, that is, joy
• And when he had brought them into his own house, he laid the table for them, etc. Rabanus. The best example of both: entering the house and the setting of the table.
16.35:
**“And when the day was come, the magistrates sent the serjeants, saying, Let those men go.”**
• this is said to the gaoler
• lest more believe
• as though they were despised
16.37:
**“They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned”** — without any certain guilt pronounced by the judges
**“men that are Romans”** — having declared their census
**“and have cast us into prison”** — a secret casting out displeased, because the flogging had been public
**“and now do they thrust us out privately? Not so; but let them come”** — at what Paul had said
16.40:
**“went out of the prison, and entered into the house of Lydia”** — the region
**“having seen the brethren”** — the Christians living in Lydia
**“they comforted them”**
• the apostles
• by their coming, by example and teaching
**“and departed”** — after the word of comfort

17.1: **“when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia”** — these are the names of cities
17.2:
**“according to his custom”** — of the Jews, or of Paul
**“Paul went in unto them, and for three sabbath days he reasoned with them out of the scriptures”** — Out of the scriptures, etc. Bede. He suggests both alike from the Scriptures, namely that it behoved Christ to suffer and to rise again, and that the passion and resurrection pertained to no one other than Jesus. For the Jews, who could not deny the passion and resurrection, awaiting Antichrist, denied that these pertained to Jesus; and therefore Paul not only preaches the mysteries of Christ but teaches that in Christ Jesus all things have been accomplished.
17.4:
**“were associated to Paul and Silas; and of those that served God”** — God; to Jews, namely the devout
**“and of the Gentiles”**
• who before did not worship
• And of those that served God, and of the Gentiles, that is, of those who had changed the Gentile rite to Judaism, and of those who had remained Gentiles, many flocked to Christ.
• Rabanus. The first cause of malice is that they were of the common people. The second, that they were also wicked beyond the common people.
**“a great multitude, and of noble women not a few”** — therefore the women believe first, so that they may more easily draw the men.
17.5:
**“But the Jews, moved with envy”** — those who had believed.
**“taking unto them some wicked men of the vulgar sort, making a tumult”** — because of the disturbed mind.
**“set the city in an uproar”** — they stir up to an assembly.
**“the city”** — Thessalonica.
**“besetting Jason's house”** — the faithful man.
**“sought to bring them out unto the people”** — Paul and Silas.
17.6:
**“And not finding them”** — thinking them to be hidden.
**“they drew Jason and certain brethren”** — They drew Jason, etc. Bede. In Greek: Jason and certain other brothers; whence it is to be understood that Jason was a brother and a faithful man.
17.7:
**“Whom Jason hath received; and these all”** — the apostles and those who received them.
**“another king”** — Another king. Rabanus. Besides Caesar, which was against Caesar’s decree. Whence in the Gospel: “Whosoever maketh himself a king speaketh against Caesar.” But the apostles contradicted that Christ is king of the Jews, that is, of those who confess him; whence also the Jews accused Christ himself.
17.8:
**“And they stirred up the people”** — they themselves, first stirred up, stir up the people.
**“and the rulers of the city”** — the rulers also stirred up along with the people.
17.9:
**“And having taken satisfaction of Jason”** — because he denied that he had received them, or professed repentance.
**“and of the rest”** — who defended and excused them.
**“they let them go”** — Jason and the others.
17.10:
**“But the brethren immediately sent away Paul and Silas by night unto Berea”** — it is a city.
**“Who, when they were come thither, went into the synagogue of the Jews”** — the strength of faith is shown, because they do not cease to speak, not even because of the persecution of the Jews.
17.11:
**“Now these”** — who received them in Berea.
**“were more noble”** — by birth or by mind, who persisted in hearing and searching the word.
17.12:
**“And many indeed of them believed”** — of the Bereans.
**“and of honourable women that were Gentiles, and of men not a few”** — or: ‘of men’.
17.13:
**“And when the Jews of Thessalonica had knowledge”** — who were.
**“that the word of God was also preached by Paul at Berea”** — who was the leader of the word.
**“by Paul”** — He who was the leader of the word; and therefore afterwards he alone was sent away to go from Macedonia to the sea.
17.14: **“And then immediately the brethren sent away Paul, to go unto the sea; but Silas and Timothy remained there”** — Berea.
17.15:
**“And they that conducted Paul, brought him as far as Athens”** — which is a city of Attica or Achaia.
**“and receiving a commandment”** — either by word alone or by letter.
**“from him”** — Paul.
**“to Silas and Timothy, that they should come to him with all speed, they departed”** — They departed, etc. Rabanus. From Athens, those brothers who had conducted Paul. Some think it was said of Silas and Timothy that they had set out from Macedonia to Paul.
17.16: **“Now whilst Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was stirred within him”** — my
17.17:
**“He disputed, therefore, in the synagogue”** — the inspiring Spirit
**“with the Jews, and them that served God, and in the marketplace”** — with the Gentiles
17.18:
**“Epicureans”** — Rabanus. They are called after their founder, who is said to be the champion of pleasure. ‘Stoics’ in Greek, in Latin ‘elements,’ who contended that sins are equal, that is, that every sin is uniform.
**“And certain philosophers of the Epicureans and of the Stoics”** — Bede. The Epicureans, following the tradition of their teacher, placed man’s happiness in the pleasure of the body alone; the Stoics, in the virtue of the soul alone. Though at odds with each other, they unanimously attack the apostle, because he taught that man is blessed in soul and body, not in the present life nor of himself, but by the grace of God through Jesus Christ in the resurrection.
**“disputed with him; and some said: What is it, that this word sower would say?”** — What does this sower of words want to say, etc. A seminiverbius is one who sows the word. Or seminiverbius, that is, a sermologus, because the seed is the Word of God. Whence: “If we have sown unto you spiritual things,” etc.
*Augustine:* We read that the apostle Paul was called a sower of words; this was said by those who mocked, but it was not to be rejected by those who believed; for he was indeed a sower of words, but a reaper of morals. And we too, though little ones and not to be compared with him, sow the word of God in the field of God, which is your heart, awaiting a rich harvest or fruit from your morals.
**“But others: He seemeth to be a setter forth of demons”** — Rabanus. They had heard from the Jews that the word demons is abominable, and therefore they compare Paul’s teaching to this abomination. Or it is the Jews who say this, that is, the Sadducees.
17.19: **“to the Areopagus”** — Rabanus. It is the name of a court at Athens, named after the idol of Mars, which among them is called Arios.
17.20: **“For thou bringest in certain new things to our ears. We would know therefore what these things mean”** — what kind they are and to what they tend
17.21:
**“Now all the Athenians, and strangers that were there, employed themselves in nothing else, but either in telling or in hearing some new thing”**
• not that they might firmly believe, but only that they might marvel
• therefore also a few asked about the teaching, what sort it is, so that they might believe
17.22:
**“But Paul standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: Ye men of Athens”**
• or the kinds of men, or in all doctrines
• Ye men of Athens, etc. What therefore you worship, without knowing it, that I preach to you, etc. He answers to what they had said or had put forward. You bring in some new things; as if he were to say: the new things that I bring in, you have among your old ones. He says this to persuade them not to reject his words as though they were new.
**“I perceive that in all things you are too superstitious”** — or: ‘I see’
17.23:
**“For passing by”** — therefore I judge you superstitious, because passing by, etc.
**“and seeing your idols”** — of the gods who are known to you
**“I found an altar also”** — besides the altars of other gods
**“on which was written:”** — each altar had its title
**“To the unknown God.”**
• as if this altar were dedicated to an unknown god
• Bede. God was known in Judea but not received. God was unknown in Achaia, though sought through many things; and therefore he who ignores will be ignored. The transgressor will be condemned; neither is free from guilt, but more excusable is he who did not offer faith to Christ, whom he did not know, than he who laid hands on Christ, whom he knew.
**“To the unknown God”** — Rabanus. To the unknown God, that is, the true God, whom no one knows as he is: “For no one knoweth the Son, but the Father: neither doth any one know the Father, but the Son.” And according to this sense he is called by Paul the unknown God. But otherwise, in their own sense, this altar was dedicated to an unknown God, that is, to that God whom the Gentiles do not know. Therefore either it was written, “dedicated to the unknown God,” or something like it which is passed over in silence, or simply it was written, “To the unknown God.”
**“What therefore you worship, without knowing it”** — as the altar confesses
**“you worship”** — because you have its altar
**“that”** — not new, as you say, but this same thing, namely the unknown
**“that I preach to you”** — so that God may not be unknown
17.24:
**“God, who made the world”**
• through creatures he makes the Creator known
• God who made, etc. Bede. Note the order of this discourse: first he teaches that there is one God, author of the world and of all things, in whom we live, move and are, and whose offspring we also are, so that he is shown to be loved not only for light and life but also for kinship of race. Afterwards he destroys by reason the opinion about idols: that the maker and Lord of the world is not shut up in temples of stone; that the giver of every benefit does not need the blood of victims; that the creator of men and governor of all cannot be moved by the hand of man. Lastly he teaches that God, to whose image man was made, is not like metals. He says the remedy of error is zeal for repentance. But if he had first destroyed the ceremonies of the idols, the Gentiles would not have heard him. When therefore he had persuaded them of one God, he added: that salvation was given to us through Christ, yet naming him man rather than God, and beginning from those things which he did in the body, he shows him to be above man, who rose again, having conquered death; for faith grows little by little, so that when he is shown to be above man, he may be believed God. It does not matter in what order anyone believes; perfect things are not asked for at the start, but from beginnings one ascends to perfect things.
**“and all things therein”** — the fruits and inhabitants of heaven and earth
**“he, being Lord of heaven and earth”** — the world, which is signified by the name of heaven and earth
**“being Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands”** — is not enclosed in a small place nor adorned with various colours, as idols are
17.25:
**“Neither is he served with men's hands”**
• is made
• as though by those who make him
**“as though he needed any thing”** — for this purpose, that he be worshipped as God
**“seeing it is he who giveth to all life”** — the soul which he breathes into them
**“and breath”** — air
17.26:
**“And hath made of one”**
• man
• Adam
**“Of one, all mankind”** — Bede. In Greek, from one blood, because blood signifies the lineage of flesh, and through flesh man is understood.
**“to dwell upon the whole face of the earth, determining appointed times”** — of ages and kingdoms
**“and the limits of their habitation”** — that is, the boundaries of the individual nations
17.27:
**“That they should seek God”**
• by faith
• to this end he made the human race, that it might seek God
**“if happily they may feel after him”** — by love
**“or find him, although”** — he is sought by man, although he is near
17.28:
**“For in him we live”**
• in both lives
• Augustine. Because he works in us that we live, move and are. And this is the work by which he holds all things together, because his wisdom “reacheth from end to end mightily, and ordereth all things sweetly.” Through this ordering we live, move and are in him. But if he were to withdraw this work of his from things, we should neither live nor be moved nor be.
*Augustine:* In the things which he created, God is shown to work unceasingly; for we are not in him as though in his substance, as he is said to have life in himself. But though we are other than he, we are not other in him, except that he works that we live, move and are; and a little after: not heaven and earth and all things that are in them, that is, the whole spiritual and corporeal creature, remains in itself, but in him of whom it is said: “In him we live, move and are”; because if a part can be in the whole of which it is a part, the whole itself is only in him by whom it was made; nor is this said according to the body, because the same could be said likewise of the world, in which we are, move and live. Therefore it is to be understood of the mind, which is to be taken as according to the image of God in a certain excellent and intelligible way; for what is not in him of whom it is said: “Of him, and by him, and in him, are all things”?
**“and move, and are”**
• in both ways, namely by motion of the limbs and movement through places
• bodily or spiritually
**“as some also of your own poets”** — He speaks to those who did not receive the prophets: not the testimony of Moses, nor of Isaias, nor of any of the prophets, but of their own authors, placing a verse of Aratus; and from their own falsehoods, which they could not contradict, he keeps and confirms his own truth.
**“said: For we are also his offspring.”** — not by nature but born of his Spirit, created by his will and re-created by adoption; and therefore it is most rightly said: we are his offspring
**“For we are also his offspring”** — This testimony is taken from the poet Aratus, not from the divine page, lest he seem to bring in something new.
17.29:
**“Being therefore the offspring of God, we must not suppose”**
• the work of God ought not to adore the works of men
• Being therefore the offspring of God, we must not suppose, etc. Rabanus. Man stands in the middle, having God above him; gold and silver and other such things are lower, and ought not to be compared to him.
17.30:
**“And the times”** — past
**“indeed, of this ignorance”** — by which God was unknown
**“Having winked at”** — Rabanus. That is, forgiving as venial, and then looking past, that is, judging unworthy by his own knowledge.
**“now declareth”** — through the apostles
**“unto men”** — to the wise
**“that all”** — persons
**“everywhere”**
• in every place
• no person, no place is excepted or refuted
**“do penance”** — all these things are said to this end: that they do penance, which is in the heart, in deed
17.31:
**“Because he hath appointed a day”**
• because for God nothing is future
• the appointed day is for the sake of penance
**“wherein he will judge the world”** — he introduces what those hated who did not believe in the resurrection of the dead
**“in equity”** — not according to the acceptance of persons
**“by the man”**
• by the man, manly or strong
• By Christ: “For neither doth the Father judge any man, but hath given all judgment to the Son.”
**“giving faith to all”** — Rabanus. By the example of his own resurrection, or he has appointed to judge; and afterwards it is to be joined thus: giving faith to all, that they will rise again.
17.32: **“And when they had heard of the resurrection of the dead, some indeed mocked, but others said: We will hear thee again concerning this matter.”** — as if they said: for now we neither believe it nor reject it
17.33: **“So Paul went out from among them.”** — as if excommunicating them
17.34:
**“But certain men adhering to him, did believe”** — not remaining through fear
**“among whom was also Dionysius, the Areopagite”** — a judge of that court, which is called Areopagus
**“Dionysius”** — Bede. This is the Dionysius who afterwards, ordained bishop of the Corinthians, ruled the Church well. For its benefit he also left many volumes, taking his surname from the place over which he presided. The Areopagus is the court of Athens, drawing its name from Mars, who is called Arios in Greek; pagus: a village.

18.1: **“After these things, departing from Athens”** — Paul
18.2: **“And finding a certain Jew, named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with Priscilla his wife, (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome,)”** — Because Claudius had commanded them to depart, etc. Bede. Josephus relates that this was done in the ninth year of Claudius. Suetonius says that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome.
18.3:
**“And because he was of the same trade, he remained with them, and wrought; (now they were tentmakers by trade.)”**
• making tents or ropes, for skenos in Greek is rope in Latin
• skene are called tents, which give shade
• Bede. Tents, or tent-work, are coverings which the ancients made of skins, or of the leafy branches of trees, or of brushwood. Mystically. As Peter drew men out from the waves of the world by the nets of faith, so Paul, raising up shelters of protection, defended them by word and deed from the shade of crime, the heat of temptation, and the winds of ambush.
**“tentmakers by trade”** — Tentmakers by trade. Bede. As exiles and pilgrims they build tents for themselves to use on the way.
18.5:
**“And when Silas and Timothy were come from Macedonia, Paul was earnest in preaching”** — of the gospel
**“testifying to the Jews, that Jesus is the Christ.”** — that God is; or that Jesus, that man, is the Christ, that is, God
18.6:
**“But they gainsaying and blaspheming”** — that Christ is not
**“he shook his garments”** — fulfils the precept of the gospel: “Shake off the dust,” etc.
**“and said to them: Your blood”**
• let the guilt of your death fall
• Your blood, etc. Rabanus. I have declared to you your iniquity. If you do not declare to the wicked man his iniquity, I will require his blood at thy hand.
• Bede. Titus Justus either had this as his proper name, or was so surnamed for the merit of his justice. This was not the Titus, disciple of Paul, to whom he wrote an epistle and whom he ordained bishop of Crete, with whom also Barnabas, going up to Jerusalem, conferred the gospel with the apostles, inquiring in their council whether he rightly preached that the Gentiles are saved by the baptism of faith without circumcision, not because he himself doubted of this, but to confirm the minds of the doubting by the authority of the apostles.
**“Super caput vestrum”** — the soul
**“Mundus ego ex hoc”** — to signify cleanness from this blood he shook out his garments
18.7:
**“And departing thence, he entered into the house of a certain man”** — a Gentile
**“one that worshipped God”** — this is not said in vain; therefore he worshipped God because he heard the law from close at hand
18.8:
**“And Crispus”** — this is the one whom Paul says he baptized: “I baptized none of you, but Crispus and Caius”
**“the ruler of the synagogue”** — the ruler of that synagogue, to which his house was joined
18.9:
**“And the Lord said to Paul in the night, by a vision: Do not fear”** — shows the imminent temptation
**“but speak”** — the gospel
**“and hold not thy peace”** — the truth, through fear
18.10: **“Because I am with thee”** — I am with you even to the consummation of the world
18.12:
**“But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia”** — of the region in which Corinth is
**“the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat”** — where the proconsul sat
18.13: **“Saying: This man persuadeth men to worship God contrary to the law”** — another Jesus or the God of the Jews, but he commands him to be worshipped otherwise, that is, as a Father
18.14:
**“And when Paul was beginning to open his mouth”**
• according to that: “hold not thy peace, because I am with thee”
• Rabanus. By fulfilling that: “hold not thy peace, because I am with thee.” And from this it appears that God was with him.
**“Gallio said to the Jews: If it were some matter of injustice, or an heinous deed”** — a crime manifest even to the Gentiles, and great
**“O Jews”** — for he speaks to the Jews
**“I should with reason bear with you”** — I would be a judge among you
18.15:
**“Of word and names”** — As if he said: concerning the word now declared and related in the gospel, and the names of Jesus and of God, or of God the Father.
**“But if they be questions of word and names”** — In Greek: all the Greeks seizing Sosthenes.
**“and of your law”** — not ours, nor known to us
**“look you to it: I will not be judge of such things”** — judge
18.17:
**“And all laying hold on”** — believing in Christ
**“Sosthenes”** — unbelieving
**“the ruler of the synagogue”** — the Jews being driven from the tribunal with disgrace, the Gentiles treated their ruler, beating him with greater insult
**“beat him before the judgment seat; and Gallio cared for none of those things”** — cura for the ablative, or cure for the dative
18.18:
**“But Paul, when he had stayed yet”** — a greater persecution, or delay
**“many days”** — a year and six months
**“the brethren”** — Christians
**“taking his leave”** — blessing
**“sailed thence into Syria”** — he returned from Europe to Asia, but briefly anticipates
**“and with him Priscilla and Aquila”** — faith changed the order, whence there is neither male nor female
**“having shorn his head”**
• Having shorn his head, etc. Rabanus. Paul or Aquila. As many think, Paul, either from fear of the Jews or from eagerness to convert them.
• It is said ambiguously, but according to Jerome it is to be understood of Paul.
**“in Cenchrae”** — Bede. It is a port of Corinth, where, about to board a ship, he shaved his head because of a vow; according to the law, those who had vowed themselves to God let their hair grow while they wished to become Nazarites, and afterwards shaving it they gave it to the fire. Paul therefore did this, not forgetful of what he had decided at Jerusalem with the other apostles about the abolition of the law, but, lest he scandalize believers from among the Jews, he made himself as a Jew that he might gain the Jews. Some copies have: “Priscilla and Aquila shaved their head,” but Augustine and Jerome interpret it of Paul in the singular number. Jerome puts it thus: he sailed to Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila, and he shaved his head in Cenchrae. For he had a vow.
18.19:
**“And he came to Ephesus”** — going
**“and them”** — Priscilla and Aquila
**“there”** — in Ephesus
18.21: **“But taking his leave, and saying: I will return to you again, God willing”** — according to that: “If God will, and if we live, etc.”
18.22:
**“And going down to Caesarea”**
• of Cappadocia or of Palestine
• so called from Caesar Augustus
**“to Caesarea”** — Rabanus. Caesarea is the metropolis of Cappadocia; he had not yet come to Syria of Phoenicia.
**“he went up”** — For the place or for merit.
**“and saluted the church”** — The faithful.
**“and so came down to Antioch”** — Of Syria.
18.23:
**“And after he had spent some time there”** — As he was accustomed before.
**“he departed, and went through the country of Galatia and Phrygia, confirming”** — Because they had believed before.
**“all the disciples”** — His own, or Christians.
18.24:
**“Now a certain Jew”** — It was said above: he came to Ephesus and left them there.
**“named Apollo, born at Alexandria”** — Born of Alexandria.
**“an eloquent man, came to Ephesus, one mighty in the scriptures”** — In the old.
18.25:
**“This man was instructed in the way of the Lord”** — The faith of Christ.
**“and being fervent in spirit”** — With his own, or the Holy (Spirit).
**“spoke”** — He preached Jesus.
**“and taught diligently the things that are of Jesus, knowing only the baptism of John”** — Which was only in water without the Spirit.
18.26:
**“This man therefore began to speak boldly”** — To preach to the Jews with confidence.
**“in the synagogue. Whom when ... had heard”** — Preaching.
**“Priscilla and Aquila took him to them”** — To their home, or to a private conversation.
**“and expounded to him the way of the Lord more diligently”** — Saying that the Spirit is necessary.
18.27:
**“And whereas he was desirous to go to Achaia”** — To the Corinthians.
**“the brethren exhorting”** — Priscilla and Aquila and the other faithful.
**“wrote to the disciples”** — Who were at Corinth.
**“That they should receive him.”** — That they not fear him as a Jew.
**“Who, when he was come, helped them much”** — “Consolation: I have planted, Apollo watered, God gave the increase.”
**“helped them much”** — Another translation: he helped believers much through grace, that is, what the apostle writes: “I planted, Apollo watered,” etc.
**“who had believed.”** — Earlier, to Paul preaching.
18.28: **“For with much vigour he convinced the Jews”** — So he comforted, because by convincing the Jews he comforted the Christians.

19.1:
**“And it came to pass”** — It was said: Apollo came to Ephesus; there also Paul returns, where he left Priscilla.
**“while Apollo was at Corinth, that Paul having passed through the upper coasts, came to Ephesus, and found certain disciples.”** — Baptized perhaps by Apollo or John, according to Augustine.
19.2: **“Have you received the Holy Ghost since ye believed?”** — Whether after baptism you received the laying on of hands by which the Spirit is given.
19.3:
**“In what then were you baptized?”** — By the baptism, namely of penance or of forgiveness.
**“In John's baptism.”** — Of penance, namely.
19.4:
**“John baptized the people with the baptism of penance”**
• John baptized with the baptism of penance. Bede. He did not remit sins but taught penance. For as circumcision in the patriarchs was the seal of the faith which they had, so too the penitent people received this washing as a kind of seal of their devotion, which prefigured the baptism of Christ, in which remission takes place.
• Rabanus. It is not baptism if it is not given in the name of the Trinity; those baptized by Judas are not rebaptized, because they were baptized in the faith of the Trinity; but those baptized by John are, because John baptizes only in water, Christ in the Holy Spirit. When therefore a good or a wicked minister baptizes, if the faith of the Trinity is full, the Lord baptizes. But those baptized by John in water alone were rebaptized by Paul.
**“Bede. The question is: whether one who, through ignorance, was perhaps baptized by one not baptized, yet rightly in faith, ought to be rebaptized? which I think is explained in this chapter. For what difference is there whether then, before the beginning of Christ's baptism, or now, someone were baptized by anyone without receiving the same? Since, John baptizing in faith and in the name of the Christ to come, declared that those were to be baptized again, saying: “I baptize in water; he shall baptize in the Holy Ghost.””** — baptizing
**“saying: That they should believe in him who was to come after him”** — As though it were said, to believe in the Holy Spirit is not contrary to John. Rabanus. Of whom he was the forerunner.
**“that is to say, in Jesus.”** — saying: “Go ye, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.”
19.5: **“Having heard these things, they were baptized”** — not rebaptized, because what they had heard agreed with John
19.6:
**“And when Paul had imposed his hands on them”** — of completion
**“the Holy Ghost came upon them, and they spoke with tongues”** — the usual sign of receiving the Holy Spirit
**“and prophesied.”** — by teaching or by foretelling the future
19.7: **“And all the men were about twelve.”** — And all the men were about, etc. Rabanus. The judgments of God are a great deep: behold, Asia, first unworthy of the visitation of the apostles, is now hallowed by the apostolic number, and is raised up by the gift of prophecy. And it must be noted that the Holy Spirit showed the signs of his coming here upon twelve disciples, and above upon a hundred and twenty (which number is made up by twelve multiplied ten times): that one in Jerusalem, this one in Ephesus, which is a city of the Greeks; whereby it is shown that he fills with the Spirit only those, whether of the Jews or of the Gentiles, who are in catholic unity.
19.8: **“And entering into the synagogue, he spoke boldly for the space of three months”** — abbreviating, he is silent about what he spoke
19.9:
**“But when some were hardened, and believed not, speaking evil”** — not only not believing
**“the way of the Lord”** — teaching
**“before the multitude, departing from them”** — avoid a heretical man after the first and second correction
**“he separated the disciples”** — lest they be infected by the blasphemies of unbelievers
**“disputing daily in the school of one Tyrannus.”**
• that is, in the building in which Tyrannus taught
• he preaches in that place so that where faithlessness abounded, faith may flourish
• Disputing daily in the school. Bede. From the fifth hour to the ninth and tenth, as is handed down by some, because he gave five hours to work, another five to teaching, and two to food and prayer; which is not confirmed by any authority.
**“in the school of Tyrannus”** — In the school of Tyrannus. Rabanus. Either as a title of dignity or as a proper name; and it is interpreted as restraining them or confirming them.
19.10:
**“And this continued for the space of two years”** — disputation in the school
**“for the space of two years”** — For the space of two years. Bede. At this time Paul wrote the first epistle to the Corinthians in Ephesus.
**“so that all they who dwelt in Asia”** — Minor (Asia)
19.11:
**“And God wrought by the hand of Paul more than common miracles.”**
• nothing was impossible to God, who is hindered by no place
• not small; no power of God is small
19.12:
**“So”** — he did
**“so that even”** — in his own manner he shortens the narrative
**“there were brought from his body to the sick, handkerchiefs”** — with which the sweat of the sufferers is wiped
**“or aprons”** — a belt, or a kind of garment, or a handkerchief
**“aprons”** — Semicinctia. Rabanus. Garments hanging from one side, or belts, or night garments, or a kind of cloth which the Hebrews use on the head.
19.13:
**“Now some also”** — inconstant
**“of the Jewish exorcists”**
• exorcist, one who adjures
• who had the art of exorcising
**“exorcists”** — Bede. Josephus says that Solomon devised and taught his people methods of exorcism, that is, of conjuration, by which unclean spirits, when driven out, did not dare to return to men. Now this is done through the reprobate to their own condemnation and to the profit of those who see and hear; for although they despise those who work the signs, yet they honour God, at whose invocation it is done.
**“attempted to invoke over them that had evil spirits, the name of the Lord Jesus, saying: I conjure you”** — behold, the exorcism
**“by Jesus, whom Paul preacheth.”** — we do not preach; behold the sign of unbelief
**“Now there were”** — Bede. In the Greek, “Erant autem” is the proper name of a certain priest, Sceva, which is interpreted “a crying or speaking little fox.”
19.14:
**“Now there were certain sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, seven, who did this.”** — likewise
**“seven sons”** — Bede. Since “Satan transformeth himself into an angel of light,” he colours his ministers also with the same pretence. Whence, since the grace of the Holy Spirit is designated by the number seven, in which figure Christ after the resurrection feasted with seven disciples, the sons of Sceva, as about to cast out evil spirits, are reckoned by the number seven; and because they invoke the name of Christ and of the apostles not by believing but by tempting, they are justly condemned not only by God but also by the demons, under the guile of falsehood. And rightly are they called sons of Sceva, which is interpreted “a crying little fox”; which animal of guile and shrewd cunning shows at once the Jews, Gentiles and heretics lying in wait for the Church and clamouring with chattering voice, of whom, as the guardians of the Church, it is commanded: “Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vines.”
19.15:
**“But the wicked spirit, answering, said to them: Jesus I know”** — Of this Aratus says in verse: “Know your madness, hostile race: the demon confesses to reign, whom you deny to have come; and by this you are convicted, by the very one whose goading you rush on.”
**“and Paul I know; but who are you?”** — trying to invoke the name of Jesus Christ
19.16:
**“And the man in whom the wicked spirit was, leaping upon them”** — grievous in harming
**“and mastering them”** — they did not dominate him
**“both”** — of the two exorcists
19.17:
**“And this became known”** — namely, that it prevailed
**“became known”** — that is, made public
**“to all the Jews and the Gentiles that dwelt at Ephesus. And fear fell”** — because of this deed
19.19:
**“But many”** — philosophers
**“of them who had followed curious arts”** — Many who followed curious arts, etc. Bede: The diligence of the magic art, whose followers rightly burn their books, though valued at a great price, because they see the demons they had served calling on Jesus and his apostles being honored.
**“brought together their books, and burnt them before all.”** — leaving an example
**“and counting the price of them”** — which could have been had from them if they were sold, or for which they had been bought
**“they found the money to be fifty thousand pieces of silver.”** — this is said so that their faith may be greater
**“fifty thousand pieces”** — Bede. In the gospel also, debts are remitted to debtors under the number fifty, we who, subsisting in this life by the five senses of the body, transgress the precepts of the decalogue; here, however, on account of the enormity of the magical crime, a thousand is added. Otherwise: the number fifty refers to penance and the remission of sins. Whence the fiftieth psalm is the psalm of penance, and the fiftieth year is the year of remission.
19.20: **“So mightily grew the word of God, and was confirmed.”** — because they burned the books, as was said above
19.21:
**“And when these things were ended”** — for two years
**“Paul purposed in the spirit”** — in the Holy Spirit or his own
**“when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem”** — because it had already been preached there, and therefore passing through sufficed
**“saying: After I have been there, I must see Rome also.”** — he places the future account first
**“see Rome”** — Rabanus. Which perhaps he had not seen before; or because he regarded as light the tribulation he was to suffer there, he says only to see it, not that he would suffer many things.
19.22:
**“And sending into Macedonia”** — although he had proposed to pass through, nevertheless he sends envoys again to prepare the alms, which he was to bring to Jerusalem, so that the collections would not be made when he himself came
**“Into Macedonia”** — Rabanus. He wished to pass from Asia, in which Ephesus is, into Europe, where Macedonia and Achaia are, and so again to go into Asia, that is, to Jerusalem, with the alms about which he wrote to the Corinthians.
**“two of them that ministered to him, Timothy and Erastus, he himself remained for a time in Asia.”** — The lesser.
19.23: **“Now at that time there arose no small disturbance”** — dissension between Paul with the faithful and Demetrius with the unfaithful
19.24:
**“Demetrius”** — Bede. While he strives to disturb the way of the Lord, he fulfils his own name in his deeds. For it is interpreted “one who persecutes exceedingly,” whence he builds temples of Diana in silver. For silver signifies eloquence, and the cunning of the Gentile is wont to build up his religion by the bare polish of speech.
**“For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver temples for Diana, brought no small gain to the craftsmen”** — to those working the same things
19.25: **“Whom he calling together, with the workmen of like occupation, said: Sirs, you know that our gain is by this trade”** — because they had gain from the price of the craft
19.26:
**“And you see and hear, that this Paul by persuasion hath drawn away a great multitude, not only of Ephesus”** — where it is
**“but almost of all Asia, saying: They are not gods which are made by hands.”** — they condemn themselves by their own mouth
**“which are made by hands”** — Bede. Wondrous is the folly of the heathen, to worship such things as they know can be set up or destroyed by man.
19.27:
**“So that not only this our craft is in danger”** — to sellers and buyers
**“Not only this our craft”** — Bede. That is, not only will our works be shown to be vain and unworthy of wages, but our religion will also be dishonoured, if Paul’s teaching prevails and idols are shown not to be gods.
**“craft”** — the acquisition of gain
**“is in danger to be set at nought”** — because it will be found at fault
**“great Diana”** — Bede. Because Demetrius said Diana would perish, they on the contrary marvel that she is great.
**“the temple of great Diana shall be reputed for nothing”** — for thus Paul taught, saying an idol is nothing
19.28: **“Having heard these things, they were full of anger, and cried out, saying:”** — cannot be destroyed
19.29:
**“And the whole city was filled with confusion”** — of this outcry, or of the two parties
**“they rushed with one accord into the theatre”** — the spectacle, where criminals were punished; and there they wished to punish Paul with his companions
**“into the theatre”** — Bede. A place having the shape of a semicircle, in which the people standing looked on at stage plays. Whence also from the spectacle it received in Greek the name theatre. Of this Arator: It was not fitting that the cause and merit of Diana be handled in any other place than a wanton forum; the shameful arena takes up the work of a foul counsel, etc.
19.30:
**“And when Paul would have entered in unto the people”** — the theatre, because he did not fear to be punished
**“the disciples suffered him not.”** — his own people, or faithful friends of Paul
19.31: **“And some also of the rulers of Asia, who were his friends, sent unto him, desiring that he would not venture himself into the theatre.”** — where the assembly of the people was
19.32:
**“Some cried one thing, some another.”** — Rabanus. That they might come into the theatre. Or they were shouting another great god, or another idol. Or insults against Paul.
**“For the assembly was”** — Catholic
**“confused”**
• from the worshippers of Diana
• Rabanus, that is, that gathering which was present at the theatre was mixed, the faithful and the faithless together, shouting different things.
19.33:
**“they drew forth Alexander out of the multitude”** — out of reverence
**“Alexander”** — lest he be killed, or lest he defend Paul
**“the Jews thrusting him forward. And Alexander beckoning with his hand for silence”** — while he is dragged, he asks for silence with his hand
**“would have given the people satisfaction.”** — that is, that the people should give the reason for the assembly, or he himself should give it on behalf of Paul and his people
19.34:
**“But”** — Alexander
**“as soon as they perceived him to be a Jew”** — against the God of the Jews
**“all with one voice”** — Great Diana, etc. Rightly the Jews drag Alexander the scribe out of that crowd, which wholly adored Diana.
19.35:
**“And when they had called”** — scarcely
**“had appeased”** — to silence
**“the town clerk had appeased the multitudes, he said: Ye men of Ephesus”** — perhaps this is the reason
**“what man is there that knoweth not”** — no one contradicts your outcry
19.36: **“For as much therefore as these things cannot be contradicted, you ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rashly.”** — against Paul and his people
19.37:
**“For you have brought hither these men”** — he speaks in general terms deliberately, so as not to seem to defend Paul
**“who are neither guilty of sacrilege”** — Neither guilty of sacrilege. Rabanus. Those are called sacrilegious from profane care. For sacred signifies the clean, and profane signifies the unclean.
19.38:
**“But if Demetrius and the craftsmen that are with him, have a matter against any man”** — Of Christians.
**“the courts of justice are open”** — The courts of justice are held: in the forum, where cases are argued, not in the theatre, where the condemned are punished.
**“and there are proconsuls”** — that they may judge.
**“let them accuse one another.”**
• Demetrius and his followers.
• let them dispute before the proconsuls.
19.39:
**“And if you inquire after any other matter”** — Apart from the case of the craftsmen.
**“it may be decided in a lawful assembly.”** — In the lawful assembly, where matters of law are handled, not of killing.
19.40:
**“For”** — For; so let it be done.
**“we are even in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar”** — and we are in danger of being accused of today’s sedition; we shall be thought to stir up sedition against some people.
**“there being no man guilty”** — since no one is liable: guilty and worthy to be killed.
**“of whom we may give account”** — of whom we can give account: the reason for assembling.
**“of this concourse. And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.”**
• of this crowd. Alexander left it, or caused it to be dismissed.
• And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly. Rabanus. He said this as a Jew, not wanting the Jews to be killed by the worshippers of idols, or as a Christian has spoken.

20.1: **“And after the tumult was ceased, Paul calling to him the disciples, and exhorting them, took his leave, and set forward to go into Macedonia.”** — as he had purposed.
20.2:
**“And when he had gone over those parts, and had exhorted them”** — In his usual way he shortens the history.
**“with many words, he came into Greece”** — Athens.
**“into Greece”** — Bede. Which is the province of Achaia. Paul came to this after Macedonia, because he had so purposed, as said above: “when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem.”
20.3:
**“Where, when he had spent three months, the Jews laid wait for him, as he was about to sail into Syria”** — The Jews lay in wait for him on the road, watching for him as he was about to sail.
**“In Syria”** — to Jerusalem.
**“And he determined to return through Macedonia”** — by fleeing the ambush.
20.4:
**“And there accompanied him Sopater”** — telling of the scattering, or saving the scattered.
**“Sopater”** — Bede. The ancients punctuated thus: Sosi, father of Pyrrhus, as if it were said: Sosi, who was the father of Pyrrhus, as though the son Pyrrhus were more illustrious than the father. Otherwise: Sosipater accompanied him, so that Pyrrhus is one name, understanding “son”. In Hebrew Sosipater is interpreted “telling of the dispersion” or “saving the dispersed”.
**“the son of Pyrrhus”** — loosening, or loosed.
**“of Berea”** — nominative case.
**“and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus”** — the proper name is interpreted as lifting up, or lifted up; where others have Secindus.
**“and Gaius of Derbe”** — from the city.
20.5:
**“These going before”** — by the direct route, for they did not fear ambush.
**“stayed for us at Troas”** — Paul and Luke and the others coming around by a roundabout way.
20.6: **“But we sailed from Philippi after the days of the Azymes”** — which is the first part of Macedonia.
20.7:
**“On the first day of the week”**
• that is, on the Lord’s day, which is the first after the sabbath.
• The name of the day is given so that there may be a preparation for doing and saying what is virtuous.
• Bede. Allegorically. The upper room: “the height of the gifts”; the night: “the obscurity of the Scriptures”; the lamps: “expositions of secrets”; the Lord’s day: “the remembrance of the resurrection of Christ or of ours”. Here the spiritual teacher is admonished, allured by the sweetness of the resurrection and the joy of life, to urge his hearers to the highest things, and by long discourse to reach the secrets of the Scriptures, and, for the sake of the weak, to light up the same with the lamp of full exposition, according to the Apostle, who, having said: “Abraham had two sons,” etc., added: “For these are the two testaments.”
**“when we were assembled”** — that is, we were gathered to celebrate the mysteries.
**“to break bread”** — bodily or spiritual.
**“Paul discoursed with them, being to depart on the morrow”** — therefore he discourses in the night because he was to depart on the morrow.
20.9:
**“Eutychus”** — Bede. In Hebrew it is amens; in Greek it is interpreted fortunate. The one fits him who through the pleasure of youth has fallen from the height of virtues; the other fits him who by the condescension of the preacher has returned to the heights of virtue.
**“sitting on the window”** — historically or mystically: faith.
**“being oppressed with a deep sleep”** — fleshly or spiritual.
**“deep”** — because of the weakness of faith.
**“as Paul was long preaching”** — this is the cause of the sleep: the length of the discourse.
**“by occasion of his sleep fell from the third loft down”**
• historically, or it indicates some error about the Trinity.
• From the third loft. Bede. The three lofts, in the highest of which Paul discourses: “faith, hope, charity; but the greater of these is charity.” So he who through sloth, by forsaking, begins to slumber amid the apostle’s words is already counted among the dead; for offending in one point, he is become guilty of all.
**“and was taken up”** — from the earth, or from the perversity of sense.
**“and was taken up dead”** — in flesh or in spirit.
**“was taken up dead”** — Bede. Amid the words of preaching the occasion for healing arises, so that the speech is strengthened by the sweetness of the miracle and of the teaching, the labour of vigils is kept off, and the memory of the master, now about to depart, is more tightly fixed in the mind.
20.10:
**“To whom, when Paul had gone down”** — from the upper room, or by sympathizing.
**“when Paul had gone down, he laid himself upon him”** — Bede. He went down and lay upon him; he embraced him. This is what Paul says: “My little children, of whom I am in labour again, until Christ be formed in you.” For the raising up of those who sin through negligence is more laborious than of those who sin through necessity and infirmity; and this is expressed by Eutychus, that by Tabitha raised by Peter. Therefore she dies by day, he in the middle of the night. She after death is placed in the upper room; he dies, having fallen from the third loft. He died with the teacher present and teaching; she with the master absent; she sat up as soon as Peter was seen; he, dead in the night, at last rises in the morning, and, the sun of justice breathing upon him, is brought back alive.
**“for his soul is in him”** — Rabanus. His soul did not depart wholly, or it returned; he said this on account of unbelievers, as “the maid is not dead, but sleepeth”; for so despair is taken away.
20.11: **“Then going up, and breaking bread and tasting”** — a little food.
20.12: **“And they brought the youth alive, and were not a little comforted”** — it is to be read passively.
20.13:
**“But we, going aboard the ship”** — Paul making his journey by land.
**“sailed to Assos”** — it is a city or an island.
20.14: **“And when he had met with us at Assos, we took him in, and came to Mitylene”** — it is an island which is opposite Asia; for it is interpreted “declining” or “transmigrating”; or a city in the island of Cyprus.
20.15:
**“And sailing thence, the day following we came over against Chios”** — a city or an island.
**“and the next day we arrived at Samos, and the day following we came to Miletus”** — it is an island.
20.16:
**“For Paul had determined to sail by Ephesus”** — to or past.
**“lest he should be stayed any time in Asia. For he hasted, if it were possible for him, to keep the day of Pentecost”**
• or of Pentecost, that is, of the fiftieth day.
• Bede. By the precept of the law all Jews gathered in Jerusalem three times a year, that is, at Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles; and the apostle, the bonds of the world broken, hurries to keep the fiftieth day, that is, of forgiveness and of the Holy Spirit.
**“Pentecost”** — Bede. It is agreed that the time of Easter and Pentecost was celebrated in the times of the apostles.
20.17:
**“And sending from Miletus to Ephesus”** — not sailing to Ephesus.
**“he called the ancients of the church”** — that is, presbyters, as it has in Greek.
20.18:
**“And when they were come to him, and were together, he said to them: You know”** — he does not boast, but sets himself forth as an example for them to imitate.
**“from the first day that I came into Asia”** — as has been said: “And he came to Ephesus,” etc., above in chapter 18.
20.19: **“Serving the Lord with all humility, and with tears, and temptations which befell me by the conspiracies of the Jews”** — not yours
20.20:
**“How I have kept back nothing that was profitable to you”** — of words
**“but have preached it to you”** — by word
**“and taught you”** — by deed
**“publicly”** — against heretics
**“and from house to house”** — in secret
20.22:
**“And now, behold, being bound”**
• as if compelled to that journey
