• Bound, etc. Not knowing, etc. Bede. He openly shows that he knew what was to come not by its being revealed to himself but to others concerning him; among whom was Agabus the prophet, and those disciples at Tyre who warned him through the Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem.
**“in the spirit”** — by the Holy Spirit foreknowing, or by my own mind
20.23:
**“Save that the Holy Ghost in every city”** — everywhere, not once in one place
**“witnesseth to me, saying”** — both through me and through others
**“That bands and afflictions wait for me at Jerusalem”** — so that where once he persecuted the Church, there now he might teach for the peace of the Church
20.24:
**“But I fear none of these things, neither do I count my life”** — life, which is breathed into by the soul, temporal, which he counts as nothing who awaits the joys of eternal life
**“more precious than myself”** — that is, my soul
**“so that I may consummate”** — in the manner of a soldier, whence: I have finished the course
**“my course and the ministry of the word which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God”** — of the remission of sins, or of spiritual grace
20.25: **“And now behold, I know that all you shall see my face no more”** — who are in the provinces to which I preached
20.26:
**“Wherefore I take you to witness this day”** — therefore, because: “You shall see my face no more”; or I leave a testament, because I am clean, etc.
**“that I am clear from the blood of all men”** — because I did not spare their vices
20.27:
**“For I have not spared”** — I did not omit or shun any word of teaching
**“to declare unto you all the counsel of God”** — especially concerning the incarnation
20.28:
**“Take heed to yourselves”** — he says this to the elders
**“and to the whole flock”** — that is, guard yourselves and the whole flock committed to you from heretics
**“wherein the Holy Ghost hath placed you bishops”** — watchmen
**“hath placed you bishops”** — Bede. It was said above that the priests of Ephesus were called to Miletus, whom he now calls bishops, that is, overseers. For one city did not have several bishops, but by the name of bishops he means the same priests. For the rank is joined, and in many things almost wholly alike.
**“to rule”** — not for the name or honor alone but that you may rule
**“the church of God”** — not ours
**“which he hath purchased with his own blood”** — not at a small price
**“of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood”** — Bede. He does not hesitate to say the blood of God, because of the unity of person in the two natures of Jesus Christ, for which it is said: “the Son of man who is in heaven.” Let Nestorius cease to separate the Son of man from the Son of God and to make two Christs.
20.29:
**“I know”** — therefore you must be attentive
**“ravening wolves will enter in”** — who are outside and outside the Church
**“after my departure”** — concerning the world, as if he says: then you must fear when I am absent
**“ravening wolves, not sparing the flock”** — heretics, crafty in faith, strong in disputation, cruel in killing
20.30:
**“And of your own selves”** — besides those who will enter from outside
**“shall arise men speaking perverse things”** — John says of these: “They went out from us, but they were not of us”
**“to draw away disciples after them”** — in the elation of pride
20.31:
**“Therefore watch, keeping in memory”** — because they will enter in and arise
**“keeping in memory”** — Rabanus. What he had said was to be kept in memory; for memory is no small guard of the divine precept.
**“that for three years”** — Because for the space of three years. Arator briefly explains this, saying: He who sings of the Church often sets forth three teachings, the volume sounding the historical, the moral, and the typical. Hence Judea, lying barren, and called a tree, awaits fruit from three years and has brought none.
20.32:
**“And now”** — He designates bishops as frail.
**“I commend you to God”** — that God may keep you, the guardians of others
**“and to the word of his grace”** — the Holy Spirit who spoke in Paul; or the word of grace, which gives grace to those who hear
**“who is able to build up”** — you into one house, that is, the Church
**“and to give an inheritance”** — heavenly, that is, that he may build, and give an inheritance in the saints, that they themselves may be his inheritance
20.33: **“silver and gold”** — wolves are known by this, that they covet this
20.34: **“You yourselves know, for such things as were needful for me and them that are with me, these hands have furnished”** — the example of working is also for bishops, a sign by which they are distinguished from wolves
20.35:
**“all things”** — examples especially of working
**“I have shewed you all things”** — Bede. That is, not only must one persist in teaching amid pressures and tears, but one must labour with one’s hands so that none of the weak be burdened; this is what is said elsewhere: “Whatsoever thou shalt spend over and above, I, at my return, will repay thee,” the gospel, namely, to preach, and not to seek maintenance from the gospel.
**“how that so labouring you ought”** — as I, whose hands ministered
**“to support the weak”** — to minister to the weak, as I did for those who are with me
**“It is a more blessed thing”** — Rabanus. This is not read in the gospel. For not all things were written; but Paul perhaps heard this from the apostles, or received it from the Holy Spirit; or it can be said that, if not the words, Jesus indicated this sense when he said: “Give to every one that asketh thee,” and elsewhere: “Do not possess gold,” etc.
**“and to remember the word of the Lord Jesus, how he said: It is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive”** — Bede. He does not set rich almsgivers before those who, having left all things, followed the Lord; but he glorifies above all those who, renouncing in themselves all that they possess, nevertheless labour, working with their hands, that they may have wherewith to give to him that suffers need.
20.37: **“And there was much weeping among them all”** — in commending them to God he prayed also for himself, who was about to depart, chiefly because of his own departure and the coming of the wolves

21.1: **“Coos, Rhodes, Patara”** — Rabanus. Coos, Rhodes and Patara are islands.
21.2: **“And when we had found a ship sailing over to Phenice”** — the province of Syria, where are Tyre and Sidon
21.3:
**“And when we had discovered”** — we drew near so that we might be seen
**“leaving it on the left hand”** — going back toward the west, by the customary manner of sailors
**“we sailed into Syria”** — that is, Phenice
**“and came to Tyre”** — the city of Phenice
21.4: **“And finding disciples, we tarried there seven days”** — knowing that he was to be bound, by their own spirit or the prophetic spirit
21.5:
**“And the days being expired”** — the seven aforesaid
**“departing we went forward”** — we went forth, from Tyre
**“they all bringing us on our way”**
• escorting us to Jerusalem
• Bringing us on our way, etc. Bede. Here was fulfilled the prophecy which says: “And the daughters of Tyre with gifts, yea, all the rich among the people, shall entreat thy countenance,” etc., to the end of the psalm. For no city received, held, and sent away the apostle with greater sweetness; indeed, to this day the place on the sands is shown where they prayed together.
21.6:
**“And when we had bid one another farewell”** — one another
**“we took ship; and they returned home”** — men of the city
21.7:
**“But we having finished the voyage by sea”** — so far they are carried by sea
**“having finished”** — or completed
**“from Tyre came down to Ptolemais”** — it is a city
21.8:
**“And the next day departing”** — by land
**“we came to Caesarea”** — of Palestine
**“And entering into the house of Philip the evangelist”** — not the apostle but the preacher who evangelized in Samaria and to the eunuch
**“Philip the evangelist”** — Bede. For the ready performance of the office of preaching, he merited to be called an evangelist.
**“who was one of the seven”** — to the deacons
21.9:
**“And he had four daughters, virgins, who did prophesy”** — as in Joel: “And your sons and your daughters shall prophesy,” etc.
**“And he had”** — Rabanus. Elsewhere the daughters of Philip the apostle are read to have prophesied, but the truth of this place is not to be contradicted, unless perhaps both are understood to have had prophetess daughters.
21.10: **“from Judea”** — Bede. This is said because Caesarea, where they were staying, belongs to Samaria, situated on the border of Phoenicia and Palestine.
21.11: **“Thus saith the Holy Ghost”** — Bede. He imitates the ancient prophets, who used to say, Thus says the Lord God, because the Holy Spirit is Lord and God just as the Father and the Son are, and their operation cannot be separated, whose nature and will are one.
21.13: **“Then Paul answered, and said: What do you mean weeping and afflicting my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but to die also in Jerusalem”** — by this the strength of faith in Paul is shown
21.14:
**“And when we could not persuade him, we ceased, saying: The will of the Lord be done”**
• concerning the life or death of Paul
• We ceased, saying. Let Paul go to Jerusalem as he had said: “Behold, I go bound in the spirit to Jerusalem.”
21.15: **“And after those days, being prepared”** — to the will of the Lord, whether to die or to live
21.16:
**“with whom we should lodge”** — Rabanus. Or bringing this one, that is, Philip the evangelist, or bringing this one, that is, Jason, for this purpose.
**“one Mnason a Cyprian, an old disciple”** — formerly a believer
21.18:
**“the day following, Paul went in with us”** — the apostle, son of Alphaeus, who was bishop of Jerusalem
**“unto James”** — Bede. This James, the brother of the Lord, was the son of Mary, the sister of the mother of the Lord; after the passion he was at once ordained bishop by the apostles. He ruled the Church thirty years, that is, until the seventh year of Nero, and was buried near the temple, where he had been cast down.
21.20:
**“glorified God”** — giving thanks to him
**“and said to him”** — they say by asking
**“Thou seest, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews that have believed; and they are all zealous for the law”** — zealots for the law against you
21.21:
**“Now they have heard of thee”** — hence is the zeal
**“that thou teachest those Jews to depart from Moses”** — that is, from the law of Moses
**“saying that they ought not to circumcise”** — Bede. For in the doctrine of Christ you condemn as sacrilegious, and as not written by God’s command, the things that were ministered by Moses. They said this of Paul, not those who knew how the faithful Jews observed these things, namely, to commend the authority of God and the holiness of those sacraments, not to obtain the salvation which, revealed in Christ, was given through baptism. But those had spread this report who so observed the legal things as though necessary for believers. For Paul, a vehement preacher of grace, opposed them, teaching that man is justified not through those things but through the grace of Christ, which was foretold in the shadow of the law. And therefore they were striving to stir up persecution against him as an enemy of the law and of the commandments of God; this false accusation he fittingly refuted by celebrating the very things he seemed to condemn. Thus showing that the Jews were not then to be forbidden them as wicked, nor the Gentiles to be compelled to them as necessary. Yet the apostles had already decreed that no one should compel the Gentiles to judaize, but the Jews were not forbidden.
**“nor walk according to the custom”**
• ancient
• Bede. At that time the Jews believing in Christ were not forbidden to walk according to the law, the temple and its religion still standing, although they were to have salvation in the sacraments of the New Testament; but believers from the Gentiles were forbidden to be converted to the law, though they were commanded to observe diligently the commandments of the law that pertain to morals and cleanness of body, as: “Thou shalt not covet,” etc. This was the fourth synod held at Jerusalem. The first was on the election of another apostle in place of Judas. The second, on the election of the seven deacons. The third, on circumcision not to be imposed on those who believed from among the Gentiles. This fourth, on the Jews not being forbidden at that time, where necessity required, to be initiated into the legal ceremonies, on account of the scandal of those who thought that the apostles condemned the law of Moses like the doctrines of idolatry.
**“walk”** — in the synagogue, or to live in the law
21.22:
**“What is it therefore?”**
• in their assembly
• what they have heard about you
• or what is to be done by you
**“the multitude must needs come together”** — it is necessary or fitting
21.24:
**“Take these, and sanctify thyself with them; and bestow on them”** — join thyself to them
**“for the things which they have heard of thee are false”** — Bede. For thou dost not reprove the things of the law as it is said. But if he celebrated for this reason, to hide his opinion by a feigned action, James would not say this.
21.25:
**“But as touching the Gentiles that believe”** — as if he said: we are not now speaking against the law
**“we have written”** — not only saying
**“decreeing”** — that they keep nothing of that kind, except that they observe themselves from idolatry, etc.
21.26:
**“Then Paul took the men”** — having four men under a vow
**“the next day being purified”** — shaving the head
**“entered into the temple with them”** — until an offering should be made, etc.
**“giving notice of the accomplishment”** — the end
21.27:
**“But when the seven days were drawing to an end”** — Minor
**“When the seven days were drawing to an end”** — Bede. They were not yet completed, but their course was still being run; whence in the Greek it is said more expressly: When the seven days were beginning to be completed; otherwise it would not stand. For he himself, five days after his arrival at Caesarea, said to the governor: “That there are yet but twelve days since I went up to adore in Jerusalem.” For if to these seven days and those five are added the day of the council, on which he himself divided the Pharisees and Sadducees, and that on which the Jews wished to kill him, more than twelve days are found.
**“stirred up all the people”** — Bede. Because they saw that the Gentiles, followers of grace, rarely observed the ceremonies of the law and the solemn rites of the temple, they feared lest the Romans should come and take away both place and nation.
21.28:
**“Men of Israel, help: This is the man that teacheth all men everywhere against the people, and the law, and this place”** — because he taught believers that the true Jerusalem is, and preferred the new law, and said that the whole Church is God’s place
**“and moreover hath brought in Gentiles into the temple, and hath violated this holy place”** — the city of Jerusalem or the temple
21.29: **“For they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city”** — Jerusalem, not in the temple
21.30: **“And the whole city was in an uproar: and the people ran together”** — lest he flee back into the temple
21.32: **“Who, forthwith taking with him soldiers and centurions, ran down to them”** — who were ready or had already begun
21.33:
**“Then the tribune coming near”** — Or: approaching
**“took him, and commanded him to be bound with two chains”** — until his case should be judged
21.34:
**“But others”** — various ones said various things, because they had no certain cause
**“cried one thing, some another, among the multitude”** — which brings forth a confused judgment
**“And when he could not know the certainty for the tumult, he commanded him to be carried into the castle”** — of his soldiers, lest the Jews kill him
21.35:
**“And when he was come to the stairs”**
• by which one ascends to the temple
• When he came to the stairs, etc. Bede. The stairs signify a descent from the temple but an ascent into the castle.
**“it fell out that he was carried by the soldiers, because of the violence of the people”** — therefore he was carried by the strong
21.36:
**“For the multitude of the people followed after, crying: Away with him”**
• for death, do not inquire into the cause
• this was said of this man which was also said of Christ
21.37:
**“And as Paul was about to be brought into the castle”** — while his leading in was being prepared, yet he had not yet gone out from the steps
**“he saith to the tribune: May I speak something to thee? Who said: Canst thou speak Greek?”** — Canst thou speak Greek? Rabanus. A question or an affirmation, because, as is thought, the tribune spoke the Greek language, or lest the Jews should know it.
21.38:
**“Art not thou that Egyptian”** — Bede. A certain Egyptian had come into Judea, who, procuring belief in himself as a prophet by magic art, gathered thirty thousand of the Jews; leading them through the desert he came to the Mount of Olives, prepared to rush upon Jerusalem and subjugate it to himself; but Felix met him with armed men, the Egyptian was put to flight with a few, and the others were slain.
**“who before these days didst raise a tumult, and didst lead forth into the desert four thousand men that were murderers”**
• of gladiators; for sica is called a sword
• Four thousand, etc. Bede. There is no controversy to be raised over this number of followers between the tribune who spoke this and Josephus who wrote about the Egyptian. For he could have come at first with a few exercising tyranny, and afterwards joined more to himself by public fraud. In the time of Felix, moreover, this kind of robbers arose, who, carrying sicae, that is, short swords, in the hand, mingled with the people and wounded in secret, so that death forestalled complaint and the striker lay hid.
21.39:
**“But Paul said to him: I am a Jew”** — not an Egyptian
**“of Tarsus in Cilicia”** — Rabanus. Whither, having been taken captive, he migrated with his parents.
**“a citizen of no mean city”**
• some books have “civis” for “municeps”
• taking up public duties, that is, the census
**“And I beseech thee”**
• as if to say: having declared himself a Roman at the census
• because I am yours
21.40: **“And when he had given him leave, Paul standing on the stairs, beckoned with his hand to the people; and a great silence being made, he spoke unto them in the Hebrew tongue, saying”** — that the whole people might understand, or that they might be more silent

22.3:
**“And he saith: I am a Jew, born at Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city”** — in Jerusalem
**“at the feet of Gamaliel”** — for service, or because as a boy and humble he sat at the feet of the teacher
**“born at Tarsus”** — Bede. Paul was born in a town of Galilee named Giscala; when it was taken by the Romans he migrated with his parents to Tarsus of Cilicia, and coming to Jerusalem for zeal for the law, he was taught by Gamaliel. He does not call himself a citizen but a townsman, from municipium, that is, the territory of that city in which he was brought up. It is called a municipium because it renders only munia, that is, the tributes or duties owed. Although born at Giscala, he nevertheless calls himself a Tarsian. So Christ, born in Bethlehem, was called a Nazarene.
**“taught according to the truth of the law of the fathers, zealous for the law”**
• imitator, or zealot against Christians
• Bede. In Greek: being a zealot of the law of God, according to that testimony: “For I bear them witness, that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.”
22.4:
**“Who persecuted this way”** — of Christ, which I now preach
**“persecuted unto death”** — of Christians, or of Stephen, or ready to die for the law
**“binding and delivering into prisons”** — of prison
22.5:
**“As the high priest”** — he calls him as one experienced to witness
**“doth bear me witness”** — the high priest had given testimony of the words in the present, or of the letter
22.6:
**“And it came to pass, as I was going, and drawing nigh to Damascus at midday”** — so that it is known that the light which shone round him was brighter than the sun
**“suddenly from heaven”** — from God
22.7:
**“And falling on the ground, I heard a voice saying to me: Saul, Saul”** — the name is repeated in rebuke
**“Saul, Saul”** — Rabanus. Some copies have “Saul Saul,” so that it may be shown that Saul is named Saul from the name of Saul.
22.8: **“And I answered: Who art thou, Lord?”** — he believed him to be God who spoke from above
22.9:
**“And they that were with me, saw indeed the light, but they heard not the voice”**
• not the face
• Bede. Above, the history tells of this vision: that his companions stood amazed, hearing indeed the voice but seeing no one. Whence it is gathered that they heard the sound of the voice confusedly, not the distinction of the words.
**“heard”** — Rabanus. They understood, but only the sound of Paul’s voice, or of him who spoke to Paul.
22.10:
**“And I said: What shall I do, Lord?”** — knowing you, I will obey you
**“And there it shall be told thee”** — Rabanus. An example of humility, against teachers not to dispute, nor to presume about ourselves as if we were taught by God.
22.11:
**“And whereas I did not see for the brightness of that light”** — which had blinded me
**“by the hand”** — by the hand, not by the eye
22.12:
**“And one Ananias, a man”** — fit
**“according to the law, having testimony”** — he had testimony from God, but was believed more by the Jews
22.13: **“Brother Saul, look up”** — Rabanus. There were two things in Paul’s eyes, blindness and illumination, and therefore he rightly believed.
22.14:
**“But he said: The God of our fathers”** — not a new God, as the Jews thought
**“hath preordained thee”** — Rabanus. A fitting order: first preordained in God’s foreknowledge; then he knows the truth, sees the Just One, and hears from his mouth; afterwards he becomes a witness of those things which he knew, saw, and heard.
**“that thou shouldst know his will, and see the Just One”** — Christ or the gospel
**“and shouldst hear the voice from his mouth”** — of Christ, not of the apostles: “Not from men, nor by man,” etc.
22.15:
**“For thou shalt be his witness to all men”** — through Scripture and his own report; or to all ages, conditions, tongues, and sexes
**“of those things which thou hast seen”** — in the shining light
**“and heard”** — in the calling voice
22.17:
**“And it came to pass”** — he passes over place and time
**“when I was come again”** — after a great circuit he returned from Damascus
**“to Jerusalem”** — the holy city
**“and was praying”** — lest Satan should deceive him
**“in the temple”** — the house of God
**“that I was in a trance”**
• in ecstasy; others say in fear, others in distraction
• That I was in a trance, etc. Rabanus. He does not tell this for self-exaltation but out of necessity, so that he may be seen as fit to preach the gospel to the Gentiles.
22.18:
**“And saw him”** — Christ
**“saying unto me: Make haste”** — from necessity, and at God’s admonition he did all things
22.19: **“And I said: Lord, they know”** — the example of my conversion would suffice for them
22.20:
**“And when the blood of Stephen thy witness was shed”** — of the martyr
**“I stood by and”** — also
**“consented”** — Rabanus. By confessing that he consented, he shows that he did not kill, unless “consenting” is taken for “killing”.
22.21:
**“And he said to me: Go”** — as if to say: although they know, yet they would not receive it
**“for unto the Gentiles”** — not the Jews
**“afar off, will I send thee”** — as much in faith as in place
22.22:
**“And they heard him until this word”** — I will send you to the nations
**“and then lifted up their voice, saying”** — to the tribune
22.23:
**“And as they cried out and threw off their garments”** — that they might kill him, or as a sign of grief
**“threw off their garments”** — Bede. In the passion of Christ only the priest, leaping from his throne, rent his garments, because then the old priesthood was to be changed. But now, because the whole nation was to be stripped of the glory of the kingdom, all cast off their garments and raise to heaven a cry mixed with dust, according to that: “The pride of them that hate thee ascendeth continually.”
**“and cast dust into the air”** — either from grief or from the manner of brute animals
22.24:
**“The tribune commanded him to be brought into the castle”** — because it had been prepared before; now it is fulfilled
**“that he should be scourged and tortured”** — that they might be satisfied with his torments
**“to know for what cause they did so cry out against him”** — therefore he commanded that he not be killed
22.25:
**“And when they had bound him with thongs”** — for scourging
**“Paul saith to the centurion that stood by him: Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?”** — convicted by no judicial order and of no guilt
22.28:
**“And the tribune answered: I obtained the being free of this city with a great sum”** — I obtained with a great sum, etc. Bede. Another edition makes clearer what the tribune said. The tribune said: Do you now so easily say that you are a Roman citizen? For I know at what price I possessed that citizenship.
**“the being free of this city”** — Bede. That is, social intercourse among citizens, or the administration of the commonwealth. For it was not that the tribune could not be a citizen of the Roman city, but he had bought a share in the citizenship that he might be a partaker. Paul was the more a Roman citizen in that he had it not by purchase but by birth.
**“But I was born so”** — Bede, that is: I am a Roman more than you in this, because I did not buy the Roman name, having been born elsewhere, but was begotten in their citizenship.

23.1:
**“And Paul looking upon the council, said: Men, brethren, I have conversed with all good conscience”** — because I persecuted in ignorance
**“good”** — I am not guilty
23.2: **“And the high priest Ananias commanded them that stood by him to strike him on the mouth”** — as of one boasting imprudently
23.3:
**“Then Paul said to him: God shall strike thee”** — he will destroy
**“shall strike”** — Rabanus. Not “may he strike”: for it is a prophecy, not a curse, since Paul says: “Bless, and curse not.” And again: “Bless them that curse.” This is to be understood not only of Ananias but also of the priesthood of the Jews, which he compares to a whited wall for the old law and its feigned surface. Other copies have “may he strike,” which the Apostle said not from anger but by divine inspiration.
**“God shall strike thee, thou whited wall”**
• because you appear to be what you are not
• Bede. He did not say this moved by disturbance of mind, for that priesthood, like a whited wall, was to be struck and destroyed when the priesthood of Christ came upon it, which was revealed as the apostles preached. And therefore he says: “Shall strike,” signifying that it will be. That he said this with a calm mind the following answer shows: “I knew not, brethren, that he is the high priest.”
**“For sittest thou”** — on the seat of Moses
**“to judge me”** — with a perverse judgment and a feigned appearance, from your own opinion
**“according to the law”** — which says: “Bring forth the blasphemer without the camp, and let all the people stone him.”
**“and contrary to the law commandest me to be struck”** — saying: the innocent and just you shall not oppress or curse
23.4: **“Dost thou revile the high priest of God?”** — They say this to show that he is liable to a blow.
23.5:
**“Thou shalt not speak evil of the prince of thy people”**
• therefore I say “I did not know” because, if I knew he was the prince, I would be guilty
• Bede. And even if he truly knew that in the New Testament this man was not prince of the priests, nevertheless, teaching others to behave more modestly toward those in whose power they are, he answers with moderation.
**“I knew not, brethren, that he is the high priest”** — Bede, that is: I did not know that it was Ananias; or he subtly says he does not know the prince, because the priesthood of the Jews has been rejected.
23.6: **“And Paul knowing”** — Bede. As the unity of the good is useful, so the unity of the wicked is always harmful to the good; therefore Paul strives to divide his persecutors, that those who had surrounded him united might release him divided. So the Red Sea, which had hemmed in the children of Israel when whole, delivered them when divided from Egypt. And that he declares himself a son of Pharisees, or according to the Greek a son of a Pharisee, is the same as what he boasted above, that he had learned the prophets and the law at the feet of Gamaliel, who was a Pharisee.
23.7: **“And when he had so said, there arose a dissension between the Pharisees and the Sadducees; and the multitude was divided”** — dismissed, so that it might return to its own places
23.8:
**“For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, neither angel, nor spirit”** — Holy
**“but the Pharisees confess both”** — The Pharisees, however, confess both. Rabanus. The angel and the Holy Spirit, or the resurrection and the angel, so that the angel is the same as the spirit.
23.9:
**“And there arose a great cry; and some of the Pharisees rising up, strove”** — for Paul against the Sadducees
**“saying: We find no evil in this man. What”** — What is wonderful
**“if a spirit”** — Holy
**“What if a spirit hath spoken to him”** — “What if a spirit has spoken to him?” Rabanus. Here it appears, according to Jerome, that the Sadducees do not confess the Holy Spirit or angels. And therefore they name spirit and angel, because they knew this to be contrary to them.
23.10:
**“And when there arose a great dissension, the tribune fearing”** — should be torn
**“lest Paul should be pulled in pieces by them”** — That he should not be torn in pieces by them. Rabanus. The Sadducees wishing to seize him, or both sides striving together for him.
23.11:
**“the night following the Lord standing by him, said: Be constant”** — timely comfort is applied
**“for as thou hast testified of me in Jerusalem, so must thou bear witness also at Rome”** — it signifies that he will labor thereafter; or it is a consolation to one who wishes him to bear witness before many
23.12:
**“And when day was come, some of the Jews gathered together”** — they bound themselves with a curse
**“bound themselves under a curse, saying”** — Neither eat nor drink, etc. Bede. Whereas the Lord says: “Blessed are they that hunger and thirst after justice,” these on the contrary hunger after iniquity and thirst for blood, so that they even give up food until they are filled with the death of the just man; but “there is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord.” For Paul is snatched from their plots that, preserved, he may give testimony to Christ at Rome.
23.15:
**“Now therefore do you with the council signify”** — not that we have sworn, but that he bring him forth; and do all this with the cunning of the council, by common consent, to conceal the conspiracy
**“to the tribune, that he bring him forth to you, as if you meant to know something more certain touching him”** — that is, his cause and his guilt
23.21: **“But do not thou give credit to them; for there lie in wait for him more than forty men of them, who have bound themselves by oath neither to eat, nor to drink, till they have killed him”** — what you promise
23.22: **“The tribune therefore dismissed the young man, charging him that he should tell no man, that he had made known these things unto him”** — to the tribune
23.23:
**“Then having called two centurions, he said to them: Make ready”** — Make ready soldiers, etc. Rabanus. This is so that the Jews might not carry him off, and that the tribune himself might not be accused of crime before the governor, as though he were going to receive money from the Jews and the price of Paul’s death.
**“two hundred soldiers”** — foot soldiers
23.24:
**“and provide beasts”** — for Paul and his companions
**“that they may set Paul on, and bring him safe to Felix the governor”** — the tribune sends the case to the governor as a lesser sends to a greater
23.31: **“Then the soldiers, according as it was commanded them, taking Paul, brought him by night to Antipatris”** — a city called by the name of Antipatris
23.32:
**“And the next day, leaving”** — seventy
**“the horsemen to go with him”** — foot soldiers
**“they returned to the castle”** — from Antipatris
23.35: **“I will hear thee, said he, when thy accusers come; and he commanded him to be kept in Herod's judgment hall”** — of the former governor

24.1:
**“And after five days the high priest Ananias came down”** — to accuse Paul
**“the high priest Ananias, with some of the ancients, and one Tertullus an orator”** — who would speak against Paul
24.2:
**“And Paul being called for”** — for the conversation
**“Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: Whereas through thee we live in much peace”** — O Felix
**“and many things are rectified”** — works
24.3: **“We accept it always and in all places”** — many works
24.4: **“But that I be no further tedious to thee”** — I may lengthen
24.5:
**“We have found this to be a pestilent man, and raising seditions among all the Jews throughout the world, and author of the sedition of the sect of the Nazarenes”**
• of the Nazarenes, that is, of Jesus
• Of the Nazarenes. Bede. At that time Christians were called Nazarenes as a reproach. Afterwards among the Jews there arose a heresy called that of the Nazarenes, who believe Christ the Son of God to have been born of Mary, to have suffered and also risen again, while keeping all the commandments of the old law. But while they wish to be both Jews and Christians, they are neither.
24.6:
**“Who also hath gone about to profane the temple”** — by bringing Gentiles into it
**“whom, we having apprehended”** — In this place some of our copies have fewer verses, which in the Greek are read thus: whom we apprehended and wished to judge according to our law; but Lysias the tribune, coming upon us with great violence, took him out of our hands, commanding his accusers to come before thee, that thou thyself, judging, mayest know of all these things, etc.
24.8:
**“Commanding his accusers to come to thee”** — to the tribune
**“of whom thou mayest thyself, by examination, have knowledge of all these things”** — the truth of them
24.10:
**“Then Paul answered”** — making a sign with the hand
**“Knowing that for many years thou hast been judge over this nation”** — as if he said: I know your friendship
**“I will with good courage”** — with confidence
**“answer for myself”** — I will excuse myself.
24.11:
**“For thou mayest understand”** — by witnesses
**“that there are yet but twelve days”** — it is not an ancient time
**“since I went up to adore in Jerusalem”** — to violate the temple
24.12: **“And neither in the temple did they find me disputing with any man”** — questioning
24.14:
**“But this I confess to thee, that according to the way”** — of the Nazarenes
**“which they call”** — saying: we have found the author of sedition
**“a heresy”** — division
**“the way, which they call a heresy”** — Bede. The Greek has it better: “according to the way which they call a heresy, so I serve the Father God.” For it is not fitting that one who spoke in Greek should say “sect which they call heresy,” since “sect” in Latin is the same as “heresy” in Greek. But he says: so I serve the Father God according to that way which unbelievers call heresy, that is, sect, as if they had more obstinacy in following whatever they please than diligence in discerning what is right.
**“so do I serve the Father and my God, believing”** — as the Pharisees, not as the Sadducees, rejecting certain of those things that are in the law and the prophets
**“the Father and my God”** — Rabanus. I am shown to be his son, not his servant, as is found in other copies.
24.15: **“Having hope in God”** — concerning the resurrection of the dead
24.17: **“Now after many years, I came to bring alms”** — in Jerusalem
24.18:
**“In which I was found purified in the temple”** — keeping the law with shaven head
**“Jews of Asia”** — Asians
24.19: **“But certain”** — found me in the temple
24.20:
**“Or let these men themselves say”** — Ananias with the elders and Tertullus
**“if they found in me any iniquity”** — now
24.21: **“Except for this one voice only”** — Except for this one voice only, etc. Rabanus. He said this by antiphrasis, for he knew this pleased them, as if to say: I committed nothing except that I preached what they themselves also believe.
24.22:
**“And Felix put them off”** — to judge between them
**“having most certain knowledge of this way”** — concerning the way of truth that was in Paul, or concerning the way which they made for Paul
**“saying: When Lysias the tribune shall come down”** — He says this so as to defer judgment, and because Paul had said: from whom you will be able to know the truth.
24.23:
**“And he commanded a centurion to keep him”** — Paul
**“that he should not prohibit any of his friends to minister unto him”** — To minister to him of their own. Rabanus. To disciples and companions. Otherwise he commanded not to forbid anyone to minister to him from his goods or means.
24.25:
**“And as he treated of justice, and chastity, and of the judgment to come”**
• frightened with servile fear
• Terrified and hoping, etc. Rabanus. Join terrified and hoping thus: for these two reasons he released him into free custody, through fear of God and hope of money.
**“Felix, being terrified, answered: For this time, go thy way”** — he granted free custody
24.26:
**“Hoping also withal, that money should be given him by Paul”** — because he hoped for money
**“for which cause also oftentimes sending for him”** — Paul
24.27:
**“But when two years were ended”**
• the governorship of Felix; or from when Paul was brought to Felix, and this seems better
• Bede. The two years are said of Paul’s stay at Caesarea and not of the governorship of Felix, since it was said above that he had been judge of that nation for many years, especially as the histories relate that the apostle was sent to Rome in the second year of Nero. Claudius Caesar, at the time when he appointed Agrippa, the son of Herod whom the angel struck at Caesarea, king of the Jews, also sent Felix as procurator of the whole province, of Samaria and of Galilee.
**“Felix had for successor Portius Festus. And Felix being willing to shew the Jews a pleasure”** — by not releasing Paul
**“left Paul bound”** — Rabanus. Whether he left him living or dead? It is uncertain, but it seems better that, living, he granted the favour to the Jews.

25.1:
**“into the province”** — Rabanus. Of Palestine; as the governors of Palestine, one always succeeding another, were sent by the Romans.
**“after three days”** — from when he came
25.2: **“And the chief priests, and principal men of the Jews, went unto him against Paul”** — about to speak against
25.3: **“Requesting favour against him, that he would command him to be brought”** — Paul
25.4: **“But Festus answered: That Paul was kept in Caesarea”** — that is, more quickly
25.9: **“But Festus, willing to shew the Jews a pleasure, answering Paul, said”** — he gives the option because he was a Roman citizen
25.10:
**“Then Paul said: I stand at Caesar's judgment seat”**
• which was done for Caesar in Caesarea
• is the place of judgment
**“where I ought”** — he says this so that he might appeal to Caesar
**“to be judged”** — because here is the place of judgment
25.11:
**“For if I have injured them, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die”** — even if you wish to grant the Jews a favour
**“I appeal to Caesar”**
• I flee to his name
• I appeal to Caesar. Bede. In that he appeals to Caesar, because he hastens to go to Rome, he does so that, by persevering longer in preaching, with many believers, he may go on to Christ crowned.
25.13:
**“And after some days, king Agrippa and Bernice”**
• his wife, according to some, or a certain husband
• King Agrippa and Bernice. Bede. This Agrippa, who came to Caesarea with his wife. He was the son of Herod Agrippa, whom an angel killed, and who held the kingdom of Judea until the overthrow of Jerusalem.
25.15:
**“About whom, when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests, and the ancients of the Jews, came unto me, desiring condemnation against him”**
• of death
• according to the Roman laws
• the condemnation of Paul would be pleasing to the Jews
25.16: **“To whom I answered: It is not the custom of the Romans to condemn any man, before that he who is accused have his accusers present, and have liberty to make his answer”** — the opportunity to clear himself
25.17: **“When therefore they were come hither”** — Caesarea
25.18:
**“Against whom, when the accusers stood up, they brought no accusation”** — or evil things
**“of things which I thought ill of”** — Rabanus. By these causes, or matters, or words, of which I suspected, that is, which I expected from the accusers; or the evils of which I suspected. Otherwise: of whom, that is, of the accusers I suspected evil, who brought no cause worthy of death.
25.19:
**“But had certain questions of their own superstition against him”** — Rabanus. He called the law of both, that is, of Paul and of the Jews, superstition.
**“and of one Jesus deceased”** — according to the sense of the Jews
25.20:
**“I therefore being in a doubt of this manner of question”** — which I did not know
**“asked him whether he would go to Jerusalem”** — where wiser men
25.21:
**“But Paul appealing to be reserved unto the hearing of Augustus”** — of Nero
**“I commanded him to be kept”** — judgment
25.22: **“And Agrippa said to Festus: I would also hear the man”** — for vellem, now
25.23:
**“And on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice were come with great pomp”**
• Rabanus. That is, with a great crowd surrounding them, or with great desire to hear Paul.
• Bede. For 'ambition' the Greek has phantasia, that is, a manifold display and royal pomp of office, by which he was surrounded and thronged on every side.
**“and had entered into the hall of audience”** — a house where cases are heard before judges
25.24:
**“And Festus saith: King Agrippa”** — Jewish
**“and all ye men who are here present with us”** — Ananias and the Jews present
**“you see this man, about whom all the multitude of the Jews dealt with me at Jerusalem, requesting”** — not only at Jerusalem but also in this place, that is, at Caesarea
25.26: **“Of whom I have nothing certain to write to my lord”** — from the testimonies of someone on whose behalf he was bound

26.1: **“Thou art permitted to speak for thyself. Then Paul stretching forth his hand”** — in the manner of those preaching, or to make silence
26.2:
**“I think myself happy, O king Agrippa, touching all the things whereof I am accused by the Jews”**
• to be spoken by you
• Of all things whereof I am accused, I think myself. Bede. Another translation has this verse thus: I think myself happy before thee, beginning to give an account today. Which Jerome with his exposition puts thus: Of all things whereof I am accused by the Jews, O king Agrippa, I think myself happy, since I am to defend myself today before thee, who knowest all the customs and questions of the Jews. For he had read that saying of Isaias: Blessed is he who speaks into the ears of a wise man; and he knew that the words of a speech profit only so far as the judge’s prudence has understood them.
**“since I am”** — or you are
26.3:
**“Especially”** — I think myself blessed
**“as thou knowest all”** — because you are experienced in Jewish custom
**“that are among the Jews”** — well
**“both customs and questions”** — badly
26.5: **“Having known me from the beginning (if they will give testimony) that according to the most sure sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee”** — before you Gentiles
26.6:
**“And now for the hope”** — of the resurrection
**“that was made by God to the fathers, do I stand subject to judgment”**
• before the tribunal
• your
26.7:
**“Unto which”** — in hope of rising again
**“our twelve tribes, serving night and day”** — to God, on account of that hope
**“hope to come.”** — to be found alive or perfected
**“For which hope”** — that is, because I preach that Christ has risen
**“I am accused by the Jews.”** — O
26.8: **“Why should it be thought a thing incredible”** — Why is it judged incredible, etc. Rabanus. Or thus: King, what do you say? It is judged incredible among you, etc., by way of question, as if he said: it is not incredible; for he raised the dead beforehand as an example of what is to come, or he raises them.
26.9: **“And I indeed did formerly think, that I ought”** — as these now think
26.10:
**“Which also I did”** — not only did I think
**“when they were put to death, I brought the sentence.”** — Rabanus. Another edition: I brought sentence on those to be killed; that is, how they were to be killed, I myself gave the sentence.
**“I brought the sentence.”** — Rabanus. I judged that they should be killed. He does not say 'to be killed' unless perhaps what follows, 'punishing them, etc.' and 'raging yet more, etc.', pertains to the killing.
26.11:
**“And oftentimes punishing them, in every synagogue, I compelled them to blaspheme: and being yet more”** — than before
**“being yet more mad”** — in the likeness of a wolf
**“I persecuted them”** — from great eagerness
**“even unto foreign cities.”** — not only to the nearby ones situated in Judea
26.12:
**“Whereupon”** — in the cities or the works of that madness
**“when I was going to Damascus”** — the metropolis of Syria Phoenicia
26.14:
**“And when we were all fallen down on the ground, I heard a voice speaking to me in the Hebrew tongue”** — in which God had formerly been accustomed to speak to the fathers, so that what is said may be more readily believed
**“Saul, Saul,”** — he repeats the proper name, to show that the vision pertains to him himself
**“why persecutest thou me?”** — in the members
**“to kick against the goad.”** — Rabanus. Hitherto you have resisted without the goad; but now if you resist against the goad, you will kick, which is hard enough: the goad is correction itself.
26.16:
**“But rise up, and stand upon thy feet: for to this end have I appeared to thee, that I may make thee a minister, and a witness of those things which thou hast seen,”** — in this first vision
**“and of those things wherein I will appear to thee,”** — afterwards in many visions
26.17: **“Delivering thee from the people, and from the nations, unto which”** — or into both
26.18:
**“To open”** — for they are blind
**“their eyes,”** — inner ones
**“that they may be converted from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan”** — these are the darkness
**“to God,”** — that is, the light
**“that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and a lot”** — the inheritance
26.19: **“Whereupon, O king Agrippa, I was not incredulous to the heavenly vision”** — because that vision was shown from heaven
26.22:
**“But being aided by the help of God, I stand unto this day”** — I persevere, or I do not fall into death
**“witnessing both to small and great”** — in age or in person
26.23:
**“That Christ should suffer,”** — will be
**“that he should be the first that should rise from the dead,”**
• this is the sense of those things which the prophets foretold, and Moses
• because he rose first, not going to die again
**“should shew light to the people,”** — Israel
26.24:
**“As he spoke these things, and made his answer, Festus said with a loud voice: Paul, thou art beside thyself”**
• you are changeable, from doctrine to doctrine
• Thou art beside thyself, Paul. Bede. He thinks it madness that a man in chains, having received a place to defend himself, speaks not of the false charge which presses him but of the conscience in which he glories, and runs through the revelation by which from a persecutor he was changed into an apostle. Moreover, he discourses of the dispensation of the Redeemer and the resurrection of the dead in the manner of one preaching. But as it is a foolish madness that the son, forsaking his father, fed swine, so there is a spiritual madness of which Paul says: “Whether we be transported in mind, or whether we be sober, it is to God,” and the prophet: “He hath not had regard to vanities and lying follies.”
**“much learning doth make thee mad.”** — Rabanus. The philosophers of the Gentiles, by reading much, changed their sects.
**“mad.”** — Rabanus. Of changeableness. Or he calls madness the resurrection of the dead, which he proclaims.
26.25: **“And Paul said: I am not mad, most excellent Festus, but I speak words of truth and soberness.”** — falsehood and wantonness are proper to madness
26.26:
**“For the king knoweth of these things”** — which he told about himself and about Christ
**“to whom also I speak with confidence. For I am persuaded that none of these things are hidden from him.”** — which I have told about me or about Christ
26.27:
**“Believest thou the prophets, O king Agrippa?”** — He says this to persuade him.
**“I know that thou believest.”**
• whatever has been said about the predictions or about Christ.
• Bede. He spoke this not by flattery but truly. For Agrippa, steeped in the rite and laws of the Jews, believed that the prophets had spoken truth, but he did not know that this truth reached to Christ; although it is read that in a certain assembly held with the Jews he said: But you presume about the help of religion, since the disciples of Jesus have now filled the world; not without the will of God, we think, does that religion grow.
26.29:
**“And Paul said: I would to God”** — that is, I pray to God or Christ.
**“that both in a little and in much,”** — in age or in person, as above.
**“not only thou, but also all that hear me, this day, should become such as I also am,”** — namely Christian.
**“except these bands.”** — For I do not wish you to be bound.
26.32: **“And Agrippa said to Festus: This man might have been set at liberty”** — to be loosed from the bonds.

27.1:
**“And when it was determined”**
• Agrippa decided.
• And when it was determined, etc. Bede. In the Greek: when it was determined that we should sail into Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion.
**“that he should sail into Italy, and that Paul, with the other prisoners, should be delivered to a centurion, named Julius, of the band Augusta,”** — from the name of Augustus, who had sent soldiers.
27.2:
**“of Adrumetum”** — Rabanus. That is, sailing to Rome, according to some; but it is better derived from the name of the city in Africa which is called Hadrumetum.
**“we launched, meaning to sail by the coasts of Asia”** — they began to sail not to Italy but near the places of Asia, to the north.
**“Aristarchus, the Macedonian of Thessalonica, continuing with us.”** — The president.
27.3:
**“And the day following”** — we went out to Caesarea.
**“we came to Sidon.”** — to the north.
**“treating courteously”** — thinking.
**“Julius permitted him to go to his friends”** — into the city of Sidon in Phoenicia.
**“to go, and to take care of himself.”** — the management of the voyage.
27.4:
**“from thence”** — from Sidon.
**“when we had launched, we sailed under Cyprus”** — to the west.
**“because”** — therefore we came near Cyprus.
27.5:
**“we came to Lystra”** — Bede. In Greek, Smyrna is written instead of Lystra. But Jerome reads myrrh.
**“which is in Lycia”** — city.
27.6:
**“And there the centurion finding a ship of Alexandria”** — just as this one is called Alexandrian, so that one is Hadrumetine.
**“sailing into Italy, removed us into it”** — from one ship into another.
27.7:
**“And when for many days we had sailed slowly, and were scarce come over against Gnidus”** — island.
**“Gnidus”** — Bede. Or opposite Chios. But it is better read in some copies, opposite Gnidus, which is an island opposite Asia.
**“the wind not suffering us”** — therefore we sailed slowly.
**“we sailed near Crete”** — it is an island.
**“by Salmone”** — name of a place.
27.8:
**“And with much ado sailing by it”** — Salmone.
**“we came into a certain place”** — in Crete.
**“which is called Good-havens”** — from goodness, or it is a proper name.
27.9:
**“The fast”** — Rabanus. A great hunger in the ship, making the sailors weaker. Others say it was the forty days' fast before the Lord’s nativity, which is not probable. Better is it to think it the seventh fast, in which Goliath had been slain. Or the day of the tenth fast, in January, when the captives in Babylon learned that the temple had been destroyed.
**“was now past, Paul comforted them”** — exhorted.
27.10: **“Saying to them: Ye men, I see”** — from signs of the storms, or by the Spirit of prophecy.
27.11:
**“But the centurion believed the pilot”** — the lord of the ship.
**“and the master of the ship”**
• that is, to the shipmaster, who was the lord of the ship.
• to the shipmaster, which also signifies the lord of the ship.
27.12:
**“And whereas it was not a commodious”** — good.
**“the greatest part gave counsel to sail thence, if by any means they might reach”** — back whence they had come.
**“Phenice to winter there”** — the island or city in Crete.
**“which is a haven of Crete”** — Rabanus. The harbour of Crete is said to be that which is in Phenice, opposite Crete. They sought the harbour of Crete because they were sailing along Crete.
**“looking towards the southwest”** — toward the southwest quarter, which took its name from Africa.
**“towards the southwest”** — Bede. The southwest wind blows between the southern and western quarter, inclining more toward the west; the northwest wind, between the north and the west, turned more toward the west. And the province of Phenice had Crete to the west.
27.13:
**“And the south wind gently blowing”** — from Crete.
**“the south wind”** — because the harbour of Crete was from Boreas.
**“thinking that they had obtained their purpose”** — to reach the harbour of Crete.
**“when they had loosed from Asson”** — Rabanus. Name of the place so called, because from there ships were loosed, going forward into the sea.
27.14:
**“But not long after, there arose against it a tempestuous wind”**
• from the name of the region.
• typhos, a blowing.
**“tempestuous wind”** — Another translation: a stormy wind.
**“called Euroaquilo”** — Rabanus. Euroaquilo, that is, Boreas, a wind between the north and the east; this wind was contrary to the ship sailing for Phenice.
27.15:
**“And when the ship was caught”**
• by the wind.
• Bede. Another translation says more plainly: The ship being caught, when they could not meet the wind, the ship being given up to the waves, they began to gather in the sails; then we ran past an island which is called Cauda, which they could not take. But a boat being sent out, they began to help the ship, girding it round and drawing it, fearing lest they should run into the Syrtes. From this it is clear that, ropes having been let down on both sides from the middle of the ship’s side around its forward parts, they fastened anchors to those things that were dragged; this was done to slow the vessel, lest by a too hasty rush they should fall into the Syrtes, terrible by hearsay alone, because they snatch everything to themselves.
**“and could not bear up against the wind”** — against.
**“giving up the ship to the winds, we were driven”** — with the rowing ceased.
27.16:
**“running under a certain island, that is called Cauda, we had much work to come by the boat”**
• the boat had almost escaped.
• Bede. It is a light little boat, also made from a single hollowed tree.
**“the boat”** — Bede. It is a light little boat made of wicker, covered with raw hide, called in Greek from contemplating; because by it sailors or pirates look out over the lands and the shore. So when they had let this down into the sea to help the larger ship, they could hardly, with the surge boiling, keep it from slipping away.
27.17:
**“Which being taken up”** — from the waves.
**“they used helps”** — of the boat.
**“they used helps, undergirding the ship”**
• equipping themselves for the storm.
• By making it heavier with some vessel, whence it follows: the vessel being lowered.
**“fearing lest they should fall”**
• ship and skiff.
• Fearing lest they fall into the Syrtes, etc. Bede. Another translation: fearing lest they should fall into the Syrtes, they lowered the sail-yard and so were driven.
**“the quicksands”** — Rabanus. Narrowness or tribulation.
**“they let down the sail yard”** — that is, the skiff.
**“and so were driven”** — contrary wind.
27.18: **“And we being mightily tossed with the tempest, the next day they lightened the ship”** — the casting out of those things which were in the ship.
27.19: **“the third day they cast out with their own hands the tackling of the ship”** — implements.
27.21:
**“And after they had fasted a long time”** — voluntary because of the danger, or necessary because of want.
**“Paul standing forth in the midst of them, said: You should indeed, O ye men, have hearkened unto me, and not have loosed”**
• others: ‘to go out’.
• You should indeed, O men, having heard me, not to have loosed etc. Rabanus. As if he said: since you did not listen, whence Paul had exhorted them above. Or: I ought to have been heard, that is, that you should hear me.
**“from Crete, and have gained”**
• and thus.
• to avoid, by antiphrasis.
**“this harm”** — of the tempest.
**“and loss”** — of the vessels.
27.22:
**“And now I exhort you”** — although you did not listen to me.
**“I will with good courage”** — sound and strong.
**“to be of good cheer. For there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but only of the ship”** — that is, the loss of the ship; or except that there will be the loss of the ship.
27.23:
**“Stood by me”** — Bede. He does not say this boastfully but calls them to faith; for the sea was also stirred up so that, through what was not heard and through what was heard, a special grace might appear in him.
**“For an angel of God, whose I am”** — the apostle.
**“and whom I serve”** — in the gospel.
27.24:
**“Saying: Fear not, Paul”** — the danger of the sea.
**“thou must be brought before Caesar”** — you will not be sunk by the waves but will be in danger at Rome.
**“and behold, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee”** — and there is no need to fear even for your companions.
27.26: **“Unto a certain island”** — Rabanus. As it were a sign, the prophecy of the truth about the island is given, so that when they come to it they are certain of their safety.
27.27: **“in Adria”** — Rabanus. The region to which they were sailing. Or the name of a certain strait in the Tyrrhene sea; but it seems rather the name of that land from which the Adriatic gulf is called. Otherwise Adria is taken in the plural for Rocks, and therefore the sailors thought a region appeared. In the book of Hebrew names, Adria is said to mean containing evils, or place of evils.
27.28:
**“Who also sounding”** — the weight of lead by which the depth of the sea is explored.
**“found twenty fathoms; and going on a little further, they found”** — in the depth of the sea.
**“fifteen fathoms”** — as the land draws near.
27.29: **“Then fearing”** — because it was still night.
27.30:
**“But as the shipmen”** — who had always been in the ship.
**“sought to fly out of the ship, having let down the boat”** — that is, had let go
**“the boat into the sea, under colour”** — by occasion
**“as though they would have cast anchors out of the forepart of the ship”** — so that they might steady the ship
27.31: **“Except these stay in the ship”** — Bede. Because in a shipwreck the skill of the sailors, who were experienced in the sea, was more useful than the soldiers' arms; therefore they rightly held the boat rather than let the sailors go.
27.32: **“Then the soldiers cut off the ropes of the boat, and let her fall off”** — lest they give occasion for flight
27.33:
**“And when it began to be light, Paul besought them all to take meat”**
• so that they would be stronger for enduring the labour
• To take meat. Bede. No one escapes the storms of the world except one who is fed with the bread of life, and who in the night of tribulations leans upon wisdom, fortitude, temperance and justice; with the help of the Lord shining forth, he reaches the harbor of salvation, so that, freed from the world, he seeks the flame of love by which the inward parts are warmed.
**“saying: This day is the fourteenth day that you have waited”** — or without food, because perhaps they did not eat during the day
27.35:
**“And when he had said these things, taking bread”** — so that he might be an example to the others
**“he gave thanks to God”** — according to the customary practice at meals, and for the safety of those sailing
27.36: **“Then were they all of better cheer”** — by the word of exhortation and the example of his work
27.37: **“And we were in all in the ship, two hundred threescore and sixteen souls”** — Rabanus. He does not say “men,” because perhaps there were also women. Or it is said thus on account of the confusion of the Christian soldiers and sailors.
27.38:
**“And when they had eaten enough”** — made stronger and no longer in need of the wheat
**“they lightened the ship”** — made it lighter
27.39: **“And when it was day, they knew not the land; but they discovered a certain creek that had a shore”** — not a cliff but an easy approach
27.40:
**“And when they had taken up the anchors,”** — from the sea into the ship
**“they committed themselves to the sea,”** — without any effort of sailing
**“loosing withal the rudder bands; and hoisting up the mainsail”** — sail
**“the mainsail”** — Bede. The artemon is a small sail, adapted to steering the ship rather than to speed.
**“to the wind”** — according to the way the wind carried them
27.41:
**“And when we were fallen into a place where two seas met”**
• that is, two-seas
• Rabanus. Bithalassum, where by the interposition of land two seas meet, which sea is called in Greek thalassum.
**“where two seas met”** — Bede. The Greeks call the sea thalassa. Bithalassum means a shore stretching out into the sea, and the sea dividing itself, surrounded on this side and that.
**“they run the ship aground”** — they drove the ship onto that ridge thrown into the sea
**“and the forepart indeed, sticking fast, remained unmoveable”** — And the forepart indeed, sticking fast, remained unmoveable, etc. Bede. This ship perished because it did not glide lightly over the waves, but, driven and fixed into the bottom of the sea, it is partly held by the ground and partly borne by the force of the waves, and so is broken. Such is the fall of a soul given to the world, which, not treading down the desires of the world, fixes the prow of its intention in the earth, and so looses the framework of the work that follows by the waves of cares; but those who escaped from the broken ship make for land, because by the example of those who perish others act more cautiously.
**“but the hinder part was broken”** — was broken apart
27.42: **“And the soldiers’ counsel was, that they should kill the prisoners”** — bound
27.43: **“But the centurion, willing to save Paul, forbade it to be done; and he commanded that they who could swim, should cast themselves first into the sea”** — before the bound men
27.44:
**“And the rest”** — not swimming
**“some they carried on boards, and some on those things that belonged to the ship”** — except the planks

28.1:
**“And when we had escaped, then we knew that the island was called Melita”** — others: Mytilene
**“the island was called Melita. But the barbarians”** — inhabitants of the island
28.2:
**“For kindling a fire”**
• with fire
• Pyre. Rabanus. Some say that pyra is the name of a kind of wood.
**“they refreshed us all”** — with heat
28.3:
**“And when Paul had gathered together a bundle of sticks”**
• twigs of vines, that is, small branches supporting grapes, which, once dried, were burned
• And when he had gathered together, etc. Bede. The apostle, having come out of the sea, kindles a fire, because the fire of love warms the hearts which by teaching he rescues from the waves of the tempests. The sticks are exhortations kindling charity, plucked from the wholeness of the Scriptures, as from branches with their leaves cut off.
**“On the fire”** — Upon the fire. Bede. With the same fire by which he warms his own, he burns the beast; because by the same virtues the saints make progress, and the impious, envying along with their author, fail. Whence the prophet: “Zeal shall take hold of the unlearned people”; and: “Now the fire shall devour the adversaries.”
**“a viper coming out of the heat”** — fleeing the heat
**“fastened on his hand”**
• entered in, did not destroy
• A viper coming out of the heat, fastened on his hand, etc. Bede. Because the unclean spirit, driven from the hearts of the faithful by the flame of virtues, pours into the teachers of truth the poison of persecution, by which he may wound the hand, that is, hinder the good work.
28.4:
**“And when the barbarians saw the beast hanging on his hand, they said one to another: Undoubtedly this man is a murderer”** — because they knew that a murderer ought to die
**“who though he hath escaped the sea, yet vengeance”** — divine vengeance
28.6:
**“But they supposed that he would begin to swell up”** — according to the custom of those struck by serpents
**“and that he would suddenly fall down and die. But expecting long”** — that is, hoping that Paul would die
**“and seeing that there came no harm to him, changing their minds”** — that is, turning their faces toward one another
28.7: **“Now in these places were possessions”** — vineyards or fields
28.8:
**“And it happened that the father of Publius lay sick of a fever”** — fever from heat
**“lay sick of a fever, and of a bloody flux”** — a flux of the bowels
**“of a bloody flux”** — Dysentery, or disinteria. Bede. It is a disease of the bowels.
28.11:
**“And after three months”** — from when they first came from Asia, or from when they arrived on the island
**“we sailed in a ship of Alexandria”** — another
**“that had wintered in the island”** — Mytilene
**“that had wintered”** — of the island
**“whose sign was the Castors”**
• another reading: Castrorum
• The sign of the Castors. Rabanus. Because perhaps some camps had once been built there in ancient times. Or, to what ship: because the emblems on the sails, woven in by the sailors, were in the form of camps, or of camps, that is, of the people.
• Bede. Without the R. The twin Castors are Castor and Pollux, whom the Gentiles on this account invoke as gods at sea, because among the portents of sailors, if single stars appear on the ship or the yards, they are dangerous, but if twin stars, they are heralds of a prosperous course. Another translation: whose sign was the sons of Jove, because the fables report that Castor and Pollux were sons of Jove.
28.12: **“And when”** — And when. Bede. Why does he save the unbelieving sick man by prayer, yet of the faithful sick, Timothy and Trophimus, heals one and leaves the other, unless because the one, who was not living within, was to be healed outwardly by a miracle, whereas those who lived healthily within did not need this.
28.13:
**“From thence, compassing”** — sailing around, around Sicily
**“we came to Rhegium.”** — the city of Sicily
**“and after one day, the south wind blowing”** — which they needed, about to sail to Rome
**“the second day we came to Puteoli.”**
• the island
• many read Puteolosin
**“Puteoli”** — Puteoli is a place beyond Rome where Virgil made medicinal baths, each one inscribed with its own title, as it is said, showing against what sickness it was effective. Whence the men of Salerno, moved by envy, coming upon them with a strong hand, destroyed the titles and mutilated the buildings.
28.15:
**“the brethren had heard”** — When the brethren had heard. Rabanus. Christians living at Rome. Whence it is evident that Paul did not first preach to the Romans.
**“they came to meet us as far as Appii Forum”** — built by Appius Claudius, next to the sea
**“and the Three Taverns.”** — three houses placed on the shore, built from one foundation
**“whom when Paul saw, he gave thanks to God, and took courage.”** — he feared less
28.16:
**“And when we were come to Rome, Paul was suffered”** — by the chief of the strangers, to whom the strangers were committed
**“to dwell by himself”** — not with the other strangers
**“with a soldier that kept him.”** — that is, with one man, or with the soldiers of Lysias the tribune and of the governors Felix and Festus
28.18: **“Who, when they had examined me”** — that is, what I had done
28.19: **“But the Jews contradicting it, I was constrained to appeal unto Caesar; not that I had any thing to accuse my nation of.”** — before Caesar
28.20:
**“For this cause therefore”** — because there is no cause of death in me
**“I desired to see you, and to speak to you. Because that for the hope”** — of the resurrection
28.22: **“But we desire to hear of thee what thou thinkest; for as concerning this sect”** — of the Christians
28.23:
**“And when they had appointed him”** — the Jews, or those with Paul
**“a day, there came very many to him unto his lodgings”** — or very many
28.25:
**“And when they agreed not among themselves,”** — the faithful and the unbelievers
**“they departed, Paul speaking this one word: Well did the Holy Ghost speak”** — Well did the Holy Ghost. Bede. This prophecy, which the Apostle declares was spoken by the Holy Spirit, the prophet declares was spoken by the Lord. From this it is shown that the will and nature of the Lord and of the Holy Spirit are one, and that in the name of the Spirit the name of the Lord is also understood.
28.26:
**“Saying: Go to this people”** — Mystically, this is said to Christ and to every teacher
**“and say to them: With the ear you shall hear”** — the teaching
**“and shall not understand; and seeing”** — the signs
28.27:
**“For the heart of this people is grown gross”** — Grown gross. Bede. Lest the thickness of the heart and heaviness of the ears be thought to belong to nature and not to will, he adds the fault of free will, saying: “they have shut their eyes, lest perhaps they should see with their eyes.”
**“and with their ears have they heard heavily,”** — because they were deaf
**“lest perhaps they should see with their eyes”** — Bede. That is, they themselves by their preceding merits were the cause that God shut their eyes; or it is to be joined to what goes before, the Lord saying to the prophet: Go to the people and reproach them with the sins by which they deserved blindness, if perhaps even so they may hear and be converted to me.
**“and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them.”** — as if to say: and if they understood and were converted, I would heal them
28.28:
**“Be it known therefore to you, that this salvation of God is sent to the Gentiles”** — Christ, or the gospel
**“and they will hear it.”**
• not as the Jews
• within
28.30:
**“And he remained two whole years in his own hired lodging”** — the lodging which he himself had rented
**“hired lodging”** — Rabanus. Free custody, through which he was conducted, or in his own assembly, in which he disputed against the Jews.
**“and he received all that came in to him,”** — not only the Jews but also the Gentiles, whom he had said were to be saved, the Jews having been rejected
28.31:
**“Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching the things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, without prohibition.”**
• because no one forbade him or could forbid him
• Rabanus. In the twenty-fifth year after the Lord’s passion, that is, the second of Nero, at the same time that Festus succeeded Felix as procurator of Judea, Paul was sent to Rome in chains, and for two years, remaining in free custody, he disputed daily against the Jews concerning the coming of Christ. But it must be known that Paul was released by Nero, whose rule was not yet strengthened, in order that he might preach the gospel in the west; the time of this permission is thought to have been ten years, since the end of that two years falls at the completion of the twenty-seventh year after the Lord’s passion, that is, of Nero’s fourth year. In the twenty-seventh year of the Lord’s passion, that is, the fourteenth of Nero, Peter and Paul were crowned with martyrdom.
**“without prohibition.”** — Bede. Not only was he not forbidden to preach at Rome, but neither while Nero’s rule was still strengthened, nor while such crimes were breaking out, was he released from preaching in the western parts. Afterwards, however, that is, in the last year of Nero, he was held back by him and crowned with martyrdom.
*Jerome:* Paul enters Rome in chains that he might free those bound by the errors of superstition. Staying in a hired lodging for two years, that he may render to us the eternal gift of both Testaments. By this exposition we are taught that the other things which in this volume are written of Paul or of others not only show forth the fruit of ecclesiastical doctrine, but also have the marrow and power of the spiritual sense.

1.1:
**“Paul”**
• in Hebrew, quiet; in Greek, small; in Latin
• Bede. On the Acts of the Apostles he says that Paul came to the faith in the year of the passion and resurrection of Christ; and that in the thirteenth year after Christ’s passion he received the apostleship of the Gentiles, with Barnabas, and the name of Paul. For before he was called Saul, after Saul the persecutor, because as that one persecuted David, so this one persecuted the Church. In the fourteenth year, according to the agreement of the apostles, he set out for the teaching of the Gentiles.
*Augustine:* He chose this name for himself for no other reason than to show himself small, as the least of the apostles. Not from any boasting, but from Saul he was made Paul, that is, from proud, little. For Paul is interpreted “little” and “quiet”; Saul, “restlessness” and “temptation.”
*Ambrose:* Moreover, he is said to have done this according to the custom of the holy apostles, who, advancing in virtues, were called by a changed name, so that they might be new even in the name itself, as Cephas and the sons of thunder.
*Jerome:* Paul took this name from the first spoil he brought to the Church, namely from Sergius Paulus the proconsul, whom he converted at Cyprus.
*Origen:* In the Scriptures we find some with two names, some with three, as Solomon, who is also Ecclesiastes and Idida, and Matthew, who is also Levi. According to this custom, then, Paul also seems to us to have been called by a double name, as is plainly shown in the Acts, where it is written: “Saul, who also is Paul.”
*Jerome:* Paul means wonderful or chosen. The Lord himself called him “a vessel of election,” and made him wonderful both in life and in teaching.
**“a servant”**
• a name of humility, so that he may call others to it
• Servant. From a servant and a humble man God made an apostle and a sublime one; so may you too be humble: “he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.”
*Haimo:* Origen. A servant through love of sonship and humility, not of fear: “For you have not received the spirit of bondage,” etc. Likewise: “Therefore now he is not a servant, but a son.” And again: “I will not now call you servants, but friends.”
**“Jesus”** — the Saviour, to whom all are rightly servants, whom to serve is to reign
**“Christ”**
• king and priest
• Jesus Christ. Ambrose. Christ: in Greek; Messiah: in Hebrew; in Latin: Anointed. Christ indeed is the anointed king and priest, with invisible oil, the fullness of spiritual grace; whence: “Thy God hath anointed thee,” etc.
• Jesus Christ: he sets down the one name for the Jews, the other for the Gentiles. For “Christ” is the name known to the Jews, by which name they see and hear the Son of God designated as promised in the law; and even if he preached another, they would not believe. But to the Gentiles, because they had not read it anywhere, he puts first the saviour, that is, Jesus.
• Christ. Although it is not a proper name but a name of sacrament, like prophet and priest, it is rightly set forth as known to the Jews. Though these names were given to many, still they are only figures; for here he alone is the true king and priest.
*Augustine:* Haimo. By placing both, he testifies that there is one person of God and man.
**“called”** — by eternal election and temporal sending
**“an apostle”**
• ‘sent’, ‘envoy’ or ‘messenger’
• An apostle. Behold, from lowly, exalted. Called: not by himself but by God; or called by men, named by the privilege of the name. Separated from the teaching of the scribes and Pharisees; this is against the Jews. Or separated from the other apostles in body and not in mind; whence: “Separate me Barnabas and Paul for the work whereunto I have taken them.”
**“separated”** — from the womb of the Synagogue, in which he was as one dead
**“unto the gospel of God”**
• to be preached
• behold the office
• commendation of the gospel by the four
• Gospel. Haimo. It is a good announcement that leads to salvation; and it concerns those things that pertain to faith and morals. Of God, not invented by man.
1.2:
**“Which”**
• from the time
• fulfilment
• It came not suddenly but was promised long before its fulfilment. Whence in this word the saying is true: “It is one man that soweth, and it is another that reapeth.”
**“he had promised”**
• from the author
• God the Father
• freely
• as a useful and necessary thing
**“by his prophets”**
• by the commended witnesses
• who are great from God, not from themselves
• Through the prophets. Haimo. Whence Jeremias: “Behold the days shall come, and I will perfect a new testament unto the house of Israel, and unto the house of Juda.” And likewise: “I will make an everlasting covenant with you.” The others likewise.
**“in the holy scriptures”**
• lest they give them over to forgetfulness
• not only in words
• Holy. Not of the Gentiles.
• Holy, because they condemn vices and contain the sacraments of the one God and the incarnation of the Son of God.
1.3:
**“Concerning”** — made
**“his Son”** — because all lead to the Son
**“his”**
• his own. Commendation of the gospel from its subject matter.
• His. His own, consubstantial with himself, coeternal, coequal. Made: only according to the flesh.
*Augustine:* And though unmade according to the divine nature. So great is the union of both natures that the whole is called God, the whole man; and in turn man is called God, and God man; which is not so in the substances of man.
**“who was made to him”**
• to his honor
• Who was made to him. Who was made according to the flesh, by the work of the Holy Spirit, of the Virgin, that is, born. This meets the impiety of the heretics, who with dull heart, understanding this passage, take Christ to be only man. For by adding “according to the flesh,” he reserved to the divinity its own dignity, in which Christ is the Word of God, by whom all things were made.
*Origen:* He was made according to the flesh, God made man, who even in assuming flesh did not cease to be God, remaining unchangeable, while the changeable man was assumed, the nature of man assumed not diminishing his nature.
