*Augustine:* He who was, was made; the Word was, the Son of God was; he was made the son of man. He took up humanity; he did not lose divinity. Born according to the truth of nature of God, the Son of God; and according to the truth of nature of man, the son of man; so that not by adoption or by name, but truly, in each nativity, he would have the name of son by being born.
*The same:* The Son of God is therefore equal to God the Father in nature, less in condition; in the form of God, the Word begotten of God. In the form of a servant he was made of a woman. In the form of God he made man. In the form of a servant he was made man; in each, both God and both man.
*The same:* The Word was made flesh, yet not converted and changed into what was made, but clothed with flesh, that he might appear suitably clothed for those of flesh.
**“John Damascene”** — Both forms are in Christ, because both substances are true and full in Christ. For the natures are united to each other without change and without alteration, neither does the divine depart from its own simplicity, nor is the human either changed into the nature of the deity or into non-existence, nor was one composite nature made out of the two.
*Augustine:* Christ therefore is one person of twofold substance; yet God and man cannot be called a part of this person. Otherwise the Son of God, before he took the form of a servant, was not whole, and grew when man was added to his divinity.
*Ambrose:* “Not always to have been made” refers to creation, as there: “Lord, thou hast been made our refuge.” For the definition or publication of creation is not declared here, but he is said to be a refuge for us, which he was not before.
*Augustine:* Who was made, etc. This word signifies something. For because the flesh of the Lord was not conceived from human seed in the Virgin’s womb and made a body, but by the working and power of the Holy Spirit, therefore the Apostle says made, not born.
*The same:* Although the seed of man did not intervene in the conception of the Virgin, yet because Christ was formed from that flesh which comes from seed, he is rightly said to be made of the seed. Yet he is not therefore a creature. Whence: “All things were made by him.” It says “all things” only of what were made, that is, every creature; whence it plainly appears that he is not made, by whom all things were made.
**“Hilary”** — For he is the true and proper Son by origin, not by adoption; in truth, not in name; by birth, not by creation.
**“of the seed of David”**
• commendation of the author from four things, first from origin
• Of the seed of David. Augustine. Haimo. Because Mary was of David. The promise was made to Abraham and to David, but he preferred here to say David, who was also sinful, not Abraham the just, so that he might be thought born of him not by merit but by grace; and so that he might be shown born of a king according to the flesh, as he was born a king of God before the ages.
**“according to”** — made, lest he be thought man only and not according to divinity
**“the flesh”** — because: “And the Word was made flesh,” etc.
1.4:
**“who was predestinated the Son of God”**
• according as man, chosen by grace alone, that he might be the Son of God, in the same power and virtue of divinity with the Father, through the union of the Word
• commendation from power
• Who was predestined. Predestination is the preparation of grace, by which from eternity God prepared, without merits, good things for the man Christ and for all whom he foreknew, to be made conformable to the image of his Son.
• Foreknowledge concerns good and evil; predestination is only of the just.
• Predestination is not foreknowledge, which pertains equally to good and bad. But it is the ordering and preparation of helping those whom divine providence finds worthy; it is properly said only of the good.
• Ambrose. Whatever the Word of the Father has by nature, the son of the Virgin has by grace.
*Ambrose:* Who was predestinated: he who lay hidden in the flesh as to what he was, was predestinated, that is, foreknown from eternity to be manifested the Son of God in the power of rising again; but when they rise. And he says not “by the resurrection of Christ” but “of the dead,” which is a greater power, because his resurrection makes the general resurrection. Whence he seems to have destroyed death in order to redeem us; wherefore he also calls him our Lord, who gave both such grace and the power of the apostleship in his stead.
*Augustine:* This so great and so lofty a union of the human nature was predestinated, so that it would have nowhere higher to be raised; just as for us the divinity itself had nowhere lower to abase itself than by taking up the nature of man with the infirmity of flesh even to the death of the cross.
*Haimo:* The Apostle here speaks not of the Word but of the man, who did not exist before he was made. For that humanity, which was not before, was predestined.
*Augustine:* For the most brilliant light of predestination and grace is the mediator of God and men himself, “the man Christ Jesus.” For that man, that he might be assumed by the Word, co-eternal with the Father, into the unity of person and be the only-begotten Son of God, whence did he merit this? What good of his, of whatever kind, went before, that he should come to this ineffable excellence? It was by the Word of God making and receiving him. The man himself, from the moment he began to be, began to be the only Son of God. That woman full of grace conceived of the Holy Spirit; of the Virgin Mary the only God was born, not by the desire of the flesh, but by the sole gift of God. In that man the will was free, and the more so the less he was able to sin.
*The same:* Rightly indeed is the Son of God said to be predestinated, not according to that which he is, the Word of God, God with God. For why should he be predestinated, when he already was, who was already everlasting, without beginning and without end? But that was to be predestinated which was not yet, that so in its own time it should come to be, as before times it had been predestinated that it should come to be. Whoever therefore denies that the Son of God was predestinated, denies that same one to be the Son of man. Jesus therefore was predestinated, that he who was to be according to the flesh the son of David, should be in power the Son of God.
**“in power”** — which can be seen from this, that he was conceived of the Holy Spirit
**“according to”** — according to; is also confirmed
**“the spirit of sanctification”**
• commendation from grace
• According to the spirit of sanctification. Let it be joined thus: “Who was made to him of the seed of David, according to the flesh.” Made indeed according to the Spirit of sanctification, that is, according to the operation of the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies men and who sanctified Christ the man in the virginal womb.
*Augustine:* Or the Son of God is proved because he gave his own the Spirit of sanctification, beginning from the resurrection of the soul, that is, the remission of sins, of those dead in sins, of Christ’s own, whom no other could heal. For there is a twofold resurrection, of the soul and of the body. Of the resurrection of the soul the Apostle says in what follows: “Rise thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead: and Christ shall enlighten thee.”
**“by the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead”**
• because he made to rise with himself the dead who were his, that is, who were to be raised by him
• Whence many bodies of those who had slept rose again with him.
• Of the dead of Christ. “Of Christ” for “of his” or “of his own”: he put the proper name for the pronoun, after the Hebrew manner; this way of speaking is most usual in the Scriptures, especially the old ones, as: “Moses did as the Lord commanded Moses.”
1.5:
**“By whom”**
• Behold what the author is to him.
• commendation from liberality
**“we have received grace”**
• remission of sins, endurance of labours
• and other gifts
**“and apostleship”** — authority or commission to preach
**“for obedience to the faith”** — that I might make them obey the faith
**“in all nations”**
• Jews by cohabitation are among the Gentiles.
• Among all nations. Not only to the Jews, among whom, since they were called without the law, they ought not to act under the law.
**“for his name”**
• in his place, or extending his name
• For his name. For his glory, not ours, as you do.
1.6:
**“Among whom are you”**
• that he may admonish them more familiarly, he turns himself to them
• among which nations
**“you also”** — Romans
**“the called of Jesus Christ”**
• by grace from him, through inner calling; or that you may be his through outer calling
• Called of Jesus Christ. That is, from him, but of Jesus Christ: the genitive for the ablative, after the Greek manner.
1.7:
**“To all”** — To all: he writes.
**“that are at Rome, the beloved of God”**
• who are at Rome, beloved of God; not to others
• Beloved of God. For he loved us first, before all merits, so that we, being loved, might love him in return.
**“called to be saints”**
• that is, those whom he loved, so that he might call them to holiness
• Called saints. Not called because they are saints, but made saints because they are called, and called because they are beloved.
**“Grace to you”**
• first greets
• remission of sins
**“and peace”**
• reconciliation and tranquillity of mind
• Grace to you and peace. Augustine: In this greeting the Trinity itself and likewise the unchangeable unity is recognized. The unity by this, that he says: from God.
*Haimo:* He did not put the name of the Holy Spirit, because he comprehends him in his gifts, that is, in grace and piety.
**“from God”** — to God
**“our Father, and from the Lord”** — from him who wills and is able
**“Jesus Christ”** — without whom there are no goods for us
1.8:
**“First indeed”** — first to soothe, afterwards about to rebuke severely
**“I give thanks”** — I give thanks. To give thanks is to perceive that all things are given by God, and to praise him for them in heart, voice and deed.
**“my God”**
• whom I make mine, which you do not
• To my God. Not idly. For this word can belong only to the saints, of whom God is said to be the God, as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. For although there is one God of all by nature, yet he is said to be properly theirs by grace, who are proved by the merit of faith and justice to be his worshippers.
**“through Jesus”**
• mediator of God and men
• not through the law, not through prophecy
**“Christ”** — because he himself is the minister of God’s benefits
**“for you all”**
• that you yourselves also should do
• For all of you. Although for others, first for you, from whom great benefit comes, through Christ the mediator, through whom God gave you all good things.
**“because your faith is spoken of”**
• he does not praise their faith as perfect, but their readiness and desire toward Christ
• even if not perfect
• Because your faith. Ambrose: He rejoices in the good thing begun by them, by which he shows love toward them and exhorts them to progress. He says he does this above all, because their faith benefits many.
**“in the whole world”** — because Rome is the head of the world, whence many might profit
1.9:
**“For God is my witness”**
• the authority set forth above
• and therefore it is not safe to lie
• A witness: I impute to the Lord that you have faith, for I pray to him that it be had. Or he explains when he gives thanks in prayers, namely also how without ceasing.
• A witness. An oath is to be made in necessary matters when men are slow to believe what is useful to them. An oath is not good in itself, yet not evil when it is necessary, although it proceeds from the evil of weakness in those to whom something is said.
*Jerome:* On Jeremiah, in the second chapter. It must be noted that an oath has these companions: truth, judgment and justice; but if these fail, it will by no means be an oath but perjury.
**“whom I serve in my spirit”**
• that is, with the will, or with spiritual things, namely by faith and charity
• not in the flesh, that is, by carnal observances
**“in the gospel”**
• in which
• preaching, not in the law, not in circumcision, not in what Moses the servant handed down, but
**“of his Son”** — which the Son handed down, not by writing but by inspiring minds
**“that without ceasing”** — of you
*Ambrose:* God is mindful when he gives, forgetful when he ceases.
**“I make a commemoration of you”** — I make a commemoration of you, etc. He says this so that they may love him and desire to hear him.
1.10:
**“Always”** — at the set hours appointed for prayer
**“in my prayers”** — which for me and for others
**“making request”**
• not only do I pray but also beseech
• testing
• In my prayers beseeching. Prayer is for obtaining good things. Beseeching is a strict prayer in necessity. It is also an adjuration to God by sacred things, as by his passion, by his death or nativity, and the like.
**“if by any means”**
• prosperous or adverse
• for whatever cause, easily or with difficulty
**“at length”** — after long desires
**“now”** — in winter or summer
**“I may have a prosperous journey”** — as if: which I do not reckon to be a prosperous journey unless I arrive at you
**“by the will of God, to come unto you”**
• not as the wicked in their wickedness
• for then the coming is profitable
1.11:
**“For I long”**
• therefore I beseech
• For I long. That what he could not persuade with words, he might persuade in person by the power of miracles.
**“to see you”** — because what he writes can be taken perversely, and to persuade by power
**“that I may impart”** — that is, I will make you partakers
**“unto you some spiritual grace”**
• of the gratuitous benefit of God
• of teaching
**“to strengthen you”** — because you already have something
1.12:
**“That is to say”**
• for such strengthening is so welcome, as if
• namely, that you be strengthened
**“together”** — as if: my comfort will be made
**“may be comforted in you”**
• because he grieves over the not upright faith
• or: 'that is, that we may be comforted with you,' another reading
• that strengthening from God is welcome to me, as if he said that, namely that you be strengthened, is my being comforted in you; he adds 'together', as if to say this my comfort will be made together with you, because you too will be comforted
• To be comforted. Now I am desolate, so are you, even if you do not feel it; but thus we would be comforted.
**“by that which is common to us both, your faith and mine”**
• that is, common, or which works through love
• or: your faith and mine
• not a new faith but mine and yours, which is mutually common, that is, if we are of one and the same faith in Christ
1.13:
**“And I would not have you ignorant, brethren”**
• Haimo. Why then do you not come? Because I am hindered, which I want you to know, and you think it is your fault, so that you now make yourselves worthy
• concerning the faith, because I purposed
• Brethren. Because they are reborn and some are upright. Whence above, called saints.
**“that I have often purposed to come unto you”** — not only did I wish
**“and”** — with some hindrances, God so doing
**“have been hindered”** — to come
**“hitherto”** — until the present
**“that I might have some fruit among you”** — that is, that you might bear fruit through my preaching, or that I might gain a reward for you. As if to say: therefore I desire to come.
**“even as among other Gentiles”** — By the example of these he provokes them.
1.14:
**“to the Greeks and barbarians”**
• which I do therefore because I am a debtor to all nations
• Greeks and barbarians. He is silent about the Jews, because he is the teacher of the Gentiles.
• Greeks. He puts the Greeks first, because all worldly philosophy took its beginning from them.
• Barbarians. He calls barbarians those who are, as it were, outside the laws, who are neither Hebrews, nor Greeks, nor Latins.
**“to the wise”**
• so that no one from either people is excluded
• Haimo. Taught in worldly reasonings
**“and to the unwise”** — unskilled in those reasonings
**“I am a debtor”**
• to evangelize
• and as I owe to others, so also to you, because I am a debtor to all
1.15:
**“So, as much as is in me”** — and as I owe to others, so also to you, because I am a debtor to all
**“I am ready to preach the gospel to you also that are at Rome”** — As if to say: even if I am prepared for these things, therefore the fault of another has remained.
1.16:
**“For I am not ashamed of the gospel”**
• ready in me
• touches those who had handed down what was not right
• For I am not ashamed of the gospel. Like those who preach falsehoods; or who think the cross of Christ a disgrace. Therefore I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is a power, that is, because it announces the power of God, not weakness; wisdom, not folly. For “the weakness of God is stronger than men; and the foolishness of God is wiser than men.” Or it is a power to the believer, by which sin is forgiven, and when the matter requires, miracles are done by which the doctrine is commended.
**“For it is the power of God”**
• to us, not to others
• binds to faith, gives salvation to every believer, remits sins, justifies, and preserves from the second death
• For the power of God. Because the incredible preaching is confirmed by signs, which is not the case with false preachers.
**“unto salvation”** — being strong
**“to every one that believeth”** — what it says, “to everyone,” determines
**“to the Jew first”**
• believing
• To the Jew first. Hesychius. As if to say: especially, and to all, the Jew first. He puts the Jew forward, because of the fathers; yet here too he needs the gospel. What need then is there of the law?
**“and to the Greek”** — to all Gentiles
1.17:
**“For the justice of God”**
• is for salvation to the believer, because it is to him for justice, which is clearly shown in the gospel itself
• For the justice of God. Haimo. Ambrose. It is that by which he freely justifies the ungodly through faith without the works of the law, as elsewhere: “that I may be found in him, not having my justice, which is of the law, but that which is of the faith,” which the gospel reveals while it gives faith to man, by which he is justified who believes God to be just and true in his promises. This is against the Jews, who deny that this is the Christ whom God promised.
**“is revealed”** — Is revealed. Augustine. He attacks the Gentiles according to their former state, because they boasted of a good nature and excused their shameful deeds by ignorance. But the Apostle says on the contrary that they had earlier had knowledge, and lost it by fault, and that the good nature left to themselves was cast headlong into all evils. Having commended the piety of faith, by which, being justified, we ought to be pleasing to God, he adds, detesting the contrary, that puffed up by themselves they fell into idols.
**“from faith unto faith”**
• from faith is justice, and so salvation, as Habacuc says, not from the law
• From faith: of God promising, unto the faith of man who believes him. Or from faith unto faith, on account of all the parts of faith: from the faith of the Old Testament, where there is one God, unto the faith of the New, where there are the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. From the faith of the first coming unto the faith of the second. From the faith of the first resurrection unto the faith of the second. From the faith of promise unto the faith of fulfilment. From the faith of the preachers unto the faith of the peoples. From the faith of the sowers unto the faith of the reapers. He has justice who passes from faith to faith, so that the Jew and anyone else may pass from the faith of the Old Testament to the faith of the New, and from the faith of words and hope to the faith of realities and of sight.
*Augustine:* “Faith is that by which are believed those things which are not seen.” There is also faith when one believes, not by words but by present realities, what will be when God shall give himself to be seen. He says therefore from the faith of words, by which we believe what we do not see, unto the faith of realities, by which we shall obtain what we believed.
**“as it is written: The just man liveth by faith”**
• Augustine. The just man lives by faith, and so lives eternal life, which is the reward of faith. “The just man liveth by faith.”
• As it is written. In Habacuc it is thus: “But the just shall live in his faith.” But this and many other testimonies which he sets down seem to differ from the translation of the Hebrew truth which we now use, because sometimes he takes from the Septuagint interpreters, and sometimes, as speaking by the same Spirit as the prophets, he takes only the sense, using his own words and his own arrangement.
1.18:
**“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven”**
• coming to judgment
• Is revealed, etc. From faith is justice, and thence salvation; because from ungodliness is injustice, and thence wrath, that is, punishment; and this same is revealed in the gospel. Or it is revealed from heaven, because it accuses them, for it showed them the creator or the saviour. For from the very fabric of heaven God is shown angry with them, who made the stars so beautiful that from them it might be known how great and how wonderful their creator is, and so he alone be adored.
**“against all ungodliness and injustice”**
• not all the impious, but all the parts of impiety and injustice
• idolaters
• Against all ungodliness. Ungodliness is sinning against God, iniquity against men. Or the impious is the unbeliever, as the idolater is. The unjust is one who by the wickedness of his work departs from fairness.
**“of men”** — which proceeds from their fault
**“of those that detain the truth of God”**
• having true knowledge of God concerning God
• Of those who detain the truth. As if: why is there wrath against them for ungodliness, since they have not known God? To which: they could indeed have known, but they take it from themselves, preferring to dwell unjustly in their pleasure.
**“detain in injustice”**
• remaining in evil work
• since it offers itself to them willingly
• They hold the truth of God. Because it is said that what is knowable of God is in them. As if: they have within themselves that by which they may know, namely natural reason.
• They hold in injustice. The good is what they hold, but the evil is where they hold it. For they hold the truth, but in iniquity. You have found God, you have found truth, and you hold it in injustice; and what you knew through the works of God, you have lost through the works of man.
*Augustine:* You have considered the whole order of things and do not want to attend to the fact that the world is the work of God, an idol the work of a craftsman. If the craftsman, as he gave the idol its shape, were to give it a heart too, the craftsman would be adored by the idol itself. Who then is your God? Is it not he who made you?
1.19:
**“because that which is known of God”**
• For there are many things about God that cannot be known through nature, such as the mystery of redemption and incarnation
• that is, knowable of God
• What is known of God. Gregory. It is what we can attain from the disposition of this world and its natural order. The unknown of God, however, is what lies hidden from every creature, such as the substance or nature of his being, and the mystery of human deliverance.
**“is manifest in them”**
• by the guidance of reason
• It is manifest in them. Augustine. Because not only did natural reason help toward this, but God also helped daily, lest natural reason seem to suffice alone.
**“For God hath manifested it unto them”** — through his work, not through teaching or inspiration
1.20:
**“For the invisible things of him”**
• The Father.
• what is known of God is manifest in them, because
• The invisible things. Haimo. He shows what they could know of God. He speaks in the plural, because he is known in many ways, namely, that he is eternal, almighty, and the like. The invisible things understood by the things that are made: because through heaven and earth and the other creatures, which they understood to be immense and everlasting, they perceived with the mind the Maker himself, incomparable, immense, eternal.
**“from the creation of the world”**
• or from the constitution of the world
• from man, not only from angels
• From the creation. From man, by excellence, because he excels among the other creatures; or on account of the fitness he has with all creatures. For he is in place locally with bodies, he feels with the animals, he understands with the angels. Whence: “Preach the gospel to every creature.”
**“by the things that are made”** — through those things, even if not through the law
**“are clearly seen, being understood”** — not by a bodily or imagined vision but by an intellectual one
**“his eternal”** — who governs all things
**“his power”**
• The Son.
• is seen
**“and divinity”**
• The Holy Spirit.
• goodness which fills all things
**“so that they are inexcusable”** — concerning this
1.21:
**“when they knew”**
• through natural reason and the revelation of creation
• When they knew, etc. Augustine. They saw whither they ought to come, but, ungrateful to him who had granted them to see, they wished to ascribe to themselves what they saw, and, having become proud, lost even what they saw. For what they found by curiosity they lost by pride. For what God had given freely he took away from the ungrateful.
**“God”** — so much so that they confessed one principle of all things
**“have not glorified him as God”** — by living well and worshipping
**“or given thanks”** — concerning the knowledge; but they attributed it to themselves, in which they were vain and false
**“but became vain”** — thinking themselves to be some thing, whereas they are nothing
**“in their thoughts”** — that is, from themselves, not from God
**“and”** — therefore
**“their foolish heart was darkened”**
• gradually, until their heart was led down to foolishness
• the swelling of pride overshadowing
• Obscured. Ambrose. For a mist of error has covered their heart, because when they had known the Creator from creatures, and no longer glorified him as God, they became dull
**“their heart”** — that is, reason, which was believed by them to be
1.22:
**“For professing”** — by mouth or by heart
**“themselves to be”** — behold how they became vain
**“wise”** — from themselves, not from God
**“they became fools”**
• in God
• behold how the heart was darkened
• They became fools. Behold how the heart was darkened, which is vengeance: wise in the natures of things, foolish in God
1.23:
**“And they changed”**
• they sinned not only in sense but also in deed
• as far as concerns themselves
**“the glory of the incorruptible God”**
• the worship due to the incorruptible God
• And they changed, etc. Augustine. Here he condemns the idols of the impious; some worshipped earth, others the sun and such things
**“into the likeness of the image of a corruptible”**
• into the image of him to whom it was likened
• first
• Into the likeness of the image. He exaggerates the folly to show the heaping up of dullness
**“man”**
• afterwards
• greater dullness
**“and of birds”** — thence
**“and of fourfooted beasts, and of”** — then
**“creeping things”** — Of man, and of birds, and of fourfooted beasts. From of old it was the custom among the Romans to worship images of men, as of Romulus, Jupiter, and others, especially from the coming of Aeneas into Italy. But of birds and fourfooted beasts and creeping things, from the time that Alexandria was conquered by Augustus and subjected to Rome.
1.24:
**“Wherefore”** — idolatry, namely
**“God gave them up”**
• by withdrawing grace he permitted them to be delivered
• Delivered up. Because nothing happens without his permission. First into the desires of their heart, which was theirs, left to themselves by God; and afterwards into uncleanness in act so great that they applied bodies naturally repugnant by a certain force, and made them more fit for vice
*Augustine:* It is manifest that God works in the hearts of men to incline their wills wherever he wills, whether to good things by his mercy, or to evil things according to their deserts, by his judgment, at times hidden, at times open, but always just.
**“to the desires”** — in the desires; behold vengeance
**“of their heart”** — that is, prepared thus by themselves, not by God.
**“unto uncleanness”** — afterwards in act.
**“to dishonour”** — as far as concerns themselves, or as far as concerns nature.
**“their own bodies”**
• likewise vengeance.
• Dishonour. Gregory. For a sin which is not washed away by penance soon by its own weight draws to another. Whence it comes about that it is not only a sin but also the cause of sin. For from it the following fault arises. But the sin that arises from sin is not only a sin but also the punishment of sin, because by just judgment God darkens the heart of the sinner, so that by the desert of the preceding sin he falls even into another.
**“among themselves”** — not having it from elsewhere but from themselves, or in their own sex.
1.25:
**“Who”** — they affect
**“changed the truth of God into a lie”**
• that is what above he called the glory of God
• what is true of God they gave to the idol, namely that it is God
• Because they defiled. He pursues the fault and the punishment more fully, part by part, so that it may be compared.
• Who changed. He shows that they changed the glory of God in parts, namely that they thought him God who was not, and worshipped him. And he follows out the parts of uncleanness: women with women, men with men, in which he compares the punishment to the fault, that as they sinned against nature, they might be punished in their own nature. Whence he concludes: and the recompense is due.
• They changed the truth into a lie. Ambrose. Because they gave the name of God, who is true, to those who are not gods.
*Augustine:* The truth of the creature is from God but is not God; they turned it into a lie, worshipping creatures as the Creator.
**“and worshipped”**
• by carefully adorning
• And they worshipped. But lest they say, I do not worship images but their realities, such as the sun, he adds: and they worshipped, etc.
**“and served the creature”**
• in deed
• by actions
• They served the creature. Here he condemns what they understood in the images.
**“rather than the Creator”** — as if that were better
**“who is”**
• yet
• although he is deprived of his honor by them
**“blessed”** — exalted above all things
**“for ever”** — without end
**“Amen.”**
• What they say is falsehood.
• Amen. As if to say: this is true, that to the true God there is blessing forever, but to the gods of the nations impiety gives honor for a time. Therefore what they say is falsehood.
1.26:
**“For this cause”**
• Likewise vengeance.
• because they so sinned against nature.
• as if: because they so sinned against the creating nature.
• again vengeance is repeated, as the fault was before.
**“delivered them up”** — He permitted them to be given up.
**“God delivered them up to shameful affections”**
• first in the burning of lust, which is a passion of nature and not to be named; afterwards in act.
• Passions. That is, pleasures, which, even if they delight, are passions of nature.
• Ignominy. Haimo. It is said as if 'without the name of dignity'. Ignominious is he who ceases to have the name of dignity, when he is caught in some crime.
**“For”** — and truly.
**“their women have changed”** — or exchanged.
**“the natural use”**
• lawful husbands.
• The natural use. Do you think, Julian, that the Apostle praised lust by this, because he said that the use of the woman is natural? You will be compelled to praise every use of a woman, and by this you will also praise the debaucheries committed with women, because there too the use is natural, though it is to be condemned because it is not lawful. Whence the children born of it are called not lawful but natural. So the Apostle did not praise the concupiscence of the flesh in that word, but called natural use that use by which human nature can continue by being born. He did not say conjugal use, but wished that to be understood as natural which takes place in members created for this, that by them both sexes may be joined for generation.
• Ambrose. And by this, when someone is joined with a harlot with the same members, the use is natural, yet not praiseworthy but blameworthy. For if anyone, even with his wife, uses that part of the body which was not appointed for generation, it is against nature and shameful.
**“into that use”** — acting among themselves.
1.27:
**“And, in like manner, the men also, leaving the natural use of the women, have burned in their lusts”**
• sin of the will.
• behold, sin of the will or of desire.
**“one towards another”** — which is from themselves, not from God.
**“men with men”**
• not only burned, but also
• Men with men. Augustine. For by the judgment of the most just God they were delivered up, whether by forsaking them or in some other way, explicable or inexplicable, to shameful passions, that crimes might be avenged by crimes. And the punishments of sinners are not only torments, but also increases of vices.
**“working that which is filthy”** — in act.
**“and”** — so.
**“receiving the recompense which was due”** — it was vengeance, fitting and worthy of the sin.
**“of their error”**
• for the error.
• And receiving the recompense which, etc. Augustine. But few see these punishments; therefore the Apostle especially recalls them, and enumerates many things which are sins and punishments of sin. For between the sin itself of apostasy and the last punishment of eternal fire, the things in between are both sins and punishments.
• It was fitting. Here the cause, on account of which they were delivered up, is shown without any doubt.
**“in themselves receiving”** — avenging God in their own nature.
1.28:
**“And as”**
• or 'because'.
• And as. Likewise, because they do not yet repent, they fall into others for the same fault. By 'as' he likens the punishment to the sin. For those sinning in agreement with God are punished in what is their own.
**“they liked not to have God in their knowledge”** — Because they did not know God, whom reason proves; or because they thought God did not know and disregarded evils, he delivered them up.
**“God delivered them up to a reprobate sense”**
• that they understand nothing except what is remote from uprightness
• And because they did not approve. Because they did not keep God in their knowledge, which reason approved, or because they thought God did not know of evils and neglected them: He delivered them up, etc.
**“to do those things”** — in deed
**“which are not convenient”** — to reason or to nature
1.29:
**“Being filled”** — them
**“with all iniquity”**
• having not a little
• With all iniquity. He enumerates the parts that he may accuse more plainly. Malice is when someone plots harm against another. Wickedness is rashness, when one dares what he cannot, or lack of self-restraint. Contention is the assault upon truth by confident clamour. Malignity is ill will, when it can do no more, or the failure to return thanks for benefits.
**“malice”** — by parts
**“fornication”** — fornication: every use outside lawful marriage
**“avarice”** — which is to acquire much and not to distribute the superfluous to the poor
**“wickedness, full of envy”** — by grief at another’s good
**“murder”** — in the plural because they are acts of the will
**“contention, deceit”** — when one thing is pretended and another done
**“malignity, whisperers”** — sowing discords among friends
1.30:
**“Detractors”** — Detractors: those who deny or pervert the goods of others.
**“hateful to God”** — Hateful to God. Lest whispering or detraction be thought a light matter, because they are in words, he adds of them: hateful to God, so that they may understand that by whispering and detraction alone they can incur eternal damnation.
**“contumelious”** — who inflict insults and shameful things by words or deeds
**“proud, haughty”**
• in honours
• Haughty: those who will not suffer a superior or an equal.
**“inventors of evil things”** — who devise a new kind of any evil by word or deed
**“to parents”** — to carnal or spiritual parents
**“disobedient”** — but more untamed than wild beasts
1.31:
**“Foolish”** — not discerning between good and evil
**“dissolute”**
• in dress and gait
• Disorderly: disorder of works or of the body shows the quality of the mind.
**“without affection”** — by love of neighbour
**“without fidelity”** — in fellowship
**“without mercy”** — do not sympathize with the wretched
1.32:
**“Who”**
• Likewise they also fall further
• before
**“having known the justice of God”** — the just God
**“known”** — with reason as their guide
**“did not understand”** — yet
**“that they who do such things are worthy of death”**
• eternal
• Worthy of death. Lest they be thought to be punished only by those things in which they delight, he adds the final death, eternal death.
**“not only they that do them, but they also that consent to them that do them.”**
• that no one be excused
• Who consent. To consent is to keep silent when you could rebuke, or to foster error.

2.1:
**“Wherefore thou art inexcusable”**
• because everyone who does and consents is worthy of death
• Wherefore thou art inexcusable. Here he speaks commonly of the Gentiles and the Jews. The Jew judged the Gentile on account of his former state; the Gentile the Jew; each a man, not a spirit. If the Jew judges the Gentile for idolatry, they too are idolaters. If the Gentile judges the Jew for transgression of the law, he too is a transgressor of the natural law.
• Inexcusable. Because you yourself are a witness to your own condemnation, while you judge another: why this? Because you do the same things.
**“O man, whosoever thou art that judgest.”**
• both Jew and Gentile alike
• Who judge. In which he shows himself to be what he is not, that is, just.
• Thou that judgest. This is on account of the Jews, even if he does not yet name them expressly, who glory in the law and do what they condemn; and because he does not yet name them expressly, therefore he says: “Wrath upon every soul of man that worketh evil, of the Jew and of the Greek.” And glory to every one that worketh good, to the Jew and to the Greek.
**“For wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself. For thou dost the same things which thou judgest.”** — For you do the same things. The Apostle destroys by his own authority the empty excuse of the Gentiles and of the Jews; for a Jew could plead an excuse for his sin: even if I do the same things, my race and the law defend me as a Jew, and ignorance me as a Gentile; the Apostle speaks against this.
2.2:
**“For we know”**
• As if to say: you think so, but we know.
• or truly you are inexcusable
**“For”** — or 'but'
**“that the judgment of God is, according to truth”** — the equity of the matter, not persons
**“against”** — against
**“them that do such things.”**
• whether Jews or Gentiles
• Who do such things. Haimo. Those who do the things they rebuke in others. Those who in judgment regard the persons of the powerful, the rich, and their relatives.
2.3:
**“And thinkest thou this”**
• a rebuke with irony
• we know so, but you think
• you suppose
• But do you think? This chapter is commonly read against Jews and Gentiles; yet it can also be read specially against any superstitious prelate of the Church.
**“O man”** — fleshly
**“that judgest them”** — Augustine. Because this power is given to you, and there is no one in the world who judges you; this as regards prelates.
**“who do such things”** — those mentioned above
**“and dost the same”** — that is, this
**“that thou shalt escape”**
• in whatever way
• That thou shalt escape. You sin the more gravely while you promise yourself impunity, because you despise the goodness of God and do not know that you despise it; and do you do this? A rebuke as if in wonder.
**“the judgment of God?”** — why then does he not punish now? Because he is good and waits, which you do not know; or the riches
2.4:
**“Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness”**
• abundant goodness
• Or despisest thou the riches. Ambrose. Abundant is the goodness which bestows many good things on sinners, or on many sinners, coaxing them to draw them to penance. Abundant is the patience which bears with so many and such great sinners and does not punish quickly. And this is of longsuffering, because it is not for an hour, but waits long through many times. He despises these who does not use them for penance as God intends, but turns them to impunity.
**“and patience”** — patience and longsuffering
**“and longsuffering?”**
• Augustine. Because now is the time of mercy.
• Of patience and longsuffering. Augustine. Patience is that by which he does not at once punish those who sin through pride and a froward mind. Longsuffering is that by which he long bears with those who sin through weakness and not through the malice of a deliberate mind, waiting for penance.
**“Knowest thou not, that the benignity of God”**
• he speaks severely, because the mind is not recalled except by fear
• behold, you do not know God to be merciful
• Knowest thou not. Three degrees of sinners are noted in these three verses: the first, while you promise yourself impunity, there: Thinkest; the second and graver, because you despise the goodness of God, there: Or despisest thou; the third and gravest, because you do not know that you despise, there: Knowest thou not, etc.
**“leadeth thee”** — as far as it is in itself
**“to penance.”** — or to penance
2.5:
**“But according to thy hardness and impenitent heart”**
• but because you are hard and obstinate in your evil, for which you do not repent in heart
• According to thy hardness. For there are some who are displeased with the evils they do, and who, led by repentance of heart, labour to get out of them, insofar as it is granted them to get out; of these he does not speak here.
• There are some who like evils and, presuming too much on the mercy of God, persist in them obstinately; in this they show his patience, and heap up their own burden by sinning worse. And there are others who are indeed displeased by their evils, but because they understand them to be grave, think that they can no longer be forgiven, like him who said: “My iniquity is greater,” etc.
• Those, therefore, by excessive hope think God is not just. These, by despair, think God is not good. Therefore both will be in peril, and labouring by hoping and by despairing, with contrary things and contrary affections, they will perish.
**“thou treasurest up to thyself wrath”**
• to be exercised
• Thou treasurest up. Thou accumulatest vengeance for thyself by sinning the worse; this impenitence and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.
• These two kill souls: despair and perverse hope. By these two blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is committed. Whence in the gospel: “Whosoever shall speak a word against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, nor in the world to come.” Of which John in his canonical epistle: “There is a sin unto death: for that I say not that any man ask.”
• The sin against the Holy Spirit is committed in two ways, namely by obstinacy or by despair. Obstinacy is a hardened stubbornness of mind in malice, through which a man becomes impenitent. And this impenitence is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Despair is that by which a man utterly distrusts the goodness of God. And both are called “the sin against the Holy Spirit.”
*Ambrose:* Truly they sin against the Holy Spirit who think their malice exceeds the goodness of God.
*Haimo:* Let it not seem to you that God is so merciful that he does not seem just, nor so just that he is unwilling to show mercy.
*Augustine:* Some call that sin unforgivable because those who sin in this way cannot repent, having hearts hardened like stones. Of which Job: “His heart shall be hardened as a stone.” Others call it unforgivable because those who sin in this way never repent although they could, and therefore it is never forgiven them. Whence it is said above on Matthew: so great is the stain of that sin that it cannot, by humility, attain the usefulness of prayer, even if with an evil conscience it is forced to acknowledge and declare the sin. On Mark it is said that one who sins so cannot repent worthily. But briefly it seems to be understood thus: that he cannot, except scarcely, with difficulty, and rarely. Whence Augustine: the Lord, as if unwillingly, takes vengeance on the guilty, who from the beginning established men for life, not for death. The same: This impenitence, or impenitent heart, cannot be judged as long as anyone lives in this flesh; for one must despair of no one, as long as the patience of God leads to penance.
**“against the day of wrath, and revelation of the just judgment of God”** — when all things will be opened, and when that will be revealed which is now unknown to us
2.6:
**“Who”** — the just
**“will render to every man according to his works”**
• or 'his own'
• Who will render to every man. He who now does not render to those whom he frees, whose goodness even toward the wicked is now bounteous. But in the future he will render evil for evils, because he is just; good for evils, because he is good and just. Only “evil for good” he will not render, because he is not unjust.
• It belongs to justice that those whose mind in this life never wished to be without sin should never be without punishment, and that no end of vengeance be given to the wicked man, who, as long as he was able, was unwilling to have an end of his crime; wherefore it is no objection that a man is punished eternally for a temporal sin.
*Ambrose:* No evil unpunished, etc. Hence it is that some hold that an evil will in the reprobate is only a punishment, and not a fault, because it merits nothing. Others, however, say it is both fault and punishment, even if it merits nothing, just as a good will in the good does not remain unrewarded, because it is in itself a reward; or they say this is to be understood only of the state of the present life.
2.7:
**“To them indeed, who according to patience”** — having well used the patience of God, they work well
**“in good work”** — are
**“glory”** — because “the just shall shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father”
**“and honour”** — because they have been made at the right hand of God
**“and incorruption”** — because what they will have will remain
**“seek eternal life”** — those who have worked good works with this good intention, not so that they may be seen like hypocrites
2.8:
**“But to them”** — as you Romans
**“who are contentious”** — or who strive against God, unwilling to repent
**“and who obey not”** — are
**“obey not the truth”** — when it is said to them
**“but give credit”** — distrusting the future judgment
**“to iniquity”** — impunity
**“wrath”**
• punishment
• after judgment
**“and indignation”**
• will be on the day of judgment
• which they will be indignant at themselves
• Indignation. Lest it seem that he is angry and does not avenge, whence tribulation and anguish.
2.9:
**“Tribulation”**
• before judgment
• which first wrath
**“and anguish”**
• which indignation
• Tribulation and anguish. Meanwhile in the soul alone, before judgment. But after judgment, wrath and indignation.
**“upon every soul of man that worketh evil”**
• both Jew and Gentile
• Upon every. What above was said indefinitely there: “But to them that”. Here universally, so as to include Jew and Gentile.
• Soul. He says this because it speaks of the soul of the unbeliever, which, on account of its unbelief, will be afflicted with spiritual punishment.
**“of the Jew first”**
• especially because he also had the written law
• The Jew first. Ambrose. He always puts the Jew before, because, believing on account of Abraham, he is more honoured; the unbelieving one is to be treated worse, because he rejected the promises made to the fathers.
**“and also of the Greek”** — Gentile
2.10:
**“But glory, and honour, and peace to every one that worketh good”** — which above is incorruption
**“to the Jew first”** — in time; or because, better instructed, he works better
**“and to the Greek”** — Gentile
2.11:
**“For there is no respect of persons with God”** — For there is no respect of persons, etc. He makes the Jew and the Gentile equal in punishment and glory, because God judges not according to persons but according to merits, since he condemns each of them according to the measure of sin.
*Ambrose:* The prerogative of birth does not follow, so that the cause of the fathers takes up the unbelieving one, or casts away from himself the believing one because of the unworthiness of his parents; but each one, by his own merit, either is rewarded or is condemned.
2.12:
**“For whosoever”** — because
**“without the law”**
• written, that is, the Gentiles
• Without the law. Augustine. For the Apostle here speaks of that law which Moses gave to the people of Israel. Therefore he called the Gentiles without law because they had not received that written law which the Jews boasted they had received.
**“have sinned without the law, shall perish”**
• not for transgression of the law
• will be condemned
**“and whosoever have sinned in the law”**
• that is, the Jews
• having the written law
• In the law. Augustine. From those who have known the divine commandments the excuse which others have from ignorance will be taken away. But neither will they be without punishment. And although it is graver for a man to sin knowing than not knowing, yet one must not therefore flee to the darkness of ignorance. For it is one thing not to have known, another not to have wished to know.
**“shall be judged by the law”**
• also for transgression of the law, by which he aggravates them
• Shall be judged. Not that they may be saved as it were by fire, as some say, but they will utterly perish. For Christ says that it shall be more tolerable for Sodom in the judgment than for the Jews who did not believe in Christ, and likewise that they will have no excuse for the sin of unbelief, because he came and spoke to them; of which they have an excuse, those to whom he spoke neither by himself nor by his own, who yet will not escape condemnation because: “Whosoever have sinned without the law, shall perish without the law.” But they will suffer lighter things, because from him to whom more is committed, more is required; because “that servant who knew the will of his lord, and did not according to his will,” etc.
2.13:
**“For not the hearers of the law”**
• that is, not for hearing the law
• For not the hearers. Ambrose. Does the law alone not save? No, because it does not make men just. And this is: not for hearing but the doers, whoever they are, which indeed is by grace.
**“are just before God”** — even if before men
**“but the doers of the law”**
• that is, grace justifies them so that they fulfil the law, because they do not do in order to be justified but are justified so that they may do
• But the doers. That is, those who believe in Christ, whom the law promised, whoever they are; which is only by grace.
• Doers. Of the law shall be justified, that is, shall be reckoned just or shall be made just by God, that they may be doers. It is not that those who were doers before are afterwards justified; as if it were said: men shall be created, because it is by the Creator that there come to be men; so these are not those who were doers and are then justified, because the Gentiles also. And this is: For when the Gentiles.
**“shall be justified”**
• will be held just
• the doers will be justified, because also the nations; and this is: for when
2.14:
**“For when the Gentiles, who have not the law”**
• written
• For when the Gentiles. For when he had said that the Gentile is condemned if he works ill and saved if he works well, yet since he does not have the law, as if he did not know what is good or what is evil, it would seem that neither ought to be imputed to him. The Apostle answers against this: although he does not have the written law, he has the natural one, because he understands and is conscious to himself what is good and what is evil. And therefore he is to be believed to work well or ill, and deservedly to be saved or condemned. I say to work well and to be saved, which is not possible except through grace and faith, which renews the natural image of God in man, lulled asleep by vice and age; without this renewal he works ill and is condemned, his conscience accusing him; for vice is against nature, and this grace heals. For the image of God in the human soul has not been so far worn away by the stain of earthly affections that no lineaments remain in it. What was impressed there through the image of God when man was created has not been wholly blotted out. Hence, vice being healed through grace, the things of the law are done by nature. Not that grace is denied by the name of nature, but rather nature is restored through grace; by which grace, the inner man being renewed, the law of justice is written anew which guilt had destroyed.
**“do by nature”** — Origen. Enlightened by natural reason they discern what is to be done and what avoided, which the law would do
**“those things that are of the law do”** — that is, what the law commands, namely to believe in God and in Christ
**“such”** — although
**“the law”** — written of Moses
**“these having not the law are a law to themselves”** — they are for themselves a law
2.15:
**“Who shew the work of the law”**
• by the signs of their works, while they praise these and condemn those
• The work of the law. It is the faith which they have of their own accord in their hearts, that is, in the inner affection where faith works through love.
**“written in their hearts”** — firmly fixed in their reason
**“bearing witness”** — whence they themselves will be witnesses to themselves, the good or the bad, knowing thereby that they are deservedly condemned or saved
**“their conscience bearing witness to them”** — even if it does not seem so to others
**“and their thoughts between themselves”** — not only the conscience of works but also of evil and good thoughts; or genitives for ablatives, after the manner of the Greeks
**“accusing one another”**
• or accusing ones
• this of unbelievers
**“or also defending”**
• or defending ones
• this of believers
2.16:
**“In the day”** — of judgment
**“when”** — rendering testimony
**“God shall judge”** — that is, they will be made open
**“the secrets of men”** — which now are hidden
**“according to my gospel”** — which is all certain according to the gospel, etc.
**“my”** — that is, of Paul, which Paul announces
**“by Jesus Christ”** — because: “For neither doth the Father judge any man, but hath given all judgment to the Son.”
2.17:
**“But if thou”** — The Gentile has only natural law; you Jew, more
**“art called a Jew”**
• the name came to you from Judah the patriarch by kinship
• But if you are a Jew. Here he attacks the Jews, accusing them more severely of sins, because they had more helps.
**“and restest in the law”** — you do not wander in errors as those who are without law
**“and makest thy boast of God”** — from the knowledge of God
2.18:
**“and knowest his will”** — from the redemption which he announced to you through the prophets
**“and approvest the more profitable things, being instructed by the law”** — from useful things you know how to choose more useful ones
2.19:
**“Art confident that thou thyself art a guide of the blind”**
• as if not understanding
• Leader of the blind. He calls the Gentiles blind, who are both deprived of reason and blind; and if they know anything, still they are in darkness.
**“a light of them that are in darkness”** — which you could also enlighten
2.20:
**“an instructor of the foolish”** — of the not yet advanced Jews
**“a teacher of infants”** — of Jews who do not know how to discourse about the law
**“having the form of knowledge and of truth in the law”**
• that is, the perfection of knowledge
• Having the form. That you may be to others an example of the knowledge of the law and of truth. For some have the knowledge and understanding of some book and so understand it as the author himself understood it, yet they do not thereby have the truth, because they do not know how it is true, nor even that it is true; but the Jew boasts that he has the sense of the law and knows that sense of the law to be true, so that he may be a model for others who wish to have it.
2.21:
**“Thou therefore that teachest another”**
• since you have all these things
• Why?
**“teachest not thyself: thou that preachest that men should not steal”** — as the law says
**“stealest”** — the sense concerning Christ in the law
2.22:
**“Thou that sayest, men should not commit adultery, committest adultery”** — you take away the truth of Christ from the law and put in a lie
**“thou that abhorrest idols, committest sacrilege”**
• by denying Christ
• by giving the worship of God to idols, which the Jews often did
2.23:
**“Thou that makest thy boast of the law”** — while you pass over the sense of the law, which concerns the incarnation and divinity
**“by transgression of the law dishonourest God”** — that is, you are the cause why they dishonour God, and truly
2.24:
**“For the name of God through you is blasphemed among the Gentiles”**
• He puts the words of the prophet Ezechiel for his own
• today, because in Christ the Father is blasphemed, as he himself says: “He that receiveth me doth not receive me only, but him that sent me.” Just as formerly the Gentiles seemed to have overcome God in the Jews
• For the name of God, etc. The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through the Jews, because the Jews strove to persuade believers that Christ ought not to be called God. Or because formerly the Gentiles did not observe that the Jews were handed over to them for their own offences, but gave glory to their idols for the victory, as if they had conquered the God of the Jews in the Jews.
**“as it is written”** — concerning contemporaries, by Ezechiel
2.25:
**“Circumcision”**
• and since you are such, circumcision does not profit
• Circumcision indeed. He shows that circumcision alone does not help them above the law.
**“profiteth”**
• to you who are of the stock of Abraham
• Profits. Because by obeying God it makes a sign of truth while the simple people is kept under the fear of God.
• Profiteth. He says this here, and in what follows: “If you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing.” He wishes this to be understood according to the state of different times. For according to the state of the Old Testament circumcision once profited, but it did not profit unto salvation without the observance of the spiritual law. But now, that is, in the time of grace, after the truth has been shown forth, it profits nothing.
**“if thou keep the law”**
• you believe in Christ and keep it spiritually
• If you keep the law. Ambrose: that you put off all filthy things, that you circumcise the heart and believe in Christ.
**“but if thou be a transgressor of the law”** — if you do not fulfil what circumcision demands, namely that you believe in Christ
**“thy circumcision”** — carnal
**“is made uncircumcision”** — is worth no more than uncircumcision
2.26:
**“If, then”** — from contraries
**“the uncircumcised”** — any Gentile
**“keep the justices of the law”** — the command through which a man is justified, or faith in Christ, whom the law foretold would come to justification
**“shall not this uncircumcision be counted for circumcision?”**
• so that he may be a son of Abraham, who is the father of faith; as no one can deny this
• Shall not. By comparison with himself he shows you to be condemnable, who knew through the law, and not through nature or circumcision, what he knew through nature, that is, Christ.
2.27:
**“And shall not that which by nature”** — restored by grace
**“is uncircumcision”** — Shall judge the uncircumcision. He seems therefore in the present place to mean the Gentiles who came to the faith of Christ in the uncircumcision of the flesh; these, keeping the spiritual law, he compares and prefers to the Jews, who by the letter and the circumcision of the flesh are transgressors of the law, and he says that these are to be judged by them.
**“if it fulfill the law, judge thee”** — perfecting
**“Who”** — although you are learned
**“by the letter”** — through the written law
**“and circumcision”** — which is the sign of putting off vices
2.28:
**“For it is not he”**
• A Jew is one by name and by nation who confesses with his lips, and is far from it in his heart.
• For not he who, etc. Whence a Jew can become a Gentile, and a Gentile a Jew: For not, etc.
**“is a Jew”**
• truly
• Jew. It means 'confessing.' For he who truly believes and rightly confesses is truly a Jew.
**“nor is that”** — made by hand is
**“which is outwardly in the flesh”** — removal of the skin
**“circumcision”** — true
2.29:
**“But he is a Jew, that is one inwardly”**
• confessing in heart
• is true
**“and the circumcision”** — cleansing
**“of the heart”**
• is true
• Circumcision of the heart. Origen: It is that which purifies the soul and cuts away the stains of vices.
**“in the spirit”** — made through the Holy Spirit
**“not in the letter”** — not with stone knives, as the letter teaches
**“whose praise”** — Whose praise is not. Ambrose. God praises the believer who is not circumcised in the flesh. The praise of the Jews is from men, who, if they do what the law commands without the spirit, yet from fear of punishment, not from love of justice, and so what appears before man is not before God.
**“is not of men”** — Not from men. Augustine. It is that circumcision by which unlawful concupiscence is imputed, which is not done by the letter teaching and helping, but by the Spirit helping and following.
**“but of God”** — that is, by which true praise is not from man but from the grace of God.

3.1:
**“What advantage then hath the Jew”**
• according to the former state
• from the law and legal observances
• What advantage then. He raises an objection that he sees can be raised, in order to resolve it. Since indeed the Jew becomes a Gentile, and the reverse, what then is the advantage of the Jew, who is called the peculiar people of God, over the Gentile, who is called an unclean dog? Or what has he gained from circumcision? It was indeed once of value for this, but not so that they were therefore worthier in faith. And this is: much every way, according to the former state, and that in every way. Every way is either in the administration of temporal things or in the unlocking of spiritual things; in both of which God did much for the Jews that he did not for the Gentiles, and so according to the former state they were worthier.
3.2:
**“Much every way”** — according to the former state, but in the faith of Christ nothing
**“First indeed, because the words of God were committed to them”**
• the law and the prophets
• First indeed. As if to say: that I may pass over other lesser matters concerning temporal things, I set down this as first and chief, that the words of the Lord, that is, the law and the prophets, were committed to them as to friends, that through them they might understand about the future redemption. But you will say: not therefore more, because some of them did not believe the words so as to receive the promised Christ. To this: it did not therefore profit believers the less; and this is the point. For if some did not believe, shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect?
3.3:
**“For what if”** — therefore more
**“some of them have not believed? shall their unbelief”** — Shall their unbelief, etc. Is it that, because some refused to believe, the rest of the Jews are prejudiced, lest they be judged unworthy to receive what God promised to the faithful, since the promise was made to profit believers?
**“the faith of God”**
• not therefore made less for believers
• The faith of God. Or some believed God, or what God had promised to men.
**“make without effect”** — made unfulfilled
**“God forbid”**
• that it is made void
• but rather
3.4:
**“But God is true”** — for
**“God is true”** — fulfilling his promises
**“every man a liar”**
• and so unworthy of the promise
• insofar as it is from himself
• but
• But every man a liar. He adds this that it may appear that the promise of God was made and fulfilled not on account of any dignity of man but on account of mercy, that grace may be given to the unworthy and grace be the more commendable. God is called true, that is, unchangeable both in essence and in promise. Man is a liar, neither having true being and falling away through sins.
• Every man a liar, who denies that God has fulfilled his promises. This above all the Jew, whom God has conquered, who does not give the promises.
• Every man a liar. The Jew also, lest he seem more worthy in the new state.
**“as it is written”** — God is true
**“That thou mayest be justified in thy words”**
• concerning the promise of the Son, or the pardon of one who groans
• That thou mayest be justified. As if: I have sinned, so that by sending the Son from my stock, as you promised, you may be proved just and to have fulfilled the promise from the justice of the promise alone, not from my merits; and may overcome by fulfilling the promises, when you are judged as one who ought not to fulfil them on account of my sins. Or: I say to you alone that I have sinned, so that while I and all sin, you alone may appear just in all your promises, and surpass all in justice when you are compared with others. Or: man overcame God when he was judged, because on account of that humility God “hath given him a name which is above all names.” This does not belong to the argument above, but is added from abundance.
**“and mayest overcome when thou art judged”**
• either not having sent the Son or not giving pardon
• That thou mayest be justified and mayest overcome. The just judge was judged by sinners, and saw it in himself; so to him, who has no sin, David says: “To thee only have I sinned,” that thou mayest be justified, who surpass all judges, who alone art judged unjustly.
3.5:
**“But if our injustice”**
• this sense was unjustly drawn from the words of David
• But if our injustice, etc. He said that God is true and every man a liar, and that he gives good things to the unworthy, in which his justice and grace appear the more commendable; whence the carnal man, saying that God uses the wicked as an instrument to his own glory, brings the matter to this, that he calls God unjust who punishes sins that profit him. This he removes, saying: Is God unjust, who executeth wrath?
**“the justice of God”** — and the holiness of God
**“commend what shall we say? Is God unjust who”**
• on account of sins
• Is God unjust? God is true and man a liar. If then this is so, and thus our injustice commends the justice of God, what seems to follow? That God is unjust. But is God unjust who inflicts evils?
**“executeth wrath”** — vengeance and condemnation
**“I speak according to man”**
• as if this question is of the carnal
• but
3.6:
**“God forbid”** — that he be unjust
**“otherwise”**
• unless it is that he is not unjust; he cannot be a more just judge
• if unjust
**“how shall God judge this world?”** — as if: namely giving evil to the good and good to the evil
3.7:
**“For if”** — because
**“the truth of God”**
• justice
• here, what above is justice
• For if the truth. With the removal interposed, he returns to the proof of the carnal man, that God is unjust if he punishes: for if he is the more glorious from it, why am I also yet judged, not only in the future, as a sinner, which I am not? Or “yet,” that is, after conversion, after he gave gifts to the unworthy. For before, he was not more glorious from my things; as if he said: what could seem so before forgiveness ought not to seem so after, namely that I should be judged a sinner, because now it is certain that the truth of forgiving would not have abounded to glory unless I had sinned. He adds: And not as we are slandered, etc. As if: and if this is so, why do we not do evil that good may come? As this is imputed to us, to think this, which is blasphemy, and even to preach it on the occasion of words like these: “Where sin abounded, grace did more abound.” Or “for if”: let it be joined more closely: how will he judge if unjust? As if: not rightly, because he would not now justly judge me as a sinner, which I am not.
**“through my lie”**
• through my sin
• what above is injustice
**“hath more abounded”** — increased
**“unto his glory”** — that is, if from my sin it is more glorious
3.8:
**“And”** — what

• Circumcision was commended to Abraham, that being under the law of command his obedience might be proved. It was instituted first for obedience; second, as a sign of Abraham’s faith; third, that that people might be distinguished from the other nations; fourth, that the chastity of mind and body might be shown by keeping modesty, and for this reason it was done in the virile member; fifth, because it could not be better signified that original sin is taken away through Christ. It was done on the eighth day with a stone knife, because in the eighth age, which will be that of the risen, all corruption of flesh and spirit will be cut off from the elect by the rock, Christ. There are therefore two things of that sacrament, namely, circumcision from sins in the present and from all corruption in the future. It conferred in its time what baptism does in ours. Likewise, what the water of baptism does among us, among the ancients faith alone did for infants, the virtue of sacrifice for adults, and the mystery of circumcision for those of the stock of Abraham. It was changed by baptism because the sacrament of baptism is more perfect, more common and fuller of grace; for it remits sins, increases virtues, conferring grace to cooperate, and it is common to both sexes, which circumcision is not.

Those to whom it was promised did not yet exist, but those to whom it was promised were themselves also promised. For posterity is not wont to be named from the woman but from the man. Or because the woman is of the man and the two are one flesh, so whether it be said from Eve or from Adam, both belong to the first man; and by this the Apostle meant original sin to be understood as of propagation, whose prince is Adam, not of imitation, whose prince is the devil. **“In whom all”** — Augustine. That in the matter not only by his example, and all were that one man. Or in which sin. For other sins are personal.

• It must be known that most Latin copies read thus: Death reigned from Adam until Moses over those who sinned after the similitude of the transgression of Adam; so that they understand those to have sinned after the similitude of the transgression of Adam who sinned in him, that they might be created like him, namely, as men from man, so sinners from a sinner, mortals from one about to die, and those to be condemned from one condemned.
**“from Adam unto Moses”**
• that is, up to the law promulgated by God through Moses
• through whom the knowledge of God returned
**“even over them also who have not sinned”** — not only on those who seemed to have deserved death by transgressing of themselves, but also on children who had deserved nothing of themselves by transgressing against any law
**“after the similitude of the transgression of Adam”** — that is, like the transgressor Adam
**“who is a figure”**
• likeness
• Adam is called the figure of the one to come, because God had already then decided, in mystery, to give through the one Christ what had been sin through the one Adam. Whence it is said in the Apocalypse: “The Lamb was slain from the beginning of the world.”
**“Who is a figure”** — Adam is the figure of Christ, because as he is the father of all according to the flesh, so Christ is according to faith; and as Eve was formed from his side, so from Christ’s side flowed the sacraments, by which the Church is saved; and therefore as Adam could communicate sin and death to his sons, so Christ can communicate to his own his justice and life; and moreover Christ confers more good on his own than Adam did evil, and therefore he can save more than Adam could destroy. That is, Christ and Adam are alike, but not the offence, that is, the sin of Adam is not so effective to condemnation as the grace of Christ to salvation. That is, their causes are not equal, nor are the effects of the causes equal. This is what is said there: “And not as it was by one sin.” The cause of Christ is abounding grace, from which comes all good to man, without which he has nothing of good. The cause of Adam is that sin of which all who are born carnally are guilty. The other sins have much from themselves, even if from that original sin they are more prone to sinning; and well does this cause of Christ profit all his own, because if the cause of Adam harmed all his own, then this cause also could profit its own; and this is: “For if by the offence of one many died.” For the effect of the cause of Adam, that is, of the sin which he brought in, is not all condemnation but that which is due for that one sin; for there are also other condemnations from our own added sins. The effect of the gifts of Christ, with all sins removed, original and actual, is all justification and eternal life; and well is this for his own through the one Christ, because if that was for his own through the one Adam, then this also could be.
**“of him who was to come.”**
