He grieves that his own race is deprived of the benefit of Christ. “I wished,” he says, not “I wish,” because he knows that such a man cannot be separated from Christ; yet he shows his affection for them, of whom he enumerates many praises, that he may strike grief into all on their behalf, who are so much worse than the Gentiles, in that they have lost the prerogative of the fathers and of the promise; for it is more grievous to have lost a dignity than not to have had it.
**“I lie not”**
• in some part
• although you do not believe
**“my conscience bearing me witness”** — rooted and founded
**“in the Holy Ghost”**
• and the Spirit is the witness
• of this, that
9.2:
**“That I have great sadness”** — stupor of mind
**“and continual”** — not hourly
**“sorrow”** — of compunction
**“in my heart”**
• not in appearance only
• and I rightly grieve
9.3:
**“For I wished myself”** — who now am an apostle
**“to be an anathema from Christ”** — separation from others
**“for my brethren”**
• for the Jews, who are brethren in the law, whose law I wished to defend
• who err from Christ
**“For my brethren”** — Or for the drawing back of those who are now brethren in faith, who are also my kinsmen; and so I was sinning more grievously.
**“who are my kinsmen”** — and therefore to be helped more
**“according to the flesh”** — of the tribe of Benjamin
9.4:
**“Who are Israelites”** — true Israelites according to the good, or by race
**“to whom”** — to whom belongs
**“belongeth the adoption as of children”** — which is
**“and the glory”** — because a peculiar people, or now through the miracles they work
**“and the testament”** — new
**“and”**
• of whom
• of whom
**“the giving of the law”** — which the old (testament) bore through figures
**“and the service of God”** — the worship of the one God
**“and the promises”** — to whom the promises were made
9.5:
**“to whom”** — praise from the forefathers
**“the fathers”** — are
**“and of whom is Christ”** — praise from what follows
**“according to the flesh”** — whence man is born in her
**“who is”** — although he was born according to the flesh of the fathers
**“over all things, God blessed for ever”** — whence also the Highest founded her
**“Amen.”**
• it is true that he is God
• as if to say: I who was contradicting this truth now confirm it
• it is true
9.6:
**“Not as though”**
• although I have labored so, and although all do not believe, yet the word has not fallen away
• the promise is not void, although not all are saved, because not all
**“hath miscarried”**
• or “that it has fallen away”
• Not as though the word of God hath miscarried, etc. The Apostle consoles his sorrow: God, foreknowing, did not of old decree that these should be saved, “not a respecter of persons.” For he condemns no one before he sins, crowns no one before he conquers, but by foreknowledge he has determined what the will of each one is to be, from which he is condemned or crowned.
• Because he grieved over the Jews, he consoles himself, finding it written that not all are to be saved, but only those like Isaac. In these words he shows that the grace of God alone makes the sons of God.
**“Not as though the word of God hath miscarried.”** — He said that the promise of the eternal inheritance was made to the Jews, but because the greater part of them did not believe, the word of God seemed not to have been fulfilled. To which he answers that although it has not been fulfilled in some, yet it has in others, that is, in the believing Gentiles, who are now the true sons of Abraham.
**“Not as though the word of God hath miscarried”** — As if: although I have labored so, and although not all believe, yet the word of God has not fallen away, or I do not say that it has fallen away. For the word of God to fall away is not to fulfil promises.
**“the word of God. For all are not”** — according to the flesh
**“Israelites that are of Israel”** — truly belonging to Israel
9.7:
**“Neither are all they that are the seed of Abraham”** — according to the flesh
**“children”** — that is, heirs
**“but in Isaac”** — but those like Isaac, because Scripture so says
**“In Isaac”**
• That is, in Christ, by calling grace they are gathered.
• They were prefigured by the promise: not those who make themselves just, but those whom God makes, these are the children of the free woman “which is above, which is our mother.” The children of the flesh are of the earthly Jerusalem, which is in bondage with her children. As Isaac did not merit that he should be promised as one to be born, so neither did these; but by grace alone the adoption of children was given to them as promised.
**“shall thy seed be called”** — because by God’s calling someone is of Abraham
9.8:
**“That is to say, not they that are the children of the flesh”** — explains the authority
**“are the children of God”**
• are not the sons of God by human work
• this is the same as sons of Abraham
**“but they, that are the children of the promise, are accounted”** — that is, those who are begotten by God’s promise alone, like Isaac
**“for the seed”** — spiritual
9.9:
**“of promise”**
• or Isaac from the promise
• certainly
**“For”** — because
**“this is the word”** — that is, in Genesis
**“According to this time”** — that day, the year having turned round
**“I will come”** — O Abraham.
**“and”** — and I will do this.
**“a son”** — either conceived or born; for it does not determine.
9.10:
**“And not only it”** — namely, Sara had the promise.
**“And not only she.”** — Sara had the promise, but Rebecca also had the promise, having, that is, two sons by one conception, of Isaac our father. He says “by one conception,” lest the difference seem to be in the merits of the parents of those begotten; but of the father, that is, of our founder, whom we should imitate if we wish to be sons of God. The promise made to Sara shows that no one is saved on account of race. This one made to Rebecca shows that no one is chosen on account of any merit of his own or of his parents, but by grace alone.
**“But when Rebecca also had conceived at once, of Isaac our father.”** — two sons.
9.11:
**“For when the children were not yet born”** — lest anyone think it comes from their merit.
**“For when”** — Rebecca had this promise: the elder shall serve the younger, that is, Esau by persecuting will advance Jacob.
**“nor had done any good or evil”** — or had done any good or evil, because they might seem to have merited something even in the womb by wrestling.
**“that the purpose of God, according to election, might stand”** — therefore then, that the purpose, that is, the foreknowledge of God, might remain, that is, be fulfilled according to election, that is, the grace which chose as he foresaw, not according to the due of merits, because he himself makes those who are to be chosen; he does not find them.
**“Not of works, but of him that calleth”** — by the grace of God who calls.
9.12:
**“Not of works”** — Because the future good or evil things would not be future, unless grace were added or withdrawn.
**“it was said to her”** — to the mother.
**“The elder shall serve the younger”**
• this is of foreknowledge.
• This is literally so, because the Idumeans, who come from Esau, who is also called Edom, were subject to the sons of Israel; but this prophecy is aimed rather at this: that the people of the Jews, the elder, that is, first in the worship of the one God, would serve the younger, that is, the later Christian.
9.13:
**“As it is written”**
• as if: thus it was said by grace, as Malachi said of things already past, that Jacob was chosen by grace, not by merit.
• Esau, grace withdrawn, rejected.
**“Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated.”**
• this again is of judgment.
• because he chooses this one without merit and rejects that one.
• Jacob I have loved, etc. In Jacob he found nothing to be loved, except the gift of his mercy. In Esau he hates nothing, except original sin. But how is this right, when they had done nothing? Because the matter is astonishing, he puts the objection to himself: “What shall we say then?” It is of mercy, to will and to run, which appears in others of the same mass to whom perdition is due; for the Scripture saith.
9.14:
**“What shall we say, then?”**
• looking back at what was said before.
• What then? Because he chose this one without merit and will reprobate that one, will God be called unjust? No, because he chose this one through mercy, and reprobated that one through justice. In neither is there injustice: this one through mercy, because Moses says so; that one through justice, because the Scripture says so, bringing in God speaking to Pharao.
**“Is there injustice with God? God forbid.”** — that is, will God be called unjust? No.
**“God forbid”** — It is agreed that no one is freed except by free mercy, and no one is condemned except by most equal justice. But why this one rather than that one is freed, let him who is able search out so deep a judgment; nevertheless let him beware of the precipice.
9.15:
**“For he saith to Moses:”** — God, brought in by Moses.
**“I will have mercy”** — by calling inwardly.
**“on whom I will have mercy”**
• by predestining.
• I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy, that is, on whom I foreknow that mercy is to be shown, knowing that he will be converted and will abide with me; this is to give to him to whom it is to be given, and not to give to him to whom it is not to be given, so that he calls him whom he knows will obey; as David, who after pardon stood so well. Saul, not heard in his prayer, did not stand firm, but was turned to idols. Whence he seems justly to have been reprobated by the one who foreknows.
**“and I will shew mercy”** — behold, no merits go before in justifying.
**“shew”** — by giving eternal life and perseverance.
**“to whom I will shew mercy”**
• by calling.
• because out of mercy he prepares those whom he wills and calls.
9.16:
**“So then it is not of him that willeth”**
• is to will good.
• It is not of him that willeth, etc. As if he said: the will of man alone is not enough if the mercy of God is not also there. To which it is said in reply: the mercy of God also is not enough if the will of man is not there. And if that was rightly said, why on the contrary is it not also rightly said: it is not of God that hath mercy, but of man that willeth? It remains therefore that this be understood as rightly said so that the whole be given to God, who both prepares the good will of man to be helped, and helps it when prepared; he goes before the willing man that he may will, and follows him as he wills lest he will in vain.
*Augustine:* Who, moreover, is so impiously foolish as to say that God cannot turn the evil wills of men, which he wills, and when he wills, to good, since nothing resists his will? But when he does it, he does it through mercy; when he does not do it, he does not do it through judgment. He has mercy indeed according to grace, which is given freely. But he hardens according to judgment, which is rendered to merits; whence it is given to be understood where the hardening of God occurs: it is his not willing to have mercy, so that nothing is inflicted by him whereby a man becomes worse, but only that what would make him better is not bestowed. Therefore it was not said in the same way, “It is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy,” as it was said, “not of him that willeth nor of him that runneth, but of God that hardeneth”; because he does not harden by imparting evil, but by not bestowing good, which he does by his equity, as he bestows grace out of his mercy.
**“nor of him that runneth”** — is to run, that is, to work.
**“but of God that sheweth mercy”** — Behold, not because of future things which he foresaw, he chooses.
9.17:
**“For the scripture saith to Pharao”** — Good things come from added grace, and evil things from withdrawn grace; and this indeed is through justice.
**“To this purpose”** — into this same wickedness, so that you may become worse, because “he that is filthy, let him be filthy still.”
**“have I raised”**
• Another reading: I raised up.
• Another reading: I preserved.
• I raised thee up, or “I roused thee,” or “I preserved thee.” Ambrose. For this very purpose I preserved you, when you were unworthy to live. Or I raised you up, because, though he was dead before God, he received a short time so that in him all nations might learn the power of God.
**“Have I raised”** — You were wicked, but as if asleep; but I, showing you signs, stirred you up into the same wickedness, so that you might become worse. And this is just: “He that is filthy, let him be filthy still.” Nor is this useless, but that, you being hardened, I might show my power by the signs of Egypt.
**“thee, that I may shew my power in thee”**
• that is, through.
• or against.
**“thee”** — hardened.
**“my power”**
• and uses the wicked well.
• in signs and miracles.
**“and that”** — through the power shown.
**“my name may be declared throughout all the earth”** — The example of Pharaoh pertains to Esau, who was rejected by the just judgment of God, though hidden, as Jacob was chosen.
9.18:
**“Therefore”** — because “Jacob have I loved,” etc.
**“he hath mercy on whom he will”** — freely.
**“Therefore he hath mercy on whom he will”** — There is no merit of mercy; the merit of hardening is the sin of the whole condemned mass. Nor does he harden by imparting malice, but by not imparting mercy, since they are not worthy; which he does by a hidden equity, remote from human senses, which the Apostle does not disclose. But he marvels: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom.”
**“and whom he will”** — because Esau and Pharaoh.
**“he hardeneth”** — by just judgment.
**“He hardeneth”** — Not as though he forced anyone to sin. But only that to some, because they sin, he does not grant the mercy of his justification, and for this reason he is said to harden them, because he does not have mercy on them, not because he impels them to sin. And he does not have mercy on those to whom he judges, by a most hidden equity, most remote from human senses, that grace is not to be offered.
9.19:
**“Thou wilt say therefore to me:”** — because from the will.
**“Why doth he then find fault?”**
• if we take offence.
• from someone, so that he may do good.
• Why doth he then find fault, etc. Since it is agreed that it is from the will of God, why is it asked whence one is good and another evil? There is no need, because each one will be such as God wills him to be, and therefore he unjustly condemns one and saves another. Or: why doth he find fault, that is, why does anyone strive to act well, when he can do nothing except what God wills? Or: why does God complain of the sins of men, when they cannot avoid what he himself wills? Thus carnal men, living in pleasures, are wont to murmur against God, and to impute to his will, not to their own fault, that they are evil. The apostle rebukes them for this presumption: O man, flesh, not spirit, wretched one, who art thou? Of what strength? Who answerest God, that is, understandest what God does, namely why he has mercy on this man and hardens you; as if to say: if it were said to you, you would not know how to answer, that is, to understand, because of your carnality; and neither does your wisdom help you to this, nor any virtue of yours. Or: what shall we answer, that is, by what reasons shall we argue against God, that he unjustly chooses or rejects.
**“for who resisteth his will?”** — who hardens us.
9.20:
**“O man,”**
• the Apostle checks this impudence.
• consider you and him.
**“O man”** — He does not answer from lack of reason to be given, but calls man back to himself.
**“who art thou”**
• you man, he God.
• you flesh, he spirit.
**“that repliest against God?”** — to whom it is displeasing that God complains.
**“Shall”** — he takes this from Isaias.
**“the thing formed”** — so you too are formed.
**“say to him”** — by whom it was made
**“that formed it”** — who owes him nothing
**“Why hast thou made me thus?”** — the work cannot complain against its maker
9.21:
**“Or”** — truly it cannot say this, because
**“hath not the potter power”** — just
**“the potter over the clay”** — who works from clay
**“of the same lump”** — Thus the whole lump of the human race is justly corrupt and miry; if from it a vessel is made unto honour, it is mercy; if unto contumely, it is just, because this was from nature. Behold the justice in those who have no time for working. But concerning those who have time he adds: “What if God, willing,” that is, what would you answer to God.
**“to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?”** — Another unto dishonour. The vessel is not for honour but for dishonour, if it is base; it has the clay from itself, not from the potter.
9.22:
**“What if God, willing”**
• namely, what you should answer God
• or “what if willing”
• As if to say: it has now been shown that even if God gives nothing good, yet he is not unjust. But what will you say if he has also given good things to some, namely when they were fitted for destruction, and endured them with much patience, and meanwhile, while he waited, showed it by many signs, either by sometimes punishing the man himself, or others in their sight, that they might beware of the wrath to come for themselves. And in this, that he endured and showed his wrath, he made his power known, because through the wicked he purges the good; as if to say you can say that he justly withdraws grace and condemns those who, though so waited for, would not repent, but abused this grace.
**“to shew his wrath”** — in the lost
**“and to make his power known”** — because, when he was thought not to be going to avenge, since he dissembles, he will be seen as powerful in avenging
**“his power”** — in those to be saved
**“endured”**
• He endured. God endures the wicked so that he may destroy them in order, and he uses them as an instrument for the salvation of the good.
• For God would create none, either of angels or of men, whom he foreknew would be wicked, unless he likewise knew to what good uses he would turn them.
**“with much patience vessels of wrath, fitted for destruction”** — long awaited, they are inexcusable; and therefore God waited for them, though he knew they would not believe
9.23:
**“that”** — thus
**“he might shew the riches”**
• in the future age
• he shows how much he did for them, when those others have the punishment that was owed equally to all
• Note that to some he does not add grace, while to others he brings it in as though they were forced. Whence Ambrose: from foreknowledge he judged Pharao to be condemned, knowing that he would not amend. But the apostle Paul he chose, foreknowing that he would be faithful. But to some grace also was given for use, as to Saul, Judas, and those to whom he said: “Your names are written in heaven,” and afterwards they went back. Of whom Ambrose: but this was on account of the justice which they served, because it is just that it answer to each according to merit. As if he said: you are now worthy of eternal life, because they were good, and their names were written in heaven on account of the justice which they served. But according to foreknowledge they were in the number of the wicked. For God judges from justice, not from foreknowledge. Whence he says to Moses: 'If anyone shall sin before me, I will blot him out of the book of life,' so that according to the judgment of the judge he seems then to be blotted out when he sins, yet according to foreknowledge he had never been in the book of life. Whence John: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” Conversely, one seems then to be written in when he ceases to be evil, who according to foreknowledge was never lacking. Since then from free mercy he adds grace to whom he will, and frees whom he will, his rich and glorious goodness is plainly shown.
**“That he might shew”** — As if to say: to this end he bears with the wicked and shows his wrath beforehand, and draws them to the knowledge of himself, that he might shew “the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy,” that is, in the elect through mercy, “the riches of glory,” that is, how rich and how great and glorious his mercy is: for this reason he gives so many good things to the wicked, that he may convince them that they are justly condemned, and that the faithful, for whom he has preserved this very grace, may love him the more.
**“his glory”** — either through the furnace or through comparison
**“on the vessels of mercy, which he hath prepared”**
• by similarly waiting
• for all
**“unto glory”** — to come
9.24:
**“whom also he hath called”**
• through preachers
• inwardly
**“Even us, nor only of the Jews”** — from one lump of Adam
9.25:
**“As in Osee he saith:”** — not Osee but God in him
**“As in Osee”** — Since it has been shown that they are children from grace alone, he begins to prove through the prophets that these are from both peoples.
**“I will call that which was not my people”** — the Gentiles who have not known me
**“my people”** — that they may know me
**“and her that was not beloved”** — namely the Gentiles
**“beloved”** — that he may serve out of love
**“and her that had not obtained mercy”** — I will call
**“that hath obtained mercy”** — that they may attain to eternal life
9.26:
**“And”** — that which I say
**“it shall be, in”** — that is, that
**“the place”** — in the whole world, or among the Jews who said, You are not the people of God
**“where it was said unto them, You are not my people; there”**
• that is, in the whole world
• by those same Jews
9.27:
**“And Isaias”** — So Osee
**“concerning Israel”** — for the Jews
**“crieth out”**
• saying
• openly
**“If the number of the children of Israel be”**
• although they are innumerable, or barren, the root of the patriarchs has not therefore perished
• If the number, etc. Behold, thus the salvation of the Jews is spoken of, so that the greater part is blinded.
**“as the sand of the sea”** — on account of barrenness
**“a remnant shall be saved”** — that is, those whom I now leave, when I have cast off others; or who are left by others as base or few
9.28:
**“For he shall finish his word”** — namely of the gospel
**“For his word”** — The prophet adds through what they are saved, that the glory of works may be excluded. The word of the gospel leads to perfection and shortens all the legal things in one Christ, yet in equity with the former, so that nothing is wanting to justice from all the things prefigured; or it keeps what is equitable, such as the moral precepts, and cuts off as figures what it is right to take away.
**“he shall finish his word, and cut it short in justice”** — the shortened word is charity, on which the law and the prophets depend
**“cut it short”** — That by the shortcut of faith he saves through grace, not through countless observances.
**“that”** — because, lest anyone doubt it, the prophet confirms it by repetition, saying
**“a short word”** — against the ancient word, which is agreed that God also made
**“shall the Lord make upon the earth”**
• who first made the word of the law long
• being on earth, made man
9.29:
**“And as Isaias foretold: Unless the Lord of Sabaoth”** — of hosts
**“Unless the Lord of Sabaoth”** — The Lord made the word. And it was so necessary that unless there were a seed, that is, the word, etc. Or: the remnant will be saved, and unless through them the nation would have perished. And this is: unless the Lord of hosts, when he blinded others, had left us, that is, for our profit, a seed, that is, the apostles, from whom the harvest of Christ grew.
**“had left us a seed”** — or Christ
**“we had been made as Sodom”** — mute in confessing
**“like unto Gomorrha”** — rough without grace, having worked with the thorns of vices
**“we had been like”** — as equals in punishment because alike in guilt
**“as, and like unto”** — He put both, to note the likeness of guilt and punishment. As if to say: we would be equal in punishment, because we would be alike in guilt.
9.30:
**“What shall we say, then?”** — Having heard Osee and Isaias, he inquires into the understanding of the prophets, lest the Jews should twist it otherwise
**“That the Gentiles, who followed not after justice”** — by works of the law
**“have attained”** — suddenly and firmly
**“to justice”** — not any kind
**“even the justice that is of faith”** — by grace
9.31:
**“But Israel, by following”**
• as if: the Gentiles have attained justice; but Israel, by following
• and this also from the prophecy of Isaias
**“But Israel”** — But he followed the law as if backwards, because he never attains spiritual understanding.
**“justice”** — by legal works
**“by following after the law of justice”** — The law of Moses is the law of justice, if it is rightly understood. Or the justice that comes from fear of punishment, not from love of justice.
**“is not come unto the law of justice”**
• that is, innocence and the other things that the law truly teaches
• elsewhere 'the law of justice'
9.32:
**“Why so?”** — as if: attend carefully
**“Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were of works”** — they sought to be justified, but by works of the law, as if these could justify
**“not by faith”** — For he did not seek justice by faith, because he did not ask of God; he did not believe in him who justifies the ungodly. Not believing that God works in man so that he may be justified.
**“For they stumbled at the stumblingstone”** — Why do they not have faith? Because they suffered offence, that is, blindness, in Christ.
**“They stumbled”** — Like a small stone, which is not guarded against, Christ was apt to cause stumbling, lying hidden in humility. To this Isaias bears witness: Behold I lay in evidence, that is, I make to be born, in Sion, that is, among the Jews, Christ, whom as small one does not guard against, and a rock of scandal, that is, utterly crushing, saddening in the future. Christ is called a stone of stumbling according to the state in which he appeared here to the wicked; a rock of scandal according to what he will do to the wicked in the future.
9.33:
**“As it is written: Behold I lay”** — openly and in plain view
**“in Sion”** — to the Jews
**“a stumblingstone”** — Christ, from whom one does not guard oneself as from a small pebble
**“and a rock of scandal”**
• the same Christ, who will utterly crush the wicked in the future
• And a rock before polishing: Christ before the passion, at which time the Jews were scandalized, angry and indignant because he made himself the Son of God. The stone, through polishing: Christ in the passion, when they were most offended and blinded.
**“whosoever believeth in him”**
• whether Jew or Gentile
• not only will he be an offence to the wicked but also salvation to the good
**“shall not be confounded”** — when he comes in the future

10.1:
**“Brethren”**
• yet
• Lest he seem to speak out of hatred, or lest the Gentiles should cast them off entirely, he adds: Yet, brethren, the will of the heart indeed, etc.
**“the will of my heart, indeed”** — not feigned
**“and my prayer to God”**
• here he hints that it is given by grace
• For the will, that it may be moved to believe true things, is not sufficient for itself unless God helps it by grace. Whence: “No man can come to me, except it be given him by my Father.”
**“is”** — by me
**“for them”** — for those who stumble
**“unto salvation”** — that God may give them faith through which they may be saved
10.2:
**“For I bear them witness”** — it is right that I pray, because they must have zeal for God, though not according to knowledge, I who was once like them
**“I bear them witness”**
• I
• I bear them witness. Ambrose. He speaks of those who did not receive Christ out of envy but out of error, to whom Peter says, “I know that you did this through ignorance.”
**“that they have a zeal of God”**
• a zeal for God
• they think they act from the special love of God
**“they have, but not according to knowledge”** — of loving
**“but not according to knowledge”** — For it is foolish to venerate the law and to persecute the God of the law.
10.3:
**“For they”** — truly, not according to knowledge
**“not knowing the justice of God”**
• which is through the faith of Christ, which is from God
• Not that by which God is just, but that which is from God to man.
**“and seeking their own”** — which is through observances of the flesh
**“seeking”** — or 'wanting'
**“to establish”** — as the proud
**“have not submitted themselves to the justice of God”**
• by which God justifies believers
• Have not submitted themselves to the justice of God, etc. This is the justice of God, which is established not in the precept of the law by which fear is instilled, but in the help of Christ’s grace.
10.4:
**“For the end of the law is Christ”**
• they are ignorant of the justice of God, because Christ, who is the giver of justice, who fulfils what the law foretold
• who also avails
**“the end”** — Not consuming but perfecting. He therefore perfects justice through faith without the works of the law.
**“unto justice to every one that believeth”** — Christ alone is justice for salvation, because the justice of the law avails only for the present life
**“Christ, unto justice”** — Justice is from Christ, because if it were by the written or natural law, and not by faith in Christ, then Christ would have died in vain.
**“unto justice”** — Not human but divine. For there is both human and divine justice: of the human, there: “Moses”; of the divine, there: “but that which is”.
10.5:
**“For Moses wrote”** — elsewhere 'wrote'
**“wrote”** — In Numbers and Leviticus, where it is so given: “He that doth those things, shall live in them.”
**“that the justice which is of the law”** — which is from fear, not from love
**“the man that shall do it”** — as if without the aiding grace
**“shall live by it”**
• he will not be punished with legal penalty
• This has the reward that he is not punished with that death. For it is no great justice to fear, nor does it have merit with God.
10.6:
**“But the justice which is of faith speaketh thus”** — of that thus; but of the justice of faith Moses speaks thus, or it itself speaks thus in the heart of man: kept, it leads to heaven; not kept, it leads to the abyss
**“Say not in thy heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? that is”**
• Say not in your heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? that is, because
• to think
**“Say not”** — The justice of faith is that there be no doubting of the hope of God, which is in Christ; that one not distrust that Christ spoiled hell and ascended to heaven with the souls, whence one is made just.
**“Say not in thy heart”** — That is: do not even think who shall ascend, that is, no man shall ascend, because he who thinks this denies that Christ ascended. Or do not think who shall descend, that is, no one shall descend, which is said for the law not observed, because to think this is to call Christ back from the dead, that is, to believe that Christ did not descend into hell, because if those who do not observe justice do not descend, Abraham and the ancient fathers descended much less. But if they did not descend, then neither did Christ, who descended only to free them. Or thus: when you have heard, he says, that Christ after the resurrection ascended into heaven, do not say in your heart: it is a lie. For who shall ascend? Because this unbelief, as much as is in you, brings Christ down from heaven to earth. Likewise when you also hear it preached that Christ descended into hell, do not say: it is a lie; for who shall descend into the deep? Therefore do not say this, because to say this is to call Christ back from the dead, as much as is in you.
**“Christ”** — words of the apostle by which he opens the sense of the preceding words of Moses
**“to bring down”**
• as far as you are concerned
• That is, to bring Christ down, that is, to deny that Christ ascended.
10.7:
**“Or who shall descend into the deep? that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead”**
• words of the apostle
• do not say this, but rather believe this word which Scripture says
10.8:
**“But what saith the scripture?”** — in Deuteronomy
**“nigh”** — useful, because it justifies and saves
**“is the word”**
• Christ, or his preaching
• Christ, who is the Word in the beginning with the Father
• The word is near: that is, it is useful, or there is nothing unsuitable either to say or to believe. Near, not far from the nature of souls and the manner of speaking, which is said to us that we may believe.
**“in thy mouth”** — for confessing
**“and in thy heart”** — for believing
**“This is”** — expounds the Scripture of Moses
**“the word of faith, which we preach”**
• by which baptism is also consecrated
• ought to be near
**“This is the word”** — Of which the Lord says: “Now you are clean by reason of the word which I have spoken to you.” He did not say by baptism. Why? Only because even in the water it is the word that cleanses; take away the word, and what is water but water? The word comes to the element, and it becomes a sacrament; whence comes this so great power of water, that it touches the body and washes the heart, except by the working of the word, not because it is spoken but because it is believed? For even in the word itself, the sound is one thing, passing, the power another, remaining.
10.9:
**“For if thou confess with thy mouth”**
• when someone attacks
• If thou confess, etc. Behold the praise and the reward of faith. The praise of faith is if you believe that Jesus is Lord, that is, saviour, and that he rose again. The reward is eternal salvation.
**“the Lord Jesus”**
• not the works of the law
• that he rose again, or that he himself is Lord and Jesus, that is, saviour
**“and believe in thy heart that God hath raised him up from the dead”** — or 'raised up'
10.10:
**“For, with the heart, we believe unto justice”**
• believing gives salvation, because justice, which is the cause of salvation
• that is, by faith of the heart a man is justified, that is, from impious he becomes pious
**“with the heart, we believe”** — The rest one can do unwillingly, but one cannot believe unless willing.
**“but, with the mouth”** — after faith of the heart it has no other value
**“confession is made”** — which is added over faith, as in martyrs
**“confession”** — To confess is to say what is in the heart; to speak otherwise is not to confess. What is in the heart ought to be in the mouth, because on the forehead, that is, in the seat of shame, the sign of the cross is made not without cause, lest the Christian blush at the reproaches of Christ. It was a sin in Peter to deny with the mouth, though he believed with the heart. For when he washed away with tears what he had denied with the mouth, what he held in the heart was working for his salvation. For the truth is both to be believed and to be spoken.
**“unto salvation”** — not only to justice
10.11:
**“For the scripture saith”** — truly, with the heart one believes unto justice
**“the scripture saith”** — through Isaias
**“Whosoever believeth in him”** — not only the Jew but also the Gentile
**“shall not be confounded”** — shall be ashamed in the future, even if here he seems to be confounded
10.12:
**“not”**
• all
• but in every nation he that feareth him is acceptable to him
**“For”** — because
**“There is no distinction”** — there is no distinction
**“For the same”** — creator
**“Lord over all, rich unto all”** — sufficient to enrich all
**“that call upon”**
• call upon him with faith and works
• The one praying calls upon him, but this he cannot truly do unless he first believes.
• Who therefore call upon him: they not only believe but also pray, so that once a person has believed, his mind does not cease, with his whole heart and in watchfulness, to ask for what God has promised, because believing gives the forgiveness of sins. Calling upon him obtains the promises of God.
**“him”** — not rich to others
10.13:
**“For whosoever”** — from the authority of Isaias he proves what he had said
**“whosoever”** — Jew or Gentile
**“shall call upon the name of the Lord”** — by submitting himself well
**“shall be saved”** — in eternal blessedness
10.14:
**“how”** — but this cannot be done by one who is turned away
**“then”** — or 'but'
**“shall they call on him, in whom they have not believed”**
• as if: they will not call upon him unless they believe
• How shall they call, etc. Having proved that both are taken from the people, he shows through what, namely through the forgiveness granted to both, which whoever has not received is inexcusable.
• How then, etc. Invocation saves; therefore it is necessary to believe, because: How shall they call on, etc. To believe is from hearing, to hear from preaching, to preach from the sending of God, so that the whole may descend from the fountain of grace. Preaching is from sending, because God sends even false preachers who announce good things, for he knows how to use evil for good. Sometimes he also sends the wicked to the wicked in anger, that in turn they may perish by themselves, as is just.
**“Or how”** — he is not believed in to whom obedience is refused
**“shall they believe him, of whom they have not heard”**
• nor did anyone ever believe who had not in some way heard
• they will not believe unless they hear
**“And how”** — they will not hear unless it is preached to them
**“shall they hear, without a preacher”** — he who resists the preacher does not receive the author
10.15:
**“And how shall they preach unless they be sent”**
• they will not preach unless they are sent
• they are not true apostles unless they are sent
• See, it appears that preachers were also sent to the Gentiles; and so the Apostle refutes those who thought the gospel was to be preached to the Jews only.
**“as it is written”**
• in Isaias or in Nahum the prophet
• but sent because
**“How beautiful are the feet”**
• the coming of the apostles who enlighten the world
• Because they enlighten the world, in which it appears that they were sent by God; otherwise they could not have done this.
**“that preach the gospel”**
• announcing
• He announces well who fulfils by deed what he preaches by mouth.
**“of peace”**
• reconciliation
• Reconciliation between people and people, the dividing wall of the legal rite being broken down among the Jews and of idolatry among the Gentiles; and between God and the wicked through faith justifying, and men believing in him.
**“of good things”** — things to come
**“that bring glad tidings of good things”** — Peace upon peace, because the kingdom of God is peace too.
10.16:
**“But all do not obey the gospel”**
• as if: all heard through the apostles
• for since hearing comes from grace, another grace is also necessary which moves the heart
**“For Isaias saith”** — that some, not all, obey
**“Lord, who”** — as if: someone, not everyone
**“hath believed our report”**
• to those things which they hear from us, or which we hear from you
• For Isaias says: Lord, who hath believed? God, foreknowing, foretold the unbelief of the Jews, but he did not cause it, nor would he have foreknown their evils unless they had them. So too he blinds by forsaking, not by doing, and the will deserved this. If it is said that the Jews cannot believe because Isaias foretold it, I say: they cannot because they will not, which God foreknew and foretold, but did not cause. They cannot, while proud, while such as to attribute all things to their own strength, so as to deny that divine help is necessary for them to work well.
10.17:
**“Faith then”** — because someone believes from hearing, though not everyone
**“cometh by hearing”** — sometimes, though not everywhere
**“Faith cometh by hearing”** — Even if God teaches inwardly, yet the preacher announces outwardly.
**“and hearing by the word”** — not our merits
**“of God”**
• otherwise: of Christ
• By the word, etc. That is, through the grace of Christ sending us the teachers of the gospel word. For unless something is said, it can neither be heard nor believed.
10.18:
**“Have they not heard”** — they believed from hearing, but those who did not believe, did they not hear? As if by this they are excusable.
**“Yes, verily, their sound hath gone forth into all the earth”**
• that is, not only the nearest but also the farthest have heard
• Indeed: or truly, that is, certainly; and so they are inexcusable, as David shows in the Psalm, saying: “Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth,” etc.
• Into all the earth, etc. Nor was this fulfilled in the time of the apostles. But by the revelation of the Holy Spirit he sees that it is to be fulfilled in later generations. He spoke therefore in the past tense on account of the certainty of prophecy. In saying therefore “their,” he wished it to be understood not only of the apostles but also of their successors. So also that: “You shall be witnesses unto me, even to the uttermost part of the earth.”
**“their sound”** — report
**“unto the ends of the whole world”** — from every side
**“their words”** — the words themselves
10.19:
**“But I say”** — All heard. But I speak specifically of the Jews: Hath not, etc.
**“Hath not Israel known”** — they indeed knew, because Moses, who was first, that is, greatest, and others after him
**“But I say: Hath not”** — Because they could both have heard and not known, he affirms that they did know.
**“Israel known”** — Because he could not contradict by reason or authority, but did not truly know, so that it sat well in their minds.
**“First, Moses saith: I will provoke you to jealousy”** — out of envy, concerning the conversion of the Gentiles
**“to jealousy”** — It stirs envy in the Jews, while the Gentiles say God is theirs, and that the promises and the law and the prophets of the Jews pertain to themselves.
**“I will provoke you”** — I will allow to be brought.
**“by that which is not a nation”**
• that is, the Gentiles, who before were not a nation, or now are not a nation.
• The Gentiles were not formerly called a holy nation, or now a not-nation, because they were not such as had been born.
**“by a foolish nation”**
• which had not known God.
• “In”: that is, against a foolish nation, that is, against the Gentiles who had not known the true God.
**“I will anger you”** — I will allow them to be angry at you and to persecute you; and when this is done, let them see and heed what has come.
10.20:
**“But Isaias is bold”**
• although he foresaw punishment was impending, yet he dares.
• not only Moses says this, but also Isaias.
**“and saith”** — in the person of Christ.
**“I was found”**
• I offered myself of my own accord.
• and hence the envy of the Jews.
**“by them that did not seek me”** — of himself.
**“I appeared openly”** — openly.
**“to them that asked not after me”** — by others.
10.21:
**“But to Israel he saith”** — so too to the Gentiles.
**“All the day long have I spread my hands”**
• works and affection.
• Or this may be understood of the hands stretched out on the cross, so that the whole is put for a part. “All the day,” therefore, that is, a part of the whole day. “Have I stretched out,” on the cross. “My hands” to a people not believing but contradicting, which is worse.
**“All the day long”** — For the whole time that I dwelt with them and enlightened the world. Or, the hands on the cross; or, I enlarged works and affection.
**“I have spread my hands”** — As if: I showed greater things to the Jews, because he denied them no benefit. For he raised their dead and cured their various infirmities. For he is said to stretch out his hands who generously bestows benefits on those who ask.
**“my hands”** — This is said not of the hands stretched out on the cross but of the works which he showed to that people.
**“to a people”** — of the Jews.
**“that believeth not, and contradicteth me”** — which is worse.

11.1:
**“I say then”**
• I seem to say that God has rejected the people.
• but have I said this, or
• Because he had refuted the Jews with so many authorities, the Gentiles could insult them, saying they had been wholly rejected; against whom he begins thus.
**“Hath God cast away”** — wholly.
**“his people”**
• or “his people.”
• the Jews, to whom he did so many [things].
• or inheritance.
**“God forbid”** — if I say the unbelieving Jews, not however all of them
**“For”** — because he did not reject me and the other predestined
**“I also am an Israelite”** — that is, a Jew, not a proselyte, but of the seed of Abraham through the line of Benjamin
**“of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin”** — lest it be thought that he is of Ishmael
11.2:
**“God hath not cast away”** — just as he did not reject me, likewise
**“his people, which he foreknew”** — predestined
**“foreknew”** — He put 'foreknew' for 'predestined'. For that is how it ought to be understood, as is clear from what follows. He said 'foreknew', however, lest the Jews again become proud because he said they were not rejected and are God’s people.
**“Know you not what the scripture saith”** — the book of Kings
**“Know you not”** — As if: so there are remnants at this time, as when Elias seemed to himself alone; if he did not know of others reserved besides himself, it is no wonder that these men are ignorant.
**“of Elias”**
• where he speaks of Elias
• that is
**“how he calleth”** — between himself and them
**“on God”** — judge
**“against”** — or 'against'
**“Israel”** — saying
11.3:
**“Lord, they have slain thy prophets”** — this was done under Jezebel
**“they have dug down thy altars”** — they overthrew from the foundation
**“and I am left alone, and they seek my life”** — he thought himself alone
11.4:
**“But what saith the divine answer to him? I have left me”** — I have reserved through grace
**“seven thousand men”** — all good
**“Seven thousand”** — By the seven the whole is signified; by the thousand, perfection.
**“that have not bowed their knees to Baal”** — the god of Achab and Jezebel
11.5:
**“Even so then at this present time also”**
• where more easily
• of grace
**“Even so then”** — As if: because there were then many, even if Elias did not know it. Therefore so, that is, thus secretly or through the same grace.
**“a remnant saved according to the election of grace”**
• through the grace by which they are chosen
• not merits
• Whence: “You have not chosen me: but I have chosen you”
**“there is a remnant saved”**
• or 'were made'
• I said: to be saved through grace
11.6:
**“And if by grace”** — that is, they were saved by grace
**“it is not now by works”** — of the law
**“otherwise”** — that is, if they are saved by the works of the law
**“grace”** — which yet is agreed to be
**“grace is no more grace”** — but a debt
11.7:
**“What then?”**
• is to be said
• that is, this
**“That which Israel sought”** — righteousness from works
**“What then? That which Israel sought”** — Having heard that the remnant was saved by grace, not by works: what then is to be said?
**“he hath not obtained, but the election hath obtained it”** — the elect received righteousness through grace, by faith
**“but the election hath obtained it”** — Election is of grace, not of merits. But blinding is of merits. For they were blinded because they would not believe, as the others believed because they willed. Mercy therefore and judgment were wrought by God in the very wills: for the former by adding grace through mercy, the latter by permitting them to be blinded through judgment. For whoever, when he has understood, has refused to believe, ought to obtain what he wills, that henceforth he may not be able to believe. In their own will therefore they were helped, so that, since knowingly they said the true was false, henceforth they should not understand; this is what the envy of an evil will deserves, not so in those who do this through error.
**“the rest”** — not only did not obtain it, but
**“have been blinded”**
• by judgment
• or “were”
11.8:
**“As it is written: God hath given them”**
• he allowed them to have bad remorse
• He hath given them. This signifies bad remorse, because it often happens that even good is troublesome to a man, as the teaching of Christ was to the Pharisees; and so he calls the envious mind, by which they envied the teaching of Christ, “the spirit of compunction.”
**“the spirit”** — that is, evil
**“of insensibility”** — reason, which can see by itself, but they are thus
**“eyes”** — reason, which can see by itself, but they are thus
**“that they should not see”** — by itself
**“and ears that they should not hear”** — reason, which understands by another’s teaching, but they are thus, until
**“until this present day”** — That is, as long as the present day can be called “today”, that is, until the present day, of all to whom this writing comes.
11.9:
**“And David saith”** — adding
**“Let their table be made before them”** — the malice which they offered me
**“their table”** — That is, Scripture. Of them, that is, first taken away from them. And set before them, because they delight in its carnal observances. Or before them, because if they were willing to attend to reason they could understand.
**“a snare”**
• so that their own iniquity may entangle them
• Just as they offered me vinegar, so let it be made for them before them, because they knew wickedness and persisted in it.
• Into a snare, etc. The Scripture, which is bread to those who understand, ensnares when it is ill understood, and in its place the preaching of Christ is rejected. It was also a cause of captivity, when out of zeal for it they killed Christ; and in that captivity a cause of stumbling and reproach; and afterwards a cause of eternal damnation, which is specially called recompense.
**“and a snare”** — so that it may hold them
**“and a stumbling block”** — as a cause of reproach
**“and a recompense unto them”** — of eternal damnation
**“that they see not”** — that they sin
**“always”** — weigh down with sins
11.10:
**“Let their eyes be darkened”**
• reason, which sees
• Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see, etc., because they did not see without cause, let it be done to them not to see.
• Let their eyes be darkened, etc. These words are spoken not by the wish of one desiring them, but by the office of one foretelling them.
**“and bow thou down their back”** — free will, which ought to be raised up
11.11:
**“I say then”**
• I seem to say
• Have they so stumbled, that they should fall? Because I say they are blinded on the authority of the prophets, do you think they are beyond recovery and without profit? But their fall profits, and they can be restored, lest anyone despise them.
**“have they so stumbled, that they should fall?”**
• without restoration and profit
• only
**“God forbid”** — that their fall be not useless but rather useful
**“But by their offence, salvation is come to the Gentiles”** — Whence, because you have rejected the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.
**“salvation”** — While they are scattered through the world as witnesses that the prophecies about Christ are not invented.
**“that”** — so
**“them”**
• the Gentiles
• others
**“they may be emulous”**
• The Jews, by zeal for the law and the fathers.
• envy and hold in hatred
**“That they may be emulous of them”** — This has often been done, and will be done more fully at the end of the age, when the Jews will follow the Christians in the faith of Christ.
