Or that they may be moved by a zeal for God against their evil works.
11.12:
**“Now if the offence of them”**
• because they killed God or rejected the word
• if the world has been enriched by their offence
**“Now if the offence”** — Now if the offence of them. He said the offence of the Jews profits; if so, then their conversion is all the more.
**“the riches of the world, and the diminution”** — that is, rejection
**“of them, the riches of the Gentiles”** — few of them converted, as the apostles, enriched the Gentiles
**“how much more the fulness of them?”**
• who will be converted at the end of the world
• How much more, etc. That is, if God turns their evil into good, that is, into the riches of the world, much more their good, since at the end their fullness, converted, will enrich the Gentiles by teaching and example; in which he shows that their fall is neither useless nor beyond recovery.
11.13:
**“For I say to you”** — and as if someone asked whether they could be converted, he says: they certainly can
**“Gentiles”** — who are mine in particular
**“as long indeed”** — that which always is
**“As long indeed”** — Although I am the apostle of the Gentiles, yet I will honour my ministry by adding beyond what I owe, so that, also laboring among the Jews and trying, if this way does not succeed, I shall attempt another, which I would not do if I despaired of their salvation.
**“indeed as I am the apostle of the Gentiles”** — not of the Jews
**“apostle”** — because sent to the Gentiles
11.14:
**“if by any means”** — either with prosperity or with adversity
**“to emulation”** — that is, to imitate me
**“I may provoke”** — may be able to provoke
**“them who are my flesh”** — the Jews
**“and”**
• or 'that'
• so
**“may save”** — with the grace of God helping
**“some of them”** — at least
11.15:
**“For if”** — and therefore I labor for them, because their taking up will be useful for the instruction of the Gentiles. And truly
**“the loss of them”** — unbelief
**“be the reconciliation of the world”** — will be
**“the receiving”** — of the rest
**“but life from the dead?”** — of the Gentiles; because they were dead
11.16:
**“For if the firstfruit be holy, so is the lump also”**
• can be sanctified
• But if the firstfruit. I have said that their taking back will be very profitable; lest you say it cannot happen, as though the whole race were rejected. For if the firstfruit, that is, the few of them taken up, as the apostles and the other disciples, is holy, so is the lump, that is, the race can be sanctified.
*Ambrose:* The firstfruit is a small taking from some thing, as a sample of the whole mass, as from food or drink. And the root, that is, the patriarchs, from whom the saints draw the moisture of faith. And the branches, which sprang from their stock, are grounded in them.
11.17:
**“And if some”**
• he proves that the Jews can still be taken up, so as to restrain the Gentiles
• that is, but
**“of the branches”** — natural
**“be broken”** — cut off from the promise
**“and thou”** — O Gentile
**“being a wild olive”** — naturally barren and bitter
**“art ingrafted”** — joined by another’s working
**“in those things”** — in the place of the broken
**“and art made partaker”**
• you were made
• partaker
**“partaker”** — In the hope of the promise this is against custom. For a good tree is wont to be grafted into a not good one; here, a not good one into a good one.
**“of the root”** — of the patriarchs and prophets
**“and of the fatness”** — of the apostles, who above all have the spirit of the root
**“of the olive tree”** — of the fruitful Jewish people before the coming of Christ
11.18:
**“Boast not”**
• if, I say, this is so
• because, though the olive is pruned, it is not cut off.
**“boast”** — that is, to insult at another’s evils.
**“against the branches”** — broken.
**“But if thou boast”** — you, a Gentile.
**“thou bearest not the root, but the root thee”** — It is said to you, because that people has nothing from you, but you have faith from it.
11.19:
**“Thou wilt say then”** — O Gentile.
**“The branches were broken off, that I might be grafted in.”**
• Thou wilt say then: The branches were broken off, etc. As if to say: though you stand, it is nevertheless not permitted you to boast against those who were cast out on account of my grafting in. The Apostle answers this: you speak well, because it is true that they were broken off for unbelief, and you stand by faith, that is, not by your merit but by the grace of God; and therefore be not proud, lest you also be broken off through pride as they were through unbelief.
• You are not steadfast if you destroy those through whom you stand.
• He is easily deceived who rejoices in others' evils.
11.20:
**“Well”** — You say.
**“because of”** — But.
**“unbelief they were broken off”** — that is, by their own fault; whence the opportunity of salvation is yours, not because of you.
**“But thou standest by faith”** — and therefore.
**“Faith”** — It is God’s gift that you stand, not your merit.
**“be not highminded”** — to be proud.
**“but fear”**
• to offend.
• chastely.
• fear what you ought, because
**“But fear”** — Lest you lose the benefit of so great grace and fall into punishment. For chaste fear is when the soul takes care lest God, forsaken, forsake her.
11.21:
**“For if God hath not spared the natural branches”**
• the prerogative of the fathers to whom the promise was made.
• but see.
**“For if God”** — God did not spare the Jews, who drew their origin from the holy fathers, from whose people he also took flesh; much less will he spare you if you withdraw from faith or swell up in pride.
**“lest perhaps”** — that this happen, which indeed can happen.
**“he also spare not thee”** — to another.
11.22:
**“See then”** — because you stand by faith.
**“the goodness”**
• he persuades by goodness, terrifies by severity.
• learn to be humbled by both.
**“and the severity of God”**
• that is, strict justice.
• because broken off through unbelief.
**“towards them indeed that are fallen, the severity; but towards thee, the goodness of God”** — by which he confers a benefit on you.
**“when”** — if yet.
**“abide in goodness”**
• that you may attribute all to God
• those things
**“otherwise”** — unless you remain
**“thou also”** — as they
**“shalt be cut off”**
• from the holy root
• feeling the severity of God
11.23:
**“And they also, if they abide not still in unbelief, shall be grafted in”**
• as if: not only will you be cut off if you do not remain in good
• therefore not to be despised
**“for God is able”** — if they do not remain in unbelief, which certainly can happen
**“to graft them in again”** — to himself, because he was also born from that
11.24:
**“For if thou”** — able to graft. For they will be grafted in, and this is argued from the less
**“wild olive tree, which is natural to thee”** — because born from it
**“wert cut out”** — by the power of God
**“wild olive tree”** — by the rites of sterile Gentiles
**“and, contrary to nature”** — because idolatry and such things are by custom natural to the Gentiles
**“Contrary to nature”** — It is said to be against the custom of nature that a shoot bear the fruit of the root. God, however, does nothing against nature, because what he does is nature. The highest nature is the work of God, against which nothing is done, but against what is customary for us.
**“wert grafted into the good olive tree”** — joined by faith to the patriarchs and apostles, who had the richness of the Holy Spirit
**“olive tree”** — Here the faith of the fathers is understood.
**“how much more”** — if this is so, how much more, etc.
**“they that are the natural branches”** — taught by the law the worship of God
**“be grafted into their own olive tree”** — will be joined to their own people
11.25:
**“For I would not have you ignorant, brethren”** — the Jews will be grafted in; and truly, both in the meantime some, and at last the fullness; and I want you to know this
**“of this mystery”**
• the hidden judgment of God
• I say mystery, lest you think you can discern this by your own wit
**“lest you should be wise in your own conceits, that blindness in part”** — not all blinded
**“has happened in Israel”** — not from nature but from fault
**“until the fulness of the Gentiles should come in”** — that is, until, or up to which, so that the cause and the limit are noted
11.26:
**“And so”** — after it has entered
**“all Israel”** — with Elias and Enoch preaching
**“should be saved”** — by the Gentiles provoking to emulation
**“As it is written”**
• Israel should be saved
• in Isaias
**“There shall come”** — according to the flesh
**“out of Sion”** — from the Jews
**“he that shall deliver”** — by force, which is at times when someone is hardly converted
**“and shall turn away”**
• willingly
• at the end, when it is easy
**“ungodliness”** — unbelief
**“Ungodliness”** — The worship of the observance of the law. The worship of the Jews since the coming of Christ is ungodliness.
**“from Jacob”** — by the Jews
11.27:
**“And this”** — will be
**“to them”** — because I myself will do what I promised
**“covenant”**
• the promise will be fulfilled
• or 'testimony'
**“when I shall take away”**
• I will remit
• When I shall take away. This will be at the end, when by the preaching of Elias and Enoch the Jews will be converted; whence through Malachias: “I will send you Elias the Thesbite, who shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to the fathers,” that the children may understand as the fathers, that is, as the prophets understood.
11.28:
**“As concerning”**
• that is, on account of
• then they will be converted, but now enemies; behold why part is blinded and part enlightened
**“the gospel”**
• which is against their law, not on account of the Gentiles
• According to the gospel, etc. Augustine. Or thus: Then they will be converted, but now indeed they are enemies of Christ. And indeed of ours. Again, of themselves, that is, by their own fault. But this is according to the gospel and on your account, that is, for the perfecting of the gospel and of yours.
**“indeed, they are enemies”** — so that there might be room for you to enter into the faith
**“for your sake”**
• for your benefit
• Enemies on account of. He shows this comes from the disposition of God. For of themselves they can be enemies, which profits the gospel, God using evils for good, so that although they act against the will of God, the will of God is fulfilled, wisely disposing all things.
**“according to”** — as if to say: some are enemies according to the gospel and on your account, but some are most dear or beloved according to election
**“but as touching the election”** — not on account of merits
**“most dear for the sake of the fathers”** — that is, on account of the promises made to the fathers
**“For the sake of the fathers”** — The elect are beloved for the sake of the fathers, to whom these things were promised, not by that calling by which many are called who are not foreknown and yet perish, of which it is said: “Many are called, but few are chosen,” but by that by which the elect are called, which is without change; for “he who hears of the Father cometh to the Son,” who loses nothing of all that is given, but whoever perishes was not of them. Whence: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.”
11.29:
**“Without repentance”**
• change
• According to the election and for the sake of the fathers they are to be saved, because the gifts, that is, the promises, and the calling, that is, the election, are from eternity. Without repentance, that is, without change of God’s counsel. Or I therefore say according to the election, because those into whom God breathes faith, he breathes it without any repentance of theirs going before.
• Without sin. The grace of God in baptism does not require groaning or lamentation or any work, only faith, and freely pardons all things. This is so that they may not think those cannot receive mercy because they do not see them grieving.
**“are the gifts”**
• remission of sins in baptism
• promises
**“and the calling of God”**
• or election from eternity
• inward and gratuitous
• which no one’s merit has gone before
• to faith
11.30:
**“For as”**
• so it was needful that some should be enemies and others chosen
• That is, for what reason God once allowed you not to believe: namely, that you might not have cause for pride afterwards, when converted.
**“you also in times past”** — for a long time, more than these
**“did not believe God”** — which availed so that now you might believe in humility
**“but now”** — lately
**“have obtained mercy”** — proved that nature fails, that is, that you could not be helped by free will
**“through their unbelief”** — which is a certain cause of your mercy
11.31:
**“So these also”** — Jews
**“now have not believed”** — so that they may not have matter for boasting afterwards, once converted
**“for your mercy”**
• coming
• that is, they have not had the grace of faith through God’s mercy as you have
**“that they also”** — humbled
**“That they also”** — Having learned that salvation is not by the law but by grace, so that thus, through humility, they too might obtain mercy.
**“may obtain mercy”** — the grace of faith
11.32:
**“For God hath concluded”** — therefore it was so done with both
**“Hath concluded”** — That is, he permitted. “Concluded” here seems in some way to set forth a mystery. For God has concluded all in unbelief, that, confounded by repenting of the bitterness of their unbelief, and turned by believing to the sweetness of God’s mercy, they might remain more humble, so that the grace of the gift might be most welcome, and they might cry out: “O how great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord.”
**“all”** — Jews and Gentiles
**“in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all”**
• because otherwise they would fall through pride
• And why so? Do not suppose it can be comprehended?
• All. That is, of Jews and Gentiles: not that he will condemn none, as some falsely supposed.
• For we have a very small understanding for examining the justice of God’s judgments, for examining grace freely given, rendered by no preceding merits. Nor does it move us so much that grace is given to the unworthy as that it is equally denied to others who are unworthy.
*Augustine:* I know that as there is no impossibility, so there is no iniquity with God, and I know that “God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.” But this is obscure: why he gives to some who are unworthy, and denies to others; there is therefore something in the hidden depth of God’s judgments. Nor is this clear: why he saved Jews and Gentiles in such a way that he first permitted them to be concluded in unbelief.
11.33:
**“O the depth of the riches”** — because he knows many things, and deep ones
**“O the depth”** — If anyone asks why they are saved in this way, since there are many other ways of salvation, the Apostle by his wonder signifies that he does not know this. Note: from the fact that we behold creatures as having come into being, we have no doubt at all that there is God the Father, from whom all things have their beginning. Again, since if he were without reason he would seem as it were a foolish thing, we know beyond doubt that he has a reason, by which he proceeds from himself, not he from the reason, that is, the Son, through whom we see all things so reasonably ordered, and we faithfully believe that he has proceeded from the Father. And we know that God the Father rejoices because he has such a reason, and the reason rejoices because he has proceeded from such a Father. We therefore know that that joy and goodness is the Spirit proceeding from both. We do not at all doubt that in this Spirit all things consist, and that joy and kindness reach even to creatures; and so the Spirit is said to proceed, that is, to be given, not as regards the Father and the Son but as regards men, because if we see anything good in anyone, we believe it was given to him through the Spirit by the Father and the Son. It is to be noted that to say that the reason is from the Father, and that goodness and joy proceed from both, as Augustine says, is nothing other than to beget the Son; but when the Spirit is said to proceed from the Father and the Son, this means he is sent, given, and also from himself.
**“of the wisdom”** — concerning spiritual things
**“and of the knowledge of God”** — concerning worldly things
**“How incomprehensible are”** — just as his wisdom and knowledge are incomprehensible, so too are the judgments by which he has acted from wisdom and knowledge
**“his judgments”** — that is, dispositions concerning all things
**“his ways”** — That is, the fulfilments of the disposition, because what he has disposed cannot be known even in its carrying out.
11.34:
**“For who hath known”**
• truly high wisdom and knowledge
• this Isaias says
**“the mind of the Lord”** — in wisdom and knowledge
**“Or who hath been his counsellor”** — in the arrangement and carrying out of things. Who was there whose condition would act, or who would know his counsel
**“His counsellor”** — He is his only-begotten Son, who is also called “the angel of great counsel.” But of men and angels none was his counsellor.
11.35:
**“Or who hath first given to him”** — faith and good works
**“Or who hath first”** — And if we cannot know the judgments, this at least is certain: that he gives from grace alone.
**“and recompense shall be made him”**
• by God
• recompense from this, that he first gave his faith
11.36:
**“For”** — no one, because rather
**“of him”**
• from the Father, from whom the Son
• For of him, etc. “Of him,” “by him,” “in him” indicate the distinction of persons; “him,” the same pronoun repeated, the identity of substance; and because such glory is his, not that of the just themselves. All things are of him, not out of him. For heaven and earth are of him because he made them, but not out of him, because not out of his substance. In him are all things which he established, yet those who sin do not defile him, of whose wisdom it is said: “She reacheth everywhere by reason of her purity, and nothing defiled cometh into her.”
*Augustine:* It is fitting that, beholding the creator with the mind through the things that are made, we understand the Trinity. The trace of this Trinity appears in creatures. For in that Trinity is the highest origin of all things, and the most perfect beauty, and the most blessed love. And so those three seem to be distinguished from one another, and are also infinite in themselves, so that each is in each, and all in each, and each in all, and all are one. What the Apostle says is therefore not to be taken confusedly: Of him, and by him, and in him. Of him, he says on account of the Father; by him, on account of the Son; in him, on account of the Holy Ghost. Nor did he say “of him” wishing the Father to be understood in such a way that you would understand all things to be from the Father so as to deny that all things are from the Son or from the Holy Ghost. Since it can rightly be said that all things are of the Father and by the Father and in the Father. The same can be said likewise of the Son and the Holy Ghost. But by this, when it is said: Of him, and by him, and in him, are all things, the equality of the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost is without doubt shown. And since he had not named before the Father or the Son or the Holy Ghost, but God and Lord, which the Trinity itself can be called, he wished each of these three to be referred to each.
**“and by him”** — the Son through whom all things
**“and in him are all things”** — the Holy Spirit, because by love alone he created and preserves all things
**“All things”** — Those things which are natural are not sins; those which spoil nature, which arise from the will of sinners, are. In creatures appears the trace of the Trinity. In the Trinity is the supreme origin of all things, and perfect beauty, and most blessed delight.

12.1:
**“I beseech you therefore”**
• because in him are all things
• Hence is the moral admonition, after the treatment of the law and of faith and of the nature of the Jewish and the Gentile people.
**“I beseech”**
• Up to here he has sufficiently humbled both parts, and has annulled the glory of the former state; now, as if the business were finished, he proceeds from here on to morality.
• Up to here, lest the one should be proud against the other; from here on, that the one should labour for the other’s profit. I beseech you by the mercy of God, that is, by the apostleship mercifully committed to me by God, or the mercy given you by God.
**“brethren”** — what brotherhood requires me to ask
**“by the mercy of God, that you present”** — offer
**“bodies”** — not only minds, although the flesh resists
**“a sacrifice”** — in the mortification of carnal desires
**“living”** — through good works
**“A living sacrifice”** — Augustine. Formerly a victim was killed, so that men, subject to death because of sin, might be shown; now, because they are free from sin, a living victim is offered as a sign of eternal life.
**“holy”** — firm in good things
**“pleasing unto God”** — so that you may do it with good intention
**“your reasonable”** — with discretion, nothing too much
**“service”**
• all in the aforesaid things
• let it be
12.2:
**“And be not”** — for it is in your own hand
**“conformed to this world”** — to take on the form of secular concupiscence
**“Be not conformed”**
• Augustine. Here the soul becomes a sacrifice to God: kindled with the fire of love, it loses the form of worldly desire, and referring itself to God, it is reformed, made subject to him as to an unchangeable form.
• A general prohibition. But “be reformed” is a general command. There, continence; here, justice; this relates to not coveting, that to loving; that to turning away from evil, this to doing good. For by not coveting we are stripped of the old nature, and by loving we are clothed with the new.
**“but be reformed”** — deformed in Adam, or again and again, as if from day to day
**“Be reformed”** — Because the image of God is partly lost, so that it begins to be reformed by him by whom it was formed. For it cannot reform itself as it could deform itself.
**“in the newness”** — after the manner of the new man
**“of your mind”**
• by which sin is not ruled over
• or 'vestre'
**“that you may prove what is ... the will of God”**
• by testing, what God wills
• What is the will, etc. The will of God is spoken of either as that by which he wills, which is in God, or as that which he wills. Here is understood the will of God by which he wills, which is always fulfilled, and which is sometimes called the good pleasure or the disposition of God. Of which the prophet says: “He hath done all things whatsoever he would.” And the Apostle: “Who resisteth his will?” God therefore wills that all the good things that come to pass be done, of which he himself is the author. But evil things he does not will to be done, yet neither does he will that they not be done. For if he willed that they not be done and they were done, something would resist his will; but he only foreknows that they are done. Besides, the will of God is said to be his working or permission. Whence Augustine: Nothing is done that the Almighty does not will to be done, either by permitting it to be done or by himself doing it. Likewise the will of God is sometimes said to be his counsel or approval.
**“good”** — because whatever God wills is good
**“and the acceptable”** — for those who understand well and have proved it
**“and the perfect”**
• by precepts
• in all goodness, so that nothing is better
12.3:
**“For I say”** — that I beg; but this I forbid
**“by the grace”** — of the apostleship
**“For I say, by the grace”** — This is the sacrifice of Christians: that the many are one body in Christ. For this is shown to the faithful, by their desire, in the sacrament of the altar, in which the Church is signified in the thing which it offers. For as bread is made of many grains, so the holy Church is made of many members of the faithful, who rejoice together in the participation of their creator, by whose gift they are holy; which is also shown in what follows, where he says: “We, being many, are one body in Christ,” which cannot be done unless they be wise unto sobriety, which he here commands.
**“that is given me, to all that are among you”** — because not all act
**“not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise”** — to inquire into divine mysteries
**“to be wise”** — That it not go beyond the bounds of justice, that it be useful only to us and harm no one.
**“but to be wise unto sobriety”** — without presumption
**“and according as God hath divided to every one the measure”**
• according to quantity or quality
• And to every one. As he warned them not to be proud of their former state, so neither of the good things they received in faith.
• And to every one, etc. To the greater or the lesser, by the reason by which God divided out the measured gifts that faith deserves. He did this so that the Church should not be in want, and that there be matter for serving one another, so that there be mutual love. Whence he adds: For as, etc.
**“to every one”** — If it is nourished by its own strength, an infant grows; otherwise it fails.
**“of faith”** — by which God also divides faith in measure to each one: this is faith working through love
**“the measure of faith”** — And God divides faith in measure, without which there are no good works. The Spirit was not given to Christ by measure, but to all others. Whence John says of Christ: “For God doth not give the Spirit by measure.” Not the Spirit indeed is divided to the others, but his gifts.
12.4: **“For as in one body we have many members, but all the members have not the same office:”** — therefore he divided by measure, because they are many, one body; and therefore all necessary things are to be given, not in one
12.5:
**“So we being many”** — through diverse gifts
**“are one body in Christ”** — by serving one another
**“and every one”**
• no one is excluded
• greater or lesser
**“members one of another”** — serving others, needing others
**“Every one members”** — Having gifts different for this purpose. Or: we are individually members; therefore let this be done in different gifts. Whether we have prophecy, let us be members of others, that we may prophesy to them. I say, having it according to the rule of faith, because prophecy is given as the faith of them or of the hearers requires.
12.6:
**“And having”** — or 'therefore'
**“different gifts, according to the grace that is given us”** — that is, we are members one of another.
**“either prophecy”** — of things future, or of any hidden things.
**“Either prophecy”** — He begins with prophecy, because believers, having received the Spirit, will prophesy.
**“to be used according to the rule of faith”** — than beyond the measure.
12.7:
**“Or ministry”**
• having the ecclesiastical office.
• as presbyters.
**“in ministering”**
• we are members of others.
• constantly.
**“or he that teacheth”** — who has the grace of teaching.
**“in doctrine”** — in setting forth doctrine, let him be a member of another.
12.8:
**“He that exhorteth”** — who has the grace of exhorting.
**“in exhorting”** — let him be a member of another.
**“he that giveth”** — alms.
**“with simplicity”** — let him be a member of another, not in duplicity of present and future glory.
**“he that ruleth”** — as a leader.
**“with carefulness”**
• as one who acts carefully.
• let him be a member of another.
**“he that sheweth mercy”** — who has the grace of helping or sympathizing with the oppressed.
**“He that sheweth mercy”** — A daily medicine for daily wounds, even if lighter ones. Nevertheless: “Judgment without mercy to him that hath not done mercy.” Whoever, as if too just and secure, awaits judgment without mercy, provokes wrath against himself. This mercy is manifold: to forgive the one who sins, to help the oppressed, etc.; and therefore he adds, since it was said before, he that giveth, with simplicity. Simplicity excludes hypocrisy; cheerfulness shows joy, resting on the hope of the future.
**“with cheerfulness”** — let him help with a cheerful mind.
12.9:
**“Love”** — this is the love by which diverse goods are united.
**“without dissimulation”** — and so each will be a member of the other.
**“Hating that which is evil, cleaving to that which is good”** — so that the love of a friend does not make one love evil, nor evil make one give up good.
12.10:
**“Loving one another with the charity of brotherhood”** — that is, the love which brothers have among themselves, or those wishing to be loved in return by brothers.
**“with honour”** — in every reverence.
**“preventing one another”** — there is no brotherly love unless they anticipate one another with mutual services.
12.11:
**“In carefulness”** — be careful in heart.
**“not slothful”**
• in work.
• and therefore.
**“Not slothful”** — Cursed is he who does the works of God negligently; the slothful man is without hope. And therefore, that the cold of sloth may be driven away: Be fervent, etc.
**“In spirit fervent”**
• even if in deed you cannot fulfill what you wish.
• with the fire of charity
**“fervent”** — The spirit is the fire by which charity glows; whence the Lord says: “I am come to cast fire on the earth; and what will I, but that it be kindled?”
**“Serving the Lord”**
• or 'to the time'
• that which you believe, at hand, you are to devote to the Lord
• Serving the Lord, or 'the time'. Although fervent, do not thrust the words of God everywhere and unseasonably, but serve the time, that is, the opportunity.
12.12:
**“Rejoicing in hope”**
• and in these things hope only for eternal ones
• Rejoicing in hope. Those certain of the future rejoice, and therefore are patient in tribulation.
**“Patient in tribulation”** — and if evils meet them among these goods
**“in prayer”** — that you may be able to endure
**“Instant”** — because the thing is deferred for this purpose
12.13:
**“Communicating to the necessities of the saints,”** — suffer, and make your goods common to the saints who suffer
**“Pursuing hospitality.”**
• and receive the saints in hospitality
• by the example of Abraham and Lot
**“Bless”** — that is, pray good things
**“them that persecute you,”** — removes from common custom
**“bless”** — again and again
**“and curse not.”** — as if to say: without any admixture of bitterness
12.15:
**“Rejoice”** — and you ought
**“with them that rejoice,”** — concerning progress
**“weep with them that weep.”** — concerning the matter for which weeping is due
12.16:
**“Being of one mind one towards another.”**
• with joy or weeping
• and for all these
**“Not minding high things,”** — at least in heart
**“but consenting to the humble.”** — imitators of the humble
**“Consenting”** — This is not done with the mouth only, because then is humility true if it is not in the tongue alone, lest those presuming on themselves should not sympathize with others but reproach them.
**“Be not wise in your own conceits.”** — that is, do not exercise your prudence only among yourselves but rather among your neighbours, even if any of them offends you
12.17:
**“To no man rendering evil for evil. Providing good things”** — he warns that lawful things not be done with scandal
**“not only in the sight of God”** — in the secret of the heart
**“but also in the sight of all men.”** — so that scandal not arise but a good example; because that is to be done which is not displeasing to God, and which is not a scandal to a brother
12.18:
**“If it be possible, as much as is in you,”** — that they may agree; if not, at least do as much as is in you; or “if it can be done,” because it is difficult; yet what is “from you,” that is, from your power, is possible
**“have peace with all men.”** — Whence also: “With them that hated peace I was peaceable.”
12.19:
**“Revenge not yourselves, my dearly beloved,”** — Referring to adversaries.
**“but give place unto wrath.”** — to God’s judgment, or to their wrath.
**“Give place unto wrath”**
• He gives place to wrath who allows the adversary to do what he wants.
• He does not command that they be unwilling to be avenged by God, namely that the saints condemn, not indeed to satisfy hatred, but: “The just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge.” But he commands that they not avenge themselves, but give place to the wrath of God, who says: “Revenge is mine, I will repay.” If then the good man wishes God to punish his enemy, is this not to render evil for evil? Or in this way he neither loves nor does good to his enemy. But the good man rather desires the enemy to be corrected than punished; even when God punishes he does not delight in the punishment, because he does not hate him, but in the justice of God, since he loves God; for God too, whom he follows in this, though he rains upon the just and the unjust, yet even in this world corrects with hardships, and at the end condemns the stubborn.
**“for it is written:”** — In Proverbs.
**“Mine”** — and so whoever does not do this despises God.
**“revenge”** — Reserve.
**“I will repay,”** — I will avenge.
**“saith the Lord.”** — not only do not defend yourselves.
12.20:
**“But if thy enemy be hungry”** — Note the unusualness of the conjunction “but.” For it is to be followed up as though neither conjunction were interposed.
**“For, doing this, thou shalt heap coals of fire”** — the fervour of charity, or of the Holy Spirit, or the burning of penance.
**“upon his head.”** — the mind.
12.21:
**“Be not overcome by evil,”** — even if he does not repent, yet because if you strike back you will become like him, wicked.
**“but overcome evil by good.”** — by suffering.
**“Overcome evil by good”** — Contend against him with goodness, and it is a wholesome contest, so that there are not two evil ones.

13.1:
**“Let every soul be subject to higher powers”** — secular powers, good or bad.
**“Every soul”** — Even if you are so perfect in the body of Christ, yet “every soul,” that is, every man, by the part the whole, you should serve as it were not only in body but also in will. For it seemed that unbelieving lords ought not to rule over the faithful, even if the faithful ought to be equals; this pride too the Apostle removes.
**“higher”** — in that they are high, that is, in worldly matters; or the cause is noted, that is, because they are higher
**“be subject.”** — and therefore ought to be subject.
**“for there is no power but from God.”** — Whence: “Thou shouldst not have any power against me, unless it were given thee from above.”
**“For there is no power”** — Power is from God, but what is from God is ordained; therefore power is ordained. And so “he that resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God.” Of good power it is clear that God has made it perfect. Reasonably it can be seen of evil power as well, since the good are purified by it and the wicked are condemned and it itself is cast down into the worse. And know that by the name of power is sometimes understood the power itself which is given to someone by God, sometimes the man himself having power; let the diligent reader distinguish this. The malice of men has of itself the desire to harm, but power, if God does not give it, it does not have; and therefore the devil, before he took anything from Job, said to the Lord: “Put forth thy hand,” that is, give power. Because even the power of those who harm is only from God, as it is written, wisdom speaking: “By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree just things.” Whence Job also says of the Lord: “Who maketh a hypocrite to reign for the sins of the people.” And of the people of Israel the Lord says: “I gave them a king in my wrath.” Power to harm the good is given, I say, to the wicked, that the patience of the good may be proved and the iniquity of the wicked punished. For by the power given to the devil Job was proved, that he might appear just; and Peter was tempted lest he presume on himself, and Paul buffeted lest he be exalted, and Judas is condemned that he might hang himself.
**“those that are, are ordained of God.”**
• reasonably disposed.
• Those that are, are ordained of God, etc. That is, reasonably disposed by God. Job says: “God doth not cast away the mighty, whereas he himself also is mighty.”
*Gregory:* He desires indeed to imitate God who administers the height of power intent on the advantages of others and not on his own praises; who, set over others, seeks to profit them, not to rule over them. For it is the swelling of pride, not the order of power, that is in fault. God distributes power; the malice of our mind finds the pride of power. Let us then take away what we have added of our own, and the things we possess by the Lord’s bounty are good, since it is never just power but wicked action that is condemned.
13.2:
**“Therefore he that resisteth”** — by force or by fraud.
**“the power”**
• in those things that pertain to power.
• that is, tributes and such like.
**“resisteth the ordinance of God.”** — that is, to one who has power by God’s ordinance.
**“And they that resist”**
• which is so grave.
• Augustine. If he commands what is not lawful, then indeed despise the power in fearing a greater power; therefore if the emperor commands one thing and God another, the former being despised, one must obey God.
**“purchase to themselves damnation.”**
• and therefore one ought not to resist but to be subject.
• they will deservedly acquire damnation.
13.3:
**“For princes”** — good or bad.
**“Princes”** — He says: those who are created for the correcting of life and the restraining of adversities, having the image of God, so that the rest may be under one.
**“are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil.”**
• to fear for those who do good
• Not a terror, etc. If the prince is good, he does not punish the one who acts well, but loves him. If he is bad, he does not harm the good but purifies him. The bad man ought to fear, because princes are appointed to punish evils.
**“Wilt thou then not be afraid”** — as if: they are a terror to those who act badly; but you, etc.
**“of the power?”** — whatever it may be
**“Do that which is good:”** — and there is nothing for which you should fear
**“and thou shalt have praise from the same.”** — even if it is bad, while for you it is the cause of a greater crown
**“Thou shalt have praise”** — If it is just, by the praise of the one who praises; if unjust, by the one who offers you the occasion of praise.
13.4:
**“For he is God's minister to thee, for good.”**
• truly you will have praise from him, because he is God’s minister doing good to you, whether he is good or bad
• he is not to be feared by the good
**“For he is God's minister”** — Therefore rulers are given, so that evil things may not be done.
**“But if thou do that which is evil, fear.”** — he is to be feared, because he holds the sword of judicial power not without cause, but so that he may punish the wicked; and this is what “for he is God’s minister” means: he avenges in God’s place
**“For he beareth not the sword in vain. For he is God's minister: an avenger to execute wrath upon him that doth evil.”** — that is, to his harm
**“An avenger to execute wrath”** — That is, for the avenging of God’s wrath, or: an avenger for the showing of God’s wrath, because this punishment shows that those who persist in evil are to be punished more severely.
**“Qui male agit: "he that doth evil"”** — because he is God’s minister
13.5:
**“"Wherefore be subject of necessity"”**
• or by necessity, the necessary ordinance
• as if from necessity
**“"not only for wrath"”** — to be avoided, of the prince or of God
**“"but also for conscience' sake"”** — that your mind may be pure in loving the one set over you
13.6:
**“"For therefore also you pay tribute"”** — this is the proof of subjection
**“For therefore”** — You ought to be subject, because also for this reason, that is, to show subjection, you pay tribute, as to those who will give back, because they give back while they fight for the country and while they carry out judgments; you pay it as serving God. For by the fact that you give them tribute you serve God, because they are ministers of God. Or you pay tribute because they are ministers of God, that the good may be praised and the wicked punished. I say they are serving you for this, while they defend the country.
**“"For they are the ministers of God, serving unto this purpose"”** — for this very tribute they serve you in the defence of the country
13.7:
**“"Render therefore to all men their dues"”**
• because they are ministers of God
• namely, that the evangelical discipline may be praised
**“"Tribute, to whom tribute"”**
• you owe
• which the regions pay
**“tribute”** — render
**“"custom, to whom custom"”**
• you owe
• the stipend which is given to lords when they are carried through the country
**“custom”** — render
**“Tribute”** — Tribute. Or customs duty, which is paid at home. Tribute, which is carried to the house of the Lord.
**“"honour, to whom honour"”**
• you owe
• that you stand up
**“honour”** — render
**“"fear, to whom fear"”** — that we fear lordship and reverence persons
13.8:
**“"Owe no man any thing"”**
• discharge the rest so that you owe nothing
• Owe no man anything, etc. Peace to all, love among brothers. For otherwise they are not truly brothers.
**“"but to love one another"”** — discharge charity so that you always owe
**“love”** — Mention is made here of charity because it avails for this humility. For charity alone is that which, even when paid, always keeps the debtor. For it is paid when it is bestowed, but it is owed even if it has been paid, because there is no time when it is not to be bestowed. Nor is it lost when it is paid, but rather is multiplied by paying; for it is paid by having, not by lacking, unlike money, which cannot be paid unless it is had, nor had unless it is paid; rather, when it is paid by a man, it grows in the man, and is acquired the greater, the more people it is paid to.
**“"For he that loveth his neighbour, hath fulfilled the law"”**
• and he shows this by parts
• He loveth his neighbour. Since there are two precepts of charity, one is often put for both, because neither is God loved without the neighbour, nor the neighbour without God, or can he be. Love of neighbour appears in deeds; love of God lies more hidden. Therefore he puts this one more specially, of which the Lord says: “A new commandment I give unto you: That you love one another,” where that greater commandment of the love of God seems to be passed over. But to those who understand well, both are found in each, because he who loves God cannot despise the neighbour whom God commands to be loved; and he who loves the neighbour in a holy and spiritual way, what does he love in him but God?
**“neighbour”** — Every man must be understood, because there is no one with whom evil is to be done. He therefore who loves men ought to love them either because they are just or because they are unjust. For so he ought to love himself too, namely either because he is just or that he may be just. For he who loves himself otherwise loves himself unjustly, because he loves himself to this end, that he be unjust; to this end therefore, that he be wicked, he therefore does not now love himself: “But he that loveth iniquity hateth his own soul.”
13.9:
**“"For Thou shalt not commit adultery: Thou shalt not kill: Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness: Thou shalt not covet"”** — through Moses
**“"in this word"”** — which Moses wrote in Leviticus
**“"is comprised"”** — is contained, is fulfilled
**“"Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself"”** — in good, since he that loveth iniquity hateth his own soul
13.10:
**“"The love of our neighbour worketh no evil"”** — he who loves does good, because no evil; and therefore the fullness of the law
**“"Love therefore is the fulfilling of the law"”** — he who loves fully fulfils the law
13.11:
**“"And that knowing the season"”** — we know that love works no evil
**“"And that knowing"”** — Another commendation of charity. For it does no evil and prepares the opportunity of doing good.
**“knowing”** — Namely, because it is the hour; or, as some books have, this time, namely knowing grace. Since we have had love, it is the hour, that is, the opportunity, but brief.
**“"that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep"”** — from sluggishness
**“sleep”** — Sleep is negligence or ignorance.
**“rise”** — by working well
**“"For now"”**
• we ought to rise
• Reasons inserted why we ought to rise.
**“"our salvation is nearer"”**
• more due through good works

**“nearer”** — He who works well is near eternal life. For baptism is for pardon, a good life for the crown.
**“"our salvation"”** — the eternal, which is promised to us
**“"than when"”** — then
**“"we believed"”**
• because we have believed and worked, it is more shameful unless we rise
• yet
13.12:
**“"The night is passed"”** — Again, why they ought to rise is shown: because the night of unbelief and ignorance
**“passed”** — That is, it has passed, but is now no more; its memory warns you to be on your guard. Day: eternal blessedness.
**“"The night is passed, and the day is at hand"”** — Is at hand, while sins are forgiven, while the just are made so through grace.
**“night”** — The old man, who passed away in baptism. Day: the sun of justice, by whose light they have learned the truth, so that they may know what is to be done.
**“"Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness"”** — because of the many causes crowded in
**“"the works of darkness"”** — Evil works that come from the darkness of ignorance, or that love darkness and lead to darkness.
**“"and put on"”** — as an ornament
**“armour”** — virtues
**“"of light"”** — which light, that is faith, requires
13.13:
**“"Let us walk honestly, as in the day"”** — having received the virtues, let us exercise ourselves in their act, as befits the day of faith
**“"not in rioting and drunkenness"”**
• These are the works of darkness.
• luxurious feasts
**“"not in rioting"”** — Note that these things are touched upon in these Romans, and therefore they have no right to glory. Pride is the mother of these diseases, and the greed for human praise, which often begets hypocrisy as well; this is not resisted unless fear and charity are instilled by frequent testimonies of the divine books.
**“"not in chambering"”** — laziness in sleeping
**“"and impurities"”** — and lust, which comes from excessive food and drink
**“"not in contention and envy"”** — as they were wont, each putting himself before the other, in which the lesser envied the greater
13.14:
**“"But put ye on"”** — as if to say: do not do the things said above
**“"the Lord Jesus Christ"”**
• that is, the form of Christ
• having put him on, you will not be compelled to serve the flesh
**“"and make not provision for the flesh in its concupiscences"”**
• unlawful ones
• not in things necessary for sustenance

14.1:
**“"Now him that is weak"”**

• him who does not yet believe perfectly, as is to be believed
• It belongs to perfect faith to distinguish no food, or to think it unclean, because: “All things are clean to the clean.” But because the weak judged that some foods were to be abstained from, there was therefore contention among the Romans. And if it is unknown with what mind someone does it, not to dispute about it.
**“Take unto you”**
• as Christ does the sick
• to heal
**“not in disputes about thoughts”** — so that you may judge the guilty person from what is hidden
**“Not in disputes”** — One is not to be condemned whose thought is not open, or of whom we do not know what he will be afterward.
14.2:
**“For one believeth”** — such a one can take in others
**“that he may eat”** — to be able
**“all things”** — given for human uses
**“but he that is weak, let him eat herbs”**
• this one needs to be received, who is allowed to eat herbs, in which there is no dispute
• and since these things are so

For the fatness of meats and delicate feasts provoke the body to lust.
**“Weak”** — He who distinguishes foods, thinking some clean and some unclean, because the Jews were forbidden to eat, says he is to be left to his own judgment, lest he eat with scruple.
14.3:
**“Let not him that eateth”** — all things without distinction

**“despise”** — because it is a matter of will to eat or not to eat

But those things of which it is doubtful with what mind they are done, let us interpret in the better part, as with foods, because any human foods can be taken indifferently with a good mind and a simple heart, without the vice of concupiscence.
**“For God”** — neither the other; for each is a servant of God
**“him”** — eating or not eating
**“hath taken him to him”**
• to faith
• and with this, therefore it is

• this concerns the predestined
• he will be able to stand to his Lord

14.5:

**“another judgeth every day”**
• of them
• to be chosen in abstinence
**“Let every man”** — so that he who eats should eat with thanksgiving, and he who abstains should do so for God
**“in his own sense”**
• that is, according to his own conscience

**“abound”** — in better part
14.6:

• that is, he does it to the honour and praise of the Lord
• to God
• he thinks to please God
**“He that regardeth”** — I say in his own sense, as one who abounds; for he who regards the day, whether every day or one day among the days, regards it for the Lord.

• all things

• to the honour of the Lord

**“of us”** — of us, the faithful

**“and no man to himself”** — but to the Lord
**“dieth”**
• in vices
• and truly no one to himself, because to the Lord
14.8:
**“For whether we live”** — the life of virtues

• and judge both

For this is a perverse doctrine handed down by the foolish; but it is better that Christ be said to rule over both and to judge both, as it were: “To them he gave power to be made the sons of God,” these even now and after death reign with Christ. But his saints reign with him in one way now, in another way they will reign then. Now they reign because they “mind the things that are above and seek them.” Finally they will reign with him, so that they will be in his kingdom and will also themselves be his kingdom, because the souls of the pious dead also are not separated from the Church. Which even now is the kingdom of Christ, because it now reigns with Christ in the living and the dead. Or he died to free the dead from sins; for while he lived, he showed the living the way of salvation; he rose again that he might make those justified live with him.

• Christ ought to rule and to judge; but you, etc.
• eating all things
**“thy brother”** — not eating

• eating
• you ought not to do so

14.11:
**“for it is written:”** — In Isaias.

**“every knee shall bow to me”** — in judgment
**“every knee”** — even of enemies
**“and every tongue”** — knowing in conscience that I am God
**“shall confess”** — what he has done
**“to God”** — to me
14.12:
**“Therefore”** — and because Scripture says
**“every one of us”** — to be judged by God
**“shall render account to God for himself”** — he will not evade by circumlocutions
14.13:
**“Let us not therefore”** — and because each will render account for himself
**“any more”**
• as we have done hitherto

Let us not blame things when we do not know with what mind they are done, or even if they are open, let us not blame them so as to despair of recovery. **“judge one another”** — we, from opinion
**“But judge this rather”** — namely
**“judge this rather”** — discern what is to be observed as profitable
**“that you put not a stumblingblock”** — so that he may perish, one doing the same through your example

**“I know”** — by this
**“and”** — because
**“of itself”** — after his coming, or through his creator

**“to him”** — This is the weak man of whom above: He that is weak eateth herbs.
**“it is common”** — for conscience
14.14:
**“I know and am confident”** — As if I say: put not a stumblingblock before your brethren. **“that nothing is common”** — unclean
14.15:
**“For if, because of thy meat, thy brother be grieved”**

• I do not say he is scandalized, but what is less, at least
**“now”** — from this alone it is evident that
**“thou walkest not now according to charity”** — in which you sin, namely that you do not walk according to charity.

**“for whom Christ”** — only consider what he did, that

14.16:

• since the brother is grieved or lost, therefore not

14.18:
**“For he that in this serveth Christ”**

• in justice, peace and joy.
**“pleaseth God”**

• According to that joy which is in the Holy Ghost. One another: the Jew toward the Gentile and the Gentile toward the Jew.
14.19:
**“Therefore let us follow after the things that are of peace”** — because dispute begets discord
**“and keep the things that are of edification”** — by teaching with peace
14.20:
**“Destroy not the work of God for meat”**
• let us follow these, but let us not destroy the work of God.

• and I do not say, because of food, that it is not clean, because

14.21:
**“It is good not to eat flesh”** — From these, for the sake of a stumbling block, you ought to abstain, because you ought to abstain also from all flesh.
**“and not to drink wine, nor”** — to do anything
**“whereby thy brother is offended”** — in which there is for him a cause of condemnation
**“is offended”**
• Disturbed, not knowing what to hold.
• One who departs from right faith.
**“or scandalized”** — is saddened
**“or made weak”** — so that he doubts, and if he is not offended
**“made weak”** — One who does not depart but begins to doubt.
14.22:
**“Hast thou faith?”**
• you can do this well, because you lose nothing of your good
• in the heart, which no one will take away
**“faith”** — By which you believe all things to be clean and to be eaten.
**“Have it”** — only
**“before God.”**
• not before the abstainer, lest you harm him
• because
**“Have it before God”** — That you keep peace with your brother, which is useful before God.
**“Blessed is he that condemneth not himself”** — who does not make himself blameworthy by harming others with his good
**“Blessed”** — He calls blessed the one who does nothing other than what he approves as useful, but judges him to be condemned by his own judgment, who does not do what he says he ought to do.
**“in that which he alloweth.”** — judges it good
14.23:
**“But he that”** — not that one is blessed, but he who
**“discerneth,”** — some foods clean, others unclean
**“if he eat,”** — and with that conscience
**“is condemned; because not of faith.”** — eats
**“For all”** — good also
**“that is not of faith is sin.”**
• what is done against faith, that is, against conscience, so that it is believed to be evil
• But all that is not of faith, etc. Yet not everything that is done with faith is good, because ignorance that comes from fault does harm.
• Every life of unbelievers is sin, and nothing is good without the highest good, where recognition of eternal truth is lacking; it is false virtue even in the best morals.
• Works that seem commendable apart from faith are like great strength and very swift running outside the way.
• Not of faith. Your faith wills that a man do what he rightly understands is to be done, and it is sin if something is done otherwise than what has been approved.

15.1:
**“Now we that are stronger, ought”** — the weak man, if he eats, is condemned; but we
**“the infirmities of the weak”** — since they cannot raise themselves up to us
**“to bear”** — to bear, to raise up, not to provoke, not to despise
**“and not to please ourselves.”** — not to obey our own will
**“Not to please ourselves”** — That is, not to claim what pleases us, but what pleases the brother, since we ought to take care for one another.
15.2:
**“Let every one of you”** — studying charity
**“please his neighbour”** — take care to please
**“unto good”**
• to that which is useful
• which is of worth
15.3:
**“For”** — and truly we ought not to please ourselves
**“Christ did not please himself,”**
• he did not do what pleased the flesh
• For Christ also, etc. Whence: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him that sent me.” The reproaches: that is, when I did thy will, O God, the Jews said that I sinned against thee, who rather by not receiving me whom thou hadst sent sinned against thee. They reproached, and therefore they killed me. Thus the sins of those who sin against God fell upon Christ, because the innocent is killed by sinners as a blasphemer.
**“but”** — but to God the Father
**“As it is written”**
• in the Psalm
• because I cast them out of the temple, which had made it a den of thieves, therefore
**“The reproaches of them that reproached thee, fell upon me.”** — were the cause of my oppression
15.4:
**“For what things soever”** — what does this have to do with us?
**“were written”** — concerning Christ, whose life is the discipline of our life and manners
**“Were written”** — In the divine books. Whence he said: it is written.
**“were written for our learning: that through patience and the comfort of the scriptures, we might have hope.”**
• that through those writings we may be taught to suffer with our neighbours, and be comforted in this through the example of Christ, and so hope for what Christ received
• Scripture is for teaching, but
15.5:
**“Now the God of patience and of comfort”** — the giver
**“grant you”** — without distinction
**“to be of one mind one towards another”** — that one feels so that the other may feel
**“To be of one mind”** — As if to say: unless you are of the same mind, you will not be able to honour God.
**“according to Jesus Christ:”** — not apart from Christ, but in him, so that you may be of one mind according to his teaching
15.6:
**“That with one mind”** — with the same will
**“with one mouth”** — with the same confession of voice
**“you may glorify God”**
• because God is essence
• because creator
**“and the Father”** — and the Father, and because kind in sending Christ
15.7:
**“Wherefore”** — that you may honour God
**“receive one another,”** — the weak
**“as Christ also hath received you”** — the weak, as Christ also received you
**“unto the honour of God.”**
• that he might make them immortal
• he received, because [he received] the Jews, so that he might be their minister, that is, their apostle and preacher, and so that he might be true in the promises and fulfil the promises which he made to the fathers, namely Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
15.8:
**“For I say that Christ Jesus was minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm”** — that is, to be verified
**“the promises made unto the fathers.”** — Of the circumcision, that is, of the Jews to whom he came in the flesh. Whence: “I was not sent but to the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel.”
**“For the truth”** — He did not reject the Jews, to whom truth belongs properly; the Gentiles, to whom mercy belongs, and to whom there was no promise.
**“The promises”** — For he had promised Abraham: “In thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.” And David: “Of the fruit of thy womb I will set upon thy throne.” And likewise Jacob said: “There shall rise a star out of Jacob.”
15.9:
**“But that the Gentiles”** — And he received the Gentiles through mercy.
**“but”** — I say
**“for his mercy”** — concerning
**“are to glorify God”** — in the Psalm, about the Gentiles, of whom it would seem less
**“because of”** — or “therefore”
**“Therefore will I confess to thee, O Lord, among the Gentiles”**
• that is, I will make the Gentiles sing to you
• I will make those confessing from among the Gentiles
**“Will I confess”** — But confession is not only of sins, but also of praise.
**“and will sing to thy name.”**
• praising with joy a new canticle
• a new canticle, and praising you with joy
• Verse of Master Prepositinus: “A new thing is sung that does not grow old with time. / Would you sing new things? First make yourself new.”
15.10:
**“And again he saith:”** — Isaias
**“Rejoice, ye Gentiles”** — because you have been taken up that you may be one fold
**“with his people.”** — to the Jews, because you are one with them
15.11:
**“And again:”** — David
**“Praise the Lord, all ye Gentiles”** — because they have been taken up
**“And magnify him”** — because he increased the number of his people by the Gentiles being added
**“all ye people.”** — the twelve tribes
15.12:
**“And again Isaias saith:”** — to the same (point)
**“There shall be a root of Jesse”**
• the father of David, who is also Jesse
• And from this root will be he who shall rise.
**“a root of Jesse”** — David is the tree, which through a branch, that is, Mary, bore fruit, that is, Christ.
**“and”** — from which he
**“he that shall rise up”** — from death
**“to rule the Gentiles”**
• by faith and good works
• and therefore
15.13:
**“Now the God of hope”** — I admonish you to receive one another.
**“of hope”** — who gives hope, or in whom we hope.
**“fill you with all joy and peace”**
• spiritual
• that none of you may grieve as you used to grieve in strife.
**“and peace”** — That you may be able to rejoice, let him give peace and concord to one another, and this will be if the faith is sound.
**“that you may abound”** — That is, that through these things held you may be more certain of eternal blessedness, and may abound in the power of the Holy Spirit, that is, the strength of good work which is given by the Holy Spirit.
15.14:
**“For I am sure”** — and though I thus admonish you to receive one another, yet not all of you need this admonition.
**“also”**
• concerning you
• o
**“I myself also am assured”** — Lest the Apostle seem to understand all as discordant and foolish in need of correction, he removes this; and therefore he begins in order to admonish the more perfect about the correction of the lesser. And then he sets himself forth as an example, who labours for others, and it is necessary that these do this, since he himself, hindered by others, cannot come to them.
**“my brethren, and I myself”** — who speak thus
**“of you, that you also”**
• you
• not only I
**“are full of love”** — by which you wish good
**“replenished with all”** — of the old and new law
**“knowledge”** — by which you may be able
**“replenished with all knowledge”** — Through this praise he provokes to better things in the manner of one exhorting. Whence he does not say teach but admonish, as if what is known but slips from the mind. For this is usually admonished: what, though known, sometimes slips from the mind or is held negligently.
**“so”** — you are filled with these two
**“that you are able”** — unless your fault remains
**“one another”** — in turn
**“to admonish”**
• you, not to say teach
• but yet
15.15:
**“But I have written more boldly”** — although full of love and knowledge, nevertheless somewhat boldly
**“I have written to you, brethren, in some sort”**
• of the Church or of the epistle
• I have written to you more boldly, etc., on account of the apostleship, as if: I could not omit it for my office.
**“as it were putting you in mind”** — to you in part, that is, to the more perfect; not as thinking you foolish, but as making you mindful what you ought to do, in which, as if you had forgotten, he subtly rebukes you
**“because of the grace which is given me”** — He does not write rashly, but the Apostle of the Gentiles dares to write to all the Gentiles, by the authority handed to him through grace.
15.16:
**“That I should be the minister of Christ Jesus”** — that I should be the minister of Jesus Christ, whom he himself, not another, appointed
**“among the Gentiles; sanctifying the gospel of God”** — showing and confirming that it is holy, by good work and miracles
**“that the oblation of the Gentiles may be made acceptable and sanctified”** — that the Gentiles whom I offer may be acceptable to God by the perfection of faith, and sanctified by good work
**“in the Holy Ghost.”**
• by whose grace there is faith and good work
• and because I do so
15.17:
**“I have therefore glory”**
• merit worthy of glory
• So also you, if you labour for the brethren.
• He says this so that they may prove that they can be no less than the apostles who had been with Christ.
**“against”** — through
**“in Christ Jesus towards God.”**
• to be referred
• glory
15.18:
**“For I dare not to speak”**
• that is, I speak only those things which he works through me
• as pseudo
**“of those things which Christ worketh not by me, for the obedience of the Gentiles”** — that the Gentiles may obey the gospel
15.19:
**“by the virtue of signs and wonders”** — through my preaching in word and deed and good work, and through the power of lesser and greater miracles done in the power of the Spirit
**“in the power of the Holy Ghost”** — by which he works such things in me; by which, he working in me, I have so laboured
**“so that from Jerusalem round about”** — all around
**“as far as unto Illyricum”** — the sea
**“I have replenished”** — I have fully preached
**“the gospel of Christ.”** — or “of God”
15.20:
**“And I have so preached”** — in such a place
**“this gospel, not where Christ was named”**
• by the pseudo-apostles
• Not where Christ was named, etc. Because he knew that false apostles and others were teaching false things under the name of Christ, which it would be a very great labour to correct afterwards, therefore he was careful to forestall this and to deliver the truth whole, where Christ had not yet been announced; which he proves by the testimony of the prophet.
**“lest I should build upon another man's foundation.”**
• for if I did that, this would thence happen
• that is, lest I should preach to those already converted by others, not that I would not do this if it had happened
15.21:
**“But”** — I did so
**“As it is written”** — in Isaias, that it happens so
**“They to whom he was not spoken of”** — before
**“of him”** — Christ
**“shall see,”** — will believe
**“and they that”** — and those who before
**“have not heard”**
• the preaching of someone about God
• And they that have not heard, etc. That the understanding of the word of God might be true, he hastened to imbue the Gentiles with the truth.
**“shall understand.”** — that my prediction is true
15.22:
**“Wherefore”** — because I have preached so much
**“I was hindered very much”** — so that he might exclude the wicked inventions of the false apostles
**“to come to you”** — as he said at the beginning of the epistle
15.23:
**“But now”** — the reason for delaying
**“having no more place in these countries, and having a great desire”** — because he also hurries to forestall these
15.24:
**“When I shall begin to take my journey into Spain”** — where the journey is difficult for false apostles, and so it was allowed to delay
**“I hope”** — as if to say: I can do nothing of myself
**“that as I pass, I shall see you”** — because you do not need a long stay, but meanwhile prepare yourselves, lest you hold me back from the others
**“and be brought on my way thither by you”** — into Spain
**“if first, in part”**
• that which is now at variance
• of time, that is, for some while

15.25:
**“But now”** — because I have no place here, and I long for you; therefore now

15.26:
**“For it hath pleased them”**
• I did not compel them
• They have approved, etc. He invites the Romans to works of this kind, because whoever lives by the mercy of God ought to be kind to his brother.
**“of Macedonia and Achaia to make a contribution for the poor of the saints”** — or “saints”
**“that are in Jerusalem”** — To the poor of the saints who, etc. These gave themselves wholly to divine service, caring for nothing worldly, giving the faithful an example of good conduct.
15.27:
**“For it hath pleased them”** — they were pleased
**“and they are their debtors”** — he so wishes them to be merciful that he says this is owed even by him who expects mercy
**“For if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things”** — of the Jews, who sent preachers to them
**“the Gentiles have been made partakers”** — surely
**“they ought”** — they themselves
**“in carnal things to minister to them”** — to the Jews
15.28:
**“When therefore”** — because it pleased them, namely to make a contribution for the saints who are in Jerusalem
**“I shall have accomplished this”** — that is, when I have completed the work of ministry

15.29:

15.30:
**“I beseech you therefore, brethren, through our Lord Jesus Christ”** — if you love him.
**“and by the charity of the Holy Ghost”** — if there is in you the charity which the Spirit makes.
**“that you help me”** — through
**“in your prayers for me to God”**
• having
• That you help me in your prayers. Many small ones, when gathered together in one mind, become great; and it is impossible that the prayers of many should not obtain. If therefore they desire to see him, let them pray that they may receive him set free with the joy of charity.
15.31:
**“That I may be delivered from the unbelievers”** — lest they take away what I bring.
**“that are in Judea, and that the oblation of my service”** — enjoined on me.
**“may be acceptable”** — as if: sufficient, not diminished.
**“acceptable”** — So that, their charity toward him being understood, they may with him in one mind give thanks to God. For he is great and perfect, through whose ministry many, made glad, praise God.

15.32:
**“That I may come to you with joy, by the will of God”** — He says this to show that he does all things with the will of God.
**“and”** — or “that”

16.1:
**“And I commend to you”** — I show her to be commendable.
**“I commend to you”** — Henceforth he sets forth many whom the Romans ought to believe. As if to say: do as I have said, but imitate these.

• in faith

**“our sister”** — or “my”
16.2:
**“That you receive her”** — for
**“in the Lord as becometh”** — as it is worthy for saints to receive, or to be received.
**“saints”**
• by you
• Or: “that you esteem the saints worthily.” As other copies have, that is, very honorably and with respect.
**“and that you assist her”** — help
16.3:
**“Salute Prisca and Aquila”** — who is also called Priscilla in the Acts of the Apostles
**“Aquila”** — The husband of Priscilla, who, as Paul’s helpers, had come to Rome for their strengthening. So also all the others whom he greets.
**“my helpers in Christ Jesus”** — in the preaching of Christ
16.4:
**“Who have for my life”**
• that is, life
• to be delivered
**“laid down their own necks”** — by serving me
**“laid down”** — to the sword
**“the churches of the Gentiles”** — Because these labour for the advancement of the Gentiles, exhorting them to the faith of Christ, and they did not refuse to suffer dangers for the Apostle. Whence the Romans ought to obey them.
16.5:
**“and”** — greet
**“the church which is in their house”** — that is, the household
**“Salute Epenetus”** — who laboured more earnestly for their exhortation
**“my beloved”** — who first was born again in Christ
16.6:
**“Salute Mary”** — who laboured more earnestly for their exhortation
**“who hath laboured much among you”** — because she endured dissension for the apostle
16.7:
**“Salute Andronicus and Junias, my kinsmen”** — because they were Jews
**“and my fellow prisoners”** — having suffered captivity for the cause of the faith
*Augustine:* Augustine. Because as long as we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord, and in this way they are fellow captives.
**“who are of note among the apostles”** — among the preachers
**“who also were in Christ before me”** — in the faith of Christ
16.8:
**“Salute Ampliatus”** — this man was a friend of the apostle in the Lord, and not a fellow captive
**“most beloved to me in the Lord”** — or 'in Christ'
16.9:
**“Salute Urbanus, our helper”**
• in exhorting to the faith
• a partaker of the work
**“of us”** — to me and to others
**“in Christ Jesus, and Stachys, my beloved”** — who was my own friend, and if not a helper, that is, a partaker of the work
16.10:
**“Salute Apelles, approved”**
• that is, approved
• Apelles was found faithful in Christ through temptations, though not his friend or partner in the work.
**“Salute them that are of Aristobulus' household”** — Aristobulus used to gather brothers in Christ, whom he greets, thereby proving his deed.
16.11: **“Of Narcissus' household”** — Narcissus is said to have been a priest who, by travelling, strengthened the holy brothers; since he was not then present, he greets his own, and because he did not know the merits of all of them, he distinguishes them by adding: “who are in the Lord,” that is, those whom you see to be worthy.
16.12:
**“Salute Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labour in the Lord”** — in the ministry of the saints and in distresses
**“Salute Persis, the dearly beloved, who hath much”** — more than those named above
**“hath laboured in the Lord”** — in the ministry of the saints, or in distress
**“Hath laboured”** — This labour is that of which the Apostle speaks more often, in exhortation and in the ministry of the saints, and in pressure and in want for God’s sake.
16.13:
**“Salute Rufus, elect in the Lord”** — because he was advanced to carry out the affairs of the Lord, namely to the priesthood
**“and his mother”** — by the flesh
**“and mine”** — by benefits
**“His mother and mine”** — Because of his holiness he calls his mother his own, whose son he preferred for the ecclesiastical office.
16.14: **“Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren that are with them”** — he greets together those whom he knew joined in Christian friendship
16.15: **“Salute Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympias; and all the saints that are with them”** — and these were like-minded, of one mind
16.16:
**“Salute one another”** — all
**“with an holy kiss”**
• in the peace of Christ
• And all, etc. He bids all to whom he writes and whom he names to greet one another with a holy kiss, that is, in the peace of Christ, so that the kisses may be devout, not carnal.
**“All the churches of Christ salute you”** — of these places
**“of Christ”** — They who trust in Christ, not in any other thing.
16.17:
**“Now I beseech you, brethren”** — Greet and imitate these, but avoid those.
**“to mark”** — discern
**“them who make dissensions and offences”** — who make you disagree and offend one another
**“To mark them”** — He touches on the false apostles, whom he warns are to be avoided throughout the whole epistle.
**“contrary to”** — going beyond
**“the doctrine”** — because they burned with zeal for the law and compelled believers to Judaize
**“which you have learned”** — from the true
**“and avoid them”** — and you ought to turn aside
16.18:
**“For they that are such, serve not Christ our Lord”** — our
**“but their own belly”** — for some they flatter, others they slander, so that they can fill their belly
**“by pleasing speeches and good words, seduce the hearts of the innocent”** — for with fine-sounding words they commended their own teaching, by which they deceived the hearts of the simple
16.19:
**“For your obedience”**
• your ability to obey
• Therefore I warn you to avoid, because your faith and obedience is praised everywhere, because you are in the head of the world, and so by your example others could now be corrupted. Or I ask you to avoid, because you readily obey what is good, and I rejoice in that; but I wish you to be wise in discerning the good and without any part of evil.
**“is published in every place. I rejoice therefore in you. But I would have you”** — and safely
**“to be wise”** — that is, that you may be
**“in good”** — by discerning
**“and simple in evil”** — without any part of it
16.20:
**“And the God of peace”**
• giver
• And the God of peace. Be you wise; God shall crush Satan, that is, false preachers, or any man opposing you, or the devil.
**“crush Satan under your feet”** — that it may not be able to harm you
**“Under your feet”** — As the head: that you may despise the first stirrings of suggestions, as was said of Eve in the figure of the Church.
**“speedily”**
• namely at my coming
• that this may be done
**“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you”** — be
**“The grace”** — He now wishes for them the grace which he promised at his coming.
16.21:
**“saluteth”** — thus
**“you, Timothy”** — as if you were in his care
**“Timothy, my fellow labourer, saluteth you”** — So many and such great men rejoice in your undertaking, and therefore it befits you to persevere.
**“my fellow labourer”** — as if co-bishop
**“and Lucius, and Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen”** — by birth or by faith
16.22:
**“I Tertius salute you”** — by name, not by number
**“who wrote this epistle in the Lord”** — notary of the apostle, to whom he granted to greet under his own name
16.23:
