**“And the whole church”** — And above he had said all the churches, but here he speaks of the church of another province, whence Gaius was.
**“Saluteth you, Erastus, the treasurer”** — from the chest, as a prince; or rather from the citadel, the treasurer of the city
**“of the city”** — of the Athenians
**“and Quartus, a brother.”** — a proper name
16.24:
**“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ”**
• thus these greet, or also I myself
• or thus these named greet you, and I myself subscribe with my own hand
**“with you all.”** — be
**“Now to him who is able”** — to God the Trinity
**“To him who is able”** — Thus I admonish. To him who is able to strengthen you be glory, from whom alone are all things. In which epistle the sum is noted.
**“to confirm you”** — in perfect faith
**“according to”** — according to
**“my gospel”**
• from which the preaching of Christ does not differ
• according to
16.25:
**“and the preaching of Jesus Christ”** — which is the gospel and the preaching
**“according to the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret in eternal times”** — that is, according to what has been revealed to me of the hidden counsel of God, kept silent from eternity; or it reveals the mystery itself
**“According to the revelation of the mystery”** — According to the revelation of the mystery. He means the incarnation of Christ, etc., which “was kept secret from eternal ages,” because although in some part it had been known to the ancient fathers, yet it was fully known by none until in its own time it was revealed through Christ himself. The scriptures of the prophets being opened by him, giving testimony to this preaching. Made known to all nations for obedience, that is, that they may obey the faith by working well. Hidden from others but known to God alone, because even if it is now revealed to men, yet it is known to God alone, because he alone knows why it was so done. In which he checks the inquirers who ask why God delayed so long? Why he allowed so many nations to perish?
16.26:
**“which now is made manifest”** — by the Holy Spirit
**“by the scriptures of the prophets”** — unlocked
**“according to the precept of the eternal God”** — who from eternity ordained this, is not feigned
**“of the eternal God”** — God alone is properly called “eternal,” because he is without beginning and without end. Not so eternal fire, which, though without end, yet has a beginning. That, then, is true eternity which is true immortality; this is that highest unchangeableness which God alone has, that he cannot be changed at all. For it is one thing for something not to be changed though it can be changed, another not to be able to be changed at all. So, then, man is called good, yet not as God, of whom it is said: “None is good but God alone.” So the soul of man is called immortal, yet not as God, of whom it is said: “Who only hath immortality.” So also man is called wise, yet not as God, of whom it is said: “To God the only wise.” So fire is called eternal, yet not as God, whose immortality alone is itself true eternity.
**“for the obedience”** — that they may obey
**“of faith,”** — by working well
**“known among all nations”** — known among all nations, I mean of the mystery
16.27:
**“To God the only wise”** — This error has crept in upon some, who suppose that the Father alone is signified here, and that he alone is truly wise; whereas it is not said, “to the only wise Father,” but “to God the only wise,” and the one God is the Trinity itself, so that we understand God alone to be wise as we understand God alone to be powerful, that is, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, who is the one and only God whom alone we are commanded to serve. Yet if the Apostle had said, “to the only wise Father,” he would not thereby separate the Son or the Holy Spirit. As in the Apocalypse it is read of the Son, who “hath a name written which no man knoweth, but he that receiveth it”; yet the Father, from whom the Son is inseparable, is not therefore said not to know this name. As, then, the Father knows what no one is said to know but the Son, because the Father and the Son are inseparable, so also, had it been said “to the only wise Father,” the Son and the Holy Spirit would have to be understood together with him, because they are inseparable.
**“through Jesus Christ”** — revealed
**“to whom”** — to God alone, or to Christ
**“honour”** — honour from us
**“To whom be honour”** — If you take away “to whom,” the reading is complete. Blessed Augustine says it is put in, and discusses how it ought to be taken.
*Augustine:* That “to whom be glory” is added, when “to him glory” would have sufficed, is a manner of speaking unusual in our tongue, not an ambiguous sense. It is the same to say, in an unusual order of words, “to him glory through Jesus Christ, to whom glory,” which in the usual order is “to him, to whom through Jesus Christ glory.” Through Christ glory is to the Father, that is, clear knowledge with praise, because through him God the Trinity has become known to men, which is a mystery.
**“and glory”** — in himself

For they are not called Peter’s but Christ’s, that there might be no hope in man, and that there might not be as many baptisms as servants. Christ gave his servants the ministry of baptizing, but kept the power to himself, which, if he wished, he could give to his servants, so that there would be as great force in the baptism of a servant as there is in a baptism given by the Lord; and therefore it makes no difference whether the one who happens to have the ministry of baptizing, baptizes well or ill. Hence also no one says “my baptism,” though he says my gospel, my prudence, my glory, although these are from God, and in these there is a difference. For in these one is more learned than another, and one works better than another. But in baptism it cannot be said that one is baptized more or less than another, whether he is baptized by a lesser or by a greater.

Or: I say to them that perish, as it is written, that he would destroy it and make it reprobate and false. Where is the wise? Prove it. The Apostle scorns false wisdom. Where? As if to say: it is worth nothing. And it is an invective against the Jews and against the Gentiles. • which according to the reasoning of this world
• Or: the world, by its own wisdom, imprudently did not know God in the wisdom of God, that is, because the wisdom of the world before did not know God through the wisdom of God, that is, through this magnificence of the world and the adornment of a work so wisely established, it did not venerate the wisdom of its creator.
**“The wisdom of this world”** — Where the foolish and weak thing of God is despised, which is according to the reasonings of the world, which judges impossible what it does not see in the natures of things.
**“The wisdom of this world hath God made foolish”** — For through foolishness he saves them that believe. And why he shows by what he has said before: that the world by its wisdom knew not God, so that faith and salvation might be from God, not from wisdom. But in the wisdom of God, which “shineth in darkness,” therefore: “The Word was made flesh.” For as a cure is the way to health, so the medicine of wisdom through the taking of man’s nature is fitted to our wounds, so that we are cured by some things as by contraries and by some as by likes. For by the cunning of the serpent, that is, by wisdom, we were deceived; by the wisdom of God we are set free. And as that wisdom was called wisdom and was foolish, so this which is called foolishness is wisdom. Behold the contraries. The likes are that, as he freed by a woman those deceived through a woman, so, born of a woman, Christ, a man, freed men, a mortal, mortals.

• For both the Jews, etc. “The world by wisdom knew not,” because the Jews seek signs of power, being accustomed to it from of old. And the Greeks seek wisdom, whether nature can bear what is preached. But we, on the contrary, preach Christ crucified, which is not to the Jews a sign of power but a scandal, because they are angered against the preachers through the shame of their own crime. Or: what we preach seems foolishness for this reason, that the Jews ask signs and the Greeks wisdom, and we do the contrary, and yet through this foolishness God saves them that believe. And there follows: But to them that are called, which join thus: I said that the Jews ask signs and the Greeks wisdom, and in the crucifixion which we preach there is the great power of God and the great wisdom of God, even if to the reprobate it seems otherwise; yet to those who are called to life, not by the common calling but by that by which the foreknown are called, the passion of Christ appears as power and wisdom, namely that salvation may be from God, not from the choice of Jew or Greek.

1.24:
**“But unto them that are called”**
• to life, not by common calling but by that by which they were foreknown.
• Or: To them that are called. We preach Christ, that is, the faith or passion of Christ, namely the power of God, because by faith their sins are forgiven and demons are driven out and, when the case requires, miracles are done. And the wisdom of God, because those who believe in Christ crucified understand that Christ is the wisdom of God. For Christ is the wisdom of the Father, as he is also the power of the Father. He is the Word and the hand of the Father, by whom as by hand and word the Father made all things. Whence: “The heavens are the works of thy hands.” And again: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.” Beware of understanding the Son to be called the wisdom of God as though he alone were understanding and wise for himself and the Father and the Holy Spirit, as though the Father were not wise of himself but of the Son. For God the Father is wise by that which he himself is, his own wisdom; and the Son, the wisdom of the Father, is wise of the wisdom which is the Father, of whom the Son is begotten. So also the Father is understanding by that which he himself is, his own understanding. But the Son, the understanding of the Father, is understanding of the understanding which is the Father, of whom he is begotten.

• enlightening us to the truth
• Who is made unto us wisdom, etc. That is, enlightening us to the truth. But he is said to be wisdom to us because in time, that is, from some time, we are turned to him, that we may remain with him for ever. And that wisdom itself “was made flesh, and dwelt among us.” And this he does, that is, he enlightens us. Because he is made unto us justice, that is, because he first justifies us by good work. For the justice which lives in itself, without doubt is God, and lives unchangeably. But as, though he is life, he becomes justice to us when we are made partakers of him, so, though he is justice in himself, he on the contrary becomes justice to us when by cleaving to him we live justly. And through this he himself is justice to us, because he is first sanctification, that is, because he first amends us in baptism. And this is so because he was first made redemption to us, that is, because he first redeemed us by suffering. And all this was done that no one may glory but in the gifts of God.

**“They would never have crucified the Lord of glory”** — Augustine. He was crucified in the form of a servant, and yet the God of glory was crucified. For such was that taking up which made God man and man God. But let the prudent and diligent reader understand what is said on account of what, and what according to what. For behold, we say that according to what he is God he glorifies his own, that is, according to this, that he is the Lord of glory; and yet the Lord of glory was crucified, because God is rightly said to be crucified, not from the power of the divinity but from the weakness of the flesh. For Christ, God and man, is one person; therefore it is said: “No man hath ascended into heaven, but he that descended from heaven.” If then you attend to the distinction of substances, that is, of natures, the Son of God descended and the son of man was crucified; but on account of this unity of person he said not only that the son of man had descended from heaven, but also that he was in heaven while he spoke on earth. But far be it that Christ so felt death that, as far as in him lay, life lost life. For if this were so, the fountain of life would have lost life. He felt death, therefore, by participation in the human feeling which he had willingly taken up; he did not lose the power of his nature by which he gives life to all things. So in the sepulchre he did not forsake his flesh by dying with it, as in the virgin’s womb he formed it by being born with it. He died, therefore, without life departing; so he suffered, without power perishing. “No man taketh it away from me; but I lay it down of myself, and I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again.” At one and the same time, therefore, he was truly dead and truly living, in whom the taking up of mortality admitted death, and the divinity did not lose life. The Son of God therefore neither endured death in his soul, nor felt it in his majesty. Yet by participation in weakness the king of glory was crucified.

Another builds upon this foundation wood, hay, stubble: he, namely, who thinks on the things that are of the world, how he may please the world. The work of the former is not burned, for he did not love those things whose loss would torment him. But the work of the latter is burned, because what has been possessed with love does not perish without sorrow. But since, if either condition were set before him, he would rather be without them than without Christ, and does not forsake Christ for fear of losing such things, though he grieves when he loses them, he is saved indeed, yet so as by fire. By gold, silver, precious stones he signifies “excellent doctrine”; in the other three, vain doctrine is signified, which, though it deceives for now, will appear in the fire, because it will burn while the good remains, and for the good doctrine, that is, there will be the reward of eternal life. Wood, hay, stubble are built by those who, though they do not seize what belongs to others, yet cling with some love to things allowed to infirmity; who according to their ways of loving will endure the fire longer, as wood, or less, as hay, or least, as stubble. But rather by wood, hay, stubble are understood neither good works, nor evil ones which are damnable, but venial sins. **“The temple”** — Augustine. Those in whom God dwells by faith. The temple of God, that is, of the Holy Spirit. Whence he adds: And the Spirit of God dwelleth. Note how the Spirit is here called God; for when he had said before: You are the temple of God, he does not add: And God dwelleth, but: THE SPIRIT OF GOD DWELLETH IN YOU, in which he plainly shows that the Spirit of God is God. For the Holy Spirit is present everywhere to regenerate men to eternal life. The Holy Spirit therefore sits in the heavens with the Father and the Son, and dwells in his temple, that is, in the saints, who are the temple of God, now walking by faith. And they will be the temple of God at some time also according to sight, as even now the angels of God are his temple.
*Augustine:* But someone might say: before God made heaven and earth, before he made the saints, where did he dwell? God dwells in himself; he dwells with you and is with himself. So the saints are not the house of God in such a way that, if it were taken away, God would fall; rather God dwells in the saints in such a way that, if he departs, they fall. Besides, it must be known that it can be said only most foolishly that the Spirit has no place in our body, which our soul has filled entire. It is said more foolishly still that the Trinity is hindered somewhere by narrowness, so that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit cannot be together anywhere. But that is much more wonderful, that although God is everywhere whole, he does not nevertheless dwell in all. Who, moreover, would dare to suppose, unless he were utterly ignorant of the inseparability of the Trinity, that the Father or the Son could dwell in anyone in whom the Holy Spirit does not dwell? Or the Holy Spirit in anyone in whom the Father or the Son does not? It must be confessed, therefore, that God is everywhere by the presence of his divinity, but not everywhere by the grace of indwelling. For on account of this indwelling, where the grace of his love is recognized, we do not say: Our Father, who art everywhere, though this too is true, but “who art in heaven.” This also is wonderful, that God is the indweller of some who do not yet know God, and not of some who know him. For those do not belong to the temple of God who, knowing God, do not glorify him as God. But there belong to the temple of God little children sanctified by the sacrament of Christ, and regenerated by the Holy Spirit, who cannot yet know God. **“And you are Christ's”** — That as these things are ours, so we may be subject to Christ. And Christ is God’s: doing his will, so that we also do his. Why then do you hope anything from men to the injury of Christ?

4.1:
**“Let a man so account of us”**
• and since this is so, think of us neither too much nor too little
• Let a man so account of us. Hitherto he has spoken of the glory of the false ones; here he treats of his own contempt.
**“So account of us”** — The Apostle says this because they thought less of him; but let a man think of him as God does, who chose him.
**“as of the ministers”** — not lords
**“of Christ,”** — that not as false ones
**“and the dispensers”** — Augustine. Not only the good but also the wicked are dispensers. For unless it were dispensed through the good, the Apostle would not rightly say: “Be ye followers of me.” Again, if not through the wicked, the Lord would not say of certain men: “What they say, do ye; but what they do, do ye not.” For they are dispensers through whose ministry one comes to eternal salvation. For to be a dispenser of that salvation through word and sacrament is not to be a partaker of it.
**“of the mysteries”** — or of mysteries
**“of God.”** — we divide mysteries or ministries according to the measure of each
4.2:
**“Here now it is required among the dispensers”**
• namely who
• the order: that among the dispensers anyone be found faithful, one who can be trusted to dispense well
**“Here now it is required”** — Here now it is required. We are to be so esteemed; but here, among you, it is sought, which it is not elsewhere. Now, in the present, when one ought to have waited until God judges.
4.3:
**“But to me it is a very small thing”** — as if: here among us it is sought, which should not be sought, but whatever others do
**“to be judged by you,”** — as if an unfaithful dispenser
**“or by man's day;”** — by the understanding, which does not see hidden things and can be deceived
**“by man's day”** — That is, by all while they are in their own day, and it is not the day of the Lord. Human, because there is also the day of the Lord on which he will judge, when each one will render account for himself, and then the secrets of hearts will be laid open.
**“but neither do I judge my own self.”** — who know myself better than you do, and so it is dangerous for you to judge things unknown
**“do I judge my own self”** — It is dangerous for you to judge the unknown things of my heart or of others. For what depth must be believed to be in a man, lying hidden even from the man in whom it is, as in Peter the depth of weakness lay hidden when he promised he would die with the Lord.
*Augustine:* Since then each one, about himself, can either not at all or hardly pass a true judgment, how can he judge about another, since no one knows what goes on in a man except the spirit of the man?
*Augustine:* The Apostle forbids judgment, because the hearts of men are hidden from us. In these things our credulity is for the most part deceived. But we must beware lest we be deceived by a pernicious opinion, so that we, who cannot search out the conscience of men, should hold a true and certain verdict about the things themselves. But this belongs to human temptation, without which this life is not led. Whence the Apostle: “Let no temptation take hold on you, but such as is human.” If therefore we cannot avoid suspicions, because we are men, yet we ought to refrain from judgments, that is, definitive and firm verdicts. If therefore we suspect, which is human temptation, let us at least not judge, when there is no error in the matters themselves, so that the disapproval of vices and the approval of virtues may be right. Surely if there is error about men, human temptation is venial.
4.4:
**“For I am not conscious to myself of any thing,”** — conscience does not sting me in anything
**“yet am I not hereby justified;”**
• that is, I do not therefore think myself just, because it may be that I do not know; for who understands sins?
• neither I nor you, but
• I know myself better than they do; but God knows better than I.
**“But he that judgeth me”** — that is, he who can and ought to judge me.
**“is the Lord.”** — who knows all things.
4.5:
**“Therefore”** — and because the Lord is.
**“judge not before the time”** — of judgment.
**“until the Lord come,”** — that is, until.
**“until the Lord come”**
• to judge.
• Otherwise, an injury is done to the judge, because it is an injury to the judge if a sentence proceeds from a servant before his judgment.
**“who both will bring to light”** — and because then all things known to all will be able to judge both themselves and others.
**“will bring to light”** — That is, he will make open the hidden things of darkness, that is, of sins.
**“the hidden things of darkness,”** — deeds and thoughts will then be open.
**“and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts;”** — even good thoughts.
**“and then shall every man have praise”** — reward.
**“shall every man have praise from God.”** — according to his measure.
**“and then shall every man have praise from God”** — For one who does good or thinks good; but here it is not known who is worthy of praise.
4.6:
**“But these things, brethren,”** — I said that we must not boast in ourselves.
**“I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollo”**
• since you were not to boast in us.
• I have put forward the figure for all, so that it may be shunned by all as it is by us.
*Ambrose:* Ambrose. By this he sets aside the glories and perverse traditions of the false apostles under his own person and that of Apollo, marking them out summarily and not one by one, lest a greater discord should arise.
**“for your sakes;”** — your humility.
**“that”** — namely this.
**“that in us you may learn,”** — who are greater.
**“that one be not puffed up”** — by acting beyond.
**“above that which is written.”**
• in Jeremias.
• “He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.”
**“against the other for another”**
• himself or his teacher.
• Or he rebukes those same men who boasted of the false teaching: as if to say, you glory in those men, but what have you from them that you did not have from me? And if from me, why do you glory against me, since you received the same from me?
**“that one be not puffed up against the other for another”** — Than another, that is, better than he; that is, as though one were other than he, who is nothing so far as concerns himself, or so far as concerns the ministry. For who distinguisheth thee from the mass of the lost? No one but God. Or if you were baptized by Peter, how will you be distinguished from him who was baptized by Paul? He is nothing, you are nothing.
4.7:
**“For who distinguisheth thee?”** — from the lost, except God.
**“Or what hast thou”**
• which, if you say your faith or prayer or righteousness, again I ask: what have you that you did not receive?
• “What hast thou that thou hast not received?” etc. He tries to remove another kind of arrogance, namely that man should be proud, thinking that he has by himself, or from a minister, some grace given him by God.
**“that thou hast not received?”** — by God
**“And if thou hast received,”** — from God
**“And if thou hast received”** — This is against those who, hearing the same things they had received from the Apostle, were glorying in the teaching of the false apostles, who, commending themselves through eloquence, turned the glory to themselves, whereas the Apostle had made himself seem contemptible, that he might give the glory to God. Therefore the Apostle speaks to them ironically, as if conceding what seemed to them about themselves, when he adds.
**“why dost thou glory”** — in yourself or in those
**“as if thou hadst not received it?”** — as if from God, but from yourself or from them
4.8:
**“You are now full”**
• so quickly
• but you
• full
• As if: I rebuke you, saying: why do you glory, etc. But I do not seem to do this rightly, because you are already, etc.
• Already rich: ironically, as if he said: it is not so. For these are the words of one angry, not of one affirming.
**“You are”**
• by the Holy Spirit
• as if: you are able to satisfy others also
**“you are now become rich”** — ironically
**“you reign without us”**
• so they thought, glorying over the false apostles
• you rule
**“and I would to God you did reign”**
• truly
• and he wishes this kindly for them
**“did reign”** — To reign truly is to be secure in the hope and promises of God, and to rejoice in adversity.
**“that”** — so
**“that we also might reign with you”** — let us follow you, since you disdain to follow us, whom indeed you ought to follow, because we truly reign; but I fear lest without you
4.9:
**“For I think that God hath set forth us apostles, the last”** — most vile, or like Elias and Enoch
**“For I think”** — As if to say: it is by no means to be thought. For he speaks ironically. Therefore, without us, because through the evils which we suffer, God shows us the apostles as most vile, whom he does not care for, as appointed to death, that is, to no use, but reserved for death. What is seen by this? That they gather to our spectacle as to a monster, through which we are the more proved friends of God. Or: therefore you ought to reign with us, because I think and am certain that we are like the last, Elias and Henoch, in tribulations.
**“as it were men appointed to death”** — As those who were kept for death by the victors, to which spectacle the people gathered, so then for the derision of Elias, and now the wicked of the apostles.
**“we are made a spectacle to the world, and to angels”** — either by the good, that they may strengthen, or by the evil, that they may insult
**“and to angels, and to men”** — Good angels and good men praise, the wicked mock. These are the right hand and the left, but neither lifts up the former nor breaks the latter.
4.10:
**“We”** — and
**“fools for Christ's sake”** — rebuke with irony, as if the whole thing were the opposite
**“for Christ's sake”** — Whose cross we preach, while you, keeping silent, seem prudent in Christ.
**“but you are wise in Christ; we are weak”** — afflicted
**“but you are strong”**
• by power
• secure
**“you are honourable”** — revered
**“but we without honour”**
• despised
• and
4.11:
**“Even unto this hour”** — that is, continually, that is, up to this time
**“we both hunger and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no fixed abode”**
• on account of persecution we change places
• we are driven off, lest we teach more
• We hunger and thirst, etc. Ambrose. Preaching the truth, they do not have favour among men.
4.12:
**“And we labour”** — that is, for our necessities
**“working with our own hands”**
• which no one gives
• and
**“we are reviled, and we bless”** — exhorting others to good
**“persecuted”** — torments
**“we suffer it”** — patiently
4.13:
**“We are blasphemed”** — as magicians, evildoers
**“and we entreat”** — God for them, or that they may not blaspheme us
**“as the refuse of this world”**
• by which the world is defiled and cleansed by being cast off
• As the offscouring of this world, etc. Through all these things we are proved in Christ to be wise and strong.
**“we are made”** — considered
**“the offscouring of all”** — the refuse of iron, or of fruit, and whatever of any material is cast away so that it may be made cleaner
**“even until now”**
• continually, up to this time
• even if I have said you are puffed up, etc., nevertheless
4.14:
**“I write not these things to confound you”**
• that is, I shall make you ashamed
• As a healing physician softens harsh things with gentle ones.
**“but I admonish you as my dearest children”** — for whom I have suffered so much
4.15:
**“For”** — sons, for I am the father
**“if you have ten thousand”** — a finite number put for an infinite
**“instructors”**
• teachers who did not beget
• While he names tutors, he signifies boys.
**“have in Christ, yet”** — yet
**“not many fathers”** — who had begotten
**“For in Christ Jesus”** — in the faith of Christ, not in me
**“by the gospel, I”** — only
**“I have begotten you”** — He added “by the gospel,” lest what is God’s be thought to be his own. For the Lord says in the gospel: “Call not yourselves father upon earth; for one is your Father, God.” This is said not that the name be taken away from the rest, but that the grace of God, by which we are begotten unto eternal life, be not ascribed to the nature or power, or even the holiness, of any man.
4.16:
**“Wherefore I beseech you”** — because I begot you, I therefore beseech you as a debt owed
**“be ye followers of me”** — not falsely
4.17:
**“For this cause”** — that you may imitate me
**“have I sent to you Timothy”** — through him the letter is believed to have been sent
**“who is my dearest son”** — in faith
**“dearest”** — by acting well
**“and faithful in the Lord”** — in preaching
**“who will put you in mind of my ways”** — my instructions
**“which are in Christ Jesus”** — and therefore to be kept
**“as”** — I
**“everywhere”** — of the lands
**“I teach everywhere in every church”**
• and therefore authoritatively
• it was necessary to be sent, because
4.18: **“As if I would not come to you, so some are puffed up”** — about the philosophers, whose earthly wisdom they glory in
4.19:
**“But I will come to you shortly”** — after the admonition he promises to go to them
**“if the Lord will”**
• unless your fault hinders
• Therefore he says it, to show that if he did not go, God had not willed it, the cause certainly being their unworthiness.
**“and will know”** — I will test
**“not the speech of them”** — of human wisdom
**“that are puffed up”** — by the pride of high wisdom and of judging the rest
**“But the power.”**
• in faith and good working
• as if: therefore I will not seek the speech, because
4.20:
**“For the kingdom of God is not in speech”** — the cause of the kingdom of God
**“but in power.”** — as if: not the speech of human wisdom but power is the cause of the kingdom of God
4.21:
**“What will you?”** — I will truly come, but which of these?
**“With a rod”** — Augustine. He brings in words of terror, that the puffed-up might be humbled and prepare themselves to receive him. Far be it that dutiful sons should say: If you are coming with a rod, do not come. For it is better to be taught with a father’s rod than to perish by the flattery of a plunderer.
**“shall I come to you”** — of correction; where, even if there is, love does not appear to be
**“or in charity”** — in open affection, so that I may supply good things
**“and in the spirit of meekness?”** — so that I may spare their sins

5.1:
**“It is absolutely heard”**
• there is need of the rod unless you correct yourselves
• that is, by all
• He begins to treat of fornication, and rebukes that fornicator who kept his father’s wife, and those who tolerated him. For they too were partakers with him, while they suffered a matter of so great a sin to go among them uncorrected. So he showed that not only that man was guilty of death, but that those who adhered to him were not free from the crime.
**“among you”** — who are puffed up and do not correct
**“fornication,”** — a shameful thing
**“and such”** — is that
**“fornication”** — so as to show that this sin is grave; nor does he say it is admitted even among those who do not know God
**“as the like is not among the heathens; that one should have his father's wife.”** — this publicly, where there is no need of witnesses
**“That one should have his father's wife”** — Ambrose. Publicly he had his stepmother in the place of a wife, and the crime could be covered by no evasion. And for this cause he begins with fornication; afterwards he will speak of every sin, both carnal and spiritual.
5.2:
**“And you are puffed up”**
• although there is such a crime among you, yet
• what ought rather to be done
**“Are puffed up”** — By the wind of pride, which drives out mercy; as if: one member suffers, the others suffer with it, and so on.
**“and have not rather mourned”** — grief for his sin
**“that”** — so that
**“he might be taken away from among you”** — because you are all partakers
**“that hath done this deed.”** — who did this deed, which in no way could be hidden
5.3:
**“I indeed, absent in body”** — you did not bear it, you who were present
**“but present in spirit”** — by care of mind and providing for you
**“have already judged, as though present”** — as if I were present
5.4:
**“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ”**
• I have judged
• that is, in his place; or you, gathered together, deliver in the name of the Lord, whose glory is in judgment of this kind, not out of your hatred
**“In the name of the Lord”** — In this way I have judged: that you, gathered together into one without any dissension, with whom my authority and the power of Christ will cooperate, should deliver such a one to Satan.
5.5:
**“to deliver”** — the guilty one
**“such a one to Satan”** — To deliver to Satan. He is said to have had this power, that when he could not remove someone from folly, he might deliver him to the devil to be vexed, until professing penance he should desist from evil. Or: To deliver to Satan is to expel from the Church, to withdraw admonition from him, to make it free for him to go to the destruction of the flesh, that is, to act according to what his flesh desires, leading him to destruction. But not out of the bitterness of hatred, but with this intention, that this repulsion may avail to call him back in the day of the Lord, that is, if ever the Lord should visit his heart, if ever the Lord should shine in his heart.
**“for the destruction of the flesh,”** — so that the devil may torment him bodily, and so he may come to his senses
**“that the spirit”** — of the common Church
**“may be saved in the day”** — of judgment
**“That the spirit may be saved”** — Augustine. Thus the Apostle delivers to Satan not cruelly but lovingly, as Moses judged only a few of the worshippers of idols, frightening for the present and establishing discipline for the future. So too Elias and other good men, because thus fear is struck into others and sin is lessened in the sinners themselves. Whence Christ does not reprehend this example of Elias in his disciples, but because from hatred and not from love of correction they desired the vengeance of fire upon those who had not given them lodging. So too Peter is read to have taken vengeance on Ananias and his wife. Or he delivers them so that the Holy Spirit, of whom the defiled are stripped, may be saved to them, not lost, in the day of judgment.
5.6:
**“Your glorying is not good.”**
• as if: such fornication among you
• because among you there is such
• although among others there is no good
• because this prevents all these good things
**“Know you not that a little leaven”** — the consent to this sin, or this one fornicator, corrupts others by example
**“corrupteth the whole lump?”**
• they all defile who, though they could rebuke, keep silent
• because it corrupts, therefore
**“The whole lump”** — They were partakers while he suffered the guilty one. But if anyone does not have the power, or cannot prove the one he knows to be guilty, he is free from blame. And it is not for a judge to condemn without an accuser, just as Christ did not cast out Judas.
5.7:
**“Purge out the old leaven”** — by casting out him who corrupts, who is a member of the old man, and sour
**“that you may be”** — that is, that you may persevere
**“a new paste”** — renewed in virtues, without the corruption of sin
**“Paste”** — It is flour bound together with water without leaven, the same as unleavened bread. He wishes therefore that they be one thing through love, pure from the corruption of sin, having put on the new man, just as in baptism they were made unleavened. Zyma is Greek, fermentum is Latin.
**“as you are unleavened.”** — made so in baptism
**“For”** — therefore pure
**“Pasch”** — It is not, as some think, a Greek name but a Hebrew one. Yet in this name a certain agreement of the two languages happens very fittingly. For because to suffer is called paschin in Greek, Pasch is therefore thought to be passion. But in the Hebrew language Pasch is called “passage,” because the people of God first celebrated the Pasch then, when fleeing out of Egypt they passed over the Red Sea. But now that prophetic figure is fulfilled, since Christ was led “as a sheep to the slaughter,” and with his blood smeared on our door-posts, that is, our foreheads signed with the sign of the cross, we are freed from the perdition of this world as from Egyptian captivity, and make a most saving passage, when we pass from the devil to Christ.
*Ambrose:* The Pasch is a sacrifice, not a passing over, as seems to some. For first the Pasch, and so the passing over, because first comes the example of the Saviour, and so salvation.
**“is sacrificed”** — through whom we have to pass from this world to the promised country
**“Christ our”** — whom we ought to eat
5.8:
**“Therefore let us feast”** — because otherwise we would not pass over
**“not with the old leaven,”** — with the old corruption
**“nor”** — by parts
**“with the leaven of malice”** — into another
**“and wickedness;”** — into itself
**“but with the unleavened bread”** — in sincerity from vices, and in the truth of good works, which are signified by the unleavened bread
**“of sincerity”** — from vices
**“Of sincerity”** — Of the new life and truth without any deceit: so that sincerity may make life pure, and truth may exclude all deceit.
**“and truth.”** — of good works
5.9: **“I wrote to you in an epistle”** — I now advise you to purge yourselves of this, but you ought to have done so even without this admonition, because I have already written in another epistle
5.10:
**“not”** — so the former ones had understood it
**“with the fornicators of this world”** — that is, the Gentiles
**“covetous”** — this too he had forbidden in that epistle, which they ought to observe now as well
**“extortioners”** — but not from the Gentiles
**“otherwise you must needs go out of this world”**
• if I had commanded you not to mix with the Gentiles, you would have had to go out from worldly company, since such people are everywhere
• Or otherwise, that is, if you mix with them, it would be better for you to die.
**“Otherwise you must needs go out of this world”** — Such people could not be gained for Christ if they avoided their conversation and table; whence the Lord also ate with publicans and sinners.
5.11:
**“But now I have written to you”** — because it is not of those; therefore now, that is, in this present, it appears that
**“But now”** — Then I wrote to you, and you did not take it well; but now I write plainly.
**“not to keep company”**
• with fornicators
• in this manner
**“if any man that is named a brother”**
• even if he is not
• Or: who is named a brother, that is, is publicly known as a fornicator, etc.
**“that is named”** — Augustine, On Penance. He wished that naming to be understood which is made against someone when the sentence is delivered in judicial order and with integrity. For if naming suffices, many innocent men must be condemned, because they are often falsely named in some crime. By these words he shows well enough that the wicked are to be removed from the communion of the Church not rashly and in any way whatever, but by judgment. Or if they cannot be removed by judgment, they should rather be tolerated, lest anyone, by perversely avoiding the wicked and departing from the Church, bring to hell those whom he seems to flee.
**“be”** — In all these he marks them.
**“fornicator”** — named
**“covetous, or a server of idols, or a railer”** — that is, a slanderer
**“or a drunkard”** — by habit
**“or an extortioner: with such a one”** — and others like these
**“not so much as to eat”**
• much less to pray
• not even to eat, so that being shamed he may be corrected.
5.12:
**“For what have I to do”** — I speak of these.
**“them that are without”** — outside the Church
**“to judge”**
• these are to be coaxed
• nothing
• but
**“Do not you”** — in these the rot is to be cut away
**“judge them that are within”**
• by name and profession
• but
5.13:
**“For them that are without, God will judge”**
• he has not committed to us
• and because I command not to mix with such, therefore
**“Put away the evil one”** — man
**“evil”** — That is, that fornicator, as the Greek word forces us to understand, or consent.
**“from among yourselves”**
• by whom you are defiled
• made the same

6.1:
**“Dare any of you”**
• and when you ought to judge those who are within
• By occasion of this kind of judgment he begins to treat of judgments in which they sinned in many ways: that, the faithful being despised, they went to unbelieving judges, or appointed foolish judges, and quarreled and defrauded and did other things of this kind.
**“having a matter against another”** — a believer
**“go to be judged before the unjust”** — unbelievers
**“unjust”** — Unbelievers are unjust to the faithful in whatever way they can, and either utterly despise the divine laws, or, in order to oppress the good, interpret them by false exposition.
**“and not”** — rather
**“before the saints”** — who, fearing God, would keep justice, and in judging would serve the truth of the laws with charity preserved, and charity with truth preserved.
6.2:
**“Know you not”** — Ought not the saints to judge of such things?
**“that the saints shall judge this world”** — who is in error, since there is also another, higher one.
**“the saints shall judge”** — Because by the example of their faith the unbelief of such people will be condemned.
**“shall judge”** — with authority and power
**“And if the world shall be judged by you”** — that is, through you
**“shall be judged, the world”** — because you have some saints who will judge
**“are you unworthy”** — as if: not
**“to judge the smallest matters”** — these
6.3:
**“Know you not”** — Truly you can judge of these.
**“that we shall judge angels”** — the apostates, who, though created worthy, have fallen, whereas these stand frail, and because when attacked they were overcome
**“shall judge”** — we shall show to be condemnable
**“how much more”** — we shall be able to judge
**“things of this world”**
• concerning worldly things
• and when you ought to judge
6.4:
**“If therefore you have judgments of things pertaining to this world”**
• because they are not to be held, but rather despised
• Or: Secular, therefore. Because the Apostle had said that they could judge the least things, he determines who are to be appointed to settle business of this kind, namely the contemptible ones who are in the Church. For the greater ones ought to attend to spiritual things. As if to say: and because you ought to judge, therefore if you have secular judgments, appoint to judge those who are contemptible, that is, some wise men who are nevertheless of lesser merit. For the apostles, going about preaching, had no leisure for such things.
*Augustine:* He wished, then, wise men who dwelt in the places, faithful and holy, not those who ran hither and thither for the gospel, to be the examiners of such business. From these we cannot excuse ourselves even if we would. For I call Christ to witness that I would rather work something with my hands at fixed hours each day, and have the other hours free for reading and praying, or for doing something about the divine letters, than suffer the most tumultuous perplexities of lawsuits about secular business, whether to be settled by judging or cut short by intervening.
**“the most despised”**
• irony
• undiscerning, worthless
**“who are the most despised in the church, set them to judge”** — as if: this is what you have done, whence brothers, compelled, run to those, namely unbelievers
6.5:
**“I speak to your shame”**
• as if: I do not command but remind, that you may be ashamed
• Let those who have perceived the wisdom of outward things examine earthly causes. But those who are endowed with spiritual gifts ought not to be entangled in earthly business, so that, not being compelled to arrange lower goods, they may be able to serve higher goods. Yet care must be taken that those who shine with spiritual gifts do not wholly abandon the affairs of their weak neighbours, but either commit them to others to whom it is fitting to handle them, or manage them themselves.
**“Is it so”** — because
**“there is not”** — that is, so
**“any one wise man, that is able to judge between his brethren”** — so that it is necessary for you to set up fools, and these rather are to be set up, than that one go to unbelieving judges when wise men are lacking
6.6:
**“But brother goeth to law with brother”** — which is evil
**“and that before unbelievers”** — which is worse
6.7:
**“Already indeed there is plainly a fault among you”**
• that is, from this alone, that you have lawsuits
• It is a fault to have a lawsuit against another. **“All things are lawful to me,”**

• Note that something can be lawful and not expedient. But what is expedient cannot be unlawful. And so not all things that are lawful, that is, that are forbidden by no precept of the Lord, are expedient. But all unlawful things are not expedient. Therefore let us try to distinguish by some fixed limit between what is lawful, and what is not lawful and therefore not expedient. I confess that those things seem to me lawful and not expedient which are permitted by the justice that is before God, but which on account of the offence of men are to be avoided, lest by them men be hindered from salvation. But those things are unlawful, and for that reason not expedient, which are so forbidden by justice itself that they are not to be done, even if they are praised by those to whose knowledge they have been brought. But if this is so, only unlawful things are forbidden by the Lord; so that those things which are lawful and not expedient are avoided not by the bond of law, but by the free kindness of love and the counsel of charity. These are the things that are laid out further for the wounded man, who was brought to the Samaritan’s inn to be healed by that man’s compassion. These are not commanded by the Lord, although they are urged by the Lord to be offered. That is never said to be lawful which is forbidden, as Ambrose proves. Whence it is said: “It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother’s wife.” And the Lord: “It is not lawful to cast the children’s bread to dogs.” And therefore: “All things are lawful to me” is never said of evil things.
**“All things are lawful to me”**
• Because he had said that it is better to bear than to plead causes badly, lest anyone think that his own is in no way to be asked back, he adds: All my things it is lawful for me to ask back, but nevertheless I will not ask back, because not all things are expedient for my course but hinder it. Likewise for another reason: they are lawful but I will not ask back, because since I am free, I do not wish to be brought under the power of a judge, or I do not wish to be under the dominion of any thing, so that on account of it I should offend a brother.
• That is, let someone suppose it is lawful, not because those things are lawful to him, but because legal torments no longer threaten.
• Which the natural law has, for his fellow apostles also, not the law of Moses, who forbade many things because of the hardness of the people. He says this because it was lawful for him to take support, as one who would act afterwards too. But he would not, because he cannot urgently reprove one from whom he receives. Whence he says: But I will not be brought under the power of any. But false apostles, who preach for the sake of gain, do not wish to be loved by sinners.
• He speaks of those things that pertain to food. All things are lawful, but I will not be brought under the power of any; which I would do, if I ate with offence. For so I would offend my brother through love of food, because meat is for the belly. Whence afterwards: “Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, eat”, but not with scandal, because then it is not expedient. And elsewhere: “I will never eat flesh, lest I should scandalize my brother.” Likewise elsewhere: “All things indeed are clean: but it is evil for that man who eateth with offence.” These things are the more welcome the more they are not owed. Unlawful things are forbidden; lawful things that are not expedient are to be freely avoided.

• He that is joined to God is one spirit, etc. Not by identity of substance but by participation, when he is joined to him in this way, approaching by faith, so that he is a partaker of his blessedness; which will then be fully the case when his desire shall be satisfied with unchangeable goods, namely in the Trinity itself, his Lord, whose image he is. Therefore the spirit of man is not one with the Spirit of God in the way that the Son is one with the Father and one God. For so we say of the Father and the Son “they are one,” because they are two of one substance. And we say “he is one,” but we add which one, namely one God. Attend carefully: when “he is one” or “she is one” is said of two or more things, it can be said both of those that are of different substance and of those that are of one substance. For the spirit of man and the Spirit of God are of different substance, and yet it is said: He that is joined to the Lord is one spirit, etc. But where it is said of two or more “they are one,” and it is not added what one, they are not understood as different, but as being of one substance; so it is said: “He that planteth, and he that watereth, are one.” Likewise: “I and the Father are one.” If therefore it is rightly said of those who are of different substance that they are “one spirit,” how much more are those who are of one substance rightly said to be “one God.”
6.18:
**“Fly”** — therefore
**“Fly fornication.”** — With other vices one may await a struggle. But flee this one, do not draw near to it, for it cannot be overcome better in any other way.
**“Every sin”**
• other sins only stain the soul
• No sin so dishonours and defiles the body as that one. Or otherwise. Every sin is without the body, that is, without the wife, who is said to be one body with her husband, except this one. For they ought to be separated for no other, but for this. And they are separated for this reason, that they sin against the unity of the body, and against the faith of the marriage bed, and against the intention of offspring. Otherwise. He who sins criminally is called a beast, not a man, and sins without his body, that is, without the Church, because for venial sins one is not separated from the Church. But he who commits fornication sins without his own body, that is, without the Church, so that he is cast out from it.
• Every sin, etc. Because other sins, even if they are carried out through the body, do not nevertheless make the soul so bound and subject to carnal concupiscence as happens in the work of bodily fornication alone. For the force of lust acting in the body in carnal fornication makes the soul mingled with the body itself; for it so glues the soul to the body that in that very moment it is not permitted to a man to think or attend to anything else, because the very submersion, and the swallowing up of lust and carnal concupiscence, subjects the mind itself as captive. Whence it is said: “He that committeth fornication, sinneth against his own body.”
*Jerome:* A man placed in marriage, whatever sins he commits, does not darken his own wife. But if he commits fornication with others, he stains her so that she is not lawful, but as an adulteress, so that the husband ought to receive penance, if she suffers her husband to remain in adultery. Hence we have it that unless the husband repents, the wife ought to put him away.
*Augustine:* In other sins it is permitted to the mind to work at one thing and attend to another, but not in fornication, where the whole man is flesh. But there is a general fornication, when someone not adhering to God adheres to the world. Whence it is said: “The friend of this world is an enemy of God.” He therefore who clings to the world and is far from God sins against the body, because by bodily concupiscence the mind is drawn away to all manner of temporal things, serving the creature rather than the Creator. But he who clings to God and not to the world, if he sins through human frailty, by ignorance or by negligence, is without the body, because he does not sin by bodily or temporal concupiscence, but by human temptation, which is easily forgiven.

• Wedlock or matrimony is the marital union of a man and a woman, keeping an undivided habit of life. And wedlock is a good thing, one of the sacraments of the Church, holding the image of the union of Christ and the Church; whence: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak in Christ and in the church.” For Christ, approving matrimony, was present at a wedding, and commended it by a miracle. God also instituted the first marriage among our first parents. The efficient cause of matrimony is marital consent in the present, expressed by words; whence it is not intercourse but will that makes matrimony.
**“Concerning the things”** — Taking occasion from the fornication which he forbids, he continues about marriage, about which they had asked. And he treats it in three ways: according to counsel, according to indulgence, according to precept.
**“John Chrysostom”** — Not the deflowering of virginity but the marriage contract makes a marriage. The cause for which it ought to be contracted is the procreation of children and the avoiding of fornication. There are also other honest cases, such as the reconciliation of enemies and the restoration of peace.
*Augustine:* What is beyond the intention of generation is not an evil of marriage, but venial on account of the good of marriage. Which is threefold: faith, offspring, sacrament. Faith, that one not consort with another man or woman; offspring, that it be brought up religiously; sacrament, that the marriage not be separated. By these three goods carnal intercourse between spouses is excused, so that it is either no sin, or venial. For when they come together for the sake of offspring, it is excused so that it is no sin; but when for the sake of satisfying or restraining concupiscence, it is venial.

• Someone will say: if the Apostle conceded this by indulgence, then marriage is a sin. For to what is indulgence granted, if not to sin? Plainly, what the Apostle conceded to weakness by indulgence, I dare to say is a sin. For in granting indulgence the Apostle has regard to the intercourse of the married, where there is the evil of incontinence. The evil of incontinence is that the husband knows his wife even beyond the necessity of begetting children; but even there is the good of marriage. For it is not because the evil of incontinence is there that the union which is beyond the intention of generation is therefore not good. Rather, this good is not made blameworthy on account of that evil; but that evil is made venial on account of the good of marriage. This good of marriage the Apostle does not reprove, but the evil of incontinence. Intercourse for the sake of begetting is necessary for them, blameless, and it alone is properly of marriage. But that which goes beyond necessity obeys not reason but lust. Since, therefore, intercourse with the intention of begetting is not blameworthy, and this is what is properly to be attributed to marriage, what does the Apostle concede by indulgence, if not that spouses demand the debt of the flesh, not by the will to propagate but by the pleasure of lust? Which pleasure, however, does not fall into guilt on account of marriage, but on account of marriage receives pardon. Wherefore marriages are praiseworthy even from this, that they bring it about that even what does not pertain to them is forgiven for their own sake. For this intercourse, by which concupiscence is served, is not done so that the offspring which marriage seeks may be fulfilled. Altogether, therefore, marriages are good in their own kind, because they keep faith of the marriage bed, and unite both sexes for the sake of receiving offspring, and shudder at the impiety of separation.

*Augustine:* For there is only one God, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, that is, the Trinity itself, from which God is. And no division of parts is made in the unity of the deity. For God the Father is not a part of God. For the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are three persons, and these three, because they are of one substance, are one, and are supremely one, because there is no diversity of natures and no diversity of wills. For if they were one in nature and were not so in consent, they would not be supremely one. But if they were unequal in nature, they would not be one. Further, Christ is one person of twofold substance, because he is both God and man. Yet neither God nor man can be called a part of this person. Otherwise the same Son of God before he took the form of a servant was not whole, and grew when man was added to his divinity. But if in one person God cannot be a part, how much more can any one of the three not be a part of the Trinity. Of this Trinity, therefore, one is not a third part, nor are all anything greater than each single one.
