9.8:
**“Speak I these things according to man?”** — namely, I prove this only by human comparison
**“Or doth not the law also say these things?”** — does not the law of Moses prove the same?
9.9:
**“For it is written in the law of Moses: Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn.”** — you shall not forbid the preacher to live by preaching
**“Is”** — but lest this seem to be said only according to the letter, he adds
**“for oxen?”**
• that a command about these might be given in the law
• not for the oxen, but for us alone: Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn.
9.10:
**“Or doth he say this indeed for our sakes?”** — These things are for our sake, because other things also look to the same end; and this is
**“For these things are written for our sakes”** — These
**“that he that plougheth, should plough in hope”** — Not for hope.
**“he that plougheth, should plough”**
• He opens the hearts to faith.
• not that this is the principal intention.
**“and he that thrasheth”** — He separates the grain from the chaff.
**“in hope to receive fruit”** — of wages.
9.11:
**“If we have sown unto you”** — again he proves by reasons.
**“spiritual things”** — which quicken your spirit, or which are given by the Holy Spirit.
**“is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?”** — for support.
9.12:
**“If others be partakers of this power over you”** — again from the lesser.
**“be partakers”** — they make such powerful use of yours as you yourselves do.
**“why not we rather?”** — who labour for the sake of your salvation.
**“Nevertheless, we have not used this power”** — behold, it is lawful for us to receive.
**“but we bear all things”** — because perhaps they would say that he was not in need; against this he adds.
**“lest we should give any hindrance”** — because if the Apostle received, the false apostles would then receive freely, and so would persist in preaching, and thus a hindrance would be made to the gospel.
**“hindrance”** — Perhaps these too were greedy, either thinking they had bought a license to sin, or that the Apostle would diminish the freedom of rebuking.
9.13:
**“Know you not that”** — Likewise he proves that he has this power by the likeness of the priests of the Gentiles or of the Jews.
**“Know you not”** — He returns again and again, commending that it is lawful for him and yet he does not do it. Natural reason has this, that one lives by that where he labours.
**“they who work in the holy place”**
• in the temple.
• or this of the Gentiles.
**“work”** — as craftsmen.
**“eat the things that are of the holy place; and they that serve the altar”** — as the priests of the Jews.
**“partake with the altar?”** — because they have a share of those things that are offered.
9.14:
**“So also the Lord ordained”** — and as happens here, so the Lord reasonably ordained concerning preachers, that they might be freer to preach the word of God.
**“the Lord ordained”** — “Behold, I send you,” etc. And a little after: “And in the same house, remain, eating and drinking such things as they have.”
**“that they who preach the gospel, should live by the gospel.”** — for the labourer is worthy of his hire.
9.15:
**“But I have used none of these things.”**
• it is established in so many ways that it is lawful, either by authority or by example.
• but nor do I wish to use it.
**“But I have used none”** — He abstains from expenses, lest there be a pattern for the greedy false apostles.
**“Neither have I written these things”** — that it be permitted to receive
**“that they should be so done unto me”** — these things, that is, that I should receive
**“for it is good for me to die”** — because if I took it I would lose the glory; and I prefer to die, or I want rather to die, that is, to be afflicted
**“rather than that any man should make my glory void.”** — which would be if he received it with offence
**“my glory”** — For whoever does not wish to use what is owed to him spends more on the Church. The Apostle therefore had the greatest glory before God, by not demanding a stipend from the weak, or by getting his daily food from his own labours.
*Ambrose:* This is what the Lord says to the innkeeper, to whom the wounded man who fell among robbers was brought: “Whatsoever thou shalt spend over and above, I at my return will repay thee.” The Apostle spent more, who served as a soldier at his own charges. Or he means his glory which he has with God in this, that he kept the false apostles from preaching, by not receiving, since they preached only for temporal things.
9.16:
**“For”** — whether it be made void
**“if I preach the gospel”** — only
**“it is no glory to me”** — there is no glory from this alone, because it is necessary by command, nor do I dare to give it up, because woe will be
**“glory”** — Which he has before God, sympathising with the weak. NECESSITY, of sustaining this life. WOE, because I have nothing to live on. IF WILLING, without any necessity of this life. IF UNWILLING, so that what I am compelled by necessity to do, I do for the profit of others, not of myself.
**“woe is unto me if I preach not the gospel”** — as it has been enjoined on me
**“For if I preach the gospel”** — For a reward. Or, if I preach thus, it is not. GLORY, because then it would be from necessity, because WOE, that is, want, would be, as with the false apostle.
9.17:
**“For if I do this thing willingly”**
• if I do this from necessity there is no glory, but if will is joined to necessity, so that I preach out of love, then there is glory for me
• For if I do this thing willingly. Because the reward is from the will, let us see how: namely, if I so act out of love that I would rather suffer want than misuse power.
**“I do this thing; I have a reward”** — but
**“but if against my will, a dispensation is committed to me”**
• although I have no reward, I dispense to others and profit
• We ought not to preach the gospel in order to eat, but to eat in order to preach the gospel; so that food may not be the good that is sought, but the necessary thing that is added, that this may be fulfilled: “Seek ye first the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you.” For the kingdom of God alone we ought to do all things, not to contemplate a temporal reward alone, or together with the kingdom of God.
**“a dispensation is committed to me”** — Here such a dispensation is understood: that as a servant dispenses another’s revenue, from which he himself takes nothing beyond food. Elsewhere a steward is called one who, as a son, ministers the gospel to his co-heirs.
9.18:
**“What is my reward then?”** — that is, this
**“That preaching the gospel, I may deliver the gospel without charge”** — I may establish
**“the gospel, that I abuse not”** — which would be if I received
**“my power in the gospel”** — because he would not freely rebuke
9.19:
**“For”** — certainly I will do what I said, for I have done even more
**“whereas I was free as to all”** — bound by the merits of no one
**“I made myself the servant of all”** — that I might serve the advantages of all
**“that I might gain the more”** — I might make gain of my preaching
9.20:
**“And I became”** — and I accommodated myself to all
**“to the Jews, a Jew”** — in foods and such things, and because he circumcised Timothy
**“a Jew”** — Jerome. Not truly a Jew, just as not truly a Gentile, to whom he yielded in foods and the like; nor yet in the worship of idols, because in Christ neither circumcision is anything, nor uncircumcision. He therefore pretended by way of dispensation to be a Jew. But Augustine says that this is done out of the compassion of mercy, not by pretense; as he who ministers to the sick man becomes as it were sick, not when he falsely claims to have fevers, but when with the mind of one who suffers with him he thinks how he would wish to be served if he were sick.
*Augustine:* As a Jew. Not by the cunning of pretense, so as to feign himself a Jew, as some think. For he did those things freely, as he says: “Let him not become uncircumcised” who is circumcised. Truly, then, not feignedly, he lived as a Jew (which he was), just as he did not deceitfully feign himself a Gentile, but lawfully allowed himself the use of all foods, to whom every creature was good, not in pretense but in truth. As therefore he took up these rites of the Gentiles truly, so also the sacraments of the Jews he took up not deceitfully, so as to be single toward the one and double toward the other, having one thing in his heart and another in show. So also when he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” he did not pretend another’s weakness, but grieved. So also that he became weak to the weak was not a lie, but he truly said that expenses were owed to him, and yet he abstained, lest he seem a seller of the gospel. His pretense, then, is not deceitful and crafty, but his merciful compassion suits all, and he bears their weakness in compassion, helping them as he himself would have wished to be helped if he were in those things, as though he himself had their weaknesses. For he who ministers to the sick man becomes as it were sick, not when he falsely claims to have fevers, but when with the mind of one who suffers with him he thinks how he would wish to be served if he were sick; he did not pretend the things he did like the Jews, just as he did not pretend the things he did like the Gentiles.
*Jerome:* To Augustine. There is not much difference between my opinion and yours, because I say that both Peter and Paul, through fear of the faithful and of the Jews, practised the law, or rather pretended to keep its commands. But you assert that they did this fearing, not with the craft of one who lies but with the feeling of one who suffers, provided it be agreed by them that out of fear or mercy they pretended to be what they were not.
**“that I might gain the Jews”** — to Christ
9.21:
**“To them that are under the law”**
• to the Samaritans
• The Samaritans, who receive the books of Moses, which the Jews do not use. They are of Persian origin, whom the king of the Assyrians placed, when Israel was taken away, or the king of the Persians, to inhabit the places of Samaria.
**“as if I were under the law”** — since he does not deny that the law was given by God, but from it teaches Christ
**“whereas myself was not under the law”** — servilely
**“that I might gain them that”** — likewise
**“were under the law. To them that were without the law”** — to the Gentiles
**“as if I were without the law”** — while I agreed with them, according to natural reasons, that the world was made by God, and such things
**“whereas I was not without the law of God, but was in the law of Christ”** — not Jewish
**“that I might gain them that were without the law”** — that is, the Gentiles
9.22:
**“To the weak I became”** — in faith
**“weak”** — by abstaining from lawful things
**“that I might gain the weak”**
• because
• behold
**“I became all things to all men”**
• what, through each detail
• as if I were of all sects
• Not with the craft of one who lies but with the feeling of one who suffers with them; that is, not by deceitfully doing all their evils, but by mercifully healing the evil of all as though it were his own, doing for others what he would wish done to himself if there were need. For he thinks that, as a man, he could have been in those vices in which others are. Whence elsewhere he says: “Considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.”
**“all things to all men”** — He yielded to all, yet did not go beyond religion.
9.23:
**“And I do all things”** — behold why he adapts himself to all
**“for the gospel's sake”** — that he may run without hindrance
**“that I may be made partaker thereof”** — of his promise, that is, of justice and eternal blessedness
9.24:
**“Know you not that they”** — He shows how great is the profit of our law, in which the palm is promised not to one but to all, and he who came first waits to be crowned together with the later one.
**“Know you not that they that”** — All things for the gospel, because unless I do all things and abstain from all the things that are against it, I shall not have the reward. Or I press on thus in all things because all can have the crown; or because if “many are called, yet few are chosen,” so that thus at least few may be chosen out of many.
**“all run indeed”** — here all are equal in labour
**“but one”**
• as if rare, not all
• there one, here all who run perseveringly receive
**“receiveth the prize?”** — The prize (bravium) is the reward of the race.
**“Is it so”** — So you, however
**“run that you may obtain”**
• by working well
• because not every runner receives, therefore run so perfectly: So run that you may obtain.
9.25:
**“And every one that striveth for the mastery”** — and truly so one must strive, because even in the lesser case, where one receives
**“every one that striveth for the mastery”** — Many comparisons are drawn from things not to be praised, as in the Gospel of the unjust judge who would not hear the widow, and of him who out of weariness lends loaves; so here athletic and playful things are not commended.
**“refraineth himself from all things”** — so you from stumbling-blocks
**“and they indeed”** — and they abstain
**“that they may receive a corruptible crown”** — as if: and truly we ought to abstain, because the matter is greater here
**“but we an incorruptible one”** — and therefore we ought to abstain from all things
9.26:
**“I therefore”**
• he sets himself forth as an example
• and because such a one
**“so run”**
• by working
• so lawfully
**“not as at an uncertainty”** — that I may be uncertain of the reward
**“not as at”** — He runs to an uncertainty who does such things that he can hope from some and despair from others.
**“so fight”** — against enemies
**“Not as one beating the air”** — I strive not in words but in deeds, or not vainly, as one who strikes the air for an enemy
9.27:
**“But I chastise my body”** — I restrain the unlawful movements of the body
**“and bring it into subjection”**
• of reason
• while he strives toward another
**“lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway”**
• with its trembling the ram frightens the lambs
• rejected by God
**“Lest perhaps”** — What could happen quickly, others must then guard against the more, lest by offending they be reprobate.

10.1:
**“For I would not have you ignorant, brethren”** — so it is to be done
**“For I would not have you ignorant”** — For one who wishes to understand, it must be done thus: for baptism and the sacraments do not suffice, as some think, just as God’s benefits did not avail the Jews when afterwards they sinned.
**“that our fathers”** — founders of our faith
**“That our fathers”** — By the example of the Jews, who by their negligence gave offence, he makes them watchful.
**“all”** — both good and bad
**“were all under the cloud”** — protecting from the heat, and against the Egyptians so that they might not be seen by them
**“Under the cloud”** — Augustine. Because all things were in figure of ours.
**“and all passed through the sea”** — Augustine explains “passed through the Red Sea”: if the figure of the sea was of such power as to lead the people to the manna, how much more Christ’s baptism, the enemies being drowned.
10.2:
**“And all in Moses”** — under the leadership of Moses
**“were baptized, in the cloud”** — by the Spirit
**“In Moses baptized”** — Cleansed under the leadership of Moses by those visible signs. Or they received the sign of baptism, which availed the same for believers.
**“Baptized in the cloud”** — Because they were both delivered from death and through it cleansed from the ignorance of God which weighed upon all the nations, and prepared to receive the law. Or they are said to be baptized because they bore the form of our sacrament: Moses signifies Christ, the cloud the Holy Spirit, the sea baptism.
**“and in the sea”** — by water
10.3:
**“And did all eat the same spiritual food”** — Food. Christ is the bread “which cometh down from heaven: if any man eat of it, he shall not die.” But it belongs to the power of the sacrament, not to the visible sacrament: he eats within, with the heart, not without; not he who presses with the tooth.
**“did eat”** — the manna, which signified Christ and effected the same for believers. Others ate and died, which Moses and the other good men did not.
10.4:
**“And all drank the same spiritual drink”**
• water from the rock
• a sign of the blood of Christ, and it effected the same for believers
**“Food and drink”** — He calls manna and water spiritual, because they were prepared not by nature but by the power of God, having the figure of a future mystery.
**“the same and the same”** — The same in faith, different in time, different in appearance.
**“the same food, the same drink”** — The food is the same in mystery, and the drink of those people was the same as ours: the same in signification, not in outward form, because the same Christ was figured to them in the rock and was made manifest to us in the flesh.
**“spiritual”** — That is, signifying something spiritual. When he says spiritual, he shows that it is to be understood spiritually in Christ, and he hints this of all of them when he explains one: “the rock was Christ.”
**“spiritual, the same”** — For the one food was bodily, the manna; ours is another, that of the fathers, ours and not theirs. Spiritual: which we have; the one was other, and we other; but in visible form it was different, which nevertheless signified the same by spiritual power.
**“and they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them”**
• which signifies Christ, and was the same of faith
• by which
**“rock”** — That is, Christ followed, because where human help failed, he was present.
**“the rock that followed them”** — That is, satisfying their will, because wherever they went, the flowing waters followed them; so Christ accompanies his own in the desert of this world. Or following, that is, signifying the truth that is to follow.
**“and the rock was Christ”** — in a sign
**“and the rock”** — A thing that signifies is usually named by the name of the thing it signifies: “was Christ.” Not by substance, but by signification.
**“the rock Christ”** — Augustine. In different signs the faith is the same; but they believed that things were to come, we believe that they have come. There the rock was Christ; for us, what is placed on the altar is Christ. If you look at the visible appearance, it is one thing; if at the intelligible signification, they drank the same spiritual drink.
*Augustine:* In the sign the rock was struck twice with the rod. The double striking signifies the two beams of the cross. Water was brought out of the rock when the rod came to it, because when the wood came to the rock, Christ, spiritual grace flowed out.
10.5:
**“But with most of them”** — the Jews used all these benefits according to the letter
**“of them”**
• of those who offended the Lord
• of the Jews
**“God was not well pleased: for”** — from this it appears
**“they were overthrown in the desert”**
• lest you think men had now invented these things; he says
• these things were done not for them only
10.6:
**“Now these things were done in a figure of us”**
• thus
• considering their punishments
**“that we should not covet evil things”** — lest we so sin, lest we likewise perish
10.7:
**“Neither become ye idolaters”**
• through idol-offerings
• He touches those who feasted in an idol’s temple, thinking themselves free from guilt.
**“as some of them, as it is written”** — in Exodus
**“The people sat down”**
• so that you in the idol’s temple
• some of the people
**“to eat and drink”** — before the calf
**“The people sat down to eat and drink”** — By recalling those, he notes the things that are among the Corinthians, showing how severely they were punished among the Jews.
**“and rose up to play”** — to make games in veneration of the calf
**“to play”** — That is, to adore, which is like a children’s game. For childhood is easily inclined to play. But what is so like childish play as to adore idols?
10.8:
**“Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication”** — as some among you
**“committed fornication”** — with the Madianite women
**“and”** — therefore
10.9:
**“Neither let us tempt Christ”** — as do those who despair of the resurrection
**“Neither let us tempt”** — Note: Christ is God, whom the Jews tempted, and therefore they perished by serpents until the brazen serpent was raised up, and those who looked upon it were healed from the bites.
**“as some of them tempted”** — saying: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?”
**“and perished by the serpents”** — until the brazen serpent was raised up
10.10:
**“Neither do you murmur”** — as you do against me, or those who have lesser gifts of the Spirit against God
**“as some of them murmured”** — against Moses
**“and were destroyed by the destroyer”** — by the angel who struck them beyond the bounds of the promised land
10.11:
**“Now all these things”** — these things happened to them because of their own sins, and not only for this but also that they might foreshadow that we would perish for like sins
**“all these things in figure”** — of us
**“In figure”** — Behold, he shows why those signs are no longer observed, since the matter is now plain for our correction.
**“happened to them: and they are written for our correction”** — otherwise the punishment will be greater
**“Are written”** — For us alone. Augustine. For by these examples we are provoked to a more correct life, so that we may merit either a reward if we are obedient, or a heavier punishment if we are disobedient.
**“And they are written”** — Behold, here it appears why those letters of the Old Testament are received by us.
**“upon whom”** — namely we
**“the ends of the world are come.”** — the sixth age
**“The ends of the world”** — Because we are in the last age, and should be corrected all the more by so many examples of those before us. Or, the ends of the age have come upon us; worldliness is brought to an end in us, and therefore it is more shameful if we sin.
**“Therefore”** — because they, although they had enjoyed benefits, perished
10.12:
**“he that thinketh himself to stand”** — by good things
**“let him take heed lest he fall.”**
• by sinning, or by causing sin
• for he who stands, stands from God; he who falls, falls from himself
**“Lest he fall”** — As those who, presuming on knowledge, ate idol-offerings to the scandal of the brethren, and boasting falsely, judged the Apostle when they themselves were guilty.
*Augustine:* Let him see that he does not fall. He cuts off pride, lest through it they be tempted as the Jews were tempted and perished, because those who slandered Moses tempted God; so these who slander the Apostle tempt God.
**“Let him take heed lest he fall”** — Not that anyone is entirely without fall, but temptation, that is, delight in sin, does not seize him, that is, reason does not lead him to consent. Except human, that is, except of those things without which this life is not lived.
10.13:
**“Let no temptation take hold on you, but such as is human”**
• although it happens, which God permits, which is to test the good and to punish the wicked
• He exhorts that human temptation, and no other, seize them. For human temptation is that in necessity or distress a man does not despair, seeking human help from God. Therefore to suffer for Christ is human temptation, through which one advances before God.
*Augustine:* A human temptation is to think otherwise than the matter stands, even with a good mind. But to love one’s own opinion too much, or to envy one’s betters, to the point of cutting off communion and founding a schism or heresy, is the sacrilege that comes of diabolical presumption. In nothing to think otherwise than the matter stands is angelic perfection. A human temptation, then, I believe, is when someone with a good mind nevertheless, according to human frailty, slips in some counsel, or is irritated against a brother in zeal to correct him, but more than Christian tranquillity demands. And because we are men, but angels in hope, to whom we shall be made equal in the resurrection, if the perfection of an angel is not in us, let the presumption of the devil not be.
**“And God is faithful”**
• I exhort you
• true in what he permits, who promised to be the protector of his elect
**“who will not suffer you to be tempted”** — afflicted for themselves
**“above that which you are able”** — to bear, because he either does not allow them to fall or raises them from a fall
**“but will make”** — who gives licence to the tempter, gives mercy to the tempted
**“also with temptation issue”** — an increase of virtue
**“that you may be able to bear it.”**
• that you may not fail in the struggle but may conquer
• perseveringly
**“You may be able to bear it”** — This is done through humility. For humility guards in every temptation, so that those do not crack in the furnace who have no wind of pride.
10.14:
**“Wherefore”** — Because the sacraments alone do not save, and because he who falls is punished, and because the help of God is not lacking, flee from the worship of idols. Or let not the wise commend things offered to idols, to the offense of the weak, to whom they would seem idolaters. Or let not the weak themselves be idolaters; and that you may flee, I speak something lofty, as to the prudent, and therefore judge diligently. Or now I speak to the weak as above to the prudent.
**“my dearly beloved, fly from the service of idols”** — lest through this a temptation against God arise, that is, provocation
**“Fly”** — Let no one be constant in an idol’s temple; let him hope nothing from it. For to hope from it is to doubt God, as also Saul, who returned to idolatry hoping something from it.
10.15:
**“I speak as to wise men”** — something lofty
**“judge ye yourselves”** — diligently
10.16:
**“The chalice of benediction”**
• the drink of blood, through which those who partake are blessed
• chalice, that is, the sharing of the chalice; is it not indeed the sharing of Christ? That is, does it not make us have a certain communion with his life?
• Or, the chalice of blessing was blessed not only by Christ at supper, but also we priests bless it.
**“The chalice”** — Therefore one must flee the worship of idols, because as one who eats what was sacrificed to idols is one with a demon, so through the body of Christ one is one with Christ.
**“which we bless”** — that is, which we the faithful exalt by believing and giving thanks
**“is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? And the bread, which we break”**
• the partaking of the bread broken on the altar
• The bread which we break, etc. Augustine. When Christ is eaten, life is eaten. But who dares to eat his Lord? And yet he himself, inviting us to eat, says: “He that eateth me, the same also shall live by me.” Nor is Christ killed that he may be eaten, but he gives life to the dead when he is eaten; he refreshes and does not fail; he lives when eaten, because he rose when slain. Nor when we eat do we make parts of him. Indeed in the sacrament it is so. The faithful know how they have eaten the flesh of Christ. Each one receives his own part; whence the grace itself is called parts; he is eaten by parts and remains whole. He is eaten whole by parts in the sacrament, and remains whole in heaven. For he is also whole in your heart. For he was wholly with the Father when he came into the virgin and filled her, and did not depart from him. He came into flesh that men might eat him, and remained whole with the Father that he might feed the angels.
**“is it not the partaking of the body of the Lord?”** — does it not make us one with Christ?
10.17:
**“For we, being many, are one bread, one body”** — of that head, which is Christ
**“For we, being many, are one bread”** — He explains how the chalice of blessing and the bread become to the recipient the flesh and blood of Christ.
*Augustine:* For by the unity of the bread and the unity of the body charity must be understood; if this is lacking, he who receives takes judgment to himself. Typically, moreover, the Church of Christ is called one bread and one body, because as one bread is made of many grains and one body of many members, so the Church of Christ is joined together of many faithful by the binding of charity. Because we are one bread. One bread, by the union of faith, hope and charity, one body through the supplying of charity; because we are one, we ought to be said to be of one mind, that as faith is one, it may have one sense and work.
10.18:
**“Behold Israel”**
• that is, the carnal one, keeping the precepts of the law, serving also in the shadows of the sacrifices
• Or: Behold Israel. That is, learn, you men who see God, how carnal things stand, that is, idolatry. For as we, partaking of one bread and one chalice, are made conformable to the body of Christ, so those who eat the victims offered to an idol are partakers of the altar of error, that is, of the devil.
**“Behold”** — It is a likeness, to understand what has been said above. As if: are not those who eat those sacrifices of the law, namely carnal Israel, partakers of the altar? Indeed they are, because so those who eat the flesh of Christ and drink his blood are partakers of him.
**“according to the flesh”** — there is also Israel according to the spirit
**“are not they, that eat of the sacrifices, partakers of the altar?”**
• those of carnal Israel
• as if they indeed are
• so you of Christ
10.19:
**“What then? Do I say, that what is offered in sacrifice to idols, is any thing?”**

• Gloss of the Lombard: And he gave it in this species because the thing of this species bears an express likeness to both realities of this sacrament, namely, the contained and signified, and the signified and not contained. The thing contained and signified is the flesh of Christ, which he took from the Virgin, and the blood which he shed for us. But the thing signified and not contained is the unity of the Church in the predestined, called, justified and glorified. This is the twofold flesh of Christ.
• There are therefore three things in this sacrament. One which is “only sacrament,” as the visible species of bread and wine; another which is “sacrament and thing,” as the proper flesh and blood of Christ. The third which is “thing and not sacrament,” as is the mystical flesh of Christ. For a sacrament is the sign of a sacred thing. And that species signifies both things and bears an express likeness to both. For as bread, beyond other foods, refreshes and sustains the body, and wine gladdens and inebriates man, so the flesh of Christ spiritually refreshes and fattens the inner man more than other graces, and the blood spiritually gladdens, and so inebriates as to make sober; whence: “My chalice which inebriateth me, how goodly is it!” It has also a likeness to the thing signified only, which is the unity of the faithful, because one bread is made of many grains, and wine flows together into one from many grapes, so the unity of the Church consists of many persons of the faithful. Of this also the sacrament is the proper body of Christ, which he took from the virgin, because as the body of Christ consists of many members, pure and free from every stain of sin, so also the ecclesiastical unity consists of many clean and spotless persons. In figure of this thing the ark of the Lord was made of Sethim wood, which is incorruptible and like the white thorn.
• He gave it under two species for this reason, that it might be shown that Christ assumed the whole human nature, that is, body and soul, that he might redeem both. For the bread refers to the body, the wine to the soul, because wine produces blood, in which the seat of the soul is said by the physicians to be. And therefore it is celebrated under two species, that the taking up of soul and flesh in Christ and the freeing of both in us may be signified.
• Water is added for this reason, that our redemption may be shown to have been wrought by the passion of Christ, and his passion to have been undertaken for love of us. For water signifies the human race. Whence in the Apocalypse: “The waters which thou sawest are peoples,” whose salvation could not be without the Lord’s passion, nor the Lord’s passion without love of the people; for unless he loved us, he would not deliver himself to death for us.
• That the true body of Christ is on the altar the Truth itself testifies when he says: “Take ye, this is my body.” And the authorities of the saints, brought forward, confirm it. For Ambrose says: Before it is consecrated it is bread and wine; but where the words of Christ have wrought, of the bread is made the flesh and body of Christ. Likewise: The word of Christ, which could make out of nothing what was not, can it not change things that are into what they were not?
• Likewise, Eusebius: The invisible priest, by his word and his secret power, changes visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood.
• Likewise. Even the wicked receive the true body of Christ. There is also in sinners who receive unworthily the true flesh of Christ and the true blood of Christ, but in essence, not in saving effect. And the Apostle: “He that eateth and drinketh the body of the Lord unworthily,” etc. By which we are taught how much care must be taken not to receive a good thing badly; for behold, it has been made evil, while the good is badly received. But what Augustine says seems to contradict this: The good man receives the sacrament and the thing of the sacrament, but the wicked man the sacrament and not the thing. To which we say: The good man receives the sacrament, that is, the proper flesh and blood of Christ, and the thing, that is, the unity of the faithful, and increase of grace, but not so the wicked man. The same: He who does not eat, eats; he who eats, does not eat; that is, he who does not eat sacramentally eats spiritually, and he who eats sacramentally does not eat spiritually. Likewise the Truth said: You are not to eat this body which you see, and to drink that blood which they will shed who will crucify me, but I have commended to you another sacrament; that is, you are not to eat in this species, but in the sacrament, not torn and mangled by bites (as you suppose) but whole and unharmed.
• It is to be known that in the utterance of those words, “This is my body,” and, “This is the chalice,” etc., the mystery is consummated and the bread is converted into the body of Christ. But what is that conversion? That it is not formal is manifest, because the form of the bread and wine remains. Whether it is substantial is not clear. For some say that the substance passes or is converted into the substance in such a way that this becomes that, yet that is not increased. Nor do they concede that it can truly be said that this is that. Others say that this passes or is converted into that in this sense: that under those accidents under which the substance of bread and wine was before, after the consecration there is the substance of the body and blood, by which accidents, however, the body itself is not affected. We therefore, leaving the uncertain things aside, profess what is certain from the authorities, namely that the substance of bread and wine is converted into the substance of the Lord’s body and blood. But we are not ashamed to confess that we do not know the manner of the conversion. The accidents that remain of the former substance, namely color, taste, form, weight, neither affect the body of Christ itself nor are founded in it. But if it is asked in what they are founded, we say that it seems to us rather that they are without a subject than in a subject.
• As to the breaking, of what thing it is, or in what thing it takes place: it is manifest that it is not in the body of Christ, since that is incorruptible, impassible and immortal. Whence also Christ rebuked the carnal sense of the disciples, who thought that the flesh of Christ, like other flesh, was to be divided into parts and torn with bites. Therefore many say that there is no breaking there, but it only seems to happen. To them is objected what Ambrose says: Nothing false is to be supposed in the sacrifice of truth, nor as in the tricks of magicians, where the eyes are deceived by a kind of delusion so that what is not seems to be. To this they reply: Our sight does not deceive us, nor is anything deceived, as would be the case if it were believed to be broken as it seems. Nor is it an illusion, since it is done for the profit of faith, not for deception. Others say that there is indeed a breaking there, not indeed in the body of Christ, but in the sacramental form of the bread itself, which the Apostle seems to mean when he says: “The bread which we break,” etc.
• Likewise Augustine: When Christ is eaten, life is eaten. Nor when he is eaten do we make parts of him, and yet in the sacrament it is so done. Likewise: each one receives his part; he is eaten by parts and remains whole. From which it is plain that the whole and incorrupt body of Christ is eaten, and if there is a breaking or dividing there, it seems to be not in him but in the sacrament. Others say that there is a breaking there but of no thing, because nothing is broken there. For as the accidents are there without a subject, so there can wonderfully be a breaking in an accident, or without any thing that is broken. For great and unsearchable is this mystery. Whence Ambrose: Why do you seek the order of nature in the body of Christ, when the very birth of the Lord from a virgin was beyond nature? We are bidden to believe, we are not permitted to discuss. It is to be known that although the species of bread and wine are different there, yet they ought not to be called two sacraments but one, because under either species the same is received.
• It must be known that the body of Christ is not taken by brute animals, even if it seems so. What does a mouse take? What does it eat? Perhaps either nothing, or the substance of the bread brought back under its own appearance.
• After this let us see what those parts that seem to be made there signify. The body of Christ is threefold: the part of the host put into the chalice shows the body of Christ that has already risen; the part eaten, him still walking upon earth; the part remaining on the altar until the end, the bodies of the saints lying in the tombs until the end of the age.
• Note that the body of Christ was mortal and passible by will, but by nature neither mortal nor passible but immortal; it was given to the disciples as neither mortal nor passible but immortal, even if at that time it was mortal.
• Note that the disciples received the Lord’s body at the supper, before the resurrection, such as it was in nature, namely immortal, not such as it was by will, that is, mortal. While it was still mortal it could not be immortal for Peter by nature, but by the power of him by whose will it was mortal, and not by the right of nature. For he alone died by will, all others by necessity.
• We ought to believe that the bread and wine which Christ gave the disciples at the supper to eat and drink were converted there into the true body and true blood of Christ, when before it was true bread and true wine. Nor is it to be wondered at, as Augustine says: if he bore himself immortal in mortal hands, since in the transfiguration he who was then and afterwards mortal showed himself to Peter and James and John in the glory of immortality and impassibility.
**“Take ye, and eat: this is my body”** — After the old Passover was celebrated, the Lord gave his body and blood to the disciples, to show that the sacraments of the Old Testament were to cease.
**“Moreover”** — It is usually asked, if there is no substantial conversion there, as some hold, but this is said to pass or be converted into that by a figure of speech, namely that it is received under those accidents under which the substance of bread or wine was, what has become of the substance itself of the bread or wine? To this they answer: either it is resolved into the pre-existing matter, or reduced to nothing, which he can do there also who created all things from nothing.
**“It is asked also”** — If some water is not added through forgetfulness or negligence, is it void? Since this is not certain to us from authority, we say what seems to us, without asserting it. If it is omitted not with the intention of introducing heresy but by forgetfulness, it is no less effected, but yet it is to be severely punished. Nor do the Greeks add water.
**“which shall be delivered for you: this do”** — what I said, that is, take and eat my body, so that as I went before, so you may follow.
**“for the commemoration of me.”** — that is, in memory of my passion and death.
11.25:
**“In like manner also the chalice,”** — for our salvation and exhortation.
**“after he had supped”** — the old Passover now finished.
**“saying: This chalice is the new testament in my blood,”** — as if: this chalice is my blood, by whose being poured out the New Testament is confirmed, because a testament is confirmed over the dead; or it is a new promise, not of temporal but of eternal good.
**“this do ye, for the commemoration of me.”** — therefore you ought to take it in memory of the passion, because:
11.26:
**“For as often as you shall eat this bread, and drink the chalice, you shall shew the death of the Lord”** — you will represent it as made for you.
**“As often as”** — He explains: in which commemoration of Christ, that is, of his death.
**“until he come.”** — the Lord, to judgment.
**“Until he come”** — Because this will not be changed, like the sacraments of the Jews.
11.27:
**“Therefore”** — because it must be taken in remembrance of the death
**“whosoever shall eat this bread, or drink the chalice of the Lord unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and of the blood of the Lord.”** — he will pay the penalty for the death of Christ, or will contract a stain from the good thing taken amiss
**“unworthily”** — Augustine. In the fifth book, On the One Baptism: Because someone does not receive it unto salvation, it is not on that account less the body and blood which he has received.
*Augustine:* On John, Homily eight. Even holy things harm the wicked; therefore one must beware of receiving the good badly. And evils profit the good, as the angel of Satan did Paul.
**“unworthily, shall be guilty”** — Ambrose. He is unworthy who celebrates the mystery otherwise than as instituted by Christ. Guilty is he who makes his benefit void.
*Augustine:* On John, homily twenty-four. They are worthy if he repents of grave sins as much as venial ones displease him, even though through the frailty of the human condition he knows he will straightway return to them. No sin is venial when it pleases, however small, as if it were mortal; if it truly displeases, none is judged.
11.28:
**“prove”** — let him examine
**“But let a man prove himself”**
• If the sins are daily ones, or not deadly, and are forgiven the brother, let him who is about to approach the altar say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive,” etc. And let him approach securely, and eat of that bread and drink of the chalice. As if to say: see whether you forgive. For if you do not forgive, you lie, and you lie to one whom you do not deceive. You can lie to God, you cannot deceive him.
• Augustine. He receives unworthily who receives when he ought to be doing penance; therefore let him first judge himself and exercise himself in the truth of penance, that he may be judged by himself and not be judged by the Lord. For divine vengeance ceases if human confession goes before. It is asked whether the Eucharist is to be received daily, or whether days are to be chosen on which a man, living more purely and continently, may approach so great a sacrament more worthily. He answers this question rightly who advises that one remain above all in the peace of Christ, and that each do what he piously believes according to faith is to be done. For Zacheus and the centurion, when the one received Christ into his house rejoicing, and the other said: “Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof.”
• Both honoured the Saviour, though in a different and, as it were, contrary way. To this likeness also it applies that among the ancient people the manna tasted in the mouth of each of the pious according to his own will; so in the mouth of each Christian the body of Christ, received either daily or on certain days. For one, out of reverence, does not dare to receive it daily, and another, out of reverence, does not dare to omit it on any day. Contempt alone that food will not bear, as the manna would not bear loathing.
**“and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of the chalice.”** — one must approach devoutly, because it is the Lord, so that we may seem to render glory to the Redeemer
11.29:
**“For he that”** — for he who otherwise
**“eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment”** — damnation
**“to himself”** — not to you
**“eateth and drinketh,”** — a good man endures evil so that you may come to the rewards of the good; and Judas could associate with Peter, but could not defile him
**“eateth and drinketh judgment to himself”** — It is asked how this is so, since the Lord says: “He that eateth me, the same also shall live by me.” But there are two ways of eating: one sacramental, in which the good eat as well as the wicked; the other spiritual, in which only the good eat. And this is not only to eat Christ and to receive his body in the sacrament, but to abide in him and to have him abiding in oneself. For he eats spiritually who abides in the unity of the Church, which the sacrament itself signifies. For he who is at variance with Christ neither eats the flesh of Christ nor drinks his blood, even if he daily receives the sacrament of so great a thing to his judgment. Of which Augustine also says: Why do you prepare your tooth and your belly? Believe, and you have eaten.
**“not”** — because
**“discerning the body of the Lord.”** — he takes it indiscriminately and carelessly, as with other foods
11.30:
**“For this cause”** — because they receive unworthily
**“many among you”** — this is an image of the future judgment, so that from this they learn that sin goes not unpunished
**“Therefore are there many infirm and weak among you”** — This is done for the correction of others.
**“infirm”** — by fevers and other sicknesses
**“and weak”** — by long weakness
**“and many sleep.”** — they die
11.31:
**“But if”** — so these evils come from unworthy reception, but
**“if we would judge ourselves”** — by doing penance
**“we should not be judged.”** — we would be punished
11.32:
**“But whilst we are judged”** — but nor is judgment useless to others
**“whilst we are judged”** — For those who suffer, the punishment is sometimes also a purging, as for the prophet Abdo, who ate though forbidden, who while alive could be terrified or saddened over what he would not feel when dead. For it was said to him: “Thy dead body shall not be brought into the sepulchre of thy fathers.” And by this the disobedience of the prophet could be punished, lest his soul be snatched away to the punishment of Tartarus.
**“we are chastised by the Lord”** — according to others
**“we are chastised”** — The correction of all is in a few, because others are amended by fear of our punishment.
**“that we be not condemned with this world.”**
• with the lovers of the world
• he is like an unbeliever who approaches thoughtlessly
11.33:
**“Wherefore, my brethren,”** — lest a similar punishment befall you
**“When you come together”** — in likeness of the Lord’s supper
**“wait for one another”**
• fasting
• but
**“Wait for one another”** — Ambrose. That the offering of many may be celebrated together and served to all.
11.34:
**“If any man be hungry, let him eat at home”**
• let him take his own food, and not after the Eucharist
• let him feed on earthly food
**“that you come not together unto judgment. And the rest I will set in order, when I come”** — concerning the same; but you cannot be without these

12.1:
**“Now concerning spiritual things”** — about those; afterwards, but
**“Concerning spiritual things”** — Concerning the good things of the Holy Spirit, for the greater of which some were proud, while the lesser they envied and despaired of, as though they would never have them.
**“I would not have you ignorant, brethren”** — which truth has, that there be no schism among you but peace
12.2:
**“You know that”**
• about to say that all good things come from the Holy Spirit, he sets before them likenesses of the contrary
• as those who have experienced it
**“when you were heathens”**
• reason opposes that impiety
• Gloss of the Lombard: Ambrose. By these words the Apostle sharply rebukes those who attributed divine benefits to men, showing that no benefit is human, but a gift of God, when he says, “No man, speaking by the Spirit, saith Anathema to Jesus,” which voice is from human error, as is everything false; and “no man can say the Lord Jesus, but by the Holy Ghost,” from whom is all that is true. “For every truth, by whomsoever it is spoken, is from the Holy Spirit.”
**“You know that when you were heathens”** — About to hand down spiritual things, he recalls former ones, that as then there was the image of idols, so now of God. You know, as having experienced it, that when you were Gentiles, that is, living as Gentiles, you were going. “Going,” a word as of constant action, is thus known because through the individual gifts they gave glory to men rather than to God, not knowing that this was supplied by the Holy Spirit. “Except in all”: he shows that praise and grace belong to God, so that as then, with the image of the idol, all the evil was from man, so now all good things may be believed to be from the Spirit of God. Therefore, because you know that the evil spirit, drawing you back from the good, led you to so irrational an evil, that is, idolatry, by this I easily make known to you that by the Spirit of God one is kept from evil and good is done; and this is: no man speaking by the Spirit of God, in thinking, speaking, working. He says likewise in three ways, namely in heart, mouth and deed, any separation from Jesus, that is, any sin, which voice is from human error, as is everything false that exists. By the Spirit one is kept from evil. Or: he does not say anathema. To whom? To Jesus, so as to say that he is either not from God or less than God. And no one, however great he may be, says truly, that is, in thought, word and deed, “Jesus is Lord,” and I am his servant, except by the Holy Spirit, from whom is all that is true. To work well is by the Spirit. For Jesus is not called Lord by the flattery of men, as in the idols which are called gods by men though they are not. Therefore it is not the favour of men and a kindness that Jesus is called Lord, but a gift of God, who has made known his mystery to men. He who says this does not bestow a benefit on religion but receives one. And it is by the favour of men that idols are called gods though they are not; whence their priests also are subject to them. But here it is otherwise; whence they ought to be humbled, that they may suffer themselves to be rebuked, and not seek to be soothed by flatteries.
**“you went to dumb idols, according as you were led”** — by the evil spirit
**“going”** — you were
12.3:
**“saith”** — He says it properly who declares his will and mind by voice. Generally, however, there: “Not every one that saith to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven,” etc.
**“Anathema to Jesus”** — Then he who breaks himself off from the body of Christ does not have this from the Holy Spirit.
**“And no man can say the Lord Jesus”** — truly by word, that is, by thought and deed, Jesus is Lord
**“but by”** — that is, by
**“the Holy Ghost”** — as if: no one can avoid evil and do good except through him; but nevertheless
**“But by the Holy Ghost”** — As if: to work well and every good is through the Holy Spirit; and therefore then the greater should not despise the lesser, because he has nothing except from the Holy Spirit.
12.4:
**“Now there are diversities of graces”** — of the gifts of the Spirit
**“Now there are diversities”** — This is common to all, but the graces are divided so that the lesser may not despair, and the greater, hearing of the graces, may not be proud.
**“diversities”** — Just as he who says “the Lord Jesus” has it from grace, so in the offices of the Church grace is not divided among persons, but the work of the three persons is one, without distinction.
**“diversities of graces”** — He calls graces the very virtues given freely by God, such as faith and hope and the like, of which the effects are, as to neighbours, ministration, and as to oneself, operation; which is what he says: the Spirit, the Lord, God. The same substance is understood entirely, but a Trinity in persons. “But the same God who.” He says this lest the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit seem to work in some separate way, from the fact that he had assigned graces to the Spirit, ministrations to the Lord, and operations to God; referring all things to one God, he adds: because God, namely, worketh all.
**“but the same Spirit”** — giver, equally, as far as he himself is concerned, kind to all
12.5:
**“And there are diversities of ministries”** — by which some serve others
**“but the same Lord”**
• giving to each at his own will
• Son
12.6:
**“And there are diversities of operations”** — greater works, namely, and lesser
**“but the same”** — giver
**“but God”** — Father
**“who worketh all”** — necessary
**“All in all”** — He gives all things not to one, but works all things in all, so that what each does not have in himself, he may have in another; and so charity and humility remain.
**“in all”** — If you love unity, whoever has something in it has it for you. The eye alone sees, but not for itself alone; this charity is a gift of the Spirit, which surpasses all things, as he will say afterwards.
12.7:
**“And the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man”** — that is, grace through which it is made plain that the Spirit is in him
**“To every man”** — The goods are divided, and are given not singly to the merit of anyone, but for the profit of building up the Church.
**“unto profit”**
• of the Church
• because even the lesser profits
12.8:
**“To one indeed”** — by parts he defines what he had said
**“by the Spirit, is given”** — not through merit
**“the word of wisdom: and to another, the word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit”** — not only wisdom, that is, understanding of divine things, and knowledge of human things, but also the speech of these, so that they can express them to others
**“Of wisdom, of knowledge”** — Wisdom is in the contemplation of eternal things, knowledge in the action of temporal things. Whence in Job: “Behold, piety,” that is, the worship of God, “is wisdom,” which in Greek is “theosebia.” And what is his worship but love and knowledge of him? To abstain from evils, moreover, is knowledge, and evils are in temporal things, among which one must move with caution and prudence. He to whom wisdom is given is as the sun; he to whom knowledge, the moon in the night of the world; those to whom the rest are given are stars, because these also are necessary in the night. Whence: “The moon and the stars to rule the night.”
12.9:
**“to another, faith in the same spirit”**
• steadfastness of faith, or speech
• To another, faith. Faith too is among the gifts and bounties of God. Therefore not charity alone, but charity with faith, is given us by God.
**“to another, the grace of healing”** — healing the sick
**“in one Spirit”** — the same for all
12.10:
**“to another, the working of miracles”** — of miracles against nature
**“to another, prophecy”** — to foretell future things
**“to another, the discerning of spirits”** — so that he discerns what he hears, by which spirit it is said, good or evil, because the devil also speaks good things deceitfully
**“to another, diverse kinds of tongues”** — that is, to speak in diverse tongues
**“to another, interpretation of speeches”** — of tongues or of visions, as with Joseph
**“Of speeches”** — Or the words are, allegorically, the declarations found in the prophets and the gospels.
12.11:
**“But all these things”**
• that is, even if not diverse
• See that the Apostle says here that the Holy Spirit gives the gifts. Elsewhere he says that he was given. Christ also said: “Receive ye the Holy Ghost.” Whence, when they hear the Holy Spirit called the gift of God, let them recognize that kind of speech which the Apostle uses. In the stripping off of the body of the flesh there is nothing other than the flesh itself; so the gift of the Holy Spirit is nothing other than the Holy Spirit.
*Augustine:* So far is it a gift of God, insofar as it is given to those to whom it is given. But God is with himself, even if it is given to no one. For when it is given by his will, he himself, the same, gives it and works all things, dividing to each as he wills.
**“worketh”** — in substance
**“and the same”** — unchanging
**“one and the same Spirit”** — Augustine. What he said above, that the Spirit works these things, is said because what the one works, the three work, being of one nature. One and the same, lest they be thought as many as the works; not that the Spirit works without the Father and the Son. For the operation of the Trinity is inseparable.
**“dividing”**
• not himself divided
• as he who is God
**“to every one according as he will”** — therefore he gives diverse things to diverse persons because
**“Dividing to every one”** — Whence let not this one grieve, nor that one be proud. As he wills, who alone knows what is fitting, and freely, not for the merit of men.
12.12:
**“For as the body is one”** — by the joining of the members
**“and hath many members”** — diverse
**“and all the members of the body”** — although
**“many members, is one”** — yet
**“body, are”** — ministering
**“So that”** — and all the faithful are
**“so also is Christ”**
• not to say the body of Christ, because Christ himself, the lesser as well as the greater, are
• One Spirit will do all things in the members of the body of Christ, as one soul sees in the eye, hears in the ear, and does all things in all the rest.
**“So also is Christ”** — Christ is called head and body, on account of the ineffable unity of the head and the members.
12.13:
**“For”**
• because
• He shows how the body of Christ is one: because all, washed in one Spirit, were led into this, that afterwards we might be one body, of one mind through that one Spirit, so that the whole body is quickened by one soul. And because we have all been made to drink, in the receiving of the various gifts of the Holy Spirit, in one Spirit, because he directs all the gifts to the making of one; the person of no one is to be despised or preferred, nor the glory of God given to men, because it is one and the same in all.
**“in one Spirit”** — in the Holy Spirit
**“were we all baptized into one body”** — led
**“were baptized”** — we were baptized, washed
**“whether Jews”** — or: Jew
**“whether Gentiles”**
• or: Gentile
• differing in nation
**“whether bond”** — or: servant
**“whether free”** — or: free
**“and in one Spirit we have all been made to drink”** — and we were all made to drink in one Spirit, in the receiving of diverse gifts
12.14:
**“For”** — indeed all are one
**“the body also”** — to which the Church is similar
**“For the body also”** — Ambrose. He shows by the likeness of the human body that the unity of the body of Christ, that is, of the Church, has a variety of offices, and that this diversity does not take away unity, just as the unity of the human body does not consist in singleness but in many members, that they may render one another what they owe.
**“is not one member”**
• so also in the Church
• not all of one office and gift
**“but many”** — because the same Spirit gives all things
12.15:
**“If the foot should say”** — someone to whom a lower gift is given
**“because I am not the hand”** — as worthy as he to whom the working of powers is given
**“I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body?”** — as if because he is not of the first, he is therefore not necessary
12.16:
**“And”** — similarly
**“if the ear should say”** — one who has knowledge
**“because I am not the eye”** — as one who has the word of knowledge or wisdom
**“I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body?”** — is surely still, because if that is not, another can be
12.17:
**“If the whole body were the eye, where would be the hearing?”**

• of things to come

Whence: “You have the key of knowledge, but you enter not in yourselves, and those that were entering in you have hindered.” The wicked also have these things, and they will confess in the judgment, where they will not dare to lie, and it will be said to them not, “You had not,” but “I know you not,” because they had them without charity.

By this garment the cold is driven off by which Peter was chilled, warming himself at the fire of Caiphas. This alone divides between the sons of the kingdom and of perdition. Other gifts also are given through the Spirit, but without charity they profit nothing; whence the Lord says: “For he that hath, to him shall be given: and he that hath not, that also which he hath shall be taken away from him.” They have indeed the grace of possessing the Christian name, but they do not have the charity of using it, and therefore what he hath shall be taken away from him.
13.3:

**“poor”** — not of the rich who might repay

And therefore to give a cup of cold water is as much as it was for Zacheus to give half of his goods. By charity the disciples of Christ are known, not by prophecy, faith, and the other things which those also have who are not disciples.

13.9:

13.10:
**“But when that which is perfect is come”** — but all that is in part will be destroyed: that is, When that which is perfect is come, etc.
**“Shall be done away, that which”** — It is the destruction of imperfection when what is imperfect is fulfilled in the true. Here it is objected by some that by the same reasoning charity ought to be said to be done away, because now it is in part by comparison with the future state. To which some say that it is not knowledge itself, that is, the gift of knowledge, that is done away, but its manner, because now we know in a riddle and in shadow and obscurely, but then by sight, that is, most clearly. But to this too, they say, all now love imperfectly, but then most perfectly; therefore the manner of loving will be done away. So then charity can be said to be done away like knowledge. To which they answer: it is true that of charity as of knowledge all imperfection will be taken away. But as there are two things to be loved, God and neighbour, so also there are two principal manners, namely God for his own sake and neighbour for God’s sake. These manners will not be done away in the future, but the manner of imperfection will be taken away. Others say: not only the manner of knowledge, but also the act, or the very knowledge which now is, will be done away in the future. Of the act and use of knowledge itself it is probable that it will be done away, but the knowledge itself, not so; for it is from God. For knowledge is itself a quality of the mind, whose act is that very vision by which we now see, from which we shall be led to another. Whence: “We know, that, when he shall appear, we shall be like to him.”

14.1:
**“Follow after”** — therefore
**“charity”** — with all desire
**“be zealous for spiritual gifts; but rather that you may prophesy”** — desire also the other gifts of the Spirit, such as tongues and others, but after charity, prophecy rather than tongues
14.2:
**“For he that speaketh in a tongue”**
• unknown and foreign
• When the one speaking in a tongue did not understand himself, as if someone knew the pronunciation of some language but not its meaning.
*Augustine:* Or so that tongue be taken otherwise, and a distinction be made between spirit and mind; for since in the tongue, in that member which we move in the mouth when we speak, signs of things are given, not the things themselves brought forth, therefore by a transferred word he here calls tongue the utterance in which there are significations, like images of things, which, in order to be understood, need the mind, that is, the understanding of the mind. But while they are not understood they are said to be in the spirit, not in the mind. For mind here is taken as the higher power of the soul, spirit as the lower power of the same soul, on which the images of things are impressed. Tongue, however, is any utterance of signs; therefore when understanding comes, which belongs to the mind, there comes either revelation, or knowledge, or prophecy, or doctrine. It must be known that one speaking with a tongue sometimes did not understand; sometimes he understood but could not explain to others, though perhaps another interpreted; sometimes he both saw and understood and interpreted. As for example Pharao saw in spirit seven ears of corn and seven kine, and their utterance was as a tongue, but he did not understand what they signified, and therefore was not a prophet. Hence one to whom likenesses of things were shown in the spirit, if he did not understand, was not yet a prophet. And he is rather to be called a prophet who interprets what another sees, as Joseph rather than Pharao. Pharao saw in spirit, Joseph by mind. His spirit was formed to see the images, this man’s mind enlightened to understand the truth. Therefore in the former was tongue, in the latter prophecy, because in the former was the imagining of things, in the latter the interpretation of the imagining. He is therefore less a prophet who sees the images of the things signified by the spirit alone; more a prophet who is endowed with the understanding of them alone; but most of all he who excels in both, as Daniel, who both told the king’s dream which he had seen and opened what it signified.
**“speaketh not unto men”**
• to the understanding of men
• some signs without understanding
**“but unto God”**
• to God, whose praises he speaks
• not to men
**“for no man”** — no one who is a man, that is, carnal
**“heareth”** — understands
**“Yet by the Spirit he speaketh”**
• not himself
• not the mind, but the lower power of the soul
**“mysteries”** — concerning God, secret things
14.3:
**“For”** — concerning this one I say that not to men; for he who prophesies
**“he that prophesieth”**
• by understanding with the mind and by opening up through interpretation
• expounds the Scriptures, which are hidden from many
**“speaketh to men unto edification”** — of beginners
**“and exhortation”** — of the advanced
**“and comfort”** — of the desolate
14.4:
**“But he who”** — likewise, for this reason
**“speaketh in a tongue”** — because it is by the spirit
**“himself”** — so that he is edified more

**“but he that prophesieth”** — that is, to speak with the mind
**“edifieth the church”** — so far as concerns himself
14.5:
**“And I would have you”** — although I thus put prophecy before the tongue, nevertheless
**“all to speak with tongues”** — that it is a gift of God, and therefore I will not forbid it
**“but rather to prophesy”** — because it profits more
**“For greater is”** — more worthy
**“he that prophesieth”** — explains
**“than he that speaketh with tongues: unless perhaps”** — which rarely
**“he interpret”** — is able to explain what he says
14.6:
**“But now”** — when the faithful
**“brethren”** — But now, brethren. I have said that he who prophesieth is greater than he that speaketh with tongues. But in myself you can see that the tongue does not profit, prophecy does. Now, when the faithful are concerned, what then when the unbelievers?
**“if I come to you speaking with tongues, what shall I profit you”** — nothing
**“unless I speak to you”** — unless by signs, that is, unless understanding is added to the tongue, so that it is done not by the spirit only but also by the mind
**“either in revelation”** — by sudden showing
**“Either in revelation”** — Or in revelation. That I may explain revelation. Revelation is when certain mysteries are shown through figures, as in the Apocalypse.
**“or in knowledge”** — Or in knowledge. That I may explain the things that pertain to knowing. These are the things that illuminate faith, such as the nature of the Godhead.
**“or in prophecy”** — Or in prophecy. That I may explain the Scriptures that deal with future things.
**“or in doctrine”** — Or in doctrine. That I may explain the Scriptures that form morals.
**“or in doctrine?”** — Or revelation is the sudden showing of certain things through the Spirit; whence afterwards: “If any thing be revealed to another sitting.” Prophecy is as with Isaias or the rest, which the Holy Spirit reveals little by little without human effort. Knowledge is of those things which one has learned by his own study. Doctrine is of those things learned from another’s teaching.
14.7:
**“Even”** — although you so desire tongues; yet

**“whether pipe or harp, except they give a distinction of sounds”** — distinct and intelligible sounds
**“how shall it be known”** — that is, who will be able to judge the modes or harmonies of the song
**“what is piped or harped”** — pipe
14.8:
**“For”** — another likeness
**“an uncertain sound”** — truly it will not be known of these, since not even from the trumpet

**“who shall prepare himself to the battle?”** — who will prepare himself for battle? It will not be known; the outcome shows it, because no one prepares himself.
14.9:
**“So likewise you”** — speaking
**“except you utter by the tongue plain speech”**
• by the tongue, unless plain speech, by interpretation
• of whatever signs, or unknown
**“you utter”** — who ought to exhort against the demons to war
**“how”** — as if: in no way
**“shall it be known”**
• it will be understood
• by you
**“what is said? For you shall be”** — it will not be known
**“speaking into the air”** — not to the hearts of men
14.10:
**“There are, for example, so many”** — as if uselessly
**“so many kinds of tongues in this world”** — there are many

Because “so many kinds of tongues,” the meaning of this saying is as much as if you spoke in all tongues, which no one would ever understand, and of all things in each tongue, because there is nothing without its voice in each tongue. Or: so many as there are kinds of tongues; in this they are many, because you speak in all tongues and of all things.
**“There are in this world”** — in the whole
**“world; and none is without voice”** — understanding
**“and none is without voice”** — There are many tongues, but they have their own meanings; they are uttered so that they may be understood.
14.11:
**“If then I know not the power of the voice”** — the interpretation of the meaning of the voice which I utter
**“If then I know not”** — And because others without an interpreter would not understand, therefore I shall be a barbarian.
**“I shall be to him to whom I speak”** — to him to whom I must teach
**“a barbarian”** — not understanding
**“and he that speaketh”**
• teaches

**“a barbarian to me”**

14.12:
**“So you also”**

**“but my understanding is without fruit”** — the understanding of those things that I say

14.15:
**“What is it then?”** — is useful

**“I will pray also with the understanding”** — understanding of the mind
**“I will sing with the spirit”** — the melody of the song, which is less

14.16:
**“Else”** — but otherwise
**“if thou shalt bless”** — you say some good things
**“with the spirit”** — tongue given through the Spirit
**“how shall he that holdeth the place”** — as if: no one, not even a wise man, because he does not understand
**“of the unlearned”** — unlettered and rude
**“how shall he say”** — as if: in no way. BECAUSE HE DOES NOT KNOW WHAT YOU SAY
**“Amen”** — Augustine. Note that this word “amen” is neither Greek nor Latin, but Hebrew, and is interpreted “true.” And though it could be said, “true” is not said but “amen.” Yet neither Greek nor Latin translator dared to render it, lest it become cheap if laid bare, but that it might have honour from the veil of secrecy.
**“to thy blessing”**
• here is the place of the unlearned
• also very attentive so that he may understand
**“because he knoweth not what thou sayest”** — Therefore I say, at your blessing; or I note this, that the unlearned has no place. For I do not note this or accuse you that you do this; he says this so that he would not seem to find fault with the gift of the Spirit.
14.17: **“For thou indeed givest thanks well”** — in the tongue
14.18:
**“I thank my God”**
• as if I did not blame you for what I do not have in myself
• He sets himself forward as an example that they ought not to speak in tongues except for edification, as he himself does, who knows them all.
**“I give thanks”** — Lest he seem to speak as a rival through envy, belittling in others what he does not have in himself, he shows that he speaks in the tongues of all of them, saying: I THANK.
**“I speak with all your tongues”** — with which any one of you speaks
14.19:
**“But in the church”** — to which I ought to be useful
