He is the end, which he briefly concluded above, and afterwards sets forth member by member. All, so that none of those united to him may love his own will against him, and then it may be manifest what is said: “What hast thou that thou hast not received?” All, because God will be that whereby they are satisfied. All things that are honestly desired: life, health, glory, peace, the end of desires. In unequal brightness there will be equal joy, because it is of one thing, so that what each will have will be common to all, because the glory of the head also will be of all through the bond of charity.
**“that God may be all”** — One with the Father and the Holy Spirit. All things. That can be desired in all his members, because he who gave the virtue will himself be the reward of virtue, since God will be that by which they are satisfied.
15.29:
*Otherwise:* the dead will rise.
*Otherwise:* if there is no future resurrection of the dead.
**“what shall they do”** — they.
**“that are baptized for the dead”** — That is, for the removal of sins. Or for those who are made dead to themselves after the likeness of Christ’s death: what will they do, since they are not going to have life?
**“if the dead rise not again at all?”**
• it does not prove their practice, but shows a firm faith in the resurrection.
• Or there were certain unlearned men who were baptized for those who had departed from this life without baptism, thinking it profited them. Whence he says: What shall they do? That is, what will it profit those who are not to rise again? Even if they do not rise at all, why is one baptized, since sins are not remitted except for the sake of the future resurrection? As if to say: if fools are so certain of the resurrection, you ought not to doubt.
**“if the dead rise not again at all”** — As if Christ had not risen: why are they baptized, when they are not forgiven, if Christ has not risen?
**“I protest by your glory”** — To swear truly is not a sin, but one is not therefore to swear in doubtful matters, and it is safer not to swear than to perjure oneself by the habit of swearing. But to swear falsely is a most grave sin. An oath is not against the precept when it is not from the evil of the one swearing but of the unbelieving or weak man, who otherwise does not believe.
**“why are they then baptized for them?”** — as if they, that is, the dead
15.30:
**“Why also are we”**
• distinguishes from what was said before
• who seem to be wise
**“in danger every hour?”** — we suffer dangers
15.31:
**“I die daily”** — I not only suffer dangers but
**“I die”** — I undergo the dangers of death
**“by your glory”**
• that you may attain glory
• or I swear by your glory
**“brethren, which I have”** — now in hope
**“in Christ Jesus our Lord”** — that is, while I consider that he himself was glorified through the passion; or as not human but eternal
15.32:
**“If (according to man) I fought with beasts at Ephesus”** — against those who are wise in a bestial way
**“what doth it profit me, if the dead rise not again?”**
• They rise: this alone remains
• again, if not
• What doth it profit me, if I fought, that is, disputed. According to man. That is, acting reasonably, because it is man’s part to believe that man does not die as a beast does.
**“Let us eat and drink”**
• this is from Isaias, and is the voice of the Jews despairing in captivity
• This is on account of those who, as if nothing were to be after death, care only for the belly like cattle, saying: who has come from there? I have not heard the voice of anyone coming from there. To whom it is said: fool, if your father rose, would you believe? The Lord of all has risen, and you do not believe? He who willed to die and rise, that we might all believe one, lest we be deceived by many. You would believe a father about to die again, and you do not believe him now immortal, who finally has testimony in heaven, testimony on earth, testimony from the angels, testimony from the dead below.
**“tomorrow”** — in the near future
15.33:
**“Be not seduced: Evil communications corrupt good manners.”** — on account of all these things: do not be seduced by false teachers, nor converse with them, because their conversations kill virtues while they make men not hope for the resurrection
**“Be not seduced”** — From the false teachers, who seek a wound in the medicine and try to twist a bond out of the Scriptures, whence they cast the snare of death.
15.34:
**“Awake, ye just”** — against them
**“Awake”** — These things, do not. But awake from the body and so you will be just; and afterwards: Do not sin, by consenting to them, because they are ignorant of God.
**“and sin not”** — which the justice of God requires
**“For some have not the knowledge of God”** — who, namely, said it was foolish to believe that the dead would rise
**“I speak it to your shame”**
• let it shame the ignorant to believe
• and this
• that you should be ashamed to agree with them
• or shame
• that is, profit
15.35:
**“But some man will say”**
• not knowing God
• Thus far he has proved by reasons; now he shows that it can be done by the very nature of things. As if to say: it is proved by these. But yet he says, as though it could not happen by nature: And with what body shall they rise? As if to say: it cannot be other than now, that is, passible and mortal. Foolish man, who do not attend to what you see daily.
**“How do the dead rise again”** — how can it be
**“the dead”** — who is now ashes
**“or with what manner of body shall they come”** — proof of how they will rise again
**“With what manner of body”** — Whence, because such a man here rejects faith in the resurrection through knowledge of natural things, and seems wise to himself when he is not, the Apostle fittingly answers him: Senseless man, etc.
15.36:
**“Senseless man, that which thou sowest”** — who do not consider that the grain
**“is not quickened”**
• is quickened
• That which thou sowest is not quickened, etc. So the dead can live with a better body, so that what you sow rises better.
**“except it die first”** — rots
15.37:
**“And that which thou sowest”** — proof with what body
**“thou sowest not the body”** — he does not deny the substance, but the fitting quality, when it grows up
**“which”** — what kind of
**“that shall be”** — the same in substance, different in quality
**“but bare grain, as of wheat”** — grain
**“or of some of the rest”** — of seeds
15.38:
**“But God giveth it”** — to the grain
**“But God giveth”** — As therefore the bare grain is sown and by God’s will rises somehow clothed, having many increments with it, so the dead by God’s power can live and rise with a better body.
**“a body as he will”** — with chaff and ear
**“and to every seed its proper body”**
• as wheat, of wheat
• not the same body for all grains
**“to every seed its proper body”** — So also for us, our own ancient body, as Job says: “Whom I myself shall see, and not another.” But there will be difference in glory and dignity, although from the same matter. As not all flesh is of the same dignity, although from the same elements.
15.39: **“All flesh is not the same flesh”** — of the same dignity
15.40:
**“And there are bodies”** — Every flesh is a body, but not conversely, as wood.
**“celestial”**
• is no longer called ‘flesh’
• Those of the risen that are earthly before they die come from Adam; as Christ is heavenly, so from him the bodies are called heavenly and are no longer called flesh. But from Adam, because he is earthly, the bodies are earthly.
**“and”** — are
**“bodies terrestrial: but, one is the glory of the celestial, and another of the terrestrial”** — not only do the earthly differ among themselves but also from the heavenly
15.41:
**“One is the glory of the sun”**
• the heavenly themselves also differ among themselves
• One is the glory of the sun, etc. As these bodies, though of one nature, are yet diverse in brightness, so also men, though of one kind, will be of unlike glory in the resurrection. So that the dignity of those who have the hundredfold will be equal to the brightness of the sun; to the brightness of the moon, those of the sixtyfold; and to the stars, those who sought the thirtyfold. But the resurrection of the faithless is like the dark stars and the last of all. For unbelief cannot have a bright resurrection, because as a coal covered with its ash is darkened, so these, surrounded by faithlessness and the darkness of error, will lack light.
• Since they are of unequal brightness, God is all in all, as because ‘God is charity,’ and through charity it will come about that what each has is common to all.
**“another the glory of the moon”** — although of one nature they are of diverse brightness, so men in the resurrection
**“and another the glory of the stars. For star differeth from star in glory”** — they differ from those too, since also among themselves
**“For star differeth from star”** — Augustine. “In my Father’s house there are many mansions,” although the same denarius, that is eternal life, is for all. For there is one blessedness which the just receive, and an unequal quality of reward.
15.42:
**“So also is the resurrection of the dead”** — so the dead shall rise with a different body
**“It is sown in corruption”**
• but this all share in common: that they will rise incorrupt; but
• is buried or mortified
• Is sown. That is, although man, from the time he is conceived until dissolution, is in corruption, yet he shall rise in incorruption.
**“it shall rise in incorruption”** — that is, immortal and impassible
15.43:
**“It is sown”** — dies and is buried
**“in dishonour”** — without any honour
**“it shall rise in glory”** — glorious
**“It is sown in weakness”**
• immovable, unruled, because it is not able to move or rule itself
• because such a body is one which anything may harm
**“it shall rise in power”** — powerful, to which nothing can do harm
15.44:
**“It is sown”** — truly living and vigorous
**“body”** — what, through its parts
**“natural”** — that is sustained by food
**“a natural body”** — That is, it has nothing from the soul, except that it is given sense by it, as the animals are. It shall rise a spiritual body, passing into the nature of spirit, because agile, light, not needing food. When he said that the body would pass to incorruption, he makes mention of corruption, that the greater dignity of the resurrection may be shown.
**“it shall rise a spiritual body”**
• that no longer needs these
• He does not say “spirit,” as though the body were turned into spirit, as some think. Whence the Lord: “Handle, and see: for a spirit hath not flesh and bones.” But “spiritual,” because it will be fully subject to the spirit, will no longer resist, nor will it need food, as man needed it before sin.
**“If there be a natural body, there is also a spiritual body”** — if indeed it is animal, it is also spiritual. That it is animal he proves from Genesis, where the first man was made a living soul; the last is spiritual.
**“If there be a natural body”** — Truly a spiritual body shall rise, because if it is now natural, it is, that is, it is agreed that it will one day be spiritual. For as we are natural, because our father was made carnal into a living soul, so we shall be spiritual in the resurrection, because our spiritual father was made in his resurrection into a quickening spirit. Which he explains thus: As it is written, in Genesis, that we are natural, begotten of a natural father. Into a living soul, that is, able to live only by means of sustenance. Not quickening; Christ into a quickening spirit, that is, one who would so quicken the body that it would need no further sustenance, nor be dissoluble, nor be as the natural body, as though by relatives. When it is said “body,” “natural” is added in vain, unless there is another, spiritual, in contrast to which it is called natural.
**“as”** — or as
**“as it is written”** — here he explains what an animal body is
15.45:
**“The first man Adam was made into a living soul”** — that is, able to live; that is, giving life to the body through the sustenance of food, yet quickening the body
**“The first man”** — The whole human race is two men: the first and the second. Born of the one, reborn of the other. Christ is called Adam because of the same matter. Last, because after him no other man succeeds who is the head or author of the human body.
**“the last Adam”** — the Apostle adds this
**“into a quickening spirit”** — here, what is spiritual
**“quickening”** — who takes away corruption
15.46:
**“Yet that was not first which is spiritual”** — in Christ, each one who has experienced this should expect the same for himself
**“Yet that was not first”** — He said that our bodies will be spiritual. But lest anyone doubt whether the natural can become spiritual, he proves it by the likeness of Christ. As if to say: he was made into a quickening spirit. But what is spiritual was not first in him, but what is natural, then the spiritual. So it can also come about with us.
15.47:
**“The first man”** — The first into a living soul, because of the earth and therefore earthly, that is, natural and passible by nature. The second spiritual because from heaven, that is, because the divine nature was united to the human, and therefore heavenly, that is, spiritual in the resurrection. And because the first father was earthly, all are such.
**“Celestial”** — Conceived and born not by human custom but by divine will.
15.48:
**“As is the earthly, such also are the earthly”** — that is, animal
**“and such as is the heavenly, such also are they that are heavenly”** — that is, spiritual
15.49:
**“Therefore”** — that we may be heavenly
**“as we have borne the image of the earthly”** — as by the example of Adam we have loved earthly things
**“let us bear”**
• that is, we should wholly subject ourselves to him
• after baptism
**“and the image of the heavenly”** — that is, obedience; but if we do not bear it, we shall not be heavenly; and this is: Now this
15.50:
**“Now this I say”** — The Jews believed in a future resurrection, but in the manner of this life, so that they married and begot children. Whence they could not answer the Sadducees, which the Apostle removes.
**“that flesh and blood”** — By flesh and blood he signifies “the belly” and “lust,” that is, the works of the flesh, which will not be there.
**“cannot possess the kingdom of God”** — that is, given over to vices, which arise from flesh and blood
**“nor”** — because
**“corruption”** — which is the effect of flesh and blood
**“neither shall corruption”** — Flesh. But lest you think this is said according to the substance of the flesh, he made it plain. Therefore I said: flesh shall not possess the kingdom of God, because of the corruption of mortality, which is signified by the name of flesh. And as if he said: how will it be flesh and not be flesh? He explains: Behold, I tell you a mystery.
**“possess incorruption”** — itself immortal
15.51:
**“Behold, a mystery”**
• which is hidden from many
• Because he said that they will rise to glory, and afterwards: flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God, he explains how this is to be distinguished.
**“I tell you”** — that is, this
**“we shall all indeed”** — both good and bad alike
**“rise again”** — because even those found living will die when Christ comes
**“We shall all indeed rise again”** — Or, according to Jerome, who assert that those found living will not die, writing to Marcella: All the dead will rise, but not all the living found will be changed, only the saints.
*Jerome:* To Marcella. You had asked what the Apostle says, that at the coming of the Lord the Saviour some living are caught up to meet him in the clouds, so that they are not prevented by those who have slept in Christ. And you wish to know whether they meet him in their bodies in such a way that they do not die first, since our Lord also died, and Enoch and Elias, according to the Apocalypse of John, are said to be about to die, that is, that there be no one who has not tasted death. This can be known from the very context of the place: that the saints who at the coming of the Lord the Saviour are found in the body meet him in those same bodies, yet so that the corrupt and mortal is changed into glory, and into incorruption and immortality, so that the bodies of the living also are transformed into the same substance as the bodies that are to rise. Whence the Apostle says in another place: “Because we would not be unclothed, but clothed over, that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life,” that is, that the body be not abandoned by the soul, but that, the soul dwelling in the body, what was before inglorious may become glorious. Concerning Enoch or Elias, who the Apocalypse reports will come and will die, this is not the time for dispute, since that whole book is either to be understood spiritually (as we think) or, if we follow a carnal interpretation, we must acquiesce in Jewish fables, that Jerusalem be built again and victims offered in the temple, and, spiritual worship being diminished, carnal ceremonies prevail.
**“but we shall not all be changed”** — into immortality
15.52:
**“In a moment”** — in the very briefest, smallest and narrowest span of time
**“in the twinkling of an eye”** — so that the resurrection may be more wonderful
**“In the twinkling of an eye”**
• Because in a moment there is delay. He adds: in the twinkling of an eye, that is, as quickly as the eye strikes at what it sees or the eyelid is struck, that is, with the greatest speed.
• That is, as quickly as the ray of the eye passes to distant things and flies over the middle ones; and though there is a before and after there, the whole is nevertheless done as though it were alike.
**“at the last trumpet”**
• and this by the trumpet, that is, by a great and clear voice, after which there will be no other
• At the last trumpet, that is, at the last sign that will be given that these things may be fulfilled. This trumpet is a cry, whence it is said: “At midnight there was a cry made: Behold the bridegroom cometh.” By the name of trumpet is meant some evident and illustrious sign, which is elsewhere called the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God. And in the Gospel: “The voice which the dead that are in the graves shall hear, and shall come forth,” etc.
**“for the trumpet shall sound”** — or there will be a sound
**“and the dead”** — sinners or all
**“shall rise again incorruptible”** — without loss of limbs
**“and we shall be changed”** — the good into the glory of immortality and impassibility
**“We shall be changed”** — He explains how this happens, or what the change is. For this corruptible must. According to this the flesh is said not to possess the kingdom of God, because there will be no corruption and mortality there, that is, not according to these qualities, but the same substance. For in saying “this” he, as it were, points with a finger to the same flesh, that the same flesh which seems to be about to rise may be shown: For this corruptible must put on incorruption. And this not only for a time, which he shows there: And this mortal must put on immortality.
15.53:
**“For this corruptible must”** — we shall be changed; because it is fitting, for that we served well, or because promised
**“put on this”** — as an ornament
**“incorruption”** — so that it no longer hungers or is in any way harmed
**“and this mortal”** — that is, this body which is shown
**“must put on immortality”** — so that it no longer dies or is dissolved
15.54:
**“And when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption and this mortal shall have put on immortality”** — truly it will put on immortality, because then it will be done, that is, fulfilled, and never otherwise would it be fulfilled
**“then shall come to pass the saying”** — lest anyone think it said of the inner death, which has already happened
**“that is written”** — In Isaias. Or Osee thus: “O death, I will be thy death.”
**“Death is swallowed up”**
• eternally
• Is swallowed up, that is, destroyed in the victory of Christ. Or in this, that it exceeded the measure of conquering by attacking Christ. Or in this, that the servants of God conquer the lust of the flesh.
**“death”** — dissolution, or the devil, already partly swallowed up, will in the future be swallowed up more completely
**“in victory”** — in the resurrection of Christ
15.55:
**“O death, where is thy victory?”**
• the power by which you were dissolving all men for a time
• “Where is thy victory, O death?” Words of the prophet, or of the Apostle rejoicing and mocking death in the person of the risen, so that the resurrection may be more certain.
• You conquered in the dying; you are conquered in the risen. Or death is the delight of sin, which comes from the act of sinning.
**“O death, where is thy sting?”** — original sin, whence death comes, as he himself explains; not what death did. For by sin we die; we do not sin by death.
15.56:
**“Now the sting of death is sin”** — which pricks
**“and the power of sin is the law”**
• The increase: lest anyone say that anyone is helped by the law, but by God alone
• Because the law, by forbidding, increases the desire for sin, unless the Spirit pours out charity.
15.57:
**“But thanks be to God”** — I give
**“who hath given us the victory”** — of sin and death
**“through our Lord Jesus Christ”** — not through the law
15.58:
**“Therefore, my beloved brethren”** — because through Christ we conquer
**“be ye steadfast”** — in faith of the resurrection
**“and unmoveable”** — so that you cannot be moved by the false
**“always abounding in the work of the Lord”** — in hope of the resurrection
**“knowing”** — that is, having hope
**“that your labour is not in vain”** — without reward
**“in the Lord”** — in the word of the Lord

16.1:
**“Now concerning”** — I have admonished about other matters
**“Concerning the collections”** — Augustine. After other matters, he briefly admonishes about the collections to be made for the saints who were at Jerusalem. Which is not against that: “Be not solicitous for tomorrow.” For it is not being solicitous for tomorrow if one thinks of these things in the human way; it is so if one serves God for the sake of these things, so that in his works he looks not to the kingdom of God but to the acquiring of these things.
**“that are made for the saints, as I have given order”** — therefore it is to be held
**“in the churches of Galatia”** — for the use of the saints
**“so do ye also”**
• gather
• So do ye also, etc. The Apostle commands all the people to assemble at the Church on the Lord’s day, and to bring there what each wished to give for the work of the saints. And lest it perish through wicked ministers, if they left it with the Church, he commands them to carry it with them and lay it up in a safe place until he himself should come. And they did this on each Lord’s day, because what is gathered little by little is neither burdensome and is found to be much.
16.2:
**“On the first day of the week”**
• one day of the week
• Or, on one day of the sabbath, that is, on the Lord’s day. For one day of the sabbath, or one of the sabbaths, or the first of the sabbath, is called among the Jews the day we now call the Lord’s day.
**“every one of you”** — gather
**“put apart with himself”** — lest you say he is not a faithful steward whom you trust
**“laying up”** — and taking care lest he take it again for himself
**“what it shall well please him”**
• not that it may burden [you]
• therefore before
**“that when I come, the collections be not then to be made”** — because it would burden [you] if they gave it all at once, suddenly together
16.3:
**“And when I shall be with you”** — you judge worthy
**“by letters”** — that is, with my letters and your letters of praise and commendation, of those carrying and sending
**“them will I send to carry your grace”** — gift
16.4: **“And if it be meet”** — if the matters are great
16.5:
**“Now I will come to you, when I shall have passed through Macedonia”** — when I have passed through all places as far as Macedonia
**“For I shall pass through Macedonia”** — because where there is no need, one should not linger there
16.6:
**“And with you perhaps I shall abide, or even spend the winter”** — because many things there need correcting
**“I shall abide”** — As a physician stays where many are sick.
16.8: **“But I will tarry at Ephesus”** — hence he sent a letter
16.9:
**“For a great door is opened unto me”** — many hearts prepared to listen
**“great and evident”** — because they do not contradict the preaching
**“and many adversaries”**
• because
• who try to hinder
• as though: Why then is there need to stay there? He answers: adversaries, etc.
16.10:
**“Now if Timothy come”** — to you
**“see that he be with you without fear”** — Augustine. Perhaps he had already feared the disturbance caused by the strife of the false apostles.
16.11: **“Let no man therefore despise him, but conduct ye him on his way in peace: that he may come to me. For I look for him with the brethren”** — who are with him
16.12:
**“And touching our brother Apollo”** — who was their bishop, ordained by the Apostle
**“I give you to understand, that I much entreated him”** — because the Corinthians had asked for him, who, since he could not settle them, went to the apostle at Ephesus
**“to come unto you with the brethren: and indeed it was not his will at all to come at this time”** — because he fears the uncorrected
**“But he will come when he shall have leisure”**
• opportune
• when you have been corrected
16.13:
**“Watch ye”**
• but you
• against the cunning of the devil
**“stand fast in the faith”** — sleep does not creep upon the one standing
**“do manfully”** — It is the inconstancy of women.
**“and be strengthened”**
• in the Lord
• that there may be progress in your strength
16.14:
**“Let all your things”** — correction also
**“be done in charity”** — not for the sake of empty glory
16.15:
**“And I beseech you, brethren”**
• who
• I beseech you. The order of this text looks back and depends as far as there: “that you also be subject.”
**“you know the house of Stephanas, and of Fortunatus, and of Achaicus”** — These were with the apostle in the preaching to the Corinthians.
**“that they are the firstfruits of Achaia”** — They were the first to believe in Achaia.
**“and have dedicated themselves to the ministry of the saints”** — that they might minister to the saints.
16.17:
**“And I rejoice in the presence of Stephanas, and Fortunatus, and Achaicus”** — because they are present with you, from whom you have progress; or because they came to minister to me on your behalf what you ought to have done.
**“because that which was wanting on your part, they have supplied”** — They ministered to me what you did not do.
16.18:
**“For they have refreshed”**
• whom they fed
• The spirit: mine by joy, yours by charity.
**“both my spirit and yours”** — who preserved the apostle
**“Know them”** — Honour.
**“therefore, that are such”** — those
16.19:
**“The churches of Asia salute you”** — All desire what I write.
**“Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord”** — with whom I lodge
**“with the church that is in their house”** — that is, by the assembly of brothers
16.20:
**“All the brethren salute you. Salute one another with a holy kiss”**
• from a true heart
• as a sign of peace
16.21:
**“The salutation of me”** — so that they may know the letter is his. He adds: Salute, etc.
**“Paul, with my own hand”** — written
16.22:
**“If any man”** — I salute the faithful, but
**“love not our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema”**
• or condemned
• separated from God
**“maranatha”**
• until the Lord comes, or at the coming of the Lord
• Maranatha is composed of Greek and Syriac; in Latin it is interpreted 'the Lord comes.'
• Augustine. Maranatha: 'the Lord comes.' It is composed of Syriac and Greek.
• Maranatha, that is, until the Lord come, or at the coming of the Lord. For Maranatha is interpreted “the Lord cometh,” and is composed of Syriac and Greek. It is more Syriac than Hebrew. Anathema is interpreted “condemned” or “separated.” So he uses a word both Greek and Syriac together.
16.23:
**“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ”** — This is the salutation of Paul.
**“be with you”** — be.
16.24:
**“My charity”** — Love one another with that love by which you love God, or love God with that love by which I love you or God.
**“be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen”** — Not according to the love of the world.

1.1:
**“Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will”**
• not by usurpation
• Paul, an apostle, etc. He first sends ahead the greeting, as is usual. Then he gives thanks to God for the good things conferred through grace, speaking to the perfect; afterwards he invites them by his own example to endure suffering; then he rebukes the false apostles by putting them down, exposing their craftiness. And he commends himself in many ways. Finally a moral admonition is added, with a repeated blessing. Sending the greeting first, then, against the pride of the false apostles he calls himself Paul; and against presumption of heart he names himself Apostle, saying: Paul, etc.
**“of God”** — not of men
**“and Timothy our brother”** — who went with the First Epistle to the Corinthians and reported to the apostle all that was happening among them
**“to the church of God that is at Corinth, with”** — and
**“all the saints”**
• reborn by the grace of the Holy Spirit
• to the presbyters
**“that are in all Achaia”** — whose metropolis is Corinth
1.2:
**“Grace unto you”** — behold the greeting
**“and peace”** — tranquillity of mind
**“from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ.”** — without whom the Father gives nothing
1.3:
**“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,”** — although in himself his glory cannot be increased or diminished, he is exalted in his own, in whom he is said to be exalted through their knowledge and their progress
**“the Father of mercies,”** — to us who are sons of Christ
**“and the God of all comfort.”** — the consolation is no less than the tribulation
**“Blessed”** — First he speaks to the perfect about tribulation, setting himself forth as an example of patience and of consolation received from God, counting as praise what others count as disgrace. God: the creator of all things, the Father of Christ, through whom he is also our Father, the Father of mercies, in a father’s way giving forgiveness of sins and good works and constancy in tribulation; and God, the giver of all perfect comfort, as much as it befits God to give to those who suffer for Christ. That he is the God of comfort is plain from this, that he comforts.
1.4:
**“Who comforteth us”** — ministers
**“in all our tribulation;”** — of soul and body
**“that we also may be able”** — is comforted by God
**“also”** — desolate, that is, deprived of human help
**“to comfort”** — by the example of our consolation
**“them who are in all”** — that is, any
**“distress, by the exhortation”** — by such consolation as urges us toward greater things
**“wherewith we also are exhorted”**
• us
• By which we are exhorted, that is, which God gave for this purpose, not only that he might comfort us but that he might also exhort us; and so our consolation is also of use for exhorting others, so that we may truly be able to comfort.
**“by God.”** — that we may truly be able to comfort
1.5:
**“For as the sufferings of Christ abound”** — which are inflicted for Christ, that is, in the name of Christ, or which we suffer in likeness to Christ
**“in us”** — in us, who are their place
**“so”** — no less
**“so also by Christ doth our comfort abound.”** — since either here we are set free, or we understand the fatherly kindness in the scourges, because he scourges every son whom he receives
1.6:
**“Now whether we be in tribulation”** — but all this is for you
**“it is for your exhortation”**
• because by our example God warns you to suffer, whence eternal salvation is yours
• that you may be encouraged to greater things and may hope for salvation
**“For your exhortation and salvation”** — In bitter things salvation and a reward are promised.
**“or whether we be comforted”** — in the hope of reward
**“it is for your consolation”**
• that you may hope for the like
• because by our example God warns you to suffer under the hope of reward, so that you may bear it more lightly
**“or whether we be exhorted”** — to heavier things, or once the evils are ended, or by the power of patience given to us
**“and salvation,”** — for salvation, I say
**“which worketh the enduring”** — salvation works, that is, intends to work in you; that is, we intend that it work patience in you
**“of the same sufferings”** — as you ought, by our example, to suffer the same things which we also suffer
1.7:
**“That our hope”**
• is worked by God
• because we hope that you will suffer
**“for you may be steadfast,”**
• we suffer, I say
• for your benefit
**“knowing that as you are partakers of the sufferings, so shall you be”**
• because equal glory will be repaid to your labour
• in the future
**“also of the consolation.”** — eternal
1.8:
**“For we would not”** — explains the tribulations
**“have you ignorant, brethren,”**
• because it will profit you to know
• For we would not have you ignorant, etc. So that the Corinthians would not fail, suffering tribulations from unbelievers, the Apostle gives himself to them as an example, so that, as he himself, they may be strengthened in their tribulations.
**“of our tribulation”** — They falsely glory in their own glory; but we glory in tribulation
**“which came to us in Asia, that”** — what happened in it, that is to say
**“out of measure”** — of the preceding tribulations
**“we were pressed”**
• by the weight of sufferings
• and
**“above our strength,”** — human
**“so that”** — so much
**“we were weary”** — we who are accustomed to rejoice at evils
**“even of life.”** — not only to speak, and to do the rest
1.9:
**“ourselves”** — Not only others about us but also in us, because our nature promised nothing but death or failure. He signifies that so great an insolence of iniquity had risen up against the preachers of the faith that they had death before their eyes. For they had been so afflicted that they despaired of the present life.
**“in ourselves”**
• not only did it weary us to live, but also
• For “cursed is the man that trusteth in man.”
**“we had the answer of death”** — a complete certainty of dissolution
**“that we should not trust”** — therefore God permitted them only to be afflicted
**“but in God”** — in whom securely, because he is
**“who raiseth the dead.”** — to whom it is like that he delivered me from those aforesaid. Whence he adds: “Who hath delivered and doth deliver us out of so great,” etc.
1.10:
**“who hath delivered us out of so great dangers”** — brought us back to safety
**“hath delivered”** — Because God does not deny his faithfulness to those placed in necessity.
**“in whom we trust”** — stretching out in the desire of the mind
**“that”** — hereafter
**“And yet”** — That thanks may be given to God by many, from persons of many kinds converted to God on account of the preaching of the erring, for their preaching, having that gift of faith which is in them. By persons of many faces he means infants, boys, and the other ages, according to the condition of each sex.
**“will deliver”** — daily
1.11:
**“helping”** — Not only to us and to others, but also
**“you in prayer”** — by your prayer or prayers
**“for us”**
• made or for others
• so your prayers will help us that through many
**“that by the persons of many”** — that is, from persons of diverse ages
**“By the persons of many”** — Another translation: that in the face of many, of that which is in us, etc. This letter is read thus, as if: your prayers will so help us that thanks may be given to God by many for us. Thanks, I say, for that gift which is in us; these are not changed: let them be given, I say, in the face of many.
*Augustine:* That is, among many and before many, this because the grace of God comforts the apostles on account of many, that is, of all believers, on whose account also pressures were heaped on them. And therefore all those believers should render thanks to God for deliverance.
**“of that which is in us”** — or you
**“is a gift”** — is of the gift, of deliverance and of other good things
**“Gift”** — Proceeding from persons, that is, honest men, as to you and others of many faces, that is, of discretions or of discreet merits, and of diverse virtues, as the face of Job was patience, David’s humility, Moses' meekness.
**“that by many thanks may be given for us”**
• By many; thanks be given for us
• Ambrose. Therefore I do not distrust God’s help, because the conscience is pure from all pretence.
**“By many”** — Expounds what he had said above: from persons of many faces.
1.12:
**“For our glory is this”**
• this whence we glory
• Therefore both you and others ought to pray for us. Or therefore your prayers can help us, because this whence we glory is so honest.
**“The testimony of conscience”** — There are good works which bear witness outwardly to what is in conscience.
**“the testimony of our conscience”** — Witness of conscience, that is, conscience not accusing but bearing witness that in sincerity, etc.
**“that in simplicity”** — not having one thing in the mouth and another in the heart
**“and sincerity”** — preaching the sincere truth about God, not also the observances of the law
**“of God”**
• because this glory of conscience is from God: simplicity and sincerity
• As conscience is a great punishment to the wicked, so it is a joy to the pious, not as though they glory in it proudly, but give all to God. Therefore he rightly does not say: our glory is the testimony of another’s malice or of lesser grace, but of our conscience. Because it is hidden, it is not subject to another’s judgment, and so let no one presume either to think or to pronounce a sentence against it.
**“not in carnal wisdom”** — Which is to love pleasures, to avoid labours; or to preach according to the natures of things and not against them, as the false apostles did, whose painted preaching he refutes.
**“but in the grace of God we have conversed”** — that is, according as the Spirit freely showed me
**“in this world”** — in this world, where so many evils
**“and more abundantly”** — we have conversed simply
**“towards you”**
• towards you
• to whom we yielded our right, because when he had received from others, he would not receive from these
1.13:
**“For we write no other things to you”** — MORE ABUNDANTLY TO YOU, because nothing was required in the first epistle, nor in this
**“than what you have read”** — in the first epistle
**“and known”** — in the experience of works
**“I hope”** — Ambrose. He hopes they will advance, because they had begun to become better, the apostle’s affection toward them being known, and they took pride in it.
**“that you shall know unto the end”** — and as you have known me until now, so henceforth you will know
**“you shall know”** — me in the same
1.14:
**“as also you have known us in part”** — not wholly, because although you know that I abstained, yet you do not know with what discretion I did this
**“That we are your glory”** — You will know that we are your glory, that is, through us you ought to obtain eternal glory, and we through you, being well instructed, which would not be so if I were to receive from you with a stumbling block.
**“as you also are ours”** — which will be glory
**“in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ”**
• coming, that is, at the time of judgment
• when all things will be laid open
1.15:
**“And in this confidence”**
• now some of you have been corrected
• or I kept simplicity toward you more abundantly, and trusting in this, or in this, that we hope to be glorified through one another
**“In this confidence”** — Because the life of some was clean or amended, he wished to see those whom it had been unworthy to see before. If therefore he did not go, it is on account of others who are now purging themselves.
**“I had a mind to come to you before”** — I wished first to come to you
**“I had a mind”** — Augustine. Previously, because in the former epistle he had promised that he would come, and had not come, and so seemed false and fickle, he now excuses this. For he did not do this except because of their fault. One is not to be judged a liar who says what is false which he thinks true, because so far as it lies in him he does not deceive but is himself deceived. On the contrary, he lies who says what is true which he thinks false; nor is he free from lying who unknowingly speaks the truth with his mouth, but knowing it is not true, lies in his will.
**“that you might have a second”** — through my presence
**“grace”** — confirmation after faith, or you who had faith before
1.16:
**“and by you”** — by your guidance
**“to pass by you into Macedonia, and again from Macedonia to come to you”** — so that I might strengthen you in many ways
**“and to be brought on my way by you towards Judea”** — so that I might carry alms to the saints who were there
1.17:
**“Whereas then I was thus minded”** — I therefore wished to come for this, and did not come
**“was minded”** — and did not do it
**“did I use lightness?”** — so that what I did not propose by reason but by impulse of mind I dismissed with the same lightness
**“Or the things that I purpose”** — so that I proposed it for a carnal advantage, and because it was not, I dismissed it
**“do I purpose according to the flesh”** — things to be done or to be left undone
**“that there should be with me, It is, and It is not?”**
• so that by these causes there is with me, that is, in my intention, affirmation and negation of the same thing
• THAT THERE SHOULD BE WITH ME IT IS AND IT IS NOT, that is, that I should prefer my will to usefulness. As if to say: not so, because usefulness is to be preferred to will, and so I did.
1.18:
**“But God is faithful”** — But God is faithful. In this I am not to be believed a liar, because in nothing else have I lied to you. And this can be believed, because God is faithful, who promised teachers of the truth. Or: God is truthful, a witness to me in this, and this is, it seems to me, the “It is and It is not”; but God is faithful in his promises, because in all that discourse of ours which was among you there is not “It is and It is not,” that is, falsehood. In our discourse there was not “It is and It is not,” because in that Son of God, that is, in the preaching of him who, being the Son of God, was preached by us, there was not “It is and It is not,” but “It is”; that is, only the affirmation of truth was in him. For if we were liars, so would he be, because we preach only what he taught. The Son of God is truthful, because the promises of God are in him, that is, through him, “It is.” Or also “It is,” that is, truth and fulfilment, because in him they were fulfilled and shown forth. And it is not to be believed that he is a liar through whom the Father appeared truthful. And because the promises of God were fulfilled through Christ, therefore we through him say “Amen” to God, that is, that he is truthful. And that Christ and God are truthful, is. To our glory, because by this we are proved to preach the truth. Ours, I say; I do not ascribe it to us alone, but to God, because he who confirms is God.
**“for our preaching which was to you was not It is and It is not”**
• that is, a lie, as in pseudo
• that is, I did nothing other than what I knew was to be done, because usefulness is to be set before the will
1.19:
**“For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us”** — that is, in the preaching of him who is the Son of God, Jesus Christ
**“by me, and Sylvanus, and Timothy, was not It is and It is not”** — that is, a lie
**“but It is was in him”**
• he never wished anything other than what is useful
• the Son of God is truthful, and truly, because
1.20:
**“For all the promises of God are in him, It is”** — or according to another reading, truth and fulfilment
**“therefore”** — or also
**“and by him amen to God unto our glory”** — through whom this is made manifest
1.21:
**“Now he that confirmeth”** — in true preaching
**“us”** — the Jews
**“with you”** — because the Gentiles also were confirmed with the Jews
**“in Christ”** — in the true preaching of Christ
**“With you in Christ”** — Then, if you are firm in Christ, it is all the more certain of us, through whom you were confirmed.
**“and that hath anointed us”** — into kings and priests through the Spirit in baptism; whence Peter: “We are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood”
**“is God”** — is
1.22:
**“Who also hath sealed us”** — he wrote in the book of life, or distinguished from others by the sign of the cross
**“and given the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts”** — the Holy Spirit as a pledge; or the gifts are the pledge, in that the Spirit is in them
1.23:
**“But I call God to witness”**
• he explains why he did not come to them as he had said
• lest they think themselves despised
**“But I”** — I did not leave off for fickleness or earthly advantage, but sparing. Then the spiritual man does not fulfil what was arranged, when he plans something more providently for salvation.
**“upon my soul”**
• not only against the body but also against
• if I lie
**“that to spare you, I came not”**
• lest he grieve many
• lest, corrected more harshly, they be turned to sedition; he wishes therefore first to soften
**“any more to Corinth”**
• the first time after I departed from you
• therefore I say, sparing
1.24:
**“not because we exercise dominion”** — not because faith suffers domination and compulsion
**“Not because we exercise dominion”** — Lest they be indignant as if about lordship, because he had said, sparing you I did not come, he adds: Not because we have dominion over your faith, etc.
**“over your faith”** — which belongs to the will, not to necessity
**“but we are helpers”** — if you wish to cooperate
**“of your joy”** — eternal; or because the amended will rejoice
**“for in faith you stand”** — which works through love, not by lordship

2.1:
**“But I determined”** — Sparing you, I did not come, but I determined this same thing that I did when I sent the first letter: namely, that I should not come again, or that there should not again be sorrow, as there was when their sins were heard of.
**“this with myself, not to come to you again in sorrow”** — grieving you
2.2:
**“For if I make you sorrowful, who is he then that can make me glad, but the same who is made sorrowful by me?”**
• no one except he who is grieved by me, which is better done by letter than in person
• For if I make you sorrowful, etc. By correcting, rebuking in any way, either by letter or in person. And who, etc.? As if to say: and do you make me sorrowful, if not he who is made sorrowful by me, that is, according to my will, so that he may repent?
2.3:
**“And I wrote this same to you”** — that no one makes me glad except he who is grieved by me.
**“that I may not, when I come”** — concerning lack of correction
**“have sorrow upon sorrow”** — concerning sins
**“have”** — concerning you
**“from them of whom I ought to rejoice”** — not only now but formerly, when you grieved me and so gravely sinned
**“having confidence in you all”** — that I shall no longer have sorrow
**“Having confidence”** — As if to say: see then that I do not trust in vain that it will be my joy, and you ought to do what pertains to my joy, because my joy, etc.
**“that my joy is the joy of you all”** — that is, when I rejoice, you rejoice
2.4:
**“For out of much affliction”**
• I had sorrow
• with labours, watching for you and praying
**“and anguish of heart”** — with care, with grief
**“I wrote to you”** — the first letter
**“with many tears”**
• which are a judgment of what was inside
• I relate these
**“not that you should be made sorrowful”** — through the memory of them
**“but that you might know”** — that the desire of amending
**“Not that you should be made sorrowful but that you might know”** — Ambrose. For he rebuked for this purpose, that he might show with what love he loved them, over whose sins he grieved more than they did; he who does not rebuke with this feeling, makes sorrowful. For he who does not grieve with a brother mocks him.
**“the charity I have”** — or which I may have
**“more abundantly”**
• shown, because he loves all as himself
• which you thought
**“towards you”** — which I yielded from my right
2.5:
**“And if any one”** — like that fornicator
**“have caused grief”** — I wrote through tears; but nevertheless forgive him
**“And if any one have caused grief”** — He orders that the fornicator be received, whom he had earlier judged to be handed over to Satan, because he was corrected.
**“not”** — only
**“he hath not grieved me, but in part”** — you also
**“But in part”** — I do not impose the burden of sorrow on all, on account of those who grieved over their sins.
**“that I may not burden you all”** — not all; so that I will not impose this on all. Which is said in rebuke, or it would burden those who did not grieve for the sin.
2.6:
**“this rebuke is sufficient”** — yet
**“To him who is such a one”** — to him who has sinned so gravely
**“this rebuke, which is given by many”** — because such a one would easily despair if he were punished too harshly
**“This rebuke”** — Though this rebuke seems a penalty not worthy enough in length of time or in some other way, yet in this it is not to be thought small, that it is done by many, by whom, gathered together, he was delivered to Satan. He certainly suffers great sorrow who sees many shudder at his sin. And so it is enough that he was rebuked by many.
2.7:
**“So that on the contrary, you should rather forgive”** — because the more he is forgiven by many, the more he is to be forgiven
**“and comfort him”**
• him
• that through the example of David and of others to whom pardon was granted
**“you should rather forgive him and comfort him”** — He rightly commands forgiving a man afflicted for sin, and helping him by consolations. For if the one corrected grieves in mind, he soon has fruit; for this is true penance: to cease from sin.
**“comfort him”** — Through the words of the Lord by the prophet saying: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live.” And again: “In whatever hour the sinner groans, I will not remember all his iniquities.”
**“lest perhaps”** — by penance too harsh, despairing
**“be swallowed up”** — by the devil
**“with overmuch sorrow”** — so that he might wish to use the world
2.8:
**“Wherefore”** — lest he be swallowed up
**“I beseech you”** — who could command
**“that you would confirm”** — by forgiving him what you also ought to do
**“towards him”** — towards him, or to him
**“your charity”** — which you had by casting him out
2.9:
**“For to this end also did I write, that”** — now
**“that I may know the experiment of you”** — with what mind you did it in casting him out
**“For to this end also did I write, that I may know the experiment”** — Since I wrote on account of receiving him, I also wrote for this too: that I may know whether those whom I have found obedient to me in the casting out are obedient in all things.
2.10:
**“And to whom you have pardoned any thing”** — To whom you have forgiven anything, I beg: you ought to forgive.
**“I also”** — I forgave what I was well able to
**“For, what I have pardoned”** — like the other apostles
**“if I have pardoned any thing”** — because this was not done rashly and at random
**“for your sakes”** — I did it
**“have I done it in the person of Christ”** — in the person of Christ, as if Christ himself forgave, lest such forgiveness, which is for friends, seem void
2.11:
**“That we be not overreached”** — Therefore we ought to pardon, lest we be deceived by Satan through excessive harshness. For often, because of harsher punishments, the weak man is cast down into despair.
**“by Satan”**
• that he may make him despair
• He who cannot deceive them by their consent makes them too harsh.
**“For we are not ignorant of his devices”** — cunning
2.12:
**“And when I was come to Troas”** — sparing you, I did not come to Corinth
**“And when I was come”** — After the interposed matter about receiving the fornicator, he returns to them, showing that as it was their fault that he did not come to Corinth, so too that he made no progress in Troas, while Titus was detained among them, without whom he could not make progress there, because perhaps Titus could use their language more expressly.
**“for”** — to preach
**“for the gospel of Christ, and a door was opened”** — hearts prepared
**“unto me in the Lord”** — God working
2.13:
**“I had no rest in my spirit”** — I could not satisfy my will
**“because I found not”** — there, as we had agreed
**“Titus my brother”**
• who, hindered among you, did not come there
• who was needed there
**“Because I found not Titus”** — Because he alone could not both instruct the faithful and resist the clamouring unbelievers.
**“but bidding them farewell”**
• who had been converted
• in whom a door was opened
**“I went into Macedonia”** — but not uselessly, because there I was, as it were, a conqueror
2.14:
**“Now thanks be to God”**
• I give
• Hitherto of tribulations, and whose fault had not come. Here he begins to commend himself and to belittle the false apostles.
**“who always maketh us to triumph”** — makes to triumph
**“in Christ Jesus”** — in the preaching of Christ, by which he prepares hearts to believe
**“and the odour of his knowledge”** — The odour of knowledge, that is, Christ, who as a scent proceeding from the Father makes known him who is invisible, as a thing not seen is known by its smell and it is understood in what place it is. Or the miracles or the words of teaching by which one comes to knowledge of him.
**“and manifesteth by us”** — not through false ones
**“in every place”** — wherever we preach
2.15:
**“For”** — through us
**“we are the good odour of Christ unto God”**
• and sweet to God, even if it does not so seem to you
• A SWEET SAVOUR, namely, as once the legal sacrifice, so now true preaching and the sincere report of the apostles.
• God the Father’s odour is Christ; the apostles are the odour of Christ.
• The odour of Christ is the apostles, in whose life and preaching Christ is shown and not blasphemed. As it is said of the wicked: “The name of God through you is blasphemed among the Gentiles.”
*Ambrose:* He calls the preaching of Christ an odour, because as things not seen are known by smell, so invisible God willed to be understood through the preaching of Christ.
*Augustine:* This good odour is signified in Scripture by the naming of certain spices and ointments. For the bride of the Lord says: “After the odour of thy ointments we will run.” Because of this odour it is said in the gospel: “The house was filled with the odour of the ointment, the alabaster box being broken,” that is, the world was filled with the good fame and teaching of Christ and the apostles. This odour quickens those who love, and kills those who envy; as though he who envies the fame of Christ or of Paul dies by the good odour, and he who loves it lives in the good odour. If there were no brightness of the saints, the envy of the wicked would not arise; but if any such by persecuting break the flask, the odour of the ointment is spread the more widely.
**“in them”** — good, both with respect to those who are saved thereby and to those who, despising it, perish, because we act with a good intention
**“that are saved”** — mercy
**“and in them that perish”** — judgment
2.16:
**“To the one indeed”** — good to God, but to other men we seem an odour of death
**“the odour of death unto death”** — of envy and of ill opinion, leading to eternal death
**“The odour of death”** — That death may proceed from our preaching, to those who are found in eternal damnation.
**“but to the others the odour of life unto life”** — of love and good opinion, leading them into eternal life
**“And for these things”** — we are the odour, and through us God works these things: And for these things, etc.
**“who is so sufficient”**
• as we true apostles; as no one
• of the false apostles
2.17:
**“For we are not as many, adulterating the word of God”** — mixing in false things for pleasure, not preaching as the offspring of God
**“As many”** — Ambrose. Here he touches on the false apostles, who by corrupt teaching violated the truth, of whom Isaias says: “Thy wine-sellers mix water with wine.”
**“but with sincerity”** — with sincere intention, not for gain, and without admixture of corruption
**“but as from God”**
• who taught us
• and we do this
**“before God”**
• that is, for his cause alone
• that we may please him
**“in Christ we speak”** — In Christ. Never going beyond him, as those who act by the law, preaching legal things.

3.1:
**“Do we begin”**
• as if always new in this
• as in the first
**“Begin”** — Because he knew they took his commendation amiss, as in the first epistle, as if he sought his own glory, he begins, against their opinion, to show that he seeks not his own glory but God’s.
**“ourselves”** — not God
**“to commend”** — with these praises
**“Or do we need”** — you think we need
**“as some do”** — false [ones]
**“epistles of commendation”** — whom no virtue commends
**“epistles”** — sent by others
**“to you”** — to others
**“from you?”** — we do not need, because
3.2:
**“our epistle”** — our instruction
**“You are”** — in whom my knowledge and life are shown to others
**“written in our hearts”** — because I always have care for you
**“which is known”** — that, taught through us
**“and read by all men”** — who through you learn to imitate us
3.3:
**“Being manifested”**
• us

**“the letter killeth”** — Augustine. Mark what letter the Apostle says kills, to which, as if in contrast, he brings in the quickening spirit. It is surely the decalogue, written on those two tables, because “the law entered in that sin might abound.” Yet these precepts are so useful and wholesome to him who does them that unless one does them he cannot have life. So the letter is not called killing because the law is evil, but because, forbidding sin, it does not give life to man, but increases concupiscence and heaps up sin by transgression, unless grace frees through the law of faith. It appears therefore that the oldness of the letter, if the newness of the Spirit be lacking, makes men guilty by the knowledge of sin rather than freed from sin. Whence: “He that addeth knowledge, addeth also sorrow,” not because the law itself is evil, but because it has a good commandment only in the letter showing it, not in the Spirit helping. If this commandment is kept from fear of punishment, not from love of justice, it is done servilely, not freely, and so it is not done at all. For the fruit is not good which does not rise from the root of charity. But if faith be present, working by love, there comes delight in the good, which is the good not of the letter but of the Spirit.
*Augustine:* Letter and spirit are said in another way of law and grace. The law then is good, but with grace; as knowledge with charity profits, without it kills, so the law without grace kills, since it is the power of sin; for when it commands what is impossible without grace, it shows man that he is weak, that he may seek grace. **“WHO IS THE IMAGE”** — Augustine. It is to be known that image, equality, and likeness are to be distinguished. For where there is an image, there is at once likeness, but not at once equality. Where there is equality and likeness, there is not at once an image. Where there is likeness, there is not at once image or equality. For example: in a mirror there is image and likeness, but not equality, because many things are lacking to the image which are in the thing from which it is expressed. There can also sometimes be an image in which there is equality, as in parents and children there is found image and likeness and equality, except for the time by which the parents precede; because the likeness of the son is expressed from the parent so that it is rightly called an image, and it can be so great that it is rightly called equality. There can also sometimes be likeness and equality, although there is no image, as in two equal eggs. But Christ is called the image of the Father in such a way that none of these is lacking: so that he is not only his image and likeness, because he is an image, but also an equality so great that not even an interval of time is an impediment, because God did not beget the Son in time.

And therefore, since it is so dissolved, that the condition and cause be set forth first. From this it can be seen that we shall have it. For: not only for the present dwelling but also in this, that is, in the consideration of this so great glory. We groan: from the delay of desire, which we would not do unless we were certain. In figure of which matter Axa, the daughter of Caleb, asked the upper watery ground and the nether watery ground, that we may pour out tears not only for the misery of our present sojourn, but for the delay of the glory above. We groan, because we desire, over and above the renewal of the soul which we have already received, to be clothed upon with our habitation, that is, that there be given to the soul a garment not of the earth, corruptible, but from heaven, that is, immortal and impassible, in the likeness of the heavenly. We who are more perfect groan for the delay, because the less perfect also, who cherish the flesh, among whom the Apostle mentions himself, lest they think less of themselves. And this is: For we also who are in this tabernacle, who love the habitation of this body, of which there is no need to take care since it is a tabernacle only for a time, groan with desire of the heavenly, I say we, burthened, etc. Or: it is no wonder if we groan, because we are removed from blessedness. For we groan even over this lesser thing, because we are stripped of this body. And this is: for we are in this tabernacle, though burthened with it, that is, therefore we groan because we would not, etc. If this could be done. Or: we groan with desire of the heavenly. • Or “be separate,” that is, be apart, ready against them as before for them. This was said literally to the Jews dwelling in Babylon.
*Augustine:* Some evil men are to be tolerated for the sake of peace, and one does not withdraw from them bodily, but spiritually. To go out is to do what pertains to the correction of the wicked, as far as is permitted, according to each one’s rank, with peace preserved. To touch not is to be displeased. For the prophets who said these things did not abandon their people, but dwelt among those whom they rebuked, entered one temple with them, and celebrated the same sacraments; this is to go out: to spare not in speech, but to refute, correct, admonish. This is to touch not the unclean thing: not to consent in will. We commit a greater evil in the separation of the good than we flee in the mixture of the wicked. That is, when we separate ourselves bodily from the good on account of the wicked, how great is the evil which we flee by not remaining in union with the wicked; that is, how great is that which we flee in fleeing the union of the wicked. Let each one therefore withdraw spiritually from the wicked. To such a one God does not impute his own sins, because he did not commit them; nor those of others, because he did not approve them; nor negligence, because he did not keep silent; nor pride, because he remained in unity.

**“By an equality”**
• Let him divide as much as he has with the saints, since no more is demanded than that he give what he keeps for himself. So Zacchaeus gave half his goods to the poor.
• I do not say this indeed according to parity, but that they may be sustained from your goods as you are, that their abundance also may supply your want. For those who live in this world do not have merits sufficient for eternal life. But because the poor of Christ, whose is the kingdom of heaven, would make friends and debtors to themselves through alms, through their merits they will obtain what they do not merit by themselves. That then there may be an equality: not that they do not differ in brightness, but because to all there will be the same, and for all a sufficiency. As it is written of the manna, as a sign of this thing. He that gathered much, namely of the manna, that is, more than a gomor, had no more, that is, he had no more than a gomor. And he that gathered little, that is, less than a gomor, had no less, that is, he had no less than a gomor. In Exodus he says: “Neither had he more that had gathered more: nor did he find less that had provided less.” By this it was signified that both those who have greater merits and those who have lesser will have the same refreshment at the eternal feast.
