**“or our brethren, the apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ.”** — namely, for those others who are our brothers and apostles, and by whom he was asked
**“Or our brethren”** — Or else: through your fathers, the apostles of the churches, to the glory of God; that is, that they themselves are apostles of the churches, which is of the glory of Christ God, that is, to the glory of Christ, because in them the glory is not of men but of Christ.
**“the glory of God”** — to the glory of Christ
8.24:
**“Wherefore shew ye”**
• because we sent such men
• that they may approve the good things they have heard of you, and the rest of the churches may recognize what they have heard of them
• Therefore show: that is, your charity which you showed to others, and our glory which you likewise showed to be true; now show it well by receiving them, and this in the sight of the churches, so that others may take an example from you.
**“the evidence of your charity, and of our boasting on your behalf; shew ye to them, in the sight of the churches.”** — namely, that the rest of the churches may recognize that the good things they heard of you are true

9.1:
**“For”** — I warn concerning the receiving of these
**“concerning the ministry that is done towards the saints, it is superfluous”** — superfluous
9.2:
**“For I know your forward mind: for which I boast of you to the Macedonians.”** — saying
**“That Achaia also”** — whose metropolis is Corinth
**“is ready from the year past”** — drawn on by the rivalry of the Macedonians
**“and your emulation”** — love and zeal of your giving
**“And your emulation”** — By the rivalry of the Corinthians, while other churches hear that they, who were once entangled in errors, afterwards became men of good will, were stirred up to a good work.
**“hath provoked very many.”** — to give alms
9.3:
**“Now I have sent the brethren,”** — why then do you send them ahead?
**“that the thing which we boast of”** — not that they should exhort you to this, but that you may be ready
**“concerning you, be not made void”** — wholly
**“in this behalf,”** — if you are commanded
**“that (as I have said) you may be ready:”** — you ready for them
9.4:
**“Lest, when the Macedonians shall come with me, and find you unprepared, we should be ashamed”** — who were boasting of you
**“We should be ashamed”** — For if this was not found, which he testified of them, then he himself will blush, and they will be confounded all the more.
**“not to say ye”** — to blush, which is the greater thing, that is, which ought to be
**“in this matter.”** — in this giving of alms which sustains the poor
9.5:
**“Therefore I thought it necessary”** — that this not be
**“to desire the brethren”** — namely Luke, Titus and Apollo
**“that”** — me
**“that they would go to you before, and prepare this blessing before promised”** — often promised
**“this blessing”** — that is, the alms which is rightly called a blessing, because it is the cause of eternal blessing
**“to be ready,”** — when we come
**“so as a blessing”** — so that it may be a work of charity and a great one
**“not as covetousness.”** — so that they may grieve over what was given, and what they give may be little
9.6:
**“Now this I say:”** — let those prepare; I however prescribe why you should give generously
**“He who soweth sparingly”**
• gives
• He does not sow sparingly who, having little, gives little, if his mind is ready to give more if he had more.
• He says 'sows', not 'gives', because to give is not to lose but to sow: to go without for a time, so that more may be had in the future.
**“shall also reap sparingly”** — recompense
**“and he who soweth in blessings”** — where the mind is weighed more than the wealth
**“in blessings”**
• of God
• from the generosity of God’s gifts
**“shall also reap.”** — recompense
9.7:
**“Every one”** — namely, let him give
**“as”** — as much
**“hath determined”** — he has determined, because if they gave unwillingly it would profit them nothing
**“in his heart”** — by the counsel of reason
**“not with sadness, or of necessity”** — that is, sad or compelled, but willingly
**“Not with sadness”** — He who gives unwillingly, out of present shame, has no reward.
**“for a cheerful giver”**
• who from good will
• He gives generously who has the desire to give, even if he has nothing to give.
**“For a cheerful giver”** — He who gives so as to be rid of the annoyance of the petitioner, not to refresh the entrails of the needy, loses both merit and the thing.
*Augustine:* Whatever good you do, do it with cheerfulness, and then you do it well. But if you do it with sadness, what is done is made of you, and you do not make it.
**“God loveth”** — approves, rewards.
9.8:
**“And God is able”** — as if I so advise: and do not distrust.
**“to make all grace abound”**
• that is, all the gifts of the Holy Spirit.
• not only this but also this with others.
**“to make in you”**
• or in your hearts.
• so.
**“that in all things”** — in every state of yours.
**“always, having all sufficiency”** — for he who chooses only sufficiency will be able to walk or abound in God’s work.
**“having”** — considering to have.
**“may abound to every good work.”** — in the giving of alms, as also in other things.
**“May abound to every good work”** — For although what one who has little gives is small, it nevertheless abounds, because it is done with right judgment, since it is not asked how much, but with what mind it is given.
9.9:
**“As”** — is: is not this indeed good?
**“it is written:”** — in the Psalm.
**“He hath dispersed abroad”** — not bestowing everything on one but dividing it among many.
**“he hath given”** — freely.
**“to the poor”** — not to the rich, who could repay; how much more to the saints.
**“his justice”**
• and this.
• that is, also the reward of justice.
**“His justice”** — He is just who reckons the goods of the world as common, for the sake of the end of eternal reward.
*Ambrose:* By this example he invites us to give generously to the saints. For if the reward of him who gives to the poor is great, how much greater is that of him who ministers to the saints? For those who are wicked can also be called poor.
**“remaineth for ever”** — for eternity, without end.
9.10:
**“And he that ministereth”**
• not only from this is life given.
• that is, God.
**“seed to the sower”** — whence alms are made.
**“bread”** — necessities of life.
**“to eat”** — not for superfluity.
**“will give”** — and so far; and therefore let no one fear to give through this fear.
**“and”** — which.
**“will multiply your seed”** — whence you may do more alms.
**“and increase the growth of the fruits”** — the will and the means of giving alms.
**“The growth of the fruits”** — Righteousness is holiness and a good life, and from these come fruits, that is, eternal reward. The increases of almsgiving, for which here too virtues and in the future glory will be increased.
**“of your justice”** — from which righteousness and life proceed
9.11:
**“That being enriched in all things, you may abound”** — He will increase both the means and the will to give to such a degree that in every condition, according to your reckoning, that being enriched in all things, you may abound, etc.
**“unto all”** — perfect
**“simplicity”** — generosity made with a simple heart
**“which worketh through us thanksgiving to God”**
• and therefore to be done
• That which works through us thanksgiving, that is, the very giving is the cause why thanks are rendered to God, of whose giving we are the ministers.
9.12:
**“Because”** — therefore thanks are given because there are many good things in this
**“the administration”** — our ministry
**“of this office”** — of this office of ours
**“doth not only supply the want of the saints, but aboundeth also”** — because many give thanks in the working of God
**“aboundeth also by many thanksgivings in the Lord”** — and this
9.13:
**“By the proof of this ministry”**
• that is, those who praise this our ministry
• who moves them to give thanks
**“glorifying God for the obedience of your confession”** — not only for your generosity but, having taken occasion thence, for faith and every good
**“unto the gospel of Christ”** — because you obeyed the gospel of Christ in submission of mind, glorifying God
**“and for the simplicity”** — because with a simple heart, or by your example to others, they share their goods with others
**“of your communicating”** — because you count your things as common
**“unto them”**
• done
• the aforesaid saints
**“and unto all”** — other nations
9.14:
**“and in their”** — of the saints
**“praying for you”** — also glorifying God because those saints pray for you
**“being desirous of you”** — desiring to see you in eternal blessedness or even here
**“because of the excellent grace”** — that is, charity
9.15:
**“Thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift”** — and because from this, in so many good things, I give thanks for charity, which cannot be told how useful it is, or unspeakable, that is, which ought to be told
**“Thanks be to God”** — Of the other want and the other supplying of the want of Christ’s provincials and Christ’s soldiers. He dealt here with carnal things toward those. Then, however, from spiritual things toward these, exclaiming as one full of joys: I give thanks.

10.1:
**“Now I Paul myself beseech you”** — not others who falsely put themselves before me
**“Now I Paul myself”** — He begins on the uncorrected, who followed the false apostles and thought him fierce, as if to say: I invite the corrected to almsgiving. But you others I beseech, I Paul, truly humble, not proud, I who advise others to almsgiving; I say to you the same that I beseech of those, etc.
**“by the mildness and modesty of Christ”** — if you wish me to be lenient as Christ
**“who in presence”** — outwardly
**“indeed”** — as you say
**“am lowly among you”** — while present
**“but being absent, am bold toward you”** — as if I do not fear, rebuking you sharply
10.2:
**“I beseech you”** — not only do I beseech but also I ask
**“that I may not be bold when I am present”** — when I come
**“be bold”** — I will punish boldly
**“with that confidence”** — as much as I am thought to be bold when absent, so much will I do when present, in the matter
**“wherewith I am thought to be bold, against some”** — the unreformed
**“who reckon us as if we walked according to the flesh”** — after the manner of the carnal
10.3:
**“For though we walk in the flesh”** — in the flesh, that is, although living in the flesh, which is frail
**“we do not war according to the flesh”** — For we do not wage the warfare given you by God according to the flesh, that is, for earthly gain; this is what he says: “in the flesh.”
10.4:
**“For the weapons”** — not according to the flesh
**“of our warfare”** — powers, miracles, by which we wage war in preaching
**“are not carnal”** — weak
**“but mighty to God”** — but mighty through God
**“unto the pulling down of fortifications”** — of heretical philosophers
**“Unto the pulling down of fortifications”** — Unto the pulling down of fortifications. That they may destroy counsels fortified by diverse cunning of men or of demons.
**“fortifications”** — Fortifications are the hearts of unbelievers, which the devil holds and fortifies with various errors, so that the word of God may not be able to enter by faith; or by likeness to fortifications. And the weapons of the Apostle’s warfare are strong to overcome these, and he shows the parts of that fortification, namely counsels.
**“counsels”** — fortified arguments
**“destroying”**
• we wage war not according to the flesh, for
• they can destroy, for we destroy
10.5:
**“And every height that exalteth itself”** — the depth of understanding of the lawyers as well as of the philosophers or of the impious
**“against”** — while they attack the virgin birth and such things
**“the knowledge of God”** — which is of God
**“and bringing into captivity”** — we lead captive even unto the obedience of Christ
**“every understanding”** — all who understand proudly
**“unto the obedience of Christ”** — that they may humbly obey the faith of Christ, which they had before resisted
10.6:
**“And”** — also
**“having in readiness”** — according to life and power
**“And having in readiness”** — And having in readiness to revenge all disobedience. Because nothing gnaws at us to make us hold back from daring.
**“to revenge all disobedience”**
• that we are not like the false apostles, who preach for carnal things, and flatter vices, and are conscious to themselves
• which we will do
**“when your obedience shall be fulfilled”** — after I have known the obedient through love, then I will truly punish the disobedient
**“To revenge all disobedience, when”** — For then he avenges disobedience, when he condemns it through obedience. Then he destroys it, when he leads those who resist to faith. And this is worthy vengeance, that perfidy be condemned by those by whom it was defended.
10.7:
**“See the things that are according to outward appearance”**
• we true apostles are such as I showed above: But the things that are according to the face, etc.
• as if the things I say are open
• I have said many things by which I have shown you that we ought rather to be followed than the false apostles. As if to say: though what I have said does not suffice for you, why should you follow me rather than the false apostles? See these other things that are according to the outward appearance, that is, are as evident as the things that lie before the eyes, namely these: if any of those false apostles trusts through something, that is, through faith or something else, that he is Christ’s, by the same we also are, or: see the things that are according to appearance, that is, diligently consider their works, who do good only in your sight, lest perhaps they seduce you so that you would wish to prefer them to us, which you ought not.
**“If any man trust to himself, that he is Christ's”** — he says this of the presumptuous
**“let him think this again with himself”** — that he not exceed the measure of reason, either on account of hatred of us or for his own honor
**“that as he is Christ's”** — through whatever things
**“so”** — through the same things
**“so are we also”** — we truly are Christ’s, for we are even more excellent through the power which they do not have; and this is what he says: For even if, etc., as they also are
10.8:
**“For if also I should boast somewhat more of our power”** — of the apostleship
**“which the Lord hath given us”** — not to them
**“unto edification, and not for your destruction, I should not be ashamed”**
• that we may build you up in virtues, so that we may not corrupt you by perverse teaching or example, as the false ones do
• I should not be ashamed. Because it is both true, and said not for my glory but for your advantage.
10.9:
**“But that I may not be thought as it were to terrify you”** — I have power for building up and not for destruction; but yet it might seem to them that I ought therefore to flatter, because he received the power for building up and not for destruction.
**“But that I may not be thought”** — Here he says that when he is present he will fulfil in deed what he threatens in word when absent. He says this on the occasion of that saying, “ready to revenge all disobedience”; so he says, that I may not be thought by you as it were to terrify by words and not in deed, that you may know that I, who am less in words, shall fulfil in deeds what I shall fulfil in words.
**“by epistles”** — only
10.10:
**“For his epistles indeed”** — Paul’s
**“say they”** — some
**“are weighty”** — weighty to understand
**“and strong”** — to terrify
**“but his bodily presence”** — not daring to exercise severity
**“is weak”** — against the strong
**“and his speech”** — because I speak like an unlearned man, without argument
**“contemptible”** — against the weighty
10.11:
**“Let such a one think this”** — who thinks this of me
**“that such as we are”** — how harsh
**“in word by epistles, when absent, such also we will be indeed when present”** — avenging all disobedience
**“such”** — Because if we flattered your vices, then we would not build up but destroy.
10.12:
**“For we dare not match”** — I will truly avenge, because I ought not to flatter, lest I perish as they do
**“For we dare not”** — We shall be such in deed, because we are not like the false apostles, who usurp power for themselves and flatter vices. And this is it: we do not insert ourselves among some, that is, the false apostles, who commend themselves, that is, usurp power; which is: we do not put ourselves in their number so as to usurp power, but we have received it from God. Or: we do not compare ourselves with them, so as to flatter you as they do and soothe your vices, which one who has power could also do. But rightly we do not do this, because we dare not, lest we perish as they do. Not this, but we measure ourselves, not by anything other than what has been enjoined, without usurping. And we compare you with ourselves, because we act according to what our office requires. And in doing this we will not glory beyond measure. Not so we, as if to say: as those who by usurping glory beyond measure.
**“or compare”** — in deeds
**“ourselves with some, that commend themselves”** — not God them
**“that commend themselves”** — not sent by God
**“but we measure ourselves by ourselves”** — we are
**“and compare ourselves with ourselves”** — as the nature of each one’s office requires
10.13:
**“But we”** — that they
**“will not glory beyond our measure”** — beyond our measure
**“but according to the measure”** — we will exercise power
**“of the rule”**
• the people whose rule I am, for directing, under which measure you also
• According to the measure of the rule, etc. For by the will of God he was directed to preach the gospel to the Corinthians. For it had been apportioned to each one to whom he was to be sent in preaching, so that each would have certain peoples of his own, of whose faith they might glory. But to the rule of the Apostle belonged all those whom he had founded in the faith, he who had been sent by God to all. Whence he adds: Which measure God hath measured to us.
**“which God hath measured to us, a measure”** — I say
**“to reach even unto you”**
• by the admonition of God
• God has measured; for it is not overextension
• he therefore who resists God sending him
10.14:
**“For we stretch not ourselves beyond our measure, as if we reached not”** — we reach
**“unto you”** — because
**“For we are come as far as to you in the gospel of Christ”** — in the preaching of the gospel
10.15:
**“Not glorying beyond measure”** — where another had laid the foundation of faith
**“In other men's labours”** — That it would be beyond measure to glory; but having hope in you, that is, to be magnified through you among others and to preach according to our rule, that is, according to what has been enjoined by God, not having hope to glory in another’s rule.
**“but having hope of your increasing faith”** — through growing faith from virtue to virtue
**“in you”** — because through you we are proved to be such true apostles
**“to be magnified”** — by others
**“according to our rule”** — governance
**“our rule abundantly”** — not in another
**“abundantly”**
• not in few places
• but
10.16:
**“Yea, unto those”** — places
**“that are beyond you, to preach the gospel, not to glory in another man's rule”** — nor are those who are in faults of another’s governance
**“in them”** — explains
**“that”** — namely
**“are made ready”** — by other preachers, because he preached to those to whom it had not been announced, so that he might seek glory by his own labour
**“to glory”** — I will glory in the things said before and in others; but all this, of which there is cause for glorying, is from God, and therefore
10.17:
**“But he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.”**
• that is, let him attribute his confidence and glory to the Lord.
• which he cannot do who does not have power from God.
**“But he that glorieth”** — I will not glory in another’s rule. Likewise he who glories, that is, wishes to exercise power in the Lord, that is, let him glory in the measure given by God.
10.18:
**“For not he who commendeth himself”**
• he who glories apart from God, attributing to himself what is God’s.
• he who preaches without being sent, who is not fit but a presumptuous man.
**“is approved”** — by God or by men.
**“but he, whom God commendeth.”** — by miracles and powers.
**“But he, whom God”** — God commends and approves him whom he holds worthy, and sends him to preach his gift; whom he does not send, he does not commend, because one not sent preaches.

11.1:
**“Would to God”** — but
**“you could bear with”** — without indignation.
**“Would to God you could bear with”** — As if to say: I glory in my government, which seems foolishness; but “Would to God you could bear with some little of my folly,” etc. Or he calls the glorying according to the flesh foolishness, lest he seem inferior to them in that which he himself does not care about, but which profits the Corinthians.
**“some little”** — because I am able to glory more.
**“of my folly”** — of glorying, which seems foolishness.
**“my folly”** — Because it is said: “let not thy own lips praise thee, but those of thy neighbour.”
**“but do bear with me.”** — I desire that you bear with me, but I also command it.
**“do bear with”** — As if to say: though it is grievous, you should nevertheless bear it patiently.
11.2:
**“For I am jealous”**
• as subjects their prelate.
• I love.
**“I am jealous”** — Augustine. Jealousy is a movement of the mind on account of another’s state, either toward good or toward evil; this one is of love, not of envy, because he loves them with the jealousy of God, that is, which God inspires by his Spirit; by this he shows that what he will say, he will say out of love for them, not that they may advance to his praise but to their own advancement.
**“of you with the jealousy of God.”**
• for the honour of God, not mine; not with zeal, the bride of God as mine, but for God.
• I truly love you, because I am the friend of the bridegroom.
**“For I have espoused you”** — with the ring of faith.
**“to one husband”**
• not to many.
• to the lawful Christ, the true bridegroom.
**“as a chaste virgin”**
• not to an adulterer.
• All one virgin, on account of the unity of whole faith, firm hope and charity; virgin, because they are undefiled by evil work; chaste, because they have no heat of evil will.
**“you as a chaste virgin”** — He passes from the plural to the singular, wishing it to be understood that the whole Church is a virgin, and that in all her true members she keeps the virginity of the mind, even if not of the body. Virginity of the flesh is the untouched body, and this virginity belongs to few. Virginity of the heart is uncorrupted faith, and this belongs to all the faithful. Whence in the Apocalypse: “These are they who were not defiled with women: for they are virgins,” etc. By women he signified error, because error began through a woman.
**“that I may present ... to Christ.”** — that is, so that I may present you on the day of judgement.
11.3:
**“But I fear”** — and therefore I speak to you with zeal, saying true things about myself.
**“lest, as the serpent”** — the devil through the serpent.
**“But I fear lest, as the serpent”** — Augustine. These Corinthians are like Eve, the false apostle like the serpent, the light of faith like paradise. Those, then, whose faith is corrupted are cast out of paradise, because they prefer a lie to the truth. Those, then, who build up a lie in men drive the truth away from them, and bring in the devil, and so shut out Christ. For if you say anything against the faith, rottenness enters from the serpent’s poison, and the worms of lies are bred, and nothing remains whole. And therefore, as for our fathers there was need of patience against the lion, so for us there is need of watchfulness against the dragon. For then he compelled, now he teaches; then he brought violence, now snares. Then he was seen roaring, now he is slippery and wandering, and is hard to see. Therefore the Apostle fears lest, as Eve was seduced by the serpent, so the Church be corrupted by heretics in the virginity of faith which she bears in her heart. Now, therefore, my soul, keep your virginity, to be made fruitful afterwards in the embrace of your spouse. Hedge in your ears with thorns. For the serpent still murmurs, and is not silent. What was done even in that paradise is done in the Church. Let it suffice that we correct what we fell into or experienced there.
**“seduced Eve”** — casting her out of paradise.
**“by his subtilty”** — by promising false things
**“so your minds should be corrupted”** — through similar deceptions
**“minds”** — understanding
**“your minds and fall from the simplicity”** — from the paradise of simple faith, which receives nothing foreign
11.4:
**“For if he that cometh”** — but you ought not to suffer them, because it is nothing other than what I preach, and the same, but worse; why then do you esteem us inferior to them?
**“if he that cometh”** — Not sent, or selling, because he acts for temporal gain.
**“another Christ”** — more excellent than I, which cannot be
**“preacheth whom we have not preached; or if you receive another Spirit”** — better, which it is not; but rather through us
**“receive whom you have not received”** — through us
**“or”** — if
**“another gospel”** — another redemption or preaching, which cannot be
**“which you have not received”** — through us
**“you might well bear with him.”** — as if: if they preached something greater, you would rightly suffer; but because this is not so, you do not rightly suffer them. For I have done no less in these things than the great apostles, and so it is established that I am not less than they, the false apostles.
**“you might well bear with him”** — If something greater is done for you through them than through us, then you would rightly suffer. He says anathema to the Galatians, if they received something else, which would certainly not be greater, but contrary.
11.5:
**“For I suppose that I have done nothing less than the great apostles.”**
• I mean myself, then set aside
• I suppose, etc. The great apostles. The great apostles, in the eyes of these men, are Peter and the others who were with the Lord. Or he says this on behalf of the false apostles, to whom he shows he has done no less. For the Church of the Corinthians was tossed about by various errors. Some favoured the apostles who had been with the Lord in the flesh. Others favoured the false apostles, from whom, in composed words, they heard the same things as from the Apostle. Against these he speaks here. As if to say: they preach to you nothing other than I do. And because it could be said that even if the same, yet better than Paul, he removes this: For I suppose, etc.
**“I suppose”** — Above, about the false apostles; now about the true ones, to whom Paul seems inferior because he had not been with Jesus.
**“For”** — no less
11.6:
**“For although I be rude in speech”** — because I do not adorn words, or because my tongue is hindered as to ornament, in the case of the false apostles
**“rude”** — This is not said of the apostles, since they were not eloquent, but of the false ones, who composed words. One unskilled in speech is not guilty before God, but one who lacks the knowledge of God, which pertains to salvation.
**“yet not in knowledge”** — but not in knowledge; I know whatever is great
**“in all things”** — But you can be witnesses of them to me. And therefore it is worse that, knowing this, you put me after them.
**“but in all things we have been made manifest to you.”** — but I have been made manifest to you; as if you have experienced all things that happen in me
11.7:
**“Or did I commit a fault”** — not less, though less; did I sin in this?
**“humbling myself”** — by working with my hands
**“that”** — so
**“you might be exalted?”**
• from death to life; the false ones removed
• the false apostles being removed
**“Because”** — because you do not think you have bought a license to sin
**“freely”** — without expense
**“preached the gospel of God”** — or: I preached
**“Because the gospel of God freely”** — I did not do less but more, because freely. Therefore you are angry with me and set others before me, although this is not a sin but a glory.
11.8:
**“other churches”** — from what then were you living
**“I have taken”** — because I spent no small things on you
**“receiving”** — from others
**“wages for your ministry”** — that I might preach to you

Let no one, when he thinks he has good angels as friends, have evil demons as feigned friends, and endure them as enemies all the more harmful as they are more cunning and deceitful. For neither are the holy and faithful worshippers of the one true God safe from their deceits and manifold temptation. In these evil days, where this anxiety is not useless, lest when Satan transforms himself by deceiving he seduce to something ruinous. For when he deceives the bodily sense but does not move the mind from the true and right opinion by which anyone leads a faithful life, there is no danger in religion. Or when, feigning himself good, he does or says things that agree with good angels, even if he is believed good, the error is not dangerous or deadly. But when through these foreign things he begins to lead to his own, great watchfulness is needed that no one go after him, which no one can do without God. And this very difficulty is useful for this, that each one have no hope in himself, nor one man in another, but in God alone.

**“whether in the body, or out of the body”** — The Apostle did not know this: whether when he was caught up the soul was in the body, or went out of the body altogether, so that the body lay dead; or whether, in some other manner, of a living body, wherever the soul was, his mind was taken up to see or hear the ineffable things of that vision. And because this was uncertain, therefore perhaps he said: whether in the body, or out of the body.

**“such a one caught up to the third heaven”** — shows also God, in the life in which he is to be seen for eternity
**“caught up”** — Lifted up beyond nature, up to the third heaven, that is, to the knowledge of the Godhead.
**“to the third heaven”** — The first heaven is the air, the second the firmament, the third spiritual, where the angels and holy souls of God enjoy contemplation.
*Augustine:* Or the three heavens are understood as three kinds of visions, so that the first heaven is bodily vision, when certain things are seen bodily by the gift of God, as Eliseus saw the fiery chariots when Elias was taken up; and Baltasar the hand writing on the wall: “Mane, Thecel, Phares.” The second heaven is imaginary or spiritual vision, when someone in ecstasy or in sleep sees not bodies but images of things by the revelation of God, as Peter the sheet. The third heaven is intellectual vision, when neither bodies nor their images are seen, but the gaze of the mind is fixed, by the wondrous power of God, on incorporeal substances. To this the Apostle was caught up, that he might see God himself in himself, not in any figure. But whether in the body or in the separated soul, he says he does not know. As if to say: I did not see by human sense, so that, even if in the body, it is not against that word of Moses: “Man shall not see me and live.” For then the Apostle did not live as a man, that is, according to the use of the senses of the body, but every sense of man was taken away. Or, according to Dionysius, who established three orders of angels, placing three in each: in the first, angels, archangels, virtues; in the second, principalities, powers, dominations; in the third, thrones, cherubim and seraphim, the third of which contemplates God more nearly; in likeness to these the Apostle is said to have seen God. Or the first heaven is the knowledge of the heavenly bodies, the second the knowledge of the heavenly spirits, the third the knowledge of the Godhead.
*Augustine:* The third heaven, which is not seen through the body, nor imaginatively but properly, is seen by that vision which surpasses all. Through the body are seen heaven, earth, and all things visible to the eyes. The spirit holds bodily images, either true ones or such as it feigns. The intellect grasps incorporeal things, which have no images. These are the three kinds of visions. By the first vision Baltasar saw the hand, and did not know what it signified, which Daniel, a prophet, better by the proper vision of the mind, explained. By the second Peter saw the sheet in ecstasy, where not the body but the image, and afterwards the mind divinely aided, saw what it signified. Borne up to this, the mind without any image sees the clear truth; there the powers of the soul are without any labour; there the whole power is one: to love what you see, and the highest happiness is to see and to have what you love. For the sake of this vision of the truth, where God is seen, not by bodily vision as on Sina, or spiritual, as Isaias and John in the Apocalypse, but “by sight, not in a riddle,” every labour is undertaken. In this way Moses asked to see God, that is, in the substance which is God, whom yet he had seen in many figures, and to whom he had spoken face to face. Because there, that is, in that species, he is seen far more ineffably and more powerfully, and speaks hidden things, where no one living in these senses sees. This is the third heaven, where God is seen face to face. This is paradise, if it can be called paradise, because both the present Church is called paradise and the place in which Adam lived bodily.

**“But other of the apostles I saw none, saving James the brother of the Lord”**
• because he was the son of Joseph, who was called the father of Jesus
• The brother of the Lord. It is the custom of the Jews to call male kinsmen of the same family brothers.
• James the brother of the Lord. Jerome: Because this James was the son of Joseph, who was called the father of Jesus. But this is not sound, since Joseph is believed to have been a virgin. Another reason, then, must be sought why he is called the brother of the Lord, as are Joseph and Simon and Jude. Whence it is said in the gospel: “Behold, thy father and thy mother and thy brethren,” etc., so that it may therefore be clear why they are called brethren.
• For in the divine Scriptures we call people brothers in four ways, namely by nature, by race, by kinship, by affection: by nature, as Esau and Jacob; by race, as all the Jews among themselves, whence in Deuteronomy: “If thou buy thy brother,” etc. And likewise: “Set over thee a prince whom the Lord shall choose, who is of thy brethren.” Further, those are called brothers by kinship who are of one family, when a multitude spreads out from one root, according to which Abraham in Genesis calls Lot brother, saying: “Let there be no quarrel between me and thee, for we are brethren,” and Jacob and Laban are called brothers. They are also called brothers by affection, according to which all Christians are called brothers, as there: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together,” etc. And the Lord says: “Go, and tell my brethren.” Further, in general all men are called brothers, because they are born of one father. Understand therefore that those were called brothers of Christ by the privilege of kinship.
*Ambrose:* It is to be known that Mary, the mother of the Lord, was the daughter of Joachim and Anne, and she married Joseph, and so Joseph was the reputed father of Christ. But when Joachim was dead, Cleophas, the brother of Joseph, took the same Anne to wife and begot of her a daughter whom he called Mary, who married Alpheus, who begot of her sons, namely James, Joseph, Simon, Jude. But when Cleophas was dead, one Salome married the same Anne and begot of her a daughter named Mary, who married Zebedee, and he had of her sons, namely James, who was called the greater, and John the evangelist. Anne therefore had three husbands and three daughters. Now it is to be seen why James the son of Alpheus was called both the less and the brother of the Lord. He was called the less to distinguish him from James the son of Zebedee, who was called the greater not according to time but because he followed the Lord first; and so James the son of Alpheus is the less because he adhered to Christ later. He was called the brother of the Lord, as some are pleased to hold, because he was the son of the maternal aunt of Christ; or on account of likeness of holiness; or because he was the nephew of Christ’s paternal uncle, that is, of Cleophas. For the Hebrews call brothers those joined by close kinship on the fathers' side. Whence Jerome says that this James and his brothers are understood as brothers of the Lord, in these words: Some, following the ravings of the apocrypha, suppose that the brothers of the Lord who stood outside were sons of Joseph by some little woman. But we ought to understand here by the brothers of the Lord his cousins, namely the sons of Alpheus and of the maternal aunt of his mother, the mother of James the less and Joseph and Jude.

**“Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith”** — It should be known that he now treats chiefly of the works that are in the sacraments, which are not necessary where the grace of faith is. For the works of the law are twofold: some are taken in the sacraments, some in morals. To the sacraments belong circumcision, the sabbath, the new moons, sacrifices, and countless observances of this kind. To morals: “Thou shalt not kill”, “Thou shalt not commit adultery”, and the like. In the observances, if they are not understood, there is servitude alone. But if they are observed and understood, not only do they do no harm, but they even profit, if they suit the time. Every sacrament, when it is understood, is referred either to the contemplation of truth or to good morals. The contemplation of truth is founded in the love and knowledge of God alone. Good morals, in the love of God and of neighbour, “on which two commandments dependeth the whole law and the prophets”.
3.3:
**“Are you so foolish”** — and since you are of faith, are you therefore so foolish?
**“whereas you began in the Spirit”** — holy
**“began”** — you had the beginning of salvation
**“would now be made perfect by the flesh”** — since, though you are more advanced, you seek to be made perfect through the flesh, that is, carnally, from whom a beginning could not even be had
3.4:
**“Have you suffered so great things”** — you are not made perfect, but you lose what you have held. And altogether
**“in vain”**
• that is, without profit
• John says that they had already endured much for the faith, and in those very sufferings had overcome fear by love. So they suffered such great things without cause, who wished to slip back to the law from the love which had sustained such things in them.
**“If it be yet in vain”** — I confirm this, because it is in you; if you wish, it will profit. He says this so that they may not despair.
3.5:
**“He therefore who giveth”**
• by ministry, not by authority
• Since you received the Spirit not from works, which you never had, but from faith, you can therefore see that I, who had the works of the law, yet received the power of giving the Spirit and of working miracles not through them but through faith. Concerning him who had been under the law it may be doubted, but by the likeness of these it is clear.
**“giveth to you the Spirit, and worketh miracles among you”** — miracles
**“among you”** — among you
**“by the works of the law, or by the hearing of the faith”**
• not indeed by works but by faith; although these things do not help me, who there was strong, why do you seek them?
• so the Spirit is from faith, just as righteousness is also
3.6:
**“As it is written: Abraham believed God”** — to believe
**“it was reputed to him unto justice”** — a sufficient cause
**“unto justice”** — Here he calls righteousness the remission of sins and the observance of a good life.
3.7:
**“Know ye therefore”** — because Abraham was just from faith
**“they who are of faith”** — whose being is from faith
**“the same are the children of Abraham”** — just
3.8:
**“Foreseeing”**
• Not only righteousness from faith, but also blessing, because Scripture says: “In thee shall all nations be blessed”, which is in conformity with your faith. And lest the truth say that Moses thought otherwise: foreseeing that God justifieth the Gentiles by faith.
• That is, showing long before it was done that this was provided, namely that he declared from faith, not from works; that is, he showed it. Or “foretold,” that is, he showed that it was foretold that they would be blessed in eternal beatitude. “In you”: in the imitation of your faith.
**“that God justifieth the Gentiles by faith, told unto Abraham before: In thee shall all nations be blessed”**
• that is, in your seed.
• in the imitation of your faith.
**“all nations”** — not only the Jews.
3.9:
**“Therefore”** — because authority says this.
**“shall be blessed with faithful Abraham”**
• as Abraham was blessed through faith.
• and therefore it is not to be understood otherwise than as he expounded above, so that it is said “in thee,” that is, in the likeness of thy works.
• those who are of faith will be blessed, for it is not from the works of the law but they will be cursed.
3.10:
**“For as many as are of the works of the law, are under a curse”** — of transgression.
**“For as many as”** — This is to be understood not of the works that concern morals, but of those done in those observances. The law written on tablets is profitable; the rest are a burden.
**“are”** — so that they cannot escape the curse.
**“For it is written: Cursed is every one, that abideth not”** — not merely knows it.
**“For it is written”** — Those who are of the works of the law are accursed, because, as it is written by Moses in Deuteronomy: “Cursed is every man,” etc. As if he said: I have commanded many things, which no one will be able to fulfil, but they were given as a burden, and therefore all are accursed. In which he intimates that a saviour is to be desired, who may put an end to these things and free us not only from other sins but from the curse of the law. Why then do the Galatians pass from grace to the curse?
**“in all things”**
• not only some of them.
• which no one can do. Whence: “Why now do you tempt God, to put a yoke upon the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?”
**“which are written in the book of the law”** — so.
**“to do them”** — not only wish it but fulfil it in deed.
3.11:
**“But that in the law”** — the curse is from the law, but that justice is not from it.
**“no man is justified with God”**
• although among men, who are deceived.
• He is justified before God who worships him freely, that is, not from desire to seek anything from him besides himself, or from fear of losing it. For in him alone is our true blessedness, and it is perfect.
**“it is manifest”** — from the words of Habacuc.
**“because the just man liveth by faith”** — eternal life.
3.12:
**“But the law is not of faith”**
• that it be fulfilled for things to come, but for temporal things.
• Justice and life are from faith; but the law is not from faith. For it might seem that the works of the law were done from faith, so that for them they might hope for eternal things, which is not so; but they kept those things from fear of punishment.
**“He that doth those things”**
• it commands nothing to be believed.
• but for fear.
**“shall live”** — otherwise to be punished.
**“in them”** — not before God.
**“shall live in them”** — He does not say: he who shall do it shall live in it, when he had said before: the law is not of faith, that you may understand the law in this place to be put for the very works which were done in those observances. But those who lived in these works feared, of course, that if they did not do them they would suffer stoning or the cross or something of the kind. He therefore who shall do them shall live in them, not with God, that is, he will have a reward, that he may not be punished by this death. But he who lives by faith, when he has departed hence, will then have the more a reward most present. Therefore whoever either desires or fears the present things that are seen does not live by faith, because faith in God pertains to things invisible.
3.13:
**“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law”** — the curse is from the law, not justice; but Christ redeemed us Jews who were under the curse. Why then do you strive for that?
**“being made a curse for us”**
• while, as a guilty man, he is put to death.
• that you may be his disciple.
**“being made”** — That is, reckoned not only as cursed but even as a curse. Or he was made in truth of the thing, cursed, that is, mortal.
**“for it is written”** — In Deuteronomy.
**“Cursed”**
• therefore he was reckoned accursed because he was hanged.
• That is, dead, because death is from the curse, and every sin is a curse. Or the very thing that is done in order that punishment may follow. Or the very punishment, which is also called sin because it comes from sin. Accursed of God, because God hates sin and our death, since he sent his Son to destroy it. Every one: even Christ, lest heretics to come deny his true death. Foolish honour separates Christ from the curse which is joined to death. The punishment of sin, therefore, since it does not necessarily come from blessing, comes from the curse by which it is said: “If you touch it, you shall die the death.” Or accursed, that is, mortal: but mortality is from sin.
**“every one”** — he truly died; every man, so that no one may exclude Christ.
**“that hangeth on a tree”**
• for his own crimes; which Christ did not do.
• The curse is twofold: of guilt and of punishment. Whence also accursed is said in two ways, namely actively and passively, that is, according to guilt and punishment. For one is not accursed because he is crucified, but because he has fallen into such guilt that he deserved to be crucified, which Christ did not. And therefore, although he was reputed so, yet he was not accursed with the curse of punishment, though with that of guilt.
**“Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree”** — As if it were punishment enough that the guilty man dies hanging, and that he remains there until evening, so that then he is taken down and buried, lest, if he remained there longer, the disgrace and stain would be greater for his family.
*Jerome:* In the Hebrew copies and in our present ones it is found in Deuteronomy: “Cursed is he of God.” In the ancient copies of the Hebrews, however, the name of God is not found. And I think it was added by someone after the Lord’s passion, to defame Christ for us who believe him accursed by God. But this is not to the Lord’s reproach: what wonder if he is called accursed of God who has in himself what God hates, that is, reproves and grieves over, namely sin and death?
3.14:
**“that in the Gentiles”** — so he redeemed us Jews, that also among the Gentiles, who are not under the curse of the law.
**“the blessing of Abraham might come in Christ Jesus, that”** — at length to both.
**“the promise of the Spirit”** — that is, the blessedness which the Spirit, given as a pledge, promises.
**“we may receive by faith”** — by faith, not by works.
3.15:
**“Brethren, after the manner of man”** — that is, human custom.
**“I speak”** — I prove that same thing.
**“Brethren, I speak after the manner of man”** — As if: I have proved by reasons and authorities that the Spirit, justice, and blessedness are given through faith, not through the law. Now I say, that is, I prove, the same according to human custom, in which, although there is often no firmness, yet a man’s testimony is firm, that is, what is made by a man for his heirs. Likewise the law does not make void the testament of God, but it sets before it him to whom it was made, that is, Abraham, so that from the dignity of the giver and the receiver the promise may be seen to be unchangeable. And to his seed, that is, Christ. Not that the promise was made to him, but it pertained to him, because through him the blessing was promised to be given. And that this seed is Christ, not another, he marks from the words of Scripture, which is: “And in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.” Scripture does not say in seeds, as it would if it wished to be understood of many, but in seed, as of one; and that one is Christ, says the Apostle. For no other can be found who has blessed all nations.
**“yet a man's testament, if it be confirmed”** — by witnesses and by the death of the testator.
**“no man despiseth”** — so that he says it is not valid, not rightly made.
**“nor addeth to it”**
• so that he may arrange those matters otherwise; but it is in the authority of all.
• likewise.
3.16:
**“To Abraham”** — whom God would not deceive.
**“the promises were made”**
• in the plural.
• because often the same thing, that is, eternal blessedness, is promised.
**“and to his seed”** — to Christ.
**“his”** — to Abraham.
3.17:
**“Now this I say, that the testament which was confirmed”** — from the promise to Abraham.
**“Now this I say, the testament”** — God promised this to Abraham, and this testament, confirmed by oaths, I say and affirm the law does not make void; it might be thought otherwise of the law because it was given only for a time, since the law was given a long time after the promise made to Abraham; and if the blessing were from it, the men of that time, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, would not have had it.
**“after four hundred and thirty years the law was made, doth not disannul”** — the law does not weaken the promise; but it signifies what things are future, and when.
**“the law doth not disannul”** — That is false, which it would do if the blessing were given through it. For that promise did not say that it was through the law, but through the seed, because if the blessing were through the law, he promised to the seed in vain, and the seed itself came in vain. The law does not make void what would then avail to empty the promise, for it would be false and God would be made a liar. For if the inheritance, that is, eternal blessedness, is from the law, then it is not from what the promise said. He destroys the consequent: but it is given from the promise, which he shows in part because to Abraham, of whom it is certain that he was without the law, God gave it by the repromise, that is, through Christ often promised.
3.18:
**“For if”** — from the works of the law.
**“the inheritance, it is no more of promise”** — the promise is excluded and Abraham is frustrated.
**“To Abraham”** — of whom there is no doubt that he has it.
**“But God gave it to Abraham by promise”** — by faith.
3.19:
**“Why then was the law? Because of transgressions”**
• or so that it might make them transgress, that the physician might be desired.
• or so that through fear they would cease to transgress, so that at some time they would do the same by will.
**“Why then was the law”** — Augustine. In the book of Retractations. Formerly, when I was expounding this chapter, I thought it should be so divided that there would be a question: What then? And then an answer: the law was because of transgression, etc. This indeed is not far from the truth, but this division seems better to me: that the question be: What then is the law? And the answer follow: because of transgression, etc. As if, since the law is not for justice or for blessedness: what then is its usefulness? Why was it given by God? Then, lest it seem given in vain, he explains why it was given, saying: The law was set in the midst because of transgression, etc.
**“it was set until”** — and therefore it is now not to be kept.
**“It was set because of transgressions”** — It was set in the midst between the promise and the seed to whom the promise was made, that is, between Abraham and Christ, to instruct the people of God in the fear of God, that it might become worthy to receive the promise, which is Christ. Or because of transgressions, that is, that man, proudly trusting in his own strength, might receive precepts in which, failing and made a transgressor, he might seek a deliverer and saviour. The law was therefore given to tame man’s pride and to reveal his weakness. It was given also to the hard-hearted as a scourge. It was given also as a sign of things to come, that it might bear witness to the future by figures. Behold the four causes of the giving of the law briefly distinguished, which are more fully explained in the epistle to the Romans, where it is said: “The law entered in,” etc.
**“the seed should come, to whom”**
• of whom.
• God.
**“he made the promise”** — he had promised: that through him all nations would be blessed; against him acts he who brings the law back.
**“being ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator”**
• who is God and man, between God and man.
• It was done by the great counsel of God that after man’s fall the law was not given at once, nor the Son of God sent. For unless man’s pride had first been tried, it would have claimed for the freedom of his own will a sufficiency, and would have judged the law to have been given needlessly and the Son of God to have come in vain. Again, unless the written law had first been given, by which he might prove what he could do, he would have judged Christ’s coming superfluous. Therefore, that man might have no occasion for disparaging or murmuring, God left him first in the freedom of the will under the natural law, that so he might know the powers of his nature; yet when he failed there, seeing that free will was not sufficient for him unto justice, he did not even so humble himself to ask for grace, but proudly, thinking the written law joined to the law of nature sufficient for him, cried out: There is no lack of one to fulfil, but of one to command. So that he might be convicted concerning this law also, before he sent the Son, he gave the law, which partly laid bare the disease, but did not consume it. When it was given, the disease grew strong and the weakness increased, not by the fault of the law but of nature, and by the urging of the devil, that so, the insufficiency of both laws and his own weakness being known, he might cry out to the physician and seek the help of grace; and so it was done. For when the sicknesses were multiplied, afterwards they hastened to the physician, who coming in the form of a servant healed the wounds of the languishing man. This is that Samaritan who drew near to the wounded man who had fallen among robbers and bound up his wounds, whom the priest and the Levite had passed by without mercy, that is, the old law and the priesthood, because the law led no one to perfection. This is that Eliseus who sent his staff to raise the son of the Sunamite; and since the boy did not rise by it, at length Eliseus himself came, contracted himself and fitted himself to the dead child, and the dead one arose. This is also that angel at whose descent the water was moved and one was healed. This is the almighty Word who came from the royal seats, “while all things were in quiet silence.” The first silence was before the law, the second under the law, the third will be in glory. The first, ignorance of the sickness; the second, despair of the cure; the third, the obtaining of health. For before the law man did not recognize his disease, and therefore was silent and sought no remedy. But when the law came in and showed the sick their wounds, at once the silence was broken and the sick began to ask for a remedy. But wishing to be healed by the works of the law, where there is no salvation, they could not find what they sought. At length man, considering that no one can be saved or justified by the law, as though wearied by long crying out and despairing, ceased to speak again, and the second silence followed. Then therefore the almighty Word of the Father, clothed in the form of a servant, came from the royal seats into the world; as Samaritan he drew near to the wounded; as “angel of great counsel” he descended to the pool; as Eliseus he came to raise the dead; that is, the Son of the highest King came from the throne of the Father to bear the death of the passion, from equality of majesty to the gibbet of the cross, from the royal seat to the workshop of sin, from the light of heaven to the darkness of the world or of hell; and coming he spoke peace, gave grace, set forth mercy, promised pardon; and so, the silence being broken, the sick began with pure faith and true confession, as with great outcries, to demand a remedy and to hasten to the physician, by whom their wounds might be healed and their disease cured. Health therefore being received, and the happiness of future immortality given, nothing further will remain to be asked. And then there will be the third, blessed silence.
• Or in the hand of a mediator. And because a mediator is between two extremes, it might seem either that Christ is not God, or that there would be two gods. To this he answers: although the mediator is not of one but of two extremes, yet he is one God with God the Father by the divine nature, between whom and men he mediates by the human.
**“being ordained by angels”** — I say the law was ordained by angels, that is, by Moses and other ministers of God; or given to men by the ministry of angels, in which angels was indeed the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; at times God was figured through them without any distinction of person. And note that he does not say “given” but “ordained,” as if given in due order, between the time of the natural law, of which they were convicted that it could not help, and the time of grace, before which they had to be convicted concerning the law. He who therefore now brings it back acts against the order of the angels.
**“in the hand”** — In the power of Christ, so that it stood while he willed, or ceased; therefore you act against him who destroyed it.
3.20:
**“Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one.”** — A mediator. The law which the mediator has belongs to the Jews only; but yet the mediator himself is not of one people only, that is, of the Jews who had the law, but also of the Gentiles; and therefore do not seek the law that you may have a mediator. The mediator is not of one, but yet he is one, sufficient to reconcile all to God, because he is God; and therefore add nothing else.
**“Now a mediator is not of one”** — Augustine. But of two, because he made peace in himself, the corner stone, between two discordant peoples; taking away from one side the number of gods, from the other the rites of the law, by which they were at variance, and making the two into one in himself. But according to these men, Christ is not the arbiter of two, who, being led into the law, made one people of two; and of one people there is no mediator; but God is one. He says this lest Christ, who as man is mediator, by preaching God, should seem to preach one contrary to the one God, since he himself as man, insofar as he is God, is one with the Father. For the Father and the Son are one God.
*Augustine:* If the Son of God had remained in the natural equality of the Father and had not emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, he would not be mediator of God and men, because the Trinity itself is one God, the same in three, namely in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, the eternity and equality of the deity remaining constant. If then Christ has but one nature, how will he be a mean? For unless you grant such a one between God and men, who is so a mean that he is God by reason of the divinity and man by the nature of humanity, you do not show how human things are reconciled to divine. For he, coming, first joined in himself human things to divine by the communion of both natures in one and the same person; then he reconciled all the faithful to God the Father, since all who by believing loved the humility of Christ, and by loving imitated it, were healed from the impiety of pride.
3.21:
**“Was the law then against the promises of God? God forbid.”** — It is not hostile to the promise but confirms it.
**“Was the law then against”** — Since the law is because of transgression, is it therefore against the promises, so that through it the promise might be fulfilled otherwise than as it was promised? No: because from the law there is no life, that is, eternal blessedness; for if life were from it, then justice also. But justice is not from it. And this is: but hath concluded all; the law itself shut up the Jews entirely under the dominion of sin. Or it shows that all men are shut up under sin.
**“For if there had been a law given which could give life, verily”** — not only from opinion.
**“justice should have been by the law”** — but since this is not so, rather it condemns and shuts up under sin.
3.22:
**“But the scripture hath concluded all under sin”**
• that is, the law remaining and written, or which does not give the quickening Spirit.
• but it is only Scripture.
• why then was it given?
• The law was given so that grace might be sought.
• But the scripture hath concluded, etc. That is, it shows that all men are concluded under sin. For the law was given not to take away sin, but to show all things concluded under sin. It was given to convict of his sickness the sick man who seemed to himself well, that sins might be demonstrated, not taken away. It was given that man might find himself, not that the sickness might be healed, but that, the sickness growing in transgression, a physician might be sought. He therefore who denies his sickness judges the saviour superfluous; therefore let us both praise the creator in our nature, and for the fault inflicted upon us seek the saviour.
**“But the scripture hath concluded”** — The same as to the Romans: “God hath concluded all in unrighteousness, that he may have mercy on all”; with sins made known through the law they are shut up, so that they cannot excuse themselves, but seek mercy.
**“that the promise, by the faith of Jesus Christ, might be given to them that believe.”**
• therefore God so ordered that men, by their own weakness and that of the law becoming known, might hasten to grace and by believing obtain the promises.
• The law shut up under sin, but nevertheless was useful.
3.23:
**“But before the faith came”** — by the burden of the law, or against their will.
**“we were kept under the law”** — not free but slaves.
**“shut up”** — compelled to serve as if in dungeons.
**“unto that faith which was to be revealed”** — because hidden among the ancients.
3.24:
**“Wherefore”** — because the law kept us toward faith; therefore.
**“the law was our pedagogue”** — restraining boys from unlawful things and directing them to right things by fear of punishments.
**“in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith”**
• while we were untaught the law was our pedagogue.
• Before (that is, therefore after) faith came, which is spontaneous, which no merit called forth. We were kept, not free but slaves. Shut up, that so, being accustomed, we might be led into it, that is, into so good a faith, which was to be revealed in the time of Christ, when many things that were before obscure were made plain. Behold the honour of the law, that it kept us as a pedagogue; but this is not great, because it belongs to boys, not to adults. A pedagogue in Christ, in the instruction of Christ, who therefore instructed us, that so coming to faith like boys we might be justified unto perfection. Or in Christ, that is, in carrying out the precepts of Christ.
3.25:
**“But after the faith is come”** — soon, or in this life we have this good and a greater in the future.
**“we are no longer under a pedagogue”** — that is, the compulsion which is not necessary for free men.
3.26:
**“For you are all the children of God by faith, in Christ Jesus.”**
• being.
• one and the same with him, not by nature but by the bond of charity.
**“For you are all”** — We Jews, in the time of faith, forsake the pedagogue, because you Gentiles, who had not the law, are all sons; what then we forsake by a true example, do you take up? As if he said: you ought not to do this.
3.27:
**“For as many of you as”** — by faith you are in Christ; hence whoever, that is, of whatever condition or sex.
**“in Christ”** — In the institution of Christ and in the likeness of his death.
**“have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ.”**
• in which Christ, that is, in whose faith.
• Put on. That is, you have been made conformed to him, which is for you honor and protection against heat. That Christ is a garment the apostle explains elsewhere, saying: “Put ye on our Lord Jesus Christ.”
*Augustine:* Of baptism. Men put on Christ sometimes as far as the receiving of the sacrament, and sometimes also as far as the sanctification of life. And the first is common to good and bad, but the second is proper to the good.
3.28:
**“There is neither Jew”** — because none is more worthy on account of any of these; therefore let no one Judaize, as if by this he were more worthy.
**“nor Greek: there is neither bond nor free: there is neither male nor female. For you are all”** — none of these is in Christ, since you are all Gentiles.
**“For you are all one”** — not differing in anything.
3.29:
**“And if you be Christ's”** — as if you are in Christ.
**“then are you the seed of Abraham”** — that is, righteous through faith, as Abraham was. Although you are the seed of Abraham. What then is more to the Jews? Nothing.
**“seed of Abraham, heirs according to the promise”**
• that is, according to faith in the promised Christ, not according to fleshly observances.
• I say you are the seed of Abraham, and therefore.
**“Then are you the seed of Abraham”** — Jerome. Above, Christ is called the seed of Abraham, where it is read that the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. But here the sons of Christ, that is, all believers, are called the seed of Abraham. But whenever Christ is named the seed of Abraham, it is to be understood bodily, because he is begotten of his stock. But whenever we who believe in him are called the seed of Abraham, then we ought to receive it spiritually, as the seed of faith.
**“heirs”** — of the kingdom.

4.1:
**“Now I say, as long as the heir is a child”** — in age and knowledge.
**“Now I say”** — Now you Gentiles and we Jews are Christ’s, and the seed of Abraham, and heirs; but formerly we Jews were under the law, like an heir who is to be, and appointed by the Father. Behold again why the law is not to be kept.
**“he differeth nothing from a servant”** — compelled, has no power.
**“though”** — although.
**“he be lord”** — about to be.
4.2:
**“But is under tutors”** — who defend him against enemies.
**“and governors”** — appointed, at which the freedom of himself and his people is given to him.
**“until the time appointed”** — by knowledge of God and by strength.
**“Until the time appointed”** — For after he is grown up, he has the freedom of himself and of his own things; otherwise he is rightly disinherited. The law was a pedagogue, because it restrained by fear and compelled them to serve the precepts of God. It was tutor and agent to the Jews, whom God appointed heirs, while they were little children in the knowledge of God and in strength to resist sins. In that time they were also slaves under the penalties of the law, terrified from evils, stirred by promises; and what was condemned was not themselves but their vices, nor were their own things condemned, that is, the eternal inheritance, although they were lords of these, appointed by God. For them the law stood in the place of a tutor, while it defended them against the assaults of malignant spirits and the persuasions of the Gentiles, who would draw them to idolatry, by admonishing, rebuking, sometimes punishing. It preserved eternal goods for them, since Christ freed many of them from hell. It was also an agent, because it pleaded their cause before God, while through sacrifices and expiation it appeased God for them; and this until the time appointed, that is, until the coming of Christ, in whom God ordained that they should become perfect and free and obtain the inheritance, otherwise they would be disinherited.
4.3:
**“So we also, when we were children, were serving under the elements of the world”** — under the law, which is the first instruction to faith and righteousness.
**“under the elements”** — Ambrose. In the elements he signifies the new moons, that is, the lunar days, and the sabbath; not that they hoped in the elements as the pagans did, but that in these they worshipped God.
**“of the world”** — Augustine. Because the law promised not heavenly but earthly things, or transitory things like the world; or the new moons, that is, the lunar days and the sabbath, are in the elements.
**“were serving”** — both frightened by threats and captivated by flatteries.
4.4:
**“But when the fulness of the time was come”**
• that is, after the preceding time was fulfilled; or because in it the gifts of the Spirit are given in fullness.
• Or the fulness of time, that is, after that whole span was fulfilled during which the law was to last, then God sent.
**“The fulness of the time”** — He knew when he ought to come, or also to suffer, etc. For the hour is not his or ours except by his will. Yet a long series of heralds had to be sent before.
**“sent”** — made visible to men.
**“God sent his Son, made of a woman”** — also.
**“God sent his Son”** — Whence: I, he says, came out from the Father and came into this world. And yet of him the evangelist John says: “He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not.” Then he adds: “He came unto his own.” Therefore he was sent to where he already was. Whence also the prophet says: “Do not I fill heaven and earth?” We must therefore ask how this sending is to be understood, if we are to think soberly what is worthy of the Son of God. We ought to understand him as sent for this reason: that out of that incomprehensible and unspeakable secret of majesty the Word of God gave himself profoundly to be comprehended by our minds, not only when he emptied himself, but also when he dwelt in us, as it is written: “I will dwell in them.”
**“made of a woman”** — The usage of Hebrew speech calls women not corrupt ones but females.
**“made under the law”** — under the burden of the law, as under other penalties.
**“Made under the law”** — That he might appear circumcised, as a son of Abraham, to whom he had been promised, bearing the sign of him to whom he had been promised, in whom circumcision was fulfilled, and therefore the sign might now cease. For Abraham believed that he would have a son in whom all nations would be blessed, which we believe is now done.
4.5:
**“That he might redeem them who were under the law”** — not that they might be cleansed from it, but that he might free them from it, as from penalties.
**“redeem”** — that is, the good things that are given through grace, by which they are sons.
**“that we might receive the adoption of sons”**
• as our nature partakes, so he adopts us to his own.
• That is, that we might be partakers of the divine glory. For as he himself shares in our nature, so he adopts us to see his own. For from this we receive adoption, that the only Son of God did not disdain to share in our nature, being made of a woman, so that he might be not only the only-begotten, but also become the firstborn among many brethren. But he says adoption that we may distinctly understand the only Son of God. For we are sons of God by benefit and by condescension; he is Son by nature, who is what the Father is.
• He said “might receive,” not “might take,” to signify that we lost this in Adam, from whom we are mortal.
*Augustine:* Against Faustus. For God has one only Son, whom he begot of his own substance. But us he did not beget of his own substance. For we are his creature, which he did not beget but made. And therefore he adopted us, that he might make us brethren of Christ after our manner. This manner, therefore, in which God, when we were already not born of him but created, begot us, instituted by his Word and his grace, that we might be his sons, is called adoption. Whence: “He gave them power to be made the sons of God,” etc.
4.6:
**“And because you are sons”** — not only we Jews who believe are sons, but also you Gentiles; which the effect proves, because he sent.
**“God hath sent”** — Father.
**“the Spirit”** — whom the Son also sends.
**“God hath sent the Spirit”** — Ambrose. That we might be proved adopted as sons by God, he gave us his Spirit, who shows the Father’s sign in the sons, so that, because we would not dare to say this on account of our weakness and unworthiness, he suggests it so that we may dare to say it.
**“of his Son”** — who proves that you are sons.
**“the Spirit of his Son”**
• Note that the Spirit is also the Son’s. And note here also the Trinity. Augustine on John: If perhaps someone asks whether the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son. For the Son is the Son of the Father alone, and the Father is the Father of the Son alone. But the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of one of them, but of both. Whence the Lord says: “The Spirit of your Father that speaketh in you.” And the Apostle says here: “God hath sent the Spirit of his Son.” And there are many other testimonies by which it is clearly shown that he is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son, who in the Trinity is called the Holy Spirit. Nor do I think he is properly called the Holy Spirit for any other reason, since even if we are asked about each singly, we cannot call the Father and the Son anything but Spirit, since God is a Spirit. What therefore they are called in common, they are also singly. It was fitting that he be properly called this who is not one of them, but in whom the communion of both appears. Why then should we not believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son, since he is also the Spirit of the Son? For if he did not proceed from him, he would not, presenting himself to the disciples after the resurrection, have breathed on them, saying: “Receive ye the Holy Ghost.” For what else did that breathing signify, but that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him? To this also pertains what he says of the woman with the issue: “Somebody hath touched me; for I know that virtue is gone out from me.” For that the Holy Spirit is called by the name of virtue is clear from what the angel said to Mary: “And the power of the most High shall overshadow thee.” And the Lord, promising the disciples, says: “Stay you here till you be endued with power from on high.”
• This is the virtue which went out from him and healed all. Yet the Son himself says that he proceeds from the Father, because he is accustomed to refer to him even what is his own, from whom he himself is, as elsewhere: “My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me.” From whom the Son has it that he is God: for he is God of God; from him he has it that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from him.
**“into your hearts”** — of Jews as well as Gentiles.
**“crying: Abba, Father.”** — who makes us cry out what we would never presume unless the Spirit taught.
**“crying”** — Jerome. Note that in the Scriptures “cry” is understood not as the utterance of a great voice but as the greatness of knowledge and intention.
**“Abba, Father”** — He elegantly put two words meaning the same thing on account of the whole people, which was called from Jews and Gentiles into the unity of the faith, so that the Hebrew word pertains to the Hebrews, the Greek to the Gentiles. But both words have the same meaning, for the unity of the same faith and Spirit.
4.7:
**“Wherefore”** — because the Spirit cries in you: 'Father.'
**“now he is not a servant”**
• from the time of grace.
• anyone of us who believe in Christ, as once.
**“but a son”**
• from the time of Christ.
• serving out of love.
**“And if a son, an heir”** — in the future.
**“through God”** — through the working of God.
4.8:
**“But then indeed”** — now sons; but then, when unbelievers.
**“not knowing God”** — and so there was some excuse.
**“them, who, by nature”** — not of themselves but by the opinion of men.
4.9:
**“But now”**
• when the truth is revealed.
• Who by nature are not gods. Ambrose. He shows that there is one nature of the true God, namely of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. But what is it to be God by nature, except to be the true God? Whence the Apostle elsewhere: “You turned to serve the living and true God.”
**“after that you have known God”** — and so sin more gravely than formerly.
**“or rather are known by God”** — that you were approved and loved, not by you but rather by the grace of God.
**“or rather are known”** — Scripture frequently uses this kind of speech. Whence: “So in the sanctuary have I come before thee, to see thy power and thy glory,” that is, you saw me that I might see you. God knows us, that is, he gives us knowledge of himself. For it is not from ourselves that we know him; from eternity indeed he knows, but he is then said to know when he makes himself known.
**“how turn you”** — from the faith.
**“again”** — as before conversion.
**“to the weak”** — because they are changed in unstable appearance.
**“weak”** — Truly the law, which is needy because it does not justify perfectly, insofar as it helps, does so not by itself but in respect to grace.
**“and needy”** — because they lack the highest and stable form of the Creator, so that they may be as they are.
**“needy”** — Elements are so called that need one another in order to govern the world. Days, as when they say: today nothing is to be begun. Months, when those who study the course of the moon say: under such a moon nothing is to be begun. Times, as when they say: now is the beginning of spring. Years, when they say: it is a new year. But there ought to be no suspicion of these things, because whatever is done simply in devotion to God can turn out well. They were doubly subverted, so as to be turned back to the law and to their former errors.
**“elements”** — that is, the initial law for the worship of God.
**“how turn you again”** — As if the law after Christ did not differ from ancient idolatry.
**“you desire to serve”** — You wish to serve the elements; and truly, since you already observe days in the Jewish rite, as sabbaths.
4.10:
**“You observe days, and months, and times, and years.”** — This you already do, but I fear worse.
**“You observe days”**
• It would not be thought grave by God unless the Apostle said: “I am afraid lest perhaps I have laboured in vain.” Those observe this who wish or refuse to begin on certain days, months or years, as if times were lucky or unlucky.
• Those are blamed who follow the constellations, not those who know the natural effects of the elements in the well-ordered revolution of the stars, so as, for example, not to sail in a tempest, not to sow in autumn; of which, when they were made, it is said in Genesis: “And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years.”
**“Months”** — As the new moons. Times, as of the going out from Egypt. Years, the sevenths and the seventh of the seventh decade, which after the captivity, returning to Jerusalem, they observed in place of the fiftieth, which is called the jubilee.
