*Jerome:* Days: as from the tenth of the first month to the fourteenth, on which the lamb was sacrificed, and from the fourteenth to the twenty-first of the same month, when unleavened bread was eaten. Also the seven weeks which the Israelites reckon by the Jewish rite, and they keep Pentecost, and also the sounding of trumpets on the first of the seventh month. Also on the tenth of the same month the atonement and fast, and on the fifteenth the Feast of Tabernacles. Months: as the new moons. Those also keep months who observe the first and the seventh month. And the seventh years. I think indeed that this is said of the seventh year of remission and of the fiftieth, which is called by them the jubilee, which the Jews at times could not keep in its order, being oppressed by captivity. When this was ended, they kept in its place the seventh year of the seventh decade. This can be understood either as the sixty-seventh year, in which leave to return from Babylon was granted them by Cyrus and Darius. Whence, when seventy years were completed, they returned. Or rather the seventy-seventh, which, having returned to Jerusalem, they observed in place of the fiftieth, which is called the jubilee.
4.11:
**“I am afraid of you”** — Your fickleness, not otherwise.
**“lest perhaps ... in vain”** — For profit; which is, if you fully receive the law.
4.12:
**“Be ye as I”**
• Who dismissed the law.
• Be as I. Because I also, who had the law, am now without the law, as you also are and ought to be as I, because I beseech you. Nothing excuses me, because false teachers had said Paul was an enemy to the Galatians, nor had he wished them to be taught what he preached in other churches.
**“because I also am”** — I was once under the law.
**“as you”** — Now you wish to be so, and I dismissed it not without reason.
**“Because I also am as you”** — A man corrected from error; and so you can be corrected.
**“brethren, I beseech you”** — As if to say: I beseech, and I can do so safely, as those whom I rightly love.
**“Brethren, I beseech”** — He restores those corrected harshly by good deeds.
**“you have not injured me at all”**
• And so the cause of enmity is not with you.
• You did not injure me, but received me with honour when you had a reason to despise me.
4.13:
**“And you know, how through infirmity”** — When I suffered persecution.
**“of the flesh”** — Because my flesh was afflicted.
**“I preached the gospel to you heretofore”** — And for so long a time you did not despise me, etc.
4.14:
**“and your temptation”** — That is, me troubled; through which the devil tempted you that you would not believe.
**“your”** — By which it might be seen what kind of people you are.
**“Your temptation”** — For they were tested, when the apostle suffered tribulation according to the flesh, whether they would desert him through fear or embrace him in love.
**“in my flesh, you despised not”**
• After conversion, that I might be more base.
• As one base before conversion.
**“nor rejected”**
• So that you would shrink from being turned from this.
• So that you would not share in my danger.
**“but received me as an angel of God”** — As if an angel had come, or you believed me an angel.
**“even as”** — As if he himself had come.
**“Christ Jesus”**
• Who in him.
• And because then you did so.
4.15:
**“Where is then”**
• as if to say: it is indeed wonderful that you have fallen from the good.
• Wondering at their spiritual work, he commends it, so that, considering this, they may not fall into carnal fear. And because they had changed for the worse, he rebukes them. For although they received him as an angel, he does not on that account spare to cut and to burn, because he seeks not his own but the things of Christ; he seeks not milk and wool from the sheep, that is, the profit of supplying need and the favour of honour, but the salvation of all.
**“your blessedness”**
• by which you were called blessed, fervent in good beginnings and, as it were, in certain steps of advancing.
• as if to say: be ashamed that you have been changed.
**“For I bear you witness”** — you were truly blessed, or: you received me as an angel and as Christ.
**“that, if it could be done”**
• for the profit of the Church.
• it cannot be done that is not done justly.
**“If it could be done”** — Augustine. Could not that have been done which the Apostle says? What is not justly done cannot be done. So also Job: “Oh that I could kill myself.” And the Lord to Lot: “I cannot do anything till thou go in thither.” He said he could not, because he undoubtedly could by power, but could not by justice.
**“you would have plucked out your own eyes”**
• which among all things is dearest to you.
• and therefore more is to be grieved over you.
**“and would have given them to me”** — for the profit of my preaching.
4.16:
**“Am I then become your enemy”** — and since this is so, it is therefore credible that I have become an enemy.
**“I tell you the truth”**
• as if I seem an enemy by this, because I tell the truth; but if I were deceiving, I would be thought a friend.
• Because whoever rebukes one who wants no one to point out his error seems an enemy.
4.17:
**“They are zealous”**
• they love.
• I am not an enemy, but they are zealous, etc. For they are zealous not well, who do not so much desire that those men be better as that they wish to make them worse and drag them backward by perverse zeal.
**“in your regard not well”** — not profitably.
**“but they would exclude you”** — from faith to the law, or from my love.
**“that you might be zealous for them”**
• in legal matters.
• but you.
4.18:
**“that which is good”** — namely me and men of that kind.
**“But be zealous”**
• love, imitate.
• and this.
**“in a good thing”** — that is, love for this reason, because in it is virtue and good work, not for any other thing.
**“always”** — so that by persevering step you may arrive at the end of the good work.
**“and not only”** — be zealous for good.
**“when I am present with you”** — but especially when absent.
4.19:
**“My little children”**
• because now you are weak and need perfect steps.
• That which is born in you; for it was not yet born of her. Thus little ones are born in the bowels of the Church, until, being formed, they come forth.
*Augustine:* My little children. Again he begins to show from the law itself why it is not to be kept. Imitate me, because you are my sons. Or: not only is it proved from what has been said that the law is to be set aside, but the authority of the law itself shows this. Say, little children; answer; for the sentence hangs on thus far. And that is inserted: of whom I am in labour again, etc. Have you read the law or not? Whatever they choose, they are proved fools. If they have not read it, they ought not to receive what they do not know. If they have read it, it itself proves that it is to be set aside. And if they do not understand, they are fools.
**“of whom I am in labour again”** — as before, with pain and labor, I beget to the light of faith.
**“until Christ”** — Whom you have deformed, let him be beautiful in you. Or that he may appear beautiful to others through you. It is said more weightily, as if he said that they be formed in Christ.
**“I am in labour again until Christ be formed in you”** — Until Christ be formed, etc. That is, that you may receive his likeness, which you lost by real fault. For very few consider what labour there is in preachers, first, and with what pains they bring souls to birth in faith and right conduct. Whence the Apostle had first begotten them through faith in baptism, but afterwards they were deformed by false teachers and made weak; now he reforms them with pain. Whence he adds: until Christ be formed in you. For those who conceive faith, but do not attend to the sense of the faith, are denied to have Christ formed in their souls.
*Augustine:* For Christ is formed in the heart of believers, when the sacraments of grace are opened to them and those things that seemed obscure become clear.
4.20:
**“And I would willingly”**
• as if: I have just now used soft words, calling you brothers and sons.
• so that the apostle might be confounded by blushing
• Knowing that a word spoken to those present has greater force, the Apostle desires to change the apostolic voice, contained in letters, into presence. For divine Scripture edifies when read, but it profits much more if it is changed from letters into voice. For the living voice has great force, a voice resounding from the mouth of its author, which is uttered and distinguished with that pronunciation with which it was begotten in the heart of the man. The sense, therefore, is: because I am ashamed for you, I would willingly utter the voice of the letter in person from my own mouth, that I myself might rebuke you more severely than usual; because a letter cannot express the voice of one who reproaches, cannot sound the cry of one who is angry, nor unfold the grief of the heart with its strokes. For I do not have the fruits which teachers are wont to have from their disciples, and without it the seed of doctrine has been cast. So that I may say with Jeremias: “I have not profited, neither hath any man profited me.”
**“be present with you now, and change”** — to reproach
**“my voice”** — that I might say to you things worthy of you, which I am unwilling to write, lest they remain among you
**“because I am ashamed for you”** — I am ashamed before others on your account
4.21:
**“Tell me, you that desire to be under the law”**
• carnally
• you have read but have not understood
4.22:
**“For it is written”**
• therefore I ask whether you have read; for in it indeed it is written that Abraham had two sons; which, if you had attended to, you would never return to it
• It is written that he had two, though he had more; but Scripture spiritually follows up each of the two, hinting that something outstanding is foreshadowed in these.
**“had two sons”** — Ismael and Isaac
**“Two sons”** — Augustine. He had more: for after the death of Sarah he begot others by another wife, namely Cethura, who do not pertain to this signification.
**“the one”** — namely Ismael
**“by a bondwoman”** — Agar
**“and the other”** — namely Isaac
**“by a free woman”** — namely Sara
**“The one by a bondwoman, and the other by a free woman”** — Nor did he distinguish the two sons of Abraham in vain, but by a different working: because he who was of the bondwoman was born according to the nature of the flesh, by which a young woman is wont to conceive of an old man; he who was of the free woman, not according to the force of the flesh, as a barren old woman of an old man, but by the working of God who promised. The one, therefore, custom showing nature begot; the other, promise signifying grace gave. There human usage is shown, here the divine benefit is commended. Allegorically: Abraham is God the Father, who is the father of many nations; the free woman is the New Testament giving to all through Christ new grace; Agar, the Old Testament. In both God begot sons for himself who should serve: but in the old the Jews are servants, because of fear of punishment and promises of temporal things, and this is according to the flesh, which both dreads punishments and loves sweet things; the grace of the New Testament brings forth free men who serve out of love, not by the force of the flesh but by the work of God. For who would believe things impossible according to nature, who would despise what is pleasant in the present, unless he hoped for things unseen, unless the power of God worked here in him?
4.23:
**“But he who”** — The Jews and all slaves of sin
**“was of the bondwoman, was born according to the flesh”** — born by no miracle but by the law of nature
**“But he”** — the free Christian
**“of the free woman, was by promise”** — was born miraculously
4.24:
**“Which things are said by an allegory”** — by another understanding
*Allegorically:* It is said that something seems to sound one thing in the words and to signify another in the meaning, as here by Abraham God the Father is meant; for he is the father of many nations. For Abraham means father of many, and of nations is understood.
**“For these are”** — the bondwoman and the free woman are, that is, signify
**“the two testaments. The one”**
• the Old Testament
• was given
**“from mount Sina, engendering unto bondage”** — because they served through fear, or were slaves of sin
**“From mount Sina”** — That in such a place signifies that they were proud of the commandment against other nations, or that they themselves were proud and puffed up against the commandment itself. As witness to this is Agar, that is, signified by Agar: Agar means alienation, because it estranges from the inheritance.
**“which is Agar”**
• alienation
• truly the Old Testament begets into slavery, because
4.25:
**“For Sina”** — the Old Testament given on that mountain
**“is a mountain in Arabia”** — not in the land of promise where the sons are, but where as it were they are slaves and strangers
**“Arabia”** — Humility or affliction, because they were afflicted under carnal observances.
**“who”** — a mountain in all things
**“hath affinity”** — that is, like
**“which mount”** — Ambrose. In all things it is joined and like to that Jerusalem, that is, to the Jewish people which now is, that is, which serves for a time; the whole people is the mother, the individuals are the sons. Or the proselytes, who all serve for fear of punishment, in all these things; except that the old law is not to be held, but the new, which is above, which is free.
**“to that”** — to the Jewish people that now is
**“Jerusalem which now is”**
• this is the Synagogue, which begets under sin
• which loves earthly things
**“and is in bondage with her children”** — this Synagogue serves through fear or under sin
4.26:
**“But that Jerusalem”** — the Church gathered from the Gentiles
**“which is above”** — which rejoices with the Lord in hope
**“Which is above”** — The heavenly city is that of the saints, although in some whom it here brings forth it is still a pilgrim. Sara the barren signifies that the nature of the human race, corrupted by sin and therefore condemned, deserved nothing of true happiness for the future. Isaac born by the promise signifies the sons of grace; and because this was to come about not by regeneration but by generation, therefore circumcision was then commanded, when a son was promised from Sara. For circumcision signifies nature renewed, having put off its oldness. That he commands all sons and servants to be circumcised testifies that this grace pertains to all.
**“Jerusalem is free”** — because it loves and serves out of love
**“which is our mother”**
• of believers, namely
• truly that which is above is free, because Scripture says this
• which is the mother, because each, instructed by its word and example, serves out of charity
**“Which is our mother”** — Augustine. The heavenly city is called our mother, because we are called to it. And it is therefore called heavenly, because heaven is its seat. And those whom it begets will be there with it.
4.27:
**“For it is written”** — in Isaias
**“It is written”** — That she is free and a mother, he proves by the authority of Isaias, adding:
**“Rejoice”** — Rejoice, break forth, cry out, pertain to freedom, because “many are the children” pertains to the mother. Isaias, looking to the time of Christ, addresses the Church of the Gentiles, before barren, then fruitful, saying: O barren Church, who in the time of the law bearest not by the power of a miracle, because at that time she begot as it were none, nor travailest, because she had not yet an adornment, rejoice in heart, break forth, show the joy of thy mind outwardly. Cry out, preach thy joy to others, because the children of thee, once desolate, are more than of her that is bringing forth in the meantime; Isaias would say this superfluously of the ancient Sara.
*Augustine:* For the Church was barren among all the Gentiles, before this offspring which we see arose.
*Ambrose:* The heavenly Jerusalem is barren because it does not bear according to the flesh nor suffer pains, but begets spiritually without passion, crying out in joy.
**“for many are the children”** — from Adam
**“of the desolate”** — by childbirth, not by the love of the husband
**“more than of her that hath a husband”**
• the law for begetting
• which begets carnally under the law
*Ambrose:* The Synagogue, therefore, is that which has a husband, that is, the law. But the desolate and wandering multitude of the Gentiles, living without any power of a husband, is that which was also barren, bringing forth the offspring of no lawful word.
*Augustine:* But nature, corrupted by sin, begets the citizens of the earthly city. But grace, freeing nature from sin, begets the citizens of the heavenly city.
**“her that hath a husband”** — The Synagogue indeed had a husband, that is, the law, and was once fruitful in children. But the barren Church, without a husband, Christ, without any word of a bridegroom, lay long in the desert. But after that one received a bill of divorce and turned every ornament of the husband to the ornament of the idol, then the husband, the former girdle rotting, wove for his loins another belt, another girdle from the Gentiles; which, as soon as she was joined to the husband, conceived and brought forth. Whence Isaias cries out: “Enlarge the place of thy tent, and lengthen thy cords.”
4.28:
**“Now we, brethren”** — there are two sons: one according to the flesh, the other by the promise of nature
**“as Isaac was”**
• after the likeness of Isaac
• Isaac: laughter, that is, those who serve in gladness, not out of sadness or necessity
**“are the children of promise”** — begotten through grace
**“are”** — we are sons according to Isaac
4.29:
**“But as then”** — Ismael, or also Esau
**“he that was born according to the flesh persecuted him”** — Isaac or Jacob.
**“persecuted”** — I do not think we can easily find where Ismael persecuted Isaac, but only that when the son of the Egyptian was playing with Isaac, Sara was indignant.
*Augustine:* For Sara understood the sport to be persecution, because the sport of the greater toward the lesser is mockery and deception, because, intending other things, he feigns certain things to the boy, that is, the weak one, and works frauds; so also now those persecute more who seduce by mocking. And as Sara then understood that sport, so now the Church understands this sport to be persecution.
*Augustine:* All who in the Church seek earthly happiness from the Lord belong to Ismael. Cast out. This will be when the threshing floor begins to be winnowed; and the ancient ministers of the Old Testament, seeking grace, are sons of the promise.
**“him that was after the spirit”**
• holy
• those who according to the flesh persecute those who according to the Spirit
**“so also it is now”** — by this we are proved to be sons of promise
4.30:
**“But what saith the scripture”** — we suffer from them, but it is not to be cared for, because what Scripture reports Sara to have said
**“Cast out the bondwoman and her son”** — so the law and the Jews, cast out from the Church and from the grace of the Father
**“for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman”** — that is, the wicked with the good, the Jews with the Christians. For just as now they are unlike in their way of life, so they will be in future in recompense
4.31:
**“So then, brethren”** — because we suffer from the Jews and other evils, so Isaac from Ismael
**“we are not the children of the bondwoman”** — because we are not slaves of sin or of the law
**“but of the free”** — namely of the heavenly Jerusalem
**“By the freedom”** — Augustine. The freedom by which we are set free by Christ is the forgiveness of sins, and justification by faith working through love.

5.1:
**“by the freedom wherewith Christ has made us free.”** — not in any other way but through that freedom by which he who was free from sin, obedient through love, set us free
**“Stand fast, and”** — and because we are free
**“be not held again under the yoke of bondage.”** — this servitude is no lighter than idolatry
**“be held”** — nor even by circumcision, because
5.2:
**“Behold, I Paul”** — who am of noted authority
**“tell you, that if you be circumcised”**
• that you may have hope of salvation in him
• circumcision now not only does not profit but harms
**“If you be circumcised”** — Augustine. Circumcision and the other legal observances are not harmful to those born and instituted under them, though not necessary; it was more harmful to forbid them as if harmful. But the Gentiles are not to be compelled to such things; yet if they do not wish to conform to them, as Timothy did, they are not to be forbidden; but if they trust in them, they are lost. It is therefore lawful for these to hold them, that they may not seem rather condemned than ended; but they are not to be imposed on the Gentiles, lest they seem either not to have been instituted as a cause of promising Christ, or still to promise him; but by their ceasing it is now clear they were signs of the future, which were to be buried with honor by being gradually abandoned, not fled from as the sacrileges of the Gentiles.
*Jerome:* Or he said that these legal observances after the passion of Christ are harmful, whether hope be placed in them or not, to those who observe them, unless they are kept by way of dispensation. Whence he says: Before the new preaching began it was fitting to be circumcised. But now, faith succeeding the law, circumcision added will profit the believer nothing but will hurt.
*Ambrose:* For it is a greater evil to become a slave from being free than to be born one.
5.3:
**“testify”** — nor will this be the only evil for you
**“again”** — as formerly before faith
**“to every man”** — to Jew and Gentile
**“circumcising himself”** — for the sake of having righteousness
**“that he is a debtor to the whole law.”**
• that is, out of obligation he must fulfil all the legal observances which circumcision requires
• for just as baptism demands its own justification, so circumcision demands its own
• Christ will not profit, because you who were earlier full of the grace of Christ
**“A debtor to the whole law”** — He says this so that, by the terror of the countless observances written in the law (lest all be compelled to fulfil them, which neither the Jews themselves nor their fathers could fulfil, as Peter says), they should abstain from those things to which some wished to subject them.
5.4:
**“You are made void of Christ”** — by the virtues of Christ
**“who”** — I mean you.
**“in the law”** — otherwise circumcision would not harm.
**“are justified”** — you believe to be justified.
**“you are fallen from grace.”**
• future, that is, you are unworthy of eternal blessedness.
• already possessed.
• has fallen from grace, which came so that, the burden ceasing, it might justify; he who brings back this burden loses this grace.
5.5:
**“For we in spirit”** — who does not deceive.
**“For we”** — He who trusts in the law loses grace, which can seem to be the opposite, since justice and hope come from faith, that is, eternal blessedness; and we do this through the Spirit, lest we be thought to be deceived.
**“by faith, wait for the hope of justice.”** — by faith, because not from another source.
**“The hope of justice”** — That is, the hope which justice hopes for, namely eternal life; or by which justice itself is hoped for. For faith, hungering and thirsting for justice, hopes to be renewed and to advance in it; or the hope of justice is Christ, from whom justice itself is hoped for.
5.6:
**“For”** — to those who are.
**“in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision”**
• circumcision is equated with uncircumcision.
• For in Christ Jesus, etc. For those who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus, virtues are to be sought and vices fled. But the things in between, which lie between virtues and vices, are neither to be sought nor fled, such as circumcision and uncircumcision, which avail nothing in Christ.
**“availeth any thing, but faith”** — which is not idle.
**“But faith”** — Augustine. Without love faith is empty. Faith with love is that of a Christian; the other is that of the demon. For “the devils also believe and tremble.” But those who do not believe are slower and worse than the demons. But it is very uncertain whether one believes that he is Christ or believes in Christ. For the demons believed that he is Christ, yet they did not believe in Christ. For he believes in Christ who hopes in Christ and loves Christ.
**“that worketh by charity.”**
• of God and neighbour.
• or charity.
**“worketh”** — and this once was in you.
5.7:
**“You did run”** — by perfecting [yourselves] through the works of faith.
**“well.”** — because from love.
**“You did run well”** — Here he praises the Galatians, and blames those through whom they were led to want to Judaize, and warns that they not consent to them.
**“who hath hindered you”** — or bewitched.
**“the truth”** — which thrusts itself forward unasked.
**“not to obey?”** — they labour in every way to hinder your course, but do not consent to any of them.
**“No one”** — of them.
**“consented.”**
• at least by listening to them, because they urge that the works of the law must be kept.
• as if: 'therefore do not consent, because'.
5.8:
**“This persuasion”** — by which they wish to put you under the yoke of the law.
**“is not from him”** — namely of God.
**“that calleth you.”**
• to life.
• but from the devil.
5.9:
**“A little leaven”** — do not consent, because a little leaven, that is, those few sour things, or this persuasion, or circumcision and a little of the law.
**“A little leaven corrupteth”** — Augustine. Do not think the plots of a few men are to be despised; for a spark is a small thing, and almost when it is seen it is not seen. But if it has laid hold of tinder and found nourishment for itself, it consumes walls, the widest cities, forests and regions. And as leaven seems a small thing and of no account, yet when mixed with the flour it corrupts the whole mass, and all that is mixed passes into its power; so also perverse doctrine, beginning from one, at first in the beginning scarcely finds two or three hearers, but little by little it creeps like a cancer in the body. And according to the common proverb, the scab of one sheep defiles the whole flock. Therefore the spark must be put out as soon as it appears, and the leaven removed from the neighbouring mass, and the scabby animal driven away from the folds of all.
**“the whole lump.”** — the congregation of the Church of the faithful; that is, or of the virtues
5.10:
**“I have confidence”**
• I exhort this and am confident.
• He says he is confident about these men because they erred not willingly but by being deceived. And therefore, now that the true way has been shown, he believes they will easily return.
**“among you”** — because they are good
**“in the Lord”** — God working
**“that you will not be of another mind.”**
• than what I taught
• as if: I am confident in you, but he
**“But he that troubleth you”**
• as if the pure fountain of your understanding
• troubles, that is, so that, the order being changed, you may be carnal instead of spiritual.
**“shall bear the judgment”**
• he will undergo condemnation
• he shall not be spared by anyone
**“whosoever he be.”** — even if he be a son of Abraham according to the flesh
**“Whosoever he be”** — They say he tears at Peter in secret, to whose face he wrote above that he had withstood him, because he did not walk with a right foot to the truth of the gospel. But neither would Paul speak with so bold a curse of the prince of the Church, nor would Peter be worthy to bear the judgment of the Church. Whence it must be judged that it is said of some other, who either had been with the apostles, or had come from Judea, or had believed from among the Pharisees, or was some great man so esteemed among the Galatians, that he should bear the judgment of the troubled Church.
5.11:
**“And I, brethren,”** — But I do not trouble by preaching legal things.
**“And I”** — For it was laid to him by false teachers that he preached circumcision elsewhere, but he did not want to reveal his opinion easily to them.
**“brethren, if I yet preach circumcision”** — as formerly
**“why do I yet suffer persecution?”**
• I suffer from the Jews for no other cause.
• Why do I yet suffer persecution, etc. For he endured very frequent persecutions from the Jews, because he taught that believers from among the Jews ought not to be circumcised.
**“Then”** — even if I preach it
**“is the scandal of the cross made void.”** — the Jews would not be angry about the cross if I asserted that circumcision justifies
**“The scandal of the cross”** — Augustine. The preaching of the cross was a scandal to the Jews, because it made void the sabbath and circumcision. But if he admitted circumcision, it would not be a scandal to them and they would be at peace.
5.12:
**“I would they were even cut off, who trouble you.”** — These words are not so much of anger against adversaries as of love for the Church of the Lord; for he did not so much curse them as pray for them.
**“I would they were even cut off”** — They themselves trouble you, but would that they were cut off: not carnally, but that they may lose the power of generating in you, or may profit nothing in others; not only circumcised but cut off, so that they may have no power of generating at all; and I rightly wish this, lest they bring you back into the servitude of the law. For you have been called by God to liberty.
**“were cut off”** — With an elegant ambiguity he wishes a good: “For there are eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven.”
5.13:
**“For you, brethren, have been called unto liberty”** — that you may serve not from fear but from love, and that you, who before were bound by sins, receiving grace, may be free
**“only make not liberty an occasion to the flesh”**
• and since this is so, this alone is necessary: that you not abuse liberty
• because then you were slaves
• that, because you are free and the fear of the law does not press upon you, you should follow the desires of the flesh
**“make not liberty an occasion”** — The sense is: beware lest, having heard the name of liberty, you judge that you may sin with impunity.
**“but by charity of the spirit”** — which proceeds from the Spirit
**“But by charity of the spirit”** — Augustine. Charity is to be had not through affection of the flesh, but through the Spirit.
**“serve one another”** — because then you are free
5.14:
**“For all the law”** — therefore charity is to be had
**“All the law”** — Augustine. For both those things that pertain to good morals and those that are in the sacraments, when they are rightly understood by free men, and not observed carnally by slaves, must be referred to charity.
**“in one word”** — that is, by the one precept of charity; because whoever fulfils that precept neither does evil and as far as he can does good
**“is fulfilled”** — by this, namely
**“Thou shalt love thy neighbour”**
• without which God is not loved either
• Augustine. This is written in Leviticus, in which he rightly says the whole law is fulfilled, although there are two commandments of charity on which the whole law hangs, and the prophets, because the love of God is contained in the love of neighbour; and therefore in this commandment is the perfection of salvation, because God is not loved without the neighbour. For he that loveth not his neighbour, whom he seeth, how can he love God, whom he seeth not? Since therefore both commandments are such that neither can be kept without the other, it suffices to mention one of them.
**“as thyself”**
• “He that loveth iniquity hateth his own soul.”
• in the love of the neighbour the law is fulfilled
**“As thyself”** — Augustine. Just as he who does not love himself cannot love his neighbour as himself. Now he does not love himself who loves iniquity. For “he that loveth iniquity hateth his own soul.”
5.15:
**“But if you bite one another”** — you detract in some respect
**“and devour”**
• you devour the whole, blaming everything under the pretext of charity; this vice touched them
• Devour. Or accuse one another, laying crimes on each other.
**“take heed you be not consumed one of another”** — these are the cause of your consumption
**“You be not consumed one of another”** — Through schism in the Christian religion, through vain glory and vain victory, the occasion of charity being changed, he touched this vice of theirs, because dissension is the enemy of love. For by this vice especially of contention and envy, ruinous quarrels were nourished among them, by which society and life are consumed.
5.16:
**“I say then”**
• through the faith of Christ and never otherwise
• He shows how sufficient the faith of Christ is without the law, because through it they overcome the flesh and its works and follow the spirit; as if he said: “Make not liberty an occasion to the flesh, but by charity of the spirit serve.” And this I say can be yours in Christ and never otherwise.
**“spirit”**
• by reason
• by the Holy one; for the spirit of man cannot do this
**“walk”** — make progress by working well
**“and”** — then
**“the lusts of the flesh”** — the delights that the flesh suggests
**“you shall not fulfill”**
• in act
• but this is serious
**“You shall not fulfill”** — He does not say “you will not do” or “you will not have,” because they could not not have them, but “you will not perform,” that is, you will not fulfil their works by consent of the will.
5.17:
**“For the flesh”** — or indeed
**“lusteth”**
• always new in this
• For the flesh lusteth, etc. Augustine. The flesh is said to lust because the soul does this according to the flesh, as the ear is said to hear and the eye to see, when rather the soul hears through the ear and sees through the eye. For the flesh lusts for nothing except through the soul. But it is said to lust when the soul by carnal concupiscence struggles against the spirit. For the cause of carnal concupiscence itself is not in the soul alone, nor in the flesh alone: for it comes about from both, because without both no delight is felt.
**“against the spirit”**
• this is clear in good people where the Spirit of God is
• but one must not despair or fail
**“But the spirit”** — reason aided by the grace of God
**“against the flesh; for these are contrary one to another”** — these against each other, because to such an extent that you are not permitted to do whatever good or evil; and therefore in this fight one must yield to the better, that is, to the spirit by which we wish good things, even if we do not perform them; for we wish that there be no concupiscences, but this we do not perform
5.18:
**“But”** — he says this so that they not be slack in the fight
**“if”** — these two fight against each other; but see to whom one must yield
**“spirit”** — by the Holy one, the governor and ruler of your spirit
**“are led”** — As if: ‘if, I say, this is the case’
**“you are not under the law”**
• Ambrose. It is set down for those who act wickedly.
• These are opposed to one another.
**“But if you are led by the spirit, you are not under the law”** — Jerome, to Augustine. From this it appears that he is under the law not by dispensation but truly, so that you understand him not to have the Holy Spirit.
**“You are not under the law”** — You now have this advantage, and therefore this part is to be chosen. He says that those are damnably under the law whom the law makes guilty, not fulfilling the law while, not knowing grace, they presume upon themselves.
*Augustine:* Augustine, On Nature and Grace. He is under the law who refrains from evil through fear, not love, being guilty in will.
*The same:* In the same work. Under the law is that which instils fear, not love.
*Augustine:* All these are not of the will of the flesh but are vices of the soul. To believe also that all evils befall the soul from the flesh is an error, lest we clear of all these the devil, who has no flesh. But by the name of flesh he signified the whole man, who by living according to himself falls into these. For not by having flesh, but by living according to himself, that is, according to man, did man become like the devil, because he too wished to live according to himself, when he “stood not in the truth.”
5.19:
**“Now the works of the flesh are manifest”** — that is, evils appear of themselves
**“which are”** — broadly or strictly
**“fornication”** — the work of lust
**“uncleanness”**
• even if it is not carried out in deed
• or what is against nature
**“immodesty”**
• not to keep modesty
• not to live modestly
**“luxury”** — any excess
5.20:
**“Idolatry, witchcrafts, enmities”** — persevering
**“contentions”** — in words
**“emulations”** — when two strive for the same thing
**“wraths”** — a sudden storm of the mind
**“quarrels”** — when in anger they strike one another
**“dissensions”** — when they form parties in the Church
**“sects”** — in Greek: heresies
5.21:
**“Envies”** — over others' goods
**“murders, drunkenness”** — constantly
**“revellings”** — excessively
**“And such things as I foretell to you”** — before judgment, while it is still permitted to repent
**“As I foretold”** — before this letter
**“That they who do such things”**
• he did not say all
• because even single ones take away the kingdom
**“Shall not obtain the kingdom of God”** — Augustine. There is no middle place: whoever will not be in the kingdom will be in punishment.
5.22:
**“But the fruit”** — these are of the flesh, but these are the works of the Spirit, which themselves are fruits because they are to be sought for their own sake
**“Of the Spirit”** — holy, or enlightened by the grace of reason
**“Is charity”** — which calls from earth to God
**“Charity”** — He put the head first, from which the members follow. He does not rejoice well who does not love the good in which he rejoices. He has not true peace with anyone unless he loves him. He is not longanimous in waiting with perseverance unless he burns in loving. He is not benign unless he loves the one he helps. He is not good except by loving. He is not faithful in a saving way except by that faith which “worketh by charity.” He is not meek who is not moderated by love. A man does not restrain himself from that by which he is disgraced unless he loves that by which he is honoured. Rightly therefore he so often commends charity, as if it alone were to be commanded, since it cannot be had without the rest, by which a man is made good.
**“Joy”**
• which pleases itself well
• The purity of conscience. Whence: “There is no joy for the wicked, saith the Lord.”
**“Peace”** — when they do not disturb themselves
**“Patience”** — of adversities
**“Longanimity”** — of expectation
**“Goodness”** — sweetness of soul
**“Benignity”** — generosity with goods
**“Mildness”** — which is not intractable
5.23:
**“Faith”** — certainty about invisible things
**“Modesty”** — which keeps measure in words or deeds
**“Continency”** — which abstains from lawful things
**“Chastity”** — when it rightly uses what is lawful
**“Against such there is no law”**
• why should I speak of each one singly; the law is not laid down for the just but for the unjust
• but against evils
5.24:
**“And they that are Christ's”** — those whom it is necessary to follow the Spirit
**“And they that are”** — As if the law were laid down against the wicked; but for the good the cross is laid down. This is why he says: And they that are Christ’s, etc.
**“Have crucified their flesh”**
• they have mortified
• fighting
**“With the vices”**
• of works
• They have crucified their flesh with the vices, etc. Augustine. In the sermon on Lent. For it befits our devotion that we who celebrate the passion of the crucified Lord should make for ourselves a cross of restraining carnal pleasures. On this cross indeed the Christian ought always in this life to hang, that he may be fixed with nails, even the precepts of justice, as Christ was fixed on the cross with nails.
**“And concupiscences”**
• of desires
• here in many copies the sixth chapter begins
5.25:
**“If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit”** — those who are Christ’s act as I have said; and let us, because we are Christ’s, walk in the Spirit, because we came to this life with the Spirit as leader and author.
**“If we live in the Spirit”** — What he said above in general to those to whom he writes, he turns back and counts himself among them, thereby showing that he does not tell them what he himself would not wish to keep. As if: I do not say to you what I myself would not want.
5.26:
**“Let us not”** — also
**“Be made”** — as he adds
**“Vain”** — worldly
**“Desirous of vain glory, provoking one another”**
• to contention and strife and other unlawful things
• This evil is caused by vain glory.
• of vain glory, which is to wish to conquer where there is no prize.
**“Envying one another”** — if we do not dare to provoke.
**“Envying”** — It must be known that, although the power of the ancient enemy is poured into the human heart through every vice, in the zeal of envy the serpent shakes all his inward parts, and in impressing this malice he has, as it were, moved the doorpost; this zeal has no measure, remaining continually without end, while other crimes come to an end. And the more the one who is envied advances with better success, the more the envious man burns into a greater blaze with the fires of spite. Hence the threatening countenance, the grim look, paleness in the face, trembling in the lips, gnashing in the teeth, raging words and unbridled abuse, and the hand ready for violence, though meanwhile empty of the sword, yet armed by the hatred of a frenzied mind.

6.1:
**“Brethren”** — Do not do what I have said, but if a man is overtaken.
**“And if a man be overtaken”** — as one who has fallen through lack of thought.
**“Brethren, and if a man be overtaken”** — Hitherto, to the whole Church, by condemning the law and commending grace; now to prelates, how they should treat their subjects, namely gently, because they are brethren, though superiors.
**“A man be”** — so that he cannot avoid it; and it is no wonder, because he is a man.
**“In any fault”**
• not sinning by daily habit.
• Augustine. A fault is to turn aside from the good; a sin is to do evil. Or a fault is what is done in ignorance, a sin what is done by one who knows. Yet they are used without distinction. Being overtaken is when, even for an hour, it is not seen what is to be done, or when one who has seen is overcome so that evil is done, either because the truth lies hidden or because weakness compels.
**“You”** — do not therefore despise him.
**“Who are spiritual, instruct such a one”** — not one who melts away through each single sin, even if at some time he slips.
**“Instruct in the spirit of meekness”** — reasonably and gently.
**“Of meekness”** — Lest, if you do otherwise, he will not suffer himself to be reproved, but begin to defend himself, lest he seem shameful.
**“Considering”**
• as if: ‘do so as I have said.’
• each of you.
**“Thyself”**
• because you too are frail.
• Considering thyself, etc. Augustine. Nothing so inclines to mercy as the thought of one’s own danger.
**“Lest thou also be tempted”** — lest, God permitting, you fall into the like.
6.2:
**“Bear ye one another's burdens”** — instruct gently, and help with prayers and other means, as if the burden were your own.
**“And so you shall fulfill the law”**
• charity.
• Augustine. That is, charity. For out of charity Christ bore our sins, and he also commanded that we love one another.
**“Of Christ”** — of Christ: who bore our sins.
6.3:
**“For”** — Do so; for if anyone does otherwise he deceives himself, and this is
**“If any man think”** — judges proudly in his own mind.
**“Himself to be some thing”** — great in comparison with the sinner.
**“Whereas he is nothing”**
• of himself.
• nothing in comparison with the spiritual man, who gives all to grace.
**“He deceiveth himself”**
• divides himself
• from the truth.
• let no one think so, but rather
• For it is not his praisers who deceive him, but rather he himself, because, since he is more present to himself than they are, he prefers to seek himself in them rather than in himself.
6.4:
**“But let every one prove his own work”**
• If he considers his actions, knowing that if he has any good, he has received it from God, and if any evil, that it is from himself and not from God.
• Prove, let him carefully examine, his own work, not another’s sin, like the Pharisee who said: “I am not as the rest of men,” who was just not in reality but deceitfully.
**“And so in himself”** — That God, who is in him, may be his glory and nothing else.
**“Only glory”** — Of a pure conscience.
**“and he shall have glory”**
• In consideration of himself and not of another.
• Or thus: and so, that is, if he considers his actions, knowing that no one ought to boast that he has a clean heart. In himself, etc.
**“in himself only”** — That is, within, in his pure conscience. He will have glory, that is, he will glory and rejoice.
**“and not in another”** — That is, in another’s praise, namely when the other praises him. For he who has the consciousness of a good work ought not to glory of this before another and pour out his praise abroad, but humbly glory in himself.
**“and so in himself only”** — Augustine. Ambrose. That is, if we consider our own acts, we set ourselves before no one nor judge anyone. The truly just man puts another before himself, because he knows his own evils better than another’s, and the knowledge of these is his glory. For he rejoices while he recognizes his own sickness, which he desires to heal.
6.5:
**“For every one”** — Let him prove his own work; for he will be judged on his own.
**“burden”** — sin
**“shall bear his own”**
• Burden. Augustine. There are some works of sharing in weakness, of which above: “Bear ye one another’s burdens.” Others are works of rendering an account to God, of which here. Against those who think that a man is defiled by the sins of others he says: “Every one shall bear his own burden.” Against the negligent, who care to correct no one, being secure that they are not contaminated by the sins of others, he says: “bear ye one another’s burdens.” We bear one another’s burdens of weakness when with gentleness we endure another’s anger, and when we pardon him who has injured us, if he asks.
• He will offer in the day of judgment the sheaves of works, whence: “But they that come shall come with joy, carrying their sheaves,” and this is taken of good works only.
• Each his own burden. No one is defiled by another’s sin.
*Jerome:* Or by burden is understood good and evil work. For in the Scriptures burden is taken in both a good and a bad sense. And so each, good or bad, will bear his own burden, that is, will receive the reward of his works.
6.6:
**“communicate”**
• Let him share. Or make his goods common to him, and not make excuse, because God cannot be deceived.
• Let him communicate: this is said to subjects; so too to prelates. But let him who is catechized, that is, instructed, even if he communicates with him by word only and not by example, in all the good things which he shall say, that is, let him show himself a sharer with him by receiving them and fulfilling them in deed. And lest anyone say: I ought to do only what I see in him, he adds: “Do not err,” etc., because it is an error.
*Jerome:* For it is a customary precept that he to whom the word of God is preached should supply the necessaries to the preacher of it, which he rightly signified by the name of good things; as also the Lord in the gospel, speaking with his disciples, says: “When you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children”; and foreseeing that some would pretend poverty and wish to elude the precept, he added: “Do not err, God is not mocked.” As if to say: let no one excuse himself vainly, because God cannot be deceived. For he knows your hearts, he is not ignorant of your means. A plausible excuse can appease a man, it cannot deceive God.
**“him that is instructed”** — that is, is instructed
**“in the word, to him that instructeth him, in all good things”** — Not in evils, if he does them so that the law may be your guide, not man.
6.7:
**“Be not deceived, God is not mocked”**
• cannot be deceived
• but from him each one receives what he deserves
**“For whatsoever a man shall sow”** — by the labour of the present life
*Ambrose:* Even if you excuse yourselves before men, God cannot be deceived; truly he is not deceived, because he will repay according to merits. And this is: For whatever a man shall sow, etc.
**“that also shall he reap”** — he will receive the reward of these
**“For”**
• who thinks carnally of the law
• who, though he does whatever he does as good works, does them so that it may go well with him carnally
**“he that soweth”** — carnal vices
**“in his flesh”** — that from the flesh
**“corruption”** — nothing suits the flesh better than corruption
6.8:
**“He that soweth in his flesh”** — He adds “his own.” But when he says in the spirit, he does not add “his own,” because carnal seed is from man. But spiritual seed is from the Spirit of God. The harvest, however, is promised here at the end. And therefore perseverance is needed in sowing.
**“of the flesh shall reap”** — a harvest suited
**“But he that soweth in the spirit”**
• who gives assent to the Spirit
• Jerome. Augustine. That is, he who gives assent to the spirit from faith, with charity, serving justice and understanding the law spiritually.
**“in the flesh, in the spirit”** — Ambrose. This consists of spirit and flesh. Therefore he sows from both; moreover, man, even Christian, is flesh in comparison with the Holy Spirit.
6.9:
**“And in doing good”** — as if: let prelates be so toward subjects, and subjects toward prelates, as I said; and both, namely prelates and subjects.
**“let us not fail”**
• Another reading: let us faint.
• If man puts no end to his work, neither does God put an end to the reward. As much as we have sown in works, so much shall we reap in fruits. And as far as the eagerness of him who seeks has enlarged itself, so far will the hand of him who repays open itself to the reward, because each will receive according as he does, for he who is strong to sow will be strong to reap.
**“For in due time”** — one who will not fail in reaping ought not to fail in working.
**“in due time”** — in due time and fitting.
**“In due time”** — God does not at once do whatever is prayed for unto salvation, nor on that account does he deny it because he delays; but he grants it in his own time, that is, at a fitting time.
6.10:
**“Then”** — because we shall reap.
**“whilst we have time”** — in this life.
**“Whilst we have time”** — The time of sowing is the present life in which we run. In this it is allowed us to sow what we will. But when it has passed, the time of working is taken away. Whence: “Work whilst it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.”
**“let us work good to all men”** — so that there may be perfect love.
**“to all men”**
• Ambrose. Jerome. Mercy is to be shown to all, in which the just, who are of the faith, are to be preferred. That we are to do so to all, even to our enemies who are wicked and persecute the Church, the Lord is witness: “Do good to them that hate you: love your enemies,” for they too are men, on whom the Lord in this respect makes it rain and gives the sun.
• Augustine. For eternal life is to be desired for all with equal love, although the duties of love that are chiefly to be shown to the brethren cannot be shown to all alike.
*Augustine:* Yet Scripture says: “Give to the merciful and uphold not the sinner.” And “to the ungodly and to sinners repay vengeance; do good to the lowly and give not to the ungodly, for the Highest hateth sinners and will repay vengeance to the ungodly.” Which means: do good to no one because he is a sinner, but because he is a man, so that you may not be slack in avenging nor inhuman in helping. Hate in him what God hates, that is, what is evil, and rebuke and pursue it so as to destroy it, and preserve what he is as a man; and “uphold” him not, so as to wish him safe in that he is evil, and give not on account of his being evil, but because he is a man, so that mercy may be closed to no man and impunity granted to no sin. Let us therefore pursue in the wicked their own iniquity, and have mercy on them in their common condition.
*Ambrose:* Jerome. Because we ought to be readier and more inclined to good toward the brethren, because we are members one of another. For if the reins of liberality are loosed toward all, they are loosed most of all toward the household of the faith, that is, Christians, who have the same Father and are reckoned by the name of the same Master. Mercy therefore is to be shown to all, in which the just, who are of the faith, are to be preferred.
*Augustine:* On Christian Doctrine. Every sinner, as he is a sinner, is not to be loved. And every man, as he is a man, is to be loved for God’s sake, but God for his own sake. And if God for his own sake, he is to be loved more than every man. Each ought to love God more than himself. Likewise another man is to be loved more than our body, because all these things are to be loved for God’s sake, and another man can enjoy God with us, which the body cannot. But all men are to be loved equally. But since you cannot benefit all, you must take counsel chiefly for those who, by the opportunities of places and times or of any circumstances, are joined to you more closely.
**“but especially to those who are of the household of the faith”** — who are of our household through faith.
6.11:
**“See”**
• so that you may hold the aforesaid more firmly.
• Augustine. After exhorting them to moral works, he returns to that from which he had been speaking before, namely, that legal observances are not to be held.
*Jerome:* Lest anyone under his name deceive the incautious, he guards against it by completing the end of the letter with the note of his own hand. For from this place to the end he wrote with his own hand.
**“what a letter I have written to you with my own hand”**
• so that you may know that this letter was sent by me, and by this obey the more.
• there was need that I write, because false apostles press on.
6.12:
**“For as many as desire to please”** — to unbelieving Jews.
**“in the flesh”** — by carnal observance.
**“They constrain you”** — Ambrose. These were false teachers who so preached Christ that they also taught the law was to be kept.
**“they constrain”** — They preached the cross, that they might have gain from the faithful; the law, that they might please the Jews.
**“you to be circumcised”** — they do not lead by reason but by wickedness.
**“only”** — on account of this.
**“the persecution of the cross of Christ”** — that which is inflicted for the cross.
**“The persecution of the cross of Christ”** — Jerome. Perhaps he says this because the Roman emperors Caius Caesar and Octavian and Augustus promulgated laws that the Jews, wherever they were, should live by their own rite and serve their ancestral ceremonies. For whoever was circumcised, though he believed in Christ, was held among the Gentiles as a Jew. But he who, being uncircumcised, professed by his foreskin that he was not a Jew, became liable to persecutions from Gentiles as well as Jews. Those therefore who had perverted the Galatians, wishing to avoid these persecutions, persuaded the disciples to circumcision as a defence. For neither could the Jews persecute them, nor the Gentiles, whom they saw both circumcising proselytes and themselves keeping the things of the law.
**“that they may not suffer”** — by unbelieving Jews.
6.13:
**“For neither they themselves who are circumcised keep the law; but they will have you to be circumcised”** — so only; for they do not please by the law, nor do they do this from love of the law.
**“that they may glory in your flesh”** — that is, concerning carnal circumcision, in which there is pain for you.
**“your flesh”** — by your pain.
**“that they may glory”**
• among the Jews, because they make so many proselytes.
• they glory in the flesh.
6.14:
**“But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ”**
• Whence the philosopher of the world blushed; there the apostle found treasure.
• For what does it profit?
**“God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross”** — Augustine. Therefore the cross is fixed on the forehead of believers, where is the seat of shame, that faith may not blush at his name and may love the glory of God rather than that of men. The sign of the Old Testament was circumcision in hidden flesh, the sign of the New is the cross on the open forehead: for there is concealment, here revelation; that is under a veil, this is in the face. But the Lord, bearing the cross on his shoulder as the rod of his kingdom, commended it to us that we might glory in it. Let us therefore not blush at this reproach and deformity of Christ, but venerate it. For it is not a great thing to glory in the wisdom of God, or in his majesty or power, but in the cross. Whence: the ungodly man insults and the philosopher mocks.
**“by whom”** — What seemed foolishness to them has become wisdom and glory to the apostle.
**“the world is crucified to me”** — Augustine. It often happens that a man does not hold the world in his mind. Yet the world binds him in its occupations; and the man is dead to the world, while the world looks on him as if alive, striving to snatch him away when he is intent on other things in his own acts. But neither did Paul desire the world, nor the world him, so that, as between two dead men, neither sees the other; since therefore neither did Paul seek the glory of the world, nor was he himself sought by the glory of the world. Therefore he glories that he is crucified to the world and the world to him.
**“and I to the world.”** — The lusts of the world do not have dominion, nor does the world now thrust itself in; and I am strong against it.
**“and I to the world”** — I desire nothing in the world, nor does it recognize anything of its own in me. As the Lord says: “For the prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not any thing.”
6.15:
**“For in Christ Jesus”** — For in Christ Jesus; therefore I glory only in the cross.
**“neither circumcision availeth any thing”** — As if circumcision and uncircumcision were equal before God.
**“nor uncircumcision, but a new creature”** — Ambrose. New life, that is, regeneration.
6.16:
**“And”** — And I glory in the cross.
**“whosoever shall follow this rule”** — Rectitude.
**“shall follow”**
• Of mind.
• From God.
**“upon them”** — The Gentiles.
**“and mercy”**
• That is, remission of sins.
• Concerning sins.
**“and”** — Also.
**“upon the Israel of God”** — The Jews, not the fleshly but those of God, that is, the spiritual.
**“Upon them and upon Israel”** — Here he signified two parts, upon whom the peace and mercy of God remain: namely, of the faithful Gentiles and of the believing Jews.
6.17:
**“From henceforth”**
• in a way; or 'de cetero' as two words, that is, 'of another' beside faith, that is, of legal matters
• He does not wish weariness to be caused him through troublesome contentions about a matter already sufficiently expounded; or as it is read in the Greek: Henceforth, let no man bring or afford trouble, namely, that there be again a necessity in you
**“I bear”** — Augustine. Jerome. For he offers labour to the teacher who thinks otherwise than he taught.
**“let no man be troublesome to me”**
• So that I am again compelled to write about the same thing.
• To me, to whom no trouble is to be made.
**“For I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus”** — The marks of Christ’s soldiery, which prove that I am his.
**“The marks”** — Augustine. A stigma is a mark or brand made with some iron. He therefore calls them stigmata, as if they were marks of the punishments from the persecutions which he was suffering. And the sense is: therefore no trouble ought to be made for me, because I have other conflicts and struggles which contend with me in the persecutions that I suffer.
**“in my body”** — For the faithful, as if he said: ‘which you do not heed.’
**“bear”** — That it is not feigned.
6.18:
**“Grace”** — Grace, not law.
**“The grace of our Lord”** — The conclusion of the epistle, as a signature, which he also uses in some other epistles. As if: that you may hold to what has been said.
**“of our Lord”** — Grace: not dissension, not bondage to the law, not strife, not quarrelling.
**“of our Lord Jesus Christ with your spirit”** — By reason, so that you always understand the truth.
**“brethren. Amen”** — By this Hebrew word he shows that the things he has spoken are true.

1.1:
**“Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, by the will of God”**
• not by my merits; so you, through it, whatever you are
• It should be known that this epistle, which we have as written to the Ephesians, the heretics and Marcionites entitle to the Laodiceans.
**“Paul, an apostle”** — In his usual way he puts the greeting first. Then he gives thanks to the Lord, setting forth first the benefits granted to the human race, then those specially bestowed on the apostles themselves, then showing the Ephesians themselves by whom and to what they have been called. Then he shows the dignity and pre-eminence of Christ; afterwards he invites them to patience and charity, commending the unity of faith and of the Church and listing the gifts of grace. Finally, exhorting them to the contest against the princes of darkness, he describes the armour of the Christian warfare.
**“to all the saints who are at Ephesus”** — he writes or commands, or I Paul write or command
**“To the saints”**
• To the perfect, and not only to them but also to the faithful, who, if not holy, are at least sound in faith.
• By the exercise of virtues. And to the faithful: by the right faith which is in Christ Jesus. Ambrose. He rightly put those two; for a good life then profits, if there is faith in Christ Jesus. Then they are truly saints, if they are faithful in Christ. Or distinguish between saints and faithful, so that you understand the saints as the greater and more perfect, the faithful as the less perfect.
**“and to the faithful”** — then a good life profits, if there is faith in Christ
**“in Christ Jesus”** — by the work of Christ, not by their own merits
1.2:
**“Grace be to you”**
• he greets before other things
• of justification
**“and peace”** — tranquillity of mind and reconciliation to God
**“from God the Father”** — through whom all things were created and restored
**“and from the Lord Jesus Christ”** — without whom no good things are given to us
1.3:
**“Blessed be the God”**
• in heart, in mouth, in deed
• let it be from me, from you, from all
**“Blessed”** — With the greeting put first, he begins with thanksgiving, indicating that all things are from God.
**“Blessed be and blessed”** — One word of blessing, indeed, but it must be understood variously according to the fitness of the person. God is blessed by man when he is exalted with fitting praises. But man is blessed by God, when God bestows the gifts of his grace on him, not for his merits but by his mercy.
**“and Father of our Lord”** — by eternal generation
**“Jesus Christ”** — for whom he does good to us
**“who hath blessed”**
• he will bless, that is, in the future he will exalt, giving immortality
• He sets down four: two predestinations and their two effects.
**“Who hath blessed”**
• He lists the benefits which have been given by God through Christ to the whole human race: two preordinations of God and their effects, of which one is of the present, unto justice, the other of the future, unto the crown. They are not called two as though there were not one predestination of God, which is God himself; but because the eternal preordination of God itself concerns two things, namely justice in the present and glory in the future. God, before the foundation of the world, when no one had deserved anything, preordained that in the time of grace he would separate some from the lost, and make the just into the unspotted. He preordained also that he would bring those just ones to eternal blessedness. Of these preordinations, the one he fulfils in that he makes men just; the other he will fulfil in the future, which will be the perfection of all. He begins from the consummation of all, using the past tense for the certainty of the future thing. He who has blessed us will exalt in the future, by giving immortality, those cursed by our own merits.
• The effect of the second predestination, which will be fulfilled in the future, from which he begins, because it is the highest good, when he says: “Who hath blessed.”
**“us”** — cursed by our merits
**“with every spiritual blessing”** — with every kind of exaltation, which will be wholly spiritual, even in bodies which will then have the nature of spirit
**“in heavenly places”** — held in heaven, whence more commendable
**“in Christ”** — Christ working
1.4:
**“As”**
• the first predestination
• so he will do this freely
• freely
**“he chose us”** — by predestining
**“in him”** — through Christ himself
**“before the foundation of the world”** — that is, before we were
**“As he chose us before the foundation of the world”** — Augustine. Let no one therefore think that souls are eternal with God, and that they then merited something, according to the error of those who say that before these visible things there were certain holy souls, and that therefore they were then chosen.
**“As he chose”** — Here he sets down the first preordination, which is of the present, touching its effects. As if to say: he will bless us in the future, which, though it seems to be from merits, yet will be as freely given as the first preordination is free, because the merits which precede the life to come are from grace and are gifts of God. For God crowns in us his own gifts, not merits which are from ourselves.
**“that we should be”**
• he chose it so that we should be in the time of grace
• he chose that we should be, not because we were future
**“holy”**
• through good works
• by virtues
**“he chose that we should be holy”** — Augustine, On Predestination. For how would he choose those who were not yet, except by predestinating? He chooses us, therefore, by predestinating. And as he did not choose us because we were then holy, so neither because we were to be holy; but rather he chose us for this, that in the time of grace we might be holy by good works. He did not therefore choose us because we were to be so, but that we might be holy. For we were to be so precisely because he himself, predestinating, chose that we should be such by his grace. But the Pelagian, resisting the truth, says: God foreknew who would be holy and unspotted by the choice of free will; and therefore he chose them in his foreknowledge as such as he foreknew they would be. He chose, I say, before they were, predestinating as sons those whom he foreknew would be holy. He foresaw not that he himself would make them so, but that they themselves would make themselves so. The apostle refutes him here, saying: “That we should be holy,” etc.
**“and unspotted”** — from crime, from evils
**“in his sight”**
• that is, within, where he sees; not outside, where men see
• or that we may see him
**“his”** — not of men
**“in”** — in charity he did this, not by merits
**“charity”** — of God, or of themselves
1.5:
**“Who hath predestinated us”**
• another and second predestination, to eternal life
• he himself, surely, chose us
• by grace alone he chose beforehand
**“Who hath predestinated”** — Predestination, which pertains to justice and holiness of the present life, having been set down, another is set here, pertaining to eternal life, the effect of which he noted above.
**“unto the adoption”**
• by free will
• to the good things which the sons are to have
**“of children”** — the sons are those believing in him
**“through Jesus Christ”** — not through merits
**“unto himself”**
• who are to come
• to have the same things with Christ
**“according to the purpose”** — he predestined according to the will set forth long before, and openly to all
**“of his will”** — not by our pleasure
1.6:
**“Unto the praise of the glory of his grace”**
• that is, that we may praise the glorious grace
• As if to say: the glory of graces is eternal adoption.
**“in which”** — grace
**“hath graced us”** — he made us pleasing to himself
**“in which he hath graced”** — The effect of the first preordination, to justice.
**“in his beloved son”**
• through the Son, for whom he also loves us
• Ambrose. For God the Father, loving his only-begotten, bestows divine bounty also on those whom he loves and to whom the Son wills it.
1.7:
**“In whom we have”** — Behold, through what we were made grateful.
**“redemption”** — That we may be able to return from the captivity in which we served the devil, sold under sin.
**“through his blood”** — and
**“the remission of sins”** — in baptism
**“In whom we have redemption, the remission”** — Ambrose. He shows a twofold grace, because he both redeemed and did not impute our sins.
**“according to”** — because he remits all and destroys all the right of the enemy.
**“the riches of his grace”** — according to his rich and abundant grace.
1.8:
**“Which hath superabounded”**
• when he had abounded in all things.
• he abounded more than in others.
• Thus far of those things he gave to the whole human race; now of those he gave singularly to the apostles.
**“in us”** — to the apostles
**“in all wisdom”**
• in this
• by all knowledge of divine things.
**“and prudence”** — foresight of temporal things.
1.9:
**“That he might make known unto us”** — to all, so that he made known.
**“the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure”** — that is, his will hidden from others, namely to restore all things not by merits but according to good pleasure.
**“which”** — good pleasure or mystery.
**“he hath purposed in him”**
• long before, or openly offered to all for fulfilment, I say
• to the Son
1.10:
**“In the dispensation of the fulness of times”**
• to be fulfilled not at another time but in the dispensation.
• In the dispensation, that is, in the fulness of time dispensed by God, that is, in this time of grace, in which by divine providence he reasonably dispensed the fulfilment of what had been promised or prefigured in the other times. For if men were wholly ignorant, not taught beforehand, they would not receive Christ; and unless they had first been convicted by the natural and the taught law, the proud would have thought little of Christ’s coming.
**“to re-establish”** — to lead back to the first state all things destroyed through sin.
**“To re-establish”** — Augustine. Those things in heaven are restored when what fell from there among the angels is restored from men. Those things on earth are restored when the very men who are predestined to eternal life are renewed from the old age of corruption.
**“all things in Christ, that are in heaven”**
• while what fell from there is restored from men.
• that is, the angels themselves.
• All things that are in heaven, that is, the angels. Or to restore, that is, to supply; that are in heaven, that is, to fill up the diminished number of angels.
**“That are in heaven”** — Augustine, in the Enchiridion. Christ did not die for the angels; but whatever of men is redeemed by his death is done for the angels, because with them man returns into grace after the enmities between men and the holy angels, and the loss of the angelic fall is repaired. And surely the holy angels, taught by God, in whose truth, contemplated in its threefold nature, they are blessed, know how great a number, to be supplied from the human race, the completeness of that city awaits.
**“and on earth”**
• the men themselves.
• That are on earth, that is, men who had been corrupted by sin. Or
• That are in heaven, that is, the souls of the saints who are in heaven; and that are on earth, that is, the saints who are still on earth; and this 'in him', that is, through Christ.
**“in”** — that is, through Christ.
**“him”** — for the coming of Christ is salvation both to the saints who are already with Christ and to those who are yet to be.
1.11:
**“In whom”** — by whom
**“we also”** — that you
**“called by lot”** — by divine election
**“In whom we also are called by lot”** — Lest the apostles, in whom grace abounds, should seem to have deserved better than others, he shows that they were called thus freely, not by merits, as the others also were.
**“By lot”** — Lot is said of grace, because the choosing is not of man but of the will of God. Whence the tunic of the Lord, woven from above, which signifies charity, fell by lot.
**“are predestinated”** — first prepared
**“according to the purpose”** — through inner grace
**“his”** — not through merits
**“who worketh all things”** — also in the apostles
**“Who worketh all things”** — Augustine. Ambrose. Even to will that we be, that no one may glory in man. For it is true: “You have not chosen me: but I have chosen you,” etc. But the praise of God’s glory is when many are brought to faith, as the physician’s glory is when he cures many.
**“according to the counsel of his will”**
• as if: we do not know how he chose us more for the office of apostleship, but nevertheless he did it by counsel, not rashly
• that is, according to the will that is from reason
1.12:
**“That we may be”** — that through us others may praise his glory
**“unto the praise of his glory”** — and therefore we ought to be such that others may praise through us
**“we who before hoped”** — we
1.13:
**“In whom you also”**
• in whose faith you also are, through this that you heard the word of truth. As if: we hoped in Christ
• Now he comes to the things he gave to the Ephesians.
**“after you had heard”** — as if not before but after
**“After you had heard”** — Here “when” marks both cause and time.
**“the word of truth”** — that is
**“the gospel of your salvation; in whom also believing”** — believing by whose working
**“you were signed with the holy Spirit of promise”** — separated from the devil’s flock through the Holy Spirit who was promised, or who promises the inheritance and is its pledge
1.14:
**“Who is the pledge”** — or pledge
**“of our inheritance, unto the redemption”** — that the enemy may no longer rule over us
**“of acquisition”** — he redeemed so that he may keep, not so that he may lose
1.15:
**“Wherefore”** — With the benefits conferred on the human race, or on the apostles, or on the Ephesians, enumerated, the Apostle adds what he thinks of their benefits, namely that he gives thanks and asks that more be added, so that they not grow proud but strive further.
**“I also, hearing of your faith”** — as if, when you had heard the gospel, you believed
**“that is in the Lord Jesus”** — by which you believed in Christ without admixture of the law
**“and of your love towards all the saints”** — works of charity shown
1.16:
**“Cease not to give thanks for you”**
• I know well what you are, and therefore I praise not you but God, who has done this
• Thanks are given to God, for it is he who made them.
• for the goods had.
**“making commemoration of you in my prayers”** — imploring further things for you.
**“Commemoration”** — Augustine. Thanksgiving is fittingly placed first for things already given. For he who is to be prayed to that he may act, to him thanksgiving is to be rendered when he has acted; that is: Making commemoration, etc.
1.17:
**“That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ”**
• according to the humanity.
• Distinguish: God is Father, and he is the God of Christ and the Father. But he is the God of Christ according to the humanity, that is, because Christ was born a man of a woman. Whence he says in the psalm: “From my mother’s womb thou art my God.” Showing that the Father is his God because he was made man. For as man he was born of his mother’s womb, and according to the man God was born of a virgin, so that not only was he Father to him whom he begot from himself, but he was also God to him whom he created as man from his mother’s womb. As if, then, he is Father to the Son from his own womb, but God from the mother’s womb, not from his own. Whence he himself says: “I ascend to my Father and to your Father, to my God and your God.”
**“That God”** — As if: to obtain, not pleading merits, but that God and Father of Christ, etc.
**“the Father of glory”**
• of Christ according to the divinity.
• also according to the humanity.
**“may give unto you”** — even though already wise.
**“the spirit of wisdom and of revelation, in the knowledge of him”** — namely.
1.18:
**“The eyes of your heart enlightened”** — so that you do not think God is reached by bodily sense.
**“of your heart”**
• where the image of God is, in which you are renewed in the knowledge of God.
• of reason.
**“The eyes of your heart”** — In his image, therefore, know its author, who is not reached by bodily sense. Do not think, then, that God is reached by bodily sense, but hear him with the eyes of the mind. In the body, where there are different members, you hear in one place, you see in another. But in your heart, where different members are not found, there you hear where you see; to this end may he enlighten the eyes.
**“that you may know”** — more fully than now.
**“what”** — how great.
**“the hope is of his vocation”** — the thing hoped for, to which he calls believers.
**“that you may know what the hope is of his vocation”** — He says this that they may be more eager. Ambrose. Because when they fully know what is the fruit of believers, they will become more eager in tending religion. Or so that hope is taken in its proper sense. And it is: that you may know what it is, namely his call, that is, how much avails the hope of eternal life to which he calls. And that you may know what is the fulfilment of that hope. Which he says thus: And what are the riches of his glory.
**“and what are the riches of the glory”** — this is the hope.
**“And what are the riches”** — Here he makes clear what he understood by the name of hope. For he takes hope to mean the thing hoped for.
**“of his inheritance”** — of the glorious eternal inheritance, namely blessedness, which is called an inheritance because it will be held firmly.
**“in the saints”** — in common.
1.19:
**“and what is”** — that is, that we apostles will have glory above others, so that you may not stand still but strive toward something greater which we will have.
**“What is the exceeding”** — For the greatest teachers will have a certain increase of glory beyond what all will have in common. For all will have the same penny, but “star differeth from star in glory,” and: “There will be many mansions in the house of the Father.” And among others the apostles, shining more brightly, will sit higher. Whence in the tabernacle of the Lord a crown of open work, four fingers high, was made upon the table, covering the whole table, and upon it another little golden crown. By the crown four fingers high, which covered the table, is signified the glory of eternal life which all the elect will enjoy, which is also announced by the four books of the gospel written with the finger of God, that is, the Holy Spirit. And it was of open work for the diversity of merits. The little golden crown above it is the perfection of the reward of those who excel among the teachers.
**“greatness”** — of glory.
**“of his power towards us”**
