• to be given to us by the power of God.
• the apostles.
• concerning that blessedness, insofar as he powerfully worked in Christ.
1.20:
**“which he wrought in Christ”**
• of whom we are members.
• and therefore we believe we shall have the same things with him.
**“raising him up”**
• that is, in this way.
• Raising him up, etc. The example of the glory of the saints consists in the resurrection of the Saviour, that in it the faithful may know what is promised to them. For in like manner they are lifted up above the heavens with Christ, as he himself says: “Father, I will that where I am, there my minister also may be.” Because the body of Christ also, which is the Church, will be at that right hand, that is, in that very blessedness. For although our body is not yet there, yet our hope is already there. And therefore the Lord after the resurrection commanded the disciples who were fishing to cast the nets on the right side. He also said that in the judgment he will set the lambs on the right, the kids on the left.
**“from the dead and setting”**
• firmly.
• that is, showing that the man Christ is eternally blessed.
**“on his right hand”**
• in judicial seat and power of judging. Whence: “Hereafter you shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of the power of God.”
• because the Father has given all judgment to the Son
**“On his right hand”** — The right hand is eternal blessedness, which is given to the saints; the left is misery, which is for the wicked. For God is not confined and enclosed by any bodily form.
**“in the heavenly places”** — dignity from place
1.21:
**“Above all principality”** — He says this on account of the incarnation of the Son of God, so that the man made also is said to be above all heavens, and above every creature, having his name by nature, not by adoption.
**“and power, and virtue, and dominion”** — the dignity of these orders
**“and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come”** — not only above these four but above every name that can be named, either already known or to be known in the future
1.22:
**“And he hath subjected all things”**
• not only does he precede all in dignity, but also in power, because they too are under him
• because they were made through him
**“under his feet”** — fully, or under his humanity
**“Under his feet”** — The full subjection is signified by the feet, by which all things are rightly subject to him, because they were made through him.
*Ambrose:* Or under his feet. That is, by the humanity, which is signified by the feet; for as the foot is the lower part of the body, so in Christ the humanity is the lower nature, which even the angels worship.
**“And”**
• that is, because
• because he is high by God
**“And he himself”** — After he has recalled the dignity of Christ, he returns to us, showing that his dignity pertains to us. As if: so God exalted Christ. And this exaltation of his pertains to us, because he is the head and we the body, so that we may share in him.
**“hath made him head”** — in whom all the spiritual senses of the Church, namely the gifts of grace
**“Head”** — Augustine. According to the Godhead, because all were made by him. Also according to the humanity, by which the Church is joined to him in nature and grace. “For of his fulness we all have received.”
**“over all the church”** — who in heaven and on earth, while they confess that this is the one through whom they were made
1.23:
**“which is his body”** — united to him in nature and grace
**“and the fulness”** — filling him so that he has all members
**“The fulness of him”** — Ambrose. Because he is filled up through them; yet being all in all here and in the future. The same. When they come in to confession and bend the knee, Christ is filled up, because those who withdraw seem to empty him.
**“who is filled all in all”** — because they are from him
**“All in all”** — Because the members confer nothing on him, but he gives all things to the members, because by his power they are what they are.

2.1:
**“And you, when you were dead”**
• formerly, before faith
• not knowing your evils
• He recalls former things, that they may be humbled in man, and that it may be certain that if these things were given to enemies, much more will those things be given to friends which the apostle desires; as if he said: he is the head of the whole Church and of yours, because he “hath quickened you together with,” that is, although you were dead; or we who have believed have the hope of the inheritance, and you believed according to it. But God quickened, or raised up Jesus, etc.
**“in your offences”** — by neglecting what is commanded
**“and sins”** — by doing what is forbidden
2.2:
**“Wherein in time past”** — that is, before faith
**“you walked”** — turning from one thing to another
**“according to”** — the way of life that entices you
**“the course of this world”** — and
**“according to the prince”**
• The prince: namely, that is, Beelzebub, who is prince of the evil spirits; or, intransitively, the spirit as prince.
• He calls the prince of error the spirit of the air in which he rules.
**“of the power of this air”** — that is, who has power in this murky air now with men in the world; and because invisible spirits are so near us, they are the more to be feared.
**“Of this air”** — The murky air is the hell of the demons.
**“of the spirit that”**
• prince
• Spirit, that is, of spirits; for the singular genitive is put for the plural.
**“now worketh on the children”**
• still; therefore those who have been snatched away should be grateful to the deliverer
• as far as God permits
**“of unbelief”** — who distrust eternal things, or of whom, that is, of whose salvation we despair
**“On the children of unbelief”** — What? Nothing but his own evil works, and chiefly this, that he works in them distrust itself and unbelief, by which they are enemies of the faith through which he knows they can be cleansed. Augustine. When therefore God is often said to work wicked obstinacy, he does so not by urging and inspiring but by forsaking, so that those, that is the evil spirits, work in the children of unbelief what God justly permits.
2.3:
**“In which”** — sins
**“also we all”** — Jews and Gentiles
**“conversed in time past”** — living our life
**“in the desires”** — doing
**“of our flesh”** — desires which come from the flesh
**“fulfilling”** — also in act
**“the will of the flesh”** — those things in which the flesh delights
**“and of our thoughts”**
• that is, those things in which the flesh does not delight but the soul thinks, such as heretical perversities
• and the will
• or of minds
**“and were”** — we Jews
**“by nature”** — that is, through the fathers
**“And were by nature”** — As if he were saying: since these things aforesaid were in us, let not the Gentile despair of becoming equal to the Jews.
**“children”**
• debtors
• through original sin
**“of wrath”** — of eternal punishment
**“Children of wrath”** — Augustine. Mortals are born with the wrath of God, because when Adam sinned, vice grew into nature. For the human race was held under just condemnation, and all were by nature children of wrath. Of this wrath the Lord says: “He that believeth not in the Son hath not life; but the wrath of God abideth on him.” He does not say “comes,” but “abideth.” With this wrath indeed every man is born. This is that wrath with which we were all born, to which by being born we clung. Wrath from the stock of iniquity, from the mass of sin.
*Augustine:* In the book of Retractations. The nature of man is truly and properly said to be such as he was first created from the beginning without fault. But we use the word in a transferred sense when we speak of nature also as such as man is born. According to this way of speaking it is said here: We were by nature children of wrath.
*Augustine:* In the Enchiridion: In this wrath, since men had become so much the more grievous and destructive as they had added greater or more numerous sins besides, a mediator and reconciler was necessary, who would appease this wrath by the offering of a single sacrifice.
**“even as the rest”** — Gentiles
2.4:
**“But God”**
• although you were dead, God quickened you together
• not another
**“who is rich in mercy”** — because he forgives both actual and original sins
**“for his exceeding charity”** — not on account of our merit
**“wherewith he loved us”**
• the Jews or the Gentiles
• or: “you”
2.5:
**“Even when”** — not only after we are just, but also when
**“we were”** — or: “we were”
**“dead in sins, hath quickened us together in Christ”** — after the likeness of Christ, and this by the grace of Christ
**“Hath quickened us”** — Or: us Jews likewise and you Gentiles; and this is that by whose grace you Gentiles are saved. And he raised up both together.
**“by whose grace you are saved”** — by whose grace you are saved, as we Jews
2.6:
**“And”** — with Christ
**“hath raised us up together”**
• he states as completed what is future
• already in hope
**“and hath made us sit together in the heavenly places”** — as judges
**“Hath made us sit in the heavenly places”** — It is not vainly spoken, but faithfully he already reckons as done what he does not doubt will be. For certainly Christ already sits in the heavenly places, but we not yet. But we hold it by sure hope.
**“in Christ Jesus”**
• by this, that you are in Christ
• in the faith of Christ
2.7:
**“That he might shew in the ages to come”** — so here he made it in hope, that he might fulfil it in reality on the day of judgment; or therefore, that to our posterity
**“the abundant riches”**
• gifts of grace, abundant
• “That eye hath not seen, nor ear heard”; so that as much is given as the mind cannot search out
**“in the ages to come the abundant riches”** — Augustine. For in the future age the gift of God will appear, in the reward of believers, “that eye hath not seen, nor ear heard.” And these are the abundant riches, that so much is given as the mind cannot search out.
**“of his grace”**
• given
• not by merits
**“in his bounty”** — his
**“towards us in Christ Jesus”**
• more than we deserve; or beyond our understanding, which we cannot fully grasp
• being
2.8:
**“by grace”**
• in goodness
• going before, that is, by God’s gratuitous will
**“For you are saved through faith”** — because faith cooperates with the good will or grace of God
**“and that”** — that is, faith
**“not of yourselves”**
• that is, by the power of your nature
• And that not of yourselves, etc. Augustine. Lest perhaps you say: I deserved, and therefore I received. Do not think you received by deserving. Grace went before your merit; not grace from merit, but merit from grace. For if you bought grace by merit, you did not receive it freely. Grace goes before all merits, that my merits may follow as gifts of God. And lest anyone understand otherwise, on account of the arrogant and those who wish to establish their own justice, he opens it more plainly by adding: For of him, etc.
**“for it is the gift of God”** — purely, not partly from your works
2.9:
**“Not of works, that no man”** — no one
**“may glory”** — be lifted up by works
**“that no man may glory”** — Augustine. To Boniface. He does not say this because good works done with pious thought are made void, since God renders to every man according to his works, and the glory is God’s who works the good; but because works are from grace, not grace from works. It is therefore good for man not to presume on the strength of his own will; for he who thought he could keep by himself, without God’s help, what he had been given, “took his journey into a far country,” and living riotously wasted all, and worn down by misery and “coming to himself,” said: “I will arise, and will go to my father”; which good thought he would not have had unless the most merciful Father had inspired even this in him in secret.
2.10:
**“For we are his workmanship”** — No one ought to glory, because we are created in faith and in works; we are his workmanship, that is, his work; or we are created through workmanship, that is, operation; and so one is not to glory in works through faith, since faith and all things come from grace.
**“created in Christ Jesus”**
• through Christ
• Created, etc. Augustine. This is the grace that prepared. This is predestination, because predestination is the preparation of grace. Grace is the gift itself, which is also the effect of predestination; and predestination cannot be without foreknowledge. But foreknowledge can be without predestination. By predestination indeed God foreknew those things which he himself was to do. But he is able to foreknow also what he himself does not do, such as any sins; for although there are some things which are sins in such a way that they are also punishments of sinners. Whence it was said: “God delivered them up to a reprobate sense,” etc. There it is not the sin of God but his judgment. The predestination of God, therefore, is of that good whose effect is good. He therefore works and keeps man good who is unchangeably good; and we must always cling to him, from whom we ought to be made and perfected.
**“Created”** — Augustine. Not by that creation by which we were made men, but by that of which he spoke who already was a man: “Create a clean heart in me, O God,” etc.
**“in good works, which God hath prepared”** — before you were able to rise to them
**“that we should walk in them”** — not that, trusting in the grace of God, we should be idle
2.11:
**“For which cause”**
• that is, because you have these goods from God, be mindful, so as to be more grateful
• that is, because you have this
• that you may know all things to be from the grace of God
• That you may know all things to be from the grace of God. He had compared Jews and Gentiles, that both are under sin; now he shows that the Gentiles were less worthy and suffered reproach from the Jews, so that now, made equal to the Jews, they are the more bound to the grace of God.
**“be mindful that you, being heretofore Gentiles”**
• before conversion
• as those born and living as old sinners
**“heretofore Gentiles”** — In some copies it is found written “who there, you who were Gentiles,” and accordingly it is read suspended up to “But now in Christ,” etc., the sense remaining the same.
**“in the flesh”** — in the carnal
**“who are called uncircumcision”** — uncleanness
**“by that which is called”** — and is not truly so
**“circumcision in the flesh”** — not in spirit
**“made by hands”**
• not by God
• and be mindful that you who now are such
2.12:
**“That you were”** — because you were in evil
**“at that time without Christ, being aliens”** — the promise of Christ which was made to the Jews
**“from the conversation of Israel”** — which the Jews did not count you among
**“and strangers”**
• even though you have received the law and the prophets
• you were
• foreigners
**“Strangers”** — A guest, as if “foot of the door,” because when he was received into the house, the master of the house set his foot upon the threshold, and the one received, with right hands given, swore that his coming in was peaceful.
**“to the testament”** — that is, of the law of Moses and of the prophets
**“of the promise”** — of the promise made to the sons of Abraham, such as concerning the eternal inheritance
**“having no hope, and without God”** — knowledge of God
**“in this world”**
• you were
• so evil
2.13:
**“But now”** — in the time of grace
**“in”** — through
**“in Christ Jesus, you, who some time were afar off”** — from God and from Israel, not in place but in merit
**“are made”** — although you were far, yet
**“nigh”** — to God, and not to carnal but to spiritual Jews
**“by the blood of Christ”** — that is, Christ; but not in just any way but in the blood of Christ
2.14:
**“For he is our peace”** — between us Jews, that is, and the Gentiles, and God
**“who hath made both”** — both peoples
**“one”** — in faith and morals
**“Who made both one”** — For he himself is the corner stone, in whom the two peoples, like walls coming from different corners, are joined to one another as if in the kiss of peace.
**“And”**
• because
• by this he united
**“the middle wall”**
• the obstacle that was between these two peoples
• The wall, that is, the obstacle on one side from the law, on the other from idolatry.
*Ambrose:* A partition wall is a heap of stones without mortar, as is made around gardens. So the wall was a partition wall, which would easily be destroyed when grace came, which both removed the law and turned the hearts of the Gentiles from idolatry. It was in the middle, so that neither people agreed with the other. And while this wall stood, there were enmities, wrath and envy, between them, which were abolished when the wall was destroyed.
**“of partition”**
• because it was not stable nor of any strength
• and by this
2.15:
**“the enmities in his flesh”** — assumed or sacrificed
**“the law”** — he explains the wall as regards the part of the Jews
**“of commandments”** — as regards those things it commanded, that is, carnal observances, not as regards the truth which it foreshadowed
**“contained in decrees”** — the precepts of the gospel which are from reason
**“Making void, that he might make the two”** — joins in his faith those previously divided by the law
**“in himself”** — or himself
**“into one”** — or one
**“new”** — or new
**“man”**
• or man
• Ambrose. Of himself alone, there is no newness from elsewhere.
**“making peace”**
• the enmities having been destroyed
• Making peace, etc. He makes peace between them, so that he may reconcile both to God the Father.
2.16:
**“And might reconcile both”** — placed
**“in one body”** — of the Church
**“to God”** — through this he reconciles them to God, because he offered himself for sin and enlightened them through the gospel.
**“in himself”** — Not otherwise than through the cross, that is, by death, he slew the enmity which was between God and men, that is, he put away sins. For the death of the Saviour profited all men.
2.17:
**“And coming”** — appearing through the assumed humanity
**“he preached”** — although not in his own person but in the apostles
**“peace”** — to be made peace with God through himself
**“to you”** — to the Gentiles
**“who were afar off”**
• from God
• because they were idolaters and without law
• and therefore more thankful
**“were afar off”** — Augustine. If you love God with affection, you are near. If you hate, you are far off.
**“and peace to them that were nigh”** — to the Jews, who worshipped the one God
2.18:
**“For”** — the effect shows that he made peace, because we both have the means of coming near
**“by him we have access both”** — and this
**“in one Spirit”** — through the same Spirit, who is given to all through Christ
2.19:
**“Now therefore”** — and because the Gentiles have access, therefore now from the time of faith
**“you are no more strangers”**
• less worthy
• You are not strangers, that is, less worthy in faith, as those formerly received under the law.
**“and foreigners”**
• strangers to God
• And strangers, that is, aliens from God. But fellow citizens, that is, of the same right and dignity in the house of God. Of the saints: not the carnal Israel. And domestics, that is, members of the household. Of God: to whom he reveals secrets.
**“but you are fellow citizens”** — against strangers
**“with the saints”** — advanced from good to better
**“and the domestics of God”** — against foreigners
**“fellow citizens and domestics”** — Augustine. Two loves make two cities: the love of God makes Jerusalem, the love of the world Babylon. Let each one ask himself what he loves, and he will find whose citizen he is.
2.20:
**“Built upon”** — resting
**“upon the foundation”** — Christ or the doctrine, that is, the Old and New Testament, because what the apostles preached the prophets foretold. Whence: “The foundations thereof are in the holy mountains”
**“of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself”** — being present
**“In himself”** — Augustine. Lest the apostles or prophets, on whom the city is founded, should hold themselves in themselves and not in Christ, the whole rests on the first foundation, which is the foundation at the top, not at the bottom as in a bodily building.
**“chief”** — because he completes it.
**“corner”** — because he joins the two.
**“stone Jesus Christ”** — because he firmly supports.
2.21:
**“In whom”** — through whom.
**“all the building, being framed together”** — both from the Gentiles and from the Jews.
**“groweth up”**
• in faith.
• by growth until it is the temple of God.
**“GROWETH UP”** — No one is so perfect that he cannot grow.
**“into an holy temple”** — by the removal of vices.
**“in the Lord”** — by the working of the Lord.
2.22:
**“In whom you also”** — Ephesians, like the others.
**“are built together”** — you are built after the likeness of the others.
**“into an habitation of God”**
• or: dwelling.
• that you may be a dwelling.
**“in the Spirit”** — working.

3.1:
**“For this cause”**
• Having shown that peace and reconciliation were made through Christ, here he sets out through what means they are built together: because God revealed that salvation pertains to the Gentiles, and sent him to preach to them, and makes him suffer for them, that they may be more pleasing to God. But he begins from the end, saying:
• For this cause, that is, for this matter pleasing to me, that you may be built together; or for the grace of God to be fulfilled in this matter.
**“I Paul, the prisoner”** — who am now held at Rome.
**“Jesus Christ”** — for Christ Jesus.
**“for you Gentiles”** — because I preached the word of salvation to the Gentiles.
3.2:
**“If yet you have heard”** — If yet you have heard, that is, understood the grace, that is, the apostleship, dispensed by God, who knows why he chose me for this office. Or the apostleship through which we dispense different things to different people. Ambrose. By this he wishes them to know that by the judgment of God he was sent by Christ to preach to the Gentiles the mystery of the grace of God.
**“of the dispensation of the grace of God which is given me towards you”** — I say for you, if you know that I am your apostle, which no one is ignorant of; and since I am bound for the apostleship, then especially for you.
3.3:
**“How that, according to revelation,”**
• the dispensation is given me toward you, because the divine hidden thing has been made known to me.
• that is, not obscurely but openly.
**“the mystery has been made known to me,”** — by God.
**“the mystery”** — the hidden thing of God.
**“as I have written above”** — he himself is our peace.
**“in a few words”** — in brevity.
**“As I have written above in a few words”** — According to “he himself is our peace.” For there he summed up the substance of the mysteries revealed to him in a brief discourse, not so much setting out all that he knew as showing it from a little.
3.4:
**“As you reading, may understand”**
• although briefly, yet openly.
• attentive.
• What, namely?
**“my knowledge”** — Had.
**“in the mystery of Christ”** — in recognizing this hidden thing
3.5:
**“which”**
• Mystery.
• that the Gentiles are to be saved through Christ
**“in other generations”** — in past ones, namely in any whatever
**“was not known”** — not so fully as now
**“to the sons of men, as”** — how fully
**“it is now revealed”** — when it is seen to be fulfilled
**“to his holy apostles and prophets”**
• who interpret the Scriptures
• to the new ones
**“and prophets”** — The earlier prophets indeed foresaw long ago this about the Gentiles, that they were to be called and to share in the future gift of God; but this lay hidden, that salvation would come to them without the law, through faith, namely in Christ.
**“in the Spirit”** — through the Spirit
3.6:
**“That the Gentiles should be”** — that is, the mystery, namely
**“fellow heirs”** — in the future
**“and of the same body”** — now in the Church with the Jews
**“and co-partners”** — because to them, as to the Jews
**“of the promise”** — made to Abraham, about the inheritance and the common body
**“in Christ Jesus, by the gospel”** — all this through the incarnation of Christ and through my preaching; for the incarnation profits nothing unless it is preached
3.7:
**“Of which I am made a minister”** — of the gospel
**“By the gospel I am made a minister”** — Ambrose. Through his preaching the gift of God was made known, which God gives to the Gentiles according to the working of his power by which he raised up Christ, in whom all are saved without the works of the law.
**“a minister”** — For it is not mine, and so no thanks are to be rendered to me but to God.
**“according to”** — according to his free gift
**“the gift”** — not by my merits
**“of the grace of God”** — that the Apostle was a persecutor; for this is like any miracle
3.8:
**“To me”** — I say
**“to me, the least of all the saints”** — not in power, but more humble than the earlier ones
**“is given this grace”** — so great
**“to preach among the Gentiles”** — among the Gentiles
**“to preach the unsearchable”**
• which cannot be understood at all
• or: inestimable
**“unsearchable”** — By their own nature, but through the grace and revelation of the Holy Spirit, they are unsearchable to the faithful.
**“the riches of Christ”** — many gifts
3.9:
**“And to enlighten all men”**
• through preaching and miracles
• concerning this matter, how wondrous, and out of how great love
**“what is”** — these are the unsearchable riches
**“the dispensation”** — the fulfilment of the secret redemption
**“of the mystery which hath been hidden”** — hidden from the creatures of all ages, and existing in the sole knowledge of God who made all things
**“from eternity”** — not in the ages
**“which hath been hidden in God”** — Augustine. In the world are hidden the rational causes of all things which come to pass naturally, as Levi was hidden in the loins of Abraham when he was tithed. In God are the causes of those things which come to pass by grace, or of those which are done wonderfully, not naturally, to signify these, and which were done by the ministry of angels. Whence he says thus: hidden in God, that it might be made known to the princes. God does not need messengers, that he may learn from them these lower things, he who steadfastly knows all things. But he has messengers for our sake and for their own, because it is good for them to stand before God, that they may take counsel concerning lower things and obey his commands. The mystery of the kingdom of heaven was not hidden from them, which in due time was revealed for our salvation, by which, set free, we are joined to them. To them therefore it was made known from the ages, because every creature is not before the ages but from the ages, with which the Son began before the ages. Whence in the person of wisdom: “Before the ages he founded me.”
**“in God”** — For God has in himself hidden the causes of certain deeds, which he does not make subject to created things, and he fulfils them, not by that work of providence by which he established natures that they might be, but by that by which he governs as he wills those which he created as he willed. There also is the grace by which sinners are saved. For man is restored not by nature depraved by vice, but by the grace of God.
3.10:
**“That the manifold wisdom of God may be made known”** — thus hidden from the ages, yet so that it might be made known
**“That may be made known”** — It is given to me to preach and to enlighten. See how great this is, because by this something was added to the angels, who learned many secrets in these things.
**“to the principalities”** — the different orders of angels
**“to the principalities and powers”** — Blessed Jerome says that the dignities mentioned did not understand the mystery purely until the passion of Christ was completed and the preaching of the apostles was spread abroad among the nations. Whence in Isaias the angels, wondering, said: “Who is this that cometh from Edom?” And in the Psalm: “Who is this King of Glory?”
**“in heavenly places”**
• which are in heaven, where we also shall be
• Because the Church was first there, whither after the resurrection this Church also is to be gathered, that we may be equal to the angels of God.
**“through the church”** — which receives the gifts of God
**“the manifold wisdom of God”** — concerning the restoration of men
**“manifold”** — In the Greek, “multifarious.” Not only various but distinguished by many a variety. For Christ is immense, yet he is conceived; he is an infant who cries in the manger, yet is praised by angels in heaven. Herod persecutes, but the Magi adore. The Pharisees are ignorant, but a star points him out. He is baptized by a servant, but the voice of the thundering Father is heard. He fears to suffer, but goes willingly to the passion. He wishes the chalice to be transferred, yet he rebukes Peter, who feared the chalice.
3.11:
**“According to the eternal purpose, which he made, in Christ Jesus our Lord”**
• to be fulfilled, or made, that is, fulfilled
• According to the eternal purpose, etc. For that which is simple in its own nature is manifold, according to the things that are done in the world, which God foreordained, that is, preordained, when it is varied in many ways. And lest the teachers of sacred Scripture seem to contradict themselves in the aforesaid sentences, what has been said can be determined thus: that to those who are of greater dignity, and through whose ministry those things were announced, they were known in part, as to intimates and messengers; so to those who are of lesser dignity they would be unknown.
3.12:
**“In whom”**
• because God the Father fulfilled it through Christ
• in Christ
**“we have boldness”** — against tribulations, or the certainty of future inheritance
**“and access”** — in the thing itself, to the Father
**“with confidence”** — by the merit of the confidence had
**“by the faith of him”** — that is, because you have access and the other goods that have been spoken of above
3.13:
**“Wherefore I pray you not to faint”** — from faith and good work
**“at my tribulations”**
• on account of my tribulations
• which are
**“my tribulations for you”** — to be tried
**“which is your glory”**
• if you stand in them and do not fail
• and
3.14:
**“For this cause”**
• that is, that you not fail from faith
• I bow
• I ask you and beseech God that grace may cooperate with you. And this is what he adds: For this cause. In which he shows that they have the power of free will in their own right. But lest they think that this suffices, he adds: I bow my knees.
**“I bow my knees”** — the sense of the mind, or the outward knees of the body
**“to the Father”** — Found only in the Greek. But because the Latin copies add “of our Lord Jesus Christ,” it fits well that he prays so that we may obtain by the merit of him to whom the Father belongs properly and naturally, but to us by adoption.
**“of our Lord Jesus Christ”** — that we may obtain by his merit
3.15:
**“Of whom”** — God the Father
**“all paternity”** — by whose dispensation there are fathers to us, and in heaven angels providing for us, and on earth prelates
**“in heaven and earth is named”** — I bow my knees to the Father
**“all paternity is named”** — Is named. Even if it is not truly so, as with God, who is Father of all by creation and by the re-creation of the faithful, whom he adopted as sons. Or “is named” means “is nameable.” For from him who is the Father of all, both the angels in heaven and men on earth received that they should call others fathers. And note that Christ, the only-begotten of God by nature, by the benefit of adoption signifies that he is Father, saying: “Son, thy sins are forgiven thee.” Likewise also the Holy Spirit, through whom the just are adopted as sons. But man is called father either by nature or by authority, by example or by reason of a benefit.
3.16:
**“That he would grant you, according to the riches”** — abundance
**“of his glory”** — of his majesty
**“to be strengthened with might”**
• constancy, by which you may be strengthened in the inner man, who cannot be reached by enemies; and this through the Holy Spirit
• thence it will be not to fail
3.17:
**“That Christ may dwell by faith”**
• and let him first grant
• for there are sometimes strong heretics in whom Christ does not dwell
**“in your hearts”** — whence secure about help
**“That Christ may dwell by faith in your hearts”** — Augustine. Your faith is of Christ; Christ is in your heart.
**“in charity”** — order, that in charity
**“being rooted”** — from the likeness of trees
**“being rooted and founded in charity”** — I pray also that they may be rooted, that is, firmly planted, from the likeness of a tree, which the more it is fixed in the earth, the more it grows and yields more abundant fruit.
**“and founded”** — from the likeness of a house, because the Holy Spirit dwells in them
3.18:
**“You may be able to comprehend”** — perfectly understand
**“with all the saints”** — as all the saints
**“With all the saints”** — Augustine. This is the fellowship of the heavenly commonwealth. These do not seek their own but what is Christ’s, that is, they do not pursue private advantages, but in the communion where the salvation of all is, they take counsel.
**“what is”** — how great it ought to be
**“the breadth”**
• of charity
• Or what is the breadth of charity, which ought to be extended even to enemies, and to do good with cheerfulness, because he who gives sadly loses what he gives. There is need, then, of the breadth of charity, lest whatever good you do perish. But because, iniquity abounding, the charity of many grows cold, there is need of length. Whence he adds: And what is the length of charity. This is the long-suffering of perseverance, wherein in some manner one perseveres. Whence: “He that shall persevere to the end, he shall be saved.” And what is the height of charity. This is that the heart be directed upward, that God be looked for as the reward. For if you do good even to enemies, and give cheerfully, you have breadth. And if in these you persevere to the end, you have length. But if you do not do all these things for the heavenly reward, you have not height, and so already neither breadth nor length. For to have height is to think of God, to love God, and to love him freely, to count him your helper, your crowner, and finally your reward, expecting from him nothing other than himself. If you love, love freely. If you truly love, let him whom you love be your reward. And what is the depth of charity, that is, that you may be able to understand the hidden judgment of God, why he gives to this man and not to that; for from the depth of the judgments of God, which we cannot search out and contemplate, proceeds all that we can do. What I can do I see; whence I can I do not see, except that I know it is from God. But why he gives to one and not to another is far beyond me; it is an abyss and a depth. Now therefore charity itself is exercised in good works for the succour of others, and is extended even to enemies, and this is the breadth. Now with long-suffering it bears adversities and perseveres in what it has truly held, and this is the length. But all this it does to obtain the eternal homeland, which is promised to it on high, and this is the height. But that charity exists from a hidden source, and this is the depth.
• Ambrose. That you may be able to comprehend what is the breadth, etc., that is, to know God as immeasurable and beyond estimation, exceeding all things in the majesty of his power. But when he says this he signifies that, as in a sphere, where all these are equal, that is, what the immensity of God is, exceeding and filling all things, not enclosed in them, but containing all things within himself, after the immensity of the Father. He wishes them also to know that the charity of Christ is above the knowledge of men: that God is man, that the just man dies for the ungodly, etc. That you may be filled, for then nothing is lacking to the Christian when he knows the Father and the Son so. Otherwise the profession of the Godhead is not whole.
**“what is the breadth”**
• Augustine. In the works of charity, which is extended even to the loving of enemies, as Christ, who prayed for his enemies, which was shown on his cross, which was stretched out in breadth from right to left, where the hands were fastened, by which works are signified, which ought to be done with cheerfulness. And what is the length of charity, namely that it endure to the end; whence: “Having loved his own, he loved them unto the end.” Which was signified by the length of the cross from above down to below. And what is the height, that is, whither charity tends, namely to eternal blessedness, which is marked by the part of the cross placed above. And what is the depth of charity. That it bears the whole, as the part of the cross fixed in the earth, in a hidden place, which is not seen, that is, the mercy of God, which comes from the hidden judgment of God, through which charity in us is long, broad and high. Or the depth of charity is the sacraments of the Church, which are deep and unsearchable, and are the foundation of charity, without which it has no strength.
• What the mystery of the cross is. Augustine. It is to be known that in these words the figure and mystery of the cross is shown. For he died because he willed, and as he willed he died. Not in vain, then, did he choose such a kind of death, in which he who had said, “Take up thy cross and follow me,” might be a master to you of this breadth, and length, and height. The cross is taken up when the deeds of the flesh are put to death by the spirit. As long, then, as the body of sin is made void, as long as “the outward man is corrupted, the inward man is renewed day by day,” it is the time of the cross. He, then, in whose power it was to die or not to die, and to die thus or not thus, not in vain chose the cross, where he might crucify you to this world. For the breadth in the cross is the transverse beam, where the hands are fastened, which pertains to good works, because there the hands are stretched out. The length is from that part of the wood which extends from the transverse beam to the earth, and from it to the earth is visible; there the body is crucified and in a manner stands, which standing signifies perseverance. But the height in that wood is what rises from the same transverse beam upward toward the head, by which the expectation of heavenly things is signified. But the depth is in that part of the wood which does not appear, which, fixed in the earth, is hidden. Whence the whole rises. This signifies the depth of gratuitous grace, in which the wits of many are worn away, striving to search it out.
**“and length”** — where one persists by standing
**“and height”** — as God the reward
**“and depth”** — the hidden judgment why he gives to this one and not to that one
**“Depth”** — The will of God, whose causes are not searched out. Whence: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God!” Height is a name common to the high and the deep. But when it is said of the high, the eminence of sublimity is commended; when of the deep, the difficulty of investigation and knowledge.
3.19:
**“To know also”** — that you may be able in part, so that you may imitate; which surpasses and cannot be fully known; or charity surpasses knowledge, which is to another charity, because the better it is understood the more it is loved
**“the charity of Christ, which surpasseth all knowledge”** — the love by which he loved you, and which surpasses yours
**“that you may be filled”**
• through these knowledges
• going on
**“unto all the fulness of God”** — here, of the virtues, after the beatitudes
**“unto all the fulness”** — Not that they may be full God, as some in error wished, but that they may be perfectly filled with God.
3.20:
**“Now to him”** — I pray this for you: now to him be glory who is able to do
**“who is able to do all things”**
• to fulfil in us
• Or, who is able to do all things. According to the power that works in us, in which there are some things that no one would ask for or understand, such as God dying as man for men, and other things of this kind.
**“more abundantly than we desire or understand”** — because we understand more than we ask
**“according to the power that worketh in us”** — he can do this in you, as he has already done in us apostles
3.21:
**“To him be glory”** — to him himself, that is, to God alone, not to a man, who has nothing of himself
**“in the church, and in Christ Jesus”** — for those things he did in the Church and in Christ
**“unto all generations, world without end. Amen”** — of him who contains all ages

4.1:
**“I therefore”** — because God can do all things, or that glory be to him from you
**“I beseech”** — Thus far he has shown what is to be attributed to grace; hence he admonishes concerning morals, first all in common, afterwards by individual orders.
**“I, a prisoner”** — to whom compassion is due
**“in the Lord”** — for the Lord’s sake
**“that you walk worthy”** — from good to better, so that your walk may agree with my preaching
**“of the vocation in which you are called”** — that is to say, thus
4.2:
**“With all humility”** — inward and outward
**“and mildness”** — that you may be tractable
**“with patience”** — of adversities
**“supporting one another”** — if trouble arises from a brother, or bear one another’s burdens
**“in charity”**
• not feignedly, or for some earthly reward
• Augustine. To Eudoxius. For this is the action of the straight course, which always has its eyes on God. Such action is neither broken by business, nor turbulent, nor languid, nor bold, nor fleeing, nor headlong, nor lying down.
4.3:
**“Careful”** — eager, cautious, attentive
**“to keep”** — that it be kept as most sacred
**“the unity of the Spirit”** — that you be one body by the work of the Holy Spirit, or the church unity which the Holy Spirit makes
**“in the bond of peace”**
• living
• because this peace is the nourishment of spiritual unity
• In the bond of peace, that is, keeping peace. This peace exists if we love one another’s good things, if we bear with sins which cannot be uprooted without harm to the wheat, or with hope of salvation for those who are to be corrected, until the last harvest.
4.4:
**“One body”**
• in ministering
• by helping one’s neighbour
• You ought to keep unity, so that you may be one body by serving your neighbour, and one spirit with God by willing the same; or one spirit with the brethren, with whom you ought to will the same and refuse the same; or you ought so to keep the unity of the spirit, because you ought to be one body by the joining together of many members, and you are able, because “one Spirit dwelleth in you.”
• Augustine. On account of the fellowship which the Holy Spirit makes, not without the Father and the Son. The Church has received this gift, that in the Holy Spirit there be made the remission of sins; and although the Trinity makes this remission, yet it is understood to belong properly to the Holy Spirit. For he is the spirit of the adoption of sons. He is the love and bond of the Father and the Son; to him therefore belongs the fellowship by which we are made one body of the only Son of God. For as the one body of a man consists of many members, and one soul quickens all the members, making in the eye that it may see, in the ear that it may hear, and so in the rest, so the Holy Spirit contains and quickens the members of the body of Christ, which is the Church. And as a member of the human body, cut off, retains indeed the form by which it is known, but by no means has the spirit by which it lives apart from the unity, so whoever is divided from the unity of the aforesaid peace retains the sacrament indeed as a form, but does not live by the spirit apart from the unity. In vain therefore does he glory outwardly in the form unless he is quickened inwardly by the spirit. Those on whom he first came spoke with the tongues of all, because through tongues the union of the human race is made, and so the fellowship of the members of Christ to be in all nations is prefigured. He has the Spirit who stands in the unity of the Church, who speaks with the tongues of all.
**“and one Spirit”**
• by will
• by which the body lives
**“as you are called”** — you ought to be as those called to the same thing
**“in one hope of your calling”** — to the one thing hoped for, which is the effect of the calling
4.5:
**“One Lord”**
• is for us
• You ought to keep unity, because we have one Lord, not three, on account of whose differing wills you would need to disagree. And you are bidden to believe the same and to work in the same manner. And you have one God, Creator of all and Father by providing, and therefore no one can set himself above another. Who is God over all, that is, he surpasses all creatures; let his dignity invite you. And diffused through all things, because he is everywhere, and therefore to be feared, since he can nowhere be escaped. And in us all, by grace, who keep unity. And so this is understood not singly of one person, but commonly of all, that is, of the Trinity.
**“one faith”**
• from God
• The things that are believed are one thing; faith, by which they are believed, is another. For those things are in reality which are believed to be, or to have been, or to be going to be. But faith is in the mind of the believer, and is visible only to him whose it is.
**“One faith”** — Not by number but by kind, because it is alike in all.
**“one baptism”** — equal from whoever gives it, and it cannot be repeated
4.6:
**“One God and Father of all, who”** — the Father
**“is above all”**
• whom you cannot avoid
• because he owes his being to no one, and surpasses all creatures
**“and through all”** — the Son, through whom all our works are restored
**“and in us all”** — is the Holy Spirit
**“us”** — in the faithful by grace, and in all creatures by essence; whence: “The Spirit of the Lord hath filled the whole world”
4.7:
**“But to every one of us is given grace”** — lest unity take away subjection, he adds that the gifts are diverse, which is not contrary to the aforesaid unity
**“according to the measure of the giving of Christ”** — a free gift, according as Christ the giver measured it, to one this, to another that. But to Christ alone the Spirit is given without measure. But to all others not without measure
4.8:
**“Wherefore he saith”**
• the prophet
• To prove that Christ as man gives various gifts, the Holy Spirit says in the psalms; truly Christ gives according to his humanity, for the prophet says that ascending he gave, and he said ascending with respect to descent, and so he hints that descending also he gave. And it is agreed that Christ descended according to his humanity, and ascended; therefore he gave according to his humanity, because according to the Godhead, which is everywhere, he neither descended nor ascended. But according to the soul he descended to hell; according to body and soul he ascended to heaven. Or thus: ascending, which is according to the humanity, he gave. But what is it that the humanity ascended, that is, how could the humanity ascend unless because the Godhead first descended into the lower parts of the earth, which are lower than the air, that it might be united to human nature? And because he had said the humanity ascended, the Godhead ascended, lest therefore they should seem two, he adds: He that descended, that is, the Godhead, and he that ascended above the heavens, that is, the humanity. He is one and the same person, that he might fill all things with his gifts; and so he filled them that he himself gave some apostles, and some prophets, etc. Behold how he gave to some more, to others less. To men he gives by measure; he himself did not receive by measure.
**“Ascending on high”** — in place and dignity
**“he led captivity captive”** — behold a happy captivity. They were captives because they were subdued, sent under a light yoke, freed from sin, made servants of righteousness
**“He led captivity captive”** — That is, those whom the devil had captured from paradise and had made his own, of the world and of hell. Christ made them captives again when they are led back to heaven.
*Augustine:* He gave gifts to men. He speaks with apostolic authority. In the Psalm it is read thus: “Thou hast received gifts in men.” For so many copies have it, and especially the Greek, and so we have it translated from the Hebrew. But the Apostle said gifts, as the prophet did, not a gift. But though the prophet said, Thou hast received in men, Paul, by apostolic authority, preferred to say, he gave gifts to men; that from both words, one prophetic, the other apostolic, since in both is the authority of the divine word, the fullest sense might be rendered. For both are true: that he gave to men, and that he received in men. He gave to men as the head to his members. He received in men, the same himself, namely in his members. Christ himself therefore both gave from heaven and received on earth. He gave, because he is God with the Father, according as he gives. He received: the prophet says he received, because he himself is with his own in the Church, in which he receives; this is, to receive in men. The Spirit is a gift, but gifts in the plural, because through the Spirit each has his own things, not all things each singly, as one soul does all things in all the members.
**“he gave gifts”** — the Spirit
**“to men”** — to rational beings
4.9:
**“Now that he ascended, what is it, but because he also descended first”** — the prophet said ascending. But what is this, unless that he first descended, with respect to whom he said ascended?
**“into the lower parts of the earth”** — that is, to the dead, the proof of which is set down before, because he led captivity which he drew from there
4.10: **“He that descended is the same also that ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.”** — therefore, since the words of the prophet so imply, it is the same who descended and ascended, so that he might fill all things with gifts, or all things foretold of himself
4.11:
**“And he gave some apostles”** — vicars of his preaching
**“and some prophets”**
• concerning future things, or interpreters of the Scriptures
• as Agabus
**“Prophets”** — Ambrose. In the New Testament, prophets are called expounders of the Scriptures; yet there were some at the beginning of the faith who foretold future things, as Agabus and the seven daughters of Philip.
**“other some evangelists”**
• as the seven deacons under the apostles
• as Mark, Luke
**“Evangelists”** — who are also deacons, because although they are not priests, they can nonetheless preach the gospel.
**“other some pastors and doctors”** — as bishops, who ought to teach by word and example; and therefore he joined pastors and teachers. For a pastor is not one unless he has the teaching by which he feeds the flock.
4.12:
**“For the work of the ministry”** — All these he gave for the work of the ministry, that each may be able fully to do the work of the ministration entrusted to him. For if one had all, he would not perform each singly in a perfect way. And this is for the perfecting, that is, that they may perfect those who are already saints; and for the edifying, that is, that they may build up into the body of Christ those who are still strangers.
**“for”** — or: in
4.13:
**“Until we all meet”**
• this prelacy will last as long as until we meet, not after; and therefore it is not to be borne heavily.
• Until, that is, on the day of judgment, we all who are in one and not discordant faith, and in one and not differing knowledge of the Son of God, either in the virtues by which the Son of God is known in us, or by which we shall know him in the future, may meet one another from the various parts of the world; or meet Christ himself, as if running with desire to joy.
**“into the unity of faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man”** — not in sex but in perfection of virtue; for here we are children in the strength of body and mind.
**“Unto a perfect man”** — That each one may be a perfect man, and have the same age, which is the measure and limit of age, beyond which nothing naturally is added to a man; in which age Christ had the fulness of years and of body, in which he passed from this world. For all will rise again in the same age in which Christ died and rose again, of whatever age they died. Or: unto a perfect man, that, head and members, we may all be one perfect man, to whom nothing is lacking and to whom nothing afterwards is to be added. A perfect man, because there will be the measure and limit of age. Limit, that afterwards nothing be added in number or in strength. Measure, because Christ will be full, having all, who now grows through individuals; and all in him immortal and blessed with him, and then there will be no need of prelacy.
**“Unto the measure of the age”** — Augustine. He does not say the measure of body or of stature, because each one will receive his own measure, which he either had in youth, even if he died old, or would have had if he had died before. But the age will be that to which Christ came, that is, youthful, about thirty years. Now it is not right to say that in the resurrection a size is added to the body which it did not have, nor are bodies to be brought back to greater size according to the measure of the Lord’s body. For much of them would perish, since not even a hair will perish. For nothing taken away in any way from the human body will perish. For that matter will be so ordered in each that nothing of it perishes. And what is lacking to anyone, he will supply who made from nothing what he willed. And if anything in some part has abounded excessively, it will be spread through the whole. For nothing unseemly will be there, but whatever is to be will be fitting. The bodies of the dead therefore will rise without any deformity. Nor will that earthly matter which, when the soul departs, becomes a corpse be so restored in the resurrection that the things which fall away, though they return to the body, must return to the same parts of the body from which they fell away; otherwise an immoderate and unseemly size would be given to hair and nails.
**“unto the measure of the age of the fulness of Christ”** — Christ is called anointed. And in the Old Testament kings were anointed.
4.14:
**“That henceforth we be no more”**
• up to that: he gave these ministers, that we may now no longer be as formerly, etc.
• he gave, I say, these prelates
**“children”** — in understanding
**“tossed to and fro”** — wavering through our weakness
**“and carried about”** — and not be carried about, another urging us
**“with every wind”** — the teaching of the wicked is like a storm wind
**“of doctrine”** — made
**“by the wickedness”** — on account of which they are blinded
**“of men, by cunning craftiness, by which they lie in wait to deceive”**
• made
• through malicious men, cunning in themselves and for deceiving the simple
• so that under the pretext of truth he may deceive more, drawing them to error
4.15:
**“But doing the truth”**
• let us not be such, but doing
• good things according to the teaching
• in deed
**“in charity”** — not feignedly or out of fear
**“we may grow up”**
• by the assertion of faith
• through the members
**“in him”** — he cooperating, who is the head, providing for us, and Christ able to govern
**“in all things who is the head, even Christ”** — in every spiritual gift
4.16:
**“Of whom”** — well, in him, because through him
**“the whole body”** — The Church
**“being compacted”** — through faith
**“and fitly joined together”** — by the bonds of charity
**“by what every joint”** — that is, through faith and charity, which join together and make the members of Christ minister to one another
**“supplieth”** — offered not only by will but according to what each member can do
**“according to the operation in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body”** — it increases those who are the body
**“in”** — tending
**“unto the edifying of itself in charity”** — that is, it builds up into its own fellowship those who are not yet, and all this from love; when this is done there will be the measure of age
4.17:
**“This then I say”**
• I do not beseech as before
• He warns them to beware of the old custom of the Gentiles. As if to say: since God has given so many helps for keeping unity, and since you are able to grow and to meet him, therefore I say, I do not beseech as before.
**“and testify”** — as if I command
**“in the Lord”** — under the witness of God
**“That henceforward”** — from the time of faith
**“you walk not”** — live
**“as also the Gentiles walk”** — namely
**“in the vanity of their mind”** — because they love the transitory things that sensuality suggests
4.18:
**“having their understanding darkened”** — from darkness
**“darkened”** — Not a little, and therefore less surprising, than concerning you who are enlightened and have the hope of life.
**“having their understanding”** — natural
**“being alienated”** — without hope of immortality
**“from the life of God”**
• from God, who is the life of the soul
• because God forsakes them
• Augustine. There are two lives: one of the body, the other of the soul. And as the life of the body is the soul, so the life of the soul is God. And as the body dies if the soul leaves it, so the soul dies if God leaves it. The soul, departing from the light of justice, the more it seeks what it may find against justice, the more it is driven back from the light of truth and is sunk in darkness.
**“through the ignorance”** — because they do not know the life of God
**“that is in them”** — remaining
**“because of”** — because they have closed their eyes to preaching
**“the blindness”** — others: hardness
4.19:
**“of their hearts. Who”** — also
**“despairing themselves”**
• because of their own shamefulness
• concerning the future life
**“Despairing”** — Or insensible, which is drawn from the Greek, that is, not grieving for sin.
**“have given up”** — by will
**“to lasciviousness”** — to fornication
**“in”**
• and then they gave themselves up
• in a vehement and insatiable desire
**“the working of all uncleanness”** — so that they left out nothing at all that is unclean
**“unto covetousness”**
• or by itself, concerning another vice
• others: covetousness
4.20:
**“But you”** — the Gentiles walk so
**“have not so learned Christ”** — that Christ is to be imitated
4.21:
**“If so be that you have heard him, and have been taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus”** — you understood his preaching, or you heard him speaking inwardly, so that you were taught the truth
**“as the truth is in Christ Jesus”** — He says this because there are some in the Church who, under the name of Christ, do not follow the truth that Christ taught.
4.22:
**“to put off”**
• that is, this one
• that you put off
• or: put off
• not according to substance but according to conduct
**“Put off”** — He does not command that the body be put off, but that life be changed for the better. Ambrose. For the inner man, if he follows his former vices, is called “old”; but if he walks in newness of life, a stranger to worldly error, he is called “new.” He is therefore corrupted by that by which he grows old. Therefore he says: Put off, that is, the oldness by which the inner man becomes old and is corrupted.
**“the old man”** — Some think that the old man is the body and the new man is the soul. But the body is the outer man and the soul the inner man, and it is in the inner man that this oldness and newness are at work.
**“who is corrupted”** — although he delights
**“according to the desire of error”** — also not only according to works; and therefore put off also the desires that come from error or lead into error
4.23:
**“And be renewed”** — daily
**“in the spirit of your mind”**
• through the Holy Spirit, who leads the reason of your mind in spiritual fashion
• that is, by the spirit that is the mind
• Augustine. On the Trinity. He did not mean two things there, as if the mind were one thing and the spirit of the mind another; but because the mind is spirit. A similar saying is: “In the despoiling of the body of the flesh,” that is, of the flesh which is the body.
• Augustine. On Genesis. The mind, or reason, or understanding, which is set over the rest by man, is the image of God; and man, created in the knowledge of God, after he lost his wisdom through sin, is renewed in the same, so that that image begins to be reformed by him by whom it was formed.
4.24:
**“And put on”** — by work
**“the new man”** — the new man: the likeness of Christ
**“who according to God”**
• For he was conceived in the virginal womb by the work of the Holy Spirit, from the seed of a woman without the seed of a man; this was new. Whence Jeremias: “The Lord hath created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall compass a man.”
• Or according to God, that is, created to the image of God in justice and holiness, which he lost by sinning.
**“is created”** — is created: not by human nature but by the power of God
**“in justice”** — by common action, granting good things to all
**“and holiness”** — perfect
**“of truth”** — not hypocrisy
4.25:
**“Wherefore putting away lying”** — because the old man is to be put off
**“Wherefore putting away”** — He pursues the parts of the old and new man.
**“speak ye the truth”** — because the new man is to be put on
**“every man with his neighbour”** — with any man
**“with his neighbour”** — Even to a Gentile: because every man is a neighbour by the condition of first birth, or by hope of conversion; all ought to be considered neighbours.
**“for we are”** — that which is fitting
**“members one of another”** — by serving
4.26:
**“Be angry”**
• as if: I unwillingly bear what cannot be avoided. But concerning anger, do not come to the act of sin, and let it not last until the setting of the sun.
• Bernard. That is, be indignant with yourselves with such vehemence that you cease to sin, because the sun of justice does not set over this anger, but rather shines upon it.
• Ambrose. Which is a natural movement of the mind against sinners; but lest you sin by exceeding measure, by rebuking too harshly. Whence Solomon: “Be not over just: for there is one that perisheth in his justice.” Justice, therefore, is to be tempered, as God also bears with the wicked that some of them may be corrected.
**“and sin not”**
• for yourselves concerning past sins, that is, to repent
• cease to sin any further
**“Let not the sun go down”**
• He wills that anger not last, because if it lasts an occasion is given to the devil. For the angry man thinks evil, and thus the devil inserts himself, so that he pays out evil.
• Christ does not desert the mind that never dwells with anger.
**“upon your anger”** — the splendour of reason, or God; lest by anger, as by an interposed mountain, it be obscured to you
4.27:
**“Give not place to the devil”**
• if one also provokes, which is the temptation of the devil
• by persevering in anger
**“Give not place”** — Augustine. On Psalm 61. There are two gates by which the devil enters: desire and fear of earthly things. With these turned to the opposite, God enters. Those are to be shut, these opened.
4.28:
**“He that stole”** — other parts of the old man
**“let him now steal no more”** — by some deceit take anything away
**“but rather let him labour”** — not only through servants
**“the thing which is good”** — not wicked works of gain
**“that he may have”** — not only that he may live, but also
**“that he may have something to give to him that suffereth need”** — or: to the one who suffers
4.29:
**“Let no”** — also
**“evil speech proceed from your mouth”**
• even if it has been conceived in the heart
• Let no evil speech, etc. Ambrose. For in the servant of God all good things ought to be seen, nor should his purity be stained in any part.
**“but that which is good, to the edification”** — as if he were not to be called good to no purpose
**“that it may administer”** — so that he proceeds opportunely and circumspectly
**“grace to the hearers”** — that is, that he may be pleasing to the hearers
4.30:
**“And grieve not the holy Spirit of God”**
• he rejoices if we make progress in him; otherwise he is grieved, that is, he departs
• driving him away from you by evil works
**“And grieve not”** — By disobedience to the preacher of truth, which is to grieve the Holy Spirit, so far as concerns you. This you ought not to do, you in whom, as if sealed in wax, his image has been left to you. Or you are signs, that is, distinguished from the wicked.
**“grieve not the holy Spirit”** — Augustine. The Holy Spirit is in himself unchangeable, but in the saints he makes them rejoice at the progress of others and grieve at their falls, which comes from the charity which he makes; and so he is said to be grieved because he does this in his own, as God is said to know when he makes to know, and to rest from the works which he had made very good, because he makes us rest when we have done good works.
**“In whom”**
• because he is
• by whose grace
**“you are sealed”** — as wax, the form of the new life impressed on you by a seal
**“unto the day of redemption”**
• that is, on the day of baptism
• and
4.31:
**“Let all bitterness”** — by biting words and deeds
**“and anger”** — sudden fury
**“all bitterness and anger”** — Ambrose. Even these, if they arise from occasions that arise, must nevertheless be moderated.
**“and indignation”**
• which, if it is smaller, is lifted up
• comes from anger
**“and clamour”**
• from indignation, like the voice of a madman
• contention
**“and blasphemy”**
• from clamour
• where false things are said about God
**“blasphemy”** — Augustine. It is that by which false things are said about God himself. And therefore it is worse to blaspheme than to perjure, because in perjuring God is called as witness to a false matter. In blaspheming, false things are said about God himself.
**“be put away from you”** — because, when these are pressed down, evil could be kept in the heart; he adds
**“with all malice”**
• of the heart
• because they could cause destruction
• against God and the saints
4.32:
**“And be ye kind”** — he goes on to the parts of the new man
**“kind”** — generous with your goods
**“merciful”**
• in affection and compassion of mind
• even if there is nothing to give
**“forgiving one another”** — for the wrongs committed against you; otherwise God will demand back what was forgiven, as is read in the gospel of the wicked servant
**“even as God hath forgiven you in Christ”** — through Christ

5.1:
**“Be ye therefore”**
• and because God has given
• now
**“followers of God”** — one another, by forgiving you
**“as most dear children”** — then: dearest children
5.2:
**“And walk”**
• not only forgive, but
• by the showing of works
**“in love”** — laying down their lives for the brethren, if there is need
**“as Christ also”** — so sincerely
**“hath loved us, and hath delivered himself for us”** — while he was wronged with spittings, buffetings and the like
**“an oblation and a sacrifice”** — while he was slain on the cross
**“for an odour of sweetness”**
• because he was slain for justice
• of whom it was said in the law
• Augustine. If the death of Christ was a sweet odour to God, then he gladly accepted his death. Therefore those who crucified him did not sin. But it is not so, because they unjustly killed the just one. He was first offered by his own will; and Judas, what has he but sin in betraying Christ? Yet unless Christ had delivered himself up, Judas would not have betrayed him. Judas betrayed Christ, Christ delivered himself. But the one was carrying on the business of his selling, the other of our redemption. Therefore the one sinned impiously, the other acted mercifully.
5.3:
**“But fornication”** — with the free from the husband
**“and all uncleanness”** — incontinence pertaining to lust, in whatever way it is done
**“or covetousness”** — immoderate desire of having
**“let it not so much as be named among you, as becometh saints”** — let there be no suspicion: among you
5.4:
**“Or obscenity”** — as in kisses and embraces
**“or foolish talking”** — as by flattering words
**“or scurrility”** — which is called courtliness by fools, which is wont to move laughter
**“which is to no purpose”**
• to profit
• although it is done with great labour
**“but rather giving of thanks”** — let it be named among you
5.5:
**“For know you this”** — by the reason of the mind
**“and understand”** — because the Scriptures say so
**“Avaricious”** — He equates covetousness with idolatry, because he means the covetous man whose god is money; or because he usurps for himself the goods of God, which God wills to serve the needy, and hoards them and prefers them to God, as idolatry does the honour of God.
*Ambrose:* Or the covetous man is an adulterer, who seizes for himself the goods of others, that is, another’s wife.
**“which is a serving of idols, hath no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God”** — which is of the Father and the Son
5.6:
**“Let no man”** — against this
**“deceive you with vain words”** — promising impunity from the mercy of God, or preaching natural things, like the false ones who say good things and do not do them
**“with vain words”** — All their arguments are empty words, void of fruit, drawing to punishments.
**“For because of these things cometh the anger of God upon the children of unbelief.”** — of the devil, whom we distrust, or who distrust
5.7: **“Be ye not therefore partakers with them.”** — like
5.8:
**“For you were heretofore”** — and therefore it is no wonder if these evils were then in you
**“darkness”** — sinning through ignorance
**“but now light”** — doing good from discernment, and justified through faith and baptism, and sons of God by adoption, who is the true light
**“in the Lord”** — not in you
**“as”** — and therefore
**“Walk then as children of the light.”**
• that is, in the life of the sons of God, in the course of good works, holily and blamelessly
• because these works are of the light
5.9:
**“For the fruit”**
• or: 'for'
• Works of this kind, however, are the fruit and work of the light.
**“of the light is”** — that is, to live
**“in all goodness”** — that you be good
**“and justice”** — do what is just to your neighbours
**“and truth”** — that you speak true things
**“and justice, and truth”** — Or justice and truth are parts of goodness. And the sense is: In all goodness; and in place of it: and justice and truth.
5.10:
**“Proving”** — walk, first proving and discerning by reason
**“what is well pleasing to God”** — as if your works are so carefully watched that they may be pleasing to God
5.11:
**“And have no”** — walk as sons of the light
**“fellowship with the unfruitful works”**
• that with the good there be a share of the evil
• be separated from the evil in heart, not in body
**“of darkness”** — or: 'of the dark ones'
**“but rather reprove them”**
• not neglecting the correction of your own
• yet with a gentle mind
**“reprove them”** — As the Apostle says elsewhere: Do this, that outwardly the rebuke may sound terribly, and inwardly the love of gentleness be kept. They join two things: namely that they not share in it by consenting, and that they reprove. For in these two ways the wicked man does not stain you, if you do not consent, even if you reprove. The Apostle embraced both, saying: Have no fellowship, do not consent, praise or approve. And because it is little not to consent, he adds: But rather reprove, that is, rebuke, correct, restrain. And the sense is: be not consenting to the wicked by approving, nor negligent in reproving, nor proud by reproving insultingly.
5.12:
**“For the things that”**
• do not have fellowship
• you ought not to have fellowship either
**“are done by them in secret”**
• that is, in thought
• in this it appears that they are shameful
• in a place not open to view
**“it is a shame even to speak of”** — not only to do
5.13:
**“But all things”**
• especially the wicked
• or: 'for'
**“But all things that are reproved”** — But they are to be reproved, because thus they are often made manifest through confession and penance, and therefore they must be reproved, because what is thus made manifest is turned into light. Or those wicked are made manifest to themselves that they are wicked, and so are to be reproved, because thus they begin to be light. Or: reprove; but all things, etc. For all that is made manifest, that is, the wicked man when he comes to know himself to be wicked, is light, that is, through penance he begins to be converted to good.
**“by the light”**
• by the enlightened
• holy and good men, who are the sons of light
**“are made manifest”**
• to themselves, that they are wicked
• before, they are not known
**“for all that”** — wicked, especially
**“for”** — or “for”
**“that is made manifest”**
• thus
• through confession and penance
**“is light”**
• it is turned into light, because it is good that sin is made manifest through penance and confession
• Is light, that is, not ambiguous, nor can it be excused, what is said openly.
5.14:
**“For which cause”** — namely, because what is made manifest becomes light
**“he saith”** — the Holy Spirit says through me
**“Rise thou that sleepest”**
• who are sluggish and do not know yourself in sins
• forgetful of God
• Rise through confession, and arise through satisfaction.
**“and arise from the dead”** — from future damnation
**“and shall enlighten thee”** — here through faith, and in the future through sight
**“Christ”** — who is the sun of justice
5.15:
**“See therefore”** — because it is profitable to reprove
**“how”** — by what moderation
**“you walk circumspectly”** — by living and by reproving
**“not as unwise”** — indiscreet
**“But as wise”** — namely, providing in all things
5.16:
**“redeeming the time”** — preparing the opportunity to serve God and to be free for divine things, which is necessary, because today men are wicked
**“Redeeming the time”** — Or: what you have done too little at one time, make up at another, halving the days which the impious do not halve. For some halve the days, others fill them, others do not even begin them; that is, some die in Egypt, others in the desert, others in the holy land. Nor is it a wonder if you have done less, because the days are evil, and not everything can be done at pleasure.
**“because the days are evil”** — that is, in this life many hindrances occur
**“the days are evil”** — The days are called evil on account of the wickedness and misery of men. For otherwise, as far as the spans of the hours go, these days are well ordered. For the seasons take their turns and run their course: the sun rises and sets, and the times pass. To whom are the times troublesome, if men are not troublesome to themselves? The days are called evil, then, as I said, on account of the misery and wickedness of men. But misery is common to man; wickedness therefore ought not to be common. For since Adam fell from paradise there have never been any but evil days, as the child shows who is born, who begins with weeping. He does not yet speak, and already he prophesies that he will be in toil and fear. Let us therefore redeem the time. He redeems who loses, that is, gives of his own that he may have leisure for God, as if he gave money for wine: you give money and buy wine. You give one thing, you receive another; you lose something, you gain something. So you lose coins, that you may buy yourself something. So may you lose of your own, that you may buy yourself quiet. Whence: “If a man will contend with thee in judgment, and take away thy coat, let go thy cloak also unto him,” that you may have a quiet heart, lest you lose the time of leisure for God, from whom he wishes to call you away by loss and lawsuits.
5.17:
**“Wherefore”** — because the days are evil
**“become not unwise”** — thoughtless
**“but understanding”** — but seek what pleases God
**“what is the will of God”** — that all things be done with moderation
5.18:
**“And be not drunk with wine”** — nothing is less fitting for one who reproves others
**“In whom”** — from which an evil movement proceeds, whence the authority to rebuke is removed
**“is luxury; but be ye filled with the holy Spirit”** — the gifts of the Holy Spirit
5.19:
**“Speaking to yourselves in psalms, and hymns, and spiritual canticles, singing and making melody to God”** — In this way you will be able to be filled with the Spirit, if you understand and instruct yourselves inwardly about what you say, namely psalms, which admonish to good work; and hymns, which are of the praises of God; and canticles, which are of eternal joy. And therefore spiritual things are to be understood spiritually; and after speaking these, singing, praising God, and exulting in eternal things, as the hymn and canticle teach, and making melody by deed, as the Psalm teaches.
**“in your hearts to the Lord”** — by spontaneous will
5.20:
**“Giving thanks always”** — for the glory of the Lord, not your own
**“for all things”**
• for prosperity or adversity
• gifts
**“in the name”** — exalting
**“Of our Lord Jesus Christ”**
• through whom he adopted us, and through whom we have known him
• because God is by believing
**“and the Father”** — because the Father is eternal by the nature of Christ, and by the grace of adoption to us
5.21:
**“Being subject”** — humbly taking care
**“Subject one to another”** — Ambrose. Not only hearers to prelates, but also prelates to those under them, serving them in charity and humbly taking care of them. For even if the dignity belongs to the greater, it is nevertheless administrative. Whence the Apostle: “I have made myself the servant of all.” It is therefore the part of the greater, their dignity nevertheless preserved, to serve, as it is the part of the lesser to obey humbly; and this ordered subjection, of the greater as of the lesser, ought to be in the chaste fear of Christ, who commanded humility.
**“in the fear of Christ”** — by the chaste fear of God, who commanded humility
5.22:
**“Women”** — Up to here he has spoken generally about conduct; now he exhorts certain persons in each rank.
**“be subject to their husbands, as to the Lord”**
• in simplicity
• like Sara, who called Abraham lord
5.23:
**“Because the husband is the head”**
• ruler
• and author, whence he began
**“of the wife, as Christ is the head”** — ruler, author
**“of the church”** — Christ
**“He is the saviour”** — is and
**“of his body”** — that is, of the Church
**“of him”** — of Christ
5.24:
**“Therefore as”** — Christ is the saviour of the Church; which the husband is not of the wife; but nevertheless as the Church
**“as the church is subject to Christ, so also let the wives be to their husbands in all things”** — which is not against God
5.25:
**“Husbands, love your wives”** — of whom you are the head
**“as Christ also loved the church”** — of whom he is the head
**“and delivered himself up for it”**
• so much did he love that
• so also you for your wives, if there is need
5.26:
**“That he might sanctify it”** — the righteousness of the good life
**“cleansing it”**
• before
• from sins
**“by the laver of water”** — sanctify
**“in the word of life”**
• who is given life
• by whose coming to the element it becomes a sacrament
5.27:
**“as”** — to this end
**“present”** — in the future
**“to himself a glorious church”**
• glowing in soul and body
• adorned with a double robe
**“not having”**
• now or then
