• Now, Spot or wrinkle, but that she should be holy. Here, through good works. And without blemish, in abstinence from evil. Or: then holy through glory, without blemish through the removal of corruption. As Christ shed his blood to wash the spot of the Church, and stretched himself on the cross to take away the wrinkle, so also husbands, if need be, ought to die to save their wives, and to instruct them with the word of life, that they may present them to God.
**“spot”** — something criminal
**“or wrinkle”** — mortal sin lying hidden within, as deceit and duplicity are called a wrinkle
**“not having spot or wrinkle”** — Because through good action she is clean from spot, and through hope stretched out to the things above; therefore his garment on the mountain shone as white as snow, which signified the Church cleansed from every spot of sin, who through the stretching out of Christ on the wood of the cross is stretched free from wrinkle, and by desire toward heavenly things.
**“or any such thing”** — some sin for which one is condemnable
5.28:
**“So also”** — likewise
**“ought men to love their wives as their own bodies”**
• that is, as themselves, because both are one flesh, and the wife is a portion of the husband’s body
• because
**“He that loveth his wife, loveth himself”** — because the wife is the husband’s body, and the husband the head of the wife
5.29:
**“For no man ever hated his own flesh”** — ought to love his wife, who is his own flesh, because no one hates his flesh
**“hated”** — although the saints mortify the flesh, they do not hate it but the sin that is in it
**“No man ever hated his own flesh”** — He who wishes to be without a body hates not the body but its corruptions and its weight.
**“but nourisheth”** — with food and drink
**“and cherisheth it”**
• with garments
• as his own flesh, and indeed as his own flesh, because it is his body, and we are all members of this body: some of the flesh, that is the weak; others of the bones, that is the perfect
**“as also Christ doth the church”** — So let a husband do toward his wife, who is his flesh, because so also Christ nourishes the Church with the food of his body, and cherishes it with the spiritual garments of the precepts, the virtues and good works.
5.30:
**“Because we are members of his body, of his flesh”** — as the weak, who need to be sustained by the strong
**“of his flesh”** — Augustine. In Genesis Adam says: “This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.” As Eve, made from Adam, drew from him flesh and bones, so we, established by Christ, are some like bones, strong, others like flesh, weak, from his flesh, that is, in respect of a like weakness which he had in his manhood. To show this, how much he loved the Church, it is written in Genesis: Christ as man shall leave the Father, by taking the form of a servant, and the mother, that is the Synagogue, from whom he was born according to the flesh, and shall cleave, that is, join himself, to the Church; and the two, that is Christ and the Church, shall be in one will and one flesh. Genesis says these are the words of the first man. But Christ in the gospel says they are God’s, when he says: “Have ye not read, that he who made man from the beginning, made them male and female? And he said: For this cause,” etc., that you may know that on account of the ecstasy of sleep which came upon Adam, in which he was within the angelic court, he could have said this by divine inspiration, as a prophet. Christ and the Church are one flesh, because God, with God, through the flesh became a sharer with us. Christ, head and body, is one, like a whole man, because the woman also was made from the man and belongs to the man. Christ left the Father, because he did not appear to men in that dignity in which he is with the Father.
**“and of his bones”** — as the perfect and strong, who are sustained in Christ alone
5.31:
**“For this cause”** — because he loves his wife
**“shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they shall be two in one flesh”** — here Moses speaks of the union of marriage, which is the sign of a great thing, namely the joining of Christ and the Church
5.32: **“This is a great sacrament; but I speak in Christ and in the church”** — This is a great sacrament, etc. And lest anyone think it is meant of the man and the wife according to the bodily union of both natural sexes, which adds a mingling: I speak in Christ and in the Church. According to this, then, what has been said is taken as of Christ and the Church: They are no longer two, but one flesh. And as bridegroom and bride are spoken of, so head and body. Whether, then, head and body is said, or bridegroom and bride, understand one thing. For from two there is made, as it were, one person, namely from head and body, from bridegroom and bride; which wonderful and excellent unity Isaias commends, in whom Christ speaking says: “As a bridegroom decked me with a crown, and as a bride adorned me with her jewels.” The sacrament of this spiritual unity was that which is said in Genesis, literally, of the union of marriage.
5.33:
**“Nevertheless”** — although this is said not only according to the letter but is a sign of another thing, nevertheless let the husband also love his wife according to the letter, following the mortality of the history
**“let every one of you in particular love his wife as himself. And the wife”** — let not only love but also
**“fear her husband”** — be subject to her husband

6.1:
**“Children”** — as subjects
**“obey your parents”** — carnal
**“in the Lord”** — according to the faith and justice of the Lord
**“For this”** — and you ought to
**“for”** — for, because
**“is just”** — because it is the precept of the law
6.2:
**“Honour thy father and thy mother”** — To honour a father is to show him reverence and supply his necessities.
**“the first commandment”** — Among the commandments that concern man, in the second table. For the decalogue pertains to the two precepts of the charity of God and of neighbour. To the first precept, of God, three cords pertain, that is, three commandments, because God is a Trinity. But to the other precept, namely of neighbour, seven cords, that is, seven commandments. And those three pertaining to God were written in the first table, and the other seven, to the neighbour, in the second. Among these this is rightly the first, because as God is principally the origin of man, so, secondarily, are parents. A promise is added to this commandment, which is not in the others.
**“with a promise”** — which is not in the others
6.3:
**“That it may be well”** — so that
**“with thee”** — in the present: in carnal and spiritual things
**“And thou mayest be long lived”** — in eternal life
**“upon”** — founded
**“earth.”** — of the living
6.4:
**“And you, fathers, provoke not your children to anger”** — because so they will not keep the law. For in anger no one will know what is useful.
**“but bring them up”** — while they are boys, so that they do not despise the law
**“in the discipline”** — of words
**“and correction of the Lord.”** — of blows, so that they may make progress in the things of the Lord
6.5:
**“Servants, be obedient”**
• which he took from sin
• Augustine. On John. Servitude began from sin, for the first cause of servitude is sin, that man should be subjected to man by the bond of condition; which was not except by God’s judgment, with whom there is no iniquity, and who knows how to distribute different punishments according to the deserts of the guilty.
**“to them that are your lords according to the flesh”** — not only spiritual and good
**“with fear”** — reverence, which sons too
**“and trembling,”** — which is of slaves
**“in the simplicity”** — He makes servitude free who serves not with fear under deceit but with faithful love, until iniquity passes away and all power is emptied.
**“of your heart”** — so that as you show outwardly, so may it be in your will; so that if you cannot be made free by your lords, you may serve freely
**“as to Christ.”** — obey, since he himself commanded this for the preservation of humility
6.6:
**“Not serving to the eye, as it were pleasing men,”** — obey, I say, not serving to the eye while you are seen, like those who seek to please men
**“but, as the servants of Christ doing the will of God from the heart,”**
• with Christ commanding; serve not men as servants but Christ
• so also you
6.7:
**“With a good will serving,”** — to your lords
**“as to the Lord, and not to men.”** — so that in that, thinking you serve God and not men only
6.8:
**“Knowing”** — I say to you
**“that whatsoever good thing any man shall do, the same shall he receive from the Lord, whether he be bond, or free.”** — For he shall not receive less than the free man.
6.9:
**“And you, masters, do the same things”** — like in good will
**“forbearing”** — if the servant sins
**“threatenings,”** — not only blows
**“knowing that the Lord both of them and you is in heaven; and”** — that
**“there is no respect of persons with him.”** — For God is a just judge, who discerns causes, not persons. Therefore, by what measure a man has measured, the same shall be measured back to him.
6.10:
**“Finally, brethren,”** — he admonishes in general
**“Finally”** — After the particular precepts by which he admonished the individual orders, he now admonishes all in common. Until now you have lived by word and deed; now henceforth, in the future, for the remaining time.
**“be strengthened”** — against the war of the devil
**“in the Lord”** — with the help of the Lord
**“and in the might of his power.”** — who gives mighty strength to those who wish to fight
6.11:
**“Put you on”** — thus you ought to be strengthened
**“the armour of God,”** — virtues
**“that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil.”** — because he plots evil from hiding
6.12:
**“For our wrestling is not”** — it is necessary that you stand, because
**“against flesh and blood,”** — the war is near; not against men, who are visible and frail, nor only against those vices that come from flesh and blood
**“but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world”** — demons who rule over others, and against those who have power over them, who are to be feared because they govern worldly men and are lovers of the world’s darkness, these evils, that is, those whom they hurl into dark works
**“Rulers of the world”** — Not because they rule the world, which consists of heaven and earth. But he calls sinners the world, of whom it is said elsewhere: “And the world knew him not.” Such a world they rule, against whom we have perpetual enmities, because they also make men troublesome to those who suffer them. For they instigate and inflame them, and move them as their vessels, and touch them like instruments. Against them we have a hidden struggle, for which the Apostle arms us.
**“of this darkness”** — Lest it be thought that demons rule this invisible world, he adds what he meant by the name of the world of this darkness, that is, of sins. As if to say: the demons do not rule the world, which consists of heaven and earth, but sinners.
**“Against spiritual things”** — As if to say: the enemies are to be feared, because they are spiritual and invisible, and because they are wicked, and they fight not for a small matter but to take away the heavenly inheritance. Or he calls virtues heavenly, in which we suffer the warfare of the demons. Or the spirits of wickedness are in heavenly places, that is, in this lower air. For they fight like horsemen on horses, that is, men. Let us therefore kill the horses and possess the horsemen.
**“against the spirits of wickedness in the high places.”** — against the spiritual and wicked enemies
6.13:
**“Wherefore”** — because such enemies and of so great a matter
**“take unto you the armour of God,”** — by which God arms his own
**“that you may be able”** — because otherwise you would not be able
**“to resist”** — to resist
**“in the evil day,”** — in this life, where there is temptation
**“and to stand in all things”** — both in prosperous and in adverse things
**“perfect.”** — to stand perfect in virtues
6.14:
**“Stand therefore, having your loins girt”**
• because the armour of God is necessary
• manfully, as often as you are provoked
• GIRDED LOINS: that is, restraining carnal desires with the girdle of chastity, not in pretence, but in truth or through charity.
**“about with truth,”**
• that is, truly, on account of Christ
• or with charity
**“and having on the breastplate of justice,”** — Augustine. Justice, by rendering each man his right, is to be the breastplate, lest a place be open to the enemy.
6.15:
**“Shod”** — Mark says the apostles are shod with sandals or soles, so that the foot is neither covered nor bare on the ground, that is, lest the gospel be hidden, nor rest on earthly advantages.
**“and your feet shod”** — Feet, that is, the affections, should be fortified with virtues, lest they be assailed by vices, so that they may thus be ready to preach the gospel, which announces peace between God and man, or so that they may be ready to fulfil the precepts of the gospel.
**“with the preparation of the gospel of peace.”** — that is, that you may be prepared to preach the gospel or to fulfil its precepts
6.16:
**“In all things”** — in battles
**“taking the shield of faith,”** — the faith of things which we do not see
**“The shield of faith”** — Augustine. Faith is the shield under which justice is safe, as under the defence of all the virtues. It is held out before all the weapons, and the devil attacks it first. Whence faith, about to fight, first seeks the field under the uncertain front of the battle.
**“wherewith you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts”** — all the wiles
**“of the most wicked one.”** — of the devil
**“extinguish all the fiery darts.”** — which set fire from vice to vice
6.17:
**“And take unto you the helmet of salvation”** — rejoicing in the hope of eternal salvation
**“And the helmet”** — The helmet is eternal salvation, whose memory wraps the mind lest it fail.
**“and the sword of the Spirit”** — which the Holy Spirit gives
**“And the sword of the Spirit”** — Augustine. On the Psalm. The word of God is a two-edged sword, teaching of things temporal and eternal; promising the comfort of the former in the Old Testament, the perfection of the latter in the New. For what is promised us temporally belongs to one side of the sword, but what is promised for ever belongs to the other side of the sword. For this reason too there are said to be two testaments, because the old promises earthly things, the new eternal. Of this sword the Lord says: “I came not to send peace, but the sword.” This sword is truly sharp, because it divides the one whom it strikes from the world.
**“which is the word of God”** — to strike the enemy
6.18:
**“By all prayer”** — through all things which are to be prayed for
**“and supplication praying”** — and by petitioning with adjuration
**“at all times”** — not by the hours
**“in the spirit”** — not in words but in mind
**“In the spirit”** — He prays who prays with a clean conscience and sound faith. He prays in the flesh who, with a polluted mind, is about to sin again, not by chance but by purpose.
**“and in the same watching”** — attentive
**“with all instance”**
• that is, that they press on in all virtues
• not carelessly
**“and supplication”** — keeping watch
**“for all the saints”** — made
6.19:
**“And for me”** — namely
**“that speech may be given me”** — by God
**“that I may open”**
• which tribulation may dull
• In opening, that is, that I may openly relate the mystery of the gospel, that is, the secrets of the incarnation and passion. Lest the pressure of tribulation, by its very fear, blunt the point of the teaching.
**“my mouth”** — of my word
**“with”** — that “freely and without hindrance I may make known that mystery”
**“confidence, to make known the mystery of the gospel”** — freely, without hindrance, I may make known that mystery
6.20:
**“For which I am an ambassador”** — for not even for my chains do I cease from my embassy
**“I am”** — now at Rome
**“in a chain”** — placed
**“so that”** — with confidence
**“in him”** — in preaching the gospel itself
**“I may be bold to speak according as I ought”** — amid all evils
6.21:
**“But that you also may know”** — lest, on hearing of the tribulations, they should be moved; he says Tychicus is to make everything known to them, adding:
**“the things that concern me”** — concerning me; because there were many tribulations for him which, as it were, surrounded him, or rather were certain because they did not touch his inner self
**“what I am doing”** — how constant I am amid those things
**“Tychicus will make known to you all things”** — so that they may listen well; he commends him
**“my dearest brother”**
• therefore listen to him
• my brother in faith
**“faithful minister in the Lord”** — in those things which are of the Lord
6.22: **“Whom I have sent to you for this same purpose, that you may know”** — that he may tell you the plain truth
6.23:
**“Peace”** — He wishes them peace, which is the gate of love.
**“Peace be to the brethren and charity with faith, from God the Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ”** — through peace they will remain in charity, which comes from faith
6.24:
**“Grace be with all them that love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption. Amen”**
• after the likeness of the spouse who does not admit corruption
• in the integrity of faith, or in eternal life

1.1:
**“Paul”** — He sends ahead a greeting, as is his custom. Then he gives thanks to God for them, begging greater goods for them, that growing in virtues they may come to perfection. Then he urges them to patience in tribulations by the example of himself and of Christ. Afterwards, that they beware of the craftiness of the false apostles. Finally he inserts a moral admonition, and near the end he says that he rejoices over the gift which they had sent him at Rome by Epaphroditus.
**“Timothy”** — He names him here, because he was about to send him to them; commending him in a way, so that they may receive kindly what he writes by him.
**“servants”** — with chaste fear
**“Servants”** — He called them servants, so that they too might bear hard things for the Lord; of Christ, so that they might stand firm against false teachers.
*Augustine:* As there are two fears, so there are two servitudes, which make two kinds of servants: for there is a fear which perfect charity casts out, and there is a servitude like it which is to be cast out with it. There is also a chaste fear, remaining for ever and ever, to which another servitude is joined, not remaining for ever in the house.
**“the servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints”** — sanctified by baptism
**“in Christ Jesus”**
• Christ working
• or established
• in the faith of Christ
• who believe God and man
**“who are at Philippi, with the bishops”** — that is, and
**“With the bishops”** — He calls the presbyters bishops. For there would not be several bishops in one city, nor would he pass over the presbyters and descend to the deacons. And by the deacons he signifies the greater, by the saints the lesser; because he puts the lesser first, he invites to humility; and because he adds these also, he shows that no one is so perfect as not to need admonition.
**“and deacons,”**
• who equally wished their good
• with the greater and the lesser, or he writes together with these
1.2:
**“Grace”**
• and
• remission of sins
**“be unto you, and peace”** — tranquillity of mind and reconciliation to God
1.3:
**“I give thanks to my God”**
• of all
• by whose will all good things come to all
**“I give thanks”** — As if to say: do what you do, because such things are why I praise God.
**“my God”**
• by my private benefit
• who does for me what I wish in you
**“in every remembrance of you,”**
• as often as I become mindful of you
• which indeed I am
1.4:
**“Always”** — at fitting times
**“in all my prayers making supplication for you all”** — held
**“you”** — prelates or subjects
**“with joy;”** — not sad about fault
**“making supplication”** — praying that you may persevere
1.5:
**“For”** — I say with joy held
**“your communication”**
• because you have shared with me in the faith and works of the gospel
• YOU HAVE SHARED. Or you have made your shared things in preaching the gospel.
**“in the gospel”** — which is
**“of Christ, from the first day”** — of your conversion, and therefore henceforth one must stand more firmly
1.6:
**“Being confident in the Lord Jesus”** — not in you
**“of this very thing, that he who”** — God
**“Being confident”** — As if: I beseech that you stand, and I trust that this very thing which I pray for be done by you, not something else; but see that I do not trust in vain.
**“hath begun”** — working
**“a good work in you,”** — Or, IN YOU. Through succession, until the common day of judgment.
**“will perfect”**
• cooperating
• what he began by working
**“Will perfect”** — Augustine. On Grace and Free Will. Because he himself, beginning, works that we may will; and, perfecting, cooperates with those who will.
**“unto the day of Christ Jesus.”** — until the end of life, when God will be seen
1.7:
**“As it is meet for me”**
• he ought not to think otherwise of such good men
• So I give thanks, I beseech and trust, as it is right to think, that is, so to wish. And he sets out the cause: because I have you in my heart, whether bound, knowing that you too are bound, or defending the gospel, which you also do.
**“to think this for you all, for that I have you in my heart,”**
• in the innermost affection of love
• not with lips only
**“and in my bands,”** — because you suffer with me
**“and in the defence,”** — against those who attack
**“and confirmation of the gospel,”** — of the weak in teaching
**“you all are partakers of my joy”** — that in the future you may be partners
**“you all are partakers”** — even the lesser
1.8:
**“For God is my witness”** — I pray for all of you for this reason, because I desire that you all be in the bowels of Christ, so that you may be loved by Christ as his bowels; and hence (he is) witness.
**“how”** — with what affection
**“I long after you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ.”**
• May I desire you all in the bowels, that is, in the inmost love of Christ, that you may be perfectly loved by him; or that you may love God and neighbours with the same effect with which Christ loved, who laid down his life.
• Or it refers to what he said above, that he desires them to be partners of his joy, and specifies how: namely, with the love of Christ, not human, so that he may have them as sharers in God.
1.9:
**“And this I pray”** — also
**“that your charity may more and more abound”** — may grow
**“in knowledge,”** — that they may know in what things they ought to love God and neighbour, and when they have known, may have sense, that is, memory and attention, in all things
**“and in all understanding,”** — memory
1.10:
**“That you may approve the better things, that you may be sincere”** — in you
**“That you may approve the better things”** — Again, let your charity grow into knowledge, so that you may prove and discern, not only evil and good but also among goods which are better; so that after testing you may be sincere in yourselves, without works of corruption, and as regards the neighbour, without offence.
**“and without offence”** — toward the neighbour
**“unto”**
• and this perseveringly
• unto
**“the day of Christ,”** — that is, the end of life
1.11:
**“Filled with the fruit of justice”** — not only without evils but also full of fruit, that is, of works which are the fruit of justice, which is a habit of the soul
**“Filled with the fruit”** — That is, with the reward of justice, so that you may be the glory and praise of God, so that for you it may be said: “God is wonderful in his saints.”
**“through”** — and this
**“Jesus Christ”** — not by your own strength
**“unto the glory and praise of God.”** — by this, about to pass into eternal glory, whence you may praise God
1.12:
**“Now, brethren, I desire you should know”** — because he said he desired these to be sharers of his joy; therefore make known what his preaching has achieved, as to dear ones
**“Now, I desire you should know”** — Thus far he has spoken in general; from here he sets down in particular the things that persuade to endurance. I give thanks for you. I trust; but I would have you know, brethren, as if he were saying: since you are so perfect, persevere and beware, lest the tribulations pressing upon you diminish this your perfection, but look to my example.
**“That the things which”** — the abundance of sufferings on every side surrounding me from without
**“me”** — or therefore around, because they do not reach the inner parts
**“have fallen out, rather”** — rather than to my harm, as the wicked intended
1.13:
**“So”** — to the furtherance
**“That”** — the usefulness of the bonds appears in Christ, who is more proclaimed on account of the bonds
**“my bands are made manifest in Christ”**
• or the bonds themselves, that they were in Christ, that is, that I was bound on account of him and not for another crime
• That my bands are made manifest, etc. Jerome. Because I patiently endure whatever evils, it is clear that it is not a crime of falsehood, which a just vengeance strikes against me, but a certain power of truth, which the strength of enduring magnifies.
• Or they spoke of my bonds, or preachers made known in all the praetoria.
**“in all the court,”** — where the greater men assemble
**“and in all other places”**
• places
• And in all other places. For when the Apostle at Rome, bound, had been thrust into prison in the house of the emperor, and was teaching the gospel and encouraging the weak and working many miracles, many believed through him, so much so that he made the house of the persecutor a church; then indeed his bands were made manifest in Christ. Or: In all the court and in all other places, that is, to the emperor, to all the consuls and princes, and to the lesser, that he endured such things for Christ.
1.14:
**“That many”** — so they have benefited the gospel, which I endure
**“of the brethren in the Lord”** — not in themselves
**“growing confident by my bands,”** — by consideration of the bonds
**“are much more”** — than before
**“bold”** — against those attacking
**“to speak the word of God without fear.”** — as if: by my example they dare to preach confidently, saying thus: if the bound man speaks, why not rather we?
**“Bold without fear”** — They dared without fear. Augustine. For his constancy encouraged many not to fear to preach the gospel.
1.15:
**“Some indeed”** — different from the former, because they are wicked
**“and”** — and preach
**“out of envy and contention,”** — because they envy the glory of my apostleship and strive to have it
**“but some”** — different from these, the good
**“and for good will”**
• for the love of God and of neighbour, the example of my good will
• that they may save others
1.16:
**“Some”** — not different
**“out of charity,”** — a private matter, so that they might fill his place for the apostle while he is in chains
**“out of contention preach Christ not sincerely, supposing that they raise affliction”** — to increase
**“Supposing affliction”** — Ambrose. Therefore these announced Christ with the craftiness of pretence, that they might be able to stir up seditions against the Apostle, as the author of them, who had gathered many into his company. Behold, he has distinguished four kinds of teachers: two of the good and two of the evil, who all announce Christ, but not with the same mind.
1.17:
**“knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel.”** — that is, I am set for the defence, in chains, or set, that is, I am firm and steadfast in the defence
**“But some”** — different from these, because they are wicked
*Augustine:* For the wicked announced Christ not with a simple and truthful heart; but the good, with a pure heart and sincere faith, all alike advanced the gospel. Whence he says that the wicked are to be tolerated, adding: For what?
**“But some out of contention”** — Convicted in the contention by me, they preach, according as they ought to be convicted of preaching.
**“Out of contention”** — From private hatred, which they once had against me, and were refuted. And lest they seem corrected, he adds: not with a pure heart, but supposing that, if any accuse them about the preaching, they would vindicate its author against me.
1.18:
**“But what then?”**
• while even the wicked advance it; for what matters the intention
• He does not forbid hired workers but permits them, because they too are useful for some things.
**“so that by all means, by occasion,”**
• of earthly gain
• as the wicked do
**“or by truth”**
• as the good do
• with a true heart
**“Or by truth”** — Augustine. Some announced the truth, though not through truth, that is, not with a true mind. For they preached the gospel on occasion, seeking from men their own advantages; taking counsel for earthly desires, they announced the kingdom of heaven, having truth in the tongue, but not chastity in the breast. These are useful to those whom the Lord instructs. Whence he says: “All things therefore whatsoever they say to you, observe and do: but according to their works do ye not.” For whoever seeks anything from God other than God does not seek God chastely. We find three persons, if we diligently search the words of the Lord in the gospel: the shepherd, the hireling, the thief. The shepherd announces the truth for the sake of the truth. The hireling, on the occasion of a temporal thing. The thief and robber denies the truth and takes it away. The shepherd, therefore, is to be loved, the hireling tolerated, the robber to be guarded against.
**“Christ”**
• the truth of Christ
• not falsehood. Whence: “Do what they say,” etc.
**“be preached. And in this”** — because through occasion as well as through truth
**“rejoice,”** — now
**“yea”** — or not only progress for others but joy for me too
**“and will rejoice.”** — afterwards
**“Yea, and I will rejoice”** — Therefore I rejoice over my wicked fellows, or over the advance of the gospel, because from it comes my salvation.
1.19:
**“For I know that this”**
• to suffer for Christ
• or the advance of the gospel through my preaching
**“shall fall out to me”** — in the future
**“unto salvation,”** — which they prepare for me unto death
**“through your prayer”** — not only by my merit
**“and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ,”** — that is, through the Spirit who supports me from beneath, as a column holds up one who is about to fall
1.20:
**“According”** — as if to say: it will be as great as I expect in the future and hope for in the present
**“to my expectation and hope, that”** — this I hope
**“unto”** — in prosperity or adversity, so that in some way I might give up preaching
**“nothing I shall be confounded,”** — state
**“In nothing”** — Haimo. Because both the hope is great, and the thing is true and honest.
**“but with all confidence, as always”** — from the time of conversion
**“so now also”** — while I labour in chains
**“shall be magnified”** — among the Gentiles
**“Christ”** — the fame and glory of Christ
**“in my body,”** — even in what is more fragile
**“whether it be by life,”** — if I live, teaching
**“or by death.”** — leaving an example
1.21:
**“For to me, to live is Christ”** — by life, because I live for his sake, that I may magnify him, not for any other reason
**“For to me”** — As if: I rightly magnify Christ whether by life or by death. For to me “to live is Christ” means that here my life is through faith and hope, and in the future through sight. For this life he gives up his mortal body, that he may receive it immortal for eternity.
**“and to die is gain.”** — by death, because Christ is the reward of death; or dying itself is gain, because by death, freed from these miseries, I pass over to blessedness; or because by death he gains many for God
1.22:
**“If to live”**
• and to work well
• Christ is to me to live, that I may magnify him. But if this is so, then I do not know what to choose, to die or to live. As if, were it not for this fruit, there would be no doubt that I would choose to die, that I might have Christ as my reward; and therefore do not doubt about dying.
**“in the flesh”** — which seems strange
**“this is to me the fruit of labour”** — that is, so worthy from my work, namely to magnify Christ
**“what”** — behold
**“I shall choose”** — much less do I desire
1.23:
**“But I am straitened”**
• that is, I not only do not know but am also straitened
• therefore I do not know because
• or I do not know what to choose: for I am straitened between two, etc.
• I am straitened, etc. Augustine, On Christian Doctrine. It is not to be punctuated so as to say: I am straitened, and afterwards it follows, having a desire out of the two, namely of being dissolved and of remaining in the flesh; which is judged from the very text of the sentence, as follows: to be dissolved and to be with Christ is far the better. For it is plain that he says he has the desire of that which is best, so that, though he is straitened between two, he has desire only for the higher one, and for the other a necessity on account of the brethren. So, then, it is to be punctuated thus: I am straitened, or compelled, between two. Then follows: I say, having a desire, or longing, to be dissolved from these miseries, by which I am bound as if with fetters, and to be with Christ in presence. And as if it were asked why he has desire for this rather: He adds: because it is far the better, as far as concerns me. And as if it were asked again: why then are you compelled between two? He adds: because there is a necessity of remaining, saying: “But to abide still in the flesh, is needful for you,” not for me. As if: that is better for me, this is necessary for you; therefore I desire that, and this I do not refuse.
**“between two: having a desire to be dissolved”**
• from the desire to be dissolved and the necessity of living
• from these miseries
• because bound
**“and to be with Christ”** — in presence
**“a thing by far”** — as far as I am concerned
**“the better”** — but
1.24:
**“But to abide still in the flesh, is needful”** — that is better; this is necessary
**“But to abide still”** — Behold, he chooses not what is better for himself but what is profitable for many, for the sake of love, which is to be chosen above all.
**“for you”** — not for my sake
1.25:
**“And having this confidence, I know”** — because it is necessary for you; or I know, not doubtfully but confident in the mercy of God.
**“that I shall abide, and continue”** — not briefly indeed but for a long time
**“with you all”** — to the greater and the lesser
**“for your furtherance”** — that you may grow through good things
**“joy of faith”** — That we may rejoice in your faith, or that you may rejoice in faith, making progress in it. This is not except where there is a clean conscience.
1.26:
**“That your rejoicing may abound”** — that is, that you may give thanks abundantly to God with joy
**“in Christ Jesus”** — who has done good to you
**“for me”**
• preserved for you
• that is, freed
**“by my coming again”** — to come
**“to you”** — to strengthen you
1.27:
**“Only let your conversation”** — I shall come if only
**“the gospel of Christ”**
• the Lord’s discipline
• because according to your merit life will be given to me for your work
**“let your conversation be”** — so worthily, etc.
**“whether I come and see you, or, being absent, may hear of you”** — that is, this
**“that you stand fast in one spirit”** — holy, to which no contrary spirit clings; and as he is one, so you are of one mind without dissension
**“with one mind”**
• in will
• for every battle undertaken with one mind brings forth victory
• and
**“labouring together for the faith of the gospel”** — with all strength to fulfil what faith requires
1.28:
**“And”** — and after this
**“in nothing”** — in no danger
**“be ye terrified by the adversaries”** — who terrify you by harsh things
**“which to them is a cause of perdition”** — eternal
**“but to you of salvation”** — eternal
**“and this from God”** — Also, that you suffer is not from you but from God, because by the merit of Christ, who obeyed the Father, this is given to you among other graces.
1.29:
**“For unto you it is given”** — because it is given to you as a reward
**“for Christ”** — whom you love
**“not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him”**
• whence greater glory

• he humbled himself
**“Emptied”**
• Augustine. How? Not by emptying the substance, not by changing the form of God. Taking the form of a servant: the form of a servant came to him without losing the form of God; the form of God did not depart.
• To empty oneself is to show oneself visible from the greatness of one’s invisibility.
**“being made in the likeness of men”** — Augustine. Let us see, then, Christ Jesus, God and man, both maker of things and made among things, both creator of man and created man. Christ as God is equal to the Father, he is as great as he, such as he, he is what he is. He is not he who he is, because that one is the Father, this one the Son. But he is what he is, because that one is God and this one, that one almighty and this one, that one unchangeable and this one; therefore it was not robbery to be equal to God, because it was by nature; as he is born, so also always born, and as always born, so always equal.
**“taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men”**
• The same. He did not therefore beget one unequal, nor add equality to him already born, but by begetting gave it, because he begot an equal, not an unequal. Not without reason, then, does Scripture say both: namely, that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Father is greater than the Son. The one is on account of the form of God, the other on account of the form of a servant, on account of which he was made less not only than the Father, but even than himself and the Holy Spirit; and also: “Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels”; therefore he was both made man and remained God. Therefore it is very reasonable that Christ the man is less than the Father, and that the same Christ, God, is equal to the Father. For Christ, the Son of God, is both God and man: God from eternity, man in time. God, because he is God the Word. Man, because in the unity of person a rational soul and flesh were joined to the Word. For when he was the only Son of God, in order that he might also be “full of grace,” the one Son of God was made the son of man, and the same is the son of man. There are not two sons of God, God and man, but one Son of God, God without beginning, man having received a beginning.
• Likewise. For just as the number of persons is not increased when flesh is joined to the soul, so that there is one man, so the number of persons is not increased when a man is joined to the Word, so that there is one Christ.
• The same. God is therefore read to be man, that we may understand the singularity of this person; not that we may suppose the divinity changed into flesh. For by that assumption neither of the two was converted and changed into the other, nor was the divinity changed into a creature so as to cease to be divinity, nor was the creature changed into divinity so as to cease to be a creature.
**“made”** — According to the form of a servant. He who was uncreated according to the form of God and also in his own. In habit, that is, in conduct. Found, by one wishing to test him, as another man, because he eats, drinks, sits, etc.
**“in habit”** — Habit is the assumption of a man, like a garment which does not change what it clothes.
*Augustine:* God the Son, not changing his own form, but taking the form of a servant, and not converted or transmuted into man with his unchangeable stability lost, “was made in the likeness of men.” He is himself the one who assumes, in assuming a true man; this likeness expresses a true man. “And in habit found as a man,” that is, by having man he was found as a man by those to whom he appeared in man. When he says: As a man, it is such as that: “As of the only begotten of the Father.” For it expresses the truth. Has not the habit, then, sufficiently signified how he had said he was made in the likeness of man, because he was made so not by transfiguration into man but by habit, when he was clothed with the man whom, uniting him to himself, he in a manner conformed and joined to immortality and eternity?
2.8:
**“and in habit found as a man”** — “Habit” is said of a thing that comes to a person in order to be had. Yet there is this difference: some of the things that come so as to make a habit are not changed but change, as wisdom, which makes a wise man of a fool, remaining itself whole and unshaken. Others both change and are changed, as food, which loses its appearance when it is turned into the body, and changes weakness into strength. A third kind neither changes nor is changed, as a ring placed on the finger; this kind is very rarely found. A fourth kind: the things that come are changed, not in their nature, but are in a manner formed, and receive another appearance and form, as a garment, which when cast off and laid aside does not have the form it takes when put on. For put on the limbs it receives a form it does not have when taken off; this kind fits here. And according to this: He emptied himself.
**“He humbled”** — also
**“Humbled”** — Behold, we have in Christ humility, and thence the remedy for pride. Why then do you swell up, O man? O dead skin, why do you stretch yourself? O foul matter, why do you puff yourself up? Your prince is humble and you are proud. The head is humble and the member is proud.

**“God also hath exalted him”** — by giving impassibility and immortality
**“God hath exalted him”** — He exalted him according to his humanity, which was made more glorious in the resurrection. In which the divine nature also can be said to be exalted according to its showing forth, because it began to be known what it was; just as in the assumption of weakness it is said to be emptied, because what it was did not appear.
*Ambrose:* After the cross it is made manifest what he received from the Father when begotten. For he did not receive it then, when his divinity and majesty began to be known by creation. The name of God, which is above all names, is not given to man by title alone but by nature, but to him who is equal, who emptied himself, whose all things are from the Father.

*Augustine:* He gave to the man the name which is above all names, not to God, so that in the form of a servant the only begotten Son of God is named, in which he died, in which he ascended and sits at the right hand of the Father; in that same form, so honoured, so glorified, and changed by heavenly habit, he is both the son of David and the Lord of David, who is also Lord of heavenly, earthly and infernal things.

But perhaps it might be said that the man is God by adoption. And so Christ would be partly true God and partly adoptive. But the creature does not bend the knee to an adoptive God but to the true. It is established, however, that Christ is true God, to whom the knee is bent, not adoptive.

**“That the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of the Father”** — How can it happen that a man is in the glory of God the Father? Even if a man were adopted as God, he could not be in the glory of God the Father.
*Ambrose:* In the book On the Trinity he says: God the Word certainly has glory. But the glory of that Word is the same as the Father’s, so that the glory of the Father and the Son is one; whence the Son himself says: “I seek not my own glory,” that is, divided from the Father. For this belongs to him who is born of God, because to be in the glory of God the Father is to differ in nothing from him, so that the glory of the Father and the Son is one through common substance and power. Beware how you understand the aforesaid words of the illustrious men Ambrose and Augustine, lest they be thought to contradict each other. Know therefore that there is a natural gift and there is a gratuitous gift. By natural gift the Father gave the name above all names to God the Son, not to the man, that is, to Christ according as he is God, not according as he is man. Nor was this anything other than to beget one equal to himself. But by gratuitous gift he gave it to Christ the man, not to God, because Christ, not as God but as man, received the name of God by grace, and not by the grace of adoption but by the grace of union, so that he is not an adoptive God but the true God, to whom every knee is bent.

**“For Christ”** — Lest I should show the coming of Christ to be either not yet made or superfluous. For all these were empty hindrances, so that grace should not be approached.
3.8:
**“Furthermore I count”** — Not only for the sake of having Christ have I so judged. Nevertheless, that is, but even if I could not attain him. For this alone, namely for the knowledge which we have of Jesus, surpassing other knowledge. Or which stands out in him more than in others. Or it goes with the same as the preceding verse. All these things of the law I have, truly, that is, but yet not in part, but: I count all things loss. For the love of whose Christ, not only do I count all things loss, but I have also done so, by teaching and by living spiritually, that it might appear to others that all things are loss.
**“all things to be but loss for the excellent knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord; for whom”** — Christ to be honored
**“I have suffered the loss of all things, and count”** — that which is more
**“as dung”** — As if to say: not only the losses of goods, but those things which defile one who already observes the law; and this so that in the future I may have Christ as my reward, and here be a member in him, which cannot otherwise come about unless I esteem those things as dung.
3.9:
**“And may be found”** — to one attending reasonably
**“in him”** — a member joined to him by charity
**“not having”** — in this way he can be in him
**“my justice”** — by which one fears punishment and does not love justice
**“My justice”** — Whence elsewhere: “Seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted themselves to the justice of God,” that is, to the grace of God.
**“which is of the law, but that which is of the faith of Christ Jesus, which”** — justice from faith
**“My justice, which is of the law”** — If justice is from the law, how is it yours? Did you impose the law on yourself? God gave the law and imposed it. God commanded you to obey his law. But it is yours too, because you presume about the law, by your own will, thinking you are able to fulfil the law.
**“But that which is of the faith”** — Which is obtained from God, which takes away fear and gives love, which God alone works in us. For it is better to be just than to be a man. If then God made you a man, he makes you also just, which is better. He made you, not you yourself, but without you. For you applied no understanding that he should make you. He therefore who made you without your knowing justifies you when you are willing. And since our justice is from faith, what need is there of the law also? It is to be taken away altogether, according to the shadow of the legal figures.
**“of God”** — not from us, although the faith is ours
**“justice in faith”** — availing
**“Justice in faith”** — Justice, that is, being in faith; just as it is born of faith, so it has no existence except in faith.
3.10:
**“That I may know him”**
• perfectly in the future
• this seems to say of faith not having time for working, which nevertheless avails for this
• Or justice in faith, that I may know him. As if to say: He who thinks to be justified in the law does not know Christ. But I wish to be justified by faith that I may know him, why he was born, why he suffered, and may know what is the power of his resurrection, that is, the justification of believers, and may know the fellowship of his sufferings, which he knows well who believes that through it he will come to the joys of heaven.
**“To know”** — He adds the commendation of faith through the many things it does. For it makes us know God perfectly also in the other life, who is believed by faith here. And to have the resurrection, which is the power of our resurrection, and the efficacy of the resurrection of Christ. And in this life to have fellowship in suffering. For except through faith no one would suffer so much. And conformity to his death, that we may die as he did, if need be.
**“and the power”** — that is, to bring about our resurrection
**“of his resurrection”** — because he rose for our justification
**“and”** — to
**“the fellowship of his sufferings”**
• that is, that we may be partners of Christ in suffering
• of faith having time for working
• which is through charity
**“being made conformable”** — I may be found, configured with him
**“to his death”**
• that is, that I may die, if need be
• an imitator of his death and passion
3.11:
**“if”** — I despising
**“by any means I may attain”** — to Christ in the air
**“I may attain”** — Giving to God what he has given to me, and through this about to come to the resurrection. Or I may meet Christ in the judgment, which belongs to the saints only, coming first to the true and glorious resurrection, which is not among the dead but far from the dead; for although all rise on the day of judgment, only the just will be gloriously changed, and will meet the Lord, carried up into the air by angels. But the wicked will remain on earth until they receive the terrible sentence of the judge.
**“to the resurrection”** — true and glorious
**“which is from the dead”** — not among the dead
3.12:
**“Not as though”** — if somehow; because it is not true that here already
**“I had already attained”**
• some glory
• the power of the resurrection
**“Not as though I had already attained”** — He says this of himself, lest those whom he praises be puffed up as men, but that they may add labour, as he himself does, who is so great.
**“or were already perfect”**
• in knowledge
• of the knowledge of Christ
**“but I follow after”** — advancing, trying
**“But I follow after”** — Augustine. Not with the steps of the body, but with the affections of the mind and the conduct of life, that I may be able to be a perfect possessor of justice; I who, advancing by the right road from day to day in spiritual renewal, am already perfect as a traveller of the same justice. For he was a perfect traveller, but not yet one arrived at the perfection of the journey itself.
**“if I may by any means apprehend”** — I may be able to know perfectly Christ, who is the highest blessedness
**“wherein”** — in that way
**“If I may by any means apprehend”**
• Because it is difficult. And lest it seem superfluous to suffer so much, since he has faith and other goods, he adds: Rightly do I labour so much for that glory, because I do not say that I have already received anything; for if I have received any glory, it is nothing in comparison with the future. Or if I have received anything, as of the knowledge of Christ, I do not say that I am perfect in it; and if so of me, what of others?
• Behold how great is the faith that asks so great a thing.
**“I am also apprehended”**
• even now
• In that in which I was apprehended, that is, through mercy, by which I was sought out and found by the presence of God.
**“by Christ Jesus”**
• that I may see him as he is, as he himself sees me as I am
• or that I may see him in that brightness in which he appeared to me on the way, when he apprehended me
3.13:
**“Brethren”** — He opens more clearly what he had said, and determines what that is which he has not yet apprehended but follows after that he may apprehend. And as to those wondering what he means when he says, I have not received, I am not perfect: Brethren, he says, I do not count myself - who know myself better - to have apprehended one thing, namely. Many things indeed I have, but not yet the one. Whence: “One thing I have asked of the Lord.” What then do you do, Apostle? What do you set before me to imitate? He says: The things that are behind, etc.
**“I do not count myself”**
• I have not apprehended, for I do not reckon
• whatever others may think of me
**“to have apprehended”** — myself; but I pursue not surely three or two, but one, which truly is one, in which are all goods; in this way giving to forgetfulness those things that are behind, that is, the earthly things that I left
**“But one thing I do”** — earlier evils
**“One thing”** — This is that of which Philip says: “Lord, shew us the Father, and it is enough for us.”
**“But one thing I do: forgetting the things that are behind”** — giving to forgetfulness
**“the things that are behind”** — Ambrose. Earlier deeds, not because they are evil but small, as to merit; but stretched out toward better things, so that he always advances for the better.
*Ambrose:* Forgetting now the merits already past, stretching with all intention toward heavenly things, which are prior to earthly ones. Or toward merits yet to come, from which if he ceased he would also lose those past.
**“to those that are before”** — heavenly things
**“stretching forth myself to those that are before”** — with all desire, with all intention, toward a thing not yet possessed
**“stretching forth myself”** — Augustine. For he stretched himself forth to heavenly things according to intention, not according to anticipation, not according to apprehension; so that we too, lest we fall back through love of temporal things from which we have already leapt away, and lest we remain in those things to which we have already come, may run and press on. For we are on the way; let us not look back, but be stretched forth to the things before by intention and desire. The life of a good Christian is a holy desire. But what you desire you do not yet see, yet by desiring you are made capable, so that when it comes you may be filled with what you see. For by deferring the thing God stretches our desire; by desiring he stretches the soul; by stretching he makes it capable. Let us therefore desire, because we are to be filled. This is our life, that by desiring we be exercised. And desire exercises us just so much as we have cut off our desires from the love of the world.
3.14:
**“towards the mark”** — the prize
**“I press”** — Until I come to the appointed good, namely.
**“to the prize”**
• namely
• To the prize: which is appointed for me, and promised by God, and toward which I have set myself to run. And since I am thus, therefore be you, Philippians, of this mind; but he numbers himself with them, saying: “As many as,” etc., as if to say: even if you do this, God will give it to you. But if in any way you are minded otherwise than is to be thought in the future, because now you see through a glass, this also he will reveal, because he will make you clearly know both himself and all other things which you now see obscurely. Or also, that you are now minded otherwise both of God and of all things, even this imperfect knowledge God has revealed to you through the Spirit. Or thus: if you are minded otherwise, that is, if you think you have the perfect knowledge of Christ, God will reveal this also, that is, that you are minded ill, through mercy. Likewise he will free you from other errors for the sake of a good life. For he will do this if you are humbly minded and think humbly of yourselves. For he who remains in catholic peace, if he is minded otherwise than he ought, God will reveal it to the humble. But if the proud man defends it, God casts him away, because “God resisteth the proud, but to the humble he giveth grace.”
• Or thus: I do not reckon that I have apprehended. Here make a distinction. I have not apprehended.
**“One thing”** — I assert to you concerning myself that I too forget those things that are behind; but stretching myself toward those things that are before, I pursue, etc.
**“supernal vocation of God in Christ Jesus”**
• that is, to that which God calls me, through his Son, to be given in the heavenly places
• Of the heavenly calling, that is, of eternal life to which God calls; and therefore it is a worthy and certain thing.
3.15:
**“Let us therefore, as many as”** — runners, in comparison with others
**“are perfect”**
• we run perfectly
• Augustine. It must be known that the justice by which “the just man liveth by faith” is now true justice; which, although not undeservedly it may be called perfect in some of the just according to the capacity of this life, is nevertheless small compared to that great one which the equality of the angels has received; he who did not yet have it said that he was perfect on account of that which was already in him, and imperfect on account of that which was still lacking. But the lesser justice makes the merit, the greater is the reward. Therefore he who does not follow this one does not attain that one.
**“Let us therefore, as many as are perfect”** — Augustine, On the Trinity. As if to say: I do not speak to the imperfect, who are still given milk to drink and are not fed with solid food, but to those who understand the equality of the Word with the Father. Although they see thus here, yet not yet as it is to be seen, face to face. For certain faith in some measure begins knowledge. For certain or perfect thought is not perfected except after this life, when we shall have seen face to face. Let us therefore be minded in this: that we know the desire of seeking true things to be safer than presuming unknown things as known. So then let us seek as those who are to find, so let us find as those who are still to seek; about things to be believed let us doubt with no unbelief; about things to be understood let us affirm with no rashness. In the former authority is to be held; in the latter truth is to be sought out.
**“be thus minded”** — that we are imperfect in comparison with the future, and let us strive thither
**“Be thus minded”** — That we are not yet perfect, so that we may be perfected there to which we are still running perfectly, “that when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away,” that is, it is now no longer in part but wholly, because the very thing seen will succeed to faith and hope. But charity, which is the greater among these, will not be taken away, but will be increased and fulfilled. In which fullness that precept of charity will be fulfilled: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God,” etc. For while there is still something of carnal concupiscence, God is not loved altogether with the whole soul. The flesh is then not said to lust, except because the soul lusts carnally. Then he will be just without any sin, because there will be no law in the members fighting against the law of the mind. Then he will altogether love God with his whole heart, whole soul, whole mind, which is the greatest precept. Why then should this perfection not be commanded to man, although no one has it in this life? For one does not run rightly if it is not known whither one is to run. But how would it be known if it were not shown by any precepts?
**“and if in any thing you be otherwise minded”** — And if in any thing you be otherwise minded, that is, if you have devised anything better for the worship of God, know that this also is a gift of God, because he will reveal this to you. But lest any presumption should arise from this, he adds, “whereunto we are come, that we be of the same mind,” that is, not to be wise outside the rule of discipline, but what is common and modest in the truth of the gospel.
**“this also God will reveal to you”** — he will not only give the prize
**“will reveal”** — or will reveal
3.16:
**“Nevertheless”** — although otherwise, nevertheless it is necessary
**“whereunto we are come”** — let us hold to that
**“Nevertheless whereunto”** — Though we of imperfect measure think otherwise now, yet it is necessary that we all think the same of that to which we have come, and that we complete it by faith and knowledge and work.
**“That”** — that is
**“the same”** — of that
**“be of the same mind”** — by believing
**“let us also continue in the same”** — and so God will reveal what we think otherwise
**“rule”**
• of the teaching of faith and of life
• by the rectitude of living
3.17:
**“Be ye followers of me, brethren”**
• that as I believe, teach, and work, so you also do
• and in these things, namely in faith and the rule of living
**“and”** — although you do not have me present, imitate those like me
**“observe”**
• look carefully
• Observe them. He wants them to be watchful, lest they be caught by the subtlety of the wicked.
**“them who walk so as you have our model”** — the pattern of our life
3.18:
**“For many”**
• those who so; for many otherwise
• not thinking with us about the abolition of the law but preaching that the law is to be kept along with the gospel
**“walk, of whom I have told you often”** — while I was present
**“and now tell you weeping”** — both for their ruin and for the overthrow of the simple
**“that they are enemies of the cross of Christ”** — to be

3.19:
**“Whose end is destruction”** — in their end there will be eternal punishment
**“whose God is their belly”** — Augustine. A man worships that which he loves above others.
**“God is their belly”** — Augustine. Ambrose. As if salvation lay in food, so that the belly is their god; and they glory in their circumcised shameful parts, which is to mind earthly things.
**“Whose God is their belly”** — Because whatever they do, they do for the belly. Or they make a god of the foods that belong to the belly, while they say that these justify men; and their glory is in such things. Whence they can be confounded and blush, while they say they are justified by animals. Or their temporal glory will lead them to eternal confusion. They walk so perversely, but: “Our conversation is in heaven,” that is, both in living and in understanding let us be like the angels. “From whence,” that is, besides the advantages which we already have, also: “we look for the Saviour, our Lord.”
**“and whose glory is in their shame”** — or in their circumcised shameful parts
**“who mind earthly things”** — in earthly things they understand nothing but what they see
3.20:
**“But our conversation”** — although we are still on earth

**“from whence also the Saviour”** — of souls, and now and then also of bodies
**“we look for”** — coming
3.21:
**“Who will reform”** — as if: we look for this from him, that as he has already reformed souls, so he will reform bodies too, when he gives them the second robe along with the souls

**“of our lowness”** — of abasement
**“made like”**

**“thee also”** — O
**“my sincere companion”** — own

4.4:
**“Rejoice”**

• As if to say: because their names are in the book of life. And that the same may be most surely believed by you. Rejoice in the Lord, that is, set every good in which one should rejoice in the Lord, not outside. And this is necessary for you from God, that I say again: Rejoice in the Lord, not as certain other things said once, because this is modesty and the right measure, that all joy be in the Lord, and that others learn this through you. Or modesty toward all, believers and unbelievers, that they may imitate, so that they cannot find fault. And because the Lord is nigh, that is, ready to give whatever is needed in spiritual or temporal things. Be nothing solicitous and fearful. But let your petitions for those things which you wish to obtain be made known, that is, be so earnest, not lukewarm, that they reach God, that is, be fulfilled.
**“in the Lord always”**
• not in the world, in which they rejoice who take delight in the impunity of their wickednesses
• Rejoice in the Lord, that is, in truth and not in iniquity, in the hope of eternity and not in the flower of vanity.
4.5:
**“Let your modesty”** — a reasonable way of life
**“be known to all men. The Lord is nigh.”** — by their example he wants others to be gained
4.6:
**“Be nothing solicitous”** — without worldly anxiety, to keep the promises of God before the eyes
**“but in every thing, by prayer”** — which is common
**“in every thing, by prayer”** — Prayer and entreaty, in common, for oneself or for others, concerning any things. Petition concerning things specifically necessary.
**“and supplication”** — which is with adjuration
**“with thanksgiving”** — he who wishes to obtain other things should be thankful for past things
**“your petitions”** — to be to us
**“be made known”** — This knowledge comes by constancy and watchfulness of prayer. Then at last peace keeps the hearts in Christ. He says this because whoever has peace with God does not fear an adverse mind.
**“to God”**
• Or, to the angels, who offer them to God. Whence: “When you prayed, I offered your prayer before God.” Or: let them be made known to us before God through patience, not before men through boasting.
• Augustine. On the Grace of the New Testament. The angel is not said to offer our prayers to God as though God then learned what we wish or what we need, who knows all things before they happen, as also after they have been done. But it is because the rational creature, obeying God, must refer temporal causes to the eternal truth, whether by asking what may be done for itself, or by seeking counsel what it should do. In which it also bears witness that there is no good by which it is made blessed, but that unchangeable good, by whose participation even the wise man is made wise.
• Augustine, On the Trinity, book 15. For to know all things God’s own perfection suffices him; yet he has messengers, that is, angels, not that they should announce to him what he does not know. For there is nothing he does not know; but it is good for them to consult his truth about their works.
4.7:
**“And the peace of God”**
• I admonish you to ask, and I pray God, without whom human labour is useless, that he grant the result
• The peace of God, that is, God, who is the highest peace, which cannot even be thought; and therefore there is no need of anything outside him.
**“which surpasseth all understanding”** — understanding
**“surpasseth all understanding”** — Ours, not of those who always see the face of the Father. Or, the peace by which God himself is at peace surpasses all understanding except his own. For we cannot know it so, nor can any angel.
**“keep your hearts and minds”** — wills and understandings, that you desire or understand nothing outside Christ
4.8:
**“For the rest, brethren”**
• Hitherto I have admonished to patience and to caution.
• I admonish you to these things.
**“As to the rest”** — Hitherto I have warned against persecutors and against false preachers. But henceforth, in conclusion, he sets out what pertains to perfection.
**“whatsoever things are true, whatsoever modest”** — which pertain to the true faith, both because of the truth in them and because through them chastity is kept with God
**“whatsoever just”** — Just: toward one’s neighbour. Holy: in one’s own life; and, to say less: whatsoever things are lovely, that is, worthy to be loved, such as a modest walk, humble speech, and the like. And whatsoever things are of good fame, because holy and just men ought so to be that no evil opinion but a good one be held of them, that they may profit others. Which things of good fame I mean: if there be any virtue in them, or praise of Christian discipline. For good fame is not to be sought from strength, or the knowledge of the world, or other secular things. Or distinguish it thus: namely, that this, “if any praise,” is referred to fame; and that, “if any virtue,” is referred to the other things said before. In this way: Think on whatsoever things are true, etc., if there be any virtue in them. And think on whatsoever things are of good fame, if there be any praise of discipline in them.
**“of good fame. Augustine.”** — Our life is necessary for us, a good name for others. For whoever guards his life from the charges of disgraceful deeds does good to himself. But whoever is merciful also in regard to his reputation is merciful toward others.
**“if there be any virtue”** — this applies to other things
**“if any praise of discipline”** — this refers to good fame
**“the same”** — which pertain to perfection
**“think on”** — turn them over in memory
4.9:
**“The things”** — all things
**“you have both learned”** — I teaching
**“and received”** — that they be worth holding
**“and heard”**
• from others
• likewise therefore to be thought over, because you heard and saw these things in me
**“and seen”** — through you
**“for me”** — to be
**“these do ye”** — not only think them but also fulfil them in act, and God will be helping to do these things
**“and the God of peace shall be with you”** — given
4.10:
**“Now I rejoice”** — I exhort to the future; but of the past, which he is able to recall, for incitement

**“in the Lord exceedingly”** — who did this not as a gift
**“that now at length”** — after many times
**“at length”** — At some time, because they could not do so for all. You have flourished again. By ministering to me the necessities; which ministry is called a flower, because from it the fruit of eternal life comes forth.
**“hath flourished again”**
• as formerly
• or you have sprouted again, from the likeness of trees, because they had dried up from barrenness and had as it were withered
• ministering to me
**“for me”**
• for my benefit
• Because your compassion profits me. Lest, however, they should seem to have ceased for some bad cause, he adds: now you have flourished again; but before you were busy and hindered by some adversities.
**“think”** — so that you felt what was pressing upon me, as formerly
**“as you did also think”** — with merciful compassion
4.11:
**“Non”** — that I rejoiced
**“I speak not”**
• as if for things consoling the want
• I speak not as it were for want, etc. He rejoices not on his own account, but at their progress.
**“For I have learned”** — I have had it as a habit
**“to be content therewith”**
• content with these
• always
• because
4.12:
**“I know both how to be brought low”**
• because I am not broken by this

**“I know how to abound”** — because I am not lifted up by this
**“everywhere”** — in every place, before princes or any others
**“in all things”** — in every kind of thing
**“I am instructed”** — by God, not by myself
**“to be full”** — lest fullness harm
**“to be hungry”** — lest I fail
**“To abound, to be full, to be hungry”** — He who is not lifted up by the things he has received, who does not twist them to the use of vain glory, who does not possess alone what he has received but divides it mercifully with the needy, knows how to abound. He who, having received food, uses it not for the gorging of the belly but for the preparation of strength, and gives the flesh no more than necessity asks, knows how to be full. He who bears want of food without murmuring, and for the necessity of living does nothing by which the soul may fall into the snare of sin, knows how to be hungry.
**“to abound”** — as if to say: I am not saddened by want, nor do I exult in abundance, knowing that abundance often lifts up, and that want endured gains heavenly riches
**“to suffer need”** — I have been instructed
4.13:
**“I can do all these things”** — not only do I know, but I can carry it out, with him strengthening who taught me
**“I can”** — to do
**“in him”** — by his help
**“who strengtheneth me”** — in Christ, who gives me the ability
4.14:
**“Nevertheless”** — as if to say: I do not rejoice over the things given, which I could do without, but over your good
**“you have done well”**
• he rejoices thereby because they have done well
• well, as far as you are concerned, who do what is just
**“in communicating to my tribulation”** — your good deeds
**“In communicating to my tribulation”** — Sharing in my tribulation. Augustine. He rejoices and is nourished thereby because they did well, not because his distress was relieved.
4.15:
**“And you also know”** — you share, but the others do not
**“O Philippians”** — like the others
**“that in the beginning of the gospel”** — he recalls these things so that they may be more eager, as deserving praise
**“when”** — namely
**“when I departed from Macedonia, no church communicated with me as concerning giving and receiving, but you only”** — so that he might reasonably consider that he ought to give carnal things, since he received spiritual things
4.16:
**“For unto Thessalonica also”** — not only while I was preaching to you, but also
**“once and again”** — beyond which nothing is to be sought
**“you sent for my use”** — necessities
4.17:
**“Not that I seek the gift”**
• I say you have done well
• not that I may be filled, but that you may not be empty
• Not that I seek, etc. Augustine. The gift is the thing itself that is given as a present: food, drink, and the like. But the fruit is the good works, and the right will of the giver. Whence the Lord in the Gospel does not say simply: He who receives a just man or a prophet; but he added: “in the name of a just man” or “of a prophet.” For to receive a prophet or a just man is a gift; to do this in the name of a just man or prophet is fruit. Elias is read to have been fed by a raven and by a widow. But by the raven, who was fed without being given in the name of a just man; by the widow, with fruit, who knew that she was feeding a man of God.
**“but I seek the fruit”**
• of the gift, because this is good, whence many goods come forth
• But I seek the fruit, that is, a good and right will joined to good work. For he rejoices not so much that his need has been relieved, as he congratulates them on their fruitfulness.
• Or, the fruit that abounds, that is, that the fruit of your justice may abound when you have rendered account to God of your deeds.
**“that may abound to your account”** — that for the work of mercy your account may have the grace of the Holy Spirit
4.18:
**“But I have all”** — I do not seek the gift; yet I have all things.
**“and abound”** — not that I lack in one thing as in another, but
**“I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus”** — gifts
**“the things you sent”** — to me
**“an odour of sweetness, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God”**
• these are the sacrifice by which is given to you to overcome enemies, which God receives gently
• you have filled me
**“An odour of sweetness”** — Which please God like the sweetest smell. For they are compared to prayer, which is God’s incense; whence it is said: “Give alms, and it prays for you to God.”
4.19:
**“And may my God supply all your want”**
• not in earthly things but in glory
• that nothing may be lacking to you
**“supply want”** — Not in earthly things but in glory. Or the glory of Christ is to fulfil the desires of the saints, or that he himself may be glorious thereby.
**“according to his riches”** — according as he is rich, and can give more than anyone deserves
**“in glory in Christ Jesus”** — through whom all things
4.20:
**“Now to God”** — May God fulfil; then thanks to him.
**“and our Father be glory”** — unto
4.21: **“Salute ye every saint in Christ Jesus”** — that which is holy is from Christ
4.22: **“The brethren who are with me, salute you. All the saints salute you; especially they that are of Caesar's household”** — These signify that they have a more favorable affection toward those.
4.23: **“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen”** — by reason, that it may always be sound and abound in spiritual things

1.1:
**“Paul”**
• the name being known to all
• He prefixes the salutation in the usual manner. This done, he gives thanks to God for their good things, and, commending their faith and love, prays that they may be made perfect in Christ, whose benefits and primacy according to both natures he commends; then, recalling the dignity of his ministry, he warns them not to fall away from Christ, led astray by philosophy or the ceremonies of the law. Finally he instructs all together morally, according to sex and age and condition, and at the end he admonishes Archippus to be careful of the ministry he has received; and prefixing the salutation he says: Grace, etc.
**“an apostle”** — Note the dignity: to all. He rightly calls himself an apostle here, because he was an apostle also to those to whom he had preached through his disciples.
**“of Jesus Christ”** — behold the authority of what is to be said
**“by the will of God”** — that he is not a false apostle
**“and Timothy, a brother”**
• who is a man of great authority
• wrote
1.2:
**“To the saints, who are at Colossa”** — to the greater ones
**“and faithful”** — to the lesser ones
**“brethren in”** — and because they are holy and faithful
**“Christ Jesus”** — through the grace of Christ, not in the law
**“Grace be to you”**
• in this way he greets
• forgiveness of sins
**“and peace”** — reconciliation of the mind to God
**“from God our Father”** — because God the Father is able and willing
1.3:
**“We give thanks”** — He shows the good things they received, while he gives thanks for these.
**“to God, and the Father”** — because God the Father is able and willing
**“of our Lord Jesus Christ”** — through whom all things are to us
**“always for you”** — also
**“praying”** — that you may grow into better things
1.4:
**“Hearing”** — behold, from where he gives thanks
**“your faith”** — by which you believe him to be God and man
**“in Christ Jesus”** — to be
**“and the love”** — not idle
**“which you have towards all the saints”** — shown through the display of work proceeding from it
1.5:
**“For the hope”**
• not for human praise, not for earthly gain
• a thing hoped for
**“that is laid up”** — it does not appear now
**“for you in heaven”** — to be rendered only from eternity
**“which you have heard”**
• how then is a thing so hidden hoped for
• that you might hold it as certain
**“in the word of the truth of the gospel”** — which is to be held, because the message is both fully true and good; so do not seek that hope elsewhere, which you first understood.
1.6:
**“Which”** — the gospel.
**“is come unto you”** — You did not have it first, but it came to you through others; nor do you alone have it.
**“as also it is in the whole world, and bringeth forth fruit”** — makes it bear fruit.
**“and groweth”** — makes it grow.
**“even as it doth in you”**
• is.
• As also in you, that is, as purely and truly as it came through me and others into the whole world, and still remains in it. As if to say: it has been done for you no less than in the other Churches. Since the gospel is in the world, it bears fruit there by good works and grows by increase of knowledge or in the number of the faithful. Not that they have more than you, but it does this just as it is in you, and therefore you ought to add nothing to it.
**“since the day you heard”**
• through Archippus.
• not through those added later, but through the first.
• by believing.
**“and knew”** — by discerning.
**“the grace”** — that is.
**“of God”** — all of which is from God.
1.7:
**“As you learned of Epaphras”**
• From the first day you heard the truth, as afterwards you learned it to be the truth through Epaphras. “In the mouth of two every word stands.”
• confirming the preaching of Archippus.
**“our most beloved fellow servant, who is for you a faithful”**
• for your salvation.
• not for your temporal goods.
**“for you”** — Desiring their salvation, he began to help Archippus.
