• The same. We are therefore saddened at the deaths of our own by the necessity of losing them, but with the hope of receiving them back. Thence we are afflicted, hence we are consoled. Thence weakness affects us, hence faith restores us. Thence the human condition grieves, hence the divine promise heals. But it may move one how God wept for the dead man who was at once to live at his command. Whence: The Lord wept not for the dead man but for death, which man drew upon himself by sinning. For if sin had not gone before, death without doubt would not have followed. The death of the body therefore followed, which the death of the soul preceded; it preceded by forsaking God, and the death of the body followed when the soul departed. The soul forsook God willingly. It was forced to forsake the body unwillingly. As if it were said to it: You departed from him whom you ought to have loved; depart from him whom you have loved. For who wishes to die? No one at all; and so no one, that it was said to Peter: “Another shall gird thee, and lead thee whither thou wouldst not.” If there were no bitterness of death, there would surely be no fortitude of martyrs.
**“That you be not sorrowful”** — Augustine. It is necessary that you be saddened, but where you are saddened, let hope console you. For the most truthful custom of Scripture calls them sleepers for this reason, that when we hear of them sleeping, we may by no means despair that they will awake. There is therefore, for the dead who are loved, a kind of sadness that is in a way natural. For nature shrinks from death, and death would not have befallen man except from preceding guilt. Hence, then, it is necessary that we be sad when those we love leave us in dying, because we also desired that they not leave us forever remaining behind, but go on ahead for a little while and we follow; yet death itself, which nature flees, when it seizes the beloved, saddens in us the affection of that very love.
**“even as others”**
• unbelievers
• As also the rest, etc. Augustine. On the pomp of funerals. Therefore the pomp of the funeral, the costly trains of mourners, the care of burial, the rich construction of monuments, are some kind of comfort to the living, not helps to the dead. But that the dead are helped by the prayers of the holy Church, and by the saving sacrifice, and by the alms which are given for their spirits, is not to be doubted, so that the Lord may deal with them more mercifully than their sins have deserved. For the whole Church observes this, handed down by the fathers: that for those who have died in the communion of the body and blood, prayer is made when at the sacrifice itself they are commemorated in their place, and it is also commemorated that the offering is made for them. And when works of mercy are performed for the sake of commemorating them, who would doubt that he helps those for whom prayers are not offered to God in vain? For it is not to be doubted that these things profit the dead, but such as lived before death in such a way that these things can be useful to them after death. For those who have departed from the body without faith working through love and its sacraments, the offices of this piety are rendered for them by their own in vain, for they lacked the pledge of it while they were here, not treasuring up mercy for themselves but wrath. Therefore new merits are not acquired for the dead when their own do some good for them, but these consequences are rendered to their preceding merits. And so each one, ending this life, cannot have after it anything except what he has merited in it. Let the pious hearts of loved ones therefore be permitted to be saddened by the deaths of their own with a curable grief, and let them shed consolable tears by the mortal condition; yet let the joy of faith restrain these, by which the faithful, when they die, are believed to depart from us for a little while and to pass over to better things. Let there be, according to one’s means, care for burying and building tombs, because in the holy Scriptures these are reckoned among good works, and not only in the bodies of the patriarchs and other saints, but also in the body of the Lord himself, those who did these things are praised. Let men therefore fulfil toward their own the duties of the last service and the soothings of their human grief; but those things which help the spirits of the dead, namely offerings and alms, let them render for them much more carefully and abundantly.
• But God could have granted this to believers, that they should not even experience the death of this body. But if he had done this, a certain happiness would be added to the flesh, and the strength of faith would be diminished. For men so fear this death that they would call Christians happy for no other reason than that they could not die at all; and by this no one would hasten to the grace of Christ for the sake of the future life, but to remove the trouble of death, and thus in a manner softly would men believe in Christ. He has therefore given his faithful more grace. For what great thing is it, seeing that those who believed did not die, to believe that one will not die? How much greater, how much stronger, how much more praiseworthy, to believe in such a way that one who is to die hopes to live without end. Whence also his dear ones who survive can be consoled in the sadness of a friend’s death.
• The same, on the words of the Apostle. For what wonder is it if you are saddened that the body which lives by the soul becomes lifeless when the soul departs; he who walked lies still, he who spoke is silent, the closed eyes do not take in the light, the ears are open to no voice, all the offices of the limbs have ceased. There is no one to move the steps for walking, the hands for working, the senses for perceiving. Is not this the house which some invisible dweller adorned? He who is not seen has departed; what is seen with sorrow has remained.

**“Then we who are alive”** — Ambrose. At the coming of the Lord, those who shall be found alive will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air, having suffered death as a kind of slumber. For in the rapture itself they will have death and resurrection, and when the soul in the rapture itself has gone out from the body, the body will remain earth, but this death will last so short a space that it can be neither thought of nor weighed.
*Augustine:* It is commonly asked whether those whom Christ will find alive are never to die at all, or whether at the very moment of time in which they are caught up to meet Christ they will pass over to immortality with wonderful swiftness. For it must not be said that it cannot be that, borne aloft through the air, they die and come to life again in that space; and to this sense, that we should suppose that those whom the Lord will find alive here will, in that small space, both suffer death and receive immortality, the Apostle seems to urge us where he says: “In Christ all shall be made alive.” And elsewhere: “That which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die first.” But why should it seem incredible to us that that multitude of bodies is in a manner sown in the air and there comes to life again immortally and incorruptibly, since we believe that the resurrection will be in the twinkling of an eye, and that the dust of the most ancient corpses will return into limbs that will live without end, with such ease and such immeasurable swiftness? Nor do we think that those will be exempt from that sentence in which it was said: “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt go,” that is, you will go into this, life lost, which you were before you took life; you will be this, lifeless, which you were before you were enlivened.

**“Wherefore, comfort ye one another”** — Augustine, on the words of the Apostle. Let sorrow perish where there is so great a consolation; let grief be wiped from the mind; let faith drive out pain. In so great a hope the temple of God ought not to be sad. There dwells the good comforter; there the promiser who does not deceive. For why do we mourn the dead so long? You will say: because death is bitter; but the Lord also passed through it. Let us therefore be comforted. But you will say: can the human heart not grieve for a dearest one departed? Rather, it is better for the human heart to be healed by grieving than to become inhuman by not grieving. For Mary sought the Lord, and grieved for her dead brother.

So many who are here quite secure will then find that they have nothing good. For this reason he began with the times, to warn them to take care for themselves, lest they be so caught.
*Augustine:* In the letter to Hesychius. It is therefore needed to know not after how much time this will be, but how it will be, that those who do not wish to be caught by that hour as by a thief in the night may take care to be children of light and to watch with a prepared heart. For if, to guard against this evil, that is, lest the hour of the Lord find one unprepared like a thief, it were necessary to know the spans of times, the Apostle would not say that there was no need for him to write this, but would rather judge that it ought to be written. **“but unto the purchasing of salvation”**
• salvation will not be given to the idle
• and this
**“by our Lord Jesus Christ,”** — without whom neither hope nor anything else would help us
5.10:
**“Who died for us”** — we may live in the flesh
**“whether we watch or sleep”** — we shall have died
**“we may live together with him.”** — joined to him in likeness to him
5.11:
**“For which cause”** — because this hope is ours
**“comfort one another”** — in this misery
**“one another”**
• each grieving with the others over the death of their own
• you
**“edify one another”** — not knowing
**“one another, as you also do”** — one another, that you may nevertheless do so no less than now
5.12:
**“And we beseech you, brethren”**
• do this, all of you; but you, the lesser
• and if subjects
**“to know”** — show that you know
**“them who labour among you”** — in your governing and teaching
**“and are over you in the Lord”** — by the ordinance of the Lord
5.13:
**“that you esteem them”**
• as those equal to what is right
• so know
**“more abundantly in charity”**
• he wills that they honor the priests out of charity
• That you esteem them more abundantly, etc. Haimo. By ministering necessities to them and showing reverence to their dignity. For what does it profit to have honor without fruit? As riches beget neglect of salvation, so poverty, while it seeks to be satisfied, turns aside from justice. Therefore in another epistle he commands that priests be held worthy of double honor.
**“for their work's sake. Have peace with them”** — and even if they rebuke or punish severely, knowing that their work requires this, have peace with them
5.14:
**“And we beseech you, brethren”** — prelates
**“And we beseech you”** — Haimo. Here he admonishes prelates to bear patiently the wickedness and impatience of their subjects, while they grumble against them in something.
**“rebuke”** — yet
*Augustine:* He who ceases from it, lest he lose what they used to give him, is a hireling.
**“the unquiet”** — the busybodies, the wanderers
**“comfort the feeble minded”**
• against adversity
• or those despairing because of sins
**“support”** — as physicians to heal
**“the weak”** — in faith
**“be patient”** — if in this office anything is inflicted
5.15:
**“See that none render evil for evil to any man”**
• not only suffer, nor withhold good for evil, so that you neglect to rebuke
• Evil for evil. For then evil is returned for evil if he who should be rebuked is not rebuked, but is neglected by a wicked pretence.
**“but ever follow”** — in prosperity or adversity
**“ever”** — Or in general, to all: rejoice always.
**“that which is good”** — is profitable
**“towards each other, and towards all men”** — even unbelievers
5.16:
**“Always”**
• Always, whatever happens to you
• not only endure it, but also
**“rejoice”** — Whence elsewhere: “Rejoicing in tribulation”
5.17:
**“Pray without ceasing”**
• of certain hours
• Without ceasing, that is, always live justly and desire eternal things.
*Augustine:* The just man never ceases to pray, unless he ceases to be just; he always prays who always does good. For good desire itself is prayer. And if the desire is continual, the prayer is continual.
**“pray”** — also for those who persecute
5.18:
**“In all things”** — and for adversities
**“give thanks”** — to God
**“For this”** — to do all these things
**“is the will of God”** — who taught this through Christ
**“in Christ Jesus”**
• this to you through Christ
• Or the will of God is shown in Christ, because these things were in Christ, in whom nothing displeased God.
**“concerning you all”** — to greater and lesser
5.19:
**“Extinguish not the spirit”**
• or do not hide grace
• If anyone explains the sayings of the prophets and preaches them for edification, do not despise him.
• Because it is the will of God to do all these things, you elders, who have through the Holy Spirit the gift of understanding, do not hide it, for by that merit you would also be lost. You subjects, do not despise their prophecies; yet do not accept all things indiscriminately, but prove, that is, examine by reason, and hold that which is found good.
• That is, just as the Holy Spirit reveals something for a time, do not forbid to speak what he feels. Or, we extinguish the Holy Spirit who is given to us, not as far as he is in himself but in us, when we drive him away by sinning.
5.20: **“Despise not prophecies”** — Behold what he said of the Spirit.
5.21: **“But prove all things”** — are to be proved. For certain things need no testing.
5.22:
**“From all appearance of evil refrain yourselves”**
• from every thing that presents an appearance of evil, as from a wicked interpretation
• if anything presents an appearance of evil, and even if it is not evil, do not act rashly.
• For unclean spirits are wont to speak good things deceitfully, and amid these to introduce evil, so that through these things which are good, the evil things are received.
5.23:
**“And may the God of peace himself”**
• giver
• who can remove restlessness
• I admonish prelates and subjects thus; but God himself, who can.
**“sanctify you in all things”** — which I taught
**“that your whole spirit”** — of which elsewhere: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind”, which spirit is mine, which serves the law of God
**“your whole spirit”** — Let reason be kept whole by not consenting to the flesh until the coming of the Lord, that is, until the end of life. And soul, that is, sensuality, whole by serving reason. And body without blame, so that you do nothing by its ministry for which anyone may complain. Sometimes the soul is defiled by an evil thought, and yet the body is clean. And therefore he says that the spirit ought to be whole in man. But if an evil life or thought intervenes, the spirit will not be whole.
**“and soul, and body”**
• and if not without sin, for in many things we all offend.
• Or spirit is put for its gifts, that is, let the grace of the Spirit which was given in baptism be kept uncorrupted and whole, lest by our fault or uncleanness it be corrupted or driven away. For when a man does what the Holy Spirit hates, his grace withdraws from him entirely or is diminished.
**“spirit, and soul, and body”** — Augustine. He has set down three things of which man consists, namely spirit, soul and body: that by which we understand, that by which we live, and that by which we are visible and tangible. These in turn are called two, because the soul is often named together with the spirit.
**“Without blame”** — Augustine says: Not without sin, concerning the perfection of a just man. It is one thing to be without sin, which in this life was said of the only-begotten alone. It is another to be without blame, which could be said of many just men even in this life. For there is a certain measure of good life in which, even in this present conduct, there can be no just complaint. For who justly complains of a man who wishes evil to no one and counsels faithfully those he can, and against the injuries of anyone does not hold the desire of revenge, so that he may truthfully say: “as we also forgive our debtors,” and yet by the very fact that he says this he declares that he is not without sin: “In many things we all offend.”
5.24:
**“He is faithful who hath called you”** — unto life
**“Faithful”** — I pray that he sanctify, so that he keeps the sanctified; nor is there any doubt about this, because he who called is true in his promises.
**“who also will do it”** — will perfect the work of grace.
5.26:
**“Salute”** — on our part
**“all the brethren with a holy kiss”** — which is the sign of love
5.27:
**“I charge you”** — Greet them, and show the letter.
**“by the Lord, that this epistle be read to all the holy brethren”** — to those sanctified in baptism, or made perfect, that they may progress from there

1.1:
**“Paul, and Sylvanus, and Timothy”**
• These are the three in whose name this and the first epistle is written.
• Paul and Sylvanus. Because in the first epistle he said certain things about the coming of the Lord and the resurrection of the dead, he now writes another epistle, in which he signifies, though obscurely (for he cannot do so openly), the abolition of the Roman kingdom, and Antichrist, and the restlessness of certain persons.
• The apostle again writes this epistle to the Thessalonians. For a graver tribulation having arisen among them, he again admonishes them to patience, showing the just judgment of God, that the good may obtain glory, the wicked punishment. He also writes that the day of the Lord is not at hand, as it seemed to be on the occasion of the former epistle. For when, in reading the former epistle, they had come to that place where the Apostle says: “The dead shall rise first at his coming. Then we who are alive, who are left, shall be taken up together with them,” etc., they were troubled and exceedingly terrified, thinking the day of the Lord near, lest they should be condemned because, having come late to the faith, they were imperfect. And therefore, having learned this, he wrote to them that the day of judgment is not imminent, but will come in its own time, lest the apostle, having lied in this, should be rejected in everything, or lest the devil should mock those who await these things by some deceit. He also rebukes the restless more sharply.
• And the Apostle’s intent is to admonish the good and peaceful to patience, to correct the restless, and here to make somewhat plain what he had said obscurely in the previous epistle.
• First he greets them; then he gives thanks for their good deeds; afterwards he admonishes them to patience and constancy. Then he asserts that Antichrist will precede the coming of Christ, and announces some signs, though obscure, of the coming of Antichrist, treating of the abolition of the Roman kingdom and the slaying of Antichrist. Near the end he begs them to rebuke the curious.
**“to the church of the Thessalonians”** — writes, or they write
**“in God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ.”** — existing
1.2: **“Grace unto you, and peace from God”** — from whom these come, not from us
1.3:
**“We are bound to give thanks”**
• as if: hold fast what you hold, because it is a good for which we must always give thanks and can never repay, as is fitting
• We ought to give thanks, etc. Here he gives thanks to God for their good things, lest perhaps they, having so great a good which they had from God, be lifted up as if having it of themselves.
**“We are bound to give thanks always to God”** — from whom this comes, not from us
**“always for you, brethren, as it is fitting.”** — because for great goods great thanks are to be given
**“because your faith groweth exceedingly”**
• beyond what it was before, it does not decrease in tribulations
• more and more
**“and the charity of every one of you towards each other, aboundeth”** — towards you
**“Towards each other”** — So that he who is loved loves others and shows charity by mutual services.
1.4:
**“So”** — so much does it grow
**“So that we ourselves also”** — the apostles
**“in you”** — we who would not glory in a small thing
**“glory in the churches of God”**
• to whom we give an example about you; see therefore that you are not an example of failing
• we glory on account of you, and especially
**“for your patience and faith”** — kept
**“in all your persecutions”** — from place to place
**“and tribulations”** — torments
**“which you endure”** — in which they show what is to be given in judgment to those who suffer and to those who inflict
**“Which you endure”** — Therefore we glory because you endure, so that you are an example and proof to others that God judges justly when he permits his own to be afflicted and the wicked to prosper. For they see you advancing from evil to better, and them growing worse from prosperity; and so you are an example to them, that they may not be wearied when they are corrected by God, who scourgeth every son whom he receiveth, with whom it is just that judgment should begin at his house; whence Peter says: “It is time that judgment should begin at the house of God.” I say of a just judgment, which can be seen even in respect of present things, when the good become better and the wicked worse. Yet I say “just” on this condition: “If it be just with God,” etc. As if to say: the judgment by which God now judges appears just. If the future judgment be considered, where justice is manifest to all, when he renders to each according to merits, by which present things also are proved just, namely finally, if it is just to give these punishment and you rest: for whoever considers this end does not say it is unjust that the good are purified and the wicked grow foul, as each has deserved by his own life. David says something like this: “I studied that I might know this thing, it is a labour in my sight, until I go into the sanctuary of God, and understand concerning their last ends.” But yet it can be seen from present things; whence he adds: “But indeed for deceits thou hast put it to them: when they were lifted up thou hast cast them down,” etc.
1.5:
**“For an example of the just judgment of God”**
• therefore
• glorious among others
• Of the future. For if he punishes sins so severely in the penitent, what will he do to the hardened? So that it may be understood that he who spares not the just does not spare the wicked. Just, if yet it be just, which is certain. For “if yet” is not put here for doubt but for affirmation; whence another translator says: Since indeed it is just, etc.
**“that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God”** — in eternal blessedness, or the Church which he here rules
**“for which”** — that you may be worthy
**“also you suffer”** — you not only work good things
1.6:
**“Seeing it is a just thing”** — another translator says: Since indeed it is just
**“with God to repay tribulation”** — in the pure and simple nature of justice
1.7:
**“And to you who are troubled, rest with us”** — equal to us
**“when the Lord Jesus shall be revealed”**
• manifestation
• As if to say: it is just that they be given punishment, and you rest; which will certainly come to pass in fact.
**“when shall be revealed”** — He begins to show how dreadful the tribulation will be for them, and how joyful the rest will be for these.
**“The Lord Jesus”** — Of him coming in a flame of fire: not that he is surrounded by flame, but by effect, because he will burn up his enemies. Or he says “in a flame of fire” because there will be a fire in the world which will go before him, occupying as much space of air as the water occupied in the flood, which will burn up the earth and the thickness of the air and will purify the elect.
**“from heaven”**
• of him coming
• then glory; to these, terror; to those.
**“with the angels of his power”** — by whose ministry the power of God will appear, while they choose the good and cast the wicked out.
1.8:
**“In a flame of fire”** — there will be fire in the world.
**“giving”** — bringing on.
**“vengeance to them who”** — who have not received the faith.
**“know not God, and who obey not”**
• as to heretics and false Christians.
• who do not carry out what they have received.
**“To them who know not”** — For there are some who do not know the law; and who do not obey, because there are others who know but do not carry it out.
**“the gospel”** — which ought to be obeyed, because it is the Lord’s.
1.9:
**“Who shall suffer eternal punishment”** — increases the punishments.
**“shall suffer eternal punishment”** — That is, they will undergo. For “to give” is sometimes put for “to undergo,” and so this fits well here. For he who suffers gives to him whom he offended punishments, as though pleasing to him.
**“in destruction”** — to both, namely those who do not know and those who know.
**“eternal”** — not ending by the dissolution of body and soul.
**“in destruction, eternal”** — As if to say: they will always feel the punishments, yet the punishments will not always fail.
**“from the face”** — removed.
**“of the Lord, and from the glory of his power”** — so that they may not see him, and the glory which his power will give to the saints.
1.10:
**“When”** — and these things foretold will come to pass.
**“he shall come to be glorified in his saints”**
• so he will glorify them that he will appear glorious in them.
• behold what glory of the saints.
**“and to be made wonderful in all”** — even to the lesser ones.
**“who have believed”**
• even if they had no time for working.
• When he shall come to be glorified, etc. And to be made wonderful, etc. For he will be seen glorious and wonderful in those who believe. But he will appear severe toward the unbelieving when he will confine them in eternal punishments. And the short sense of these words is: He will come to punish the wicked and glorify the good.
**“because our testimony was believed upon you”** — although it was above human understanding; or, ruling over you who did not seek a reason.
**“Because our testimony”** — Therefore he will give rest with us to you who are troubled, because you believed the testimony, that is, whatever we said about that day of judgment: about the glory of the good and the punishment of the wicked.
**“in”** — that is, concerning.
**“that day”**
• or, in that day, that is, on account of that day, that you may then be freed.
• of the revelation of the Lord.
1.11:
**“Wherefore also we pray always for you; that our God would make you worthy of his vocation”**
• judges worthy those whom he calls to the kingdom through grace
• In which, too, the order of the words is this: In which day we always pray that he would make you worthy, etc., that is, judge you worthy. Or: in which, that is, for which, or in avoiding the danger of which day, I also pray always for you. For one must always pray to avoid the danger of that day.
**“and”**
• meanwhile
• for, that is
• that he may fulfill
**“fulfill all the good pleasure of his goodness”** — that he may fully accomplish every good will
**“the work of faith in power”**
• steadfastness
• The work of faith, etc. That is, the confession, which is properly the work of faith in power, so that they cannot in any way be turned from the confession. Or the work of faith: every good thing that faith requires, and without which faith is dead.
• Or in the power of perseverance, that is, that he may give you perseverance to the end.
1.12:
**“That”** — so that he may fulfill that
**“may be glorified”**
• in this life
• in you
• with famous renown and honor
**“the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him”** — you will be glorified in the future
**“according to the grace”** — more than you are worthy, or as Christ the man was glorified

2.1:
**“we beseech”** — we not only pray but beseech
**“And we beseech you, brethren”** — Hitherto he said that he gives thanks to them and prays. Here he determines concerning the day of judgment, beseeching them not to take up lightly and easily an opinion about the coming of the Lord, as of something close at hand, lest they receive it or be terrified.
**“by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ”**
• if you wish that the future coming of Christ may profit you
• to judgment
**“and”** — and by the coming
**“of our gathering together”**
• of all the saints
• if you wish to be in it
• to come
• tending
**“unto him”**
• Christ, as to the body of the eagle; or into sameness, that we may live in mind and body, we who now strive in different directions
• what?
2.2:
**“That you be not easily moved”** — nor waver at all
**“Be not easily moved”** — As if: “If you are moved quickly,” for nothing is brought against you that lasts long.
**“from your sense”** — with pure understanding
**“nor be terrified, neither by spirit”** — nor be terrified, nor by the spirit, as for a nearby danger, that is, as if the day of the Lord were at hand
**“Neither by spirit”** — That is, if a wicked spirit, appearing like an angel of light in a vision, should persuade you of this. Or if someone should say, by the Holy Spirit revealing, that he has known that the day of judgment is imminent.
**“nor by word, nor by epistle”**
• of some false apostle who explains this from the Scriptures
• Nor by epistle, etc. For deceivers are wont, in order to deceive, to forge a letter under the name of some famous man, so that the authority of the name may commend what could not be received on its own.
**“as sent from us”** — sent under my name
**“as if the day of the Lord were at hand”**
• not that he wishes them to be ready
• As if the day of the Lord were at hand. Not that he wishes them to have their loins girded and lamps burning in their hands, waiting until the Lord returns from the wedding.
*Augustine:* To Isicius. For in whatever state a man’s last day finds him, in that the last day of the world will take hold of him, because as each one dies on that day, so will he be judged on that day; and therefore every Christian ought to watch, lest the coming of the Lord find him unprepared. For that day will find unprepared the one whom the last day of this life finds unprepared. And therefore he does not say only “be not terrified,” or seduced, but adds: “As if the day of the Lord were at hand.” He says this lest, through this very disturbance, being found off their guard, they might be seduced into adoring the devil, who was working to appear under the name of Christ and make himself adored; that he might not be able to do so, the apostle foretold the time and the signs of the coming.
2.3:
**“Let no man”** — in each particular
**“deceive you by any means”**
• also by something other than what has been said
• but the day of the Lord does not press unless first the nations depart from the Roman empire, not that immediately after
**“for unless there come a revolt first”** — or: dissension
**“For unless there come”** — He speaks covertly of the destruction of the Roman empire, lest he provoke them to persecution of the Church. Or he says this of the spiritual empire of the Roman Church, or of departure from the faith.
**“Unless there come”** — Refuga first. Augustine. Some codices have it thus. There is no doubt that he said of Antichrist, whom he calls refuga, namely a runaway from the Lord God, that very thing. For if this may rightly be said of all the impious, how much more of this one.
**“and”** — unless
**“the man of sin be revealed”**
• whose appearance already goes before
• not God
• wholly
**“the son”** — a servant and a source
**“of perdition”** — of the devil, who destroyed men, or because he himself is to be destroyed and destroying others
**“The son of perdition”** — Antichrist is so, not by nature, but by imitation.
2.4:
**“Who opposeth”**
• to Christ and his members
• whence he is called Antichrist
**“and is lifted up”** — lifts himself up
**“above all that is called God”** — either by false opinion, as the gods of the Gentiles, or by grace of benefit, as the saints
**“or that is worshipped”** — as God the Trinity
**“so that he sitteth in the temple of God”**
• or into the temple
• that is, in the Church, or in the temple destroyed by the Romans, which the Jews will then rebuild
**“In the temple”** — Or into the temple. Augustine. Some wish that here not only the prince himself but his whole body, that is, the multitude of men belonging to him together with their prince, be understood, and think it more correct to say, as it is also in the Greek, not “in the temple” but “into the temple of God he sitteth,” as if: he with his own is the temple of God, which is the Church, as it is said: he sits “in a friend,” that is, as a friend.
*Haimo:* Antichrist will be born in Babylon of the tribe of Dan, according to what Jacob says: “Let Dan be a snake in the way, a serpent in the path.” And when he comes to Jerusalem he will circumcise himself, saying to the Jews: I am Christ, promised to you. Then all the Jews will flock to him and will rebuild the temple destroyed by the Romans, and he will sit there, saying that he is God.
**“As if he were God”** — For as in Christ all the fullness of the Godhead dwelt, so in Antichrist will dwell the fullness of malice and all iniquity, because in him will be the head of all evils, namely the devil, who is king over all the children of pride.
2.5:
**“Remember you not”** — thus you ought to believe, since I said the same long ago
**“that when I was yet with you, I told you these things”** — about the coming of Antichrist and the day of judgment
2.6:
**“And now”** — you retain this
**“what withholdeth”**
• what is the cause in his manner
• that is, that the falling away is not yet
**“you know”** — Because he says that they know what withholdeth, and does not expound it openly, and therefore we do not know, save that some suspect it was said of the Roman empire, until it be taken away or be made out of the midst. And that the apostle therefore did not wish to write this openly, lest he should incur the charge of having ill-wished the Roman empire, when it was hoped to be eternal. And this which he said, “For the mystery of iniquity already worketh,” they wished to be understood of Nero, whose deeds seemed those of Antichrist; whence some suspected that he was either snatched away alive and hidden until he be revealed in his time, or that, having been slain, he would rise again and be the future Antichrist. Some think this was said of the wicked and feigned who are in the Church, so long until they come to so great a number as to make a great people for Antichrist. And they say this is the mystery of iniquity because it seems hidden. And that it was said of this: “And now you know what withholdeth.” And when he says, “only that he who now holdeth, do hold,” they say the apostle exhorts the faithful to persevere steadfastly in the faith which they hold, until the mystery of iniquity, which is now hidden, go out of the midst of the Church. And the sense is: This only remains to be done, that he who now holds the faith do hold it, that is, persevere firmly in it, until iniquity, that is, the feigned, which is now hidden, go out of the midst of the Church, that is, openly depart from it, whence “they went out from us, but they were not of us”; so then openly.
**“that he may be revealed”**
• yet so
• be made manifest
**“in his time”**
• in its own fitting time, as God has ordained
• that is, after the falling away has come
**“In his time”** — Jerome. When the approach to the Roman empire and to obedience to the Roman Church is completed, there will come a departure from both empires; when this is fulfilled, that wicked one will come. When the time of mercy is fulfilled, in which the fulness of the Gentiles enters into the faith, the departure will be revealed, and so the day of the Lord will be at hand.
2.7:
**“For the mystery of iniquity already worketh”**
• it will be revealed in its own time; for the iniquity now works in secret, not in its own person, that is, in the wicked and false who are in the Church
• For the mystery, etc. Iniquity is already found in the very beginnings of its approach, but mystical, that is, cloaked under the name of piety, so that they wish to be held as ministers of Christ, when they are pseudo
**“For the mystery”** — Haimo. Already the devil was secretly killing martyrs through Nero and others, as through him he will then openly do, killing Elijah and Enoch and very many others; and Nero and the others are a shadow of the coming Antichrist, as Abel and David are of Christ.
**“only that”** — this remains
**“he who now holdeth”**
• rules
• the Roman empire or the faith
**“do hold, until he be taken out of the way”** — Until he be taken out of the way, that is, until that power of the Roman empire be taken out of the midst of the world, because all from every side flowed together to Rome as to the head. Or: let him who holds the faith hold it until it grow cold. Or: let him who withholds him, that is, the approach to the faith, withhold until it be taken out of the way. Or: until iniquity, which is now mystical, be made out of the midst, that is, as among common things, so that a man is not ashamed to commit adultery or to steal, as neither to walk or to speak.
**“be taken out of the way”** — That is, the falling away, that is, it appears plainly; and then, the falling away being revealed from the true God and charity already grown cold, he will be revealed from the abundance of iniquity, etc.
2.8:
**“And then”** — the seat being prepared
**“shall be revealed”** — will be made manifest
**“that wicked one”**
• Antichrist
• who is not to be feared now nor then, because it follows: whom the Lord, etc.
**“whom the Lord Jesus shall kill with the spirit of his mouth”** — by command, by power
**“with the spirit of his mouth”**
• That is, by the power of the Holy Spirit, who is called the Spirit of his mouth because he proceeds from him.
• That is, by the power of his command, whether by himself or through Michael. He will be slain, as the teachers hand down, on the Mount of Olives, in his tent and on his throne, in that place opposite which the Lord ascended into heaven. When he is slain Christ will not come at once, but, as is understood in Daniel, forty-five days will be granted to the elect for penance; how long after that the Lord will come is wholly unknown.
**“and shall destroy”**
• saying: “Go, you cursed, into everlasting fire”
• him with all his members at his bright coming
2.9:
**“him, whose”** — that is, of Antichrist
**“coming is according to the working of Satan”** — because at the devil’s instigation he will do everything, yet not without sense, as madmen are, who bear no guilt for the evils they do
**“in all power”** — in all power of human might and riches
**“and signs”** — lesser
**“and lying wonders”** — greater
**“lying”**
• because by a magic art, not true but by illusion, he will deceive men, as Simon Magus did to a certain man, who, thinking to kill him, beheaded a ram
• because the lie confirms him, namely, that he is God
• Augustine. Or because they are not true as they appear but illusory. Or if they are true, by God’s permission they draw men to a lie.
2.10:
**“And in all seduction of iniquity”** — by threats, flatteries, and all means
**“to them that perish”** — who are given over to perdition
**“because they receive not the love”**
• That is, therefore.
• That is, Christ, who showed love to all.
**“of the truth”** — That is, of Christ, in whom the promises are fulfilled.
**“they receive not, that they might be saved”** — by receiving which they might be saved.
2.11:
**“Therefore”** — because they did not receive the truth.
**“God shall send them”** — he will permit to come upon them.
**“the operation of error”** — him who is malice itself, because he is the father of all malice and iniquity. Therefore God will send them, etc.
*Augustine:* God will permit the devil to do these things by a just judgment, though he will do them with an unjust and malicious counsel. Therefore, being judged, they are led astray, and being led astray, they will be judged; but being judged by the secretly just and justly secret judgment of God, they will be led astray. And being led astray they will be judged in the last and manifest judgment by Christ, who most justly will judge him who was most unjustly judged.
**“to believe lying”** — that Antichrist is God.
2.12:
**“That all may be judged”** — at last openly, meanwhile secretly.
**“who have not believed the truth”** — Christ, who is truly God.
**“but have consented to iniquity”** — Antichrist.
2.13:
**“But we”** — Concerning those, thus you, however, will come to salvation, because you have received the truth; whence we give thanks to God. And this is what he says: But we
**“ought to give thanks to God always for you, brethren, beloved of God, for that God hath chosen”** — from eternity.
**“us”** — you.
**“God hath chosen you firstfruits”**
• of faith.
• Firstfruits. That is, that we might believe in Christ and confess the faith not in that perilous last time but in the primitive Church. Or we, the apostles, the firstfruits of all believers, because the apostles were the first to believe, and this for the salvation of all nations.
**“unto salvation”** — eternal.
**“in sanctification”** — placed in sanctification.
**“of the spirit”** — who sanctifies in baptism.
**“and faith of the truth”** — of Christ.
2.14:
**“Whereunto”**
• faith, as he freely chose you from eternity, so also he freely called you.
• he adds by what means they came to faith.
**“he hath called you”** — turned away.
**“by our gospel, unto the purchasing”** — that through faith you may acquire glory.
**“unto the purchasing”** — Or that you may be an acquisition in which God is glorified.
**“of glory”** — which Christ has.
2.15:
**“Therefore”** — because these things are good for you, and the day of the Lord is not at hand.
**“brethren, stand fast”**
• in faith.
• unmoved.
**“and”** — and that you may stand.
**“hold the traditions”** — from us
**“which you have learned”** — up to understanding
**“whether by word”** — present
**“or by our epistle”** — I admonish, but
2.16:
**“Now our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God”** — by the power by which he is creator of all things
**“and our Father, who hath loved us”**
• by affection, by the sweetness of charity
• giving the Son for us
**“and hath given us everlasting consolation”**
• Christ, in the miseries of the age and in the future
• And has given consolation. By promising the kingdom of heaven.
**“and good hope in grace”** — that from this very exile we shall come to the homeland
**“in grace”** — That is, through the grace he gave we hope for eternal things. Or grace, not by our merit.
2.17:
**“Exhort”** — he who has already done so many
**“your hearts”** — wills
**“and confirm”** — against assailants

3.1:
**“For the rest, brethren, pray for us, that the word of God”**
• the gospel that God gave you, or that which treats of God
• Pray for us, etc. He urges that prayer be made, that God may deign to direct his teaching with tireless course and pour it through the mouths of the apostles into the ears of hearers, and from the ears into hearts, so that the uprisings of evil men may be restrained; whence he adds: that we may be delivered.
**“may run”** — without hindrance to all nations, that many may quickly be converted
**“and may be glorified”** — let it become clear and intelligible to all
**“even as”** — ran
3.2:
**“And that we may be delivered”** — from the false
**“we may be delivered”** — From false brethren, lest they lead our people astray or lay snares for us. Or: that we may be delivered from importunate men, that is, unbelievers, who resist the word of God and do not stand in the harbour of rest. And from evil men, who persecute the faithful. Therefore I say, “that we may be delivered,” because not yet have all received the faith through me who are to receive it. Or: all who are importunate have not faith, but you who have it God will confirm; whence he adds: “faithful,” etc.
**“from importunate”** — by disputing with the wicked
**“and evil men”** — who preach falsehoods
**“for all men have not faith”**
• that is, of whom none has faith, but what they hold is error
• pray that we may be delivered
• “For all men have not faith,” that is, even with you praying, not all are going to believe, but only those foreordained to eternal life, predestined to the adoption of sons.
• For all men have not, etc. God makes those who do not yet believe to believe through the prayers of believers, in order to show that he himself makes it so. For no one is so unskilled, so slow of wit, as not to see that God does what he commanded to be asked of him that he may do. And it must be known that to be able to have faith, as to be able to have charity, is of the nature of men; but to have faith, as to have charity, is the grace of the faithful. But when the will to believe is prepared by the Lord in some, it must be discerned what comes of his mercy and what of his judgment; for “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” Unsearchable, therefore, are both the mercy by which he freely delivers and the truth by which he justly judges.
3.3:
**“But God is faithful”** — true in his promises
**“who will strengthen you”** — lest the importunate deceive
3.4:
**“And we have confidence”** — I have said all these things to you, and I do not think in vain
**“concerning you in the Lord”** — who will work in you
**“that the things which we command, you both do, and will do”** — that this may be so
3.5:
**“And the Lord direct”** — if anything is twisted
**“your hearts”** — that their wills may be
**“in the charity of God”** — which God gives, or that you may love God
**“and the patience of Christ”** — that you may be patient, as Christ also was
3.6:
**“Charge”** — you will do what we command; but whoever is unwilling, let him be excommunicated
**“We charge”** — He begins about the meddlesome and the idle, warning the good to rebuke them.
**“brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ”**
• we command through Jesus, or it is the honour of God if the diseased sheep is shut out
• in the honour of Christ
**“that you withdraw yourselves”** — do not have fellowship with them
**“from every brother walking disorderly”** — otherwise than the order of nature requires
**“and not”** — walking
**“according to the tradition which they have received of us”** — that is, not according to the teaching which we handed on to them
3.7:
**“For yourselves know”**
• therefore you ought to withdraw yourselves
• For yourselves, etc. And when they do not do these things, you ought to avoid them. Or: they do not walk according to the tradition; for you know how I conducted myself, which you do not see in them. As if to say: There is no need for me to expound to you that tradition, because you know it, that we were not disorderly, as those who mind other men’s business, wandering hither and thither.
**“how”** — in which
**“you ought to imitate us”** — truly we ought to be imitated, because we are good
3.8:
**“Neither”** — without labour
**“did we eat any man's bread”** — as if taken from others
**“but in labour”** — the opposite of gratis
**“and in toil”** — even to weariness
**“we worked night and day, lest we should be chargeable to any of you”** — the opposite of from anyone
3.9:
**“Not as if we had not power”**
• therefore all the more those who do not have this power ought to live by their own labour
• therefore we did not receive
**“but”** — but for a different reason here than among the Corinthians: for here he abstained in order to give an example, there in order to repel false apostles
**“that we might give ourselves a pattern unto you”**
• that you may imitate us and lay aside idleness
• But that we might give ourselves a pattern, etc. It is to be noted that the apostle taught not only by words but exhorted also by deeds. For it belongs to a fit teacher to fulfil in works what he teaches in words. For although it is not unknown that what is taught is true, yet if it begins to be neglected by the teacher, it does not readily profit. For works persuade hearers more than words. And therefore those who profit from words alone, when their teachers are negligent, are to be rewarded with great praise. The apostle, then, was a pattern also to those among the people who were slender in substance, that they might learn not to lose their freedom. Whence also Solomon: “Withdraw thy foot, he says, from the house of thy neighbour, lest having his fill he hate thee.” For he who frequently comes to another’s table, given to idleness, must needs flatter him who feeds him, whereas our religion calls men to freedom.
**“to imitate us”** — I worked among you as an example to you, for so I taught that it should be done
3.10: **“If any man will not work”** — Augustine, On the Work of Monks. Some say that the apostle commanded this concerning spiritual works; otherwise, if he spoke of bodily work, in which farmers or craftsmen labour, he would seem to think against the Lord, who says in the Gospel: “Be not solicitous what you shall eat,” etc. But they strive in vain to draw a darkness over themselves and others, so that what charity usefully admonishes they are unwilling not only to do but even to understand, though in many other places of the epistles the apostle most openly teaches what he means here. For he wishes the servants of God to work with their bodies whence they may live, so that they be not compelled by want to ask for necessaries; nor is it against what was said before: “Be not solicitous what you shall eat,” etc. For this was not said so that they should not provide, as far as sufficient for necessity, whence they could honestly, but that they should not look to these things nor, for the sake of these, do whatever they are commanded to do by the preaching of the gospel.
3.11:
**“For we have heard”**
• therefore I command this
• the reason why he made mention of his labour
**“there are some among you who walk disorderly, working not at all, but curiously meddling”** — about other people’s affairs
**“meddling”** — in this way they deserve to be fed
**“curiously meddling”** — The Lord’s teaching abhors this deed, for “whose god is their belly” is said of those who with shameful care provide for their own necessities.
3.12:
**“Now we charge them that are such, and beseech them by the Lord Jesus Christ, that, working with silence”** — not noisy
**“they would eat their own bread”** — of their own labour
**“they would eat”** — He added this lest, by this occasion, they should cease to minister to the poor.
3.13:
**“But you, brethren, be not weary in well doing”**
• to the poor
• we command that they work, etc.
**“be not weary”** — Because even if they work, they may still be in need of some things. And he warns them in God’s name that those who had the means to provide the servants of God with necessities should not grow slack on this occasion. For he who is kind in giving does not come under reproof, but he who, though he could bear labor, wishes to spend his life in idleness.
3.14:
**“And if any man obey not our word”** — to this one
**“our word”** — God’s command
**“by this epistle, note that man”**
• that he be made known to me or reproved
• or by your letter, mark him for us
**“and do not keep company with him, that he may be ashamed”** — let him be ashamed, cast out by all, and so submit himself
3.15:
**“Yet”** — yet
**“do not esteem him as an enemy”** — that you hold him in hatred
**“but admonish him as a brother”** — out of love
3.16:
**“Now the Lord of peace himself give you everlasting peace”** — here and in the future
**“in every place”** — that is, both among the household and among strangers
**“The Lord be with you all”** — that you may have peace
3.17:
**“The salutation”** — is written
**“The salutation of Paul with my own hand; which is the sign in every epistle. So I write”**
• as
• Which is the sign in every epistle, etc. Because of the corrupters of the Scriptures, he testifies that he subscribes the greeting with his own hand at the end of all his epistles, so that no epistle is received under his name that was not subscribed by his hand.

1.1:
**“Paul, an apostle”** — that is, legate.
**“of Christ Jesus”**
• He puts the name of dignity first, so that Timothy, fortified by this authority, may resist the false apostles.
• and this.
**“according to the commandment”**
• not by usurpation.
• command and will.
• According to the command. Whence: “Separate me Paul and Barnabas for the work whereunto I have chosen them.”
**“of God”**
• of the Father.
• Whoever resists him resists the command of God, who saves, and of Christ, from whom is the hope of glory. Whence he who resists the Apostle shows that he has hope of salvation neither in Christ nor in God.
**“our Saviour, and of Christ Jesus our hope”** — in whom eternal life is to be hoped for, not in carnal observances.
1.2:
**“To Timothy, his beloved son in faith. Grace, mercy”** — here grace is for the gift of the Holy Spirit, and mercy for the forgiveness of sins.
**“Grace and mercy”** — In this greeting he sets down three things that he wishes for him, whereas in the others he set down only two. Mercy is taken here for what is called grace in the other epistles, that is, the remission of sins. Peace is tranquillity of mind, a foretaste of eternal peace; this he is wont to wish for all in common. But grace, which he adds here, is wished for bishops, that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit, by which the ministers of God are armed.
**“peace from God the Father, and from Christ Jesus our Lord”**
• that is, of the king and of the priest.
• Pope Gelasius. Christ, that is, anointed. But the bodily anointing was made not in the Son of God, but in Christ; that is, in him is the abundant fullness of spiritual holy power. Whence he, fortified with so great an anointing according to his humanity, is alone sufficient to govern the two principal offices, that is, the royal and the priestly. He is the good priest, because he laid down his life for us, blotted out our sins, and reconciled us to the Father. Likewise he is the true king, because he conquered the enemy, redeemed us when captive, and powerfully protects us for ever. But after him, since in human frailty no one can be found who alone in the Church would be in any way sufficient for these offices, therefore Christ himself commands that for these same two offices two distinct persons also be chosen: a king, who from without may defend the Church against enemies in a secular manner, and a priest, who from within may rule in a different way, by the spirit. He also joined them in so great a bond that each needs the other: the king in any spiritual matters humbly obeys the priest, and the priest, on the other hand, renders the same service to the king in secular affairs.
1.3:
**“As”** — namely, do so, no less.
**“I desired”**
• I did not command as to an equal, but as to a lesser.
• He says I asked, so as to show the feeling of love and the form of humility.
**“As I desired”** — After the greeting he begins here first to deal with repelling the false apostles, who teach that the law is still to be kept.
**“to remain”** — to set in order the Church.
**“at Ephesus”**
• which is the metropolis city of Asia.
• Metropolis, that is, mother city: metro means mother; polis means city. Or whence archbishops are also called metropolitans, as prelates of the mother cities.
**“when I went into Macedonia, that”** — therefore.
**“charge some”**
• both to the hearers and to the teachers.
• those separated from the catholic faith, both teachers and lesser men.
**“not to teach otherwise”** — than we do.
1.4:
**“not to give heed”**
• subject.
• to the teachings of those who preach that the law is necessary together with grace.
**“to fables”** — because what they say about the law is a fable, not a fact.
**“and endless genealogies”**
• which are without end, or forbidden.
• Fables: of the Jews, who say that the first man had two women, Eve and another, from whom they say many sons were born, which the sacred page nowhere relates. Genealogies: in which they relate that they are of the race of Abraham and David, as though salvation were owed them from this; or in which they relate that Christ is not of David.
**“Fables and genealogies”** — Augustine. A certain heretic, an enemy of the law and the prophets, supposes that the Apostle in this place called the divine words fables, as also elsewhere when he says: “But avoid profane and old wives' fables.” Who would not thus err greatly as a heretic? Why then did he himself do the same, if he judged these to be old wives' fables? Why does he say, Abraham had two sons, and other such things? But it is better said that, besides the lawful Scriptures, the Jews have unwritten traditions, which they teach from memory and call deuterosis, where they say that God created two wives for the first man, from whom they weave endless genealogies, making most fruitless questions; and these he calls fables.
**“which furnish questions”** — quarrels.
**“rather than the edification”** — rather than the edification of righteousness.
1.5:
**“Now the end”**
• or indeed.
• The building up of God is in faith, because from faith comes hope, and from hope charity, which is the fulfilling of the law. Or they teach and attend to fables and genealogies, but the end and fulfilling of the law is charity, wherefore there is no need of other things.
**“of the commandment”** — For: of the commandments, whose fulfilment is the love of God and of neighbour. Whence: “On these two commandments dependeth the whole law and the prophets.” End is called a boundary; end is consumption; end is also called fulfilment and completion. For bread is ended in one way, a tunic in another, a field here and there in another. Bread, that it may be consumed and be no more. A tunic, that it may be completed and be perfect. A field, that, shut in by its furrows and boundaries, it may extend no further.
**“of the commandment is charity”** — For the end of the commandment, etc. Augustine. For charity, by which we love God and neighbour, and which is the root of all good things, securely possesses the whole greatness and breadth of the divine words. Whence: on these two commandments dependeth the whole law and the prophets. If, then, you have no leisure to search all the sacred pages, to unroll all the volumes of discourses, to penetrate all the secrets of the Scriptures, hold fast charity, on which all things depend, because the end of all is the love of God and neighbour. No kind of things to be loved is passed over in these two commandments. For since the love of God comes first and the love of neighbour follows, nothing seems to be said of your love of yourself. But when it is said, “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself,” the love of yourself by you is at the same time not passed over. Now he lives holily and justly who has an ordered love, so that he neither loves what is not to be loved, nor loves equally what is to be loved less or more, nor loves less or more what is to be loved equally. Every man, insofar as he is a sinner, is not to be loved; but insofar as he is a man, he is to be loved for God’s sake, and God for his own sake. And each ought to love God more than himself. Likewise another man is to be loved more than our body, because all these things are to be loved for God’s sake; another man can enjoy God with us, which the body cannot, because the body lives by the soul, by which we enjoy God. But all are to be loved equally, to equal goods; but since you cannot benefit all, counsel is to be given especially to those who, by the opportunities of places and times, or of any circumstances whatever, are joined to you more closely, as by a kind of lot. This, then, is the sum of all: that it be understood that the fullness of the law and of the divine Scriptures is charity, toward the thing which is to be enjoyed and the thing which can enjoy that thing with us, that is, God and neighbour; for it is commanded that God be loved and the neighbour, but that each love himself there is no need of another special commandment. The same: This charity is the love of God and of neighbour. The love of this world is called cupidity; cupidity is lessened as charity grows. Let cupidity, then, be restrained, and charity be stirred up.
**“from a pure heart”**
• what kind of charity proceeding from a pure heart is here defined, so that it is defined neither everywhere nor nowhere
• proceeding
• a pure understanding, so that nothing is loved except God and what is of God
**“and a good conscience”** — Augustine. Conscience for hope. For he despairs of attaining what he loves who has the sting of a bad conscience.
**“and an unfeigned faith”**
• or feigned, that is, fragile, but strong against adversity
• pretended
• Or not earthen and fragile; or one in which each man does not feign for himself whatever he likes, but the catholic faith.
1.6:
**“From which things”**
• he disapproves of the adversaries
• by faith, hope and charity
• Here he disapproves of the adversaries who taught legal matters, saying “from which” etc.
**“some going astray”** — not knowing the mystery of the law and the prophets, which extends to Christ
**“are turned aside”** — from legal matters
**“unto vain babbling”** — which is worse
1.7:
**“Desiring to be teachers of the law, understanding neither the things they say”** — what they affirm
**“nor whereof”** — by which, as testimonies of the prophets, or conversely: that is, not understanding what they say in proving what they intend; nor concerning which they affirm, that is, what they intend to prove
**“they affirm”** — Understanding not, etc. For whenever they begin to be rebuked and convinced of their wrong and false opinion, to defend what they have said with the lightest rashness and the plainest falsehood, they utter many words from the holy books, wishing to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say nor whereof they speak.
1.8:
**“But we know”**
• they do not understand, but we understand; for so that this may be shown in some way
• He approves his own side.
• Lest he should seem to accuse the law, he adds: But we know, etc. But lest he should seem again to bring it in, he subjoins: “Knowing this, that the law is not made for the just man,” because he is not just from it, but from faith. Why then is the law necessary for him? But it was given for this: either to punish the guilty, or to restrain one unwilling to sin. The just man, however, though he does not need it, uses it, that so he might be an example of authority to others, and might bear witness by his deeds to things to come.
**“that the law is good”**
• but according to those who understand only carnally, not good
• How good, if it was not laid down for the just? But the just man no longer needs a tutor; the unjust does, that he may become just.
**“if a man”** — just or unjust
**“use it lawfully”**
• spiritually, as it itself teaches; or so that through it he recognizes the disease and seeks the physician
• He who knows it was given for a time and under Christ abandons it. Now the just, by remission, have no need of the law, from which they are free through Christ.
• There are many ways of using the law lawfully, so that in one respect the just man, and in another the unjust man, is rightly said to use the law lawfully. For the unjust man uses it lawfully when, understanding why it was given, he is led by its threat, as by a tutor, to the grace by which he may be made just. But the just man uses it lawfully too, when, holding to it, he lays it upon the unjust, so that when the disease of inborn concupiscence begins to increase in them through the incentive of prohibition and the heaping up of transgression, they may flee to justifying grace, and through it, delighted by the sweetness of justice, may escape the penalty of the threatening letter.
1.9:
**“Knowing this”**
• that not for him
• however
• also
**“that”** — and since he is just in faith, what is the law to him?
**“the law is not made for the just man”** — that it may lord it over him
**“that the law is not made for the just man”** — That is, imposed, so that it is above him to lord it over him. For he is rather in it and with it than under it, because he is a friend of justice; the one who does not sin only from fear of punishment is its enemy. But he is a friend who does not sin from love of it.
**“but for the unjust”** — acting against the law of nature
**“and disobedient”** — although they were well admonished by reason
**“for the ungodly”**
• part by part
• against God
**“and for sinners”**
• against themselves and their neighbour
• Or: to sinners, the wicked in themselves and the defiled toward their neighbour.
**“for the wicked”** — to whom crime itself is pleasing
**“and defiled”** — who either consent through fear, or through some favour
**“for murderers of fathers, and murderers of mothers, for manslayers”** — because the law of nature had fallen into disuse among them; it was restored in writing to restrain them
1.10:
**“for fornicators, for them who defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers”** — who inflict blows of any kind on their neighbours
**“for liars, for perjured persons, and whatever other thing is contrary to sound doctrine”** — to the moral and natural law
1.11:
**“Which”** — sound doctrine
**“is according to the gospel”**
• not against
• every truth agrees with the gospel
**“The gospel of the glory of the blessed God”** — which preaches or gives glory
**“which hath been committed to my trust”**
• as to a faithful man
• whence
1.12:
**“I give thanks”** — Here he shows that the evils were his under the law. But those things being set aside, the good is that he is faithful and placed in the ministry; whence, strong, by which he shows that the law, after the gospel, is uselessly followed.
**“who hath strengthened me”** — that neither death nor life may separate from Christ
**“hath strengthened me”** — He strengthened the mind, which before thought impossible what was preached of the Lord’s power and majesty and hope.
**“to Christ Jesus our Lord, for that he hath counted”** — when under the law he was unfaithful
**“me faithful”**
• by certain knowledge
• foresaw
**“putting me in the ministry”** — of preaching
1.13:
**“Who”**
• as if: but whether this was mine through the law, and not because I was a blasphemer under it
• behold the evils he had under the law
**“before was a blasphemer”** — against God
**“and a persecutor”** — of the saints
**“and contumelious”** — inflicting insults on those who were seized
**“But I obtained the mercy of God”**
• forgiveness, not through my merits
• Those who sin knowingly, as David did, also obtain mercy; and those who are ignorant, which is more easily forgiven.
**“mercy”** — Concerning what I did in ignorance. Or: the cause is not proper, though the ignorance was evil, but the mercy is free.
**“because I did it ignorantly”** — Under the law there was ignorance, and therefore unbelief; now on the contrary faith and knowledge of the truth. Behold, it is plain that he did not dismiss the former things out of levity.
**“in unbelief”** — living
1.14:
**“Now the grace of our Lord hath abounded exceedingly”** — I have obtained not only mercy, but also faith and love and the grace of gifts.
**“hath abounded exceedingly”** — Greater goods than the evils of old. It hath abounded, because he not only forgave sins but gave faith and love; of which no one is to doubt, because Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners. And this saying is faithful, that is, true; and acceptable, because useful. Of all acceptation, because it saves body and soul.
**“the grace of our Lord”** — who gave diverse gifts with faith and love, that is, with the perfection of faith and love, because remission of sins is given to no one without faith and love.
**“with faith and love, which is in Christ Jesus”** — not in the law
1.15:
**“A faithful saying”** — Or: this saying is human, another reading has it, not to say divine; because if a man who receives a man into his house is called humane, how much more humane is he who takes man into himself.
**“and worthy of all”** — not one
**“worthy of all acceptation”** — because here and in the future he saves
**“that”** — that is, he
**“Christ Jesus came”**
• as if subject to suffering with others
• That Christ Jesus came, etc. Christ had no cause for coming except to save sinners. Take away diseases, take away wounds, and there is no cause for medicine. But the great physician came from heaven; a great sick man lay throughout the whole globe of the earth. That sick man is the human race, which had wholly perished, since one man sinned, in whom was the whole. But one came without sin, to save from sin. For “the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost”; he came by that in which he was man. For by that in which he was God, he was always here, he who said: “Do not I fill heaven and earth?” So he was both in the world and came into the world: he was here by his divine majesty, he came by human weakness. Why did he come? From mercy, namely because he willed to take away sins and save sinners. For not our merits but our sins drew him from heaven to earth; whence: “And thou shalt call his name Jesus.” Why? Hear: “For he shall save his people.” From what? “From their sins.” Do little children belong to this people? They plainly do. So believe, and with this faith bring little children to the grace of Christ. Why do you say to me: he is healthy, he has no fault? Why do you run with him to the physician, if he has no fault? If he were healthy, Jesus would not cry out: “Suffer the little children to come unto me,” etc.
**“into this world”** — so wretched
**“to save sinners”** — whoever, even little ones, who though born of the baptized, that is, only in the flesh and not in the spirit, not from what is renewed; because if the spirits were from transmission, a cleansed spirit would descend cleansed
**“of whom”** — among whom
**“I am the chief”** — who in the law
**“Chief”** — That is, worse, because he was a persecutor, than which he was not earlier. For no one was fiercer among persecutors; therefore no one was first among sinners. He was first, then, not in order of time, but in magnitude of iniquity.
1.16:
**“But for this cause have I obtained mercy”**
• a sinner
• In me, whom God appointed a fit preacher to the Gentiles, in whom he showed so great an example of his mercy.
**“first”** — that is, the greatest sinner; or first, that is, before it was shown in others; or first, that is, chiefly in me; or before
**“Christ Jesus might shew forth”** — that is, perfect
**“all patience”** — because he has endured so much, and for the future reserves no wrath
**“for the information”**
• that no one may despair because of the enormity of his crimes
• what he will do for a friend, who has done this for an enemy
**“of them that shall believe in him unto life everlasting”**
• tending
• that they may have eternal life
• therefore
• for the aforesaid
1.17:
**“Now to the king”**
• to the Trinity
• according as God is with God
**“of ages, immortal”** — unchangeable
**“invisible”** — incomprehensible
**“the only God”**
• who alone creates
• God is invisible to all in nature, according to that: “No man hath seen God at any time.” Yet he is seen when he wills, and as he wills, not as he is, but in whatever form he wills to appear. In the future, however, the sons will see him as he is.
• To the invisible, only God: because the other gods are visible, not only invisible; and because there are also some invisible creatures, such as the soul, and yet they can be grasped by sense, because all its powers can be known, which is not so of God.
**“The only God”** — Who alone is God by nature, that is, alone the creator, which is understood of the Trinity itself. Not of the Father alone, as some would have it, because he does not say: to the Father alone, but to God alone. For the Trinity is preached by us as the one and only God. And the Only-begotten also, as he is God with God, and the Holy Spirit in his own nature, is immortal and invisible.
**“be honour”**
• be
• from creatures
**“and glory”** — in essence
1.18:
**“This precept I commend”**
• because all salvation is from Christ, not from the law
• it is not permitted to conceal
**“I commend to thee”**
• as to one about to go to war
• This precept I commend, etc. After he has recalled what and how great are the benefits of the Father and Christ toward sinners, he shows how ecclesiastical discipline instructs the people.
**“O son Timothy; according to the prophecies going before on thee”** — that is, according to the knowledge of the prophets that is in you, or according to what the Spirit has shown me about you
**“that thou war”** — that you may be soldiers in deed
**“in them”** — in them, by expounding them and fulfilling them in work
**“a good warfare”**
• good, useful to many
• warfare, by the habit of teaching yourself and others, and by carrying out in deed what you preach with your mouth
1.19:
**“Having”** — which you can
**“faith”** — right
**“and a good conscience”** — lest the teacher blush, conscious of a bad life; for it is shameful to do one thing and preach another
**“Which”** — good conscience
**“some rejecting”**
• by shameful deeds
• as one who is in filth, that is, still
**“concerning the faith”** — near, but not within
**“have made shipwreck”** — that is, they also lost the faith, drowning others with them
**“Have made shipwreck”** — Haimo. Shipwreck is called the breaking of a ship. And as he loses his goods who suffers shipwreck, and moreover himself perishes, so those who reject a good conscience lose the truth of the faith, and moreover perish eternally.
1.20:
**“Of whom”** — to false teachers who lost the faith
**“is Hymeneus and Alexander”** — he names them so that nothing of doubt remains
**“whom I have delivered up to Satan”** — so you too excommunicate
**“Whom I have delivered up to Satan”** — I have excommunicated both, so that in this way he is shut out from Satan, the kingdom of Satan.
*Augustine:* For there is no creature, whether one that abides in truth giving glory to God, or one that did not stand in charity, seeking its own glory, which, willing or unwilling, does not serve divine providence. But the willing one does with it what is good; and as for the one that is unwilling, what is just is done concerning it. Yet it is not repaid for what is justly done concerning it, but for the spirit in which it acts, because God has neither denied free will to the rational creature, nor kept back the power by which he justly orders the unjust to himself.
**“I have delivered up to Satan”**
• Not that they should perish, because Satan can do nothing unless permitted, he who harasses those given to him. Whence: “Sin no more, lest some worse thing happen to thee.” But since she is “a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan hath bound, lo, these eighteen years, ought she not” etc.
• Augustine. Because the apostolic power itself used that for the correction of men; for the transgressing angels with their prince the devil are rightly called the stewards or agents of divine providence, and the devil is called the magistrate of this world. But a magistrate under so great an emperor does nothing except as much as is permitted him, and the stewards and agents of this world do nothing except as much as the Lord allows. Therefore he says: I have delivered up to Satan, etc., because Satan can do nothing unless permitted.
**“that they may learn not to blaspheme”** — not that they may perish, but that they may be so corrected
*Haimo:* Now the Apostle was of such power, and had such grace, that he could deliver by a word to the devil those who fell away from the faith. And this delivering is this: the Apostle, moved by their blasphemies, pronounced sentence against them. And the devil, who is prepared for this, to take into his power those turned away from God, having heard the sentence, chastises them; which the Apostle therefore did, that being corrected they might learn not to blaspheme.

2.1:
**“I desire therefore”** — because Christ came to save sinners, and because in this you ought to be a soldier; teach to pray so that what must be done may be obtained
**“I desire”** — Thus far concerning false apostles; here concerning prayers.
*Haimo:* Directing these words to Timothy, in that he gave the Church the pattern of how it ought to celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass and make supplication for all.
**“first of all”** — Augustine. Haimo. That is: before all things, that supplications be made. The order of the Mass is shown here, which is a special kind of prayer. Supplications or entreaties, that is, those which are made near or before the consecration. Prayers, in the consecration itself. Petitions or intercessions, as though from what is owed, that what is done here may be perfected in eternal life, as when the people is blessed by the bishop. Thanksgivings for what has been done, which conclude the whole, as though the whole were from God, as when we say, Let us bless the Lord.
**“first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made”** — Or supplications are adjurations for difficult matters, as for the conversion of the wicked, for the removal of evils. Prayers, as when virtues and good things are prayed for on behalf of those already converted. Thanksgivings, for all things in general. Petitions, as when heavenly glory is prayed for on behalf of the already just.
**“for all men”**
• or of every kind
• For all men: that we may follow the mercy of God, because God wills all to be saved, although according to justice he condemns some. Whence Jerome: in those who perish he shows judgment, in the saved mercy.
2.2:
**“For kings”** — even if they are wicked
**“and for all”** — dukes, counts
**“all that are in high station”**
• which will also profit us, because the Church is to be gathered from every kind of people; also from those who seem to stray from faith and humility through worldly pride and arrogance
• because the Church is to be gathered from every kind of men; even from those who, by worldly pride and arrogance, seem to wander away from faith and humility
**“that we may lead a quiet and a peaceable life”** — we too use the peace of Babylon
**“That we may lead a quiet”**
• Quiet, without disturbance, which profits the tender members of the Church.
• In the peace of princes the quiet and government of the Churches is preserved. For in wars tranquillity is scattered, piety grows lukewarm, discipline is loosed, and when it is loosed, the chastity of the weak is violated. In the peace of Babylon our peace is indeed a bodily one, which is common to good and bad, while we are held captive among the Babylonians, whom we are commanded to serve and to pay tribute.
**“That we may lead a quiet and a peaceable life”** — Augustine. For we too make use of the peace of Babylon, so long as the two cities, namely Jerusalem and Babylon, are intermingled. From which the people of God is so freed by faith that meanwhile it lives as a pilgrim in it. Therefore the Apostle admonished the Church to pray for kings and all in high station, being inspired by the same Holy Spirit as Jeremias, who sent a letter to the Jews who were in Babylon, that they should pray for the life of Nabuchodonosor and of his sons and for the peace of the city, saying that in their peace would be your peace.
**“in all piety”** — that is, worship and religion
**“and chastity”** — integrity of faith
2.3:
