**“For this”** — to pray for all
**“is good”** — useful to the Church
**“For this is good”** — Lest anyone think that these things are not to be done for those whom the Church suffers, he adds: For this is good. And lest anyone think that salvation is possible by the worship of the one God and a good life without participation in the body of Christ, that is, without the faith of the Church, he says: one God, and one mediator, so that all men may never be saved except through the mediator; not God the Word, who always was, but the Word made flesh.
**“and acceptable”** — pleasing to God
**“in the sight of God our Saviour”** — do not despair
2.4:
**“Who will have all men”** — just as we also do
**“to be saved”**
• through mercy, even if he condemns through justice
• not that all are saved, but that no one is saved except whom he wills to be saved; and therefore he is to be asked that he may will it, because then it will be done
• Who will have all men, etc. If God, who is called almighty, wills all men to be saved, why is this his will not fulfilled? But in this manner of speaking a sense and a condition lie hidden; whence Peter says: “All Scripture needs interpretation.” God therefore wills all men to be saved, if they come to him; for he does not so will it that they be saved against their will. But he wills them to be saved if they themselves also are willing; otherwise he would have excluded some from salvation and the knowledge of the truth.
• Or: Who will have all men to be saved. Although it is certain to us that not all are saved, yet we must not on that account detract anything from the will of the most almighty God. The Almighty is not to be believed to have willed something to be done which was not done. But we ought to understand what is written thus: he wills all men to be saved: no one is saved except whom he wills. Not that there is no man except one whom he wills to be saved, but that no one is saved except whom he wills. And therefore he is to be prayed to that he may will, because it must needs be done if he himself wills. For so we understand that also: “who enlighteneth every man,” not that all are enlightened, but that no one is enlightened except by him. And “in Christ all shall be made alive,” because without him no one.
• Or: Who will have all men to be saved. Not that there is no man whom he would not have saved, he who refused to work miracles of power among those who he says would have done penance if he had done them. But let us understand “all men” as every kind of men, distributed through whatever differences, because the Church gathers Jews, Gentiles, kings, private persons, rich, poor, learned and unlearned. This manner of speech the Lord used when he said: “You tithe mint and rue and every herb,” that is, every kind of herbs.
• Or: Who will have all men to be saved, that is, makes all to will. And it can be understood in any other way, provided we are not forced to believe that the Almighty willed something to be done and it was not done, because the Almighty cannot be frustrated in willing whatever he has willed by the will of his own essence. Or he wills, that is, he counsels, commands, exhorts.
**“and to come to the knowledge”** — and therefore he wills it
**“of the truth”** — of Christ, who is the way, the truth and the life
2.5:
**“one”** — truly all, because one, etc.; as if he wills all men to be saved
**“For there is one God”** — creator of all
**“one mediator of God and men”**
• to make peace, as a middle arbiter
• made man for all
**“mediator”** — This is that arbiter whom Job desires, saying: “Would that there were an arbitrator between us.” Augustine. It was fitting that a mediator between God and men should have something like God and something like men, lest, being like men in all things, he be far from God, or, being like God in all things, he be far from men, and so be no mediator. And so Christ, the true mediator, appeared between mortal sinners and the immortal just One: mortal with men, just with God. Therefore Christ is called mediator of God and men, because between God and mortal man there is God made man, reconciling man to God. He is mediator insofar as he is man. But insofar as he is the Word he is not in the middle, because he is equal to God, and God with God, and together one God. It was fitting that he neither fail to become mortal, nor remain mortal: made mortal indeed, not by the weakening of the Word’s divinity, but by taking on the weakness of flesh. But the good angels cannot be mediators between wretched mortals and the blessed immortal One, because they are blessed and immortal with God in such a way that they are not mortal or wretched with men. The evil angels, however, are in a way mediators, because they are immortal with God, wretched with men. But they are not true and good mediators, because the mediator who is immortal and wretched puts himself between so as not to allow us to pass over to blessed immortality. The good mediator is contrary to him, because he both willed to be mortal for a time and was able to remain blessed in eternity, and did not put himself between so as to forbid passing over to blessed immortality. But he put himself between, mortal and blessed, so that, our mortality having passed, he might make us immortal from dead, and blessed from wretched. One mediator, then, is evil, who separates friends; another good, who reconciles the enemies of Jesus Christ.
**“the man Christ Jesus”** — for he mediates in no other way than through a man
2.6:
**“Who gave himself a redemption”** — in this he is judged to will to save all
**“for all”**
• he excepted no one who would wish it
• Who gave etc. Another translation: Who gave himself a redemption for all, a testimony in his own times.
**“a testimony”**
• or, of which thing witnesses also went before, namely the prophets; and in due time all was completed.
• that is, this thing was attested by witnesses, the angels and apostles.
2.7:
**“Whereunto”** — in which thing to be preached.
**“I am appointed a preacher and an apostle”**
• preacher is the name of the act, apostle of the dignity.
• which is more.
**“I say the truth”** — and in these things, that Christ gave himself, and that I am an apostle.
**“I lie not”** — in some part.
**“a doctor of the Gentiles”** — to whom one must believe, because he teaches faith and truth.
**“in faith and truth”**
• future, which is the matter of faith.
• which is the end of God’s commandments.
**“and truth”** — Augustine. Which is the future reality and the reward of faith. You seek the reward: let faith go before. For we believe that we may know, we do not know that we may believe. For what is faith, but to believe what you do not see? Faith, then, is to believe what you do not see; truth is to see what you have believed.
2.8:
**“I will therefore that men pray”** — because he is teacher of the Gentiles, or because it is good to pray.
**“in every place”** — wherever they are, not only in the church.
**“lifting up”** — lifting toward eternal things, not pressing down to earthly things.
**“pure hands”** — the hands signify the affection of the heart which embraces God.
**“without anger”** — hatred of someone.
**“and contention”**
• where a storm of anger or hesitation does not please God.
• Anger against the neighbour. Contention against God.
2.9:
**“In like manner”** — let them lift up hands without anger and contention.
**“women also”** — so that they may be heard as humble while they pray.
**“In”** — their religion adorning them.
**“in decent apparel: adorning themselves with modesty”** — not with a worn-down brow, as harlots have.
**“and sobriety”** — of mind.
**“adorning themselves”** — with other virtues, with modesty and sobriety.
**“not with plaited hair”** — adorning themselves with curled locks, or with gold or silver in braids, not adorning themselves.
**“or gold, or pearls, or costly attire”** — not adorning themselves.
**“Precious,”**
• which are beyond the custom of the country.
• Not with plaited hair or gold, etc. That they should not strive, by all these things beyond the measure and manner of their person, to stir up lust by occasion, but rather be professing by all good works and showing forth outwardly the piety of the soul.
2.10:
**“But as becomes women professing godliness,”** — but they should be professing through works and showing outwardly the piety of the soul, which becomes women; or adorning themselves through works, which becomes women professing piety.
**“As becomes women”** — Which becomes women. Ambrose. For she who wishes to be heard should bow down, with pomp put away from her, so that she may call forth the mercy of God; for a proud dress neither obtains it nor makes her be believed upright.
2.11:
**“The woman”** — to pray is common with men; but not to speak, rather.
**“in silence”**
• not asking anything
• Augustine. He who speaks is more aroused to lust, and arouses it.
**“The woman in silence”** — He said that the office of prayer belongs to all, and how, and for whom, and why, and that prayer is to be made everywhere. Now he says that the office of teaching belongs to men alone, and determines what sort of men ought to be appointed to it.
**“learn”** — what she does not know
**“with all subjection.”** — not upright, and such like
2.12:
**“But to teach”**
• in the Church
• over the man
• But I suffer not, etc. Ambrose. Behold, he has taught that a woman should have not only a humble and modest bearing, but he has also denied her the authority to teach, and commanded that she be subject to man, so that both in bearing and in obedience she be under the power of the man from whom she takes her origin.
**“I suffer not a woman, nor to use authority”** — by any spiritual prelacy
**“over the man,”** — even in her own sex, as in a cloister
**“but to be in silence.”** — that she not chatter with her neighbour
2.13: **“For Adam was first formed, then Eve.”** — the order of creation shows that the woman is subject to the man
2.14:
**“And Adam was not seduced,”** — in the same way as the woman
**“Adam was not seduced”** — Augustine. Although the Apostle calls him a transgressor, in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, yet he denies that he was seduced; whence also, when questioned, he did not say: “The woman seduced me,” but “she gave me, and I did eat.” But the woman said: “The serpent deceived me.” This the Apostle properly called seduction, by which what was being urged, though false, was thought true, namely that God had forbidden them to touch that tree because he knew that if they touched it they would be as gods, as though he begrudged divinity to them, he who had made them men. But even if some desire of experiencing it, on account of some elation of mind (which could not be hidden from God, the searcher of inward things), stirred the man, when he saw that the woman had not died after taking that food, yet I do not think that he, if he was already endowed with a spiritual mind, in any way believed what the devil suggested. Therefore he says: Adam was not seduced first, nor in that in which the woman was, so as to believe that to be true: “You shall be as gods.” But he thought that both could be done: that he might gratify his wife and obtain pardon through penance. He therefore sinned less who thought of penance and of God’s mercy. For after the woman was seduced and ate, he ate what she gave him, so that he might eat with her; he did not wish to grieve her, whom he believed would pine away without his comfort and, estranged from him, perish altogether; not indeed from carnal craving for the food, which he had not yet felt, but from a certain friendly goodwill, by which it often happens that God is offended lest a friend be offended; which that he ought not to have done, the vengeance of the divine sentence showed. Therefore in some other way he too was deceived. For being inexperienced in the divine sentence he could be mistaken in this, that he believed what was committed to be venial. But by that serpentine guile by which the woman was seduced, I think he could in no way have been seduced.
**“but the woman being seduced”** — by consent
**“was in the transgression.”**
• if she had ruled, she would more easily be seduced
• in deed
• that is, made him transgress
2.15:
**“Yet she shall be saved through childbearing, if she continue in faith”**
• of God and of neighbour
• a woman ought not to teach in the Church, but she has an increase of salvation from this, if she begets sons for God by instructing them daily, so that they remain in faith and love
• It seems from these words to be a hindrance to a woman if she has no sons, or if she has some and is unwilling to continue in good works. But elsewhere the Apostle says: “She shall be more blessed, whether virgin or widow, if she so remain.” Whence, when he says: She shall be saved through the childbearing of a son, it can be understood that he has secretly figured a mystery of the matter: that the sons of the woman are the good works of the flesh, which are chiefly wont to be practised in the offices of mercy; but works of mercy profit nothing either pagans or Jews who do not believe in Christ, or any heretics and schismatics, where faith and love and sober sanctification are not found. And therefore he adds: If they continue. Otherwise, if it is taken according to the letter, what he says is as it were empty: She shall be saved through the childbearing of sons. What of the continent woman? What of the virgin rather? But the woman is a type of the flesh, Adam of reason, which flies to God, as the sparrow to its house. The flesh begets sons, that is, works, which however profit not pagans, and the like, except only in faith and love. This is the turtledove that lays her young ones in the nest, that is, in the unity of the Church; this is she who is first deceived and deceives the man.
**“Yet she shall be saved”** — And though the woman was the cause of sin, yet she shall be saved, not only the virgin and the continent, but also the married woman, even if never ceasing from the work of marriage, but who, proceeding through the begetting of children, has departed from this world, if she continue in faith and love and sanctification, so that besides her own husband she know no other. With sobriety, that is, temperance, so that even her own husband she use temperately.
**“and sanctification”** — which they received in baptism
**“with sobriety.”** — temperance against the heat of vices

3.1:
**“A faithful saying:”** — a man can preside; and it determines who it is that desires to work and to benefit many, not to lord it proudly, if blameless, etc.
**“if a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work.”** — If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work. Jerome to Oceanus. Work: not dignity, but labour; not delights; not to grow in loftiness, but to grow less in humility, that he may become the servant and minister of men for Christ’s sake; that, leaving aside Rachel, fair of face, but not forsaking her, he may go in with Jacob to Lia, bleary-eyed. And that he may come down from the mountain with Moses to the plains, and from the leisure of contemplation to the labour of action. For no one ought to be so at leisure as not to think, even in that leisure, of his neighbour’s profit, nor so active as not to seek the contemplation of God. In leisure, idle rest ought not to delight, but either the inquiry into or the finding of truth, that each may advance in it and not envy another what he has found. In action, however, honour in this life or power is not to be loved, because all things are vanity under the sun, but the work itself which is done through honour and power, so that it is done rightly and profitably, namely so as to avail for the salvation of those under him. Whence: If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work. He wished to explain what the episcopate is, because it is the name of a work, not of an honour; for it is a Greek word and the name is derived from this, that he who is set over those over whom he is set, oversees them, bearing the care of them. For scopos is intention, epi is over. Hence in Latin bishop is called “overseer,” that he may understand that he is not a bishop who has loved to preside, not to profit. For the episcopate is an intention over one’s own life and that of others. So no one is forbidden from the study of knowing the truth, which belongs to praiseworthy leisure. But the higher place, without which a people cannot be ruled, even if it is held and administered as is fitting, is sought unbecomingly. Therefore in leisure the profit of the neighbour is to be thought of; in action the contemplation of God is to be sought. The love of truth seeks holy leisure; the necessity of charity undertakes just business. If no one lays this burden on you, you must be free for truth. If it is laid on, it must be taken up because of the necessity of charity. But even so the delight of truth is not to be abandoned, lest that sweetness be withdrawn and this necessity overwhelm.
3.2:
**“It behoveth therefore”** — so that he can work well
**“a bishop to be blameless,”** — not liable to reproach
**“Blameless”** — The same as to Titus: “without crime.” A thing almost against nature, to be without sin. But let such a man be chosen that, by comparison with him, the rest may be called a flock.
**“the husband of one wife”** — That is, monogamous after baptism. For if he had a wife before who has died, it is not imputed to him, since the things that were done before, such as fornications or other things, do not harm him at all once he is wholly new.
**“Sober”** — The ministers of the temple are forbidden to drink wine and strong drink, lest their hearts be weighed down by drunkenness, and so that their senses may always be vigorous and clear.
**“prudent,”** — in all things to be done
**“Prudent”** — Against those who under the name of simplicity excuse the folly of priests.
**“of good behaviour,”**
• in bearing and gesture
• Adorned, either with virtues, or with movement and gait, dress and common speech.
**“chaste,”** — modest
**“given to hospitality,”** — who has been accustomed to this beforehand
**“a teacher,”**
• who has the grace of teaching
• A teacher: because a blameless way of life without speech profits as much by example as it harms by silence. For wolves must be kept off by the barking of dogs and by the staff. Whence: “Cursed is the dog that cannot bark.”
3.3:
**“Not given to wine,”** — who does this often
**“Not given to wine”** — Jerome. Because the belly seething with wine soon foams into lust. Noe uncovered his thighs by drunkenness. Lot, whom Sodom did not overcome, the wines overcame.
**“no striker,”**
• so irascible and disturbed in mind that he strikes when he ought to be patient
• Not a striker, so that he may follow him who turned his back to the scourges, that is, Christ.
**“but modest,”** — who keeps the measure of his spirit
**“not quarrelsome,”** — who is wont to do this
**“Not quarrelsome”** — Nothing is more shameless than the arrogance of rustics, who think garrulousness authority, and, ready for quarrels, thunder swollen against subordinates.
**“not covetous,”**
• who would easily turn aside from the just
• Not covetous, as the apostles, seeking nothing beyond food and clothing.
3.4:
**“one that ruleth well his own house,”** — thus
**“Ruling well his own house”** — Not so that he may increase wealth, but so that he first exacts from his household what he is about to prescribe to the peoples.
**“having his children in subjection”** — lest they imitate the sons of Eli, who slept with women in the porch of the temple, and, thinking religion plunder, turned to their own delights what was in the sacrifices
3.5:
**“But if a man know not how to rule his own house,”** — to the lesser, of which a more intimate care
**“know not how to rule, how shall he take care of the church of God?”** — to the greater, where there are so many and strangers, as if in no way
3.6:
**“Not a neophyte,”**
• not a novice
• why
**“Not a neophyte”** — Yesterday a catechumen, today a pontiff; yesterday in the theatre, today in the church; in the evening in the circus, today at the altar; lately a patron of actors, now a consecrator of virgins.
**“lest being puffed up with pride,”** — puffed up with pride, thinking himself more worthy than the others, as if religion needed him
**“Lest being puffed up with pride”** — The momentary priest does not know humility, either in the manner of persons or to despise himself; he has not fasted, not wept, not corrected himself, not given to the poor. Into arrogance, which is the ruin of the devil, fall those who in a moment of an hour become masters before they are yet disciples.
3.7:
**“Moreover he must have a good testimony of them who are without:”**
• not only from the faithful
• Have a good testimony, etc. This clause agrees with the beginning, that he be blameless not only by his household but by outsiders, Jews, Gentiles, heretics, so that those who detract from religion may not dare by right to detract from him.
**“lest he fall into reproach”** — contempt among unbelievers or believers, and so into hatred and the snares of the devil among others
3.8:
**“Deacons”** — unless he took bishops for presbyters, he would not omit anything about them, going down to deacons
**“in like manner”** — it is necessary to be
**“chaste, not double tongued”** — so that those who sow discords
**“not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre”** — that is, to buy and to sell at a higher price
**“Not greedy of filthy lucre”** — Haimo. It is shameful for those in this profession to devote themselves to gain.
**“holding”** — as those who often do this
3.9:
**“Holding the mystery of faith”** — let them know what of the faith is hidden from others
**“in a pure conscience”** — remaining
3.10:
**“And let these”** — He does not say simply 'these', but says 'And these'; in this he hints that bishops too are to be tested.
**“also first be proved: and so let them minister”** — found such
**“no”** — that is
**“No crime”** — Augustine. A crime is a grave sin most worthy of accusation and condemnation.
3.11:
**“The women in like manner”**
• of those to be ordained: who, if they have been wicked and harlots, the husbands necessary for ruling them are not to be taken from them
• Ambrose. When he commands that a holy man be made bishop and deacon, he wishes the people not to be unlike, even in the lowest rank of women, that the Church may be clean; but on the occasion of these words the Cataphrygians say that deaconesses ought to be ordained, which is against authority.
**“chaste, not slanderers, but sober, faithful in all things”** — in words and deeds
3.12:
**“deacons”** — also
**“Deacons”** — After the interruption about women, he speaks again of deacons.
**“be the husbands of one wife”** — whom God has appointed for man, with whom he is blessed; that is, not with a second one
**“husbands who rule well their children, and their own houses”** — because such men will minister well, and those who have ministered well, as if this were a burden to no one
3.13:
**“For they that have ministered well”** — that they may become bishops
**“to themselves a good degree”**
• more excellent
• useful to men
**“shall purchase, and much confidence”** — of eternal glory
**“in the faith”** — and this through faith
**“which is in Christ Jesus”** — though I hope to come
3.14: **“These things”** — necessary from God
3.15:
**“But if I tarry long”** — I wish
**“that thou mayest know”**
• yet
• meanwhile
**“how thou oughtest”** — according to the differences of individuals
**“to behave thyself in the house of God”** — therefore it is to be done cautiously
**“which is the church”**
• all the more cautiously
• because many are there
• The church is the gathering of many to the worship of the one God.
**“of the living God”** — and so life is in them
**“the pillar”** — which is clear, because it bears so much for Christ
**“and ground of the truth”** — a support for those already wavering, about to fall
**“The pillar and ground of the truth”** — Bearing the truth well in itself, so that it does not fall, though it is afflicted.
3.16:
**“And evidently great is”**
• Great, because there is no end to its greatness.
• And manifestly great, because it appeared through preaching and through many miracles.
**“of godliness”** — in the Church, therefore the cause of religion is to be kept more carefully
**“the mystery”**
• Christ according to his divinity is said to be hidden
• A hidden thing is called a sacrament. The same is also a mystery. This, then, is called a sacrament: the Word of the Father, which in the nature of deity or divinity, in which he is equal to the Father, remains invisible. And this is the sacrament of godliness, that is, of all holy religion and true worship, and therefore the Church must be kept the more carefully.
**“which”** — invisible in itself
**“was manifested”** — to the Church, lest he be negligent of her, for whom he did so much
**“in the flesh”**
• assumed
• that is: by works and power shown in the flesh, it became clear who it was who was in the flesh
**“Was manifested in the flesh”** — He says the mystery, which is Christ, was manifested in the flesh. For born a man, the Son of God, who was in secret with God, declared himself to the creature by work and preaching.
**“was justified in the spirit”** — He was shown to be holy and just, because conceived of the Holy Spirit
**“appeared”** — which also
**“unto angels”**
• who profited from him
• He who was first seen humble appeared in majesty, death having been conquered, so that the angels, recognizing the mystery which before lay hidden, now declared in the flesh, bending the knee to him, might give thanks as to God, because they had learned the truth
**“Appeared unto angels”** — What was hidden is made known to the angels not only in God, but here too it appears to them, when it is brought about and made public.
**“hath been preached”** — behold again a great mystery
**“unto the Gentiles, is believed in the world”** — remaining
**“In the world”** — So that the unbelief of the world cannot earn pardon for its error. As the Lord says of the Jews: “If I had not come, and spoken to them, they would not have sin,” etc.
**“is taken up”** — from this mortality
**“in glory”** — above every creature, having the name which is above all names

4.1:
**“Now the Spirit manifestly saith”** — to me, in the heart
**“Now the Spirit manifestly”** — What the Holy Spirit has revealed to him as to come, he does not keep silent, for the instruction and caution of the Church, saying that there will be men of pestilent doctrine, that the Church, forewarned, may be watchful, lest she be circumvented by such men, as though the house of God were so worthy; but the Spirit saith manifestly. And therefore, because of its loftiness, do not lay aside the care.
**“that in the last times”** — against which more must now be provided for or watched
**“shall depart”** — Whence: unless there come a falling away first
**“some”** — notable ones
**“from the faith, giving heed”** — as if eagerly
**“to spirits of error”** — because in them evil spirits will speak
**“and doctrines”** — not indeed of men, but
**“of devils”** — of men who have demons
4.2:
**“Speaking lies in hypocrisy”** — by pretence or feigned religion, so that they may deceive the more
**“and having their conscience seared”**
• burnt with the fire of an evil conscience and marked with the sign of an open lie, so that all may beware
• corrupted by a wicked thought
• namely this
**“seared”** — A cautery is an iron, so called from cavendo, to beware.
4.3:
**“Forbidding to marry”** — that is, to abstain from marriages, which they say were instituted by an evil author
**“to abstain from meats”** — and commanding
**“from meats”** — As if unclean, not for the sake of bodily discipline.
**“which God”** — not as the prince of darkness lies to them
**“hath created to be received”** — so that man, for whose sake all things are received, might thence give thanks
**“Whom God created”** — This is the teaching of the saints; that is the teaching of demons.
**“with thanksgiving to the faithful”** — who believe rightly about foods, and who understand what they believe, which not all do
4.4:
**“For”** — this, namely
**“every creature of God is good,”**
• by its nature
• certain animals were called unclean, not by nature but by signification
**“and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving,”** — is accustomed to be received
4.5:
**“is sanctified”**
• so that the devil may not harm through it
• Is sanctified. Food is made holy and wholesome, not harmful to soul or body; the word sanctifies, prayer obtains, but the devil tempts through food.
**“for it is sanctified by the word of God”** — the Son, through whom the Father created
4.6:
**“These things”** — which I said about creatures and marriages
**“proposing to the brethren,”** — before or publicly
**“good”** — in deed and in opinion
**“thou shalt be a minister of Christ Jesus,”** — you who can do so well, because
**“nourished up in the words of faith”** — by others
**“and of the good doctrine”** — in conduct
**“which thou hast attained unto.”**
• from infancy
• also by your own effort
4.7:
**“But avoid”** — where there is no fitness
**“and old wives’ fables”**
• or empty, without fruit, even if reason seems to be there, as in the legal matters
• which old women are accustomed to tell.
**“avoid fables, exercise thyself”** — It is not enough to avoid those things unless he confirms what is true; he adds “exercise,” as if to say: set these things before the brethren, but
**“unto godliness.”** — to the worship and reverence of almighty God, and to works of mercy.
4.8:
**“For”** — I admonish about godliness, therefore.
**“bodily exercise”**
• the bridling of the flesh.
• in which you toil.
**“For bodily exercise”** — It is given to be understood that he exercised himself in vigils, fasts, prayers and good works, not intent on God, nor on works of mercy.
**“is profitable to little”** — so that, vices being avoided, he may be free from punishment.
**“but godliness is profitable”** — when he studies for the salvation of all.
**“godliness”** — Godliness, which works good for the brethren, avails to merit God.
**“is profitable to all things, having promise of the life”** — that here he may abound in spiritual goods and have sufficiency of temporal things.
**“of the life that now is”** — Having here riches and glory, in the future eternal life. Whence: “His left hand under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.” Whence also: “In her right hand is length of days, and in her left hand riches and glory.” And the Lord in the gospel: “You shall receive in this time a hundredfold,” that is, a multiplication of riches and glory, “and in the world to come life everlasting.” The whole sum of our discipline is in mercy and godliness; whoever follows it, if he suffers the slipperiness of the flesh, will be beaten. But if anyone has had only bodily exercise, he will suffer everlasting punishments.
4.9:
**“A faithful”** — true.
**“saying”** — and this one is about godliness.
**“and worthy of all acceptation.”** — because it is profitable.
4.10:
**“For therefore”**
• which I show in myself.
• in this, that godliness has the promise of this life and of the future.
**“we labor”** — namely, the apostles.
**“and are reviled,”** — we suffer reproaches.
**“because we hope in the living God”** — or to God.
**“living”**
• or to the living.
• as God, who gives life, has promised.
**“who is the Saviour”**
• who maketh his sun to rise upon the good and the bad.
• who saves carnal men along with beasts.
**“of all men, especially of the faithful.”** — here and in the future, according to body and soul.
4.11:
**“These things command”** — to those who know.
**“these things”** — that they avoid fables; but exercise thyself.
**“and teach.”** — to those who do not know.
**“These things command and teach”** — He admonishes him that his progress should be an example to others in all things, that in a young man a wonderful and serious discipline might be seen, that his acts might excuse him, and that he might be held not as a youth but as an elder; and that his elders might be ashamed if they did not show themselves, in conduct and morals, grave according to the pattern of this.
4.12:
**“Let no man”** — so maturely, that no one
**“despise thy youth: but be thou an example”** — so that, seeing your conduct, they may profit by your example.
**“of the faithful in word,”** — so that they may speak by your example.
**“in conversation,”** — honest among others
**“in charity,”** — of God and of neighbour
**“in faith, in chastity.”** — of mind and of body
4.13:
**“Till I come,”** — that you may be able to do this
**“attend unto reading, to exhortation”**
• after reading
• of those now willing
**“and to doctrine.”** — of those not knowing
4.14:
**“Neglect not”** — because you were appointed to this
**“the grace”** — of the episcopate
**“that is in thee, which was given thee by prophesy”**
• therefore do not make it void, lest you be disobedient to those to whom you bowed your head
• according to the election, in which he seems to say, from past things, what kind he will be
**“by prophesy”** — He calls it the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, through which he foreknew what he was to do concerning this man and the others. Therefore he says: “which was given thee by prophesy,” because, the Spirit revealing it, the Apostle knew that Timothy was worthy of episcopal honour.
*Ambrose:* Prophecy is that by which he is chosen, as one who will be a fit teacher. The words of the laying on of hands are mystical, by which the one chosen for this work is confirmed, receiving authority with his own conscience as witness, so that he may dare to offer sacrifice to God in the Lord’s stead.
**“with imposition of the hands of the priesthood.”** — Of the priesthood, for of the priests, because there cannot be fewer than three. And he calls the bishop a priest; or because one lays on the hand, the others assenting. Or of the priesthood, because the priesthood is the cause why they lay on hands; or because the laying on of hands gives the priesthood to the one ordained.
4.15:
**“These things”**
• the things said above pertaining to your office
• because you were chosen for this
**“be wholly in these things”** — that is, carry these out in constant practice
**“that thy profiting may be manifest to all.”** — so that no one may be ignorant that you profit to all
4.16:
**“Take heed to thyself”** — that you may profit
**“and to doctrine,”** — how you live and teach
**“Take heed to thyself and to doctrine”** — which are of value to you and to others
**“For in doing this thou shalt both save thyself and them that hear thee”** — a double reward

5.1:
**“An ancient man”** — in age or in manners
**“rebuke not”**
• yet one must press on, but with discretion
• Rebuke not, lest he, bearing it unworthily to be corrected by a younger man, be exasperated rather than profit.
**“but”** — out of respect for age
**“entreat”** — so that he may more easily receive it, for he may fear that afterwards he will be rebuked. Yet an old fool is to be rebuked vehemently, as Gregory says.
**“as a father: young men, as brethren”** — with feeling of love
**“as brethren”** — So that, seeing that they are admonished out of love, they may more easily correct themselves.
5.2:
**“Old women, as mothers”** — so that they may be taught with gentle speech and thus profit honourably
**“young women, as sisters”** — so that they may readily be able to receive the discipline of good conduct
**“in all chastity”**
• that not even a nod be made against them
• In speaking to young women, the young man is rightly admonished about chastity.
5.3:
**“Honour widows”** — by supporting them from the Church’s resources and cherishing them with comforts
**“that are widows indeed”**
• as to a husband, so are they cut off from love of the world
• not all, however, but “If any”
• Jerome. That is, those who are destitute of the help of all their own, and who cannot work with their own hands, whom poverty weakens and age wears out, whose hope is God and whose whole work is prayer. From this it is given to understand that young widows, except those whom infirmity excuses, are to be left to their own labour or to the service of their children and kinsfolk, and are not to be received. Honour, moreover, is here taken either for alms or for a gift, as in that: “Let the priests that rule well be esteemed worthy of double honour: especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.” And in the gospel the Lord explains the commandment of the law in which it is said: “Honour thy father,” that it ought to be understood not in the sound of words, since the want of parents can be mocked by empty flattery, but in supplying the necessaries of life. For when God commanded that children should feed their poor parents and repay to the old the benefits which as little ones they had received, the scribes and Pharisees on the contrary taught children not to entrust to their parents corban, that is, “the gift which I have promised to the altar and have vowed to the gifts of the temple; if you receive food from me, it will be turned to your refreshment”; and so it came about that, while father and mother were in need, the children offered a sacrifice, which the priests and scribes consumed.
5.4:
**“But if any widow have children, or grandchildren”** — in which it will be proved, so that at last the widow may be worthy to be called a widow of the Church; for merits must go before, that due honour may be paid
**“and to make a return of duty to her parents”** — who have nourished her
**“to her parents”** — Parents are the same as children and grandchildren above, whence also in the secular law a parent is commanded to succeed a parent by degree. To them we return a mutual favour, since we were reared by our fathers; we in turn nourish others by the same law.
**“For this”**
• to rule the little ones
• not only to serve in the Church
5.5:
**“But she that is a widow indeed”** — she who is truly a widow and is desolate, that is, not having a house, let her trust, etc., that is, let her be received in the Church, and continue. For if otherwise, she is dead; and let her be blameless; or it is a definition of “truly,” as if to say: receive the true one, and this one is the true one. She who is true hopes and continues; for the other does not.
**“and desolate, let her trust”**
• this is what she ought to hope
• or she hopes
• “Desolate, she hopes.” Seeing that she has no support from any quarter, she is devoted with her whole soul to God, from whom alone she hopes for help of life and salvation.
**“in God, and continue”** — or she persists
**“in supplications”** — for the removal of every evil
**“and prayers”** — for the attaining of good things
**“night and day”** — she persists; and this means: For she who. And charge these also that they not be in delights, and that they be blameless
5.6:
**“For she that liveth in pleasures”** — of the world
**“she that liveth in pleasures”** — It is a kind of deceit to wish to have the honour of a widow and not to obey God, to do one thing and profess another, since she professes religion.
**“is living”** — in common life
**“is dead”** — in soul
5.7:
**“And this give in charge”** — to widows
**“that they may be blameless”** — because now there is no occasion of the world in them
5.8:
**“But if any man have not care of his own”**
• if a true widow has a household, let her rule it; but if she neglects this
• as household members: parents to children, or children to parents
• as parents, brothers, and the like are
**“have not care”** — Care is to be given to parents, as Jesus commended his Mother to John.
**“he hath denied the faith”** — by works, though not by words, because she does not love her neighbour
**“and is worse than an infidel”** — because this one does not yet know the truth, which he promised
5.9:
**“Let a widow be chosen”** — let the true and desolate widow be chosen, but of such an age, etc.
**“be chosen”** — or is chosen
**“of no less than threescore years of age”** — where the tinder of lust is extinguished
**“who hath been the wife of one husband”** — because of the sacrament mentioned above
5.10:
**“Having testimony for her good works, if she have brought up children”** — faithfully
**“if she have received to harbour”** — the poor
**“if she have washed the saints’ feet”** — of preachers, whom it was then dangerous to receive
**“she have washed the saints’ feet”** — Augustine. Let us, humble, do this for one another, which the Most High did humbly. There is great commendation of humility in this. And brothers do this for one another even by the visible work itself; and those who do not do it with the hand, do it in the heart. But it is much better that it be done also with the hands. Nor let the Christian disdain to do what Christ did; for when one is bowed down at the feet, the effect of humility is stirred up in the heart, or, if it is already there, it is strengthened.
**“if she have ministered to them that suffer tribulation”**
• in prison or the like
• what, in each case
**“if she have diligently followed every good work”** — humbly
5.11:
**“But the younger widows avoid”**
• whose blood is hot
• because this often happens
**“avoid”** — The same: do not care so much for their vows of chastity that you take them on to be sustained by the alms of the Church.
*Ambrose:* He forbids young widows to be received into this profession. For the slippery age ought not easily to be trusted.
**“For when they have grown wanton”** — after the vow of continence they have lived wantonly in food and other things
**“in Christ, they will marry”**
• as if then it were not a sin to marry
• I do not say they marry
5.12:
**“Having damnation”**
• for the broken faith of the vow
• Having damnation, etc. Augustine. In the marriage bond, indeed, if chastity is preserved, damnation is not feared. But in widowed continence and virginal excellence the virtue of a greater gift is sought; once it is sought and chosen and offered by vow, it is now damnable not only to take up marriage, but even, though one does not marry, to wish to marry. For to those who vow virginity or widowhood it is damnable not only to marry but even to wish it. Everyone of this kind is like the wife of Lot, who looked back.
**“because they have made void their first faith”** — that is, the vow; or in the violated vow, the faith of baptism
**“their first faith”** — Augustine. Although not by marrying, yet by willing it: not because marriages are condemned, but the deceit of purpose and the broken faith of the vow are condemned; and the will that departs from its purpose is damnable, whether marriages follow or not.
**“have made void”** — by willing also
5.13:
**“And withal being idle”** — with the aforesaid evils
**“they learn to go about from house to house”**
• harmful to religion
• shameful things
5.14:
**“I will therefore”** — lest these things happen
**“that the younger should marry”** — which is good
**“bear children”** — and this likewise good
**“be mistresses of families”**
• likewise good
• wherefore this
• and so
**“give no occasion to the adversary”** — to the unbeliever, to whom it is pleasing to speak evil of us
**“to speak evil”** — that is, of speaking evil
5.15:
**“already”** — I will so
**“For”** — because
**“some are turned aside”** — after the vow
**“after Satan”** — and such are not to be received, but
**“turned aside after”** — Augustine. By looking back from that excellent purpose of widowhood or virginal chastity, they fell and perished.
5.16:
**“If any of the faithful have widows”** — the young
**“minister to them”** — the things that are necessary
**“let not the church be charged”** — as if they had nothing from elsewhere, the Church would give them, yet they would not be received
**“that there may be sufficient for them that are widows indeed”** — that which the Church has
5.17:
**“Who”** — Command these things also about the priests
**“the priests that rule well, double honour”**
• obeying spiritually and supplying outward things
• Augustine. It is of necessity to receive, of charity to give; yet the gospel is not for sale, so as to be preached for these things, but for eternal ones. For if they sell it so, they sell a great thing for a cheap price. Let them therefore receive from the people the support of necessity, and from the Lord the reward of their stewardship. For it is not paid by the people as a reward to those who serve them in the charity of the gospel, but only a maintenance is given, by which they are fed that they may be able to labour.
• Who rule well. He treats here of the honour of priests, as if to say: Observe what I said about widows. And command this also about priests, that priests who rule well be held worthy in life and teaching.
• Gloss of the Lombard: Augustine, On the Baptism of Little Ones. “It is therefore of necessity to receive that by which one lives, of charity to give; yet the gospel is not for sale, so as to be preached for these things. For if they sell it so, they sell a great thing for a cheap price. Let them therefore receive the support of necessity from the people, and the reward of their stewardship from the Lord. For it is not paid by the people as a reward to those who serve them in the charity of the gospel, but is given as a stipend, by which they are fed that they may be able to labour”; and that double honour is to be shown to all priests indeed, but especially to those who labour in the word, that is, in the exhortation of those who know, and doctrine of those who know not.
**“double honour”** — For good and faithful stewards ought to be forestalled not only with lofty honour but also with earthly honour, that they may not be saddened by want of means, and may rejoice in the obedience of spiritual men. For he becomes more earnest if he is not humbled by poverty, and authority grows in him when he sees that he receives the fruit of his labour even as a price, not that he may abound, but that he may not fail. For so great a reward must be given to him who preaches the kingdom of God, that he be neither saddened nor puffed up.
**“worthy”** — by their subjects
**“be esteemed, especially they who labour in the word”** — by exhortation to those who know
**“and doctrine”** — to those who do not know
5.18:
**“For the scripture saith”** — he proves it concerning outward honour
**“Thou shalt not muzzle”**
• that is, you shall not forbid it to take what is necessary
• or you shall not muzzle
**“the ox that treadeth out the corn; and, The labourer is worthy of his reward”**
• that it may restore its strength for labour
• likewise the Lord in the gospel
*Ambrose:* A person of so high an order, that he stands in the place of Christ, is not to be easily accused.
5.19:
**“Against a presbyter”**
• But.
• He who rebukes is wont not to be loved. And therefore, when an occasion is given, he is easily accused. Against this he warns, saying.
**“but under two or three witnesses”** — two suffice if they are so approved
5.20:
**“Them that sin reprove before all”** — but these, proved guilty by testimony, or who are manifest
**“before all”** — Augustine. On the Words of the Lord. Sometimes you ought to rebuke the sinner between yourself and him alone, as the Lord says in the gospel; sometimes before all, that the rest may fear. The former is when he has sinned against you, that is, when you know that he has sinned; then in secret, lest you be not a corrector but a betrayer, as Joseph, who alone suspected adultery of Mary. But when the sin is committed openly, it is to be reproved openly.
**“that the rest also may have fear”** — priests or subjects
5.21:
**“I charge thee”** — that a priest not be accused
**“before God, and Christ Jesus”** — who will judge
**“I charge thee before God”** — Let God be my witness that I have saved my soul; beware.
**“and the elect angels”** — that they separate the good from the bad
**“that thou observe these things”**
• which I commanded
• and
**“without prejudice”** — by prior examination
**“doing nothing”** — or you will do
**“by declining to either side”** — by examination, that you not decline to other than examination finds
5.22:
**“Impose not hands lightly”** — and after all these things, do not ordain quickly, but test often

*Ambrose:* Now he gives him special counsel, that he rule himself by wholesome teaching; for God wishes to be served prudently, not that men become weak through excess and afterwards seek the aids of physicians. **“Some men's”** — Therefore there is need of examination; or: drink wine, because although your good intention has not at once become clear, it nevertheless cannot be hidden, as is also the case with evil.
*Augustine:* On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount. He calls manifest those about which it is clear with what mind they are done; these go before to judgment, because if judgment follows these, it is not rash. The hidden ones follow after, because neither will they lie hid in their time, when the time of Christ shall come, in which they shall be made manifest; so also with the good. About these, then, let us judge; those let us leave to the judgment of God.

*Augustine:* Nothing is said here that does not befit the Trinity, because in truth the Trinity is one God, both “blessed and only mighty, the King of kings, and Lord of lords,” who alone hath immortality, because he alone is immutable by nature, not by anyone’s grace, but by his own nature. He neither could nor can be changed by any turning, nor could nor will he be able to sin by any change. But when it is granted to any rational creature that it cannot sin, this is not properly of its nature, but of the grace of God. God alone, therefore, hath immortality and “inhabiteth light inaccessible, whom no man hath seen, nor can see.” Nor must the Son be understood as separated from this, because the Son is eternal life with the Father, and therefore is rightly understood here. Whom, according to the nature by which he is God, no one has seen or can see; but he will be able one day, if he is among those of whom it is said: “Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God.”

Great is the mind that is not tempted by this disease amid riches. He is great who does not think himself great because he is rich. But he who thinks himself great for that reason is proud, is needy; he swells in the flesh, bursts in the heart, begs; he is puffed up, not full.

**“profane”**
• As hypostasis is a word that relates both to person and to substance, whence also heretics, by multiplying this name, wished to introduce three substances.
• Augustine. Those things that are against religion are not the other ones to be avoided; for some novelties of words agree with the teaching of religion, such as the very name Christian, of which it is written when it began to be spoken. For in Antioch, after the ascension of the Lord, they were first called Christians, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles. Also against the impiety of the Arians the Fathers handed down the new word homoousion, but by such a name they did not signify a new thing, for that is called homoousion which is of one and the same substance. For if every novelty were profane, it would not be said by the Lord: “A new commandment I give unto you,” nor would the Testament be called new, nor would the whole Church sing a new canticle.

He adds: “The husbandman that laboureth,” etc. As if: even if you do not entangle yourself in secular businesses, there is nonetheless whence you can live, because it is necessary, etc.
**“must first partake of the fruits”** — The husbandman that laboureth, that is, the preacher, who in the field of the Church tills the hearts of the hearers with the hoe of the word of God. First partake, that is, take. Of the fruits, that is, the necessaries from the hearers, because “the labourer is worthy of his reward”; as the husbandman or vinedresser first tastes the first fruits of his labour, so the Apostle bids him who is first take first, and so distribute to the rest. For he ought first to supply his own need from what he has received, and afterwards minister to others from what remains. Thus he makes the chaste evangelist secure, one who does not preach the gospel in order to sell the gospel, and wishes him to understand that he may take necessaries for himself from those among whom he serves as a soldier of God, and whom, like a tiller, he works as a vineyard, or, like a shepherd, feeds as a flock. For it is not begging, but a right. Now Timothy was of such abstinence that, restraining himself even from things lawful, after the example of Paul he wished to live by the labour of his hands, although the Lord has decreed that he who preaches the gospel should live by the gospel.

• Saying that the resurrection is past already, etc. Or: so that it is understood of the resurrection of the soul. For there are two resurrections: the first is that which takes place in the soul through faith, when he who was dead in unbelief and other sins is made alive through faith and baptism, whence: “He that believeth in me shall pass from death to life.” The other is that of bodies, which will be on the day of judgment. The Apostle here speaks of that resurrection which takes place in the soul through faith, when he says: saying that the resurrection, of minds namely, has taken place in baptism and in faith, and that there will be no resurrection of bodies. All sects that profess religion grant the resurrection of minds in faith. For otherwise they would not seem worth hearing. Wishing therefore to be believed, even all who founded the sect of any false religion could not deny this resurrection of minds; all agreed about it. But the resurrection of the body many have denied, like these whom the Apostle names.

The number of such is “a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed up,” a well of living water, a paradise with the fruits of apples. Of this number some live spiritually, and enter upon the more excellent way of charity. Others, still carnal, earnestly exercise their progress, and that they may become fit for the food of the spiritual, are nourished with the milk of the holy mysteries; and what in evil morals is manifest even to popular judgment, they avoid in the fear of God, and hold firmly the rule of faith diligently inquired into, and if they depart from it, are quickly corrected by catholic authority, although in its words, because of the carnal sense, they still waver amid various onsets of fancies. There are also some of that number who still live wickedly, or even lie in heresies or in the superstitions of the Gentiles, and yet even there the Lord knows who are his. For in that ineffable foreknowledge of God many who seem to be outside are within. Of all these, therefore, who, so to speak, are inwardly and in secret within, that is, whom the Lord knows, no one is led astray into eternal damnation. For the Lord knoweth who are his. For the judgment has not yet appeared, but it is already made in the knowledge of God. For he knows who will remain for the crown, and who for the flame; he knows the wheat and the chaff. Then he puts the other part of the seal from the book of Isaias, adding: “And let him depart from iniquity,” etc.

**“vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood”** — For as vessels of wood and earth serve that the golden and silver may be cleansed, so the wicked profit for the advancement of the good. And as those, when broken, are cast out of the house, while other broken vessels are carefully put back, so the wicked when dead will be cast into the exterior darkness, but the good will be placed in eternal life. The great house, therefore, is the Church, in which are vessels of gold and silver, that is, the good and faithful and holy servants of God, dispersed everywhere and bound by spiritual unity, living in the same communion of the sacraments. And vessels of wood and earth, that is, those who are in the house yet are not in the framework of the house, nor in the peaceful fellowship, and yet are still in body together with the good. For before the time of the last separation one must by no means withdraw from the unity of the Church on account of the mixing of the wicked, so that before the winnowing of the threshing floor wheat and cockle, grains and chaff, are alike; for the Lord did not allow the apostles to separate the cockle from the wheat; who then would dare this?

No fire, no floods of the world, no rivers of temptation extinguish it. Of this it is said: “Love is strong as death.” For as when death comes it cannot be resisted, so against the violence of charity the world can do nothing. The likeness is given by contrast. • Note that the animosity of heretics is always restless; the Apostle here says they have the endeavour of the magicians of Pharao, comparing them to the magicians of Pharao. Jeremias compares them to the foolish little bird, the partridge, saying: “The partridge hath hatched eggs which she did not lay: so is he that hath gathered riches, and not by right: in the midst of his days he shall leave them, and in his latter end he shall be a fool.”
*Augustine:* Against Faustus. Contentious heretics are like the partridge. The contentious animal cries out and gathers what it has not borne; so also the heretic gathers Christians, whom he would make his riches. Not by right, but with rashness; but afterwards he is forsaken and is a fool, as is said here, but they shall proceed no further.
