• Out of season. You act in season, but you seem out of season to him who does not willingly hear, which yet sometimes profits him. You therefore, knowing that what seems out of season to him is in season for him, keep your love and care for his health with a mild and modest mind. For many, though they seem to depart more disturbed from the physician, have yet been healed little by little, the vigour of the word penetrating the marrow; and although the Scripture says: “In much talk thou shalt not avoid sin,” it is not to be said that this man has spoken much, even if the Apostle says: Be instant in season, out of season. For in few words there is not much that is necessary.
**“entreat”**
• adjure
• the willing
**“rebuke”**
• the negligent
• persisting with harsh words
• the unwilling
**“in all patience”**
• that you may patiently bear with those who resist, and teach those who receive
• of those who resist
**“and doctrine”**
• of those who receive
• Reprove in all patience, etc. He counsels patience to this one, who is the fiercer; to Titus, who is too patient, he gives command.
4.3:
**“For there shall be a time”** — It is now necessary that you preach this, so that the Church is prepared against these things.
**“when they will not endure sound doctrine”** — as if: they will not bear the burden of hearing salvation
**“but, according to their own desires”**
• that they teach those things which they wish
• But according to their own desires, etc. That is: who teach what they wish. It is a prophecy of the holy apostle, who, foreknowing the future, commands that we be instant in doctrine, that the Church may be prepared against what was to come. For he says there will be such men as wish to be taught according to their own desires, so that they turn away from teachers who are steadfast and truthful to those who will teach them what they gladly hear, because the truth will seem harsh to them, so that, having left true doctrine, they give themselves to fables.
**“they will heap to themselves teachers”** — many
**“having itching ears”**
• themselves
• by desire of hearing, yet not a good one
• Teachers with itching ears, etc. Augustine. On John, Homily 43. Solomon means these teachers by the woman, of whom he says: “The foolish woman and clamorous, and full of allurements, and knowing nothing at all, sat at the door of her house, ... calling to them that pass by: ... Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant.” Though she is ignorant of the truth, she promises the knowledge of the truth, which by that very concealment she commends and, as it were, seasons, that it may be heard the more willingly. The seduced steal the hearing of it, which is forbidden. This concealment causes an itching in the ears of those who fornicate spiritually, as by the itching of lust in the flesh the integrity of chastity is corrupted. For wicked teachers by that very concealment season their poisons for the curious, so that they may think them to be saying something great because they have a secret, and may drink in more sweetly the folly which they think knowledge, and hear more pleasantly what is forbidden to be said and believed openly in the Church. That woman, on account of her unlawful and punishable secrets, is called not only foolish but also bold. For under the Christian name she has set up many wicked heresies, has fashioned abominable fables, and such dirges as are sung in the theatres are laughed at without hostile scurrility. And not such things as we grieve that such folly could have devised against God, and we marvel at its boldness.
4.4:
**“And will indeed turn away their hearing from the truth”** — which are harsh to them
**“but will be turned unto fables”** — so it will be
4.5:
**“But be thou vigilant”**
• in church discipline and in explaining the Scriptures
• while you have time
**“in all things”** — you will teach men of every kind
**“labour, do the work of an evangelist”** — what you preach with your mouth, you attest by this work
**“Do the work of an evangelist”** — Attesting by works what you preach with your mouth, so that they turn back as the turtledove’s to its wings, and there are pomegranates and bells at the lower edges of the hyacinth tunic.
**“fulfill thy ministry”**
• namely the episcopate
• to such an extent that you may fulfil your ministry
**“fulfill”** — by knowledge, life and teaching
**“Be sober”** — By which you will be able to fulfil, because this virtue tempers all the others. He says this especially so that he would not afflict himself too much on account of the precept just given.
4.6:
**“For I”** — For this reason it is fitting thus
**“am even now ready to be sacrificed”** — I begin to be offered to God as an acceptable sacrifice
**“ready to be sacrificed”** — Delibor. We say libare: to taste, to pour out, or to sacrifice. Hence delibare, which however here is put for the sacrifice itself; for he calls his passion a delibation. For he is sacrificed to God who suffers for his justice.
**“and the time of my dissolution”** — of death
**“is at hand”** — is near
4.7:
**“I have fought a good fight”** — How do you know this? Because by the prevenient grace of God I have fulfilled what I owed. Or: I am about to depart soon, but I have fought the good fight, as if to say: I leave this example to you.
**“I have fought”** — I have run against the rebels, where the passage is easy. I have finished: the Church firmly established. In all things I have kept the faith, that others may do the same. He says this not as a thing fully accomplished, for there still remained the struggle of his own passion, but with firm hope, from the fact that the passion had been revealed to him; and therefore what he presumed would be, he declared as though done.
**“my course”** — of preaching
**“I have finished, I have kept the faith”**
• and in all adversities
• The faith, which is the head of the Christian religion. I have kept: this cannot be had without God’s mercy, because it is the house of God; whence he says elsewhere: “I obtained the mercy of God,” not because I was faithful, but that I might be faithful. For we find that the Apostle obtained the grace of God without any good merits, indeed with many vices, the God who renders good for evil. He, as his passion now draws near, recalls his good merits, he who will obtain the crown the more, who after evil merits obtained grace, which, unless it had first been given freely, the crown would not be rendered. Therefore his merits are not his as though they were his own, that is, procured by himself for himself, but are gifts of God.
4.8:
**“As to the rest”** — in the future
**“there is laid up for me a crown of justice”** — which no one takes away; the same you too may hope for
**“which the Lord will render to me in that day”** — because
**“will render”** — For if faith is grace, eternal life too is as a reward of faith. God seems indeed to render eternal life as a debt to the faithful man to whom he owes it, because he has deserved it through faith. But because faith is grace, and eternal life is grace for grace, therefore he will render it.
**“the just judge. And not only to me, but to them also that love his coming”**
• the wicked fear, since there they are to be condemned; but the good love it, since there they are to be saved
• The just judge, etc. Surely he is just in rendering good for good; yet he is first merciful in rendering good for evil, and that very justice by which good is rendered for good is not without mercy.
4.9:
**“Make haste to come to me quickly”**
• because the time of my dissolution is at hand
• because
**“Make haste”** — And also for this reason, because those whom I used to have with me, I now do not have.
4.10:
**“Demas”** — a proper name
**“For”** — or indeed
**“hath left me”** — in time of adversity
**“loving this world, and is gone to Thessalonica, Crescens”** — sent by me into the ministry
**“into”** — for
**“Galatia, Titus into Dalmatia”** — sent by me
4.13:
**“The cloak that I left at Troas”** — The cloak was a consular garment, with which the Roman consuls were clothed when entering the senate house. Whence it is reported that the Romans had this custom, when they were gaining the monarchy of almost the whole world, that whatever nation met them with peace and crowns, they gave it freedom, so far that they were called their brothers, and were named Roman citizens. And they gave them power to build a senate house and to have consuls, as they themselves had. So the father of Paul, having been moved from the town of Gilohalum, where he had been born, to Tarsus in Cilicia, at a certain time when the Romans came through Cilicia, went out to meet them with the other men of Tarsus, as a noble, and they received them with peace. Then the Romans granted them the aforesaid things. And there Paul’s father received a cloak, and after his death Paul kept this garment for himself in memory of him.
**“The cloak”** — According to Haimo, this cloak was given to Paul’s father by the Romans as a mark of distinction, when he was received as an associate and a Roman citizen; whence Paul also calls himself a Roman citizen.
**“at Troas”** — otherwise Carpus
**“when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, especially the parchments”** — that there I may write my letters
*Jerome:* I unroll the Hebrew scroll, which Paul calls a cloak, according to some.
4.14:
**“Alexander”** — but
**“the coppersmith”** — or a smith or keeper of the bronze
**“hath done me much evil”** — at Athens
**“the Lord will reward him”**
• it is the word of one foretelling, not of one cursing
• he declares, he does not wish
4.16:
**“At my first answer”**
• when I first began to defend the gospel against him
• it hints at a frequent encounter against him
• Tribulation is a defence for Christians, because it defends them on the day of judgment.
• This Alexander is the one mentioned above, who returned to apostasy, who made shrines of Diana at Athens and stirred up everyone against the apostle. Defence. Or he calls the affliction and tribulation brought upon him a defence.
**“no man stood with me”** — helper
**“but all forsook me: may it not be laid to their charge”** — because it belongs to man to fear
**“may it not be laid to their charge”** — He does not pray for Alexander, who sinned by envy in attacking the brotherhood. But for those who had not broken off their love, but had yielded through fear, he prays that they be forgiven. For there is a great difference between those who sin in this way and those who sin in that way.
4.17:
**“But the Lord stood by me”** — the more he was forsaken by all
**“and strengthened me, that by me the preaching may be accomplished, and that all the Gentiles may hear: and I was delivered”** — also
**“out of the mouth of the lion”**
• of the devil or of Nero
• That is, of Nero, from whose hands he was delivered by the Lord, when he came to Rome, brought by those who governed Judea, because he had appealed to Caesar. For when he had come to Rome he remained two years in free custody; afterwards he also passed to other nations that were around Rome.
**“of the lion”** — Of the devil, who, as Peter says, “as a roaring lion goeth about, seeking whom he may devour”; who, when he cannot remove him from justice, wishes to take him from life, lest he benefit others; and because he cannot, the Apostle taunts him.
4.18:
**“will deliver”** — or he has delivered
**“The Lord”** — also
**“from every evil work and will preserve me”**
• it is permitted for you to hope the same
• leading
4.19:
**“Salute Prisca and Aquila”** — And Aquila. Aquila was the husband of Prisca; the apostle was lodged with them.
**“and the household of Onesiphorus”** — household
4.20: **“Erastus remained at Corinth”** — Therefore he names them, so that, coming, he may visit these through them.
4.21:
**“Make haste to come before winter”** — he warns on account of rains and cold, that he should come in autumn
**“Eubulus and Pudens”** — or Pudens
4.22:
**“The Lord Jesus”** — after the greeting of the brethren he himself greets, as if signing off in this way: The Lord, etc.
**“Grace be with you”**
• that is: may it remain with your beloved
• lest, being admonished, you grow angry, but rather
**“Amen”** — that is: let the things I have said so far be true.

1.1:
**“Paul”** — by name
**“a servant of God”**
• humility does not take away power and dignity
• A servant by condition, yet not by the wretched slavery of sin, but by a certain nobility of God; as Moses and David are called servants, and Mary a handmaid.
**“an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith”** — holding and preaching the faith
**“of the elect of God”** — According to the faith. That is, which the elect of God hold or by which they are saved, and therefore one must labour the more for it.
**“and”** — according to
**“the acknowledging of the truth”** — is truth in the liberal arts, which is nothing to the Christian religion
**“which is according to godliness”**
• that is, the religion of Christ
• and this is
1.2:
**“Unto the hope”** — that is, by this hoping for eternal life
**“of life everlasting”**
• which, the more certain it is, the more solicitous the minister ought to be
• Unto the hope of eternal life. This is the fruit of the apostolic office here. By this he commends that the apostolic office is not to be carried out half-heartedly.
**“which”** — eternal life
**“God, who lieth not, hath promised before the times”**
• all things
• He promised. But how did he promise, when there were not yet men to whom he might promise? Because in his eternity, and in the Word himself, coeternal with him, what was to be in its own time was already fixed by predestination. He promised therefore before the times, because in himself, the eternal, he had so fixed it before time was, which began with creatures. For we cannot say that there was any time when God had not yet made anything.
• Before the times, etc. Not a recent promise but before the times of all ages, and so that it may be the more certain.
**“of the world”**
• or eternal
• which is the same
1.3:
**“hath manifested”**
• not only the effect of the thing but also in the preaching, etc.
• He manifested. In fitting times, namely the Word, that is, the Son; this is eternal life.
**“But in due times his word”** — namely
**“in preaching, which is committed to me”** — as to a faithful one
**“according to the commandment of God our Saviour”**
• to whom you are a partner
• in whose matter of men’s salvation we obey less, if in any way we are slack
1.4:
**“To Titus”** — Paul, I say, writes this epistle
**“my beloved son, according to the common faith”** — To a son according to the common faith. That is, catholic, not private to anyone; in Greek catholicon is called common or universal in Latin.
**“grace”** — and in writing he greets first in this manner
**“and peace”** — these things are plain
1.5:
**“For this cause”** — For this cause. First he tells what he ought to do and what kind of priests to ordain, beginning thus: for this cause, etc. While he recalls these things, as he had arranged for him, he advises him to carry them out.
**“I left thee in Crete”** — when I was leaving there
**“that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting”** — toward completion
**“set in order”** — the evils in sinners, adding to the good: those things that are lacking, etc.
**“and shouldest ordain”** — every
**“priests in every city”**
• bishops
• Presbyters: so that the burden of pastoral care may be borne more easily, being divided among many.
**“as I also appointed thee”** — that is, such as I taught should be appointed
1.6:
**“If any”** — that is
**“be without crime”**
• not by sin
• by criminal sin or criminal infamy
• Without crime. If he had said “without sin,” no one could rightly be ordained a minister in the Church. For many baptized faithful are without crime; but without sin in this life I would say no one, not because any sin remains that is not remitted in baptism, but because in us, who remain in the weakness of this life, there do not cease to arise daily those things which are daily forgiven to those who pray faithfully. Examine however just a man as much as you like in this life, he is nevertheless not without sin. Whence John: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” But plainly, many just men are called without complaint, which is understood as without crime. For no complaint is just against those who have no crime. Crime therefore is a complaint, that is, a grave sin most worthy of accusation and condemnation, such as murder, adultery, some uncleanness of fornication, theft, fraud, and the like; when a man begins not to have these, he begins to lift up his head toward liberty. But this liberty is begun, not perfect.
**“the husband of one wife”**
• in which is the appearance of continence and a sacrament
• The husband of one wife. After baptism, because to the new man neither fornications nor any things that were before are a hindrance. Augustine contradicts this opinion in these words: They understand more keenly who judged that neither the man who as a catechumen or pagan had another wife should be ordained, because it is a matter of the sacrament, not of sin. For in baptism all sins are forgiven. And he who said: “If a virgin marry, she hath not sinned,” sufficiently declared that marriage is not a sin. But for the sanctity of the sacrament, as a woman, if she was defiled as a catechumen, cannot after baptism be consecrated among the virgins of God, so it was seen, not absurdly, that the twice-married man has not sinned but has lost the rule of the sacrament, necessary not for the merit of life but for the seal of ecclesiastical ordination. And as many wives of the ancient fathers signified the churches that were to be from all nations, subject to one husband, that is, Christ, so our prelate, that is, the bishop, as the husband of one wife signifies the unity from all nations subject to one husband, Christ. And so, as it is not lawful “to serve two masters,” so it is not lawful to apostatize from the one God and go over to the superstition of another.
**“having faithful children”**
• of sound faith
• Having faithful children. Not even accused of lust, or not subject to him. Otherwise there is no hope in him of correcting others, nor has one who lives with such men the face to correct others.
1.7:
**“For a bishop must”** — For a bishop must, etc. Such a man ought to be appointed. For it is necessary for the handling of the office that he be without crime, that is, a bishop beyond reproach. Here he plainly shows that under the name of presbyters bishops were designated above.
**“be without crime, as the steward of God: not proud, not subject to anger, not given to wine, no striker”** — that is, not striking the minds of others by speaking otherwise than is fitting, or not fierce, not cruel.
**“not greedy of filthy lucre”** — worldly
1.8:
**“But given to hospitality, gentle, sober, just”** — to his neighbour
**“holy”** — to God
**“continent”** — from unlawful things: anger, pride, and the like
1.9:
**“Embracing”** — with love
**“that faithful word which is according to doctrine”** — truthful
**“that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine, and to convince the gainsayers”**
• by speaking against or by living badly
• Gainsay. For those who gainsay are not to be understood in one way: very few indeed gainsay us by speaking, but many by living badly. For who dares by speaking openly to gainsay the truth? Many gainsay not with the tongue but by life; to rebuke them is a good work, a great burden, a steep hill.
1.10:
**“For there are also many”** — in Crete
**“disobedient”** — in themselves
**“vain talkers”** — to others
**“and seducers: especially”** — by deceptions and frauds of every kind
**“they who are of the circumcision”** — that is, of the Jews who under the name of Christ taught Judaizing; for, reborn in Christ, they were not pure Christians, because they wished to venerate partly the law and partly Christ.
1.11:
**“Who must be reproved, who”** — therefore, because they themselves are
**“whole houses”** — the whole household
**“subvert, teaching things which they ought not”** — and they do this
**“for filthy lucre's sake”** — for the sake of earthly gain, or that they may make proselytes, as the Lord said to the scribes and Pharisees: “You go round about the sea and the land to make one proselyte”, for acquiring earthly things.
1.12:
**“said”** — they truly are such
**“of them”**
• who knew them
• One of them, etc. It is lawful to take from any source whatever testimony that one has found true, for the divine authority; as also Paul, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, when speaking to the Athenians, said of God: “In him we live, and move, and are; as some also of your own poets said.” And of the Athenian altar’s inscription he says: “I found an altar on which was written: To the unknown God.” So divine authority takes from wherever it finds what is necessary, but does not confirm that everything written there is to be accepted. Whence in the law it was commanded to the Jews that if they bought a Gentile slave, his hair should be shaved and the growth of his nails cut off. Then he was taken to domestic uses; so, the vain and superfluous things of the superstitions of the Gentiles and the sayings of the poets having been shaved off and cut away, what is found pure is to be taken for the service of the house of God.
**“One of them, a prophet of their own, said”** — Augustine. This was Epimenides the Cretan, in whose books this is found; this man is not found among the prophets of God, nor does his prophecy belong to those oracles of God which were entrusted to the Jews, and therefore the Apostle did not mention his name, as he is accustomed to mention the prophets of God, saying: “as David also saith,” or “Isaias.” Or, when he passes over their names, he says “as it is written,” and that Scripture is understood in which is the authority of God. But an unlearned man, a raging dog barking against the truth, has dared to say that this man, of whom the Apostle speaks, was among the prophets of the Jews.
**“their own”**
• because he set forth well their nature
• which was surely said so that he might not seem to be a prophet of God
**“of their own”** — although also of others
**“a prophet”** — not of God
**“The Cretians are always liars, evil beasts”** — thirsting for blood
**“slothful bellies”** — gluttonous, and therefore slothful
1.13:
**“This testimony is true”** — do not believe him less, because the Apostle commends his words, though he is a Gentile
**“Wherefore”** — they teach what is not fitting
**“rebuke them sharply”** — not gently as you are wont
**“That they may be sound”** — that is, that they believe rightly
1.14:
**“Not giving heed”** — because they do not know the force of the Scriptures of literal observance, in which no one is justified before God
**“and commandments of men”** — now not of God
**“Commandments of men”** — Because the commandments of the law, after the truth was made manifest, are now commandments of men, not of God.
**“who turn themselves away”** — or of those turning away
**“from the truth”**
• for they teach about the distinction of foods, when there is none
• as if they truly turn themselves away, because
• Of them that turn themselves away from the truth. Of spiritual understanding. For whatever is set against the truth is human inveteracy. Therefore he calls “commandments of men” and “fables” the things they narrate, because, not knowing the force of the Scriptures and the inner meaning of the words of the law, they follow the colour, not the savour. For they think that one must never depart from what Moses handed down, as for instance about the difference of foods.
1.15:
**“All things are clean”** — granted for human uses
**“to the clean”**
• who take them in good faith and are just
• All things are clean, etc. This they deny, because in the law Moses forbade certain things and separated the clean from the unclean. But he did not wish this to be understood according to the natures which God created, but according to significations. All things therefore are clean to the clean, according to their natures. Whence in Genesis: “God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good.” According to significations, certain things are unclean to the Jews, and not all things are suitable for us, either for the health of bodies or for the custom of human society.
**“but to them that are defiled”** — through sin
**“and to unbelievers”** — who do not believe in God or to God
**“nothing is clean”** — because they are not worthy of the gifts of God
**“but both their mind and their conscience are defiled”**
• as if their defilement is not from food but from an evil understanding and the conscience of sins
• because
1.16:
**“They profess”** — in words
**“that they know”** — indeed
**“God; but in their works they deny him”** — Whence John: “He who saith that he knoweth God, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar.”
**“In their works they deny him”** — If denial is made not only by the tongue but also by deeds, surely we find many antichrists, who confess Christ with the mouth and in their conduct dissent from him. Whoever denies Christ by deeds is an antichrist. Such are all bad Catholics, who deny not by words but by deeds. Do not therefore be as though secure about the faith; join to faith a right life, that you may confess Christ both by teaching true things in words and by living well in deeds. For if you confess in words and not in deeds, the faith of such conduct is nearly the faith of demons.
**“being abominable”** — hateful to God
**“and incredulous”** — nor fit to believe
**“and to every good work reprobate”**
• reprobated by God, so that they have no grace to work well
• They teach what is not right.

2.1:
**“But speak thou”** — those things
**“the things that become sound doctrine”** — that is, the teaching of sound faith
**“Sound doctrine”** — These are the things that pertain to good morals.
2.2:
**“The aged men”** — namely, exhort
**“be sober, chaste, prudent”** — providing the things necessary for faith
**“sound in faith”** — that they may have it whole
**“in love”**
• likewise sound
• of God and of neighbour, and in the very order of charity
**“in patience”** — of temptations and tribulations
2.3:
**“The aged women, in like manner”** — exhort also
**“in holy attire”**
• to be
• In holy attire: so that their walk, movements, countenance and speech may show forth holiness.
**“not false accusers”** — laying charges on others, as they are wont to do to young women
**“not given to much wine”** — Not given to much wine, etc. For there are commonly certain women who, when the body’s lust has grown cold, have given themselves to wine for the sake of pleasure.
**“teaching well”** — Teaching well. Not indeed publicly to men, but privately.
2.4:
**“That they may teach the young women to be wise”** — or that they teach the young women prudence, or exhort the young women
**“That they may love their husbands”** — Those whom they naturally love with natural affection, let them love also with chaste love, so that, namely, with modesty they render to their husbands what is due rather than demand it.
**“to love their children”** — not only with carnal but also with spiritual love
2.5:
**“To be discreet”**
• let them teach them also to be
• in understanding of mind
**“chaste”** — in continence of body
**“sober”** — in food and drink
**“having a care of the house, gentle, obedient to their husbands”** — that, not puffed up with riches or nobility, they not desire to be unequal to their husbands
**“that the word of God be not blasphemed”** — if they behave badly
**“That the word of God be not blasphemed”** — This can refer to the old men and to all the above, as if: exhort the old men and old women and young women to conduct themselves as I have said; and they ought to do this so that the word of God be not blasphemed, etc.
**“the word of God”**
• the evangelical teaching
• if they have unbelieving husbands, to whom they ought the more readily to submit for the fear of God, so that seeing this they do not blaspheme the name of God.
2.6: **“Young men, in like manner, exhort that they be sober”** — Exhort the young men likewise. Because youth is more prone to falling, it is bidden to restrain itself; and that this may be easier, he bids the teacher be a pattern, so that what he teaches in words he shows in deeds, and so the profane may be ashamed.
2.7:
**“In all things shew thyself an example”**
• Augustine. Otherwise a shepherd kills the sheep, as far as he is concerned, even if they live.
• In all things shew thyself, etc. For everyone who lives badly in the sight of those over whom he is set, as far as in him lies, kills them, even if they live by the mercy of God.
**“of good works, in doctrine, in integrity”** — of life or of body
**“in gravity”** — not light but authoritative
2.8:
**“The sound word”** — let it be thine
**“that can not be blamed”** — said in place and time
**“that he, who is on the contrary part”** — that is, your opponent
2.9:
**“Exhort servants”** — exhort
**“to be obedient to their masters”** — to whomever, as much to good as to bad
**“in all things pleasing”** — which are not against God
**“not gainsaying”** — in this way they can please, when they do not mutter when their masters have ordered them something
2.10:
**“Not defrauding”** — the due of servitude
**“but in all things shewing good fidelity”** — even in the smallest things
**“that they may adorn the doctrine”** — this refers to all
**“of God our Saviour”**
• with good works and faith
• That they may adorn the doctrine of the Saviour, etc. This refers to all those named above, namely to old men and old women and servants, as if exhorting all those named to conduct themselves as has been prescribed, so that they may adorn in their actions the doctrine of the Saviour, etc.
• May adorn. The ornament of a teacher is the honest life of a disciple.
**“in all things”** — in their actions
2.11:
**“For the grace of God our Saviour hath appeared”**
• through the flesh
• Hath appeared. As if all are to be warned, because he was born for all; he excluded no one.
**“For the grace of God”**
• God, through grace, though invisible
• Or grace, that is, Christ, who is the grace of God. Or the grace of God is saving, etc., that is, our God and Saviour, namely the Son of God, although he is invisible, nevertheless in the form of God appeared through grace in the form of a servant.
**“our Saviour to all men”**
• for the benefit of every kind of men, without whom it would not have profited to be born
• as far as in him
2.12:
**“Instructing us”** — by the example of life and teaching, in which you ought to follow him
**“denying ungodliness”** — of vain worship and ignorance
**“worldly desires ... soberly”** — in us
**“and justly”** — toward our neighbour
**“and godly”** — toward God
**“we should live ... in this world”** — so frail
2.13:
**“Looking for”**
• through this
• certain and watchful
**“the blessed hope”** — eternal glory
**“and coming of the glory”**
• or manifestation
• And the coming of glory, etc. He who will come not in weakness as before but in glory and power, to give rewards according to merits; he who in his first coming was so humble that he not only taught but also gave, etc.
**“of the great God”** — not of a weak man, not mortal, not passible as before
2.14:
**“Who gave himself”** — not only taught
**“for us”** — by this we are sure of hope
**“that he might ... us”** — to this end
**“redeem us”** — by his blood
**“from all iniquity, and might cleanse to himself”** — both from original and from actual
**“a people acceptable”** — or peculiar, that is, his own
**“A pursuer of good works”** — Because Christ redeemed us to this end, that we, pursuing a pure life and filled with good works, might be heirs of God.
2.15:
**“These things speak”** — to those who do not know
**“and exhort”** — to those who know
**“and rebuke”**
• negligent or rebellious
• Rebuke. It is now not taken harshly, since it is known to be done for salvation.
**“with all authority”** — thus with authority
**“Let no man despise thee.”** — for simplicity

3.1:
**“Admonish”** — and even if you have spiritual authority, nevertheless admonish
**“them ... princes”** — to kings and leaders
**“and powers”** — to lesser ones
**“to be subject ... at a word”** — of them
**“to obey ... to every good work”** — never to evil
**“to be ready”** — To every good work, etc. As if to say: admonish them to be slow to evil but ready for good, knowing what ought to be paid to each, because they are ready for each.
3.2:
**“speak evil of no man”** — even if they are oppressed by them
**“not to be litigious, but gentle: shewing all”** — in words and deeds
**“mildness”** — because thus unbelievers and faithless ones can be called to future hope
**“towards all men”** — good or bad
3.3:
**“For we ... were”** — For we were: we ought to do this because we too were once such as they; so they too can be what we are, through the same grace
**“ourselves also were some time unwise, incredulous, erring”**
• through evil works
• Even we ourselves were once foolish. Even if some of us were philosophers, we were nonetheless lacking in true wisdom.
**“slaves to divers desires”** — of the mind
**“and pleasures”** — of the flesh
**“divers ... living in malice”** — in harming
**“and envy”**
• at the successes of others
• if it was not permitted to harm
**“living”** — our life
**“hateful”** — hateful to God or to other men
3.4:
**“But when the goodness and kindness”**
• God, both made man and kind, or the generous mercy and clemency of God
• Kindness. Through which he bestows upon us spiritual gifts in abundance.
**“kindness ... appeared”**
• to the world through the flesh
• or to us through faith
• appeared, that is, shone upon men
3.5:
**“Not by the works of justice”** — because we had done no good works
**“which we have done, but according to his mercy, he saved us”**
• so perhaps also those who are still unbelieving
• already by the hope of future salvation
**“by the laver of regeneration”**
• of baptism
• in which, the old man being laid aside, the new man is begotten
**“and renovation of the Holy Ghost”** — because he who believes is renewed day by day more and more through the Spirit given in baptism
3.6:
**“Whom”** — the Spirit
**“he hath poured forth upon us abundantly”** — for the forgiveness of all sins, for the abundance of virtues
3.7:
**“That”** — to this end, that he may add this
**“being justified”** — meanwhile, in the present
**“by his grace, we may be heirs, according to hope”** — that we may be heirs, according to hope, although not yet in reality
3.8:
**“faithful”** — truthful
**“saying”** — that Christ has saved and made heirs
**“And these things”** — of the aforesaid things
**“I will have thee affirm”**
• others
• or I want you to affirm, namely those who believe in God, that they may take care
**“that they ... may be careful to excel in good works”**
• to excel in good works, for many others or for themselves
• Or to excel, that is, to make more progress and become better themselves.
**“who believe in God. These things”**
• the aforesaid things
• therefore I want you to confirm others about the aforesaid things, because
**“These things are good”** — in themselves
**“and profitable unto men”**
• to others
• to confirm about these things
3.9:
**“But avoid foolish questions”** — where neither salvation nor useful knowledge
**“and genealogies”** — enumerations of origins
**“and contentions”** — which they make about the law, as about foods, some asserting they should be distinguished, others not
**“and strivings about the law”** — as when Scripture, uncorrected, seems to hold contrary or impossible things about the years of Methuselah and other such matters
**“For they are unprofitable”** — without fruit
**“and vain”** — false
3.10:
**“A man that is a heretic”**
• not only avoid these things, but also after you have given correction twice
• A heretic. A heretic is one who attacks the law through the words of the law; for he asserts his own sense from the words of the law, so that by the authority of the law he confirms the perversity of his mind. They are to be avoided because, being corrected more often, they would be more practised in evil.
**“after the first and second admonition, avoid”** — why
3.11:
**“Knowing that”** — lost
**“he, that is such an one,”** — incorrigible
**“and”** — and because he sins knowingly, or and although he is
**“sinneth, being condemned by his own judgment”** — He condemns himself by his own judgment who praises error and condemns truth.
3.12:
**“When I shall send to thee Artemas or Tychicus”** — so that meanwhile they may provide for the Cretans until you come to me
**“make haste to come unto me to Nicopolis”** — therefore he says this because he wishes to see him out of affection, and to confirm him more fully in ecclesiastical discipline
3.13:
**“Send forward Zenas, the lawyer”**
• so it was in the synagogue
• Zenas, the lawyer, etc. He says this not because Apollo is more skilled, but because this profession was in the synagogue.
**“and Apollo”**
• who was perfect in the Scriptures
• Apollo. He was a bishop of the Corinthians, who on account of a sedition stirred up against him by the false apostles had departed with Zenas his companion to Titus, bishop of Crete. But the Corinthians now being quieted, through the letters of Paul he commands Titus that before he comes to Nicopolis he send them ahead, so carefully that nothing may be lacking to them for the journey.
**“with care, that nothing be wanting to them”**
• those things which are necessary for them for the journey
• so diligently
• That nothing be wanting to them, etc. Therefore he orders necessary expenses to be given them, because it was fitting that those who handed down spiritual things should not lack carnal things.
3.14:
**“And let our men also learn”** — whence also the things for them
**“and our men”** — that is, the Cretans, as well as others
**“to excel in good works”** — for themselves
**“for necessary uses”**
• Giving to the ministers
• not to whatever
**“that they be not unfruitful”** — because according to the parable the tree that bears not good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire
3.15:
**“All that are with me salute thee”** — On account of brevity, it signifies all the greeters together.
**“All that are with me salute thee: salute them”** — not feigned
**“salute them that love us in the faith”** — that is, with faithful affection

1.1:
**“Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus”**
• for whose sake also you ought to have mercy.
• Paul, a prisoner. He does not say “apostle,” a name of dignity, but of humility, because he does not command but entreats. As if to say: he whom you ought to pity should not be the cause of sorrow, if you, merciless, should torment the son?
**“a prisoner”** — The Apostle does not say what is a name of dignity, but “prisoner,” which is a name of humility, because he does not command but entreats. For here there is an intercession for Onesimus. Therefore he recalls what belongs to humility, beginning from his own injury, that he might give dignity to his epistle. For as to be bound for the cause of sin is a disgrace, so on the other hand to endure the chains of custody for Christ is the greatest glory. For at that time he was in custody. Therefore he says: Paul, a prisoner, etc. As if to say: he whom you ought to have mercy on should not be the cause of grief; what will you be, if, merciless, you torment a son?
**“and Timothy, a brother: to Philemon, our beloved”**
• brother
• by the progress of virtues
**“Beloved”** — Or worthy of love, as is found in the Greek, that is, one who deserves to be loved.
**“our fellow labourer”** — by the ministry of preaching
1.2:
**“And to Appia, our dearest sister”** — his wife, so that she too may pray for her husband
**“and to Archippus, our fellow soldier”** — his son, minister of the Colossians, so that he too may entreat the father
**“and to the church which is in thy house”** — to the whole household, so that they too may pray
1.3:
**“Grace to you”** — and before other things he greets in this manner
**“and peace”** — of mind, and reconciliation to God
1.4:
**“I give thanks”**
• the remembered goodness can move to pardon
• After the greeting he gives thanks for good things, commending faith and love, which he recalls so that the remembered goodness may move him to pardon.
1.5:
**“Hearing of thy charity and faith”** — that is, the commendation of your faith and love
**“which”** — faith and love
**“thou hast in the Lord Jesus”** — for the works of faith and love, he serves the saints
**“and towards all the saints”** — or to all the saints
**“which thou hast in the Lord Jesus, and towards all the saints”** — For he believed in Christ and loved him, and believed the saints and loved them, and through the works of faith and love served Christ and the saints.
1.6:
**“That the communication of thy faith”**
• your faith sharing in our faith; or that what you share with others is evident, so that it is rightly recognized that every good is in you through Christ.
• That the communication, etc. As if you have faith and love in Christ and in the saints, so that the communication of your faith becomes evident, that is, that your faith, sharing in our faith; or that what you impart to others from your faith is evident. And this:
**“in the acknowledgment of every good work, that is in you in Christ Jesus”** — That is, so that it is evident, and it is rightly known that every good is in you through Christ, that is, the sufficiency of all good things.
**“may be made evident in the acknowledgment of every good work, that is in you in Christ Jesus.”**
• The Apostle prays this: that his working be done with knowledge of goodness, that is, that he work with such a mind that he may thereafter expect a reward from it.
• Or thus. I am mindful of you and give thanks in my prayers held concerning this: that the communication of your faith, that is, the working of the faith by which you serve Christ and the saints, may be made evident in the acknowledgment of every good work that is in Christ Jesus, that is, with the knowledge of the eternal good, that it may be looked for as a reward. For the Apostle prays this, that his working may be done with the knowledge of goodness, that is, that he may work with such a mind that for the future he may look for Jesus Christ from it as reward, not the repayment of temporal things.
1.7:
**“For I have had great joy”** — in the heart
**“and consolation”** — in adversities
**“in thy charity”**
• this
• which flourished not only in the habit of virtue in the heart but was also made manifest outside in deed.
**“because the bowels”** — of inward affection
**“of the saints”**
• because he supplied the saints with necessities
• The bowels of the saints, that is, the dearest sons of the saints; or the saints' affection toward you, more inclined, found rest, you of course consoling, and was refreshed, because they found you good in all things.
**“have been refreshed by thee”** — or toward you
**“brother”** — worthily receiving them, as they are somewhat refreshed from their labours.
1.8:
**“Wherefore”** — because, for other servants, much more for me; because he is ready to do well.
**“much confidence”** — I do not say power against your lawful things.
**“have in Christ Jesus”** — through Christ Jesus.
**“to command”** — even.
**“thee that which is to the purpose”** — your advantage.
1.9:
**“For charity sake”** — mine or yours.
**“I rather beseech”** — Whence above: “An ancient man rebuke not, but entreat him as a father.”
**“I beseech thee”** — It is great if one who is lofty, not one who is humble, bows himself down and entreats.
**“whereas thou art such a one”** — by life and age.
**“as”** — I.
**“Paul an old man”** — for which reason you ought the more to be moved.
**“an old man”** — One should defer more to an old man, out of likeness of age.
1.10:
**“I beseech”** — I say.
**“thee for my son, whom I have begotten”** — and therefore I love him more tenderly, when I was in the faith.
1.11:
**“Who hath been heretofore unprofitable to thee”** — while unbelieving.
**“unprofitable”** — by taking away your goods.
**“hath been, but now is profitable both to me and thee”** — by serving, and through me to you, to whom belongs whatever your servant has done for me.
1.12:
**“And do thou receive him as my own bowels”**
• as a son, or as mine in that affection.
• As my own bowels, etc. The apostle Paul baptized Onesimus, a fugitive returning to divine help while he was in prison, seeing in him a hope of usefulness; whom he so commends that he signifies his own heart to be received in him.
**“receive”** — my most dear son; in many copies this is lacking.
1.14:
**“But without thy counsel”** — with consent.
**“I would do nothing”** — that not.
**“as it were of necessity”** — against your will.
**“thy good deed might be”** — That your servant serves me. Yet God brings it about that he wills it, who works in us both the willing and the doing, for good will.
1.15:
**“For perhaps”** — He says perhaps because all human things are doubtful, and there could be another cause why God so disposed it.
**“For he therefore departed for a season from thee”** — receive him, because his flight was useful.
**“that thou mightest receive him again for ever”** — here and in the future.
1.16:
**“Not now as a servant”** — only.
**“but instead of”** — or: more.
**“a servant, a most dear brother”** — Instead of a servant, which is before; or a most dear brother, more than a servant; for brothers are more dear than servants.
**“especially to me”**
• dear
• To me your master, a brother; and lest the lord be puffed up against the servant, he humbles him, calling him brother; and in the flesh, because all come from one Adam; and in the Lord, through faith.
• To me, your teacher, Onesimus is a brother; for, having offended his own master, he fled to the Apostle, to this end that, his sins being blotted out, he might return useful, so that he would become not only equal to his master in merits, but a brother to the teacher himself. And lest Philemon, because he is the master, be puffed up against the servant, he humbles him by calling him brother, both in the flesh, because all are from one Adam, and in the Lord, through faith.
**“but how much more to thee”**
• than before, or than to me
• ought to be dear
**“both in the flesh”**
• through the condition of first birth
• because your servant
**“and in the Lord?”**
• through faith
• because a faithful brother
1.17:
**“If therefore thou count”** — wish to have
**“me a partner, receive him as myself.”** — as if, if you do not receive him, you are not a partner
1.18: **“Put that to my account”** — Now he cuts off all excuse, when he says it is to be charged to himself if he has either harmed or owes anything.
1.19:
**“I Paul have written it with my own hand: I will repay it”** — either here or in the future
**“not to say to thee”**
• I say, I will repay
• I demand less than you owe
**“that thou owest me thy own self also.”** — not merely your own things
1.20:
**“Yea, brother.”** — an adjuration
**“May I enjoy thee in the Lord.”** — I will rejoice over you in the kingdom of God.
**“Refresh my bowels”**
• a son or understanding
• a son or affection
• So I will enjoy you, etc. That is, I will rejoice over you in the kingdom of God if you do what I ask. And what is it he adds: Refresh my bowels, etc.
**“in the Lord.”**
• or: Christ
• that is, on account of Christ or the Lord
1.21:
**“Trusting in”** — or: in
**“thy obedience, I have written to thee: knowing that thou wilt also do more than I say.”** — Trusting in thy obedience, etc. He provokes him by flattering him so that he does no more than is asked of him. For it tends to happen that one who sees himself well thought of shows himself better.
1.22:
**“But withal prepare”**
• or here he moves him to grant pardon
• But withal prepare, etc. He signifies that he will come to him, so as to make him more anxious and more ready to obey; because this too can move him to grant pardon.

1.1:
**“Manifold”**
• by many speeches
• In every kind of speaking: as by figures, by visions, by dreams, by speeches of angels; and in many ways by the creation of things, as in the forming of Adam, in the passage of the Red Sea, and in similar acts.
**“in divers manners”**
• by many kinds
• Of old. It is not new. God: who is unchangeable, then and now. Speaking: because what he did then, he does now also. To the fathers: who in flesh and in the worship of God are fathers to us. By the prophets: for it was not they but God in them. At sundry times, that is, many times, to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the rest, and often to the same. And in divers manners: because now by dreams, as to Daniel, now by open voice, as to Moses, now by inward inspiration, as to David. Or at sundry times: in many and different kinds of speech, as by dreams or inspirations or open voices. And in divers manners: signifying things to come by different mysteries of things. Spoke: because the same, now as formerly, to us, the sons of those fathers; lest he be thought to have spoken to us of other things than to them, which might have seemed so if he spoke to another people.
**“God, speaking in times past to the fathers by the prophets”**
• to servants by servants
• Because he put “speaking” and “has spoken,” the present for the past and the past for the present, it signifies that he speaks through the Son what he spoke through the prophets; except that in the prophets the truth was hidden and still to be fulfilled, but in the Son it is open and completed.
**“in times past to the fathers by the prophets, last of all to us in his Son”** — For the Lord appointed a time for his promises, and a time for fulfilling what he had promised. The times of the promises had prophets inspired and filled with the word of God until John; but from him to the end is the time of fulfilling what was promised. The only Son of God was to come to men, to assume man, and through that to become man, to die, to rise again, to ascend, to sit at the right hand of the Father, and to fulfil his promises among the Gentiles.
**“by the prophets”** — Augustine. He had to be foretold, so that when he came he would not be dreaded as something sudden, but awaited as one already believed in.
1.2:
**“last of all”**
• because after this no other speaking follows
• at the end of times
**“in these days”** — as if to say: there are still those living who heard and saw
**“hath spoken to us”** — to sons
**“by his Son”**
• who is greater than the prophets, whence he commends him according to both natures
• Who is greater than the prophets. For he is the Lord, the fulfiller and sanctifier of the prophets. For he is a prophet in such a way that he is also the Lord of the prophets. So also Christ is an angel and the Lord of the angels. For he himself is called “the angel of great counsel.” And it was said to Moses of him: “I will raise them up a prophet like to thee.” If Christ announced nothing, he would not be called an angel. If he prophesied nothing, he would not be called a prophet. From the fact that he announced what was present, he was an angel; and from the fact that he foretold the future, he was a prophet. From the fact that “the Word was made flesh,” he was the Lord both of angels and of prophets.
**“whom he hath appointed”** — according to his humanity. Whence: “Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance”
**“hath appointed”** — Now unchangeable.
**“heir of all things”** — because the Son never loses anything of all that the Father has given
**“Heir of all things”** — That is, the possessor of every creature. For now “the portion of the Lord is not Jacob only, and Israel the lot of his inheritance, but all the nations of the world” altogether. He uses the name of heir in order to establish and show two things by it, namely that the Son is his own, and that no loss of the gift befalls him. In saying heir, then, he showed a mark of humility. Then he passes to a higher and loftier step, saying: By whom, that is, by the Word coeternal with the Father. He made, not only the eternal and invisible and unchangeable things, which are less known to us, but also the world, that is, the visible and changeable things.
**“by whom also he made”** — as through the Word
**“the world”** — not only eternal things, which are less known
1.3:
**“Who being”** — according to his divinity
**“the brightness of his glory”**
• from the Father and the same as he
• light from light
• Who, being the brightness of his glory, etc. Here he commends him according to the divine nature, showing Christ to be coeternal and coequal with the Father and of the same substance with him, but another in person. Note how here he enters upon two ways: the one calling us back from the impious error of Sabellius, the other from the error of Arian impiety; lest the Father be thought either not to have an only-begotten, or the Son to subsist as a stranger to the Father. For there are some who rave that he is a stranger, which was Arius’s wicked view. Others labour to feign not one Father and another Son, but the same at one time Father, at another Son. He therefore warns with a complete account both that he is the Son of God, and that he does not exist as alien from him. But we ought to take this with a religious understanding, and if anything absurd perhaps occurs, to drive it from the eye of the mind. For everywhere we have need of a religious understanding, but most of all where we either say or hear something about God; for neither is the tongue sufficient to speak worthily of God, nor does the understanding avail to perceive. For we understand many things of God which we are utterly unable to speak, and we rightly speak many things which we are not fit to understand. For example: that God is everywhere we know and say, but how he is everywhere we do not grasp by understanding. Likewise: that there is a certain incorporeal power which is the cause of all good things we know, but what it is we utterly do not know. There are also some things which cannot be said, although they are grasped by the mind, so that we see even Paul himself in some such matters as if wavering, and not setting forth complete examples, as here when he says: Who being the brightness, etc. Using improper names, because he could not find proper ones, and the likeness of temporal things to show the truth of eternal things, that is, the coeternity of the Father and the Son, although temporal things cannot be compared with eternal things in a complete comparison. For in eternity there is stability, in time variety; in eternity all things stand, in time some succeed others. In creation we find nothing coeternal, because nothing is eternal, but it suffices for the likeness that we find the coeval. For we call coeval whatever have the same measure of times, nor is the one preceded by the other in time. Yet we say both began to be. Even if we can find coeval things in creation, yet not a begetter and begotten, as in the Trinity, generally, the coeternal only-begotten. For in creatures the begotten does not begin from the moment the begetter does. But in the Creator the begetter did not precede the begotten. Therefore temporal things cannot be compared with eternal in a complete comparison, but yet, by some slight and small likeness, the coeval can be compared with the coeternal. Let us therefore find coeval things. For we are admonished by the Scriptures to these likenesses. For we read it written of wisdom itself: “She is the brightness of eternal light.” Likewise: “and the unspotted mirror of God’s majesty.” Behold, wisdom itself is called the brightness of eternal light, that is, the image of the Father, and a mirror. And here the Apostle says: Brightness of glory. For the Son is coeternal with the Father, as brightness is coeval with fire. For if I wish to light a lamp, there is not yet fire there nor brightness, but as soon as I have lit it, the brightness exists likewise and with the fire. Therefore the Son of God is called the brightness of glory in this respect, that the Father is always his, in that he has one of whom he is; not in the sense that the Father was first and afterwards the Son, for always the Father, always the Son is of the Father. Therefore the Son is always born, the Father is always, and the image always from him. Behold, you could not find coeternal things in creatures and you have found coeval ones, by the proportion of which you understand the Son coeternal with the eternal begetter. For what is coeval with the temporal, this is coeternal with the eternal. But it must be observed that although in these, namely fire and brightness, there is coevality, yet there is not complete equality there, because the brightness which is poured forth there from the fire shines less than the fire itself; so these have a likeness, but not complete equality. Therefore by the proportion of other temporal things, of which one is from the other, though not coeval, yet consubstantial, the Son is shown to be consubstantial with the Father. For man is born of man, and horse of horse. Nor is either of these coeval with the other, because the one born is preceded in time by him of whom he is born; but yet both that man and this man, and that horse and this horse, that is, are of the same substance; they are different in time, but are not different in nature. Likewise God the Son is born of God the Father, and since he is coeternal with him he is also of the same nature, not less than he, because God of God, as man born of man is of the same substance, and horse of horse. Behold another kind of likeness: here equality is praised, there coevality. Join therefore this: that everything praiseworthy in creatures, to which something is lacking, is together in the Creator, to whom nothing is lacking; yet what we find there, that is, man and man are two men, but here Father and Son are one God. Therefore the Apostle says: Who being the brightness of glory. The Father is glory, the Son the same with him, and making him known, made man, as the ray the sun.
**“and the figure”**
• or character
• a full showing of the Father’s essence
**“The figure of his substance”** — Behold, otherwise: personally, as the figure is from him whose figure it is. But equal, because not at all unlike, as he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father in me”; and “he that seeth me seeth the Father also.”
**“of his substance”** — Note that these names, namely light and glory, are sometimes referred to the divine nature, sometimes to the person. And when they are referred to the person, now they are referred to the Father, now to the Son. For we say the Father is light and the Son is light. Likewise the Father is glory, the Son is glory, and these two are one glory and one light, not two. And the Son is called glory of glory, as light of light, and principle of principle, and God of God, yet not two gods but one, not two principles but one. But brightness and figure, like image, are properly referred to the person of the Son and are said relatively.
**“and upholding all things”**
• as they were created by him, so they are preserved by him
• Upholding all things, etc. It was said above that through him he made all things. Here he now attributes to him the highest authority, because with authority he governs and contains all things. For as all things were created by him, so by him they are preserved unchanged. For the omnipotence of the Creator is the cause of the subsisting of every creature, and if this power should ever cease from ruling the things it has founded, the form and nature of all things would alike fall to ruin. And therefore the Lord says: “My Father worketh until now; and I work,” showing a certain continuation of the work of him who at once contains and administers all things. In this work his wisdom also perseveres, of which it is said: “She reacheth from end to end mightily, and ordereth all things sweetly.” God, therefore, almighty, in unchangeable eternity, will and truth, ever the same, moves the spiritual creature through time, and moves the bodily creature also through time and place, that by that motion he may minister to the natures which he has founded. When, therefore, he does anything of this kind, we ought not to suppose that his substance, by which he is God, is changeable in times and places, or moveable through times and places, since he is both within every thing, because in him are all things, and without every thing, because he is above all things; and older than all, because he is before all things; and newer than all, because the same himself is after all things, that is, after the beginnings of all things. And therefore, commending his power, the Apostle says: Upholding all things, etc. And note that it is said by way of likeness. For by saying this he wished to signify the ease of upholding, by a metaphor from those who without any labour move or effect something by a word or a finger; so Christ without labour contains and governs the mass and greatness of creation. Observe that although the Apostle here says that Christ contains all things, he said above that the Father made all things through him, where he says: “By whom also he made the world.” As though he could not himself make, unless the Father had stretched out his right hand to him, or as though he had been some instrument of the Father working. But if all things are governed by him, were they not made by him? So he was not, as you, heretic, vainly suppose, some instrument, nor is the Father said to have made through him as though he could not himself make. But as the Father is said to judge through the Son, because it is agreed that he begot him as maker. For if the Father is his cause according as he is Father, much more is he the cause of those things which are declared to have been made through the Son.
**“by the word”**
• by likeness
• by command alone
**“of his power”** — which is no less in governing than in creating
**“making purgation of sins”** — this now cleansing us from sins, he who is such through the humanity according to which he endured the passion and death of the cross
**“Purgation”** — After he has shown his excellence by which he created and governs all things, here he commends the kindness of his humility. For he reminds us of the cross, then of the resurrection and ascension, where he says: He sits, etc.
**“sitteth”** — he rests and reigns with him
**“on the right hand of the majesty”** — exalted to equality with the Father
**“on high”**
• placed
• above all in place and dignity, not in paradise whence Adam fell but higher
**“On high”** — By saying this he does not confine God to a place, but shows the man Christ higher than all and more eminent than all. So also by the right hand he did not disfigure God, but showed likeness of honour. For sitting together shows nothing else but equality of honour. Contemplate the wisdom of Paul; rather, not the wisdom of Paul, but marvel at the grace of the Holy Spirit. For he did not produce his understanding from his own mind, but the Holy Spirit poured it in. Consider, then, by what steps the apostolic wisdom lifts them up, and how it leads them to the very summit of piety. Where again, before they fail and darkness seizes them, see how he called them back to lower things. For at one time he speaks of what belongs to lowliness, at another he thunders higher things, and neither always remains in lowly things nor continues in the heights, but as by certain steps is now raised to lofty summits, now brought down to lower things. For as one who wishes to raise some little child gradually to higher things and upward does this by steps, climbing from lower to higher; then, when he has come up, seeing him wearied by obscurities and failings, after the heights sets him down on lower ground, where he may breathe and refresh his spirit; and again, when he has been refreshed, lifts him up to other heights. So the blessed Apostle does with the Hebrews, whom he raises little by little to the knowledge of God, mentioning lowly things among high ones, everywhere following the footsteps of his master. For he himself did so: at one time he raised his disciples to higher things, at another he called them back to lower things for the sake of their weakness, nowhere allowing them to remain a long time on either side. So in this whole series the Apostle first recalls high things, saying “in his Son,” where the Son is understood properly, who is higher and more excellent than all. Then he descends to lowly things, saying: “Whom he hath appointed heir.” Then he returns to high things, saying: “By whom also he made the world.” Afterwards he comes to a step higher than all, saying: Who being the brightness, etc. Then he speaks of lowly things: Making purgation of sins. Thence he returns to high things by narrating: He sitteth on the right hand of the majesty.
1.4:
**“so much better”** — more worthy

**“So much better than the angels”** — Yet in the Psalm he says: “Thou hast made him a little less than the angels.” Here he is called better than they. And as that was said according to the human nature, so this too might be understood as said according to the divine, were not an effect added by which it is made plain that he speaks this of him according to the flesh. For according to that by which he is acknowledged consubstantial with the substance of the Father, he was not made but born; so the discourse concerns him according to the human nature, according to which he was both less than the angels in his passion, and greater and better also in the fullness of grace, of which the angels themselves receive by measure.
**“being made”** — made evidently according to the man
**“as he hath inherited a more excellent name than they”** — the honour, because he rose and ascended
**“A more excellent name”** — While mortal he had a different name, because angels ministered to him.
1.5:
**“For to which”**
• above the angels

**“Thou art”** — because

**“Today”** — Lest the begetting seem past. For although that day also can be understood on which Christ was born according to the man, yet because “today” signifies presence, and in eternity nothing is past, as though it had ceased to be, nor future, as though it were not yet, but only present, because whatever is eternal always is, it is taken more divinely of the everlasting begetting of the wisdom of God, which the most sincere and catholic faith preaches.

For we were outside, away from God, like those bound in chains outside the royal halls, who have some offence with the king because of faults. Christ, then, going out thus to us, that is, taking flesh, and speaking with us, made known the king’s commands, and so, amending us of our sins and turning us to God, like an excellent mediator he brings us into the royal hall. Rightly, therefore, the coming of his flesh is called both entrance and going out.
**“Again bringeth in”** — Visible, the flesh being assumed, he who before was invisible in the world; for the assumption is called a going out from the Father, and the introduction, an entrance to the inheritance, where he is commanded to be adored.

And hence the will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily forms and movements. Concerning the heavens, then, from which the birds are called birds of the heaven, there is no doubt that they perished in the flood and will perish by fire. But concerning the higher heavens of the heavens, whether they too will perish by fire is a question and a more scrupulous dispute among the learned. And there will be a burning of the world, not burning the saints of God. For what the king’s furnace was to the three children, this the burning world will be to the just, signed in the Trinity.
