• of the sons
• Author: Christ. Of their salvation: that is, of the children. For he is the Son by nature, whose heirs we shall be, who are sons by adoption. See how much lies between us. He is the Son, and we are sons. But there is this difference: he saves, we are saved. He sanctifies, we are sanctified. Now Scripture joins us together, now it separates us. “Many sons,” it says; here it joined; “the author of their salvation”; here it distinguished.
**“by his passion”** — of death
**“to perfect”**
• which he intended in the resurrection
• to perfect
• Which began in the resurrection, when he was raised up to the glory of immortality. And it was carried on in the ascension, when he ascended to the right hand of the Father. And it will be perfected in the judgment, “when all things shall be subject to him, and God shall be all in all.”
**“to perfect by his passion”** — Because otherwise man, not redeemed, would perish; and if it were so, all things would have been made in vain. For other things serve man, and man serves God. Nor would God be glorified in some, since all things were made for this; and the predestination concerning the bringing of the sons would be false.
2.11:
**“For both he that sanctifieth”**
• Christ
• He proves that it was fitting for Christ to suffer for our deliverance. For it seems unbecoming that the author of salvation should suffer, but it is not unbecoming, because he depends on God and is subject to him, as other men are, and therefore it is fitting that he suffer if there is need. And that there was need he says afterwards, there: Because then the children, etc., and he himself in like manner hath been partaker of the same. Unless it were a man who conquered the devil, man would be taken from him not justly but by violence; but if man conquers him, he rightfully loses man; and that man may conquer, it is necessary that God be in him, who may make him to be without sin. For if man by himself, or an angel in man, would easily sin, since it is agreed that he knew both natures by himself.
**“sanctifieth”** — the predestined in Christ
**“and they who are sanctified”** — by him, that is, us
**“are all of one”**
• are from God and depend on him
• But he is the proper Son; we are adopted. When he says he is not ashamed to call them brethren, he shows that our brotherhood is not natural to him but of mercy. This he proves through the prophet, lest it be thought new.
**“all”** — equally
**“For which cause”** — he proves that all are from one
**“for which cause”** — that is, because both head and members are from the same
**“he is not ashamed”** — or: Christ is not ashamed, although free from sin
**“to call them brethren”** — who by sinning are degenerate
**“saying”** — in the psalm
2.12:
**“I will declare”**
• after the resurrection
• or 'I will tell'
**“thy name to my brethren”** — the fame and glory of the godhead throughout the whole world
**“in the midst of the church”**
• throughout the whole world on every side
• placed as a pillar
2.13:
**“And again”**
• He proves the same by the authority of Isaias.
• He proves the same by the authority of Isaias.
**“I”**
• Christ
• that he was not except from him
**“will put my trust”** — as a man
**“in him”** — the Father
**“Behold I”** — is ready to serve
**“and my children”** — the apostles and other faithful
**“whom God hath given me”**
• as members to a head, in unity of nature and grace
• in this it is clear that they are of God
2.14:
**“Therefore because the children”**
• who are to be sanctified
• Because therefore. As if to say: it is clear that he himself is of God, and so are those who are sanctified; and so it does not dishonour him if it be needful. But what need was there to suffer? Therefore, because all are of God, the children also have shared.
**“Therefore because”** — As if, since all are from one. And because the children who were to be sanctified had communicated, that is, were men, corruptible, of soul and body, the body being understood by the blood. And Christ himself. Hath been partaker of the same children. Or of the same, that is, of flesh and blood, and in like manner, that is, passible and mortal, that he might be able to die and so destroy the devil, and by death make void the law and make the Jews free by grace, who through fear of punishments were slaves of the law.
**“are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself in like manner”** — sanctifying
**“hath been partaker of the same”** — the children, or flesh and blood
**“hath been partaker”** — Behold true brotherhood in Christ, and not feigned humanity.
**“through death”** — What is the marvel? Death was the weapon by which the devil conquered, and by it he was conquered by Christ. And might deliver. How great a good has death wrought! Through fear of death they were subject to servitude; for they were slaves who feared death, and suffered all things lest they die. Now the saints, about to pass to the kingdom, laugh it to scorn. Whence: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.” And this is the victory of faith, which would certainly have been lacking if immortality had followed at once upon believers. God could indeed have given this to believers, that they should not experience even the death of this body. But if he had done this, a certain happiness would be added to the flesh, but the strength of faith would be diminished. For men so fear this death that they would call Christians happy for no other reason than that they could not die at all; and by this no one would hasten to the grace of Christ for the sake of that blessed life which is to come, but men would believe in Christ more softly, for the sake of removing the trouble of death, and faith would be enervated and weak. What great thing would it be to believe, seeing that those who believed did not die? How much stronger to believe so that one hopes, while about to die, to live without end, by the example of Christ, who after death rose in glory and lives a blessed life without end. Let us therefore desire the life of Christ, because we hold the pledge, the death of Christ. For how will he not give us his goods, who suffered our evils? In these lands and in this wicked world, what abounds but to be born, to labour, and to die? These are the wares of our region. A merchant gives and receives in exchange for such wares. He gives what he has and receives what he has not. Christ also in this trade gave and received. But what did he receive, except what abounded here, namely to be born, to labour, and to die? And what did he give? To be born again, to rise again, and to reign for ever. O good merchant, we give thanks, because thou hast bought us; we drink thy blood, we read the gospel, our bill of sale; we are thy servants, we are thy creature; thou hast made us, thou hast redeemed us. A man can buy a servant; he cannot create him. But the Lord both created his servants that they might be, and redeemed them by death, that they might not be captives always. So also he tasted death, that the faithful might overcome the fear of death. For as a physician, having no need, tastes of those foods, to persuade the sick man to take them more readily, so also the Lord, since all men feared death, persuading them to approach death with confidence, himself also tasted death, having no necessity of death.
2.15:
**“And might deliver”**
• by grace
• Power, that is, the devil. He is the author of death, because of sin, from which comes death; of whom: “Behold, the prince of this world cometh,” that is, the devil, who had the power of death, “and in me he hath not any thing,” because he found nothing in Christ for which he should die; but by the will of the Father he himself willed to die, not having a cause of death from sin under the author of sin, but from obedience and justice: “he became obedient unto death,” by which he redeemed us from the servitude of the devil. For we had fallen upon the prince of this world, who seduced Adam, and made him a slave, and began to possess us as home-born slaves; but the redeemer came and the deceiver was conquered. And what did the redeemer do to our captor? He stretched out a mousetrap, his cross; he set there as bait his blood. But he shed the blood not of a debtor, by which he was commanded to release debtors; he shed the blood of an innocent man, and was commanded to withdraw from the guilty. For he shed his blood for this, that he might blot out our sins. Whence therefore the devil held us, it was blotted out by the blood of the redeemer. For he held us only by the chains of our sins. These were the chains of the captives. He came, he bound the strong one with the chains of his passion, he entered into his house, that is, into the hearts of those in whom he himself dwelt, and took away his vessels. We are those vessels, which he had filled with his bitterness, which he gave to our redeemer to drink in gall. But our God, taking away his vessels and making them his own, poured out the bitterness and filled them with sweetness.
**“who through the fear of death”** — of the body or of the soul, who kept the law; whom Christ freed from hell or from the yoke of the law
**“were all their lifetime subject”** — subject
**“to servitude”** — were in the bondage of the law
2.16:
**“For no where doth he take hold of the angels”** — the angelic nature, so as to redeem the angels
**“For no where”** — He shared with them so as to sanctify men. And this is rightly placed here, because if he were not going to free them, he would not share with them. This appears in the case of the angels, because nowhere, that is, in no Scripture, is it read that he took hold of angels.
**“but of the seed of Abraham he taketh hold”**
• that is, the flesh of Abraham, so that he might save his children
• He taketh hold. He says taketh hold, not assumed, as one pursuing him who flees far off. In this can be understood the dignity of human nature, and the mercy and grace with which he did this, and the care which he had for us. For he took hold of human nature, which was fleeing before him, and fleeing far off, for we were far away, pursued; he took hold not of angelic but of human nature; this dignity was given to it, that God should be joined to it in one person.
2.17:
**“Wherefore”** — because he took hold of the seed of Abraham
**“it behoved him in all things to be made like unto his brethren”** — that he might be passible and mortal
**“Throughout all things”** — That he was born, brought up, grew, suffered, died. He who was called above the figure of the Father’s substance.
**“that”** — therefore, in this way, that
**“merciful”** — that which was in nature
**“he might become”** — in act
**“and faithful”** — deceiving no one
**“priest”**
• mediator
• a bridge to God
**“before God”** — offering himself
**“and that he might be a propitiation for the sins of the people”** — being called near, he might remove
**“For in that”**
• that which he can
• in the lower substance, namely in the flesh
**“In that”** — In the flesh which he took he suffered many cruel things. And he knows by experience what this tribulation of those who suffer is.
**“who are tempted”** — God tempts that he may prove, the devil that he may deceive, man that he may know what he does not know.
2.18:
**“wherein he suffered”** — by Pilate
**“himself being tempted”**
• or experienced
• by the devil

3.1:
**“Wherefore”**
• O you
• From all the above he infers that he is powerful, that he suffered for us, and that he is able to help.
**“holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly vocation”** — called to heavenly things, that is, to have the heavenly inheritance
**“partakers”** — of the inheritance with Christ
**“consider”** — by loving, and by doing what he commands
**“the apostle”** — whom God sent to you
**“and high priest”**
• mediator
• through whom one goes to God
**“of our confession”**
• of faith
• whom we confess
**“Jesus”** — Jesus Christ; we have no need of another
3.2:
**“Who”** — Christ
**“is faithful to him”**
• faithful to God the Father
• Christ is faithful to the Father, as Moses was, in all the house of the Jews and of the Gentiles. For of the greater: as if to say, what his becoming faithful shows, because he is worthy of glory as Moses was. Because also of the greater before Moses, that is, one who is greater than Moses or who is before Moses in merit.
**“Who is faithful”** — He begins to compare him with Moses, as above with the prophets and angels, so that he is faithful before Moses, because he sought not his own glory but the Father’s, nor hid his commands.
**“that made him”**
• who made him of the seed of David according to the flesh
• as man
**“as was also Moses”** — was faithful
**“in all his house”** — of the Jews
**“his”**
• not of Moses, because he was a servant, not the master
• of Jesus or of the Father
3.3:
**“For this man was counted worthy of greater glory than Moses”** — by so much of greater
**“by so much as he that hath built the house hath greater honour”** — by how much greater honour he has than he who administers in it as a servant
**“the house”** — house, that is, made in the house or from the house, which is to be understood of spiritual things
**“Who”** — who, as Lord
3.4:
**“For every house is built by some man: but he that created all things, is God”**
• a house is made by someone; but he who makes both the house and all things is God, whom it is agreed presides over all; and so Christ, because he is creator and God, is above Moses
• therefore also of greater glory
• Who indeed made both the house. And God is the maker of all things. For God is the maker of both houses, which Moses and Christ governed.
**“For every house”** — He built it, I say. For it cannot be made of itself, but by someone. Is it then by Christ? Truly, because God, who made all things. Even all things and the house.
3.5:
**“And”** — that is, because
**“And Moses indeed”** — He shows that Christ is worthy of greater glory than Moses, because Christ is the builder of the house, not Moses. Here he shows the same by another reason: Christ is the Son, Moses the servant, who handed down carnal things to the carnal, but Christ spiritual things.
**“was faithful in all his house”** — not his own but
**“of him”** — of him, of the Father or of Christ
**“as a servant”** — as a servant, who does not love the house so much as one whose own it is
**“for a testimony of those things which were to be said”** — not so as to give grace, but so as to bear witness to those things which were fitting to be said to the carnal, who could not yet grasp spiritual things
3.6:
**“But Christ”** — is faithful
**“as the Son in his own house”** — who is heir with God the Father
**“which house”** — whose house
**“are we”** — we are, having been reborn
**“if we hold fast the confidence”** — that is, hope with confidence, not doubting
**“and glory of hope”** — glorious hope, which is of heavenly joy
**“unto the end, firm”** — that is, lasting to the end of life, when what is now hoped for will be had
3.7:
**“Wherefore”**
• because in this way we are the house of Christ: “Take heed,” etc., or “Harden not”
• As above, when he had commended Christ above angels and prophets in many ways, he added that we ought not to neglect what we have heard from him. So now, having commended him above Moses.
• Here he begins to frighten them, lest they be unbelieving toward Christ through the likeness of the fathers; and afterwards he coaxes them, lest they lose rest, and by the opportunity of the time.
**“as the Holy Ghost saith”** — so I say this as the Spirit says in David: Today, that is, in the time of grace, which was present to David in the Spirit: if you hear, which will truly be, harden not.
**“Today”** — Now he speaks in his own person, who before spoke through heralds: if then you were hard, now be soft.
**“today”** — The history is about this, that they sent to see the land, and when they heard that there were unconquerable men there, forgetting the power of God so often proved, they said: let us return into Egypt. Whence the Lord swore that they should not enter into the promised land, which was to be the rest of their labors, and so they all perished except two. He recalls three rests: one of the sabbath, the second in Palestine, the third the true one, which is in heaven, of which he here speaks, speaking to the true Israelites and saying: Be not hard toward Christ speaking, as the Holy Ghost forewarned, lest you suffer things like your fathers, who then heard the voice of God through Moses, you now through him himself.
**“if you shall hear his voice”** — Of Christ speaking in his own person.
3.8:
**“Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation”** — Doing as your fathers did.
**“in the day of temptation”** — Do not harden according to the day, that is, as they were hardened in the day of temptation; this is one of the provocations.
**“in the desert”** — where they most needed help; so in the desert of this world, beware lest you tempt God and perish as they did.
3.9:
**“Where your fathers tempted me”** — Fathers according to the flesh. See that you do not, according to the spirit.
**“proved”**
• they found it provable, because they saw.
• That is, from curiosity they sought to find out whether he could be greatly offended and angered to blame.
**“And they saw”** — with their eyes.
**“my works”** — of great power.
**“Forty years”** — in which years they experienced that I could do all things.
3.10:
**“For which cause”** — because they tempted.
**“offended”** — angry.
**“Offended”** — Or near, by applying the scourges of correction.
**“I was offended with this generation”** — so badly.
**“and I said”** — about them.
**“They always err in heart”** — from their own deliberate choice, because they sin seriously; and although I warned them thus, they would not acknowledge my works; and therefore, if they enter, I say this as I swore, that is, I firmly decided when I was angry; and therefore, brethren, take heed.
3.11:
**“In my wrath”** — He is said to be angry by the figure anthropopathy.
**“If they shall enter”** — It is aposiopesis, that is, they shall not enter.
**“into my rest”** — therefore.
3.12:
**“Take heed, brethren”** — because on account of unbelief rest was denied to your fathers.
**“lest perhaps there be in any of you”** — because it can easily happen.
**“an evil heart of unbelief”** — because he does not doubt that many of them are perfect.
**“An heart of unbelief”** — That you think Christ is not sufficient without the law, which is evil because thus a man falls into many sins. Nor is this slight, because this is the heart of departing.
**“to depart from the living God”** — from whom whoever departs loses life.
3.13:
**“But exhort”** — concerning the increase of virtues.
**“one another”** — one another, or each one himself.
**“every day, whilst it is called today”**
• as long as.
• the time of grace.
**“Whilst it is called today”** — That is, the time of grace, of which the prophet spoke above in the psalm, because grace for salvation is now given to believers no less than when Christ himself was present. For if anyone sins, as long as it is today he can return. Let no one therefore despair while he lives.
**“is called”** — because not less now than when Christ himself was present
**“that none of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin”** — for you know that the devil deceives the one who is hardened, whence afterwards he falls into sin
**“Through the deceitfulness of sin”** — That is, the devil being the cause of sin.
3.14:
**“For we are made partakers”**
• having a share with Christ in the inheritance
• You ought to exhort one another and not be hard, because what we were not, we have been made by grace, having a part with Christ in the inheritance, yet on this condition: if we hold the beginning of the substance, that is, of faith, which is the beginning of good things, through which God dwells in us, and through which we are made divine and partake of the divine substance, firm unto the end.
**“of Christ”** — he the head, you the members
**“we are made”** — through the grace by which we are united to him
**“yet so, if we hold the beginning of his substance”** — of life
**“hold firm”** — that we never forsake it
**“Whilst”** — as long as
**“it is said”** — to us
**“Harden not”** — As the fathers, because some of them were hard and therefore perished.
**“your hearts”** — as the fathers hardened theirs
**“as in that provocation”** — that is, the fathers hardened them, so that he may deter by their punishments; he adds this
3.16:
**“For some who heard”** — the voice of God in the desert
**“did provoke”**
• they were unbelieving and hard
• They provoked. Some hearing. He says this so that no one may think it is enough to hear about rest, because they all heard too, but not all arrived.
**“but not all”** — that is, all provoked, not like Caleb and Josue; may you be similar to these
**“that came out of Egypt by Moses”** — so we from darkness through Christ
3.17:
**“And with whom was he offended”** — with these provoking him, or not?
**“forty years”** — by which our whole life is signified
**“Forty years”** — For the number forty indicates the completeness of the ages, and signifies our whole life. He is therefore said to be angry with them for forty years, because God is angry with those sinning until the end of their life.
**“Was it not”** — as if there were no doubt
**“with them that sinned, whose carcasses”** — in this the wrath of God appears
**“were overthrown”** — without burial
**“in the desert”** — to beasts and birds
**“And to whom did he swear”**
• not only laid low but also swore
• Sedulius. As he who speaks cannot lie, so he who does not desire to swear will not be able to forswear. Oath-taking therefore is to be avoided, nor to be used except by necessity alone. It is not against God’s precept to swear, but when we make a practice of swearing we incur the crime of perjury. Let him never swear who fears to forswear. By whatever art of words one swears, God, who is witness of the conscience, takes it just as he to whom the oath is made understands it. An oath is not to be kept by which evil is rashly promised, as if someone should promise an adulteress a perpetual faith of remaining with her in the shame of debauchery. “To swear, in God, is not to overturn what he has established by providence. To repent, in God, is a change of things. Not to repent, in God, is not to change what is established.”
**“but to them”** — and to no others
**“who were unbelieving”** — to the Lord promising
**“into his rest”** — eternal, as not into the land of promise
3.18: **“that they should not enter into his rest”** — the eternal rest which was signified by the land of promise, or into the land of promise itself, literally
3.19: **“And we see that they could not enter”** — he swore they would not enter into rest; and so we see and openly know

4.1:
**“Let us fear therefore”**
• because they lost the rest
• if we do not do this out of love or fear
**“Let us fear”** — Lest anyone be thought wanting, as if it did not pertain to us. For it does pertain. For it was also announced to us, and we shall enter by believing, as they lost it by not believing.
**“lest the promise being left”** — by this, that the frequent promise of God is left and despised, or which we made to God in baptism
**“of entering into his rest”**
• which the land of promise signifies
• by true judgment, even if he presumes shamelessly from it
**“any of you should be thought to be wanting”** — from rest
4.2:
**“For unto us also”** — and rightly, because we cannot be excused as if the matter had not been told
**“it hath been declared”**
• in the time of grace
• through the Son
• of eternal rest, as to them through the figure of the land of promise
**“in like manner”** — through the servant
**“unto them”** — it was announced to them, but
**“But the word of hearing did not profit them”** — because it was not believed
**“the word of hearing”** — the promise of rest
**“not being mixed with faith”**
• that word and faith might be joined together
• Not mixed with faith, etc. For having gone out of Egypt, when they had traveled a long way and had received many signs of the power of God in Egypt, at the Red Sea, in the wilderness, they made a plan to send spies who should examine the nature of the land. When they had gone, they returned, saying that it was a province of great fruits, and a producer of unconquerable and strong men. On hearing this, those who had sent them were stupefied, not believing the promise to be true.
**“of those things”** — on account of these
**“they heard”** — by the spies
**“Of those things”** — That is, on account of these. Of those things they heard: by the spies, who brought back bad reports, they did not believe; or of the faith taken from those things they heard.
4.3:
**“For we shall enter”** — it was announced to us; we shall enter, indeed; or because they did not believe, it did not profit; because it profits us who believe
**“into rest”** — true
**“who have believed, as he said”**
• we who believe; as, on the contrary, the Holy Spirit said of the unbelievers, whereby it is clear that those who believe will enter
• What did he say? This, namely:
**“As I have sworn in my wrath; If they shall enter into my rest”** — they not into Palestine, nor into the true one; we into the true one
**“and this indeed when the works”**
• which he made
• Or: it was announced with the works finished. For he said.
**“And this indeed when the works”** — Because he had said that rest was announced, he says when. Both before the law, after the completion of the works of the seven days, through the rest of the sabbath; and under the law, when it was signified through the promised land; and in the time of grace it was announced in David; and so, indeed, when the fulfilment of this true rest and of the one signified was not yet come, since no one had yet obtained it. And again in this. Finished. Which was done when man was made, for whom all things were made, and who himself was to be glorified with God. He rested on the seventh day. In six days he made all things, so that afterwards nothing should be made except from the matter made there, or after the likeness of things made. On the seventh he rested, which signifies rest. So too in the sixth age man was born into the world for labor; on the sixth day and at the sixth hour of the day he suffered; on the seventh he rested. So also we, while we live, work under the works of the six days; going out from there we rest, if however our works be found very good.
**“from the foundation of the world”**
• beginning
• that is, from when the world began to be established, because he himself made all things
**“were finished”** — after he could rest
4.4:
**“For he spoke”** — The Holy Spirit.
**“in a certain place”** — in a certain place of Scripture.
**“of the seventh day”** — by which eternal rest is signified.
**“thus: And God rested”** — from a new work.
4.5:
**“And”** — the Holy Spirit says.
**“in this place”** — place.
**“And in this place”** — Of the second, which is signified by the sign and figure of the rest of the promised land.
**“again”** — of the same rest, through the sign
**“If they shall enter into my rest.”** — the promised land, which signifies the true rest that Moses had promised.
4.6:
**“Seeing then it remaineth”**
• remains after the promise.
• Or this text, “Seeing then,” etc., can be read in another order of the words. As if to say: in this way and in that the heavenly rest was promised and signified; therefore it remains that some enter into that rest. And since this is so. And because this would not suffice to infer what he is about to infer, he adds another thing, namely: “And they to whom,” etc. So that from these two a third is necessarily inferred in this way, as if to say: And because this is so, namely, since it remains that some enter in; and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief; therefore he again appoints a day, as if to say: because it was necessary to say in David “to-day,” after so long a time, from when those words were spoken to the fathers and the children of Israel had entered into the land of promise. Whence it is clear that this is that rest. As, etc., which are not changed.
**“Seeing then”** — Twice, through the seventh day and the promised land, rest was signified and promised. And because this is so, again, that is, under the designation of the same rest, the Holy Ghost fixes and defines a certain day, that is, the excellent time of grace, namely at the coming of Christ, saying in David: “Today”; David represents to the future time of grace the words spoken to the fathers. After so much time since those words were spoken to the fathers in the desert. Whence it is clear that it is not about the promised land, which had long since been possessed. Therefore he fixes the day of entering, since it remaineth that some enter in; and unless he saw that there would be those who would enter, he would not fix it. David, though placed under the law, in mind was in the time of grace, saying “Today”; the third time he announces that rest is to be consummated in that time.
**“that some”** — certain
**“are to enter into it”** — to enter that eternal rest which was signified.
**“and they, to whom it was first preached”** — and what need was there for them to be told, harden not your hearts, because those to whom before
**“did not enter because of unbelief”** — into the true rest which the promised land signified, to which they did not come.
4.7:
**“Again”** — the Holy Spirit.
**“limiteth”** — limits

**“A certain day, Today”** — Of the third signified, and when it is given, though obscurely, which is promised to believers through Christ.

**“The division of the soul and the spirit”** — By the soul we live with the beasts; by the spirit we understand with the angels. And therefore by the soul are understood carnal sins, that is, those which are done by act of the body, such as lust; by the spirit, spiritual sins, that is, those which are of the mind, such as pride. And the word of God discerns between carnal sins and spiritual, whatever one does and with what intention.
**“Of the soul and the spirit”** — The word of God reaches with unsurpassable knowledge, because it knows how sensuality is divided from reason, and sensuality itself from itself, while, given more to the lowest things, it is lower, or, recalled from them, it is worthier; so too it sees how the spirit is divided from itself, either when it aspires to God, thinking of the divine essence, or considers heavenly things lower down. Or again, lower down, on earth, it deals with the right conduct of worldly affairs; or how the spirit, that is, reason, is separated from sensuality, when what is lower in itself surpasses what is higher in that. “Joints” means the joining of sensuality itself and reason, which the Son of God sees, namely how they cohere with each other in something; or how this and that, that is, reason and sensuality, agree with each other in their differences, when the higher difference of sensuality, by consenting, agrees with the differences of reason. Or the lower difference of reason, pressed down and captive, sometimes consents to the lower difference of sensuality. “Marrow,” which is inward, means whatever is more inward and subtle in the soul or spirit, which also the Son of God sees. He also discerns thoughts, that is, what different things different men think. He discerns also the intents of those thoughts, to what end each tends, to good or evil. And, to say more, no creature, earthly or heavenly, is invisible to him, but all things are naked and uncovered, and even open, because fully seen on every side. Or he calls the joints the conjunctions of thoughts, the marrow their intents. This he himself says more openly: of thoughts and intents. And the order is: discerner of the joints. For if one thought is joined to another, he knows which is according to God and which according to the world. He knows whither the intent of them tends.

But those who with a weak and unexercised mind cannot do this, unless they are held by a certain milk of faith, so that they may believe the invisible things which they do not see and the intelligible things which they do not yet understand, are surely easily led astray to vain and sacrilegious fables by the promise of knowledge, so that they think of good and evil only by bodily images, and suppose that God himself is nothing but some body, and cannot think evil to be anything but a substance, whereas it is rather a certain defect, from the unchangeable substance, of changeable substances, which that same unchangeable and highest substance, who is God, made out of nothing. Whoever not only believes this, but, being exercised in the inner senses of the soul, understands, perceives and knows it, is no longer to be feared lest he be led astray by those who, by thinking evil to be a substance which God did not make, make God himself a changeable substance, as the Manichees do, or any other plagues that are so foolish.

**“the foundation”** — these are the beginning
**“The foundation”** — What he before called the word of the beginning, here he calls the foundation, because it is first set before those coming to the Christian religion, and upon it what belongs to perfection is built. This foundation he divides into six things, which are the beginning: namely penance, faith, baptisms, doctrine, imposition of hands, resurrection and judgment. Whoever converts anyone to the faith first makes him do penance, believe in God, be baptized for remission, be confirmed by the imposition of hands, and await the resurrection and the day of judgment.
**“of penance”**
• that is, penance as a stone in the foundation
• which is
• that is, of
**“from dead works”** — because there the earlier works were made void by sinning
**“dead”** — that is, by sins
**“From dead works”** — Dead works he calls the sins that kill. Or the former good works, which, following evil, were dead. To do penance for these is to lay the foundation, without which nothing will be built. For what is it to do penance from dead works, but from those things that must be put to death that we may live? Let us be borne on to perfection, laying the foundation of penance from dead works, and the foundation of faith, which is toward God, that he may have all the parts of faith and not think justice is to be had from elsewhere. Also the foundation of the doctrine of baptisms, in the plural, because there is baptism in water, in penance, and in blood; for man is cleansed from sins by penance or the shedding of blood just as by the washing of baptism. Yet it is called one baptism, because the form is one and it cannot be repeated. There the working of the three persons is one. It is not therefore said that baptism is made in penance and in blood because the sacrament of baptism is celebrated as in water with the word added, but because the shedding of blood for the name of Christ takes the place of baptism. And so also faith and penance, there at least where the point of necessity, not contempt of religion, excludes the sacrament of baptism. And therefore that is to be understood thus: “Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God,” that is, he who has not been regenerated by that regeneration by which they are born again who are born again of water and the Holy Ghost will not be saved. Men are born again in different ways: some by penance, some by the shedding of blood, some by baptism. Therefore he said baptisms in the plural. Also the foundation of the imposition of hands, because unless one believes that by the imposition of hands the Spirit is given for remission and strengthening, he is not grounded. Also the foundation of the resurrection of the dead, for unless one believes that the resurrection of Christ brings about the resurrection of the dead, he has nothing on which to build. Also the foundation of eternal judgment, because whatever is decreed there will last for ever; and he who does not believe that judgment has no foundation. Unless all these have come first in the foundation, no one can work well. And because all these are necessary for them, he says laying all these, as a stone is laid in a foundation. Not again, that is, not as formerly, that as they fell before, they should believe again. Or not laying again, that is, let us so lay now that there be no further need to lay.
**“and of faith towards God”** — against this did those act who seek righteousness in the law

**“the word of God”** — the divinity of Christ or the angelic teaching

6.6:
**“And are fallen away”** — after all these things, grievously

**“again”** — which is allowed here, not there

**“penance”** — to penance, that they be rebaptized after penance
**“crucifying again to themselves the Son of God”**
• because they cannot bring it about that the crucifixion of Christ may again avail for them; for there would be a second crucifixion of Christ if they crucified their flesh with its vices and concupiscences, which is allowed here
• To be renewed again to penance. Here the Apostle denies the repetition of baptism, but does not exclude penance. For to be renewed is to become new. And to make new belongs to the washing. Whence: “Thy youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.” This is done in baptism. And the sense is: it is impossible for those who have once received this to be renewed again, that is, rebaptized, though moved to penance; I mean those, if they are rebaptized, crucifying again the Son of God and holding him in derision, as far as they are concerned. For they do not crucify in fact, but are like mockers and crucifiers, because the one death of Christ consecrated one baptism, which suffices against all sins, even those that follow. If penance is practiced for them, as that one death, it suffices to take away all sins. But he who repeats baptism, as if that one death and the one baptism from it were not enough, repeats the death also, that from it repeated there may be repeated remission. Or they crucify in themselves the Son of God and hold him in contempt, who, despising his grace, lie in sins. And this is the reason why they ought not, having left the first faith, to fall into sins. For they can no longer be rebaptized for the remission of sins. For it is impossible to be rebaptized, because they can drink only the rain, that is, the doctrine of Christ, by which through penance they may bear fruit; and this is: for the earth, namely.
**“crucifying again”** — Because in baptism we are made conformable to his death and burial. He who thinks to be baptized a second time, as far as he is concerned crucifies Christ a second time, which is to hold him as a mockery and derision; as he died once, so we die once to sins in baptism, not a second or third time.
**“and making him a mockery”** — nor can they have Christ for display, that they imitate him in newness of life

**“For the earth”**

• in another life it is impossible to be renewed, because only here, where it drinks the rain
• or he had said: let us be carried on to perfection, adding below, and we will do this now; he adds: and it is just, because the earth, that is, the mind of the hearers
**“the rain which cometh often upon it”** — from God
**“which cometh often”** — Because if rare it does not suffice; if constant it becomes cheap.
**“that drinketh in”** — in likeness of the dry earth
**“the rain”**
• teaching
• Holy teaching is the dew of heaven, which the heavens rain on the thirsty earth, that is, the preachers of the word of truth.
**“and bringeth forth herbs meet”**
• faith and good works
• fitting
**“bringeth forth herbs”** — It signifies that they often drank through the law and the prophets the word of heavenly teaching, and yet were not so ready to bring forth the buds of faith.
**“for them by whom it is tilled”**
• who will thence be glorified; or according to that: and they bore the fruit of their birth
• not only to the doers but to their preachers
**“by whom it is tilled”** — The tillers of the earth, who cut up the shrubs with the spiritual ploughshare and cut away the harmful things with the pruning-hook of the word of God. Or for those by whom it is tilled, that is, the very same who strive to imitate themselves in good works, namely their elders, according to that: “And they brought forth the fruit of birth,” because they imitate their fathers who begot them in the faith.
**“receiveth”** — otherwise it would not bring forth
**“blessing”** — here the increase of virtues; in the future, the reward
**“from God”** — and the earth
6.8:
**“bringeth forth”** — into the open, so that they may be seen
**“But”** — or 'for'
**“thorns”** — sins that prick
**“and briers”** — heavier ones that pierce more sharply
**“is reprobate”** — by God
**“and very near unto a curse”** — to damnation
**“near”** — it has not yet fallen into the curse, but is near, and it is still possible to turn back
**“whose end”** — its end, if it persists
**“to be burnt”**
• it will be
• of eternal fire
6.9:
**“But”** — I rebuked harshly, but when
**“We trust”** — We do not say this thinking that you are such, but fearing that you may be such. I frighten you with words, lest you suffer the thing itself. We trust. Because he has nothing in the present for which to praise them, he lifts them up with the hope of things to come, to which he draws them by things past; and he revives their spirits and strengthens them, calling the old things to their mind, and makes them think that God has not forgotten the good things they have done. For as their former good deeds had died and been made void by the evils that followed, so these same deeds will live again through penance and the other good deeds that follow.
**“of you, my dearly beloved”** — because you are of such a disposition
**“better things”** — than the burning
**“and nearer to salvation”** — than the thorns and briers are
**“though we speak thus”**
• harshly frightening, rebuking
• therefore we trust concerning you, because formerly you did many things, for which, if you repent of evils, God will do well by you
6.10:
**“Work”** — He bore great witness to them. He commends three good things in them, namely that they made all their goods common to the saints. Behold the work, and this from love, which shapes actions; behold eagerness, and this for the glory of God. Behold pure and right intention.
**“and the love which you have shewn”** — namely, from which you did those good works
**“in his name”** — for the honour of God
**“you who have ministered”** — this is the work
**“and”** — still
6.11:
**“And we desire”**
• as if I praise you for the past; but for the future I desire good things for you
• We desire, etc. He shows great love toward them, and shows the same care for each one; for he likewise bears care for the evil and the lesser, and loves all.
**“every one of you”** — so that not one be missing
**“the same”** — which you formerly had
**“shew forth”** — to show frequently
**“carefulness”** — of ministering to the saints
**“to the accomplishing of hope”** — so that in the future there may be fulfilled in you what you now hope
**“unto the end”** — of your life
6.12:
**“That you become not slothful”** — to show thus
**“become”** — in this care
**“followers of them”** — of the saints
**“who through faith and patience”** — not by lineage
**“shall inherit the promises”** — the blessedness often promised
**“The promises”** — He knew the Jews liked the promises of the fathers to be recalled, so now he raises them with those praises, whom above he terrified by the example of the hardened. But in this he chose Abraham above all, whose sons they will be if they believe.
6.13:
**“For Abraham”**
• whether promises were made, at any rate
• He says three things: that the promise was made, and confirmed by an oath, and already fulfilled in Abraham.
**“God making promise”** — therefore by himself
**“because he had no one greater by whom he might swear”** — himself
6.14:
**“Saying”** — O Abraham
**“Unless blessing”** — in those who are as the stars
**“I shall bless thee”**
• by the increase of virtues
• continually
**“and multiplying”** — without faith

6.15:
**“And so”** — And so Abraham, being certain,
**“patiently”** — amid many adversities
**“enduring”** — waiting patiently for a long time
**“he obtained”** — at last
**“the promise”** — the blessing often promised, that is, eternal blessedness
6.16:
**“For men”** — Therefore God swore because men swear; therefore by himself, since he had no greater, because men swear by a greater.
**“swear by one greater than themselves”** — because by God, who alone is true of himself
**“and of all their controversy”** — of dispute
**“is the end”** — valid
**“for confirmation”** — of the other party
6.17:
**“Wherein”** — because as among men
**“more diligently”** — Wherein more abundantly, etc. As if to say: If indeed a man, who is a liar, is believed by oath, how much more must God be believed, who cannot lie.
**“God, meaning to shew the promises”** — God, wishing to show the promises abundantly by the promise, but more abundantly by the oath
**“to the heirs”** — that is, to those who were to have what was promised
**“the immutability of his counsel”**
• because scarcely anyone knows that men are saved through the faith of Christ

**“interposed”** — between the promise and the fulfilment
**“an oath”** — condescending to human custom, so that he might make them certain
6.18:
**“That by two immutable things”** — the promise and the oath
**“in which”** — in which
**“it is impossible for God to lie, we may have the strongest comfort”** — which makes us strong in every adversity, willing to suffer for an hour so that we may reign for eternity
**“may have”** — in the storms of temptations
**“who have fled for refuge”** — in adversities
