**“to hold fast”** — not to be abandoned because of adversities
**“the hope set before us”**
• already fulfilled for us in Abraham
• that is, declared in all
6.19:
**“Which we have as an anchor of the soul, sure and firm”** — which is not destroyed by the onslaught of tribulations
**“Which we have as an anchor”** — As an anchor holds a ship, so hope holds the soul, lest it be sunk in the sea of this world by consenting to iniquity. And firm, lest it at least totter.
**“and which entereth in”**
• making it enter
• because it leads into the thing
**“even within the veil”** — that is, the inner and veiled blessedness which no one has seen
6.20:
**“Where the forerunner”** — that is, into which the inner things are; and thus it is open that we can follow
**“forerunner”** — For he ran ahead for this, that we may follow. He is rightly called a runner, because no fault hindered him, according to that: “He hath rejoiced as a giant to run the way.” And elsewhere: “He hath not stood in the way of sinners.” And a forerunner, because he ran before us and for us.
**“is entered for us”** — for those to be introduced
**“Jesus”** — for us
**“according to the order of Melchisedech”** — Whence it is fitting that Christians, whose high priest is superior, be superior to the Jews by as much as lies between Christ and Aaron, and have a better sacrifice, namely a reasonable service, which leads to heaven, not cattle. But what is a reasonable service, if not what is offered through the soul and according to the Spirit, as the virtues are? “For God is a spirit; and they that adore him, must adore him in spirit and in truth.” Behold with what sacrifices God is appeased; let us therefore offer these. Those belong to riches and the rich, but these to virtues. Those are outward, these inward. Anyone can perform those, but few these. For by as much as man is better than cattle, by so much is this sacrifice better than those. For here you offer your soul in sacrifice; there cattle were offered.

7.1:
**“For this”** — I speak well, according to the order of Melchisedech
**“Melchisedech”** — melchos or melchi: king; sedech: just, or justice
**“For this Melchisedech”** — Now he begins to show how Christ was made like to the Son of God according to the order of Melchisedech. Melchisedech is called “king of justice,” that is, Christ, who rules his own by justice amid the storms of the world. Christ is king of peace, because those whom justice rules here he does not cease to rule in eternal peace. Priest of God, who offered himself on the altar of the cross. He meets and runs to meet each of the faithful by giving grace after the slaughter of the vices that creep in through the five senses and bear rule; and he blesses him, by giving increase of good work. He gives bread and wine, that is, his body and blood, by which, fed, they are cleansed from past sins and strengthened for the future. To him Abraham, that is, the faithful man, gives tithes of all, that is, he ascribes to him all his perfection: first Melchisedech, that is, king of justice; afterwards king of Salem, that is, of peace, because first he rules his own here in justice, afterwards in the future he rules them in peace. Without father according to the flesh, without mother according to the divinity. Without genealogy, because he had no sons of the flesh. Having neither beginning nor end, coeternal with the Father according to the divinity. Although all the patriarchs and prophets were a figure of Christ, Melchisedech more especially, who, not of the race of the Jews, went before as a type of the priesthood of Christ. According to the order of Melchisedech in many ways. Because he alone was king and priest, and exercised the priesthood before circumcision, so that the Gentiles did not receive the priesthood from the Jews, but the Jews from the Gentiles. He was not anointed with visible oil as Moses appointed, but with the oil of gladness and the purity of faith; nor did he sacrifice animals, but with bread and wine he dedicated the priesthood of Christ. Not truly without father or mother, since Christ according to his two natures had both a Father and a mother. But because in Genesis he is brought in as suddenly meeting Abram, and neither before nor after is his name found in a genealogy. By his example the Apostle affirms that the priesthood of Aaron had both a beginning and an end, but the priesthood of the Church is eternal, both in the past and in the future.
**“king of Salem”** — was
**“priest of the most high God”** — God through himself, not through a man
**“who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings”**
• Returning from the slaughter of the kings, etc. As we read in Genesis: Four kings fought against five and conquered them. Lot was living under the five who were defeated, and was taken by the four. When Abraham heard this, with three hundred and eighteen homeborn servants he pursued them and struck them, and brought back Lot and all the substance which they had taken. So as Abraham was returning, Melchisedech met him and blessed him, etc.
• The Hebrews hand down that Melchisedech was the son of Noe, and that when Abraham was born he was three hundred and ninety years old, and that he met Abraham as his grandson, and offered bread for the refreshment of him and his men, and as priest of God received tithes. Most say Salem is Jerusalem, but it was a town of the region of Sichem, which is called Salem even today, where from the greatness of the ruins the palace of Melchisedech is shown. Whence also in the gospel it is said: “John also was baptizing in Ennon near Salim.”
**“and blessed him”** — to Abraham
7.2:
**“To whom”** — to Melchisedech
**“Abraham divided the tithes of all”** — gave from the choicest
**“first indeed”** — was called Melchisedech
**“who first indeed by interpretation, is king of justice”** — here truly Christ, who makes the just and rules them
**“and then also”** — was called
**“and then also king of Salem”** — of peace. For Salem is interpreted as peace
**“that is, king of peace”**
• Christ, who makes peace both in heaven and on earth
• being
7.3:
**“Without father, without mother”** — not because he did not have them, but because Scripture providently does not mention them, in the figure of Christ
**“without genealogy”** — not having offspring
**“neither”** — Scripture being silent, in the figure of Christ
**“beginning of days”**
• that Scripture says
• Neither beginning, etc. Christ had altogether neither beginning nor end.
**“having neither end of life”** — in all the things premised
**“but likened unto the Son of God, continueth”** — not in himself but in Christ
**“a priest for ever”**
• that is, his priesthood endures for ever, no other succeeds him, as in Leviticus
• he was such
**“for ever”** — Because Scripture is silent that anyone succeeded him. Or mystically he speaks through him of the priesthood of Christ.
7.4:
**“Now consider”** — also from the deeds
**“Consider”** — He dwells on commending the dignity of Melchisedech and of his excellent priesthood, preferring him to Abraham himself, the father of all, and to all the Levites.
**“how great”** — he is preferred to Abraham, whom the Jews extol, of whom they boast, whom they wished to set above Christ: “Are you greater than our father Abraham?”
**“this man is”** — Melchisedech
**“to whom also gave tithes”** — as the lesser to the greater
**“out of the principal things”** — this is what he said above: divided
**“Abraham the patriarch”** — Prince. of our fathers
7.5:
**“And indeed they that are of the sons of Levi”**
• here he prefers him to the Levites
• So great is the excellence of the priesthood that even those alike in birth are much more worthy than their brethren. Whence Abraham would not have given tithes to an uncircumcised foreigner unless he were more excellent. In which also those Levitical priests paid tithes.
**“And indeed”** — And from this consider how great he is, because some of the sons of Levi, in that they receive the sacrifice, though they would not otherwise dare, have a commandment in the law, without whose authority they would never presume.
**“who receive the priesthood, have a commandment to take tithes of the people”**
• receiving the priesthood, they have a commandment to take tithes from the people
• humble
**“according to the law”**
• not otherwise than the law commands
• According to the law, etc. Melchisedech, however, received tithes from the patriarch under no law, since he was a foreigner, and in this he was more worthy.
**“that is to say, of their brethren”**
• in whom it is permitted to trust better
• namely, from the people
**“though they themselves also came out of the loins of Abraham”** — in that they take tithes they preside, though they too came out, etc., that is, they are alike in birth
7.6:
**“But he, whose pedigree is not numbered among them”** — the sons of Levi from their brethren; but Melchisedech, whose descent is not reckoned among the Jews. As if: he who was a foreigner took tithes on his own authority, without the command of the law, etc.
**“received tithes of Abraham”** — as one more excellent
**“and blessed him”** — namely Abraham
**“that had the promises”** — that is, to whom the promises were made
**“blessed him that had the promises”** — at the time of greater dignity
7.7:
**“And without all contradiction”**
• although in the receiving of tithes it is objected that he is not greater, because the sons of Levi also receive them from their brethren
• blessed
**“that which is less, is blessed by the better”**
• the type of Christ is better, having the promises
• in this way too, consider the dignity of Melchisedech
7.8:
**“And here indeed, men that die, receive thithes”** — that is, in the Levitical priesthood
**“but there”** — where it speaks of Melchisedech
**“he hath witness”** — Scripture
**“He hath witness”** — As I, or the same, say in many places.
**“that he liveth”** — because it says nothing of his death, in the figure of Christ
**“he liveth”** — For he bore the type of our high priest, whose excellence of power is shown through the likeness of that one. For through Melchisedech, in whom the figure went before, the priesthood of Christ is distinguished from the priesthood of Levi; and in figure of this Christ it is said that Melchisedech lives. Whence he who offered himself is called priest forever, not from any necessity but from the will of his own power.
7.9:
**“And (as it may be said)”**
• in this way also more worthy
• by a certain figure and manner of speaking
• for Levi, a circumcised priest, did not give tithes to the uncircumcised nearly in his own person
**“paid tithes in Abraham”** — as through a material cause
**“even Levi”** — the Levitical order
**“who received tithes”** — from [his] brethren
**“paid tithes”**
• he gave tithes to Melchisedech
• through Abraham
**“For he was yet in the loins”** — As when Adam sinned, those who were in his loins sinned, so when Abraham gave tithes, those who were in his loins were tithed. But this does not follow in Christ, although he was in the loins of Adam and Abraham, because he did not descend from there according to the concupiscence of the flesh. Since then Levi and Christ were, according to the flesh, in the loins of Abraham when he was tithed, they were not therefore tithed alike, because Christ was not there in the same manner in which Levi was there. For Levi was there according to that seminal principle by which he was to come into his mother by conjugal union; according to that principle the flesh of Christ was not there, although according to it the flesh of Mary was there, as Levi’s was, according to carnal concupiscence; but Christ was to come from there according to bodily substance. For since there is in the seed a visible corporeal mass and an invisible principle, both ran down from Abraham, or even from Adam himself, to the body of Mary, because she too was conceived and born in that way. But Christ took the visible substance of flesh from the flesh of the virgin. The principle of his conception, however, did not come from virile seed, but from far otherwise and from above. Therefore according to what he received from his mother he too was in the loins of Abraham. He, then, was tithed in Abraham who was in his loins as Abraham himself was in the loins of his father; that is, who was born of father Abraham as Abraham was born of his own father, through the law, namely, in the members, warring against the law of the mind, and an invisible concupiscence, although the chaste and good life of marriage does not allow it to prevail, except so far as by it they can provide for the continuance of the race. But he was not tithed there whose flesh drew from there not the heat of the wound but the material of the remedy. For the tithing itself pertained to prefiguring the medicine; that in the flesh of Abraham was tithed which was being cured, not that by which it was cured. For the same flesh of Abraham, or of the first man himself likewise, held both the wound of transgression and the remedy of the wound. The wound of transgression is in the law of the members warring against the law of the mind, which is as it were transcribed through all the flesh propagated from there by the seminal principle. But the remedy of the wound was taken from there, without the work of concupiscence, from the Virgin, in bodily matter alone, by the divine principle of conception and formation.
**“when”** — when, namely
**“met”** — or met
**“Melchisedech”** — the father of Levi, Abraham
7.10: **“For he was yet in the loins of his father”** — when Abraham gave
7.11:
**“If then”**
• because Christ is according to Melchisedech, and this priesthood is over the Levitical; therefore, if you can, you Jew, solve this: “If then perfection”
• Ambrose. Here he begins to give the differences between the Old and New Testaments. If then a translation of the priesthood is of necessity also a translation of the law, for a priest cannot be without testament and law and precepts. We must therefore pass from the law to the gospel.
**“perfection”** — perfection
**“If then perfection”** — Or: hitherto he has set forth the priesthood of Christ, which is according to the order of Melchisedech, above the Levitical; now he adds that the priesthood of Christ destroys the Levitical, and when it is destroyed the law is necessarily destroyed also. As if to say: if the Levitical priesthood made perfect, another would rise in vain according to the order of Melchisedech. But another rises, which is noted there by the priesthood being transferred, which he also proves there: “For he of whom these things are spoken,” and there: “And it is yet far more evident.” I: it did not make perfect.
**“was by the Levitical priesthood”** — because Aaron was of Levi
**“was”** — that it ought to be
**“for under it the people”** — interposition
**“under it the people received the law”**
• priesthood, so that it is in his hand
• This translation was prefigured in Samuel, who was chosen a priest by the Lord from the tribe of Ephraim, the sons of Heli being rejected, the Lord saying: “Whosoever shall glorify me, I will glorify him; and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed,” etc.
**“under it”** — Because the law is in the hand of the priest, and through him the law is fulfilled, which is called to perfect.
**“what further”** — after the old would perfect
**“need was there”** — to be said by the prophet David
**“according to the order of Melchisedech”** — this would not be said if that were better
**“another”** — another, according to rite and tribe
**“should rise a priest”** — to rise, a priest who freed from sin, which the other did not
**“and not be called according to the order of Aaron”** — Therefore I say the law is under the priesthood, because I note thus that when the priesthood is destroyed, the law is destroyed, which is only under it.
7.12:
**“For the priesthood being translated”**
• For the priesthood being translated, etc. That another arises, he afterwards proves both by tribe and by rite. By tribe there: For in whom these things are said, etc. By rite there: And more, etc.
• Because both were given at once, and by the same giver, and under the same promise, what is said of the one must be understood of the other.
**“it is necessary that a translation also be made of the law”** — Therefore I say the law is under the priesthood, because I note thus that when the priesthood is destroyed, the law is destroyed, which is only under it.
**“For in whom”** — Christ, in whose regard
**“of which no one”** — another
**“at the altar”** — or altar
**“was present”** — truly of another
7.13:
**“these things are said”** — “Thou art a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedech.”
**“in whom these things”** — The priesthood is truly transferred and another arises, which is the same as saying, because by tribe and by rite. He shows first about the tribe, afterwards about the rite.
**“is of another tribe”**
• of Juda
• not of the tribe of Levi
7.14:
**“For it is evident that our Lord sprung out of Juda”**
• so that the same is priestly and royal, as Melchisedech was king and priest
• For it is evident that out of Juda: the priesthood was transferred from tribe to tribe, from the priestly to the royal, so that the priestly and the royal might be the same. And behold the mystery. First it was royal, afterwards it was made priestly. So Christ was always king, but was made priest when he took flesh, when he offered sacrifice.
**“our Lord sprung”** — Christ
**“in which tribe Moses spoke nothing concerning priests”** — so that some priest might be of it
7.15:
**“And it is yet far more evident”** — this is the firmer proof, by rite
**“far more evident”** — Because if the tribe was changed in Samuel, the rite was not however.
**“yet”** — than through the tribe
**“is evident”** — that he is transferred and another rises
**“if”** — because
**“according to the similitude”** — the rite
**“according to the similitude of Melchisedech there ariseth another priest”** — as that one gave bread and wine to Abraham, so here he gives to the disciples, under the same species, flesh and blood
7.16:
**“Who”** — another
**“not according to the law”**
• according to the precept of the law
• Or, not according to the law. That is, according to the carnal understanding of the law, so as to act according to carnal observances; but according to the power of the law itself, that is, its spiritual understanding, which those who carry it out have as eternal life.
• There is a difference between priesthood and priesthood: the one carnal, this one spiritual; the one temporal, this one eternal.
**“of a carnal commandment is made”** — which the law only commanded and promised carnal things
**“but according to the power of an indissoluble life”** — the divinity that is in him, through which he gives eternal life as the divinity pleased
**“of an indissoluble life”** — For God the Father testifies with an oath: “Thou art a priest for ever.”
7.17:
**“For he testifieth”**
• that the authority testifies according to Melchisedech
• FOR HE TESTIFIETH. David testifies with me, or with many other Scriptures, that Christ is according to Melchisedech; but more faithfully he sets down the very words of David: “Thou art a priest for ever.”
7.18:
**“Reprobation indeed”**
• that there may be room for grace
• It gives the cause why the old is set aside, since God gave it and substituted the New Testament, because in the time of its standing it was weak and now altogether useless. This, however, completes what serves the praise of the new priest.
**“is made of the former commandment,”**
• is made of the preceding commandment, because something must follow
• of the old law
**“because of its weakness”**
• which it had while it stood: not malice, as heretics charge me with having said
• although it did something, it did not fully justify
**“and unprofitableness:”** — which it did not have, since now it is not only weak but even harmful, if one holds to it
**“Unprofitably”** — Because after the coming of Christ it is useless for those things to be done which were done formerly to foretell these. For circumcision and the other things of this kind were given by God to the former people through the Old Testament to signify things to come, which had to be fulfilled through Christ. When these came, those things remained, yet to be read by Christians for the understanding of the prophecy that went before, but not necessarily to be done, as if it were still to be awaited that the revelation of God should come which was signified by them as to come. Therefore now whoever of the Christians shall likewise wish to celebrate them, as one raking up dead ashes, will not be a pious conductor or bearer of the body, but an impious violator of the sepulchre.
**“for nothing”** — the law was weak then
**“the law brought to perfection:”**
• although some were then made perfect, not through it but through faith, as they were to come
• it perfected no one by justification
**“but the bringing in”**
• that is set aside
• is made through the aforesaid high priest
7.19:
**“of a better hope,”**
• there temporal things were hoped for; here, heaven
• that is, of the law through which glory is hoped for
7.20:
**“And inasmuch as”** — this likewise is to commend the new priest, concerning the quality of whose ordination is discussed here
**“not”** — that
**“without an oath,”** — Jesus was made priest
**“the others indeed”** — Levitical.
**“were made priests without an oath;”** — as if to be changed at some time
7.21:
**“But this”** — Jesus
**“with an oath”**
• was made priest
• made
**“by him”** — God the Father
**“that said unto him:”**
• Jesus
• He said: “Thou art a priest for ever”; and that the Lord swore for ever.
**“The Lord hath sworn”**
• confirmed with unshaken truth
• the prophet says this
**“and he will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever.”** — he will not change what has been done
7.22:
**“By so much”**
• that it is with an oath, and that through him we draw near to God
• as the priesthood goes before, and its law
• By so much, etc. From the praise of the priesthood he infers the commendation of the law.
**“of a better testament”** — than the old one
**“Better”** — Because it promises better things, that is, eternal ones; the old promises temporal ones.
**“surety”** — that is, surety
7.23:
**“And”** — in this same way Jesus is more worthy, because
**“the others”** — Levitical.
**“indeed were made many priests, because by reason of death they were not suffered to continue,”** — in this life
7.24:
**“But this”** — Jesus
**“for that he continueth for ever, hath an everlasting priesthood,”** — But this, because he continueth, etc. As he remains, so also does the law which he brought, in which is true remission of sins and perpetual grace; which, because the old law could not give it, was cast out. But that he remains for ever he shows from the high priest, because he is one, which he would not be unless he were immortal, whereas in the law there are many because they are mortal.
7.25:
**“Whereby also”** — because remaining, he has an everlasting priesthood
**“Whereby also he is able to save”** — Having shown that through the priesthood of Christ the old priesthood and law are destroyed, he commends his act by lowering, by contrast, the act of the old priesthood.
**“is able”** — Jesus himself drawing near to God
**“coming”** — or drawing near
**“to God by himself,”**
• not through others' victims but through himself, the living victim
• not through another high priest
• Whence: “No man cometh to the Father but by me”
**“always living”** — therefore he is able to save, which others are not
**“to make intercession for them.”** — By the representation of himself: for from that nature by which he is high priest, that is, the human nature which he brought into the heavens, he intercedes for us.
7.26:
**“For it was fitting”** — Approaching through himself.
**“that we should have”** — For us: they had others, sons of a servant.
**“a high priest, holy,”** — By the disposition of virtues and in mind.
**“innocent,”** — Toward the neighbour.
**“undefiled,”** — By the removal of evils.
**“separated”** — Not only unpolluted but always without sin.
**“from sinners,”**
• that is, the earlier priests.
• Holy: inwardly; innocent: in hands; undefiled: in body; separated from sinners, that is, free from all sin.
**“and made higher”** — whom all angels adore.
**“than the heavens;”** — made higher than the heavens, by every heavenly creature.
7.27:
**“who needeth not daily”** — who nevertheless were figures of him, who do not have this necessity.
**“Who needeth not daily”** — Since he is such, he has no necessity to offer daily. Not that he ever needs to, but to remove from him what befits them.
**“as the other priests,”** — Levitical.
**“to offer sacrifices first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, in offering himself.”** — does not have this necessity. For this, that is, to offer, he did, not for his own but for the people’s sins, once, because it suffices for all and therefore there is no need to repeat it.
**“For this he did”** — So great is the sacrifice that, although it is one and offered once, it nevertheless suffices for eternity.
7.28:
**“For the law maketh men priests, who have infirmity:”**
• of sinning and dying; and therefore they offered for themselves.
• For the law makes men priests. They have the necessity to offer daily, because they are weak; here once suffices, because he is the perfect Son.
**“but the word of the oath, which was since the law,”** — spoken through David.
**“the Son”** — appointed priest.
**“for ever”** — to endure for eternity.
**“who is perfected.”** — perfect, by grace and truth.

8.1:
**“Now of the things”** — I have said many things of him, but now I make a summary.
**“The sum”** — As if he had said few things, he briefly embraces his dignity, above what he said before. A chapter is a brief embrace of many things, so called because it briefly grasps the whole sum.
**“concerning those things which are said:”** — above those things that are said: more worthily containing the praise of Christ than those said before.
**“We have such an high priest”** — We have such an high priest. Here the chapter begins, and it ends at: God and not man.
**“who sat down”**
• who sat: it is now long since he rests and reigns according to divinity.
• because he is God who is man, who is “a giant of twin substance,” in whom two natures are united.
**“on the right hand of the throne”** — in the equality of the sitting deity, that is, of the Father, who rests and judges.
**“sat down in the heavens”** — Either above the material heavens, or above thrones and dominations; there: minister of the holies, because he ministers eternal life to the saints. Or in heaven he ministered glory, signified by the holy of holies. And minister of the true tabernacle, that is, of the truth which the old tabernacle prefigured, namely justice in the present Church, glory in the future. Which true tabernacle God fixed that it might remain for ever. But the shadowy one was not fixed but portable. And not man, because God also set up the old one, but by a man as minister.
**“of majesty”** — of majesty: this is the judgment of divine power and majesty.
**“in the heavens”** — placed according to human nature
8.2:
**“A minister of the holies”**
• this is mercy
• He ministers to the saints the increase of virtues and eternal life.
**“and”** — for, that is
**“of the true tabernacle”** — not of shadows but of the true tabernacle, which is the souls of the saints, to whom he gives eternal joys
**“which the Lord hath pitched, and not man”** — the tabernacle, that is, the heavenly and the present Church
8.3:
**“For every high priest”** — Christ is the minister, because every high priest is appointed to minister. And this is
**“is appointed to offer gifts”** — such as loaves, incense and the like
**“and sacrifices”** — from animals
**“is appointed”** — and because everyone is appointed to offer
**“wherefore it is necessary that he also”** — Whence it is necessary that this one too
**“should have some thing to offer”** — Christ, to have something to offer, that is, flesh from us, or which he had not had before
8.4:
**“If then he were on earth”**
• what Jesus offers
• Or: If then. Augustine. As if to say: and since Christ is appointed to offer, therefore he is either an earthly or a heavenly priest. But not an earthly one, because “if he were on earth,” that is, if he were an earthly high priest like Aaron, “he would not be” surely a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech, nor would it be necessary: “seeing that there would be,” etc.
**“If then he were”**
• Ambrose. If he were an earthly high priest like Aaron, he would certainly not be a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech. But because Aaron is dead, he is not a priest. But Christ, because he lives, is a priest for ever, not such as those are who bear the shadowy priesthood.
• Jerome. Because everyone offers; if there were any earthly man who could cleanse the human race, he would not be a priest according to the order of Melchisedech, since there would be enough who would offer the legal gifts; but because those were mortal and sinners, and therefore unable to cleanse the human race, Christ came, who would suffice. “But now,” that is, in this last age, “he hath obtained a better ministry” of priesthood, by so much as his law is better. Now he passes from the priesthood and sacrifice to the difference of the testaments.
**“If then”** — Lanfranc. The reason why Christ offered himself: because if he were on earth, though what could worthily be offered for the sin of the whole world could be offered, he would yet not be a priest worthy to offer, since, that is, although there were those who would offer; and therefore the clean offered himself for the world, clean. For a true sacrifice could not be duly offered except by a just and holy priest. But what priest is so just and holy as the only Son of God, who had no need to purge his own sins by a sacrifice, neither original nor added? Or thus: “if then,” as if to say: and because every priest is appointed to offer, therefore Christ also offered, by the merit of which deed he also ascended into heaven. And so it had to be done, because if he were on earth, that is, if he had not yet entered into the holy of holies, that is, into the inner parts of heaven, he would not be a priest, that is, the rite of his priesthood would not be celebrated, since the priesthood according to Aaron still remained. It remains therefore that he offer himself.
*Ambrose:* What he offers, if he also offers something, will be either on earth or heavenly; but not on earth, for if this were so he would not now be a priest; therefore what he offers is heavenly.
**“Chrysostom”**
• Whatever is offered for the unspiritual, or on behalf of the carnal, is on earth.
• For what could be offered so fittingly for men as human flesh, and what so apt for immolation as mortal flesh? And what so clean for the worldly vices of mortals as flesh born, without any contagion of the channel of concupiscence, in and from a virginal womb? And what so weighty could be offered and received as the flesh of our sacrifice? So that—since four things are considered in every sacrifice, namely, to whom it is offered, by whom it is offered, what is offered, for whom it is offered—the same one and true mediator, reconciling us to God by the sacrifice of peace, remaining one with him to whom he offered, might make one in himself those for whom he offered, himself being the one who offered and what was offered.
**“he would not be a priest”**
• nor would he be a priest,
• much less a high priest; he would not be
**“seeing that there would be others who offer”** — since there would be others who offer, many, and so he would superfluously offer carnal things
**“gifts according to the law”** — gifts according to the law, that is, on earth
8.5:
**“Who”** — lest Jesus seem to offer the same things more worthily, he adds “serve,” that is, they fully fulfil all things, as was said to Moses; and so Jesus would in vain take up this priesthood, by which he would offer something carnal
**“serve unto the example”** — figure
**“Who serve unto the example”** — Ambrose. By “example and shadow” he means the figures, which are both a pattern and an example of different things. A pattern is that after whose likeness something is made; an example is the likeness drawn from it. God showed Moses the truth on the mountain, that is, the order of the heavenly court: how the angels obey God, praise and love him, love one another and love us, and are zealous for our progress, and other such things in which they are to be imitated by us. But because the carnal people could not grasp it, he commanded that it be imagined by figures. In these the childlike people, being nourished, might at some time come to the truth; and so the thing first shown is called the pattern of the figures made after it.
**“Chrysostom”** — Again, the figures are called the pattern of the truth, which was afterwards fulfilled, as those figures foreshowed. According to this he says these serve the pattern, that is, the figures. And because a pattern is sometimes the truth, not a figure, he adds “shadow,” because those things were nothing but the shadow of the truth, destined to grow slight at the coming of Christ.
**“and shadow of heavenly things”**
• of mysteries
• heavenly things, he means the Church, of which one part reigns in heaven, and the part that follows is a pilgrim on earth
**“As it was answered”** — as it was answered
**“to Moses, when he was to finish the tabernacle”** — by the Lord; what was answered him?
**“It was answered to Moses, when he was to finish”** — Not when he was beginning, since he had already expressed many things by figures, but when he could not do it by himself, he consulted the Lord, who taught him about the figures as well as about the truth.
**“See (saith he)”** — See, he says, the Lord
**“all things”** — all things. He says all, both of the construction of the tabernacle and of the sacrifices which they were to offer in it
**“that thou make according to the pattern”** — make according to the pattern, that is, the truth
**“which was shewn thee on the mount”** — which was shown you on the mountain, because he showed him by sight on the mountain what he was to make
8.6:
**“But now he hath obtained a better ministry”** — They serve the copy and shadow; but Jesus has the better ministry, because he both ministers to spiritual things and gives spiritual things, which is now plain, since it has been shown that he does not offer upon earth; and this is: Now however, etc.
**“by how much”** — by so much the better ministry, by how much
**“and of a better testament”**
• because it promises eternal things
• namely of the new
• Of a better testament, etc. Now see, he passes from sacrifice and priesthood to the difference between the testaments, preferring the new to the old, because the new is in better promises, etc.
**“he is a mediator”** — he is the giver, a mediator between God and man
**“which”** — new
**“is established on better promises”**
• therefore he said better
• because it promises heaven
• than the promises of the old were
**“which is established on better promises”** — The precepts are almost all the same: the moral ones certainly, such as “Thou shalt not kill.” The ceremonial ones are not the same, etc. The sacraments are indeed not the same, because those promise, these give salvation. The promises are not the same, because there they are earthly, here heavenly.
**“is established”** — it is confirmed so that it may endure
8.7:
**“For if that former”**
• the first testament
• He proves that Christ’s testament is better than the old. For that one is not free from fault; this one is. For if it had been free from fault, a second would not be given, but it is given. And so it appears that that one was imperfect, and this one perfect.
**“had been faultless”**
• that is, if its observers were blameless
• that is, had perfectly cleansed man
• He says this as if the law itself had the fault, since it seems so while it commands without grace and makes transgressors.
**“there should not indeed a place”** — opportunity
**“have been sought for a second”** — It would be sought by the Lord, who first gradually instructed and brought up the people, so that afterwards he might give a perfect testament.
8.8:
**“For finding fault with them”**
• but it is sought, and this on the authority of Jeremias
• If it be asked of us why we do not worship God with the rite with which the Hebrew fathers worshipped him? We answer that God commanded us otherwise through the fathers of the New Testament. Nor is this against the Old Testament, since in it too this was foretold. For so it was announced through the prophet Jeremias, as follows: “For finding fault.” As if to say: if that had been free from fault, no place would be sought for a second. But it is sought; for Jeremias, finding fault, etc.
**“them”** — who go astray in the law
**“he saith: Behold, the days shall come”** — because light to the world
**“saith the Lord”** — Gradually the time of Christ draws near; he calls it the day, because with the darkness driven off, “the light which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world” appeared in the world.
**“and I will perfect”**
• I will fulfil
• or, bringing to completion I will give
**“unto the house of Israel”** — that he may rule over them
**“and unto the house of Juda”** — the Jews, who after Solomon were divided into two kingdoms
**“a new testament”**
• in which will be done what was promised to Abraham
• which is not of earthly things like that old one, namely the law given on Sinai
8.9:
**“Not according to the testament”** — Here it is prophesied that the old will not endure, but that a new will come. And although the same is signified and foretold in many places, yet the new itself is not read expressly. Indeed in the old books mention of the New Testament, so that it is called by that very name, is either nowhere read or hardly, apart from this prophetic passage. Consider therefore diligently the difference between the two testaments, new and old. There the letter, which alone killeth; here the spirit, which giveth life. The one is old because it does not free from the oldness of sin; the other new because it renews.
**“not according to”** — If it be asked why we hold the authority of that testament whose rite we do not observe, we answer that these things ought to be read and received lest we extinguish the prophecies, because all those things were done in shadow of things to come, as the Apostle says: “These things happened to them in figure.” When therefore something is read in the instrument of the Old Testament of such a kind as is either commanded or forbidden to be observed by us in the New Testament, what it signifies is to be inquired into, not reproved; because by the very fact that it is no longer observed, it is proved not condemned, but fulfilled.
**“which I made to their fathers”** — And because he had made it with certain ones in particular, he specifies. “Which I made in the day,” that is, the law which was given after the departure from Egypt. For what he said to Abraham before the law: “In thy seed shall all the nations be blessed,” he fulfilled in the gospel. For that was a spiritual promise, pertaining to grace.
**“on the day when I took them by the hand”** — as one who cannot rise from bed by himself, or as a nurse of little children
**“to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because”** — I took hold, but.
**“they continued not”** — Behold how he has censured them.
**“They continued not”** — He imputes it to their fault that they did not continue in the Testament, lest the law which they then received seem to be blamed. For it is that which Christ came not to destroy but to fulfil. Yet it does not justify without grace, because of the harm of the old man, who, because he is not healed by the letter commanding and threatening, is called old in that testament and new in this, on account of the newness of the spirit, who heals from the vice of oldness which he plainly lays open. “This is the testament,” etc. “Giving my laws into their mind.” Not in tables of stone, not with ink, but by the Spirit, by whose presence, who is the finger of God, charity is poured forth in hearts, which is the fulness of the law. They are not frightened from without, but love justice within; whence this reward. “And I will be to them,” that is, they shall live from me and for me, and in the future shall see me, which is perfection, so that one teach not another. This is the distance between the old and the new: that the former is in stone, the latter in the heart; there the reward is the land, here the vision of God.
**“in my testament”** — the law given on Sinai, because “They made also a calf in Horeb: and they adored the graven thing.”
**“and I regarded them not, saith the Lord”** — do not be indignant if I say they were neglected, because the Lord says it.
8.10:
**“For this is the testament”** — truly new, not according to that one, because this is the testament.
**“which I will make”**
• in an orderly way.
• I will dispose it thus by giving laws. Behold the testament; and I will also write it, so that they may remain for ever, as something which ought to remain over them and rule them.
**“to the house of Israel”** — of all who see God.
**“after”** — not only but.
**“those days”** — appointed beforehand.
**“saith the Lord”** — believe, because the Lord says it.
**“giving”**
• or I will give.
• behold the testament.
• through the Holy Spirit.
**“my laws into their mind”** — understandings.
**“of them, and in their heart”**
• into wills, because they will keep them both by understanding and by will.
• that in stone.
**“will I write them”** — so that it may remain forever.
**“and”** — so.
**“I will be their God”** — because God is truly said to be in them, and they are the people of God.
**“and they”** — that is, they will live from me.
**“shall be my people”** — this indeed in this world.
8.11:
**“and they shall not teach”** — that in the future.
**“They shall not teach”** — What lay hidden in the letter, and what the people learned through the traditions of the masters, this the Spirit, coming, taught the apostles; and this is what the prophet says: “They shall not teach every man his neighbour,” because all shall know, as is said in the gospel: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures.”
**“every man his neighbour”** — whom he loves.
**“and every man his brother”** — whom he loves more.
**“Saying”** — thus.
**“Know the Lord, for all”**
• therefore one will not teach another.
• therefore I will do all these things in both lives.
**“shall know me”**
• they will see me as I am, which is perfection.
• as if this too perfectly by itself, not from a greater.
**“from the least”** — Augustine. It makes no difference whether it is said conversely, from the greater to the least.
**“to the greatest of them”** — in time or in dignity
**“The greatest”** — Chrysostom. The greater, either in time, as those earlier, who awaited us, the later, in receiving the penny; or more worthy in knowledge or virtue, who namely were able to understand the incorporeal and unchangeable light, as far as is possible in this life, which the lesser could only believe. When therefore “that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away,” then he who, having taken flesh, appeared to the flesh, will show himself to those who love him; then all shall know him from the least to the greatest, because even the least will then know perfectly, when instructed by himself and not by a greater.
8.12:
**“Because I will be merciful”** — I will do all these things to them in both lives.
**“to their iniquities”** — sins against one’s neighbour are in themselves sins; but more closely, since he does not punish this in the future, it will no longer be remembered, when he will not punish.
**“and their sins”** — in some books, sin is taken as original sin.
**“I will remember no more”** — to eternal punishment
8.13:
**“Now in saying a new”** — The prophet said new.
**“he hath made the former old”** — shows the old, or it has become old; and if the old must come to an end.
**“And that which decayeth”** — in inanimate things
**“and groweth old”** — in animate things
**“is near its end”** — things made old and old age are heralds of death.

9.1:
**“The former had”**
• Nevertheless it had, though near its end.
• He shows how necessary Christ was, since through all these things no one entered heaven.
**“indeed”** — or nevertheless
**“The former indeed had”** — Up to here he has shown the difference between the Testaments, and that the New surpasses the Old and changes it. Now he shows the same from the very plan of the tabernacle.
**“also”** — testament
**“justifications of divine service”** — not true ones but carnal, according to the manner of carnal worship.
**“Beda”** — A holy place not spiritual but worldly. Because it was thought holy by men, and truly it had a worldly holy place, because there was a first tabernacle and a second. It is to be known, therefore, that the tabernacle had thirty cubits in length, and ten in breadth, and as many in height. It had a veil woven of four precious colours, and hung upon four gilded pillars, which divided, at twenty cubits and ten, the holy places that were outside from the holy of holies placed within. For the outer holy place had twenty cubits of length, and the inner holy place, that is, the holy of the holy, ten. And the Apostle calls that the first tabernacle, and this the second tabernacle. In the first, candlesticks in the plural, because although it was one, it had seven branches. For in the middle was a shaft from which three branches proceeded on the right side and three on the left. The table, that is, the altar, after the entrance. And upon the table twelve loaves set before God, which were of fine flour, and every sabbath they were all changed. But if before the sabbath any were needed, it could not be taken unless another were at once put in its place. And upon the bread was shining frankincense. The first is called the holy places because of the veneration of that time, chiefly because it signified the present Church, which is holy. The second is called the holy of holies, because it was in greater veneration and because it signifies the “supercelestial Church,” where there is no sin. The ark was of setim wood, having two cubits and a half in length, and one and a half in breadth, as much in height. And at each corner a golden ring, two on the right and two on the left, in which golden bars were continually set for carrying. The propitiatory, or oracle, was a table over the ark of the same length and breadth. Over it stood the cherubim, and toward it, restraining themselves, they ever looked with faces turned toward each other. All this is a parable. The first tabernacle is the present Church, in which we fight for God before we come to heaven. In it the candlestick, that is, Christ shining in power and wisdom in the midst of the faithful, who are themselves golden candlesticks, because they shine with wisdom. Christ himself is the stem which bears three branches on the right and three on the left, because he is the vine on whom three orders are founded, which in the time of grace are on the right, that is, more worthy before grace, on the left. These are Noe, Daniel and Job, that is, rulers, the continent, the married. Who also, according to the gospel, are said to be in the field and in the bed and at the mill. The first part of the shafts was like golden reeds, then cups, then golden little spheres, lastly lilies. The reeds are the saints, who have been nourished in the waters of the divine fountain, and are hollow for pouring the liquid over to others. The cups themselves, while they give others to drink what they have drunk, namely the wisdom and knowledge of God. Then the little spheres, that is, round and perfect and mobile, whom nothing may hold back until they come to the lilies of eternal joy, who have neither the corner of fear nor the haughtiness of pride. Upon these were set seven lamps, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which remained most fully in Christ, and have been distributed to the faithful according to his will. The table at the door is divine Scripture, which remains, which is set before those who enter, which, while it shows the eternal joys and how they are reached, supplies the food of life. On it the clean loaves, that is, the twelve apostles and their successors, who offer to God the frankincense of prayers; if any of them dies, another must at once be put in his place. But in the seventh age all would be taken away. The second, after the veil, is the heavenly Church, which is veiled as long as we live here. The censer: Christ, full of the fire of charity, always making intercession for us. The ark: Christ, “in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.” Golden on every side, because in his knowledge and speech and work there is nothing but pure truth. The length: perseverance of doctrine, which is signified by one cubit, and of operation, which is signified by the other cubit; for the perfection of which human understanding is imperfect, which the half cubit signifies. The breadth: perfection of charity; the height: perfection of hope, to which we are halves, that is, imperfect. The four rings: the four perfect evangelists, by whom he is carried into the four parts of the world. To which the golden bars always cling, that is, preachers shining with wisdom, always ready against enemies. In the ark an urn having manna, that is, the soul of Christ containing full wisdom, by which even the angels are refreshed. The rod signifies the “priestly power of Christ”; the tables, that he is the giver of the law; the propitiatory: Christ, who is propitiated to us; the two cherubim: all the orders of heaven which exist in him, who are joined together by love, and who, although wise, yet overshadow him as far as in them lies. Into the first the priests entered daily, because here the faithful ought daily to sacrifice themselves, mortifying their flesh with its vices and concupiscences. For otherwise they will not be able to come to the heavenly. The high priest who once a year entered the second, that is, the holy of holies, with blood, is Christ, who in the year of kindness once entered heaven through his own blood, which he shed for the sins of men. According to the parable gifts and sacrifices are offered, because these also signify something in the present time.
9.2:
**“For there was a tabernacle made the first”**
• which was for a time
• in the figure of this second, in which holy priests minister daily, kindling the light of teaching and feeding the people with the bread of God, which is ready upon the table from the sabbath of hope to the sabbath of sight
• The first tabernacle had inside it the altar of incense before the doors; the altar of burnt offerings under the open sky; or what is outside signifies the Old Testament, and is a figure; the figures within, the New.
**“wherein were the candlesticks, and the table”** — The candlesticks are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which shine in the Church.
**“and the setting forth of loaves, which is called the holy”** — the bread is ready from the sabbath of hope, where in Christ we are safe from the whirlwind of the age, until the sabbath of sight, where hope will be fulfilled.
9.3:
**“And after the second veil”** — because the veil set between divides the first from the second.
**“second”** — was
**“the tabernacle”** — signifies heaven, within which our priest Christ entered, not without blood.
9.4:
**“Having a golden censer”**
• by which is signified Christ, full of the fire of charity.
• in which the prayers of the saints are offered.
**“and the ark of the testament”** — which contained the Testament.
**“and the ark”** — The ark is the flesh of Christ, in which is the manna of the divinity, and the tables of the two Testaments, and the rod for the priesthood of Christ. The urn is the people, in whom Christ is the bread from heaven.
*Augustine:* The ark signifies the secret of God. In the ark the law and the manna and the rod of Aaron were commanded to be placed. In the law are precepts; the rod is power; the manna is grace, because without grace there is no power of doing the precepts. But because the law is not fulfilled by anyone, above is the propitiatory. For to this end it is needful that God be propitious. It is above, therefore, because mercy exalteth itself above judgment. The two cherubim overshadow with their wings, that is, they honour by veiling, because these are mysteries. They look at one another, because they agree. For these are the two Testaments. Their faces toward the propitiatory, because they either reconcile or commend the mercy of God, in which is hope. Or the cherubim, that is, the rational creature, two for charity, overshadow the propitiatory with their wings, because they ascribe the wings to God, not to themselves, that is, they honour God. Their faces toward the propitiatory, because there is no hope but in the mercy of God. • The ashes of an heifer, etc. Of the red heifer, whose ashes the law commanded to avail for the water of sprinkling and for the cleansing of those who had touched the dead, we must not be silent. For the New Testament is most evidently prefigured in it. Of this it is said in the book of Numbers that the Lord said to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel. And let them bring thee a red cow without blemish, in which there is no blemish, and upon which no yoke hath been laid. And thou shalt deliver her to Eleazar the priest, and they shall bring her forth without the camp into a clean place, and shall immolate her in his sight. And Eleazar shall take of her blood, and sprinkle it over against the face of the testimony seven times, and they shall burn her in his sight; and her skin, with the flesh and blood, shall be burnt with the dung. And the priest shall take cedar wood, and hyssop, and scarlet, and shall cast it into the midst of the flame which consumeth the cow, and a clean man shall gather up the ashes of the cow, and shall lay them without the camp in a clean place; and it shall be for the children of Israel and for the strangers a law for ever, or eternal.” From this ash was made the water of sprinkling, by which they were cleansed from contact with the dead. For he says thus: “Every soul of man that toucheth the dead shall be unclean seven days. He shall be purified on the third day and the seventh, and shall be clean. But if he be not purified, he shall not be clean. Every one that toucheth the dead, and is not purified, defileth the tabernacle of the Lord, and that soul shall be cut off from Israel.” Again he says: “And a clean man taking hyssop shall dip it in the water, and shall sprinkle the house, and the vessels, and the souls.”
• The heifer, female: the weak flesh of Christ, red, bloody with the passion. They receive her from Moses, who is a figure of the law, because according to the law they thought they were slaying Christ, since according to them he broke the sabbath and profaned the legal observances. The heifer is without blemish, because the flesh of Christ is free from sins. And for confirmation he repeats, saying: “which hath no blemish in her.” Or for a distinction, namely that although in others who are his members it has blemish, yet in itself it has none. “And on which no yoke was laid,” because it is not subjected to iniquity; nay, finding men subjected, he freed them, and broke their bonds, and had power to lay down his life and to take it up again. It is said to be given not to Aaron but to Eleazar, because the Lord’s passion was to come not to the time that then was, but to the successors of that priesthood. It was cast out without the camp; so also the Lord was cast out without the city. And it was cast out into a clean place, because the Lord had no evil cause. It was slain in the sight of Eleazar; so the flesh of Christ was slain in the sight of those who were to be the priests of the Lord in the New Testament. Its blood he sprinkled over against the face of the testimony seven times, because Christ, according to the Scriptures, shed his blood for the remission of sins. Therefore over against the face of the testimony, because it was declared in no other way than it had been foretold by the divine testimony; therefore seven times, because that number pertains to spiritual cleanness. It was commanded to be burnt without the camp of Jerusalem. To be burnt, according to the Greeks, is named from suspension, because fire is moved upward and what is burnt is turned into it, which is a sign of the resurrection. It is said to be burnt in the sight of Eleazar, because the resurrection of Christ appeared to those who were to be a royal priesthood. Its skin is said to be burnt with the flesh and blood and dung, because not only the mortal substance of the body of Christ, which is signified by skin, flesh and blood, but also the insult and rejection of the people, which is signified by the name of dung, was turned into glory, which the flame of the burning signifies. The priest casts into the midst of the burning cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet. The cedar wood is hope, which dwells firmly in the heights. Hyssop: faith, which, though lowly, clings by its roots to the rock. Scarlet: charity, because by its fiery colour it bears witness to the fervour of the spirit. These three ought to be cast into the midst of the burning, that is, into the resurrection of Christ, that our life may be hid with him. The ashes, that is, the remains of the burning, are the fame that followed after the passion and resurrection. A clean man gathered this ash and laid it up in a clean place without the camp, because this fame was most famous among those who were not of the fellowship of the Jews, and were clean from the killing of Christ and outside the celebration of the Jewish custom. From this ash is made the water of sprinkling, by which baptism is signified, whence men were cleansed from contact with the dead, because from iniquity by the baptism of Christ. By that water proselytes as well as Gentiles, or Jews, were cleansed, because baptism profits Jews and Gentiles. That water was sprinkled with hyssop, which signifies faith, because hearts are cleansed by faith, and without faith baptism does not profit. This was done by a clean man, because the ministers of the Church, who bear the person of the Lord, ought to be truly clean.

**“Hast fitted”** — That is, a fitted and suitable body, because you gave me a body without sin, both passible and mortal, which may be offered for the redemption of all.
10.6:
**“Holocausts”** — by many sacrifices one thing was signified, as if: if one thing were said in many words, so that without tedium it might be much commended
**“for sin”** — which seemed worthier than others, which were wholly burnt, and were made for sin; some also not for sin
**“did not please thee”** — from when the truth came
**“Did not please”** — Augustine. In those figures the truth was foretold. Many who knew celebrated the figures as figures of the thing, but more who did not know; and these had to cease once the thing was shown.
10.7:
**“Then”** — When I saw all those things displeasing, and the body given to me suitable for this.
**“said I”** — without any delay
**“Behold I come”**
• because
• I said, I come, to offer myself, that I may do and fulfil thy will, because thou art my God. Therefore I come to fulfil thy will, because so it is written and prefigured of me in the counsel of the Godhead, which is my head, who am, as man, the book of the human race, in which they may read all things necessary for themselves; and therefore there is no need of the law.
**“it is written of me: that I should do thy will, O God”**
• in many copies “my” is added
• so that what the law could not do may be fulfilled through me
• according as man
**“In the head of the book”** — in the first psalm, “Blessed is the man,” which is called the head of the psalter
10.8:
**“In saying before”**
• saying above, he reveals what he understands from that Scripture
• As if to say: this authority marks not only that the old victims did not make men perfect, but that Christ’s victim alone does; and moreover the taking away of the Old Testament and the establishing of the New, if the words are diligently noted, because “saying before” that thou wouldest not those, he adds: Then said I. For behold, he takes away the first sacrifice, and with it the Old Testament, and establishes, as lasting, the new sacrifice, and with it the New Testament.
**“Sacrifices, and oblations, and holocausts for sin thou wouldest not”** — already, although before
**“neither are they pleasing to thee, which”** — yet
**“which are offered according to the law”** — lest they should seem displeasing, because they were not according to the law
10.9:
**“Then said I: Behold, I come to do thy will, O God: he taketh away the first”** — which was given through Moses
**“that he may establish”** — the gospel
**“that which followeth”** — as something stable
10.10:
**“In the which will”** — that is, in his own offering, according to the will of God
**“we are sanctified”** — and therefore this is established; the first falls away, because it could not do this
**“by”** — namely
**“the oblation of the body of Jesus Christ once”** — made
**“We are sanctified by the oblation”** — With the cleansing of sins made, reconciled to God.
10.11:
**“And every”** — he more fully sets out the power of this sacrifice
**“priest”** — of the law
**“And every priest indeed”** — Lest the blood offered once a year by the high priests should seem to have profited less, and the sacrifices made daily by the priests to make men perfect, he adds this. As the high priest, offering every year, did not arrive at consummation, so also every priest always offers, and yet by those things is never consummated.
**“standeth”** — stands ready as one willing
**“daily ministering”** — ministering daily; prayers and many gifts
**“Ministering”** — Ambrose. To minister is of servants, to sit of lords. Therefore the Apostle shows those to be servants, but Christ the apostle.
**“and often”** — and often the same, because they do not cleanse entirely
**“offering the same sacrifices”** — offering victims, of animals
**“which can never”** — which never, in that time however much
**“take away sins”** — can take away sins from the conscience
10.12:
**“But this”** — but this Christ, whose sacrifice is sufficient
**“one sacrifice for sins”** — one for the sins of all
**“offering one sacrifice”** — offering the victim which can save
**“for ever sitteth on the right hand of God”** — obedience completed, he rests for eternity. For he has no need to offer again
**“Sitteth on the right hand of God”** — He can well bring to completion who has so deserved to be exalted.
10.13:
**“From henceforth”** — Henceforth, that is, of what remains, namely the glory of the good and the punishment of the wicked.
**“expecting”** — not that he suffers anything on account of his own or his followers' imperfection, but until
**“until his enemies be made his footstool”**
• that is, they are fully subdued and the subjected appear
• this can also be, but he suffers until the common judgment
**“Footstool”** — Because even if now they resist him and do not appear to be subdued, then they will all appear subject to him, under whose command they will be subject to punishments.
10.14:
**“For by one oblation”** — For by one offering; therefore he offered only once
**“hath perfected”** — he sanctified from sin, and perfected the saints in all things
**“for ever them that are sanctified”** — as long as this age shall last
10.15:
**“And the Holy Ghost also doth testify”** — not only do I affirm this, but the Holy Ghost also confirms our words concerning sanctification and perfection
**“to us”** — or to us
**“And the Holy Ghost. For after that he said”**
• the Holy Ghost in Jeremias
• For after, etc. As if to say: what now does not avail for our proof, he added other things which strengthen both of what we say: namely, “giving my laws,” which pertains to consummation; and “their sins and iniquities I will remember no more,” which pertains to sanctification.
10.16:
**“And this is the testament”** — a true testament, for the things it promises are true, and it commands only what is just; that is, the new
**“which I will make unto them”** — those reckoned beforehand to me
**“after those days, saith the Lord”** — I will testify
**“my laws”** — not as I gave to the fathers on tables of stone, but
**“in their hearts”** — in their understandings
**“and on their minds”** — in their wills
**“will I write them”** — my precepts
**“Will I write”** — He does not say I will write, but I will write over, because those laws are above the powers of men, in whose fulfilment none would suffice unless by the help of grace. In these words it is said that he perfects with virtues. And here it is said of sins that he sanctifies.
10.17:
**“And their sins”**
• in themselves
• And of their sins, etc. He added below: “And their sins and iniquities I will remember no more.” And therefore a sacrifice is no longer necessary, as he makes plain: “Now where there is remission of these.”
**“and iniquities”** — against the neighbour
**“no more”**
• that is, after the time of grace
• neither here nor in the future
**“I will remember”** — to eternal punishment
10.18:
**“Now where there is a remission of these”** — It can be seen from this authority not only that Jesus sanctifies and perfects, but that an offering is no longer to be made for sins after the time of grace, when remission has been made.
**“there is no more an oblation for sin”** — Behold, here it is said that remission of sins has been made; where this is, the offering of the law ceases.
10.19:
**“Having therefore”**
• O
• The great discourse on the great high priest, and on his new law and sacrifice, which he preferred to the old, being finished, a moral instruction is added, in which he exhorts them to many things, but chiefly to faith, patience, peace, purity, and the brotherhood of charity. And he draws the conclusion from all the foregoing, as if to say: because one victim consummates, and because the priest is according to the order of Melchisedech, and because so great a difference has been shown, that those things were lesser and these greater, therefore having.
**“brethren, a confidence in the entering into the holies by the blood of Christ”** — certain that we shall enter into the holies of holies, the heavenly ones, through the blood of Christ
10.20:
**“which”** — which way made for us, that is, which entrance
**“he hath dedicated for us”** — Christ, who first ascended, and through this we are certain
**“A new way”** — because no one entered before him
**“and living”** — abiding, because afterwards it was closed to no believer
**“through the veil”**
• Because faith has no merit where human reason provides proof.
• By this that way remains open, because the faithful take as viaticum the flesh of Christ veiled from every sense. For it appears to be bread, and yet it is truly the flesh of Christ; and by this, that that priest always intercedes for us.
**“that is to say, his flesh”**
• flesh veiled the deity
• or because it is taken under the veil of faith by the faithful.
10.21:
**“and”** — by himself
**“a high priest”**
• Christ
• who always lives “to make intercession for us”
**“high”** — above all
**“over the house of God”** — the people of God
10.22:
**“Let us draw near”** — to the entrance of the saints
**“true”** — not feigned
**“heart”** — understanding
**“in fulness of faith”** — that is, this cannot be done at least with full faith.
**“In fulness of faith”** — Because none of these is now visible, neither priest nor victim.
**“having our hearts sprinkled”**
• which we ought to do, because we also have our hearts cleansed by spiritual sprinkling.
• those bodies
**“sprinkled”** — By this it is shown that not faith alone but life with virtue is sought. Washed with water, that is, by baptism.
**“from an evil conscience”** — from a conscience of wickedness
**“and our bodies washed with clean water”**
• that is, bodily original sin, namely, is washed away by the water of baptism.
• and whatever meets it
10.23:
**“Let us hold fast the confession of our hope”**
• which concerns eternal things
• which is its cause
**“without wavering”** — that we may not turn aside to earthly things
**“for he is faithful that hath promised”**
• hope is not empty; it does not confound
• Hence he exhorts to those things that belong to faith.
• Let us have faith and confession as far as concerns ourselves, and let us consider one another: the more perfect by exhorting others, the lesser by imitating the more perfect.
**“For he is faithful”** — As God is faithful in his promises, so he wills us to be faithful to him in our promises.
10.24:
**“And let us consider”** — which we hope for
**“one another”** — one another: not that one envy and plot against another, but that one be provoked by the example of the other to love and to doing good.
**“to provoke unto charity”** — which is in the mind
10.25:
**“Not forsaking”** — in time of persecution
**“our assembly”** — gathered with us in faith
**“as some are accustomed”** — for there are those who either give way through fear of persecution, or through their own presumption withdraw from sinners, or from the imperfect, so that they may seem righteous.
**“As some are accustomed”** — He blames those who break the unity of charity, as if they could not dwell among others because of their own holiness, when rather by their example they ought to have comforted them.
**“some”** — of you
**“but comforting”** — them
**“But comforting”** — He comforts the one labouring, who persists together with him in the labour, because the relief of labour is the sight of a fellow-labourer, as happens on a journey.
**“and so much the more”** — let us comfort
**“as you see”**
• that is, the more the suffering presses on, lest any fault of yours be lacking
• that is, the nearer you are to the end and the reward
**“the day approaching”** — of recompense
10.26:
**“For if we sin wilfully”**
• charity is to be held fast and evil is to be ceased from; for if we sin wilfully, no other sacrifice is left, which some perhaps would presume to believe
• That is, to us who remain in the will to sin, Christ, who is the victim for sins, does not profit, now in this present life, whence it is clear that neither will he in the future, after the knowledge of the truth has been received, that is, although we have come to the faith, in which some are secure as if never to perish. He does not say “willingly” but “wilfully,” because he is wilful who is constant in something, willing it; he is merely willing who sins for a time, or even if we sin in will, let alone in act.
**“after having the knowledge of the truth, there is now left no sacrifice for sins”** — Christ further
**“There is now left”** — As in the old law it was given that victims be offered often for sin. For Christ is not to be sacrificed again for sins, for what was done once is done, and a second time there is no need. But rather there is need to remain in faith and truth. Otherwise judgment awaits you, unless you are renewed by penance. Therefore he adds: But a terrible. In this he did not exclude penance, but a second baptism. He does not say there is no more penance or remission. But a victim, that is, a second cross, because one suffices, wishing that we should not wait beyond this, but do penance.
10.27:
**“But a certain dreadful”** — as if to say: no sacrifice is left for sins, but a certain expectation is left, etc.
**“a certain expectation of judgment”** — this is the punishment in the meantime
**“and the rage of a fire”** — assault
**“which shall consume the adversaries”** — of Christ
10.28:
**“making void”** — He proves it by the less
**“A man making”** — that is, the transgressor
**“the law of Moses, dieth without any mercy under two or three witnesses”** — convicted
**“under two or three witnesses”** — Convicted. What then of those against whom the angels and the saints bear witness, and their own conscience?
**“dieth”** — by the death which the law commands
10.29:
**“How much more”** — therefore
**“do you think he deserveth worse punishments, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God”** — he cheapens it, so as not to believe it sufficient for salvation but as animals
**“hath trodden under foot”** — He tramples Christ who sins freely without fear, and without penitence, and who partakes of him unworthily. He counts the blood polluted if, having been cleansed by it, he returns to vomit and neglects to repent. He is injurious to the Spirit who does not receive his benefit gratefully.
**“and hath esteemed the blood”** — of Christ
**“of the testament”** — the confirmer of the new
**“hath esteemed unclean”** — not able to cleanse sins
**“esteemed the blood unclean”** — He who believes that sins are forgiven through carnal observances, from which the blood of Christ draws us back, is thus polluted and pollutes us, if he draws us back from him from whom remission comes.
**“by which he was sanctified”** — he received remission, and so sins more gravely against him
**“hath offered an affront to the Spirit of grace”**
• such a one will be punished
• He does an affront to the Spirit of grace, that is, to the Holy Spirit given freely, or he who gives grace does an affront, who ascribes to carnal observances the remission which the Spirit himself makes, or who casts him away from himself by living badly.
10.30:
**“For we know him that hath said”** — how true, how powerful
**“Vengeance belongeth to me”**
• of your injuries
• keep
**“and I will repay”** — if he avenges the injuries of others, also his own
**“And again: The Lord shall judge”**
• separating the good from the bad
• will purge
**“the Lord shall judge his people”** — how much more will God punish enemies, and not lightly
10.31:
**“It is a fearful thing”** — He falls who does not foresee but is caught suddenly.
**“into the hands of the living God”** — always, he who is both effective and powerful to do what he wills
10.32:
**“call to mind”**
• or remember
• he refreshes the frightened by praise of former things
• Remember. He invites them by things done before.
**“Chrysostom”** — Call to mind, etc. As the best of physicians, when they have cut others, and by the incision have increased the pain, bring the comfort of a lesser medicine and a remedy to that place where the pain is, and refresh the troubled soul; so the Apostle does: after he has shaken them from their evils and terrified them, he refreshes them by praise of their former deeds, namely by recalling their former good works, that he may more easily rouse them to the rest. As if to say: that you may not fall into the hands of God: Call to mind, etc.
**“the former days”**
• it is long since you believed, and therefore more accustomed
• Former days, etc. If the untrained endured, it is shameful if now they fail.
**“wherein, being illuminated”** — by faith, for which tribulation came
**“you endured a great fight of afflictions”**
• through sufferings they fought against them, so as to wrest from them patience and faith
• A great fight, etc. There were sufferings for them, both from their own pains and from the pains of others with whom they suffered.
10.33:
**“and”** — because
**“on the one hand”**
• in the other part of the fight
• so great
**“indeed”**
• you yourselves suffering
• in
• And on the one hand, etc. As if to say: you endure a fight of suffering, both in your own sufferings and in the sufferings of others with whom you suffer; and these are the two parts of those fighting against us, suffering alone.
**“by reproaches and tribulations, were made a gazingstock”** — you are to all
**“A gazingstock”** — Spectacle. Disgrace is grave, and graver when it is made a spectacle to men; it is not reproached in secret.
**“on the other”** — in the other part of the fight, namely in the grief you have for the other apostles and others of this kind, having shared their suffering
**“became companions”** — companions, by whose example you ought to suffer
**“of them that were used in such sort”** — constantly suffering
10.34:
**“For”** — so companions
**“had compassion on them that were in bands”** — and to the bound, who could not seek their necessities for themselves
**“you had compassion”** — by ministering, for which cause, your goods being taken from you, you rejoiced
**“took with joy the being stripped of your own goods”** — Because you hope for better things, namely eternal ones.
**“took”**
• as a gift.
• therefore because.
**“knowing that you have a better”** — that is.
**“and a lasting substance”** — eternal life.
10.35:
**“Do not therefore”** — because having thus had compassion and trusted in the better and lasting substance, do not give up.
**“lose your confidence”** — through impatience.
**“which”** — and will not only have it.
**“hath”** — here, now, while he hopes.
**“a great reward”** — and therefore its loss is not slight.
10.36:
**“For patience”** — Shows how confidence is not lost: “In your patience, he says, you shall possess your souls.”
**“is necessary for you”** — this one thing is your work.
**“that”** — through it.
**“doing the will of God, you may receive”** — what you sow here.
**“the promise”** — the promised life.
10.37:
**“For yet a little”**
• that is, in a little time.
• Patience must be held fast, for it is neither long nor violent.
**“and a very little while”** — one must not suffer violently.
**“he that is to come”** — and soon.
**“is”** — at some time.
**“will come”** — the rewarder.
**“and will not delay”** — because for martyrs glory comes at once after death.
10.38:
**“But my just man”**
• the words of God through the prophet Habacuc.
• meanwhile God says.
**“liveth by faith”** — by me, not by carnal observances.
**“he liveth”** — The eternal life which he merits by faith. As if to say: not only he who suffers, but he also who has faith alone, if no passion threatens, will be saved. Behold how much faith avails, which alone saves. And that he lives by faith he proves by the contrary, because if he withdraws himself from faith he does not live. Or: meanwhile the just man lives by faith, and therefore here let him not seek the crown but bear the labour. By faith is the life, the winning of the soul.
**“but if he withdraw himself”** — of faith.
**“he shall not please my soul”** — to the will of God.
10.39:
**“But we”**
• he who withdraws himself does not live.
• But we, etc. Or: we are not sons of the pagans, but of the faithful prophets.
**“are not the children of withdrawing unto perdition”** — of apostasy, because they had not yet utterly apostatized but were born of faith, and therefore ought not to withdraw themselves.
**“but of faith”** — which avails

11.1:
**“Now faith is the substance”**
• Faith is not of things seen, but recognition.
• Now faith is, etc. It is a commendation of faith, of which he gives the description. In it he notes three things, namely what it effects in us, and that it is the foundation of all good things, and that it is of things that do not appear. Of which more fully was said in the epistle to the Romans.
