Faith is the substance of things to be hoped for, that is, the cause which will make the things to be hoped for at some time subsist in us, which is, will make us attain the future goods. And faith is properly called substance, because it stands under the things to be hoped for and makes them to be in believers in the other life. And it is the foundation of all good things, which no one can change, and without which there is no good building; or it already makes the things to be hoped for to be in the heart of the believer. The evidence, that is, the certainty of things that appear not, and, if anyone doubts of it, the proof, where the future resurrection is still being proved, because so the patriarchs, apostles and other saints believed. Faith is the cause of things to be hoped for, because the cause of justice, through which they are to be hoped for. And this is: in this is the testimony of justice, that God bore witness that they were just. The ancients: not that they were old in age, but the predecessors of these; and so it is clear that faith is not new but is to be held, since the ancients held it.
**“of things to be hoped for”** — Nor did Thomas believe what he saw, for he saw a man, he believed God. But if things which are seen are said to be believed, as each one says he believed his own eyes, that is not the faith which is built up in us; but from the things that are seen something is done in us so that the things that are not seen may be believed.
**“the substance”** — foundation
**“of things”** — as if they were already in us
**“The argument of things not appearing.”** — foreshowing of future things
11.2:
**“For by this”**
• because of this
• of righteousness
**“the ancients obtained”** — by God or by men
**“a testimony”** — the ancient fathers
11.3:
**“By faith we understand”**
• that faith is the evidence of things not seen, that is, we ought to believe what does not yet appear; so also by faith alone we understand that the ages were fitted together by the word, that is, by the command of God, when all things were together in matter.
• He uses examples to commend faith, to show that faith is not of things that appear.
**“that the world was framed by the word of God”**
• wisely arranged
• These visible things, surely, before they were made, were not. How then were they known to God, since they were not? And again, how would he make what was not known to him? For he made nothing in ignorance. Therefore he made known things; he does not know them as made. Hence before they were made they both were and were not. They were in God’s knowledge, they were not in their own nature; but I dare not say that they became known to God himself in any other way when he had made them than in that by which he knew them in order to make them: “with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration.”
**“the world”** — Augustine. In the beginning God made heaven and earth, a formless and confused matter (which is called chaos), from which all things were made; by the name he signifies heaven and earth (which were to come from it), that is, by the names of visible things, on account of the weak who are less fit to comprehend invisible things. Then there was darkness, that is, the absence of light. As the place where there is no body is called emptiness, the same matter is called earth, because earth is the least beautiful among all things, invisible on account of obscurity. The same matter is also called water, above which the Spirit of the Lord is borne, as the will of the artificer over the things to be fashioned. It is called water because all things on earth begin to be formed and nourished from moisture; the same is called the abyss. An unknown thing is named by known words, and not by one only, lest it be thought to be that which men were accustomed to understand in that word.
*Augustine:* From invisible things. Before forms were given to things, there were darkness and invisible elements, but light was born in their separation. Or the invisible world was in the wisdom of God, and this visible world was made after its likeness.
**“that from invisible things visible things might be made.”** — formed from formless elements, or from the intelligible world
11.4:
**“By faith”**
• the elders obtained it, as appears in Abel
• that is, through much faith
**“By faith Abel offered to God a sacrifice exceeding that of Cain”** — He shows that the ancient fathers obtained testimony of righteousness through faith, setting forth another example to commend righteousness.
**“a sacrifice exceeding that of Cain, offered by Abel to God”** — more acceptable, that is, of greater worth than Cain’s
**“by which”** — faith
**“a testimony”** — Whence Jesus: “from the blood of Abel the just.”
**“he obtained a testimony that he was just”** — through faith he obtained much, because through faith he was just
**“God giving testimony to his gifts”** — because he accepted them, which became evident when he consumed them with heavenly fire
**“and by it”** — faith
**“he being dead yet speaketh.”** — it was so great that death did not extinguish it
**“he being dead yet speaketh”** — That is, there is matter for us to speak, that we may give an example of his faith. For death has not extinguished the fame of his faith. From the faith and patience of those who went before he comforts these. Abel yet speaketh, because by his example he admonishes others to be just. Death indeed killed him, but did not with him kill his glory and memory.
11.5:
**“By faith”** — by the merit of faith
**“Henoch was translated”** — into paradise, whence Adam was cast out
**“that he should not see death”** — as if he were not to see death from afar in others
**“and he was not found”** — lest he be thought to be in another part of the world
**“because God had translated him”** — who could hide him
**“for before his translation”** — translated through faith, because he was just through faith; just, because he pleased God
**“he had testimony”** — That is, many bore witness that he pleased God.
**“that he pleased God.”** — He pleased by faith, but
11.6:
**“But without faith”** — For indeed
**“it is impossible to please God.”** — so necessary is faith
**“For he that cometh to God must believe”** — he cannot please without faith, because neither can he draw near
**“before God”** — to believe this, namely that
**“that he is”**
• God
• THAT HE IS. To be belongs properly to God, because he is unchangeably.
**“and”** — and that
**“them that seek him”** — what then is the law to them
11.7:
**“By faith Noe”** — By faith Noe, etc. He sets down another example, of Noe, to commend faith, saying:
**“having received an answer concerning those things which as yet were not seen”** — because he believed God saying, “the end of all flesh is come,” even though he saw no signs of the flood
**“moved with fear”** — so much did he believe what he did not yet see, that by fear of it, etc.
**“framed the ark for the saving of his house”** — faith, or the ark
**“by the which he condemned”** — he showed it to be worthy of condemnation
**“the world;”** — because when they saw it being built, they did not believe
**“and was instituted heir of the justice which is by faith”** — That is, he was just by faith, like his fathers; for unless he had been just, God would not have commanded him this.
11.8:
**“By faith”** — through faith
**“he that is called Abraham”** — whereas before he was Abram
**“By faith he that is called Abraham”** — Here he comes down to the fathers of the Jews, and shows that in them and in those before them all justice had its origin from faith. And he gives the example of Abraham.
**“obeyed”** — What God said to him, “Go forth out of thy country, and from thy kindred,” he had already done. For this was said when he had already gone out from the land of the Chaldeans and was already settled in Mesopotamia. Therefore the Lord turned away not his body but his mind from his land, that he might not wish to return. For he had not gone out from there in mind if he was held by a desire of returning, which desire, at God’s command and help and with Abraham obeying, had to be cut off.
**“to go out into a place which he was to receive for an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.”**
• so greatly did he believe God
• of a better land, that is, of eternal life
11.9:
**“By faith he abode in the land”** — he was as a stranger, and in cottages, because he adds: “he looked for a city that hath foundations”
**“as in a strange country”** — although promised to him
**“dwelling in cottages, with Isaac and Jacob, the co-heirs of the same promise.”** — That is, Isaac and Jacob dwelt there; for they did not dwell together at the same time.
11.10:
**“For he looked”** — Why so?
**“foundations”** — Because stable.
**“a city that hath”** — Heavenly.
11.11:
**“By faith also Sara herself, being barren”** — In her own person, not in a substitute.
**“received strength”** — Fruitfulness.
**“to conceive seed”** — barren, even in old age
**“even past the time of age”** — by this faith
**“because she believed that he was faithful”** — At first she laughed, though from joy, yet not with full faith; but after the angel’s words her faith was strengthened. Abraham too had laughed when the promise was made to him. But that laughter was of wonder and joy, not of doubt.
11.12:
**“For which cause”** — because she believed him faithful
**“From one”** — From the womb, or Abraham, from one as good as dead, as to his being older. For an older woman, even if the usual courses of women still flow in her, cannot bear from an old man; from a young man she can. An older man also can beget, but of a young girl; so Abraham after the death of Sara was able to beget of Cetura, who was young.
**“sprung, and this one as good as dead, as the stars of heaven in multitude”** — from one, so many, which is wonderful
**“as the stars of heaven in multitude”** — He says this as regards the good, that is, those who by the light of their virtues and their multitude are compared to the faithful.
**“and as the sand”** — He uses a word taken from sailors, who look far off at the cities they long for, and greet them before they enter. So he speaks from the metaphor of sailors. And saluting, that is, rejoicing in them and desiring them, as sailors do when cities are seen from afar. And therefore they confessed that they were pilgrims, who indeed have nothing in a foreign country.
11.13:
**“died according to faith”** — that is, adhering to faith; or they died without having received the promises on earth; and these things according to their faith, for they hoped that heavenly, not earthly, things were promised to them
**“All these”** — except Enoch, who was translated
**“not having received”** — fully
**“the promises”** — to be fulfilled
**“but beholding them afar off”** — after their death, at the coming of Christ
**“and saluting them, and confessing”** — applauding the promises, though they were remote
**“that they are pilgrims and strangers on the earth”**
• though dwelling there
• Strangers. Those who are not of the country; and these confessed that they were not of the world, and that they had nothing in the world; therefore they confessed this. For those who say this give it to be understood that they seek another country, which they themselves wished to signify. And lest anyone should think that they sought the one from which they had come out, he adds: And truly, etc.
11.15:
**“And truly if they had been mindful”** — it is clear that they did not wish to return
**“Therefore”** — and because they seek this
**“he is not ashamed”** — is not ashamed
**“O God”** — who is called God of angels
**“to be called their God”** — Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
**“their God”**
• He is honored in these, as he is blasphemed by the wicked.
• Augustine. On John. Who is the God of every creature, yet he did not give them this honour in vain, but because he knew in them a sincere and special charity, and because in these three he completed the wonderful sacrament of the future people. For they begot through free women, and for freedom, as Abraham by Sara, and Isaac by Rebecca, and Jacob by Lia and Rachel; and for slavery, as Esau, begotten of Isaac by Rebecca, to whom it was said: “Thou shalt serve thy brother.” Through handmaids not only for slavery, as Abraham by Agar, Ismael, but also for freedom, as Jacob by Balaam, Dan and Nephtali, and by Zelpha, Gad and Aser. So through spiritual men even the good are free, as through Paul those of whom he himself says: “Be ye followers of me, as I also am of Christ.” And the wicked are slaves, as Simon Magus through Philip. And through carnal men not only the wicked but also the good, to whom it is said: “All things whatsoever they say to you, observe and do; but according to their works do ye not.” Whoever prudently recognizes this sacrament in the people of God keeps “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” to the end, cleaving to some, bearing with others.
**“for he hath prepared for them”** — they seek the heavenly one; or he is not ashamed, because they are his citizens
**“a city”** — in which they will be his fellow citizens
11.16: **“they now desire a better, that is, a heavenly one”** — homeland
11.17:
**“By faith”** — not in deed but in will
**“offered Abraham Isaac, when he was tried”** — that is, when God showed who he was, as an example for others
**“when he was tried”** — God did not test Abraham to make him believe, as if He did not know his faith; but so that Abraham himself and the world might know the unity and firmness of his faith.
**“and offered up his only begotten son, in whom he had received”** — that is, in whom the promises were made
**“the promises”** — these
11.19:
**“accounting”** — how then did he believe God to be truthful
**“that God is able to raise up even from the dead”**
• as to make out of nothing
• Accounting that God is able to raise up even from the dead, etc. Abraham did not tremble to believe when the promise was made, he did not tremble to offer when it was demanded. His right hand is lifted up to the sacrifice, that he might die, whose heart was lifted up to faith, that he might be born. Nor was the religion of the believer contrary to the devotion of the one obeying. The pious father faithfully held the promise, which had to be fulfilled through him whom God commanded to be offered. He did not hesitate that he who could be given unhoped for could be given back to him when sacrificed. He did not raise a question for himself, as though about contrary words of God, which opposed him, promising that a son would be born and afterwards saying: Kill thy son for me. But in his heart there was an unshaken and unfailing faith, by which he believed that God, who had granted that he should be born of aged parents, could also restore him from death.
**“God is able to raise up”** — because he had such faith
**“whereupon also he received him”** — that is, the signification
**“for a parable”** — By faith Abraham offered, not only in fact but also in signification. For he understood that Christ was signified, whose divinity does not die; but the ram sticking by the horns among the briers, that is, the flesh labouring among the Jews on the horns of the cross, crowned beforehand with the Jewish thorns, could be offered to God.
11.20:
**“By faith”** — held
**“and of things to come”** — which were not seen
**“Isaac”** — He had faith, not only that the blessed one would be the better, but he also believed that the Christian people would supplant the Jews in the blessing.
11.21:
**“By faith Jacob dying, blessed each”** — because, with his hands crossed, he gave the blessing to each, and placed his right hand upon Ephraim and his left upon Manasseh, preferring the younger to the elder
**“of the sons”** — Ephraim and Manasseh
**“of Joseph, blessed”** — because he gave each his own blessing
**“and adored the top of his rod”** — Christ, through whom he had dominion and the rod of discipline in Egypt, or the kingdom of Christ, which was signified in him as future among the Gentiles
**“adored the top of his rod”** — Perhaps he had taken the rod from his son, when the same son swore to him, and while he holds it, after the words of the one swearing, he at once adored God. For he was not ashamed to carry it, as a mark of his son’s great power, in which a figure of a great future thing was foreshown, and of the future kingdom of Christ among the Gentiles.
11.22:
**“By faith”** — held by faith concerning future things
**“Joseph, dying, of the going out”** — Joseph dying, concerning the departure from Egypt, where the redemption of the faithful from sins was signified
**“of the children of Israel made mention, and gave commandment”** — by faith in the future resurrection
**“gave commandment concerning his bones”** — Adjuring the children of Israel to carry them to the land of promise and lay them in the sepulchre of their fathers, namely in the double cave in which Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the other fathers were buried, where Adam and Eve also rested. This they wished because they foresaw that Christ would be born in that land, that they might rise again with him.
11.23:
**“By faith Moses”** — of the parents, who believed that God would do something great through him, since he was of such elegant form
**“when he was born, was hid three months by his parents, because they saw”** — because from his birth great grace of beauty was poured into him, not by nature but by the gift of God
**“and they feared not the king's edict”** — his parents
**“the king's edict”** — By which he had ordered all the male Hebrews to be put to death.
11.24:
**“By faith Moses”** — through faith in things invisible
**“when he was grown up, denied himself to be the son of Pharao's daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God”** — it is especially of faith to despise the pleasure
11.25:
**“than to have the pleasure of temporal sin”**
• that is, transitory
• he thought it a sin to rejoice in the court while his brothers were afflicted
11.26:
**“esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure of the Egyptians”** — which he endured from his own, as Christ from his own
**“the reproach”** — The reproach: that he would suffer for Christ. Or he signified the future reproaches of Christ. Or that which Moses endured from his brethren, whom he wished to free, as Christ from his own, whom he had come to redeem. They said to Christ: “Thou hast a devil.” And these to Moses: “Wilt thou kill us, as thou didst kill the Egyptian?” which nevertheless he bore patiently, as Christ also did.
**“For he looked unto the reward”**
• the eternal one to which he was going
• of those who endure patiently
11.27:
**“By faith he left Egypt”** — leading out the sons of Israel
**“not fearing the fierceness of the king”** — Not fearing, etc. Chrysostom. That he had earlier fled into the land of Madian was not fear but faith, because he believed that he would be freed by God. He would not remain there, lest it be a cause of boasting if he cast himself into open danger and tempted God, which is diabolical. For the saints, so long as they have something they can do, ought not to tempt God, as the Lord also gave place to the Jews. He also commanded his own: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another.”
**“for he endured as seeing him who is invisible”** — he endured God, whom he did not see, as if he saw him, and trusted in him, waiting for what he had promised, and therefore did not fear
**“he endured”** — that is, he waited and trusted in him
11.28:
**“By faith”** — because he so believed the people was to be saved
**“he celebrated”** — Moses
**“By faith he celebrated”** — Namely because he believed the people was to be saved: those, that is, from Pharaoh, and us from the devil.
**“pasch”** — which was the cause of the passing over
**“and the shedding of the blood”** — by which they smeared the doorposts and lintels of the house
**“that he, who destroyed”** — the angel striking
**“firstborn”** — of the Egyptians
**“might not touch them.”** — terrified by the blood, which was in figure of those to be freed through the blood of Christ
11.29:
**“By faith”** — by which they believed God promising
**“passed through the Red Sea”** — They passed through the sea, etc. So also by baptism the faithful pass over, their sins forgiven, as the Egyptians were drowned with the devil, prince of darkness.
**“as by dry land”** — and lest this should seem to have been done by chance and not by faith, he adds that they experienced it, or lest it should seem to have been an illusion
11.30:
**“By faith the walls of Jericho fell down, by the going round them seven days.”** — so the obstacles of this world fall at the voices of preachers, while in this time the Church is renewed, going round the circle of the lands
**“the going round them seven days”** — When it was completed by the Levites carrying the ark of God and sounding the brazen trumpets.
11.31:
**“By faith Rahab the harlot perished not with the unbelievers”** — because she believed the land was to be given to the Jews by God, and therefore received the spies
**“receiving the spies with peace.”** — what then will you do, you who have heard the prophets and Christ?
**“receiving the spies”** — As if to say: so you too ought, by believing, to receive the two Testaments through the apostles as spies sent by Christ, and thus you will not perish with the unbelievers.
11.32:
**“And”** — I have spoken of many deeds of faith
**“what shall I yet say?”** — as if they were infinite
**“For the time would fail me”** — of this letter or of life, if I wished to pursue each one
**“of Gedeon”** — How, having received a sign from the Lord by the fleece, he went against the Madianites with three hundred men, and overcame them by night.
**“of Barac”** — Of whom it is read in the book of Judges that, when Jabin, king of Chanaan, was afflicting the children of Israel, Debora the prophetess, who at that time judged Israel, commanded Barac the son of Abinoem to take with him ten thousand fighting men and go against Sisara, the captain of Jabin’s army. He said that he would go if she would go with him. So she also went with him. But the Lord struck terror into the army of Jabin, which Sisara had gathered at the torrent Cison. And Sisara fled to the tents of Jahel, the wife of Haber the Cinite. When he had fallen asleep there, hidden, Jahel drove a nail of the tabernacle, struck in with a hammer, into his brain, to the ground, and he died. And behold, Barac came pursuing Sisara. And Jahel went out to meet him and said to him: “Come, and I will shew thee the man whom thou seekest.” When he had entered, he saw Sisara lying dead. So God that day “humbled Jabin the king of Chanaan before the children of Israel.”
**“Samson”** — Who, as is read in the Book of Judges, sorely afflicted the Philistines.
**“of Jephthe”** — Who, when he went to battle against the enemies, vowed to the Lord that if on returning he obtained triumph over the enemies, he would offer to God whatever first met him; and his daughter met him, whom he sacrificed.
**“Jephthe”** — Jephte is not praised because he killed his daughter, but because by faith, with God helping, he overcame the enemies.
*Augustine:* In the first book of The City of God. Why Abraham is not blamed but praised because he was willing to kill his son. And it is rightly asked whether it is to be held as by the command of God that Jephte killed his daughter as he had vowed. Nor is Samson otherwise excused for having crushed himself with his enemies, except that the Spirit, who worked miracles through him, had secretly commanded this.
11.33:
**“Who by faith”** — And although he refuses to say what each one did, nevertheless he has said what certain men wrought by faith.
**“conquered kingdoms, wrought justice”** — just judgment
**“obtained”** — by faith
**“the promises”**
• which promised, as victory or other things
• from God or Christ
• He wisely avoids the recounting of the histories, lest he prolong his discourse, touching briefly on certain things. For he has neither kept altogether silent, nor become tedious by speaking; he flees density and length, lest he weary the hearer.
**“promises”** — Many promises were made to David, as to Abraham.
**“stopped the mouths of lions”** — They conquered by faith not only men but also beasts, and Daniel
**“stopped”** — Augustine. The plural for the singular: Daniel alone is meant to have shut the mouths of lions, Isaias alone to have been sawn asunder; as in the Psalm: “The kings stood up,” for Herod, “and the princes,” for Pilate. It is to be noted that in the Old Testament temporal happiness is often shown to have been bestowed upon the fathers in the things that have been said, and in others of this kind. But the time of such things is not in the New Testament. He gave such things first, so that besides him no other giver might be understood, even of earthly happiness, which belongs to the old man. In Christ, the new man, he promises new things to the new, that is, eternal things. Whence he himself dies mocked in the sight of his enemies. But he showed his resurrection not to others but to his own, that there they might learn what to hope for themselves. Whence also Jacob: “You have heard of the patience of Job, and you have seen the end of the Lord,” as if to say: suffer as Job did, but do not hope for his end, that is, the temporal things which returned to him increased, but for the eternal things which went before in Christ.
11.34:
**“Quenched the violence of fire”** — as the three boys
**“escaped the edge of the sword”** — an army girded with the sword, as Josue, David and many others
**“recovered strength from weakness”** — as Ezechias and Job
**“became valiant”** — as Josue, Judas Machabeus, and others
**“in battle”** — in battle
**“put to flight the armies”** — into flight
**“of foreigners”** — of enemies
11.35:
**“Women received”** — as through Elias and Eliseus
**“their dead raised to life again”** — coming, that is, raised again
**“But others”** — behold how much they did through faith; now how much they suffered for faith
**“were racked”**
• on the rack and in other torments
• Others were racked, etc. Augustine. Even in those fathers of the Old Testament, though rare, there were nevertheless examples of patience, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zacharias, whose blood the Lord says is to be required of those who persisted in the iniquity of their fathers by whom those were slain. And in the New Testament there were not lacking those abounding in temporal happiness, that in this we may experience the mercy of God.
**“not accepting deliverance”** — escape from the hand of enemies
**“that they might find a better”** — by that redemption
**“resurrection”** — eternal life
11.36: **“And others had trial of mockeries and stripes, moreover also of bands and prisons.”** — by this he notes that these things were in the same persons
11.37:
**“They were stoned”** — as Jeremias in Egypt, Ezechiel in Babylon
**“they were cut asunder”** — as Isaias
**“they were tempted”** — by promises
**“put to death by the sword”** — done by the sword
**“were put to death”** — as Urias, Josias
**“wandered about”** — many places of the world
**“in sheepskins”**
• as Elias and others
• Melote, etc. Melote is a garment of camels' hair, or better, it is an animal which is also the badger, whose skin is called melote.
**“in goatskins, being in want”** — lacking necessities
**“distressed”** — by anxiety of mind
**“afflicted”** — by labours
11.38:
**“Of whom”** — That is, of whose conversation the world was not worthy, and therefore lest they be held cheap on account of tribulations. Or they were so cheap to men that they were not worthy to stand or dwell among them.
**“in which”** — Or those earlier ones did not at once receive the promised life, until Christ. Why not? Because God had something better for us: that he might assume our nature and exult more gloriously with us. And if they held the faith who waited so long for rest, much more should we hold it, who receive it at once.
**“the world was not worthy”** — lovers of the world
**“wandering in deserts, in mountains”** — as Mathathias and his followers, and before them Elias and the sons of the prophets under Jezabel
**“and in dens”** — in caves, which are natural
**“and in caves of the earth.”** — in caverns of the earth, which come about by some chance
11.39:
**“And all these”** — And all these: so great things did the faithful of old do or suffer through faith
**“being approved by the testimony of faith”** — which faith bore witness to concerning them
**“now”** — as yet
**“received not the promise”**
• two robes, though each one
• the full blessedness of body and soul
11.40:
**“God providing some better thing for us, that they should not be perfected without us”** — that in the common joy of all, the joy of each one may become greater
**“be perfected”**
• might be made perfect
• Be made perfect, that is, they might enjoy rest and the vision of God.

12.1:
**“And therefore”** — because these endured
**“and”** — also
**“And therefore we also”** — After the commendation of faith, he returns to what he had begun, exhorting them to patience by many means, and especially by the example of Christ himself.
**“having so great a cloud of witnesses over our head”**
• as an example of faith and works
• after
**“a cloud of witnesses”** — That is, the multitude of saints who are witnesses of faith, who like clouds cool us in the heat of tribulations by their example, and rain upon us with their teachings.
**“laying aside”** — or renouncing sins which surround us on every side
**“every weight”** — of sins which already exist, or of weariness which comes through tribulation
**“and sin which surrounds us”** — which surrounds and threatens even if it is not yet within
**“by patience”** — girded up and unencumbered
**“let us run”** — without hesitation
**“proposed to us”** — which is set before us
**“the fight”** — of martyrdom
12.2:
**“Looking on Jesus, the author and finisher of faith”** — because he is so great a giver of faith we ought to run, and because the same one perfects us with full blessedness, and because he himself suffered
**“and finisher of faith, Jesus, who having joy set before him”**
• eternal joy, to which one goes through suffering
• That Jesus endured the cross ought to encourage you, because this too is less than the contradiction. As if to say: Look to Jesus, who endured the cross. For consider, that you may follow.
**“who having joy set before him”** — So we too, with eternal joy set before us, ought to run, having set aside shame. Or, with the joy of an earthly kingdom set before him, because the crowds wished to seize him to make him king, which he refused, since it was the way of humility.
*Augustine:* Christ despised all earthly goods, that happiness might not be sought in them. He endured all earthly evils, that unhappiness might not be feared in them. For he was born of a mother who, though she conceived untouched by man and remained always untouched, was nevertheless betrothed to a craftsman, in which he also extinguished the swelling of all carnal nobility. He was born also in the city of Bethlehem, which was small among all the cities of Juda; he would not therefore have anyone glory in the eminence of an earthly city. He was made poor, he whose are all things, that no one might be puffed up by earthly riches. He would not be made king by men, because he had shown the way of humility to the wretched. He hungered, who feeds all. He thirsted, who is the fountain of the thirsty. He was wearied from the journey, who made for us the way to heaven. He became dumb and deaf, through whom the dumb spoke and the deaf heard. He was bound, who looses the bonds of infirmities. He died, who raised the dead. Therefore for love of him let us suffer like things. For then the law will be fulfilled, when whatever he commanded is done not from desire of temporal things but from the love of him who commanded.
**“endured the cross, despising the shame”** — human shame being disregarded
**“and”** — therefore
12.3:
**“For think diligently upon him that endured such opposition”** — so violent
**“from sinners against”** — which was unworthy
**“himself”** — not only in the members
**“opposition”** — in all adversities
**“that you be not wearied, fainting in your minds.”**
• if the body fails, let the mind stand firm
• Likewise, you ought not to faint, because you have forgotten the consolation; as if to say: You ought not to forget.
• Fainting, etc. To faint is to deny the faith through fear of tribulation.
12.4:
**“For you have not yet”** — You ought not to faint.
**“unto blood”** — although you have lost your goods.
**“resisted, striving against sin”** — unbelief from the other.
**“striving”** — which is good; and therefore you must still do the same and not faint.
12.5:
**“And you have forgotten the consolation”** — of Christ, comforting in Scripture.
**“which speaketh to you, as unto children”** — of him, that is, of Christ, from whom the consolation comes.
**“speaketh, saying: My son”**
• the words of Christ in the Proverbs of Solomon.
• so.
**“neglect not the discipline of the Lord”** — the tribulations by which you are instructed.
**“neither be thou wearied”** — even to fainting.
**“whilst thou art rebuked by him.”** — because it cleanses past sins.
12.6:
**“For whom”** — that he may crown.
**“the Lord loveth, he chastiseth”** — here he makes him chaste by correcting.
**“scourgeth”** — by justice.
**“But”** — in whatever way.
**“every son”** — otherwise he receives none.
**“Every son”** — Augustine. Even the only-begotten without sin. If therefore you are exempt from the suffering of scourges, you are exempt from the number of sons. That only-begotten, born of the substance of the Father, equal to the Father in the form of God, the Word by whom all things were made, had nothing in which he could be scourged. But for this he was clothed with flesh, that he might not be without the scourge. He who scourges the only-begotten without sin leaves out the adopted, who is with sin. The only-begotten without sin, yet not without the scourge, set before us an example in his sufferings. Therefore we ought not to be troubled when some holy man suffers grievous and unworthy things, if we have not forgotten what the just one of the just and the holy one of the holy endured. And observe here the justice and mercy of God. Justice is in that he scourges; mercy in that he receives.
**“whom he receiveth.”**
• by mercy.
• into the eternal inheritance.
• and therefore.
12.7:
**“Persevere under discipline.”** — by bearing patiently.
**“as”** — because.
**“God dealeth with you as with his sons”** — in that he gives discipline, he shows himself a Father, which is said by way of comparison: For what son.
**“for what son is there, whom the father doth not correct?”**
• that is, to whom his father does not give discipline.
• Sons, stand firm in discipline.
• What son is there, etc. Augustine. He gives discipline that he may not take away mercy. He strikes the stubborn that he may give back the inheritance. If you have rightly known the promises of the father, do not fear to be scourged, but to be disinherited. Run under the hand of the father who scourges, because while he scourges he trains you for the inheritance. Do not be of an unjust, childish mind, so as to say: my father loves my brother more than me, for he allows him to do whatever he wishes, whereas if I move against his command I find scourges. Rather rejoice under the scourges, because the inheritance is kept for you.
**“Chrysostom”** — Note that he does not say: everyone who is scourged is a son. But every son is scourged; for otherwise no one is received.
12.8:
**“But if you be without chastisement”** — which you ought not.
**“whereof”** — discipline.
**“all are made partakers”** — sons.
**“then are you bastards”** — that is, you are adulterine, or the possession of the devil.
**“Then are you bastards”** — Note that he is not rightly called a father who has begotten children by adultery, because those born of him are not called lawful sons.
**“and not sons”** — of God
12.9:
**“Moreover”**
• also the reason why they ought to be under discipline
• at last
**“we have had fathers of our flesh”** — not of the soul
**“we have had fathers, for instructors, and we reverenced them”** — shall we not then
**“We reverenced”** — To reverence is to pay honor with fear.
**“shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits”** — of souls, which are not from matter as bodies are from fathers
**“and live”** — also because through him we shall live forever
12.10:
**“And they indeed”** — And they indeed. Also another reason why we must obey God.
**“for a few days, according to their own pleasure, instructed us”** — in those things which they wished, namely in vain things
**“But this”** — Father of spirits
**“for our profit”**
• to faith and a good life
• Or to the profitable, namely in receiving sanctification.
**“that we might receive his sanctification”** — if we receive the discipline which sanctifies us
12.11:
**“Now all chastisement”**
• in a state of discipline, but it is true that it is grievous, which they could object; therefore he says this that he may resolve it
• Discipline, which in Greek is paideia, is instruction through troubles, when someone suffers evils for his sins, so that he may be corrected; this is what is understood here. There is also a discipline which is called knowledge, and takes its name from learning, and is called in Greek epistemon.
**“for the present indeed seemeth not to bring with it joy”** — but it is not so, if one thinks now of future things
**“but sorrow: but afterwards”** — in another life
**“the most peaceable fruit”** — to be possessed in all quiet
**“them that are exercised”** — that is, the peace than which there is none greater
**“by it”** — discipline
**“will yield ... of justice”** — which justice merits
12.12:
**“For which cause”** — that you may have such fruit
**“the hands which hang down”** — slothful in almsgiving
**“and the feeble knees”** — by strength by which one stands firmly on the knees
**“hands”** — That is, the affection of charity by which you once embraced God; raise them up again to God. And the knees, that is, the strength which is loosened, cooled from charity.
**“lift up”** — upward to God, so that you neither grow numb with idleness nor waver through weakness
12.13:
**“Straight steps”** — That is, that your faith may walk rightly, confessing what it believes, and if need be suffering; faith is rightly called a foot because it carries the whole. Straight, so that no one may turn aside from the true way of faith, like him who receives carnal observances, which is to err. And let him not halt, like one who wavers from fear of suffering, but let him be healed if he has erred or feared.
**“And make straight steps with your feet”** — Or straight steps are right intention in works.
**“that no one, halting, may go out of the way”** — from the way of rectitude
**“but rather be healed”** — from sins, by right intention in doing good works
12.14:
**“Follow peace”** — so far as to endure, that you may have peace even amid tribulations, which is love and concord
**“Follow peace with all men, and holiness”** — perfection in works, because faith alone does not suffice
**“Holiness”** — That is, chastity of mind and body. Whence: “Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God.”
**“without which”** — from what you desire, it frightens you
**“no man shall see God”** — peace and holiness are so necessary. For by contending with others we extinguish the eye of the mind
**“Without which no man shall see God”** — Behold how he frightened the lover of the good, that is, of the vision of God. He did not say: he will be cast into the fire, or: he will be given to tireless tormentors, which things are nevertheless true. But wishing you to be a lover of the good, that is, of the vision of God, not a dreader of evil, he says: without which no man shall see God, etc. He frightens you by the very thing you desire. It is one thing to fear punishment, another to love justice. If you do not do evil from fear of hell, there is indeed faith in you, because you believe in the future judgment of God. I rejoice in your faith, but I still fear your malice. Let there be in you therefore peace and holiness, without which God will not be seen. For we shall have nothing with which to see God, if by contention we have put out the eye in us. Let us be peacemakers, that we may be acknowledged sons; let us be clean of heart, that we may see God: “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.” “Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God.”
12.15:
**“Looking diligently”**
• follow peace
• with great attention
• Do not doubt that you can be so patient, for the grace of God is at hand; but lest you be wanting to it, in this way you can retain grace. Lest any root of bitterness: the delight of sin is more truly called bitterness, and therefore to be avoided.
**“lest any man be wanting”** — not only you. As if to say: let there also be care for others
**“to the grace of God”** — which the merit of human wickedness often repels
**“lest any root”** — an evil thought
**“of bitterness”** — of harmful delight, from which bitterness [comes]
**“Root of bitterness”** — An evil thought which does not produce sweet fruits, that is, works, but bitter ones, by which the way to heaven is hindered.
**“springing up”** — sprouting upward, coming to consent and action
**“do hinder”** — that grace
**“and by it”** — bitterness
**“many be defiled”** — by example, and therefore it is grave
12.16:
**“Lest there be any”** — through the parts in which he notes some
**“fornicator”**
• be
• Lest there be any fornicator, etc. Here he shows how they ought to look, lest any root of bitterness sprout, through the parts in which he notes some of them.
**“or profane person”**
• estranged from God
• Or, lest there be any fornicator, such as holds carnal observances together with faith, as a concubine, which is spiritual fornication. Or profane, wholly neglecting the faith. Or there were some among the Jews who were followers of Esau in fornication and gluttony.
**“Profane person”** — As if: afar, that is, far from the fane, that is, the temple of God, that is, utterly irreligious.
**“as Esau”** — behold how far from religion is he who for his belly gave away the blessing
**“As Esau”** — He is called ‘fornicator’ because he took foreign wives against the will of his father and mother. He is called ‘profane’ because he was a glutton, that is, a slave of the belly, and greedy, selling his firstborn rights for a red lentil.
**“who for one mess, sold his first birthright”** — dignity
**“First birthright”** — Or his firstborn things: here he calls “first things” the honor and dignity of the priesthood, because before the priesthood of Aaron all the firstborn were priests, as Sem was. And this was a great dignity, because he also took a greater portion of the paternal substance and inheritance. And the richer adornment of garments shone upon him, and the blessing was given to him. Behold how far from religion Esau was, who for his belly gave up the blessing. His deed he therefore mentions, that he may dissuade from likeness to him.
12.17:
**“For know ye”** — that you be not like Esau, because he was rejected
**“that afterwards, when he desired to inherit the benediction”** — so we must beware that when after death they ought to receive the blessing, they be rejected and repentance not avail them
**“he was rejected”** — by God, Isaac confirming the blessing of Jacob
**“for he found no”** — he lacked the blessing, not because he did not repent, but because he did not repent as he ought, saying: “The days will come of the mourning of my father, and I will kill my brother Jacob.”
**“place of repentance”** — of pardon, and a place of blessing through penance.
**“although with tears he had sought it”** — from indignation and grief at the lost honour, against his brother, not from true penance.
**“and whirlwind”** — or the threat of the law itself.
**“and darkness, and storm, and sound of trumpet, and voice of words”** — These things were done in the giving of the law, that the hearts of the Jews might be struck with fear, lest they dare to transgress the law. There is no such terror here in the gospel.
**“Which they that heard, entreated that there might be no word more spoken to them”** — Let not the Lord God speak to us, lest perhaps we die.
**“For you are not come”** — He had said that no one should fall short of grace, by these means which he subjoined; for grace is prepared. And this is: You have not come to the harshness of the law, which he describes, that the sweetness of grace may be understood by contrast. Not to the fire, but to the Holy Spirit, who is a fire consuming sins, to whom one goes not by motion of the body but by the spirit. The whirlwind: the whirlwind is the force of the winds with hail and rain, and signifies the onset of vices, which were more dominant under the law; now one comes to the serenity through the grace of the Spirit. The darkness: because the law was obscure, now the understanding is clear. And the storm is greater than the whirlwind, that is, a tempest that drives wherever it will; this is the slavery of sin according to the working which drew men through the law, but now there is rest from vices in the perfect. The sound of the trumpet, which is a sign of the movement to battle, that is, the movement of pleasure, which is quenched not through the law but through grace. The voice of words: such a voice is the precept of the law and its threat, which the people thought heavy and intolerable, because it was precept alone, without grace helping.
**“For they did not bear what was said.”** — For they could not bear what was said; they could not bear the voice of the angel for fear, seeing the whole mount Sina smoking, and hearing the storms, the thunders and the voices of trumpets.
**“For they did not bear”** — Because without grace they were insufficient to observe the precepts. And “if so much as a beast shall touch the mount, it shall be stoned.” The mount is the divinity, the beast is the lack of reason, which is when a word of blasphemy is uttered against God. To touch is to offend. The beast therefore touches the mount who offends God by blasphemy, whom the law commands to be stoned without mercy. But in the Church, if he wishes to return, he is mercifully received. Moses was terrified, because the harshness was so great that even the perfect were frightened, since grace was not there to help. But now the precept is burdensome not even to the imperfect, since the yoke is sweet and the burden light. Not to such harsh things. But you are come: these things depend on what went before, where he says to what they have come, after the removal of those things; and he does not set down the contraries of those things, which are understood by opposition as was assigned above, but first what follows from them, that by this he may the more persuade that grace is to be held. To Sion, that is, to those who behold God on high, for to behold is a great reward. And the city of God, because God dwells in them, because he justifies them: another reward. To God the judge of all, and to the God of the spirits of the just and perfect, that is, to God who will be the possession of the just when he shall be all in all. He will be also of the others, but more of the perfect, and by this he urges perfection. Or you are come to the spirits of the just, whose companions you are in faith and work. Or to the Holy Spirit, who makes the just perfect. And through what they have all these things he subjoins: the mediator of the new testament, that is, through Jesus who gave the testament, and through the blood of Christ. Speaking better than Abel, who was the first just man, whom he also put for all the others, whose blood could effect no remission; then much less the blood of animals, but the blood of Christ did. Or he speaks better, that is, he makes us speak, that Jesus is the Son of God, by whom we are redeemed, more than the blood of Abel, which makes us say that Abel was a just man and was slain in a figure of Christ. The darkness signifies the obscurity of the law, the whirlwind the threat: “Whoever shall do this shall die the death.” The storm, the vengeance itself. The sound of the trumpet, the coming of God, whence: “With the trumpet of God he shall come down from heaven,” that is, in the voice of angels, the voice of words, not of God himself but of angels. For he spoke to Moses through an angel.
*Augustine:* See therefore the difference. There, after the Pasch, which is done by immolation, on the fiftieth day it was celebrated, God came down upon Sina in fire, but frightening the people standing far off, and writing with his finger on stone, not on the heart; but here the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God, came where the faithful were gathered together in one, in tongues of fire, not frightening from afar, but rather he sat upon each one of them. Indeed a sound came suddenly from heaven, as of a mighty wind coming; it sounded, but no one was afraid. There, fire and smoke; but here, a bearing fire.
**“And if a beast”** — so the Lord commanded.
**“touch the mountain”** — Moses said: Stand far off, because if even a beast
**“it shall be stoned”** — By hail.
12.18:
**“For you are not come to a palpable”** — that is, tangible.
**“and kindled fire”** — by which one might draw near by a bodily motion.
12.21:
**“And”** — It was very terrible, which terrified even Moses, as is added below: Moses, etc.
**“And so terrible was that which was seen”** — so terrible was what was seen, that they did not dare to approach.
**“Moses said”** — What then of the others?
12.22:
**“But you are come to mount Sion”** — that is, to those who look upon God on high, which to look upon is a great reward.
**“and to the city of the living God”** — that is
**“the heavenly Jerusalem”** — to the vision of heavenly peace.
**“and”** — to
**“the company of many thousands of angels”**
• with more, greater blessedness.
• of whom you are to be companions.
12.23:
**“and”** — to
**“the church of the firstborn”**
• of the apostles.
• who first believed.
**“who are written in the heavens”**
• “whose names are written in the book of life.”
• in the likeness of the conscript fathers.
**“who are written”** — As if to say: Do not doubt that you will come to the angels, since your predecessors have come. And this is: Who are written, that is, they are written with those who are in heaven, that is, they are in their order.
**“and to God the judge of all”**
• that is, Christ, to whom the Father gave all judgment.
• and so you will judge with him.
**“and to the spirits”** — spirits, that is, souls.
**“of the just made perfect”** — or of spirits
12.24:
**“and to Jesus the mediator of the new testament”** — through whom they can become companions of the angels
**“Jesus the mediator”** — For because it seemed incredible what God promised, namely that from this mortality, corruption, abjection, from shapeless dust, men would be made equal to the angels of God, he not only made Scripture for men that they might believe, but also set a mediator of their faith, not any prince or angel, but his only Son, that by the Son himself he might show and provide the way by which he would lead us to that ineffable immortality and to equality with the angels. For it was too little for God to make his Son a shower of the way; therefore he made him the way, that we might go by it. A physician was therefore sent, whom the sick man did not know. And therefore he killed him; but even the sprinkled blood of the physician availed for the medicine of the sick man. He came that he might visit; he was slain that he might heal.
**“and the sprinkling of blood”** — to the cleansing of the blood of Christ
**“that speaketh better than Abel”** — because this one brings pardon, that one vengeance; this one salvation, indeed even pardon to his persecutors, when he says: “Father, forgive them,” etc. That one cries out for damnation.
12.25:
**“See”** — and because you have come to Jesus, whose blood speaks better, etc. Therefore
**“that you refuse him not that speaketh”** — through the gospel: he who forbids carnal things and commands spiritual things
**“For if they”** — our fathers
**“escaped not”** — the punishment
**“who refused him”**
• that is, Christ, who gave earthly things, that is, carnal observances, through Moses, and promised earthly things
• Moses or the angel
**“that spoke upon the earth; much more shall not we, that”** — shall not escape
**“turn away from him that speaketh to us from heaven”** — the same one, speaking to us spiritual things and promising eternal things
12.26:
**“Whose voice”** — because the same
**“moved the earth”** — that he might threaten them, lest they refuse
**“then”**
• when he spoke upon the earth
• when he gave the law on Sinai
**“but now he promiseth”** — he does not threaten but promises, and therefore you ought much less to refuse
**“Saying”** — this is read in Aggeus
**“Yet once more, and I will move”** — As if they had already been moved. But ‘yet I will move’: by ‘once’ he signifies that they are not to be moved again.
**“but heaven also”**
• below
• aerial
• What is lower, namely the air, whence they are called the birds of heaven. Almost all this windy air, which Scripture calls heaven or the heavens, these lowest ones indeed, not those highest ones where the sun and moon and stars are placed, Scripture says here are to be moved, and elsewhere to perish, on account of a certain great change of themselves.
12.27:
**“And in that he saith, Yet once more”** — he expounds the sense of this authority
**“he signifieth the translation of the moveable things”** — he declares the removal of moveable things by ‘yet’ (moveable)
**“as made”** — which he can do, because he made them
**“that those things may remain”** — this he notes by ‘once’
**“which are immoveable”**
• afterwards, eternally
• As if: ‘that which they are’, because whatever they shall be, whether in their principal essences or in forms received from outside, they will be immovable in that respect.
12.28:
**“Therefore receiving an immoveable kingdom”**
• now in hope
• Because he promises an immovable heaven and earth, it is clear that we have grace, without which we could not attain that promise; but through it we receive that immovable kingdom, and therefore no one is lacking grace.
**“we have grace”** — because God is also judge of all
**“or let us have grace”** — That is, faith, hope and charity with holy work. Or let us have grace, that is, let us give thanks for all things, not murmuring in anything, because thus God is served well.
**“whereby let us serve, pleasing God, with fear and reverence”** — through love of honour, because the Father, that is, loving him as Father.
12.29:
**“For our God is a consuming fire”**
• We can please through grace, because God consumes all sins; and by this, that he cleanses and makes us serve in virtues, we please God.
• Our God, etc. Made a fire, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is both the gift and that grace, because he is given to us freely.

13.1:
**“Let the charity of the brotherhood abide in you”**
• Hence the Apostle instructs morally:
• let there be charity among us, because you are brethren.
13.2:
**“And hospitality do not forget”** — because they had this before they were despoiled of their goods.
**“for by this”** — Abraham and Lot
**“have entertained”** — were pleasing to God
*Augustine:* Abraham, offering the duties of humanity, which cannot be necessary except to weak flesh, a wonder, unless he thought them men; but in whom he understood God to speak, afterwards by certain signs he knew them to be angels, when they went into heaven while he was looking. So also Lot, who ran to meet them and adored, understood them to be angels, but again when he invites them to refreshment he thinks them men. It appeared therefore by certain signs that they were sent by God, yet they were believed to be men. He therefore showed hospitality, as to holy men in whom he knew God to be, although, like Abraham himself, he did not know them to be angels. Abraham knew God in three, Lot in two, when they spoke to them in the singular, yet they thought them men when they provided refreshment. Some: as Lot, not knowing that they were angels, yet knowing who was in them.
*Augustine:* Another translation: For by this some, not knowing it, received angels as guests, as Abraham and Lot received them, not knowing they were angels but thinking they were men in whom God was and spoke.
13.3:
**“Remember them that are in bands”**
• Remember those in bonds: which besides guests,
• for the faith of Christ, by sympathising with them in this way,
• by doing good to them,
**“as if you were bound with them”** — so sympathise and help them as if you were bound
**“As if”** — As you would wish to be helped if you were bound or labouring.
**“and them that labour”**
• and of those who labour, on whom labour hangs,
• by doing good,
**“as being yourselves also in the body”** — as being yourselves also in the body; through which you have learned what is necessary for those who labour.
13.4:
**“Marriage honourable”** — not to be prostituted
**“marriage”** — that a lawful wife be taken for love of children, and that she be abstained from at fixed times
**“in all”** — be
**“and the bed undefiled”** — not adultery
**“For fornicators and adulterers God will judge”**
• he will damn eternally
• although some think otherwise, saying that God does not care about sins of the flesh
13.5:
**“Let your manners”**
• Let life
• After they had lost their goods, they wished to gather again what he forbids. But lest they say, what if necessary things fail, he adds a consolation. Almighty God himself says: “I will not leave thee.” This he says to everyone hoping in him; as Josue, so he is with us, that we may say confidently: “I will not fear what man shall do to me.” Man, every adversary, even the devil, who is called man from his office, namely in that he deceives man.
**“without covetousness”**
• by tightness in giving
• lest they be tight-fisted with what they have
**“Without covetousness”** — He is covetous who is tight in giving, greedy in receiving.
**“contented with such things as you have”** — lest they be greedy for what they do not have
**“for he hath said”** — to Josue the son of Nun
**“I will not leave thee”** — indeed necessary things; and therefore a man should not be tenacious
**“neither will I forsake thee”** — He would be left who perished of hunger; but since this is not so, a man should not be covetous.
13.6:
**“So that we may confidently say”**
• this promise is not made to the tenacious, not to the covetous; whence it adds: So, etc.
• namely, he is with us
**“The Lord is my helper”**
• supplying necessary things
• and therefore
**“I will not fear what man shall do to me”** — even if he takes away my things
13.7:
**“Remember your prelates”**
• that you may imitate them, because they were good, namely the apostles and their successors
• Remember your prelates, etc. Because it is long to speak of each one, he advises following the teachers.
**“who have spoken to you”** — because they themselves are
**“who have spoken the word of God to you; whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation”** — that you may imitate them in death, if need be, by dying for Christ as they did, and in the conduct of good life and in faith not yet perfect
13.8:
**“Jesus Christ, yesterday, and today; and the same for ever”**
• that is, without end
• Jesus Christ yesterday, etc. This pertains to the preceding sentence, where he testified that God had said: “I will not leave thee, neither will I forsake thee.” For it might seem to them that this promise pertained to Josue alone; to which he answers that as he helped him, so he will help us. As if to say: it is not to be doubted, because he who yesterday, that is, in the past, helped Josue, today, that is, in the present, helps and will help those to come through all ages.
13.9:
**“Be not led away with various”**
• that is, diverse
• from mine
• With various doctrines, etc. Because through grace it is lawful to use all foods, some preached that it was no sin to abound in foods, but good. Others, however, superstitiously taught that one must abstain from certain foods which the law forbids, while permitting others; and by the difference and observance of foods they led many astray; against these the Apostle speaks. Doctrines which are various from ours, that is, different. As if to say: you ought to strengthen the heart by grace, which permits all things by freeing from the law, and not to be zealous about foods, because they have not profited unto salvation those who walk in them; I do not say those who sustain themselves, but those who persevere zealously in them. Or by discriminating or by abounding too much. Abstinence indeed, by which one abstains from sin, profits. But that keeping of foods profited nothing, but faith did. Likewise to abound in the gifts of graces profits; but to overwhelm the belly with a mass of foods harms.
• These are not absurdly compared to lepers, who, not having the knowledge of the true faith, profess various doctrines of error. For they do not hide their ignorance, but bring it to light as supreme skill and display the boastfulness of their speech. Moreover there is no false doctrine which does not mingle in some truth. Therefore truths mixed disorderedly with falsehoods in one discussion or narration are compared to the appearance of leprosy: as in a body of one color, so human bodies varying with diverse colors are compared to leprosy; such men are to be avoided, as the Apostle here teaches.
**“and strange”** — strange
**“Be not led away”**
• from the truth
• believing “all things are clean to the clean”
**“For it is best that the heart be established with grace”** — that you may have perfect faith
**“not with meats; which have not profited”** — not indifferent and abundant amounts of foods
**“those that walk in them”** — observers and discerners of foods, and those flowing in the abundance of foods
13.10:
**“We have an altar, whereof”**
• that is, of the body of Christ
• We have an altar, etc. Likewise one should not be concerned with foods, because we have an altar, that is, the body of Christ in faith, by whose offered prayers and works are acceptable to God.
**“We have an altar”** — He refers the custom of the law to the mystery and the spiritual sense. The precept of the law was that on the tenth day of the seventh month after the paschal feast, namely on the feast of propitiation, they should take a calf and a goat and sacrifice them within the camp, and only the high priest would carry their blood into the holy of holies to pray for the people. But the flesh was to be burned outside the camp, and it was not lawful for anyone serving the tabernacle to eat of it. Christ, however, is that calf and goat; for he is the calf which the loving father sacrificed at the return of the prodigal son. He is also the goat which was offered for sinners. He is also the high priest who entered heaven, interceding for us. Within the camp of Jerusalem he was sacrificed by the voices and judgment of the Jews, but outside, on the cross, his flesh was burned by the fire of the passion. The altar where the flesh was burned outside the camp is the altar of the Church, where the body of the Lord is consecrated. Of this they have no power to eat who serve the body, that is, fornicators and drunkards and the like. As Christ, so also his own, outside the camp, that is, the conversation of seculars, being kindled by the Holy Spirit, consume whatever is carnal in them, mortifying themselves and putting to death their members with the vices and concupiscences. Or also by martyrdom their blood, that is, a life praiseworthy to God, is presented through Christ. Or blood, that is, their souls are borne into heaven. On the altar, that is, they are offered by faith. To which the carnal who love the world dare not approach. To fulfil which mystery Jesus suffered outside the gate.
**“they have no power”** — permission
**“who serve the tabernacle”**
• to the body’s pleasure and abundance of foods
• That is, by the observances of the law, as those who discriminate foods and keep other such legal things, which he signifies by the name of tabernacle because they were imposed for a time. Or the body is rightly called a tabernacle, because one is to remain in it for a time, and therefore it is not to be served in its desires.
**“to eat”** — entirely
13.11:
**“For the bodies of those beasts”** — For the bodies of which, etc. By a twofold allegory, one of the Old and the other of the New Testament, he proves that the body of Christ is not to be eaten by those who serve the tabernacle. For to this end the bodies of the animals are burned outside the camp, and for this reason Christ suffered outside the gate, that we who wish to be cleansed from sins by his body and blood, being about to suffer reproaches and hardships, may forsake the delights of the tabernacle.
**“of those beasts”** — Christ was signified by those animals. He is a lamb according to meekness and innocence. A goat, because his flesh was passible and mortal. A ram, because he drove out vices with the twin horn of charity. A bull, by the strength of the resurrection. But what is burned is made ashes. By ashes the memory of a past thing is understood. To be outside the camp is to go out from the pleasures of the body. For those, then, who are outside the camp the body is burned, that is, a memorial is made; for if anyone lives voluptuously, he does not have an effective memory of Christ. But his blood was carried into the holy of holies by the high priest, because through himself as priest he was offered to the Father, that so we might enter into the heavenly holies. Or the bodies of these saints are burned, that is, are afflicted by fasts and other labors. Their blood is carried in outside the pleasures of the flesh, because the blood of Christ belongs only to those to whom it profits, through which they enter the holies. Which is the whole: the blood of Christ profits only those who forsake pleasures and afflict the body.
13.12:
**“For which cause”**
• not on account of himself
• that is, to signify this, that we may live outside the lusts of the flesh
**“Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people by his own blood, suffered without the gate”** — The gate is the sense of the body, in none of which Christ sinned, and therefore he suffered outside. And we, with the door of the senses closed to vices, should suffer outside.
13.13:
**“Let us go forth therefore”**
• by faith and charity
• because he himself is outside the camp
**“to him”** — To be imitated.
**“without the camp”** — the delights and pleasures of the body
**“bearing his reproach”** — of the cross, which seems so to unbelievers
**“bearing”** — bearing it patiently, as he did
13.14:
**“For we have not”** — Let us go out.
**“here”** — in this state
**“a lasting city”** — the remaining body
**“but we seek one that is to come”** — the body according to its future state
13.15:
**“By him therefore let us offer”** — that we may attain the city to come and bear the reproach
**“By him therefore”** — He who is for us the way, from whom we take the example for martyrdom.
**“the sacrifice of praise always to God”** — which was signified by the former things
**“confessing”** — Augustine. Therefore you that fear the Lord, praise him. But that you may worship him freely, learn to love him whom you fear, and you will be able to praise him whom you love. For the men of the Old Testament, fearing him, because of the letter that scorched and killed, not yet having the life-giving Spirit, ran with sacrifices to the temple, and, in figure of the blood of Christ by which we are redeemed, though not knowing what was prefigured, offered bloody victims. But now in the grace of the New Testament the spiritual sacrifice of praise is offered, by which God is honored, of which invisible sacrifice that visible sacrament was the sign.
**“to his name”** — that is, let us confess his name, which is the praise of God and the sacrifice and the fruit, because others are drawn to the faith through it.
13.16:
**“And do not forget to do good”**
• of almsgiving and generosity toward others
• Beneficence: that is, generosity toward others. And even if your substance has been taken away, nevertheless give alms from what you have. As above: “Not forsaking the assembly.”
**“to do good”** — Having set aside the judgment of the wicked about gluttony, it returns to morals.
**“and to impart”** — of charity, by which all things are held to be common
**“do not forget”** — not in those old sacrifices
**“for by such sacrifices God's favour is obtained”** — because through alms enemies are conquered, sins are extinguished. Whence the prophet: “I will have mercy, and not sacrifice.”
13.17:
**“Obey”** — Haimo. Prelates and preachers are indeed to be obeyed, insofar as their doctrine and conduct are holy and pious. But if they deviate from the way of rectitude, let us not do such things as they do, but such as they say, unless perhaps they err also in doctrine. Whence the Lord says: “What they say, do ye; but what they do, do ye not.” They have indeed dignity, though their lives be lost; and therefore look not to their life but to their conduct.
**“your prelates”** — as to the precepts, that is, that you do what the Church commands through them
**“and be subject to them”** — that you show reverence
**“For they”** — by preaching, by giving a good example, and by providing for outward matters
**“watch”** — they are anxious
**“as being to render an account of your souls”** — Obey.
**“that ... with joy”** — when they see you progressing
**“That ... with joy”** — Augustine. Let us by all means do these things with joy, when we see men advancing in the words of God. For then the laborer works with joy in the fields, when he looks at the trees and sees the fruit, when he looks at the crop and sees the abundance. Then he understands that he has not labored without cause, not without cause bent his back, not without cause worn out his hands, not without cause endured cold and heat.
**“do this”** — let them watch
**“and not with grief”** — with murmuring and sadness
**“For this is not expedient”** — not groaning, because then their care will not profit you
**“for you”**
• I do not mean for them, to whom it is profitable even to grieve over you.
• Or let them do this, that is, render account to God, secure about the reward, and not groaning anxious or doubting about your damnation.
**“Is not expedient for you”** — Augustine. I do not say it is not expedient for those for whom it is profitable to be sad on your account. For when those prelates are grieved over your evils, that very sadness is expedient for them, but not for you. Therefore let us together work good in the Lord’s field, prelates and subjects, that together we may rejoice in the reward.
13.18:
**“Pray for us”** — It strikes the pride and haughtiness of mind of certain prelates, who disdain to ask their subjects to pour out prayers for them.
**“For we trust”** — of you
**“we have a good conscience”**
• of past things
• the will
**“A good conscience”** — Our conscience does not accuse us, nor are we aware that we have laid snares for you; we have uttered nothing with pretence, we have done nothing for the sake of gain. Therefore do not think anything amiss.
**“we have ... in all things”**
• not only among the Gentiles
• The testament is eternal, because no other will succeed it.
**“In all things”** — He was accused of neglecting his own people, but he shows that he has affection for all Jews or Gentiles, in whose past good things he rejoices and for whom he wishes better things in the future.
**“being willing to behave ourselves well”** — both Jews and Greeks
**“behave ourselves”** — in the future
13.19:
**“And I beseech you the more”** — not only for my sake but rather for your advantage
**“to do this”** — to pray for me
**“that I may be restored to you the sooner”** — I urge you toward the good
13.20:
**“And may the God of peace”** — who can fit them, because he is the giver of peace, that vices may not be sought
**“who brought again”** — raised up
**“from the dead”** — from the tomb, which is properly the place of the dead
**“the great pastor of the sheep”**
• of the humble
• made shepherd also by the shedding of his blood, who confirmed the New Testament
13.21:
**“Fit you”**
• will make fit
• that you may will
**“in all goodness, that”** — also
**“you may do”** — in deed
**“his will”** — by that which he himself wills
**“his”** — he himself, because not from you
**“doing in you”** — Doing in you. For you can have nothing good unless he goes before and follows after.
**“that which is well pleasing in his sight”** — and this
**“through Jesus Christ”** — not through carnal observances
**“To whom”**
• to Christ together with the Father and the Holy Spirit
• not by carnal observances
**“glory for ever and ever. Amen.”** — as a confirmation, as it were: so be it, or it is true what I said
13.22:
**“And I beseech you, brethren, that you suffer”** — patiently
**“this word of consolation”** — that is, the epistle, which is consolation and exhortation, lest I say admonition
**“For in a few words”**
• not as an apostle have I written to you
• For I have written to you in a few words, etc. As if: no one can refuse the length of a discourse; for this is what the adversaries did, and therefore he touches on it covertly.
**“I have written to you”** — also by serving and honouring
13.23:
**“Know ye that our brother Timothy”** — fellow apostle and co-worker in preaching
**“is set at liberty”** — by me, on the journey he wished, either directed to preaching or perhaps from the prison in which he was previously held
**“with whom (if he come shortly) I will see you”** — in this he makes them attentive and more gentle
13.24:
**“Salute all your prelates”** — Salute all your prelates, etc. As he writes generally to all, so he generally wishes salvation to all prelates and subjects. For to salute is to wish salvation.
**“and all the saints”** — subjects sanctified in baptism
**“The brethren from Italy salute you”** — by this note that he wrote from Rome
13.25: **“Grace”** — the cleansing of sins and the other gifts of God

1.1:
**“James”**
• supplanter of vices, or wrestler
• a famous person placed in office, who urges that his precept and counsel be observed with reverence
• He, sent to preach after the apostles, took up the care and government of the Church of Jerusalem.
**“the servant of God, and of our Lord Jesus Christ,”** — a notable office
**“the twelve tribes”** — not to all, but to some of all
**“The twelve tribes”** — To have a special care for these belonged to the twelve apostles, who discharged an embassy for the Lord to the circumcision. Whence Paul also says: “James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship: that we should go unto the Gentiles, and they unto the circumcision,” etc. Therefore he writes to them especially, and because he himself had been ordained bishop over them by the other apostles.
**“which are scattered abroad, greeting.”**
• faith and steadfastness
• or he wishes eternal life
1.2:
**“All”**
• not temporal or passing, but perfect
• eternal
**“count it all joy”**
• tribulation in the present increases the crown of justice in the future
• there is nothing for you to grieve over, nothing to doubt
**“All joy”** — Be not indignant if the wicked flourish in the world, or if you suffer, because it is not of Christian truth to be exalted in temporal things but rather to be cast down. The wicked have nothing in heaven, you nothing in the world. By hope of that good toward which you strive, you ought to rejoice in whatever happens on the way.
**“My brethren,”** — because they are from the same Father and are to have the same things
**“when you shall fall into divers temptations”**
• which tempt in various ways
• either from persecution or from concupiscence
• various temptations come from the devil, or from a neighbour, or God tempts
**“shall fall into”** — as if from on high, of your faith
**“When you shall fall into divers temptations”** — He begins with the more perfect, concerning temptations from outside.
1.3:
**“Knowing”** — that is, the tribulation by which faith is proved
**“of your faith”** — which our faith requires
**“worketh patience.”** — causes them to understand and to have the power of patience
**“The trying of your faith worketh patience”** — The same sentence is read in Paul, but in converse order: “Knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience trial; and trial hope.” For patience works trial, because he whose patience is not overcome by tribulations is proved perfect; which sentence is also said here: patience hath a perfect work; and trial works patience, which is tribulation, given for the trial of faith; it causes to be exercised by patience that by which perfect faith is proved.
1.4: **“And patience hath a perfect work; that you may be perfect and entire, failing in nothing.”** — that is, makes them work perfectly; for this reason it follows: that you may be perfect, not failing in torments, and entire in the future, receiving full blessedness
1.5:
**“But if any of you want wisdom”**
• by which he may understand how useful tribulation is
• Such is the usefulness of tribulations that if anyone is ignorant of it, he is not yet enlightened by the Holy Spirit; let him therefore ask that his understanding be opened by the Holy Spirit, and he will know with what love the Father corrects the sons whom he receives. Nor let anyone conscious of his own frailty distrust, because he gives to all: “He hath blessed all that fear the Lord, both little and great.” And because many ask what they do not deserve to receive, he adds how they ought to ask: but let him ask in faith, nothing wavering.
**“let him ask of God”** — the Spirit who enlightens
**“who giveth to all men”** — to those who ask devoutly: “Not every one that saith to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven”; nor does he give to every just man what he asks if he asks against his own salvation, as to Paul, to whom it was said when he asked that the sting be taken away: “My grace is sufficient for thee”
**“abundantly,”** — because his gifts are not by measure
**“and upbraideth not”** — his frailty
**“and it shall be given him.”** — that very wisdom which comes from heaven
1.6:
**“But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering.”** — so let him believe and so live that he is worthy to be heard, for “he that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be as abomination”
**“For he that wavereth”** — He who, pressed by the consciousness of sin, doubts of the heavenly rewards, easily abandons the state of faith when the wind of temptations comes upon him, and is drawn away to error according to the tempter’s will and becomes a stranger to God.
**“is like a wave of the sea, which is moved by the wind”** — because he is moved by the wind of temptation like a wave
**“and carried about.”** — For he who doubts is like a wave of the sea.
1.7:
**“Therefore let not that man think”** — The carnal man who doubts
**“that he shall receive any thing of the Lord.”**
• by merit
• either here or in the future
1.8:
**“A double minded man”**
