• He who doubts does not receive, because he who doubts is double-minded, and the double-minded does not receive.
• He is double who bends the knee in prayers, and, his conscience gnawing, distrusts that he will obtain. Double is he who wants to rejoice with the world and rejoice with God, who in the good things he does seeks not God but favor. Whence it is said: “Woe to them that go into the land by two ways.”
**“is inconstant in all his ways.”** — he is easily terrified by adversity and entangled by prosperity, so that he turns away from the truth
1.9: **“But let the brother of low condition glory in his exaltation:”** — made poor and cast down among the wicked, let him understand this humiliation as exaltation before God
1.10:
**“And the rich”**
• He calls rich the one who places all hope in riches; it does no harm to have riches, but to love them.
• Let him glory, ironically. As if to say: he ought not to glory in his glory, by which he is proud and oppresses others, because it is to be ended and brought low in hell. Or let him glory in his humility, that is, let him not be proud but humble himself by serving others with his riches.
**“because as the flower of the grass”** — quickly loses his grace
**“shall he pass away.”**
• this glory
• truly the flower passes quickly because
• For as the flower of the grass, etc. “The just shall flourish like the palm tree,” the unjust like hay, because the former remains, the latter quickly passes away. The flower of the just is hope, which awaits the fruit; the root of the just is charity, which remains unmoved. The root of the wicked is cupidity; the flower, delight in temporal things.
1.11:
**“For the sun rose”** — Christ of righteousness
**“with a burning heat, and parched the grass, and”** — then
**“the flower thereof fell off, and the beauty of the shape thereof perished.”**
• with the flower falling, all the beauty of the hay perishes
• the honor of the world, friends, and such things
**“so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways.”**
• he will perish in his deeds because he neglects the straight way of the Lord
• truly you ought to suffer temptation
• The rich man in his ways, etc. The ways of the rich are temporal things by which he seeks to be made blessed, which will quickly be destroyed. The heat of the sun is the coming of the stern judge, either unforeseen at each one’s death, or at the judgment in common. In which the just man will remain like a fruitful tree.
1.12:
**“Blessed is the man”** — Because it is hard to exhort to contempt of the world, he adds about the greatness of the reward.
**“Blessed is the man that”** — You ought to suffer not only blows and prisons, but also the loss of temporal things, which are base and transitory, and whose lovers are to be punished.
**“that endureth temptation”** — because through the exercise of temptations the perfect one is proved in faith; on account of which he is also tempted
**“for when he hath been proved”** — the true believer through temptation
**“he shall receive a crown of life”** — as conquerors
**“which God hath promised”** — through the prophets and apostles
**“to them that love him.”** — not worldly things
1.13:
**“Let no man, when he is tempted,”**
• is caught by inner temptation
• Thus far of outward temptations. Now of those which we bear inwardly, from the devil’s instigation, or also from the frailty of nature. Here he also destroys the error of those who said that evil thoughts, like good ones, are inspired in us by God, and that man sins as if of necessity.
**“say that he is tempted by God.”** — as if God sends in evil thoughts
**“that he is tempted by God”** — God sends the outward temptation for the proving of his own, but the inward, by which theft, adultery and murder are often conceived, God does not send.
**“For God is not a tempter”** — is not the sender
**“of evils”** — of temptations
**“is; for he tempteth no man.”** — he brings no one into temptation
1.14:
**“every man is tempted”**
• by God none; but rather
• When we build wood, hay, stubble upon the foundation, the devil lays fire on top. Let us build gold, silver, precious stones, and he does not dare to tempt, yet he does not altogether desist but “sitteth in ambush in private places, that he may kill the innocent.”
• God and the devil tempt with different intent. The devil tempts that he may cast the tempted into sadness, into bitterness, into murmuring against God and into despair. God tempts that he may show to a man who acknowledges and confesses his weakness that strength stands in the hope of divine mercy alone. Whence: “For virtue is known or made perfect in weakness.” And in the Psalm: “It was weakened, but thou hast made it perfect.” In temptations sadness is driven away by joy; in successes, however, pride is pressed down by fear.
**“Every man is tempted”** — There are two kinds of temptation. One proves, as God tempted Abraham; the other deceives, since God tempts no one.
*Augustine:* Temptation is carried out in three ways: by the suggestion of the enemy, by delight, or also by the consent of our frailty. If we do not consent to the suggestion, the temptation turns out to us for victory. If we offend by delighting in the enticing suggestion, yet we do not yet incur death. But if the delight in the sin conceived in the heart is followed by the birth of a wicked deed, the enemy departs as victor, and we are guilty of death.
**“by his own concupiscence”** — either when the flesh seeks sweet things for itself or when the devil sends in incitements
**“Drawn away”** — from the right way
**“and allured”** — to evil
1.15:
**“Then when concupiscence”**
• by delighting or consenting
• a deed in the heart
**“bringeth forth sin”** — brings forth to the act openly
**“But sin, when it is completed, begetteth death”**
• through the act and led into the habit of a wicked life
• and because sins are not from God
**“Begetteth death”** — As one who is tempted and overcomes wins the rewards of life, so one who is enticed by desires and is overcome rightly incurs the ruin of death.
1.16:
**“Do not err, therefore”** — thinking that the temptations of vices come from God
**“my dearest brethren”**
• to whom I would persuade nothing useless
• as if he said: you ought not to dissent from us
1.17:
**“All”**
• evils not from God, rather good things
• because the first grace and its increase is from God
**“best gift”** — such as chastity and other virtues
**“and every perfect gift”** — the carrying out of those virtues, or eternal life, which is perfect
**“is from above, coming down from the Father of lights”**
• as a ray of the sun from the sun
• Every gift, etc. Having shown that vices are not from God to us but from ourselves, he shows on the other hand that whatever good we do is not from ourselves but from God. Whence he calls him Father of lights, that is, the author of all spiritual gifts. “Gift” (datum) refers to nature, “gift” (donum) to grace; and the donum of grace is wont to be ascribed to the man himself to whom it is given. But the good of nature also is from God. In baptism grace is the best gift; and in the giving of the Holy Spirit the perfect gift can be understood.
**“with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration”** — in whose nature there is no mutability but sameness, and not only in nature but also in the distribution of gifts, because he sends only gifts of light and not the darkness of errors
**“Nor shadow of alteration”** — No shadow interrupts his light, so that he would send any evils. But always the good gifts of light; in us sometimes the gifts of God, which, coming upon us, overshadow sins, which is not in God.
1.18:
**“Of his own will”** — Every good is from God, and you came to this not by your merits but by the sole grace of the divine will.
**“hath he begotten”** — through the water of regeneration into sons of light
**“us”** — before, sons of darkness
**“by the word of truth”**
• the teaching of the gospel
• to this
**“that we might be some beginning of his creatures”** — That we might be some beginning, etc. Let us not think that by this begetting we are what he is. But by adoption he has granted us a certain pre-eminence among creatures. Whence another translator: that we might be the firstfruits of his creatures.
1.19:
**“You know, my dearest brethren”** — that you had from yourselves to slip into vices; to be enlightened by the Lord’s heavenly grace
**“And let every man be swift”**
• and that the beginning of the creature, to which you were begotten, may persevere in you
• But let every man be, etc. Above he admonished to endurance of temptations; next he instructs with moral precepts.
• First he admonishes to lend the ear to the teacher, and to open the mouth to teach late, because it is foolish for a man to preach to others what he has not learned. Let him therefore who loves wisdom first ask it of God, then seek out a master of truth, and restrain his tongue not only from idle talk but even from preaching the truth which he has but lately received. Whence Solomon: “A time to keep silence, and a time to speak,” because truth is more safely heard than preached.
**“to hear”** — from the teachers of truth
**“but slow to speak”** — lest he presume to teach before the time
**“Slow to anger”** — Let him not be angry rashly and without cause, whether against subjects who sin, or against any brethren, or against the prosperity of the wicked, because the maturity of wisdom is perceived only with a tranquil mind. And he who judges in anger, even if he judges justly, yet cannot imitate the justice of the divine judgment, in which no disturbance falls.
1.20:
**“For the anger of man”** — because
**“worketh not the justice of God”** — an angry man, though among men, is not just before God
1.21:
**“Wherefore”**
• because you ought to be attentive to hearing
• Wherefore. He admonished to seek doctrine and to receive it, and that they may make progress in it, he exhorts to cleanness of body and soul. He who does not turn aside from evil cannot do good.
**“casting away all uncleanness”**
• in external things
• of soul and body
**“and abundance”** — according to wicked men abounding in riches
**“of naughtiness”** — malice properly refers to the depravity of the inner man
**“with meekness”** — against anger
**“receive”**
• with great honour
• and receive it not by hearing only but also fulfil it by work, because the righteous are not hearers of the law but doers
**“the ingrafted word, which is able to save your souls”** — even if you suffer temptations or even death in the body
**“The ingrafted word”** — What we impose on your hearts by preaching, or the word which was ingrafted and sown in the day of redemption, when God begot you: now receive it more perfectly and fulfil by works what you hold in mystery.
1.22:
**“But be ye doers of the word”** — by work
**“and not hearers”** — without works
**“deceiving your own selves”** — if you think you are to be saved by hearing alone
1.23:
**“For if a man be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he shall be compared to a man beholding his own countenance in a glass”** — in the bodily mirror, where only the shadow shines back
**“Beholding his own countenance”** — Allegorically. He who purposes in his mind to consider in the Scriptures, as in a mirror, the face of his birth, how man is born, how frail, what he is to be, how short of life, placed in how great miseries, has conceived great compunction and the will to repent, and presently, seduced by some temptation, forgets his compunction and returns to sins. With his inconstancy is compared he who gladly hears the word and neglects to fulfil it. And there is a likeness between him who of his own accord, without a teacher, has applied himself to the Scriptures, and him who hears the Scriptures from another, since neither has fulfilled them. A child when it is born cries, by which is shown the sorrow of the soul, that it enters unwillingly into the miseries of the flesh; which sorrow it afterwards forgets, accustomed to the allurements of the flesh.
1.24:
**“For he beheld himself, and went his way, and presently forgot what manner of man he was”**
• because he saw not the thing but only the shadow; so too he who has the shadow of words, not the body of work
• he who thinks he is saved by hearing alone is deceived, but
1.25:
**“But he that hath looked into the perfect law of liberty”** — by hearing the word of the gospel
**“In the perfect law of liberty”** — The law of perfect liberty he calls the grace of the gospel, which makes men perfectly free from the servitude of fear. Those who held the law served in fear. Whoever transgressed it was stoned without mercy. This law brought no one to perfection, because although it compelled men to serve by fear, it did not give grace that it might be fulfilled by love, and it could not free from the punishments of hell. But the charity which is given in the gospel “casteth out fear” and leads to life.
**“and hath continued therein”** — by continuance of work
**“not becoming a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work”** — not in hearing
**“this man shall be blessed in his deed”** — in the future, even if here miserable
1.26:
**“And if any man”** — Not only be doers of the word, but also bridle the tongue.
**“think himself to be religious”**
• by the faith which he has, and by the works of faith.
• If any man think himself, etc. He had warned them to hear the word of God not only but also to fulfil it. Now, that he may make them fortified on every side, he adds that all these things avail nothing unless the tongue also be restrained from detractions, lies, blasphemies, foolish talk, much talking, because: “Evil communications corrupt good manners.”
**“not bridling his tongue, but deceiving his own heart”** — not understanding that he is to be punished for the sin of the tongue.
**“this man's religion is vain”** — this religion is useless, not clean.
1.27:
**“Religion clean”** — in the intention of the heart.
**“and undefiled”** — in the carrying out of the work.
**“Religion clean, etc. Because he had said the doer of the work is blessed, he now says what deeds most please, namely mercy and innocence. For in that he bade us visit the fatherless and widows, he suggests all that we ought to do toward our neighbour. In that he bids us keep ourselves unspotted from the world, he shows all the things in which it becomes us to keep ourselves chaste. Among these are also those things he warned should be observed above, as slow to speak, slow to anger. Before God and the Father”** — who is not deceived in judging as men are, and who kindly cares for his sons and repays.
**“is this: to visit”** — to help.
**“the fatherless and widows”** — who lack the protection of fathers and husbands, of whom it is said: “As long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.”
**“in their tribulation”** — in time of need.
**“and to keep one's self unspotted from this world”** — he who loves the world does not keep himself unspotted from the world.

2.1:
**“My brethren”**
• and that you may be unspotted.
• My brethren. He shows that those to whom he wrote were steeped in faith but empty of works, and gave the alms he preached not to the poor for eternal things but to the rich for temporal advantages; hence he rebukes them.
**“have not with respect of persons”**
• whoever chooses the rich man for his riches and rejects the poor man for his poverty sins in both respects.
• Do not, in respect of persons, etc. As if: the Lord would invite the rich to faith and despise the poor. It is not so, because the Lord chose the poor in this world and endowed them with faith.
• The world casts out the poor and honors the rich; the faith of Christ teaches the contrary, because “all the glory of the rich as the flower of grass,” mercy toward the poor flourishes forever.
**“Of glory”** — He names the Lord of glory, so that obedience be given to him who rewards with everlasting glory whatever is given to the poor for love of him.
2.2: **“For if there shall come into your assembly”** — or “our assembly.”
2.3:
**“And you have respect to him that is clothed with the fine apparel, and shall say to him: Sit thou here well”** — in an honorable place.
**“But say to the poor man: Stand thou there, or sit under my footstool”** — Sit thou, etc. Stand thou, etc. Augustine. If we refer this distinction of sitting and standing to ecclesiastical honours, it is not to be thought a light sin to have “the faith of the Lord of glory with respect of persons.” For who could bear that a rich man be chosen for the seat of honour in the Church, while a poor man, better instructed and holier, is despised? But if he speaks of daily gatherings, who does not sin here? Yet he does not sin unless he so judges within himself, that the richer a man seems the better he seems to him; for this he seems to have signified by adding: “Do you not judge within yourselves, and are become judges of unjust thoughts?”
2.4:
**“Do you not judge”** — that is, do you not work sin?
**“within yourselves”** — not from God.
**“and are become judges of thoughts”** — that is, you ought to judge among yourselves that you think wickedly in respect of persons.
**“unjust”** — that is, of men.
2.5:
**“Hearken”** — Attend more diligently, because those who are richer in the world are not better in the divine judgment, and therefore are not to be preferred. For God has chosen not the rich but the poor, that is, the humble, for their contempt of visible things, but in the faith of invisible riches; they appear contemptible to the world, yet he has made them illustrious and noble by the expectation of the future kingdom.
**“my dearest brethren: hath not God chosen the poor in this world”**
• needy in temporal goods, but
• Did not God choose? God chose the poor, saying: “Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you a kingdom.” He also chose poor parents, by whose service he would be nourished.
**“rich”** — Do not the rich, etc.? He shows more plainly whom he meant above by the rich, namely those who prefer riches to Christ, and who, themselves strangers to the faith, oppress by power those who believe, and drag them to the judgments of the more powerful. And this is another reason why they are not to be chosen, that they bring evils upon the faithful.
**“in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which God hath promised to them that love him”** — not worldly things.
2.6:
**“But you have dishonoured”** — or “you have honored.”
**“the poor man”** — by saying: “You stand there.”
**“Do not the rich oppress you by might?”** — by taking away goods, by beating.
**“and do not they draw you before the judgment seats?”** — and they make you condemned without fault.
2.7:
**“Do not”** — also
**“blaspheme”** — In the times of the apostles, many of the Gentiles, and especially the chief men of the Jews, are found to have done this.
**“the good name”** — the saving name of Christ
**“that is invoked upon you?”** — for your protection
2.8:
**“If then the law”**
• of grace
• Because he had spoken harshly of the contempt of the rich, and in a manner contrary to the divine law, which commands that all be loved, he adds this, lest the rich be thought altogether to be despised. As if to say: for the aforesaid reasons they are not to be chosen. But yet if you fulfil this law which says, “Thou shalt love thy neighbour,” you do well; because although the rich are not to be chosen on account of riches, yet for God’s sake they are not to be loved the less.
**“you fulfill the royal”**
• excellent among the others
• Or, the law that says “Respect not the person of the poor, nor honour the countenance of the mighty”; and elsewhere, “There shall be no difference of persons, you shall hear the little as well as the great, because it is the judgment of God.”
**“Royal”** — That is, excellent, or because it is common to all and embraces all.
**“according to the scriptures”**
• as the Scriptures testify
• namely this
2.9:
**“But if”** — or indeed
**“have respect to persons”** — that is, you cast off the poor because of their poverty and advance the rich to honours because of their wealth
2.10:
**“And whosoever”** — Lest they think it a slight sin to transgress the law in this one thing, he adds: Whosoever.
**“shall keep the whole law”** — has resolved in mind to keep
**“but offend in one point”**
• But offend in one point, etc. Truly he who offends in one is a transgressor of the whole law, because he who sins against the author of the law acts against him whom he neglects in his law, and against charity, which is the cause and mother of the whole law.
• Let us see this sentence by a likeness. If someone offended me, he would offend all my brothers and friends in me, and in a way would sin against all of them. So he who neglects one commandment makes the rest, which seemed to be fulfilled, useless to himself.
• Or otherwise. “Charity is the fulfilling of the law,” on whose precepts the whole law depends. But he who acts against charity is rightly guilty of all. For no one sins unless he acts against charity, since he neither truly loves God whose law he neglects, nor the neighbour against whom he offends. Since therefore he had shown above that they sin against charity when they say to the poor man, “Stand thou there,” he fittingly adds: He who offends in one, that is, in charity, which is the root of all the precepts, is accused by all the precepts, which are as it were the children of charity. But when that one in which he had offended is reconciled, all the rest are reconciled. Why then are the sins not called equal? I do not know, unless perhaps because he who sins more gravely acts more against charity and offends the Church more, and he who sins more lightly, less.
**“is become guilty of all”** — not from human frailty but by thinking it slight
**“guilty of all”** — With God, who lets nothing go unpunished, who knows how necessary the law he gave is: he who neglects a commandment believes it was instituted by God in vain.
2.11: **“For he that said, Thou shalt not commit adultery, said also, Thou shalt not kill. Now if thou do not commit adultery, but shalt kill, thou art become a transgressor of the law.”** — and so a despiser of the lawgiver
2.12:
**“So speak ye”** — to neighbours
**“and so do”**
• so be merciful to your neighbours as God is to you
• Otherwise. He is judged more gravely who despises the law of Moses than he who despises the natural law. More gravely also he who despises the law of grace than he who despises the law of Moses. As if to say: speak well and do well, because if you neglect this you will be condemned more gravely than those who lived in the time of Moses; for to whom more is committed, from him more is required. The greater the mercy a man obtains from the Lord, the more unjustly he denies mercy to his needy neighbour, and the more justly he pays the penalties of impiety.
**“So speak ye, and so do”** — Since indeed it is evil that the rich man be chosen for his riches and the poor man cast out, and since it is good, for God’s sake, to love even the rich, and to visit orphans and widows, therefore so speak and so do. In speaking and doing this, take care that by loving your neighbours you may deserve to be loved by God, and that, showing mercy, you may be found worthy of mercy. The law of liberty is the law of charity, which he called royal above, by which it is said: “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” By this law God judges you when he gives great mercy, because you are not judged by the law of punishments and servitude, but by the law of grace, which calls the willing to penance and forgives sins.
2.13:
**“For judgment without mercy to him that hath not done mercy.”** — and you ought to act mercifully, for he who could and did not show mercy, before he is judged, will be judged without mercy
**“And mercy exalteth itself above”**
• it is placed above judgment and as it were lights up judgment, which is with mercy; for through mercy itself it is more commendable and pleases more
• But mercy exalteth itself above judgment, etc. As in the judgment he who has not done mercy will grieve, so he who has done it, being rewarded, will exult and rejoice. Otherwise: It exalteth itself above. Mercy is set above judgment in him in whom a work of mercy shall be found; even if he have something in the judgment for which he may be punished, the fire of sin is extinguished by the work of mercy as by water. Otherwise: Mercy exalteth itself. Many are gathered in through mercy, namely those who have shown mercy: “Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.”
• Here he disputes more at large about works of mercy, that he may console those whom he had terrified by the preceding sentence, teaching by what remedies daily sins are expiated, without which life is not lived, lest those who offend not in one point only but in many be found in the judgment guilty of all.
**“judgment”** — or judgment
2.14:
**“What shall it profit, my brethren, if a man say he hath faith”** — you ought to act well, because those are deceived who believe faith alone suffices
**“but hath not works”** — when he has time to work
**“Shall faith be able to save him?”** — faith without works is dead, but faith that works through love saves
2.16: **“And one of you say to them: Go in peace, be ye warmed and filled; yet give them not those things that are necessary for the body, what shall it profit?”** — your charity to them
2.17:
**“So faith also, if it have not works”**
• or without works
• by which it may revive
• What is read: “He that believeth and is baptized, shall be saved.” It is to be understood of perfect faith, which works through love.
**“So faith also, if”** — As mere kind words do not refresh the naked or the hungry unless food and clothing are also given, so faith kept only in word does not save.
**“is dead in itself”** — against itself, because what it promised in words it does not fulfil.
2.18:
**“But some man will say”**
• mockingly
• to you
• someone
• Not only for the reasons given above ought you to be urged to do good works, but also so that you do not suffer reproach from others. For someone, confident in his works, wishing to show that faith alone is worth nothing, will say by way of reproach: “Thou hast faith, etc.”
**“Thou hast faith”** — without works
**“and I have works”** — of faith
**“shew me thy faith without works”** — Because you have no works. If you can, show by some certain signs that I may believe you are faithful; but you will not be able, since the works are lacking.
**“and I will shew thee, by works, my faith”** — but I can prove by the works I have that I am faithful.
2.19:
**“Thou believest”** — He has proved that those who have no works do not have true faith. Now he reveals what sort of faith they have, lest they magnify that kind of faith.
**“that there is one God. Thou dost well”** — I do not condemn it, but it is not enough.
**“the devils also”** — do not think you are doing anything great, for even devils
**“believe”** — believe that God is one.
**“And the devils also believe”** — It is written: “Devils went out from men, crying out and saying: Thou art the Son of God”; but the legion also that possessed the man cried out in fear: “What have I to do with thee, Son of the most high God? I adjure thee by God that thou torment me not.” Therefore those who do not believe in God, or do not fear what they believe, are slower and more shameless than the devils.
**“and tremble”** — which is more
2.20:
**“But wilt thou know”**
• I will use not only reasons but also example and authority.
• Having proved that faith without works is dead, in order to invite them more clearly to good work, he sets before those who had believed from the circumcision the fine example of good work in the patriarch Abraham, that as good sons they may imitate their good father in temptation and in work.
**“O vain man”** — without works
2.21:
**“Abraham our father”** — That Abraham is said to have been justified by faith without works is understood of the works that went before; for he was not just by the works he did, but by faith alone. Here the matter concerns works that follow faith, by which he is further justified, since he had already been just by faith. Whence Paul: “By faith Abraham, when he was tried, offered Isaac.” This offering is a work and a testimony of faith and of justice. Paul praises in Abraham the constancy of faith; James praises the magnificence of works, because Abraham was perfect in both, and is set forth as an example in both.
**“was not justified by works”** — Although Abraham was just through the faith he had, yet he was justified also through the works he had; and he added “more,” that is, he was justified more; for had he not done them, he would have lost the merit of his preceding faith.
**“offering”**
• namely from these
• that is, wishing to offer
**“Offering”** — Great the temptation when he was commanded to kill his son; great the faith when he believed that he could receive seed even from the dead. Great the work when he did not hesitate to offer his most beloved.
**“Isaac his son”** — for he thought that God is able to raise even the dead
2.22:
**“Seest”** — Because he offered him in whom he had received the promise, the great power of faith appears: even as he offered, he believed the promise would be fulfilled, because he believed God powerful even to raise the dead.
**“faith did co-operate with his works; and by works faith was made perfect”** — Before, by faith, he was just; and faith led to works, and through works faith itself was increased and proved; and so through that faith which led to works the truth of Scripture appears: he believed the son promised, and was bidden to sacrifice him.
2.23: **“And the scripture was fulfilled, saying: Abraham believed God, and it was reputed to him to justice”** — Abraham believed God, etc. Augustine. To believe in God is one thing, to believe God another, to believe that God is another. To believe that he is, is to believe that he is God. To believe him is to believe that what he says is true. To believe in him is to tend toward him with charity. The first and the second are not doubted to belong to demons and to many wicked men. The third belongs only to the good.
2.24:
**“Do you see”** — because so it is in Abraham
**“that by works”** — of faith
**“a man is justified”** — who has time to work
**“and not by faith only”** — without works
2.25:
**“In like manner”** — Lest they should plead that works could not imitate so great a father, especially since now no one compels sons to be offered, he adds the example of a sinful woman who by works of mercy and hospitality was freed from her sins, and was enrolled as a citizen of the people of Israel and numbered in the generations of the Saviour.
**“Rahab”** — Broadness, which signifies the Church enlarged by faith. By her example he warns us, in order to avoid the ruin of a perishing country, to receive by works of mercy the messengers of Christ, and to keep them and send them back to Jesus; as blessed Gamaliel is read to have done.
**“was she justified by works”** — not only Abraham through greater works but also Rahab through lesser works was justified
**“receiving the messengers”** — Josue
**“and sending them out another way”** — that they might not be killed by the men of the city
2.26: **“For even as the body without the spirit is dead; so also faith without works is dead”** — truly Abraham was justified by the works of faith, because without works even Abraham himself would not have been just, much less others

3.1:
**“Be ye not”**
• only those who are discreet and taught in the Scriptures
• As I warned you to do works, so I warn you to avoid foolish teachings.
• Be not many, etc. There were many in the times of the apostles who came down from Judea to Antioch, not well instructed in the law of faith, and taught that believers from among the Gentiles ought to be circumcised, and brought in other errors, which gave the true preachers no small labour of controversy. He therefore removes these from the office of the word, lest they hinder the true preachers.
**“many masters”** — or in several churches, or several in one; do not wish to be teachers
**“My brethren,”** — to whom I wish good things
**“knowing that you receive the greater judgment”** — Greater judgment. He who, untaught, presumes the office of teaching, and does not proclaim Christ sincerely, deserves a greater damnation than if he alone perished by his own crime. Just as, on the contrary, he who ministers well acquires for himself a good rank.
**“receive”** — by presuming to teach
3.2:
**“For in many things we all offend”**
• because we are imperfect both in word and in other things; for he alone is perfect who does not offend in word
• In many things, etc. It is truly dangerous, because not only you who are less learned but we all, even the greater preachers, offend in many things: some by teaching ill, others by living ill, and in other ways. He numbers himself with them that he may rebuke the more freely. The just man offends in one way, the wicked man in another. The just man, through the frailty of the flesh, does not cease to be just. Whence Solomon: “A just man shall fall seven times, and shall rise again.” As the offence is daily, so the remedy of prayers and good works is daily. But the wicked fall into evil.
**“If any man”** — He wishes to show the unavoidable offence of the word, so as to deter the unskilled from desiring preeminence, because whoever desires to be over others must be more perfect than they, lest he offend while he ought to benefit. But the unskilled cannot avoid offending in preaching.
**“in word”** — That is, of that offence which human frailty can avoid: such as a word of deceit, of detraction, of pride, of boasting; but also of idle and superfluous speech.
**“offend not”** — not another
**“the same is a perfect man”** — he who can guard against offence of the word can all the more easily lead about all the members of the body, which are more easily corrected, to good works, that it be not turned aside from the right path.
3.3:
**“For if we put bits into the mouths of horses”** — Understand: and we ought much more to put them in our own mouths. Some books have: “Now if we put bits into the mouths of horses,” etc., and it is joined to what follows: “As we put bits into the mouths of horses, etc., so also the tongue is indeed a little member, and boasteth great things.”
**“If we put bits into the mouths of horses”**
• The comparison with horses shows the fitness and capacity to bridle the tongue. The comparison with ships also sets forth the reward or the penalty for restraint, while it says the tongue boasts great things.
• Allegorically. The great ships on the sea are the minds of men in the world; the winds by which they are threatened are the desires of the mind, by which they are naturally driven to do something through which they come to a good end or to a bad. The rudder is the intention of the heart, by which the good, having passed the waves of the world, seek the harbour of salvation, while the reprobate perish as though on Scylla or Charybdis. And because “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh,” he rightly adds: So also the tongue is a little member.
**“that they may obey us”** — it is fitting that we put bridles of restraint in our own mouths, so as to agree with our Creator, so that through guarding the tongue we also obtain uprightness of works, because it is so in this likeness
**“and we turn about their whole body”** — or of them
3.4:
**“Behold”** — I bring in another comparison to prove the same thing
**“ships, whereas they are great, and are driven by strong winds”** — or: strong
3.5:
**“Even so the tongue is indeed a little member, and boasteth great things”** — or: exults
**“and boasteth great things”** — That is, it boasts great rewards, if the impulse of the one directing it governs it well. If ill, it boasts great perdition for himself and his own. Whence Solomon: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue”: it exalts life if he teaches the Church well; death, if ill. For he acts against those who, destitute of both life and knowledge, presumed to teach.
**“boasteth great things”** — Some books have “and exulteth in great things,” because, despising the words and sense of others, it boasts itself alone as wise and eloquent. Against which: “Do not multiply to speak lofty things, boasting.”
**“Behold how small a fire”**
• how small or slight
• or: behold, a small fire
**“Behold how small a fire kindleth a great wood”** — So too an unrestrained tongue makes a great store of good works perish. And since it is almost impossible for even the perfect to avoid sin of the tongue, not just anyone ought to seek the office of teacher.
3.6:
**“And the tongue”** — by speaking evil it devours the forest of virtues
**“is a fire”** — it itself is
**“a world of iniquity”** — Because through it nearly all crimes are either plotted, such as robberies and rapes, or committed, such as perjuries and false witness, or defended, as when any impure man, excusing the crime he committed, pretends the good he did not do.
**“The tongue is placed among our members”** — among the members
**“which defileth the whole body”**
• by perjury and in other ways
• And because the tongue is such, it defiles the whole body and makes it reckoned unclean in the sight of God; and therefore it is grave to undertake the office of teaching, because it is set among our members, one of our members, very near to us.
**“and inflameth the wheel of our nativity”** — It defiles the whole course of temporal life until death; or, as we are driven by a running wheel. Or the wheel of our nativity, because, cast out from inward happiness by the merit of the first transgression, we are hurried hither and thither with a wandering mind, so that we do not know where the danger is or where the safety. This wheel of nativity is inflamed by the fire of the tongue when the vice of native disorder is heaped up even with foolish and harmful speeches.
**“being set on fire by hell”**
• that is, by the suggestion of the devil
• and truly an evil tongue
**“hell”** — The devil, for whom hell was made. As hell always burns, so the devil, wherever he is, whether in the air or under the earth, carries with him the torments of his flames, and, moved by this punishment, he suggests the flame of vices to men; and what he has suggested to them out of envy, he opens through the incontinence of the tongue, and compels it to be carried into effect through the other members.
3.7:
**“For every nature of beasts, and of birds, and of serpents, and of the rest, is tamed”**
• daily
• Otherwise. Some are beastly in sense and action, some birds in fickleness, others serpents in cunning to harm; they can be converted more easily than the tongue can be restrained by a teacher.
**“For every nature”** — We read in Pliny of a most savage asp, tamed in Egypt by a certain householder, which came out of its cave daily and was accustomed to receive its food from his table. We read in Marcellinus of a tigress made tame, sent from India to the emperor Anastasius.
**“For every”** — The tongue of the wicked surpasses beasts in fierceness, birds in lightness, serpents in venom. Some are beastly, who have “sharpened their tongues like a sword.” Some are winged, who “have set their mouth against heaven,” and “whose mouth hath spoken vanity.” Some are serpentine, of whom it is said: “The venom of asps is under their lips.”
**“and hath been tamed”** — already before
3.8:
**“But the tongue no man can tame”** — no teacher can restrain the talkative tongue of his subjects; no one is there who at some time does not offend in the tongue
**“an unquiet evil”**
• it does not rest in one, so that only the talkative man sins, but like poison it creeps from one into another by passing over; he who detracts from a brother provokes him to speak ill, of whose atrocity of poison he adds more
• it cannot be tamed, because it is
3.9:
**“By it we bless God and the Father”** — by giving thanks or praising
**“and by it we curse”** — by detracting
**“men, who are made after the likeness of God”**
• rational, as he himself is, or as he himself chiefly presides over all, so also men preside over the other creatures
• by the dishonour of the creature we offend the Creator
3.10:
**“Out of the same mouth”** — and because we bless God and curse men
**“proceedeth blessing and cursing”**
• which is unfitting
• but
• My brethren, these things ought not so to be, etc. Truly it is not fitting that with the same mouth we bless the head and curse the members, since the sweetness of blessing is consumed by the bitterness of cursing.
• Which is shown by a likeness. If you mix sweet and bitter water together and they come out through the same opening, the sweet is turned into bitter by the mixing of the bitter, not the bitter into sweet by the mixing of the sweet. So the sweetness of the tongue does not please if it is mixed with bitterness. For “a little leaven corrupteth the whole lump,” and “praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner.”
**“Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing”** — Others, seeing what we do, are led by our example to bless and curse likewise.
**“ought not so to be”** — it is not useful
3.11:
**“Doth a fountain”** — Otherwise. The preacher must sometimes use sweet preaching and sometimes bitter preaching, drawing and rebuking; which is quite difficult, since he can do both with different words tending to the same end.
**“send forth, out of the same hole, sweet and bitter water?”** — as a tree which has lost its natural fruit does not bear the fruit of another tree, so the one who speaks evil, even if he seems to speak well, does not have the fruit of blessing
3.12: **“Can the fig tree”** — Must the teacher be a fig tree, by the sweetness of the blessedness to which he admonishes, and use sweet words; and be a vine, making men forget all temporal things, in which he must use harsh words? But can the same teacher be a fig tree by drawing with sweet things, and be a vine by drawing back from the love of earthly things with harsher ones? As if to say: it is difficult. So neither can salt water make sweet water, that is, a preacher who sharply bites at the manners of others cannot in the same teaching be sweet to the same people.
3.13:
**“Who is a wise man, and endued with knowledge”**
• Having refuted those who have neither holiness of life nor continence of tongue, he admonishes those who seemed wise to themselves, or even were so, to show their wisdom more by living with discipline than by teaching others; because he who is more inclined to teaching than to doing sometimes incurs boasting, or contempt, or envy against other teachers, and many other evils.
• You ought not quickly to become teachers; for who among you is so wise in knowledge and disciplined in practice that he dares to take the office of teacher upon himself? Let him first learn to work well before teaching others, so that by his conduct among you he may be able to be an example to others; and this in meekness, lest on account of his wisdom and good working he despise others.
3.14:
**“But if”** — as regards God and as regards neighbour
**“you have bitter zeal”** — if you have zeal for souls, doing good works, and from the conscience of good works you are bitter toward your neighbours and despise them, and disfigure them with indignant words
**“and tremble”** — which is less
**“there be contentions in your hearts”** — even if they do not break out into words
**“glory not”** — lest you think you will have glory for things done from pride and for the humbling of others
**“and be not liars against the truth”** — And do not lie to God, whom in baptism you promised to renounce the pomps of the devil; which you do not do when you boast of good things.
3.15:
**“For this is not wisdom”** — puffed up and indignant
**“descending from above”** — from God, who is the giver of spiritual goods
**“but earthly”** — desirous of earthly glory
**“sensual”** — not spiritual, but, like the animals, seeking only sensible things
**“devilish”** — it savours and does only what the devil poured into human nature through transgression, namely that it turns itself to mad and harmful things
3.16:
**“For where”** — truly it is not from God, because where there is zeal of God and contention against neighbours
**“envying”** — in the mind
**“and contention”** — in words
**“there is inconstancy”** — of a mind tossed hither and thither, because it neglected to fix itself to the one anchor of the heavenly vision
**“and every evil work”** — in the sight of God, even if it seems right to men
3.17:
**“But the wisdom, that is from above”** — But the wisdom that is from above, etc. This is the gentleness which he said above must be had, opposed to bitter zeal and contentions.
**“first indeed is chaste”** — understands and works chastely
**“First indeed chaste”** — Unless chastity first sits in the mind, no perfection will follow in the work.
**“then peaceable”** — does not separate itself from God through pride, or from fellowship with neighbours
**“modest”** — in whatever it does, it does not go beyond measure, nor stop short
**“easy to be persuaded, consenting to the good”** — what it sees pleasing to good men does not displease it
**“Easy to be persuaded, consenting to the good”** — If it falls short in any way, whether through ignorance or through negligence, it gives assent to the persuasion of good things.
**“full of mercy”** — in the mind
**“and good fruits”** — by works of mercy, fasts, vigils, and prayers
3.18:
**“And the fruit”** — After distinguishing wisdom through its separate virtues, that it may more easily invite to it, he adds its fruit.
**“in peace”** — It does not demand to seem more learned or holier than it is, nor tears down a neighbour to commend itself, which is what contentious wisdom does.
**“of justice in peace”** — Not only on account of the aforesaid ought you to seek this kind of wisdom, but also because by those who make peace, as by those sowing, this seed is sown, and in peace the fruit of eternal blessedness is prepared, that is, the reward of justice, which is repaid for just works. He who here studies peace, and sprinkles the earth of his heart with works of peace as with seed, it is right that he have eternal peace as the fruit of this seed.
**“is sown to them that make peace”** — works of peace

4.1:
**“From whence are wars”** — as if from wisdom come peace, both here and in the future; but on the contrary, in you
**“and contentions among you?”** — unless from zeal and contention
**“From whence are wars and contentions”** — He had forbidden zeal and contention, whence he also argues more broadly, adding also other vices that follow from them. From contention come desires; from desires, wars and quarrels. For whoever desires to be preferred, or to abound in temporal things, hates, envies, kills.
**“Are they not hence, from your concupiscences, which war in your members?”** — because what the wicked mind suggests, the hand and tongue obey immoderately
4.2:
**“You covet”** — truly from desires, for in this order
**“and have not”** — what you desire
**“you kill”** — and that you may have
**“and envy, and”** — yet
**“can not obtain. You contend and war”** — even for temporal glory
**“and you have not, because you ask not”** — worthily of God
**“Wherefore”** — On account of these things, namely, that you do not worthily ask God; for if you asked him with pious intercession, he would give not only eternal things but also temporal things necessary for use. And because they could say, “You say we do not ask; surely we ask daily.” The answer: You do indeed ask sometimes, and yet you do not receive, because you ask amiss.
4.3:
**“You ask, and receive not; because you ask amiss”**
• ungrateful to God the giver
• because you love those things more than God
• for superfluity
4.4: **“Adulterers”** — He had said above of the open enemies of God: “Do not the rich oppress you by might? and do not they draw you before the judgment seats?” etc.; but lest these alone be thought to be enemies who openly blaspheme and persecute, he treats here also of all lovers of the world, that they are enemies of God. You ought not to spend yourselves on concupiscences, because by these you are proved lovers of the world and so adulterers, because, having left the love of heavenly wisdom, you turn aside to the embraces of the world, and by this you are enemies of God.
4.5:
**“Or do you think”** — Or do you think, etc. The spirit that dwelleth, etc. You ought not to quarrel, for the spirit which is in you does not covet to envy, but rather makes you of one mind; and Scripture says this. And do you think that Scripture is empty?
**“the scripture”** — Restraining the faithful from fellowship with the wicked, it speaks thus through Moses: “Thou shalt not enter into league with them, nor with their gods.” And again: “Thou shalt not do their works, but shalt break their statues.”
**“saith in vain: To envy doth the spirit covet”** — covets to envy, that is, desires that you envy: not
**“To envy doth the spirit covet”** — Or the spirit covets against envy, that is, it desires that envy be taken away; or it desires that you envy the world and not love it. Or the spirit of any man covets temporal things to envy, because he envies others what he does not have.
**“the spirit”** — holy, who is given in baptism
4.6:
**“greater”** — The spirit of grace does not make men envy, but rather gives grace, that is, free gifts greater than the riches of the world. Wherefore, that is, that we may know to whom he gives and to whom he does not give, Scripture says.
**“But he giveth greater grace. Wherefore he saith:”** — in the Proverbs of Solomon, according to the old translation
**“God resisteth the proud”** — God punishes all the wicked, but he is said to resist the proud in particular, because they are punished with greater penalty who neglect, by repenting, to submit to God. But he gives grace to the humble, who in the wounds of their vices submit themselves to the hands of the true physician.
**“and giveth grace to the humble”** — eternal life: good work
4.7:
**“Be subject therefore to God”** — because he gives grace to the humble: fulfil the will of God
**“but resist the devil”** — to the one suggesting evil
**“and tremble”** — so
4.8:
**“Draw nigh to God”** — by good works, by humility
**“and he will draw nigh to you.”** — by giving grace, that you may be advanced to better things, and by freeing from straits
**“Cleanse”** — and therefore you who until now have been sinners, cleanse your hands; have innocence of hands, and do not be double-minded, so that you love eternal and temporal things at the same time
**“your hands”** — have innocence of hands
4.9:
**“Be afflicted”** — mindful of the crimes which you, being wretched, committed, or by which you made others wretched; enduring the miseries of this world and poverty
**“and mourn, and weep.”** — in heart, for the sins committed
**“your laughter”** — which was of the lightness of the world
**“be turned into mourning, and your joy into sorrow.”** — of the mind, for the committing of some sin
4.10:
**“Be humbled in the sight of the Lord”** — and so in every way be humbled, bearing poverty and tribulation for love of him, casting yourselves down
**“and he will exalt you.”** — in eternal life
4.11:
**“Detract not one another, my brethren.”** — not only should you so conduct yourselves toward God, but also be good toward brothers; the vice of detraction looks to the poison of the tongue
**“He that detracteth his brother, or he that judgeth his brother”** — for some slight sin, or for some knowledge or something of the kind
**“detracteth the law”** — The law, which forbade detraction, as if he said: the law did not act rightly. Or he who detracts from a brother who keeps the law detracts from the law, and judges the law, why it gave such commands, which bid the injuries of brothers to be forgotten.
**“and judgeth the law. But if thou judge the law,”** — lest they think it a slight sin to detract from the law, he adds that they are to be punished as transgressors
**“thou art not a doer of the law, but a judge.”** — a reviler
4.12:
**“There is one lawgiver, and judge,”** — and you ought not to judge, because you would be judged by God; because he who gave the law that it might be fulfilled judges those not fulfilling it, and he himself is able
**“that is able to destroy”** — those who do not fulfil it
**“and to deliver.”** — those who fulfil it
**“But who art thou”** — But who art thou? You should avoid detraction not only so that you may not be judged by God as a transgressor, but also because perhaps you excel in nothing those whom you blame.
**“that judgest thy neighbour?”** — perhaps you are worse than he, and you yourself can fall into greater sins, and he can rise to good things
4.13:
**“Behold, now”**
• I said that detraction is to be avoided. Behold, another judgment.
• behold, you are those who say
**“you that say:”** — proposing for yourselves a span of life with foolish levity of mind
**“Behold, now you that say”** — After rebuking detraction, he reproves the rashness of those who, not having certainty of life, through desire of temporal things promise themselves life and gain for the future.
**“Today or tomorrow we will go into such a city, and there we will spend a year”** — He notes manifold folly, because they both busy themselves with increase of gains, and reckon that they will live a long time, and think it is in their power to spend a year; and in all these things they scorn to call to mind the judgment of the supreme judge.
4.14:
**“Whereas you know not what shall be on the morrow.”** — otherwise, what will be on the morrow
**“For what is”** — you ought not to promise these things to yourselves
**“your life?”**
• short
• For what is your life? He does not agree with those who say that there is nothing after death, and that death itself is nothing; but he teaches that the life of the wicked is short in the present, which eternal death will nevertheless follow in the future.
**“a vapour”** — smoke
4.15:
**“For that you should say:”** — and I say all these things to you so that you may not, in hope of a longer life, promise yourselves the gains of future time, but rather say: if the Lord
**“If the Lord will”** — leave all things to the will and power of God
**“and if we shall live, we will do this or that.”** — not only do you promise yourselves a span of life and the gains of future time, but also
4.16:
**“But now you rejoice in your arrogancies.”**
• that is, in riches, which make men proud
• as if they were true goods
**“All such rejoicing is wicked.”** — which is for the humbling of others
4.17:
**“To him therefore who knoweth”** — Throughout the whole text of the epistle he shows that those to whom he was writing had the knowledge of doing good and had learned the right faith, so that they presumed to become masters of others; and yet they had not attained perfection of works, nor humility of mind, nor continence of speech. Therefore, among other words of rebuke and exhortation, he now terrifies them greatly, because those who know how to do good and do not do it have a greater sin than if they did not know; although ignorance of the good is itself a great sin, since it is written: “He that knoweth not, shall not be known.”
**“to do good, and doth it not, to him it is sin.”** — because you exult and are proud, therefore you will be punished severely, because you know the good and do not do it

5.1:
**“Go to now, ye rich men,”**
• hitherto you have sinned thus, but now do penance
• in money
• in sins
**“Go to now”** — While the time is given, in the day of salvation, redeem the punishments to come by weeping and almsgiving.
**“weep”** — in the heart
**“and howl”** — by manifestation of deed and voice
**“in your miseries”** — with respect to the miseries to come
5.2:
**“Your riches are corrupted”** — in which you trust, and have gathered up superfluously.
**“and your garments”** — which are for adornment of the body, with which you could have clothed the needy.
**“are motheaten.”** — not worn out by necessary use.
5.3:
**“Your gold and silver is cankered,”**
• more precious among riches, and more durable.
• which you gathered not for the use of life, will fail through its own weakness.
**“and the rust of them”** — And the rust of them, etc. Not only will the fire of visible hell torment the merciless rich, but also the memory of empty riches, with which they could have redeemed their sins, will burn their souls before the judgment, and their flesh also after the resurrection, when they begin to be angry with themselves that they did not redeem their sins by almsgiving. Whence it is said to the rich man: “Son, remember that thou didst receive good things in thy lifetime, and likewise Lazarus evil things.” Behold, the rust of money is turned into a testimony of wickedness and an increase of punishment, because he understands that he gathered wrongly what he did not need for the use of life, and therefore will be punished more severely.
**“for a testimony”** — That is, for the increase of punishments; that is, that by looking on this visibly you may endure greater torments.
**“shall eat your flesh”** — The bodies, or carnal desires: because the raging flame will torment lustful souls outwardly, and the pain pricking inwardly will accuse them of their tenacity.
**“like fire.”**
• the superfluous gathering of those things which, since they were not necessary, rotted when gathered.
• Like fire. Just as fire consumes metals and other things, so will rust consume your flesh.
**“You have stored up”** — Truly so you will suffer, because when, neglecting the care of the poor, you were gathering treasures of money, you heaped up for yourselves the wrath of the inner judge; which, though it does not yet appear, remains most certain for the last days.
**“to yourselves wrath against the last days.”** — to be revealed.
5.4:
**“Behold the hire”**
• Great iniquity, when they are unwilling to receive the poor, and unwilling to pay even to hired workers and servants the wage due for their labour. Whence Job: “If my land cry against me, and with it the furrows thereof mourn; if I have eaten the fruits thereof without money.”
• Wages, etc. Cries out. And even if the poor, bearing everything patiently, do not cry out, the wage withheld cries out.
**“of the labourers”** — you will be condemned not only because you do not give your own, but also because you keep back what is another’s.
**“who have reaped down your fields”** — who have gathered the harvests.
**“which by fraud has been kept back by you, crieth: and the cry of them hath entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth.”** — Sabaoth, that is, of hosts; for the terror of those who think the poor have no defender, but the Lord almighty will look into the causes of each.
5.5:
**“You have feasted”**
• You have sinned not only by superfluously gathering and seizing what is another’s, but also by spending superfluously.
• Neglecting the heavenly joys, to which one must come through fasting and affliction, you love carnal feasts, which such great hunger and thirst will follow in the future, so that not a drop of water can be found by which the burning tongue may be cooled.
• It is plain that he addressed those rich men, from the fact that he says: “Go to now, you rich men,” who had conspired for the death of the Lord, and had not yet received the faith by which they might be saved. Of whom he also speaks above to the believers: “Do not the rich oppress you by might? and do not they draw you before the judgment seats? Do not they blaspheme the good name that is invoked upon you?” And because he writes to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad, he thus admonishes the faithful to do the works of faith, so that he may persuade even those who had not yet believed to be converted to the faith and its works. Reproaching them with the death of the Son of God, and since, as though they had done no evil, they lived luxuriously and avariciously, to them properly applies what he says: that avarice will devour their flesh like fire, and that they have “stored up to themselves wrath in the last days”; for this was fulfilled in them after the slaying of James, when Jerusalem, indeed all Judea, was stormed and laid waste by the Romans in vengeance for the Lord’s blood and the other crimes which they had done.
**“upon earth: and in riotousness you have nourished your hearts.”** — you have used every pleasure and have no care for the sustenance of the poor.
**“in the day of slaughter.”** — when the opportunity of killing was given you.
5.6:
**“have condemned”** — you have condemned to judgment.
**“the Just One”** — the Lord Jesus.
**“and tremble”** — but.
**“he resisted you not”** — because “He was led as a sheep to the slaughter.”
5.7:
**“Be patient therefore”** — because you see them to be punished.
**“Patiently”** — Having rebuked the proud and unbelieving, he turns again to those who had been oppressed by the wickedness of such men, inviting them to patience, because the oppressions will soon end, either by the just being taken up to the Lord or by the persecutors being deprived of power.
**“until the coming of the Lord”** — which begins at the end of each.
**“Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, patiently bearing”** — if he labours so patiently for the fruit of the earth which he hopes for, how much more should you for the heavenly.
**“till he receive”** — the first-fruits.
**“the early”** — So you shall receive the early, that is, the life of the soul after death; and the latter, that is, the incorruption of the flesh. Or the early in the works of justice, the latter in the reward of labours. Whence the Apostle: “You have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end life everlasting.”
**“and latter rain”** — therefore.
5.8:
**“Be patient therefore”** — if he makes delay
**“you also”** — as a farmer
**“strengthen your hearts”** — although heavy things are brought upon you
**“for the coming of the Lord is at hand”** — that you may be caught up to glory, and they to punishment
5.9:
**“Grudge not, brethren, one against another”** — as though you suffered greater things than your merits, and your persecutors, when they have done evil, seem to bear nothing adverse
**“that you may not be judged”** — you be condemned, because you find fault with the just judge as if he judged unjustly
**“Behold”** — because
**“the judge”** — who will give rewards to you and punishment to enemies
**“standeth before the door”** — because either he is near to know what you do, or he will soon come to repay both you and them
5.10:
**“Take, my brethren, for an example of suffering evil, of labour and patience, the prophets, who spoke”** — The prophets who spoke. The prophets, who were so holy that the Spirit of God spoke his mysteries through them, had an evil end, suffering death from unbelievers, like Zacharias, and others in the Old and in the New Testament: John, Stephen, and others. Nor did they groan over this end, but wished to bear it with long-suffering. Others endured long labours without murmuring, like Noe in building the ark, Moses in rebuking and leading the people, David, Joseph. And for both, firm and unchangeable, he adds an example: of Job as to labours, of the Lord as to the end of death.
**“in the name of the Lord”** — by invoking the name, or to extend the name
5.11:
**“Behold, we account them blessed”** — because we consider and revere them as great
**“who”** — them
**“have endured. You have heard of the patience of Job”** — Job, to whom temporal things were restored as to the old man
**“The patience of Job”** — He does not say the end of Job, to whom temporal things were restored, but the patience of Job. And the end of the Lord, because by the example of Job he invites to suffering, and yet not so that they receive temporal things, as Job the old man did, but eternal things as Christ the new man.
**“and you have seen the end of the Lord”** — to Christ the new man all adversities in the world, but at the end resurrection is given
**“And you have seen the end of the Lord”** — You have heard in reading, you have seen with your eyes the one who patiently endured on the cross, but you have also learned through evangelical preaching of the glory of the resurrection and ascension.
**“that the Lord is merciful”** — therefore you ought to imitate
**“the Lord”** — in nature
**“and compassionate”** — in the bestowals of graces
**“And compassionate”** — So that either in the present he frees his own from temptations and glorifies those living for constancy of faith even before men, or after death in secret crowns them. And not even so does he take away from men the memory of praise they have deserved.
5.12:
**“But above all things, my brethren, swear not”** — Because he desires to drain out entirely the deadly poison of the tongue in his hearers, he who forbade backbiting one another, who forbade judging a neighbour, who forbade groaning in adversities, which are open sins, adds also this, which seems light to some, in order to take away the habit of swearing, since “every idle word that men shall speak, they shall render an account for it in the day of judgment.”
**“nor by any other oath”** — Therefore I restrain you from the guilt of swearing, lest by frequent swearing you sometimes fall even into perjury while swearing what is true. But you will stand the farther from perjury if you are unwilling even to swear truly unless necessity compels. But he too falls under the guilt of judgment who, although he has never forsworn falsely, yet swears the truth more often than is needful. As he had given counsel to the sorrowful, so he gives it to the sick, how he may guard himself from the folly of murmuring, and set the measure of the remedy according to the measure of the wound. Let the sorrowful pray for himself. Let him who is sick in body or in faith, because he bears a greater wound, remember to seek a cure by the help of many, and this by that of the elders.
5.13:
**“Is any of you sad”** — Because he forbade groaning in troubles, now he shows what on the contrary is to be done.
**“any of you”** — either for an injury inflicted, or for some fault, or domestic loss, or any matter
**“Let him pray”** — Let him not murmur or find fault with God’s judgments, but run to the Church with knees bent, that God may send consolation. Let him pray. Lest the sadness of the world, which works death, swallow him up, and by the frequent sweetness of psalmody drive the harmful plague of sadness from the heart.
5.14:
**“Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church”** — not to younger and less learned men should he report the cause of his weakness, lest perhaps through them he receive some harmful speech or advice
**“and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil”** — consecrated, or when he is anointed
**“in the name of the Lord”** — let the name of the Lord be invoked
5.15:
**“And the prayer of faith shall save the sick man”** — brother
**“and the Lord shall raise him up”** — from bodily infirmity
**“and if he be in sins”** — even if it happens that he dies
**“And if he be in sins”** — Many are struck with death, even of the body, on account of their sins. If, then, the sick are in sins, and having confessed this to the priest with a perfect heart have forsaken them, and have been careful to amend, they are forgiven. For sins cannot be forgiven without confession of amendment. Whence it is rightly added: “Confess your sins one to another.”
**“they shall be forgiven him”** — by grace
5.16:
**“Confess therefore”** — therefore
**“one to another”** — to equals
**“your sins”** — let us declare to the priest the daily and light sins, and the uncleanness of a graver leprosy, and take care to cleanse ourselves in the time he shall order
**“and pray one for another, that you may be saved. For the continual prayer of a just man availeth much”** — note: just and continual
5.17:
**“Elias was a man like unto us”**
• by the origin of his flesh
• although second to no man in virtue
• not yet taken up
• Elias was a man, etc. Lest our frailty tremble, reckoning that it cannot do the like of so great a prophet, who deserved to be taken up to heaven in a fiery chariot, he, about to speak of his prayer, prudently began from humility. Elias, passible like us, weak in the flesh, is fed by a widow; weak in mind, terrified by the threats of one poor woman, he fled through the deserts.
**“passible”** — as we are, by the frailty of mind and flesh
**“and with prayer he prayed”** — to convince the pride of the king and the hardness of the idolatrous nation
**“with prayer he prayed”** — He shows by example how much the continual prayer of a just man avails, since Elias, by one prayer alone, by praying, so long a time kept back the heavens, turned away rains from the earth, and denied fruits to mortals.
5.18: **“And he prayed again”** — When he perceived the time, when he saw the heart of the proud king and of the idolatrous people turned to penance by the wasting of a long famine, he prayed with one prayer, and restored to the earth the fruits and the waters which he had denied. So great things did one Elias obtain by one prayer; how much more, then, many faithful by many prayers?
5.19:
**“But if any of you”** — Having shown the efficacy of prayer, he shows how great a merit it is to pray for the brethren, and to call them back to safety; so that he who in the earlier part removed from our tongue malicious and idle speech, might at the end of the epistle show what we ought to speak. Let us pray and sing psalms whenever we are beaten by adversities; let us confess our sins; let us pray for one another that we may be saved; for the salvation of our neighbours, not only temporal but rather eternal. For if it is of great reward to rescue from death a body that is some day to die, how great is the merit to free from death a soul that is to live without end in the heavenly country?
**“err from the truth, and one convert him”** — either by good admonition or, with the tongue silent, by showing examples of good action
5.20:
**“shall save his soul from death”** — Some copies have: “He shall save his own soul from death.” And truly, he who corrects one who errs thereby wins for himself greater joys of the heavenly life.
**“and shall cover a multitude of sins”** — he hides from the sight of the inner judge by the superimposition of a better life

1.1:
**“Peter”**
• a famous name
• In the time when the Church began, the apostle comforts those of the Gentiles who had gone over to Judaism, who had believed God, who suffered for the faith and were scattered. He writes from Rome in the time of Claudius Caesar.
**“Elect”** — To this end, that by the gift of the Spirit they might be sanctified, cleansed from all sins, that they who had perished through disobedience might begin to obey Christ, that, sprinkled with the blood of Christ, they might escape the power of the devil, as Israel went out of Egypt by the blood of the lamb. In the old law whatever was to be sanctified was wont to be sprinkled with the blood of victims.
**“Strangers”** — Advena in Latin, in Greek: proselytes. So the Jews called those who, born of the Gentiles, wished to believe in God, and, having received circumcision, to live in the Jewish manner according to the law of God. He therefore calls them elect strangers who from heathenism came to the acceptance of the law and afterwards to the acceptance of the faith. But we also, if we can truly say with the prophet: “For we are strangers with thee on the earth, and sojourners, as all our fathers were,” ought to believe that the epistles of blessed Peter were written to us also, and to read them as sent to us. Finally, in these same epistles he admonishes us as having our country elsewhere: “Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, to refrain yourselves from carnal desires.”
**“strangers”** — Or strangers, that is, strangers scattered from Jerusalem by the persecution that was made under Stephen, and by many other persecutions, afflicted both by the Jews and by the Gentiles for the faith of Christ, and often expelled from their seats.
**“Dispersed”** — In the year of the ascension Stephen was dead, and many were scattered through fear.
**“Pontus, Galatia, and Bithynia”** — All these provinces are of the Greeks in Asia; but there is also another Bithynia in Europe, from which those who are in Asia, the Bithynians, had their origin. That Bithynia, however, which is in Asia is called Greater Phrygia, and is separated from Galatia by the river Hiera.
1.2:
**“According to the foreknowledge of God the Father”** — not by merits, but those whom he foreknew and predestined to be made “conformable to the image of his Son”
**“Grace unto you”** — Without the grace of Christ one never comes to the peace of his reconciliation; we can have nothing peaceable except through his grace.
**“and peace be multiplied”** — so that what you have well begun you may perfectly complete
**“And peace be multiplied”** — Let no adversity draw you back from the praises of God; let every tribulation invite you to praise, because all things are multiplied to happiness, so that what you have well begun you may perfectly complete.
1.3:
**“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord”** — of the man born in the world
**“Jesus Christ”** — of the Son consubstantial with himself
**“who according to his great mercy hath regenerated us”** — first he begot us from matter; afterwards, according to the advance of life, he regenerated us
**“Hath regenerated”** — Since by our own merits we had been begotten unto death, by his mercy he has regenerated us unto life. So did he love our life that for it he determined that the Son should die, and, death being destroyed through the resurrection, should show us hope and an example of rising again. He died that we might not fear to die; he rose that we might hope for resurrection. If of the present, he regenerated us to this end, that you should be his inheritance, whom he should possess as a man possesses an inheritance. Incorruptible, that you be not corrupted by criminal sins. Undefiled, that you be not defiled even by lesser ones. Unfading, that you not fade even by daily and venial ones. Reserved in heaven, that you may be so kept in soul and body that through cleanness you may be heaven and the seat of God.
**“unto a lively hope”** — or living
**“by the resurrection of Jesus Christ”** — through faith he rises again in us, as through unbelief he dies in us
**“from the dead”** — remote
1.4:
**“Unto an inheritance incorruptible”** — where we shall be touched by neither old age, nor sickness, nor any other sadness
**“Incorruptible”** — Naturally the soul is not incorruptible, but by the grace of God it is made incorruptible through faith and justice and understanding.
**“and undefiled”** — into which no unclean person can enter
**“and that can not fade”** — because not even in the very minds of blessed men can that heavenly way of life, from long use, ever come to be cheapened, as the luxury of the present world is wont sometimes to turn to disgust from mere or long use
**“reserved in heaven for you”**
• not to be given in the present but to be rendered to us in heaven at the appointed time
• In you, etc. He who gave you, believers, the power to become sons of God, has placed in you that perseverance by which you may receive the inheritance in heaven, because whoever does not keep the discipline of the Father does not deserve his inheritance.
1.5:
**“By the power of God, are kept”** — No one can be kept in good things by the power of his own freedom unless he perfects it from whom you have the beginning of good action. Labour from faith through faith, you who are to come to eternal salvation, which, though it does not appear now, is nevertheless ready to be revealed if we shall be ready.
**“ready to be revealed in the last time”** — when the last enemy, death, will be destroyed
1.6:
**“Wherein”** — in time
**“you shall greatly rejoice”** — as triumphers
**“for a little time”** — where eternal reward is given; what in the tribulations of the world will seem eternal and heavy will seem brief and light
**“if now you must be made sorrowful”** — because one cannot come to joys except through sadness
**“If now you must”** — If, that is, although it is necessary. Or “it is necessary to be saddened” is understood: lest we fail. Or so: if it is not necessary to be saddened, the proof of your faith is found unto praise, and then it will not be in the book.
**“in divers temptations”** — in various tribulations; or: temptations
1.7:
**“That the trial of your faith”**
• Tribulations do not come to you for harm, but so that the proof, that is, you, proved faithful in the furnace of tribulation, with all the rust of age burned out
• That the trial, etc. Unto praise. When the judge, praising it, says: “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat,” etc. Unto glory. When glorifying it he will say: “Come, ye blessed of my Father,” etc. Honour. When he will say: “Let the wicked be taken away, that he see not the glory of God,” and: “Then shall the just go into life everlasting.” Whence: “If any man minister to me, him will my Father honour, who is in heaven.” Or unto praise: that you may be praiseworthy and glorious through constancy at the revelation, that is, on the day of judgment, when it will be revealed how great is the power of God. And honour, that it may be said to you: “Come, ye blessed of my Father.”
**“much more precious than gold”** — your faith pleases the highest Craftsman, God, more than gold pleases any craftsman
**“More precious than gold”** — The patience of the saints is compared to gold, because as among metals nothing is more precious than gold, so this before God is most worthy of all praise. For as gold tried in the furnace, brought out, will show how great is its brightness, so the constancy of the faithful amid afflictions seems contemptible, but when the contest is ended, at the judgment it will be shown how great is its glory. Whence it is said: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.” Whence he adds: Be found, etc.
**“which is tried by the fire, may be found”** — at last
**“unto praise and glory and honour at the appearing of Jesus Christ”** — on the day of judgment
1.8:
**“Whom having not seen, you love”** — because although you do not now see him bodily, nor even spiritually as he is, yet you will love him through faith
**“in whom also now, though you see him not, you believe”** — the rewarder
**“and believing shall rejoice with joy unspeakable”** — because: “That eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared for them that love him.”
1.9:
**“Receiving the end of your faith”** — God himself
**“the salvation of your souls”** — about to suffer no weakness
**“Salvation of your souls”** — This salvation is greatly to be loved, because they searched much about this salvation: when, or in what order, eternal salvation would come to the world. Whence it is said: “Many prophets and kings have desired to see the things that you see, and have not seen them.”
1.10:
**“Of which salvation the prophets have inquired and diligently searched”** — those who had such knowledge of God
