**“who prophesied of the grace to come in you”** — in secret, from the Lord or from angels; whence also one of them, for great love of saving knowledge, deserved to be called “man of desires” by the Lord or by an angel
**“Prophesied”** — Speaking openly to men, and explaining what they themselves knew in the secret of inner contemplation.
1.11:
**“searching”** — searching, by daily practice
**“what or what manner of time”** — What time: in what year, or under what prince. What kind, warlike or peaceful, or in what order, through the virgin’s childbirth, or by what other means.
**“the Spirit of Christ in them did signify”** — although the Spirit was in them
**“The Spirit of Christ”** — He calls the archangels and the nearest spirits, through whom the Lord works, who are subject to Christ, spirits.
**“when it foretold those sufferings that are in Christ”** — in head and members
**“sufferings that are”**
• not only his coming but also his sufferings
• which were to be ended by the cross
**“and the glories that should follow”** — late and long desired, preceded by tribulations
**“The glories that should follow”** — There are two glorifications of the Lord according to the form of the man he assumed: one in which he rose from the dead, and another in which he ascended into heaven before the eyes of the apostles. A third remains, and that in the sight of men, when he shall come in majesty to render to every one according to his works.
1.12:
**“To whom it was revealed”**
• to whom it was revealed
• to those searching, among other hidden things, this also is made known: “As star differs from star in brightness.”
**“was”** — this
**“that not to themselves”** — they were not the masters of our salvation but its ministers. Whence: “to you,” etc.
**“But to you”**
• that salvation was to come not in their days, but rather in yours, who are born at the end of the ages
• But to you, etc. This is so that he may warn them to take care of the salvation offered, which the earlier saints loved so much.
**“they ministered those things which are now declared to you”** — all the mysteries of the Redeemer, which are now fulfilled and announced, which are hidden from many
**“by them that have preached the gospel”** — through such worthy messengers, the disciples
**“to you, the Holy Ghost”** — not falsely, not fancifully, but with the Holy Spirit dictating
**“The Holy Ghost”** — The Spirit in the prophets, the Spirit in the apostles: so it appears that prophets and apostles proclaim the same salvation. Those the coming one, these the fulfilled one. So there is one Church, of which one part went before the coming of Christ, and the other part follows.
**“Into which things the angels desire to look”** — So great is the later glory of the man who suffered for us that even the angelic powers in heaven, though perfect in eternal happiness, rejoice always to behold not only the magnificence of his immortal divinity but the brightness of the humanity he assumed. But why do they desire to see him whose face they never cease to see? Only because the contemplation of the divine presence so beatifies the angels that, though they are always filled with the sight of his glory, they always hunger insatiably for his sweetness as if new. Or: on whom, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is of such majesty and glory that the vision of him, as also of the Father himself and the Son, is always desired by the angels; whom the grace of divine mercy sent to earth for the sake of man’s salvation and poured into the minds of the faithful to enlighten them.
1.13:
**“Wherefore”** — Because such great grace is promised to you, which you see revealed and which the angels now see, take care to be all the more worthy to receive it.
**“having the loins of your mind girt up”** — that you may also cut off superfluous thoughts from the mind.
**“being sober”** — in life
**“trust perfectly”** — by persevering constantly
**“trust”** — Await securely, chaste in mind and body. For he who does not know how to please the Lord, deservedly lacking the hope of good things, fears that it may come sooner.
**“which is offered you the grace”** — is shown freely by Christ and by the saints
**“in the revelation”** — to be given
1.14:
**“As children”** — And so that you may be able to wait securely, be obedient children of the Father who corrects.
**“of obedience”** — lest you be “dogs returning to their vomit”
**“not fashioned according to the former desires of your ignorance”** — by this you were in some measure excusable before, but now you know the truth.
1.15:
**“But according to him”** — by the example of Christ
**“that hath called you, who is holy”**
• he called to this
• Who hath called you, holy, that is, sanctified and sanctifying you, that in all conduct you may be holy. Whence: “Be you therefore perfect, as also your heavenly Father is perfect.”
**“that you also yourselves may be holy”** — his sons
**“be in all manner of conversation”** — firm against vices, against tribulations
1.16: **“Because it is written: You shall be holy, for I am holy.”** — Your Father, who wills you to be such as I am
1.17:
**“And if you invoke him as Father”** — saying in prayer: “Our Father who art in heaven”
**“who without respect of persons judgeth according to every one's work”** — Without respect, etc. Not as a carnal father, who is wont to spare sinning sons more indulgently than servants. But God the Father adopts as sons obedient servants, and even enemies who give him their hand, and those who seemed more honourable under the name of sons he makes, for disobedience, strangers to the inheritance.
**“converse in fear during the time of your sojourning”** — lest through negligence and desires you be unworthy of so great a Father, and, while in the time of your exile you are secure, you be unable to reach the homeland of blessedness
**“during the time of your sojourning”** — And that you may be able to be holy, conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourning, as long as you are in the exile of this world: “Blessed is the man that is always fearful.” I say this if you invoke, as if to say: you do not otherwise invoke unless you are anxious and fearful.
1.18:
**“Knowing”** — therefore conduct yourselves so, I say, knowing
**“Knowing that you were not redeemed with corruptible things”** — The greater the price by which you were redeemed from the corruption of carnal life, the more you ought to fear lest by turning back to the corruption of vices you offend the mind of your Redeemer.
**“gold or silver”** — by these prices sins are customarily redeemed among men
**“from your vain conversation of the tradition of your fathers”** — also from the transgression of the law
1.19:
**“But with the precious blood”** — Order: but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb uncontaminated and spotless. Here it touches on the Levitical and priestly rites. It signifies, moreover, a soul made clean through the righteousness that is offered to God.
**“as of a lamb”**
• because free from every sin
• of a meek lamb not opening his mouth, clothing us with his wool in his preaching.
**“unspotted”** — from the actual
**“and undefiled”** — from original
1.20:
**“Foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world”** — preordained by God that redemption would be made through him
**“manifested”** — through the assumed humanity
**“but in the last times for you”** — to be saved
1.21:
**“Who through him”** — through his institution
**“are faithful in God”** — as members
**“who raised him up from the dead, and hath given him glory”**
• in the ascension
• that you may hope to have the same glory through him
**“that your faith and hope”** — All this not because he himself needed it, but that your faith
**“might be in God”** — that you may hope to have the same grace through him
1.22:
**“Purifying your souls”** — therefore love one another, I say, purifying your souls, that they may keep faith to one spouse
**“in the obedience of charity”** — that from love of God you be obedient in bearing all things
**“with a brotherly love”** — even if brothers harm you
**“from a sincere heart”** — With a sincere heart. Not for any advantage or disadvantage: “Not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.”
**“love one another earnestly”** — than hitherto
1.23:
**“Being born again”** — therefore do this
**“not of corruptible seed”** — not of the flesh, not from the law, which fails in many things, but from the unchangeable gospel
**“not of seed”** — As from corruptible seed is born flesh, which is corrupted, so through water consecrated by the word of God a life which knows no end will be granted; which is also fittingly confirmed by the testimony of the prophet: “All flesh is grass.” As the price of the Lord’s passion, by which we are redeemed, is incorruptible, so also is the sacrament of the holy font, by which we are born again, incorruptible. These are so joined to one another that the one cannot confer salvation without the other. For so the Lord at the time of his incarnation redeemed you all by his blood, that we also in our own time, each one for the regeneration of baptism, may deserve to attain to a share in the same regeneration.
**“but incorruptible, by the word of God”** — the word, that is, the Son of God or the gospel, cannot be corrupted
**“who liveth and remaineth for ever”** — I say this birth is incorruptible because the other birth is corruptible
1.24:
**“For all flesh is as grass”** — transitory
**“and all the glory thereof”** — all the pleasures of the flesh
**“as the flower”** — because they promise something of themselves yet bring forth no fruit
**“of grass”** — or: of the field
**“The grass is withered”** — by sickness or death
1.25:
**“But the word of the Lord endureth for ever”** — The word of the Lord, etc. Just as the corruptible begets the corruptible, so the word that endures for ever gives eternal life to those “born again of water and the Holy Ghost.”
**“And this is the word which by the gospel hath been preached unto you”** — through me and the other apostles

2.1:
**“Wherefore laying away”**
• the will to harm others
• Laying away all malice, etc. Augustine. What is malice but the love of harming? What is guile but to do one thing and pretend another? What is flattery but seduction by deceitful praise? What is envy but hatred of another’s happiness? What is detraction but a censure more biting than truthful? Malice delights in another’s evil. Guile makes the heart double. Flattery, the tongue. Detraction wounds reputation.
**“and all guile”** — deception
**“and dissimulations”** — when one thing is in the heart and another in the mouth
**“and envies”**
• of the heart
• against the success of others
**“and all detractions”** — in words
2.2:
**“As newborn babes”** — Because you have thus been born again and made sons of the eternal, be such through zeal for good conduct as infants newly born are by the nature of their age.
**“desire the rational milk without guile”** — without the wrinkle of duplicity
**“Rational without guile”** — Although infants through put-away malice, yet reasonable through wisdom; and let no reason draw us to the cunning of the world, but be without guile. Whence: “Be ye therefore wise as serpents and simple as doves,” etc.
**“Desire the milk”**
• seek the simple rudiments of faith from the breasts of the mother Church, that is, from the teachers of both testaments who have written the divine words or preach them by living voice
• He touches those who come to hear the sacred readings with disdain, ignorant of that thirst and hunger of which the Lord says: “Blessed are they that hunger and thirst after justice,” and therefore arrive more slowly at the perfect increase of salvation, by which they might be refreshed with the solid food of the word, that is, know the divine mysteries or do greater good works.
**“that thereby”** — That also by learning well, through the sacraments of the Lord’s incarnation, you may come to the contemplation of the divine majesty.
2.3: **“If so be you have tasted”** — In this way, with the malice of the heart purged, desire the living food of Christ, if you have tasted how great the divine sweetness is. For he who tastes nothing of its sweetness, it is no wonder if he does not avoid soiling himself with earthly desires.
2.4:
**“Unto whom coming”** — by faith and imitation
**“Unto whom”** — As if: come to him, because coming to him by faith you are built up, since: “For other foundation no man can lay, but that which is laid; which is Christ Jesus.”
**“stone”** — Upon whom the eternal city is founded: not a material stone but a living one, which could be cast down by no shocks; so neither can those who are founded on him.
**“rejected indeed by men”** — when they said: “We have no king but Caesar.”
**“by God”**
• who is not deceived in his disposition
• fear not to be rejected
**“chosen”** — that he might make both one
**“made honourable”** — in miracles, in the ascension
2.5:
**“Be you also as living stones”** — you also as stones, that is, solid in faith, living in virtues
**“As living stones”** — Through unbelief they are hard and insensible, but through discernment instructed they are made alive and fit to be joined together in love in God’s building.
**“built up”** — Be built up, etc. To offer good works, alms, prayers, and yourselves.
**“a spiritual house”** — against rains, winds, floods
**“a holy priesthood”** — I mean you, being priests, worthy, anointed with the oil of gladness
**“to offer up spiritual sacrifices”** — not as in the old law
**“by Jesus Christ”** — This refers to all: you are built up, you are priests, you offer; and all this through Jesus Christ, by whose grace you have all things.
2.6:
**“Wherefore”** — To be confirmed: that the Lord is rightly called a stone because of his firmness.
**“it is said in the scripture”** — Isaias
**“Behold, I lay in Sion”** — because born in Judea
**“a chief corner stone”** — solid
**“chief”** — more perfect than all
**“corner”** — joining two peoples
**“chosen”** — from all
**“precious”**
• the price of redemption
• who is given as the price
**“And he that shall believe in him”** — by imitating him
**“shall not be confounded”** — neither shall he be ashamed in the present from a fall, nor in the future will he be empty of reward
2.7:
**“To you therefore”** — from the authority of the prophet
**“To you therefore that believe, he is honour”** — So that stone, rejected by these as by those, here, that is, for those who believe, is made the head of the corner; and for unbelievers it is made “a stone of stumbling, and a rock of scandal.”
**“that believe, he is honour”** — The Father will honour those who believe in the Son, and at his coming they will not be confounded
**“but to them that believe not, the stone which the builders rejected”** — which the Jews, carnally confirming that their law is to be kept and wishing to establish all their own righteousness, were unwilling to place in the foundation of their heart
**“to them that believe not, the stone which the builders rejected, the same is made”** — Because just as they rejected him in their building, so he in his coming will reject them from being received into the building of his house, which is in heaven.
**“the same is made”** — and yet
**“the head of the corner”** — in Christian building
2.8:
**“And a stone of stumbling”** — is made
**“And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of scandal”** — Though he is the stone on which the good are supported and rest secure, to the unbelieving he will be a cause of stumbling in the present, to those who do not believe in him, and therefore they fall from vice to vice. And in the future a rock of scandal, because against him whom they trampled upon as lowly their steps are dashed, and they will fall into everlasting fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels.
**“to them who stumble at the word”** — by the word, because those who speak evil of God will blush when they see his so great glory
**“stumble at the word”** — He stumbles at the word who, because he has heard the word, stumbles in mind, in that he does not believe what he has heard, and so heightens his own folly. Nor do they believe in that wherein they were also set. By nature men were made for this, that they should believe God and obey his will.
**“neither do believe”** — or because
**“whereunto also they are set”** — because: “In him we live, and move, and are.”
2.9:
**“But you”** — This testimony of praise, once given to the ancient people through Moses, the Apostle gives to the Gentiles who believe in Christ, who, like the corner stone, gathered the Gentiles into that salvation which Israel had in itself.
**“a chosen generation”**
• through faith
• Chosen. Chosen through faith and set apart from those who, rejecting the stone, became reprobate.
**“a kingly priesthood, a holy nation”** — as far as itself is concerned
**“a kingly priesthood”** — United to the body of the high priest, who ought to hope for the kingdom and offer to God sacrifices of unspotted conduct.
**“a purchased people”** — in the blood of his redemption
**“purchased”** — In the blood of his redemption, by which the people of Israel was once redeemed with the blood of the lamb out of Egypt. Whence also in the following verse it mystically recalls the old history and teaches that this was fulfilled especially in one people.
**“that you may declare his virtues”** — no longer living in passions and desires, but living holily and justly
**“declare”** — As those freed from Egypt sang a triumphal song to the Lord, so we, after the darkness is dispelled and after forgiveness received through Christ, being about to be led to the homeland of heavenly brightness, ought to render to God thanks worthy of heavenly benefits.
**“who hath called you out of darkness”** — as he led them in a pillar of fire
2.10:
**“Who in time past were not a people”**
• that is, who were estranged from the way of life of the people of God
• Who once were not a people, etc. Hence it is proved that he writes this epistle to those who came to the faith from the Gentiles. These verses are taken from the prophecy of Osee, in which the calling of the Gentiles is treated.
**“but are now”** — in the time of grace
**“the people of God”** — united to his people
**“Who had not obtained mercy”** — who had not known how to hope for mercy
2.11:
**“Dearly beloved”** — Thus far he has instructed the Church in general, explaining either the benefits by which God has called us to salvation, or the gifts with which he has deigned to honour sometimes the Jews, but now us. Here he carefully exhorts the various persons of the faithful, that by living carnally they may not render themselves unworthy of so great a glory of the Spirit, nor degenerate from the glory of the nobility promised to them; and he teaches first how freemen and servants, then women and men, lastly elders and young men, ought to conduct themselves; and he openly admonishes the free to abstain from carnal desires, because the freedom of a more relaxed life is wont to endure the greater dangers of titillating enticements.
**“I beseech you”** — because you have obtained mercy, therefore
**“as strangers and pilgrims”**
• Strangers are those who dwell in a foreign place. He adds pilgrims, who always pass from place to place.
• not in this world, but having their homeland elsewhere
**“as strangers”** — Therefore set your mind less on earthly things, since you remember that you have your homeland in heaven. The reprobate here have a homeland whose desires they gape after; therefore they will be banished into perpetual exile, lacking pleasures.
**“to refrain yourselves from carnal desires which war against the soul”** — while the flesh is weakened and subdued by flattering lusts, thence the army of vices is firmly armed against the soul
2.12:
**“Having your conversation good”** — doing good works
**“That whereas they speak against you”** — thinking you foolish, because you have left their gods; and they believe that you are afflicted in the world on account of your sins
**“As evildoers, by the good works”** — by your chaste conduct
**“Which they shall behold in you”** — your dignity
**“By the good works which they shall behold in you”** — It often happens that pagans who reviled the Christian faith, afterwards considering their good conduct, began to praise Christ.
**“In the day of visitation”** — In the time of visitation, the unbelievers already now recognize how great the glory is that God will give you, when they have seen you follow him constantly through every danger. Or, of visitation: when the Lord will visit them, by converting them.
2.13:
**“Be ye subject”**
• both to the faithful and to the unbelievers
• And that your conversation may please all, resist not any dignity of men, any person, any authority to which God has willed you to be subject, because there is no power but from God, and he that resisteth the power resisteth the ordinance of God. And he sets out the creature part by part.
**“To every human creature for God's sake, whether it be to the king as excelling”** — lest the faith of the Christian religion be disparaged even in this, that through it the rights of station are overturned
2.14:
**“Or to governors as sent by him”** — to the king or to God
**“As sent by him”** — God often allows some evil man to exercise tyranny, so that the wicked may be confounded and the good may be more proved.
**“For the punishment”**
• punishment
• For the punishment. Not that it always happens so, but it simply states what the action of a leader ought to be; who, even if he condemns the good, contributes no less to their praise by what he does, if the good bear his wickedness patiently and wisely resist his cunning.
**“Of evildoers, and for the praise of the good”** — of those rewarded
**“And for the praise of the good”** — For so, etc. Truly, whatever rulers do, the good gain praise, because God wills this, who makes use even of the wicked for good; so that you, making use of them also for good, whether they be good or wicked, may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men. So that those rulers, not knowing how you use them for good, and through them deserve praise, may find nothing to blame in you, while you honour even them and bear with them though they be unclean.
2.16:
**“As free”** — and do these good things as free
**“And not as making liberty a cloak for malice”** — the greater the liberty you enjoy among men, the more freely be subjected to the service of God
**“But as the servants of God”** — the service of God requires humility
**“Not as making liberty a cloak for malice”** — Not having your liberty for a cloak of malice. Let not your liberty wrap round your hearts, so that you sin the more freely the less you are weighed down by servitude, and let you not cover your fault under the name of liberty. But he wills them to be free from the servitude of sins, that they may remain good and faithful servants of the Creator. Whence he adds: “But as the servants of God.”
2.17:
**“Honour all men”**
• “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s”
• each one according to his measure
**“Love the brotherhood”**
• by obedience
• And among all things, love the brethren, even those who are subject to you by temporal condition; love them as brethren in Christ.
**“Fear God”** — In all obedience let the fear of the Lord go first
**“Honour the king”** — as to one who excels, venerate him with greater honour
2.18:
**“Servants, be subject”**
• that you may neither offend God nor refuse to obey your masters
• Thus far he has exhorted the free to subjection; now he speaks to servants, that they too may be subject to their masters.
**“To your masters with all fear. Not only to the good”** — in faith, life, and morals
**“And gentle”** — to those who command and forgive with moderation
**“But also to the froward”** — Not only to the good, etc. Another translation: Not only to the good and modest, but also to the more difficult.
**“To the froward”** — That is, the undisciplined. “Scola” is Greek; in Latin, “place,” in which they gathered to hear the masters of the liberal arts; whence “scola” is interpreted “leisure,” because there they had leisure for studies. Scholastics, therefore, are the learned; the discoli are the unlearned and rustic. See how above he admonished them to be subject to the human creature for God’s sake.
**“For this is thankworthy”** — that is, by this a man is made pleasing to God, and this the grace of faith requires.
**“If for conscience of God”** — If anyone, suffering for God, who knows a good intention, is beaten unjustly by his Lord, though he serves him well, he endures, that is, counts the sorrows light; this is grace, and by this a man is made pleasing to God, and this the grace of faith requires.
2.19:
**“If for conscience of God a man endure sorrows”** — let him count the sorrows light.
**“Suffering wrongfully”** — If you suffer unjustly, you gain the grace of God. For if you patiently bear the punishments inflicted by your masters, I mean you who sin by refusing to obey them and are buffeted by those masters, that is, often corrected by them so that by blows you may be led to obey, what grace will there be to you from that? You will receive nothing from God for this.
2.20:
**“For what glory is it, if committing sin, and being buffeted for it, you endure? But if doing well”** — although they do well.
**“You suffer patiently”** — the evils inflicted by their masters.
2.21:
**“For unto this are you called”**
• and by this example of Christ
• that you may suffer
• He greatly honors the condition of slaves, whom he declares to be imitators of the Lord’s passion when they do well and are beaten without fault by cruel and wicked masters.
**“Because Christ also”** — Since above he instructed slaves in particular, now he instructs the whole Church, so that he may also call to the memory of masters what their Author suffered for their salvation and deliverance.
**“Suffered for us”** — as if you rejoice, because Christ died through you; attend to what follows: leaving you an example
**“Leaving you an example”** — of insults, tribulations, scourges, the cross and death
2.22:
**“Who did no sin”** — although he suffered
**“Neither was found”** — by the Jews and Pharisees observing him
**“Guile in his mouth”** — nor did he sin with his word
2.23:
**“Who, when he was reviled”** — as a seducer and one possessed
**“Did not revile”** — he did not cast up to them the evils which were true of them
**“But delivered himself to him that judged him unjustly”** — Those judging according to an unjust law, since he was righteous, he handed over to God the Father those judging unjustly, that is, those who most wickedly condemned him and pressed for his death, so that, taking up punishment, they might be instructed.
**“When he suffered, he threatened not. But delivered himself to him that judged him unjustly”** — He touches on the gospel parable, that the faithful shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the desert, came to visit the one that had perished.
2.24:
**“Who his own self bore our sins”** — that is, the punishment owed for sins
**“Our sins”** — of all in common
**“In his body upon the tree”** — he bore in his body upon the wood
**“That we, being dead to sins”** — as he himself was bodily dead
**“Should live to justice”** — as he himself lives a new life
**“By whose stripes you were healed”** — by his bruise you were healed; either his flesh was made livid in the passion by love alone, or because the Jews condemned him to death out of envy alone
2.25:
**“For you were”** — for you were weak
**“As sheep”** — torn by vices, by the thorns of vices
**“Going astray”** — without a shepherd
**“But you are now converted to the shepherd”** — in the passion of Christ, returned in body and soul to him who feeds you with the word of truth
**“And bishop of your souls”** — Or visitor, which is the same. For bishop, that is, overseer, because: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the just, and his ears unto their prayers”; and: “The Orient from on high hath visited us.”

3.1:
**“In like manner also let wives”** — as servants to masters for God’s sake
**“In like manner also”** — It seems that the wives of those who were in tribulation were despising their husbands and also, in order to please others, adorned themselves finely; he forbids this.
**“be subject”** — being patient with their husbands, or by the husbands themselves
**“to their husbands”** — not to adulterers
**“that if any”** — husbands
**“believe not the word”** — of the gospel
**“by the conversation of the wives”** — of those who conduct themselves well and humbly endure all things
**“without the word”** — of preaching
**“they may be won”**
• may be converted to the faith
• That if any believe not, etc. He wills good women to be subject to unbelieving husbands in such a way that not only do they do nothing evil at their command, but also persist unconquerable in so holy a conversation that they may be, even for the husbands themselves, an example of charity, chastity and faith.
3.2:
**“Considering”** — only
**“your chaste conversation with fear”** — held in the fear of God, kept
3.3:
**“Whose adorning let it not be the outward”** — Whose adorning let it not be, outwardly, the plaiting of the hair, or the gold put about, or the wearing of apparel, that is, let there be no festive garments in which they are clothed. But let your adorning be the inward man of the heart, known to God alone, in the incorruptibility of the spirit, I mean a spirit quiet from the assault of vices and modest, lest he who has such a spirit be proud; for though it is not manifest to men, yet it is rich in the sight of God.
**“or the putting on”** — As Cyprian says: Clothed in silk and purple, they cannot put on Christ. Adorned with gold and pearls and necklaces, they have lost the ornaments of heart and body. But if Peter admonishes even wives, who can excuse their adornments by their husband, to be restrained and moderated by religious observance according to ecclesiastical discipline, how much more is it right for a virgin to observe this, to whom no pardon for her adornment is due, and who cannot turn the lie of her fault upon another, but remains alone in the guilt.
**“the plaiting of the hair, or the putting on”** — Because your outward man is corrupted, and you have ceased to have the blessedness of integrity, which is properly that of virginity, imitate the incorruption of the spirit by abstinence, and what you cannot in the body, supply in the mind. For these are the riches Christ seeks, and these the adornments of your union. Among Pythagoras, the law of natural knowledge dictating, the same sentence is found: that the true ornaments of matrons are chastity, not garments.
3.5:
**“For after this manner heretofore”** — even before the time of grace
**“the holy women also, who trusted in God, adorned themselves”** — not in the adornment of garments
3.6:
**“As Sara obeyed Abraham”** — even in those things which seemed hard
**“calling him lord”** — out of reverence
**“whose daughters you are, doing well”** — honouring their husbands
**“and not fearing any disturbance”** — do not be disturbed by this if any evil is inflicted by the husbands
3.7:
**“Ye husbands”** — As I have commanded wives that by their holy conversation they win their husbands and serve them, likewise I command you, O husbands, that by your conversation you win your wives; and keep them, I say, dwelling with them, rendering the debt. And this according to knowledge, not in passions of desire, but as we understand God to will, namely that you beget children for the worship of the one God; I say, giving honour to the womanly vessel, as to the weaker, and providing for them in clothing and other necessaries, even if at times it pleases them to cease from intercourse. Give honour, because they are weaker. Give it also as to co-heirs of the grace given by God in the present and of the life to be given in the future, or of the life to be given for grace.
**“giving honour”** — If we abstain from intercourse, we give honour; if we do not abstain, it is plain that intercourse is contrary to honour.
**“as to the co-heirs of the grace of life”** — therefore conduct yourselves with modesty toward your wives, so that your prayers are not hindered; for if you were at discord, your prayers would not please.
**“that your prayers be not hindered”** — He recalls that prayers are hindered by the conjugal duty, because as often as I render the debt to my wife, I cannot pray. But if, according to the word of the apostle, we must pray without intermission, then I must never serve marriage, lest any hour hinder me from prayer, to which I am commanded always to be intent.
3.8:
**“And in fine, be ye all”** — I have taught different persons, different conditions, different sexes; now I admonish all together, in the cause of the Lord’s faith, that you have one heart and one soul.
**“be ye of one mind”** — that you not differ even in thought
**“having compassion one of another”** — that each count the burden and misfortune of the other as his own
**“being lovers of the brotherhood”** — that you not destroy brotherhood, and that by this you not fall away more freely from the faith
**“merciful”** — by forgiving sins, bestowing alms, and not being proud of these
**“modest, humble”** — doing all things with measure
3.9:
**“Not rendering”**
• which according to the justice of the world seems rightly possible to do
• Not only cease to render evil for evil, but also give a blessing for a curse.
**“evil for evil”** — in deed
**“nor railing for railing”** — in words
**“for unto this are you called”** — Because he had forbidden to render evil for evil, and had rather commanded to bless those who curse, he rightly confirms by the prophetic testimony that both the good and the wicked are always seen by the brotherly gaze, that we may remember that both our patience, by which we suffer the wicked, and our goodwill, by which we wish good things to our persecutors, will be rewarded with an eternal prize, and that the persecutors will be punished with a fitting torment; but if they repent, we also shall receive a crown for their salvation, for which we prayed.
**“that you may inherit a blessing”** — As the judge says: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, possess you the kingdom prepared for you.” Or the blessing with which the saints in the life to come will bless God. What therefore each one desires to come to in the future, let him strive to meditate on and to do in the present: let him bless his Creator and his brother, and make himself worthy of a brother’s blessing.
3.10:
**“For he that will love life”** — who wishes to show that he has the blessing
**“and see good days”** — since in this world the days are evil
**“let him refrain his tongue”** — inwardly, let him not murmur.
**“from evil, and his lips that they speak no guile”** — outwardly, let him not utter anything deceitful.
3.11:
**“Let him decline from evil”** — even if an occasion is given him outwardly to sin.
**“and do good: let him seek”** — as a hidden thing.
**“peace”** — with God, with a brother.
**“and pursue it”** — as a fleeing thing.
3.12:
**“Because the eyes of the Lord”** — a look of mercy.
**“are upon the just, and his ears unto their prayers”** — on account of the swift effect.
**“but the countenance of the Lord”** — judgment or manifestation.
**“upon them that do evil things”** — either in the first place, or by repaying others.
3.13:
**“And who is he that can hurt you, if you be zealous of good?”** — And who is he, etc. Therefore you ought to turn away from evil and do good, because no one can draw you back from good, nor from the crown, if you are willing to persevere; indeed they profit you while they wish to harm.
**“And who”** — If they bring insulting words, or losses of goods, or torments, they do not hurt, but exercise your patience. But if anyone, overcome by these, fails, it is not he who brought the evil but he himself who did not endure the evil that has hurt. Every house is tried, both that which is founded upon the rock and that which is founded upon the sand; but to the one the firmness of the foundation gives the crown of perseverance; the other a frail structure laid low.
3.14:
**“But if also you suffer any thing”** — not only does what is inflicted by the wicked not harm, but it even profits, because it exercises patience.
**“for justice' sake”** — to be held or to be attained.
**“And be not afraid of their fear”** — In the future you will be blessed; but in the present, do not fear their fear, that is, those things in them which can seem to be feared, such as royal power and the like.
**“be not afraid of their fear”** — by departing from faith and love.
3.15:
**“But sanctify the Lord Christ”** — Look upon the holiness of Christ, how incomprehensible its glory is, with the inmost affection of the heart; and so sanctify Christ himself in you, so that he does not depart from your memory or from your love. Whoever does not consider this holiness fails against the snares of the enemy.
**“every one that asketh you”** — Let us not refuse reasonable sums of money to one who wishes to borrow. Whence Paul: “Walk in wisdom towards them that are without, knowing how you ought to answer every man.” For those who are outside, that is, not yet faithful, wish to learn something of the hope which is in you. Let him therefore who presides over the Church’s teaching instruct the patient and stop the mouths of those who resist.
**“a reason”** — In two ways we ought to give a reason of our hope and faith: that to those who ask, whether faithfully or unfaithfully, we may make known the right grounds of hope and faith; and that we may keep that faith and hope unspotted amid pressures, showing by patience that we have learned that it is reasonably to be preserved, for the love of which we fear neither to suffer adversity nor to undergo death.
3.16:
**“But with modesty and fear, having a good conscience”**
• and have not only doctrine but also, in doctrine, modesty, which is the mother of all virtues.
• or, according to modesty and fear, so that what you show outwardly you may have inwardly.
• In the very knowledge of the teaching, it warns that the manner of teaching be observed, so that humility is shown both in living and in speaking.
**“that whereas they speak evil of you”** — who mock in words the faith and hope of heavenly things, which they cannot see, let them be confounded by your good works, which they cannot deny to be good.
**“that whereas they speak evil”** — Or, by doing good with care, so that those who detract from your good conduct may be confounded, when the time of retribution comes, seeing you crowned with Christ and themselves condemned with the devil.
**“as of evildoers”** — in most copies it is omitted.
**“they may be ashamed who falsely accuse”** — as if they are confounded at this, that they slander.
3.17:
**“It is better”** — So you ought to bear and confound slanderers, because it is safer for you to suffer for good deeds than for evil deeds. Here he reproves those who, when they are rebuked for faults by their brethren or even constrained by punishments, bear it patiently, but if anything is inflicted on them by their brethren without fault, straightway burst into anger, and those who till now seemed innocent make themselves guilty through impatience and murmuring. It was more profitable for Tobias to be struck with blindness without fault, that his patience might be proved, than for Elymas the magician, who, struck for his perfidy, is removed from the madness of the believers and prepared for eternal vengeance.
**“doing well (if such be the will of God)”** — which prepares a greater reward.
3.18:
**“Because Christ also”** — He therefore who being just suffers imitates Christ; he who is corrected by scourges imitates the thief who, having acknowledged Christ on the cross, entered paradise; he who is not corrected even by scourges imitates the thief on the left, who for his sins went up on the cross and after the cross went to Tartarus.
**“died once for our sins”** — so we die once, that is, by temporal death, for which eternal reward will be given.
**“the just for the unjust, that he might offer us to God”** — Christ offers us to God the Father, that is, he shows our life to be praiseworthy in the sight of the Father, since through mortification of the flesh we rejoice to be sacrificed for him; or he offers us to God when we are freed from the flesh, he leads us into the eternal kingdom.
**“offer us to God”** — Because then too, if any were willing to believe the preaching of the Lord, which he put forward through the life of the faithful, he rejoiced to offer them to God the Father. But those who detracted from the good as from evildoers, with the flood impending, were confounded.
**“being put to death indeed in the flesh”** — Christ offers us to God the Father, that is, he shows our life to be praiseworthy in the sight of the Father, since through mortification of the flesh we rejoice to be sacrificed for him; or he offers us to God when we are freed from the flesh, he leads us into the eternal kingdom.
**“but enlivened in the spirit”** — holy, or our.
3.19:
**“In which also coming he preached to those spirits that were in prison”** — of darkness and unbelief; or in prison, that is, living in carnal desires.
**“in prison”** — Those who have their understanding darkened by shadows. Deservedly they are said even in this life to be shut up in prison, and in this inner prison of the mind they are weighed down by unjust works, until, released from the flesh, they are cast into the exterior darkness of eternal damnation. The just also have a prison here, but of tribulations; the reprobate, however, of vices.
**“he preached to those spirits”** — by Noe
**“coming he preached”** — He who in our times, coming in the flesh, preached to the world the way of life, himself also before the flood, coming in the spirit, preached to those who were then unbelieving and had lived carnally; for through the Holy Spirit he was in Noe and in the other good men, by whose good conversation he preached to others, the wicked, that they might be converted to good.
3.20:
**“Which had been some time incredulous”** — did not believe God threatening through Noe.
**“when they waited for the patience of God”** — Although the patience of God invited them to penance, sparing them for a hundred years during which Noe was building the ark, by which was shown what was to be in the world, they did not use the patience of God for penance, but waited for it as though it would last forever.
**“Noe”** — Which is interpreted rest, signifies Christ, who gives his faithful the rest of souls.
**“when the ark was a building”** — As the ark was built of smoothed timbers, so the Church is built of the gathering of faithful souls; as when the world perished few were saved by water, so in comparison with those who perish the number of the elect is small, because: “Strait is the way that leadeth to life: and few there are that find it.”
**“wherein a few”** — they believed God
**“that is, eight souls, were saved by water”**
• by those who were drowned in the flood is signified the mortification of the flesh; by those who were saved is signified the quickening of the spirit.
• who had the hope of the eighth.
3.21:
**“Whereunto baptism being of the like form, now saveth you also”** — Baptism makes safe—baptism, I say, of like form, that is, made like in every respect to that ark—because whatever was done there carnally is done here spiritually. That the water of the flood saved none who were placed outside the ark but killed them, signified that every heretic, though having the sacrament of baptism, is to be plunged down to hell, not by other waters but by the very waters by which the ark is lifted up to heaven.
**“not the putting away of the filth of the flesh”** — I do not say that baptism saves where there is only the putting away of the filth of the flesh, that is, where the flesh is only washed outwardly, which the heretics had; but where there is the examination of a pure conscience, that is, where the baptizer questions and requires a good conscience in the one to be baptized, for such baptism saves; the other kills. An examination made and tending toward God, that by a good conscience one may be made one with God.
**“but the examination of a good conscience towards God”** — it is not enough to have a good conscience in being baptized, unless at the Church’s questioning one shows one’s faith.
**“by the resurrection of Jesus Christ”** — And this through the resurrection, that as Christ rose from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also, cleansed from vices by the water of regeneration, may walk in newness of life.
3.22:
**“Who is on the right hand of God”** — who can, because he is at the right hand, etc.
**“swallowing down death”** — What we swallow down, we so act that what has been taken in no longer appears in our bodies. The Lord so utterly consumed death that nothing could prevail against him, and, the appearance of a true body remaining, the stain of former frailty was gone. Which is also promised to us. Whence he adds: “That we might be made heirs of life everlasting.”
**“that we might be made heirs of life everlasting”** — and after death was destroyed.
**“being gone into heaven”** — As Christ, rising, ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God, so also to us through baptism he has marked out the way of salvation and the entrance into the heavenly homeland of the kingdom.
**“the angels being made subject to him”**
• angels, the first.
• We do not doubt that the angels were always subject to the Son of God, but he mentions subjection here in order to show that the humanity he assumed, thus exalted in the resurrection, is set above every power of angelic dignity. Whence: “Thou hast subjected all things under his feet.”
**“and powers”** — powers, the second.
**“and virtues”** — virtues, the third order.

4.1:
**“Christ therefore having suffered”**
• because he swallowed, because we shall be heirs.
• After he has set forth the example of the Lord’s resurrection and of our washing, from the ark and the sacrament of the flood, he returns to what he had begun: that imitating the Saviour, amid the good we do, we should patiently bear the wickedness of evil men.
• Whoever of the just submits his body to martyrdom, having nothing in the world in which to sin, is compelled to desire only this: that, the contest ended, he may receive the crown of life. Peter wishes the minds of such men always to be imitated, with the example of the Lord’s passion set before them. He commands us to be armed with the same thought against the wickedness of the perverse and against the allurements of vices, wishing it to be understood that we also, resting in the peace of the Church, if we put on the habit of one who suffers, easily, with God’s help, avoid the falls of sins.
**“in the flesh”** — not in the godhead.
**“be you also armed with the same thought”** — as he willingly, so we also willingly; as he bore all things, so we should bear; whence comes the profit.
**“for he that hath suffered”** — He who by fear of the heavenly judgments extinguishes fleshly desires in the mind, already like Christ crucified, existing as if dead to sins, lives only in the service of God.
4.2: **“not after the desires of men, but according to the will of God”** — strengthening himself in good works.
4.3:
**“For the time past is sufficient”** — truly he now ceases from sins, because, the monstrousness of the crime having been considered, it is enough to have spent the past time.
**“to”** — according to
**“to have fulfilled the will of the Gentiles, for them who have walked”** — to be fulfilled in such a way that, as the Gentiles walked from vice to vice, not steady in one vice.
4.4:
**“Wherein”** — because you have crucified the flesh with its vices and concupiscences.
**“they think it strange, that you run not with them into the same confusion of riotousness”** — into which you formerly ran.
**“speaking evil of you”** — And even if they blaspheme you, set apart from their faithlessness, yet seeing in your conduct the works of justice and piety, they marvel and in some measure revere the faith.
4.5: **“Who shall render account to him, who is ready to judge the living and the dead”** — therefore be less concerned if, doing good, you are blasphemed by the reprobate, because although you keep silent, the just judge will not be silent, who will render to them the reward of blasphemy and to you of patience.
4.6:
**“For, for this cause”**
• therefore you ought not to care, because.
• So great is God’s care that we be put to death in the flesh and made alive in the spirit, that he commanded the word of faith to be preached even to those who, entangled in greater crimes, were to be numbered among the dead, that they may be judged indeed, that is, condemned by themselves, according to men, that is, according to this, that they lived after the manner of sinners in the flesh; that is, that, with carnal desires and vices cast away, they may live in the spirit, that is, spiritually, according to the will of God. Or: that they may be judged according to men, that is, according to the reason which God gave to men, that their own reason may condemn the evils in the wicked.
4.7:
**“But the end of all is at hand”** — Because he had said that the living and the dead are to be judged, he wisely warns that no one should flatter himself about the distance of the future judgment; for although the coming of the final crisis is uncertain, yet it is certain to all that we cannot endure long in this life.
**“But the end of all is at hand. Be prudent therefore”** — not failing from the faith.
**“and watch in prayers”**
• and that you may understand the manner of praying, and be able to obtain what you have prayed for, have charity among you; not because of your outward things but within yourselves, be yourselves the cause of love.
• Let the mind think of nothing except that alone which it prays. When we stand to pray, let every carnal thought depart; let the sincere intention of the heart pray to God not with the sound of the voice but with the sense of the mind.
4.8:
**“But before all things have a constant mutual charity among yourselves”** — He who through charity admonishes, rebukes, and corrects his neighbour, through charity covers a multitude of sins; because: “He who causeth a sinner to be converted from the error of his way, shall save his soul from death, and shall cover a multitude of sins.”
**“for charity covereth a multitude of sins”** — when faults are washed away by other virtues, most of all by charity, through which debts are forgiven to our neighbours, so that our own debts may be forgiven us by God.
**“for charity covereth”** — Because of the frailty of the flesh we cannot always persist in prayer and hospitality or in the other virtues, which must be done by the service of the body and at suitable times. But charity itself, by whose impulse these things are done outwardly, and which presides over the inner man, can always be had there, though it cannot always be shown in public.
4.10:
**“As every man hath received grace”** — by God freely
**“ministering the same one to another”** — any gift of the Holy Spirit for serving others, both in temporal and in spiritual things.
**“as good stewards of the manifold grace of God”** — formed according to the desire of each one, as in the manna it had the taste according to the food each wanted.
4.11:
**“If any man speak, let him speak, as the words of God”** — If anyone has the knowledge of speaking, let him impute it not to himself but to God; let him fear lest he teach his brother contrary to the will of God or the authority of the holy Scriptures, or contrary to what is useful, and let him not keep silent what is to be taught.
**“If any man minister”**
• let him bestow either alms or some good work humbly, because he has nothing of himself to bestow, but only from God alone.
• When you have done all things well and according to his will, attribute them not to your merits but to his grace, so that others seeing your good works may glorify your Father who is in heaven.
**“as of the power, which God administereth, that in all things”** — in your actions
**“God may be honoured through Jesus Christ”** — helper and mediator
**“To him is glory”** — renown
**“and empire”** — power
4.12:
**“Dearly beloved”** — do these good things, and cease not for any tribulation.
**“Dearly beloved, think not strange”** — If you suffer the burning heat of tribulations, which are brought upon you against reason, for your proving and glory, do not therefore think yourselves exiles from the members of Christ, and do not wonder at the evils brought upon you, since through them God tries and proves you; for it is ancient and frequent for the elect of God to suffer adversity in the present for eternal salvation.
**“think not strange”** — Do not waver from the love of God, failing in faith, or be amazed.
4.13:
**“but if you partake”** — by representing
**“but if you partake of the sufferings of Christ, rejoice that when his glory”** — when every veil will be taken away
**“you may be glad”** — in mind
**“with exceeding joy”**
• in body
• because
4.14:
**“If you be reproached for the name of Christ”** — remaining
**“you shall be blessed”** — You shall be blessed, etc. He who suffers for the name of Christ is blessed. For you ought not to believe that you suffer without reward, like those who suffer for their crimes and are punished against their will. Or: let no one be ashamed to suffer for the name of Christ, but let him be ashamed to commit crimes for which he is justly punished. But if he suffers as a Christian, for the faith and confession of the name of Christ, let him not be ashamed, but rather glorify God, remaining in this name, so that it may be said: good is this Lord, who has such faithful servants.
**“for that which is of the honour, glory, and power of God, and that which is his Spirit”** — of Christ
**“resteth upon you”** — you who labour in body rest in spirit.
**“his Spirit resteth upon you”** — Because he will rest upon you who suffer, both in the present in part, for doing good, and in the future perfectly, for rewarding. What is of honour: that both in the present you may be honourable in good works, and in the future partakers of the honour of Christ. And what is of glory: in the present a pure conscience, in the future freedom from all corruption, in soul as well as in body. And what is of power: both in the present and in the future, over the devil and his members. And whence all this? He adds: and the Holy Spirit, who is his, Christ’s, shall rest upon you. For he received him fully, and gave him to his members, and in the future will give him most of all.
4.15:
**“let none of you suffer”** — here, where no reward is expected, but perhaps it is the beginning of punishment.
**“as a murderer, or a thief, or a railer”** — he suffers as a railer who, at the time of his passion, for his own salvation, is unbridled by the wrong of the persecutor.
4.16:
**“But if as a Christian”** — suffers
**“let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God”** — Whence: “But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc.
**“in that name”** — Christian
4.17:
**“for the time is that judgment should begin”**
• Whence: “Justice and judgment are the preparation of his throne.”
• For the time is, etc. Therefore we must suffer for the name of Christ, because, since no evil can pass without punishment, and God is to judge the wicked severely at the last, in the present he scourges and corrects all whom he wishes to receive to salvation. Whence Solomon: “Son, when thou comest to the service of God, prepare thy soul for temptation.”
• His judgments are two: one hidden and the other manifest. The hidden is the punishment by which each man now is either exercised for purging, or warned for conversion, or, if he despises the one who calls, is blinded for condemnation. The other, manifest, is that by which he is to come to judge the living and the dead; and now is the time for the Church to be prepared for glory through the trials of the world. But the reprobate now: “spend their days in wealth, and in a moment they go down to hell.”
**“at”** — or: from
**“the house of God”**
• that is, by the faithful
• from the time the house of God began to be
**“And if first at us, what shall be the end of them that believe not the gospel of God”** — if judgment is first made from us; if here he torments those whom he loves, if he scourges his sons, what should the most wicked servants hope?
4.18:
**“And if the just man”**
• who hears, receives and embraces the words of God, not conscious of any evil in himself
• And if the just man, etc. It is taken from Proverbs according to the old edition. In ours, which is according to the Hebrew truth, it is thus: “If the just man receive in the earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner?” That is, if the frailty of mortal life is so great that not even the just, who are to be crowned in heaven, pass through it without tribulations, because of the countless stain of vitiated nature, how much more do those who have no share in heavenly glory look to the certain destruction of their own everlasting damnation.
*Augustine:* Do you ask why the just man can scarcely be saved in God’s judgment? And why? Only because it is certain that God’s justice is so great that at times what seems just in men by our judgment is found unjust by God’s judgment. According to that: “Man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart.” It is not hard for God to deliver the just man; but to show that the whole human nature was deservedly condemned, God himself does not will to deliver it easily from so great an evil, because sins are easy, and justice is laborious except to those who love; but charity, which makes men lovers, is from God.
**“shall scarcely be saved”** — toiling, contending with great struggle
**“the ungodly”**
• against God
• who contradicts the word of God, wholly outside God
**“and the sinner”**
• against the neighbour
• who, although he receives the words, nevertheless despises him and afflicts his members
**“where shall appear”** — in a stinking place
4.19: **“let them commend their souls”** — And because “judgment begins at the house of the Lord,” and “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God.” So this remains for those who are to suffer: that when they suffer according to what God wills, that is, for justice’s sake, they commend their souls to God, presuming nothing of themselves, that here he may purge them as he wills, and in the future make them blessed, because he is faithful, rendering good things to those whom he created. I say they suffer in good deeds, not for sins.

5.1:
**“The ancients therefore”** — and because it is necessary to suffer, and those who suffer commend their souls to God, therefore suffer and labour for him
**“The ancients”** — Since above he had distinctly admonished children and servants, husbands and wives themselves, after an intervening general exhortation, here he addresses the old men and the young.
**“that are among you, I beseech”** — the old men are to be entreated
**“who am also an ancient”** — show favour to those of like age
**“and a witness of the sufferings of Christ”** — because being present, I stood by him while he suffered; for his name I bore prison and chains, and what I saw of him I wrote
**“as also a partaker of that glory which is to be revealed in time to come”** — when on the holy mountain he saw with James and John the heavenly glory of his countenance, of which he also hopes to be a partaker; or when he saw the power of his resurrection and ascension with the other apostles who were present
5.2:
**“Feed”** — As the Lord commanded Peter to have care of the whole flock, so Peter, rightly, charges the pastors who follow in the Church that each one, with whom he is, should guard the flock of God by careful government.
**“which is among you”** — among you, or you yourselves who are
**“the flock of God”** — providing for those under you in all necessary things
**“not by constraint”**
• Do not preach the gospel because of want of temporal things, so that you may live by the gospel; but willingly according to God, namely only with a view to the heavenly reward.
• Do not preach merely to avoid want. Let no gain drive you, because all works of religion ought to be voluntary, as in the building of the tabernacle, which signifies the present building of the Church, the whole multitude of the children of Israel with devout mind offered firstfruits to the Lord for the making of the work of the tabernacle, and the very craftsmen offered themselves of their own accord.
**“but willingly, according to God”** — preach nothing except according to God
5.3:
**“Neither as lording it over the clergy”** — namely, the humility which you wish your subjects to have, you yourselves first show by deed and keep with an attentive mind
**“but being made a pattern of the flock from the heart”** — through you the flock is to be formed to humility
5.4:
**“And when the prince of pastors shall appear”**
• and from that you obtain this reward
• who was first humbled
5.5:
**“In like manner, ye young men, be subject to the ancients”** — that is, from the heart
**“In like manner, ye young men”** — After he taught the elders how they should preside, he also instructs the younger to obey their fatherly care. And he admonishes nothing else than that they be subject to the elders whom he had instructed before, and look to their examples and imitate them. But lest prelates, hearing this, should think that the laws of humility are to be kept by their subjects and not by themselves, he straightway adds, admonishing generally: But all, the elders by teaching and the young by following.
**“be subject to the ancients. And do you all insinuate humility one to another”** — both old and young ought to have humility, because God resists the proud, etc.
**“insinuate”**
• show to others by word and example
• always hold in your bosom
**“for God resisteth the proud”** — By the authority of Solomon he deters from pride, which cast down the devil.
**“to the humble”** — as to penitent men.
5.6:
**“Be you humbled therefore”** — He adds what the grace is that he confers on the humble: that the more they have been humbled for his sake in the time of struggle, the more gloriously they may be exalted in the time of reward. We speak of humility either when someone begins to be wholesomely worn down to wash away sins; or when the more perfect are humbled before God and men by a spontaneous devotion of mind; or when against persecutors the unconquered mind is armed by the virtue of patience. And for every kind of humility a fitting reward of exaltation follows.
**“under the mighty hand of God”** — who are here in pilgrimage.
**“that he may exalt you in the time of visitation”** — of judgment.
5.7:
**“Casting all your care”** — of body and soul.
**“upon him”** — as an anchor in the sea.
**“for he hath care of you”** — cast them so that you also cooperate with helping grace.
5.8:
**“Be sober and watch”** — not intent on the pleasures of the world.
**“because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion”** — As a roaring lion. As the roar of a lion stops the ears so that they receive no other sound, so the devil, by terrifying the minds of the faithful and suggesting unlawful things, turns them from the way of truth, so that they do not hear the voice of Christ.
**“goeth about”** — Like an enemy besieging walls that are shut, he searches whether any part of the walls is less secure, by whose approach the interior may be entered. He offers to the eyes unlawful forms and easy pleasures, that by sight he may destroy chastity; to the ears, songs, that he may soften Christian strength. He provokes the tongue with abuse; he urges the hand to slaughter with provoking injuries; he promises earthly honours that he may take away heavenly ones. And when he cannot deceive secretly, he adds open terrors. In peace he is full of guile; in persecution, violent; against him the mind ought to be as ready to resist as he is ready to attack.
5.9:
**“Whom resist ye, strong in faith”** — let faith be as a wall.
**“Knowing”** — Have so much the greater confidence, as it is clear that you alone are not tempted, but the very suffering that wearies you is the same and common to our brotherhood, that is, to the brotherly Church which is throughout the whole world; and since from the foundation of the world the just have always suffered, be ashamed that you alone before all cannot suffer.
**“the same affliction befalls your brethren who are in the world”** — do that which is in you.
5.10:
**“But the God of all grace”**
• of faith, hope and the others.
• giver.
**“who hath called us into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus”** — being as members.
**“after you have suffered a little, will himself perfect”** — he will add to those virtues which you already have other virtues.
**“will confirm”** — to bear tribulations.
**“and establish you”** — he will bring back into unity of the Church the members loosened by fear and error.
5.12:
**“By Sylvanus”** — who was necessary to me, but for the sake of your salvation I sent him away.
**“I have written”** — To you, not commanding but beseeching and testifying, by the authority of the Scriptures, that this is the true grace which I proclaim by writing, because “Neither is there salvation in any other,” in whom you must be saved. Or beseeching you to make this grace in which you stand, with which you have been imbued, to be your true grace, and profitable to you. He who spurns grace does not diminish grace, but makes it not his own, that is, not useful to himself.
**“briefly”** — so that you may quickly understand.
**“beseeching and testifying that this is the true grace of God, wherein you stand”** — what I say to you, others also say.
5.13:
**“In Babylon”** — He calls Rome Babylon, because of the confusion of manifold idolatry in the midst of which the holy Church, still rude and small, already shone, as the Israelite people, small in number and captive, sitting by the rivers of Babylon, wept for the absence of the holy land, and did not sing the song of the Lord in a strange land; and well, while he exhorts his hearers to patience in present adversities, he says the Church which is with him is established in Babylon, that is, in the confusion of tribulations, because the holy city of God cannot be free from the mingling and oppression of the devil.
**“and so doth my son Mark”** — the evangelist, baptized by me, taught by me.
5.14:
**“Salute one another”** — as a sign of common faith.
**“with a holy kiss”** — peaceful, dovelike, not feigned, not deceitful.
**“Grace”** — it begins with grace and ends in grace.
**“be to all you, who are in Christ Jesus”** — as though what I write to the aforementioned churches, I write to all churches throughout the world.

1.1:
**“Simon”** — obeying, namely, the faith.
**“Peter”** — acknowledging the truth, steadfast in the faith.
**“Simon Peter”** — He writes this letter to the same elect proselytes of the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia to whom he wrote the first, confirming them against the false teachers who, turning away the true doctrine, were bringing in their own errors, that those who did not yield to persecutors may not yield to heretics.
**“servant”** — humble.
**“and apostle”** — A servant and an apostle. The person of the writer is commended.
**“Jesus Christ”** — a messenger of our Saviour and King.
**“Equal”** — He acknowledges them as equals to himself, not on account of circumcision, but because they had received the same grace of Christ that he himself had received, and the same faith, and practised it through works.
**“have obtained”** — by divine election.
**“In the justice”** — Human prudence did not discover this justice, nor did the instruction of the law teach it, but our Saviour showed it in the gospel: “Unless your justice abound more than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.”
**“and Saviour Jesus Christ”** — you are made equal to the ancient people of God not in the circumcision of the law but by faith, which saves without the works of the law.
1.2:
**“Grace to you”** — In the first let it be multiplied, in this let it be fulfilled, because he writes the former to beginners, this to the more perfect. Grace is multiplied in those who make good progress in this life by faith; it will be fulfilled in those who reach the other life by sight. Whence he adds: “In the knowledge of our God,” that you may know the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom he sent.
**“and peace be accomplished in the knowledge”**
• or acknowledgment.
• in which is the completion of eternal life, whence they are made perfect in one.
1.3:
**“As all things”** — gifts.
**“As all things, are given us”** — Let it be so fulfilled that through him you may know how, that is, how perfectly, all the gifts of his grace have been given to us, not gifts of weakness, as in the old law, which led no one to perfection, but gifts of his power, which are sufficient for life and godliness, because: “All things whatsoever he heard from the Father he hath made known.” Or, if it be read “which was given to life and godliness,” it is expounded thus: that you may know how the Lord has bestowed on us all the gifts of his power according to the measure of our capacity, which power was given for attaining life and godliness.
**“of his divine power which appertain to life”** — to be obtained.
**“and godliness”** — to be preserved.
**“are given”** — and this.
**“through the knowledge of him who hath called us”** — through the knowledge of the Saviour we have come to know all the mysteries of the divinity by which we are saved.
**“his own proper glory”** — when he was transfigured on the mountain.
**“proper glory”** — He sent neither an angel nor an archangel to save us; he found in us nothing good by which we might be saved, but by his own virtue and glory he restored us, weak and without glory.
**“and virtue”** — of miracles.
1.4:
**“By whom”**
• or through whom, Christ; or through which gifts.
• knowledge.
**“most great and precious promises, he hath given us”** — the more perfectly one knows God, the more he perceives the greatness of his promises.
**“Most great and precious promises he hath given us”** — That is, eternal life, which we attain through knowledge of him. Or those things he promised us about the conversion of others through us, or he gave of the coming of the Holy Spirit or of the power of miracles.
**“he hath given us promises”** — Or, therefore, to us who are Jews by nature, who made use of his teaching bodily, he unlocked all the sacraments, and therefore gave the greatest and precious promises of the Holy Spirit, that through this he might grant you also, who are of the Gentiles and have not seen Christ in the flesh, to be partakers of his divine nature; that as we have either received the promises from him or trust that we shall receive them, so you also who believe may be free from doubt about his gifts.
**“that by these”** — grace be to you and peace, that through this.
**“you may be made partakers of the divine nature”** — co-heirs of the Son of God, not by nature but by grace; yet so that you are fleeing, lest you be corrupted by concupiscence.
1.5:
**“And you, employing all care, minister in your faith, virtue”**
• of good working.
• Minister in faith. Not only flee the concupiscence of the world, but also minister virtue in your faith; as though in a servile and humble manner show to the brethren virtue, that is, the constancy of your good conduct, which is to be added to faith, lest faith be idle without works, that by your example you may confirm others in good conduct. I say, you employing all care. Let all your care be in God alone, in the secret of the heart, that you be not soft and dissolute.
**“and in virtue”** — in good conduct, learn to do well, in hope of eternal, not temporal, things.
**“knowledge”** — of discretion in knowing what, to whom, when or how; but because pleasure is wont to flatter under the appearance of discretion, therefore in knowledge minister abstinence.
1.6:
**“And in knowledge, abstinence”**
• from evils.
• from pleasures.
• When you have learned to do good, with hope of eternal life, straightway abstain from evils, both in thought and in deed, lest the knowledge of heavenly things come to nothing. If anyone does not restrain himself from the allurements of the world.
**“and in abstinence, patience”** — patience follows abstinence, so that he who restrains himself from the pleasures of the world also endures its adversities.
**“and in patience, godliness”** — so that toward those whom you endure you may be devoutly anxious out of charity.
1.7:
**“In godliness, love of brotherhood”** — Do not spend works of godliness on your adversaries with any other regard than brotherly love, so that you pray for them, that those who are unwilling to be converted by your teaching or your rebukes may be converted.
**“and in love of brotherhood, charity”**
• of God
• Charity of God, which rightly is joined to love of brotherhood, because neither God is perfectly loved without the neighbour, nor the neighbour without God.
1.8:
**“For if these things be with you and abound”**
• the wars of vices
• For if these things, etc. Therefore hold these things and minister them to others, because if all these be with you in the affection of the heart, and also abound, that is, prevail against the wars of the vices, they will make you not empty of virtues in this world, nor without fruit in the world to come. Or not empty in yourselves, like a vessel empty of every good liquor, nor without fruit in others whom you convert by your example.
**“neither empty”**
• in the present
• as regards yourselves
• will not appear empty in my sight
**“nor unfruitful”**
• in the future
• as regards others
• of virtues
• of reward
**“they will make you to be in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ”** — on the day of judgment, when Jesus will be known; or in the knowledge, that is, because you have known.
1.9:
**“For he that”** — these things are truly to be held, because
**“hath not these things with him, is blind”** — a stranger to the light of the divine sun
**“and groping”** — not having a guide of the good way
**“is blind, and groping”** — The eye signifies knowledge, the hand action. He is blind and groping who, not having knowledge of right action, does whatever seems right to himself, and, ignorant of the light of truth, stretching out his hand as it were to a work which he does not see, sets his steps on a road which he does not foresee; and therefore, wretched, he falls into the ruin of perdition which he could not foresee.
**“having forgotten that he was purged”** — through baptism or through penance
**“having forgotten”** — When a man falls from sin into sin, he seems to have forgotten the covenant which he entered into with God in baptism.
**“old”** — of original sins, or in which he had long been accustomed
**“his old sins”** — of actual sins
1.10:
**“Wherefore, brethren”** — because he is blind who does not have this
**“labour the more”** — labour with greater zeal to hold on to these
**“that by good works you may make sure your calling and election”** — that by doing good you show yourselves certainly called by God and chosen, and make yourselves certain of the reward of your calling.
**“make sure your calling”** — “Many are called, but few chosen.” The calling, then, of all who come to the faith is sure. But those who, to the sacraments of the faith which they have received, also add good works perseveringly, these make their calling, and their election too, sure to those who look on. So too those who after their calling turn to vices, when they have departed from this life in those vices, it is now made certain to all that they were reprobate.
**“For doing these things”** — supply these things, because
**“you shall not sin”** — mortally
**“at any time”** — in the future life
**“you shall not sin at any time”** — That is, you will attain to eternal life, where you will sin no more; or you will avoid mortal sins, of which he who commits them “hath no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ,” from which he remains free, the Lord helping, who has devoted himself to the virtues aforesaid. But without venial sins no one can be.
1.11:
**“For so”** — by supplying these things
**“an entrance shall be ministered to you abundantly”**
• that is, the virtues through which you will enter into life.
• For so an entrance shall be ministered abundantly, etc. Ezechiel, speaking of the building set upon the mountain, says: “And the going up to it was by eight steps.” And here Peter numbers eight steps of virtues: faith, virtue, knowledge, abstinence, patience, godliness, love of the brotherhood, charity; by which, fleeing the corruption of worldly concupiscence, we ought to ascend to the dwelling of the heavenly kingdom, of which the psalmist says: “He hath disposed ascents in his heart, in the vale of tears, in the place which he hath set; and he bringeth in, and they shall go from virtue to virtue: the God of gods shall be seen in Sion.”
1.12:
**“For which cause”** — because these things are so useful
**“I will begin”** — That there may be an open entrance for you to the holy of holies, I will admonish you again and again, and I will always be at the beginning, because there will never be an end to admonition. What is therefore not burdensome to me to repeat often, let it not be burdensome to you to hear often.
**“to put you always in remembrance”**
• or concerning these
• by eight steps
**“though indeed you know”**
• that in the present life these things can be known
• I will admonish
• Why does he wish to admonish those who know and are confirmed? Namely, that they may exercise by works the knowledge they have, and keep with firm mind the truth in whose presence they are confirmed, lest at any time through teachers of error they fall away from the simplicity and chastity of the faith.
**“and are confirmed”** — although you are confirmed
**“in the present truth”** — in the future you will see better and be more firmly confirmed, and there will be no need to be admonished
1.13:
**“But I think it meet as long as I am in this tabernacle”**
• that is, in the body, in which the journey of this life is made and the contest against the adversaries of the truth is fought
• But I think it meet, etc. Therefore I will admonish, because I think it meet (by the fact that the Lord kindly called me and confirmed me, and bade me confirm others, saying: “Confirm thy brethren”) to stir you up, as though sleeping, to these things aforesaid, being always careful in putting you in remembrance.
1.14:
**“Being assured that the laying away of this my tabernacle is at hand”** — therefore more than is right, because I shall soon be removed from you, and many false teachers will creep in, against whom you must arm yourselves
**“The laying away of this my tabernacle”** — Beautifully he calls it not death but laying down, because for the servants of God it is so to put off the bonds of the flesh as it is for travelers, when the journey is finished, to go to their own home instead of a tent; and as for soldiers, when the enemy is laid low, to return to their country.
