**“according as our Lord Jesus Christ also hath signified to me”** — as: “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again”; and elsewhere: “Thou shalt stretch forth thy hands, and another shall gird thee,” etc.
1.15:
**“And I will endeavour”** — Because I am soon to pass away, therefore meanwhile, while I live, I will endeavour, that you, namely as often as false teachers press upon you and wish to draw you away, may have these things in memory after my decease, when you will not have me present as teacher; not to have them in just any manner, but so that you make a memory of them by fulfilling them in deed and by teaching others.
**“that you frequently have”** — I wish
**“after my decease”** — The death of the saints is so called when they go out to meet the bridegroom.
**“whereby you may keep a memory of these things”** — you may have
1.16:
**“For we have not by following artificial fables”**
• therefore I am so anxious, because the matter I teach is great
• Here he touches both the pagans and the heretics. The pagans did not fear to call gods whatever delighted them. The heretics, having received the mysteries of the true God, took pains not to attend to the divine Scriptures for the rest, but rather to carry them over to an erroneous sense by interpreting them badly.
**“made known to you the power, and presence of our Lord Jesus Christ”** — by which he works and holds all things
**“and presence”** — by which he foresaw all future things from eternity
**“but we were eyewitnesses”** — rather we teach you those great things that we saw and heard about him, transfigured on the mountain
**“of his greatness”** — we are
**“but we were eyewitnesses of his greatness”** — The transfiguration of the Lord and his brightness was a sign of his resurrection and of ours. By Elias, who appeared with him, is understood the resurrection of those who were before the law; by Moses, of those under the law; by Peter and James and John, of those under grace. Or by Moses, who was dead, that of the dead; by the living, that of the living.
1.17:
**“For he received from God the Father”**
• because this was great
• as if he received from God, insofar as he is man
**“honour”** — when his face and garments shone
**“and glory”** — through the voice coming down, the glory of his divinity shone forth
**“this voice coming down to him”** — the voice coming down to him for glorifying
**“from the excellent glory”** — of such a kind from the magnificent glory: from the glorious Father magnifying and glorifying the Son
**“This is my beloved Son”** — this is my Son, consubstantial
**“in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him”** — beloved, in whom I am well pleased. Hear him. Because no one will succeed him
1.18:
**“And this voice we heard”** — Peter, James, John
**“brought from heaven”** — to prove his divine nature
**“when we were with him in the holy mount”** — Thabor, or one like it, on another mountain, that is, the Mount of Olives, when he was praying.
1.19:
**“And we have the more firm prophetical word”** — And we have the more firm. What I have told you is not fabulous but certain, and not only declared by these signs, but for the confirmation of our preaching we also have the prophetical word of David: “The Lord hath said to me: Thou art my son, this day have I begotten thee.” More firm than the other prophets, because he prophesied more clearly than the others of Christ.
**“The more firm prophetical word”** — If anyone believes our testimony less, because we saw the glory of the Redeemer in secret, no one will dare to contradict the sure prophetic word.
**“whereunto you do well to attend”** — by doing
**“Whereunto you do well to attend”** — That you may be able to have the light of knowledge, understanding this, that none of the holy prophets preached the doctrines of life to the peoples by his own interpretation, but what they had learned from God in secret, this they delivered to the people of God to be observed. The soothsayers of the Gentiles feigned things out of their own heart. As therefore the prophets wrote not their own words but God’s, so the reader ought not to use his own interpretation, lest he stray from the faith. But let him labour to attend to how he who wrote wished his words to be understood.
**“as to a light that shineth”** — or “burning”
**“in a dark place”** — In the night of this world, full of temptations and vices and errors, where scarcely anyone is found who does not offend, against which this lamp is necessary. But will it always be necessary? Not at all. But until the day dawn, in the future the brightness of God appear, and the day star, that is our clear understanding, or Christ himself, arise in our hearts. There will be love such as we now desire, and because it is not yet, we sigh for it; and what it will be, each of us will see in each other, as now we see one another’s faces. Meanwhile it belongs to the lamp of the night that we are the sons of God and it hath not yet appeared what we shall be; in comparison with the wicked we are day; in comparison with the future life we need a lamp.
1.20:
**“Understanding this first”** — Attend to the prophetical word, for it is from God, which can be proved by this, that prophecy is not written in such words and in such a manner of speech as men use in their speaking, and as secular writings are composed and interpreted; and truly the speech of the prophets is not according to their own will or that of the hearers, but according to the will of the Holy Spirit who spoke in them.
**“that no prophecy of scripture is made by private interpretation”** — that is, not by the prophet’s own will, but by the Holy Spirit speaking in him
1.21: **“For prophecy came not by the will of man”** — As it was not in the power of the prophets always to have the Spirit and always to foretell things to come, so it was not in their power to teach whatever they wished, but they taught only what they had learned from the Spirit. These things are said so that no one may expound the Scriptures at his own pleasure.

2.1:
**“But there were also false prophets among the people”** — There were, etc. Therefore I warn you thus and use so many authorities, lest you be deceived by false teachers who pretend that Christ has not yet come. Or if they confess that he has come, they bring in some errors, and they will be gravely punished for their lies together with their followers. As among the people of Israel there were false prophets who proclaimed false things and endured the judgment of everlasting damnation, so also will these.
**“even as there shall be among you lying teachers”** — they already are, but are held back by fear; but after my death they will be made manifest
**“who shall bring in”** — into your hearts
**“sects of perdition”**
• teachings which cut and separate from God, whence they will perish
• Sects: “sects” in Latin, “heresies” in Greek, when someone, by foolish obstinacy, never ceases to pursue the error he once conceived; this is proper to heretics.
**“and deny the Lord”** — Christ
**“who bought them”** — by blood
**“them”** — or “us”
**“deny the Lord”** — to be
**“bringing upon themselves swift destruction”** — having denied the truth, they bring in falsehood, for which they will quickly be endangered
**“Perdition”** — Perdition: rightly do they bring perdition upon themselves who deny their Redeemer, or deny him not as the truth shows him, but as they themselves invent and preach him; and therefore, being estranged from the Redeemer, they await nothing more certain than the pit.
2.2:
**“And many shall follow”** — from whom it is hard to be guarded, because many, etc.
**“their riotousnesses”** — having no hope of future life, they preach desires, to which carnal people easily consent
**“through whom”** — chastity and other good works
**“the way of truth shall be evil spoken of”** — Through the heretics: not only in those whom they draw in, seduced by their heresy, but also in those whom they stir up to hatred of the Christian name by their most impure deeds and the execrable sacrifices or mysteries which they perform, the unskilled supposing all Christians to be enslaved to such shameful deeds.
2.3:
**“And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you”** — not for the cause of religion but for greed, so that they may gain something, they invent new teachings; nor do they buy you for God, but from you they acquire some advantage for themselves
**“Whose”** — to whom: the teachers and their followers
**“judgment now of a long time lingereth not”** — of eternal punishment, long since prepared for them by God; they do not cease, but now torment them, and they will not be without end
**“and their perdition slumbereth not”** — the devil, deceiving now, to torment afterwards
2.4:
**“For if God spared not the angels that sinned”** — proves from the greater
**“God, the angels”**
• who is of more worthy nature
• Although they have received this lower air as a prison, which in relation to heaven is called hell, there still remains the punishment of the last judgment, because “fire is prepared for the devil and his angels.” For God does not permit them to be consumed, but keeps them that they may be punished more grievously together with their members, as Christ is to be glorified with his.
**“For if God spared not the angels”** — If God reserves the apostate angels, delivered to the punishments of hell, for greater torments on the day of judgment; if he also destroyed the world on account of its crimes; if he destroyed the Sodomites and saved Noe and Lot: it is evident that the Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly from temptation, but to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be tormented.
**“Infernal ropes”** — Ropes are the cords by which sailors hang the sails, so that, when the breeze blows, they leave the calm of the harbour and trust themselves always to uncertain waves. To these ropes the endeavours of the unclean spirits are fittingly compared; as soon as they, driven by the blast of pride, raised themselves up against the Creator, they were snatched into the depths of the abyss by the very strivings of their own elation.
**“delivered them, drawn down to the lower hell, unto torments”** — another translation: thrusting them into the dark prisons of hell, he delivered them to be kept for punishment in judgment
**“to be reserved unto judgment”** — that is, he delivered them that they might be reserved for judgment, that is, damnation
2.5:
**“And spared not the original world”** — that is, to men living according to the origin of the first sin
**“The original world”** — The world after the flood is the same as before. Yet that one was as if another, because that world perished by water, and the whole face of the earth and all that air were changed by the height of the waters.
**“The eighth person”** — There are six ages of the world. The seventh is that life where the souls of the saints enjoy a happy sabbath, that is, eternal rest. The eighth is the common resurrection. Secretly, therefore, he hints through the peril of the temporal flood at the day of the judgment to come, when, all the reprobate being condemned, the just will receive the glory of unending life.
**“but preserved Noe, the preacher of justice”** — because by doing works of justice he showed how one ought to live before God
**“bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly”**
• bringing a flood upon the world, that is, the drowning of the wicked
• but
2.6:
**“And reducing the cities”** — These cities were twice reduced to fire, for first he reduced them to ashes by fire together with the neighbouring lands. And when he afterwards covered the places of the burning with the waters of the dead sea, he still willed to preserve the region round about as an appearance of the ancient punishment. For most beautiful apples grow there, which stir up in those who look at them the desire of eating. If you pluck them, they crumble and are dissolved into ashes, and raise smoke as if they were still burning.
**“Into ashes”** — Into ashes. The fire which once punished the Sodomites signifies what the wicked are to suffer without end. That the land smokes, and that the most beautiful fruits have ashes and stench within, suggests that carnal love, though it smiles upon fools, nevertheless lays up for them in invisible things nothing but burning; or that the smoke of their torments may ascend up for ever and ever.
**“condemned them to be overthrown, making them an example to those that should after act wickedly”** — plainly signifying that those who were to be like you would utterly perish
2.7:
**“And”** — if
**“just Lot, oppressed”** — The unjust deeds and words of his neighbours tormented the just man, who, seeing them, was not able to correct them. But he kept himself in good works. Neither did he stain himself by seeing or hearing their shameful deeds; he was just in seeing and hearing, because they saw nothing in him, and heard nothing of him, but what pertained to justice.
2.8: **“For in sight and hearing he was just”** — which was difficult, to keep justice among such people
2.9:
**“The Lord knoweth”** — and if this, and that, and all these, therefore
**“how to deliver the godly from temptation”** — as Noe and Lot
**“The unjust”** — The false ones and their followers; and therefore do not follow them.
**“unto the day of judgment”** — And before the day of judgment, loosed from the body, they pay penalties, and at the judgment they await heavier ones, when they will be tormented in body and soul.
**“to reserve ... to be tormented”** — as the devil, the original world, the Sodomites
2.10:
**“And especially them who”** — will reserve
**“after the flesh”** — He means fornicators, who for the guilt of foul corruption will suffer greater torments in judgment than the general wicked.
**“walk in the lust of uncleanness”** — that is, who indulge in lust like brute animals
**“and despise government”** — they refuse to acknowledge Jesus, the just judge of all such men
**“And despise government”** — He means the proud and arrogant, who themselves are to pay heavier punishments than the general ones.
**“audacious”** — to greater crimes
**“self willed”** — in what they have committed
**“they fear not to bring in sects”** — He means heretics, who, blaspheming the faith or the life of the orthodox, bring in sects of their own name, that is, heresies, for whom a heavier tribulation also threatens.
**“to bring in sects, blaspheming”** — without fear of vengeance they separate men from God and teach them to blaspheme
2.11:
**“Whereas”** — That is, in which evils: because they despise dominion, because they are bold, and the rest that follows. For by doing these things angels deserved to become devils, and to pay the penalties of their pride; and what their nature does not allow them to do, to be polluted by carnal desires, to this they entice men, and for these things also they will be condemned.
**“Whereas angels”** — There the wicked will be tormented, where the evil angels, who had earlier been proud against God and were punished for it, now do not bear but rather cast away the judgment of being proud against God, which is execrable, against themselves, because they are grievously punished for it; and, terrified by the greatness of the punishments, they now desist from that judgment of presumption, but these wicked men do not yet desist. Or they will be tormented there, that is, with God, where the good angels do not endure but avenge it if anything execrable is said against them. As they overthrew the Sodomites, so also the apostles sometimes avenged, as when Peter slew Ananias.
**“who are greater in strength and power”** — all these are reserved for greater things, where there is such force of punishments that even the evil angels, who are greater in strength and more robust for enduring than men, do not bear it as an unbearable burden
**“bring not against themselves a railing judgment”** — as far as those who suffer, that is, the greater punishments
2.12:
**“But these men”** — masters of error
**“As irrational beasts”** — As it is natural for irrational living creatures, for the sake of food, often to fall ignorantly into capture and destruction, so heretics, likened to foolish beasts of burden, for the sake of satisfying their appetite for corruption, blaspheming the incorrupt doctrine and life of the catholic Church, weave for themselves snares of perdition; of whom, having said “blaspheming … in their corruption,” he rightly added, “shall perish.”
**“naturally tending”** — they tend
**“to the snare and to destruction”** — so these
**“those things which they know not”** — wherefore they blaspheme
**“blaspheming, shall perish in their corruption”** — in a corrupt sense
**“shall perish”** — from the fellowship of the saints
2.13:
**“Receiving the reward of their injustice”** — that he who is filthy may be filthy still
**“The reward of their injustice”** — That is, the punishment for evil works, and especially those who serve the corruption of the flesh and are held by mad errors, blaspheme the conduct of the just, and do not cease to detract from those who think soundly.
**“a pleasure”** — Pleasure is good or evil. Good pleasure is rightly called day, in which the saints delight in the Lord. Evil pleasure is night, when the reprobate perversely delight in accomplishing the works of darkness. The unjust therefore reckon the delights of defilement and stain to be the pleasure of a day, because, since they are given over to the most impure and execrable delights, they judge these to be the best and, as it were, full of light.
**“counting for a pleasure the delights of a day: stains and spots”** — and according to a bad estimation
**“sporting themselves to excess, rioting in their feasts with you”** — that there they may deceive you
2.14:
**“Having eyes full of adultery”** — they profess the wickedness of the mind even in the bearing of the body; or the eye, that is, the soul which ought to foresee; or the eye, their master, desires adulteries, either with wives or with the devil.
**“and of sin that ceaseth not”**
• or with unceasing sins.
• from which one does not easily cease, because they are as if natural, such as satiety, drunkenness, drowsiness.
**“alluring”** — Concubines are called harlots, from pollution or from the beauty of the skin by which they entice the unwary. They therefore allure unstable souls by the erroneous sects of various doctrines, as if subjecting them to the lusts of those who defile them.
**“unstable souls, having their heart exercised”** — or blinded.
**“with covetousness”** — because whatever they do, they do for the sake of greed.
**“children of malediction”** — already possessed by eternal malediction.
2.15:
**“Leaving the right way”** — For from reason they knew what they ought to believe and how they ought to live.
**“they have gone astray”** — from the state of mind.
**“having followed the way of Balaam of Bosor”** — tending to the same end as he who came to curse the people of Israel against the will of God; but it will happen to them as it happened to Balaam, whom the she-ass rebuked for his madness.
**“having followed the way of Balaam”** — Sometimes heretics put forth dogmas so execrable that even foolish pagans, who lack divine knowledge, detest them, and by their wisdom more soundly refute the madness of those men’s twisted paths, contrary to God. And what is worse, many of the catholics so love the wages of iniquity that even learned clerics are deservedly torn to pieces by unlearned laymen. They are compared to the prophet who is rebuked by the words of the ass speaking against nature. Nor yet are they held back from their purpose of a crooked way. They come from Bosor. Bosor is interpreted “fleshly,” or “in tribulation,” because for no other cause do they more adulterate the word of truth than for the concupiscence of the flesh. Whence they are also set in tribulation, not because they suffer for the Lord, but because they oppress the minds of the weak with their doctrines and perverse examples, so that these cannot look up. Balaam is “vain people,” or “headlong them,” which suits them. For those who willingly forsake the truth they have known are a vain people, and cast their hearers headlong, preaching to them not wholesome things that would correct them but erroneous things that please them; of whom it is added: “These are fountains without water.” They promise a shower of doctrines which they do not have, like prophetic clouds to which the truth of God may come, and they are tossed by the whirlwinds of demons and of vices; they speak great things, and their whole discourse is pride.
2.16: **“But had a check of his madness, the dumb beast used to the yoke”** — because the she-ass.
2.17:
**“These are”** — The false teachers are not to be imitated, because although they seem useful, there is nothing in them but vanity and uncleanness.
**“fountains without water”** — not cleansing but rather defiling.
**“and clouds tossed with whirlwinds”** — darkening by the prompting of the devil.
**“Whose”** — false teachers or heretics.
**“the mist of darkness is reserved”** — the darkness of sins is kept, so that they may become more foul, or the infernal punishments.
2.18:
**“Proud”** — Speaking proudly that they are just, though it is vain, desiring carnally and living lustfully, they allure those who barely escape, who, though like them, nevertheless somewhat shun their company and to some degree abstain from sins.
**“speaking, they allure by the desires of fleshly riotousness”** — In the desires of the flesh, etc. Unclean is everyone who exalts his heart, so that those who have fled a little from sins return to their error and strive in lust.
**“those who for a little while escape”** — they go astray and make others go astray.
**“converse”** — or having conversed.
2.19:
**“Promising them liberty”** — in their sect they promise there is liberty of eating, and drinking, and sleeping, and reigning for ever.
**“whereas they themselves are the slaves of corruption”**
• that is, slaves made corrupt, or slaves of the devil who corrupts.
• and they truly are slaves, because
2.20:
**“For if, flying from the pollutions of the world”** — and truly they are slaves acquired, because though once free, now they are compelled to serve more heavily than before.
**“through the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ”** — If in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. Fleeing the defilements of soul and body which the world sends in, and again entangled in them, as before baptism, they are overcome by those defilements; it appears that their latter state has become worse than the former, because they offend God more than before baptism, and will suffer greater punishments, because they are liars as to the promise made in baptism.
2.21:
**“For it had been better”**
• truly worse things.
• a lesser evil.
**“for them not to have known the way of justice, than after they have known it, to turn back from that holy commandment which was delivered to them”** — because, besides the evils which the transgressors of the promise do as before, they are transgressors of the promise.
2.22:
**“For, has happened to them”** — For it has happened to them, etc. It is set down in Proverbs with its exposition: “As a dog that returneth to his vomit, so is the fool that repeateth his folly.” And afterwards the apostle adds of his own: “And the sow that was washed, to her wallowing in the mire.” The dog, when he has vomited, casts out the food that weighed down his chest. But when he returns to his vomit, he is again burdened with that by which he had been relieved. So he who by confessing casts out the wickedness that pressed on the inmost part of his mind, after confession, when he repeats it, takes it up again. The sow, while she is washed in the mire, is made filthier. So he who laments his sin and yet does not forsake it subjects himself to a heavier punishment, since he has despised even the very pardon which he could have obtained by weeping, and has, as it were, wallowed himself in muddy water; because, while by his tears he withholds cleanness of life, he makes even those very tears foul before the eyes of God.
**“that of the true proverb”**
• he proves by authority, under the image of the dog, that they are wicked slaves.
• that true proverb fits them, or that part of the book which contains that proverb.

3.1:
**“Behold this second epistle I write to you”** — I have already written another epistle to drive off the false teachers. And that I may show you my great concern, see, for the same cause I write this second epistle also.
**“my dearly beloved, second epistle I write, in which”**
• epistles
• to you, to whom I write the epistle
**“I stir up by way of admonition your sincere mind”** — that I may warn you, and that you may warn others
3.2: **“That you may be mindful”** — That through those epistles you may be mindful of those words which I myself, being present, told you before. I mean the words received, from the holy prophets, which are confirmed by the authority of the holy prophets; and that you may be mindful of the precepts of the holy apostles, lest you let go from yourselves the precepts which the holy apostles gave, because of the preaching of those false teachers; and these precepts are also those of the Lord and Saviour, because the Lord himself, who came to save us, established these precepts and commanded them to be kept.
3.3:
**“Knowing this first, that in the last days there shall come”** — in the time of Antichrist, whose heralds these already are
**“deceitful scoffers”** — Scoffers: mocking the faith and hope of Christians, because they vainly promise themselves a time of resurrection to come; walking not according to the catholic faith, but after their own lusts, rejoicing in new sins and saying: “Where is his promise?” They wish to bring this upon you, that you may believe all the promises concerning Christ to be vain. As if to say: What was foretold of him in the prophets has not been fulfilled in Christ. “Or his coming?” As if to say: What sign of his coming can you show? As if to say: No coming is to be. Therefore they do not believe in a coming to be, because “since the fathers slept,” that is, from the time of the resurrection, when the fathers, wearied with waiting for him, rested, when the resurrection of the dead first began to be preached. “All things”: the course and order of all creatures. So it continues, as now, and nothing has been changed, as a witness to his coming, and this from the beginning of creation. As it was in the beginning of the world, so it still is, and therefore they do not believe any coming to be.
3.4:
**“Where is his promise”** — Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, restrains those who supposed that the day of the Lord was at hand. Peter rebukes those who assert that the coming and the promises of the Lord are delayed. Whence it is clear to all who love his coming that the mind must be held back in this opinion with greater moderation, so that we suppose neither that the day of the Lord is near and will come sooner, nor again that it comes more slowly. But let us take care of this alone, that whether he comes sooner or late, he may find us prepared when he comes.
**“for since the time that the fathers slept, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation”** — on the part of the foolish: there is no promise or coming, because since the ancient fathers died we see nothing changed in the world, nor will anything be changed except as it now is
3.5:
**“For this they are wilfully ignorant of”**
• Here the apostle, on his own part
• They say that all things continue in the same manner, either because they truly do not know, or because they pretend not to know, that they may deceive you. There are two judgments of God: one by water, which is past; the other by fire, which remains. He says this is hidden from them: that the heavens, that is, this moist and turbulent air, of which it is said: “The kite in the air hath known her time,” were before, that is, among the first creatures of the world. Or “before,” that is, before the flood. And that the earth was before, consisting out of water, that is, by the removal of the water, which, by the word of God working, was gathered together into one place, and so the dry land appeared; and consisting through water, because by divine disposition it is all full of veins of water, as the bodies of living creatures are of blood, lest it fail through dryness if the watering by water should fail. “Through which two,” that is, in which two parts, the air and the earth, the world that then was, of another kind than this one, perished, overflowed with the water of the flood. For the flood did not reach the upper parts. But the heavens that now are, and the earth, by the same word of God, set in that form which they now have, are kept in store, reserved unto fire, to be changed for the better, against the day of judgment and perdition of the ungodly men.
**“they are wilfully ignorant of this”** — those who wish this: that there will be no judgment to come
**“that the heavens”** — another translation: the heavens were of old, made from water and through water
**“were before”** — of another kind
3.6:
**“Whereby”** — through which two, that is, in which parts: in air and in earth
**“the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished”** — polluted by the sins of men, was cleansed through water
**“Whereby the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished”** — The earth perished, because, being submerged for so long a time, it ceased to bear fruit; afterwards also in very many places it received a face unlike that which it had had before. The heavens also perished, according to the appearance of this air. For the water filled all this space where the birds fly. There are also higher heavens, but whether these too are to perish by fire, or only those which perished even in the flood, is a question sometimes rather troublesome among the learned.
3.7: **“But the heavens and the earth which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of the ungodly men”** — after the flood, and are defiled by sins, are reserved so that they may be cleansed by fire with their evil inhabitants on the day of judgment
3.8:
**“But of this one thing”**
• Having proved that the judgment will truly be, he shows how effective it will be. If the false teachers tell you that you can do what you wish, because so much time remains until the day of judgment that the judge, through the length of time, will not be able to know many things, do not believe them, because whatever can be done in a thousand years he sees just as he sees what is done in one day. If they say that by doing penance for a thousand years you will not obtain pardon of your offences, do not believe it, because one day of true penance is worth as much as a thousand years, as with the thief. If they say it is not necessary to labour so long, you can rest for a day, do not believe it, because a thousand years of labour are not more sufficient for life than one day.
• And since the judgment is to be, therefore do not be led astray by the false teachers who say to you that even if there is to be a judgment, you still need not fear, because since there are so many thoughts and so many acts of men, if they must be examined one by one, thousands of years will not suffice, when the judgment is said to be in one single day, and so many things will be able to escape the judge. But let this not escape you: that one day is worth as much with God for doing something, as a thousand years are for men to do a single thing.
**“as a thousand years”** — In the knowledge of the divine power, things past, present, and future stand equally present; and the courses of time which seem long or short to us are of equal span with the maker of times, who beholds all things, great and small, equally. The Apostle therefore recalls this to convince those who said: “Where is his promise or his coming?” showing that God has by no means forgotten his promise or his coming. But since he so contemplates each day of our age with his eternal memory that he surveys the circuit of a thousand years, and a thousand years as the space of one day, without labour, it must be plainly understood that he knows most certainly the end of all those days and years, and without any doubt has also foreknown when the splendour of his coming is to be revealed, when the rewards promised to the saints are to be paid. Whence it is rightly added: “The Lord delayeth not,” etc.
3.9:
**“The Lord delayeth not his promise”** — or his promise
**“The Lord delayeth not”** — And because he sees all things, you can believe that the Lord does not delay in fulfilling his promises, because the time of fulfilling is not yet come, but at the time when he foresaw they should be fulfilled he will fulfil them. But he therefore defers, that he may first fill up the number of the elect which he foresaw. Whence in the Apocalypse: “And it was said to them, that they should rest for a little time, till their fellow servants” be filled up.
**“but dealeth patiently for your sake”** — that you may grow in virtues
**“not willing that any should perish”** — and that others who are to be converted may be converted
**“but that all should return to penance”** — or: 'to come to their senses'
3.10:
**“But shall come”** — does not delay, but rather
**“the day of the Lord shall come as a thief”** — unforeseen, seizing them for judgment
**“in which the heavens”** — in which the heavens, which passed away in the flood, because the fire of judgment will rise as high as the water of the flood rose
**“with great violence”** — with the great force of the enveloping fire
**“the heavens shall pass away with great”** — Allegorically. The heavens, that is, the saints: if there is anything in them to be purged, they will be purged by fire.
**“shall pass away”** — into another form
**“the elements”** — That greatest fire will consume the four of which the world consists. Yet it will not consume all things so far that they cease to be, but two it will consume entirely, and the other two it will restore to a better form. Whence in what follows: “We look for new heavens and a new earth, according to his promises,” etc.
**“the elements shall be melted with heat”** — Or the elements are the saints, who were to others the matter of working well; they will be dissolved for the better by temporal punishment.
3.11:
**“Seeing then that all these things are to be dissolved”** — since in so great a judgment the evil are to be changed for the worse and the good for the better
**“what manner of people ought you to be in holy conversation”** — in us
**“and godliness”** — toward others
3.12:
**“Looking for”** — through hope
**“and hasting”**
• by doing good
• so that you may be such that the Lord comes to judgment for the sake of saving them
**“unto the coming of the day”** — of judgment
**“of the Lord, by which the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with the burning heat”** — the former things will pass away, but
3.13:
**“new heavens”** — He does not say other heavens, but the old and ancient ones to be changed for the better. Whence David: “They shall perish but thou remainest: and all of them shall grow old like a garment: and as a vesture thou shalt change them, and they shall be changed.” What shall be changed? It is certain that, consumed by fire, when the fire soon departs they will take on a more pleasing appearance. Of fire and water we have nothing of the kind; rather we have in the Apocalypse: “And the sea is now no more.” We have also in the prophets: “The light of the lamp shall not shine to thee any more.”
**“and a new earth”** — or: according to
**“according to his promises”** — And the promises, etc. Allegorically. Do not believe those who say that nothing has been fulfilled of all that was promised about the birth of Christ, saying: Where are the new heavens and the new earth that were promised? We believe the new heavens to be those in which justice dwells, and the new earth those who bear the fruit of newness; and these we call the promises of God; or we, in whom justice dwells, and we know the truth: we look for the heavens, that is, the saints, to be new in the future, and a new earth, because he has promised.
**“in which”** — That is, at the time of the age to come. “Justice dwelleth,” because then to each of the faithful a crown of justice will be rendered according to the measure of the struggle, which cannot be done in this life.
**“But we look for”** — To him, that is, by the Lord: he alone is perfectly clean who is clean by divine judgment; for human judgments are often deceived.
3.14:
**“Wherefore, dearly beloved”** — because the day of the Lord comes
**“waiting for these things, be diligent that you may be found before him unspotted”** — from venial sins in the body
**“and blameless in peace”** — from grave sins in the mind
**“Be diligent, unspotted and blameless”** — These are the watches of which it is said: “Blessed are those servants, whom the Lord when he cometh, shall find watching.” He watches who keeps himself free from filth, who, as much as is in him, has peace with all men, who subjects all the allurements of the flesh to the rule of the spirit, enjoying in himself a most happy peace.
**“that you may be found”** — by him, or to the honour of him coming and knocking
**“in peace”** — made peaceful, sins being forgiven
3.15:
**“account the longsuffering of our Lord, salvation”** — Do not think that the Lord delays the promise, but understand that the Lord therefore waits patiently so that more may be saved.
**“our most dear brother Paul”** — He says that Paul wrote to them. In this he shows that what Paul wrote specially to certain churches, he wrote generally to all the churches that are throughout the world. Peter praises the wisdom of Paul. Paul says of himself: “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church.” Paul humbles himself for his former unbelief and puts the innocence of the other apostles before his own. Behold, the first of the apostles, forgetful of his primacy and of the keys given to him, marvels at the wisdom given to Paul, because it is the way of the elect to marvel more at the virtues of others than at their own, and by these to stir themselves up to progress.
3.16:
**“As also in all his epistles, speaking”** — Paul himself
**“in them”** — in the epistles
**“of these things”** — of these things that I foretold you, that you may do these things that I taught
**“in which”** — in the epistles of Paul
**“hard to be understood”** — He says that those things in the epistles of Paul are perverted by heretics, especially those in which he speaks of the grace of God which justifies the ungodly, that is, makes the just out of the ungodly. For he says: “Where sin abounded, grace did more abound.” Lest anyone should despair over sins committed, heretics so interpret it as to urge men to commit more sins, that through these they may receive greater goods. Against them Peter adds: You therefore, brethren, knowing before, because the unwise will bring in manifold errors: some denying the judgment to come, some falsifying the divine words, some interpreting badly, some loosening the reins of lust, and many other things.
**“the unlearned”** — which the unlearned wrest, without the light of justice
**“and unstable”** — and the unstable, in mind, because among the learned they do not remain until they are instructed
**“wrest”** — There is no book of the Old or New Testament in which heretics have not perverted something, whether by taking away, or by adding, or by changing. The only remedy for the unlearned is, with humble steadfastness, to give ear to the words of the teachers; and because heretics do not have this steadfastness, they are carried away from the Church by the wind of pride like light chaff; whence it is to their own destruction.
**“as they do also the other scriptures, to their own destruction”** — as also the other Scriptures to their own damnation. Another reading: perdition
3.17:
**“You therefore, brethren, knowing these things before, take heed”** — these things
**“lest being led aside by the error of the unwise, you fall from your own steadfastness”**
• of faith
• but rather
3.18:
**“But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory”** — amid daily adversities
**“unto the day of eternity”** — and especially when he will appear after long being desired

1.1:
**“That which was from the beginning”**
• that is, from the beginning, that is, from the Father
• “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word” etc.
• In the true being of the Godhead, which we have heard through the law and the prophets; which we have seen sensibly, a man coming; which we have looked upon, perceiving the divinity in the man; and our hands have handled, of the Word of life: not by chance agreeing with him who was seen in the flesh, but searching with much handling the Scriptures that bear witness of the Word himself. What someone has seen he can announce to others; what he has perfectly beheld he sometimes cannot set forth in words.
**“From the beginning”** — The Son of God was from the beginning, but the disciples saw and heard him in the flesh.
**“which we have heard”** — “And the Word was made flesh”
**“which we have seen with our eyes”**
• living among men
• “And we saw his glory.”
**“which we have looked upon”** — that is, we came to know his life and manners, and also with spiritual eyes his divine power on the mountain
**“and our hands have handled”** — a true body, not a phantasm
**“And our hands”** — Joined to him in great familiarity, we proved by touching that he had true flesh, both before and after the resurrection, to whom it is said: “Handle and see.”
**“of the word of life”** — giving life in soul and in body
1.2:
**“For the life was manifested”** — the bread of angels became known to men by the assumption of flesh, shone forth in miracles, rose, and made others rise with him; by these the life was made manifest
**“and we have seen”** — Joined to him in great familiarity, we proved by touching that he had true flesh, both before and after the resurrection; to whom it is said: “Handle, and see.”
**“and declare unto you”** — So we heard it through them, but we did not see; therefore less happy than they.
**“the life eternal”** — to be with the faithful
**“which was with the Father”** — in eternal divinity
**“and hath appeared to us”** — in time, in humanity
**“which we have seen”**
• repeats
• in the flesh
**“and we have heard”** — the words from his mouth
**“do bear witness, and declare”** — as if to say: you ought to believe those who saw and heard
**“unto you”** — who have not seen
**“may have fellowship with us”** — not for any temporal gain, but that by living well, believing well, and bearing all things patiently
**“and our fellowship”** — and through our fellowship you may pass over to fellowship with God
**“And these things we write to you”** — we announce not in passing but commit to memory
**“that you may rejoice”** — in this world in the unity of the Church, and in the future in the fellowship of angels
**“and your joy”** — that we may lead many to the same fellowship
**“your”** — or ours
**“and we declare”** — to be believed
**“unto you, that God is light”** — because it drives away the darkness of sins
**“God is light”** — Therefore whoever wishes to have fellowship with the light, let him drive out the darkness of sins, because darkness cannot have fellowship with light. Whence it follows: “If we say”. Why is it that “the Word was made flesh”? That he might announce this to the world.
**“and darkness”** — that is, ignorance or wickedness
**“If we say”**
• therefore
• puffed up with some righteousness of our own
• if we confess, we are cleansed; but if we wish to honour ourselves
• So far, the commendation of the epistle; here he shows how charity is to be had.
• If we say, etc. Those also do not have charity who, puffed up with their merits, say they are clean.
**“that we have fellowship with him”** — through faith and charity, which join us to God
**“and walk in darkness”** — in sins
**“walk”** — adding sin to sin
**“we lie”**
• in ourselves
• in word and deed
**“And walk in darkness, we lie”** — Those who persist in sins and darken others are not counted among his members. Whence: “What participation hath justice with injustice? Or what fellowship hath light with darkness?”
**“and do not the truth”** — while by our example we lead others into the same lie
**“If we walk in the light”** — So we are cleansed, but nevertheless we ought not to think that, as long as we live, we can be altogether cleansed from sins.
*Augustine:* Augustine. God is light, which place does not contain; voice, which time does not contain; fragrance, which breath does not scatter; food, which voracity does not diminish; embrace, which satiety does not tear apart.
**“and”** — and this rightly
**“we have”** — He does not say “we have not,” lest perhaps it might seem said of past things.
**“we deceive ourselves”** — to greater sins
**“and the truth is not in us”**
• because God withdraws himself from the proud
• but
**“If we confess our sins”** — out of humility
**“If we confess”** — Because we cannot be without sin in this life, the first hope of salvation is confession itself, more from humility than from necessity; then the love with which we love him to whom we humble ourselves, and charity covers a multitude of sins. Pride extinguishes charity; charity extinguishes sins; therefore let humility strengthen charity, let humility lead to confession.
**“he is faithful and just”** — God, who promised grace to the humble, is faithful in fulfilling it and just, because he truly and justly forgives the confession
**“to forgive us”** — as to the guilty
**“our sins”** — without which one does not live
**“and cleanse us”**
• after the dissolution of the flesh
• in eternal life
**“from all iniquity”** — so that we neither wish nor are able to sin
**“forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity”** — Or: we shall make the greater sins iniquity, the lesser ones a lie. God alone is truthful of himself; man is truthful from God, a liar of himself. It is impossible that any saint should at some time not fall into the least sins. Nor do the just cease to be just, because with God helping they rise again the sooner.
**“that we have not sinned”** — as if to say: we do not need to be absolved
**“make him a liar”**
• Job
• who says: not even an infant of one day is without sin
**“and his word is not in us”** — Christ, through whom remission does not remain in the proud. Or the word which he said: “The greater thou art, humble thyself in all things.”
**“And the word”** — Augustine, in the fifteenth book on the Trinity. The words we utter are signs of the things we think. Accordingly the word that sounds outwardly is a sign of the word that shines within, to which the name “word” more properly belongs. That which is uttered by the mouth of flesh is the voice of the word, and it too is called a word on account of that from which it was taken that it might appear outwardly. For our word in a certain way becomes the voice of the body, taking on that form in which it may be manifested to the senses of men, as the Word of God was made flesh, taking on that in which he might be manifested to the senses of men. And as our word becomes voice and is not changed into voice, so “the Word of God was made flesh,” and is not changed into flesh.
1.3:
**“That you also may have fellowship”** — Whoever wishes to become a partner of God must first be joined to the fellowship of the Church. Those who have believed through the apostles have this less than those who have believed through himself. Whence it is said: “Blessed are they that have not seen, and have believed.” And again: “And not for them only do I pray, but for them also who through their word shall believe in me.”
**“is with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ”** — that we may be heirs of God, joint heirs with Christ
1.5:
**“And this is the message which we have heard from him”** — And this is the declaration. Why was the Word made flesh? What new thing did he bring to the world? Why did he come to suffer? It was not in vain; see what he wished to teach, that God is light. By this sentence he shows the excellence of the divine purity, which we are commanded to imitate. Hence the Manichees are refuted, who say that the nature of God was conquered in war and corrupted by the prince of darkness.
**“We declare unto you that God is light”** — We have come to the light, and the light has shone upon us. We were darkness; now through the light we are light, and we enlighten others, while we announce that sins are forgiven and darkness is driven out.
1.7:
**“as he also is in the light”**
• if we are called light for the same cause by which Christ was called light, that is, by his example enlightening others
• God is said to be in light, because where highest goodness is, man cannot find where to advance; man walks in light because by works of virtue he advances to better things.
**“we have fellowship one with another”** — through charity
**“the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin”** — the sacrament of the Lord’s passion has loosed all sins, original and actual

2.4:
**“He that saith that he knoweth him”**
• he who keeps the commandments knows him, for he who does not keep them does not know him
• He who says he knows him, etc. It is no great thing to know that there is one God, since even demons believe and tremble.
2.11:
**“and knoweth not whither he goeth”** — because he does not understand his guilt
**“because the darkness hath blinded”** — anger troubles the eye, hatred blinds it
2.12:
**“I write unto you, little children”**
• obedient to the Father; or lately born
• little ones, not in age but in knowledge
• I write to you, little children. He puts first the reason that could draw them away from love of the world: because to those baptized in the name of Christ and invoking the name of Christ, sins are forgiven. Therefore one must cling to Christ more than to the world.
**“I write unto you, children”** — humble in spirit
2.13:
**“because you have known him who is from the beginning”** — you know that Christ was always with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and you have announced this to others
**“because you have known the Father”** — He commends and repeats: remember that you are fathers; if you forget him who is from the beginning, you lose fatherhood
2.14: **“because you are strong”** — not from yourselves but because the word of God
2.15:
**“Love not the world”**
• the abundance of the world or its beauty
• Use the world for necessity, but do not love it for superfluity and for care of the flesh; make not provision in desires.
• Love not the world. One heart does not hold two loves opposed to each other. Rooted in charity, build upon this root nothing except what agrees with charity, because “you cannot serve two masters.” As the love of God is the fountain of all virtues, so the love of the world is the fountain of all vices; whence there follows: For all that is in the world.
**“nor the things that are in the world.”**
• such as gold and silver and every flow of riches
• because
**“If any man love the world, the charity of the Father is not in him.”** — as the love of God is quenched by hatred of one’s neighbour, so it is quenched by love of the world
2.16:
**“which is not of the Father but is of the world.”**
• it is not from God, who creates and fatherly provides for us, but from our attaching ourselves to the world
• we ought to cling to the Father, not to the world, because
2.17: **“And the world passeth”** — into a new form
2.18:
**“Little children, it is the last hour”**
• the end is near for each one
• And on this account you ought to persevere, because there are many Antichrists who wish to seduce you, as you have heard that Antichrist cometh. For with as great force and error as you have heard that Antichrist will come, with so great violence these also come. We are in the eleventh hour. The Saviour has come in the flesh, and the plague of Antichrist is to follow, which will assail the heralds of salvation and uproot the vineyard which Christ tends; and many members of this most wicked head have already been sent before, of whom we must beware, because the end of the world is now at hand, or the last hour, that is, like the last. This persecution is like that future one.
**“and as you have heard that Antichrist cometh”** — contrary to God and to his Church
**“even now there are become many Antichrists”** — and because there are many Antichrists
**“Even now there are become many”** — Antichrists are all heretics, all who destroy by their deeds the faith they confess with their words, all who are opposed to Christ and bear witness against their coming head, because the mystery of iniquity is already at work.
**“Antichrists”** — Because they were baptized and anointed with chrism, through which they can deceive more easily, they are opposed to Christ and to his Church.
**“whereby we know that it is the last hour”** — without delay the day of judgment will come
**“They went out from us, but they were not of us”**
• withdrawing from catholic unity
• hence it is proved that they were not of us
• They went out from us, etc. But though there are many Antichrists, let it not terrify you if they have returned to Judaism or paganism; do not think that the Church suffers any loss from this, because though they went out from us, yet they were not truly of us. They could not have gone out unless they were contrary to Christ; whoever is not contrary to Christ remains in the body of Christ. So the false are in the Church as bad humours in the body: when they are vomited out the body is relieved; so when the wicked go out the Church is relieved.
**“For if they had been of us”** — by the predestination and election of the Lord
2.19:
**“they would no doubt have continued with us”** — for whoever perseveres to the end, this one will be saved
**“But that they might be made manifest”** — Many who are not of us receive the sacraments of Christ with us, but temptation proves that they are not of us, because when temptation comes upon them, as if at the occasion of a wind they fly outside, for they were not grain. All will then fly away when the Lord’s threshing floor begins to be winnowed on the day of judgment. Therefore, God permitting, some go out of the Church before the last division, showing that they were not of the body of Christ, so that by this it may be made plainly clear that not all are of us who, placed within with us, receive the sacraments of Christ; and therefore their separation ought not to trouble you.
2.20:
**“But you have the unction from the Holy One”** — you ought to remain, because you have baptism or the Holy Spirit, through whom every sorrow of ignorance and of sin is driven out
**“But you have the unction”** — Speaking of heretics, he suddenly turns to his own and says that they have an anointing from the Holy One, so that by contrast he shows that heretics and all Antichrists are deprived of the gift of spiritual grace, and do not belong to him who is called holy by the prophets.
**“and know”** — who are good and who are bad; nor is it necessary that you be taught, because the anointing teaches you
**“all things”**
• what must be held of the faith
• you truly know all things, for
**“know all things”** — You know the truth of the faith and are taught of life through the anointing of the Spirit, nor do you need to be taught, except that you persist in what you have begun.
2.21:
**“I have not written to you as to them that know not the truth”** — If you were ignorant of what must be held of the faith, I could give you milk as to little ones; but because you are perfect in knowledge, I write to you as to the perfect
**“but as to them that know it, and that no lie is of the truth”**
• and these things also to those who know; no lie is of the truth; and he who lies is not of Christ
• but especially
**“And that no lie”** — He had said that no lie is of the truth. But because there are many kinds of lies, unlike one another, he now singles out the lie of denying Christ, in comparison with which the rest seem either small or nothing. This is proper to the Jews, that they say: Jesus is not the Christ; but also to all who scorn to obey the commandments of Christ.
2.22:
**“Who is a liar, but he who denieth that Jesus is the Christ”** — the proper name
**“is the Christ”** — the Messiah promised in the law
**“This is Antichrist”** — Behold, we have been warned how we may recognize Antichrist: namely, whoever denies Christ.
2.23:
**“Whosoever denieth the Son”**
• that Jesus is
• Lest anyone say: I do not worship Christ, but I worship God the Father, he adds: every.
**“who denieth the Son”** — In vain does he confess God the Father who denies the Son, who proceeds from God.
**“the same hath not the Father”** — neither has the Son nor the Father himself propitious.
**“He that confesseth”** — with the heart, voice and deed.
**“the Son”** — that Jesus is Christ.
**“hath the Father also”**
• appeased
• favourable
• therefore
2.24:
**“As for you, let that which you have heard”** — through the preachers
**“from the beginning”**
• of your way of life
• What you have heard from the beginning, etc. “If any man shall say to you, Lo, here is Christ; lo, he is there: do not believe.” Hold fast to what you have heard from the apostles.
**“let abide in you”** — that you hold in memory through observance.
**“If that abide in you, which you have heard from the beginning, you also shall abide in the Son, and in the Father”** — here through faith, in the future through hope.
**“you also shall abide in the Son, and in the Father”** — Thus you will be members of the Father and the Son, so that you do not fall away from the memory and protection of the Father and the Son; and you ought to strive for this, that you be in the Father and the Son, because thence you obtain the reward.
**“in the Son”** — He puts the Son first, because: “No man cometh to the Father but by the Son.”
2.25:
**“And this is the promise which he hath promised us”** — who does not lie.
**“And this is the promise”** — Remembrance of the promised reward make you persevering in the work.
**“which he hath promised us”** — through himself and through his preachers.
**“life everlasting”** — not gold nor anything earthly.
2.26:
**“These things have I written to you”** — as if to say: be attentive to these things that I say, because I have written these things to avoid those evil men.
**“concerning them that seduce you”** — either by perverse teachings, or by other allurements, or by the adversities of the world, draw you back from eternal life.
2.27:
**“And as for you, let the unction, which you have received from him, abide in you”** — and take care to hold well the teaching I give outwardly, so that the grace of the Holy Spirit, which you obtained in baptism, you keep whole in body and heart.
**“And you have no need that any man teach you”** — and so it happens that, with the Spirit teaching you inwardly, you have less need to be taught outwardly by human instruction.
**“teach you”** — Let no one credit to the teacher what he understands from the teacher’s mouth; unless there is one within who teaches, the teacher’s tongue labours outwardly in vain; yet let not the teacher be silent, but do what he can.
**“but as his unction teacheth you of all things”**
• which are to be held.
• what I preach; those who preach otherwise are false, nor will you find eternal life unless you follow the charity of faith which you heard through me.
**“But as his unction”** — That is, the Holy Spirit, whose sacrament is in the visible anointing. Or the anointing is charity, which “is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us,” and which inflames the heart it fills to keep God’s commandments.
**“and is truth”** — and therefore, because it is true.
**“and is no lie”** — it is not changeable like the old law.
**“and is truth and is no lie”** — Another translation: and it is truthful, namely the anointing, and is not false.
**“And as it hath taught you”** — the unction
2.28:
**“And now, little children, abide in him”** — about to have this advantage
**“abide in him”**
• And now, little children, abide. By frequent repetition he presses it home, that he may fix it more firmly in their minds.
• And if you have anything good, attribute all of it to him and not to yourselves; attribute evils to yourselves and to the devil.
**“little children, abide in him”** — He who abides in the Lord among persecutors, not confounded, has hope at his coming; but he who is ashamed here will be confounded at the coming of him whose precepts he neglected.
**“that when he shall appear”** — to the reward of the good and the damnation of the evil
**“we may have confidence, and not be confounded by him at his coming”** — for him neglected or denied
**“Little children”**
• to whom I ought to provide, and you to obey me
• This charity too can be had in this way: if you love God and the world and all the things that are of it, lest you think; and these things I write to you as a useful matter. I write to all: to some as to sons, to some as to fathers, to others as to young men.
• Fathers, adolescents, young men. Therefore sons, because sins are forgiven; therefore fathers, because you have known the things of old; therefore young men, because you are strong, because you have overcome.
2.29:
**“these things I write to you”** — that you may hold it in memory
**“that you sin not”** — by saying, we have not sinned
**“That you sin not”** — Lest, hearing that you are cleansed by God, you assume a bad security, but have a useful fear.
**“If any man sin”** — If through human frailty you cannot guard against all faults, take care at least to guard against the greater and more open ones, so that temptation does not seize you beyond what is human. But if anyone falls even after my admonition, let him not despair.
**“an advocate”** — He is not an advocate except to those who call him. Let your sins displease you; cry out, and he himself hears and frees.
**“we have”** — John, a just man, tempering himself to the weak, did not say 'you have' but 'we have.' He places himself among the number of sinners so that he may have an advocate.
**“the just”** — A just advocate does not take up unjust causes; yet he will defend us as just in judgment if we accuse ourselves as unjust.
**“And he is the propitiation for our sins”** — making us propitious to God by preaching and intercession
**“not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world”** — who now live in the flesh; but for the whole Church. Do not say: 'Lo, here is Christ; lo, there is Christ.' Christ is everywhere; everywhere he is propitious.
**“And in this we know that we have known him”**
• that is, to know God is to love
• To know or to recognize is not always said on account of acquaintance, but on account of experience and union with another thing. We know God when we are united to him; he who thus knows him keeps his commandments. In this we know, that is, we have knowledge, that we have known him, being united and adhering to him.
**“if we keep his commandments”** — charity
**“If we keep his commandments”** — We ought to heed our frailty; we ought to seek an advocate for sins; and that we may obtain it, let us labour to keep the commandments, by which one comes to the knowledge of him.
**“and keepeth not his commandments”** — “This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you.”
**“is a liar: and in him”** — or: in this
**“there is not truth”** — of Christ, who says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
**“But he that keepeth his word, in him in very deed the charity of God is perfected”** — as if he said: he knows him
**“And in this we know”** — and if we keep his commandments
**“that we are in him”** — we live the true life; we do not die
**“He that saith he abideth in him”** — the commandments are truly to be kept, because after baptism we say that we abide in him, and he who says that he
**“ought himself also so to walk, as he”**
• in the way of justice and charity and patience
• who prayed for his enemies
**“walked”** — who says: “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.”
**“himself also so to walk”**
• from virtue to virtue
• according to his measure
**“Brethren”** — and these commandments are to be heeded, because it is not a commandment
**“not a new commandment”** — new and unheard of
**“I write unto you, but an old commandment”** — in use from Abel and the holy fathers, not because it belongs to the old man
**“Not a new commandment but an old one”** — The same charity is an old commandment, because it was commended from the beginning. The same is a new commandment, because, the darkness cast out, it pours in a longing for new light.
**“which you had from the beginning”** — of your faith
**“The old commandment is the word which you have heard”** — this, and this word which you have heard from me and from the other preachers, is that old commandment; therefore old because you have heard it
**“Again”** — and you ought to hold this commandment too, because I do not preach and commend it only once, but because I see it is very useful, I repeat it again and again as if it were new
**“a new commandment”** — which renews it
**“I write unto you, which is true”**
• not shadowy
• Which is true. According to what I promised, that by the keeping of God’s commandments one comes to the knowledge and love of him. And it was fulfilled in Christ himself, because he was obedient to the Father unto death, and therefore was glorified. And in you. Some of whom already glory with God through this. And it is truly new, because the darkness is now passed. Darkness belongs to the old man, but light to the new man.
**“in him and in you: because”** — in this it appears to be new and also true, because
**“the darkness is past”** — “The night is passed, and the day is at hand”
**“The darkness”** — The same passible body and the miseries of the flesh have passed away in Christ, and the true light of immortality now shines in him, whereby he enlightens also others who were the old man and darkness, but now “light in the Lord.”
**“and the true light now shineth”** — truth speaks clearly to all, but not all hear clearly
**“He that saith he is in the light”**
• of the Christian faith or of good works
• He determines which commandment he receives, that is, charity, and how that charity itself is to be held, namely love of God and of neighbor.
**“and hateth his brother”** — whom God commands to be loved
**“is in darkness”**
• that is, reckoned to the darkness of hell
• having a beam in his eye
• in the sins in which he was born
**“until now”**
• even after he has come to God through baptism
• but
**“He that loveth his brother abideth in the light”** — of good works, because then good works and the light of faith profit him.
**“He that loveth his brother”** — He is in the light of knowledge and of works; but he who hates is in darkness of ignorance, and through that very ignorance walks from vice to vice, and “knoweth not,” that is, does not foresee, whither he goes, to what punishment he is to be received. Or he knoweth not whither he goeth, that is, he is ignorant of the way by which he may be converted to the better; and this not because the way is not open, but because the darkness hath blinded his eyes. Departing from the light of Christ by sins and carnal pleasure, he is so hindered that even if he sees the good he does not follow it. He who loves his brother bears all things for the unity of charity; even if he applies correction to his brother, he is not angry, and brings no insult. “Much peace have they that love thy law,” that is, charity, “and to them there is no stumbling block.”
**“and there is no scandal in him”** — whence the eye is disturbed
**“But he that hateth his brother, is in darkness”** — of ignorance
**“and walketh in darkness”** — from vice to vice
**“his eyes”** — the invisible eyes by which God is seen
**“because your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake”** — not of Paul, not of Donatus
**“I write unto you, fathers”**
• not in age but in wisdom
• venerable old men, in whom love of the world ought now to grow cold
• whose part it is to remember the old things and to make them known to the younger
**“Young men”** — The time of adolescence is slippery because of the incitements of the flesh, but because of the strength of its age it is fit for the contest; and these, by love of the word of God, overcame the temptations of pleasures and despised persecutions.
**“Children”** — Humble in spirit: the more they humble themselves under the mighty hand of God, the more loftily they know the secrets of the divinity. Whence: “Thou hast revealed them to little ones.”
**“I write unto you, young men”**
• who by strength of mind and love of the word of God have overcome the incitements of the flesh and manfully resisted the devil
• Consider too, and again, that you are young men: fight that you may conquer; conquer, that you may be crowned; be humble, lest you fall in the fight.
**“and the word of God”** — the word of God: the Son of God; the preaching of the Son of God
**“abideth in you, and you have overcome the wicked one.”**
• and it would be shameful to be conquered by him whom you have conquered
• I write this to all of you
**“And you have overcome”** — At that time people were dragged by custom to the brothel, but these, by manfully resisting, overcame.
**“For all that is in the world”** — All lovers of the world have nothing but these three things, in which all kinds of vices are comprehended. The concupiscence of the flesh is the desire of all things that pertain to the pleasure and delights of the body, such as food, drink, carnal intercourse, and the like. The concupiscence of the eyes is all curiosity, which is shown in learning magical arts, in gazing on spectacles, in acquiring superfluous temporal things, in searching out and carping at the vices of neighbours. The pride of life is when a man boasts himself in honours and seeks great households. By these three Adam was overcome: for he coveted the forbidden food, he wished to be knowing good and evil, he wished to be as God. These three Christ overcame: for he was not caught by the love of bodily bread, he did not come down from the pinnacle, which would have been to tempt God, he would not be exalted above the kingdoms of the world.
**“the concupiscence of the flesh is”** — is the concupiscence of the flesh, when the flesh delights through touch or taste
**“Concupiscence”** — Which concupiscence and pride is not of the Father: the battle of the vices is not from God, the Father and Creator, but from the love of the world, which we prefer to God. God made men upright; they themselves entangled themselves in endless questions. God is not a tempter of evils, but every one is tempted by his own concupiscence.
**“and the concupiscence of the eyes,”** — and the concupiscence of the eyes, when it delights in sight, as in fine clothes and gold and such
**“and the pride of life,”** — all the ambition of the world
**“and the concupiscence thereof.”** — because in that day all their thoughts shall perish
**“But he that doth the will of God”** — not he who only says “Lord, Lord”
**“But he that doth the will”** — In this way too charity can be had, if you have been overcome by no instigation of heretics from the faith and the other things that belong to God. And that you may keep it, he sets forth the reasons why what you have heard from the beginning should abide in you: Little children, because it is the last hour.
**“abideth for ever.”** — because he sought eternal things
**“If you know”** — if this is established
**“that he is just,”** — chiefly the author and nature of all righteousness
**“know ye”** — and this
**“that every one also who doth justice is born of him.”** — ministering
**“Every one who doth justice”** — Perfect righteousness is scarcely found in angels or in holy men who always remain in the contemplation of God. In us righteousness begins from faith. The beginning of righteousness is the confession of sins. Righteousness will be perfected when there is no struggle with the flesh but triumph over the enemy.
**“is born.”** — from evil to good
**“is born of him”** — Now that we are born of the righteous one, we ought to follow the righteousness of the righteous Father.

3.1:
**“Behold”** — and, if you do not understand that all righteousness is from God, prove it by this
**“What manner of charity”** — With how great and what kind of gifts God has shown his fatherly charity toward us. For he gave that in this age we should be named and made sons of God, in name and in deed, and that in the future we should be so, possessing the inheritance of blessedness.
**“hath bestowed”** — freely
**“upon us, the Father,”** — from the unworthy
**“The Father hath bestowed upon us”** — That we may know and be able to love him, not as servants their Lord but also as sons their Father. Whence: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to be made the sons of God.”
**“that we should be called the sons of God”** — in this age
**“and should be.”** — in the future, by possessing
**“Therefore the world knoweth not us,”** — because we are called sons of God: the lovers of the world do not love us, do not perceive our dignity, do not honour us but afflict us
**“because it knew not him.”** — the Father
3.2:
**“Dearly beloved, we are now the sons of God;”** — although we are despised by the world
**“we are the sons of God”** — As if he said: what is the dignity of being and being called sons of God? He answers: Dearly beloved, now we are the sons of God. Now it appears through the miracles we do and through purity of life that we are sons of God, but whatever is in the present is little compared with the future.
**“and it hath not yet appeared what we shall be.”** — “It hath not entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared for them that love him.”
**“We know that, when he shall appear,”** — at the second coming
**“we shall be like to him”**
• immortal and impassible in body, like the Son himself
• We shall be like to him. When we enjoy the contemplation of the unchangeable eternal divinity, we too shall be immortal and eternal in him, not the same as he is but like him, because we are creatures and have been made in his likeness.
**“because we shall see him as he is.”** — for the vision alone makes blessed: “Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God.”
**“because we shall see”** — According as “the Word was made flesh” the wicked saw, and in judgment they will see; but how the Word was in the beginning with the Father only the just will see, and the wicked will be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.
3.3:
**“And every one that hath this hope in him,”** — that he is to come to the likeness of God.
**“sanctifieth himself”** — He does not take away free will when he says that man sanctifies himself, nor yet does he agree with the Pelagians, who say that man has no need of grace. But as we are commanded to hope for the glory of the divine likeness according to our measure, so we are bidden to imitate the purity of the divine holiness according to our capacity, that, grace going before, we may labour to avoid evils, saying to God: “Be thou my helper, forsake me not.”
**“as he also is holy.”**
• in the present he imitates the holiness of God by living piously, denying worldly desires
• “Be holy, as also your Father is holy.”
• he who has hope sanctifies himself, namely, everyone who does, etc.
3.4:
**“Whosoever committeth sin”** — by will and by deed.
**“committeth also iniquity; and sin is iniquity.”**
• let no one therefore say: I am a sinful man, but I am not wicked.
• he who sins plainly stands contrary to the equity of the divine law.
**“and sin is iniquity”** — In Greek “nomos” is law; hence “anomia,” that is, iniquity, which is against the law or without law; hence he says: Sin is iniquity. Whatever we sin, we do against the law of God. Whence: “I have accounted all the sinners of the earth prevaricators.” Not only those who despise the written law, but also those who corrupt the innocence of the natural law.
3.5:
**“And you know that he appeared”** — at his first coming.
**“And you know”** — Lest we, who cannot be without sins and iniquities, should despair of salvation, he adds that through Christ we are loosed from sins. Not only have we been made sons of God by grace, and hope that we shall be like him, but we are also freed from iniquity, because he appeared for this, that he might take away sins; from this iniquity let no one excuse himself.
**“to take away our sins,”** — “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world.”
**“to take away our sins”** — He takes away by forgiving past deeds, by helping that they not be done, by leading to life so that they cannot be done at all.
**“and in him there is no sin.”** — and he could, because there is no sin in him; if there were sin in him, it would have to be taken away from him.
3.6:
**“Whosoever abideth in him, sinneth not;”** — truly he himself is free from sin, because also those who cling to him, by the very fact that they cling, avoid sins.
**“Whosoever abideth in him”** — As if to say: and what does it profit us that he came without sin? Answer: Everyone who abides in him does not sin.
**“and whosoever sinneth hath not seen”** — by faith
**“him,”** — in humanity
**“Whosoever sinneth hath not seen him”** — And he who abides in him does not sin. And let no one deceive you in this, by saying either that righteousness is from man, or that anyone can abide in God while having sin, because all righteousness is from God and every sin from the devil.
**“nor known”** — nor knew (or: has known)
**“him.”**
• in divinity
• by tasting his sweetness; for if he tasted how sweet the Lord is, he would not by sinning remove himself from the sight of his glory
3.7:
**“Little children, let no man deceive you.”** — but
**“He that doth justice is just, even as he is just.”**
• by participation
• Even as he is just, etc. As things are not always wont to be said with equality, for example, as there is much difference between the face of a man and its image in a mirror, because here is the body, there only the image, and yet here and there are eyes, and here and there ears, so we have the image of God, the justice of God, the holiness of God, but not the image by which the Son is equal to the Father, not the justice of God by which he is just with unchangeable perpetuity. Not by believing in him whom we do not see, that we may at some time see him, not the holiness by which he is holy in eternity, are we holy, by faith.
**“He that doth justice”** — That is, he who has the act and the intention of justice is indeed just, but not of himself; rather he proceeds from the same root as that one. Justice is in him principally, in this one secondarily; in him naturally, in this one by adoption. That is, he who is just is just from him.
3.8:
**“He that committeth sin is of the devil”** — its imitator
