**“of the devil”** — Not by drawing origin of the flesh, as the Manichee wished concerning all men, but by taking from him the imitation and suggestion of sinning, as the sons of Abraham are so called by imitating his faith, and the Jews, forsaking the faith of Abraham, became not sons of Abraham but of the devil.
**“for ... from the beginning”** — beginning from the start of its creation to sin, it sins continually up to the present
**“the devil sinneth”** — it did not stand in the truth
**“For this purpose, the Son of God appeared”** — through the flesh
**“that he might destroy the works of the devil”**
• by which man is bound
• thus he loosens, because every
**“that he might destroy”** — That is, that he may destroy that nativity which we have drawn from the devil. Adam, made by God, but by sinning born of the devil, begot such as he was. We are born with concupiscence before we add our own debts. From that damnation, because we are born, we die. But Christ was born man, that he might loose the sins of men, that he might lead them back to life.
3.9:
**“Whosoever is born of God”** — in baptism
**“committeth not sin: for his seed abideth in him”**
• by this he avoids sins, because the Word, by whom he is begotten, abides.
• “A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruits.”
**“committeth not sin”** — He does not speak of every sin. “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.” But he speaks of the violation of charity, which he who has the seed of God, and the Word of God by which he is born again, cannot commit; and the words that follow look to this; or it can be taken of any criminal sin.
**“for his seed abideth in him”** — A true son of the Father cannot abandon the law. The law of the Father is: “That you love one another.”
**“and he can not sin”**
• “I have hated iniquity,” etc.
• not only does he not sin, but he cannot sin as long as he holds the Word.
**“because he is born of God”** — in whom there is no sin
3.10:
**“In this the children of God are manifest”**
• that they do not sin
• “By their fruits you shall know them.”
**“In this ... are manifest”** — Love is the sure sign by which the children of God and the children of the devil are distinguished. Other things are common to good and wicked. At this fountain no stranger shares. Have whatever you will; unless you have this alone, nothing profits you. Though you have not other things, have this, and you have fulfilled the law, because: “Love is the fulness of the law.”
**“and the children of the devil”** — in that they sin
**“Whosoever is not just”**
• because what is of God does not sin; therefore what sins is not of God.
• not repaying to God what he owes.
**“is not of God”** — Or: from.
**“nor he that loveth not his brother”**
• is not of God
• love is truly to be had
3.11: **“For this is the declaration”** — “This is my commandment, that you love one another.”
3.12:
**“Not as Cain”** — being
**“who was of the wicked one”** — the devil, who envied God and fell, envied man and cast him down.
**“and killed his brother. And wherefore did he kill him?”** — see whence the murder came forth.
**“Because his own works were wicked”**
• because he envied his brother.
• Where there is envy, there is not brotherly love. By Cain’s works being evil he means nothing but envy and hatred of his brother. By Abel’s works being just he means nothing but charity; by this men are distinguished. Let no one look to tongues or deeds. The heart, if it does not do good for its brethren, shows what it has in itself. Cain rightly offered, the creature to the Creator, but he did not divide well, when he believed that the gifts he offered, with hatred of his brother, would please. Abel offered with love and pleased.
**“his brother's just”** — just through charity.
3.13:
**“Wonder not, brethren”** — have love; nor because of the world’s hatred or persecutions let go of love, because you are tried by temptations.
**“Wonder not”** — I do not wonder if a lover of the world hates a brother set apart from love of the world, and intent on heavenly desires. Religion is an abomination to the sinner.
**“if the world hate you”**
• lovers of the world
• because of the world, love must not be diminished.
• because
3.14:
**“We know that we have passed from death”**
• eternal
• We know, etc. Let no one exalt himself on his virtues; let no one fear the poverty of his own powers. He who loves the brother gives clear judgment, because he belongs to the lot of the just.
**“to life, because”** — by this
**“we love the brethren”** — but
**“He that loveth not”** — brother
**“abideth”** — not only is he going to be in eternal death, but already he abides
**“in death”** — of the soul
**“abideth in death”** — The life of the flesh is the soul; the life of the soul is God. The death of the body is to lose the spirit; the death of the soul is to lose God. He therefore who through hatred of a brother loses God, loses life.
3.15:
**“Whosoever hateth”** — we ought to love, not to hate, because he who hates
**“Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer”** — He who out of hatred pursues his brother provokes him to anger and discord, and so, as far as in him lies, kills him in his soul. If anyone despises hatred of a brother, will he then despise murder in his heart? He does not move his hand to kill, and is already held a murderer; the other lives, and this man is judged a slayer.
**“And you know that no murderer”** — who either strikes with the sword or pursues with hatred
**“hath eternal life abiding in himself”** — and even if through faith he is seen to live here among the saints
**“hath eternal life”** — He who is held to this kind of murder, that he is at odds with his brothers, will be damned for ever with Cain.
3.16:
**“In this we have known the charity of God, because he hath laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.”** — I have proved in many ways that charity is to be had; but that I may come to the point: out of charity we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren, as Christ laid down his life for all of us.
**“In this we have known the charity of God”** — Having set forth many reasons for having charity, he finally adds concerning the perfection of charity, under the example of the Lord’s passion. Peter is admonished to have this when, the Lord asking him, he professed that he loved him; to him it is said: “When thou shalt be old, thou shalt stretch forth thy hands, and another shall gird thee, and lead thee whither thou wouldst not.” By these words he was taught to lay down his life for the sheep: “Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
3.17:
**“He that hath the substance of this world, and shall see his brother in need”**
• food or clothing
• He that hath the substance of the world. If, whether from the opportunity of the time or from human weakness, it does not happen that we lay down our lives, we ought at least to lay down our goods for our brethren; and this is the nourishment of charity. He who has learned to give his property will some day be able to lay down himself.
**“and shall shut up his bowels from him”**
• that he has no pity for his misery, or gives nothing even if he feels pity
• if you cannot give superfluities to a brother, you can lay down your soul for a brother
3.18:
**“Little children”** — Because there is no perfect charity in him who does not lay down his soul for the brethren; or who at least does not give money. Therefore, that you may have perfect charity, little sons of the same Father, let us not love, etc.
**“let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth”** — against in word and in tongue
**“let us not love in word, nor in tongue”** — In word is understood plain speech, not action. In tongue is understood manifold speech, as some wish to commend their affection by often repeated words.
**“but in deed, and in truth”** — Because if we also err in love through human weakness, we do not err in reward, because he is greater than our heart and knows with what zeal all things are done.
**“and in truth”** — That we render benefits with a simple intention, not for boasting, or for some temporal advantage, but out of regard for God alone.
**“In this we know”** — when we do works of piety in truth, it is clear that we are of God, who is truth, when we imitate his perfection according to our measure
**“we are of the truth, and in his sight we shall persuade our hearts”** — to devise better things
**“For if our heart reprehend us”** — And this is a great thing, that through love we have thoughts so pure that we wish to show them to God; because even if conscience should accuse us within, and wish to hide from God, because we did not do our good deeds with a good mind, yet we could not be hid from God, because he is greater than our heart and knoweth all things. Love therefore avails, which commends us to him from whom we cannot be hidden.
**“God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things. Dearly beloved, if our heart reprehend us not”** — in love; but we are sure that we have pure love of the brethren, seeking the salvation of the brethren and no other gain. Likewise if it does not reprehend us in the Lord’s prayer, when we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”
**“we have confidence towards God, and whatsoever we shall ask”** — from the root of charity
**“And whatsoever we shall ask”** — A great promise, and desirable to the faithful. But if anyone is so perverse that he is not delighted by heavenly promises, let him at least fear what wisdom on the contrary thunders terribly: “He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be as abomination.”
**“we shall receive of him”** — and if sometimes not to our will, yet always to salvation
**“because his commandments”** — of charity
**“we keep”** — in spirit
**“and those things”** — works of charity
**“that are pleasing in his sight”** — in secret, where he himself sees
**“do. And this is his commandment,”** — as if someone asked what that commandment is: faith and love
**“And this is the commandment”** — He puts the commandment first, in the singular, and joins two things to it, because these cannot be separated.
**“That we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ”** — because there is no other name by which we must be saved
**“and love one another”** — “This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you.” Love one another for this, for which I love you, that is, that you may attain to blessedness.
**“as he hath given commandment to us”**
• so with pure love, not as robbers or any wicked men love themselves, but not chastely
• Evil men love one another; that is, that love is infernal and worse than discord.
**“And he that keepeth his commandments”** — You do not love the king whose law you despise.
**“And he that”** — By what reward he carries out these commandments of faith and love with fervor.
**“abideth in him”**
• In God, as in a house, as in a safe refuge.
• In him abideth, etc. In the first times of the growing Church the Spirit fell upon the believers, and they spoke with tongues and worked miracles. But now the Church has no need of outward signs. Everyone who has faith and charity bears witness that the Spirit abides in him.
**“and he in him”** — as in a clean vessel, both in the present and in the future.
**“of his Spirit”** — holy.
3.19:
**“In this we know that we are of the truth”** — In that we love the truth, we know that we are of the truth; that is, we know that we have this true love from God (who is the truth); and from this love we know that we are in his sight, that is, that we deserve his sight; and in this also we persuade our hearts to think out better works.
**“and in his sight we shall persuade our hearts”** — That is, we persuade our hearts to have such thoughts as may be worthy of the divine eyes. For all who purpose to do something persuade their hearts to turn to considering the deed with faith. But he who thinks evil, if he could, would hide it from God. But those who think good persuade their hearts most easily, so that they desire what they do to be made open to the sight of God; which is a sign of great perfection, when a man rejoices that his works or thoughts be seen by God, because: “He that doth truth, cometh to the light, that his works may be made manifest, because they are done in God.”
3.24: **“And in this we know that he abideth in us”** — If we keep charity, he abides in us; and if we doubt whether he dwells in us, we can show this by manifest signs, because he gave us kinds of tongues, the grace of healings, and the other charisms.

4.1:
**“Dearly beloved, believe not every spirit”** — to the one speaking spiritually, that you should choose him to imitate, because certain gifts of the Spirit are common to good and bad alike, apart from charity.
**“Believe not every spirit”** — Many heretics, many schismatics confess that Jesus came in the flesh, but deny it by their deeds, by not having charity. By charity “the Word was made flesh”; he who has not charity denies that he came in the flesh, and here he is convicted of not having the Spirit that is of God; he who says that Jesus came in the flesh, not by the sound of the tongue but by loving and doing, has the Spirit of God. Jesus came to gather together; the heretic scatters; he has not the Spirit of God.
**“but try the spirits if they be of God”**
• whether they are spiritual according to God, whether they strive by charity, because “if I should know all mysteries and have not charity” etc.
• therefore I forewarn you, because, etc.
**“because many false prophets”**
• who under the pretence of faith preach errors and corrupt by evil examples.
• not having charity.
• Because many, etc. Those who have not charity and who rend the unity of the Church by a perverse doctrine, nevertheless contend that the Holy Spirit is in them; he adds this, that they may be proved by their fruits, whether they are false or true prophets, because “grapes are not gathered of thorns, nor figs of thistles.”
4.2:
**“By this is the spirit of God known”** — how we can prove it: the Spirit of God is known by this sign, namely, that every spirit
**“Every spirit which confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh”** — instructs the hearers by word and by work and with that charity by which God was made man.
**“Every spirit which confesseth”** — Many heretics, who wished to separate the unity of the Church by a wicked doctrine, erased this verse from the epistle, so that they might not be convicted of error through it.
**“is of God”** — and this is to be believed.
4.3:
**“And every spirit that dissolveth Jesus”** — who denies his divinity or soul or flesh, or neglects his precepts.
**“dissolveth”** — He who separates God from man, who divides the members from God, who interprets the words of God wrongly, who withdraws from God by living badly.
**“is not of God: and this is Antichrist”** — forerunner.
**“of whom you have heard that he cometh”** — with God’s judgment impending.
**“and now”** — dwelling in the minds of those who oppose Christ in word or deed, for already the mystery of iniquity is at work.
**“is already in the world”** — to the lovers of the world.
4.4:
**“You are of God, little children”** — They are not of God, but you.
**“and have overcome”** — by confessing that Jesus came in the flesh, by having charity.
**“him”** — Antichrist.
**“Because greater is he that is in you”**
• not by the power of free will, but because God is greater to protect than the devil is to attack.
• he teaches to have hope and charity.
4.5:
**“They are of the world: therefore of the world they speak, and the world heareth them”**
• but they cannot turn the hearts of spiritual men away.
• They are of the world. These spirits are not to be loved or heard, because although they call on the name of Christ and mark themselves with the sign of Christ, yet they are of the number of those who desire worldly things and are ignorant of heavenly things.
**“Therefore of the world they speak”** — By the reasoning of worldly wisdom, proving that God cannot raise a dead man, that a mortal man cannot have a dwelling in heaven, and other such things.
4.6:
**“We are of God”** — because we have charity
**“He that knoweth God”** — through charity
**“heareth us”** — preachers of the truth
**“He that is not of God”** — he who does not have charity
**“heareth us not”** — The sensual man perceiveth not these things that are of the Spirit of God.
**“By this we know the spirit of truth and the spirit of error”**
• he who hears us has the spirit of truth; he who does not hear has the spirit of error
• and because we are of God, not of the world, therefore
4.7:
**“Dearly beloved, let us love one another”**
• in word and in deed
• Dearly beloved, let us love one another. He has commended charity in many ways; now he comes to its singular praise, in which we ought most of all to hear him, namely: he that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God, for God is charity. He had said: Charity is of God; here he adds: God is charity.
*Augustine:* Charity is the affection of the mind for loving God for God’s sake, and the neighbour for God’s sake.
**“Likewise elsewhere”** — But you, Lord, are neither an affection of the mind nor a mind, but you are the Lord God of the mind. He who acts against charity acts against God, though it seems easy to act against a man; but who does not fear to act against God?
**“charity is of God”** — The Son is God of God, the Holy Spirit is God of God, and they are not three gods but one God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit; and he loves in whom the Holy Spirit dwells. Therefore love is God, but God who is of God; and so it is truly said both that love is of God and that God is love. When it is said “of God,” either the Son is understood or the Holy Spirit. Since the Apostle says: “Charity is poured forth in our hearts, by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us,” we understand that love is the Holy Spirit; this is the fountain in which no stranger shares, whereas he shares in all the other sacraments of the Church. To drink at this fountain he exhorts us, saying: let us love one another.
**“And every one that loveth his brother”** — or God
**“is born of God”** — because he abides with God
**“and knoweth God”** — both here and more fully in the future
4.8:
**“He that loveth not, knoweth not God”** — one does not come to the knowledge of God except through charity, for: “For wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul.”
**“for God is charity”**
• brotherly love leads to the knowledge of God, who is the highest love
• In God it makes no difference that he is called 'just' and 'justice', or 'loving' and 'love', because he is not called just or loving by a transfer of names from justice or love, as if he had justice or love, but because he is justice or love.
4.9:
**“By this hath the charity of God appeared towards us, because God hath sent his only begotten Son”** — invisible in himself
**“By this hath the charity of God appeared”** — In proving that God is charity and that he loves us, he wished to lead us by his example to love one another and to come to the knowledge of him. As God did not wait for us to love him, so let us not wait for others to love us, but let us love first. The love of the Father was proved because he sent the Son; the love of the Son, because he died.
**“God hath sent”** — visible through the flesh
**“into the world”** — to die for the world
**“that we may live”** — dead before
**“by him”** — raised again
4.10:
**“In this”** — in this sending
**“is charity”** — made manifest
**“not as though we had loved God, but because he”**
• he loved the wicked but not wickedness
• Not as though we had loved God, etc. Not as though we loved him first, so that he loved us as a reward for our love; but he himself loved us first, so that, his grace going before, we might love him.
**“and sent his Son to be a propitiation”** — the proof of love
**“propitiation”** — Another translation has 'propitiator', that is, sacrificer for our sins.
**“for our sins”** — for destroying our sins
4.11:
**“Brethren”** — Be ye therefore followers of God, as most dear children; and walk in love
**“if God hath so loved us”** — but not wickedness
**“we also ought to love one another”** — Love, and do what you will: whether you keep silent, keep silent in love; whether you cry out, cry out in love; from this root nothing but good can come forth.
4.12:
**“No man hath seen God”**
• “For man shall not see me and live”
• but nevertheless
**“No man hath seen God at any time”** — As these visible things, known to the senses of the body, are seen, so God is not seen. But even if he has at times been seen in this manner of seeing, he was not seen as these natures are seen, but by his will he was seen in the form in which he wished to appear, his nature remaining hidden and abiding unchangeably in itself. But in the way in which he is seen as he is, he is perhaps now seen by the angels; by us he will be seen then, when we shall be equal to the angels. But not even then will he be seen as these visible things which are discerned by bodily sight, but “the only begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he will declare him,” which pertains not to the eyes but to the sight of the mind. As, therefore, if we wished to see this sun we would cleanse the eye of the body, so, wishing to see God, let us cleanse the eye of the mind. But since this vision is hoped for in the future, what is to be done? What consolation are we to use? While we are still pilgrims in the body, let us love one another, and so God abides in us.
**“if we love one another”** — with sincere and disciplined charity, not with slack and idle gentleness
**“God abideth in us”** — by inspiring good things
**“and his charity is perfected in us”**
• by dwelling in you, God will make you perfect
• And his charity, etc. Begin to love; God has begun to be in you. Grow in love; and further, by dwelling in you God will make you perfect, so that you love even your enemy, as he himself loved his enemies.
4.13:
**“In this we know that we abide in him, and he in us”** — if we love, he abides in us; which we prove by such experience, that he has given us of his Spirit
**“In this we know”** — Whence shall we know if we have the Spirit of God? Ask your bowels: if they are full of charity, you have the Spirit of God, because: “The charity of God is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us.”
**“that we abide in him, and he in us”** — God abides in us and we in God; and let no one despair of salvation, because although the diseases of sins press us down, the almighty physician is one who saves. Let us rejoice in hope, so that we may come to the matter itself.
**“because he hath given us of his spirit”** — he makes known and speaks subtly of his divinity
4.14:
**“And we have seen”** — We prove by this that he gave of the Holy Spirit, because we have seen, that is, through the inspiring Spirit we know by faith, and through the testifying Spirit we bear witness, that not those who have not received the Holy Spirit
**“and do testify”** — because “He was in the world, and the world knew him not.”
**“that the Father hath sent his Son”** — for the knowledge of men
**“to be the Saviour of the world”** — not only saviour but also judge
4.15:
**“Whosoever shall confess”**
• we believe and bear witness through the Spirit given, and by our example, whoever has confessed through the same Spirit with a true confession of the heart, so that he may waver neither at the deceits of heretics, nor the torments of persecutors, nor the examples of carnal brothers, nor his own frailty
• He had said above that if we love, God abideth in us; here he says: whosoever shall confess that Jesus is the Son of God, God abideth in him, and he in God. Suggesting that whoever has love toward the brethren, he truly bears witness that Jesus is the Son of God. For effects agree with their causes, and the causes themselves agree.
**“that Jesus is the Son of God”** — “No man can say the Lord Jesus, but by the Holy Ghost,” etc.
**“God abideth in him, and he in God”** — God abides in him and he in God, etc. In turn they dwell in one another: he who contains and he who is contained. You dwell in God; but that you may be contained, God dwells in you; but that he may contain you, lest you fall: how shall he fall whom God contains?
4.16:
**“And we have known”**
• by Christian faith, as if we had seen
• We have seen and bear witness that God sent his Son, and we have known for what cause he did this: not because he had need, not because he owed anything, but by charity alone; having an only Son, he did not wish him to be one only, but adopted brothers for him, who might possess eternal life with him.
**“and have believed the charity”** — which deceives no one
**“which God hath to us. God is charity: and he that abideth in charity, abideth in God, and God in him”** — God is charity, etc. He had said the same above; behold, he says it again, to commend it further and to add another effect of charity. He said above that through charity the first coming of the Son of God into the world was made for the salvation of the world; here through the same charity he announces the salvation of the faithful at the second coming, on the day of judgment. While he commends love, he neither wholly passes over the love of God in silence, nor names it often; the love of the enemy he passes over entirely in silence; fraternal charity he mentions most frequently. Why is this? Since he says it is no great thing if we love those who love us, unless love reaches even to enemies? But he who has come to the love of enemies will not pass over the brethren. For it is fitting that, like fire, it should first seize what is nearest, and so descend to what is farther off. He who wishes of an enemy that he become a brother loves a brother. For he does not love in him what he is, but what he wishes him to be; as a craftsman loves wood cut from the forest, of which he is going to make something: he does not love what it is, but what he is going to make. He has therefore admonished no less concerning charity. In mutual love is the perfection of divine charity.
4.17:
**“In this is the charity of God perfected with us”** — by this we are shown to love God perfectly if we do not fear his coming of judgment; he who fears is not perfect in charity
**“In this is perfected”** — By this sign anyone can prove how much he has advanced in charity. Ask your heart and it will answer you. Someone believes in the day of judgment, but because he is not perfect in charity he begins to fear; but if he were perfect he would have confidence, and if he desired it he would not fear. When someone is converted to penance he begins to fear, but in the course of good conduct he learns not to fear, but to wish that it come, as Paul: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.”
**“that we may have confidence in the day of judgment”** — not fearing to appear before the judge
**“because as he is, we also are in this world”** — by this we have confidence, because we imitate the perfection of his love in the world, loving even enemies, as he “raineth upon the just and the unjust” in heaven
**“As he is, so are we”** — As has been expounded, “as he is” is said not always of equality but of a certain likeness; as I have ears, so also an image. If “we are made to the image of God,” why are we not as God is?
4.18:
**“Fear is not in charity”** — “Fear is not in charity”: charity, which has confidence from the merit of righteousness, and also makes present tribulations not to be feared
**“Fear is not”** — By this perfect charity is understood, because in such charity, which does good even to enemies in imitation of divine goodness, there is no fear.
**“but perfect charity casteth out fear”**
• servile
• It is one thing to fear God lest he cast you into hell; this fear, not yet chaste, will cease. It is another to fear God lest he forsake you; this chaste fear remains for ever and ever, because it desires the coming of the bridegroom.
**“casteth out fear”** — That fear of which it is said, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,” by which each one who begins works of righteousness fears, lest the strict judge come and condemn him as too little chastened: perfect charity makes perfect righteousness, and has nothing to fear, but desires.
**“because fear hath pain”** — because the conscience of sinners torments the heart, when justification is not yet made
**“And he that feareth, is not perfected in charity”** — that we may be perfect, let us love
4.19:
**“Let us therefore love God, because God first hath loved us”** — not from any necessity, but that from enemies he might make us friends, etc.
**“because God first”** — The love of God gave us that we should love him. Whence: “You have not chosen me: but I have chosen you.”
4.20:
**“If any man say”** — because many say in words, I love, it is added: if any man
**“I love God, and hateth his brother; he is a liar. For he that loveth not his brother, whom he seeth, how can he love God, whom he seeth not”** — because a thing unknown cannot be loved
**“whom he seeth not”** — He does not see God because he has no love; he has no love because he does not love his brother, for if he had love he would see God. Therefore, with the eye cleansed, let us strive through love to behold the unchangeable substance of God.
4.21:
**“And this commandment we have from God, that he, who loveth God, love also his brother”** — because if he does not love the brother, neither does he love God, whose children he does not love.
**“And this commandment”** — Lest anyone dare to say, I can love God even if I do not love my brother, he adds: And this commandment, etc., as if to say: how do you love him whose commandment you neglect?

5.1:
**“Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ”** — Messiah
**“Whosoever believeth”**
• He believes who lives as Christ commanded. Otherwise even demons believe. But works apart from faith are either nothing, or, even if they seem good, are empty, because they are apart from Christ, the way.
• Truly he who loves God loves his brother. For he who loves God the Father loves God the Son, begotten of the Father; and he who loves God the Son loves also the sons of God, the members of that head. Therefore let us love the sons of God that we may love the Son of God, whose members they are, and by loving the whole Son let us love the Father. For love joins the body of Christ together, that there may be one Christ. So he who loves his brother loves himself, for he is one with him. Nor can he fail to love Christ who loves the members of Christ; so he who loves the Son, who is necessarily the same with the Father, loves the Father also. Whosoever believeth. And truly he who loves God loves his brother also. For he who loves God who begot loves him who is begotten, according as he is begotten of him. And who is born? He that believeth, etc. And who is he that begot? God the Father. He therefore who loves God begetting, in faith, loves him who is begotten, in faith. And fittingly, speaking of love, he mentions faith; because if anyone is so hard as to neglect to love a man because he is a man, because he is in the same exile, he must be admonished to love him at least because he is born of God, because he is a partaker of the same grace. But because many love their neighbours for kinship or for temporal advantage, he determines who is the true lover of his neighbour.
**“is born of God”** — in this faith
**“And every one that loveth him”** — God
**“who begot”** — in faith
**“loveth him also”** — man
**“who is born”** — in faith
**“of him”** — God
5.2:
**“In this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God”** — he is rightly proved to love his neighbour who also loves God; and lest anyone deceive himself about the love of God by saying in words that he loves God, he adds: and we keep his commandments; the proof of love is the showing of the work.
**“and keep his commandments”** — “This is my commandment, that you love one another.”
5.3:
**“For this is the charity of God”**
• by this the charity of God is proved to be in us, if we keep his commandments, loving the children of God.
• therefore I join: that we love God and keep his commandments, because otherwise there is no love. He does not love the king who does not love his law; from love of the king his law ought to be fulfilled.
**“that we keep his commandments”** — as if to say: they are to be kept gladly, because
**“his commandments are not heavy”**
• They do not drag downward like “a talent of lead,” but lift upward, and keeping God’s commandments makes men exalted.
• “For the yoke of God is sweet and his burden light.” For the things that are by their own nature hard and rough, the love of God and the hope of reward make light. If anyone says they are heavy, he accuses his own weakness, because to the strong they are light and truly are not heavy, because everything that is born, is born of God, who loves God and his neighbour. He who so trains himself in the commandments of God that he brings them to action, he also overcomes the world: he despises the allurements or adversities of the world, he even seeks the death of the body itself, he seeks the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth. And lest anyone trust in his own strength that he can overcome the world, he adds: “And this is the victory which overcometh the world, our faith.” That faith which worketh by love, which begs the help of God.
5.4:
**“For whatsoever is born of God, overcometh the world”** — demonstratively, as if pointing with a finger, he shows the faith as standing and abiding.
**“our faith”** — Behold what faith overcomes: that which believes a true man and true God.
5.5:
**“Who is he that overcometh the world, but he that believeth that Jesus is the Son of God?”**
• who can have contempt for the world, except he who believes Jesus to be he who was foretold as Christ, and who joins worthy works to faith.
• Who is he that overcometh, etc. He specifies which faith overcomes: the faith of Christ. As if to say: truly he overcomes the world through faith, because it is not overcome by anything else.
5.6:
**“This is he that came by water and blood, Jesus Christ: not by water only, but by water and blood”** — He who was eternal came for salvation and the remission of sins by the water of baptism and the blood of the passion; and he not only deigned to be baptized for our washing and to consecrate for us the sacrament of baptism, but also gave his blood for our redemption.
**“This is he that came by water”** — Because faith alone and the confession of divinity do not suffice for salvation and for overcoming the world, he adds also the humanity.
**“And it is the Spirit which testifieth, that Christ is the truth”**
• And although he suffered according to the man, yet the Spirit was seen upon him baptized in the form of a dove. Or the Spirit, that is, every spiritual teacher, testifies this, that Christ is the truth, the true Son of God, not a phantom, the true mediator and reconciler, free from sin and sufficient to take away all the sins of the world.
• The Spirit. That is, the human soul, which he gave up in the passion. The water and blood which flowed from his side, which could not have happened if he had not had the true nature of flesh. But even before the passion “his sweat became as drops of blood”, showing the truth of the flesh. Moreover, that from the side of one already dead, against nature, water and blood flowed living, bore witness that the body of the Lord would after death live better, and that his death would give us life. And that the sweat flowed upon the earth like blood signified that with his blood he would wash the Church throughout the whole world.
5.7:
**“And there are three who give testimony in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost. And these three are one”** — one God, bearing witness of the same thing
**“And there are three who give testimony”** — By this it appears that Jesus is the truth, true God, true man, concerning both of whom we have certain testimony: concerning the divinity through the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; concerning the humanity through the soul, the water, and the blood. The Father gave testimony of the divinity when he says: “This is my beloved Son.” The Son himself gave it when he was transfigured on the mountain and showed both the power of divinity and the hope of eternal blessedness. The Holy Spirit gave it when he rested upon him baptized in the form of a dove, or when at the calling of the name of Christ he filled the hearts of believers.
5.9:
**“If we receive the testimony of men”**
• and because we have such certain testimonies, therefore we ought to accept these, since we are accustomed to accept even the testimonies of men, who can lie.
• Great is the testimony of David, a man, which he bears of the Son of God: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit on my right hand”; who also brings in the Son speaking: “The Lord said to me, Thou art my Son.” Greater the testimony of the forerunner, who says: “I baptize you with water; he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost.” But greater is the testimony of the Father, who sent visibly upon him the Spirit with whom he was always filled; as if he said: if you believe men announcing the coming beforehand, believe the Father testifying that Christ has come.
**“the testimony of God is greater”** — to be accepted better
**“For this is”** — by which I prove
**“the testimony of God, which is greater”** — namely, that he testified
**“because he hath testified of his Son”** — “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
5.10:
**“He that believeth in the Son of God, hath the testimony of God in himself”**
• but
• He understands the Father as true in the testimony of the Son; he who does not believe says the Father is a liar. Therefore the Jews say in vain that they believe in the Father, while they despise Christ.
**“in the Son”**
• or to the Son
• Because the Father testifies of the Son, let us believe in the Son; for he who believes in the Son, so that by working well he tends toward the Son himself, has the testimony of God in himself, as though God also testified of him that he, believing thus, will be in the number of the sons of God, the Son himself promising this to his own: “If any man minister to me, him will my Father honour.” If therefore you have God as witness of your faith, what does the disgrace or persecution of men hurt you? “If God be for us, who is against us?”
**“He that believeth not”** — says that he is not the Son, or less than the Father
**“maketh him a liar”** — “I and the Father are one.”
**“because he believeth not”** — a liar in this
**“in the testimony which God hath testified of his Son”** — “Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased”; and in the passion: “I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again.”
5.11:
**“And this is the testimony”** — He testified of the Son, and also of us, the adopted sons, that through his only Son he would give us eternal life, now in hope, and at last in reality.
**“And this life is in his Son”** — In faith and confession of his name, in the reception of his sacraments, because “no man cometh to the Father but by me,” and: “There is no other name by which we must be saved.” And lest it seem he had said little in saying that life is in the Son, he adds that the Son himself is that life. For as the Father hath life in himself, so he hath given the Son also to have life in himself, who gives his own eternal life.
5.12:
**“He that hath”** — by believing and imitating
**“He that hath the Son, hath life”** — but
5.13:
**“These things I write to you”** — you must give faith to these things, because
**“that you may know”** — that you may be certain of your future blessedness
**“that you have eternal life, you who believe in the name of the Son of God”** — lest you be deceived by the frauds of those who deny that Christ is the Son of God, because by the merit of faith you will have life.
5.14:
**“And this is the confidence which we have towards him”** — and you must hope for heavenly goods not only in the future, from the faith of Christ; but also in this life there is confidence that we shall obtain whatever we have asked for salutarily.
**“And this is the confidence”** — He impresses again in many ways what he had promised above, so that he may rouse us to pray more eagerly.
**“according to his will”**
• That we may ask what he wills, or come to ask being such as he desires us to be. If we desire our salvation and that of our neighbours, let us not be at odds with the will of God. If our will through ignorance departs from the will of God, the good will of God corrects our foolish one, as happened to the apostle Paul.
• Not according to our carnal desires, for we know not what we should pray for as we ought, unless he himself shows his will, who understands our advantage better than we ourselves do.
**“if we ask according to his will”** — We obtain it as when we ask for a brother, for whom we must ask.
**“he heareth us”** — who first said: “Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you”.
5.15:
**“And we know that he heareth us whatsoever we ask”**
• and not only in future time will he hear, but we also know that he has heard and hears us daily. And by this, that we are heard now, we are certain of the future.
• and not only in future time, giving effect to the petition
• We know that, etc. Because we know that we have from him the petitions we ask, let us ask for nothing adverse to him; nothing but what he has taught us, what he has inspired in us to ask for. Even if we err in something, we are at once corrected.
5.16:
**“He that knoweth”** — by confession, or even in another way
**“his brother to sin a sin which is not to death”** — not criminally, or not unto death
**“He that knoweth his brother to sin a sin which is not to death”** — He speaks of daily and light sins, which, as they are hard to avoid, so are easily cured. If you have sinned in word or thought, or by forgetfulness or ignorance, confess to your brother, as James teaches: ask that he intercede for you. And if he in turn confesses to you, do you also intercede for him. Here the Lord’s prayer suffices, and mutual confession is a light penance. But if the sin is grave, bring in the priests of the Church and be corrected by their examination.
**“let him ask”** — for him
**“and life shall be given”** — by God
**“life shall be given to him”** — because of your prayer
**“who sinneth”** — to him who sins, I say
**“not to death”**
• not criminally
• but
**“There is a sin unto death”**
• unto the death of life
• That which separates from God, as death separates the soul from the body.
• The Lord commands us to pray for persecutors; here he says we are not to pray for certain men, because there are sins among brethren that are graver than the persecution of enemies. A brother’s sin is unto death when, after the knowledge of God which was given through grace, someone attacks the brotherhood and, having been reconciled, is driven against grace by the firebrands of envy. There is a sin not unto death: if someone has not withdrawn his love from his brother, but through some weakness of mind has not performed the duties of brotherhood. Whence Christ: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” For they had not yet been made sharers through the grace of the Spirit and entered the fellowship of holy brotherhood. So also Stephen prayed for those who had not received the grace of God. Paul does not pray for Alexander, because, when he was already a brother, he assailed the brotherhood. He prays for those who had given way through fear. Whence: “All have forsaken me,” but “may it not be laid to their charge.”
5.17:
**“All iniquity is sin. And there is a sin unto death”** — Because what is not corrected in this life, pardon for it after death is asked in vain; and this can be understood of every criminal sin; whatever differs from the rule of equity is numbered among sins; but the smallest do not harm the just, while some so differ from all justice that, unless they are corrected, they plunge into punishment.
**“All iniquity is sin”** — All, as it were: we must truly pray for those who sin not unto death, because all are occupied with many sins, and no one can be without sin, because “all iniquity is sin.” But above, there is another, a sin unto death, which is not committed through human frailty, and therefore is not purged by the prayer of the just, since “they who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God.”
5.18:
**“We know that whosoever is born of God”** — who has the seed of God in him cannot sin unto death; for at the same time he cannot work righteousness and sin.
**“Whosoever is born of God”** — He who is born of God does not sin unto death; he who is not born sins. But we are of those who are born of God, therefore we will not sin, we will not be touched by the enemy; but the lovers of the world are subject to the malign enemy.
**“sinneth not”**
• sin unto death
• David sinned grievously, but because he was born of God, he belonged to the fellowship of the sons of God; he did not sin unto death but by repenting merited pardon.
**“but the generation of God preserveth him, and the wicked one toucheth him not”** — the grace by which they are reborn, according to the purpose by which the saints are called, keeps them from committing sin unto death, though in whatever things they have fallen through human frailty, it defends them that they may not be touched by the malign enemy.
**“but the generation of God”** — Because a man is the son of God voluntarily and not by nature, the text fittingly added one of this kind:
**“but the generation of God preserveth him”** — Those who persevere in the generation of God cannot sin, nor be touched by the evil one. As day and night cannot be mixed, so righteousness and iniquity, the malign one and the generation of God, touch. Therefore the malign one sits and afflicts some, but not to their harm.
5.19:
**“We know that we are of God”** — reborn in baptism
**“the whole world”** — Not only the lovers of the world, but also the recently born, who have no discernment of good and evil, belong through the first prevarication to the kingdom of the devil, unless by the grace of God they are plucked from darkness.
5.20:
**“And we know that the Son of God is come”**
• through the flesh, not except on account of our salvation
• No one can come to eternal life without divine knowledge, no one can know without the grace of God, because: “No one knoweth the Son, but the Father: neither doth any one know the Father, but the Son, and he to whom it shall please the Son to reveal him.” For the Son reveals both the Father and the Son, appearing visible in the flesh, and he made known to the world the secrets of the divinity through the gospel.
**“and he hath given us”** — to believers
**“understanding that we may know the true God”** — by believing the true Son of God
**“And we”** — by loving
**“in his true Son.”** — as members
**“This is the true God and life eternal.”** — by this we shall be God’s, living in God without end, in the living one without beginning or end
5.21:
**“Little children, keep yourselves from idols.”** — as holy vessels
**“Little children, keep yourselves”** — And because you know the true God and true man and await eternal life, keep yourselves from the teachings of heretics, who take on themselves the appearance of holiness, who by perverse doctrines change the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of corruptible things; for covetousness is the service of idols; and those who even set the world before God are idolaters.
**“keep yourselves”** — Although he has given them testimony of perfection in many things, yet it may be feared lest someone recently converted has kept the remnants of superstition in mind.

1.1:
**“The ancient”** — I, the elder, write both in age and in conduct or in wisdom.
**“lady Elect”**
• The elder, to the elect lady. This is proper, since some doubt whether these two epistles are of John the apostle. But because they are like the first both in words and in a like assertion of faith and charity against heretics, they are proved to be of the apostle, not of John the presbyter. He writes to a certain Babylonian woman, who was called by her proper name Electa, admonishing her and her children not to depart from their purpose of faith because of the heretics. By this elect lady is signified the universal mother, the Church.
• By her children are meant the lesser ones begotten of the Church in faith. He writes, therefore, to the universal Church, that the perfection of faith is not outside charity, and he detests the heretics who divide Jesus Christ.
**“and her children”** — as much by nature as by faith
**“whom I love in the truth”** — with true love, or because you persevere in the truth
**“and not I only”** — so that the authority may be greater
**“not I only”** — Being about to write against the heretics who have fallen away from the truth, he says that all who have known the truth have one love toward the saints, that by the example of the Catholics he may deter them from the fellowship of heretics. All the faithful agree in one truth; heretics disagree in their errors.
**“but also all they that have known the truth”** — who choose God to imitate and seek God alone by works of charity
1.2:
**“for the sake of the truth which dwelleth in us”** — we love you for no other cause than the truth of faith, which endures unconquerable
**“and shall be with us”** — or with us
**“shall be for ever”** — until the end of life, or lasting into eternity
1.3:
**“be with you”** — persevering
**“Grace”** — forgiveness of sins
**“mercy”** — if after baptism you have fallen in some way
**“peace from God the Father”** — that you no longer offend God or the brethren
**“and from Christ Jesus the Son of the Father”** — who is coeternal and coequal with the Father, that is, has power with the Father and works with him
**“Jesus Christ the Son of the Father”** — There were then heretics who denied that the Lord Jesus was the true Son of God; he refutes them.
**“in truth”** — of the faith which you promised in baptism
**“and charity”** — of God and of neighbour
1.4:
**“I was exceeding glad”**
• in the Lord, because of your good beginning
• As if to say: what you hold, hold; receive nothing else from the heretics; for in what you have I rejoice, and I seek that nothing else be added to you for salvation. Since therefore I rejoice in your good beginning, do not make me grieve by your falling away; for as a watchful guardian I know all that goes on around you.
**“that I found of thy children”** — some, perhaps not all
**“walking”** — by advancing daily
**“in truth”** — in true faith
**“walking in truth”** — Adam was placed in paradise that he might work it and keep it. Work signifies the effect of advancement; keeping signifies the state and constancy of perfection itself.
**“as”** — as perfectly
**“we have received a commandment from the Father”**
• and, being assured by what you already have, I ask you now with confidence for what is due
• Not as writing to you a new commandment, etc. He reproves the heretics who, leaving aside what they had heard from the apostles, introduced new things, and by this broke up the bonds of brotherly charity.
**“from the beginning”** — of the faith, or from the earlier fathers
1.5: **“that we love one another”** — so that the ancient faith and love may remain unimpaired
1.6:
**“And this is charity, that we walk”** — that is, we keep the commandments; we do not go out to any errors; we do not cease from the work of virtues
**“according to his commandments”** — that is, of that charity given
**“For this is the commandment, that, as you have heard from the beginning, you should walk in the same”** — and it is necessary that you persevere
1.7:
**“For many seducers”**
• the former confessors of the Christian name
• This can be understood of heretics who confess Jesus incarnate, but either deny his true flesh, or his true divinity, or that God is his true Father, or something of the sort; or it can be understood of the Jews, who deny that Jesus has yet come for the salvation of the world, but await the Antichrist who is to come.
**“are gone out”** — from our fellowship
**“into the world”** — to the love and doctrine of the world
**“who confess not”** — neither in doctrine nor in life
**“that Jesus Christ”** — as master and rule of holiness
**“is come in the flesh: this is a seducer and an antichrist”**
• beware of them, for such men, and those who consent to them, are so
• and therefore
1.8:
**“Look to yourselves, that you lose not the things which you have wrought”**
• by failing of that reward which you earned by working
• Look to yourselves, etc. Do not consent to such men, but rather attend to how you may be perfectly instructed in faith and steadfastness.
**“but”** — strive
**“that you may receive a full reward”**
• in the future, or here, grace
• A full reward, etc. That you may receive God in fullness with joy by persevering in the teaching handed down to you and by not consenting to their error.
1.9:
**“Whosoever”** — who pretend that they surpass others in wisdom and teaching, and out of pride depart from the humble preaching of Christ
**“revolteth, and continueth not”** — through some seduction or fear
**“and continueth not”** — If anyone separates himself from divine teaching, so as to be outside the right faith and the conduct of God’s commandments, he separates himself from God, so as not to have God through the active and contemplative life; he who is the creator of all becomes someone’s God.
**“in the doctrine of Christ, hath not God”** — but if he persevere to the end he will be saved
**“He that continueth”** — He remains in the gospel teaching who thinks and acts according to it. He separates himself from it who thinks and acts otherwise.
**“the same hath both the Father and the Son”** — for the Father and the Son are one true God; the Son is not later, nor less than the Father
1.10:
**“If any man come to you, and bring not this doctrine”**
• since through this teaching God is had both here and in the future, and not through their teaching. Therefore: if anyone
• If any man come to you. When John at Ephesus entered the baths to wash, and saw Cherinthus, he went out, saying: Let us flee from here, lest the baths themselves, in which Cherinthus, the enemy of the truth, is washing, corrupt us. So he did what he taught. For the apostles and their disciples then used such caution in religion that they would not suffer even a word of communion with any of those who had strayed from the truth.
**“receive him not into the house nor say to him, God speed you”** — not only do not consent, but do not receive him even for an hour, much less be willing to be hospitable, lest through their evil conversations your good morals be corrupted
**“nor say to him, God speed you”** — Nor say to him, God speed you. Because a greeting is taken as a sign of consent to error; for we say this to friends whose works please us. And you, if you were perhaps not deceived, others perhaps through such familiarity of yours could be deceived, who would believe that they please you, and so would believe them.
1.11: **“For he that saith unto him, God speed you, communicateth with his wicked works”** — insofar as the word is instituted, he shows himself in common with him; otherwise it is pretence, which ought not to be among Christians
1.12:
**“Having more things to write unto you”**
• about the admonition of the same matter, or perhaps also about others
• Many things, etc. Understand that this admonition will be profitable to you, because I have resolved to come to you also for its confirmation; nevertheless meanwhile I could not wholly keep silent.
**“I would not by paper and ink”** — by writing, which will not move you as much as the life and presence of the teacher
**“for I hope that I shall be with you”** — to be instructed
**“face to face”** — my
**“speak face to face”** — your instruction, or to stop the mouths of those perverse men
**“that your joy may be full”** — they being confounded, your faith being confirmed
1.13:
**“The children of thy sister Elect salute thee.”** — either literally, or perhaps the children of another mother church
**“salute thee”** — As he forbids saying hail to the adversaries of the truth, so on the contrary he greets on behalf of the elect, speaking in the person of the elect.

1.1:
**“The ancient”** — I.
**“to the dearly beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth.”** — not for the sake of temporal goods but on account of eternal ones
**“Gaius”** — Gaius, having received the faith of Christ, good in his deeds, used to receive the preachers and hearers of the word of God, and ministered to them from his means, as is made clear in the epistle. He commends hospitality, and urges him not to give it up through the example and prompting of Diotrephes; for Diotrephes asserted that hospitality was useless. Gaius seems to have been a Corinthian, whence Paul: “I give thanks to my Lord, that I baptized none of you but Crispus and Caius.” And elsewhere: “Caius, my host, and of the whole church, saluteth you.”
1.2:

• Concerning all things I make it my prayer, etc. As now abundance is yours, and a good will to give to the needy, and the means for works, so may you, with the Lord helping, always be able to lead a life full of virtues.
**“fare well”** — in body and in soul
**“as thy soul doth prosperously”**
• he makes progress in works of almsgiving
• that you may fare well as to soul and body
**“thy soul.”** — the inner intention of the mind
1.3:

**“and gave testimony to the truth in thee”** — to true charity, which does not cease from work

1.4:

1.7:

1.2: **“Mercy unto you”** — If God has begun to have mercy on you by pardoning sins, let him fulfil mercy by adding good things besides, leading you to eternal ones. If he has been reconciled to enemies, let him give eternal peace to those made friends, in which you may differ from him in nothing.
1.3:
**“Dearly beloved”**
• They are written beforehand and predestined, not so that they become impious, but, already existing as impious, they are marked out for judgment.
• Dearly beloved. I, who had necessity to provide for your salvation (on account of the false teachers who thrust themselves upon you), to write you admonitions concerning your common salvation, that is, concerning the faith, which is as much my salvation as yours and that of all the faithful, namely the faith that worketh by charity. I say, taking all care to write to you, that is, all that pertains to solicitude. I pray for you, I dispute against your seducers, and, that you may know how to provide for yourselves, I write to you about them, I lay bare their wickednesses, I show you how you ought to hold faith and charity, and, since I am so solicitous for you, you ought to receive my admonition. I say, beseeching that no other faith be added to your faith, but to contend earnestly for the holy faith once delivered to you and to all the saints by the apostles, even unto death, that for it, if need be, you may die; and therefore I wrote that I might know the state of your faith and show you my solicitude; and so that you might be confirmed in the faith.
**“taking all care”** — or: having
**“to write unto you concerning your common salvation, I was under a necessity to write unto you: to beseech you”** — you
**“to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered”** — Therefore I had necessity
**“to the saints”**
• from the saints
• to you from the saints
• under the appearance of religion, as if they preach the faith of Jesus
1.4:
**“For certain men are secretly entered in”** — under the appearance of religion, as if they preach the faith of Jesus
**“certain”** — unknown to God and to the saints, wise in human things
**“men”** — impious ones, of human wisdom
**“who were written of long ago”** — from eternity, foreseen in God’s foreknowledge by the just judgment of God, so that they grow foul and cast others into filth, and from there they will be judged to death
**“unto this judgment, ungodly men”** — I say, impious ones, using divine Scripture by some trickery to destroy the worship of God
**“our Lord God”** — or of the Lord
**“grace”** — which says over you: you have sinned, be still.
**“turning the grace into riotousness”** — The hardness and strictness of the law, which says “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth,” the grace of the gospel tempers, in which crimes committed are purged by penance and the fruit of almsdeeds. But those turn this grace into riotousness who now sin the more freely the less they see themselves examined for their misdeeds by the harshness of the law.
**“and the only sovereign Ruler”** — both of those willing and of those unwilling
**“The only sovereign Ruler”** — The Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit is the only sovereign Ruler; the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit is the only sovereign Ruler; the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son is the only sovereign Ruler. Whoever therefore, a heretic, denies the Father of Christ, the true God, good and just, denies the only sovereign Ruler and our Lord; he who denies that Jesus is the Son of God also denies the only sovereign Ruler and our Lord. He who detracts from the power of the Holy Spirit, here too the only sovereign Ruler and our Lord is denied.
**“and our Lord”**
• singularly of Christians
• with the Father and the Holy Spirit
**“Jesus Christ”**
• savior, that is, king
• our savior
• our king
1.5:
**“I will therefore admonish you”** — And because they deny and wish to lead you in, so that you deny, I want to admonish you against them.
**“all things”** — All the hidden things of the faith; and you have no need to hear new things as if holier from new teachers, that is, you know perfectly all that is to be known about the faith, and therefore there is no need for you to hear them.
**“that Jesus”** — Not the son of Nave but our Lord, who had his beginning not from the virgin birth but was eternal God, who, born of the Virgin, received the name Jesus.
**“That Jesus”**
• Having refuted the heretics, then, so that he may call back those who had believed the wicked and impious, he shows how great is the majesty of the Lord whom they deny, showing that he is the one who led the people of Israel out of Egypt.
• As the children of Israel, who cried to the Lord and were saved out of Egypt, were punished in the desert, distrusting the power of God because of the concupiscence which they had had in Egypt, so these masters of uncleanness and their followers, who by the waters of baptism came out of the darkness of ignorance as believers, are damned if in mind they return to the concupiscences of their former life. As before they deserve to be saved by faith and good works, so afterwards by murmuring and uncleanness they deserve to be damned. Or “afterwards,” that is, twice he destroyed, because he punishes the wicked both now and afterwards; for those whom present evils do not correct he leads on to those that follow.
**“the people”** — first the humble
**“out of the land of Egypt, having saved, afterwards”** — afterwards the murmurers
**“them that believed not”** — by the words of Moses in the desert
**“did destroy”** — by serpents and in other ways
1.6:
**“the angels”** — whose nature and power is greater
**“And the angels”** — And truly they are not to be imitated, who lie that Jesus is not true God but a man begotten of both sexes. For if he did not spare the sinning angels, he does not spare proud men.
**“who kept not”**
• through humble obedience
• through humility, through obedience
**“their principality”**
• by which, through the grace of God, they ruled over other subject spirits
• That is, he punished the angels who transgressed; that is, he so condemned them under the darkness of this air, and reserves the same for the day of judgment unto heavier punishments; nor does he spare wicked men who have forsaken the unity of the Church in which they were born again to God, but he will condemn them gravely before the judgment, and more gravely in the universal judgment.
**“They kept not their principality”** — So with men who do not keep their principality, by which through the grace of adoption they were made sons of God. But they leave their dwelling, that is, the unity of the Church in which they were born again, or the seats of the heavenly kingdom which they were to receive if they kept the faith; and before the judgment he will condemn them gravely, and more gravely in the universal judgment.
**“but forsook”** — through pride
**“their own habitation”**
• the heavenly, spiritual dwelling, the vision of God
• a heavenly dwelling.
**“unto the judgment”** — who will come to the judge, to whom they will be unable to resist or to hide anything
**“The chains of God”** — That is, pride and an impenitent heart, or the divine sentence which will confine them forever; or the chains are the desire for the lowest things, by which, bound, they cannot return to higher things.
**“he hath reserved under darkness in everlasting”** — those already condemned to this air he keeps for heavier punishments
1.7:
**“As Sodom and Gomorrha”** — therefore also they are not to be imitated, because from imitating them eternal death follows
**“As Sodom”** — He had given an example of the damnation of those who deny the only sovereign Ruler, by recalling the destruction of the unbelieving people or of the angels raising themselves up against God. He also gives an example of the punishment of those who turn the grace of the Lord into riotousness, by recalling the burning of Sodom.
**“and the neighbouring cities”** — of Sodom and Gomorrah
**“in like manner, having given themselves to fornication”** — outside nature
**“and going after other flesh”** — of males
**“other”**
• or not due to intercourse
• that is, against nature
**“An example of fire”** — That is, a sign of eternal burning. As they blazed with the fire of lust, so they burned with a temporal fire, which was not purgatorial, but the beginning of punishment and a sign of what is to come.
**“suffering the punishment”** — temporal
1.8:
**“In like manner”** — are to be condemned
**“these men also”** — like the Sodomites
**“the flesh”** — his own or others'
**“defile”**
• like the unbelieving people
• It must be understood: And those are to be condemned like the Sodomites, and like those who blaspheme the majesty of divine power, and like the angels who despised the dominion of their Creator.
**“Despise dominion”** — Blaspheming majesty in lesser sins; and in grave sins, being unwilling to confess humbly and do penance, having no fear nor faith in the coming judge.
**“and majesty”** — that is, the holy angels
**“blaspheme”**
• like the apostate angels
• You ought not to blaspheme, because not even Michael, etc.
1.9:
**“When Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil”** — contending
**“When Michael”** — That is, Moses, who was appointed as a god to Pharao, and who was prince and messenger as regards others, disputing with Pharao, contended; that is, he did signs in turn against the signs of the magicians, about the body of Moses, that is, the people of Israel, that he might let them sacrifice to their God. He durst not bring against him the judgment of the railing speech of this world. But said: “The Lord command thee.” Or otherwise. When the Lord Jesus contended with Pilate about the body of Moses, that is, about the Church, he would not bring any railing speech, but “was led as a sheep to the slaughter.”
**“When Michael the archangel”** — From what Scriptures he took this testimony does not appear. But allegorically it is plain. The body of Moses: the people of Israel, because Moses was a part of that people; and therefore what is read in Zacharias to have been done about the people, the Apostle perhaps rightly says was done about the body of Moses. In Zacharias it is read: “The Lord shewed me Jesus the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord: and Satan stood on his right hand to be his adversary,” and the Lord said to Satan: “The Lord rebuke thee, O Satan: and the Lord that chose Jerusalem rebuke thee.” Because Jesus the priest desired that Israel be freed from captivity and return into their own land, Satan resisted him, unwilling that the people be freed, but wishing them to be enslaved to the Gentile enemies. Therefore the angel who was the helper of the people rebuked him and removed him from the injury of the people. But wherever or whenever this altercation of the angel with the devil took place, this is to be carefully observed: that if Michael the archangel would not speak railing speech against the devil who opposed him, but restrained him with modest speech, how much more must all railing be avoided by men, and most of all against the Creator. The devil is good in substance but evil in will, and therefore he is not railed at by the angel, because the archangel reckons it railing to bring anything against a good nature; and if the devil’s nature were evil, the Lord would not rebuke him for a good work, which could not exist in an evil nature. But when the Lord rebukes, he shows that something good can proceed from a good nature.
**“contended about the body of Moses”**
• It can be supposed that the angel carried on a dispute with the devil about the body of Moses, as if he were unwilling that the burial of Moses be revealed to the Jews, lest they adore him as a god, which the devil was trying to bring about; but it is not found in authority.
• It is read otherwise: that the Lord hid the body of Moses, and perhaps for this reason, lest the people of Israel, after the manner of the Gentiles, who worshipped as gods the kings and princes who were friends to them, after their deaths, their statues having been made, should adore the body of Moses and by idolatry of this kind transgress against God. One can therefore see that there was as it were a contest and altercation of Michael with the devil, who wished to reveal the body of Moses, that he might deceive the people by idolatry, while Michael forbade it, lest the people whose prince he was should sin. And although this is never read in the Old Testament, yet on account of the authority of the apostle, who knew certain more secret things which are hidden from us, it ought not to be refuted by anyone.
• Or thus: when Moses was dead, the Lord sent an angel and took away the body of Moses, so that no one of the people over whom he had ruled knew his burial place. For the Lord had foreseen that Moses after death would be adored by the Jews, and, if they had his body, would be held as a god; and therefore the devil, desiring that the worship of the law be turned into idolatry, is said to have disputed with that angel; because he who had been sent by God is called Michael, that is, “who is like God?”
**“he durst not bring against him the judgment of railing speech”** — so that he might curse him as a bad creature
**“but said: The Lord command thee.”** — that you may be quiet
1.10:
**“these men”** — He did not dare to blaspheme, but These, etc.
**“whatever things they know not”** — that they are to be blasphemed
**“blaspheme”** — from pride, not for any cause
**“what things soever they naturally know”** — by the appetite of the flesh alone, like brute animals
**“like dumb beasts”** — with no reason distinguishing them from others
**“in these”** — in fulfilling these things

1.11:
**“Woe unto them”**
• it will be damnation
• Because heretics are shown to have fallen away from the word of truth in all things; he shows them subject to various evils.
**“for they have gone in the way of Cain”** — They are armed with the sword of bad teaching against brothers, as Cain; they deceive with bad counsel, as Balaam. They rise up against teachers, as Core.
**“Woe unto them, for they have gone in the way of Cain”** — They go the way of Cain who, through envy of those better than themselves, take on the name of teachers that they may be honoured; who are not grieved if they are cast out by God, and are unwilling to imitate their just brethren, but out of envy sometimes kill them, spiritually and bodily. They are also driven from the face of God, thinking that nothing now comes to them by the providence of God, but believing themselves the authors of all they have. They perish in the error of Balaam who, for love of earthly advantages, attack the truth which they have known.
**“have perished in the contradiction of Core”** — Those who are unwilling to be corrected by the rebuke of holy Church, but by desire for undue primacy divide themselves from the unity of the Church, and knowing how much they wrong, yet they descend to the Tartarus of crimes.
1.12:
**“These are”** — therefore also to be avoided
**“in their banquets”** — where they ought to provide for their own honour and profit, or that of those who eat
**“spots”** — Not only do they perish and are stained in carnal feasts and drunkenness, but they are also stains of others, and lead others to perish with them, turning the grace of the Lord into lust.
**“feasting together”** — striving for gluttony beyond measure
**“without fear”** — doing all evils with great contempt
**“feeding themselves”**
• not the poor of Christ
• they are not under the true shepherd
**“clouds”** — because they obscure others
**“Clouds”** — Comparing themselves with preachers who pour down justice, flashing with miracles; but they are clouds obscuring the sun, setting their mouth in heaven, teaching proud perversities without the water of wisdom.
**“without water, which are carried about by winds”** — because at the suggestion of unclean spirits they are swept into various errors of vice
**“Trees of the autumn”** — They compare themselves to trees bearing good fruit, but they are trees of the autumn. They bear good fruit late, like a tree planted in autumn, or because then the leaves fall, and the fruit. Or if the fruit grows over, it is spurious and useless. For if they do anything that seems good, they do not act with a good intention, but to uproot the good things that are in others.
**“unfruitful”** — making no profit either for themselves or for others
**“twice dead”**
• now in the soul, afterwards in the body
• by omitting and by committing
**“Twice dead”** — She dies once who does not bear good fruit; she dies twice who bears evil fruit. Or twice dead, because before the time of faith they were dead. But thence seen to rise through faith, they return again to ungodliness, and so are plucked up by the roots from the inheritance which they hoped they would have, or from the firmness of charity, in which the saints are said to be rooted.
1.13:
**“Raging waves of the sea”** — always restless, swollen, dark, bitter, assailing the stability of the Church
**“foaming out their own confusion”** — like swelling waves they rise up proudly higher; but the more they are confounded, the more they dissolve and perish like very light foam
**“Wandering stars”**
• This signifies apostates, because in the likeness of the devil they fell from the seats of the angels, and for their apostasy the darkness is reserved for them.
• They promise the light of truth in this sea of vices. But they never abide in the same state of teaching or of life, and are a cause of shipwreck to others; and for themselves, in return for the darkness which they brought into the Church of God, the darkness of hell is prepared; and those who disturbed the peace of faith with a worldly tempest will be struck down by the storm of torments.

1.14:
**“prophesied”** — Not only by my authority do I prove that they are to be punished, but also by the authority of Enoch, that wicked men who have crept in in our times to overthrow the faith were long ago marked out for such judgment.
**“Enoch”** — In the stock of Cain, Enoch, which is interpreted “dedication,” is born first. But in the line of the elect Enoch is remembered as the seventh, because the reprobate in this life, which comes first, dedicate themselves by building themselves up; but the elect await the dedication of their building at the end of time, that is, in the seventh.
**“saying: Behold, the Lord cometh”** — plainly and terribly
**“Behold, the Lord cometh”** — The statement is true, that the Lord will reprove the ungodly both for their works and for their words. But it must be noted that the book of Enoch, from which he took this testimony, is accounted apocryphal, having been composed by someone else under the name of Enoch, and in this book many incredible things are contained. Whence this epistle of Jude, which has a testimony from an apocryphal book, was rejected in ancient times by many. But nevertheless by authority, and by age and use, it has deserved to be reckoned among the holy Scriptures; especially because he took from the apocryphal book such a testimony as was not apocryphal and doubtful, but plain by the true light; for it is lawful to take a testimony of truth even from apocryphal writings.

**“These are they, who separate”** — they separate themselves from the lot of the just
**“themselves, sensual men, having not the Spirit”** — following the desires of the soul
**“having not the Spirit”** — Because they do not have the Holy Spirit, by whom the Church is gathered and made spiritual. Therefore the sensual, unlearned, not foreseeing, fall away, because they do not have the bond of charity.
1.20:
**“But you, my beloved”** — But you, in this way, dissent from them
**“building yourselves upon”** — that you may be the temple of God
**“Building”** — Of faith, that is, building yourselves up in good works upon the foundation of faith, so that as living stones you may be placed in the house of God.
**“your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Ghost”** — of God or of your sanctified
**“praying in the Holy Ghost”** — That you may not presume on your own strength, but hope in the help of divine protection, not thinking that you are saved by yourselves, but ask for the coming of the Holy Spirit upon you, that being inspired by him you may pray more ardently, lest you be separated from the Church with those who have not the Spirit.
1.22:
**“And some indeed reprove”** — convince them, for the benefit not of them but of the Church
**“being judged”** — most certainly condemned by divine judgment
1.23:
**“But others save”** — Who are not condemned before God. But those who are now close to falling into the fire, teach, that they may free themselves.
**“out of the fire”** — from the fire of vices, and thus from the fire of torments
**“pulling them”** — by some force
**“And on others have mercy”**
• or those whom you see obstinate in sin, have mercy on, grieving that you cannot save them
• to those who are penitent nearby
**“in fear”** — This is to be joined to those three. For even when anyone reproves apostates and shows them to be damnable, he ought to reprove them in fear, lest perhaps something of the kind befall himself and his own; and he who, rebuking another, snatches him from the fire of vices, should fear lest he himself also be tempted; and he who has mercy on a penitent neighbour should look about lest perhaps he show himself either more severe or more merciful than is just.
**“hating also the spotted garment which is carnal”**
• because the body is polluted by lust
• the mortal and suffering body by which the soul is veiled
